meaning: “fatso” (a very insulting name for an overweight person).
additional_notes: A harsh, offensive insult used to mock someone’s weight/body (often said directly to the person: “¡Bola de sebo!”). Literally it’s “ball of tallow/grease,” but the intended meaning is an insult, not a neutral description. Avoid using it except to understand it or to tell someone to stop.
target_language_example: No me vuelvas a decir bola de sebo.
native_language_example: Don’t call me fatso again.

additional_notes: Common exclamation used to show surprise, shock, annoyance, admiration, etc. It often comes at the start of a sentence, like in English. You’ll also see variations like “¡Ay, Dios mío!” or “Dios mío…” depending on emotion and punctuation.
target_language_example: ¡Dios mío! Olvidé mi pasaporte en casa.
native_language_example: Oh my God! I forgot my passport at home.

meaning: "God knows" (used to say something is unknown, or to strongly emphasize a statement).
additional_notes: Often used like English “God knows…” either (1) to say you don’t know the reason/answer: “Dios sabe por qué” = “God knows why,” or (2) to emphasize that something is true: “Dios sabe que…” = “God knows that…”. You also see it as “Solo Dios sabe…” (“Only God knows…”). It can be religious, but it’s also a common idiomatic expression.
target_language_example: Dios sabe cuánto lo intenté.
native_language_example: God knows how hard I tried.

additional_notes: Used as a question to suggest an action (“¿Por qué no lees…?” = “Why don’t you read…?”) or to agree/accept an idea (“—Vamos al cine. —¿Por qué no?” = “Why not?”). It can also ask why something is not happening/available: “¿Por qué no hay señal?” = “Why isn’t there any signal?” Often written with opening/closing question marks: “¿Por qué no…?”
target_language_example: ¿Por qué no vamos a comer algo después de clase?
native_language_example: Why don’t we go eat something after class?

meaning: Your Highness (a royal title used to address a prince/princess).
additional_notes: A very formal, respectful form of address for royalty. Usually written with capital letters (Su Alteza). You can also see variants like “Su Alteza Real” (Your Royal Highness). It’s used when speaking directly to the person: “Sí, Su Alteza.”
target_language_example: Con permiso, Su Alteza, ¿puedo hacer una pregunta?
native_language_example: Excuse me, Your Highness, may I ask a question?

meaning: "Your Eminence" (a very formal title of address for a high-ranking Catholic church leader, usually a cardinal).
additional_notes: Used when speaking directly to someone with the title, often followed by a name (e.g., "Su Eminencia Tremblay"). It’s very formal and shows respect; in English it’s typically capitalized as “Your Eminence.”
target_language_example: Con su permiso, Su Eminencia, quisiera hacerle una pregunta.
native_language_example: With your permission, Your Eminence, I’d like to ask you a question.

additional_notes: A very formal title used to address a king or queen directly (or to refer to them). It’s written with capital letters in formal contexts. In conversation it often appears as a polite form of address at the beginning or end of a sentence (e.g., “Sí, Su Majestad.”).
target_language_example: Con su permiso, Su Majestad, me retiraré.
native_language_example: With your permission, Your Majesty, I will withdraw.

additional_notes: Literally “to God.” Used after verbs that take an indirect object, especially agradecer (to thank), rezar (to pray), pedir (to ask). In the example, it’s part of the common idea “Agradece a Dios…” = “Thank God…”.
target_language_example: Agradece a Dios que todo salió bien.
native_language_example: Thank God everything turned out well.

additional_notes: Used when referring to an unspecified person. It can mean 'to someone' after verbs that take an indirect object, and it also appears as the personal a before a human direct object, so in some sentences it is translated simply as 'someone' (for example, ver a alguien = 'see someone').
target_language_example: No se lo digas a alguien que no conoces.
native_language_example: Don't tell it to someone you don't know.

additional_notes: Used with verbs like necesitar, tener, buscar, pedir, etc. to introduce a person who will do an action. The “a” marks a person as the direct object (“a alguien”), and “que” starts the clause describing what that person does: a alguien que + [verb in subjunctive or past subjunctive], depending on the main verb and tense.
target_language_example: Busco a alguien que me enseñe español.
native_language_example: I’m looking for someone to teach me Spanish.

additional_notes: Used to talk generally about preferences. In Spanish, the thing liked is the grammatical subject, so you use the indirect object pronoun "les" (to them) with "gustar". Often contrasted with "a otras..." (others). Change "algunas" to "algunos" for masculine/mixed groups, and use "gusta" for singular nouns/activities and "gustan" for plural: "A algunas personas les gustan los perros".
target_language_example: A algunas personas les gusta madrugar, pero a otras les gusta dormir hasta tarde.
native_language_example: Some people like getting up early, but others like sleeping in.

additional_notes: Often appears after other verbs: aprender/enseñar a bailar (“to learn/teach to dance”), ir/salir a bailar (“to go out dancing”), and as an invitation or command: Vamos a bailar (“Let’s dance”), Ve/Vete a bailar (“Go dance”). The preposition a links to the infinitive bailar.
target_language_example: Después de cenar, salimos a bailar.
native_language_example: After dinner, we went out dancing.

meaning: made from; based on; by means of.
additional_notes: Used before a noun to express the main ingredient/material (often with "hecho/a(s) a base de" = "made from") or the method used to achieve something ("a base de esfuerzo/paciencia" = "through effort/patience").
target_language_example: Aprendió español a base de practicar todos los días.
native_language_example: He learned Spanish by practicing every day.

additional_notes: Spanish uses **a + infinitive** to say why someone goes somewhere or does something (purpose), especially with verbs like **salir** (to go out), **ir** (to go), **parar/detenerse** (to stop), **venir** (to come). In **salir a beber**, it often implies going out to drink alcohol, depending on context.
target_language_example: Vamos a beber algo después del trabajo.
native_language_example: Let’s go have a drink after work.

additional_notes: Used for being inside or on a vehicle/vessel (especially ships and planes). Common in greetings like “Bienvenido/a(s) a bordo” (“Welcome aboard”). With “subir a bordo” it means “to board/get on,” and with “a bordo de + noun” it means “aboard/on board of (a ship, plane, etc.).”
target_language_example: Cuando anunciaron el embarque, subimos a bordo del avión.
native_language_example: When they announced boarding, we got on the plane.

additional_notes: Used to say someone is physically on a ship (as a passenger or crew). Often follows verbs like estar (to be), dormir (to sleep), viajar (to travel). You can swap in other vehicles: a bordo del avión (on board the plane), a bordo del tren (on board the train).
target_language_example: Los pasajeros ya están a bordo del barco.
native_language_example: The passengers are already on board the ship.

meaning: amicably; on good terms (by the nice way).
additional_notes: Used to describe doing something peacefully/without force, or being friendly with someone. Very common in the set phrase “a las buenas o a las malas” (“one way or another”). You may also hear “estar a buenas con alguien” = “to be on good terms with someone.”
target_language_example: Prefiero arreglarlo a buenas, sin discutir.
native_language_example: I’d rather sort it out amicably, without arguing.

additional_notes: Used as "a + infinitive" after many verbs, especially movement or starting an action: "ir a buscar" (go look for/go get), "venir a buscar" (come get), "pasar a buscar" (stop by to pick up), "empezar a buscar" (start looking for). Depending on context, it can mean either searching for something or going to pick someone/something up.
target_language_example: Voy a buscar a mi hermana a la estación.
native_language_example: I’m going to pick up my sister at the station.

meaning: to go (and) look for someone; to go pick someone up.
additional_notes: Used after a verb of movement (often ir/venir/mandar) to express purpose: "ir/venir + a buscar a + person". The personal "a" is required before a person (a buscar a mi padre). Depending on context, it can mean either going to find someone or going to pick them up (e.g., at the airport).
target_language_example: Voy a buscar a mi hermana a la estación.
native_language_example: I'm going to pick up my sister at the station.

meaning: to go look for her/it; to go get (fetch/pick up) her/it.
additional_notes: Used after verbs like ir, venir, ayudar, etc. to express going somewhere in order to find or fetch someone/something: ir a buscarla = “go get her/it” / “go pick her up.” The pronoun “la” refers to a feminine person or thing (her/it).
target_language_example: Voy a buscarla a la estación a las ocho.
native_language_example: I’m going to pick her up at the station at eight.

meaning: to go get it / to go look for it (or him).
additional_notes: Often used after verbs of movement like ir/venir ("vamos a...", "ven a...") to mean you’re going somewhere in order to find or retrieve someone/something. "-lo" is an object pronoun meaning "him" or "it"; the exact meaning depends on context.
target_language_example: Ahora mismo voy a buscarlo al coche.
native_language_example: I’m going to get it from the car right now.

additional_notes: Used with verbs like "montar" or "ir a montar" to talk about horse riding: "montar a caballo" = "to ride a horse". It can also describe someone/something that is on a horse: "un hombre a caballo" = "a man on horseback". In some Latin American food contexts (especially Argentina/Uruguay), "a caballo" can mean "topped with a fried egg" (e.g., "papas fritas a caballo").
target_language_example: Nos fuimos a caballo hasta el río.
native_language_example: We went on horseback to the river.

meaning: 'out' (in 'carry out'); used with 'llevar a cabo' = 'to carry out/perform/execute'.
additional_notes: Most commonly appears in the fixed expression "llevar a cabo" (and reflexive/passive forms like "llevarse a cabo"), meaning to carry out a plan, project, experiment, meeting, etc. "Llevarlo a cabo" = "carry it out". In "se lleva a cabo", it often means "it takes place" / "it is carried out" (formal-sounding).
target_language_example: Vamos a llevar a cabo el proyecto la próxima semana.
native_language_example: We’re going to carry out the project next week.

additional_notes: Used to talk about a trade or bargain: you give/do/lose one thing and receive/get another. It’s often used with verbs like dar (to give), ofrecer (to offer), prometer (to promise), or sacrificar (to sacrifice).
target_language_example: Te ayudo con la mudanza a cambio de una pizza.
native_language_example: I’ll help you move in exchange for a pizza.

meaning: to walk; (with salir) to go for a walk.
additional_notes: Uses "a" + infinitive after certain verbs to link to the activity that follows. Common with: empezar/comenzar a caminar (to start walking), ir a caminar (to go to walk / going to walk), volver a caminar (to walk again), and salir a caminar (to go out for a walk).
target_language_example: Después de cenar, salimos a caminar por el parque.
native_language_example: After dinner, we go for a walk in the park.

meaning: to sing (after another verb, like “start to sing” / “going to sing”).
additional_notes: “A” + infinitive is common after verbs like comenzar/empezar (“to start”) and ir (“to go/going to”). In “comienza a cantar,” it means “start singing.” In “va a cantar,” it’s part of the near future: “is going to sing.”
target_language_example: Cuando escuchó la música, empezó a cantar.
native_language_example: When she/he heard the music, she/he started to sing.

additional_notes: Often used with **estar**: **estar a cargo** = “to be in charge.” Add **de** to say what someone is in charge of: **estar a cargo de + noun/verb** (e.g., *a cargo de la transmisión* = “in charge of the broadcast”). Note: **cargo** here means a role/position/responsibility, not “cargo” (goods).
target_language_example: Yo estoy a cargo de la reunión hoy.
native_language_example: I’m in charge of the meeting today.

additional_notes: Used to say who has control, authority, or responsibility for a task, area, or group. Common patterns: “estar a cargo de + noun” (to be in charge of) and “poner a alguien a cargo de + noun” (to put someone in charge of).
target_language_example: Marta está a cargo del proyecto esta semana.
native_language_example: Marta is in charge of the project this week.

additional_notes: Used mainly with verbs of movement like ir, volver, llevar, and venir to mean going or taking someone/something home. Spanish often uses casa without an article here, where English usually just says "home" rather than "to house."
target_language_example: Quiero irme a casa temprano.
native_language_example: I want to go home early.

additional_notes: Used to give the cause or reason for something (usually followed by a noun or noun phrase): a causa de la reunión, a causa de esto. It can describe neutral, good, or bad causes, but it’s very common with negative situations. Often interchangeable with "por" or "debido a" (a bit more formal).
target_language_example: Llegué tarde a causa del tráfico.
native_language_example: I arrived late because of the traffic.

meaning: because of; due to (the cause of).
additional_notes: Used to give the reason for something, usually a negative situation. It’s followed by a noun phrase: a causa del ruido (because of the noise). Change it to match gender/number: a causa del (masc. sing.), a causa de la (fem. sing.), a causa de los (masc. plural), a causa de las (fem. plural). Also common: “a causa de” before words that don’t use an article (e.g., a causa de esto).
target_language_example: Llegué tarde a causa del tráfico.
native_language_example: I arrived late because of the traffic.

additional_notes: Used with verbs like invitar (to invite), quedarse (to stay), sentarse (to sit down) to talk about going to dinner or sitting down to eat dinner. For example, quedarse a cenar = “to stay for dinner,” and invitar a cenar = “to invite (someone) to dinner.”
target_language_example: ¿Quieres venir a cenar esta noche?
native_language_example: Do you want to come over for dinner tonight?

additional_notes: Used to indicate that something reaches 0 (often with verbs like "bajar" or "reducirse": "baja a cero" = "drops to zero"). Also very common in sports scores after a number: "dos a cero" = "2–0" / "two to nil".
target_language_example: El equipo ganó tres a cero.
native_language_example: The team won 3–0.

additional_notes: Used with verbs of movement/plans (like ir, venir, volver, salir) to express purpose: "ir/venir/salir a comer" = "to go/come/go out to eat". Often implies going somewhere to have a meal (lunch/dinner), depending on context. Also common in invitations: "Vente a comer con nosotros" = "Come eat with us."
target_language_example: Vamos a comer fuera hoy.
native_language_example: We’re going out to eat today.

meaning: to buy; to go (somewhere) to buy.
additional_notes: Most often used after a verb of movement or purpose to show why someone is going somewhere: ir/venir/salir + a comprar ("to go/come/leave to buy"). It can also mean "to buy" in general after other verbs (e.g., estar obligado a comprar = "be required to buy"). You’ll often add what you’re buying: a comprar naranjas / a comprar alimentos.
target_language_example: Voy a comprar pan y leche.
native_language_example: I'm going to buy bread and milk.

additional_notes: Used to introduce what comes next (e.g., on TV: “Coming up next…”), or to mean “after that” when talking about the next step in a sequence. Often placed at the start of a sentence (A continuación, …) or after a verb like hacer/decir (qué hacer a continuación = “what to do next”).
target_language_example: A continuación, te explico los siguientes pasos.
native_language_example: Next, I’ll explain the next steps.

meaning: at the expense of; even if it costs (someone/something).
additional_notes: Used to show that one thing is achieved by sacrificing something else, or that someone suffers/loses because of it. Common patterns: (1) "a costa de + noun/pronoun" = "at the expense of" (A gana a costa de B). (2) "a costa de + infinitive" = "even if it means/costs + -ing" (Lo haré a costa de perder tiempo). Can also mark the target of a joke: "La broma fue a costa de Tom" (Tom was the butt of the joke).
target_language_example: Voy a terminar el proyecto a costa de dormir poco.
native_language_example: I’m going to finish the project even if it means sleeping little.

additional_notes: Used with verbs like "ayudar" (to help) + "a" + infinitive: "Ayudé a alguien a cruzar la calle" = "I helped someone cross the street." "A" here means "to" before an infinitive.
target_language_example: ¿Me puedes ayudar a cruzar la calle?
native_language_example: Can you help me cross the street?

additional_notes: Used to say there is no restriction on the time: something can happen whenever. Often used with availability or opening hours (e.g., "está abierto a cualquier hora", "puedes llamarme a cualquier hora").
target_language_example: Si necesitas ayuda, escríbeme a cualquier hora.
native_language_example: If you need help, text me at any time.

additional_notes: Uses the personal “a” because it refers to people. Often used to mean “any person (at all),” especially in general statements like “It can happen to anyone.” You’ll also see it followed by a clause: “a cualquiera que + verb” = “anyone who…”.
target_language_example: Eso le puede pasar a cualquiera.
native_language_example: That can happen to anyone.

meaning: "because of / on account of"; also "as a deposit (partial payment) toward".
additional_notes: With a noun, it often gives a reason: "a cuenta de + sustantivo" (because of something). It’s also used with money and totals: "pagar/abonar X a cuenta de (un total)" = to pay X as an advance/partial payment toward the final amount.
target_language_example: Pagué 20 euros a cuenta del total.
native_language_example: I paid 20 euros as a deposit toward the total.

additional_notes: Used with verbs like "llevar" or "cargar" to say you’re carrying something on your back (often heavy). It can also be figurative: "llevar (algo) a cuestas" = to carry a responsibility, worry, or problem around with you.
target_language_example: Llevo la mochila a cuestas todo el día.
native_language_example: I carry my backpack on my back all day.

meaning: to go for a walk; to take a stroll.
additional_notes: Used after verbs of movement like ir, salir, or venir: "salir/ir a dar un paseo" = to go out for a walk. "Dar un paseo" literally means "to give a walk," but it’s the common Spanish way to say “take a walk,” often for leisure (in a park, after dinner, etc.).
target_language_example: Vamos al parque a dar un paseo después de comer.
native_language_example: Let’s go to the park for a walk after eating.

additional_notes: Used as a fixed phrase to introduce an honest correction, clarification, or admission—often at the start of the sentence and set off by commas: "A decir verdad, ..." It’s similar in tone to "to be honest" or "actually" in English.
target_language_example: A decir verdad, no tengo muchas ganas de salir hoy.
native_language_example: To tell the truth, I don’t really feel like going out today.

additional_notes: Used to say something happens every day or on a daily basis. It often goes at the end of the sentence (e.g., "Trabajo a diario") but can also appear earlier for emphasis. Common with routines (leer, trabajar, ir) and repeated events (ocurrir, pasar).
target_language_example: Hago ejercicio a diario.
native_language_example: I exercise every day.

additional_notes: Used to compare two people or things and highlight a contrast. It’s often followed by a noun or pronoun: "A diferencia de mi hermano..." (Unlike my brother...), "A diferencia de ti..." (Unlike you...). You can also use it mid-sentence to add a contrast: "..., a diferencia de otros, ..." (..., unlike others, ...).
target_language_example: A diferencia de ayer, hoy tengo tiempo.
native_language_example: Unlike yesterday, today I have time.

additional_notes: Used with verbs like convertir/transformar/cambiar ("to convert/turn/exchange") to talk about turning something into cash or money. Often similar in meaning to "en efectivo" or "por dinero" depending on context, but the literal idea is "to/into money."
target_language_example: Puedes cambiar los puntos a dinero en la caja.
native_language_example: You can exchange the points for money at the register.

meaning: remotely; from a distance (not in person).
additional_notes: Used to say something is done without being physically present. Common with studying/working: "estudiar/trabajar a distancia" (distance learning/remote work). It can also mean controlling or operating something from far away: "controlar a distancia" (remote control).
target_language_example: Trabajo a distancia tres días a la semana.
native_language_example: I work remotely three days a week.

additional_notes: Colloquial expression used to emphasize degree or intensity. Common with verbs like llorar (to cry), llover (to rain), trabajar (to work): “llorar a dolor” = to cry your eyes out / cry bitterly; “llovió a dolor” = it rained heavily. Not a literal ‘to pain’ translation in English.
target_language_example: Cuando se fue, lloré a dolor.
native_language_example: When he/she left, I cried my eyes out.

additional_notes: Used to talk about a destination or direction (movement). Often appears with verbs like ir, venir, volver, llegar: "Voy a donde tú vas". It’s frequently written as one word: "adonde" (same meaning). Contrast with "donde" = "where" (location, not direction): "Estoy donde tú estás".
target_language_example: No sé a donde vamos después.
native_language_example: I don't know where we're going next.

additional_notes: Used especially with movement verbs like "ir(se)" (to go) or "venir" (to come): "irse a dormir" = "to go to sleep / to go to bed"; "venir a dormir" = "to come (over) to sleep." On its own, "¡A dormir!" can be a common way to tell someone (often a child) "Go to sleep!"
target_language_example: Ya es tarde; voy a dormir.
native_language_example: It’s late; I’m going to sleep.

additional_notes: An idiomatic adverbial phrase used to say something happens only just (almost not), or that it takes a lot of effort. Common with verbs like caber (fit), poder (be able to), subir (go up), and entender(se) (understand / make oneself understood).
target_language_example: A duras penas llegamos a tiempo por el tráfico.
native_language_example: We barely arrived on time because of the traffic.

meaning: “where are you going?” / “where are you headed?”
additional_notes: Used to ask someone’s destination. Often said as a quick way to stop someone who’s leaving: “Espera, ¿a dónde vas?”. In “Ya veo a dónde vas con esto”, it’s figurative: “I see where you’re going with this” (I understand your intention/point). Note: it’s normally written with accent marks in questions: “¿A dónde vas?”.
target_language_example: ¡Oye! ¿A dónde vas tan rápido?
native_language_example: Hey! Where are you going so fast?

additional_notes: Most commonly used after verbs like "empezar a" or "comenzar a": "Empecé a echar de menos a mi familia" = "I started to miss my family." The base phrase is "echar de menos" (to miss / to feel someone’s absence). Use it with a direct object (a person/thing you miss), often with "a" before a person: "echo de menos a mi madre".
target_language_example: Cuando me mudé, empecé a echar de menos a mis amigos.
native_language_example: When I moved, I started to miss my friends.

additional_notes: Preposition + stressed pronoun. Commonly used to mark the indirect object (often together with the pronoun "le": "A ella le gusta..."). It can add emphasis or clarify who "le" refers to (especially when there could be more than one person).
target_language_example: A ella le dije la verdad ayer.
native_language_example: I told her the truth yesterday.

additional_notes: Used with verbs in the infinitive (e.g., cantar, nadar) or with a noun (e.g., la música). In Spanish, the thing liked is the grammatical subject, so it literally works like “to her, it is pleasing,” which is why you see both “a ella” and “le.” You can drop “a ella” if it’s clear who you mean: “Le gusta cantar.”
target_language_example: A ella le gusta cocinar los fines de semana.
native_language_example: She likes cooking on weekends.

additional_notes: Uses the preposition **a** + infinitive (**encontrar**) to link to another verb or adjective, often meaning “to find” as the goal of an action: **ayudar a encontrar** (help to find), **poder ayudarte a encontrar** (be able to help you find), **estar decidido a encontrar** (be determined to find). You’ll also see it after some verb phrases like **llegar a encontrar** (“to manage to find / to end up finding”).
target_language_example: Te voy a ayudar a encontrar tus llaves.
native_language_example: I’m going to help you find your keys.

additional_notes: Used with the preposition "a" + the demonstrative "esa" to point to a specific feminine noun that is a destination or target (place, event, thing, etc.). Common with verbs of going/bringing (ir, llevar) and also with some nouns/verbs that take "a" (asistir a esa fiesta/reunión; ser inmune a esa enfermedad). "Esa" usually means "that" (often something not right here/now, or already mentioned).
target_language_example: ¿Puedes acompañarme a esa reunión?
native_language_example: Can you come with me to that meeting?

meaning: (to) that woman (used when she is the direct object of the verb).
additional_notes: Spanish uses the "personal a" before a direct object that is a specific person (or a personified being): "Veo a esa mujer" = "I see that woman." Without "a" ("Veo esa mujer") sounds unnatural/incorrect when referring to a person. "Esa" means "that" (near you or previously mentioned), and "mujer" means "woman."
target_language_example: No conozco a esa mujer, pero la he visto antes.
native_language_example: I don’t know that woman, but I’ve seen her before.

additional_notes: "A" + infinitive is used after many verbs to express what someone is encouraged/able/starts/learns to do: "animar a + infinitivo" (encourage to...), "aprender a + infinitivo" (learn to...), "empezar a + infinitivo" (start to...), "ponerse a + infinitivo" (begin doing, often suddenly). Also common in comparisons with "preferir": "Prefiero leer a escribir" = "I prefer reading to writing."
target_language_example: Cuando terminó la cena, se puso a escribir un mensaje.
native_language_example: When dinner ended, he/she started writing a message.

additional_notes: Made up of a + ese. Often means "to that," as in "pertenecer a ese mundo" or "atado a ese cohete." Before a person, the a can be the personal a, which is often not translated into English: "a ese bastardo" = "that bastard."
target_language_example: No quiero hablar con a ese hombre.
native_language_example: I don't want to talk to that man.

meaning: “to that man” / “that man” (when he is a direct object).
additional_notes: Uses the preposition **a** because Spanish often adds the **personal a** before a specific person when they are the direct object: **Veo a ese hombre** (“I see that man”). It can also mean “to that man” with an indirect object: **Le dije a ese hombre...** (“I told that man...”); here **le** is the indirect object pronoun and **a ese hombre** clarifies who “le” refers to.
target_language_example: ¿Conoces a ese hombre?
native_language_example: Do you know that man?

additional_notes: Used to give an approximate time (or sometimes an approximate amount). It’s very common with clock times: "a eso de las tres" = "around three o’clock". It can also be followed by "de" + number: "a eso de 20 euros" = "about 20 euros".
target_language_example: Llegamos a eso de las seis de la tarde.
native_language_example: We arrived around six in the evening.

additional_notes: Most commonly used in the fixed phrase "a espaldas de + person" (also "a las espaldas de") to mean doing something secretly or without the other person’s knowledge: "Lo hicieron a espaldas de su jefe". Less commonly, it can be used more literally to mean “behind” someone physically, but that sense is usually expressed as "detrás de".
target_language_example: Tomaron la decisión a espaldas de Marta.
native_language_example: They made the decision behind Marta’s back.

meaning: at this time (of day); at this hour.
additional_notes: Used to talk about what is happening now or what is typically true around this time of day. It’s also common for imagining a future moment: “Mañana a esta hora…” = “Tomorrow at this time…”.
target_language_example: A esta hora, la tienda ya está cerrada.
native_language_example: At this time, the store is already closed.

additional_notes: Used to say that, given the time that has passed or the stage you’re at, you expect something to have happened (or to be true) already. Often expresses surprise, impatience, or emphasis: "A estas alturas ya deberías..." = "By now you should already..." It can also be used with "del año" to mean "at this time of year."
target_language_example: A estas alturas, ya deberían haber llegado.
native_language_example: By now, they should have arrived.

meaning: "at this time (of day) / at this hour" (often implying it’s late or unusual).
additional_notes: Used to talk about the current time or a specific moment understood from context, often with a tone of “so late/so early.” It can also mean “by now / at this point” when referring to what should have happened already (e.g., "A estas horas ya deben de estar en casa" = "By now they should be home").
target_language_example: ¿Vas a llamarlo a estas horas?
native_language_example: Are you going to call him at this hour?

meaning: 'to study' / 'to start studying' / 'in order to study'.
additional_notes: Often used after verbs like "ponerse" (ponte a estudiar = start studying) or "ir" (ir a + place + a estudiar = go somewhere to study). The "a" before an infinitive can mean either starting an action (ponerse a...) or purpose (ir a... a...).
target_language_example: Me voy a la biblioteca a estudiar para el examen.
native_language_example: I'm going to the library to study for the exam.

additional_notes: Used to state that one person or thing does not follow the general rule you just mentioned. It’s common in more formal writing, signs, and announcements; in everyday speech you’ll also hear "excepto" or "salvo".
target_language_example: Todos pueden entrar, a excepción de los menores de edad.
native_language_example: Everyone can enter, except minors.

additional_notes: Used to show support or agreement. Very often followed by "de" + noun/pronoun: "estar a favor de" (to be in favor of). You can also use it without "de" when the thing supported is understood: "Hay personas a favor" (There are people in favor). Common opposites: "en contra (de)" (against).
target_language_example: Estoy a favor de esa idea.
native_language_example: I'm in favor of that idea.

additional_notes: Used to say you support an idea, plan, or action. Common with estar: "estar a favor de" = to be in favor of. Opposite: "estar en contra de" (to be against).
target_language_example: Estoy a favor de la propuesta.
native_language_example: I'm in favor of the proposal.

meaning: 'at the end of' (with time periods); also 'in order to' (especially in "a fin de que" = 'so that').
additional_notes: Common with time expressions: "a fin de año/mes" = "at the end of the year/month". With an action/purpose, Spanish often uses "a fin de + infinitive" (more formal) or "a fin de que + subjunctive" to express purpose: "Lo hice a fin de que…" = "I did it so that…".
target_language_example: Te llamaré a fin de mes a fin de que lo tengamos todo listo.
native_language_example: I’ll call you at the end of the month so that we have everything ready.

additional_notes: Used to introduce a final conclusion, summary, or “when everything is considered” idea. Often goes at the beginning of the sentence followed by a comma (A fin de cuentas, ...) or at the end for emphasis.
target_language_example: A fin de cuentas, no era tan difícil.
native_language_example: After all, it wasn't that difficult.

meaning: at the end of (a time period).
additional_notes: Used to place something near the end of a month, year, season, etc. It’s common with dates/time periods: a finales de octubre (late October), a finales de este año (toward the end of this year). Often contrasts with a principios de (“at the beginning of”).
target_language_example: Nos mudamos a finales de marzo.
native_language_example: We’re moving at the end of March.

additional_notes: Used literally for floating on water, and very commonly in the expression "mantenerse a flote" = to stay afloat (often financially: to avoid going bankrupt; or generally: to manage, keep going). It usually goes with verbs like "estar", "seguir", "mantener(se)".
target_language_example: Con ese trabajo extra, pudimos mantenernos a flote unos meses más.
native_language_example: With that extra job, we were able to stay afloat for a few more months.

meaning: thoroughly; in depth; all the way (e.g., press fully).
additional_notes: Used with verbs like estudiar, investigar, analizar, conocer to mean “in depth/thoroughly.” With actions like pisar (the gas/brake pedal), it means “all the way/fully” (press down completely).
target_language_example: Vamos a hablarlo a fondo antes de decidir.
native_language_example: Let’s talk about it in depth before deciding.

additional_notes: Used to say that something happens as the result of continuous effort, repetition, or insistence. It’s often followed by an infinitive (a fuerza de + verb) or a noun (a fuerza de + noun). Common translations include “by dint of,” “through,” “by,” or “with,” depending on context.
target_language_example: A fuerza de estudiar todos los días, aprobó el examen.
native_language_example: By studying every day, he/she passed the exam.

meaning: by means of; through (often with repeated effort/force).
additional_notes: Used to say something is achieved using a tool, physical blows, or persistent effort. Common patterns: "a golpe de martillo" (with hammer blows), "a golpe de talonario" (by throwing money at it), "a golpe de esfuerzo" (through sheer effort). It often implies force, repetition, or determination.
target_language_example: Abrieron la puerta a golpe de martillo.
native_language_example: They opened the door with hammer blows.

meaning: shouting; at the top of one’s lungs.
additional_notes: Used with verbs like pedir, gritar, llamar, or protestar to emphasize that someone is yelling loudly (often desperately or insistently). It can also be figurative: “lo estabas pidiendo a gritos” = “you were practically begging for it / asking for it (very obviously).”
target_language_example: ¡Lo estaban pidiendo a gritos!
native_language_example: They were practically begging for it!

additional_notes: Used with verbs like estar/sentirse ("to feel comfortable") and pasársela ("to have a good time"). It can also mean doing something freely or without pressure, especially in expressions like "hablar a gusto" (to talk freely/in peace).
target_language_example: Aquí estamos a gusto; podemos hablar a gusto.
native_language_example: We’re comfortable here; we can talk freely.

additional_notes: Used most often after a verb to introduce a new topic, especially in phrases like “vamos a hablar de…” (we’re going to talk about…), “pasemos a hablar de…” (let’s move on to talk about…), or “volvamos a hablar de…” (let’s go back to talking about…). It’s followed by a noun, name, or issue you’re discussing.
target_language_example: Ahora vamos a hablar de tus planes para el verano.
native_language_example: Now we’re going to talk about your plans for the summer.

additional_notes: Often used as a + infinitive after another verb or to show purpose: ir a hacer = to go do/make, ayudar a hacer = to help do/make. hacer can mean either 'do' or 'make' depending on what follows.
target_language_example: Voy a la cocina a hacer café.
native_language_example: I'm going to the kitchen to make coffee.

additional_notes: Common structure with verbs that take **a + infinitive** (like *obligar a*, *forzar a*, *animar a*, *limitarse a*). **Hacerlo** = *hacer* (to do/make) + **lo** (it). You can change **lo** to **la/los/las** depending on what “it/them” refers to.
target_language_example: No me vas a convencer a hacerlo.
native_language_example: You’re not going to convince me to do it.

additional_notes: Common with verbs like "ir/estar a juego (con)" or "combinar a juego (con)" to say things match: "Los zapatos van a juego con el bolso". It’s often used for clothing and accessories, but can also be used for furniture/decor.
target_language_example: La corbata va a juego con la camisa.
native_language_example: The tie matches the shirt.

meaning: 'to play' (as an action you go/start/learn to do).
additional_notes: Used after verbs like ir/salir/empezar/enseñar/aprender/querer to mean “to play.” It often implies going out/starting to play: Los niños salieron a jugar = “The kids went out to play.” For specific games/sports, Spanish commonly uses jugar + a + game (jugar a póker, jugar al ajedrez) and jugar + sport without “a” in many varieties (jugar fútbol). Also used as a short command/announcement: ¡A jugar! = “Let’s play!”
target_language_example: Después de la cena, vamos a jugar.
native_language_example: After dinner, we're going to play.

additional_notes: Used to introduce the evidence or clue you’re using to form an opinion or guess. It’s followed by a noun (a juzgar por la foto), an adjective/noun phrase (a juzgar por su expresión), or a clause with "lo que" (a juzgar por lo que dices). Commonly used for deductions: "...debe de...", "diría que...", "parece que...".
target_language_example: A juzgar por su acento, es de Argentina.
native_language_example: Judging by his accent, he’s from Argentina.

additional_notes: Combination of the preposition a and the feminine singular article la. It is used before feminine singular nouns, and its exact meaning depends on context: direction or destination (a la playa), reference or topic (introducción a la jardinería), or set expressions (a la ida, a la casualidad). Unlike a + el, it does not contract.
target_language_example: Vamos a la playa este fin de semana.
native_language_example: We're going to the beach this weekend.

additional_notes: Used with verbs that take the preposition **a** to indicate the person/institution you contact, go to, or report something to (e.g., **llamar a la Policía** = to call the police; **ir a la Policía** = to go to the police; **reportar/denunciar algo a la Policía** = to report something to the police). **Policía** is often capitalized when referring to the institution.
target_language_example: Si ves algo sospechoso, llama a la Policía.
native_language_example: If you see something suspicious, call the police.

meaning: "to Grandma / to the grandmother" (sometimes "Grandma" as the person affected).
additional_notes: Used with the preposition "a" + "la" before "abuela". It often marks an indirect object (e.g., "Dile... a la abuela" = tell Grandma) and also appears with the "personal a" before a person as a direct object (e.g., "ver a la abuela" = to see Grandma; "recoger a la abuela" = to pick Grandma up).
target_language_example: Mañana voy a llamar a la abuela para invitarla a cenar.
native_language_example: Tomorrow I’m going to call Grandma to invite her to dinner.

meaning: at the level/height of; up to (the standard).
additional_notes: Used literally for physical height/level (often with de): “a la altura de la cintura” = “at waist level.” Figuratively, it means being good enough or meeting expectations/standards: “estar a la altura (de…)” = “to be up to (…).” As an instruction: “Pórtate a la altura” = “Behave appropriately / rise to the occasion.”
target_language_example: No sé si estaré a la altura del trabajo.
native_language_example: I don’t know if I’ll be up to the job.

additional_notes: Used to say someone does something in a traditional or outdated style, often meaning “the way it used to be done.” Common with verbs like hacer (to do), vestir (to dress), cocinar (to cook): “Lo haremos a la antigua” = “We’ll do it the old-fashioned way.” Not to be confused with “la antigua casa” (“the old former house”), where antigua is just an adjective meaning “old/former.”
target_language_example: Prefiero cocinar a la antigua, sin microondas.
native_language_example: I prefer to cook the old-fashioned way, without a microwave.

additional_notes: Used with verbs of movement (ir, volver, regresar, llevar) to indicate destination. It’s the contraction of "a" + "la" (you don’t say *a la* before a masculine singular noun; it becomes "al").
target_language_example: Voy a la biblioteca después de clase.
native_language_example: I'm going to the library after class.

meaning: to the head; at the head (leading/in charge).
additional_notes: Used literally for something directed toward a person’s head (e.g., "Le dispararon a la cabeza" = they shot him in the head). It’s also used figuratively to mean "at the head of" a group or effort, i.e., leading or in charge: "estar a la cabeza de". In commands like "¡Manos a la cabeza!", it means "hands on your head."
target_language_example: Ella está a la cabeza del proyecto.
native_language_example: She is leading the project.

meaning: to the street; out onto the street.
additional_notes: Used with verbs like salir (to go out), echar (to throw/kick out), tirar (to throw), and sacar (to take out) to show movement/direction from inside to outside (the street). It can be literal (go out to the street; take the trash out) or figurative in expressions like echar a la calle (to kick someone out / evict). Also appears in descriptions like dar a la calle (“to face the street”).
target_language_example: Por favor, saca al perro a la calle un momento.
native_language_example: Please take the dog out to the street for a moment.

additional_notes: Used to talk about going/putting someone into bed. Often appears after verbs like ir (go), volver (go back), llevar (take), or as a short command: «¡A la cama!» = “To bed!” / “Go to bed!”. In other contexts it can mean physically “to the bed” (movement toward the bed).
target_language_example: Estoy cansado; me voy a la cama.
native_language_example: I’m tired; I’m going to bed.

additional_notes: Used to say what time someone goes to bed. It’s normally followed by a time: “a la cama a las diez” = “to bed at 10.” (You’ll often see it with the verb “irse”: “Me voy a la cama a las diez.”)
target_language_example: Me voy a la cama a las diez.
native_language_example: I go to bed at ten.

additional_notes: Used with verbs like mirar (to look) and decir (to say) to emphasize doing something directly and openly to the person, often in a confrontational or very direct way: “mirar a la cara” = “look (someone) in the face”, “decirlo a la cara” = “say it to (someone’s) face.”
target_language_example: No te atreves a decírmelo a la cara.
native_language_example: You don’t dare say it to my face.

meaning: à la carte; ordered individually (not a set menu).
additional_notes: Most common in restaurants: "menú" is a fixed-price set meal, while "a la carta" means you choose each dish separately and pay item by item. You may see it on signs like "Menú / A la carta".
target_language_example: Hoy vamos a pedir a la carta, no el menú del día.
native_language_example: Today we’re going to order à la carte, not the daily set menu.

meaning: to the house; into the house.
additional_notes: Used with verbs of movement (like entrar, ir, correr) to show direction or destination. With entrar, many speakers use both “entrar en la casa” and “entrar a la casa” depending on region; “a la casa” is common in Latin America. In “Vayan a la casa,” it means “go to the house/home.”
target_language_example: Los niños entraron a la casa porque empezó a llover.
native_language_example: The kids went into the house because it started to rain.

meaning: "to the girl" / "the girl" (with "a" marking the receiver or a person as the direct object).
additional_notes: Spanish uses "a" in two common ways here: (1) with an indirect object meaning "to" someone: "Dáselo a la chica" = "Give it to the girl." (2) as the "personal a" before a direct object that is a specific person: "Vi a la chica" = "I saw the girl" (not "to the girl"). With verbs like "preguntar", it can also mean "ask the girl" (the person you’re asking).
target_language_example: ¿Puedes llamar a la chica, por favor?
native_language_example: Can you call the girl, please?

meaning: to the city; toward the city.
additional_notes: Uses "a" to mark direction or destination (going/leading/conducting to a place). It can also mark the affected recipient in actions like "causar daños a la ciudad" (cause damage to the city).
target_language_example: Mañana vamos a la ciudad en autobús.
native_language_example: Tomorrow we’re going to the city by bus.

additional_notes: Used after verbs of movement (like ir, bajar, subir, venir) to say someone goes to the kitchen. It’s a + la (to the + feminine singular place).
target_language_example: ¿Puedes ir a la cocina por un vaso de agua?
native_language_example: Can you go to the kitchen for a glass of water?

additional_notes: Used to coordinate an action so everyone does it at the same time. It’s said before counting (uno, dos, tres) and means the action should happen on “tres.” Often used with commands: Salta…, Tíralo…, Levántate….
target_language_example: A la cuenta de tres, lo levantamos juntos: uno, dos, tres.
native_language_example: On three, we’ll lift it together: one, two, three.

additional_notes: Used with verbs of movement or sending (e.g., ir, mandar, llevar, enviar) to indicate someone goes/is sent/is taken to jail/prison. "Cárcel" is commonly translated as "jail" in everyday speech, though it can also mean "prison" depending on context.
target_language_example: Si sigues haciendo eso, vas a ir a la cárcel.
native_language_example: If you keep doing that, you’re going to go to jail.

meaning: 'on the count of' (two/three), as in a countdown.
additional_notes: Used mostly in spoken Spanish in the pattern “A la de + número” to coordinate an action (like “on three”). You’ll often hear it as “A la de tres…”. In other contexts, “a la de + alguien” can be an elliptical way to mean “to the one belonging to …” when the noun is omitted (e.g., “a la de ella” = “to hers”).
target_language_example: A la de tres, saltamos.
native_language_example: On the count of three, we jump.

additional_notes: Used to indicate direction or location: go/turn/look "to the right" or something is "on the right" (often with verbs like estar/quedar: "Está a la derecha"). It can also be used politically to mean "right-wing" (e.g., "muy a la derecha"). Often pairs with "a la izquierda" (to the left).
target_language_example: El baño está a la derecha del ascensor.
native_language_example: The bathroom is to the right of the elevator.

additional_notes: Used literally for things floating/moving (a boat, ice) without being steered or anchored: "estar/ir a la deriva". It’s also common figuratively for plans, projects, or people that are directionless, stalled, or lacking guidance (e.g., a bill or project that "quedó a la deriva").
target_language_example: Sin un plan claro, el equipo quedó a la deriva.
native_language_example: Without a clear plan, the team was left adrift.

additional_notes: Used with verbs of movement (like ir, venir, llegar) to say someone goes/comes/arrives to school. Literally “to the school” (a + la).
target_language_example: Mañana voy a la escuela temprano.
native_language_example: Tomorrow I’m going to school early.

additional_notes: Literally “to the station.” Used with verbs of movement (ir, venir, llegar) to say someone goes/arrives at the station: “Llegó a la estación.” In some contexts (especially with llegar), English often uses “at,” even though Spanish still uses “a.” Not to be confused with “en la estación” (“in/at the station,” focusing on location rather than arrival).
target_language_example: Voy a la estación para comprar un billete.
native_language_example: I’m going to the station to buy a ticket.

meaning: to the family; for the family.
additional_notes: Used with verbs to show the indirect object (who something is said/done/served/brought to) or motion/direction toward the family (e.g., "volver a la familia"). It can also refer to a specific family group ("la familia de Chihiro") or an organization/group treated like a family ("Bienvenida a la familia").
target_language_example: Les conté la noticia a la familia.
native_language_example: I told the news to the family.

additional_notes: Used after verbs of movement or direction like ir (to go), venir (to come), llegar (to arrive), and invitar (to invite): ir a la fiesta, venir a la fiesta, estar invitado/a a la fiesta. "A" + "la" = "to the" (feminine singular), because "fiesta" is feminine.
target_language_example: ¿Vas a la fiesta esta noche?
native_language_example: Are you going to the party tonight?

additional_notes: Used to say something is done against someone’s will, using physical force or coercion. Common with verbs like tomar (to take), quitar (to take away), llevar (to take/bring), and sacar (to get/remove). As a standalone answer ("A la fuerza."), it means "Forcibly" / "We had to use force."
target_language_example: No quería ir, pero lo llevaron a la fuerza.
native_language_example: He didn’t want to go, but they took him by force.

additional_notes: Used with the personal “a” to mark people as the object of a verb. It often translates as “people” or “to people,” depending on the verb (e.g., pagar a la gente = pay people; atacar a la gente = attack people).
target_language_example: Tenemos que ayudar a la gente del barrio.
native_language_example: We have to help the people in the neighborhood.

meaning: to the room; into the room.
additional_notes: Uses the preposition **a** (movement/direction toward a place) + **la**. Often translates as **“to the room”** or **“into the room”** depending on context (especially with verbs like *entrar* “to enter”). You’ll also see it in phrases like **servicio a la habitación** (“room service,” literally “service to the room”).
target_language_example: Por favor, suba a la habitación y descanse.
native_language_example: Please go up to the room and rest.

meaning: 'when (doing something)' / 'when it comes to'; also 'at the time of'.
additional_notes: Commonly used before an infinitive to mean “when” or “when it comes to” doing something: "a la hora de escoger" = “when choosing.” It can also be more literal with a noun to refer to a specific moment/time: "a la hora de la cena" = “at dinnertime,” "a la hora de la muerte" = “at the time of death.”
target_language_example: A la hora de tomar una decisión, necesito pensarlo bien.
native_language_example: When it comes to making a decision, I need to think it through.

additional_notes: Used with verbs of movement (like ir, volver) to say someone is going to church or returning to church. It’s a + la (a = “to”, la = “the”) + iglesia (“church”); with a + el you would get al, but here it stays a la because iglesia is feminine.
target_language_example: Los domingos voy a la iglesia con mi familia.
native_language_example: On Sundays I go to church with my family.

additional_notes: Used to indicate direction or location. Common with movement/commands: "Gire a la izquierda" (turn left), "Siga a la izquierda" (keep/stay to the left). Often paired with "a la derecha" (to the right).
target_language_example: El baño está a la izquierda de la cocina.
native_language_example: The bathroom is to the left of the kitchen.

additional_notes: Used to talk about what will happen over time after a long period, often meaning that the final result will be seen later (similar to “in the long run” or “eventually”). Common with verbs like ser, pagar, pasar, resultar: "A la larga, todo se arregla."
target_language_example: A la larga, este esfuerzo valdrá la pena.
native_language_example: In the long run, this effort will be worth it.

meaning: into the light; to light (as opposed to darkness). Also: “to light” = revealed/known (in phrases like “salir a la luz”).
additional_notes: Literal meaning: “to the light” (direction/return: Regresa a la luz). Very common in the fixed expression “salir a la luz” = “to come to light / to be revealed” (a secret, truth, scandal). Also used with “la luz” meaning “light” in general (e.g., “al calor y a la luz” = “to heat and light”).
target_language_example: La información salió a la luz después de la investigación.
native_language_example: The information came to light after the investigation.

additional_notes: Used to introduce information that helps you interpret something (“in light of these facts…”). It can also be literal when talking about actual light (often with candles): “a la luz de una vela / de las velas” = “by candlelight.”
target_language_example: A la luz de lo que pasó ayer, vamos a cambiar el plan.
native_language_example: In light of what happened yesterday, we’re going to change the plan.

additional_notes: This is a nonstandard variant you may hear in some regions or in casual speech. The most common and widely accepted form is **a lo mejor** (also meaning “maybe/perhaps”). It’s used to express possibility or uncertainty and often goes at the beginning of the sentence.
target_language_example: A la mejor llego tarde.
native_language_example: Maybe I’ll arrive late.

meaning: to the table; at the table.
additional_notes: Used for going to sit/eat at the table (often as a call like “A la mesa.” = “Dinner’s ready / To the table!”). Common with verbs like “sentarse a la mesa” (to sit down at the table), “estar sentado a la mesa” (to be seated at the table), and “modales a la mesa” (table manners). With movement verbs it can also mean onto the table, e.g., “subir a la mesa” (to climb up onto the table).
target_language_example: Los niños ya están a la mesa.
native_language_example: The kids are already at the table.

additional_notes: A very strong, vulgar expression used to reject something (“A la mierda con…”, “A la mierda + noun”) or to insult/dismiss someone (“Vete/Váyase a la mierda”). Stronger than “al diablo” and not appropriate in polite situations. Often appears with verbs like “mandar a la mierda” = “to tell someone to fuck off / to send someone to hell.”
target_language_example: ¡A la mierda con este plan! Nos vamos.
native_language_example: To hell with this plan! We’re leaving.

additional_notes: Used with verbs like "estar", "verse" (to look), and "vestirse" (to dress) to say someone/something is trendy or up-to-date in fashion or style. You can negate it: "no está a la moda" (it’s not in style).
target_language_example: Ese corte de pelo está muy a la moda este año.
native_language_example: That haircut is very fashionable this year.

meaning: 'death' (as the object of a verb, often after verbs like 'fear' or 'escape').
additional_notes: Uses the personal “a” because death is treated like a person/agent in many expressions (especially with verbs like temer(le) a, escapar a, engañar a). Often appears as “le temer a la muerte” (“to fear death”) or “escapar a la muerte” (“to escape death”).
target_language_example: Mucha gente le teme a la muerte.
native_language_example: Many people fear death.

meaning: “to the woman” / “the woman” (with the personal a).
additional_notes: Used before a specific female person (la mujer = “the woman”). In Spanish, a is often required before a human direct object (the “personal a”): e.g., “Veo a la mujer” = “I see the woman.” It can also mark “to” after verbs like ayudar/saludar (help/greet someone).
target_language_example: Vi a la mujer en la estación.
native_language_example: I saw the woman at the station.

meaning: to the girl; (marking the girl as the direct object) the girl.
additional_notes: Used with the preposition "a" + "la" to refer to a specific girl. It can mean "to the girl" (indirect object/recipient: "Le dio una rosa a la niña") or "the girl" as a direct object with the personal "a" (common with people/animals: "Atacó a la niña").
target_language_example: Vi a la niña en el parque.
native_language_example: I saw the girl in the park.

additional_notes: Common (especially in Argentina/Uruguay) to mean “in the evening/at night,” often contrasting with "a la mañana". In many other places you’ll also hear "por la noche" or "en la noche." It can refer to a specific night ("Ayer a la noche") or a general time ("los domingos a la noche").
target_language_example: ¿Venís a la noche o mañana a la mañana?
native_language_example: Are you coming tonight or tomorrow morning?

additional_notes: Used most often with verbs like volver / regresar (to return) to say that a situation is returning to the usual state after a change, problem, or interruption. You’ll commonly hear: volver a la normalidad (“to go back to normal”).
target_language_example: Después de las vacaciones, todo volvió a la normalidad.
native_language_example: After the vacation, everything went back to normal.

additional_notes: Used to express movement/direction toward a workplace office (a + la = “to the”). Common with verbs like ir, venir, llegar, llevar, enviar/mandar. If you’re talking about being in the office (location), you usually use “en la oficina” (in/at the office).
target_language_example: Voy a la oficina después de comer.
native_language_example: I’m going to the office after lunch.

additional_notes: Used as an adverbial phrase to say something is done or goes perfectly. Often follows a verb (hacerlo a la perfección, dibujar algo a la perfección) or describes how things are going (Todo marchaba a la perfección). Also appears in the saying “La práctica lleva a la perfección” (“Practice makes perfect”).
target_language_example: El plan salió a la perfección.
native_language_example: The plan worked out perfectly.

additional_notes: Used with verbs of movement (like ir, irse, venir, llevar, estar rumbo) to say someone is going/heading/taking someone to the beach. It’s “a” + “la playa” (feminine singular), so the literal idea is “to the beach.”
target_language_example: ¿Vamos a la playa este fin de semana?
native_language_example: Are we going to the beach this weekend?

additional_notes: Used with verbs like llamar (a la policía) “to call the police,” informar/decir (algo a la policía) “to report/tell something to the police.” The "a" marks who receives the action (the indirect object): “to/at.”
target_language_example: Si ves algo sospechoso, llama a la policía.
native_language_example: If you see something suspicious, call the police.

meaning: to the question (as in “answer the question”).
additional_notes: Used after verbs like responder/contestar (to answer) to mark what you are answering: responder/contestar a + la pregunta. Often translates as just “answer the question” in English, even though Spanish includes “to”.
target_language_example: No contestes todavía a la pregunta; primero escucha la explicación.
native_language_example: Don’t answer the question yet; first listen to the explanation.

meaning: at the door; on the door (e.g., knock/ring).
additional_notes: Common with verbs like llamar (to knock/ring), golpear (to knock/hit), and dirigirse (to head) to describe being at the door or doing something to the door. In this context, llamar a la puerta means “to knock/ring at the door.”
target_language_example: Están llamando a la puerta, ¿puedes abrir?
native_language_example: They’re knocking at the door—can you open it?

meaning: to the meeting; at the meeting.
additional_notes: “A” marks direction (“to”) and is also used with verbs like asistir a (“to attend”), faltar a (“to miss”), and ir a (“to go to”). “Reunión” means “meeting” and is feminine, so it takes “la”. In context it often corresponds to “(to/at) the meeting” depending on the verb.
target_language_example: ¿Vas a la reunión mañana?
native_language_example: Are you going to the meeting tomorrow?

meaning: to the (room for) … / to the … room.
additional_notes: Used to indicate movement/direction to a specific room that has a purpose or function. It’s typically followed by a noun: a la sala de fumadores (to the smoking room), a la sala de masajes (to the massage room). Often used with verbs like ir (to go), volver/regresar (to return), llevar (to take), mandar (to send).
target_language_example: Por favor, llévalo a la sala de reuniones.
native_language_example: Please take him to the meeting room.

meaning: per week; a week later (with time words like "siguiente").
additional_notes: Most commonly means “per week” to express frequency: "tres días a la semana" (three days a week), "horas a la semana" (hours per week). With a time modifier like "la semana siguiente" it can mean “the following week / a week later.”
target_language_example: Voy al gimnasio cuatro veces a la semana.
native_language_example: I go to the gym four times a week.

meaning: to the lady; to Mrs. (polite, adult woman).
additional_notes: Used with the preposition “a” to mark the person who receives an action (e.g., send something to her) or the person you address in commands. With names, “la señora + surname” means “Mrs. + surname” (polite/formal).
target_language_example: Por favor, entrégueselo a la señora García.
native_language_example: Please give it to Mrs. García.

meaning: in the shade; (figuratively) in the shadow of (someone).
additional_notes: Used literally for a place not in direct sunlight: "a la sombra" or "a la sombra de + [thing]" (in the shade of a tree/building). Figuratively, "vivir a la sombra de + [person]" means being overshadowed by someone’s fame or influence.
target_language_example: Vamos a sentarnos a la sombra de la pared porque hace mucho calor.
native_language_example: Let’s sit in the shade of the wall because it’s very hot.

additional_notes: Used to say someone goes/goes over to a shop. "A" indicates direction (to/toward), and "la" is "the" (feminine singular). Often used with verbs like ir (to go), venir (to come), correr (to run): "Voy a la tienda" (I’m going to the store).
target_language_example: Voy a la tienda a comprar pan.
native_language_example: I’m going to the store to buy bread.

additional_notes: Uses "a" to show movement/direction (ir/venir/llegar a la universidad) and also commonly to talk about attending university (ir a la universidad = to go to/attend college). In many contexts it can be translated as "to college" in American English.
target_language_example: Voy a la universidad en autobús todos los días.
native_language_example: I go to university by bus every day.

additional_notes: Used with **estar** to say something is available to be bought: *Está/No está a la venta.* You’ll also see **salir a la venta** for when tickets/products become available for purchase (go on sale).
target_language_example: ¿Está a la venta esta casa?
native_language_example: Is this house for sale?

additional_notes: Used to say that two or more things happen together. Very common with "todo/todos" (all at once) and in the pattern "uno/una ... a la vez" meaning "one ... at a time" (e.g., "Una pregunta a la vez").
target_language_example: No podemos hacer dos cosas a la vez.
native_language_example: We can't do two things at the same time.

additional_notes: This is the preposition **a** + **la vida** (“life”). It often appears with adjectives and verbs that take **a** (e.g., *indispensable a la vida* = “essential to life”, *darle sentido a la vida* = “to give meaning to life”). It can also be part of set phrases like **Gracias a la vida** (“Thanks to life”) or with a modifier: *a la vida escolar* (“to school life”).
target_language_example: El amor le da sentido a la vida.
native_language_example: Love gives meaning to life.

additional_notes: Used to say that something can be seen (often in reports like “¡Objetivo a la vista!” = “Target in sight!”). Common with verbs like "estar" (estar a la vista = to be visible), "tener" (tener algo a la vista = to have it in view), and "aparecer" (aparecer a la vista = to come into view).
target_language_example: Ya está el hotel a la vista.
native_language_example: The hotel is already in sight.

additional_notes: Used to say something is visible and not hidden. Very common with people/words like todos (everyone), cualquiera (anyone), or a person: "a la vista de todos" = where everyone can see it; "a la vista de cualquiera" = where anyone can see it. Often implies it’s exposed or left out openly.
target_language_example: No dejes el pasaporte a la vista de todos.
native_language_example: Don’t leave the passport in plain sight (where everyone can see it).

a la vuelta de la esquina

target_language_multi_word_term: a la vuelta de la esquina
meaning: 'just around the corner' (very near; sometimes 'coming soon').
additional_notes: Commonly used to say a place is very close: "Vivo a la vuelta de la esquina". It can also be used figuratively to mean something is imminent or about to happen: "Veo la muerte a la vuelta de la esquina" (I feel death is near). Often intensified with "justo" (right/just): "Justo a la vuelta de la esquina".
target_language_example: La farmacia está a la vuelta de la esquina.
native_language_example: The pharmacy is just around the corner.

additional_notes: Often used with words like "moda" to mean "in the latest fashion" ("vestido a la última moda"). Depending on context, it can also mean "to the last (one)" when followed by a noun (e.g., "a la última sesión" = "to the last showing/session").
target_language_example: Quiere estar a la última, así que siempre compra ropa nueva.
native_language_example: She wants to be up-to-date, so she always buys new clothes.

additional_notes: Used to talk about effects, consequences, or plans that matter over a long period of time. It can modify a verb (Pensar a largo plazo = to think long-term) or a noun (un plan a largo plazo = a long-term plan).
target_language_example: A largo plazo, esta decisión nos ayudará.
native_language_example: In the long term, this decision will help us.

additional_notes: Contraction of **a + las**. Commonly used to mean **“to the”** when indicating direction or a recipient with a feminine plural noun: *a las cuevas* (“to the caves”), *a las familias* (“to the families”). It’s also used with clock times: *a las tres* (“at three o’clock”).
target_language_example: Vamos a las tiendas después del trabajo.
native_language_example: We’re going to the stores after work.

meaning: “to the girls, (to) them …” (introduces what is done/said to the girls).
additional_notes: Used at the start of a sentence to mark the indirect object (who something is for/to). Spanish often repeats the indirect object: **a las chicas** + **les** (even though both mean “to them”). Common with verbs like **gustar/encantar/doler** and with giving/telling: **A las chicas les gusta… / A las chicas les di… / A las chicas les dije…**
target_language_example: A las chicas les gusta el helado.
native_language_example: The girls like ice cream.

additional_notes: Used to say the time when something happens. Use **a la** with 1 o’clock (*a la una*) and **a las** with other hours (*a las dos, a las cinco*).
target_language_example: La reunión es a las cinco.
native_language_example: The meeting is at five.

additional_notes: Used to say the time when something happens. "A las" is used with most clock times (except 1:00, which is "a la una"). You can add "en punto" to mean exactly (e.g., "a las cuatro en punto").
target_language_example: La reunión empieza a las cuatro.
native_language_example: The meeting starts at four o’clock.

additional_notes: Used to say the time when something happens. It uses **a** + **las** + hour for most times (because *hora* is feminine plural in this expression). For 1 o’clock you say **a la una** (singular). In some contexts it can imply a meeting/reservation time: *Mesa cuatro, a las diez* = “Table four, (for) 10:00.”
target_language_example: Te llamo a las diez.
native_language_example: I’ll call you at ten o’clock.

additional_notes: Used to say what time something happens. With specific clock times, Spanish uses **a + la/las + hour**: **a la una** (at 1:00) but **a las dos/tres/cuatro** (at 2/3/4). You can add minutes: **a las dos y media** (at 2:30). **como a las dos** means “around/about 2:00.”
target_language_example: La reunión es a las dos.
native_language_example: The meeting is at two o’clock.

meaning: to women; by women (as the people affected).
additional_notes: "A" often marks an indirect object (who something happens to / who someone appeals to): "gustar a las mujeres" = "to be liked by women" (literally, "to please women"). "Las" is "the" (plural, feminine).
target_language_example: Le gusta contar historias a las mujeres.
native_language_example: He likes telling stories to women.

meaning: "to the girls" / "the girls" (with the personal or indirect-object "a").
additional_notes: Used before a feminine plural noun (las niñas = “the girls”) when it’s an indirect object (often translates as “to the girls”): A las niñas les gusta… (“The girls like…”). It’s also used with the “personal a” before a direct object that is a specific person: Buscaron a las niñas (“They looked for the girls”). In the idiom la niña de mis ojos (“the apple of my eye”), you can see it in comparisons like Lo cuidaré como a las niñas de mis ojos (“I’ll take care of him like the apple of my eye”).
target_language_example: Voy a darles un regalo a las niñas.
native_language_example: I’m going to give the girls a present.

additional_notes: Used to say the time something happens. With hours other than 1, Spanish uses **a las + number** (e.g., *a las nueve*). With 1 o’clock, it’s **a la una**. You can add parts of the day like *de la mañana / de la tarde / de la noche* to be more specific.
target_language_example: Nos vemos a las nueve.
native_language_example: See you at nine o’clock.

additional_notes: Used to say the time when something happens. Use **a las + [hour]** for times from 2:00 to 12:00 (a las dos, a las nueve). For 1:00, use **a la una** (singular). You can add **de la mañana / de la tarde / de la noche** if you need to specify AM/PM.
target_language_example: La reunión es a las ocho.
native_language_example: The meeting is at eight o’clock.

additional_notes: Used to state the time when something happens. With times (except 1 o’clock), Spanish typically uses "a las + [hour]": a las once (11:00). You can add precision with phrases like "en punto" (exactly) or minutes: "a las once y cuarto" (11:15).
target_language_example: La reunión es a las once.
native_language_example: The meeting is at eleven o’clock.

additional_notes: Commonly used as the indirect object with verbs like gustar/encantar/interesar ("to/for people"): A las personas les gusta… It can also mark a direct object when the verb is about acting on people, using the personal “a”: humillar a las personas, ver a las personas. Here, “las personas” means “people” in general.
target_language_example: A las personas les preocupa el futuro.
native_language_example: People worry about the future.

meaning: at the first opportunity; as soon as something starts.
additional_notes: Used to say something happens very early or at the first sign of trouble/possibility. Often appears in longer expressions like “a las primeras de cambio” (= at the first chance / right away).
target_language_example: A las primeras, se cansó y se fue a casa.
native_language_example: At the first opportunity, he got tired and went home.

additional_notes: Used to say the time when something happens. "A las" is used with all clock times except 1:00 ("a la una"). You can add parts of the day for clarity: "a las seis de la mañana/tarde/noche".
target_language_example: Nos vemos a las seis.
native_language_example: See you at six.

additional_notes: Used to say the time when something happens. With times, Spanish uses "a las" + hour (plural), and "y media" means “and a half” (= :30). You can add context like "de la mañana" (in the morning), "de la tarde" (in the afternoon), or "de la noche" (at night).
target_language_example: La clase empieza a las seis y media.
native_language_example: The class starts at six thirty.

additional_notes: Used to say the time when something happens. Use **a la** + hour for 1:00 (a la una) and **a las** + hour for 2:00–12:00 (a las dos, a las siete). You can add details like **en punto** (exactly) or **y media** (half past): *a las siete en punto*, *a las siete y media*.
target_language_example: Nos vemos a las siete.
native_language_example: See you at seven.

additional_notes: Often used after verbs like empezar a, ponerse a, and echarse a to mean “to start crying.” The preposition a + infinitive marks the start/beginning of an action (e.g., Empezó a llorar = “He/She started to cry”). By itself, llorar means “to cry.”
target_language_example: Cuando escuché la noticia, me eché a llorar.
native_language_example: When I heard the news, I burst into tears.

meaning: over the course of; throughout; along.
additional_notes: Used in two common ways: (1) time: "a lo largo de los años / de mi vida" = "over the years / over my life"; (2) place: "a lo largo de la calle / de todo el país" = "along the street / throughout the whole country". Often followed by a noun (e.g., "a lo largo de + el/la/los/las + noun").
target_language_example: A lo largo de la semana, tengo tres reuniones.
native_language_example: Over the course of the week, I have three meetings.

additional_notes: Often used as part of common patterns like: (1) “a lo que + verb/clause” = “to what/that which …” (e.g., “a lo que él dice” = “to what he says”); (2) “a lo + adjective” to talk about something abstract or general (“de lo visible a lo invisible” = “from the visible to the invisible”); (3) “a lo de + noun” to refer to a situation/topic already known in context (“a lo del puente” = “about the bridge thing / about what happened with the bridge”). By itself, “a lo” usually needs what follows to be complete.
target_language_example: Presta atención a lo que te estoy diciendo.
native_language_example: Pay attention to what I’m telling you.

additional_notes: Used to say someone does something on a large scale or in an extravagant/impressive way (spending, traveling, celebrating, etc.). With feelings, it can mean “a lot” or “seriously” (e.g., enamorarse a lo grande = to fall hard).
target_language_example: Para su cumpleaños, lo celebraron a lo grande.
native_language_example: For her birthday, they celebrated in a big way.

meaning: 'throughout' / 'over the course of' (often: "a lo largo de" = "throughout/along").
additional_notes: Most commonly used as "a lo largo de" + a time period or place. With time it means "throughout/over" (a lo largo del año = throughout the year). With space it means "along" (a lo largo de la calle = along the street).
target_language_example: A lo largo del día, beberé mucha agua.
native_language_example: Throughout the day, I will drink a lot of water.

additional_notes: Used to say something is located or can be seen/heard far from where you are. It often goes with verbs like ver (to see) and oír/escuchar (to hear): "Vimos... a lo lejos", "Oí... a lo lejos".
target_language_example: Se ve una montaña a lo lejos.
native_language_example: You can see a mountain in the distance.

additional_notes: Used to express uncertainty or a guess about what might be true. It’s common at the start of a sentence: "A lo mejor + verb". With "a lo mejor no..." it means "maybe not". It can also follow an imperative or suggestion to mean "maybe" something will happen: "Sigue, a lo mejor...".
target_language_example: A lo mejor llegamos tarde si hay tráfico.
native_language_example: Maybe we’ll arrive late if there’s traffic.

additional_notes: Used to express uncertainty or a guess about what could be true. Very common in spoken Spanish and often followed by the indicative (e.g., “A lo mejor es…”). It can also appear mid-sentence after a comma.
target_language_example: A lo mejor llego tarde porque hay tráfico.
native_language_example: Maybe I’ll arrive late because there’s traffic.

meaning: "to what" / "to that which" (referring to a thing or idea).
additional_notes: Used before a clause introduced by "lo que" to point to the specific thing being talked about. Common in phrases like "a lo que sigue" (to what comes next) and "a lo que me refiero" (what I mean / what I’m referring to).
target_language_example: No entiendo a lo que te refieres.
native_language_example: I don’t understand what you mean.

additional_notes: Used to set an upper limit on a number, amount, or degree (the maximum possible). It often appears between commas after the quantity: "tres, a lo sumo, cuatro semanas". It can also limit a statement more generally ("a lo sumo lo sospecha" = he can only suspect it at best).
target_language_example: Llegaré en una hora, a lo sumo.
native_language_example: I’ll arrive in an hour, at most.

additional_notes: Usually just the preposition a + the masculine plural article los. It can mean 'to the' or 'at the' depending on context. In age expressions, a los dieciséis años means 'at sixteen years old'. Before specific people or animals, it is often the personal a, which is required in Spanish but usually not translated into English: vi a los profesores = 'I saw the teachers.'
target_language_example: Vi a los estudiantes en la biblioteca.
native_language_example: I saw the students in the library.

meaning: to the customers / to the clients.
additional_notes: Used with verbs that take an indirect object (often translated as “to” in English), like decir, mentir, explicar. It can also appear with the “personal a” before a direct object that is a person/group, especially with verbs like recibir or atender (e.g., “Recibimos a los clientes” = “We welcome/receive the customers”).
target_language_example: Voy a explicarles el problema a los clientes.
native_language_example: I’m going to explain the problem to the customers.

meaning: to the others; to everyone else.
additional_notes: Used to include other people besides the one already mentioned. It often contrasts with “a ti/a mí” (you/me): “No solo a ti, también a los demás” (“Not just you, but the others too”). “A” is the preposition “to/for,” and “los demás” means “the others/rest (of them).”
target_language_example: No se lo digas solo a él; díselo también a los demás.
native_language_example: Don’t tell only him; tell the others too.

meaning: to/for both of them; to the two (people).
additional_notes: Used when you’re talking to or about two people at the same time (usually masculine or mixed-gender; for two females you typically say “a las dos”). Often appears with indirect object pronouns like “les” (A los dos les gusta...) or as a greeting (Buenos días a los dos).
