additional_notes: A literal noun phrase: ballena (whale) + azul (blue). In Spanish, the adjective usually goes after the noun, so you say ballena azul (not *azul ballena*). Often used with the article: la ballena azul (the blue whale).
target_language_example: La ballena azul puede medir más de 30 metros.
native_language_example: The blue whale can measure more than 30 meters.

additional_notes: A raised area of sand (usually underwater or just at the surface) that can make a boat run aground (encallar / encallarse). Common in rivers, lakes, and near the coast. Also heard as "banco de arena" for sandbars that appear at low tide.
target_language_example: Tuvimos que cambiar de ruta porque había un banco de arena cerca de la orilla.
native_language_example: We had to change route because there was a sandbar near the shore.

additional_notes: Used for a collection of information stored electronically (or organized records). Common with verbs like buscar en (to search in), estar en (to be in), and subir/cargar a (to upload/add to). Often refers to a company/system database: La base de datos de clientes (the customer database).
target_language_example: Voy a buscar tu nombre en la base de datos.
native_language_example: I’m going to look up your name in the database.

meaning: 'it's enough to' / 'all you need is to'.
additional_notes: Used to say that doing one thing is sufficient to achieve a result. It’s often followed by an infinitive (basta con + infinitive): "Basta con leer" = "You just have to read." It can also be followed by a noun: "Basta con tu apoyo" = "Your support is enough."
target_language_example: Para abrir la puerta, basta con usar esta llave.
native_language_example: To open the door, all you need is to use this key.

additional_notes: Used to tell someone to stop or to say you’ve had enough. Common patterns: "¡Basta de + infinitive!" (Basta de hablar = Stop talking) and "¡Basta de + noun!" (Basta de tonterías = Enough nonsense). It can sound firm or impatient; you can also say "¡Basta!" on its own.
target_language_example: Basta de discutir; vámonos a casa.
native_language_example: Enough arguing; let’s go home.

meaning: pretty well; quite well; fairly well.
additional_notes: Used to say something works/looks/turns out well enough, often meaning “better than okay” but not necessarily “excellent.” With skills or ability, it means you can do something reasonably well. Word order: usually after the verb (hablar bastante bien, funciona bastante bien).
target_language_example: Hoy me siento bastante bien, gracias.
native_language_example: I feel pretty well today, thanks.

additional_notes: Used to say something is good to a noticeable degree, but not necessarily “excellent.” Often corresponds to “pretty good” in English. It can describe things (un sitio web), skills (su inglés), or people (un jugador bastante bueno).
target_language_example: Su inglés es bastante bueno.
native_language_example: His/Her English is pretty good.

meaning: quite a long time; enough time.
additional_notes: Often means “a long time” in phrases like “hace bastante tiempo” (a long time ago / it’s been quite a while) or “desde hace bastante tiempo” (for quite a while). With context like “Tienes bastante tiempo”, it can also mean you have plenty of time (no rush).
target_language_example: No te preocupes: todavía tenemos bastante tiempo para llegar.
native_language_example: Don’t worry: we still have plenty of time to get there.

additional_notes: Used to comfort or reassure someone you care about. "Cariño" is an affectionate term like “honey/sweetheart/darling,” so it’s common with partners, kids, or close family. Often said after (or as part of) phrases like "Vas a estar bien" or "Todo va a estar bien."
target_language_example: Tranquilo, vas a estar bien, cariño.
native_language_example: Relax, you’ll be okay, honey.

additional_notes: Common polite reply when someone asks how you are (or how someone/something is doing): “¿Cómo estás?” → “Bien, gracias.” It can also be used to confirm that something is OK: “Está bien, gracias.” Often you’ll hear “Bien, gracias. ¿Y tú?” (“Fine, thanks. And you?”).
target_language_example: —¿Cómo estás? —Bien, gracias. ¿Y tú?
native_language_example: —How are you? —Fine, thanks. And you?

additional_notes: Used in conversation to acknowledge what was said (“bien/okay”) and then add a disagreement, concern, or different point (“pero/but”). Often appears with a pause/comma: “Bien, pero…” You’ll also see it without a comma: “Bien pero…”.
target_language_example: Bien, pero no tengo tiempo ahora.
native_language_example: Okay, but I don’t have time right now.

meaning: "..., right?" / "..., isn’t it?" (seeking confirmation, often like "well, right?").
additional_notes: Used at the end (or in the middle) of a sentence as a tag question to check that the other person agrees or to confirm something you believe is true. It often adds a conversational "well" tone (bien) plus "no?" = "right?". Common in casual speech.
target_language_example: Estás listo para salir, bien, ¿no?
native_language_example: You’re ready to go out, right?

additional_notes: Used mainly in two common patterns: (1) comparisons: "(tan / así de) bien como ..." = "as well as ..." (often with a verb), e.g., doing something as well as someone else. (2) "Está bien como está" = "It’s fine the way it is" (no change needed).
target_language_example: No hablo inglés tan bien como mi hermano.
native_language_example: I don’t speak English as well as my brother.

meaning: well with (getting along with / matching / looking good with).
additional_notes:
Common patterns:
- "llevarse bien con + person" = to get along well with someone: "Me llevo bien con mis compañeros."
- "(no) llevarse bien con + thing/situation" = to do well with / cope well with something (often used with "nunca/no").
- "combinar bien con + clothing/thing" = to match/go well with.
- "verse/quedar bien con + clothing" = to look good with / suit (an outfit or item).
In these uses, "con" means "with"; "bien" works like "well".
target_language_example: Me llevo bien con mi jefa, pero esta chaqueta no combina bien con esos pantalones.
native_language_example: I get along well with my boss, but this jacket doesn’t match those pants well.

additional_notes: Used to congratulate or praise someone (often said alone: “¡Bien hecho!”). It can also describe something that is correctly/skillfully done: “un trabajo bien hecho” (“a job well done”). You can intensify it with “muy”: “Muy bien hecho.”
target_language_example: ¡Bien hecho! Terminaste el proyecto a tiempo.
native_language_example: Well done! You finished the project on time.

additional_notes: Most commonly used as an interjection: “Bien por + [person/pronoun]” to congratulate or show approval (Bien por ti/él/ella/nosotros). Tone can be genuinely supportive or mildly sarcastic depending on context and intonation. In other contexts, “bien” + “por” may appear with different meanings (e.g., pagar bien por algo = “pay well for something”), but the congratulatory use is the most common fixed phrase.
target_language_example: ¡Bien por ti! Te lo mereces.
native_language_example: Good for you! You deserve it.

meaning: “how well” (often in **lo bien que…**) / “really; indeed” (emphasis, sometimes sarcastic).
additional_notes: Commonly appears as **lo bien que + verb** to comment on the degree/quality of an action: *Es increíble lo bien que canta* (“It’s incredible how well she sings”). It can also be used as an emphatic **bien que + verb** meaning “(you/he/she) sure does…”—often to underline a contrast or to sound ironic: *Bien que te quejas, pero no ayudas* (“You sure complain, but you don’t help”).
target_language_example: Ya veremos lo bien que te sale el plan.
native_language_example: We’ll see how well your plan turns out.

additional_notes: Common in legal and financial contexts. It refers to property that belongs to a person individually, often contrasted with "bienes gananciales" (marital/community property). "Bienes" here means assets/property (not “goods” in a shopping sense).
target_language_example: Antes de casarse, hicieron una lista de sus bienes propios.
native_language_example: Before getting married, they made a list of their own assets.

additional_notes: Used to welcome someone to a place, group, or situation. It agrees with the person being welcomed: bienvenido (male), bienvenida (female), bienvenidos/bienvenidas (plural). Often followed by a place or group (bienvenido a Boston / a la familia).
target_language_example: Bienvenido a Boston.
native_language_example: Welcome to Boston.

meaning: "Welcome to" (addressing a group, or at least one man).
additional_notes: Used to greet people when they arrive somewhere or to introduce a place/event. "Bienvenidos" is the masculine plural form; it’s also used for mixed-gender groups. For all women, use "bienvenidas a". For one person: "bienvenido a" (man) / "bienvenida a" (woman). The preposition "a" is followed by a place or event (often with an article: "a la", "al").
target_language_example: Bienvenidos a nuestra casa.
native_language_example: Welcome to our house.

additional_notes: Used to describe a person's position (lying on their stomach) or the position of an object turned so the front/top faces downward. Often used with verbs like estar/estar echado, dormir, dejar, and poner.
target_language_example: Por favor, pon el papel boca abajo.
native_language_example: Please put the paper face down.

meaning: face up; on your back (lying with your face toward the ceiling).
additional_notes: Used mainly with verbs like estar/tumbarse/dormir to describe someone lying on their back, or with poner to place something with the front/top side facing up. Common contrast: “boca abajo” = face down.
target_language_example: Si te mareas, acuéstate boca arriba y respira despacio.
native_language_example: If you feel dizzy, lie on your back (face up) and breathe slowly.

additional_notes: Literal meaning: a nuclear weapon (“an atomic bomb”). In casual speech it can be used figuratively to describe something that’s very powerful or impressive (e.g., a phone, a computer, a speaker), depending on context.
target_language_example: Ese altavoz es una bomba atómica: suena increíble.
native_language_example: That speaker is an atomic bomb: it sounds amazing.

meaning: a rowboat (a small boat moved with oars).
additional_notes: Often used with the article: "un/el bote de remos". "Remo" = oar, so it’s literally “boat of oars.” You’ll commonly see it with verbs like "cruzar" (to cross), "alejarse" (to move away), or "atravesar" (to go across) when talking about crossing a river or moving away from shore.
target_language_example: Alquilamos un bote de remos para cruzar el lago.
native_language_example: We rented a rowboat to cross the lake.

additional_notes: Literal meaning: the body part (your right arm). Figurative meaning: someone you rely on a lot at work or in life—your most trusted helper. In the figurative sense, it often appears with possessives like "mi/tu/su brazo derecho".
target_language_example: En la oficina, Ana es mi brazo derecho.
native_language_example: At the office, Ana is my right-hand person.

additional_notes: Used as a mealtime wish, like “Enjoy!” You can say it on its own (“Buen apetito.”) or to a group (“Buen apetito para todos.”). It can also be used literally to describe appetite: “tener buen apetito” (to have a good appetite) or “comer con buen apetito” (to eat heartily).
target_language_example: ¡Buen apetito! La cena está lista.
native_language_example: Enjoy your meal! Dinner is ready.

meaning: "good appearance"; (about a person) "to look well" / "to look good".
additional_notes: Used to talk about how someone or something looks, often as a quick judgment (healthy, attractive, or in good condition). Common patterns: "tener buen aspecto" (to look good/well), "no tener buen aspecto" (to not look good / look worrying), and intensifiers like "muy" ("tiene muy buen aspecto").
target_language_example: Después de dormir bien, tengo muy buen aspecto.
native_language_example: After sleeping well, I look really good.

additional_notes: Used to describe someone’s character (they are kind, generous, well-intentioned). Common patterns: “tener buen corazón” (to have a good heart) and “ser de buen corazón” (to be good-hearted). You can intensify it with “muy”: “de muy buen corazón.”
target_language_example: Sé que cometió un error, pero tiene buen corazón.
native_language_example: I know he made a mistake, but he has a good heart.

additional_notes: Used as a greeting, especially in parts of Latin America (e.g., Argentina/Uruguay). In many other places you’ll more commonly hear the plural: “buenos días.” It can also describe the weather, meaning “a nice day” (e.g., “hizo buen día” = “it was a nice day”).
target_language_example: —Buen día, ¿cómo está usted?
native_language_example: Good morning, how are you?

meaning: good taste (literal taste, or good judgment/style).
additional_notes: Used both for flavor (food/drink tastes good) and for having refined taste or good judgment in choices (clothes, art, people, etc.). In sentence 2, it means he has good taste in women.
target_language_example: Tiene muy buen gusto para elegir ropa.
native_language_example: He has very good taste in choosing clothes.

additional_notes: Used with the verb tener (“to have”) or with estar + de (“to be in”): tener buen humor (“to be in a good mood”), estar de buen humor / de muy buen humor (“to be in a good/very good mood”). You can add muy to emphasize.
target_language_example: Hoy estoy de buen humor porque descansé bien.
native_language_example: Today I'm in a good mood because I slept well.

meaning: a good eye; good judgment (for noticing/choosing things well).
additional_notes: Used to say someone is good at noticing details or judging/choosing well. Very common with "tener": "tener buen ojo". You can add "para" + infinitive or noun to specify what: "buen ojo para juzgar" / "buen ojo para estas cosas".
target_language_example: Mi hermana tiene buen ojo para elegir ropa.
native_language_example: My sister has a good eye for choosing clothes.

additional_notes: Used to say someone would make a desirable romantic partner (for their looks, personality, job, status, etc.). It can describe a man or a woman: «Tom es buen partido». Don’t confuse «partido» here with «partido» meaning “game/match” (sports) or “political party.”
target_language_example: Dicen que Marta es muy buen partido.
native_language_example: They say Marta is a great catch.

meaning: "Enjoy your meal!" (said to someone who is about to eat).
additional_notes: A common polite phrase used right before someone starts eating (similar to French “bon appétit”). You can say it to one person or a group: “Buen provecho” / “Caballeros, buen provecho.” In a different structure, “sacar buen provecho de (algo)” means “to get good use/benefit out of (something)” (e.g., “Espero sacar buen provecho de ello.”).
target_language_example: ¡Que disfrutes la cena, buen provecho!
native_language_example: Enjoy dinner—enjoy your meal!

meaning: a good while; quite some time.
additional_notes: Usually used with an article: "un buen rato". It can mean you spent a long time doing something (often longer than expected): "Estuve esperando un buen rato." It can also mean you had a nice time: "Pasamos un buen rato" (= we had a good time).
target_language_example: Te estuve esperando un buen rato.
native_language_example: I waited for you for quite a while.

additional_notes: Used to talk about pleasant weather (sunny, mild, not rainy). Common with the verbs hacer and haber: “Hace buen tiempo” / “Hizo buen tiempo” = “The weather is/was nice,” and “Habrá buen tiempo” = “There will be good weather.” You can also use it with tener: “Tener buen tiempo” (especially when talking about a day, trip, or event having good weather).
target_language_example: Si hace buen tiempo, vamos a la playa.
native_language_example: If the weather is nice, we’re going to the beach.

meaning: a nice guy; (with "tener buen tipo") good-looking / with a good figure.
additional_notes: With "ser un buen tipo", it means someone is kind, decent, or friendly (often a man). With "tener buen tipo", it refers to physical appearance: being attractive or having a good body/figure. It’s fairly informal and common in everyday speech.
target_language_example: Mi vecino es un buen tipo y siempre ayuda a los demás.
native_language_example: My neighbor is a nice guy and he always helps others.

additional_notes: Used to congratulate or praise someone for what they did. You can say it directly to someone (¡Buen trabajo!) or refer to their work with an article: “el buen trabajo” (Keep up the good work = Sigue con el buen trabajo / Sigan con su buen trabajo). In everyday Spanish, you’ll also hear “¡Buen trabajo!” and “¡Buen trabajo, chicos!”; “hombre” can be used like “man”/“buddy” in a friendly way.
target_language_example: ¡Buen trabajo! Lo hiciste muy bien.
native_language_example: Good job! You did it really well.

additional_notes: Used to wish someone well when they’re about to travel or as they leave. Often said directly as “Buen viaje” or in the more formal/subjunctive form “Que tengas/tenga buen viaje” (you/usted have a good trip). You can also use it after the trip with verbs like “Espero que hayas/hayan tenido un buen viaje” (“I hope you had a good trip”).
target_language_example: Buen viaje, ¡nos vemos pronto!
native_language_example: Have a good trip—see you soon!

meaning: a good deed; an act of kindness.
additional_notes: Used for a concrete helpful or kind thing someone does. Very common in the set phrase "hacer una buena acción" (to do a good deed), and also "mi buena acción del día" (my good deed for the day). Can be singular or plural: "buenas acciones".
target_language_example: Voy a hacer una buena acción y ayudar a mi vecino con las bolsas.
native_language_example: I’m going to do a good deed and help my neighbor with the bags.

additional_notes: Informal expression (common in Latin America) used to praise or approve what someone just did/said, or to react positively to a suggestion, joke, or idea. Often said on its own as a quick response.
target_language_example: —Voy a llevar paraguas por si llueve. —¡Buena esa!
native_language_example: —I’m going to bring an umbrella in case it rains. —Nice one!

additional_notes: Used to say someone is acting honestly and without trying to deceive or take advantage. Very common in legal/business contexts (e.g., negociar/actuar/obrar de buena fe). Often contrasts with "mala fe" (bad faith).
target_language_example: Actué de buena fe y no sabía que el documento era falso.
native_language_example: I acted in good faith and didn’t know the document was fake.

additional_notes: Used to describe someone (or a group) as kind, decent, and well-intentioned. It’s very common in everyday Spanish. It usually stays in the singular form "gente" even when talking about several people: "Son buena gente" (They’re good people). You can add intensifiers like "muy": "muy buena gente".
target_language_example: Mis vecinos son muy buena gente y siempre ayudan.
native_language_example: My neighbors are really nice people and always help.

additional_notes: Used to say something is a good suggestion/plan. Often said on its own to agree (“Buena idea.”). You’ll also hear it with emphasis: “¡Qué buena idea!” = “What a good idea!” You can add an article depending on context: “una buena idea” (a good idea) or “la buena idea” (the good idea).
target_language_example: Es una buena idea salir temprano.
native_language_example: It’s a good idea to leave early.

meaning: skill/a good touch (at something); also: a good coat/layer (of paint, etc.).
additional_notes: With "tener buena mano para/con + noun" it means you’re naturally good at something or good with someone: "Tiene buena mano para la pintura" / "buena mano con los niños". With "una buena mano de + noun" (especially "de pintura") it means a good, generous coat/layer: "una buena mano de pintura" = “a good coat of paint.” By itself, "Buena mano" can be a brief compliment meaning “Nice work / Good job.”
target_language_example: Necesito alguien con buena mano para arreglar esto.
native_language_example: I need someone with a good touch/skill to fix this.

additional_notes: Used to say someone remembers things well (names, facts, events). With the verb tener: "Tener buena memoria" = "to have a good memory."
target_language_example: Mi abuela tiene buena memoria para los nombres.
native_language_example: My grandmother has a good memory for names.

additional_notes: Used to wish someone luck (“¡Buena suerte!”). It can also refer to luck as a thing: “para la buena suerte” (for good luck), “te dará buena suerte” (it will bring you good luck). Often used with “tener”: “Que tengas buena suerte” = “I hope you have good luck.”
target_language_example: ¡Buena suerte en el examen!
native_language_example: Good luck on the exam!

additional_notes: Means a life that is pleasant/satisfying (health, happiness, comfort, etc.). It can also refer to a comfortable or enjoyable lifestyle ("living well"). In phrases like “Que tengas / Ten una buena vida”, it can sound like a warm wish, or (depending on tone/context) a “goodbye” meaning “have a nice life.”
target_language_example: Después de tantos años de trabajo, por fin vive una buena vida.
native_language_example: After so many years of work, he finally lives a good life.

additional_notes: Used as a greeting in the evening/night and also as a farewell when someone is going to sleep or you’re leaving at night. Commonly used with a comma before a name/title ("Buenas noches, Don Calogero.") or to address a group ("Buenas noches, todos.").
target_language_example: Buenas noches, nos vemos mañana.
native_language_example: Good night, see you tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used to talk about positive information or a favorable update. Often appears with verbs like traer (to bring), tener (to have), escuchar (to hear), or ser (to be): “Ella vino con buenas noticias” / “Esas son buenas noticias.” You can also exclaim it: “¡Qué buenas noticias!”
target_language_example: Tengo buenas noticias: mañana no hay clase.
native_language_example: I have good news: there’s no class tomorrow.

meaning: 'Good afternoon' (also used as a polite 'hello' in the afternoon/evening).
additional_notes: A common greeting used from around midday until nighttime (often until dinner time). It can be used when arriving or when leaving, especially as a polite sign-off (like “good day”). Often followed by a name or title: “Buenas tardes, señor/señora”, “Buenas tardes a todos”.
target_language_example: Buenas tardes, ¿cómo está usted?
native_language_example: Good afternoon, how are you?

additional_notes: Used to react to new information (often like English “good to know”). In real conversations it’s very common to add an object: “Bueno saberlo” (good to know it) or “Es bueno saberlo” (it’s good to know). You may also hear “Qué bueno saberlo” (how good to know that).
target_language_example: Ah, bueno saberlo. Gracias por avisarme.
native_language_example: Oh, good to know. Thanks for letting me know.

meaning: "Well, now..." (a transition to the next step or what happens next).
additional_notes: Used at the start of a sentence to move the conversation forward: introducing the next instruction, conclusion, or new situation. "Bueno" here works like English "well" (a discourse marker), not literally "good." Often followed by what to do next ("Bueno, ahora vas a...") or by something the speaker has just realized/confirmed ("Bueno, ahora lo sabes").
target_language_example: Bueno, ahora vamos a empezar con la primera pregunta.
native_language_example: Well, now we're going to start with the first question.

meaning: "Well, then…" (a transition to a conclusion or next step).
additional_notes: Common in conversation to wrap up what was just said and move on. It can introduce a decision (“Well then, let’s go”), a conclusion (“Well then, I guess…”), or a change of topic. Often said with a pause after "bueno".
target_language_example: Bueno, entonces quedamos mañana a las ocho.
native_language_example: Well then, we’re meeting tomorrow at eight.

meaning: "Well, it's..." (used to introduce what you’re about to say).
additional_notes: Used as a conversational filler at the start of a sentence, often to soften an opinion, react to something, or give an explanation. It’s very common in speech. You’ll usually hear it with a pause after bueno: “Bueno, es…”.
target_language_example: Bueno, es un poco tarde, ¿no?
native_language_example: Well, it’s a bit late, isn’t it?

meaning: "Well, that’s…" / "Well, that is…" (introducing a conclusion or comment).
additional_notes: Used in conversation to react and then state what something is (often summing up, clarifying, or acknowledging a point): “Bueno, esa es la cuestión” = “Well, that’s the question/issue.” You’ll typically finish it with a noun phrase (la cuestión, una teoría, una forma, etc.).
target_language_example: Bueno, esa es la razón por la que no fui.
native_language_example: Well, that’s the reason I didn’t go.

meaning: "Well, that's…" / "Well, that is…" (often reacting or concluding).
additional_notes: Used in conversation to react to what someone said (sometimes with a positive/negative opinion), or to wrap up a point. You’ll often hear it before an adjective or phrase: "Bueno, eso es fantástico." It can also stand alone as "Bueno, eso es." meaning "Well, that’s it" / "Well, that’s that."
target_language_example: Bueno, eso es todo por hoy.
native_language_example: Well, that’s all for today.

additional_notes: "Bueno," is a very common way to start a response (like “well…” in English), often to show a pause, a decision, or mild hesitation. "Lo" is the direct object pronoun meaning “it/that,” and it normally goes before the verb: "Bueno, lo entiendo" = “Well, I understand it.” In the examples, "lo haré" = “I’ll do it,” and "lo sé" = “I know it.”
target_language_example: Bueno, lo entiendo, pero no puedo hacerlo hoy.
native_language_example: Well, I understand it, but I can't do it today.

additional_notes: Bueno is often used as a conversational filler/transition meaning “well…/so…”. It’s followed by whatever you’re about to say. The "me" is the pronoun that goes with the next verb (common with reflexive verbs like "me voy" = “I’m leaving”, or with verbs where someone does something to you: "me salvó" = “(he/she) saved me”).
target_language_example: Bueno, me tengo que ir ya.
native_language_example: Well, I have to go now.

meaning: “Well, look…” (used to introduce what you’re about to say).
additional_notes: Used in conversation as a filler/discourse marker to get someone’s attention or to soften/prepare an explanation, correction, or refusal. Note: in natural Spanish you’ll much more often hear the conjugated form “Bueno, mira, …” (to one person) or “Bueno, miren, …” (to several people); the fixed form “bueno, mirar” is unusual outside of listings/labels.
target_language_example: Bueno, mirar, hoy no puedo quedar.
native_language_example: Well, look, I can’t meet up today.

additional_notes: Used at the start of a reply to disagree gently, correct someone, or backtrack/qualify what was said. Often followed by an explanation: “Bueno, no es que…”, “Bueno, no, no es mi novio.” In speech, the pause/comma matters: “Bueno, no” sounds less blunt than a plain “No.”
target_language_example: —¿Te gustó la película? —Bueno, no… me pareció un poco aburrida.
native_language_example: —Did you like the movie? —Well, no… I thought it was a bit boring.

meaning: “Well, if…” (used to introduce a condition or soften what you’re about to say).
additional_notes: Often used at the start of a sentence to sound more polite, hesitant, or to acknowledge what someone said before adding a condition. Common in spoken Spanish: “Bueno, si no es mucha molestia…” = “Well, if it’s not too much trouble…”, “Bueno, si tú lo dices” = “Well, if you say so.”
target_language_example: Bueno, si quieres, podemos hablar mañana.
native_language_example: Well, if you want, we can talk tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used at the start of a reply to soften or qualify “sí,” often when admitting something, correcting yourself, or agreeing but with reservations. It can be followed by an explanation or a contrast (e.g., “pero…”).
target_language_example: Bueno, sí, tienes razón, pero quería intentarlo de todas formas.
native_language_example: Well, yes, you’re right, but I wanted to try anyway.

additional_notes: Used to soften what you’re saying and show uncertainty or reluctance. Often introduces a suggestion, a possibility, or a polite disagreement/hedge (similar to “well, perhaps…”). Can also stand alone as a hesitant reply: “Bueno, tal vez.”
target_language_example: Bueno, tal vez podamos ir mañana si no llueve.
native_language_example: Well, maybe we can go tomorrow if it doesn’t rain.

meaning: “Well, I…” / “Okay, I…” (leading into something addressed to you).
additional_notes: Used to start a sentence in conversation. "Bueno" works like a soft transition (“well/okay”), and "te" is the indirect object pronoun meaning “to you” (e.g., te dije = “I told you”, te dejo = “I’ll leave you / I’m heading out”, te veo luego = “I’ll see you later”). Often sounds like you’re wrapping up, explaining, or emphasizing what you said/will say.
target_language_example: Bueno, te llamo mañana.
native_language_example: Okay, I’ll call you tomorrow.

meaning: “Alright, (then)…” / “Okay, now…” (used to move on, wrap up, or show “enough/already”).
additional_notes: A very common conversational opener: **bueno** = “well/alright” and **ya** often means “already/now,” but together they usually work as a discourse marker. It can signal (1) a transition to the next thing (*Bueno, ya llegamos*), (2) that something is enough/should stop (*Bueno, ya es suficiente*), (3) closing a conversation (*Bueno, ya nos veremos*), or (4) “as you already know” (*Bueno, ya sabes...*). Tone depends on context: it can sound neutral or slightly impatient.
target_language_example: Bueno, ya me voy a casa; mañana hablamos.
native_language_example: Alright, I’m going home now; we’ll talk tomorrow.

meaning: "Well, I…" (used to start your response, often emphasizing what *you* think/do).
additional_notes: Used as a conversation opener before stating your point, memory, decision, or opinion. It can also signal a mild contrast with what someone else said ("Well, *I*..."). Common in spoken Spanish; you’ll often hear it with a pause: "Bueno, yo..."
target_language_example: Bueno, yo prefiero quedarme en casa.
native_language_example: Well, I’d rather stay home.

additional_notes: Used to introduce a question, often to move the conversation along, show impatience/surprise, or get to the point (similar to “So, what…?” or “Well then, what…?” in English). You’ll usually see it followed by another clause: “Bueno, ¿qué hacemos?”
target_language_example: Bueno, ¿qué vamos a hacer ahora?
native_language_example: So, what are we going to do now?

meaning: "Well, and…?" / "So…?" (used to ask what happens next or for more details).
additional_notes: Often used at the start of a question to keep the conversation going, shift to the next point, or ask for clarification: "Bueno, ¿y ahora qué?" (So what now?), "Bueno, ¿y después...?" (And after that?), "Bueno, ¿y qué le pasó?" (So what happened to him/her?). It can also show mild surprise or impatience depending on tone ("Pero bueno, ¿y esto?").
target_language_example: Bueno, ¿y entonces qué hacemos?
native_language_example: So, what do we do then?

additional_notes: Used to say people have a friendly relationship. Often appears as “muy buenos amigos” (“very good friends”). It can also imply “just friends” in some contexts, depending on tone.
target_language_example: Somos buenos amigos desde la escuela.
native_language_example: We’ve been good friends since school.

additional_notes: Used as a greeting from morning until around lunchtime/early afternoon. It’s often followed by a comma and the person’s name/title (e.g., “Buenos días, señora”). In “los buenos días,” it can mean “the good days” (good times) in a more literary sense.
target_language_example: Buenos días, ¿cómo estás?
native_language_example: Good morning, how are you?

additional_notes: Used to talk about being polite and showing respect in social situations (for example, greeting people, saying “please/thank you,” not interrupting). It’s often used with the verb tener: “tener buenos modales” = “to have good manners.”
target_language_example: En esta casa, se esperan buenos modales en la mesa.
native_language_example: In this house, good manners at the table are expected.

additional_notes: Used when the direct object is a person (or pet) and Spanish uses the “personal a”: buscar a mi esposa = “look for my wife.” For things, you usually drop the “a”: buscar las llaves = “look for the keys.” Very common with “ir/venir a buscar a …” to mean “go/come get (someone)” (pick them up or fetch them).
target_language_example: Voy a buscar a mi hermano a la estación.
native_language_example: I'm going to pick up my brother at the station.

meaning: to look for a job; to job hunt.
additional_notes: Uses the verb "buscar" (to look for) + "trabajo" (work/job). Common with "empezar a" (to start) as in "empezar a buscar trabajo" and with movement/purpose expressions like "venir/ir a" (to come/go) to explain why someone goes somewhere: "vino a ... para buscar trabajo".
target_language_example: Tom ha empezado a buscar trabajo.
native_language_example: Tom has started looking for a job.

additional_notes: Used for a phone’s voicemail service/inbox. Common with verbs like ir/mandar/entrar: "Ir/mandar al buzón de voz" = to go/send to voicemail (the call isn’t answered); "Entrar el buzón de voz" = voicemail picks up.
target_language_example: Si no contesto, deja un mensaje en el buzón de voz.
native_language_example: If I don’t answer, leave a message in the voicemail.

meaning: a loose end; an unresolved detail.
additional_notes: Used for a remaining detail or issue that hasn’t been explained or finished. Very common in the phrase “atar cabos sueltos” (to tie up loose ends), especially when talking about investigations, stories, plans, or paperwork.
target_language_example: Antes de entregar el informe, quiero resolver cada cabo suelto.
native_language_example: Before turning in the report, I want to resolve every loose end.

additional_notes: Used to talk about something that happens annually or repeats year after year. Often goes at the beginning or end of the sentence: “Cada año…” / “…cada año.”
target_language_example: Cada año viajamos a la misma playa.
native_language_example: Every year we travel to the same beach.

meaning: each person; everyone (individually) — “to each their own.”
additional_notes: Used to talk about people one by one, emphasizing individual responsibility, preference, or situation. Common patterns: “Cada cual + verb” (Cada cual que haga lo suyo = Each person should do their part), “Cada cual a su manera” (each in their own way), “Allá cada cual” (up to each person / to each their own). Often takes singular verbs because it refers to each person individually.
target_language_example: En mi casa, cada cual prepara su desayuno.
native_language_example: In my house, each person makes their own breakfast.

additional_notes: Used to talk about something that happens daily or is repeated day after day. Often placed at the beginning or end of the sentence: "Cada día estudio" / "Estudio cada día."
target_language_example: Hago ejercicio cada día antes de cenar.
native_language_example: I exercise every day before dinner.

additional_notes: Used to talk about something that happens repeatedly once per hour (a schedule: “Toma la medicina cada hora”) or to emphasize that something changes hour by hour (“Empeora a cada hora” = “It’s getting worse every hour”). Often appears as “a cada hora” meaning “every hour / hour by hour.”
target_language_example: El autobús pasa cada hora.
native_language_example: The bus comes every hour.

additional_notes: Used to talk about something that happens regularly each morning. Often placed at the beginning of the sentence for emphasis ("Cada mañana,") or after the verb ("... cada mañana").
target_language_example: Cada mañana voy al trabajo en autobús.
native_language_example: Every morning I go to work by bus.

additional_notes: Used to talk about frequency or repetition (something happens every minute), or to emphasize how valuable/urgent time is ("Every minute counts"). Often appears in lists like "cada segundo, cada minuto" for emphasis. With "por" ("por cada minuto") it means "for each minute" when counting or measuring.
target_language_example: Me llama cada minuto para saber si llegué bien.
native_language_example: He calls me every minute to see if I arrived safely.

additional_notes: Used to emphasize that you mean all the words one by one, not just the general idea. Often appears with translation instructions (Traduce/Traduzca/Traduzcan) or for emphasis like “every word you say…”.
target_language_example: Escuché cada palabra que dijiste.
native_language_example: I listened to every word you said.

additional_notes: Used to refer to people individually in a group (“each person”). Very common with verbs like recibir, tener, dar: “Cada quien recibió…”, “Le dio … a cada quien.” It can also imply “each to their own/each one separately,” especially with actions: “Mejor vamos cada quien a casa” = “Let’s each go home (separately).” Often interchangeable with “cada uno/a,” depending on region and context.
target_language_example: Aquí cada quien paga lo suyo.
native_language_example: Here each person pays for their own.

additional_notes: Used to talk about something that happens continuously or very frequently, or to emphasize that time is extremely important (often with "cada segundo cuenta" = "every second counts"). You can also chain it with other time units for emphasis: "cada segundo, cada minuto, cada día".
target_language_example: En una emergencia, cada segundo cuenta.
native_language_example: In an emergency, every second counts.

additional_notes: Used to talk about individuals in a group, meaning “each (one) separately.” Often followed by a verb in singular (e.g., "cada uno tiene..."). It can also be used with "a" to mean “to each one/person” (e.g., "a cada uno"). You may also hear feminine/plural forms depending on context: "cada una" (each woman/each one, feminine) and "cada uno/a de + plural noun" (each of the...).
target_language_example: Al final del curso, le dieron un diploma a cada uno.
native_language_example: At the end of the course, they gave a diploma to each person.

meaning: each one of them / each of them.
additional_notes: Used to talk about people or things in a group individually. You can also say “cada una de ellas” for an all-female group, or “cada uno de ellos/ellas” depending on the group. Often followed by a singular verb: “Cada uno de ellos tiene…”. By itself (“Cada uno de ellos.”) it can be a short answer meaning “Each one of them.”
target_language_example: Cada uno de ellos tiene su propia llave.
native_language_example: Each of them has their own key.

meaning: each one of us / each of us.
additional_notes: Used to talk about the members of a group that includes the speaker. Often followed by a verb in the singular: "Cada uno de nosotros tiene..." You can change it to match other groups: "cada uno de ustedes" (each of you), "cada uno de ellos" (each of them).
target_language_example: Cada uno de nosotros tiene una opinión diferente.
native_language_example: Each of us has a different opinion.

additional_notes: Often used in two main ways: (1) "cada vez que ..." = "every/each time that ..." (introduces a repeated situation). (2) "cada vez más + adjective/adverb" = "more and more" (shows an increasing change over time): "cada vez más fuerte". By itself ("Cada vez."), it can sound like "Every time." (often implying annoyance or emphasis, depending on context).
target_language_example: Cada vez que lo veo, está más cansado.
native_language_example: Every time I see him, he’s more tired.

additional_notes: Used to say that something changes gradually over time in the direction of “more” (greater intensity, quantity, frequency, popularity, etc.). Common with verbs like ponerse/hacerse/volverse + adjective (e.g., “cada vez más oscuro”), and with gustar: “Me gusta cada vez más” = “I like it more and more.”
target_language_example: Cada vez más personas trabajan desde casa.
native_language_example: More and more people work from home.

additional_notes: Used to introduce something that happens repeatedly. It’s followed by a verb clause (often in the present tense to talk about a habitual situation).
target_language_example: Cada vez que llamo, no contestas.
native_language_example: Every time I call, you don’t answer.

meaning: “every time I …” / “whenever I …” (introduces something that happens repeatedly).
additional_notes: Used to start a time clause about a repeated situation: "cada vez que" + verb. "Me" is an object/reflexive pronoun that goes with the verb (e.g., me veo = I see myself; me muevo = I move; me pide = asks me). Often followed by the main clause: "Cada vez que me llama, contesto" (Every time he calls me, I answer).
target_language_example: Cada vez que me llama, estoy ocupado.
native_language_example: Every time he calls me, I’m busy.

additional_notes: Used to talk about who reports to whom in an organization (workplace, military, government, etc.). Often appears with verbs like “respetar” (to respect/follow) or “seguir” (to follow) and with “hay”/“existe” to say there is an established hierarchy.
target_language_example: Tienes que respetar la cadena de mando y hablar primero con tu supervisor.
native_language_example: You have to respect the chain of command and talk to your supervisor first.

additional_notes: Common legal term meaning a prison sentence for the rest of someone's life. Often used with verbs like "condenar a" / "sentenciar a" (to sentence to): "Fue condenado a cadena perpetua". In some places it can allow parole after many years, but it generally means "life in prison."
target_language_example: Lo condenaron a cadena perpetua por el crimen.
native_language_example: He was sentenced to life in prison for the crime.

meaning: to like someone; to get along (with someone).
additional_notes: Used to express that someone gives you a good impression or you find them pleasant. It’s commonly used with an indirect object pronoun: "me cae bien" (I like him/her / he/she seems nice to me), "te cae bien", "le cae bien", "nos cae bien", "les cae bien". For the opposite, use "caer mal" (to dislike / to rub someone the wrong way).
target_language_example: María me cae bien, pero todavía no la conozco mucho.
native_language_example: I like María (she seems nice to me), but I still don’t know her very well.

meaning: to rub someone the wrong way; to be (un)liked (to give a bad impression).
additional_notes: Used to say that a person (or something they did) causes a negative impression. Often appears with an indirect object pronoun: “Me cae mal” = “I don’t like him/her” (literally, “He/She falls badly to me”). You can also use it in past tense for a first impression: “Me cayó mal” = “I didn’t like him/her (when I met them / at that moment).” Opposite: “caer bien” (to be liked).
target_language_example: Ese chico me cae mal porque siempre interrumpe a los demás.
native_language_example: I don’t like that guy because he always interrupts other people.

additional_notes: A polite, common way to order coffee in a café or restaurant. Often said by itself (“Café, por favor.”) or after a request (“Dame un café, por favor.”). You can swap in other items: “Agua, por favor.”
target_language_example: Dame un café, por favor.
native_language_example: Give me a coffee, please.

additional_notes: A very common drink, especially at breakfast. In cafés, you can order it hot; the exact milk/coffee ratio can vary by country or place, but it generally means regular coffee mixed with milk.
target_language_example: ¿Me pone un café con leche, por favor?
native_language_example: Can I have a coffee with milk, please?

additional_notes: Used when ordering coffee to specify no milk (and usually no foam). It can still be served with sugar on the side; say “sin azúcar” if you want it unsweetened. In many places, “un solo” is a common shorthand for “un café solo.”
target_language_example: Para mí, un café solo, sin azúcar, por favor.
native_language_example: For me, a black coffee, no sugar, please.

additional_notes: A container/box used to store and carry tools (e.g., a hammer, screwdriver). Often used with verbs like guardar (to store), dejar (to leave), necesitar (to need), or estar en (to be in).
target_language_example: ¿Dónde está mi caja de herramientas?
native_language_example: Where is my toolbox?

meaning: music box (a small box that plays music).
additional_notes: A common noun phrase for a small, often decorative box with a mechanism that plays a tune when opened or wound up. Used with articles like "una" or "la": "una caja de música", "la caja de música".
target_language_example: Encontré una caja de música antigua en el ático.
native_language_example: I found an old music box in the attic.

meaning: “black box” (a device/record, or something mysterious with hidden contents).
additional_notes: Commonly refers to an airplane’s flight recorder (“la caja negra del avión”). More broadly, it can mean something whose internal workings or information are unknown/hidden (like “a black box in someone’s mind”), or a box/container that’s literally black in color depending on context.
target_language_example: Todavía no saben qué pasó hasta que analicen la caja negra del avión.
native_language_example: They still don’t know what happened until they analyze the plane’s black box.

additional_notes: Used in stores and restaurants for the machine where the cashier enters purchases and takes payment. You’ll often hear it with verbs like "pagar en la caja" (pay at the register) or "abrir/cerrar la caja" (open/close the register).
target_language_example: Puede pagar con tarjeta en la caja registradora.
native_language_example: You can pay by card at the cash register.

meaning: to shut up; to silence someone.
additional_notes: Often used as a strong command (e.g., “¡Calla la boca!”) or to emphasize forcing someone to stop talking (e.g., “Le hicieron callar la boca”). It’s rude/harsh, so avoid using it with strangers or in polite situations; “cállate” or “guarda silencio” are softer alternatives depending on context.
target_language_example: ¡Calla la boca y escucha un momento!
native_language_example: Shut up and listen for a moment!

meaning: a dead end (street); a dead end / no way out (situation).
additional_notes: Literally “alley/street without an exit.” Used both for a real dead-end street and, figuratively, for a situation with no solution or escape ("I'm stuck / there's no way out"). In speech it can also be said alone to mean “dead end.”
target_language_example: Seguimos caminando y terminamos en un callejón sin salida.
native_language_example: We kept walking and ended up at a dead end.

additional_notes: Used when someone decides differently than before (e.g., after thinking more or getting new information). Conjugate "cambiar" to match the subject (puedo/puedes/puede/podemos/pueden cambiar de idea). Often used with "todavía" (“still”) to suggest there’s still time to decide differently.
target_language_example: Lo pensé mejor y decidí cambiar de idea.
native_language_example: I thought about it more and decided to change my mind.

additional_notes: Used when someone stops thinking/feeling one way and decides or believes something different. Very common with verbs like “hacer” (to make someone change their mind): “me hizo cambiar de opinión” = “it made me change my mind.” Often used with “no” to say someone won’t change their mind: “No le harás cambiar de opinión.”
target_language_example: Lo pensé mejor y decidí cambiar de opinión.
native_language_example: I thought about it again and decided to change my mind.

additional_notes: Used for big ambitions or plans to make society/life better (or sometimes to radically transform things, even negatively, depending on context). It often implies making a major impact beyond just personal change.
target_language_example: Quiero cambiar el mundo, aunque sea poco a poco.
native_language_example: I want to change the world, even if it’s little by little.

meaning: to change things (to improve a situation).
additional_notes: Often used when talking about changing a situation, how something works, or the current state of affairs—not just switching one object for another. You can add context with phrases like "en mi país" (in my country), "aquí" (here), or "para mejor" (for the better).
target_language_example: Estamos trabajando para cambiar las cosas en nuestra comunidad.
native_language_example: We’re working to change things in our community.

additional_notes: Most commonly used like "camino de + place/person" to mean you are going toward a destination: "camino de casa" = "on my way home". In more descriptive writing, "un camino de + noun" can mean "a path/road of ..." (e.g., "un camino de oscuridad" = "a path of darkness").
target_language_example: Compré pan camino de casa.
native_language_example: I bought bread on the way home.

additional_notes: Literal meaning: the area where a battle is fought (often with the verb "salir/ir al campo de batalla" = "to go out to the battlefield"). It’s also used figuratively to mean a place or situation of intense conflict (e.g., "El amor es un campo de batalla").
target_language_example: Después de la explosión, la calle parecía un campo de batalla.
native_language_example: After the explosion, the street looked like a battlefield.

additional_notes: Used to refer to a prison camp where large groups of people are detained, often in wartime and especially associated with Nazi Germany in World War II. It’s a very serious, historical term. Plural: campos de concentración.
target_language_example: Los prisioneros huyeron del campo de concentración.
native_language_example: The prisoners escaped from the concentration camp.

additional_notes: Used before a noun to talk about how much of something there is. It often comes with adjectives like cierta (a certain), mucha (a lot of), inmensa (a huge), or una gran (a great/large).
target_language_example: Necesito una pequeña cantidad de dinero para el autobús.
native_language_example: I need a small amount of money for the bus.

additional_notes: Used as part of the structure "ser capaces de + infinitive" to express ability, capability, possibility, or managing to do something. It agrees in number and gender with the subject: "capaz de" (sing. masc.), "capaz de" (sing. fem. is also "capaz"), "capaces de" (plural), "capaces de" (plural fem. also "capaces"). Often used in various tenses: "somos/eran/seremos capaces de..."; "fuimos capaces de..." can imply a concrete achievement (similar to "we managed to").
target_language_example: Finalmente fuimos capaces de resolver el asunto.
native_language_example: In the end we were able to resolve the matter.

additional_notes: Used to express someone’s ability to do something. It’s typically followed by an infinitive verb (capaz de + infinitive): "Soy capaz de hacerlo" = "I’m able to do it." With "ser" in different tenses: "era capaz de" (was able to), "fui capaz de" (managed to / was able to).
target_language_example: No creía que fuera capaz de terminar a tiempo, pero lo logré.
native_language_example: I didn’t think I’d be able to finish on time, but I did.

additional_notes: Used to show orientation or position relative to something, similar to "frente a". It’s usually followed by a noun (often with an article): "cara a la puerta" (facing the door). Common in the fixed expression "cara a cara" = "face to face."
target_language_example: Se puso cara a la pared para que no lo vieran.
native_language_example: He stood facing the wall so they wouldn’t see him.

meaning: face to face; in direct confrontation.
additional_notes: Used for meeting or seeing someone in person (not online/over the phone), or for confronting something directly (a person, an enemy, reality, a problem). It can also be used as a noun phrase: "el cara a cara" = a face-to-face meeting or showdown.
target_language_example: Prefiero hablarlo cara a cara.
native_language_example: I prefer to talk about it face to face.

additional_notes: Used in science/physics to talk about the property of particles or objects that can be positive or negative (e.g., electrons = negative, protons = positive). Often appears with verbs like tener (“to have”) or with adjectives like positiva/negativa, and with intensity words like enorme (“enormous”).
target_language_example: Este objeto tiene carga eléctrica positiva.
native_language_example: This object has a positive electric charge.

meaning: "responsibility for / in charge of" (often in *hacerse cargo de*), or "the position/role of".
additional_notes:
Very common in these patterns:
- **hacerse cargo de + noun** = to take care of / take responsibility for something or someone. (e.g., *Tom se hará cargo de todo*.)
- **estar a cargo de + noun** = to be in charge of. (e.g., *Ella está a cargo del proyecto*.)
- **el cargo de + job title** = the position/role of. (e.g., *el cargo de locutor* = the announcer position.)
Be careful: **cargo** is a false friend with English **cargo** (freight). Here it usually means “responsibility/position,” not “freight.”
target_language_example: ¿Quién se hace cargo de los niños esta noche?
native_language_example: Who’s taking care of the kids tonight?

additional_notes: A common food term. It can be used generally (La carne de cerdo tiene mucha grasa) or to specify what you want in a dish (Quiero carne de cerdo). Often contrasted with other meats like pollo (chicken) or res/vacuno (beef).
target_language_example: ¿Tienen tacos de carne de cerdo?
native_language_example: Do you have pork tacos?

additional_notes: Refers to meat like beef (carne de res/vaca), pork (cerdo), or lamb (cordero), as opposed to white meat (carne blanca) like chicken (pollo) or turkey (pavo). Often used when talking about diet, nutrition, or restaurant menus.
target_language_example: En este restaurante sirven mucha carne roja.
native_language_example: At this restaurant they serve a lot of red meat.

additional_notes: A common, neutral phrase for a romantic letter written to someone you love. You can also say "una carta de amor" (a love letter) or "cartas de amor" (love letters).
target_language_example: Le escribí una carta de amor.
native_language_example: I wrote him/her a love letter.

meaning: a country house; a house in the countryside (often a weekend/summer home).
additional_notes: Used for a house outside the city, typically in a rural area. It can be a second home for weekends or vacations; in some contexts it may be quite simple (even a small house on a plot of land). Often used with verbs like ir a / estar en / pasar el fin de semana en la casa de campo.
target_language_example: Este verano vamos a pasar un mes en la casa de campo.
native_language_example: This summer we’re going to spend a month at the country house.

meaning: my mother’s house/home; my mom’s place.
additional_notes: Used to talk about a location associated with your mom. Common with verbs like ir a (to go to), estar en (to be at), venir de (to come from): «Voy a casa de mi madre», «Estoy en casa de mi madre». In everyday speech you can also say «la casa de mi madre».
target_language_example: Este fin de semana voy a casa de mi madre.
native_language_example: This weekend I’m going to my mom’s place.

additional_notes: This is usually part of a full sentence and commonly needs an article: **La casa está...**. Use **estar** to talk about the house’s location or condition/state (e.g., *La casa está lejos / limpia / abierta*). For more permanent characteristics, Spanish often uses **ser** (e.g., *La casa es grande*).
target_language_example: La casa está cerca de aquí.
native_language_example: The house is near here.

meaning: "I almost..." / "I nearly..." (something almost happened to me, or I almost did something).
additional_notes: Use "casi" before an object pronoun like "me" when the verb affects you (or you’re the one who would have done it): "Casi me desmayo" = I almost fainted; "Casi me pega" = He/She almost hits me. It’s typically followed by a verb (often in the past: "casi me morí", "casi me matan") and expresses that it did NOT actually happen, but came close.
target_language_example: Casi me caigo en la calle.
native_language_example: I almost fell in the street.

additional_notes: Used to say that very few people (almost none) do something or know something. It’s a common combination of "casi" (almost) + "nadie" (nobody) and is followed by a verb: "Casi nadie + verb".
target_language_example: En mi clase, casi nadie llega temprano.
native_language_example: In my class, hardly anyone arrives early.

additional_notes: An adverb phrase used to talk about something that happens very infrequently. It often goes right before the verb ("casi nunca como..."), but it can also come at the beginning of the sentence for emphasis ("Casi nunca como...").
target_language_example: Casi nunca salimos entre semana.
native_language_example: We almost never go out during the week.

additional_notes: An adverb phrase used to say something happens most of the time, but not 100%. It commonly goes before the main verb (e.g., “casi siempre voy…”) or right after the subject (“Yo casi siempre…”).
target_language_example: Yo casi siempre desayuno en casa.
native_language_example: I almost always eat breakfast at home.

additional_notes: Used to say something happens very frequently, but not literally daily. Often placed after the verb (e.g., "Voy casi todos los días") or at the beginning/end of the sentence for emphasis.
target_language_example: Hago ejercicio casi todos los días.
native_language_example: I exercise almost every day.

additional_notes: Often used as "un/una caso de + noun" to describe an incident or medical/legal situation: "un caso de asesinato" (a murder case), "un caso de muerte" (a case involving a death). Also appears in the common expression "hacer caso de" = "to pay attention to / heed" (e.g., "Haz caso de su consejo" = Heed his/her advice).
target_language_example: Es un caso de fraude muy grave.
native_language_example: It’s a very serious case of fraud.

additional_notes: Used to say someone (or something) is unlikely to improve, change, or succeed. It’s often said jokingly or as a criticism: “Eres un caso perdido” = “You’re a lost cause.” You can use it with ser (eres/soy) or about a situation: “Esto es un caso perdido.”
target_language_example: No intentes convencerlo; es un caso perdido.
native_language_example: Don’t try to convince him; he’s a lost cause.

additional_notes: Most commonly used as **en caso que + verb** to introduce a possible situation and what to do if it happens. It often appears with the subjunctive (e.g., *en caso que llueva*). Similar to **por si** (“just in case”), but **en caso que** is a bit more formal and explicit.
target_language_example: En caso que llegues tarde, llámame.
native_language_example: In case you arrive late, call me.

additional_notes: Usually used after an article or other determiner: **la causa de la…** (“the cause of the…”), **una causa de la…** (“a cause of the…”). If you want to say “because of / due to,” Spanish more commonly uses **a causa de la…** or **por causa de la…** (both = “because of the…”).
target_language_example: La causa de la demora fue el tráfico.
native_language_example: The cause of the delay was traffic.

additional_notes: From the verb phrase **ceder a** = “to give in to / to yield to” something. **Cedió** is the simple past (pretérito) form, so it describes a finished action in the past. You can change the subject: **Yo cedí**, **tú cediste**, **ella/él cedió**, etc. Often used with **la tentación** (temptation) but also with other things: *ceder a la presión* (give in to pressure).
target_language_example: Al final, cedió a la tentación y comió el pastel.
native_language_example: In the end, he gave in to temptation and ate the cake.

additional_notes: A common place word meaning a large building/area with many stores. Often used with ir a (to go to): ir al centro comercial. Uses masculine articles (el/al).
target_language_example: Vamos al centro comercial esta tarde.
native_language_example: We’re going to the shopping mall this afternoon.

additional_notes: Common everyday item. Often used with possessives (mi/tu/su) and verbs like usar (to use), cambiar (to change/replace), and olvidar (to forget). You can specify the type, e.g., “cepillo de dientes eléctrico” (electric toothbrush).
target_language_example: ¿Trajiste tu cepillo de dientes?
native_language_example: Did you bring your toothbrush?

additional_notes: Used to show that someone or something is physically near another person or thing. It is normally followed by de before a noun or pronoun: cerca de mí, cerca de la casa. It can also mean 'about/around' with numbers or quantities.
target_language_example: Vivimos cerca de la estación.
native_language_example: We live near the station.

additional_notes: Used to say something is nearby your current location. Often with verbs like estar, quedar, haber, vivir, or to describe where something happened (e.g., I lost it near here). You can also use it alone as a short answer: “Cerca de aquí.”
target_language_example: ¿Hay algún restaurante cerca de aquí?
native_language_example: Is there a restaurant near here?

meaning: near my house (close to where I live).
additional_notes: Used to say something is located or happened in the area around your home. Often used with "hay" (there is/are): "Hay un parque cerca de mi casa." You can swap the possessive to match the person: cerca de tu/su/nuestra casa.
target_language_example: Hay un supermercado cerca de mi casa.
native_language_example: There’s a supermarket near my house.

additional_notes: Used to say something is at a short distance from a place or thing: cerca del ascensor, cerca del puente. It can also be used with times to mean “around/about” a time: cerca del mediodía (“around noon”). It’s the contraction of cerca de + el → cerca del. With feminine nouns, use cerca de la (e.g., cerca de la estación).
target_language_example: La farmacia está cerca del hotel.
native_language_example: The pharmacy is near the hotel.

additional_notes: A noun for the animal that eats ants and termites. Despite the literal words (“pig” + “ant”), it refers specifically to an aardvark (not a pig). Usually used with the article: el/la cerdo hormiguero.
target_language_example: En el zoológico vimos un cerdo hormiguero comiendo hormigas.
native_language_example: At the zoo we saw an aardvark eating ants.

additional_notes: Literally “to close the beak.” It’s an insulting, informal way to tell someone to stop talking, often used as an imperative: “¡Cierra el pico!” You’ll also hear “Cierra el pico, por favor” (still rude despite “please”). A more neutral alternative is “cállate” (still direct) or “guarda silencio” (more formal).
target_language_example: Mejor cierra el pico y déjame hablar.
native_language_example: You’d better shut up and let me talk.

meaning: to shut up; to close your mouth.
additional_notes: Literally “to close the mouth.” In everyday speech it often means “to stop talking,” and can sound rude or like a strong command depending on tone (similar to “shut up”). It commonly appears conjugated (e.g., “cierra la boca”), but the base multi-word term is “cerrar la boca.” A frequent alternative is “cállate.”
target_language_example: Tienes que cerrar la boca un momento y escucharme.
native_language_example: You have to shut up for a moment and listen to me.

additional_notes: Simple past (pretérito) of "cerrar": "cerró" = "(he/she/it) closed". Subject is often implied in Spanish (él/ella/eso). Used for a completed action, including when something non-human causes it: "La corriente de aire cerró la puerta" = "The draft closed the door."
target_language_example: Cuando terminó la reunión, cerró la puerta.
native_language_example: When the meeting ended, he/she closed the door.

meaning: a scapegoat; someone blamed for a problem (often unfairly).
additional_notes: Used to talk about a person who takes the blame so others don’t have to. Often appears with verbs like ser (to be) or necesitar (to need): “X es el chivo expiatorio” / “Necesitan un chivo expiatorio.”
target_language_example: No me culpes a mí; no soy tu chivo expiatorio.
native_language_example: Don’t blame me; I’m not your scapegoat.

additional_notes: Used to talk about a period of 100 years, often in historical context (e.g., events that happened “hace cien años” = “100 years ago,” or that lasted “cien años” = “for 100 years”). Related phrase: “un siglo” = “a century.”
target_language_example: Mis bisabuelos llegaron a este país hace cien años.
native_language_example: My great-grandparents arrived in this country 100 years ago.

additional_notes: Used to state an amount of money. It can appear alone as a short answer (e.g., “¿Cuánto cuesta?” — “Cien dólares.”). Before a noun, Spanish uses the shortened form “cien” (not “ciento”): “cien dólares”, “cien personas”. With a specific noun like “billete” (bill/banknote), Spanish often uses “de”: “un billete de cien dólares”.
target_language_example: ¿Cuánto cuesta la entrada? Cien dólares.
native_language_example: How much is the ticket? One hundred dollars.

additional_notes: Used to state the number 100,000. It can be part of a longer phrase (e.g., "cien mil hombres") or said by itself as an answer. Before a noun, Spanish typically doesn’t add “of” like English does (“cien mil calles” = “one hundred thousand streets”).
target_language_example: Vendieron cien mil entradas en un día.
native_language_example: They sold one hundred thousand tickets in one day.

additional_notes: A common genre label for books, movies, and TV. Often used with "de": "una novela de ciencia ficción" (a science-fiction novel). It can also be said on its own as an exclamation or label (e.g., reacting to something that seems unreal or futuristic).
target_language_example: ¿Te gusta la ciencia ficción o prefieres la fantasía?
native_language_example: Do you like science fiction, or do you prefer fantasy?

additional_notes: Used before a plural noun to give an approximate large number (not necessarily exactly 200, 300, etc.). Often appears in bigger expressions like "cientos de miles" (hundreds of thousands). With time expressions it can mean "for hundreds of...": "en cientos de años" = "in hundreds of years" / "for hundreds of years."
target_language_example: Recibimos cientos de mensajes en un solo día.
native_language_example: We received hundreds of messages in a single day.

additional_notes: Imperative command using (tú): cerrar = to close, la boca = the mouth. Usually rude or aggressive; in arguments it can be a direct insult or threat. In calmer contexts it can mean “be quiet” (often to listen), but it still sounds harsh—"cállate" is similar, and "guarda silencio" is more polite.
target_language_example: Por favor, cierra la boca y escucha un momento.
native_language_example: Please, be quiet and listen for a moment.

additional_notes: Command (tú) form of **cerrar** used to tell one person informally to close the door. Often used with suggestions or urgency (e.g., **mejor** = “you’d better”, **rápidamente** = “quickly”). For a more formal command to one person, use **cierre la puerta**.
target_language_example: Por favor, cierra la puerta cuando salgas.
native_language_example: Please close the door when you leave.

additional_notes: An instruction/command using the tú form (from cerrar). It can be used literally (to shut your eyes) or as a calming/imagining prompt (e.g., before counting or listening). For other people: “cierre los ojos” (usted), “cierren los ojos” (ustedes).
target_language_example: Cierra los ojos un momento, por favor.
native_language_example: Close your eyes for a moment, please.

meaning: five years (a duration or an age).
additional_notes: Used to talk about (1) a length of time: "por/en cinco años" = for/in five years; "desde hace cinco años" = for the past five years; and (2) someone’s age: "a los cinco años" (at age five) or "de cinco años" (five-year-old). With comparisons: "cinco años mayor/menor que" = five years older/younger than.
target_language_example: Viví en México cinco años.
native_language_example: I lived in Mexico for five years.

additional_notes: Used to talk about an amount of money in dollars (USD). Often appears after verbs like pagar (to pay), deber (to owe), and with fines: una multa de cinco dólares (a five-dollar fine).
target_language_example: ¿Me prestas cinco dólares?
native_language_example: Can you lend me five dollars?

additional_notes: Used to state a duration or an amount of time. With durations, Spanish often uses "tardar + (time) + en + infinitive" (e.g., "Tardé cinco horas en manejar...") or "por" (e.g., "por cinco horas" = for five hours).
target_language_example: La película dura cinco horas.
native_language_example: The movie lasts five hours.

additional_notes: Used to express the number 5,000 before a noun (cinco mil años, cinco mil euros) or on its own as a number. Spanish uses a space between the words; it’s not written as one word.
target_language_example: Necesito cinco mil dólares para el coche.
native_language_example: I need five thousand dollars for the car.

additional_notes: Used to talk about an amount of time (duration) or someone’s age. For age, it often appears with verbs like cumplir (to turn) or tener (to be), and with expressions like a la edad de cincuenta años (at the age of fifty) and más de cincuenta años (more than fifty years old).
target_language_example: Mi tía tiene cincuenta años, pero parece más joven.
native_language_example: My aunt is fifty years old, but she looks younger.

additional_notes: Used as a number on its own (answering a question), for quantities and measurements (liters per minute, etc.), in prices (often said without a currency word, e.g., “Dos, cincuenta y cinco” = $2.55/€2.55 depending on context), and for ages with “a los … años” (at … years old).
target_language_example: El autobús llega a las cincuenta y cinco.
native_language_example: The bus arrives at fifty-five.

additional_notes: Used for the safety belt in cars, planes, etc. Common with verbs like ponerse (to put on), usar (to wear/use), and abrocharse (to fasten). You may also hear it with the article: el cinturón de seguridad.
target_language_example: Antes de arrancar, ponte el cinturón de seguridad.
native_language_example: Before starting, put on your seat belt.

additional_notes: Used to talk about surgical procedures to change or repair appearance (for example, after an accident) or for cosmetic reasons. It’s a general term; specific procedures are often mentioned with verbs like “hacerse” (to get/have done): “hacerse una cirugía plástica.”
target_language_example: Mi prima se hizo cirugía plástica el año pasado.
native_language_example: My cousin had plastic surgery last year.

additional_notes: Used to stress certainty or to make something explicit. Common patterns: **dejar (bien) claro que + clause** = “to make it (very) clear that…”, and **que quede claro que + clause** = “let it be clear that…”. In replies, you’ll often hear **claro que sí/no** = “of course (yes/no)”.
target_language_example: Que quede claro que no es una excusa.
native_language_example: Let it be clear that it’s not an excuse.

additional_notes: Used to emphasize that something is obvious, expected, or goes without saying. Often appears at the beginning of a sentence (“Claro está, …”) or as a parenthetical aside (“…, claro está.”). You may also see it as “claro está que …” = “of course/clearly …”.
target_language_example: Claro está que no puedo ir si tengo que trabajar.
native_language_example: Of course I can’t go if I have to work.

additional_notes: Used to strongly confirm or emphasize what you’re saying (often like an emphatic “yes”). It can answer a question (“Claro que sí”) or introduce a statement you’re sure about (“Claro que lo conozco”). Often followed by “sí” when responding directly: “Claro que sí”.
target_language_example: —¿Vienes mañana? —Claro que sí.
native_language_example: —Are you coming tomorrow? —Of course.

additional_notes: Used to strongly confirm something, usually followed by a verb that takes the object pronoun **lo** (“it,” “him” in some contexts). Common patterns: **Claro que lo sé** (Of course I know), **Claro que lo conozco** (Of course I know him/it), **Claro que lo soy** (Of course I am), **Claro que lo están** (Of course they are). **Lo** must agree with what you’re referring to; you may see **la/los/las** instead depending on gender/number.
target_language_example: —¿Sabes la respuesta? —Claro que lo sé.
native_language_example: —Do you know the answer? —Of course I do.

additional_notes: Used to give a strong, emphatic “no,” often in response to a question or suggestion. It can sound neutral or reassuring (“Claro que no, cariño.” = “Of course not, darling.”). You may also hear it with filler words like “pues”: “Pues claro que no.”
target_language_example: —¿Te molesta si abro la ventana? —Claro que no.
native_language_example: —Do you mind if I open the window? —Of course not.

additional_notes: Used to strongly agree or confirm something (often as a friendly, emphatic "yes"). It can sound a bit insistent depending on tone. Often interchangeable with "por supuesto" or "claro". In some contexts it can be ironic/sarcastic, like "yeah, sure".
target_language_example: —¿Vienes mañana? —Claro que sí.
native_language_example: —Are you coming tomorrow? —Of course.

additional_notes: Used to strongly confirm or emphasize what you’re saying, similar to “of course!” or “sure!” Often appears as a standalone answer (¿Vienes? — Claro que sí.) or before a statement (Claro que te ayudo.). Commonly followed by “sí” for extra emphasis: “claro que sí.”
target_language_example: ¿Me puedes ayudar? Claro que sí.
native_language_example: Can you help me? Of course.

additional_notes: Used with a subject/activity to say what class or lesson someone has: “tener clase de + [subject/activity]” (e.g., clase de piano, clase de español). It can also mean “type/kind of” in phrases like “una clase de problema” (“a kind of problem”), but in schedules it usually means a class/lesson.
target_language_example: Tengo clase de español mañana.
native_language_example: I have Spanish class tomorrow.

additional_notes: Refers to the social/economic group between the working class and the upper class. Often used with "de" to describe a person or place ("un barrio de clase media"), and can be modified: "clase media baja" = "lower middle class".
target_language_example: Ella es de clase media y vive en las afueras de la ciudad.
native_language_example: She is middle class and lives on the outskirts of the city.

meaning: social class (a person’s group in society based on wealth, education, job, etc.).
additional_notes: Used to talk about socioeconomic status (e.g., lower/middle/upper class). Often appears with adjectives like "clase social baja/media/alta" or with verbs like "pertenecer a" (to belong to) and phrases like "en cuanto a" (as for).
target_language_example: Vienen de una clase social diferente, pero se llevan bien.
native_language_example: They come from a different social class, but they get along well.

additional_notes: Meaning depends on context: (1) With plural things (often with "muchas"/"diferentes"), it means categories: "muchas clases de juegos" = many kinds of games. (2) With a subject you study, it means lessons: "tomar clases de berebere" = to take Berber classes. Often followed by a noun.
target_language_example: Hay muchas clases de comida aquí, y también doy clases de español.
native_language_example: There are many kinds of food here, and I also teach Spanish classes.

additional_notes: A common noun phrase for a car powered by electricity (often rechargeable). You’ll often hear it with verbs like cargar (to charge) or comprar (to buy). Also: carro eléctrico (more common in much of Latin America).
target_language_example: ¿Dónde puedo cargar mi coche eléctrico?
native_language_example: Where can I charge my electric car?

additional_notes: A noun phrase: coche (car) + nuevo (new). Adjectives usually go after the noun in Spanish (coche nuevo). It agrees in gender/number: coche nuevo (masc. singular), coches nuevos (plural). With a feminine noun (e.g., casa), it would be nueva.
target_language_example: Me compré un coche nuevo la semana pasada.
native_language_example: I bought myself a new car last week.

meaning: to answer the phone; to pick up the phone.
additional_notes: Used when someone answers a ringing phone (“pick up”). In much of Spain, coger is common, but in several Latin American countries coger can be vulgar, so alternatives like contestar el teléfono, atender el teléfono, or levantar el teléfono are safer there.
target_language_example: ¿Puedes coger el teléfono, por favor?
native_language_example: Can you answer the phone, please?

additional_notes: Preterite (completed past) form of "comenzar" for "ellos/ellas/ustedes". It’s usually followed by an infinitive: "comenzaron a + infinitive" (e.g., "comenzaron a hablar" = they started to talk). Similar in meaning to "empezaron a".
target_language_example: Cuando llegó el profesor, comenzaron a estudiar.
native_language_example: When the teacher arrived, they started to study.

additional_notes: Used to say someone began doing something in the past. It’s the preterite (completed past action) of "comenzar" + "a" + infinitive: "comenzó a estudiar" = "(he/she) started to study". Often you’ll include the subject (Él/Ella/La clase comenzó a...).
target_language_example: A las ocho, comenzó a llover.
native_language_example: At eight o’clock, it started to rain.

additional_notes: Past tense (preterite) of "comenzar": "comenzó" = "(it/he/she) began." Very common pattern: "comenzar/empezar a + infinitive" to say something started to happen (e.g., "comenzó a nevar" = it started to snow). "Llover" is an impersonal verb, so you don’t name a subject; in English we use "it."
target_language_example: Estábamos caminando y de repente comenzó a llover.
native_language_example: We were walking and suddenly it started to rain.

additional_notes: A very common, flexible phrase for when you want to eat but don’t specify what. Often used to suggest grabbing a bite: "Vamos a comer algo" (Let’s get something to eat). You can add adjectives or details: "algo delicioso" (something delicious), "algo dulce" (something sweet).
target_language_example: ¿Quieres comer algo antes de salir?
native_language_example: Do you want to eat something before we go out?

additional_notes: From the verb phrase "cometer errores" = "to make mistakes" (literally, "to commit errors"). "Comete" is the present tense for él/ella/usted; plural: "cometen errores". Very commonly used in general statements like "Todo el mundo comete errores" (Everyone makes mistakes).
