additional_notes: A common, neutral way to express thanks. It’s often followed by "por" + the reason (e.g., "dar las gracias por tu ayuda"). In replies, you may hear "No hay por qué" / "No hay de qué" meaning “You’re welcome / No need to thank me.”
target_language_example: Quería dar las gracias por tu ayuda.
native_language_example: I wanted to thank you for your help.

meaning: to do your best; to give it your best effort.
additional_notes: Used to encourage someone to put in maximum effort. Often appears as “dar lo mejor de ti” (“to give the best of yourself”). It can refer to effort, performance, or attitude.
target_language_example: En el examen voy a dar lo mejor de mí.
native_language_example: On the exam, I’m going to do my best.

meaning: to not matter; to be all the same.
additional_notes: Used to say something makes no difference or you don’t have a preference between options. Often appears conjugated (e.g., "me da lo mismo", "nos da lo mismo") and is commonly followed by "si..." (whether/if): "Me da lo mismo si vienes o no" (It doesn’t matter to me whether you come or not).
target_language_example: Para mí, dar lo mismo si comemos aquí o allí depende del precio.
native_language_example: For me, whether we eat here or there being all the same depends on the price.

meaning: to give rise to; to lead to (often: “dar lugar a”).
additional_notes: Most commonly used as **dar lugar a + noun/infinitive** to express that something causes or results in something else: *La decisión dio lugar a protestas* (“The decision led to protests”). In some formal contexts it can also mean “to take place,” but **tener lugar** is more common for that meaning.
target_language_example: El cambio de horario puede dar lugar a muchas quejas.
native_language_example: The schedule change can give rise to many complaints.

meaning: to lead to; to give rise to; to cause.
additional_notes: Used in more formal Spanish to talk about causes and results (A da lugar a B). Common with nouns like problemas, cambios, confusión, debate, accidentes. Not usually used for direct, intentional actions (for that, "causar" is more straightforward).
target_language_example: Un malentendido puede dar lugar a problemas.
native_language_example: A misunderstanding can lead to problems.

meaning: to scare; to be scary; to frighten someone.
additional_notes: Literally “to give fear.” Used to say something causes fear or seems scary. Common patterns: “Me da miedo…” = “I’m scared of…” / “It scares me…”, “Te da miedo” = “It scares you,” “Da miedo” = “It’s scary.” You can also use it with a specific thing: “Me da miedo la oscuridad” (the dark scares me).
target_language_example: Esa película puede dar miedo por la noche.
native_language_example: That movie can be scary at night.

meaning: to report (something), especially to the authorities; to notify.
additional_notes: Often used with an authority or superior: "dar parte a la policía" (report it to the police). You may also see "dar parte de + noun" meaning "to inform/report about" something (more formal/official-sounding than "decir").
target_language_example: Voy a dar parte a la policía del robo.
native_language_example: I’m going to report the robbery to the police.

meaning: to let (someone/something) pass; to make way (for).
additional_notes: Often used with "a": "dar paso a" = "to make way for" or "to lead to" (one thing results in another). In physical situations it can mean letting someone go through (e.g., in a crowd or doorway). In more formal contexts, "dar paso a" can introduce what comes next: "Ahora damos paso a..." = "Now we move on to...".
target_language_example: Perdón, ¿me puede dar paso?
native_language_example: Excuse me, can you let me through?

meaning: to make someone feel sorry; to make someone feel sad; to be a shame/pity.
additional_notes: Often used with an indirect object pronoun: me/te/le/nos/les da pena + infinitive or clause ("Me da pena decirlo" = "I’m sorry to say it / I feel bad saying it"). It can also mean someone/something inspires pity ("Esa situación da pena" = "That situation is sad/pitiful"). Note: "pena" can also mean "punishment/sentence" in other contexts, but in this expression it refers to pity/sadness.
target_language_example: Me da pena ver a tanta gente sin trabajo; esa situación da pena.
native_language_example: It makes me sad to see so many people without work; that situation is really sad.

meaning: to assume; to take for granted.
additional_notes: Used when you treat something as true or certain without confirming it first. Often followed by a clause with "que": "Dimos por hecho que vendrías" (We assumed you would come). It can also mean treating something as already done/settled: "Dieron por hecho el trato" (They considered the deal done).
target_language_example: No vayas a dar por hecho que voy a decir que sí.
native_language_example: Don’t assume I’m going to say yes.

meaning: to take for granted; to assume (as true).
additional_notes: Used when you treat something as already true or obvious, often without checking. Very commonly followed by a clause with "que": "Doy por sentado que..." (I assume that...). Also used in other tenses/persons: "Di por sentado que...", "Damos por sentado que...".
target_language_example: No debes dar por sentado que entiendo todo.
native_language_example: You shouldn’t take it for granted that I understand everything.

additional_notes: Used to say a plan, method, medicine, or effort is effective and achieves the desired outcome. Commonly appears as “dar buen resultado” (to work well) or “no dar resultado” (not to work). Conjugate “dar” to match the subject: “da resultado”, “dio resultado”, “ha dado resultado”.
target_language_example: Espero que el nuevo tratamiento pueda dar resultado.
native_language_example: I hope the new treatment can work.

meaning: to give (someone) time; to allow time.
additional_notes: Often used with "a" + person/thing: "Dame tiempo" = "Give me some time". Also common: "dar tiempo a + infinitive" (to give time to do something) and "darle tiempo a algo" (to let something have time to happen).
target_language_example: Necesito dar tiempo para pensarlo.
native_language_example: I need to give time to think about it.

meaning: to take a walk; to go for a stroll.
additional_notes: Common everyday expression for walking for pleasure or to get some fresh air. It’s often used with ir a (to go to): "Vamos a dar un paseo." You can also use it as a quick excuse/plan: "Solo voy a dar un paseo." In some contexts it can sound like an instruction (“You’re going to go for a walk now.”).
target_language_example: ¿Quieres dar un paseo después de cenar?
native_language_example: Do you want to go for a walk after dinner?

meaning: to take a step back; to back off.
additional_notes: Often used literally (physically stepping backward) and figuratively (pausing to reconsider, reducing involvement, or letting someone else lead). Common in advice or conflict situations: “Vamos a dar un paso atrás y pensar.”
target_language_example: Creo que es mejor dar un paso atrás y pensarlo bien.
native_language_example: I think it’s better to take a step back and think it through.

meaning: to take a walk/ride; to go for a spin; to take a lap/turn (around).
additional_notes: A very common phrase meaning to go out for a short walk or ride, often without a specific purpose ("I’m going out for a bit"). It can be on foot (dar una vuelta por la calle / por el barrio), by vehicle (dar una vuelta en el coche), or around something (dar una vuelta a la manzana = go around the block). In "Voy a dar una vuelta", the destination is often implied.
target_language_example: Hace buen tiempo, vamos a dar una vuelta por el parque.
native_language_example: The weather’s nice—let’s go for a walk around the park.

meaning: to turn/turn around; to flip (turn over).
additional_notes: Often appears as "dar la vuelta". Depending on context, it can mean turning yourself/something around (e.g., a corner, a car) or flipping something over (e.g., food in a pan). In some regions, "dar una vuelta" can also mean "to go for a walk/drive" (take a lap).
target_language_example: Tienes que dar vuelta la tortilla para que no se queme.
native_language_example: You have to flip the tortilla over so it doesn’t burn.

meaning: to thank (someone); to say thank you to (someone).
additional_notes: Uses the verb dar (“to give”) + le (“to him/her/you-formal”) + las gracias (“thanks”). It’s a polite way to thank someone: Quiero darle las gracias… (“I want to thank you…”). You can add por + reason: darle las gracias por su ayuda (“thank you for your help”). Change le depending on who you’re thanking: darte las gracias (to you, informal), darle las gracias (to you formal / to him/her), darles las gracias (to you all / to them).
target_language_example: Quería darle las gracias por venir hoy.
native_language_example: I wanted to thank you for coming today.

meaning: to act important; to put on airs.
additional_notes: Reflexive phrase used to criticize someone for behaving as if they are more important than others. Commonly used in forms like "No te des importancia" or "Se da mucha importancia"; the infinitive "darse importancia" can also be used after verbs like "dejar de" or "tender a" (e.g., "Deja de darte importancia").
target_language_example: Deja de darse importancia; solo estamos aquí para ayudar.
native_language_example: Stop acting so important; we’re just here to help.

meaning: to hurry (up); to be in a hurry.
additional_notes: A common reflexive expression meaning “to hurry.” Often used as a command: “¡Date prisa!” (to one person), “¡Dense prisa!” (to a group), and polite “¡Dese prisa!”. You can add “en” + activity: “Date prisa en vestirte” (Hurry up getting dressed).
target_language_example: Tenemos que darnos prisa, que llegamos tarde.
native_language_example: We have to hurry up; we’re running late.

additional_notes: Literally “to give you the thanks.” Used to express gratitude directly to someone you address as tú. Often followed by por + noun/clause (“darte las gracias por…” = “to thank you for…”). For usted, use “darle las gracias”; for more than one person, “darles las gracias.”
target_language_example: Sólo quería darte las gracias por tu ayuda.
native_language_example: I just wanted to thank you for your help.

additional_notes: This is the tú (informal singular) form of the idiom **darse cuenta de** (“to realize/to notice”). It’s reflexive (with **te**) and is commonly followed by **que + clause** (*Te das cuenta de que…*) or by a noun/phrase (*Te das cuenta de su valor*).
target_language_example: ¿Te das cuenta de que ya es muy tarde?
native_language_example: Do you realize it’s already very late?

additional_notes: Informal command used to tell one person to hurry. It’s the tú (informal) imperative of the reflexive phrase darse prisa (“to hurry”). You can soften it with por favor, or use the formal version: dese prisa (usted).
target_language_example: ¡Date prisa, que vamos a llegar tarde!
native_language_example: Hurry up, we're going to be late!

additional_notes: Used to indicate possession or connection to God, especially in religious expressions. Common in set phrases like “la gracia de Dios” (the grace of God) or “por el amor de Dios” (for the love of God). Word order can vary in English (“of God” vs “God’s”).
target_language_example: Pidió la ayuda de Dios en un momento difícil.
native_language_example: He asked for God's help in a difficult moment.

additional_notes: Often used to describe something happening slowly over time, step by step. Common with verbs like "irse" (to leave) and "acostumbrarse" (to get used to): "De a poco se van" = "Little by little they leave" / "they leave one by one over time." You can also use it alone as a short answer meaning “gradually / slowly.”
target_language_example: De a poco voy entendiendo el español.
native_language_example: Little by little I’m starting to understand Spanish.

additional_notes: Used to refer to a lower level/part of a place ("el quiosco de abajo" = the kiosk down below; "la estantería de abajo" = the lower shelf) or to indicate something comes from underneath something (often in the pattern "de abajo de + [object]", like "de abajo del escritorio" = from under the desk).
target_language_example: Las llaves están en el cajón de abajo.
native_language_example: The keys are in the lower drawer.

additional_notes: Uses "de + material" to say what something is made of: "una puerta de acero" = "a steel door". It can also be figurative to mean "ironclad" or "tough" (e.g., "una coartada de acero" = a rock-solid alibi; "una vejiga de acero" = a bladder of steel).
target_language_example: Compré una caja de acero para guardar mis documentos.
native_language_example: I bought a steel box to keep my documents.

additional_notes: Commonly used to show agreement or acceptance, like “okay” or “all right” (De acuerdo, vamos). In questions like “¿de acuerdo?”, it means “okay?” or “all right?”. With estar, it means “to agree / to be in agreement” (Mi tío estaba de acuerdo). In some varieties, “de acuerdo a” is used for “according to,” though “de acuerdo con” is often considered more standard.
target_language_example: No estoy de acuerdo contigo.
native_language_example: I don't agree with you.

additional_notes: Used to cite a source or criterion: de acuerdo a la radio/las noticias (according to the radio/news) or de acuerdo a la ley (according to the law). Often interchangeable with "según" or "de acuerdo con".
target_language_example: De acuerdo a mi calendario, hoy tenemos examen.
native_language_example: According to my calendar, we have an exam today.

meaning: 'according to' (based on what someone says or what a source indicates).
additional_notes: Used to introduce a source of information, opinion, rules, forecasts, reports, test results, etc. Similar to “según.” Don’t confuse with “estar de acuerdo con” = “to agree with.”
target_language_example: De acuerdo con el informe, el tren llegará tarde.
native_language_example: According to the report, the train will arrive late.

meaning: 'according to the' (referring to a feminine singular noun).
additional_notes: Used to cite a source, rule, or authority: de acuerdo con la ley / la política / la información. It must be followed by a feminine singular noun; for masculine use “de acuerdo con el”, and for plural “de acuerdo con los/las”.
target_language_example: De acuerdo con la ley, no se puede fumar aquí.
native_language_example: According to the law, you can’t smoke here.

meaning: to agree on / be in agreement about.
additional_notes: Used to say people share the same opinion about a topic: "estar de acuerdo en eso" (agree on that). With a clause, it often appears as "estar de acuerdo en que + verb" (agree that...): "Estoy de acuerdo en que es importante." You’ll also see "quedar de acuerdo en + infinitive/noun" meaning "to agree to / arrange to" do something: "Quedamos de acuerdo en salir temprano."
target_language_example: Estamos de acuerdo en que debemos salir temprano.
native_language_example: We agree that we should leave early.

additional_notes: Used with quantities/containers to say how much water there is: "un vaso de agua" (a glass of water), "una botella de agua" (a bottle of water), "un litro de agua" (a liter of water). It can also describe something related to water, like "presión de agua" (water pressure).
target_language_example: ¿Me traes una botella de agua, por favor?
native_language_example: Can you bring me a bottle of water, please?

meaning: 'from now on' (starting now, in the future).
additional_notes: Used to mark a change beginning at this moment and continuing into the future, often with rules, promises, or instructions. It can appear at the beginning of the sentence for emphasis. Common alternatives: "a partir de ahora" and "en adelante".
target_language_example: De ahora en adelante, voy a estudiar todos los días.
native_language_example: From now on, I'm going to study every day.

meaning: “from there”; in some contexts “(that one) over there.”
additional_notes: Commonly used to point something out with “ese/esa/eso + noun + de ahí” (= “that … over there”). With verbs of movement (salir, irse, venir), it means “from there” / “out of there.” Often refers to a place just mentioned or that’s obvious in the situation.
target_language_example: No puedo creer que todavía sigas de ahí.
native_language_example: I can’t believe you’re still there.

meaning: "of air" / "air-" (air-filled, air-powered, or related to air).
additional_notes: Used after a noun to specify that something is made of, filled with, or caused by air: una ráfaga de aire (a gust of air/wind), una corriente de aire (a draft), un colchón de aire (an air mattress). With quantity words it can mean “some air” (often “some fresh air” or “a breath”): Necesito algo de aire. In a poetic sense it can mean “made of air” (Soy de aire).
target_language_example: Dormimos en un colchón de aire porque no había cama.
native_language_example: We slept on an air mattress because there was no bed.

meaning: 'next door' / 'next to (it)' / 'nearby (the one next to it)'.
additional_notes: Used after a noun to mean the one next to it: "la habitación de al lado" (the next room), "la puerta de al lado" (the next door), "el perro de al lado" (the dog next door). It can refer to an adjacent place (next room/apartment/house) or the neighboring people/thing. Often implies immediate proximity (right next to), but in some contexts it can be more generally 'nearby' (e.g., "el hotel de al lado del río" = the hotel next to the river).
target_language_example: Voy a preguntarle al vecino de al lado si ha visto mi paquete.
native_language_example: I'm going to ask the next-door neighbor if they've seen my package.

additional_notes: Used after a verb (often an emotional or physical reaction) to show the reason/cause: you do something because you’re very happy. Common with verbs like gritar (to shout), llorar (to cry), saltar (to jump), bailar (to dance).
target_language_example: Cuando me dieron la noticia, salté de alegría.
native_language_example: When they gave me the news, I jumped for joy.

additional_notes: Used to say something is true or will happen, but you’re not sure exactly how or in what way. Often expresses uncertainty, approximation, or that the details aren’t important. Commonly placed at the beginning or in the middle of a sentence as a softener (like “well, somehow…”).
target_language_example: De alguna forma, vamos a encontrar una solución.
native_language_example: Somehow, we’re going to find a solution.

meaning: somehow; in some way (to some extent).
additional_notes: Used to say something will happen or be done even if you don’t know exactly how (“somehow”), or to soften/qualify a statement (“in a way / sort of”). Often used as a filler at the end of a sentence: “..., de alguna manera.”
target_language_example: Vamos a llegar a tiempo, de alguna manera.
native_language_example: We’ll get there on time, somehow.

additional_notes: Used to say the exact way is unknown or not important, or to soften what you’re saying. It can go at the beginning, middle, or end of the sentence (often set off by commas). Similar to "de alguna manera".
target_language_example: De algún modo, vamos a encontrar una solución.
native_language_example: Somehow, we’re going to find a solution.

additional_notes: Used after a noun to say something is rented/for rent: "casa de alquiler" (rental house), "coche de alquiler" (rental car). In signs/ads you may also see "Se alquila" (For rent).
target_language_example: Busco un piso de alquiler cerca del centro.
native_language_example: I'm looking for a rental apartment near downtown.

additional_notes: Used after a measurement (metros, centímetros, pisos) to say how tall something is: “X metros de altura” = “X meters tall / X meters in height.” You’ll often see it with verbs like tener (“to have”) and alcanzar (“to reach”). Also common as “a (X) metros de altura” = “at a height of (X) meters.”
target_language_example: La estatua mide cinco metros de altura.
native_language_example: The statue is five meters tall.

additional_notes: Used to refer to something that happened or existed earlier (in the past, or earlier in a conversation/story). Very common with "lo de antes" = "that earlier thing / what happened before" (e.g., "Gracias por lo de antes" = "Thanks for what you did earlier"). It can also describe older items or earlier photos/events ("fotos de antes").
target_language_example: ¿Te acuerdas de lo de antes? Necesito hablar contigo.
native_language_example: Do you remember what happened earlier? I need to talk to you.

additional_notes: Used to talk about origin or the place someone or something belongs to. With movement verbs, it often means leaving this place (for example, 'get out of here'). Before a noun, it can mean 'from here' or 'local'.
target_language_example: ¿Eres de aquí o estás de visita?
native_language_example: Are you from here, or are you visiting?

additional_notes: "De" + material means "made of" (or "of"). It’s used after a noun: "castillo de arena" (a sandcastle), "pala de arena" (a shovel full of sand). It can also describe something associated with sand, like "gato de arena" (sand cat).
target_language_example: Compré una bolsa de arena para el jardín.
native_language_example: I bought a bag of sand for the garden.

additional_notes: Used to refer to something located higher than another thing (the upstairs room, the top bunk, the upper part). Often contrasts with "de abajo" (downstairs/below). It can describe location ("el cuarto de arriba" = the upstairs room) or identify which one ("la litera de arriba" = the top bunk).
target_language_example: La oficina de arriba está cerrada hoy.
native_language_example: The upstairs office is closed today.

meaning: "of art" / "art" (used to describe something related to art).
additional_notes: Used after a noun to specify its type or focus: "clase de arte" (art class), "museo de arte" (art museum). It’s a common pattern in Spanish: noun + "de" + subject area.
target_language_example: Mañana tengo clase de arte.
native_language_example: Tomorrow I have art class.

additional_notes: Used after a noun to describe something or someone associated with a neighborhood (barrio). It can mean simply “local” (una tienda de barrio = a neighborhood shop) and, depending on context, can also suggest a humble/working-class, down-to-earth vibe (un chico de barrio = a kid from the neighborhood).
target_language_example: Vamos a comer a un bar de barrio.
native_language_example: Let's eat at a neighborhood bar.

additional_notes: Most commonly appears after the verb phrase “dejar de + infinitive” (“to stop doing something”). With “beber,” it can mean stopping drinking alcohol in general, or stopping drinking a specific drink if it’s stated (e.g., “dejar de beber café”).
target_language_example: Estoy tratando de dejar de beber alcohol.
native_language_example: I’m trying to stop drinking alcohol.

meaning: pocket-sized; for carrying in a pocket.
additional_notes: Used after a noun to describe something small/portable or designed to be carried in a pocket (e.g., diccionario de bolsillo, reloj de bolsillo).
target_language_example: Necesito una linterna de bolsillo para el coche.
native_language_example: I need a pocket flashlight for the car.

additional_notes: Uses "de" to describe something related to a firefighter or used by firefighters. Common with clothing or equipment: "traje de bombero" (firefighter suit), "casco de bombero" (firefighter helmet). It can also describe a job or role in context: "trabajo de bombero" (a firefighter’s job).
target_language_example: Mi hijo quiere un casco de bombero.
native_language_example: My son wants a firefighter helmet.

additional_notes: Used with the verb "estar" to describe someone’s temporary mood or attitude at a particular moment (e.g., "Estoy/Estás/Está/Estaba de buen humor"). The opposite is "de mal humor" (in a bad mood).
target_language_example: Hoy estoy de buen humor porque dormí bien.
native_language_example: Today I'm in a good mood because I slept well.

meaning: in good faith; with honest intentions.
additional_notes: Used to say someone acted honestly and without trying to deceive or harm anyone. Often appears with verbs like hacer (to do) or actuar (to act): “Lo hice de buena fe.” In everyday English it can also match “meaning well,” depending on context.
target_language_example: Te lo dije de buena fe, para ayudarte.
native_language_example: I told you in good faith, to help you.

meaning: 'with good …' (e.g., good intentions / good manners; politely).
additional_notes: Commonly used right before a noun to describe it: "de buenas intenciones" (with good intentions) and "de buenas maneras" (politely / with good manners). Note: "estar de buenas" is a different expression meaning "to be in a good mood."
target_language_example: Te lo pedí de buenas maneras, pero no quisiste escuchar.
native_language_example: I asked you politely, but you didn’t want to listen.

meaning: 'baseball' / 'of baseball' (used to describe something related to baseball).
additional_notes: Uses "de + [sport]" to mean something is associated with that sport: "jugadores de béisbol" (baseball players), "partidos de béisbol" (baseball games), "campo de béisbol" (baseball field). Often functions like an adjective in English ("baseball" as a modifier).
target_language_example: Me compré una gorra de béisbol.
native_language_example: I bought myself a baseball cap.

additional_notes: Used after a noun to specify that something comes from a horse or is meant for horses. In English it’s often translated with “horse” in front of the noun: carne de caballo = horse meat, mierda de caballo = horse manure. Literally it’s “of horse.”
target_language_example: ¿Tienes carne de caballo?
native_language_example: Do you have horse meat?

meaning: headfirst; upside down (with the head pointing down).
additional_notes: Often describes position or movement where the head goes first or is lower than the rest of the body: colgado de cabeza = “hanging upside down.” It also appears in common expressions like duro de cabeza (“stubborn/thick-headed”) and echar de cabeza a alguien (“to rat someone out / turn someone in,” colloquial).
target_language_example: El niño se tiró a la piscina de cabeza.
native_language_example: The kid jumped into the pool headfirst.

meaning: from beginning to end; completely (e.g., read/know something all the way through).
additional_notes: Commonly used with verbs like leer (to read) and conocer/saber (to know). It emphasizes that you read or know something in full, not just parts of it. It can also be used more generally for doing something thoroughly.
target_language_example: Me vi la serie de cabo a rabo en un fin de semana.
native_language_example: I watched the series from beginning to end in one weekend.

additional_notes: Used after a noun to describe it: "un producto de calidad" = a high-quality product. Often contrasts with "cantidad" (quantity): "calidad, no cantidad". You can also use it alone as a short evaluation meaning "(it’s) good quality".
target_language_example: Busco una chaqueta de calidad que me dure años.
native_language_example: I’m looking for a high-quality jacket that will last me for years.

additional_notes: Used to say something happens while you are going somewhere. Often appears with a destination: “de camino a/al + place” (on the way to + place). You can also use it more generally to mean “while I was on my way.”
target_language_example: De camino a casa, compré pan.
native_language_example: On the way home, I bought bread.

additional_notes: Used to say something happens while you are traveling toward your home. Often placed at the end of the sentence: "Me encontré con él de camino a casa". You can add more details after it: "de camino a casa desde la escuela" (on the way home from school).
target_language_example: Compré pan de camino a casa.
native_language_example: I bought bread on the way home.

meaning: facing; head-on (and in phrases like “de cara a…”, “looking ahead to / with a view to…”).
additional_notes: Most commonly used with “a”: “de cara a + noun” means “in preparation for,” “with a view to,” or “looking ahead to” something (often time-related: “de cara al futuro”). Without “a,” it can describe physical orientation: “estar de cara a…” = “to be facing…”.
target_language_example: De cara al futuro, vamos a ahorrar más.
native_language_example: Looking ahead to the future, we're going to save more.

meaning: with a view to; looking ahead to (in preparation for).
additional_notes: Often used before a future event, goal, or situation to mean “in anticipation of” or “in preparation for”: "De cara a las elecciones..." It can also be used more literally to mean “facing/toward” (physically), but the planning/anticipation meaning is very common in news and formal speech.
target_language_example: De cara al examen, voy a estudiar todos los días.
native_language_example: With the exam coming up, I’m going to study every day.

meaning: closely; from up close (at close range).
additional_notes: Used to talk about distance or attention: seeing something up close (Ver/Mirar de cerca) or watching/following someone closely (Seguir/Vigilar de cerca). Very common with the comparative: "más de cerca" = "closer" / "more closely."
target_language_example: Quiero ver el mapa de cerca.
native_language_example: I want to see the map up close.

additional_notes: Used after a noun to say it is chocolate-flavored or made with chocolate (e.g., torta/pastel/helado de chocolate). This is the common pattern noun + de + ingredient/flavor. Not the same as "chocolate" by itself (the ingredient).
target_language_example: ¿Tienes galletas de chocolate?
native_language_example: Do you have chocolate cookies?

additional_notes: Means “with certainty,” often used with verbs like saber or conocer: “No lo sé de cierto” = “I don’t know for sure.” It can sound a bit formal or literary; in everyday speech you’ll often hear “con certeza”, “seguro”, or “de verdad” instead.
target_language_example: No sé de cierto si va a venir.
native_language_example: I don’t know for sure if he/she is going to come.

additional_notes: Literally means “of color.” In reference to people (e.g., "persona/gente de color"), it’s often used to mean “person/people of color,” but in many Spanish-speaking contexts it can sound old-fashioned, euphemistic, or even offensive. Depending on the situation, speakers may prefer more specific terms like "persona negra" (Black person) or "afrodescendiente" (Afro-descendant). For objects, it can simply mean “colored” (not black-and-white).
target_language_example: En la foto antigua, todos salen en blanco y negro; la versión nueva es de color.
native_language_example: In the old photo, everyone is in black and white; the new version is in color.

additional_notes: Most often used with **dar**: **dar de comer (a alguien)** = “to feed (someone)” / “to give someone something to eat.” You’ll also see it in expressions like **la mano que te da de comer** (“the hand that feeds you”). On its own, it can appear in questions like **¿Qué hay de comer?** (“What is there to eat?”).
target_language_example: Le di de comer al gato antes de salir.
native_language_example: I fed the cat before leaving.

additional_notes: Used with verbs like ir/estar/salir/venir to say someone is out shopping (e.g., ir de compras = to go shopping). It often implies shopping for clothes, groceries, or general purchases.
target_language_example: Vamos de compras después del trabajo.
native_language_example: We’re going shopping after work.

additional_notes: Used after a noun to describe something connected to or meant for a community (e.g., "centro de comunidad" = community center, "servicio de comunidad" = community service). Often alternates with the adjective "comunitario/a" ("centro comunitario").
target_language_example: Este es un centro de comunidad para jóvenes.
native_language_example: This is a community center for young people.

additional_notes: Used after a noun to describe a person or thing that is trusted: "un amigo de confianza" (a trusted friend), "un informante de confianza" (a reliable informant). It can also describe a setting or relationship where people speak openly: "una reunión de confianza" (a private/off-the-record meeting).
target_language_example: Necesito a alguien de confianza para cuidar a los niños.
native_language_example: I need someone trustworthy to look after the kids.

additional_notes: Used to emphasize genuine feelings, especially in apologies or thanks ("Gracias de corazón", "Lo siento de corazón"). It can also describe something related to the heart in a more literal sense, depending on context (e.g., "en forma de corazón" = heart-shaped; "un hombre de corazón noble" = a kind-hearted man).
target_language_example: Te lo agradezco de corazón.
native_language_example: I sincerely thank you.

additional_notes: Used in comparisons with "más/menos ... que de costumbre" to mean "more/less ... than usual." You may also hear "lo de costumbre" meaning "the usual (thing)," often as a short reply when ordering or describing routine actions.
target_language_example: Hoy estoy más cansado que de costumbre.
native_language_example: Today I’m more tired than usual.

additional_notes: Used to move on to a conclusion or next point, often meaning that what was said before doesn’t change the outcome. It can also show indifference ("I don’t care anyway") or wrap up a topic ("Anyway." at the end of a conversation).
target_language_example: De cualquier forma, mañana tengo que trabajar.
native_language_example: Anyway, I have to work tomorrow.

meaning: anyway; in any case; either way.
additional_notes: Used to say the result is the same no matter what ("either way") or to move on/continue the conversation ("anyway"). Often placed at the beginning of a sentence with a comma: "De cualquier manera, ..." It can also modify an adjective to mean "in any way" (e.g., "atractivo de cualquier manera" = attractive either way).
target_language_example: De cualquier manera, tenemos que irnos ahora.
native_language_example: Anyway, we have to leave now.

meaning: Used in set phrases to mean “realize” (darse cuenta) or “pretend/assume” (haz/haga de cuenta que).
additional_notes:
You’ll almost always see it in fixed expressions:
- **darse cuenta de (algo)** = “to realize / to notice (something)”. Example: *Me di cuenta de mi error.*
- **haz/haga/hagan de cuenta que...** = “pretend / imagine / let’s assume that...”. It’s common in conversation and often introduces a hypothetical situation.
By itself, **de cuenta** isn’t usually used as an independent phrase in everyday Spanish.
target_language_example: Haz de cuenta que no escuchaste nada.
native_language_example: Pretend you didn’t hear anything.

meaning: made of leather; leather (as a material).
additional_notes: Used after a noun to describe the material something is made from: "zapatos de cuero" (leather shoes), "cinturón de cuero" (leather belt). It can also stand alone when the item is understood from context: "Éstos son de cuero" = "These are leather."
target_language_example: Quiero una chaqueta de cuero negra.
native_language_example: I want a black leather jacket.

meaning: serious; worrying; not to be taken lightly.
additional_notes: Often used after verbs like **estar** or **ser** to say that a person/situation is in a bad or delicate state: **estar de cuidado** (“to be in serious condition / to be worrying”). Also common in **cosa (o asunto) de cuidado** to mean “a serious matter” or “something tricky/dangerous.”
target_language_example: Después del accidente, su estado está de cuidado.
native_language_example: After the accident, his condition is serious.

meaning: vulgar: used to mean “(as) hell / extremely” in expressions like *caerse de culo* (“to be shocked/amazed”), or as a crude insult meaning “crappy/ass-…” (*cara/pinta de culo*).
additional_notes: *Culo* literally means “butt/ass,” and *de culo* shows up inside set phrases. Most common: **(te) vas a caer de culo** = “you’re going to be blown away / shocked.” It’s also used to insult someone’s look or attitude: **cara de culo** (“ass-face,” someone with a sour/unpleasant expression) and **pinta de culo** (“you look awful / you look like crap”). Very informal and rude—avoid in polite situations.
target_language_example: Cuando me enteré, me caí de culo.
native_language_example: When I found out, I was shocked.

additional_notes: Used after a noun to describe political orientation (e.g., un partido de derecha = a right-wing party) or to indicate position/direction (e.g., el carril de derecha = the right lane). Which meaning is intended depends on context.
target_language_example: Mi abuelo siempre vota por partidos de derecha.
native_language_example: My grandfather always votes for right-wing parties.

additional_notes: Uses "de" to link something to money. Common in phrases like "problemas de dinero" (money problems), "hablar de dinero" (to talk about money), and with adjectives/expressions like "estar escaso de dinero" or "andar corto de dinero" (to be short on money).
target_language_example: No quiero hablar de dinero ahora.
native_language_example: I don’t want to talk about money right now.

meaning: “of drugs”; used to say something involves drugs (usually illegal).
additional_notes: Common after nouns to specify what kind of thing it is: comercio de drogas (drug trade), transporte de drogas (drug transport/trafficking). In warnings/commands you’ll often hear “Nada de drogas” = “No drugs.” It can be literal (medications) in the right context, but in everyday speech it often implies illegal drugs.
target_language_example: La policía investiga una red de tráfico de drogas.
native_language_example: The police are investigating a drug trafficking network.

additional_notes: Used to talk about something happening in the daytime (not at night). Often contrasts with "de noche" (at night). You can use it after a verb to say when you do something: "Trabajo de día" (I work during the day).
target_language_example: Prefiero viajar de día.
native_language_example: I prefer to travel during the day.

additional_notes: A common question to ask someone’s origin (country, city, or region). Often used as a standalone question: “¿De dónde eres?” You can add emphasis or politeness with “Por cierto” (by the way) or the person’s name. Answer with “Soy de + place” (e.g., “Soy de México”).
target_language_example: ¿De dónde eres? Soy de Canadá.
native_language_example: Where are you from? I'm from Canada.

meaning: of them (feminine plural); from/among them; sometimes “of them” after a verb that uses **de**.
additional_notes: **Ellas** means “they/them” when referring to an all-female group or to feminine plural nouns (e.g., *las chicas, las casas*). **De ellas** is used for possession (*el libro de ellas* = “their book”), quantities/parts (*la mitad de ellas* = “half of them”), and after expressions that take **de** (e.g., *tener miedo de ellas* = “to be afraid of them”). In sentences like *No hay muchas de ellas*, Spanish usually uses **muchas** (feminine) to match *ellas*.
target_language_example: Tengo miedo de ellas, pero no son peligrosas.
native_language_example: I’m afraid of them, but they aren’t dangerous.

additional_notes: Used after a noun to indicate something is related to an emergency or is meant to be used only in urgent situations (e.g., situación de emergencia, aterrizaje de emergencia, salida de emergencia, botón de emergencia). Often translates as “emergency” as an adjective in English.
target_language_example: Solo usa el teléfono de emergencia si necesitas ayuda inmediata.
native_language_example: Only use the emergency phone if you need immediate help.

additional_notes: Used after a noun to specify that something is related to energy (often electricity or power): e.g., red de energía (energy grid), control de energía (power control), señal de energía (power/energy signal), caída de energía eléctrica (power outage/drop in electrical power). In Spanish, this often works like an English adjective before the noun (“energy network/grid”, “power control room”).
target_language_example: Necesitamos un plan de ahorro de energía en la oficina.
native_language_example: We need an energy-saving plan in the office.

additional_notes: Used after a noun to describe something as wonderful, unreal, or “perfect,” often implying it feels like a dream (e.g., equipo de ensueño = “dream team,” hombre de ensueño = “dream guy/man,” reino de ensueño = “dreamlike kingdom”).
target_language_example: Pasamos unas vacaciones de ensueño en la playa.
native_language_example: We had a dream vacation at the beach.

meaning: "at first / initially"; also "starting/entry" (e.g., starting salary, inbox).
additional_notes: Most commonly used as an adverb meaning “right away” or “to begin with”: "De entrada, no..." = “At first, I don’t...”. It can also describe something related to “entry” or “input,” depending on the noun: "salario de entrada" (starting salary), "carpeta/bandeja de entrada" (inbox), "aparato de entrada" (input device).
target_language_example: De entrada, pensé que era muy difícil.
native_language_example: At first, I thought it was very difficult.

additional_notes: Used to describe the manner or way something is done, often referring back to something already mentioned or visible in the situation. Common with negatives for correction or disapproval: "No de esa forma" = "Not like that."
target_language_example: No lo hagas de esa forma; hazlo con más cuidado.
native_language_example: Don’t do it like that; do it more carefully.

additional_notes: Used to refer to the way something is done or happens, often pointing to something already mentioned or obvious from context. Common in advice or criticism: “No lo hagas de esa manera” = “Don’t do it that way.” It can also introduce a result or plan: “De esa manera, …” = “That way, … / In that way, …”.
target_language_example: Hazlo de esa manera y terminarás más rápido.
native_language_example: Do it that way and you’ll finish faster.

additional_notes: A common combination of de + ese. It usually means "of that" or "from that," depending on context. Ese is masculine singular and is used before a masculine singular noun; compare de esa, de esos, de esas.
target_language_example: La puerta de ese edificio siempre está cerrada.
native_language_example: The door of that building is always closed.

additional_notes: Used to describe the manner or way something is done or thought. Often appears after verbs like pensar (to think), hacerlo (to do it), decirlo (to say it), or irse (to leave). Can be used in corrections or prohibitions: «No de ese modo» = “Not like that.”
target_language_example: No lo hagas de ese modo; hazlo más despacio.
native_language_example: Don’t do it like that; do it more slowly.

additional_notes: Used to refer back to something already mentioned or understood from context. Often follows verbs like hablar (to talk) and saber (to know): hablar de eso = “talk about that,” saber de eso = “know about that.” With nada/no sé: no sé nada de eso = “I don’t know anything about that.”
target_language_example: No quiero hablar de eso ahora.
native_language_example: I don’t want to talk about that right now.

additional_notes: Used to say what the real meaning, purpose, or main idea is. Very common when concluding or clarifying something: “Así que de eso se trata” = “So that’s what it’s about.” You can also add a noun/topic: “De eso se trata la vida” (That’s what life is about) or “De eso se trata esto” (That’s what this is about).
target_language_example: Ahora lo entiendo: de eso se trata.
native_language_example: Now I get it: that’s what it’s about.

additional_notes: Used for position/posture (often with verbs like "echarse" = to lie down): "echarse de espalda" = to lie on your back. It’s also used to describe things related to the back: "dolor(es) de espalda" = back pain, "masaje de espalda" = back massage. Note: "de espaldas" (plural) means "with your back turned / facing away."
target_language_example: Después de correr, me dolía la espalda y pedí un masaje de espalda.
native_language_example: After running, my back hurt and I asked for a back massage.

meaning: with your back turned; on your back (face up).
additional_notes: Describes position/orientation. **Estar de espaldas (a alguien/algo)** = facing away, with your back toward someone/something: *Estaba de espaldas a mí.* It can also describe body position: **tirado/acostado de espaldas** = lying on your back (face up).
target_language_example: Me quedé de espaldas a la puerta.
native_language_example: I stayed with my back to the door.

additional_notes: Used with feminine singular nouns to mean "of this" or "from this." It’s the preposition "de" + "esta" (feminine form of "this"). For masculine nouns, use "de este"; for plural, "de estas" (feminine) / "de estos" (masculine).
target_language_example: No entiendo el origen de esta historia.
native_language_example: I don’t understand the origin of this story.

additional_notes: Used to describe the manner something happens or to invite someone to see/understand something from a particular perspective. Often followed by “como” (e.g., “De esta forma es como…” = “This is how…”).
target_language_example: Hazlo de esta forma para que sea más fácil.
native_language_example: Do it this way so it’s easier.

additional_notes: Used to describe how something is done or how something happens. Often appears with verbs like ser (Es mejor de esta manera), terminar (terminar de esta manera), actuar (actuar de esta manera), or sentirse (sentirse de esta manera). It can also be used alone as a short answer meaning “like this.”
target_language_example: Hazlo de esta manera, por favor.
native_language_example: Do it this way, please.

additional_notes: Used to refer back to something that happened earlier today (in the morning): la presentación de esta mañana (this morning’s presentation), lo de esta mañana (what happened this morning / the thing from this morning). Often follows a noun ("la reunión de esta mañana").
target_language_example: ¿Tienes el informe de esta mañana?
native_language_example: Do you have this morning’s report?

additional_notes: Used to describe something that is scheduled for, happening in, or belonging to tonight: la cena de esta noche (tonight’s dinner), el concierto de esta noche (tonight’s concert). Often follows a noun (la reunión de esta noche).
target_language_example: ¿A qué hora es la película de esta noche?
native_language_example: What time is tonight’s movie?

additional_notes: `de` + `esta` (`this`, feminine). It literally means 'of/from this (one)'. `esta` can stand alone to mean 'this one' when the feminine noun is understood from context. With some verbs or expressions, English changes the wording: `encargarse de esta` = 'take care of this one'; `salir de esta` = 'get out of this / pull through.'
target_language_example: Tu solución es diferente de esta.
native_language_example: Your solution is different from this one.

additional_notes: Uses the infinitive estar after de in several common patterns: (1) after adjectives: "feliz de estar..." = "happy to be..."; (2) after nouns: "la impresión de estar..." = "the impression of being..."; (3) to give a cause: "me duelen... de estar sentado" = "...from/because of being seated"; (4) after "deber de" to express probability/assumption: "debías de estar..." ≈ "you must have been..." (in everyday Spanish people also say "deber" without "de").
target_language_example: Estoy contento de estar contigo hoy.
native_language_example: I'm happy to be with you today.

meaning: "to be here" / "being here" (often after a feeling like happy or glad).
additional_notes: Used after adjectives or expressions of emotion to give the reason/cause: "Estoy contento/feliz de…" = "I’m happy/glad to…" or "about…". Here, "estar" is used for being in a place (location).
target_language_example: Me alegro mucho de estar aquí con ustedes.
native_language_example: I’m really glad to be here with you all.

additional_notes: Used to indicate belonging/origin related to something close/identified: de + este + masculine singular noun (e.g., de este club = “of this club”). For feminine nouns, use “de esta”; for plural, “de estos/de estas”. Note: “de + el” contracts to “del”, but “de + este” does not contract.
target_language_example: ¿Eres miembro de este club?
native_language_example: Are you a member of this club?

additional_notes: Commonly used with verbs or expressions that take "de" (e.g., disfrutar de = to enjoy, deshacerse de = to get rid of, escapar de = to escape from, hablar de = to talk about). It refers to something close in context: "this" (esto). Often translates as "of this" or "about this" depending on the verb.
target_language_example: No quiero saber nada más de esto.
native_language_example: I don't want to know anything more about this.

additional_notes: Used with "ser" to describe a person (or group) as someone you can trust: "Es de fiar" = "He/She is trustworthy." In the negative, it often means you shouldn't trust them: "No es de fiar" = "He/She isn't trustworthy" / "He/She can't be trusted."
target_language_example: No le cuentes el secreto; no es de fiar.
native_language_example: Don’t tell him the secret; he can’t be trusted.

additional_notes: Used after a noun to describe something that goes beyond the surface ("un análisis/debate de fondo" = an in-depth analysis/debate; "algo más de fondo" = something deeper/underlying). In sports it describes endurance/long-distance events ("corredora de fondo" = long-distance runner) and "esquí de fondo" means cross-country skiing.
target_language_example: Necesitamos un análisis de fondo antes de decidir.
native_language_example: We need an in-depth analysis before deciding.

additional_notes: Used to describe how something is done or how something happens, usually followed by an adjective or adverb: de forma ordenada (in an orderly way), de forma segura (safely), de forma natural (naturally). Common in more formal or written Spanish; in conversation you can often replace it with just an adverb (rápidamente, claramente) or with "de manera" (same meaning).
target_language_example: Respira de forma lenta y profunda.
native_language_example: Breathe slowly and deeply.

additional_notes: Used for direction/position: “de frente” = in front, straight toward you (often contrasted with “de los lados” = from the sides). With verbs of speaking (decir, hablar, contar), it means speaking directly and honestly, sometimes confronting someone (“Te lo digo de frente”).
target_language_example: Prefiero que me lo digas de frente.
native_language_example: I’d rather you tell me directly (to my face).

meaning: soccer (used to say something is related to soccer).
additional_notes: “De” often means “of” or “for.” You use “de fútbol” after a noun to describe it: equipo de fútbol (soccer team), zapatos de fútbol (soccer shoes/cleats), torneo de fútbol (soccer tournament). It’s neutral and very common. In many countries “fútbol” means soccer; in the US you may also see “fútbol americano” for American football.
target_language_example: Necesito una camiseta de fútbol para el entrenamiento.
native_language_example: I need a soccer shirt/jersey for practice.

meaning: formal; dressy; for a gala (special occasion).
additional_notes: Used after a noun to describe something meant for a very formal or ceremonial event (e.g., "cena de gala" = gala dinner, "vestido de gala" = formal evening dress, "uniforme de gala" = dress/ceremonial uniform). It often implies elegant, fancy clothing or an official ceremony.
target_language_example: Esta noche es una cena de gala, así que ponte algo de gala.
native_language_example: Tonight is a gala dinner, so wear something formal.

additional_notes: Used to describe an action or change that happens unexpectedly and quickly. With actions like opening a door, it can also suggest doing it abruptly/with force (like slamming it open). Often goes with verbs like abrir, parar, terminar, detenerse.
target_language_example: Me desperté de golpe por el ruido.
native_language_example: I woke up suddenly because of the noise.

meaning: on duty (especially doing a shift, being on call).
additional_notes: Used for being assigned to a duty shift or being the person responsible at that time (e.g., hospital, security, work rotations): estar de guardia = to be on duty/on call; turnos de guardia = duty shifts/rotations. With professions it can also imply the role itself (e.g., disfrazado de guardia = disguised as a security guard).
target_language_example: Hoy estoy de guardia, así que no puedo salir.
native_language_example: I'm on duty today, so I can't go out.

additional_notes: Usually introduces the perfect infinitive: “de haber + past participle” (de haber robado = of having stolen). Common after nouns/adjectives/verbs like: acusado de…, feliz de…, suerte de…, presumir de…. At the start of a clause, “de haber + participle” can express a condition, similar to “if … had” / “had …” (De haber ocurrido…, hubiera… = If it had happened…, it would have…).
target_language_example: Me arrepiento de haber dicho eso.
native_language_example: I regret having said that.

additional_notes:
Literally “of speaking,” but in practice it’s usually part of common patterns with **de + infinitive**:
- **turno de hablar** = “turn to speak”
- **encargarse de hablar** = “to take charge of speaking / to handle the talking”
- With verbs like **dejar / parar / tratar**, it often becomes:
  - **dejar / parar de hablar** = “to stop talking”
  - **tratar de hablar** = “to try to speak”
So the English translation changes depending on the verb or noun before **de**.
target_language_example: Es hora de hablar con la profesora.
native_language_example: It’s time to talk to the teacher.

additional_notes: Used with verbs like "morir"/"morirse" or "estar muriéndose" to say someone dies or is dying because of hunger. Very common as an exaggeration in everyday speech: "Me muero de hambre" = "I’m starving."
target_language_example: Después del trabajo, me muero de hambre.
native_language_example: After work, I’m starving.

additional_notes: Used to introduce information that confirms, clarifies, or slightly corrects what was just said. Common at the beginning of a sentence (often followed by a comma: “De hecho, …”), but it can also appear mid-sentence or at the end (“…, de hecho.”).
target_language_example: No me molesta; de hecho, me alegra.
native_language_example: It doesn’t bother me; in fact, it makes me happy.

meaning: “of iron” / “made of iron”; also “iron” (very strong, strict, or tough).
additional_notes: Literal use: describes the material something is made from (un escritorio de hierro, una sartén de hierro). Figurative use: describes strength, toughness, or strict control, often in phrases like “puño de hierro” (iron fist) or “mano de hierro (en guante de terciopelo)” (firm/strict control disguised with softness).
target_language_example: Necesitamos una voluntad de hierro para terminar este proyecto a tiempo.
native_language_example: We need an iron will to finish this project on time.

meaning: man to man; frankly and directly.
additional_notes: Used to introduce a serious, honest conversation (or confrontation), often privately and without intermediaries: “Let’s talk straight.” It’s gendered/male-coded; a more neutral option is “de persona a persona” (or “de tú a tú” in some contexts).
target_language_example: Mira, de hombre a hombre: necesito que me digas la verdad.
native_language_example: Look, man to man: I need you to tell me the truth.

meaning: of English; English (as a school subject).
additional_notes: Used with nouns to specify the language is English, especially in education or language-related contexts: examen de inglés (English test), maestro/profesor de inglés (English teacher), clase/curso de inglés (English class/course).
target_language_example: Tengo clase de inglés los martes.
native_language_example: I have English class on Tuesdays.

additional_notes: Used to say something should happen without delay. Very common with commands/requests ("sal de inmediato") and with future intentions ("estaré ahí de inmediato"). Similar to "enseguida" and "ahora mismo".
target_language_example: Llámame de inmediato si pasa algo.
native_language_example: Call me immediately if something happens.

additional_notes: Combination of de + la, used before feminine singular nouns. It often shows possession, origin, source, or relation. Unlike de + el, which becomes del, de + la stays separate.
target_language_example: Vengo de la estación.
native_language_example: I'm coming from the station.

meaning: from the village; of the village.
additional_notes: Used to say someone or something belongs to, comes from, or is located in a village (la aldea). It often follows a noun: "la gente de la aldea" (the village people), "los caminos de la aldea" (the village roads).
target_language_example: El médico de la aldea llega los lunes.
native_language_example: The village doctor arrives on Mondays.

additional_notes: Used with "de" + "la" to show origin (from the library) or relationship/possession (the library's...). "De" can mean "of" or "from" depending on context.
target_language_example: Saqué este libro de la biblioteca.
native_language_example: I took this book from the library.

additional_notes:
Often used in common expressions with pronominal verbs, especially:
- sacarse algo de la cabeza / quitarse algo de la cabeza = to get something out of your head (stop thinking/worrying about it)
It can also be literal, meaning “from the head” (e.g., “born from the head of Zeus”).
target_language_example: No puedo sacarme esa canción de la cabeza.
native_language_example: I can’t get that song out of my head.

additional_notes: Most commonly used with places and directions: "al otro lado de la calle" (across the street), "en la esquina de la calle" (on the corner of the street), "al final de la calle" (at the end of the street). It can also describe people as "la gente de la calle" meaning ordinary people or people out on the street (context-dependent).
target_language_example: La farmacia está al otro lado de la calle.
native_language_example: The pharmacy is across the street.

meaning: from/out of bed; off the bed.
additional_notes: Used with movement verbs to show leaving the bed or moving away from it (e.g., salirse/levantarse/saltar/caerse de la cama = get out of bed / get up out of bed / jump out of bed / fall off the bed). It can also appear in location phrases like al pie de la cama (“at the foot of the bed”).
target_language_example: Me levanté de la cama muy temprano.
native_language_example: I got out of bed very early.

additional_notes: Used with nouns to show belonging/origin: "el corazón de la casa" = "the heart of the house." It’s the combination of "de" (of/from) + "la" (the) + "casa" (house/home). You’ll also hear it in set phrases like "vino de la casa" (“house wine”, i.e., the restaurant’s own/default wine).
target_language_example: La cocina es el centro de la casa.
native_language_example: The kitchen is the center of the house.

additional_notes: Combination of "de" + "la" ("of/from" + "the"). Used to describe something belonging to the city or located within it (e.g., "el más grande de la ciudad" = "the biggest in the city"), or to indicate movement/origin (e.g., "salir de la ciudad" = "to leave the city"). The exact meaning depends on context.
target_language_example: Es el restaurante más famoso de la ciudad.
native_language_example: It’s the most famous restaurant in the city.

additional_notes: Used with a noun to say someone/something belongs to a specific class/group (e.g., "la más alta de la clase" = the tallest in the class; "el mejor de la clase" = the best in the class). With verbs of movement or absence, it can mean “from/out of class” (e.g., "salid de la clase" = leave the classroom; "ausentarse de la clase" = be absent from class).
target_language_example: Soy el más rápido de la clase.
native_language_example: I'm the fastest in the class.

meaning: from the kitchen; of the kitchen.
additional_notes: Used after a noun to say it belongs to or is located in the kitchen ("the kitchen's" / "in the kitchen"). It’s the contraction of "de" + "la" (feminine singular), so it refers to "la cocina" (the kitchen). Common in phrases like "la luz de la cocina" (the kitchen light) or "la ventana de la cocina" (the kitchen window).
target_language_example: ¿Dónde están las llaves de la cocina?
native_language_example: Where are the kitchen keys?

meaning: of the company; from the company.
additional_notes: Used to show possession/association ("the company's...") or affiliation/where someone works ("I'm from the phone company"). In Spanish, "compañía" can mean a business/company (not just "companionship").
target_language_example: El nombre de la compañía aparece en la puerta.
native_language_example: The company’s name appears on the door.

additional_notes: Used to indicate belonging or connection to a specific company (empresa). Most often it’s possession/association: "el presidente de la empresa" (the company’s president), "el éxito de la empresa" (the company’s success). It can also mean "from the company" depending on context (e.g., "un correo de la empresa" = an email from the company).
target_language_example: Necesito la dirección de la empresa para enviar el paquete.
native_language_example: I need the company’s address to send the package.

additional_notes: Used with nouns to show possession/association ("la campana de la escuela" = the school bell, "un récord de la escuela" = a school record). With some nouns it can mean origin or leaving a place ("su ausencia de la escuela" = his/her absence from school). Also used to describe relationships formed there ("amigos de la escuela" = friends from school / school friends).
target_language_example: Mañana es el festival de la escuela.
native_language_example: Tomorrow is the school festival.

meaning: on/at the corner; around the corner (nearby).
additional_notes: Used after a noun to mean “the one on/at the corner” (e.g., la tienda de la esquina = the corner store). It often implies a nearby place people already know in the neighborhood, like a local store or house.
target_language_example: ¿Vamos a tomar un café en el bar de la esquina?
native_language_example: Shall we have a coffee at the corner café?

meaning: “of the station” or “from the station” (sometimes “of the season”).
additional_notes: “De la” usually means “of the” or “from the,” depending on context. “Estación” can mean a transport station (train/bus/metro) or a season of the year. So “de la estación” can refer to something belonging to the station (la salida de la estación = the station exit), coming from the station (llamé de la estación = I called from the station), or related to the season (depende de la estación = depends on the season).
target_language_example: Salimos de la estación y buscamos un taxi.
native_language_example: We left the station and looked for a taxi.

meaning: of the family; in the family.
additional_notes: Used after a noun or pronoun to specify that someone/something belongs to a particular family or is part of the group. Common in comparisons and roles: “el más… de la familia” (the most … in the family), “el bebé de la familia” (the baby/youngest in the family), and also in “amigo/a de la familia” (a family friend).
target_language_example: Soy el mayor de la familia.
native_language_example: I’m the oldest in the family.

meaning: 'of the party' (used after certain verbs like disfrutar de).
additional_notes: Often appears after verbs that take the preposition "de", especially "disfrutar de" = "to enjoy" something. In "disfruten de la fiesta", "de la fiesta" means what you should enjoy: the party/celebration.
target_language_example: ¡Disfruta de la fiesta!
native_language_example: Enjoy the party!

additional_notes: Used after a noun to show that something belongs to, comes from, or is related to people in general (not one specific person). Often appears in phrases like "el respeto de la gente" (people’s respect), "la vida de la gente" (people’s lives), "la aprobación de la gente" (people’s approval). "Gente" is usually singular in Spanish (la gente es...), even though it means "people."
target_language_example: Me preocupa la opinión de la gente.
native_language_example: I care about people’s opinion.

additional_notes: Used with nouns to specify something related to a particular war (e.g., el peligro de la guerra = “the danger of war”), and with verbs like hablar to mean the topic is war (hablar de la guerra = “to talk about the war”). Also appears in fixed phrases like dios de la guerra (“god of war”).
target_language_example: No quiero hablar de la guerra ahora.
native_language_example: I don't want to talk about the war right now.

additional_notes: Used after verbs of movement (salir, marcharse, irse) to say someone leaves a room. It can also mean “of the bedroom” in context, since habitación can refer to a bedroom.
target_language_example: Salí de la habitación para contestar el teléfono.
native_language_example: I left the room to answer the phone.

meaning: “in history / ever” (used to emphasize a superlative).
additional_notes: Literally “of (the) history,” but it’s often used after a superlative (mejor, peor, más grande, etc.) to mean “in history” or “of all time / ever.” You can add an adjective like “moderna” (de la historia moderna = “in modern history”).
target_language_example: Es el mejor día de la historia.
native_language_example: It’s the best day ever.

additional_notes: Used after a noun to mean it belongs to or affects all humans in general (not a specific person or group). Often appears in phrases like "la historia de la humanidad" (the history of humanity) or "un enemigo de la humanidad" (an enemy of humankind).
target_language_example: Este es uno de los mayores desafíos de la humanidad.
native_language_example: This is one of humankind’s biggest challenges.

meaning: of the church; from the church.
additional_notes: Used to show a relationship or origin: something belonging to a church (e.g., el coro de la iglesia = the church choir) or coming from a church (e.g., saliendo de la iglesia = leaving the church). It’s the combination of "de" (of/from) + "la" (the) + "iglesia" (church).
target_language_example: Las puertas de la iglesia están abiertas.
native_language_example: The church doors are open.

additional_notes: Used after a noun to describe something that belongs to the island or is associated with it (e.g., la gente de la isla = the people of the island). It can also imply origin (someone or something is from the island), depending on context. It’s built from de (“of/from”) + la (“the”) + isla (“island”).
target_language_example: Compramos comida típica de la isla.
native_language_example: We bought typical island food.

additional_notes: Used to show that someone/something is included on a list or removed from it. Very common with verbs like estar/ser (estar en la lista = to be on the list), borrar/quitar/sacar/retirar (de la lista = off/from the list). Often refers to rankings or order: a la cabeza de la lista = at the top of the list; al fondo de la lista = at the bottom of the list.
target_language_example: Por favor, quita mi nombre de la lista.
native_language_example: Please, take my name off the list.

meaning: from the rain (rain-related: protection/shelter from rain).
additional_notes: Uses "de" to indicate what something protects you from or gives you shelter from. Very common in expressions like "a pesar de la lluvia" (despite the rain), "cubrir(se) de la lluvia" (to cover/protect oneself from the rain), and "refugio de la lluvia" (shelter from the rain).
target_language_example: Nos quedamos bajo el techo para protegernos de la lluvia.
native_language_example: We stayed under the roof to protect ourselves from the rain.

meaning: in the early hours of the morning (after midnight).
additional_notes: Used with times or expressions like "a la una / a las dos / a esas horas" to specify that it’s very late at night or very early in the morning (typically from about 12:00 a.m. until dawn). Often implies it’s an unusually late/early hour: "Son las dos de la madrugada" = 2 a.m.
target_language_example: Llegamos a casa a las tres de la madrugada.
native_language_example: We got home at three in the morning (3 a.m.).

additional_notes: Used with verbs like ir/andar/caminar (to go/walk) and agarrar/coger (to hold) to say someone is holding another person’s hand: “andar/ir de la mano” = “to walk hand-in-hand.” It can also indicate that something is taken/removed from someone’s hand (more literally “from the hand”), as in “le quitó X de la mano.”
target_language_example: Los niños cruzaron la calle de la mano con su mamá.
native_language_example: The kids crossed the street holding their mom’s hand.

meaning: in the morning; of the morning.
additional_notes: Often used after a noun to specify that something happens in the morning: el sol de la mañana (the morning sun), el primer tren de la mañana (the first train in the morning). With time expressions it’s common to say a primera hora de la mañana (“first thing in the morning”).
target_language_example: Tengo una reunión a primera hora de la mañana.
native_language_example: I have a meeting first thing in the morning.

meaning: from/off the table; of the table.
additional_notes: Uses "de" + "la" ("of/from" + "the") with "mesa" (table). With movement verbs (e.g., caerse, quitar, recoger), it often means "off/from the table" (something leaves the table surface). With nouns, it can mean "of the table" (things that are on the table or related to it), depending on context.
target_language_example: Quita los platos de la mesa, por favor.
native_language_example: Please take the plates off the table.

additional_notes: Used to say something happens similarly or with the same method as something else. Often followed by "que" to compare two actions ("de la misma manera que..."). It can also stand alone to mean “the same way.”
target_language_example: Hazlo de la misma manera que te enseñé.
native_language_example: Do it the same way I showed you.

meaning: of the mountain; from the mountain.
additional_notes: Used to describe something that belongs to, comes from, or is related to a specific mountain. Very common in phrases like “al pie de la montaña” (at the foot/base of the mountain).
target_language_example: Desde aquí se ve la nieve de la montaña.
native_language_example: From here you can see the snow on the mountain.

additional_notes: Uses "de + la + muerte" to link something to death (belonging to it, caused by it, or associated with it). Common in phrases like "dios de la muerte" (god of death), "planeta de la muerte" (planet of death), and "responsable de la muerte de..." (responsible for the death of...).
target_language_example: Dicen que es el dios de la muerte.
native_language_example: They say he is the god of death.

meaning: “of the music”; “about/when it comes to music” (depending on context).
additional_notes: Most often it’s the preposition "de" + the noun phrase "la música" (= "the music"). It’s used to: (1) show connection/possession/topic: "el negocio de la música" (the music business), "amante de la música" (music lover); (2) indicate what you enjoy/are passionate about: "disfrutar de la música" (enjoy the music), "apasionarse de/por la música" (be passionate about music); (3) talk about music in general: "¿Qué hay de la música?" (What about the music?).
target_language_example: Me encanta aprender de la música de otros países.
native_language_example: I love learning about the music of other countries.

additional_notes: Used to say something appears, happens, or comes unexpectedly and without warning ("out of nowhere"). It can also mean "from nothing" in more philosophical or literal statements (e.g., "Nothing comes from nothing"). Often used with verbs like surgir (to arise), aparecer (to appear), salir (to come out), venir (to come).
target_language_example: De la nada, empezó a llover muy fuerte.
native_language_example: Out of nowhere, it started raining really hard.

additional_notes: Most common after a noun: la ley/fuerza/fenómeno de la naturaleza (“a law/force/phenomenon of nature”). Also used with plural nouns: las bellezas de la naturaleza (“the beauties of nature”). Often translates more naturally into English as an adjective (“a natural phenomenon”) even though Spanish uses “de + la naturaleza.”
target_language_example: El terremoto fue un fenómeno de la naturaleza.
native_language_example: The earthquake was a natural phenomenon.

de la noche a la mañana

target_language_multi_word_term: de la noche a la mañana
additional_notes: Used to say something happened very fast or unexpectedly, as if from one day to the next. Often goes with verbs like cambiar (to change), caer (to fall), perder (to lose value), hacerse rico (to become rich).
target_language_example: Todo cambió de la noche a la mañana.
native_language_example: Everything changed overnight.

meaning: of the office; from the office.
additional_notes: Uses "de" to show belonging/origin. Common with nouns like "la puerta de la oficina" (the office door) and events like "la fiesta de la oficina" (the office party).
target_language_example: Necesito el número de teléfono de la oficina.
native_language_example: I need the office phone number.

meaning: (hanging) on the wall; of/from the wall.
additional_notes: Used to describe something attached to or located on a wall (especially with items like cuadros, mapas, relojes: "el cuadro de la pared", "el reloj de la pared"). It can also mean movement away from the wall with verbs like "sacar" ("sacaron el retrato de la pared" = they took it down/off the wall).
target_language_example: Quité el póster de la pared porque estaba roto.
native_language_example: I took the poster off the wall because it was torn.

additional_notes: Used to indicate that something belongs to, comes from, or is part of a particular movie/film: "la escena más importante de la película" (the most important scene in the movie). It can also refer to physical film, especially in phrases like "película fotográfica" (photographic film).
target_language_example: ¿Cuál es tu parte favorita de la película?
native_language_example: What’s your favorite part of the movie?

meaning: of the police; from the police.
additional_notes: Used after a noun to say it belongs to or is connected with the police (e.g., "un soplón de la policía" = a police informant). It can also indicate origin/source ("algo de la policía" = something from the police).
target_language_example: ¿Es una orden de la policía?
native_language_example: Is it an order from the police?

additional_notes: Used to link something to a specific door: sounds (el chirrido de la puerta = the squeak of the door), location (al otro lado de la puerta = on the other side of the door), marks/traces (las huellas… de la puerta = the fingerprints from/on the door). It’s the preposition de (“of/from”) + la (“the”, feminine) + puerta (“door”).
target_language_example: No encuentro la llave de la puerta.
native_language_example: I can’t find the door key.

meaning: “that I told you about” (referring to a feminine singular noun).
additional_notes: Used after a feminine singular noun to mean “about which/that … about.” It’s a relative clause: **de** (“about/of”) + **la** (feminine singular “the”) + **que** (“that/which”) + **te hablé** (“I told you / I spoke to you,” informal *you*). It agrees with the noun: **del que te hablé** (masc. sg.), **de los que te hablé** (masc. pl.), **de las que te hablé** (fem. pl.).
target_language_example: Ésta es la casa de la que te hablé.
native_language_example: This is the house I told you about.

meaning: “over the line” (in pasarse de la raya: “to go too far”).
additional_notes: Almost always used with the verb phrase **pasarse de la raya** (also **pasarse**): to say someone has crossed a limit—being too rude, too intense, or doing something unacceptable. Very common when scolding or apologizing. Verb changes: **te has pasado**, **me pasé**, **te estás pasando**, etc.
target_language_example: Perdón, me pasé de la raya con lo que dije.
native_language_example: Sorry, I went too far with what I said.

additional_notes: Used with "de" + "la" to show a connection to a specific meeting. Often follows verbs/adjectives like "irse de la reunión" (to leave the meeting), "estar ausente de la reunión" (to be absent from the meeting), or nouns/titles like "presidente de la reunión" (chair/president of the meeting).
target_language_example: Tuve que irme de la reunión temprano.
native_language_example: I had to leave the meeting early.

meaning: "of the room" / "from the room" (often: the living room).
additional_notes: Uses the preposition "de" + "la" (="del" is used with masculine nouns). With movement verbs like "salir" or "echar", it usually means "out of/from the room" (salió de la sala = he left the room). With nouns, it can show location or association: "el sofá de la sala" = the living-room sofa. "Sala" can mean a living room, a classroom, a hall, or a waiting room depending on context.
target_language_example: Deja los zapatos fuera de la sala, por favor.
native_language_example: Leave your shoes outside the living room, please.

additional_notes: Used after a noun to mean it is a lucky object/thing (e.g., "moneda de la suerte" = lucky coin, "amuleto de la suerte" = lucky charm). Often refers to something believed to bring good luck; also used in set phrases like "los siete de la suerte" (lucky sevens).
target_language_example: Siempre llevo conmigo una pulsera de la suerte.
native_language_example: I always carry a lucky bracelet with me.

additional_notes: Used after a clock time to specify that it’s PM during the afternoon/evening period: a las cinco de la tarde = 5 PM. In many Spanish-speaking places, "de la tarde" is typically used from around 1–2 PM until it gets late; later at night people may switch to "de la noche". Common phrases: a primera hora de la tarde (early afternoon), a última hora de la tarde (late afternoon).
target_language_example: Nos vemos a las cuatro de la tarde.
native_language_example: See you at 4 PM (in the afternoon).

additional_notes: Used after a noun to say something belongs to, happens during, or is typical of a particular season/period (sports season, TV season, social season, etc.). Often refers to “the current season” in context: el evento más grande de la temporada = the biggest event of the season.
target_language_example: Este es el último partido de la temporada.
native_language_example: This is the last game of the season.

additional_notes: Used to show possession or connection to a store: el dueño de la tienda (the owner of the store), el gerente de la tienda (the store manager), la mejor cámara de la tienda (the best camera in the store). With verbs like llevarse/robar, it often means 'from the store' (took/stole it from the store).
target_language_example: Compré este cargador de la tienda de la esquina.
native_language_example: I bought this charger from the corner store.

meaning: "of the Earth / on Earth"; sometimes "from the land/place".
