additional_notes: Literal meaning is “of the earth/land/soil,” but it’s often used in set phrases to mean “in the world/on Earth,” especially in superlatives: "el/la más ... de la tierra" = “the most ... in the world.” You also see it in idioms like "la sal de la tierra" (“the salt of the earth,” a very good, honest person/people) and in expressions like "sobre la faz de la tierra" (“on the face of the earth”). In "de la tierra de + place," it can mean “from the land/region of …” (i.e., originally from there).
target_language_example: Para mí, es la mejor comida de la tierra.
native_language_example: For me, it’s the best food in the world.

meaning: of the university; from the university.
additional_notes: Uses "de" to show origin (from) or relationship/affiliation (of). It’s the contraction/combination of "de" + "la" (feminine singular), because "universidad" is feminine: "la universidad".
target_language_example: Recibí un correo de la universidad.
native_language_example: I received an email from the university.

additional_notes: Most commonly used to mean “of life” (something related to life in general: la esencia de la vida = the essence of life; los hechos de la vida = facts of life; la vida humana = human life; el juego de la vida = the game of life). In some fixed phrases it can sound more like “in life” (algo de la vida = something in life). Literal meaning: “of the life,” but usually translates as “of life.”
target_language_example: Cada etapa de la vida trae algo nuevo.
native_language_example: Each stage of life brings something new.

additional_notes: Used with "ser" ("Es de la vieja escuela") to describe someone’s habits, values, or way of doing things as traditional or from an earlier time. It can be approving (classic, tried-and-true) or mildly critical (not modern).
target_language_example: Mi jefe es de la vieja escuela y prefiere llamadas en vez de mensajes.
native_language_example: My boss is old-school and prefers phone calls instead of messages.

additional_notes: Common in set phrases: “mirar de lado” = to look sideways/with suspicion; “dejar de lado” = to set aside/ignore/put off something; “pon(er) X de lado” = to put/turn something on its side. Often used both literally (position) and figuratively (not considering something).
target_language_example: Dejemos de lado las diferencias y hablemos con calma.
native_language_example: Let’s set aside our differences and talk calmly.

additional_notes: Combination of **de** + **las** ("the", feminine plural). Used to connect nouns, often meaning possession/origin/topic: *el aroma de las pesadillas* (the smell of the nightmares), *la historia de las monedas* (the history of the coins). Very common in the pattern **uno/una de las** = "one of the".
target_language_example: Es una de las mejores ideas del año.
native_language_example: It’s one of the best ideas of the year.

meaning: (literally) “from the hands”; in irse/ir de las manos: “out of hand / out of control”.
additional_notes: Often used in the fixed expression **irse (o ir) de las manos** to mean a situation is getting out of control. It commonly appears with an indirect object pronoun to show who it’s happening to: **se me** (to me), **se nos** (to us), etc. Tenses: **se nos va de las manos** (it’s getting out of hand), **se nos fue de las manos** (it got out of hand). In a literal sense, it can also mean something slips **from your hands**.
target_language_example: La situación se nos está yendo de las manos.
native_language_example: The situation is getting out of hand.

additional_notes: Used after a noun to express irritation or contempt about that thing: "el coche de las narices" = "that damn car". It’s informal and can sound rude; common in Spain. Similar in tone to "de mierda" but usually a bit less harsh.
target_language_example: No encuentro las llaves de las narices.
native_language_example: I can’t find the damn keys.

meaning: of the people; about the people.
additional_notes: Used to indicate possession/origin/association (“of the people”) or the topic (“about the people”), depending on the verb or noun it follows. Very common after nouns (e.g., "las apariencias de las personas" = "people’s appearances") and in comparisons/contrasts with "diferente de" ("different from").
target_language_example: No me acuerdo de los nombres de las personas que conocí ayer.
native_language_example: I don’t remember the names of the people I met yesterday.

additional_notes: Used to specify the material/ingredient something is made from ("hecho de leche" = made from milk) or to indicate an amount of milk, often with words like "un poco de", "más de", or "nada de". With containers, it helps identify what’s inside ("un cartón de leche" = a carton of milk).
target_language_example: ¿Tienes café de leche o sin leche?
native_language_example: Do you have coffee with milk or without milk?

additional_notes: Used to say something is a classic, clear, or perfect example—often meaning it’s done exactly as it should be, or that it’s very typical (sometimes with irony). Common with nouns like "un ejemplo de libro" (a textbook example) or "una actuación de libro" (a perfect performance).
target_language_example: Lo que hizo fue un ejemplo de libro de cómo no se debe conducir.
native_language_example: What he did was a textbook example of how you shouldn’t drive.

additional_notes: Used to present an alternative outcome if the previous condition isn’t met. Often placed at the beginning of a sentence and followed by a comma: "De lo contrario, ..." It can also appear mid-sentence: "..., de lo contrario ..."
target_language_example: Ponte el cinturón; de lo contrario, te pueden multar.
native_language_example: Put on your seat belt; otherwise, they can fine you.

additional_notes: Used to refer to the specific thing being talked about/thought about, often after verbs that take “de” (e.g., hablar de, conversar de, saber de): “Sé de lo que hablas” = “I know what you’re talking about.” Also very common in comparisons with más/menos… de lo que: “Más potente de lo que imaginaba” = “More powerful than I imagined.”
target_language_example: No entiendo de lo que estás hablando.
native_language_example: I don’t understand what you’re talking about.

additional_notes: Used to praise someone or something as excellent quality or performance. Often follows verbs like ser/estar ("es/está de lo mejor") or describes how someone did something ("Lo has hecho de lo mejor"). It can also be expanded: "de lo mejor de + place/group" = "one of the best in + place/group".
target_language_example: Tu presentación estuvo de lo mejor.
native_language_example: Your presentation was top-notch.

meaning: very; extremely (used to emphasize an adjective).
additional_notes: Used before an adjective to intensify it, often in the pattern: “ser + de lo más + adjective” or “un/una + noun + de lo más + adjective”. It’s common in descriptions and can sometimes sound a bit ironic depending on context (“de lo más extraño” = “really strange”).
target_language_example: Tu idea es de lo más útil.
native_language_example: Your idea is extremely useful.

additional_notes: Used in comparisons, most often after "más" or "menos": "más/menos ... de lo normal" (more/less ... than usual). You’ll also see the related phrase "fuera de lo normal" meaning "out of the ordinary / unusual."
target_language_example: Hoy hay más tráfico de lo normal.
native_language_example: There's more traffic than usual today.

additional_notes: Most often used after comparatives such as más, menos, mejor, peor, antes, or lejos to introduce a clause: de lo que pensé = 'than I thought'. It can also appear after verbs or expressions that already use de, where it means 'of/about what': de lo que eres, de lo que hace Mary. In comparative phrases, English usually translates it simply as 'than'.
target_language_example: Llegamos antes de lo que pensaba.
native_language_example: We arrived earlier than I thought.

additional_notes: Used after a comparative (más/menos/mejor/peor, etc.) to mean “than you think.” It’s often part of the pattern “más … de lo que crees” (“more … than you think”). You can change the verb/person: de lo que piensas, de lo que cree, de lo que creíamos, etc.
target_language_example: Este examen es más fácil de lo que crees.
native_language_example: This exam is easier than you think.

additional_notes: Used in comparisons (especially with "más", "menos", "mejor", "peor") to say the reality differs from what you expected: "más/menos/mejor/peor de lo que esperaba". Literally "of what I expected," but in English it’s usually "than I expected." You can change the verb/person: "de lo que esperabas" (you expected), "de lo que esperábamos" (we expected).
target_language_example: La comida estuvo mejor de lo que esperaba.
native_language_example: The food was better than I expected.

additional_notes: Used after a comparative (más/menos/mejor/peor, etc.) to say the reality is different from what it appears. Very common pattern: **más/menos + adjective + de lo que parece** (e.g., *más fácil de lo que parece*).
target_language_example: El examen fue más difícil de lo que parece.
native_language_example: The exam was harder than it seems.

additional_notes: Used after a comparative (más/menos + adjective/adverb/noun) to compare reality with what you believed before: “more/less … than I thought.” You can change the verb/person: de lo que pensabas (you thought), de lo que pensábamos (we thought), etc. Often shortened in speech to “de lo que pensaba yo.”
target_language_example: Este examen fue más difícil de lo que pensaba.
native_language_example: This exam was harder than I thought.

additional_notes: Used after a comparison (más/menos… + adjective/adverb/noun) to say the reality is different from your expectation: “more/less … than I thought.” Often uses the past tense because you had an earlier expectation (pensé), but you may also hear other forms like “de lo que pensaba” (“than I used to think/than I was thinking”).
target_language_example: El examen fue más largo de lo que pensé.
native_language_example: The exam was longer than I thought.

additional_notes: Used after a comparative to say the reality is greater/different than the listener assumes: “más/menos … de lo que piensas” = “more/less … than you think.” Very common with adjectives (fuerte, listo, joven, rápido) and with “mucho” for emphasis (“Mucho más de lo que piensas”).
target_language_example: La situación es más complicada de lo que piensas.
native_language_example: The situation is more complicated than you think.

additional_notes: Used with relative clauses. Common patterns: (1) comparisons with más/menos… de lo que (+ verb): “more/less… than (what) …” (e.g., Más fácil de lo que parecía = “easier than it seemed”). (2) talking/knowing/being aware: hablar/saber/tener idea de lo que… = “to talk/know/have an idea about what…”. Often refers back to something understood from context (“what I’m talking about”).
target_language_example: No es tan complicado de lo que piensas.
native_language_example: It’s not as complicated as you think.

meaning: crazy; insane; unbelievable (often as an intensifier).
additional_notes: Used after a noun to emphasize that something is chaotic, extreme, or hard to believe: “una jaula de locos” (a madhouse), “cosa de locos” (something crazy). It’s a common, informal/colloquial way to add emphasis rather than literally meaning “of crazy people.”
target_language_example: El tráfico hoy está de locos.
native_language_example: Traffic today is insane.

additional_notes: Combination of de + los, used before masculine plural nouns. Most often it means "of the" to show belonging, relationship, or part of a group; in some contexts it can mean "from the."
target_language_example: Muchos de los estudiantes ya llegaron.
native_language_example: Many of the students have already arrived.

meaning: of the others; of everyone else.
additional_notes: Used to refer to other people/things in a group, meaning “the rest” or “everyone else.” Often appears after nouns to compare or contrast (e.g., “al nivel de los demás” = “at everyone else’s level,” “el sufrimiento de los demás” = “other people’s suffering”). Can also be used with “los de los demás” to mean “those (ones) belonging to others.”
target_language_example: No te rías de los demás.
native_language_example: Don’t laugh at others.

additional_notes: Used after a comparative/superlative or a choice word to specify you’re comparing/choosing between exactly two things: el mejor de los dos (the better/best of the two), el más grande de los dos (the bigger/biggest of the two), cualquiera de los dos (either of the two). Often refers back to two items already mentioned.
target_language_example: ¿Cuál de los dos prefieres?
native_language_example: Which of the two do you prefer?

additional_notes: Uses "de" + "los" + "hombres" to show possession or association: "el mundo de los hombres" = "the world of men/humans". In literary or fantasy contexts, "los hombres" can mean humans in general (mankind), not only male people.
target_language_example: La historia del mundo de los hombres está llena de guerras.
native_language_example: The history of the world of humans is full of wars.

additional_notes: "De" commonly expresses possession, relation, or who something is for (like English “of” or sometimes “for”). "Los niños" means “the children/the kids” (masculine plural; it can include a mixed group). Very common in phrases like "las risas de los niños" (children’s laughter), "al alcance de los niños" (within children’s reach), and after verbs like "cuidar de" (to take care of).
target_language_example: Los juguetes de los niños están en el suelo.
native_language_example: The kids’ toys are on the floor.

meaning: one of us; from our group/side.
additional_notes: Used with **ser** to show someone belongs to your group: **Es de los nuestros** (“He/She’s one of us”). Can also refer to people in your group in general: **muchos de los nuestros** (“many of our people”). It can be used alone as a short reply meaning “one of us.”
target_language_example: No te preocupes: ella es de los nuestros.
native_language_example: Don’t worry: she’s one of us.

additional_notes: Used with "otros" (others) to talk about a different group of people/things, often in contrast to someone already mentioned. Common with verbs like "aprender de" (to learn from): "aprender los unos de los otros" = "learn from each other." Also appears in questions like "¿Qué hay de los otros?" (What about the others?).
target_language_example: Aprendimos mucho de los otros durante el proyecto.
native_language_example: We learned a lot from the others during the project.

meaning: "of those who/that"; also used in comparisons like "more/less ... than".
additional_notes: Used to refer back to a group already mentioned or understood: "los que" = "those who/those that". Very common after a noun or expression like "nombres de los que..." (names of those who...), "asuntos de los que..." (matters that...), or with comparisons: "más/menos ... de los que + verb" = "more/less ... than (those) who/that...".
target_language_example: Tengo más trabajo de los que puedo terminar hoy.
native_language_example: I have more work than I can finish today.

additional_notes: Used after a noun to describe something as luxurious, upscale, or premium (e.g., "un hotel de lujo"). It can contrast with a basic option ("regular o de lujo"). Depending on context, it can also mean "excellent/top-quality" in a more figurative way (e.g., "un plan de lujo" = a great plan).
target_language_example: Reservamos una habitación de lujo para el fin de semana.
native_language_example: We booked a luxury room for the weekend.

additional_notes: Used with estar (estar de luto) to say someone is mourning, often after a loved one dies. It can refer to personal mourning or collective/national mourning (un día de luto). It may also imply wearing black or observing mourning customs, depending on context.
target_language_example: Después de la muerte de su abuela, estuvo de luto varios meses.
native_language_example: After his grandmother’s death, he was in mourning for several months.

additional_notes: Used after a noun to say what it’s made from/material (often with furniture, houses, objects): "una silla de madera" = “a wooden chair.” It can also describe traditional wooden buildings ("casas de madera").
target_language_example: Compré una mesa de madera para la cocina.
native_language_example: I bought a wooden table for the kitchen.

meaning: in the early hours of the morning (very late at night/very early).
additional_notes: Used to talk about the time between midnight and sunrise (often around 1–5 a.m.). It commonly follows verbs to say when something happened (llegó de madrugada, ocurrió de madrugada). It can also be used with a range: de madrugada a noche = “from early morning until night” (all day).
target_language_example: Salimos de madrugada para evitar el tráfico.
native_language_example: We left in the early hours to avoid traffic.

additional_notes: Used to say a situation is getting progressively worse over time. Common with verbs like ir/seguir (e.g., "va de mal en peor", "ha ido de mal en peor") and also with "vamos" to mean "things are getting worse for us".
target_language_example: Después del accidente, todo fue de mal en peor.
native_language_example: After the accident, everything went from bad to worse.

additional_notes: Used with verbs like estar, ponerse, levantarse, or despertarse to describe someone’s mood at a moment in time: estar de mal humor (to be in a bad mood), ponerse de mal humor (to get into a bad mood), despertarse/levantarse de mal humor (to wake up/get up in a bad mood). The opposite is de buen humor (in a good mood).
target_language_example: No le hables ahora; está de mal humor.
native_language_example: Don’t talk to him now; he’s in a bad mood.

additional_notes: Used to say someone does something without wanting to, often because they feel forced or not enthusiastic. It commonly goes with verbs like ir, hacer, aceptar, or irse. Literally “with bad desire/with ill will,” but in English you usually translate it as “reluctantly.”
target_language_example: Firmó el contrato de mala gana.
native_language_example: He signed the contract reluctantly.

additional_notes: Common (especially in Mexico) with verbs like "estar/ponerse/andar": "estar de malas" (to be in a bad mood), "ponerse de malas" (to get in a bad mood), "andar de malas" (to be having a bad day / sometimes also ‘to be unlucky’ depending on context).
target_language_example: No le hables ahorita: está de malas.
native_language_example: Don’t talk to him right now—he’s in a bad mood.

additional_notes: Used after verbs to say someone does something very well (Ella canta de maravilla). Also common with verbs like sentar/quedar to say something looks great on you or suits you perfectly (Te sienta / Te queda de maravilla).
target_language_example: ¡La comida está de maravilla!
native_language_example: The food is wonderful!

additional_notes: Used after a noun to mean “of tomorrow” (i.e., something happening/available tomorrow): la boda de mañana (tomorrow’s wedding), el tiempo de mañana (tomorrow’s weather), los titulares de mañana (tomorrow’s headlines). Note: in other contexts, “de mañana” can also mean “in the morning” (e.g., clases de mañana = morning classes), but in these examples it means “tomorrow’s.”
target_language_example: ¿A qué hora es la reunión de mañana?
native_language_example: What time is tomorrow’s meeting?

additional_notes: Used when you do something relying only on what you remember, not reading or checking: aprender/saber algo de memoria (to memorize/know something by heart), recitar de memoria (to recite from memory), dibujar de memoria (to draw from memory).
target_language_example: Sé tu número de teléfono de memoria.
native_language_example: I know your phone number by heart.

additional_notes:
Most often appears in set phrases:
- "echar de menos a alguien" = "to miss someone" (very common): "Te echo de menos" / "Os echaré de menos".
- "(eso) es lo de menos" = "that’s the least important thing" (used to downplay something: there are bigger problems).
target_language_example: Te echo de menos cuando no estás aquí.
native_language_example: I miss you when you’re not here.

additional_notes: Used after a noun to say something isn’t genuine or is make-believe: “un teléfono de mentira” (a fake phone), “una pistola de mentira” (a toy/fake gun). Often contrasts with “de verdad” (real).
target_language_example: Compré un reloj de mentira en el mercado.
native_language_example: I bought a fake watch at the market.

additional_notes: Used before a noun: de mi + noun = "from/of my ..." depending on context. For example, de mi mente = "from my mind" and de mi comportamiento = "of my behavior." Don't confuse it with de mí (with an accent), which means "of/from me."
target_language_example: Saca tus cosas de mi mochila.
native_language_example: Take your things out of my backpack.

meaning: “of my house/home” (i.e., “at/near/in my place,” depending on context).
additional_notes: Literally means “of my house/home,” and it’s used to locate something relative to where you live: delante de mi casa (in front of my house), en la terraza de mi casa (on my house’s terrace), la parte de abajo de mi casa (the downstairs part of my house). In Spanish, “casa” can mean either “house” or “home,” so “de mi casa” often translates naturally as “at my place.”
target_language_example: Nos vemos delante de mi casa a las ocho.
native_language_example: See you in front of my place at eight.

meaning: of my family / from my family.
additional_notes: Used with a noun to show ownership or association ("la casa de mi familia" = "my family’s house"). With verbs/adjectives, it can indicate separation or origin ("separado de mi familia" = "separated from my family").
target_language_example: Este anillo es de mi familia.
native_language_example: This ring is from my family.

additional_notes: Used with **de** to show possession or association (like **’s** in English). Common in phrases like **en casa de mi hermana** (“at my sister’s house”) and **la boda de mi hermana** (“my sister’s wedding”).
target_language_example: El coche es de mi hermana.
native_language_example: The car is my sister’s.

meaning: “of my daughter” / “my daughter’s” (showing possession); sometimes “about my daughter” after verbs like hablar/contar.
additional_notes: Most commonly used to show that something belongs to your daughter: el plato de mi hija (my daughter’s plate), la habitación de mi hija (my daughter’s room), el cumpleaños de mi hija (my daughter’s birthday). It can also mean “about my daughter” with verbs like hablar de / contar de (to talk/tell about). With certain verbs, de can mean “from” or “away from” depending on context (e.g., Sal de mi hija. = Get away from my daughter.).
target_language_example: Quiero hablarte de mi hija.
native_language_example: I want to tell you about my daughter.

additional_notes: Used with **de** to show a relationship or possession (like English **'of'** or **'my son's'**): *la foto de mi hijo* = "my son's photo" / "the photo of my son". It often follows a noun (*la boda de mi hijo*) or appears after certain verbs/adjectives that take **de** (*ser amigo de mi hijo* = "to be my son's friend"). There is **no contraction** here: it stays **de mi** (not *del mi*).
target_language_example: Hoy es el cumpleaños de mi hijo.
native_language_example: Today is my son's birthday.

additional_notes: Uses **de** to show a relationship like possession (**la casa de mi madre** = “my mother’s house”) or origin/source (**noticias de mi madre** = “news from my mother”). It also appears after some verbs that take **de**, like **despedirse de** (“to say goodbye to”). On its own, **De mi madre.** can be a short answer meaning “(It’s) my mother’s.” or “(It’s) from my mother,” depending on context.
target_language_example: Este regalo es de mi madre.
native_language_example: This gift is from my mother.

additional_notes: Used with "de" to show possession or relationship. Often corresponds to English ’s: "la casa de mi mamá" = "my mom’s house." It can also identify someone related to your mom: "el abuelo de mi mamá" = "my mom’s grandfather." With places, "en casa de mi mamá" means "at my mom’s (house)."
target_language_example: Dejé mis llaves en la casa de mi mamá.
native_language_example: I left my keys at my mom’s house.

additional_notes: Used to show possession or a close relationship. In Spanish, "de" + person often equals the English possessive with ’s. You’ll see it after a noun: "el reloj de mi padre" (my father’s watch). With "ser" it can mean something belongs to him: "Son de mi padre" (They’re my father’s).
target_language_example: ¿Es este libro de mi padre?
native_language_example: Is this book my father's?

meaning: 'from me' / 'on my behalf'; also 'on my part' (about something you did).
additional_notes: Used when you want someone to pass along something for you: a message, greeting, kiss, gift, etc. Example pattern: "Dile ___ de mi parte" (Tell ___ from me). It can also describe responsibility or behavior: "Fue (adjetivo) de mi parte..." = "It was (adjective) of me to..." / "on my part."
target_language_example: Si ves a Ana, dile gracias de mi parte.
native_language_example: If you see Ana, tell her thanks from me.

additional_notes: Used to refer to your whole life experience, often after a superlative to mean “the most … (I’ve ever experienced) in my life,” e.g. “la llamada más importante de mi vida” = “the most important call of my life.” It can also be used in “el objetivo de mi vida” = “the goal of my life.”
target_language_example: Esa fue la mejor noche de mi vida.
native_language_example: That was the best night of my life.

meaning: with fear; scared (often in phrases like “to tremble/die of fear”).
additional_notes: Used after verbs to describe the cause/intensity of the feeling: “temblar de miedo” (to tremble with fear), “morirse de miedo” (to be extremely scared). It can also be used informally to mean “awesome/amazing” (e.g., “¡Está de miedo!”), but in your examples it’s literal fear.
target_language_example: Los niños temblaban de miedo durante la tormenta.
native_language_example: The kids were trembling with fear during the storm.

additional_notes: Vulgar and highly offensive. Used after a noun to insult it or say it’s terrible (e.g., “un día de mierda” = a shitty day; “este lugar de mierda” = this shitty place). With people/labels it becomes a harsh slur-like insult (“X de mierda” = “you fucking X / X piece of shit”). Not appropriate in polite situations.
target_language_example: No quiero volver a ese trabajo de mierda.
native_language_example: I don’t want to go back to that shitty job.

meaning: barely; by a miracle (just in time / just by chance).
additional_notes: Used to say something happened only with great luck or narrowly avoided danger. Common with verbs like sobrevivir (to survive), salvarse (to be saved), and esquivar (to dodge/avoid). Often implies “it could easily have gone wrong.”
target_language_example: Llegamos al aeropuerto de milagro.
native_language_example: We barely made it to the airport.

additional_notes: Used when "de" is followed by the possessive adjective "mis" + a plural noun: "de mis + [plural noun]" (e.g., "de mis gafas" = "of my glasses"). Very common after expressions like "la mayoría de..." (most of...), "ninguna de..." (none of...), "muchas de..." (many of...), "el padre de..." (the father of...).
target_language_example: La mayoría de mis amigos vive cerca.
native_language_example: Most of my friends live nearby.

additional_notes: Used to specify that something belongs to, comes from, or is part of your group of friends. Very common after quantity words like "muchos/pocos/varios/algunos/ninguno" (e.g., "Muchos de mis amigos...") or phrases like "el único de mis amigos".
target_language_example: Ninguno de mis amigos vive aquí.
native_language_example: None of my friends live here.

additional_notes: Used after a noun (or with estar) to say something is currently popular or fashionable: “estar de moda” = “to be in fashion.” Often contrasted with “pasar de moda” (to go out of fashion) and “estar fuera de moda” (to be out of fashion). “Industria de moda” means the fashion industry.
target_language_example: Ese color está de moda este año.
native_language_example: That color is in style this year.

additional_notes: Commonly introduces a consequence: “X, de modo que Y” = “X, so Y.” It can also introduce a conclusion based on what was just said (“De modo que…” = “So…” / “So then…”). Sometimes it’s close to “so that” when it expresses the outcome or purpose of an action, but most often in everyday speech it’s the result (“therefore/as a result”).
target_language_example: No había pan, de modo que compré tortillas.
native_language_example: There was no bread, so I bought tortillas.

additional_notes: Used to say something is true only for the time being, and may change later. Common in short answers: “De momento, no.” It can also mean “for the moment” in the sense of “for now, don’t do it / not yet”: “Olvídate de eso de momento.”
target_language_example: De momento voy a quedarme en casa, pero quizá salga más tarde.
native_language_example: For now I’m going to stay home, but I might go out later.

additional_notes: Common in set phrases. With "susto" it intensifies the idea: "un susto de muerte" = a really big scare ("scared to death"). With "amenaza" or "amenazar" it can be literal: "amenaza de muerte" / "amenazar de muerte" = death threat / to threaten to kill someone. It usually follows a noun ("un susto de muerte") or the verb phrase ("amenazar de muerte").
target_language_example: Cuando vi el perro, me dio un susto de muerte.
native_language_example: When I saw the dog, it scared me to death.

additional_notes: Used to talk about excess or something beyond what’s needed. Common patterns: (1) “Está de más + infinitive” / “No está de más + infinitive” = “It’s unnecessary / It wouldn’t hurt to…”. (2) “Hablar de más” = to talk too much / say more than you should. (3) “De más” alone can mean “No need” / “That’s unnecessary.” (4) In “razón/motivo de más”, it means “one more reason (to…)”.
target_language_example: No está de más llevar una chaqueta por si hace frío.
native_language_example: It wouldn’t hurt to bring a jacket in case it’s cold.

additional_notes: de + mí is the form used after a preposition. Its exact English translation depends on the expression: it can mean "of me," "about me," or something less literal in phrases like reírse de mí ("laugh at me") or despedirse de mí ("say goodbye to me"). Note that mí has an accent and is different from me.
target_language_example: No hables de mí delante de ellos.
native_language_example: Don't talk about me in front of them.

additional_notes: Reflexive phrase used to refer back to the speaker after prepositions like de ("of/about"), often expressing feelings or talking about oneself: "hablar de mí mismo" (talk about myself), "avergonzarse de mí mismo" / "tener vergüenza de mí mismo" (be ashamed of myself). For a female speaker: "de mí misma". Note: "mí" (with accent) is the object pronoun "me" after a preposition; "mismo" adds emphasis ("myself").
target_language_example: No quiero hablar de mí mismo ahora.
native_language_example: I don’t want to talk about myself right now.

additional_notes: Used after a noun/adjective to say something is true from the moment someone was born (not acquired later): “ciego de nacimiento” (blind from birth), “alemán de nacimiento” (German by birth). It also appears in set phrases related to official records: “nombre de nacimiento” (birth name) and “partida de nacimiento” (birth certificate).
target_language_example: Soy canadiense de nacimiento, pero vivo en México desde hace años.
native_language_example: I’m Canadian by birth, but I’ve lived in Mexico for years.

meaning: "You're welcome"; also "(it’s) no use / good for nothing" (with verbs like *servir*).
additional_notes: As a polite reply to *gracias* (“thank you”), *De nada* means “You’re welcome / No problem.” In another common pattern, *servir de nada* means “to be of no use / not help at all”: *No sirvió de nada* = “It didn’t help at all.”
target_language_example: —Gracias por tu ayuda. —De nada.
native_language_example: —Thanks for your help. —You’re welcome.

additional_notes: Uses: (1) After a noun to mean "business" as an adjective: escuela de negocios (business school), viaje de negocios (business trip). (2) After verbs like hablar to mean "about business": Hablemos de negocios (Let’s talk business).
target_language_example: Mañana tengo un viaje de negocios a Madrid.
native_language_example: Tomorrow I have a business trip to Madrid.

meaning: "of snow" / "snow" (used to describe something related to snow).
additional_notes: Used after a noun to say it’s made of snow or meant for snow. Common in set phrases like: tormenta de nieve (snowstorm), bolas de nieve (snowballs), tabla de nieve (snowboard), vehículos de nieve (snow vehicles).
target_language_example: Compramos cadenas de nieve para el coche.
native_language_example: We bought snow chains for the car.

additional_notes: Used to strongly refuse or disagree (“No way!”). It can also mean “in no way / by no means” to emphasize that something is impossible or not true: “No puedo hacerlo de ninguna manera” = “I can’t do it any way / at all.” Often appears alone as a firm answer, sometimes with “no”: “No, de ninguna manera.”
target_language_example: —¿Vienes con nosotros? —De ninguna manera.
native_language_example: “Are you coming with us?” “No way.”

meaning: No way; by no means; not at all.
additional_notes: Used to strongly deny something (“No way!”) or to say something should absolutely not happen (“By no means should you…”). It can also appear with another negative word like “no” for emphasis (e.g., “No … de ningún modo” = “not at all”).
target_language_example: —¿Vienes mañana? —De ningún modo.
native_language_example: —Are you coming tomorrow? —No way.

additional_notes: Used to say something happens during the night (not just “in the evening”). Common with verbs like salir (to go out) or trabajar (to work). You’ll also see it in set phrases like "turno de noche" (night shift).
target_language_example: No me gusta conducir de noche.
native_language_example: I don’t like driving at night.

additional_notes: Common in Spain in everyday speech to talk about what typically happens or what someone usually does. It often appears at the beginning of a sentence: “De normal, …”. Similar in meaning to “normalmente” or “por lo general”.
target_language_example: De normal, salgo del trabajo a las seis.
native_language_example: Normally, I leave work at six.

additional_notes: Used with "de" to show origin/relationship: "de nosotros" = "from us" or "of us" depending on context. Common after certain adjectives/phrases like "apartado/lejos de nosotros" (away from us) or "uno de nosotros" (one of us).
target_language_example: Se sentó lejos de nosotros para poder concentrarse.
native_language_example: He sat far away from us so he could concentrate.

additional_notes: Used to show possession or association: de + nuestra + feminine singular noun (e.g., de nuestra nación = of our nation). “Nuestra” agrees with the noun that follows: de nuestro + masculine singular (de nuestro país), de nuestras + feminine plural, de nuestros + masculine plural.
target_language_example: Hablamos de nuestra familia todos los días.
native_language_example: We talk about our family every day.

additional_notes: Commonly used before a masculine singular noun: de nuestro + noun (e.g., "de nuestro lado" = "on our side"). For feminine singular, you’ll usually see "de nuestra" (e.g., "de nuestra casa" = "from our house").
target_language_example: ¿Tienes una foto de nuestro viaje?
native_language_example: Do you have a photo of our trip?

additional_notes: Used with masculine plural nouns to show possession or origin: de nuestros errores (“from our mistakes”), de nuestros ancestros (“of our ancestors”), de nuestros clientes (“many of our clients”). For feminine plural nouns, use de nuestras (e.g., de nuestras ideas).
target_language_example: Estoy orgulloso de nuestros logros.
native_language_example: I’m proud of our achievements.

additional_notes: Used to say that something happens another time. It is very common in everyday Spanish and is often interchangeable with "otra vez".
target_language_example: Quiero intentarlo de nuevo.
native_language_example: I want to try it again.

additional_notes: Used to say something happens another time or repeats. Common with commands ("Hazlo de nuevo" = "Do it again") and with "gracias" to mean "thanks again". Often interchangeable with "otra vez" in everyday speech.
target_language_example: ¿Puedes decirlo de nuevo, por favor?
native_language_example: Can you say it again, please?

meaning: made of gold; (figuratively) golden / very valuable or kind.
additional_notes: Uses "de" + material to say what something is made of: "una moneda de oro" (a gold coin), "las agujas son de oro" (the hands are gold). It can also be figurative: "un corazón de oro" means someone is very kind. In some fixed phrases it means something extremely valuable or special (e.g., "un huevo de oro" = a very valuable asset).
target_language_example: Me regaló un anillo de oro por mi cumpleaños.
native_language_example: He gave me a gold ring for my birthday.

additional_notes: Used to say something should be expressed/done differently (“in another way”), or to warn about a consequence if something doesn’t happen (“otherwise”). Often comes with the conditional: “De otra forma, + would/could…” or “..., de otra forma + ...”.
target_language_example: Explícamelo de otra forma, por favor.
native_language_example: Explain it to me in another way, please.

additional_notes: Used to describe doing something differently or having a different opinion/memory/decision. Common with verbs like ver (to see), recordar (to remember), decidir (to decide), and poder/no poder (to be able/not able): “No podía actuar de otra manera” = “He couldn’t act otherwise.”
target_language_example: Podemos hacerlo de otra manera si prefieres.
native_language_example: We can do it another way if you prefer.

additional_notes: Used to warn about what will happen if you don’t do something, or to introduce an alternative outcome. Often followed by a future tense: “De otro modo, … (will happen).” Similar to “si no” in meaning, but “de otro modo” is more like “otherwise.”
target_language_example: Date prisa; de otro modo, llegaremos tarde.
native_language_example: Hurry up; otherwise, we'll be late.

meaning: by ear; from hearing (without reading music/without being told).
additional_notes: Commonly used with music to mean playing or learning a song just by listening ("tocar de oído"). In the fixed expression "duro de oído", it means "hard of hearing".
target_language_example: Aprendí esa canción de oído, sin partitura.
native_language_example: I learned that song by ear, without sheet music.

meaning: made of paper; paper (as a material).
additional_notes: Uses "de" to describe what something is made of (material). Common with objects like "toalla de papel" (paper towel), "bolsa de papel" (paper bag), "avión de papel" (paper airplane). If you mean paper *for writing/printing*, you often use "papel" without "de" (e.g., "Necesito papel").
target_language_example: Quiero una bolsa de papel, por favor.
native_language_example: I want a paper bag, please.

additional_notes: Used to say who something comes from (a gift, message, letter, greetings) or who is sending it. Often followed by a person or group: de parte de mi esposa / de parte de todos. You can also use it in phrases like: Saludos/Un abrazo de parte de…
target_language_example: Te llamo de parte de mi jefe.
native_language_example: I’m calling on behalf of my boss.

meaning: just passing through; stopping by briefly.
additional_notes: Used to say you’re not staying long—you're only in a place temporarily or on the way somewhere else. Often with verbs like estar/ir/pasar: “Estoy de paso”, “Vamos de paso”, “Está de paso por…”.
target_language_example: Estoy de paso por Madrid, solo por dos días.
native_language_example: I’m just passing through Madrid, only for two days.

additional_notes: Common in ads, menus, and casual speech to describe food, desserts, or pleasures that feel like a guilty treat (e.g., un postre de pecado = a sinfully good dessert). It can also be used more literally in religious/moral contexts to mean “related to sin,” but the everyday use is usually “indulgent/irresistible.”
target_language_example: Este brownie está de pecado.
native_language_example: This brownie is sinfully good.

additional_notes: Common, fairly informal expression. Use it after a noun to describe something as movie-like: "una noche de película" (a movie-like night). It can also describe an experience or moment: "Fue de película" (It was like in a movie). Depending on context, it can be positive (amazing) or just dramatic/unreal.
target_language_example: La vista desde la cima es de película.
native_language_example: The view from the top is like in a movie.

meaning: in profile; from the side (side view).
additional_notes: Used to describe seeing, drawing, photographing, or positioning someone/something so you view it from the side rather than from the front. Common with verbs like mirar (to look), ponerse/estar (to be positioned), salir (to appear in a photo), and hacer (to do/make).
target_language_example: Ponte de perfil para la foto, por favor.
native_language_example: Turn sideways for the photo, please.

meaning: perfectly; great; just what you needed.
additional_notes: Common idiom used to say something is ideal or comes at the perfect time: “Me viene de perlas” = “It suits me perfectly / It comes in really handy.” In other contexts it can also be literal and mean “of pearls” (jewelry): “un collar de perlas” = “a pearl necklace.”
target_language_example: Tu ayuda me viene de perlas, porque estoy muy ocupado.
native_language_example: Your help is perfect because I’m very busy.

additional_notes: Used with "de + noun" to describe something related to dogs (e.g., "peleas de perros" = dogfights; "hablar de perros" = to talk about dogs). In some set phrases it can be more idiomatic/negative, like "vida de perros" or "cosa de perros," meaning a miserable/awful life or situation.
target_language_example: No soporto las peleas de perros.
native_language_example: I can't stand dogfights.

meaning: in weight (about body weight); of weight.
additional_notes: Used after nouns like "peso" to talk about weight. Very common in the fixed phrase "subir de peso" (= to gain weight) and its negative "no subir de peso" (= not gain weight). Also used in factual contexts like measurements: "unidades de peso" (= units of weight).
target_language_example: Desde que dejé de hacer ejercicio, he subido de peso.
native_language_example: Since I stopped exercising, I've gained weight.

additional_notes: Most commonly means “standing up” (not sitting/lying down). Often used with verbs like estar/quedarse (“to be/stay standing”) and ponerse (“to stand up”): ponerse de pie = to stand up; estar de pie = to be standing; quédate de pie = stay standing. It can also mean “on foot” in contexts like ir/venir de pie (to go/come on foot).
target_language_example: Me quedé de pie esperando el autobús.
native_language_example: I stayed standing while waiting for the bus.

meaning: made of stone; stone (as a material).
additional_notes: Used after a noun to say what it’s made of (material). Often translates as “stone” or “of stone”: "una casa de piedra" = "a stone house" / "a house made of stone".
target_language_example: La pared es de piedra.
native_language_example: The wall is made of stone.

additional_notes: Used after a noun to specify that something involves the feet. Very common in phrases like "masaje de pies" (foot massage). Also appears in set expressions like "atado de pies y manos" (“tied hand and foot,” meaning completely restrained or unable to act).
target_language_example: Después de caminar todo el día, quiero un masaje de pies.
native_language_example: After walking all day, I want a foot massage.

additional_notes: Used after a noun (or with ser/estar) to say what something is made from: “un vaso de plástico” (a plastic cup), “Es de plástico” (It’s plastic / It’s made of plastic).
target_language_example: ¿Tienes una botella de plástico?
native_language_example: Do you have a plastic bottle?

meaning: from around there; somewhere around (that area).
additional_notes: Used to talk about an imprecise place or origin. Often appears with verbs like “ser” (to be) or “venir” (to come): “Soy de por ahí” = “I’m from around here/there.” It’s vague and conversational, similar to “around there / somewhere in that area.”
target_language_example: Creo que la tienda queda de por ahí, cerca del parque.
native_language_example: I think the store is around there, near the park.

additional_notes: Used to say something is in the middle of a situation (physically or figuratively), or that there’s an additional factor involved—often in phrases like “hay + [something] + de por medio” (e.g., money, problems, misunderstandings). It can also mean “intervening” or “getting in the way.”
target_language_example: No puedo hablar del tema porque hay dinero de por medio.
native_language_example: I can’t talk about it because there’s money involved.

meaning: for life; lifelong; for the rest of one’s life.
additional_notes: Used to say something lasts for a person’s entire life (a treatment, a supply, a memory, protection, a consequence). It often comes after the noun ("un tratamiento de por vida") or after a verb ("te protegeré de por vida").
target_language_example: Tendrás acceso de por vida a las actualizaciones.
native_language_example: You’ll have lifetime access to the updates.

additional_notes: Used to describe something as being of the best quality or level: "mercancía de primera" (top-quality goods), "servicio de primera (categoría)" (first-class service). It can also stand alone as a reaction: "Es de primera" / "¡Esto es de primera!" = “It’s excellent!” Related set phrases include "de primera fila" (top-level, front-row) and "de primera plana" (front-page, headline).
target_language_example: La comida de este restaurante es de primera.
native_language_example: The food at this restaurant is first-class.

additional_notes: Used after a noun (or sometimes after what’s being described) to mean something is the best, highest quality, or highest category/service level. Common in travel and services (e.g., tren/vuelo/camarote de primera clase) and also for people or things meaning “top-notch” (e.g., un cantante de primera clase).
target_language_example: Este hotel ofrece servicio de primera clase.
native_language_example: This hotel offers first-class service.

meaning: for the first course (starter) (on a menu).
additional_notes: Used especially in Spain when ordering a set menu: *de primero* = first course, and it’s often followed by *de segundo* (second course/main dish). You’ll hear it with verbs like *tomar/pedir* (to have/order): *De primero, ensalada.*
target_language_example: De primero, voy a pedir una sopa.
native_language_example: For the first course, I’m going to order a soup.

additional_notes: Used to say something is being done with urgency or too fast. Common with verbs like "hacer" (hacer algo de prisa = do something in a hurry). Also used alone as an instruction: "¡De prisa!" = "Hurry up!" Related phrase: "tener prisa" / "tener algo de prisa" = to be (a bit) in a hurry.
target_language_example: Lo hice de prisa y se me olvidó revisar los detalles.
native_language_example: I did it in a hurry and I forgot to check the details.

additional_notes: Used to describe something that happens unexpectedly or abruptly. Often placed at the beginning of a sentence ("De pronto,") but it can also appear mid-sentence. Similar in meaning to "de repente".
target_language_example: De pronto, empezó a llover y tuvimos que correr.
native_language_example: Suddenly, it started to rain and we had to run.

additional_notes: Used after a noun to describe something meant for testing or evaluating (e.g., instalaciones de prueba = test facilities, vuelo de prueba = test flight). Also used in expressions like “vuelta de prueba” (a test drive) and “mes de prueba” (a trial month). Often translates as “test/trial” or “for testing,” depending on the noun.
target_language_example: Podemos usar una cuenta de prueba antes de pagar.
native_language_example: We can use a trial account before paying.

meaning: upright/on end; (in some expressions) extremely tense or nervous.
additional_notes: Literally refers to something being positioned or sticking straight up on its end/tip (e.g., un libro de punta = standing upright; el pelo de punta = hair standing on end). With body-related nouns like "los nervios", it’s a set expression meaning you feel very on edge: "estar/tener los nervios de punta" = to be extremely nervous/tense.
target_language_example: Con esa película de miedo, se me puso el pelo de punta.
native_language_example: That scary movie made my hair stand on end.

additional_notes: Used with verbs like caminar/andar/pasar to mean moving quietly on your toes (heels lifted), often to avoid making noise. It can also be used more figuratively to mean staying very alert or tense (e.g., something “keeps you on your toes”).
target_language_example: Entró de puntillas para no hacer ruido.
native_language_example: He came in on tiptoe so he wouldn’t make noise.

additional_notes: Used mainly to describe clothing or fabric made by knitting (with stitches), e.g., "tela de punto" (knit fabric) or "suéter de punto" (knitted sweater). In everyday speech it often refers to soft, stretchy knit material.
target_language_example: Me compré un suéter de punto porque es más cómodo.
native_language_example: I bought a knitted sweater because it’s more comfortable.

additional_notes: Used after expressions of emotion such as "estar contento/feliz" + "de que". It triggers the present subjunctive (estés) because it’s reacting to something, not just stating a fact. Often appears in full sentences like "Estoy contento/a de que estés aquí" = "I’m glad you’re here."
target_language_example: Me alegro de que estés aquí hoy.
native_language_example: I’m glad you’re here today.

additional_notes: Used after verbs like saber (“to know”) to point to a specific topic that the speaker assumes is obvious or already understood: “Sabes de qué estoy hablando” = “You know what I’m talking about.” It can also add emphasis or a slightly challenging tone (“You know very well what I’m talking about”). Often appears with ya (“already / you know”) and with tú for emphasis: “Tú sabes…”
target_language_example: No te hagas; sabes de qué estoy hablando.
native_language_example: Don’t play dumb; you know what I’m talking about.

additional_notes: Used with verbs like saber, entender, ver, decir to ask or say what a situation, topic, plan, or issue is about. Often refers back to something mentioned (esto/eso) or implied by context: “No entiendo de qué se trata (esto)” = “I don’t understand what this is about.”
target_language_example: Explícame de qué se trata la reunión, por favor.
native_language_example: Explain to me what the meeting is about, please.

additional_notes: Used with a descriptor to indicate someone’s racial category (e.g., "de raza negra/blanca"). With animals, it commonly means the animal is purebred and is often followed by the breed or origin (e.g., "un perro de raza labrador / de raza francesa"). Because it refers to race, it can be sensitive depending on context.
target_language_example: Adoptaron un gato de raza siamesa.
native_language_example: They adopted a purebred Siamese cat.

additional_notes: Used to talk about being back in a place or having returned, or about bringing/sending someone or something back. Common with verbs like estar/volver/ir/traer: “estar de regreso” (to be back), “voy de regreso a…” (I’m heading back to…), “traer … de regreso” (to bring … back).
target_language_example: Estoy de regreso en casa.
native_language_example: I’m back home.

additional_notes: Used after a noun to specify its function/type. Common with vehicles and services: "camión/camioneta de reparto" = delivery truck/van. Also used in arts/film: "actor/actriz de reparto" = supporting actor (not the lead).
target_language_example: El paquete llegó en una camioneta de reparto.
native_language_example: The package arrived in a delivery van.

additional_notes: Used to describe something that happens unexpectedly and quickly. It often goes at the beginning of the sentence ("De repente, …") or right before/after the verb ("… de repente").
target_language_example: De repente, empezó a llover muy fuerte.
native_language_example: All of a sudden, it started raining really hard.

meaning: spare; replacement (extra, kept in case it’s needed).
additional_notes: Used after a noun to mean an extra one kept as a backup: "una llanta de repuesto" (a spare tire), "piezas de repuesto" (replacement parts), "una llave de repuesto" (a spare key). Can also refer to a substitute item/person in context: "uno de repuesto" = a spare/backup one.
target_language_example: ¿Tienes una batería de repuesto?
native_language_example: Do you have a spare battery?

meaning: as a result of; because of.
additional_notes: A fairly formal expression used to introduce a cause and its consequence. It’s similar to "a consecuencia de" or "como resultado de" and is followed by a noun phrase (or something treated like a noun).
target_language_example: De resultas del accidente, la carretera quedó cerrada varias horas.
native_language_example: As a result of the accident, the road was closed for several hours.

additional_notes: Used literally for being physically on your knees (often with verbs like caer (to fall), ponerse (to get), estar (to be), and ponerse de rodillas (to kneel down)). It can also be figurative, meaning “brought to its knees” (defeated/ruined), especially about a country or organization. Common in commands: ¡De rodillas! / Póngase de rodillas.
target_language_example: Se puso de rodillas para pedir perdón.
native_language_example: He got down on his knees to ask for forgiveness.

additional_notes: Used to describe something made of or involving blood (un charco de sangre = a puddle of blood) and family ties by biology (primos de sangre = blood cousins). It’s also used in common medical phrases like examen/análisis de sangre (blood test).
target_language_example: Necesito hacerme un análisis de sangre mañana.
native_language_example: I need to get a blood test tomorrow.

additional_notes: Often used with nouns like "clase" or "categoría" to mean someone/something is lower status or lower quality: "de segunda clase", "de segunda categoría". In other contexts, it can also mean "second-hand/used" (e.g., "un coche de segunda" = a used car).
target_language_example: No quiero un producto de segunda; prefiero pagar un poco más.
native_language_example: I don’t want a second-rate product; I’d rather pay a little more.

additional_notes: Used mainly for items you buy that have had a previous owner (un coche de segunda mano, un computador de segunda mano). It can also mean “secondhand” information—information you heard from others, not directly (información de segunda mano).
target_language_example: Compré este teléfono de segunda mano para ahorrar dinero.
native_language_example: I bought this phone second-hand to save money.

additional_notes: Used after a noun to say it’s related to safety/security: "motivos de seguridad" (security reasons), "servicios de seguridad" (security services), "sistema de seguridad" (security system), "jefe de seguridad" (head of security). Often translates as an adjective in English ("security" or "safe").
target_language_example: Por razones de seguridad, no podemos abrir la puerta ahora.
native_language_example: For security reasons, we can’t open the door right now.

additional_notes: Often used as **“de seguro (que) + verb”** to emphasize that something will definitely happen or is definitely true. It’s different from **seguro** meaning “insurance” (as in *póliza/plan/número de seguro*).
target_language_example: De seguro que llegamos a tiempo si salimos ahora.
native_language_example: For sure we’ll arrive on time if we leave now.

additional_notes: Often used as part of common patterns with nouns/verbs that take **de + infinitive** (here, *ser*): *el sueño de ser…* (“the dream of being…”), *la suerte de ser…* (“the luck to be…”), *acusar a alguien de ser…* (“to accuse someone of being…”). Also appears in **deber de ser** to express a guess/probability: *Deben de ser americanos* (“They must be American”).
target_language_example: Me alegro de ser parte del equipo.
native_language_example: I’m happy to be part of the team.

additional_notes: Most common with "estar": "Estoy de servicio" = "I’m on duty / I’m working." Used for jobs with shifts (police, doctors, customer service, etc.). You may also see it in place names like "departamento de servicio" meaning the service department/desk (e.g., in a store, hotel, or company).
target_language_example: Lo siento, no puedo salir esta noche: estoy de servicio.
native_language_example: Sorry, I can’t go out tonight—I’m on duty.

meaning: more than enough; extra; to spare.
additional_notes: Used after a noun or quantity to mean you have more than you need (surplus). Common with verbs like tener (to have): "Tengo tiempo/dinero/comida de sobra" = "I have time/money/food to spare."
target_language_example: Traje comida de sobra para todos.
native_language_example: I brought more than enough food for everyone.

additional_notes: A compositional phrase: de means "of" and su is a possessive that can mean "his," "her," "your" (formal), or "their," depending on context. It often appears after nouns like foto, casa, or amigo to show possession or connection.
target_language_example: Vi una foto de su perro en el teléfono.
native_language_example: I saw a photo of her dog on the phone.

meaning: from their house/home; of their house/home.
additional_notes: “De” can mean “from” (movement/origin) or “of” (possession/relationship), so the exact translation depends on context: “salió de su casa” = “left/ran out of his/her house,” while “el tejado de su casa” = “the roof of his/her house.” “Su” can mean “his,” “her,” “their,” or “your (formal),” so you often rely on context to know whose house it is.
target_language_example: Te llamo cuando salga de su casa.
native_language_example: I’ll call you when I leave their house.

meaning: of his/her/their social class (people like him/her/them).
additional_notes: Used to talk about someone’s social class, status, or group (often implying wealth or importance). With an article it can refer to people in that group: "los de su clase" = "people of his/her class" / "people like him/her".
target_language_example: No es común ver a alguien de su clase en este barrio.
native_language_example: It’s not common to see someone of his class in this neighborhood.

additional_notes: Used to show possession or to specify who/what something is related to. Spanish “su” can mean “his,” “her,” “your” (formal/usted), or “their,” so the context tells you whose son it is. Often used after nouns like: la muerte de su hijo (the death of his/her son), el casamiento de su hijo (his/her son’s wedding), orgulloso de su hijo (proud of his/her son), hablar de su hijo (talk about his/her son).
target_language_example: Me habló de su hijo y de lo bien que le va en la escuela.
native_language_example: He/she talked to me about his/her son and how well he’s doing at school.

additional_notes: Used to show relationship or origin connected to someone's mother. In Spanish, "su" can mean "his", "her", "your (formal)", or "their", so the exact meaning depends on context.
target_language_example: Aprendió a cocinar de su madre.
native_language_example: He/She learned to cook from his/her mother.

meaning: of her husband / about her husband; from her husband.
additional_notes: Means “of her husband” (possession/relationship) or “about her husband” when talking about him (e.g., quejarse de su marido = complain about her husband). With verbs like divorciarse de, it means “from” (divorced from her husband). Note: su can mean “his,” “her,” “your (formal),” or “their,” so de su marido can also be “of his/your/their husband” depending on context.
target_language_example: Siempre habla de su marido en el trabajo.
native_language_example: She always talks about her husband at work.

meaning: 'of his/her father' (belonging to, from, or about his/her father).
additional_notes: Uses de + possessive + noun. It can show possession/connection (El carácter de su padre = her/his father's personality), origin/traits (Tiene los ojos de su padre = he/she has his/her father's eyes), or topic (habla mal de su padre = speaks badly about his/her father). Su can mean 'his', 'her', 'your (formal)', or 'their'—context tells you whose father it is. Often interchangeable with the possessive adjective: el carácter de su padre = su carácter (but 'de su padre' is clearer about who it refers to).
target_language_example: Aprendió a conducir en el coche de su padre.
native_language_example: He/She learned to drive in his/her father's car.

meaning: “of you/him/her/them” (on your/his/her/their part); also “on someone’s side.”
additional_notes: Used after adjectives or nouns to attribute a behavior, remark, or decision to someone: Es muy amable de su parte (“That’s very kind of you”); Fue un error de su parte (“It was a mistake on his/her part”). It can also mean “on someone’s side” in contexts like La ley está de su parte (“The law is on your/his/her side”). You can change the possessive depending on who you mean: de mi parte, de tu parte, de nuestra parte, etc.
target_language_example: Fue un error de su parte decirle tales cosas.
native_language_example: It was a mistake on his/her/their part to say such things to him/her.

meaning: about his/her work; from his/her job.
additional_notes: Uses de + su + trabajo. With verbs like quejarse de / hablar de / ser admirador de, it means “about his/her work.” With verbs like echar (a alguien) de, it means “from/out of his/her job” (to be fired). “Su” can mean “his,” “her,” “your (formal),” or “their,” depending on context.
target_language_example: Lo despidieron de su trabajo el mes pasado.
native_language_example: They fired him from his job last month.

meaning: of his/her life; (with «qué será de…») what will become of him/her.
additional_notes: Usually refers to someone’s life or situation. Common in the expression «¿Qué será de su vida?» meaning you wonder what happened to someone or how they’re doing now. «Su» can mean “his,” “her,” or “your (formal)” depending on context.
target_language_example: Hace años que no lo veo; me pregunto qué será de su vida.
native_language_example: I haven’t seen him in years; I wonder what became of him.

additional_notes: "Sus" means "his/her/their" (also "your" formal). "De sus" is used when something belongs to them, often after verbs/expressions that take "de" (e.g., "cuidar de", "olvidarse de", "vaciar ... de") or after nouns like "la mujer de sus sueños". "Sus" agrees with the thing owned (plural), not with the owner: "sus pacientes" = "his/her/their patients".
target_language_example: Siempre habla bien de sus compañeros de trabajo.
native_language_example: He/She always speaks well of his/her coworkers.

meaning: of his/her/their friends; from his/her/their friends.
additional_notes: Uses **de** + **sus** (his/her/their) + **amigos** (friends). It can indicate belonging/relationship (**of**) or source/origin (**from**), depending on the verb: e.g., *recordar los nombres de sus amigos* = “remember the names of his friends”; *pedir prestado... de sus amigos* = “borrow... from their friends.”
target_language_example: Ella recibió ayuda de sus amigos.
native_language_example: She got help from her friends.

additional_notes: Uses **de** (“of”) + **sus** (“his/her/their”) + **hijos** (“children/sons”). **Sus** can mean *his*, *her*, *their*, or *your (formal)* depending on context, so you often rely on the sentence to know whose children. Common after another noun to show what it’s about: **el cuidado de sus hijos** (“the care of his/her/their children”), **la custodia de sus hijos** (“custody of his/her/their children”).
target_language_example: Ella habla mucho del futuro de sus hijos.
native_language_example: She talks a lot about the future of her children.

meaning: 'of his/her/their parents' (or 'from his/her/their parents,' depending on context).
additional_notes: Used to refer to someone’s parents with the possessive "sus" (can mean "his," "her," "their," or formal "your"). Often appears after expressions like "independiente de" (independent of/from) or in phrases like "los deseos de sus padres" (their parents’ wishes).
target_language_example: No depende de sus padres para pagar la renta.
native_language_example: He/She doesn’t depend on his/her parents to pay the rent.

additional_notes: Somewhat formal. Used to say something happens or is true on its own, without needing extra help or explanation ("in itself"). Often appears with verbs like ser/estar/implicar (e.g., "no es malo de suyo" = "it’s not bad in itself").
target_language_example: La idea no es mala de suyo, pero necesitamos un plan.
native_language_example: The idea isn’t bad in itself, but we need a plan.

additional_notes: Used with verbs or expressions that take "de" (like "dudar de...") to refer back to the same male person ("himself"). For a female person, use "de sí misma"; for plural, "de sí mismos / de sí mismas". Often used for self-reflection or self-doubt.
target_language_example: A veces duda de sí mismo, pero sigue adelante.
native_language_example: Sometimes he doubts himself, but he keeps going.

additional_notes: Used especially for food/products that are available at a certain time of year (fruta/verdura, setas/hongos, etc.). When something está de temporada, it’s usually more available and often cheaper. You may also see it in phrases like final de temporada (“end of the season”) or de temporada a temporada (“from season to season”).
target_language_example: Prefiero comprar verduras de temporada porque saben mejor.
native_language_example: I prefer to buy seasonal vegetables because they taste better.

additional_notes: Used to describe something seen as inferior or not very good. Often appears with a noun like "clase" (e.g., "de tercera clase" = "third-class"), but it can also stand alone: "Son de tercera" = "They’re third-rate."
target_language_example: Ese hotel es de tercera; mejor busquemos otro.
native_language_example: That hotel is third-rate; let’s look for another one.

meaning: text; (used in set phrases like “text message,” “textbook,” “word processor”).
additional_notes: Means “of text / for text” and is most commonly used in fixed combinations: "mensaje(s) de texto" (text message(s)), "libro(s) de texto" (textbook(s)), and "procesador de texto" (word processor). It’s neutral and literal: "de" + "texto".
target_language_example: ¿Me puedes mandar un mensaje de texto cuando llegues?
native_language_example: Can you send me a text message when you arrive?

additional_notes: Usually means "about you" after verbs like hablar, saber, or oír. In some expressions, English uses "of you" instead, as in pensar eso de ti. Ti is the form of "you" used after a preposition; compare subject tú.
target_language_example: Quiero saber más de ti.
native_language_example: I want to know more about you.

meaning: all my/your/their life; for as long as I/you/they can remember.
additional_notes: Used to say you’ve known someone or something for a very long time (often since childhood). It commonly goes with verbs like conocer (to know/meet) and ser (to be): “Nos conocemos de toda la vida” = “We’ve known each other forever.”
target_language_example: Ese bar está ahí de toda la vida.
native_language_example: That bar has been there forever.

additional_notes: Used to move on from what was just said, or to say something is true regardless of objections, reasons, or circumstances. Common at the start of a sentence, often followed by a comma: "De todas formas, ..."
target_language_example: De todas formas, vamos a intentarlo otra vez.
native_language_example: Anyway, let’s try again.

additional_notes: Used to compare or refer to something within a whole group of feminine plural nouns (e.g., "la mejor de todas las joyas" = "the best of all the jewels"). Also used to mean "from/against all the..." depending on the verb: "defender a alguien de todas las críticas" = "defend someone from all criticism." It’s the feminine plural form; with masculine plural you use "de todos los."
target_language_example: Este es el más caro de todas las opciones.
native_language_example: This is the most expensive of all the options.

additional_notes: Used to say that something is true or will happen despite what was just mentioned (like “no matter what” or “regardless”). It often appears at the start of a sentence to shift back to the main point, or at the end to emphasize “even so.”
target_language_example: No tengo mucho tiempo, pero te ayudo de todas maneras.
native_language_example: I don’t have much time, but I’ll help you anyway.

additional_notes: Used to emphasize sincere, deep gratitude, acceptance, apology, or feelings. Often appears with expressions like "gracias" and "te agradezco". It’s a warm, fairly formal phrase (not slang).
target_language_example: Lo siento de todo corazón.
native_language_example: I’m truly sorry / I’m sorry with all my heart.

meaning: in the whole world; from all over the world; everyone.
additional_notes: Often used for emphasis with superlatives: el/la más + adjective + de todo el mundo (“the ...est in the whole world”). With nouns like gente/turistas, it usually means “from all over the world.” With verbs like burlarse/acordarse, it can mean “everyone” (i.e., everybody).
target_language_example: Es el mejor chocolate de todo el mundo.
native_language_example: It’s the best chocolate in the whole world.

additional_notes: Most often means “of everything” after nouns like creador/precio/final (e.g., “the creator/price/end of everything”) or after verbs like acordarse/hablar/huir/informar (e.g., “remember/talk/escape/be informed about everything”). In phrases like “hay de todo” or “tiene de todo,” it means “there’s a bit of everything / it has everything (you might need).”
target_language_example: En ese mercado venden de todo.
native_language_example: At that market they sell a bit of everything.

additional_notes: Used to refer to the entire group of something masculine plural: de todos los + noun (e.g., de todos los estudiantes = of all the students). If the noun is feminine plural, use "de todas las" instead (de todas las casas = of all the houses). Often appears after nouns like "la ubicación de..." (the location of...) or after verbs like "hacerse de..." (to get hold of...).
target_language_example: Tengo los nombres de todos los invitados.
native_language_example: I have the names of all the guests.

additional_notes: Used after a superlative (el/la mejor, el/la peor, el/la más + adjective) to mean “ever” or “in history.” It’s a very common way to emphasize that someone/something is the greatest, cutest, biggest, etc., compared to all others in the past and present.
target_language_example: Este es el mejor concierto de todos los tiempos.
native_language_example: This is the best concert of all time.

additional_notes: Used to say something is true or will happen despite other facts or objections. Often appears at the beginning or end of a sentence to add “anyway.” Similar to “de todas formas.”
target_language_example: No estoy seguro, pero iré de todos modos.
native_language_example: I'm not sure, but I'll go anyway.

additional_notes: Literally “of work.” Commonly used after a noun to specify that it’s related to work or used for work: puesto de trabajo (job/position), oferta de trabajo (job offer), ropa de trabajo (work clothes), compañeros de trabajo (coworkers), exceso de trabajo (overwork). The exact English translation depends on the noun it follows.
target_language_example: Necesito un ordenador de trabajo.
native_language_example: I need a work computer.

additional_notes: Used to express a duration, age, or time amount. Common patterns: "estar embarazada de tres meses" = to be three months pregnant; "un bebé de tres meses" = a three-month-old baby; "un adelanto de tres meses" = an advance of three months. Often appears as "de + number + (día/semana/mes/año)".
target_language_example: Mi contrato es de tres meses.
native_language_example: My contract is for three months.

additional_notes: Used after a noun to specify that it’s related to road traffic, driving, or transportation on streets. Common collocations: leyes de tráfico (traffic laws), reglas de tráfico (traffic rules), accidentes de tráfico (traffic accidents), atasco de tráfico (traffic jam). Often interchangeable with "de tránsito" in many regions.
target_language_example: Hay muchas señales de tráfico en esta avenida.
native_language_example: There are many traffic signs on this avenue.

additional_notes: Used after a noun to specify it’s about traffic or transportation (especially road traffic): accidentes de tránsito (traffic accidents), normas de tránsito (traffic rules), policía de tránsito (traffic police). In some countries, “tránsito” commonly means road traffic; in others it can also refer to public transit/transportation.
target_language_example: Hubo un accidente de tránsito en la autopista.
native_language_example: There was a traffic accident on the highway.

additional_notes: A common combination of the preposition de and tu, the singular informal word for 'your.' It can show possession or connection ('el ritmo de tu traducción' = 'the rhythm of your translation') and with some verbs can mean 'about your...' ('Cuéntame de tu primer beso'). Note that tu without an accent means 'your'; tú with an accent means 'you'.
target_language_example: No sé nada de tu hermano.
native_language_example: I don't know anything about your brother.

additional_notes: Used to describe someone’s age relative to the person you’re speaking to. Often follows “ser” (Es de tu edad.) or a noun (un hijo/una hija de tu edad). You’ll also hear “como de tu edad” to mean “around your age.”
target_language_example: Creo que ella es de tu edad.
native_language_example: I think she’s your age.

additional_notes: Used to show possession or connection with someone’s mother: *casa de tu madre* (your mom’s house), *un amigo de tu madre* (a friend of your mom). In some vulgar insults it can appear after a swear word (e.g., *… de tu madre*), but by itself it’s neutral.
target_language_example: Tengo que pasar por la casa de tu madre esta tarde.
native_language_example: I have to stop by your mom’s house this afternoon.

additional_notes: Uses "de" to show possession or relationship ("your father's"), or origin/source ("from your father"). Often follows a noun: "la casa de tu padre" = "your father's house". "Padre" is "father" (more formal/neutral); "papá" is more common for "dad".
target_language_example: Este reloj es de tu padre.
native_language_example: This watch is your father's.

meaning: “on your part” / “from you” (your doing; your responsibility).
additional_notes: Used to comment on someone’s action or behavior, often after an adjective: Es muy amable/considerado/generoso de tu parte (“That’s very kind/thoughtful/generous of you”). It can also express responsibility or blame: Fue descuidado de tu parte… (“It was careless of you to…”). Not the same as “parte” meaning “part” in a physical/object sense.
target_language_example: Es muy amable de tu parte ayudarme con esto.
native_language_example: It’s very kind of you to help me with this.

additional_notes: Used to say that something belongs to, happens in, or is the most important/best/worst within your life. Very common with superlatives: “el mejor día de tu vida” (the best day of your life), “la decisión más importante de tu vida” (the most important decision of your life).
target_language_example: Hoy es el mejor día de tu vida.
native_language_example: Today is the best day of your life.

additional_notes: Used after a noun to describe the person who is currently working that shift (often in workplaces like hospitals, security, customer service). Common patterns: “el/la [profesión] de turno” (the [profession] on duty) and “cambio de turno” (shift change).
target_language_example: ¿Puedes llamar al médico de turno, por favor?
native_language_example: Can you call the doctor on duty, please?

additional_notes: Used to show possession or association: de + tus + plural noun (masculine or feminine), e.g., de tus actos / de tus ideas. Common in set phrases like “ser responsable de tus…” (“to be responsible for your…”). Not used before singular nouns (use “de tu…”).
target_language_example: Estoy orgulloso de tus logros.
native_language_example: I'm proud of your achievements.

additional_notes: Uses de to show what something is made of or the type/category. Very common in partitive expressions like algo de té (“some tea”) and quantities like una libra de té (“a pound of tea”).
target_language_example: ¿Quieres algo de té con limón?
native_language_example: Do you want some tea with lemon?

additional_notes: Uses "de" to show (1) possession/connection: "la casa de un amigo" (a friend’s house), "el auto de un amigo" (a friend’s car); or (2) origin/source: "tomó prestado... de un amigo" (borrowed ... from a friend), "recibí ayuda de un amigo" (got help from a friend). Often appears after a noun (to say who it belongs to) or after a verb (to say who something comes from).
target_language_example: Tengo un consejo de un amigo.
native_language_example: I have some advice from a friend.

meaning: suddenly; overnight; from one day to the next.
additional_notes: Used to talk about a change that happens very quickly (often unexpectedly), or about things that vary from one day to the next. Often used with verbs like desaparecer (to disappear), llegar (to arrive/come into someone’s life), cambiar/variar (to change/vary), and in negatives to mean “not overnight”: No se logrará de un día para otro.
target_language_example: Mi jefe cambió de opinión de un día para otro.
native_language_example: My boss changed his mind overnight.

additional_notes: Used with nouns to show that something belongs to, comes from, or describes a man (possession/association): la reputación de un hombre (a man’s reputation), el sueño de un hombre viejo (an old man’s dream). Contrast: de un hombre = “of a man” (one/any man), de el hombre (del hombre) = “of the man” (a specific man).
target_language_example: La voz de un hombre se oía en la calle.
native_language_example: A man’s voice could be heard in the street.

meaning: back and forth; from one side to the other.
additional_notes: Used to describe someone or something moving repeatedly between two sides/places, often pacing in a room (restless or nervous). It can also be used more generally for moving around from place to place.
