additional_notes: An adverbial phrase meaning "completely" or "entirely." It is very common with negation: "no del todo" = "not completely," "not entirely," or "not quite."
target_language_example: No estoy del todo seguro.
native_language_example: I'm not completely sure.

additional_notes: Del = de + el. With "orgulloso del trabajo," it means “proud of the job/work” (de = “of/about”). With time expressions like "luego del trabajo," it means “after work” (de = “from/after,” referring to the time when work ends).
target_language_example: ¿Quieres tomar un café después del trabajo?
native_language_example: Do you want to have a coffee after work?

meaning: “from the train” / “of the train” (de + el tren).
additional_notes: "Del" is the contraction of "de" + "el". Common with verbs like "bajar(se) del tren" = "to get off the train". It can also show possession/association: "el jefe del tren" = "the train’s boss/manager".
target_language_example: Nos bajamos del tren en la próxima estación.
native_language_example: We’re getting off the train at the next station.

additional_notes: Used to indicate that something belongs to, comes from, or is related to the universe. "Del" is a contraction of "de + el" ("of/from the"). You’ll often see it after nouns: "la lengua del universo" (the language of the universe).
target_language_example: La historia del universo es fascinante.
native_language_example: The history of the universe is fascinating.

additional_notes: "Del" is the contraction of "de + el". With "árbol" it can mean (1) origin/movement away: "bajó/saltó del árbol" = came down/jumped from the tree; or (2) possession/relationship: "las hojas/ramas del árbol" = the tree's leaves/branches (the leaves/branches of the tree).
target_language_example: El gato no quiere bajar del árbol.
native_language_example: The cat doesn’t want to come down from the tree.

meaning: 'in front of' (in front of something/someone); also 'in someone’s presence'.
additional_notes: Used mainly for physical position: something is located or happens in front of another person/thing ("El coche está delante de la casa"). It can also mean "in front of" in the sense of "with someone present/watching" ("No lo digas delante de los niños" = don’t say it in front of the kids). Often contrasts with "detrás de" (behind).
target_language_example: No discutas delante de tus hijos.
native_language_example: Don’t argue in front of your kids.

additional_notes: Used to say something is beyond your ability (right now) or harder than you can handle. Common pattern: "demasiado + adjective + para + person" (e.g., "demasiado caro para mí" = too expensive for me). You can change the person: "para ti" (for you), "para nosotros" (for us).
target_language_example: Lo siento, esta tarea es demasiado difícil para mí.
native_language_example: Sorry, this homework is too difficult for me.

additional_notes: Used to say someone isn’t old enough to do something (often followed by an infinitive: "para + verb"). You can add emphasis with "aún" or "todavía" (“still”): "todavía demasiado joven para...". It can also be used with "para mí" to mean someone is too young for you as a partner.
target_language_example: Soy demasiado joven para conducir.
native_language_example: I’m too young to drive.

additional_notes: Use it for physical distance ("not too far from here") or to say something has gone past an acceptable limit (a joke, a situation, behavior). Often used with verbs like "ir" ("ha ido demasiado lejos") or "llevar" ("llevó la broma demasiado lejos").
target_language_example: Perdón, me pasé; fui demasiado lejos con lo que dije.
native_language_example: Sorry, I went too far with what I said.

additional_notes: Used to say something happens at an excessive speed. It can describe actions (conducir/manejar, comer, olvidar) or events (Todo pasó demasiado rápido). The form changes for gender/number: demasiado rápido (masc. sing.), demasiado rápida (fem. sing.), demasiado rápidos/rápidas (plural).
target_language_example: Estás hablando demasiado rápido; no te entiendo.
native_language_example: You’re speaking too fast; I don’t understand you.

additional_notes: Used to say an action happens after the right time, so it’s no longer possible or is harder to fix. Often appears with "ya" ("ya es demasiado tarde" = "it’s already too late") and in future warnings ("será demasiado tarde" = "it will be too late"). Also used in the encouraging phrase "nunca es demasiado tarde" ("it’s never too late").
target_language_example: Lo siento, llegamos demasiado tarde para ver el show.
native_language_example: Sorry, we arrived too late to see the show.

additional_notes: Used to say an amount or duration of time is excessive. Common with verbs like pasar (to spend) and esperar (to wait): “pasar demasiado tiempo (haciendo algo)” = “to spend too much time (doing something)”, “esperar demasiado tiempo” = “to wait too long”. Also appears with “ha pasado demasiado tiempo” = “too much time has passed / it’s been too long.”
target_language_example: No quiero perder demasiado tiempo en esto.
native_language_example: I don’t want to waste too much time on this.

meaning: 'within' / 'inside' (a limit or place); also 'in' (a certain amount of time).
additional_notes: Used for limits and boundaries (e.g., dentro de unos límites = within certain limits) and for time expressions meaning "after" a duration (dentro de cinco días = in five days). Often followed by a noun or a time expression (dentro de poco, dentro de una semana).
target_language_example: Llegaré dentro de una hora.
native_language_example: I’ll arrive in an hour.

additional_notes: Used for (1) location: “inside (of) a place/thing” (Dentro de la cueva = inside the cave), and (2) future time: “in/within + a period of time” (Dentro de cuatro meses = in four months; Dentro de instantes = in moments). Often used to say something will happen after a short/defined amount of time.
target_language_example: Te llamo dentro de diez minutos.
native_language_example: I’ll call you in ten minutes.

meaning: in two (minutes/days/etc.); two (units of time) from now.
additional_notes: Used to say something will happen after two units of time. Normally you add the time unit: "dentro de dos minutos/días/horas". In casual speech, the unit can be understood from context (e.g., in a meeting: "Vuelvo dentro de dos").
target_language_example: Te llamo dentro de dos minutos.
native_language_example: I'll call you in two minutes.

additional_notes: Used for something physically inside your body (literal) or for emotions, thoughts, or something personal that you feel "within" yourself (figurative). Often used with verbs like "estar" (to be) or "vivir" (to live).
target_language_example: Siento que hay algo dentro de mí que no puedo explicar.
native_language_example: I feel like there is something within me that I can’t explain.

additional_notes: Used to say something will happen in the near future. It often goes at the end of the sentence (e.g., "Te veré dentro de poco"), but it can also be placed earlier for emphasis. Similar in meaning to "pronto" or "en poco tiempo".
target_language_example: Voy a llamarte dentro de poco.
native_language_example: I’m going to call you soon.

additional_notes: Used to say something/someone is within an enclosed space or interior of something. It’s the contraction of “dentro de + el” → “dentro del”. With feminine nouns, use “dentro de la” (e.g., dentro de la casa).
target_language_example: Dejé el móvil dentro del bolso.
native_language_example: I left my phone inside the bag.

additional_notes: Used to say that something changes based on a condition or factor. It’s the verb depender (to depend) in the 3rd person (depende = it depends) + de (on). Often followed by a noun (Depende de tu decisión) or a clause introduced by qué/si (Depende de qué tan fuerte sea).
target_language_example: Depende del clima si vamos a la playa.
native_language_example: It depends on the weather whether we go to the beach.

meaning: "it depends on you" / "it's up to you."
additional_notes: Used to say that the decision or outcome is in the other person’s hands. Often comes after words like ahora (now), todo (everything), or eso (that): "Ahora depende de ti" (Now it’s up to you), "Eso depende de ti" (That depends on you). You can swap ti for another person/pronoun: "depende de mí" (on me), "depende de nosotros" (on us).
target_language_example: ¿Salimos hoy o mañana? Depende de ti.
native_language_example: Are we going out today or tomorrow? It’s up to you.

meaning: "it depends on the" (followed by a masculine singular noun).
additional_notes: Used to say something changes based on a condition or factor. It’s the 3rd-person singular of depender + de + el (= del). Use "depende de la" with feminine singular nouns (Depende de la hora), and "depende de los/las" for plurals (Depende de los precios / de las reglas). Often followed by a clause: "Depende de si..." or "Depende de lo que...".
target_language_example: Podemos ir mañana, pero depende del clima.
native_language_example: We can go tomorrow, but it depends on the weather.

additional_notes: Used with "de" to say you need someone/something or that something is determined by something else. Often appears with "tener que": "tener que depender de alguien" = "to have to depend on someone."
target_language_example: No quiero depender de mis padres para pagar el alquiler.
native_language_example: I don’t want to depend on my parents to pay the rent.

additional_notes: Common legal/police phrase (as in Miranda rights). Uses the structure "tener derecho a + infinitive" = "to have the right to + verb". Often appears as: "Tiene derecho a permanecer en silencio."
target_language_example: Tiene derecho a permanecer en silencio y a hablar con un abogado.
native_language_example: You have the right to remain silent and to speak with a lawyer.

meaning: civil law (non-criminal law; also the legal system based on civil codes).
additional_notes: Used in legal contexts. It can refer either to the area of law dealing with private matters (contracts, property, family law, etc.), or—depending on the country/context—to the “civil law” legal tradition (as opposed to common law). Often seen in phrases like “Código de Derecho Civil” or “estudiar Derecho civil.”
target_language_example: Está estudiando derecho civil en la universidad.
native_language_example: He/She is studying civil law at the university.

additional_notes: Used to describe a basic right that every person should have (often in legal, political, or moral discussions). Singular: "un derecho humano"; plural: "derechos humanos".
target_language_example: La educación es un derecho humano.
native_language_example: Education is a human right.

meaning: to rest a little; to take a short break.
additional_notes: Used to suggest or say you need a brief rest (physically or mentally). Very common with verbs like "necesitar" and "deberías": "Necesito/deberías descansar un poco." You can also use it as a group plan: "Vamos a descansar un poco" (Let’s take a short break).
target_language_example: Estoy cansado; voy a descansar un poco.
native_language_example: I’m tired; I’m going to rest a little.

additional_notes: Used to mark a change that begins at the present moment and continues into the future. Common in instructions, rules, and announcements. Often appears at the beginning of a sentence followed by a comma: "Desde ahora, ...".
target_language_example: Desde ahora, vamos a estudiar español todos los días.
native_language_example: From now on, we're going to study Spanish every day.

additional_notes: Used to mark the starting point of an action, distance, or viewpoint: distance (desde aquí hasta…), perspective (la vista desde aquí), or what you’ll handle/continue doing from your current position (Me encargaré desde aquí). Often pairs with “hasta” to show a range: “desde aquí hasta allí”.
target_language_example: Desde aquí puedo ver toda la ciudad.
native_language_example: From here I can see the whole city.

meaning: from the beginning; from the start.
additional_notes: Used to say something has been true or happening starting at the very beginning. Also common when restarting something: “Otra vez desde el principio” = “Again from the beginning / Let’s start over.”
target_language_example: Si no entiendes, podemos empezar desde el principio.
native_language_example: If you don’t understand, we can start from the beginning.

additional_notes: Used to mark a starting point in the past (a moment or event understood from context) and everything that has happened from that point up to now (or up to another reference time). Often followed by a present perfect (he visto) or present tense to describe what has been true since that time. Also common in phrases like "Ha pasado un año desde entonces" (A year has passed since then) and "No sé de ella desde entonces" (I haven’t heard from her since then).
target_language_example: Tuve un accidente y desde entonces manejo con más cuidado.
native_language_example: I had an accident, and ever since then I drive more carefully.

additional_notes: Used to talk about an action or situation that started in the past and continues up to now. It’s commonly followed by a time expression (e.g., "dos años", "seis meses", "mucho tiempo"). Often corresponds to English “for” (duration) or “since … ago” (e.g., "desde hace seis meses" = “for six months” / “since six months ago”).
target_language_example: Vivo aquí desde hace tres años.
native_language_example: I’ve lived here for three years.

meaning: for years; for many years (up to now).
additional_notes: Used to say something started years ago and has continued until the present (or up to the time being talked about). Often goes with the present tense (La conozco desde hace años) or present perfect (No la he visto desde hace años). Similar idea: "since years ago."
target_language_example: No hablamos desde hace años.
native_language_example: We haven’t talked for years.

meaning: for a long time; for a long while.
additional_notes: Used to say something started in the past and has continued up to now (a duration from then until now). Common with the present tense: “Nos conocemos desde hace mucho” = “We’ve known each other for a long time.”
target_language_example: Vivo aquí desde hace mucho.
native_language_example: I’ve lived here for a long time.

meaning: for a long time; for a long time now.
additional_notes: Used to say something started in the past and has continued up to now, or that a long time has passed since something happened. Often appears with present perfect (he + participle) or the present tense in Spanish (which can translate as “have been …” in English).
target_language_example: No te veo desde hace mucho tiempo.
native_language_example: I haven't seen you in a long time.

meaning: for a long time; for quite a while (from then until now).
additional_notes: Used to say something started in the past and is still true now. Often goes with the present tense (e.g., "lo conozco desde hace tiempo") or with the imperfect to describe an ongoing past situation ("había... desde hace tiempo"). Similar to "desde hace + period of time" (desde hace dos años = for two years).
target_language_example: No hablo con él desde hace tiempo.
native_language_example: I haven’t talked to him in a long time.

additional_notes: Used to mark a change that begins today and continues into the future. Often appears at the start of a sentence (sometimes followed by a comma) to introduce a new rule, decision, status, or habit. Compare: “a partir de hoy” (from today on, often for rules/decisions) and “desde hoy” (from today on, emphasizing the starting point).
target_language_example: Desde hoy, voy a estudiar español todos los días.
native_language_example: Starting today, I'm going to study Spanish every day.

meaning: from the window; out of the window.
additional_notes: Used to say where you are seeing something from (your viewpoint) or where something is thrown from. With verbs like ver (“to see”), it means you’re looking from inside/by the window: Lo vi desde la ventana. With verbs like arrojar/tirar (“to throw”), it can mean “out of the window.” You can also specify which window: desde la ventana de mi habitación (“from my bedroom window”).
target_language_example: Se oían los pájaros desde la ventana.
native_language_example: You could hear the birds from the window.

additional_notes: Used to strongly agree, confirm, or emphasize what you’re saying. Often placed at the start as a stand-alone reply (“Desde luego.” = “Of course.”) or inside a sentence for emphasis (“Yo desde luego…”). In “desde luego que…”, it reinforces the statement (“certainly/definitely that…”).
target_language_example: —¿Vienes mañana? —Desde luego.
native_language_example: —Are you coming tomorrow? —Of course.

meaning: since (I/he/she was) a child; since childhood.
additional_notes: Used to say something has been true starting in childhood and continuing up to the present (or up to another reference point). Often used with the imperfect (conocía, soñaba, era) or with the present (es, conozco). You can change the gender/number: desde niña, desde niños, desde niñas. Also common with possessives: desde niño/a ("since I was a kid") vs. desde su niñez ("since his/her childhood").
target_language_example: Me gusta la música desde niño.
native_language_example: I've liked music since I was a kid.

additional_notes: Used with a verb to mark the starting point in time of an action/state that continues up to now (or up to another moment being talked about). Often used with the present perfect (he estado, ha pasado) or with an imperfect past situation (era pequeño).
target_language_example: No la he visto desde que terminó el curso.
native_language_example: I haven’t seen her since the term ended.

meaning: “since I/he/she was…” (from the time when someone was…).
additional_notes: Used to say something started in the past at a certain life stage/age and continued afterward. It’s often followed by a noun phrase like un niño/una niña/un bebé/muy joven. You can change the verb for person/number: desde que era (I/he/she was), desde que éramos (we were), desde que eran (they were).
target_language_example: Vivo aquí desde que era adolescente.
native_language_example: I’ve lived here since I was a teenager.

meaning: "since I was a child" / "ever since I was a kid."
additional_notes: Used to say something started in childhood and has continued up to a later time (often the present). The verb is typically in the imperfect (era) because it describes an ongoing past period. You can change the person and gender: desde que era niña (since I/she was a girl), desde que eras niño (since you were a boy), desde que éramos niños (since we were kids).
target_language_example: Vivo en esta ciudad desde que era niño.
native_language_example: I've lived in this city since I was a child.

meaning: “always” / “for as long as I can remember.”
additional_notes: Used to say something has been true for a very long time, basically all your life or since the earliest time you can remember. Often used with verbs like conocer (to know), querer (to love/like), or vivir (to live): “Lo conozco desde siempre” = “I’ve known him forever.”
target_language_example: He vivido en este barrio desde siempre.
native_language_example: I’ve lived in this neighborhood for as long as I can remember.

meaning: “I wish I could…” / “I would like to be able to…”
additional_notes: Uses the conditional tense of "desear" (desearía) to express a wish or regret about something you can’t do (often because it’s not possible right now). It’s typically followed by an infinitive: "Desearía poder + infinitive" (e.g., desearía poder ir, ayudar, quedarme).
target_language_example: Desearía poder ayudarte, pero no tengo tiempo hoy.
native_language_example: I wish I could help you, but I don’t have time today.

meaning: "I wish that..." / "I would like it if..."
additional_notes: Used to express a wish about a situation, often something unreal, unlikely, or not true right now. It’s the conditional of "desear" + "que", and it typically triggers the imperfect subjunctive (e.g., "desearía que vinieras", "desearía que hubiera"). You can also use it politely to express what you’d like someone to do.
target_language_example: Desearía que pudiéramos hablar en privado.
native_language_example: I wish we could talk in private.

additional_notes: Used to politely ask someone to slow down, especially when speaking. Often said alone ("Despacio, por favor.") or with a verb like "Habla" (you, informal), "Hable" (you, formal), "Hablad" (you all, informal Spain), or "Hablen" (you all, formal/Latin America). You can add "más" or "un poco más" for "more" / "a bit more": "Habla un poco más despacio, por favor."
target_language_example: ¿Puedes repetirlo más despacio, por favor?
native_language_example: Can you repeat that more slowly, please?

meaning: bachelor party (party for a man before his wedding).
additional_notes: Used for a celebration held shortly before a man gets married. Often said with possessives: “mi/tu/su despedida de soltero”. For a woman, you’ll usually hear “despedida de soltera” or “despedida de soltera(o)” depending on region.
target_language_example: Vamos a organizarle una despedida de soltero este fin de semana.
native_language_example: We’re going to organize his bachelor party this weekend.

additional_notes: Used to refer to something happening later than another event or time. It is followed by a noun or pronoun (después de la tormenta, después de mi divorcio) or an infinitive (después de aprobar). Before a full clause, Spanish usually uses después de que.
target_language_example: Nos vemos después de clase.
native_language_example: See you after class.

additional_notes: Used to say something happens later than the action of having dinner. It’s a time expression: después de + infinitive (después de comer, después de estudiar, etc.).
target_language_example: Vamos a dar un paseo después de cenar.
native_language_example: We’re going to go for a walk after dinner.

additional_notes: Used to talk about what happens once the school day or a class period is finished. Common in school-related plans and routines: "después de clases, voy a…" (after class, I’m going to…). You can also hear "después de la clase" (after the class) for one specific class.
target_language_example: Nos vemos después de clases para estudiar.
native_language_example: See you after class to study.

additional_notes: Used to say something happens later than eating. It can be followed by nothing (after eating/after the meal) or by an object: «después de comer mi comida» (after eating my food). Often placed at the beginning or end of the sentence, with a comma when it starts the sentence.
target_language_example: Después de comer, vamos a dar un paseo.
native_language_example: After eating, we're going for a walk.

additional_notes: Used to talk about what happens next in time, referring back to an action or event already mentioned. It’s common in storytelling and giving instructions: Primero..., y después de eso.... Also often shortened to "después" when the context is clear.
target_language_example: Terminamos de comer y después de eso fuimos al cine.
native_language_example: We finished eating and after that we went to the movies.

additional_notes: Used to say something happens later than the meal (cena = dinner). Often placed at the start or end of the sentence: “Después de la cena, …” / “… después de la cena.”
target_language_example: Después de la cena, hago la tarea.
native_language_example: After dinner, I do my homework.

additional_notes: Used to say something happens following the end of the school day. It can be followed by a verb phrase (e.g., "después de la escuela + jugamos/estudio/trabajo").
target_language_example: Después de la escuela, hago mi tarea y luego salgo con mis amigos.
native_language_example: After school, I do my homework and then hang out with my friends.

meaning: 'after the war' (in the period following a war).
additional_notes: Used to place an event in time after a specific war that both speakers understand from context (often a major war). It can refer to immediately after or generally in the years following: e.g., "dos años después de la guerra" = "two years after the war."
target_language_example: Después de la guerra, mucha gente tuvo que empezar de nuevo.
native_language_example: After the war, many people had to start over.

additional_notes: Used to talk about what happens once it has rained. It commonly introduces a time clause at the beginning of a sentence (followed by a comma), but it can also appear later in the sentence. You can swap in other events: después de la clase (after class), después de cenar (after dinner).
target_language_example: Después de la lluvia, salimos a caminar.
native_language_example: After the rain, we went out for a walk.

additional_notes: Used to talk about what happens once a person has died (often in discussions about the afterlife: "la vida después de la muerte" = "life after death"). It can describe a time period (“after death”) or beliefs (“after death there is nothing”).
target_language_example: Muchas religiones hablan de lo que pasa después de la muerte.
native_language_example: Many religions talk about what happens after death.

additional_notes: Used literally to talk about the time following a storm, and also in the common saying “Después de la tormenta viene/llega la calma” (“After the storm comes calm”), meaning that after a difficult period, things improve.
target_language_example: Después de la tormenta, revisamos el techo por si había daños.
native_language_example: After the storm, we checked the roof in case there was damage.

additional_notes: Used to introduce a clause (subject + verb) that happens first, followed by the main action: "después de que + verb". With completed/past actions it’s very commonly followed by the subjunctive in many dialects (e.g., "después de que regresara"), though you’ll also hear the indicative ("después de que regresó"). If there’s no verb (just a noun/infinitive), use "después de" (e.g., "después de la cena", "después de comer").
target_language_example: Te llamo después de que termine la reunión.
native_language_example: I’ll call you after the meeting ends.

después de todo lo que hemos

target_language_multi_word_term: después de todo lo que hemos
meaning: “after all that we have …” (followed by a past participle or verb phrase).
additional_notes: This is an incomplete phrase that normally continues with what “we have” done/experienced (often a past participle): “después de todo lo que hemos pasado/hecho/vivido”. It’s used to emphasize that something should/shouldn’t happen considering everything up to now.
target_language_example: Después de todo lo que hemos pasado, no quiero discutir más.
native_language_example: After all we’ve been through, I don’t want to argue anymore.

additional_notes: Used to (1) correct or update a conclusion: "It wasn’t X, after all" / "He’s going after all"; and (2) give a reason or reminder that supports what you’re saying: "After all, she’s the judge." Often placed at the beginning or end of the sentence, and it’s common with commas in writing.
target_language_example: Parece que vamos a salir después de todo.
native_language_example: Looks like we’re going to go out after all.

additional_notes: Used to say something happens later than an event or time. It’s the contraction of “después de + el” (de + el = del). With feminine nouns, use “después de la” (no contraction): “después de la clase”. With plural nouns: “después de los / de las”.
target_language_example: Después del almuerzo, voy a llamar a mi mamá.
native_language_example: After lunch, I’m going to call my mom.

additional_notes: Used to say something happens later than lunchtime. Often followed by an action or a time (e.g., “después del almuerzo, …”). In Spanish, “después de” becomes “después del” before a masculine singular noun like “almuerzo” (de + el = del).
target_language_example: Nos vemos después del almuerzo.
native_language_example: See you after lunch.

meaning: after work; after getting off work.
additional_notes: Used to talk about what you do once your workday ends. Often appears at the beginning of a sentence or set off with commas, and can be emphasized with words like "inmediatamente" (immediately) or "directo" (straight).
target_language_example: Después del trabajo, vamos a cenar.
native_language_example: After work, we're going to have dinner.

additional_notes: Refers to a detective hired by an individual or company (not the police) to investigate something (e.g., surveillance, finding information). Often used with contratar (to hire): «contratar a un detective privado».
target_language_example: Contratamos a un detective privado para encontrar a la persona desaparecida.
native_language_example: We hired a private investigator to find the missing person.

additional_notes: Used to indicate position: something is located behind someone/something else (e.g., "detrás de María"). It can also mean going after someone/something (often with verbs like correr/ir/saltar): "corrió detrás de la pelota". Sometimes it’s used figuratively, like "detrás de las palabras" = "behind the words" (the hidden meaning).
target_language_example: El gato se escondió detrás de la puerta.
native_language_example: The cat hid behind the door.

additional_notes: Used to say something (or someone) is located on the far side of a door from where you are. Common with verbs like estar (to be), esconderse (to hide), colgar (to hang), esperar (to wait). You can also use it more figuratively (as in “Detrás de la puerta, la riqueza lo esperaba”) to mean something is “just out of sight” or “right around the corner.”
target_language_example: El gato está detrás de la puerta.
native_language_example: The cat is behind the door.

additional_notes: Used to say something (the sun, moon, etc.) is hidden/covered by clouds and not visible. Often appears with verbs like "desaparecer" (to disappear) and "ser" (to be): "desapareció detrás de las nubes", "está/es invisible detrás de las nubes". You can also say "desde detrás de las nubes" = "from behind the clouds".
target_language_example: El sol salió de detrás de las nubes.
native_language_example: The sun came out from behind the clouds.

additional_notes: Used to indicate something/someone is located or moves behind the speaker. Often with verbs like estar (to be), ponerse (to stand/get), ir/venir (to go/come): "Está detrás de mí" = "He/She is behind me."
target_language_example: No te pongas detrás de mí; no puedo verte.
native_language_example: Don’t stand behind me; I can’t see you.

additional_notes: Used to indicate position/movement at your back (often as a warning: “Behind you!”). It can also mean “following you” (walking/driving after you): “Iremos detrás de ti.” In some contexts, “estar detrás de alguien” can imply support or pursuit (“backing you” / “after you”), but the basic meaning is physical location. Also note: “ti” is used after prepositions (de, a, para, etc.).
target_language_example: ¡Cuidado, hay un perro detrás de ti!
native_language_example: Careful, there's a dog behind you!

additional_notes: "Detrás de" means "behind" in a physical sense. "Del" is the contraction of "de + el" (used with masculine singular nouns: detrás del sofá, detrás del arbusto). It can also mean "after" in the sense of pursuing or looking for someone/something: La policía va/anda detrás del asesino = The police are after the killer.
target_language_example: El gato está escondido detrás del coche.
native_language_example: The cat is hiding behind the car.

additional_notes: Usually used as the reflexive verb phrase **darse cuenta de que** (“to realize that”). In the past tense you’ll often see **me di cuenta de que...** = “I realized that...”, followed by **que + a full sentence**. (Other persons: *te diste cuenta de que*, *se dio cuenta de que*, etc.)
target_language_example: Me di cuenta de que había olvidado mi pasaporte.
native_language_example: I realized that I had forgotten my passport.

meaning: "I assumed" / "I took it for granted that".
additional_notes: This is the 1st-person singular preterite of the expression "dar por sentado que" (literally "to give for seated," but meaning to assume something is true without checking). You can change the verb to match the subject and tense: "doy por sentado que..." (I assume), "dio por sentado que..." (he/she assumed), "dimos por sentado que..." (we assumed). It’s commonly followed by a clause with "que".
target_language_example: Di por sentado que la reunión era a las seis.
native_language_example: I assumed the meeting was at six.

additional_notes: Used to report what someone says or claims. "Dice" is the present-tense form of "decir" for he/she/it or usted, and "que" introduces the statement that follows.
target_language_example: Ella dice que llega mañana.
native_language_example: She says that she's arriving tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used to report what someone claims or says. The subject of dice is often implied (él/ella/usted). What follows after que is a statement with es (“is”). You can change the verb to match the person/tense: digo que es (I say it’s), dicen que es (they say it’s), dijo que era (he said it was).
target_language_example: Mi jefe dice que es urgente.
native_language_example: My boss says it’s urgent.

meaning: "(he/she) says no" or "(he/she) says that ... not".
additional_notes: Used with a subject understood from context (often él/ella/usted). "Decir que no" can mean refusing (saying no) or denying something (saying it didn’t happen): e.g., "Dice que no" = "He/She says no"; "Dice que no lo hizo" = "He/She says he didn’t do it."
target_language_example: Le ofrecí ayuda, pero dice que no.
native_language_example: I offered him/her help, but he/she says no.

additional_notes: Used to report what someone claims or states they want. The subject is usually implied from context (él/ella/usted), and the verb that follows is in the present tense: "dice que quiere + infinitive" (e.g., quiere ser/ir/hacer). Note that Spanish "dice" means "says" (it’s not related to English "dice").
target_language_example: María dice que quiere viajar a México este verano.
native_language_example: María says she wants to travel to Mexico this summer.

additional_notes: Used to report what other people say or what’s commonly believed, without saying who exactly (“they/people”). Very common for rumors, reputation, or general opinions. Usually followed by a description with "ser" (e.g., "Dicen que es honesto").
target_language_example: Dicen que es muy bueno, pero no lo conozco.
native_language_example: They say he’s very good, but I don’t know him.

additional_notes: Past participle of decir used with haber (e.g., he/has/had) or with modals/conditionals: debiste haber dicho la verdad (you should have told the truth), si me hubieras dicho la verdad (if you had told me the truth). More generally, the base phrase is decir la verdad = “to tell the truth.”
target_language_example: Deberías haber dicho la verdad desde el principio.
native_language_example: You should have told the truth from the beginning.

meaning: “said and done” / “no sooner said than done.”
additional_notes: Used to show that something was done immediately after it was said, often to emphasize quick action or that someone kept their word. Common pattern: “Dicho y hecho: …” or “Y dicho y hecho.”
target_language_example: —¿Vamos por un café? —Dicho y hecho: en cinco minutos salimos.
native_language_example: “Shall we go for a coffee?” “Said and done: we’re leaving in five minutes.”

meaning: 'saying that' (introducing what someone claims, reports, or uses as an excuse).
additional_notes: Uses the gerund (diciendo) + que to introduce the content of what someone said. Very common after a main verb to add a message, claim, or reason/excuse: "Me llamó diciendo que..." (He/She called me saying that...), "Se fue diciendo que..." (He/She left saying that...). Often corresponds to English "saying that" or sometimes "claiming that."
target_language_example: Me escribió diciendo que llegaría tarde.
native_language_example: He/She wrote to me saying that he/she would arrive late.

additional_notes: Used to talk about a duration (for ten years), a point in the past (ten years ago), or age (at ten years old). Common patterns: "hace diez años" = "ten years ago"; "durante diez años" / "por diez años" = "for ten years"; "a los diez años" = "at (the age of) ten."
target_language_example: Viví en México durante diez años.
native_language_example: I lived in Mexico for ten years.

additional_notes: Used to talk about a period of 10 days (duration) or something that happened 10 days ago with "hace" ("hace diez días" = "ten days ago"). You can also use it with "en" to mean within a 10-day period ("en diez días" = "in ten days" / "within ten days").
target_language_example: Voy a estar de viaje diez días.
native_language_example: I’m going to be traveling for ten days.

additional_notes: Used to state a price, a payment amount, wages, or money owed. With amounts of money, Spanish often uses the verb + amount directly: “cuesta diez dólares” (it costs ten dollars), “me debe diez dólares” (he owes me ten dollars), “son diez dólares” (it’s ten dollars). In many contexts you’ll also hear “por diez dólares” (for ten dollars) and “a diez dólares al día” (at ten dollars a day).
target_language_example: ¿Me puedes cambiar un billete de diez dólares?
native_language_example: Can you break a ten-dollar bill for me?

additional_notes: Used to talk about quantities (people, money, etc.). It can be literal or used for exaggeration/strong emphasis ("not even with ten thousand men..."). In numbers: 10.000 (often written with a dot in many Spanish-speaking countries).
target_language_example: El coche cuesta diez mil dólares.
native_language_example: The car costs ten thousand dollars.

additional_notes: Used to talk about duration (e.g., a delay) or frequency (e.g., something happens every ten minutes). You can use it with time expressions like “en diez minutos” (in ten minutes) and “cada diez minutos” (every ten minutes).
target_language_example: Vuelvo en diez minutos.
native_language_example: I’ll be back in ten minutes.

additional_notes: Used to compare two (or more) things and point out how they are not the same. It’s often used with verbs like "hay" (there is/are) and adjectives like "gran" or "clara": "Hay una gran/clara diferencia entre A y B". You can also use it in definitions or explanations: "Es la diferencia entre A y B".
target_language_example: Hay una gran diferencia entre estudiar un poco y estudiar todos los días.
native_language_example: There’s a big difference between studying a little and studying every day.

additional_notes: Used before an infinitive to describe something that is not easy to do/believe/understand, etc.: "difícil de + infinitive" (difícil de aprender, difícil de creer). "Difícil" agrees with the noun it describes: difícil (singular), difíciles (plural).
target_language_example: Esta palabra es difícil de pronunciar.
native_language_example: This word is hard to pronounce.

meaning: "let’s say" / "let’s suppose" (used to introduce an explanation or an approximate/softened statement).
additional_notes: Used to frame what you’re about to say as a way of explaining, giving an example, or speaking approximately rather than 100% precisely. Often softens the statement (like “so to speak” or “kind of”). Common in speech: “Digamos que…” + clause.
target_language_example: Digamos que hoy no tengo muchas ganas de salir.
native_language_example: Let’s say I don’t really feel like going out today.

additional_notes: Used to say someone/something merits a quality or treatment. Pattern: **ser + digno/a + de + noun/infinitive** (e.g., *digno de orgullo*, *digno de admiración*). It agrees in gender/number: *digno, digna, dignos, dignas*. Often sounds formal or literary.
target_language_example: No es digno de confianza.
native_language_example: He/She isn’t trustworthy (literally: “worthy of trust”).

additional_notes: Used to introduce what you’re stating or expressing an opinion about. It can also be used with an indirect object to mean “I tell (someone) that...”, e.g., "Le digo que..." (I tell him/her that...) or "Me digo que..." (I tell myself that...).
target_language_example: Sólo digo que no es tan fácil.
native_language_example: I’m just saying it’s not that easy.

meaning: 'I say' / 'I’m the one saying it' (often: 'if you ask me' or 'that’s what I’m saying').
additional_notes: Used in conversation to emphasize that something is your opinion or your words. It can also show agreement (“Eso/Lo mismo digo yo” = “That’s what I’m saying / Same here”) or add insistence/authority (“Se lo digo yo” = “I’m telling you (trust me)”). Word order matters: “digo yo” often sounds more emphatic than plain “yo digo”.
target_language_example: Está carísimo; digo yo que deberíamos esperar.
native_language_example: It’s really expensive; if you ask me, we should wait.

additional_notes: Past tense of "decir" (to say/tell) + "que no". Often used to remind someone you already refused or set a boundary. It can stand alone (Dije que no.) or introduce a clause: "Dije que no pagamos nada" = "I said we aren’t paying anything."
target_language_example: Lo siento, pero dije que no voy a ir.
native_language_example: Sorry, but I said I'm not going to go.

additional_notes: Uses the preterite of decir (dijeron) to report what “they” said at a specific moment in the past. It’s often followed by a statement (que + clause) or by “sí/no” as a short answer: “Dijeron que sí/no.”
target_language_example: Dijeron que no tenían tiempo.
native_language_example: They said that they didn’t have time.

additional_notes: Used to introduce reported speech or a reminder of what someone previously said. "Dijiste" is the preterite (simple past) of "decir" for "tú" (you, informal singular). In English, "that" is often optional: “You said (that)…”
target_language_example: Dijiste que no ibas a llegar tarde.
native_language_example: You said you weren’t going to be late.

additional_notes: Used to quote or remind someone of what they previously said. Often followed by a verb phrase: “dijiste que no tenías…/que no estaban…” (= “you said you didn’t have…/that they weren’t…”). By itself (“Dijiste que no.”) it means “You said no.”
target_language_example: Dijiste que no querías ir, ¿te acuerdas?
native_language_example: You said you didn’t want to go, remember?

additional_notes: Used to remind someone of a past statement. "Dijiste" is the simple past of "decir" (you said), and "querías" is the imperfect of "querer" (you wanted/you used to want). Often followed by an infinitive (querías hablar/irte/hacer) or by another clause with "que" (querías que + subjunctive).
target_language_example: Dijiste que querías cambiar de trabajo, ¿todavía lo estás pensando?
native_language_example: You said you wanted to change jobs—are you still thinking about it?

additional_notes: Used to report what someone said. Dijo is the third-person singular preterite of decir (“to say” / “to tell”), so it means “he/she/it said” or “told.” In contexts with an indirect object, it can also mean “told someone to ...,” often followed by the subjunctive.
target_language_example: María dijo que llegaría tarde.
native_language_example: María said that she would arrive late.

additional_notes: Used to report what someone said in the past. The subject of era is often not stated in Spanish, so in English it may be translated as he was, she was, or it was depending on context. Dijo is the past form of decir ('to say'), and era is the past form of ser ('to be').
target_language_example: María dijo que era demasiado tarde.
native_language_example: María said it was too late.

additional_notes: Used to report what someone said about a past situation/state. "dijo" is the past tense of "decir" (to say/tell). After "dijo que...", Spanish commonly uses the imperfect "estaba" to describe an ongoing state at that time (e.g., "estaba bien/ocupado/triste"). The subject (he/she) is often implied by context.
target_language_example: Mi jefe dijo que estaba enfermo y no vendría hoy.
native_language_example: My boss said he was sick and wouldn’t come today.

additional_notes: Used to report what someone said they planned or intended to do in the past. The verb changes with the speaker (dije/dijiste/dijo/dijimos/dijeron) and you can change the subject after “que” (e.g., “dijo que yo iba a…”). In reported speech about the past, “va a” often becomes “iba a”.
target_language_example: Ella dijo que iba a llamarme después.
native_language_example: She said she was going to call me later.

meaning: "(he/she) said that (he/it/him)…" (reported speech + direct object pronoun).
additional_notes: Used to introduce what someone said in the past: dijo que… = “(he/she) said that…”. The "lo" is a direct object pronoun meaning “him” or “it,” referring to something already known from context (e.g., "dijo que lo intentaría" = “said he would try it”; "dijo que lo sentía" = “said he was sorry [about it]”). Often followed by an imperfect or conditional verb to reflect a future-in-the-past idea (intentaría, podría, etc.).
target_language_example: Mi jefe dijo que lo revisaría mañana.
native_language_example: My boss said that he would look it over tomorrow.

meaning: "(he/she) said no" or "(he/she) said that ... not".
additional_notes: Used with reported speech. It can mean a direct refusal/denial ("He said no"), or it can introduce a negative statement: "dijo que no + verb" ("said that he/she didn’t..."). In commands/advice it often appears as "me dijo que no + imperfect subjunctive": "Me dijo que no condujera..." = "He told me not to drive...".
target_language_example: Le pregunté si venía, pero dijo que no.
native_language_example: I asked if he was coming, but he said no.

additional_notes:
Used to report what someone said they wanted. 
- "dijo" is the simple past of "decir" (he/she said) and "quería" is the imperfect past of "querer" (he/she wanted/was wanting).
- Often followed by an infinitive: "dijo que quería ir" (said he wanted to go), or a noun: "dijo que quería un coche" (said he wanted a car).
- Subject is often clear from context; you can add it: "Él dijo que quería..." / "Ella dijo que quería..."
target_language_example: Ella dijo que quería hablar contigo.
native_language_example: She said that she wanted to talk to you.

additional_notes: Used as an informal command to one person. dile is the tú command form of decir with le attached, and a introduces the person receiving the message: Dile a Tom..., Dile a tu madre.... It is often followed by que + clause.
target_language_example: Dile a Sara que me llame esta noche.
native_language_example: Tell Sara to call me tonight.

meaning: Tell your… (informal command, to one person).
additional_notes: "Dile" is the tú imperative of "decir" (to tell), with "le" = "to him/her/you (formal)". It’s commonly followed by "a + [person]" to name who you’re telling (e.g., "Dile a tu jefe…" = "Tell your boss…"). "Tu" is the informal possessive "your" (your boss / your husband / your girlfriend).
target_language_example: Dile a tu hermana que llego en cinco minutos.
native_language_example: Tell your sister I’ll arrive in five minutes.

additional_notes: “Dile” is the tú command form of “decir” (to say/tell) + “le” (to him/her/you formal). “Que” introduces what you want them to say next, followed by a full clause. Often used when asking someone to pass on a message.
target_language_example: Por favor, dile que llego tarde.
native_language_example: Please tell him/her that I'm arriving late.

meaning: “tell him/her/them that I’m …” (when you can’t talk).
additional_notes: Used to pass a message through someone else: **dile** = “tell (him/her/them)” (informal tú command of *decir*), and **que estoy** introduces what you want them to say about you (usually what you’re doing right now). If you need “tell you (formal)” use **dígame**; if you’re talking to multiple people, **digan**.
target_language_example: Dile que estoy ocupado ahora y que lo llamo más tarde.
native_language_example: Tell him I’m busy right now and that I’ll call him later.

meaning: “Tell him/her that I…” (used to pass on a message about yourself).
additional_notes: "Dile" is the tú command form of "decir" + the indirect object pronoun "le" (= to him/to her/to you formal). "Que" introduces what you want them to say, and "me" means “me” (the subject of the message is usually "yo"). Common pattern: "Dile que me + verb" (e.g., "dile que me espere" = tell him/her to wait for me).
target_language_example: Dile que me llame más tarde, por favor.
native_language_example: Tell him/her to call me later, please.

additional_notes: Used to give an instruction to someone to pass on a message to a group ("them"). It’s an affirmative tú command: di + les (“tell” + “to them”), followed by que to introduce what you want said. You can add pronouns after que (me, te, lo, etc.): “Diles que me ayuden.”
target_language_example: Diles que llego en diez minutos.
native_language_example: Tell them I’ll be there in ten minutes.

meaning: “tell me how…” (ask for instructions or a description).
additional_notes: “Dime” is the informal command form of “decir” (to tell) used with tú. “Cómo” introduces an indirect question meaning “how” (how to do something, how to get somewhere, what something/someone is like, or how something went). Often followed by an infinitive: “Dime cómo llegar / usar / hacerlo…”, or by a clause: “Dime cómo se llama / cómo es…”.
target_language_example: Dime cómo lo hiciste.
native_language_example: Tell me how you did it.

additional_notes: An informal (tú) command: di (tell) + me (to me) = dime. Used to press someone to be honest, often with words like ahora (now), mejor (better), por favor (please), or solo/sólo (just). For a formal (usted) version, say: "Dígame la verdad."
target_language_example: Por favor, dime la verdad: ¿qué pasó anoche?
native_language_example: Please tell me the truth: what happened last night?

additional_notes:
Used to ask someone directly what they want (an object, a plan, a choice, etc.).
- dime = “tell me” (informal tú command of decir)
- lo que = “what / that which”
- quieres = “you want” (tú)
Often said with emphasis (Solo/Sólo dime...) to mean “Just tell me…”.
target_language_example: Dime lo que quieres comer esta noche.
native_language_example: Tell me what you want to eat tonight.

additional_notes: Used to ask someone for an explanation or reason. "Dime" is the informal (tú) command of "decir" (to tell/say). You can soften it with "por favor" or make it more formal with "Dígame por qué".
target_language_example: Dime por qué estás enojado conmigo.
native_language_example: Tell me why you’re mad at me.

additional_notes: Used to ask someone to tell you information. "Dime" is the informal (tú) command form of "decir" (to tell/say). "Qué" introduces an indirect question: "Dime qué ocurrió" = "Tell me what happened." Often followed by a full clause (qué + verb) or an infinitive: "Dime qué pensar" = "Tell me what to think."
target_language_example: Dime qué necesitas para mañana.
native_language_example: Tell me what you need for tomorrow.

meaning: money in the bank (money you have in a bank account).
additional_notes: Used to talk about money you have saved or deposited at a bank, meaning it’s in your account (not cash you’re carrying). Often used with verbs like tener (to have), depositar (to deposit), and poner (to put).
target_language_example: No tengo mucho dinero en el banco ahora mismo.
native_language_example: I don’t have much money in the bank right now.

additional_notes: Used to talk about having (or not having) enough money for a purchase. It’s usually followed by what you want to buy: “dinero para comprar un coche / una casa”. You can add “algo de” to mean “some”: “algo de dinero para comprar…”.
target_language_example: No tengo dinero para comprar entradas para el concierto.
native_language_example: I don’t have money to buy tickets for the concert.

additional_notes: Used to refer to someone’s email address. Common in formal contexts (forms, customer service, official emails). Often appears with verbs like "tener" (to have), "dar" (to give), "anotar" (to write down), or "perder" (to lose). In casual speech it may be shortened to "correo" or "email" depending on region, but the full term is widely understood.
target_language_example: He perdido tu dirección de correo electrónico.
native_language_example: I’ve lost your email address.

meaning: “I’d say…” / “I would say that…” (a tentative opinion or guess).
additional_notes: Uses the conditional of decir (“to say”) to sound less certain, more polite, or to estimate. Often followed by a number or a yes/no opinion. You can also change the subject: Él/Ella diría que… (“He/She would say…”).
target_language_example: Diría que mañana va a llover.
native_language_example: I’d say it’s going to rain tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used for a computer’s storage unit, either internal or external (e.g., “disco duro externo”). You’ll often see it with verbs like guardar (to save), borrar (to erase), and llenar/estar lleno (to be full).
target_language_example: Necesito más espacio porque mi disco duro está lleno.
native_language_example: I need more space because my hard drive is full.

additional_notes: Used with an infinitive (dispuesto a + infinitive) to show willingness or readiness: "Estoy dispuesto a ayudar." Also commonly used in the negative: "no estar dispuesto a" = "to be unwilling/not prepared to." It agrees in gender and number: dispuesto, dispuesta, dispuestos, dispuestas.
target_language_example: No estoy dispuesto a esperar más.
native_language_example: I'm not willing to wait anymore.

additional_notes: Used to talk about an age or a length of time. For age, it often appears with phrases like “a los doce años” (at age 12) or “tenía doce años” (I was twelve). For duration, it can mean a period of twelve years (“Doce años es mucho…”).
target_language_example: Viví en esa ciudad doce años.
native_language_example: I lived in that city for twelve years.

additional_notes: Literally “pain in the head.” Common with tener: Tengo dolor de cabeza / Tengo un dolor de cabeza. You can add adjectives like leve (mild) or fuerte (bad/severe). It can also be used figuratively to mean something annoying or complicated (like “a headache” in English).
target_language_example: Este papeleo es un dolor de cabeza.
native_language_example: This paperwork is a headache (a hassle).

additional_notes: Used to talk about pain in your stomach area. Often used with tener (to have): “Tengo dolor de estómago.” You can add an adjective like fuerte (strong/severe): “un fuerte dolor de estómago.”
target_language_example: Tengo dolor de estómago, así que no voy a comer mucho.
native_language_example: I have a stomachache, so I’m not going to eat much.

meaning: a nobody; an insignificant person (often insulting).
additional_notes: Used with ser (e.g., «Eres/Es/Soy un don nadie») to say someone has no importance, status, or influence. It’s usually rude/derogatory, similar to calling someone “a nobody” in English.
target_language_example: No le hagas caso; es un don nadie.
native_language_example: Don’t pay attention to him; he’s a nobody.

meaning: “where (someone/something) is / where it is” (relative ‘where’ referring to a location).
additional_notes: Most commonly, Spanish uses the accented form «dónde está» in direct questions: «¿Dónde está el mando?» = “Where is the remote?”. Without the accent («donde está»), it’s typically a relative/embedded ‘where’: «Se quedará donde está» = “It will stay where it is.” The only difference in writing is the accent: «dónde» = interrogative/exclamatory “where”, «donde» = relative “where.”
target_language_example: Si no le identifica nadie, se quedará donde está.
native_language_example: If nobody identifies him, he will stay where he is.

meaning: Literal: “where to want” / intended meaning in context: “where (someone) wants” or “wherever (someone) wants.”
additional_notes: **Nonstandard / unusual phrasing.** Spanish normally conjugates the verb **querer** (to want), so you would typically see **donde quieres** (“where you want”) or **donde quieras** (“wherever you want / anywhere you want”). Also note spelling: **dónde** (with accent) is used in direct/indirect questions (e.g., «¿Dónde quieres ir?» / «No sé dónde quieres ir.»); **donde** (no accent) is used in statements/relative clauses (e.g., «Vamos donde quieras.»).
target_language_example: En algunos apuntes aparece «donde querer», pero lo normal es decir «donde quieras».
native_language_example: In some notes you might see “donde querer,” but normally you would say “donde quieras.”

meaning: wherever you want; anywhere you like.
additional_notes: Uses subjunctive (quieras) to mean an open choice: “wherever you want.” Often used by itself to mean “wherever you want/anywhere is fine.” With movement verbs, it’s common to add "a": "ir a donde quieras", "llevarte a donde quieras" (“go/take you wherever you want”).
target_language_example: Puedes quedarte donde quieras.
native_language_example: You can stay wherever you want.

additional_notes: Used to mean an unspecified place: “any place” or “no matter where.” Often appears as **donde sea que...** (“wherever...”), and can be used alone as a short answer: **Donde sea.** = “Anywhere.” Also common with **a** after verbs of movement: **ir a donde sea** (“go anywhere”).
target_language_example: Podemos comer donde sea, pero que sea cerca.
native_language_example: We can eat anywhere, but it has to be nearby.

meaning: "as far as I know" (often used as a fragment).
additional_notes: Most commonly you’ll hear it as **hasta donde yo sé** (“as far as I know”). By itself, **donde yo sé** literally means “where I know,” but in real conversation it’s often used (or written) to mean “to the best of my knowledge,” especially when the speaker is not completely sure.
target_language_example: Hasta donde yo sé, la tienda cierra a las ocho.
native_language_example: As far as I know, the store closes at eight.

meaning: to sleep a little; to get some sleep.
additional_notes: Used to suggest or say you need a short rest or some sleep. Very common with verbs like necesitar (to need), tener que (to have to), deberías (you should), and trata de (try to).
target_language_example: Después del viaje, necesito dormir un poco.
native_language_example: After the trip, I need to get some sleep.

meaning: 'two, three, four' (often said out loud to count or keep rhythm).
additional_notes: Used when counting in sequence, especially as a cue for timing: starting an activity, keeping a beat in music/dance/exercise, or counting repetitions. You’ll often hear it repeated or preceded by “uno/una” (“one”).
target_language_example: ¡Preparados? Uno, dos, tres, cuatro, ¡vamos!
native_language_example: Ready? One, two, three, four—go!

additional_notes: Used to talk about a length of time. Common patterns: **hace (unos) dos años** = “(about) two years ago”; **durante dos años** = “for two years” (over a two-year period); **lleva + past participle + dos años** = “has been + [state] for two years” (e.g., *lleva muerta dos años* = “she’s been dead for two years”).
target_language_example: Viví en Madrid dos años.
native_language_example: I lived in Madrid for two years.

additional_notes: Used to count two items/points/ideas. Very common in conversation to introduce two points: “Bueno, dos cosas: …”. Also appears in set phrases like “dos cosas a la vez” (“two things at once”) and “una de dos cosas” (“one of two things/one of two possibilities”).
target_language_example: Espera, dos cosas: primero, necesito tu ayuda; segundo, no tengo tiempo.
native_language_example: Wait, two things: first, I need your help; second, I don’t have time.

meaning: two sons; two children (in some contexts).
additional_notes: Hijo usually means “son” (male child). In some contexts, especially in the plural, hijos can also mean “children” in general (like English “kids”), but if you want to be clearly gender-neutral you can say dos hijos/as or dos niños (depending on context). Often used with tener (to have): Tengo dos hijos.
target_language_example: Mi hermana tiene dos hijos.
native_language_example: My sister has two sons.

additional_notes: Used to refer to a quantity of two adult males. Often appears as a subject (“Dos hombres…”) or object (“Necesito dos hombres”). You may also see “los dos hombres” = “the two men” (specific/known).
target_language_example: Necesito dos hombres para mover el sofá.
native_language_example: I need two men to move the couch.

additional_notes: Used to say a duration (how long something lasts) or a time span. Common patterns: "durante dos horas" (for two hours), "(algo) duró dos horas" (something lasted two hours), "en las últimas dos horas" (in the last two hours), "solo dormí dos horas" (I only slept two hours).
target_language_example: Esperé dos horas en el aeropuerto.
native_language_example: I waited two hours at the airport.

additional_notes: Used to talk about a duration (por dos meses = for two months) or frequency/interval (cada dos meses = every two months).
target_language_example: Viví en Madrid por dos meses.
native_language_example: I lived in Madrid for two months.

additional_notes: Used for exact quantities (dos mil soldados/libros/billetes) and for years. For years, Spanish often says the number directly: "en dos mil trece" = "in 2013". For larger numbers: "dos mil millones" is "two billion" (Spain; in much of Latin America, "dos mil millones" is also understood).
target_language_example: Compré dos mil entradas para el concierto.
native_language_example: I bought two thousand tickets for the concert.

additional_notes: Used to say a duration of time or a short wait. Often appears in phrases like “Sólo dos minutos” (Only two minutes) or with fractions: “dos minutos y medio” (two and a half minutes).
target_language_example: Espérame dos minutos, por favor.
native_language_example: Wait for me two minutes, please.

additional_notes: Used to give an approximate small number, like “two or three” or “a couple/few.” It can refer to countable things (dos o tres cosas) or time periods (dos o tres semanas).
target_language_example: Dame dos o tres minutos y termino.
native_language_example: Give me two or three minutes and I’ll finish.

meaning: “two or three times” (a few times; an approximate number).
additional_notes: Used to give an approximate count, often meaning “a couple/few times,” not an exact number. Common for frequency (e.g., per month) or how many times something happened.
target_language_example: He estado en Madrid dos o tres veces.
native_language_example: I’ve been to Madrid two or three times.

additional_notes: Used to talk about a group of exactly two people. Often appears with verbs in plural (e.g., “Dos personas pueden…”). Sometimes in expressions like “una o dos personas” = “one or two people.”
target_language_example: En la mesa hay dos personas esperando.
native_language_example: There are two people waiting at the table.

meaning: "two points"; also the punctuation mark ":" (a colon).
additional_notes: Most commonly it’s the literal amount in scores/grades (e.g., “I was short by two points”). In spelling/dictation, people also say “dos puntos” to indicate you should write a colon (:). Context usually makes it clear whether it means points or punctuation.
target_language_example: En el examen me quedé a dos puntos de aprobar.
native_language_example: On the exam, I was two points short of passing.

additional_notes: A time duration of 14 days. Common with "por" (for) to say how long something lasts ("por dos semanas"), and with "en" to mean "in two weeks" ("Nos vemos en dos semanas"). You can also use it in countdowns: "Faltan dos semanas" = "Two weeks left."
target_language_example: El curso dura dos semanas.
native_language_example: The course lasts two weeks.

additional_notes: Used to say something happens 2 times. Often placed after the verb (e.g., "Fui dos veces" = "I went twice") or before a time period with "en"/"por" (e.g., "dos veces en una semana" = "twice in a week", "dos veces por año" = "twice a year"). Can also appear in set phrases and proverbs (e.g., "solo se vive dos veces").
target_language_example: Te lo dije dos veces.
native_language_example: I told you twice.

additional_notes: Used to say something happens two times each day, often for routines, schedules, or dosage instructions. You can swap the number: "una vez al día" (once a day), "tres veces al día" (three times a day).
target_language_example: Tomo esta medicina dos veces al día.
native_language_example: I take this medicine twice a day.

additional_notes: Used to express doubt or uncertainty about something. It is typically followed by the subjunctive (e.g., "Dudo que sea...", "Dudo que vaya...") because the speaker is not stating the idea as a fact. In more formal Spanish you may also hear "Dudo de que..." (especially when followed by a noun phrase), but "Dudo que..." is very common.
target_language_example: Dudo que podamos llegar a tiempo.
native_language_example: I doubt we can arrive on time.

additional_notes: Used to say someone owns or is in possession/control of something: "el dueño de la casa" (the owner of the house). It agrees in gender and number: "dueño" (male), "dueña" (female), "dueños/dueñas" (plural). Often used with businesses, property, or objects, and sometimes more broadly for someone who controls something.
target_language_example: ¿Sabes quién es el dueño de este coche?
native_language_example: Do you know who the owner of this car is?

additional_notes: A common goodnight wish, said when someone is going to sleep. Often used by itself ("Dulces sueños") or with "Buenas noches" and with "Que tengas..." ("Que tengas dulces sueños" = "Have sweet dreams").
target_language_example: Bueno, me voy a dormir. Dulces sueños.
native_language_example: Well, I'm going to sleep. Sweet dreams.

meaning: for years; for many years (over a long period of time).
additional_notes: Used to say something continued over a long span of time in the past or up to now. It often goes with past tense ("Fue mi colega durante años") or with "llevar"/"estar" + gerund to emphasize ongoing duration ("se ha estado tiñendo... durante años").
target_language_example: Viví en Madrid durante años antes de mudarme a Londres.
native_language_example: I lived in Madrid for years before moving to London.

meaning: during the day; in the daytime.
additional_notes: Used to say something happens at some point within daytime hours (as opposed to at night). Often contrasts with “durante la noche” (during the night).
target_language_example: No puedo hablar ahora; trabajo durante el día.
native_language_example: I can't talk now; I work during the day.

additional_notes: Used to say that something happens within the time period of summer. It often answers “when?” and can be used with events (viajar), habits (conservar agua), schedules (la escuela está cerrada), and repeated situations (se producen a veces).
target_language_example: Durante el verano, hace mucho calor aquí.
native_language_example: During the summer, it’s very hot here.

meaning: for hours; for several hours (for a long time).
additional_notes: Used to say an action continues over a period of many hours. Common with ongoing or repeated activities (e.g., llorar, discutir, conducir, caminar). Often emphasizes that it felt like a long time.
target_language_example: Esperamos durante horas para ver al médico.
native_language_example: We waited for hours to see the doctor.

additional_notes: Used to say something happens while the class is happening. Often followed by an action (e.g., tomar notas, hablar, dormir). You can swap in another time period: durante la reunión (during the meeting), durante el examen (during the exam).
target_language_example: Por favor, no uses el teléfono durante la clase.
native_language_example: Please, don’t use your phone during class.

additional_notes: Used to say that something happened within the time period when a war was taking place. Often used with past tense to describe events, losses, or experiences in that period. You can also place it at the beginning of the sentence for emphasis: "Durante la guerra, ..."
target_language_example: Durante la guerra, muchas familias tuvieron que mudarse.
native_language_example: During the war, many families had to move.

additional_notes: Used to say something happened at some point in the night (not necessarily all night). Very common with past tenses: "llovió durante la noche" (it rained overnight).
target_language_example: Hubo un corte de luz durante la noche.
native_language_example: There was a power outage overnight.

meaning: for a long time (for a long period).
additional_notes: Used to say something continues or was true over an extended period. Often placed at the beginning of a sentence for emphasis, or at the end to add time detail. Can also be used alone as a short answer meaning “for a long time.”
target_language_example: No te vi durante mucho tiempo.
native_language_example: I didn’t see you for a long time.

additional_notes: Used to say something happens for the entire duration of a period or event. It’s followed by a feminine singular noun (la mañana, la reunión, la película, la presentación). For masculine nouns use “durante todo el” (durante todo el día). With plural nouns: “durante todos/todas”.
target_language_example: Estudié durante toda la noche.
native_language_example: I studied throughout the whole night.

meaning: all night (long); for the whole night.
additional_notes: Used to say something happens continuously throughout the night. It can describe an activity ("Estudié durante toda la noche") or a situation/condition ("Hubo ruido durante toda la noche"). Often interchangeable with "toda la noche," but "durante" emphasizes the duration.
target_language_example: Estuvimos despiertos durante toda la noche por el bebé.
native_language_example: We were awake all night because of the baby.

additional_notes: Used to say something happens or is true for the entire year (not just in one season). Often goes at the end of the sentence. Literal parts: durante = during, todo = all, el año = the year.
target_language_example: Aquí hace calor durante todo el año.
native_language_example: It’s hot here all year round.

meaning: for a while; for some time.
additional_notes: Used to say something happens/lasts for a limited period of time (often temporary, with no exact duration). It commonly goes after the verb: “vivir aquí durante un tiempo” (live here for a while).
target_language_example: Voy a quedarme en casa durante un tiempo.
native_language_example: I’m going to stay at home for a while.

meaning: for an hour; during an hour.
additional_notes: Used to say how long something lasts. It’s common to put it at the beginning of the sentence (Durante una hora, ...) or after the verb (Estuvo en silencio durante una hora).
target_language_example: Esperamos durante una hora.
native_language_example: We waited for an hour.

meaning: for a week; during a week.
additional_notes: Used to say how long something lasts (a duration). It often answers “How long?” and commonly follows a verb: “Me quedé… durante una semana” (I stayed… for a week). You can swap in other time periods: “durante dos días”, “durante un mes”.
target_language_example: Estudié español durante una semana antes del examen.
native_language_example: I studied Spanish for a week before the exam.

meaning: 'hard (in order) to' (as in 'work hard to do something').
additional_notes: Usually used with a verb like trabajar: “trabajar duro para + infinitive” expresses making a strong effort in order to achieve a goal. Duro is an adverb meaning “hard” here (not “hard” = “not soft”). Often interchangeable with “mucho” or “mucho esfuerzo” depending on context.
target_language_example: Estoy estudiando duro para el examen.
native_language_example: I’m studying hard for the exam.

meaning: to act like / pretend to be (often in an arrogant way).
additional_notes: Usually appears conjugated with a reflexive pronoun and the fixed plural object pronoun: "(yo) me las doy de + sustantivo/adjetivo", "(él/ella) se las da de...", "(nosotros) nos las damos de...". It often implies showing off, acting superior, or speaking as if you had authority, and can sound sarcastic or critical.
target_language_example: Él siempre intenta dárselas de experto, pero nunca ha trabajado en esto.
native_language_example: He’s always trying to act like an expert, but he’s never worked in this.

additional_notes: Used to ask permission to look at something (“Déjame ver esa lista.”) or to pause while you check/think (“Déjame ver…” = “let me see…”). It’s informal and common in everyday conversation. Also appears with an object: “Déjame ver + noun/pronoun” (déjame ver eso / el tuyo / lo que tienes).
target_language_example: Déjame ver tu pasaporte, por favor.
native_language_example: Let me see your passport, please.

meaning: day by day; from one day to the next.
additional_notes: Used to talk about something that changes or progresses gradually over time. Often goes with verbs like cambiar, variar, mejorar, empeorar, crecer. You can also use it as a noun phrase meaning “daily life” in some contexts (e.g., en el día a día).
target_language_example: Estoy aprendiendo español día a día.
native_language_example: I'm learning Spanish day by day.

meaning: 'lucky day' (a day when someone has good luck).
additional_notes: Often used with a possessive to talk about who is lucky: Es mi/tu/su/nuestro/vuestro día de suerte. It can be said on its own as an exclamation (¡Día de suerte!) or used negatively (Hoy no es tu día de suerte) to mean someone isn’t having luck today.
target_language_example: ¡Hoy es tu día de suerte! Encontré tus llaves.
native_language_example: Today is your lucky day! I found your keys.

additional_notes: Used for an official holiday when businesses, offices, or schools may be closed (e.g., un día festivo nacional). It can also be used in phrases like "tarifa de día festivo" to mean a special rate that applies on holidays.
target_language_example: El lunes es día festivo, así que no hay clases.
native_language_example: Monday is a public holiday, so there are no classes.

meaning: day after day; day in, day out.
additional_notes: Used to emphasize that something happens repeatedly every day, often for a long time (and sometimes with a feeling of routine, persistence, or annoyance). It can be placed at the beginning, middle, or end of a sentence for emphasis.
target_language_example: Trabaja día tras día para ahorrar dinero.
native_language_example: He works day after day to save money.

meaning: day and night; all the time; nonstop.
additional_notes: Used to emphasize that something happens continuously or for very long periods, often with effort or intensity (work, study, worry). It can be literal (both daytime and nighttime) or more generally mean “constantly.”
target_language_example: Estuve pensando en eso día y noche.
native_language_example: I was thinking about that day and night.

additional_notes: Used to say something happens some number of days after an earlier time/event. Often appears with a number (e.g., “dos días después” = “two days later”). It can also be used without a number to mean “days later” in general. Contrast: “todos los días después de…” means “every day after …” (repeated action).
target_language_example: Tres días después, recibimos la respuesta.
native_language_example: Three days later, we got the answer.

meaning: days without eating; days not having eaten.
additional_notes: Used to say someone has gone a certain amount of time without doing something, especially with **llevar**: **llevar + (number of) días + sin + infinitive** (e.g., *Lleva tres días sin comer* = “He hasn’t eaten for three days”). Often implies hunger, weakness, or looking very thin.
target_language_example: No puedo correr hoy: llevo dos días sin comer.
native_language_example: I can’t run today: I haven’t eaten for two days.

additional_notes: Indirect question in the imperfect tense: dónde = where, estaba = was (from estar). Used after verbs like preguntar (to ask) and recordar (to remember): “No podía recordar dónde estaba.” In direct questions it normally takes ¿?: “¿Dónde estaba John?”
target_language_example: No sabía dónde estaba mi teléfono.
native_language_example: I didn’t know where my phone was.

additional_notes: Used to ask for or state our current location. Often appears inside a longer sentence after verbs like saber (to know), recordar (to remember), or mirar (to look): “Sé dónde estamos” = “I know where we are.” With question marks it becomes the direct question: “¿Dónde estamos?” = “Where are we?”
target_language_example: No sé dónde estamos; necesito un mapa.
native_language_example: I don’t know where we are; I need a map.

additional_notes: Used to talk about your location. It can be a direct question (¿Dónde estoy?) or part of a longer sentence after verbs like saber, recordar, or entender (No sé dónde estoy; Me cuesta recordar dónde estoy). The accent in dónde is used in indirect or direct questions about place.
target_language_example: Perdón, estoy perdido: ¿dónde estoy?
native_language_example: Sorry, I’m lost: where am I?

additional_notes: Used to ask or say where one person or thing is. It can appear in direct questions (¿Dónde está...?) and indirect questions/statements (No sé dónde está = I don't know where it/he/she is). Use it with singular subjects; for plural, Spanish uses dónde están.
target_language_example: ¿Dónde está el baño?
native_language_example: Where is the bathroom?

additional_notes: Used to ask for the location of multiple people/things, or of one thing treated as plural (e.g., “los huevos”). It’s also used inside a longer sentence after verbs like querer saber/decir (“I want to know/tell me where they are”): No question marks needed in that case. For one person/thing, use “¿dónde está…?”
target_language_example: ¿Dónde están mis llaves?
native_language_example: Where are my keys?

additional_notes: Used to ask where someone is right now. It’s informal/neutral and typically said to someone you address as “tú.” For a formal/polite version use “¿dónde está (usted)?”; for more than one person use “¿dónde están?”
target_language_example: ¿Dónde estás? Te estoy esperando afuera.
native_language_example: Where are you? I’m waiting for you outside.

additional_notes: Used to ask someone their location (question: ¿Dónde estás?) or inside a longer sentence to say you know/need to know someone’s location (indirect: No sé dónde estás). In indirect statements it’s usually written without opening/closing question marks, but dónde keeps its accent.
target_language_example: No sé dónde estás; mándame tu ubicación.
native_language_example: I don’t know where you are; send me your location.

additional_notes: Used to ask for or state a person’s address/location. It’s an indirect question (after verbs like saber, preguntar, no tener idea), so dónde keeps its accent: “No sé dónde vive.” You can change the verb for different people: dónde vives (you), dónde vivo (I), dónde viven (they/you all).
