target_language_example: No sé dónde vive tu profesor.
native_language_example: I don’t know where your teacher lives.

additional_notes: "Dónde" introduces an indirect question meaning "where." "Vivía" is the imperfect past of "vivir" (to live), used for an ongoing/repeated situation in the past. Often appears after verbs like "preguntar" (to ask) or "averiguar" (to find out): "Me preguntó dónde vivía" = "He/She asked me where I lived."
target_language_example: No recuerdo dónde vivía cuando era niño.
native_language_example: I don't remember where I lived when I was a kid.

additional_notes: A common loanword in Spanish (also written "email" or "correo electrónico"). Used with verbs like "mandar/enviar un e-mail" (to send an email) and "por e-mail" (by email).
target_language_example: ¿Me puedes mandar un e-mail con la información?
native_language_example: Can you send me an email with the information?

meaning: to start running; to run off (suddenly).
additional_notes: Used for an abrupt start of motion, often because of fear, urgency, or surprise. Very common in storytelling: “Y entonces echó a correr…” Conjugate only “echar” (echo, echas, echó, etc.) + “a” + infinitive “correr”. You can also say “echarse a correr” with essentially the same meaning.
target_language_example: Cada vez que oye un ruido extraño, decide echar a correr.
native_language_example: Whenever he hears a strange noise, he decides to start running.

meaning: to ruin; to spoil (food); to waste.
additional_notes: Used when something becomes unusable, damaged, or fails (plans, chances, objects). With food or machines it’s very common in the reflexive form: "se echó a perder" = it went bad / it broke down. Can also mean to waste an opportunity: "No lo eches a perder" = Don’t mess it up / don’t waste it.
target_language_example: No vayas a echar a perder la sorpresa contándole a todos el secreto.
native_language_example: Don’t ruin the surprise by telling everyone the secret.

additional_notes: Common way to say you miss a person, place, or thing. It’s often used in the future/conditional when talking about something you’ll miss after leaving or losing it: «Voy/Vas a echar de menos…». Also used to mean “notices the absence of” in sentences like «nadie lo va a echar de menos» (“no one will miss it / notice it’s gone”).
target_language_example: Voy a echar de menos a mis amigos cuando me mude.
native_language_example: I’m going to miss my friends when I move.

meaning: to blame (someone) / to put the blame on (someone).
additional_notes: Common pattern: echarle la culpa a + person/thing. The indirect object pronoun (me/te/le/nos/les) shows who is being blamed: Me echaron la culpa a mí. You can also use echar la culpa de + thing (the cause): Le echaron la culpa del accidente al conductor. Similar to 'culpar' but more everyday.
target_language_example: No quiero echar la culpa a nadie, pero fue un accidente.
native_language_example: I don’t want to blame anyone, but it was an accident.

additional_notes: Common, everyday phrase for looking at something briefly, often to check or inspect. It’s usually followed by “a” + a thing/place (“echar un vistazo a algo”), and often used politely as “Déjame/Quisiera echar un vistazo” (“Let me/I’d like to take a look”).
target_language_example: ¿Puedo echar un vistazo a tu tarea?
native_language_example: Can I take a look at your homework?

meaning: to help (someone); to lend a hand.
additional_notes: Used to offer, request, or say you will give help. Often followed by "a" + person or an infinitive (e.g., "echar una mano a mi amigo", "echar una mano a limpiar"). Conjugates like "echo/echas/echa" etc. Literal words mean "to throw a hand," but the actual meaning is "to lend a hand."
target_language_example: Oye, luego me tendrás que echar una mano.
native_language_example: Hey, later you’ll have to give me a hand.

meaning: to back down; to back out (change your mind).
additional_notes: Reflexive verb phrase. Commonly used when someone withdraws from a decision, promise, or plan after having agreed or intended to do something. It can also mean to physically move backward, but the figurative sense (“back out”) is very frequent. Example warning/encouragement: “No te eches atrás” = “Don’t back out / don’t chicken out.”
target_language_example: Iba a aceptar el trabajo, pero decidí echarse atrás a última hora.
native_language_example: I was going to accept the job, but I decided to back out at the last minute.

additional_notes: A astronomy term for when the Moon passes into Earth’s shadow. Usually used with the verb "haber" (hay / habrá) or with an article: "Hay eclipse lunar" / "Habrá un eclipse lunar". You can also refer to it as a time period: "durante el eclipse lunar" (during the lunar eclipse).
target_language_example: Esta noche habrá un eclipse lunar visible desde aquí.
native_language_example: Tonight there will be a lunar eclipse visible from here.

additional_notes: Used for the school subject/class focused on sports, exercise, and fitness. Common with verbs like tener (to have), dar (to teach), and ser/trabajar como profesor de educación física (to be/work as a PE teacher). Often shortened in conversation to “educación física” or “EF” depending on the region.
target_language_example: Hoy tengo educación física, así que necesito ropa deportiva.
native_language_example: Today I have PE, so I need sports clothes.

additional_notes: Used mainly in medical/pharmacy contexts for an unwanted or extra effect caused by a medicine, treatment, or vaccine. Often appears in plural: "efectos secundarios". You can ask about it with "¿Cuál es el efecto secundario más común?" or "¿Cuáles son los efectos secundarios?"
target_language_example: Un efecto secundario común de este medicamento es la somnolencia.
native_language_example: A common side effect of this medication is drowsiness.

additional_notes: Literally means “the ring.” When capitalized (Anillo), it usually refers to a particular famous ring (for example, in *The Lord of the Rings*, “the One Ring”). In everyday Spanish, you’d normally write it in lowercase: *el anillo*.
target_language_example: No encuentro el Anillo; ¿dónde lo dejaste?
native_language_example: I can’t find the Ring; where did you leave it?

meaning: “the King” (a king; also a title or nickname).
additional_notes: Used with the definite article (el) to refer to a specific king, often with a capital letter when it’s a title (El Rey) or when talking about a particular monarch. It can also be used as a nickname (e.g., for a famous person), sometimes placed after a name in apposition: “Harry, el Rey.”
target_language_example: Dicen que el Rey llegará mañana al palacio.
native_language_example: They say the King will arrive at the palace tomorrow.

additional_notes: Common in religious contexts to refer to God (often capitalized: “el Señor”). In other contexts, “señor” (usually not capitalized) can also mean “sir/Mr.” when addressing a man, but the religious meaning is the one used in these examples. Not the same as English “senior.”
target_language_example: Que el Señor te bendiga.
native_language_example: May the Lord bless you.

additional_notes: Refers to a (usually male) lawyer. For a female lawyer, you can say “la abogada.” Often used with “con” to mean “with the lawyer present” (e.g., “Con el abogado presente…”).
target_language_example: Necesito hablar con el abogado antes de firmar.
native_language_example: I need to talk to the lawyer before signing.

additional_notes: Most commonly means a coat (outerwear). In sentences with clothing, Spanish often uses the definite article (el/la) where English would use a possessive: "Se puso el abrigo" = "He/She put on (his/her) coat." It can also mean “shelter” or “protection” (e.g., from the cold), depending on context.
target_language_example: Hace frío, así que voy a ponerme el abrigo.
native_language_example: It’s cold, so I’m going to put on my coat.

additional_notes: Refers to an unplanned, harmful event (e.g., a car crash, workplace incident, etc.). Common with verbs like ocurrir (“to happen”), producirse (“to occur”), provocar (“to cause”), and tener lugar (“to take place”). You can also say sobrevivir a un accidente (“to survive an accident”).
target_language_example: El accidente ocurrió en la autopista, pero nadie resultó herido.
native_language_example: The accident happened on the highway, but nobody was hurt.

additional_notes: A common place word. Uses the masculine article el; plural: los aeropuertos. Often used with en (at/in): en el aeropuerto. You can also use desde el aeropuerto (“from the airport”) and al aeropuerto (“to the airport,” a + el = al).
target_language_example: Estoy en el aeropuerto.
native_language_example: I'm at the airport.

additional_notes: Agua means "water." Although agua is a feminine noun, it usually takes el in the singular because it begins with a stressed a sound: el agua fría. Adjectives and other words still stay feminine (for example, mucha agua, agua fría).
target_language_example: El agua de esta botella está muy fresca.
native_language_example: The water in this bottle is very fresh.

additional_notes: Used to describe water or make a statement about it, followed by an adjective or a noun (e.g., "El agua es fría" = "The water is cold", "El agua es vida" = "Water is life"). Note: although "agua" is feminine, it uses "el" in the singular for pronunciation reasons ("el agua"), but it stays feminine in agreement: "El agua es clara" (not *claro*).
target_language_example: El agua es fría, pero está limpia.
native_language_example: The water is cold, but it’s clean.

meaning: "the water is" (describing the water’s condition or location).
additional_notes: Used with **estar** to talk about the water’s current state (temperature, wet/dry, clean/dirty, etc.) or where it is located. Often followed by an adjective ("caliente") or a location phrase ("de ese lado"). In Spanish, **estar** is typically used for temporary conditions and locations.
target_language_example: El agua está fría hoy.
native_language_example: The water is cold today.

additional_notes: Refers to the air around us (what we breathe). It’s also used in fixed expressions like "al aire libre" (outdoors) and "en el aire" (in the air / up in the air).
target_language_example: Abre la ventana para que entre el aire.
native_language_example: Open the window so the air can come in.

meaning: the mayor (head of a town/city government).
additional_notes: Used with the masculine article (el). The feminine form is "la alcaldesa". In Spanish it often refers to the elected leader of a municipality/city hall (ayuntamiento).
target_language_example: El alcalde habló con los vecinos después de la reunión.
native_language_example: The mayor spoke with the neighbors after the meeting.

additional_notes: Usually refers to a person's soul/spirit (often in religious or philosophical contexts). It also appears in strong emotional expressions (e.g., "me parte el alma" = "it breaks my heart") and in oaths to emphasize sincerity (e.g., "por el alma de..." = "by the soul of...").
target_language_example: Siento paz en el alma cuando estoy con mi familia.
native_language_example: I feel peace in my soul when I’m with my family.

additional_notes: A masculine noun (el almuerzo). It can mean the meal itself (“Gracias por el almuerzo”) or the lunch period/event (“Te veo en el almuerzo” = “See you at lunch”). Common verbs: preparar (to make), comer (to eat), saltarse (to skip). In many places, almuerzo refers to the main meal around midday.
target_language_example: Hoy no tengo tiempo para el almuerzo.
native_language_example: Today I don’t have time for lunch.

additional_notes: Refers to love as a general idea or force, and can also mean romantic life in expressions like suerte en el amor ('luck in love'). Spanish often uses the definite article with abstract nouns in a general sense, where English usually just says 'love' without 'the'.
target_language_example: El amor cambia a las personas.
native_language_example: Love changes people.

meaning: "love is..." (used to define or describe what love is).
additional_notes: A very common sentence starter in Spanish: "El amor es + noun/adjective/phrase". Use it to make general statements, definitions, or poetic descriptions about love. It can be followed by a noun phrase ("un regalo"), an adjective ("fuerte"), or a longer idea ("la respuesta para todo").
target_language_example: Para mí, el amor es cuidar a alguien todos los días.
native_language_example: For me, love is taking care of someone every day.

additional_notes: A common proverb meaning that when people are in love, they may not notice a person’s faults or see things objectively. Often used with "dicen que..." or "se dice que..." (= "they say...") to introduce it as a general saying.
target_language_example: Aunque todos ven sus defectos, para ella el amor es ciego.
native_language_example: Even though everyone sees his flaws, for her love is blind.

meaning: an elderly man; an old man.
additional_notes: Used to refer to an older man in a fairly formal/neutral way. Often contrasts with "el joven" (the young man). For women, you’ll often see "la anciana". In everyday speech, people also commonly use "un señor mayor" for “an older man.”
target_language_example: El anciano necesita ayuda para cruzar la calle.
native_language_example: The elderly man needs help crossing the street.

additional_notes: A noun meaning a circular piece of jewelry worn on a finger. In Spanish it’s often used with the definite article (el) when talking about a specific ring: el anillo. Common phrases: ponerse el anillo (to put on the ring), llevar un anillo (to wear a ring), un anillo de oro (a gold ring).
target_language_example: Perdí el anillo en la playa.
native_language_example: I lost the ring at the beach.

additional_notes: Most commonly means a digital file (document, PDF, attachment) you send, download, attach, or delete data from. It can also mean an archive/record in a workplace or office context. Related: "archivo adjunto" = "attached file"; "borrar" un archivo = delete a file.
target_language_example: No puedo abrir el archivo; ¿me lo puedes enviar otra vez?
native_language_example: I can’t open the file; can you send it to me again?

additional_notes: Used for any weapon (a gun, knife, sword, etc.). Even though it ends in -a, it takes the masculine article for pronunciation: el arma, el arma del crimen. Plural: las armas.
target_language_example: Por favor, deja el arma en el suelo.
native_language_example: Please, put the weapon on the ground.

additional_notes: A common food word. Use it as a masculine singular noun with the article el (el arroz). In cooking contexts you’ll often see it with verbs like cocinar (to cook), hervir (to boil), dejar reposar (to let it rest), and guardar (to store/put away).
target_language_example: Deja que repose un poco el arroz.
native_language_example: Let the rice rest a little.

meaning: art; (figuratively) the art/skill of doing something.
additional_notes: Usually refers to art in general as an idea (painting, music, literature, etc.). It can also mean a skill or craft when used in patterns like “el arte de + infinitive” (e.g., “el arte de hablar” = “the art of speaking”). With careers or studies, you may hear “dejar X por el arte” meaning to leave something for art/artistic work.
target_language_example: Para mí, el arte es una forma de entender el mundo.
native_language_example: For me, art is a way to understand the world.

additional_notes: Used before an infinitive (verb in the "to + verb" form) to talk about a skill, technique, or knack: "el arte de + infinitivo". It can be meant seriously (a learned skill) or ironically (suggesting someone is good at something—sometimes not very honorable).
target_language_example: Aprendió el arte de escuchar sin interrumpir.
native_language_example: He learned the art of listening without interrupting.

additional_notes: A masculine noun used for the elevator in a building. Common verbs: tomar el ascensor (to take the elevator), subir/bajar en ascensor (to go up/down by elevator), and funcionar/dejar de funcionar (to work/stop working).
target_language_example: Perdón, ¿dónde está el ascensor?
native_language_example: Excuse me, where is the elevator?

additional_notes: Refers to a person who kills someone (especially intentionally). Common in crime/news contexts. Can overlap with English “assassin,” but is often broader. Feminine form: la asesina.
target_language_example: El asesino confesó su crimen.
native_language_example: The murderer confessed his crime.

meaning: "the matter" / "the issue" (a topic or situation being dealt with).
additional_notes: Used for a problem, topic, or piece of business under discussion or consideration: *discutir el asunto* (discuss the matter), *resolver el asunto* (resolve the issue). In set phrases: *ni voz ni voto en el asunto* = “no say in the matter.” *Tener cartas en el asunto* means “to have a stake/advantage” (literally “to have cards in the matter”).
target_language_example: No quiero hablar del asunto ahora.
native_language_example: I don’t want to talk about the matter right now.

additional_notes: Common in Latin America for “car” (also: “el carro”); in Spain, “el coche” is more common. Use it with estar/en to say you’re in the car: “estoy en el auto”.
target_language_example: Dejé las llaves en el auto.
native_language_example: I left the keys in the car.

additional_notes: Common way to refer to a bus as a form of public transportation. Often used with verbs like estar (location/condition): “Está en el autobús” (He/She/It is on the bus), and coger/tomar (to catch/take): “coger el autobús” (to catch the bus).
target_language_example: Tengo que coger el autobús a las ocho.
native_language_example: I have to catch the bus at eight.

additional_notes: Refers to an airplane. Often used with common travel verbs like “salir” (to depart/leave), “llegar” (to arrive), “volar” (to fly), and “aterrizar” (to land).
target_language_example: El avión está a punto de despegar.
native_language_example: The plane is about to take off.

additional_notes: Used to talk about something that happened in the previous calendar year. Often placed at the beginning or end of the sentence: "El año pasado fui a México" / "Fui a México el año pasado".
target_language_example: El año pasado empecé a estudiar español.
native_language_example: Last year I started studying Spanish.

additional_notes: Used to talk about the year after the current one. Very common for future plans and hopes. Often follows verbs in the future tense (e.g., viviré, volveremos) or can stand alone as a short answer: “Tal vez el año que viene.”
target_language_example: El año que viene voy a empezar un nuevo trabajo.
native_language_example: Next year I'm going to start a new job.

additional_notes: Context tells you which meaning it has: with verbs like robar (to rob) or words like federal, it usually means a bank; with verbs like pintar (to paint) or places like parque (park), it often means a bench. In Spanish, both uses are masculine: el banco.
target_language_example: Anoche robaron el banco.
native_language_example: Last night they robbed the bank.

additional_notes: Refers to a vessel that travels on water. In Spanish, "barco" can mean either "boat" or "ship" depending on size/context. The article changes with gender/number (e.g., "el barco", "los barcos").
target_language_example: El barco sale del puerto a las ocho.
native_language_example: The ship leaves the port at eight.

additional_notes: Used to talk about the room with a toilet/sink in public places and homes. Common in directions ("Ahí está el baño"), availability ("está ocupado" = "it’s occupied"), and in gendered forms: "el baño de hombres" (men’s room) / "el baño de mujeres" (women’s room). "Necesito el baño" is a common, polite way to say you need to use the restroom.
target_language_example: Perdón, ¿dónde está el baño?
native_language_example: Excuse me, where is the bathroom?

additional_notes: Refers to a baby (a very young child). Often used as a noun on its own ("El bebé se durmió"). "Bebé" can also be used more broadly to mean “the youngest one” in a family or group ("Él es el bebé de la familia").
target_language_example: El bebé está llorando porque tiene hambre ahora.
native_language_example: The baby is crying because he’s hungry now.

additional_notes: "El bebé" means "the baby." "Está" is from "estar" and is used for temporary states/conditions and locations (where someone/something is), often followed by: a place (aquí, en casa), an adjective (dormido), or a present participle to describe an action in progress (gateando, gritando).
target_language_example: El bebé está cansado.
native_language_example: The baby is tired.

meaning: “the white (one)” / “the color white”; sometimes “the target/bullseye” depending on context.
additional_notes: Spanish often uses **el + color/adjective** as a noun: **el blanco** = “the white one/thing” (e.g., a white wall, a white box, white paint). It can also mean **the white area/mark** you’re aiming for (like a target). Context tells you whether it refers to a color choice, a white object/surface, or a target.
target_language_example: Prefiero el blanco porque combina con todo.
native_language_example: I prefer the white one because it goes with everything.

additional_notes: Refers to a forest/wooded area. Uses the definite article "el" (“the”), but in Spanish you often use the article where English might say just “in forest/woods” (e.g., "están en el bosque" = “they’re in the woods”).
target_language_example: Vamos a caminar por el bosque esta tarde.
native_language_example: We’re going to walk through the woods this afternoon.

meaning: the button (a physical or on-screen control you press).
additional_notes: Often used with verbs like pulsar, presionar, apretar, or tocar (“to press/tap”). You can specify which one with de + description: el botón de en medio (the middle button), el botón verde (the green button), el botón de emergencia (the emergency button).
target_language_example: Pulsa el botón de encendido para iniciar la máquina.
native_language_example: Press the power button to start the machine.

additional_notes: Common body-part noun. Often used with "por" to mean grabbing/holding someone by the arm: "agarrar a alguien por el brazo".
target_language_example: Me duele el brazo derecho.
native_language_example: My right arm hurts.

additional_notes: Common in much of Latin America as a shorter alternative to “el autobús”. Used with the article: “el bus” (the bus).
target_language_example: Tomamos el bus al centro.
native_language_example: We took the bus downtown.

additional_notes: “Caballo” means “horse.” It’s masculine, so it usually goes with “el” (the) and “un” (a): el caballo, un caballo. Plural: los caballos (the horses).
target_language_example: ¿Dónde está el caballo?
native_language_example: Where is the horse?

additional_notes: Usually refers to head hair (similar to “pelo,” but “cabello” can sound a bit more formal/neutral). Common with verbs like dejarse crecer el cabello (to grow your hair out), llevar el cabello suelto (to wear your hair down), and recogerse el cabello (to tie/pin your hair back). Can also appear in product descriptions: champú para el cabello seco (shampoo for dry hair).
target_language_example: Me corté el cabello ayer.
native_language_example: I got my hair cut yesterday.

additional_notes: Usually refers to the drink “coffee.” It can also refer to coffee as a product/commodity (e.g., the coffee market). In Spanish it’s masculine, so it’s commonly used with el/un: el café, un café.
target_language_example: A mí me gusta más el café que el té.
native_language_example: I like coffee more than tea.

additional_notes: Most commonly refers to hot weather or high temperature: *el calor del verano* (“the summer heat”). It can also mean warmth as something that can be kept or conserved (*conservar el calor*). In some contexts (food/health), it can refer to the idea of “heat” in the body or a “heating” effect (e.g., spices that *quitan el calor* = “reduce the heat”).
target_language_example: Mi padre odia el calor del verano.
native_language_example: My father hates the summer heat.

additional_notes:
Very common with two main meanings:
- Change/improvement: *El cambio lleva tiempo.* / *El cambio fue sobresaliente.*
- Money change (cash back): *Cuente el cambio.* (Count the change.) / *Quédese con el cambio.* (Keep the change—said to a waiter/driver.) / *Se ha dejado el cambio.* (You left the change behind.)
Context usually makes clear which meaning is intended.
target_language_example: Aquí tiene su recibo y el cambio.
native_language_example: Here is your receipt and your change.

additional_notes: Often refers to a physical road/path ("cruzar el camino" = cross the road; "estar en el camino" = be in the way/in the path). It can also be more abstract: "el camino que se nos presenta" = the path/way ahead (the situation or future). In the set phrase "una para el camino", it means "one for the road" (usually one last drink before leaving).
target_language_example: No te quedes en el camino; muévete, por favor.
native_language_example: Don’t stay in the way; move, please.

additional_notes: A masculine noun used for a large road vehicle that carries goods (e.g., el camión del gas, el camión de combustible). Common patterns: "el camión de + noun" = "the ___ truck". Plural: "los camiones".
target_language_example: El camión del gas llega a las ocho.
native_language_example: The gas truck arrives at eight.

meaning: the countryside; a field; (also) a camp (e.g., concentration camp).
additional_notes: Most commonly means “the countryside” (as opposed to the city): Estamos en el campo. It can also mean “a field” (open land): El campo está lleno de flores silvestres. In some contexts it means “camp,” especially in historical phrases like campo de concentración.
target_language_example: Me encanta caminar por el campo los fines de semana.
native_language_example: I love walking in the countryside on weekends.

meaning: 'the captain' (a leader/officer in charge, especially in the military or on a ship).
additional_notes: Used with the definite article el (“the”). It can refer to a military rank (capitán), the person in charge of a ship, or the captain of a team. In direct address, Spanish often drops the article: “Capitán, venga aquí.”
target_language_example: El capitán dio la orden de avanzar.
native_language_example: The captain gave the order to move forward.

meaning: the car (also: cart/wagon, depending on context).
additional_notes: In many Latin American countries, carro commonly means “car” (synonym of coche/auto). In Spain, carro more often refers to a cart/trolley (e.g., a handcart or shopping cart), so context matters. Possession is often shown with de: el carro de ella = “her car.”
target_language_example: Dejé las llaves en el carro.
native_language_example: I left the keys in the car.

additional_notes: Used to talk about a situation or issue ("No creo que ese sea el caso" = "I don't think that's the case"), or a specific case/investigation (often police/legal: "resolver el caso"). Very common fixed phrase: "El caso es que..." = "The thing is (that)..." to introduce the main point.
target_language_example: El caso es que no tenemos tiempo para discutirlo ahora.
native_language_example: The thing is, we don't have time to discuss it now.

meaning: the center of attention; the focus of everyone’s attention.
additional_notes: Used with verbs like ser (“to be”) or querer/necesitar ser (“to want/need to be”) to talk about someone who is being noticed by everyone (sometimes with a negative idea: wanting attention).
target_language_example: No me gusta ser el centro de atención en las fiestas.
native_language_example: I don’t like being the center of attention at parties.

additional_notes: Usually literal (the organ in your head): *el cerebro humano*. In casual speech it can mean your thinking ability: *tener el cerebro encendido* (“have your brain switched on,” i.e., think before you speak). With violence it can appear in phrases like *un tiro/una bala en el cerebro* (“a shot/bullet to the brain”).
target_language_example: Necesito dormir; no me funciona el cerebro hoy.
native_language_example: I need to sleep; my brain isn’t working today.

additional_notes: Refers to a male child or young man. Depending on context, chico can mean "boy," "kid," or "guy." The article el means "the."
target_language_example: El chico está esperando afuera.
native_language_example: The boy is waiting outside.

additional_notes: A common noun usually used with the definite article (el): el chocolate. It can refer to chocolate as a food in general or to a specific chocolate item, depending on context. With gustar: Me gusta el chocolate. Also common with verbs like odiar (to hate) and encantar (to love).
target_language_example: ¿Quieres el chocolate o prefieres el café?
native_language_example: Do you want the chocolate, or do you prefer coffee?

additional_notes: Usually means “the sky” in weather/nature contexts (clouds, stars, flying, daylight/night). It can also mean “heaven” in religious or figurative contexts (e.g., "estar en el cielo"). It’s masculine singular: el cielo.
target_language_example: El cielo está lleno de estrellas.
native_language_example: The sky is full of stars.

additional_notes: Used to describe how the sky looks right now, especially for weather. Spanish typically uses **estar** (not *ser*) for temporary conditions: *El cielo está azul / nublado / despejado / gris.*
target_language_example: Mira, el cielo está despejado; podemos ir al parque.
native_language_example: Look, the sky is clear; we can go to the park.

meaning: the cinema; the movie theater; movies/film (as an art form or industry).
additional_notes: Usually means either (1) the movie theater/cinema as a place (e.g., “El cine estaba abarrotado” = the theater was packed), or (2) cinema/film in general as an art form or industry (e.g., “Me apasiona el cine mudo” = I’m passionate about silent films). Common phrase: “ir al cine” = to go to the movies.
target_language_example: El cine estaba abarrotado.
native_language_example: The movie theater was packed.

additional_notes: Most commonly means “the weather” (conditions like sun, rain, temperature) in a place and time: El clima está bien/mal, El clima cambia. It can also mean “climate” in a more general sense (typical weather patterns of a region), but beginners will often see it as “weather.”
target_language_example: Hoy el clima está muy frío y ventoso.
native_language_example: Today the weather is very cold and windy.

additional_notes: Means a specific car. Coche is a very common word for "car" in Spain; in many parts of Latin America, carro or auto is more common.
target_language_example: El coche está en el garaje.
native_language_example: The car is in the garage.

meaning: school (often an elementary/primary or secondary school).
additional_notes: Refers to a school as an institution or the building. In many Spanish-speaking places, “colegio” usually means primary/secondary school (not university). It can also refer to the students/people at the school (“todo el colegio lo sabe” = everyone at school knows).
target_language_example: El colegio empieza a las nueve y termina a las seis.
native_language_example: School starts at nine and ends at six.

additional_notes: Used to talk about the color of something (often with "de": "el color de los libros"). In Spanish, "color" is masculine: "el color", "los colores".
target_language_example: ¿Cuál es el color de tu coche?
native_language_example: What color is your car?

meaning: the committee (a group of people chosen to make decisions or organize something).
additional_notes: Used for an official group within an organization. You’ll often see it with verbs like "constar de" / "consistir de" (to consist of) and "tener una sesión" (to hold a meeting/session). Plural: "los comités".
target_language_example: El comité se reúne mañana para decidir el presupuesto.
native_language_example: The committee meets tomorrow to decide the budget.

additional_notes: A common noun for a live music event. It’s masculine (el concierto). You’ll often see it with verbs like "tener lugar" (to take place), "durar" (to last), "concluir" (to end), "disfrutar" (to enjoy), and "suspender" (to cancel/postpone).
target_language_example: ¿A qué hora empieza el concierto?
native_language_example: What time does the concert start?

additional_notes: Used for a formal written agreement, often something you read, review, and sign (firmar). Common with jobs, rentals, services, etc. Singular: el contrato; plural: los contratos.
target_language_example: Antes de firmar, quiero leer el contrato con calma.
native_language_example: Before signing, I want to read the contract carefully.

meaning: 'control' (power to manage a situation); also '(remote) control' (device).
additional_notes: Common with verbs like tener el control (to be in control) and perder el control (to lose control). In everyday speech, el control can also mean the remote control, especially when the context is TV/electronics; you can also say el control remoto for clarity.
target_language_example: Dame el control, por favor; yo pongo la tele.
native_language_example: Give me the remote, please; I’ll turn on the TV.

additional_notes: Used literally for the organ (medical/physical), and figuratively to mean the central or most important part of something ("the heart of the house/city"). Common structure: "el corazón de + [place/thing]". Also appears in health descriptions like "tener el corazón débil" (to have a weak heart).
target_language_example: Esta plaza es el corazón de la ciudad.
native_language_example: This plaza is the heart of the city.

additional_notes: Used literally (the organ) or figuratively (the center/most important part of something). In expressions like "tener el corazón de + animal/persona", it describes someone’s heart/constitution (often meaning strong, healthy, brave, etc.), depending on context.
target_language_example: Madrid está en el corazón de España.
native_language_example: Madrid is in the heart of Spain.

additional_notes: Used for physical mail (letters, packages) and sometimes the service that delivers it. Common with verbs like llegar (to arrive), repartir (to deliver/distribute), enviar (to send), and recoger (to pick up/collect). Also appears in related phrases like correo de voz (“voicemail”) and correo electrónico (“email”).
target_language_example: ¿Ya llegó el correo?
native_language_example: Has the mail arrived yet?

additional_notes: Commonly means “the room” in a house or building; in many contexts it specifically refers to a bedroom. Note: “cuarto” can also mean “fourth” (e.g., el cuarto piso = the 4th floor) or “quarter” in other contexts, but with this kind of sentence it means “room.”
target_language_example: El cuarto estaba en el más completo desorden.
native_language_example: The room was in complete disarray.

additional_notes: Definite article + noun: el = “the” (masculine singular), cuchillo = “knife”. Used for a specific knife that’s known in the context. Common with verbs like pasar (to hand/pass) and with adjectives like afilado (sharp).
target_language_example: ¿Dónde está el cuchillo?
native_language_example: Where is the knife?

additional_notes: A common body-part noun. Used with injuries and medical descriptions (heridas en el cuello, herido en el cuello) and with physical actions (agarrar por el cuello = to grab someone by the neck). In Spanish, body parts are usually mentioned with the definite article (el/la/los/las) instead of a possessive: Me duele el cuello = My neck hurts.
target_language_example: Me duele el cuello desde ayer.
native_language_example: My neck has hurt since yesterday.

additional_notes: Usually refers to a person’s physical body (human or animal). In news/crime contexts, it can mean “the corpse/dead body” (e.g., encontrar/examinar/enterrar el cuerpo). Common related uses: herir el cuerpo (injure the body), arruinarse el cuerpo (damage your health/body), en el cuerpo de… (in the body of…).
target_language_example: Después del accidente, le dolía todo el cuerpo.
native_language_example: After the accident, his whole body hurt.

additional_notes: A common, rude body-word that also appears in many idioms. Examples: "en el culo del mundo" = "in the middle of nowhere" (very far away); "partirse el culo" can mean "to laugh your ass off" (or in some contexts "to work your ass off"); "salvar(le) el culo (a alguien)" = "to save someone’s ass" / "get someone out of trouble." Use carefully in polite company; "el trasero" is a more neutral option.
target_language_example: Este pueblo está en el culo del mundo.
native_language_example: This town is in the middle of nowhere.

additional_notes: Refers to grass as a surface, especially a lawn in a yard/park. Common with verbs like cortar el césped (to mow the lawn) and in signs like Prohibido pisar el césped (Keep off the grass).
target_language_example: ¿Puedes cortar el césped mañana?
native_language_example: Can you mow the lawn tomorrow?

meaning: the code (a password/entry code, set of rules, or coding system).
additional_notes: Often refers to an access code or password (e.g., for entering a building, phone, or account): "No sé el código" / "Ingrese el código". It can also mean a system of symbols/communication like "el código Morse" (Morse code), or a set of rules (a code of conduct) depending on context.
target_language_example: Necesito el código para abrir la puerta.
native_language_example: I need the code to open the door.

additional_notes: Usually means a finger; for toes you often specify: "el dedo del pie" (toe). Common with body-related verbs (hurt, burn, cut, twist): "Me duele / Me quemé / Me corté / Me torcí el dedo". In safety contexts: "Quita el dedo del gatillo" = "Take your finger off the trigger." Also used with rings: "Se puso el anillo en el dedo".
target_language_example: Me corté el dedo cocinando.
native_language_example: I cut my finger while cooking.

additional_notes: Refers to the morning meal. Often used with en (at/for breakfast): en el desayuno. You can also specify a day/time: el desayuno de mañana (tomorrow’s breakfast).
target_language_example: Siempre tomo café en el desayuno.
native_language_example: I always drink coffee at breakfast.

meaning: the desire to (do something); the desire for (something).
additional_notes: Used to talk about a want or strong wish. It’s normally followed by an infinitive (el deseo de comer = “the desire to eat”) or a noun (el deseo de tu corazón = “your heart’s desire”). You can chain several actions after it: “el deseo de progresar, de trabajar…”.
target_language_example: Tengo el deseo de aprender español este año.
native_language_example: I have the desire to learn Spanish this year.

additional_notes: A masculine noun for a large, very dry area of land with little rain and few plants. Often used with prepositions like en (in), por (through/across), and para (to/toward): en el desierto, por el desierto, fueron para el desierto.
target_language_example: Hace mucho calor en el desierto durante el día.
native_language_example: It’s very hot in the desert during the day.

additional_notes: Used to talk about events as if they were decided by fate ("It was destiny"). It can also mean a person’s future/role in life ("your destiny") and, in travel contexts, a “destination,” but in these examples it means fate/destiny.
target_language_example: Creía que conocerte fue el destino.
native_language_example: I believed that meeting you was destiny.

additional_notes: Used literally in religious or cultural contexts (“the Devil”). It can also be used figuratively to blame bad luck, temptation, or trouble on an evil force (like saying “the devil made me do it”). Always masculine: el diablo.
target_language_example: Dicen que el diablo tienta a la gente.
native_language_example: They say the devil tempts people.

additional_notes: Which meaning depends on context: **el diario** can be a **newspaper** (often with a name, like *El Diario X*; or in phrases like *una entrevista para el diario*), or a **personal diary/journal** (often followed by **de + person/thing**, e.g., *el diario de papá*).
target_language_example: Leí el diario esta mañana y luego escribí en mi diario.
native_language_example: I read the newspaper this morning and then wrote in my diary.

additional_notes: A masculine noun, so it uses el (singular) and los (plural: los diccionarios). Commonly used with verbs like usar (to use), coger (to grab), necesitar (to need), and decir (to say) when referring to what the dictionary states.
target_language_example: No entiendo esta palabra; voy a buscarla en el diccionario.
native_language_example: I don’t understand this word; I’m going to look it up in the dictionary.

additional_notes: Means money. With the article el, it can refer to specific money ("the money"), but in Spanish it is also often used for money in general, where English may simply say "money."
target_language_example: No encuentro el dinero en mi bolso.
native_language_example: I can't find the money in my bag.

meaning: "the money and..." (used to link "the money" with the next thing).
additional_notes: This is a fragment you’ll often see before a second item or action: "el dinero y + [something else]". It can connect two nouns ("el dinero y el contrato" = "the money and the contract") or set up a deal/sequence ("Dame el dinero y..." = "Give me the money and...").
target_language_example: Tráeme el dinero y el pasaporte.
native_language_example: Bring me the money and the passport.

meaning: the director; the principal (head of a school).
additional_notes: Most commonly refers to the person in charge of an organization or department. In a school context, "el director" usually means the principal. Used with "hablar con" (to talk to), "tener una cita con" (to have an appointment with), and verbs like "regañar" (to scold). Feminine: "la directora."
target_language_example: Mañana tenemos una reunión con el director de la escuela.
native_language_example: Tomorrow we have a meeting with the school principal.

meaning: divorce (the legal ending of a marriage).
additional_notes: A common noun used with the definite article: el divorcio (“the divorce”). Often appears with verbs like querer/pedir (to want/ask for a divorce) and with time phrases like tras/después del divorcio (“after the divorce”).
target_language_example: Quieren el divorcio porque ya no son felices juntos.
native_language_example: They want a divorce because they’re no longer happy together.

additional_notes: Used to compare quantities or say something is 2× a number or amount. Common patterns: "el doble de + noun" (Pagué el doble de dinero), "el doble de + number" (el doble de 10), and "el doble de + adjective + que" for comparisons (el doble de largas que...).
target_language_example: Este bolso cuesta el doble de lo que esperaba.
native_language_example: This bag costs twice what I expected.

additional_notes: Refers to a (male) doctor. For a female doctor, you’ll often hear "la doctora". In many contexts, "doctor" can also be an academic title (PhD), but in these examples it clearly means a medical doctor.
target_language_example: El doctor me recomendó descansar unos días.
native_language_example: The doctor recommended that I rest for a few days.

additional_notes: Used for any written record: a form, contract, letter, certificate, ID paperwork, or digital file. It’s masculine: el documento; plural: los documentos. Common verbs include firmar el documento (to sign), leer el documento (to read), entregar el documento (to hand in/deliver), and está escrito en el documento (it’s written in the document).
target_language_example: Necesito el documento para completar el trámite.
native_language_example: I need the document to complete the procedure/paperwork.

additional_notes: A common noun for physical or emotional pain. It’s usually used with the article: el dolor (the pain). Common patterns: aliviar el dolor (to relieve pain), aguantar/soportar el dolor (to endure pain), sentir el dolor (to feel pain).
target_language_example: Me duele la espalda, pero este té me ayuda con el dolor.
native_language_example: My back hurts, but this tea helps me with the pain.

additional_notes: Used with the definite article "el" to talk about Sunday as a specific day. "el domingo" often means "on Sunday" when referring to an event on that day (Las elecciones son el domingo). For repeated habits, Spanish often uses "los domingos" = "on Sundays" / "every Sunday" (e.g., Voy a la iglesia los domingos).
target_language_example: Nos vemos el domingo por la tarde.
native_language_example: See you on Sunday afternoon.

additional_notes: Used to talk about the Sunday in the previous week (a specific day in the past). It often goes at the beginning of the sentence as a time expression, but it can also appear after the verb.
target_language_example: El domingo pasado, cenamos en casa de mis abuelos.
native_language_example: Last Sunday, we had dinner at my grandparents' house.

additional_notes: Refers to a specific day. It is often followed by de + noun or a clause to specify which day: el día de mi renacimiento, el día del casamiento, el día en que él está libre.
target_language_example: No olvidaré el día que nos conocimos.
native_language_example: I won't forget the day we met.

meaning: the previous day; the day before.
additional_notes: Used to refer to the day immediately before a point in time you’re talking about (often in storytelling or reported speech). In indirect speech it usually means “the day before” relative to when the person spoke or relative to the past event being described (similar to English “the day before”).
target_language_example: Llegamos a Madrid el día anterior, así que ya conocíamos la ciudad.
native_language_example: We arrived in Madrid the day before, so we already knew the city.

meaning: "the day of" (for a specific event, holiday, or occasion).
additional_notes: Used to name a particular day connected to something: el día de Navidad (“Christmas Day”), el día de pruebas (“the day of tryouts/tests”). It can also be followed by an infinitive to mean “the day when you can/do something”: el día de poder verte (“the day I can see you”). Often you’ll also hear just "día de" without "el" depending on the sentence.
target_language_example: ¿Qué vas a hacer el día de tu examen?
native_language_example: What are you going to do on the day of your exam?

meaning: 'today' (often a more formal/emphatic way to say it).
additional_notes: Used to refer to the current day, especially in speeches, announcements, or more formal writing. It can sound more emphatic than just "hoy" and is often used when highlighting the importance of what happened or will happen today.
target_language_example: El día de hoy tenemos una reunión importante.
native_language_example: Today we have an important meeting.

additional_notes: Used to introduce a clause that describes what happened on that specific day. It’s very common in memories and important events: “Recuerdo el día en que…”, “Hoy es el día en que…”. Often you’ll also see the more formal variant “el día en el que…”.
target_language_example: Nunca olvidaré el día en que nos mudamos a esta ciudad.
native_language_example: I’ll never forget the day we moved to this city.

additional_notes: Used to introduce a relative clause that specifies which day you mean. It’s often used with important past events and is followed by a verb phrase (e.g., "el día en que + nació / llegaste / empezó todo"). You can also see "el día que" in casual speech; "el día en que" is a bit more formal/precise.
target_language_example: Nunca olvidaré el día en que nos conocimos.
native_language_example: I’ll never forget the day we met.

additional_notes: Used to say something lasts for the entire day. Often appears with time expressions like “pasarse + el día entero + gerundio” (Me pasé el día entero limpiando = I spent the whole day cleaning) or with verbs like “esperar” (Te esperamos el día entero = We waited for you all day). You can also say “todo el día” with the same meaning.
target_language_example: Estuve estudiando el día entero para el examen.
native_language_example: I studied all day for the exam.

additional_notes: Used for a day when you don’t have to work or go to school. Common with verbs like "tener" (to have), "tomarse/cogerse" (to take), and in phrases like "estar de día libre". In Spanish you often say "tomarse/cogerse el día libre" (literally “to take the free day”).
target_language_example: Mañana me voy a tomar el día libre para descansar.
native_language_example: Tomorrow I’m going to take the day off to rest.

additional_notes: Used to introduce a clause that identifies a specific day by what happened (often in the past): “El día que asesinaron a Julio César…”. It can also refer to a future/conditional moment meaning “the day when (something happens)”: “El día que tengamos una segunda oportunidad…”. Often interchangeable with “el día en que”.
target_language_example: El día que te conocí, supe que quería volver a verte.
native_language_example: The day I met you, I knew I wanted to see you again.

additional_notes: Used to talk about a physical structure (a school, factory, etc.). Often followed by location phrases (e.g., en la montaña) or a relative clause (el edificio que ves...). Note: "edificio" is masculine, so it takes "el".
target_language_example: El edificio de la esquina es el hospital.
native_language_example: The building on the corner is the hospital.

additional_notes: Refers to a country’s military forces (especially the land forces). Used with the definite article: el ejército. Common with verbs like servir en (to serve in), proteger (to protect), and defender (to defend).
target_language_example: Mi hermano sirvió en el ejército durante dos años.
native_language_example: My brother served in the army for two years.

additional_notes: Used to refer to a person selected for something special (a job, role, prize, etc.), or in a romantic sense: “the one.” In stories it can sound dramatic/prophetic (“the chosen one”). Changes for gender/number: el elegido (male), la elegida (female), los/las elegidos/as (plural).
target_language_example: El próximo chico que encuentres puede ser el elegido.
native_language_example: The next guy you meet might be the chosen one.

additional_notes: Refers to a person, group, or force you are fighting against (literal or figurative). In plural: los enemigos (“the enemies”). Common in stories, war contexts, games, or conflicts: enfrentarse a el enemigo (“to face the enemy”), estar cerca (“to be nearby”). Note: in everyday Spanish, "a el" often contracts to "al" (encontrar al enemigo), but the base term remains "el enemigo".
target_language_example: El enemigo está muy cerca.
native_language_example: The enemy is very close.

meaning: the team; the equipment/gear (depending on context).
additional_notes: Most commonly means “the team” (sports, work group): *El equipo local* = the home/local team; *Todo el equipo* = the whole team. It can also mean “equipment/gear” (especially in technical/work contexts), and in that sense it often appears with more detail (e.g., *equipo de sonido*, *equipo de seguridad*).
target_language_example: El equipo necesita más tiempo para terminar el proyecto.
native_language_example: The team needs more time to finish the project.

additional_notes: “Equipo” can mean either a group of people (a team/unit) or a set of devices/tools (equipment). With “el equipo de + noun,” the noun clarifies the sense: with rescue/search/emergency it often means a team/unit (el equipo de rescate = the rescue team); with radio/transmission it often means equipment (el equipo de radio = the radio equipment).
target_language_example: El equipo de rescate reportó desde el lugar del choque.
native_language_example: The rescue team reported from the site of the crash.

meaning: the stage; the setting/scene (place where something happens).
additional_notes: Most commonly refers to the physical stage in a theater/show (subir/salir a el escenario is more often contracted to subir/salir al escenario). It can also mean the setting or scene of a place or event (e.g., el escenario del crimen = the crime scene; el escenario de los Alpes = the Alpine scenery). Figuratively, preparar el escenario means to set the stage (create the conditions for something).
target_language_example: El actor salió al escenario y el público aplaudió; después volvió a el escenario para el bis.
native_language_example: The actor came out onto the stage and the audience applauded; then he returned to the stage for the encore.

meaning: the desk; also (less often) an office/study.
additional_notes: Most commonly refers to a desk (the piece of furniture you work at). In some contexts it can mean an office or study (the room/area where you work), but beginners will usually see it as “desk.” Plural: los escritorios.
target_language_example: Dejé mi cuaderno en el escritorio.
native_language_example: I left my notebook on the desk.

additional_notes: Most commonly refers to outer space in science/astronomy contexts (often just “espacio” once the topic is clear): “El espacio está lleno de misterios.” It can also mean an empty space/gap (e.g., on a page), a physical area/room, or available capacity, depending on context.
target_language_example: El espacio está lleno de misterios.
native_language_example: Space is full of mysteries.

additional_notes: Used for an entertainment event like a concert, play, or performance. Common in set phrases like "El espectáculo debe continuar" ("The show must go on") and "Se acabó el espectáculo" ("The show is over"). You can also use it for a scheduled event: "El espectáculo es el lunes" ("The show is on Monday").
target_language_example: Compramos entradas para el espectáculo de esta noche.
native_language_example: We bought tickets for tonight’s show.

additional_notes: A masculine noun (el). Used for the object you look into to see your reflection. Common with verbs like colgar (to hang), romper(se) (to break), and adjectives like sucio (dirty). Also used figuratively in expressions like “Los ojos son el espejo del alma” (“The eyes are the mirror of the soul”).
target_language_example: Me miré en el espejo antes de salir.
native_language_example: I looked at myself in the mirror before leaving.

additional_notes: Used for the body organ and, by extension, digestion and appetite. Common beginner phrases: "Me duele el estómago" (My stomach hurts), "Tengo el estómago vacío" (I have an empty stomach), and "Me hace ruido el estómago" (My stomach is growling). In expressions like "Se me cayó el estómago", it means you suddenly felt sick/nervous or your stomach “dropped” when you saw/heard something.
target_language_example: No puedo comer mucho; tengo el estómago revuelto.
native_language_example: I can’t eat much; my stomach is upset.

additional_notes: Refers to a specific exam/test (school, class, or a formal evaluation). Use "el" because "examen" is masculine. In Spanish, "examen" can also mean a medical test (e.g., "un examen de sangre" = a blood test), but in school contexts it usually means an exam.
target_language_example: Tengo que estudiar para el examen mañana.
native_language_example: I have to study for the exam tomorrow.

additional_notes: A masculine noun used for a scientific test or trial done to learn something or check a hypothesis. Often used with verbs like empezar/comenzar (to start), terminar (to finish), and ser un éxito (to be a success).
target_language_example: El experimento salió bien y aprendimos mucho.
native_language_example: The experiment went well and we learned a lot.

additional_notes: Used to talk about Saturday and Sunday. Often appears with verbs like pasar (to spend) and hacer (to do): Pasé/Voy a pasar el fin de semana… You can also use it with time expressions like este fin de semana (this weekend) or el fin de semana pasado (last weekend).
target_language_example: Este sábado voy a descansar en casa el fin de semana.
native_language_example: This Saturday I'm going to rest at home on the weekend.

meaning: “the end of the world” (the apocalypse); also “it’s not the end of the world” = “it’s not a big deal.”
additional_notes: Literally “the end of the world.” Used for dramatic or literal talk about an apocalypse ("El fin del mundo se acerca"), and very commonly in the expression "No es el fin del mundo" to calm someone down and say something isn’t so serious.
target_language_example: Tranquilo, no es el fin del mundo si llegamos tarde.
native_language_example: Relax, it’s not the end of the world if we’re late.

meaning: “the end of the …” (before a feminine noun).
additional_notes: Used to talk about the last part of something. It must be followed by a feminine singular noun (la película, la semana, la clase, etc.). With a masculine noun, you usually say “el final del …” (de + el → del).
target_language_example: Me gustó el final de la película.
native_language_example: I liked the ending of the movie.

additional_notes: Uses the masculine singular article (el) with language names: el francés, el español, el inglés. It can refer to the language in general or to French class/subject, depending on context. Nationalities can also be the same word (un francés = a French man), but with "el" it usually means the language.
target_language_example: Estoy estudiando el francés este año.
native_language_example: I'm studying French this year.

additional_notes: Refers to cold temperatures in general or a period of cold weather. It can be the subject of a sentence ("El frío duró hasta abril") or something you feel ("Noto el frío"). Common patterns: "hace frío" (it’s cold), "por el frío" (because of the cold), and "el frío me caló hasta los huesos" (the cold chilled me to the bone).
target_language_example: No salgas sin chaqueta: el frío está fuerte hoy.
native_language_example: Don’t go out without a jacket: it’s really cold today.

additional_notes: Refers to fire/flames (e.g., a house fire, a campfire). Often used with verbs like "apagar" (to put out) and "propagarse" (to spread).
target_language_example: Llamaron a los bomberos porque el fuego era muy grande.
native_language_example: They called the firefighters because the fire was very big.

additional_notes: Refers to time that has not happened yet (what comes after the present). Often used with verbs like pensar en el futuro (to think about the future) or hablar del futuro (to talk about the future).
target_language_example: Tenemos que prepararnos para el futuro.
native_language_example: We have to prepare for the future.

additional_notes: A masculine noun (el fútbol). In most Spanish-speaking countries, fútbol refers to soccer (association football). Use it with verbs like gustar (Me gusta el fútbol) and to compare popularity (El fútbol es más popular que...).
target_language_example: Me gusta el fútbol, pero me gusta más el baloncesto.
native_language_example: I like soccer, but I like basketball more.

additional_notes: A simple statement using **ser** (permanent/defining info) to describe what something is: **X es un/una + noun**. You can add an adjective or extra info after **deporte** (e.g., **de equipo**, **emocionante**). In much of Latin America, **fútbol** can refer to soccer; in the U.S./Canada, "football" usually means a different sport, so Spanish uses **fútbol americano** for American football.
target_language_example: El fútbol es un deporte muy popular en muchos países.
native_language_example: Soccer is a very popular sport in many countries.

additional_notes: Most commonly refers to the part of a firearm you press or pull to fire. You’ll often see it with verbs like apretar (to press/squeeze) or jalar (to pull): apretar/jalar el gatillo. By extension, phrases like rápido con el gatillo suggest someone is quick to use a gun (or quick to react aggressively).
target_language_example: No pongas el dedo en el gatillo hasta que estés listo para disparar.
native_language_example: Don’t put your finger on the trigger until you’re ready to shoot.

additional_notes: Refers to a (male) cat, or to a cat in general. In Spanish, you can also say "la gata" for a female cat. The plural is "los gatos" (male or mixed group) and "las gatas" (female cats).
target_language_example: El gato duerme en el sofá.
native_language_example: The cat sleeps on the couch.

meaning: “the cat is …” (and often “the cat is [doing] …” right now).
additional_notes: "El gato" means “the cat.” "Está" (from estar) is used for location (cerca de, debajo de, sobre) and for temporary states or actions in progress, especially with a present participle: "está destrozando" = “is destroying,” "está escribiendo" = “is writing.”
target_language_example: El gato está durmiendo en el sofá.
native_language_example: The cat is sleeping on the sofa.

additional_notes: Refers to the people and institutions that run a country (and make decisions). Common with verbs like tomar una decisión (to make a decision) and with trabajar para (to work for).
target_language_example: El gobierno anunció nuevas medidas.
native_language_example: The government announced new measures.

meaning: "Modern Greek" (the Greek language as spoken today).
additional_notes: A language name. Use it with the definite article: el griego moderno. You can also say "griego" by itself when the context is clear. Often contrasted with "el griego antiguo" (Ancient Greek).
target_language_example: Estoy aprendiendo el griego moderno este año.
native_language_example: I’m learning Modern Greek this year.

additional_notes: Used to introduce a statement as a fact or piece of evidence, often followed by the subjunctive in Spanish when it expresses attitude, doubt, or evaluation ("El hecho de que estés aquí...") and the indicative when it states an accepted fact ("Nadie puede negar el hecho de que el fuego quema").
target_language_example: El hecho de que llegues tarde no me molesta, pero avísame.
native_language_example: The fact that you arrive late doesn’t bother me, but let me know.

additional_notes: A common noun for frozen water. Used for ice in nature (lakes, sea ice) and in everyday contexts (ice cubes). Masculine singular: el hielo; plural: los hielos. In Spanish, the "h" is silent.
target_language_example: No camines sobre el hielo; es peligroso.
native_language_example: Don’t walk on the ice; it’s dangerous.

additional_notes: A simple factual sentence used to state what something is. Structure: "El/La + [noun] + es + un/una + [category]" (e.g., "El oro es un metal"). "Hierro" means "iron" and is masculine, so it uses "el" and "un".
target_language_example: El hierro es un metal muy útil.
native_language_example: Iron is a very useful metal.

additional_notes: Used to identify a male person as someone’s child. It’s often followed by a name or a noun phrase: "el hijo de Renata" (Renata’s son), "el hijo de la hermana Rosa" (Sister Rosa’s son). For a daughter, use "la hija de".
target_language_example: Marcos es el hijo de mi profesora.
native_language_example: Marcos is my teacher’s son.

additional_notes: Usually refers to a specific adult male: el hombre = "the man." In more general statements, it can also mean "man" in the sense of humanity or humankind, depending on context.
target_language_example: El hombre está en la cocina.
native_language_example: The man is in the kitchen.

meaning: the white man (a white person; often referring to white men as a group).
additional_notes: Literally “the white man.” It can be a neutral description, but it’s very often used in social/political contexts to refer to white people (especially white men) as a group, sometimes critically or as a symbol of power/privilege. Use with care because it can sound charged depending on context and tone.
target_language_example: En esa discusión, hablaban del hombre blanco como símbolo de poder.
native_language_example: In that discussion, they talked about the white man as a symbol of power.

meaning: “the man with/of …” (used to identify a man by a defining trait, clothing, role, or association).
additional_notes: Used before a noun phrase to single out a man by something that characterizes him: clothing/color ("el hombre de negro" = the man in black; Spanish often uses "de" where English uses "in"), a physical feature ("el hombre de seis dedos" = the six-fingered man), a role/type ("el hombre de familia" = a family man), or association/origin ("el hombre de Jengibre" = the Gingerbread Man). The phrase is generally compositional, but it doesn’t always translate word-for-word in natural English.
target_language_example: El hombre de negro lo hace ahora.
native_language_example: The man in black is doing it now.

additional_notes: Used to talk about the man with the most money/wealth in a place or group. Often followed by a location phrase with en (e.g., en la ciudad, en el mundo). It’s the superlative of rico (“rich”): más rico = “richest.”
target_language_example: Dicen que él es el hombre más rico del país.
native_language_example: They say he is the richest man in the country.

additional_notes: Used to introduce a relative clause that describes or identifies a specific man. The verb after "que" can be in different tenses: "El hombre que llamó..." (who called), "El hombre que llevaba..." (who was carrying). In sentence 6, "el hombre que era" means "the man he used to be."
target_language_example: El hombre que vive al lado es médico.
native_language_example: The man who lives next door is a doctor.

additional_notes: A body part. With aches/injuries Spanish often uses the definite article (el) where English uses a possessive: Me duele el hombro = 'My shoulder hurts.' Common verbs: doler (to hurt/ache), lastimarse (to injure), romperse (to break), tocar (to touch).
target_language_example: Me duele el hombro derecho.
native_language_example: My right shoulder hurts.

additional_notes: A common place noun. Use **en el hospital** for being in/at the hospital (as a patient or visiting): *Estoy en el hospital.* With motion verbs, you often use **al hospital** (“to the hospital”): *La llevaron al hospital.*
target_language_example: Estuve en el hospital hace unos días.
native_language_example: I was in the hospital a few days ago.

meaning: "the hotel" (a place where you pay to stay overnight).
additional_notes: Uses the masculine singular definite article el. You’ll often see it with location phrases like "está cerca/lejos de...", "está al final de...", or "está en...". Plural: "los hoteles".
target_language_example: ¿Dónde está el hotel?
native_language_example: Where is the hotel?

meaning: the habit of; being in the habit of (doing something).
additional_notes: Used with an infinitive to talk about a repeated, regular behavior: "tener/desarrollar el hábito de" + verb (infinitive). Common with imperfect for past habits: "tenía el hábito de".
target_language_example: Estoy tratando de romper el hábito de comer tarde.
native_language_example: I'm trying to break the habit of eating late.

additional_notes: Refers to a specific language as a system of communication (e.g., el idioma español, el idioma inglés). In everyday Spanish, you’ll also hear "la lengua" with a similar meaning. Not to be confused with "idioma" in English, which is a fixed expression (in Spanish, that’s "un modismo").
target_language_example: El idioma es una de las formas de comunicación más importantes.
native_language_example: Language is one of the most important forms of communication.

additional_notes: Used when telling someone to bring/take a raincoat as a precaution. It commonly follows commands with llevar (“to bring”) or llevarse (“to take with you”): Lleva/Lleve/Lleven… or Llévate/Llévese/Llévense…. The key part is por si llueve = “in case it rains.”
target_language_example: Mete el impermeable por si llueve esta tarde.
native_language_example: Pack the raincoat in case it rains this afternoon.

meaning: hell; (figuratively) a terrible situation; used for emphasis (“as hell”).
additional_notes: Literal meaning: the religious/spiritual place of punishment (“hell”). Very common figuratively to describe extreme suffering, chaos, or a horrible place/situation (e.g., “Viven en el infierno” = “They’re living in hell”). It can also be used as an intensifier in comparisons like “como el infierno” (“as hell,” “like hell”).
target_language_example: Este trabajo es el infierno, pero necesito el dinero.
native_language_example: This job is hell, but I need the money.

additional_notes: A masculine noun. Used for a written document with information, results, or a summary (for work, school, an investigation, etc.). Common collocation: "devolver/entregar el informe" (return/hand in the report).
target_language_example: Tengo que terminar el informe hoy.
native_language_example: I have to finish the report today.

additional_notes: Refers to the English language. It’s usually used with the definite article (el), especially after verbs like hablar (to speak), aprender (to learn), estudiar (to study), usar (to use), and gustar (to like).
target_language_example: Estoy aprendiendo el inglés para mi trabajo.
native_language_example: I'm learning English for my job.

additional_notes: A masculine noun meaning the season of winter. Usually used with the definite article: el invierno. Common in time expressions like en/durante el invierno (in/during the winter), todo el invierno (all winter), and in contrasts with other seasons (verano, primavera, otoño).
target_language_example: En el invierno hace mucho frío aquí.
native_language_example: In the winter it’s very cold here.

additional_notes: Refers to a garden (an outdoor area with plants). In Spanish, nouns often take a definite article, so you’ll commonly see it as “el jardín” (“the garden”).
target_language_example: Vamos a sentarnos en el jardín.
native_language_example: Let’s sit in the garden.

additional_notes: A masculine noun, so it usually goes with "el" (the). Common with the verb "gustar": "Me gusta el jazz" = "I like jazz."
target_language_example: ¿Te gusta el jazz?
native_language_example: Do you like jazz?

additional_notes: Used for the person in charge (at work, of a department, a group, etc.). It can be formal or neutral depending on context. Also used in the expression “tú eres el jefe” = “you’re the boss” (often meaning “it’s your decision”). Feminine form: “la jefa”.
target_language_example: Necesito hablar con el jefe antes de tomar una decisión.
native_language_example: I need to talk to the boss before making a decision.

additional_notes: Used to say someone is the person in charge of a group, organization, department, or family. Often followed by a noun with or without an article: "el jefe de Recursos Humanos", "el jefe de la policía". Feminine form: "la jefa de".
target_language_example: Mi hermano es el jefe de ventas en esa empresa.
native_language_example: My brother is the head of sales at that company.

additional_notes: Most commonly means “the game” (a match, a video game, or any kind of game): El juego ha acabado / El juego se acabó = “The game is over.” It can also refer more generally to “play” or “gameplay” depending on context. In the phrase el juego de la vida it means “the game of life.”
target_language_example: ¿A qué hora empieza el juego?
native_language_example: What time does the game start?

additional_notes: Used to refer to the day of the week. In Spanish you typically use the definite article with days (el jueves, el lunes). It can mean either 'Thursday' as a general day or a specific upcoming/past Thursday depending on context. Common with prepositions like hasta el jueves ('until Thursday').
target_language_example: Nos vemos el jueves por la tarde.
native_language_example: See you on Thursday afternoon.

additional_notes: Refers to the person who presides over a court and makes legal decisions. Even if the judge is a woman, Spanish often still uses the masculine article in this job title: "la juez" exists but is less common; you may also hear "la jueza" in some places.
target_language_example: El juez escuchó a los testigos antes de decidir.
native_language_example: The judge listened to the witnesses before deciding.

additional_notes: A masculine noun for someone who steals. The feminine form is "la ladrona". Common verbs with it include "robar" (to steal), "huir" (to flee), and "escaparse" (to get away).
target_language_example: El ladrón huyó cuando saltó la alarma.
native_language_example: The thief fled when the alarm went off.

additional_notes: A masculine noun meaning a body of water surrounded by land. Use with the definite article "el" when talking about a specific lake ("El lago es grande") and without it for general statements ("Un lago puede ser profundo"). Often followed by a proper name: "el lago Lemán".
target_language_example: Vamos a nadar en el lago mañana.
native_language_example: We’re going to swim in the lake tomorrow.

additional_notes: Refers to language in general as a human communication system (not a specific language like español/inglés). It can also mean “language” in a broader sense, like the way a group communicates (e.g., el lenguaje corporal = body language; el lenguaje técnico = technical jargon).
target_language_example: El lenguaje cambia con el tiempo.
native_language_example: Language changes over time.

additional_notes: A basic noun phrase for a specific book. "el" means "the" and is the masculine singular article used with "libro."
target_language_example: No encuentro el libro en la mesa.
native_language_example: I can't find the book on the table.

additional_notes: Used to state a fact about the book. "Es" (from "ser") can describe what it’s like (Es interesante), express “of” + noun (Es de gran valor / Es de la niña = belongs to the girl), or indicate language/content (Es en japonés = it’s in Japanese).
target_language_example: El libro es muy largo.
native_language_example: The book is very long.

meaning: "the book that/which" (introduces a description of the book).
additional_notes: Used when you identify a specific book by adding a relative clause with **que**: *el libro que…* = “the book that/which…”. **Que** here means “that/which” (not “what”). It can change for gender/number: *el libro que…*, *la revista que…*, *los libros que…*, *las revistas que…*.
target_language_example: ¿Dónde está el libro que me prestaste?
native_language_example: Where is the book that you lent me?

additional_notes: Refers to a specific place/location. Often used with adjectives like "correcto" (right/correct) or "bonito" (nice/beautiful): "el lugar correcto" = "the right place."
target_language_example: Este es el lugar donde nos conocimos.
native_language_example: This is the place where we met.

additional_notes: Used to say something happens on a specific Monday. With days of the week in Spanish, you often use "el" to mean "on" (el lunes, el martes, etc.).
target_language_example: Tengo una cita con el médico el lunes.
native_language_example: I have a doctor’s appointment on Monday.

additional_notes: Used to refer to the Monday of the previous week (before today). Often used with past tenses (e.g., fui, vi) or with desde to mean “since last Monday.” In Spanish you usually include the article: el lunes pasado.
target_language_example: Empecé el trabajo nuevo el lunes pasado.
native_language_example: I started the new job last Monday.

meaning: "on Monday in the …" (used before a time of day).
additional_notes: This phrase is typically incomplete by itself: you normally finish it with a time of day, most often "mañana" (morning), "tarde" (afternoon/evening), or "noche" (night). Examples: "el lunes por la mañana" = on Monday morning; "el lunes por la tarde" = on Monday afternoon/evening; "el lunes por la noche" = on Monday night.
target_language_example: El lunes por la mañana tengo clase.
native_language_example: On Monday morning I have class.

meaning: 'the teacher'; also 'the master' (an expert or respected guide).
additional_notes: Most commonly refers to a (male) teacher at school. It can also mean a master in an art/discipline (e.g., Zen) or a respected leader/mentor. Use "la maestra" for a female teacher/master. It’s also used in titles or nicknames before a name (e.g., "el maestro Howl").
target_language_example: El maestro nos explicó la tarea y luego escribió el ejemplo en la pizarra.
native_language_example: The teacher explained the homework to us and then wrote the example on the board.

additional_notes: Often used in a general, abstract sense as “evil” (opposite of el bien, “good”), especially in moral/religious/philosophical contexts: El mal está en todas partes. It can also mean “harm” or a negative force you protect against: un amuleto contra el mal. In some contexts, mal can refer to a specific “bad” condition or problem (e.g., a sickness or issue), but that’s usually clearer with context or other words.
target_language_example: Ella siempre lleva consigo un amuleto contra el mal.
native_language_example: She always carries an amulet against evil.

meaning: briefcase; small case/bag (often for carrying documents or something important).
additional_notes: A masculine noun (el maletín). Commonly refers to a briefcase used for work papers, but it can also mean a small case/bag used to carry something important. You’ll often see it with verbs like tener (to have), dar (to give), or estar en (to be in): “Está en el maletín” = “It’s in the briefcase.”
target_language_example: Dejé los documentos en el maletín.
native_language_example: I left the documents in the briefcase.

additional_notes: Uses the masculine singular definite article "el" with "mapa". Common for a physical map, a drawn map (e.g., a treasure map), or a map of a place ("el mapa de Brasil").
target_language_example: ¿Dónde está el mapa?
native_language_example: Where is the map?

additional_notes: A masculine noun phrase used to talk about large bodies of salt water. Often appears with prepositions like en (in/on), hacia (toward), and del (= de + el, “of/from the”) as in hacia el mar or del mar.
target_language_example: Los peces viven en el mar.
native_language_example: Fish live in the sea.

additional_notes: Use the definite article with days of the week to talk about a specific Tuesday: *el martes* = “(this/that) Tuesday” or “on Tuesday.” For recurring events, Spanish often uses plural: *los martes* = “on Tuesdays / every Tuesday.”
target_language_example: Tengo una cita el martes por la mañana.
native_language_example: I have an appointment on Tuesday morning.

meaning: marriage; the institution of being married.
additional_notes: Usually refers to marriage in general (the institution) or a specific marriage (a couple’s union). Also commonly means “the married couple” in some contexts, but in these examples it’s about marriage as an idea/institution (e.g., believing in marriage).
target_language_example: Para ella, el matrimonio es una decisión muy seria.
native_language_example: For her, marriage is a very serious decision.

additional_notes: Used with a masculine noun to mean the maximum degree of something: *el mayor problema* (“the biggest problem”), *el mayor éxito* (“the greatest success”).
