It can also be used as a noun meaning “the oldest (male person/child)”: *el mayor de los hermanos* (“the oldest of the siblings”). Don’t confuse **mayor** with the English “mayor” (city leader); in Spanish that’s usually **alcalde**.
target_language_example: Este es el mayor error que he cometido.
native_language_example: This is the biggest mistake I’ve made.

additional_notes: Masculine singular form of mejor when talking about the top person or thing in a group. It can go before a noun (el mejor plan) or stand alone when the noun is understood (este es el mejor). Common related forms are la mejor, los mejores, and las mejores.
target_language_example: Este restaurante es el mejor del barrio.
native_language_example: This restaurant is the best in the neighborhood.

el mejor día de mi vida

target_language_multi_word_term: el mejor día de mi vida
additional_notes: A fixed phrase to express that something is/was the happiest or most important day you’ve ever had. Common with different tenses: "Es/Hoy es el mejor día de mi vida" (it is/today is), "Fue/Ese fue" (it was/that was), "Ha sido" (it has been), "Había sido" (it had been). You can swap "mi" for another person: "de tu vida", "de su vida", "de nuestra vida".
target_language_example: Cuando me dieron la noticia, pensé: "Este es el mejor día de mi vida".
native_language_example: When they told me the news, I thought: “This is the best day of my life.”

meaning: the menu (list of food/drinks or options).
additional_notes: Used most often in restaurants to mean the list of dishes and drinks. It can also mean a set of choices/options in another context (like on a device or in a plan). Common related phrases: "menú infantil" (kids' menu), "cambiar el menú" (change the menu), "¿Me trae el menú?" (Could you bring me the menu?).
target_language_example: ¿Nos trae el menú, por favor?
native_language_example: Could you bring us the menu, please?

additional_notes: Often refers to (1) a physical place where goods are sold (a market), or (2) the economic “market” for a product (customers and demand), as in “estar en el mercado” (to be on the market/available for sale). It can also be used in a broader, more abstract sense to talk about the market economy.
target_language_example: Este teléfono ya está en el mercado, pero todavía es caro.
native_language_example: This phone is already on the market, but it’s still expensive.

additional_notes: Used to talk about something that happened in the previous month. It’s a time expression; it often goes at the beginning or end of the sentence (e.g., “El mes pasado fui…” / “Fui… el mes pasado”).
target_language_example: El mes pasado empecé un nuevo trabajo.
native_language_example: Last month I started a new job.

additional_notes: Used to talk about something happening in the month after the current one. It can go at the start or end of the sentence. Also common: "la semana que viene" (next week), "el año que viene" (next year).
target_language_example: Nos vemos el mes que viene para hablar del proyecto.
native_language_example: See you next month to talk about the project.

additional_notes: Used to talk about the city train system that runs underground or on dedicated tracks. Common with verbs like "tomar el metro" (to take the subway) and "ir en metro" (to go by subway). Also used when asking for directions: "¿Dónde está el metro?"
target_language_example: Para llegar al centro, toma el metro en esta estación.
native_language_example: To get downtown, take the subway at this station.

additional_notes: Used to say something is identical to another previously mentioned thing/person, or to emphasize that it’s exactly that one. It agrees in gender/number: el mismo (m. sg.), la misma (f. sg.), los mismos (m. pl.), las mismas (f. pl.). Often used before a noun: "el mismo auto" = "the same car."
target_language_example: ¿Es el mismo libro que leíste el año pasado?
native_language_example: Is it the same book you read last year?

additional_notes: Used to say that someone repeats an identical mistake (often with verbs like cometer (to make/commit), repetir (to repeat), or seguir (to keep doing)). With a comparison you’ll often see: "el mismo error que..." (“the same mistake as...”).
target_language_example: No quiero cometer el mismo error otra vez.
native_language_example: I don’t want to make the same mistake again.

additional_notes: Often used to talk about the exact time something happens, or the suitable/ideal time to do something. Common patterns: "ser el momento de + infinitive" (to be the time to do something), "llegar el momento" (the time will come).
target_language_example: No es el momento de discutir eso ahora.
native_language_example: This isn’t the time to argue about that now.

additional_notes: Most often refers to a vehicle’s engine (car, motorcycle, etc.). Common verbs: encender el motor (start/turn on the engine), apagar el motor (turn off the engine), dejar el motor andando/encendido (leave the engine running).
target_language_example: ¿Puedes apagar el motor, por favor?
native_language_example: Can you turn off the engine, please?

additional_notes: Refers to a male child or teenager, and sometimes a young man depending on context. In many places it’s a common alternative to “el chico.” Plural: “los muchachos” (the boys / the guys).
target_language_example: El muchacho está esperando afuera.
native_language_example: The boy is waiting outside.

additional_notes: A common noun phrase for the world. It can refer to the planet, human society, or everything in general depending on context.
target_language_example: Quiere viajar por el mundo.
native_language_example: He wants to travel around the world.

additional_notes: Literally “the entire world.” Used for emphasis to mean all people or all places (e.g., “everyone in the world will know”). It’s masculine singular, so you’ll often see it with singular verbs: “El mundo entero está…”.
target_language_example: El mundo entero estaba mirando el partido.
native_language_example: The whole world was watching the game.

meaning: part of “todo el mundo lo …” = “everyone … it”.
additional_notes: This is usually seen as a fragment inside a full sentence, most commonly **todo el mundo lo ...** (“everyone ... it”). **Todo el mundo** means “everyone” (literally “all the world”). **Lo** is a direct object pronoun meaning “it” or “him” (often “it/that” in general). Word order: **Todo el mundo lo + verb** (e.g., lo sabe = knows it).
target_language_example: Todo el mundo lo sabe.
native_language_example: Everyone knows it.

additional_notes: Used to emphasize that something is widely known. Often followed by a clause with "que" ("El mundo sabe que..."). You can also hear variations like "Todo el mundo sabe" (more common) or "medio mundo sabe" ("half the world knows").
target_language_example: Todo el mundo sabe que a Ana le encanta el chocolate.
native_language_example: Everyone knows that Ana loves chocolate.

additional_notes: A masculine noun, so it uses the article el (el museo / un museo). Commonly used when talking about visiting a museum, finding it in a city, or its opening hours (abierto/cerrado).
target_language_example: ¿A qué hora abre el museo?
native_language_example: What time does the museum open?

additional_notes: Superlative phrase meaning “the most big/great.” Use it to compare within a group: el más grande (masculine singular). It can mean physical size (“the biggest”) or importance/skill (“the greatest”). With nouns it often appears as “el más grande + noun” (e.g., el más grande pintor). Feminine/plural: la más grande, los más grandes, las más grandes.
target_language_example: De todos los edificios, este es el más grande.
native_language_example: Of all the buildings, this is the biggest.

additional_notes: Refers to a medical doctor. Often used when talking about your doctor or a doctor you visited (e.g., "Voy al médico" = "I’m going to the doctor"). Feminine form: "la médica" (also common: "la doctora").
target_language_example: Tengo cita con el médico mañana.
native_language_example: I have an appointment with the doctor tomorrow.

additional_notes: used to replace a masculine singular noun that has already been mentioned or is clear from context. It means “mine” or “my one” in English. The form agrees with the noun: el mío, la mía, los míos, las mías.
target_language_example: ¿Dónde está mi abrigo? El mío es negro.
native_language_example: Where is my coat? Mine is black.

additional_notes: Often means a business in general (“a company” or “the business side of something”), but in everyday speech it can also mean a small local shop. In the phrase “El negocio es el negocio,” it’s like “business is business,” meaning you make decisions based on business, not feelings. Plural: los negocios.
target_language_example: Tengo que abrir el negocio a las ocho.
native_language_example: I have to open the shop at eight.

additional_notes: A masculine singular noun phrase: el means "the" and niño means "boy" or sometimes "child." It usually refers to a male child; for a girl, use la niña.
target_language_example: El niño juega en el parque.
native_language_example: The boy is playing in the park.

meaning: “the name of the” (masculine singular: of the).
additional_notes: Used to introduce who/what something belongs to or refers to: el nombre del lugar (“the name of the place”), el nombre del caballo (“the horse’s name”). It’s a contraction of de + el → del, so you use it with masculine singular nouns (el lugar, el Señor). With feminine singular you use “de la” (el nombre de la casa), and with plural “de los/de las” (el nombre de los niños). Also appears in set religious phrases like “En el nombre del Padre…” (“In the name of the Father…”).
target_language_example: ¿Cuál es el nombre del hotel?
native_language_example: What is the name of the hotel?

additional_notes: Used before a masculine singular noun to mean “the new …” (e.g., el nuevo modelo, el nuevo programa). It agrees in gender/number: la nueva, los nuevos, las nuevas. It can also be used on its own as a noun-like phrase to mean “the new one” or “the new guy/person,” depending on context.
target_language_example: ¿Quién es el nuevo en la oficina?
native_language_example: Who is the new one in the office?

additional_notes: Used to talk about how many of something there are. Usually followed by a plural noun: el número de abejas/accidentes. With it, Spanish commonly uses a singular verb because the subject is número (singular): El número de abejas está disminuyendo. It can also appear in phrases like “sin importar el número de veces” (“no matter how many times”).
target_language_example: El número de estudiantes en la clase es de veinte.
native_language_example: The number of students in the class is twenty.

meaning: the goal; the target; the objective.
additional_notes: Used for an aim or purpose ("the goal") or for the person/thing being aimed at or targeted ("the target"). Common in formal contexts (plans, work, study) and also in security/military contexts (a target). Plural: los objetivos.
target_language_example: Ir a la universidad no es el objetivo de mi vida.
native_language_example: Going to university is not the goal of my life.

additional_notes: A masculine noun, so it uses **el** (singular) and **los** (plural: *los océanos*). Often used when talking about the sea, marine life, pollution, climate change, etc.
target_language_example: Me gusta nadar en el océano cuando hace calor.
native_language_example: I like to swim in the ocean when it’s hot.

additional_notes: A masculine noun meaning a strong negative feeling toward someone or something. Common patterns: **el odio a + noun** (“hatred of/toward”) and **el odio hacia + person/thing** (“hatred toward”). With **a + el** it contracts to **al**: **el odio al matrimonio** (“hatred of marriage”). Related verb: **odiar** (“to hate”).
target_language_example: Alimentar el odio es como tomar veneno esperando que le haga daño al otro.
native_language_example: Feeding hate is like drinking poison hoping it will harm the other person.

additional_notes: Refers to the eye, literally or sometimes figuratively. Because this term includes the article el, it often appears where English would use a possessive with body parts: cúbrete el ojo = cover your eye. In expressions like guiñar el ojo, it means to wink.
target_language_example: Me duele mucho el ojo izquierdo.
native_language_example: My left eye hurts a lot.

additional_notes: A masculine noun (el olor). Often followed by "a" + noun to say what something smells like: "el olor a sudor" = "the smell of sweat." Use adjectives to describe it: agradable (pleasant), desagradable (unpleasant), espantoso (awful).
target_language_example: No soporto el olor a humo en la ropa.
native_language_example: I can’t stand the smell of smoke on clothes.

additional_notes: Common in Spain for “computer”; in much of Latin America, “computer” is usually “la computadora” or “el computador.” Use “el” because it’s masculine: el ordenador / los ordenadores.
target_language_example: Voy a encender el ordenador para buscar el horario del tren.
native_language_example: I'm going to turn on the computer to look up the train schedule.

additional_notes: Usually refers to the precious metal (“gold”). In sports/competitions, “ganar el oro” means “to win gold” (i.e., the gold medal).
target_language_example: Quiere ganar el oro en la próxima carrera.
native_language_example: He/She wants to win gold in the next race.

meaning: "the other day" (a recent day in the past).
additional_notes: Used to refer to a non-specific recent time in the past (often a few days ago). It’s commonly used to set the time of a past event. In some contexts (like "Gracias por el otro día"), it refers back to a recent meeting/occasion you both remember.
target_language_example: El otro día te vi en el supermercado, pero tenías prisa.
native_language_example: The other day I saw you at the supermarket, but you were in a hurry.

additional_notes: Used to refer to the opposite side of something (a street, a wall, the Moon) or the opposing side in a conflict (“the other side”). Often appears with de: “el otro lado de la calle / de la Luna”.
target_language_example: Nos vemos en el otro lado de la calle.
native_language_example: See you on the other side of the street.

additional_notes: Used for the remaining person or thing, often when the noun is left out because it is clear from context. It can also refer to a place or side, as in el otro lado (“the other side”). For feminine nouns, use la otra.
target_language_example: No quiero este; prefiero el otro.
native_language_example: I don't want this one; I prefer the other one.

meaning: the patient (a person receiving medical care).
additional_notes: Used in medical contexts (doctor, hospital, treatment) to refer to someone who is ill or injured and is being treated. Feminine form: la paciente. Can also be used more generally for “patient” (someone who waits calmly), but in everyday speech it most often refers to the medical meaning.
target_language_example: El doctor dijo que el paciente está estable.
native_language_example: The doctor said the patient is stable.

additional_notes: Used to identify someone as another person's father. It’s followed by a noun or name (el padre de Peng) or a pronoun: "él/ella" (formal/neutral) or "mi/tu/su" + noun (el padre de mi hijo). Note: in sentence 2, "fue el padre de mi hijo" means "was the father of my son" (biological/legal parent), not a job title.
target_language_example: Él es el padre de Ana.
native_language_example: He is Ana’s father.

additional_notes: A masculine noun, so it uses el: el pan. In plural: los panes (“the breads/loaves”). Commonly used with types of bread: pan blanco (white bread), pan integral (whole wheat bread).
target_language_example: ¿Puedes comprar el pan para la cena?
native_language_example: Can you buy the bread for dinner?

meaning: "the paper"; also "the role" (in a play/movie), and sometimes "the document/paperwork" depending on context.
additional_notes: Most commonly refers to the material you write or draw on (e.g., "en el papel" = on paper). In acting/theater, "hacer" or "interpretar" + "el papel de" + character means to play that character’s role. In bureaucratic contexts, "el papel" can mean a required document ("obtener el papel" = get the document).
target_language_example: Tom dibujó una línea recta en el papel.
native_language_example: Tom drew a straight line on the paper.

meaning: the role/part of (in a play, movie, etc.).
additional_notes: Used with verbs like hacer or interpretar to talk about acting a character: hacer el papel de X / interpretar el papel de X. You can also talk about learning the lines: Sé el papel de memoria (“I know the role/part by heart”).
target_language_example: Ella hizo el papel de doctora en la película.
native_language_example: She played the role of a doctor in the movie.

meaning: the package; the parcel; the packet.
additional_notes: Refers to something wrapped or contained (a parcel in the mail, a package you send/receive, or a packet/container of something). Common with shipping verbs like "enviar" (to send) and "recoger" (to pick up).
target_language_example: ¿Ya llegó el paquete que pediste?
native_language_example: Did the package you ordered already arrive?

additional_notes: Used when talking about an umbrella that someone left behind on the bus. It often appears with verbs like dejar(se) (“to leave behind”) or olvidar(se) (“to forget”), e.g., “Me he dejado el paraguas en el autobús” = “I left my umbrella on the bus.”
target_language_example: Creo que me he dejado el paraguas en el autobús.
native_language_example: I think I left my umbrella on the bus.

additional_notes: Used literally for a religious/spiritual “heaven” (often after death: “su alma está en el paraíso”) and figuratively for an ideal, wonderful situation (“esto es el paraíso”, “otro día en el paraíso”). You may also hear the set phrase “problemas en el paraíso” meaning that something isn’t as perfect as it seems.
target_language_example: Estar aquí contigo es el paraíso.
native_language_example: Being here with you is paradise.

additional_notes: Refers to a public park. Uses the masculine singular definite article "el". Spanish commonly uses the definite article when referring to a specific park understood from context.
target_language_example: El parque está lleno de niños.
native_language_example: The park is full of children.

additional_notes: Used for a sports match (e.g., soccer, basketball). Common with verbs like jugar (to play), ganar/perder (to win/lose), and celebrarse (to be held). Also used with tickets: entradas para el partido.
target_language_example: ¿A qué hora empieza el partido?
native_language_example: What time does the game start?

additional_notes: Used for a scheduled soccer match/event. In many Spanish-speaking countries, “fútbol” usually means soccer (not American football). You’ll often hear it with verbs like ver (to watch), jugarse (to be played), and posponerse (to be postponed).
target_language_example: ¿A qué hora empieza el partido de fútbol?
native_language_example: What time does the soccer game start?

additional_notes: Used to talk about earlier times or what has already happened. Often appears in contrasts like "el pasado" vs. "el futuro" (the future), and with verbs like "olvidar" (to forget) or "recordar" (to remember).
target_language_example: No quiero hablar del pasado ahora.
native_language_example: I don't want to talk about the past right now.

additional_notes: Most commonly refers to a cake (often a whole cake you bake/serve and then slice). In some regions, "pastel" can also refer to a pastry or even a savory pie, so context matters. Common collocations include "cortar el pastel" (to cut the cake) and "sacar el pastel del horno" (to take the cake out of the oven).
target_language_example: Corta el pastel con ese cuchillo.
native_language_example: Cut the cake with that knife.

additional_notes: Used to talk about a nation/state as a whole (its territory and people). It can also mean “the countryside” in some contexts (like being out of the city), but in these examples it means “country” (e.g., leaving the country; the whole country).
target_language_example: No puedo viajar porque no tengo pasaporte para salir del país.
native_language_example: I can’t travel because I don’t have a passport to leave the country.

meaning: the chest; the breast (front of the torso).
additional_notes: Refers to the front upper part of the body (between neck and stomach). Common in health contexts (dolor en el pecho = chest pain) and to describe body features (pecho peludo = hairy chest). For women, "pecho" can also mean "breast," but "la mama" is more specific/medical.
target_language_example: Me duele el pecho cuando respiro hondo.
native_language_example: My chest hurts when I take a deep breath.

additional_notes: Means “hair” (especially hair on your head). Spanish often uses the definite article with body parts (el/la) where English uses a possessive: “Me lavo el pelo” = “I wash my hair.” In “tener el pelo de punta,” it means your hair is standing on end (from fear, cold, surprise, etc.).
target_language_example: Me corté el pelo ayer.
native_language_example: I got my hair cut yesterday.

additional_notes: Refers to a newspaper (print or, sometimes, the news outlet behind it). In Spanish you normally use the definite article: leer el periódico = “to read the newspaper.” Can also mean “(for) the newspaper” in contexts like publicar en el periódico (“to publish in the newspaper”).
target_language_example: Mi abuelo lee el periódico todas las mañanas.
native_language_example: My grandpa reads the newspaper every morning.

additional_notes: A basic noun phrase for a specific dog. "El" is the masculine singular word for "the," and "perro" means "dog."
target_language_example: El perro duerme en el jardín.
native_language_example: The dog is sleeping in the garden.

meaning: “the dog is …” (using estar for location or a temporary/ongoing action).
additional_notes: Use **estar** (not ser) to say where someone/thing is or what they’re doing right now. Very common patterns: **El perro está + en/al lado de…** (location) and **El perro está + gerundio** (present continuous), e.g. **está ladrando/saltando/dando vueltas**.
target_language_example: El perro está durmiendo en el sofá.
native_language_example: The dog is sleeping on the couch.

additional_notes: Usually refers to fish you eat (fish meat), especially in everyday contexts like liking it, buying it, or saying it’s healthy/expensive. It’s masculine singular (el); plural: los pescados. Contrast: el pez = a fish (the animal) when talking about it alive.
target_language_example: Hoy vamos a comer el pescado con arroz.
native_language_example: Today we’re going to eat fish with rice.

additional_notes: Refers to the body part (foot). Often appears with actions done using your foot: "con el pie" (with your foot) or "darle con el pie" (kick it / hit it with your foot). Common idiom: "levantarse con el pie incorrecto" = to get up on the wrong foot (to start the day in a bad mood).
target_language_example: Me duele el pie porque caminé mucho.
native_language_example: My foot hurts because I walked a lot.

meaning: 'the left foot'; also (idiom) 'the wrong foot' / 'a bad start'.
additional_notes: Literal meaning: the left foot (used with pain, numbness, injuries, etc.): *Me duele el pie izquierdo.* Idiomatic meaning: when used with verbs like **empezar** or **levantarse** (often **empezar con el pie izquierdo**, **levantarse con el pie izquierdo**), it means things started off badly or someone woke up in a bad mood.
target_language_example: La reunión empezó con el pie izquierdo y hubo muchos problemas desde el principio.
native_language_example: The meeting got off to a bad start and there were lots of problems from the beginning.

additional_notes: In these examples, "el piso" refers to the surface you walk on indoors. It’s common with cleaning verbs like "barrer" (to sweep): "Barrer el piso" = "to sweep the floor." (In other contexts, "piso" can also mean "apartment" in some countries, but here it clearly means "floor".)
target_language_example: Hay agua en el piso, ten cuidado.
native_language_example: There’s water on the floor—be careful.

meaning: the plan; a plan (idea/strategy for doing something).
additional_notes: Usually refers to an arrangement or strategy that has been decided (or is being discussed): conversar/discutir el plan, mantener el plan en secreto. Common fixed phrase: "Todo va según el plan" = "Everything is going according to plan."
target_language_example: Mantén el plan en secreto, porque todavía puede haber cambios.
native_language_example: Keep the plan secret, because there could still be changes.

meaning: power; the ability/authority to do something.
additional_notes:
Commonly used with:
- "el poder de + infinitive" = the power/ability to do something ("el poder de amar").
- "tener el poder (para) + infinitive" = to have the power/ability ("Tengo el poder para construir...").
- "tomar el poder" = to seize/take power (often political control).
It can mean personal ability/strength, legal authority, or political power depending on context.
target_language_example: No tienes el poder para cambiar el pasado.
native_language_example: You don't have the power to change the past.

additional_notes: Used to talk about an ability or capacity. It’s usually followed by an infinitive (el poder de + verb, e.g., el poder de cambiar “the power to change”) or by a noun (el poder de + noun, e.g., el poder de la mente “the power of the mind”).
target_language_example: Todos tenemos el poder de cambiar nuestras vidas.
native_language_example: We all have the power to change our lives.

meaning: "the power of the" (of a masculine singular noun).
additional_notes: Used to talk about someone’s or something’s strength, ability, influence, or authority. It’s made of el poder (the power) + del, which is the contraction of de + el (“of the”). Use del before a masculine singular noun: el poder del rey, el poder del fuego. For feminine singular nouns, use de la: el poder de la magia.
target_language_example: Conoces el poder del dinero.
native_language_example: You know the power of money.

additional_notes: Refers to how much something costs. Common patterns: "el precio de + [thing]" (the price of...), "subir/bajar el precio" (raise/lower the price). It can also be used figuratively for "the price" of something in life (a consequence or sacrifice), e.g., "el precio de la fama".
target_language_example: El precio de este boleto incluye impuestos.
native_language_example: The price of this ticket includes taxes.

additional_notes: Used before a masculine singular noun to talk about how much something costs or how its price changes (sube, baja, aumenta, cae, varía). For feminine nouns, use “el precio de la” (e.g., el precio de la gasolina). Can also be used figuratively: “el precio del pecado…”.
target_language_example: El precio del billete incluye impuestos.
native_language_example: The price of the ticket includes taxes.

additional_notes: Used for something you win or receive for being the best (a contest, competition, raffle, etc.). Common with verbs like ganar (to win) and recibir (to receive), and in phrases like el premio fue para… (the prize went to…). It can also mean an “award” like at a ceremony.
target_language_example: Si estudias mucho, puedes ganar el premio.
native_language_example: If you study a lot, you can win the prize.

additional_notes: Used for the head of a country or organization. Often followed by "de" + a place/organization ("el presidente de Francia"). When used in the news or in context, "el presidente" can mean "the current president" without naming them. Feminine form: "la presidenta".
target_language_example: Mañana el presidente dará un discurso en la televisión.
native_language_example: Tomorrow the president will give a speech on TV.

additional_notes: Used with masculine singular nouns that come right after it: el primer año, el primer giro. It’s a shortened form of “primero” used before the noun. For feminine nouns, use “la primera …” (la primera vez).
target_language_example: Este es el primer día de clases.
native_language_example: This is the first day of class.

additional_notes: Used to talk about the beginning of something (a trip, job, relationship, etc.). In the expression “el primer día del resto de mi/tu vida” it means “the first day of the rest of my/your life,” often said to mark a fresh start. Also common in comparisons like “como el primer día” = “like on the first day,” especially about feelings staying the same over time.
target_language_example: Hoy es el primer día de mi nuevo trabajo.
native_language_example: Today is the first day of my new job.

meaning: “the first step” (the initial action in a process).
additional_notes: Used to talk about starting a process (solving a problem, learning something, making a change). Often followed by “para + infinitive” (el primer paso para resolver...) or “consiste en + infinitive” (el primer paso consiste en reconocer...).
target_language_example: El primer paso para mejorar es pedir ayuda.
native_language_example: The first step to improving is asking for help.

additional_notes: Used in contests, competitions, raffles, etc. It refers to the highest prize/award. Often used with verbs like ganar (to win) and obtener (to receive).
target_language_example: Si practicas mucho, quizá ganes el primer premio.
native_language_example: If you practice a lot, maybe you’ll win first prize.

meaning: the first train (usually of the day).
additional_notes: Refers to the earliest scheduled train, often in the morning: “tomar/coger el primer tren” = “to take/catch the first train.” It can imply getting up early to leave as soon as possible.
target_language_example: Si queremos llegar a tiempo, tenemos que tomar el primer tren.
native_language_example: If we want to arrive on time, we have to take the first train.

additional_notes: Used for a masculine person or thing that comes before all others in order, time, or importance. When it comes directly before a masculine singular noun, Spanish usually uses primer instead: el primer día, not el primero día. As a standalone phrase, el primero means 'the first one.'
target_language_example: Juan fue el primero en llegar.
native_language_example: Juan was the first to arrive.

additional_notes: Used to identify the first person/thing that does an action, followed by a verb phrase (a relative clause): «El primero que llega…». It agrees with the noun/person: «la primera que…» (feminine), «los primeros que…» (plural), etc. In English it’s often translated as “the first to + verb” (e.g., “the first to arrive”).
target_language_example: El primero que termine el examen puede salir.
native_language_example: The first person to finish the exam can leave.

meaning: the beginning; the start (also: a guiding principle).
additional_notes: Most commonly means “the beginning/start,” often in phrases like “al principio” (at first/in the beginning) or “es/eso es sólo el principio” (it/that’s only the beginning). It can also mean “principle” as in a rule or guiding idea, but in your examples it’s mainly about the start of something (including figuratively).
target_language_example: Tranquilo: esto es sólo el principio.
native_language_example: Relax: this is only the beginning.

additional_notes: A common noun phrase for a difficulty, issue, or obstacle. Even though problema ends in -a, it is masculine: el problema, un problema. It can also identify the source of trouble, as in Ella es el problema or Tom es el problema.
target_language_example: Ese es el problema.
native_language_example: That's the problem.

additional_notes: Used to point out an obstacle or the reason something can’t happen. It’s often followed by a clause with que + verb: “El problema es que no tengo tiempo.” You can also use it to politely disagree or bring up a concern before giving an explanation.
target_language_example: Quiero ir, pero el problema es que mañana trabajo temprano.
native_language_example: I want to go, but the problem is that I work early tomorrow.

additional_notes: Commonly refers to a male teacher/professor. Use **la profesora** for a female teacher/professor. In many Spanish-speaking contexts, **profesor** can mean a school teacher as well as a university professor; context tells you which.
target_language_example: El profesor nos explicó la lección con paciencia.
native_language_example: The teacher explained the lesson to us patiently.

additional_notes: Used for a planned piece of work or an organized effort (at school, at work, or a construction/engineering plan). Common collocations: "el proyecto de construcción" (construction project), "terminar el proyecto" (finish the project), "el proyecto continúa" (the project continues), "estar en marcha" (to be underway).
target_language_example: Tenemos que terminar el proyecto esta semana.
native_language_example: We have to finish the project this week.

additional_notes: Used for the next person, thing, or time in a sequence. Before a masculine singular noun, it means "next" (el próximo tren = the next train). When the noun is omitted, el próximo means "the next one." It changes with gender and number: la próxima, los próximos, las próximas.
target_language_example: Tomamos el próximo.
native_language_example: We'll take the next one.

additional_notes: Used to talk about something that will happen in the year after the current one. Often paired with the future tense (tendré) or with "ir a" + infinitive (voy a trabajar) to express future plans.
target_language_example: El próximo año vamos a mudarnos a otro país.
native_language_example: Next year we’re going to move to another country.

additional_notes: Used to talk about the weekend immediately following the current time. Often appears after verbs in the future (va a…, vendrá, espero que…). You can also say “este fin de semana” for “this weekend.”
target_language_example: ¿Qué vas a hacer el próximo fin de semana?
native_language_example: What are you going to do next weekend?

additional_notes: Used to talk about the Monday after today. It’s common with future plans and schedules (events starting, meetings, visits). In many contexts it matches English “next Monday.” If you need to be extra clear, you can say “este lunes” for “this Monday” (the coming Monday) vs. “el lunes siguiente” for “the following Monday” (after a specific Monday already mentioned).
target_language_example: Tengo una cita con el médico el próximo lunes.
native_language_example: I have a doctor’s appointment next Monday.

additional_notes: Used to talk about something happening in the month after the current one. Common with future expressions like "va a" (is going to), the simple future ("saldrá", "terminará"), and scheduled events.
target_language_example: Nos mudamos el próximo mes.
native_language_example: We’re moving next month.

additional_notes: “Pueblo” can mean either a (usually small) town/village or “the people” (the general population). Context tells you which: with verbs like “dejar / volver / llegar” it often means “town” (Tom dejó el pueblo = he left the town), while in political or social contexts it can mean “the people” (Yo no soy el pueblo = I’m not the people / I don’t represent the people).
target_language_example: El pueblo es pequeño, pero hay de todo.
native_language_example: The town is small, but it has everything.

additional_notes: A common noun for a bridge; it’s masculine, so it uses el/un (el puente, un puente). Often used with en to mean “on/at the bridge” (en el puente) when talking about meeting or where something happened.
target_language_example: Hay un restaurante cerca del puente.
native_language_example: There’s a restaurant near the bridge.

additional_notes: Used for a job position, role, or post that someone can get, lose, compete for, or be offered (e.g., ganar el puesto, perder el puesto, ofrecer el puesto). It can also mean a physical “stall/stand” (like a market stand), but in these examples it clearly means a job/position.
target_language_example: Si consigo el puesto, empiezo el lunes.
native_language_example: If I get the position, I start on Monday.

additional_notes: Refers to a group of people as spectators/listeners (at a show, game, speech, etc.) or to people in general (“the public”). Often used with verbs like aplaudir (to applaud), aburrirse (to get bored), ver (to see), and admirar (to admire).
target_language_example: El público guardó silencio durante el discurso.
native_language_example: The audience fell silent during the speech.

additional_notes: A common noun phrase: "el" (the) + "queso" (cheese). Used for cheese in general or a specific cheese already known from context (e.g., "el queso de cabra" = goat cheese). In some contexts people may say things like "Eres el queso" jokingly (literally "You are the cheese"), but it’s not a standard set compliment everywhere.
target_language_example: ¿Puedes pasarme el queso, por favor?
native_language_example: Can you pass me the cheese, please?

additional_notes: "El reloj" can mean either a clock (on a wall/table) or a watch (worn on your wrist). Context usually makes it clear (e.g., "el reloj de mi padre" is often a watch). Common related phrase: "¿Qué hora es?" (What time is it?).
target_language_example: El reloj de mi padre está atrasado.
native_language_example: My father's watch is running slow.

meaning: “the watch that/which …” (a watch with a description after it).
additional_notes: Used when you add a relative clause with **que** to identify or describe **el reloj**: *el reloj que compré* (“the watch that I bought”). **Que** here means “that/which” and is used for people or things. It doesn’t usually translate as a separate word in very natural English, but Spanish needs it to connect the noun to the clause.
target_language_example: No encuentro el reloj que me regalaste.
native_language_example: I can’t find the watch you gave me.

additional_notes: Uses the masculine singular article "el". You’ll often see it with location phrases ("está en...", "estaba lejos de...") and status words like "abierto/cerrado" (open/closed) or "vacío" (empty).
target_language_example: El restaurante está abierto hasta las diez.
native_language_example: The restaurant is open until ten.

additional_notes: Means “the rest (of it/them).” Often used by itself when the context is clear (“Ya sabes el resto.” = “You know the rest.”). You can also use it with "de" to mean “the rest of …”: "el resto de + noun" ("el resto de la frase" = “the rest of the sentence”).
target_language_example: No entiendo esta parte, pero el resto sí.
native_language_example: I don’t understand this part, but I do understand the rest.

additional_notes: Used to talk about the final effect, answer, or score of something (an exam, investigation, experiment, etc.). Very common pattern: "el resultado de + [thing]" (the result of...).
target_language_example: Todavía no sabemos el resultado del partido.
native_language_example: We still don't know the result of the game.

additional_notes: Used to talk about what something leads to or produces. Often followed by a noun ("el resultado de la guerra") or a longer phrase ("el resultado de todas las decisiones..."). You’ll also see it in cause-and-effect statements: "X es el resultado de Y" ("X is the result of Y").
target_language_example: El cansancio que siento hoy es el resultado de haber dormido poco.
native_language_example: The tiredness I feel today is the result of sleeping little.

additional_notes: Refers to a male monarch/ruler. Often used with a place or title: “el rey de + [country/city]” = “the king of …”. In Spanish you normally include the article: “el rey” (not just “rey”) when talking about a specific king.
target_language_example: El rey de España visitó la ciudad ayer.
native_language_example: The king of Spain visited the city yesterday.

meaning: "the king of" (ruler of a place; also "the best/most important of" something).
additional_notes: Used with a place or group: "el rey de Jerusalén" = the king of Jerusalem, "el rey de los animales" = the king of the animals. It can be literal (an actual monarch) or figurative to mean the top/best/most dominant. In card games, "rey" is also the "king" card (e.g., "el rey de picas" = the king of spades).
target_language_example: Mi hermano cree que es el rey de la cocina.
native_language_example: My brother thinks he's the king of the kitchen.

meaning: the risk of; the possibility of (something bad) happening.
additional_notes: Often used in the common expression **correr el riesgo de + infinitive** (“to run the risk of / to risk + -ing”): *Corres el riesgo de perder tu trabajo.* You can also use **hay el riesgo de...** (“there is a risk of...”).
target_language_example: No quiero correr el riesgo de llegar tarde.
native_language_example: I don’t want to risk arriving late.

meaning: the color red; the red one.
additional_notes: Uses the definite article (el) to talk about the color red as a noun ("Red is better") or to refer to the red option/object when choosing between items ("Buy me the red one"). Often paired with other colors: "el rojo y el verde". In instructions, it can refer to a red button/light (e.g., red = stop).
target_language_example: ¿Cuál prefieres, el rojo o el azul?
native_language_example: Which do you prefer, the red one or the blue one?

meaning: “the noise” (a sound, often annoying or loud).
additional_notes: Masculine noun: el ruido. Used for an unwanted/loud sound (e.g., traffic, a bang). Common with verbs like: hacer ruido (to make noise), oír un ruido (to hear a noise), despertar por el ruido (to wake up because of the noise), el ruido me pone nervioso (the noise makes me nervous).
target_language_example: No puedo dormir por el ruido de la calle.
native_language_example: I can’t sleep because of the noise from the street.

additional_notes: A masculine noun (el rumor). Used for information people are saying that hasn’t been confirmed. Common with verbs like circular/estar por todas partes (“to be everywhere”), extenderse (“to spread”), and resultar ser + adj. (“to turn out to be…”).
target_language_example: No creas el rumor hasta que haya pruebas.
native_language_example: Don’t believe the rumor until there’s proof.

additional_notes: Refers to a river. Used with the masculine singular definite article el. In Spanish, río has an accent mark (río).
target_language_example: Vamos a nadar en el río mañana.
native_language_example: We’re going to swim in the river tomorrow.

additional_notes: A noun phrase used for hidden information that someone doesn’t want others to know. Often appears with verbs like saber/conocer (to know), guardar (to keep), revelar (to reveal), and with the expression “salir a la luz” (to come to light).
target_language_example: No le digas a nadie el secreto.
native_language_example: Don’t tell anyone the secret.

additional_notes: Used as an ordinal number for a masculine noun (e.g., "el segundo mes" = "the second month"). For feminine nouns, use "la segunda". You’ll also hear "el segundo" by itself to mean “the second one” (the second item/person).
target_language_example: Él llegó el segundo en la carrera.
native_language_example: He came in second in the race.

meaning: the traffic light on red (red light).
additional_notes: Used to refer to the situation/status of a traffic light showing red, meaning you must stop. Often used with verbs like ver (to see), parar/pararse (to stop), saltarse (to run/ignore), and pasarse (to go through/run).
target_language_example: No cruces; el semáforo en rojo significa que tienes que parar.
native_language_example: Don’t cross; the red light means you have to stop.

additional_notes: Used as a polite title before a man’s last name (el señor Smith = Mr. Smith). It can also refer respectfully to an adult man in general (“el señor de la mesa 3”). Often contrasts with la señora (Mrs./Ms.) and la señorita (Miss). As a direct form of address, Spanish typically uses “señor” without the article (Disculpe, señor...).
target_language_example: Me gustaría dejar un mensaje para el señor Alexander.
native_language_example: I’d like to leave a message for Mr. Alexander.

additional_notes: Used to refer to the next item in a sequence (next day, next Tuesday, next train, the next one to take, the next meeting, etc.). It agrees with the noun: el siguiente (masc. sing.), la siguiente (fem. sing.), los siguientes, las siguientes. Often used before time words: el siguiente día, el siguiente martes.
target_language_example: No llego a tiempo; voy a coger el siguiente tren.
native_language_example: I won’t make it on time; I’m going to take the next train.

meaning: “the system” (an organized set of parts, rules, or processes).
additional_notes: Used for many kinds of systems: a machine/technical system (el sistema de ventilación), a computer/AI system, or an institutional system (e.g., healthcare, education, legal). It’s masculine singular: el sistema; plural: los sistemas.
target_language_example: El sistema no responde, así que voy a reiniciarlo.
native_language_example: The system isn’t responding, so I’m going to restart it.

additional_notes: Used for the paper cover you put a letter or documents in (often for mailing). Common with verbs like abrir (to open), entregar (to hand in/return), and escribir la dirección en el sobre (to write the address on the envelope).
target_language_example: ¿Pusiste la carta en el sobre?
native_language_example: Did you put the letter in the envelope?

additional_notes: Usually refers to the sun in the sky. Common with verbs like salir (to rise) and ponerse (to set), e.g. "sale el sol" / "se pone el sol". In "tomar el sol", it means "to sunbathe" (literally "to take the sun").
target_language_example: Hoy no veo el sol porque está nublado.
native_language_example: Today I can't see the sun because it's cloudy.

additional_notes: A masculine noun (el). Often used with clothing verbs like ponerse (to put on) and quitarse (to take off): Quítate el sombrero. / Se quitó el sombrero. It can refer to many kinds of hats (not just a cowboy hat).
target_language_example: Me gusta el sombrero, ¿dónde lo compraste?
native_language_example: I like the hat—where did you buy it?

additional_notes: Used to introduce what is making the sound (a voice, a bell, a battle, etc.). It often takes a noun after de: el sonido de la campana (the sound of the bell). You can also use it with a clause that identifies the source: Fue el sonido de la campana lo que le despertó (It was the sound of the bell that woke him up).
target_language_example: Me relajó el sonido de la lluvia.
native_language_example: The sound of the rain relaxed me.

additional_notes: Means the surface you walk on. It can refer to the floor inside a building ("Barrer el suelo" = sweep the floor) or the ground/soil outside ("El sol ha secado el suelo" = the sun dried out the ground/soil). Common phrases: "en el suelo" = on the ground; "caer al suelo" = to fall to the ground.
target_language_example: Dejé la mochila en el suelo.
native_language_example: I left the backpack on the floor.

additional_notes: A possessive pronoun used to replace a noun and avoid repeating it. It agrees in gender/number with the thing owned, not with the owner: el suyo (masc. singular), la suya, los suyos, las suyas. Often contrasts with another person’s possession: “Este es mi libro, no el suyo.”
target_language_example: Mi teléfono es nuevo, pero el suyo es más viejo.
native_language_example: My phone is new, but theirs is older.

additional_notes: Used to talk about Saturday. With days of the week in Spanish, you often use the article: el sábado = on Saturday / Saturday (this Saturday or Saturdays in general, depending on context). You can add time words like pasado (last) or próximo/que viene (next): el sábado pasado = last Saturday.
target_language_example: ¿Tienes planes el sábado?
native_language_example: Do you have plans on Saturday?

additional_notes: A room or level below the ground floor of a building. Often used with location verbs like estar (“to be”): Está/Están en el sótano (“He/She is / They are in the basement”). It can also refer to a safe place (e.g., during storms) or a dark/dirty storage area, depending on context.
target_language_example: Guardamos las cajas viejas en el sótano.
native_language_example: We keep the old boxes in the basement.

meaning: the theater; theatre (the building or the art form).
additional_notes: Usually refers either to the place where plays/performances happen (a theater) or to theater as an activity/art form. Common with prepositions: en el teatro (at/in the theater).
target_language_example: El teatro está vacío.
native_language_example: The theater is empty.

additional_notes: Usually means "the ceiling" when talking about the inside/top of a room (e.g., something is on the ceiling). It can also mean "the roof" when talking about the top of a building, often outdoors (e.g., cats on the roof).
target_language_example: Hay una lámpara en el techo.
native_language_example: There is a lamp on the ceiling.

meaning: the roof (top covering of a building/house).
additional_notes: Refers to the exterior roof structure (often a sloped/tiled roof). Common patterns: "el tejado de + (house/building)" and "estar en el tejado" (to be on the roof). "A dos aguas" describes a gabled roof (two sloping sides).
target_language_example: Hay una gotera en el tejado.
native_language_example: There’s a leak in the roof.

additional_notes: Refers to a telephone/phone in general (landline or mobile, depending on context). Common with verbs like sonar (to ring), colgar (to hang up), and caer(se) (to drop/fall).
target_language_example: No encuentro el teléfono; creo que lo dejé en el coche.
native_language_example: I can’t find the phone; I think I left it in the car.

additional_notes: Uses the preterite of sonar (“to ring/sound”) to describe a completed event: the phone rang (once/at that moment). Often used to set the scene with another action in progress (e.g., estaba/tomaba… cuando el teléfono sonó). For repeated ringing, you’ll often add phrases like varias veces (“several times”) or cada pocos minutos (“every few minutes”).
target_language_example: Estaba cocinando cuando el teléfono sonó.
native_language_example: I was cooking when the phone rang.

additional_notes: Used to refer to what people are talking about or the subject of a class/text (“el tema de la clase”). It can also mean an issue under discussion or debate (“el tema del aborto”). Common with verbs like cambiar/poner/retirar/dejar el tema and phrases like “sobre el tema” (about the topic) and “no tener voz en el tema” (not having a say in the matter).
target_language_example: No quiero hablar de el tema ahora.
native_language_example: I don’t want to talk about the topic right now.

additional_notes: This expression can refer to either time in general or the weather, depending on context. In phrases like perder el tiempo and pasar el tiempo, it means time. When talking about rain, sun, wind, or temperature, it usually means the weather.
target_language_example: Parece que el tiempo va a mejorar.
native_language_example: It looks like the weather is going to improve.

meaning: "time will tell" (we’ll know in the future).
additional_notes: Used to say that the truth or outcome isn’t known yet and will become clear later. Often appears as a standalone comment (El tiempo dirá.) or followed by si + clause: Solo el tiempo dirá si…
target_language_example: El tiempo dirá si esta decisión fue la correcta.
native_language_example: Time will tell if this decision was the right one.

additional_notes: Common, fixed expression used to say that time seems to go by very fast. Often used as an exclamation: “¡Cómo vuela el tiempo!” or “¡El tiempo vuela!” It’s usually figurative, not literally about something flying.
target_language_example: Ya es viernes otra vez; el tiempo vuela.
native_language_example: It’s Friday again already; time flies.

additional_notes: In home/entrance contexts, "tocar el timbre" or "llamar al timbre" means “to ring the doorbell.” ("Timbre" can also mean other things like a postage stamp in some contexts, but in these examples it’s clearly the doorbell.)
target_language_example: Si nadie abre, toca el timbre otra vez.
native_language_example: If nobody opens, ring the doorbell again.

additional_notes: Common, fairly informal way to refer to a man/person (similar to “guy”). Depending on tone and context, it can sound neutral or a bit dismissive (“that guy”). Note: "tipo" can also mean “type/kind” (e.g., "un tipo de comida" = “a type of food”), but in your examples it means “guy/man.”
target_language_example: ¿Quién es el tipo de la chaqueta azul?
native_language_example: Who’s the guy in the blue jacket?

meaning: the kind/type of; the sort of.
additional_notes: Used to classify or describe a category: "el tipo de deportes" (the type of sports), "el tipo de verde" (the shade/kind of green), "el tipo de persona" (the kind of person). With people, it can mean "the kind of person who...": "No es el tipo de hombre que...". In some contexts (especially in speech), "el tipo" can also mean "the guy," but that’s slightly different from the phrase "el tipo de".
target_language_example: No es el tipo de comida que me gusta.
native_language_example: It’s not the kind of food I like.

additional_notes: Uses "tipo" (literally "type") in a common, casual way to mean "guy" or "a person". It introduces a relative clause with "que" to describe which person you mean: "el tipo que + verb..." (the person who...). Can sound a bit informal or blunt depending on context; more neutral options include "el hombre que" (the man who) or "la persona que" (the person who).
target_language_example: El tipo que trabaja en recepción siempre nos ayuda.
native_language_example: The guy who works at reception always helps us.

additional_notes: Refers to work, labor, or a task to be done. Depending on context, trabajo can mean general work, a specific piece of work, or a job. With the article el, it usually means 'the work' or 'the job' in context.
target_language_example: Todavía no he terminado el trabajo.
native_language_example: I still haven't finished the work.

additional_notes: Used to talk about what a person, animal, or thing does (their role or responsibility), or who/what created something: *El trabajo de él es...* (“His job is...”), *el trabajo de un crítico* (“a critic’s job”), *el trabajo de hombres* (“the work of men”). Often followed by a person (*él/ella/Juan*), a group (*los hombres*), or a noun phrase (*un crítico*).
target_language_example: El trabajo de Ana es cuidar a los niños.
native_language_example: Ana’s job is to take care of the children.

additional_notes: A common noun phrase meaning sustained effort. Often used with verbs like hacer (to make/produce), agotar (to exhaust), vencer (to beat/overcome), and ser el motivo de (to be the reason for).
target_language_example: El trabajo duro siempre da resultados.
native_language_example: Hard work always pays off.

additional_notes: Common, mildly informal word for the part of your body you sit on. Often used in expressions: "un dolor en el trasero" = "a pain in the butt" (an annoying person/thing); "una patada en el trasero" = "a kick in the butt"; "meterse algo en el trasero" is a rude way to say "you can shove it."
target_language_example: Me duele el trasero de tanto estar sentado.
native_language_example: My butt hurts from sitting so much.

additional_notes: Used to talk about an agreement between people (often a negotiation). Common phrases: “cerrar el trato” (to close/finalize the deal), “el trato sigue en pie” (the deal is still on/stands), “ése/ese fue el trato” (that was the deal), “arruinar el trato” (to ruin the deal). Also note: “trato” can sometimes mean “treatment” (how someone is treated), but in these examples it means “deal/agreement.”
target_language_example: Si estás de acuerdo con el precio, cerramos el trato hoy.
native_language_example: If you agree with the price, we’ll close the deal today.

additional_notes: A literal, everyday phrase for a train. It often appears in common travel expressions like perder el tren ('miss the train') and alcanzar el tren ('catch the train').
target_language_example: El tren sale a las nueve.
native_language_example: The train leaves at nine.

additional_notes: Usually refers to road traffic and congestion, especially in cities. Common with verbs and phrases like estar atrapado en (to be stuck in), evitar (to avoid), cortar (to stop/block), and la hora punta (rush hour) as in el tráfico de la hora punta (rush-hour traffic).
target_language_example: Hoy hay mucho caos en el centro por el tráfico, así que voy en metro.
native_language_example: There’s a lot of chaos downtown because of the traffic, so I’m taking the subway.

additional_notes: Possessive pronoun meaning “yours” when the thing owned is masculine singular (e.g., el coche → el tuyo). It usually needs the definite article (el/la/los/las): el tuyo, la tuya, los tuyos, las tuyas. Used to avoid repeating a noun: “Déjame ver el tuyo” = “Let me see yours.”
target_language_example: Yo tengo mi bolígrafo; ¿dónde está el tuyo?
native_language_example: I have my pen; where is yours?

additional_notes: Common masculine noun. Use "el" for tea in general or when referring to a specific tea you’ve mentioned: "Me encanta el té" (I love tea) / "Aquí está el té" (Here is the tea). You can describe how you take it: "con/sin azúcar" (with/without sugar).
target_language_example: ¿Quieres el té con leche o sin leche?
native_language_example: Do you want the tea with milk or without milk?

additional_notes: Usually refers to the whole cosmos (space, stars, galaxies, everything that exists). It can also be used more loosely or humorously to mean “fate/life/the world” (e.g., "El universo me odia" = "The universe hates me"). Masculine noun: el universo.
target_language_example: A veces siento que el universo conspira a mi favor.
native_language_example: Sometimes I feel like the universe is conspiring in my favor.

additional_notes: Used to show a reciprocal action between two people/things (they do something to/with each other). It often appears with plural verbs and reflexive pronouns: "Nos miramos el uno al otro" = "We look at each other." It changes with gender/number: "el uno a la otra", "la una al otro", "las unas a las otras", etc. Often interchangeable with "mutuamente" in meaning.
target_language_example: Se ayudan el uno al otro cuando tienen problemas.
native_language_example: They help each other when they have problems.

additional_notes: Used with two people/things to show a mutual relationship (learning from, loving, depending on, keeping secrets from, being independent of). It often pairs with verbs or phrases that take “from/with/of” in English: aprender (mucho) el uno del otro = learn (a lot) from each other; enamorarse el uno del otro = fall in love with each other; depender el uno del otro = depend on each other; ser independiente el uno del otro = be independent of each other; no guardarse secretos el uno del otro = not keep secrets from each other. For mixed-gender pairs you’ll also see: el uno de la otra / la una del otro.
target_language_example: Tom y María dependen el uno del otro.
native_language_example: Tom and María depend on each other.

meaning: (to be) meant for each other; perfect for each other.
additional_notes: Used to say that two people (usually a couple) are a great match. It often appears after verbs like ser/estar: “(No) somos el uno para el otro” (we are/aren’t meant for each other) or in the common expression “estar hechos el uno para el otro” (to be made for each other). You can change gender/number: “el uno para la otra,” “la una para el otro,” “la una para la otra.” For plural groups: “los unos para los otros / las unas para las otras.”
target_language_example: Creo que ustedes son el uno para el otro.
native_language_example: I think you’re meant for each other.

meaning: "the value of"; in "tener el valor de", "the courage to".
additional_notes: Most commonly means the value/importance of something: "el valor de la información" (the value of information). When it appears after forms of "tener" (e.g., "tuvo el valor de"), it means having the courage/bravery to do something and is followed by an infinitive: "tuvo el valor de decir...".
target_language_example: No todos tienen el valor de decir la verdad.
native_language_example: Not everyone has the courage to tell the truth.

additional_notes: Means the season “summer.” It’s a masculine noun typically used with the definite article (el verano), especially when referring to the season in general. Common in time expressions like todo el verano (“all summer”) and antes de que empiece el verano (“before summer starts”).
target_language_example: De las cuatro estaciones me gusta más el verano.
native_language_example: Of the four seasons, I like summer the most.

additional_notes: Used to talk about something that happened during the previous summer (relative to now). Often placed at the beginning or end of the sentence as a time expression: “El verano pasado fuimos…” / “Fuimos… el verano pasado.”
target_language_example: El verano pasado hice un viaje con mis amigos.
native_language_example: Last summer I took a trip with my friends.

additional_notes: Most commonly means “dress” (a one-piece garment, typically worn by women). In some contexts, especially with adjectives like "formal" ("vestido formal"), it can mean “attire” or “outfit.” You’ll also see it with a relative clause: "el vestido que..." = “the dress that...”.
target_language_example: ¿Te gusta el vestido que me compré?
native_language_example: Do you like the dress I bought?

meaning: the trip; the journey; travel (as a noun).
additional_notes: A common noun for a trip/journey from one place to another. Often used with prepositions like durante el viaje (“during the trip”) and for parts of a trip: a la ida (“on the way there”) / a la vuelta (“on the way back”).
target_language_example: Durante el viaje, vimos muchos paisajes bonitos.
native_language_example: During the trip, we saw many beautiful landscapes.

additional_notes: Often refers to an elderly man (“the old man”), sometimes in a familiar/affectionate way. It can also be used before a name as a nickname meaning “old” (e.g., “el viejo Danny” = “old Danny”). In some contexts, “el viejo Nick” is a set phrase meaning “Old Nick” (the Devil).
target_language_example: Dicen que el viejo Antonio todavía sale a caminar todas las mañanas.
native_language_example: They say old Antonio still goes for a walk every morning.

additional_notes: Refers to moving air outdoors. Common with verbs like "soplar" (to blow) and "ponerse" to describe a change in weather: "El viento se puso más fuerte" = "The wind got stronger." Also used in phrases like "contra el viento" (against the wind) and "con el viento" (because of/with the wind).
target_language_example: Hoy hace mucho viento: el viento no me deja abrir el paraguas.
native_language_example: It’s very windy today: the wind won’t let me open my umbrella.

additional_notes: Used to talk about a specific Friday or the upcoming/known Friday. In Spanish, days of the week usually take the definite article (el) when you mean “on” that day: el viernes, el jueves. You can add time expressions: el viernes por la mañana = on Friday morning.
target_language_example: Nos vemos el viernes por la tarde.
native_language_example: See you on Friday afternoon.

additional_notes: A masculine noun meaning the alcoholic drink made from grapes. Use **el vino** for the general idea or a specific wine in context (e.g., on a menu). In Spanish, the article **el** is often used when talking about something in general: **Me gusta el vino** = “I like wine.”
target_language_example: Me gusta el vino, pero hoy prefiero agua.
native_language_example: I like wine, but today I prefer water.

additional_notes: A masculine noun for the musical instrument. Often used with the verb "tocar" (to play an instrument): "tocar el violín" = "to play the violin". Plural: "los violines".
target_language_example: ¿Sabes tocar el violín?
native_language_example: Do you know how to play the violin?

additional_notes: Commonly used with verbs like bajar/el volumen (turn the volume down) and subir el volumen (turn the volume up). You can also say "(Le) subió el volumen al televisor" to mean someone increased the TV’s volume; "le" refers to the person affected (e.g., Tom).
target_language_example: ¿Puedes bajar el volumen, por favor?
native_language_example: Can you turn the volume down, please?

additional_notes: Means “the tree” (definite article + noun). In Spanish, “árbol” takes masculine articles (el/un), even though it ends in -l. It can refer to any tree, and in a Christmas context “el árbol” often implies “the Christmas tree” from context.
target_language_example: El árbol está en el jardín.
native_language_example: The tree is in the garden.

additional_notes: Used to refer to a specific place/section or region. Common in instructions or warnings: “despejen el área” = “clear the area.” Also used with directions or labels: “el área Este” = “the east area/sector.”
target_language_example: Por favor, manténgase fuera del área restringida.
native_language_example: Please stay out of the restricted area.

additional_notes: Used for the final train service of the day on a route. Often appears with travel verbs like perder (to miss/lose) and coger (to catch/take), and in warnings or urgency: Date prisa o perderás el último tren (Hurry up or you’ll miss the last train).
target_language_example: Si no salimos ya, vamos a perder el último tren.
native_language_example: If we don’t leave now, we’re going to miss the last train.

additional_notes: Used to refer to a single person or thing with no others in the group. Before a noun, it usually means "the only" (el único asiento = the only seat). On its own, it often means "the only one." The form changes with gender and number: la única, los únicos, las únicas. Although único looks like "unique," in many common sentences it means "only."
target_language_example: Juan es el único que entiende la pregunta.
native_language_example: Juan is the only one who understands the question.

additional_notes: A more formal way to refer back to a noun (like “which/that”). It agrees with the noun’s gender/number: el cual, la cual, los cuales, las cuales. Very common after prepositions: con el cual (with which/whom), en el cual (in which), por el cual (for which). Often interchangeable with “que,” but “el cual” can be clearer in longer sentences or to avoid ambiguity.
target_language_example: Compré un libro, el cual recomiendo a todos mis amigos.
native_language_example: I bought a book, which I recommend to all my friends.

additional_notes: Used to avoid repeating a masculine singular noun. el de + phrase often means 'the one from/of/at/belonging to ...', depending on context. In more formal comparisons, it can mean 'that of' (for example, su comportamiento era el de un caballero). Feminine and plural forms are la de, los de, and las de.
target_language_example: Prefiero el de color azul.
native_language_example: I prefer the blue one.

additional_notes: Used to refer to a specific person or thing already known from context: "the one who/that...". It often avoids repeating a noun. The form changes with gender and number: la que, los que, las que.
target_language_example: Quiero el que está en la mesa.
native_language_example: I want the one that's on the table.

additional_notes: Used to refer to an unspecified person or thing, meaning it doesn’t matter which one. Often appears after a noun or with a choice: "el día que sea" (any day), "elige el que sea" (choose whichever/any one). Similar in meaning to "cualquiera" in many contexts.
target_language_example: Puedes elegir el que sea; todos son buenos.
native_language_example: You can choose whichever one; they’re all good.

additional_notes: Used to report what a woman/girl says. It’s followed by a clause introduced by que. In conversation you might also hear Ella dice: … (with a pause) without que. Verb form: dice = “(she) says” (present tense of decir).
target_language_example: Ella dice que no tiene tiempo hoy.
native_language_example: She says she doesn’t have time today.

additional_notes: Used to introduce reported speech (what a woman said). After **dijo que**, you usually follow with a full clause: **Ella dijo que + [sentence]**. In the past, Spanish often uses **imperfect** to report what someone said (e.g., *dijo que no tenía…*).
target_language_example: Ella dijo que llegaba tarde.
native_language_example: She said that she was arriving late / that she would be late.

meaning: “she was” (past tense of *ser*, describing what someone/something was like or used to be).
additional_notes: Uses the imperfect past (*era*, from *ser*) to talk about past descriptions, roles/identities, relationships, and ongoing states in the past: *Ella era actriz* (she was an actress), *Cuando ella era pequeña…* (when she was little…). Often sets background or describes what someone was like. Note: *era* can look like the English noun “era,” but here it’s a verb meaning “was.”
target_language_example: Ella era muy amable cuando la conocí.
native_language_example: She was very kind when I met her.

meaning: "she was a" (used before a feminine noun).
additional_notes: Used to describe what a woman/girl was like in the past, usually followed by a feminine noun or a noun phrase (e.g., *una corredora, una joven, una señora, una heroína*). For masculine nouns, you’d say *él era un*.
target_language_example: Ella era una excelente estudiante cuando vivía en Madrid.
native_language_example: She was an excellent student when she lived in Madrid.

additional_notes: Subject pronoun + the verb ser. Used to identify a woman/girl or describe qualities seen as more essential or characteristic. In Spanish, ella is often omitted unless needed for emphasis, contrast, or clarity.
target_language_example: Ella es mi profesora.
native_language_example: She is my teacher.

meaning: “she is the …” (referring to a woman or feminine noun).
additional_notes: Used to identify or describe someone with a feminine noun/title: ella es la juez / campeona / dueña / jefa. It’s also used before a relative clause with **la que** (“the one who/that”): *Ella es la que alimenta a nuestro perro* (“She’s the one who feeds our dog”), *Ella es la que más me gusta* (“She’s the one I like the most”).
target_language_example: Ella es la doctora que me ayudó.
native_language_example: She is the doctor who helped me.

meaning: “she is a …” (used before a feminine noun).
additional_notes: Used to identify or describe a woman by saying what she is: Ella es una + feminine noun/adjective phrase (e.g., estudiante, cocinera). The article “una” is feminine; for masculine nouns you’d use “él es un …”. Note: the full sentence can be neutral (Ella es una estudiante) but the noun you choose can be offensive (e.g., “puta” is a strong insult).
target_language_example: Ella es una buena amiga.
native_language_example: She is a good friend.

meaning: 'she was' / 'she used to be' (imperfect past of *estar*).
additional_notes: *Ella* = “she.” *Estaba* is the imperfect of *estar* and is used for ongoing/background situations in the past, temporary states/feelings, and actions in progress (often with a gerund: *estaba durmiendo* = “was sleeping”). It also commonly sets the scene: *Cuando abrí la puerta, ella estaba…* (“When I opened the door, she was…”).
target_language_example: Ayer por la noche, ella estaba muy cansada.
native_language_example: Last night, she was very tired.

additional_notes: "Está" is the form of "estar" used with temporary states, feelings, location, and ongoing actions. In Spanish, the subject pronoun "ella" is often omitted unless needed for emphasis or clarity.
target_language_example: Ella está en la cocina ahora.
native_language_example: She is in the kitchen now.

meaning: she went to / she went (in the past).
additional_notes: Uses the preterite (simple past) of **ir**: **ella fue** = “she went.” It’s commonly followed by **a + place** (Ella fue a París.) or **a + infinitive** to say what she went to do (Ella fue a estudiar / a ver a alguien).
target_language_example: Ella fue a la tienda a comprar pan.
native_language_example: She went to the store to buy bread.

additional_notes: “Fue” is the preterite (completed past) form of **ser** (“to be”) and **ir** (“to go”). In these examples it means **“she was”** (often describing who/what she was). It’s also used in the passive voice: **fue + past participle** (e.g., *fue educada* = “was educated”). Context tells you whether it means “was” (ser) or “went” (ir).
target_language_example: Ella fue la mejor estudiante de la clase.
native_language_example: She was the best student in the class.

additional_notes: Present tense of hablar with the subject pronoun ella (“she”). Use it to say what languages she can speak (Ella habla inglés.) or that she talks a lot (Ella habla demasiado.). With topics, use hablar de/sobre (“to talk about”): Ella habla sobre/de una red de energía. Often the subject pronoun is optional in Spanish, so Habla inglés can also mean “She speaks English” if the context is clear.
target_language_example: Ella habla español y francés.
native_language_example: She speaks Spanish and French.

additional_notes: “Ella” means “she.” “Hizo” is the simple past (preterite) of “hacer” (“to do/to make”), used for completed actions in the past. Often followed by a direct object: “ella hizo la tarea” = “she did the homework.”
target_language_example: Ella hizo la cena anoche.
native_language_example: She made dinner last night.

additional_notes: Not a fixed expression. Ella means "she," and le is an unstressed pronoun placed before the verb. It usually refers to "him," "her," or "you" (formal), often with the sense of "to him/her/you," though English may not always say "to." Context tells you who le refers to.
target_language_example: Ella le preparó la cena.
native_language_example: She made him dinner.

additional_notes: Used to report advice someone (ella) gave to another person (le = to him/her/you formal). It’s typically followed by the subjunctive in Spanish: «Ella le aconsejó que se fuera / leyera / viera…». You can swap «ella» for other subjects (Él/Yo/Nosotros) and «le» for «me/te/nos/les» depending on who receives the advice.
target_language_example: Ella le aconsejó que descansara y bebiera agua.
native_language_example: She advised him/her to rest and drink water.

meaning: “she told him/her that …” / “she said to him/her that …”
additional_notes: Used to introduce reported speech. “le” is an indirect object pronoun meaning “to him” or “to her” (you often need context to know which). What comes after “que” can be an order/request (often with the subjunctive: “que parara/parase”, “que siguiera…”) or a statement of information (often with the indicative: “que su padre había muerto”).
target_language_example: Ella le dijo que no viniera mañana.
native_language_example: She told him/her not to come tomorrow.

additional_notes: Past tense (preterite) of dar: dio = “gave.” Le is an indirect object pronoun meaning “to him” or “to her” (also used for “to you” in formal usted). Often followed by the thing given (direct object): “Ella le dio la llave” = “She gave him/her the key.” You can add who receives it with a clarifier: “Ella le dio leche al gato” (le = to the cat).
target_language_example: Ella le dio un regalo por su cumpleaños.
native_language_example: She gave him/her a gift for his/her birthday.

additional_notes: "Ella" means "she" (often omitted in Spanish unless emphasis/contrast is needed). "Lo" is a direct object pronoun meaning "him" or "it" (masculine singular), and it can also refer to an idea/situation like "that" (lo sé = I know it/that). It goes before the conjugated verb: "Ella lo visita" = "She visits him/it."
target_language_example: Ella lo vio ayer en el parque.
native_language_example: She saw him yesterday in the park.

meaning: 'she did it' / 'she made him/it do it'.
additional_notes: Literal pieces: ella = 'she', lo = 'it/him' (direct object pronoun), hizo = 'did/made' (preterite of hacer). Most often it means 'she did it' (e.g., Ella lo hizo a propósito = 'She did it on purpose'). With an infinitive, it can be causative: ella lo hizo + infinitive = 'she made him do (something)' (e.g., Ella lo hizo hacerlo = 'She made him do it').
target_language_example: Ella lo hizo ayer.
native_language_example: She did it yesterday.

additional_notes: A combination of ella (“she”) and me (“me” or “to me”). The exact English translation depends on the verb: ella me guió = “she guided me,” ella me sonríe = “she smiles at me.” Spanish often leaves out ella unless it is being used for emphasis or contrast.
target_language_example: Ella me llamó ayer.
native_language_example: She called me yesterday.

additional_notes: Used to report what a woman said. After "dijo que", you typically use the past tenses (e.g., "conocía", "iría", "había comprado") or the imperfect subjunctive for requests/commands (e.g., "que la viera" = "that I see/visit her"). Often shortened in speech to "me dijo que..." when it’s clear who "she" is.
target_language_example: Ella me dijo que no podía venir hoy.
native_language_example: She told me that she couldn’t come today.

additional_notes: Uses the preterite (simple past) of **dar**: **dio** = “gave.” **me** is the indirect object pronoun (“to me”). It’s followed by what was given: **Ella me dio un regalo** (“She gave me a gift”). It can also appear in set phrases like **Ella me dio la espalda** (“She turned her back on me / ignored me”).
target_language_example: Ella me dio su número de teléfono.
native_language_example: She gave me her phone number.

additional_notes: A subject pronoun plus negation: ella means "she" and no means "not." It is used before the verb to make a negative statement about a woman or girl. In Spanish, ella is often omitted unless it is needed for emphasis, contrast, or clarity.
target_language_example: Ella no quiere salir hoy.
native_language_example: She doesn't want to go out today.

additional_notes: Used to say that a woman/girl does not have a certain quality or identity. Follow it with an adjective (Ella no es joven), a noun (Ella no es mi madre), or part of a longer structure like: "no es solo X sino también Y" (not only X but also Y) and "no es..., sino..." (not ..., but rather ...). For comparisons, you’ll often see: "Ella no es menos + adjective + que..." (She is not less ... than...).
target_language_example: Ella no es de aquí; es de México.
native_language_example: She isn't from here; she's from Mexico.

additional_notes: From ella (she) + no (not) + tiene (has). Used to negate possession or to say someone lacks something: Ella no tiene dinero/hijos. It’s also used in common expressions like no tener la razón (“to not be right”) and no tener conciencia de… (“to have no awareness of…”). With quantities, no tiene más de… means “she has no more than…”, and no tiene menos de… means “she has no fewer than…”.
target_language_example: Ella no tiene tiempo para salir hoy.
