native_language_example: She doesn't have time to go out today.

additional_notes: Common way to say what a woman/girl wants to do. "Ella" = "she" and "quiere" is from "querer" (to want). Typically followed by an infinitive verb: "ella quiere + comprar/jugar/leer/saber/ser/tomar...".
target_language_example: Ella quiere aprender español este año.
native_language_example: She wants to learn Spanish this year.

additional_notes: This is not a fixed expression. ella means "she," and se is a pronoun used with many pronominal or reflexive verbs. Depending on the verb, se may mean "herself," show that the action affects her, or not be translated directly in English at all. In natural Spanish, ella is often omitted unless you want emphasis or clarity.
target_language_example: Ella se lava las manos antes de comer.
native_language_example: She washes her hands before eating.

additional_notes: Past tense (preterite) of "enamorarse de" (to fall in love with). Use "de" before the person/thing: "se enamoró de él/ella", "se enamoró de un artista". The "se" is part of the verb (reflexive) and is required.
target_language_example: Ella se enamoró de él en cuanto lo conoció.
native_language_example: She fell in love with him as soon as she met him.

additional_notes: Used to describe where a woman sat in relation to someone or something. "Cerca de" means "near/close to" and is followed by a noun or pronoun (e.g., cerca de mí/ti/él/ella/nosotros). You can change the subject and tense: "Me senté cerca de…" (I sat near…), "Se sentaron cerca de…" (They sat near…).
target_language_example: Ella se sentó cerca de la ventana para leer.
native_language_example: She sat near the window to read.

additional_notes: Used to talk about a woman/girl who does something habitually or in every case. It’s the subject pronoun "ella" (she) + the adverb "siempre" (always), usually placed before the verb: "Ella siempre se levanta...". In everyday Spanish, the pronoun is often dropped if it’s clear from context: "Siempre se levanta a las seis."
target_language_example: Ella siempre llega temprano a clase.
native_language_example: She always arrives early to class.

additional_notes: “Tenía” is the imperfect past of “tener” (to have). It often describes an ongoing state in the past, a habitual situation, or background information (not a single finished event). Common patterns include: “tenía ganas de + infinitive” (she felt like / wanted to…), “tenía en mente + infinitive” (she had in mind to…), “tenía la opción de + infinitive” (she had the option to…), and “tenía + noun” (she had + a thing/trait, e.g., defects).
target_language_example: Cuando era niña, ella tenía mucho miedo a la oscuridad.
native_language_example: When she was a child, she was very afraid of the dark.

additional_notes: A straightforward combination of ella + tiene (from tener). It is used for possession or to say that someone has a quality, feeling, or characteristic. In Spanish, the subject pronoun ella is often omitted unless needed for emphasis or clarity, so tiene by itself can also mean 'she has' depending on context.
target_language_example: Ella tiene mucha suerte.
native_language_example: She has a lot of luck.

additional_notes: Used with the verb **tener** to say that a woman has or possesses something, or to describe a characteristic (e.g., *un acento*, *un buen corazón*). **Un** is the masculine singular indefinite article, used before masculine singular nouns (e.g., *un novio*, *un rostro*). For feminine nouns, it changes to **una** (*Ella tiene una hermana*).
target_language_example: Ella tiene un coche nuevo.
native_language_example: She has a new car.

additional_notes: Used to say that a female person possesses or has something. "Una" is the feminine form of "a/an" and is used before singular feminine nouns (e.g., "una rosa", "una ventaja"). In Spanish, "tener" can be used for both physical things ("una rosa") and more abstract things ("una manera", "una ventaja").
target_language_example: Ella tiene una idea muy buena.
native_language_example: She has a very good idea.

additional_notes: Used before an infinitive verb (e.g., bajar, convencer, investigar, no llorar) to say that she made an effort to do something. In the past tense (pretérito): trató. You can change the subject: yo traté de (I tried to), él trató de (he tried to), etc.
target_language_example: Ella trató de llegar temprano, pero había mucho tráfico.
native_language_example: She tried to arrive early, but there was a lot of traffic.

meaning: "she lives" (she resides; or she is alive).
additional_notes: Most commonly used to talk about where or how a woman/girl lives: location (Ella vive cerca/de aquí/en Madrid), living situation (Ella vive sola/con sus padres), or lifestyle/conditions (Ella vive en la abundancia). It can also literally mean “she is alive,” but that usually needs context (e.g., after an accident).
target_language_example: Ella vive con su hermana en el centro.
native_language_example: She lives with her sister downtown.

meaning: “she lives in” (she resides in; or lives in a certain condition).
additional_notes: Used to say where a woman/girl lives: Ella vive en + place. It can also be figurative: Ella vive en + abstract noun (e.g., en la abundancia = “in abundance”). In Spanish you can’t drop “en” here (not *ella vive Madrid*).
target_language_example: Ella vive en este barrio desde 2020.
native_language_example: She has lived in this neighborhood since 2020.

additional_notes: "Ellos" = "they" (masculine or mixed group). "Estaban" is the imperfect past of "estar" and is used for states/conditions (cansados, listos, enamorados) or ongoing actions in the past, often with a gerund (estaban discutiendo, estaban jugando). It commonly sets background context: what was happening/what they were like at that time.
target_language_example: Cuando llegué, ellos estaban esperando afuera.
native_language_example: When I arrived, they were waiting outside.

meaning: 'they are' (temporary state/location) or 'they are' + a gerund ('they are ...-ing').
additional_notes: "Ellos" = "they" (often dropped in Spanish unless you need emphasis/contrast). "Están" is the present tense of "estar" (to be) used for temporary states, locations, and many conditions: "Ellos están a favor" (They’re in favor), "Ellos están por empezar" (They’re about to start). With a gerund (-ando/-iendo), it forms the present progressive: "Ellos están leyendo" (They are reading). For marriage, Spanish usually says "Están casados desde hace dos años" (They’ve been married for two years).
target_language_example: Ellos están en casa y están preparando la cena.
native_language_example: They are at home and are preparing dinner.

additional_notes: Used with a noun (ellos quieren más dinero = they want more money) or with an infinitive (ellos quieren estar contigo = they want to be with you). With “que” + verb in the subjunctive, it means “they want (someone) to do something” (ellos quieren que haga… = they want me to do…).
target_language_example: Ellos quieren que vengas mañana.
native_language_example: They want you to come tomorrow.

meaning: "they" + "se" (they themselves / each other), used with reflexive, reciprocal, or pronominal verbs.
additional_notes: "Se" is a pronoun that goes with "ellos" when the subject does the action to itself (reflexive: "Ellos se lavan" = They wash themselves) or to one another (reciprocal: "Ellos se saludaron" = They greeted each other). It also appears in many pronominal verbs where English often just uses a normal verb: "Ellos se escaparon" = They escaped; "Ellos se quedaron" = They stayed/ended up. "Se" usually comes right before the conjugated verb ("Ellos se van") and can attach to an infinitive ("van a encontrarse").
target_language_example: Ellos se ayudan cuando tienen problemas.
native_language_example: They help each other when they have problems.

meaning: "they are" (for a group of men, or a mixed group).
additional_notes: Used with the verb ser to identify or describe who people are (with nouns, professions, nationality, or adjectives). "Ellos" is the subject pronoun and is often omitted in Spanish when it’s clear from context ("Son jugadores de béisbol"). Use "ellas son" for a group of all women.
target_language_example: Ellos son mis vecinos.
native_language_example: They are my neighbors.

meaning: “they have” / “they’ve got”; also “they have to” (in “tienen que”).
additional_notes: Present tense of "tener" with "ellos" (“they”). Used for possession (Ellos tienen la llave), relationships/attributes (Ellos tienen un lazo sanguíneo), and with "que" to express obligation/necessity: "Ellos tienen que..." = “They have to...”. In everyday speech, Spanish often drops the subject pronoun, so you may also hear just "tienen" when it’s clear who “they” are.
target_language_example: Ellos tienen que irse ahora, pero tienen el número de teléfono.
native_language_example: They have to leave now, but they have the phone number.

additional_notes: Past tense (pretérito) of empezar: it describes the moment you began doing an action. It’s followed by an infinitive: empecé a + verb (empecé a estudiar, empecé a trabajar). For other subjects: empezó a (he/she started to), empezamos a (we started to).
target_language_example: Empecé a estudiar español el mes pasado.
native_language_example: I started studying Spanish last month.

additional_notes: used before an infinitive to say that an action is beginning: empezar a + verb. The verb empezar is usually conjugated in real sentences, as in empezó a, voy a empezar a, or vamos a empezar a.
target_language_example: Voy a empezar a estudiar ahora.
native_language_example: I'm going to start studying now.

additional_notes: Used when you begin again with nothing or with a clean slate—often after a big change (moving, a breakup, losing a job, restarting a project). It can apply to a person, a group, or a situation. Literal idea: “start from zero.”
target_language_example: Después del divorcio, decidió empezar de cero.
native_language_example: After the divorce, he/she decided to start over.

meaning: to start over; to start again.
additional_notes: Used when you restart something from the beginning, often after a mistake, failure, or a big change in life. It can be literal (redo a task) or more personal (restart your life/routine). Also commonly said as "volver a empezar".
target_language_example: Me equivoqué con el formulario, así que tengo que empezar de nuevo.
native_language_example: I made a mistake on the form, so I have to start over.

additional_notes: Preterite (simple past) of "empezar" for "ellos/ellas/ustedes": "empezaron". It’s used to say that a group started doing something at a specific moment in the past, and it’s typically followed by "a" + infinitive (e.g., "empezaron a hablar"). In the present tense you’ll often see "empiezan a" (stem change e→ie).
target_language_example: Después de la música, todos empezaron a cantar.
native_language_example: After the music started, everyone began to sing.

additional_notes: Used with an infinitive to say someone/something began doing an action at a specific moment in the past. It’s the preterite (completed past) form of "empezar": "empezó a" + infinitive (e.g., "empezó a ladrar" = started to bark).
target_language_example: Cuando sonó el teléfono, empezó a llover.
native_language_example: When the phone rang, it started to rain.

additional_notes: Past tense (pretérito): empezó = "started" (from empezar), a + infinitive is used to say you start doing something. Llorar = "to cry." Use it with a subject if needed: "Mi hermana empezó a llorar" = "My sister started to cry."
target_language_example: Cuando vio el perro perdido, empezó a llorar.
native_language_example: When she saw the lost dog, she started to cry.

additional_notes: Uses the past tense of empezar (empezó = “(it) began/started”) + a + infinitive (llover = “to rain”). Common for describing a change in weather at a specific moment; often with time phrases like de repente (“suddenly”) or tan pronto como… (“as soon as…”).
target_language_example: Íbamos a caminar, pero empezó a llover otra vez.
native_language_example: We were going to go for a walk, but it started to rain again.

additional_notes: Used with an infinitive to say that someone or something begins an action: "Empieza a hablar" (He/She starts to talk). Often follows commands or suggestions: "Empieza a practicar" (Start practicing). Note: "empieza a" can also mean "starts at" when followed by a time (not an infinitive): "La escuela empieza a las ocho y media" (School starts at 8:30).
target_language_example: Empieza a llover, mejor nos vamos.
native_language_example: It’s starting to rain; we’d better go.

meaning: "at all" (usually with a negative: "not at all").
additional_notes: Most commonly used with "no" or another negative word to emphasize a complete negation: "No... en absoluto" = "Not... at all" / "Not at all." It can also appear after a negative statement to strengthen it: "No molesta en absoluto" ("It doesn’t bother [me] at all").
target_language_example: No me gusta en absoluto.
native_language_example: I don’t like it at all.

additional_notes: Used after a noun to say there is a large amount of something (often with verbs like “haber” or “tener”): “comida en abundancia” = “plenty of food.” It’s a common, neutral phrase.
target_language_example: En esta ciudad hay trabajo en abundancia.
native_language_example: In this city there’s plenty of work.

additional_notes: Used to mark a starting point and what happens from that moment onward. It can refer to the present ("From now on...") or to a point in the past ("From that moment on..."). Common at the beginning of instructions, rules, or announcements: "En adelante, ...".
target_language_example: En adelante, vamos a comunicarnos por correo.
native_language_example: From now on, we're going to communicate by email.

additional_notes: Used when you don’t know (or don’t want to say) the exact location. Common with verbs like estar (to be), haber (there is/are), esconder (to hide), dejar (to leave/forget), and with clues/evidence: “Debe estar en alguna parte” = “It must be somewhere.” You can also use it more abstractly: “en alguna parte de…” = “somewhere in…”.
target_language_example: Mis llaves tienen que estar en alguna parte.
native_language_example: My keys have to be somewhere.

additional_notes: Used when you don’t know (or don’t say) the exact place. Very common in conversation. Often appears with verbs like estar/haber (to be/there is) and with “por aquí” to mean “around here somewhere”: “Tiene que estar por aquí en algún lado.”
target_language_example: Dejé mis llaves en algún lado y no las encuentro.
native_language_example: I left my keys somewhere and I can’t find them.

additional_notes: Used when the exact place is unknown, not specified, or not important. It can be used alone as a short answer (e.g., “En algún lugar.” = “Somewhere.”). Also common with extra details: “en algún lugar del oeste” = “somewhere in the west.”
target_language_example: Déjame las llaves en algún lugar seguro.
native_language_example: Leave the keys somewhere safe.

additional_notes: Used to talk about an unspecified time in the past or future. It can mean “eventually” when you expect something to happen sooner or later (Tenía que pasar en algún momento). It can also sound vague/noncommittal in plans (Podemos quedar… en algún momento).
target_language_example: En algún momento te llamaré para confirmarlo.
native_language_example: I’ll call you at some point to confirm it.

additional_notes: Used when you don’t know (or don’t want to say) the exact place. With verbs like estar/haber it means a location (“There’s a hotel somewhere around here”). With actions like cenar it can mean you need to choose a place (“You’ll have to have dinner somewhere”). It’s also common with leer/ver/oír: “I read/saw/heard it somewhere” (the source isn’t specific).
target_language_example: Creo que dejé mis llaves en algún sitio de la casa.
native_language_example: I think I left my keys somewhere in the house.

additional_notes: Used with verbs like "leer" (to read) or "decir" (to say) to indicate speaking so others can hear, not silently ("en voz baja" = quietly).
target_language_example: ¿Puedes leerlo en alta voz, por favor?
native_language_example: Can you read it out loud, please?

additional_notes: Used with body parts to mean they are raised: “los brazos/las manos en alto” = “arms/hands up” (often a police command). With verbs like “leer” or “hablar,” it can mean “aloud,” though the more common phrase is “en voz alta.” It can also be figurative for posture/pride: “la frente en alto” = “head held high.”
target_language_example: Cuando terminó el examen, levantó las manos en alto y sonrió.
native_language_example: When the exam ended, he raised his hands up and smiled.

additional_notes: Used to say how something looks or seems, often implying it may not match reality. Common patterns: “en apariencia, …” (apparently, …) and “X es … en apariencia, pero …” (X seems …, but …).
target_language_example: En apariencia todo está bajo control, pero todavía hay problemas.
native_language_example: Apparently everything is under control, but there are still problems.

meaning: Back then; at that time (in the past).
additional_notes: Used to refer to a specific period in the past, often contrasting it with the present ("back then... but now..."). It commonly appears at the beginning of a sentence as a time expression.
target_language_example: En aquel entonces no tenía coche, así que iba a todas partes en autobús.
native_language_example: Back then I didn’t have a car, so I went everywhere by bus.

meaning: at that moment; back then (at that time).
additional_notes: Points to a specific time in the past that’s distant from “now” (often like “at that point” or “back then”). It can appear at the start of a sentence as a time marker: “En aquel momento, …”.
target_language_example: En aquel momento, no entendí lo que estaba pasando.
native_language_example: At that moment, I didn’t understand what was happening.

additional_notes: Used to talk about people who are carrying weapons or acting as soldiers/combatants. Common in phrases like "compañeros/hermanos en armas" (= comrades/brothers-in-arms). Don’t confuse it with English "in (someone’s) arms" (= being held).
target_language_example: Los soldados están en armas desde el amanecer.
native_language_example: The soldiers have been under arms since dawn.

additional_notes: Used with verbs of movement/travel (ir, viajar, llegar) to say the mode of transportation. In Spanish, “en + [vehicle]” often means “by/in/on” that vehicle (en coche, en tren, en avión).
target_language_example: Vamos al centro en autobús porque es más barato.
native_language_example: We’re going downtown by bus because it’s cheaper.

additional_notes: Used to say how you travel (the means of transport). It often contrasts with other options: en tren (by train), en barco (by boat). You can use it alone as a short answer (e.g., to “How will you go?”).
target_language_example: Vamos en avión porque es más rápido.
native_language_example: We’re going by plane because it’s faster.

additional_notes: Used with verbs of movement (ir, venir, llegar) to say how someone travels. You can also say "ir en bici" (more casual) as a shorter version.
target_language_example: Hoy voy al parque en bicicleta.
native_language_example: Today I’m going to the park by bike.

additional_notes: Used mainly for images, photos, films, or TV that have no color. Often follows the noun (e.g., “televisión en blanco y negro”) or is used after verbs like dejar/poner (“dejar las fotos en blanco y negro”).
target_language_example: Prefiero imprimir esta foto en blanco y negro.
native_language_example: I prefer to print this photo in black and white.

meaning: blank; (figuratively) having a mind go blank / not remembering what to say.
additional_notes: Used literally for something with nothing written on it (a blank page, blank form). With verbs like estar/quedarse, it commonly means you can’t think of anything or you forget what you were going to say (often due to nerves): “Estoy en blanco” = “My mind is blank”; “Me quedé en blanco” = “I went blank / I froze and forgot.”
target_language_example: Cuando me preguntaron mi número, me quedé en blanco.
native_language_example: When they asked me my number, I went blank.

additional_notes: Used literally for photos/TV/printing without color. Also used figuratively to mean something is clear, definite, or written down as proof (e.g., “Here it is, in black and white”).
target_language_example: Lo tengo en blanco y negro en el contrato.
native_language_example: I have it in black and white in the contract.

meaning: in someone’s arms; being held/carried in the arms.
additional_notes: Used with verbs like llevar, tener, tomar/coger, and sostener to mean holding or carrying someone (often a child) in your arms. It can also be used for carrying an object held against your body (e.g., “con la TV en brazos”).
target_language_example: El bebé se durmió en brazos de su mamá.
native_language_example: The baby fell asleep in his mom’s arms.

additional_notes: Used to say something will happen in the near future. Common in announcements and more formal contexts (e.g., trains, events, weather). Similar to "pronto" but often sounds a bit more formal.
target_language_example: Volveré en breve.
native_language_example: I'll be back shortly.

additional_notes: Used to say that something is working well or hasn’t been damaged or worn out. It can also be used with health: “en buen estado de salud” = “in good health.” Often used with the verb “estar” (to be): “está/están en buen estado.”
target_language_example: El teléfono está viejo, pero todavía está en buen estado.
native_language_example: The phone is old, but it’s still in good condition.

meaning: in good hands (well cared for / in good care).
additional_notes: Used with estar to say someone is being taken care of by a capable, trustworthy person or place (a doctor, a team, a company, etc.). It can refer to safety, treatment, or good service.
target_language_example: No te preocupes: con la doctora López estás en buenas manos.
native_language_example: Don’t worry: with Dr. López you’re in good hands.

additional_notes: Used to say someone goes somewhere or does something with the purpose of finding or achieving something. Common with verbs like ir, salir, viajar, andarse/ir de viaje. Usually followed by a noun (en busca de aventuras, en busca de trabajo).
target_language_example: Salimos temprano en busca de un buen restaurante.
native_language_example: We left early in search of a good restaurant.

meaning: at the cashier / in the cash register (cash on hand).
additional_notes: Used in stores to indicate where you pay (“pagar en caja” = pay at the checkout/cashier). In accounting/business, “dinero en caja” refers to cash physically in the till (cash on hand), as opposed to money in the bank.
target_language_example: Puede pagar en caja, por favor.
native_language_example: You can pay at the cashier, please.

meaning: in the capacity of; as (in an official role).
additional_notes: Used in formal/official contexts to specify the role or function someone has (similar to “as” or “in the role of”). It often comes before a job title or position: “en calidad de representante/director/testigo”.
target_language_example: Asistió a la reunión en calidad de representante de la empresa.
native_language_example: He attended the meeting in his capacity as the company’s representative.

meaning: in bed (usually because you’re sick or resting).
additional_notes: Often used with verbs like estar/quedarse to mean someone is staying in bed, especially due to illness: "Está en cama" (He/She is bedridden / in bed). You can add a reason with "con" ("en cama con gripe" = in bed with the flu).
target_language_example: Hoy no voy a trabajar; estoy en cama.
native_language_example: I’m not going to work today; I’m in bed.

additional_notes: Used to contrast two people, things, or situations, often after stating the first one. It can go at the start of a sentence ("En cambio, ...") or after the subject for emphasis ("Yo, en cambio, ..." = "I, on the other hand, ...").
target_language_example: Yo no tengo coche; en cambio, mi hermana sí.
native_language_example: I don’t have a car; my sister, on the other hand, does.

additional_notes: Used to say someone or something is currently heading toward a destination or will arrive soon. Often with verbs like venir (to come) or estar (to be): “Vienen en camino” / “Está en camino.” In Latin America you’ll also hear “en camino” for items being delivered/shipped (e.g., answers, packages).
target_language_example: Tu pedido ya está en camino.
native_language_example: Your order is already on the way.

additional_notes: Used to say that someone is at home or staying home. In this expression, casa usually means "home," not just a physical house, and it normally appears without an article: en casa, not en la casa, unless you mean a specific house.
target_language_example: Hoy me quedo en casa.
native_language_example: I'm staying home today.

additional_notes: Used to say you are at a specific person’s home (not necessarily your own). It’s followed by a person or relationship: en casa de mi hermana, en casa de Juan. With names, you can keep or drop the article depending on region/style: en casa de Sandy / en casa de la Sandy.
target_language_example: Nos vemos a las siete en casa de Marta.
native_language_example: See you at seven at Marta’s place.

additional_notes: Used to talk about a possible situation and what to do if it happens. Common with nouns: en caso de duda/urgencia (“in case of doubt/an emergency”). You’ll also see the related structure en caso de que + subjunctive for full clauses: En caso de que lo hayas perdido… (“In case you’ve lost it…”).
target_language_example: En caso de lluvia, cancelamos el picnic.
native_language_example: In case of rain, we’ll cancel the picnic.

additional_notes: Used to explain what you should do if an emergency happens. Often appears in instructions, signs, and safety rules. You can place it at the beginning or end of the sentence, and it’s commonly followed by a command (imperative), like "llama" (call) or "presione" (press).
target_language_example: En caso de emergencia, salga por esta puerta.
native_language_example: In case of emergency, exit through this door.

meaning: "in case" / "in the event that" (introduces a possibility).
additional_notes: Used to talk about something that might happen, often as a precaution (e.g., bring something or give information just in case). It’s followed by a verb; in many cases Spanish uses the subjunctive after it: En caso de que llueva. It’s also common to use the infinitive with the shorter form "en caso de" when there’s no subject change: En caso de lluvia (in case of rain).
target_language_example: Te dejo una copia, en caso de que la necesites.
native_language_example: I’ll leave you a copy, in case you need it.

meaning: 'in a certain…' / 'to a certain…' (introduces an unspecified thing, time, way, or sense).
additional_notes: Usually followed by a noun or fixed phrases like: en cierto modo (in a way), en cierto sentido (in a sense), en cierto momento (at a certain moment). By itself, it sounds incomplete in Spanish, like the start of one of those expressions.
target_language_example: En cierto modo, tienes razón.
native_language_example: In a way, you're right.

additional_notes: Used to soften or qualify what you’re saying, meaning it’s true only partially or from a certain perspective. Often placed at the beginning of a sentence (En cierto modo, sí.) or before the verb (en cierto modo lo haces).
target_language_example: En cierto modo, entiendo lo que dices, pero no estoy de acuerdo.
native_language_example: In a way, I understand what you’re saying, but I don’t agree.

additional_notes: Used to qualify a statement: it’s true or you agree, but only from a particular perspective or partially (not completely). It often goes at the beginning of the sentence with a comma, or after the idea it modifies.
target_language_example: En cierto sentido, tienes razón, pero no del todo.
native_language_example: In a way, you're right, but not completely.

additional_notes: Used to say something will happen after five minutes have passed from now, or as a deadline: En cinco minutos quiero verte... It can also be a short standalone answer to mean “in five minutes.” Similar pattern: en + number + minutos/horas/días.
target_language_example: Llego en cinco minutos.
native_language_example: I’ll be there in five minutes.

meaning: in common; shared (by two or more).
additional_notes: Used with verbs like tener to talk about things people share (interests, ideas, experiences): Tenemos mucho en común. It can also describe something shared between places or things (e.g., una frontera en común = a shared border). Very common patterns: tener algo/nada/mucho/más en común; una cosa en común.
target_language_example: Mi hermana y yo tenemos mucho en común.
native_language_example: My sister and I have a lot in common.

additional_notes: Commonly used in two ways: (1) "estar en condiciones de + infinitive" = to be able/fit/in a position to do something (often about health, readiness, or capability): "No está en condiciones de conducir." (2) "en condiciones" = in proper condition / in acceptable shape, or describing the circumstances: "en condiciones peores" (in worse conditions). "Poner algo en condiciones" means to fix it up / get it into good shape.
target_language_example: Después de dormir un poco, ya estoy en condiciones de seguir trabajando.
native_language_example: After sleeping a bit, I’m able to keep working.

meaning: as a whole; together (as a group).
additional_notes: Used to talk about something viewed in its totality (overall) or people/things acting jointly. Often with verbs like "trabajar", "actuar", "decidir", or to give an overall opinion: "En conjunto, ...".
target_language_example: En conjunto, el equipo hizo un buen trabajo.
native_language_example: Overall, the team did a good job.

additional_notes: Used to introduce a conclusion or result (similar to “therefore/as a result”): “En consecuencia, ...”. It can also mean “accordingly / in line with that” after a decision or fact, often with verbs like “actuar” or “comportarse”: “actuar/comportarse en consecuencia” = “act/behave accordingly.”
target_language_example: No hay pruebas suficientes; en consecuencia, no podemos arrestarlo.
native_language_example: There isn’t enough evidence; therefore, we can’t arrest him.

additional_notes: Used with estar/seguir/mantenerse/ponerse to talk about staying or getting in touch with someone or something: Estoy en contacto con…, Me mantengo en contacto con…, Ponte/Póngase en contacto con…. Often implies ongoing communication (by email, phone, etc.).
target_language_example: Me mantengo en contacto con mis amigos por WhatsApp.
native_language_example: I stay in touch with my friends on WhatsApp.

additional_notes: Used to express opposition. Very often followed by **de + noun/infinitive**: *estar en contra de fumar* (“to be against smoking”), *en contra de los recortes* (“against the cuts”). You can also use it alone as a short answer: *—¿Estás a favor? —En contra.*
target_language_example: Estoy en contra de esa idea.
native_language_example: I'm against that idea.

additional_notes: Used to show opposition or being unfavorable toward someone/something. Common with verbs like estar/ir/votar/hablar: "estar en contra de" (to be against), "votar en contra de" (to vote against), "hablar en contra de" (to speak against). "No tengo nada en contra de..." means “I have nothing against…” (no objection).
target_language_example: Estoy en contra de esa propuesta.
native_language_example: I’m against that proposal.

meaning: against the war; opposed to the war.
additional_notes: Used with estar (or sometimes ser) to express opposition to something: estar en contra de + noun/infinitive. Here, de la guerra means “of the war,” so the whole phrase expresses being opposed to war (or to a specific war, depending on context). You can swap in other nouns: en contra del plan, en contra de la decisión.
target_language_example: Mucha gente está en contra de la guerra.
native_language_example: Many people are against the war.

additional_notes: Used to say you did something you didn’t want to do, often because someone pressured you or forced you. You can also change the possessive pronoun: en contra de tu/su/nuestra voluntad (against your/his/her/our will). Common with verbs like hacer, tomar, casarse, obligar.
target_language_example: Firmé el contrato en contra de mi voluntad.
native_language_example: I signed the contract against my will.

additional_notes: Used to say that what follows is true regardless of the situation, or to move on/return to the main point (similar to “anyway”). Often appears with commas in writing: “En cualquier caso, …”.
target_language_example: En cualquier caso, gracias por venir.
native_language_example: In any case, thanks for coming.

additional_notes: Used to say something can happen at an unspecified time, often soon or without warning. Common with the future tense (llegará) or near-future with ir a (van a…). It can also mean you have permission/freedom to do something whenever you want.
target_language_example: Si necesitas ayuda, llámame en cualquier momento.
native_language_example: If you need help, call me anytime.

meaning: as for; regarding; when it comes to.
additional_notes: Used to introduce a topic and comment on it. Often followed by a noun, pronoun, or phrase (e.g., “En cuanto a ti…”, “En cuanto a los perros…”). It’s a common way to shift focus to a specific subject; similar to “as far as X is concerned.”
target_language_example: En cuanto a la comida, prefiero algo ligero.
native_language_example: As for the food, I’d prefer something light.

meaning: as for me; as far as I’m concerned.
additional_notes: Used to shift the topic to your own situation/opinion. Often followed by a comma: “En cuanto a mí, …”. You can change the pronoun: “en cuanto a ti/él/ella/nosotros…”. Similar to “por mi parte”.
target_language_example: En cuanto a mí, prefiero quedarme en casa esta noche.
native_language_example: As for me, I’d rather stay home tonight.

additional_notes: Often used to mean “as soon as” to show that one action happens immediately after another. Common pattern: en cuanto + present subjunctive (for future/uncertain events): “En cuanto llegue, te llamo.” For completed past events, it usually goes with indicative: “Vine en cuanto pude.” (It can also mean “regarding/in terms of” in the phrase “en cuanto a…”, but that’s a different use.)
target_language_example: En cuanto termine la reunión, te escribo.
native_language_example: As soon as the meeting ends, I’ll text you.

additional_notes: Used to talk about a future action that will happen immediately after an arrival. After **en cuanto**, Spanish typically uses the **present subjunctive** (here, **llegue**) when the arrival is in the future or not yet certain. The subject is understood from context (e.g., “as soon as you arrive,” “as soon as I arrive,” etc.).
target_language_example: En cuanto llegue al hotel, te mando un mensaje.
native_language_example: As soon as I arrive at the hotel, I’ll send you a message.

additional_notes: Most often used with verbs like **tener en cuenta** (to keep in mind / take into account), **tomar en cuenta** (to take into account / consider), and **tener a alguien en cuenta** (to consider someone). Also appears in **tomando en cuenta...** meaning “considering...” or “given...”.
target_language_example: Toma en cuenta el clima antes de salir.
native_language_example: Take the weather into account before you go out.

additional_notes: Used to refer to the specific thing being talked about: "el tema/en asunto en cuestión" = "the topic/issue in question." It can also appear with verbs like "estar" to mean something is being questioned or is at stake ("está en cuestión").
target_language_example: El documento en cuestión no está firmado.
native_language_example: The document in question isn’t signed.

additional_notes: Used to emphasize that something happens very quickly (or within a short time), often with time units like segundos, minutos, horas, días. It commonly appears as: en cuestión de + plural time unit (en cuestión de segundos).
target_language_example: Llegó en cuestión de minutos.
native_language_example: He arrived in a matter of minutes.

additional_notes: Used to say something (a project, investigation, therapy, experiment, etc.) has started and is still happening. Common patterns: “estar en curso” (to be in progress) and “algo en curso” (an ongoing/ongoing thing).
target_language_example: El proyecto sigue en curso.
native_language_example: The project is still in progress.

meaning: in a circle; in a circular shape/pattern.
additional_notes: Used to describe (1) people or objects arranged forming a circle (e.g., sitting/standing in a circle) and (2) movement that goes around repeatedly (e.g., moving in circles). Often used with verbs like estar/sentarse (arrangement) and moverse/caminar/girar (movement).
target_language_example: Los niños estaban de pie en círculo para jugar.
native_language_example: The kids were standing in a circle to play.

additional_notes: Used after verbs like describir, explicar, contar, etc. to say something is described/explained with a lot of specific information. It often goes at the end of the sentence (e.g., “Explícalo en detalle”).
target_language_example: ¿Puedes explicármelo en detalle, por favor?
native_language_example: Can you explain it to me in detail, please?

additional_notes: Used to say something will happen after a 10-minute wait from the current moment (future time). It answers “When?” and is common with future tense or “ir a” (e.g., va a...). You can swap the number: en cinco minutos, en dos horas, etc. Not the same as “during ten minutes” (that would be “durante diez minutos”).
target_language_example: Te llamo en diez minutos.
native_language_example: I’ll call you in ten minutes.

additional_notes: Used to describe movement or orientation toward a place or point. It’s common with verbs of movement (ir, correr, volar, caminar). Often interchangeable with “hacia,” but “en dirección a” can sound a bit more formal or descriptive. It can also appear as a standalone phrase on signs or in short notes (e.g., “En dirección a Kiev.”).
target_language_example: El tren va en dirección a Barcelona.
native_language_example: The train is heading toward Barcelona.

additional_notes: Used after verbs like "dividir" (to divide) or "partir" (to cut/split) to say something is split into two pieces/groups. It can also describe being in two places, having two rooms, or taking part in two wars (i.e., the number two in a situation).
target_language_example: Vamos a dividir la cuenta en dos.
native_language_example: Let’s split the bill in two.

meaning: in two days; within two days (two days from now).
additional_notes: Used to talk about a time frame or deadline. With future events (llegará, será, llámame) it often means “two days from now.” With completed actions (hizo el trabajo) it means “in two days” as the duration it took to finish.
target_language_example: Te mando los documentos en dos días.
native_language_example: I’ll send you the documents in two days.

meaning: in two hours (from now); within two hours.
additional_notes: Used to say how long until something happens (a point in the future) or how long it will take to finish something. With other numbers: en una hora, en tres horas, en cinco minutos, en dos días, etc.
target_language_example: Termino el informe en dos horas.
native_language_example: I’ll finish the report in two hours.

meaning: "in two weeks" (from now; within a two-week period).
additional_notes: Used to say something will happen after two weeks have passed from a reference point (often now): "Vuelvo en dos semanas". It can also describe what happened over a two-week span: "Subí tres libras en dos semanas". Similar idea to "dentro de dos semanas" when talking about a future deadline.
target_language_example: Te llamaré en dos semanas para confirmar la cita.
native_language_example: I’ll call you in two weeks to confirm the appointment.

additional_notes: Used to say you pay (or want to be paid) with physical money (bills/coins), not by card or bank transfer. Often used with verbs like pagar (to pay) and cobrar (to charge/collect).
target_language_example: ¿Puedo pagar en efectivo?
native_language_example: Can I pay in cash?

additional_notes: Used to confirm, agree with, or emphasize a statement—often in a slightly formal tone. It can appear at the start of a sentence ("En efecto, ...") or inserted mid-sentence ("Puede, en efecto, ..."). Similar to "efectivamente" or "así es" in meaning.
target_language_example: En efecto, tienes razón.
native_language_example: Indeed, you're right.

additional_notes: Formed with the preposition `en` and the masculine singular article `el`. It is used before masculine singular nouns. Most often it means 'in the', but depending on the context it can also be 'on the' or 'at the'. Unlike `a + el` (`al`) and `de + el` (`del`), `en el` does not contract.
target_language_example: Estamos en el parque.
native_language_example: We are in the park.

additional_notes: Used to say that something happened during a specific accident (often a car crash). It commonly follows a verb to explain how/when someone got hurt or something was damaged: “Me lesioné… en el accidente.” You can also hear “en un accidente” (in an accident) when the accident isn’t specific.
target_language_example: Perdió un diente en el accidente.
native_language_example: He lost a tooth in the accident.

additional_notes: Used for something that happens instantly, without delay. Common with arrests/catching someone while they’re doing something ("pillaron/arrestaron ... en el acto" = they caught/arrested them in the act) and with sudden death ("murió en el acto" = died instantly/on the spot).
target_language_example: Cuando vio el error, lo corrigió en el acto.
native_language_example: When he saw the mistake, he corrected it immediately.

additional_notes: Used to say where something happens. Common with verbs like estar (to be), despedirse (to say goodbye), dejar (to drop off), recoger (to pick up), and with travel phrases like tengo una conexión (I have a connection/layover).
target_language_example: Nos vemos en el aeropuerto a las ocho.
native_language_example: See you at the airport at eight.

additional_notes: Used to say that something/someone is inside the water or happening there. Common with verbs like meter (to put in), tener (to have), explotar (to explode), estar (to be), and navegar (to sail).
target_language_example: Los niños están jugando en el agua.
native_language_example: The kids are playing in the water.

meaning: 'in the air'; also 'up in the air' (unresolved) or 'on the air' (broadcasting).
additional_notes: Literal use: something is physically in the air (a smell, smoke, energy you can feel): "Hay un mal olor en el aire." Figurative use: something is uncertain/not decided yet or left unresolved: "Dejé el plan en el aire." With verbs like "poner" or "salir": "poner/salir en el aire" = to put on the air / to air (a TV/radio program).
target_language_example: El plan todavía está en el aire.
native_language_example: The plan is still up in the air.

meaning: in the closet; in the wardrobe/cabinet.
additional_notes: Used to say something is located inside an armario (a closet/wardrobe for clothes, or sometimes a cabinet). With verbs like colgar (to hang), guardar (to store), esconder (to hide), mirar (to look). It can also appear in the idiom "un esqueleto en el armario" = "a skeleton in the closet" (a hidden shame/secret).
target_language_example: Dejé las toallas en el armario del baño.
native_language_example: I left the towels in the bathroom cabinet.

additional_notes: Used to say where something happens: inside the elevator. "Ascensor" = elevator; "en el" = in the. Common with verbs like subir/bajar (go up/down), ir (go), and rules like "No se puede..." (You can’t...).
target_language_example: Nos vemos en el ascensor a las ocho.
native_language_example: See you in the elevator at eight.

additional_notes: Used to say someone or something is inside a car. With verbs of movement you may also hear "meterse/subirse al auto" (“get into the car”) vs. "estar/esperar en el auto" (“be/wait in the car”). "Auto" is common in many Latin American countries; in Spain, "coche" is more common.
target_language_example: Los niños están esperando en el auto.
native_language_example: The kids are waiting in the car.

meaning: on the bus; in the bus.
additional_notes: Used to say where something happens while you are riding a bus. With vehicles in Spanish, both “en” (in/on) and “a” (by) can be used depending on the verb, but with actions like sitting, sleeping, talking, etc., “en el autobús” is very common. You can change the article for gender/number: “en la guagua” (bus in some countries), “en los autobuses” (on buses).
target_language_example: Hablamos en el autobús camino al trabajo.
native_language_example: We talked on the bus on the way to work.

meaning: on the plane; in the airplane.
additional_notes: Common way to say someone/something is physically inside a plane during a flight. With verbs like "ir" (to go), it can mean traveling by plane: "Voy en avión" is more common than "voy en el avión" unless you mean a specific plane/flight.
target_language_example: Nos vimos en el avión y hablamos un rato.
native_language_example: We saw each other on the plane and talked for a while.

additional_notes: Used to say someone or something is located on a specific balcony. "En" + "el" (masculine singular) becomes "en el". With places, Spanish often uses "en" where English uses "on" (e.g., sitting/smoking/standing there).
target_language_example: Hace frío, pero quiero tomar un café en el balcón.
native_language_example: It’s cold, but I want to have a coffee on the balcony.

meaning: in/on the bench; at/in the bank.
additional_notes: "Banco" has two very common meanings: (1) "bench" (a seat, often in a park) and (2) "bank" (the place for money). Context usually makes it clear: "sentarse" or "del parque" → bench; "ahorros" (savings), "trabaja" (works), or people inside → bank. With places like a bank, "en" often means "at" in English ("Estoy en el banco" = "I’m at the bank").
target_language_example: Tengo que ir en el banco a sacar dinero.
native_language_example: I have to go to the bank to withdraw money.

meaning: in the bar; at the bar.
additional_notes: Used to say someone/something is located inside a bar (a place to drink), or present there. It’s a common location phrase: en + el ("in" + "the") + bar.
target_language_example: Nos vemos en el bar a las ocho.
native_language_example: See you at the bar at eight.

meaning: on the boat; in the ship.
additional_notes: Used to say someone or something is located aboard a boat/ship. With transport, Spanish often uses “en” (not “sobre/on”) to mean “on/in” a vehicle: en el barco, en el tren, en el avión.
target_language_example: ¿Quién está en el barco?
native_language_example: Who is on the boat?

meaning: in the bathroom; in the restroom.
additional_notes: Used to say someone or something is inside the bathroom/restroom. Often answers “¿Dónde está…?” (Where is…?). With verbs like “estar” it means someone is in there (possibly using it).
target_language_example: Perdón, estoy en el baño ahora.
native_language_example: Sorry, I’m in the bathroom right now.

meaning: in (your/his/her) pocket; also figuratively, “in your control” / “in your back pocket.”
additional_notes: Literal use: describes something physically inside a pocket (often with verbs like tener, llevar, meter, ponerse). Figurative use: someone has you “en el bolsillo” if they have power over you, influence you, or can easily get you to do what they want (e.g., because you owe them something).
target_language_example: Llevo el teléfono en el bolsillo, por si me llamas.
native_language_example: I carry my phone in my pocket, in case you call me.

meaning: in the forest / in the woods.
additional_notes: Used to say that something happens or is located inside a forest. You can swap the article depending on the noun: en el bosque (in the forest), en la selva (in the jungle), en el parque (in the park). With plural you can say en los bosques (“in the forests”).
target_language_example: Hace frío en el bosque por la noche.
native_language_example: It’s cold in the woods at night.

additional_notes: Literal location phrase: en (“in/on”) + el (“the”) + bote (“boat”). Used to say someone/something is inside the boat. With boats, Spanish often uses en where English might use “in” or sometimes “on” depending on context.
target_language_example: Los niños están en el bote y nosotros estamos en la orilla.
native_language_example: The kids are in the boat and we are on the shore.

meaning: on the arm; in the arm.
additional_notes: Used to say where something is located or where an injury happened. With wounds/shots/stabs, Spanish often uses "en" (literally "in/on") where English says "in" (shot in the arm) or "on" (a mark on the arm).
target_language_example: Me hice un corte en el brazo.
native_language_example: I got a cut on my arm.

additional_notes: Used to say something is located or stored inside a drawer. Often follows verbs like guardar (to store/put away), dejar (to leave), or meter (to put in). You can change the article for gender/number: en la caja (in the box), en los cajones (in the drawers).
target_language_example: Las llaves están en el cajón de la cocina.
native_language_example: The keys are in the kitchen drawer.

additional_notes: Used to say something is inside a specific drawer that belongs to or is part of something (a desk, a dresser, the kitchen, etc.). You’ll usually add a noun after de: en el cajón de la mesa / del escritorio. (de + el → del).
target_language_example: Las llaves están en el cajón del escritorio.
native_language_example: The keys are in the desk drawer.

meaning: on the way; along the road/path.
additional_notes: Literally means “on the road/path.” Often used for travel (“on the way to…”) and sometimes more figuratively to mean “staying on track/keeping going.” You’ll also commonly hear "de camino" or "en camino" with a similar meaning (“on the way”).
target_language_example: Estoy en el camino a casa.
native_language_example: I’m on the way home.

meaning: in the countryside; in the field (e.g., on the playing field).
additional_notes: Most commonly means “in the countryside/rural area,” especially with verbs like vivir (to live) or crecer (to grow up). It can also mean “on the field” in sports or similar contexts (e.g., no había árbitro en el campo).
target_language_example: Prefiero pasar los fines de semana en el campo para descansar.
native_language_example: I prefer to spend weekends in the countryside to rest.

meaning: in the center; in the middle.
additional_notes: Used to say something is located or placed in the middle of a place or object (en el centro del pueblo/la habitación/la piedra). It can also mean “downtown” or “in the city center” in news-like contexts (Hay un homicidio en el centro). Often used with verbs like estar (to be), haber (there is/are), and poner (to put).
target_language_example: Nos vemos en el centro a las seis.
native_language_example: See you downtown at six.

en el centro de la ciudad

target_language_multi_word_term: en el centro de la ciudad
additional_notes: Used to say something is located in the central part of a city. Common with location verbs like estar, encontrarse, and ubicarse. Often interchangeable with “en el centro” when the city is clear from context.
target_language_example: El hotel está en el centro de la ciudad, cerca del museo.
native_language_example: The hotel is in the city center, near the museum.

additional_notes: Usually means “in the sky” for things you can see above you (clouds, birds, rockets). It can also mean “in heaven” in a religious or afterlife sense; context makes it clear. The phrase is literal: en (in) + el (the) + cielo (sky/heaven).
target_language_example: Mira, hay muchas estrellas en el cielo esta noche.
native_language_example: Look, there are many stars in the sky tonight.

meaning: at the movie theater; in the cinema.
additional_notes: Used to say where something happens (location). It can mean being inside the movie theater building or attending/watching a movie there. Often used with verbs like ver (to see), entrar (to go in), esperar (to wait), estar (to be), and dar (to show/screen a movie).
target_language_example: Nos vemos en el cine a las ocho.
native_language_example: See you at the movie theater at eight.

additional_notes: Used to say that someone or something is located inside a car. "En" = in/on; with vehicles like "coche" (car), it usually means "in". It can also mean riding/traveling by car in some contexts (e.g., "Voy en el coche" = "I’m going in the car").
target_language_example: Dejé mi bolso en el coche.
native_language_example: I left my bag in the car.

meaning: at school; in school (at the school).
additional_notes: Used to say someone is physically at the school building or that something happened during their time as a student. In many places, "el colegio" refers to primary/secondary school (not university), so "en el colegio" often means "in school" (when you were a kid/teen).
target_language_example: Hablamos de eso en el colegio.
native_language_example: We talked about that at school.

meaning: in the heart; deep down (inside someone).
additional_notes: Often literal (physical heart): “apuñaló… en el corazón” (stabbed in the heart) or “puso la mano en el corazón” (put his hand on his heart). Also used figuratively to mean someone’s inner feelings/true nature: “bueno en el corazón” (good at heart). You’ll also see it with "de": “en el corazón de…” = “in the heart of… / at the core of…”.
target_language_example: Aunque parecía frío, en el corazón era una buena persona.
native_language_example: Although he seemed cold, deep down he was a good person.

additional_notes: Used to say where something/someone is located. It commonly answers “Where?” (¿Dónde?) and is often used with verbs like hay (there is/are), estar (to be), and mirar (to look). In some contexts, cuarto can also mean “quarter” (1/4) or “fourth,” but en el cuarto usually means “in the room.”
target_language_example: Dejé las llaves en el cuarto.
native_language_example: I left the keys in the room.

additional_notes: Used to say where something is located or happens: an injury (herida) in the neck, something placed on the neck (a scarf, a necklace, a bandage), or kissing someone on the neck (besarle en el cuello). With body parts, Spanish often uses the definite article (el/la) instead of a possessive: "Me duele el cuello" = "My neck hurts."
target_language_example: Me puse una bufanda en el cuello porque hacía frío.
native_language_example: I put a scarf around my neck because it was cold.

additional_notes: Used to say something is located or happens in a desert. Common with verbs like estar (to be), vivir (to live), perderse (to get lost), encontrar (to find), and phrases like pasar la noche (to spend the night).
target_language_example: Pasamos dos días en el desierto.
native_language_example: We spent two days in the desert.

meaning: during the day; in the daytime.
additional_notes: Used to talk about something that happens (or is visible) in daylight hours, often contrasted with “en la noche” (at night). You may also hear “de día,” which is very common and means the same idea.
target_language_example: Trabajo en el día y descanso en la noche.
native_language_example: I work during the day and rest at night.

additional_notes: Used to say someone/something is located inside a particular building. Often answers the question “¿Dónde?” (Where?). You can change the article and noun depending on the place: “en la casa” (in the house), “en el hotel” (in the hotel).
target_language_example: Los documentos están en el edificio.
native_language_example: The documents are in the building.

meaning: in the army; in the military.
additional_notes: Used to say someone is serving/served as a soldier or was in the military at a certain time. Common with verbs like estar (to be), servir (to serve), quedar(se) (to stay), and conocer (to meet) when talking about experiences during military service.
target_language_example: Mi hermano estuvo en el ejército durante tres años.
native_language_example: My brother was in the army for three years.

additional_notes: Used to say someone is physically on a theater/concert stage (not in the audience). Common with verbs like aparecer (to appear), estar/pararse (to be/stand), and in show contexts like cuando caiga el telón (when the curtain falls).
target_language_example: Los actores ya están en el escenario.
native_language_example: The actors are already on the stage.

additional_notes: Uses the preposition phrase "en el" + noun "espacio" to mean being located in outer space. Often appears in science-fiction or astronomy contexts. Don't confuse with "en un espacio" (in a space/area/room), which can mean a physical place on Earth.
target_language_example: Los astronautas viven en el espacio durante meses.
native_language_example: Astronauts live in space for months.

additional_notes: Used with verbs like mirar(se) or ver(se) to say someone is looking at themselves or something reflected in a mirror. Can also be used figuratively (e.g., “mírate en el espejo”) to mean “look at yourself / take a hard look at your own responsibility.”
target_language_example: Me miré en el espejo antes de salir.
native_language_example: I looked at myself in the mirror before leaving.

additional_notes: Used to say where something is located: *en* (on/in) + *el estante* (the shelf). Often appears with verbs like **poner** (to put) and **guardar** (to store/put away).
target_language_example: La sal está en el estante de arriba.
native_language_example: The salt is on the top shelf.

meaning: in the stomach (in the belly area).
additional_notes: Used to say that something is located in the stomach area or that you feel something there (pain, a warm feeling, nervousness). Often follows words like dolor (pain), sensación (feeling), nudo (a knot), or describing an injury (un balazo/una bala en el estómago).
target_language_example: Me duele mucho en el estómago.
native_language_example: My stomach hurts a lot.

additional_notes: Used to talk about something happening while taking an exam (often with verbs like usar, copiar, hacer trampas). It can also introduce the specific test: en el examen de historia/biología (“in the history/biology exam”).
target_language_example: No hables en el examen.
native_language_example: Don’t talk during the exam.

additional_notes: Used to say that someone is/was outside their home country (often contrasted with “en casa / en mi país”). Common with verbs like vivir, estudiar, trabajar, viajar, morir: “vivir/estudiar/trabajar en el extranjero”.
target_language_example: Mi hermana estudia en el extranjero este año.
native_language_example: My sister is studying abroad this year.

additional_notes: Used both literally (location at the lowest/deepest part of something: en el fondo del río/de la mochila) and figuratively to mean “deep down” or “when you really think about it,” often at the start of a sentence: En el fondo, sabía que...
target_language_example: En el fondo, creo que tienes razón.
native_language_example: Deep down, I think you’re right.

meaning: at the bottom of; deep inside (figurative).
additional_notes: Used to locate something physically at the lowest/deepest part of something (en el fondo de la caja/el pozo). It’s also very common figuratively with feelings or personality: "en el fondo de tu/su corazón" = "deep down in your/his/her heart" (deep inside). Often contrasts with what seems true on the surface.
target_language_example: En el fondo de mi bolso siempre hay monedas.
native_language_example: At the bottom of my bag there are always coins.

additional_notes: Used to point out where something is located, specifically at the lowest part of something (ocean, lake, river, glass, etc.). It’s followed by a masculine singular noun: del = de + el (e.g., en el fondo del mar). For feminine nouns, you use: en el fondo de la (e.g., en el fondo de la botella).
target_language_example: Hay monedas en el fondo del bolso.
native_language_example: There are coins at the bottom of the bag.

additional_notes: Used to talk about a time after now. Very common with future plans, predictions, or things that might happen later (e.g., "en el futuro voy a...", "en el futuro pasará..."). It can refer to the near future or the distant future depending on context.
target_language_example: En el futuro, quiero vivir en otro país.
native_language_example: In the future, I want to live in another country.

additional_notes: Indicates location. Use it to say someone/something is physically inside the gym or at the gym as a place (exercise or sports facility). It’s also used for events held there (e.g., a picnic moved indoors due to rain).
target_language_example: Nos vemos en el gimnasio a las seis.
native_language_example: See you at the gym at six.

additional_notes: Used to say where something happens on someone’s body (being hit, hurt, touched, etc.). With body parts in Spanish, you usually use the definite article (el/la) instead of a possessive: "Me puso la mano en el hombro" = "He put his hand on my shoulder." Often appears with pronouns like me/le/lo/la to show who is affected.
target_language_example: Me dio una palmada en el hombro para llamar mi atención.
native_language_example: He patted me on the shoulder to get my attention.

additional_notes: Used to say something is visible far away where the sky seems to meet the land or sea. Common with verbs like aparecer (to appear) and hundirse (to sink/set) when talking about the sun or ships.
target_language_example: Veo una tormenta en el horizonte.
native_language_example: I see a storm on the horizon.

additional_notes: Used to say that food is inside the oven, usually cooking or heating. You’ll often hear it with estar (está en el horno) or dejar (he dejado… en el horno).
target_language_example: El pastel ya está en el horno.
native_language_example: The cake is already in the oven.

additional_notes: Used to say someone is physically at the hospital (often as a patient, but it can also mean being there for work or to visit). In Spanish you normally include the article: "en el hospital" (not just "en hospital"). With specific hospitals you may also hear "en el Hospital X".
target_language_example: Mi abuela está en el hospital desde ayer.
native_language_example: My grandmother has been in the hospital since yesterday.

additional_notes: Used to say where someone or something is located or where something happens. With verbs like estar/quedarse (to be/stay), dejar/olvidar (to leave/forget), encontrarse (to meet), and reservar (to book). Often implies inside the hotel or at the hotel as a place (e.g., meeting point).
target_language_example: Nos vemos en el hotel a las ocho.
native_language_example: See you at the hotel at eight.

additional_notes: Used with verbs like "estar" (to be), "arder" (to burn), or "quedarse" (to stay): "Está en el infierno" = "He/She is in hell." It can be literal (religious/afterlife) or figurative to describe a terrible situation ("this place is hell").
target_language_example: No quiero estar en el infierno otra vez.
native_language_example: I don’t want to be in hell again.

additional_notes: Used to say something happens during the winter season. Often used with other seasons too (en el verano, en la primavera, en el otoño). You can also add a specific time: en el invierno de 2023 / en el invierno de hace tres años.
target_language_example: En el invierno siempre hace frío aquí.
native_language_example: In the winter it’s always cold here.

additional_notes: Used to say where something happens or where someone/something is located. Common with verbs like estar/haber (location/existence) and with actions like trabajar, caminar, reunirse. "Jardín" can mean a private garden/yard or a landscaped garden area (e.g., at a house, school, or park).
target_language_example: Estamos en el jardín porque hace buen tiempo.
native_language_example: We’re in the garden because the weather is nice.

additional_notes: Used to say something is located or happening inside the lake (in the water), not next to it ("junto al lago") or on the shore. "En" + "el" contracts to "en el".
target_language_example: Vimos patos nadando en el lago.
native_language_example: We saw ducks swimming in the lake.

additional_notes: Used for where something is located or where to put it in a car. In Spain, *maletero* commonly means the car’s trunk/boot; in some Latin American countries you may also hear *cajuela* or *baúl*.
target_language_example: Deja las maletas en el maletero, por favor.
native_language_example: Leave the suitcases in the trunk, please.

additional_notes: Used to say something is shown or located on a map. Often used with verbs like buscar (to look for), encontrar (to find), indicar/representar (to indicate/represent), and estar (to be).
target_language_example: ¿Puedes señalar el hotel en el mapa?
native_language_example: Can you point out the hotel on the map?

additional_notes: Used to say where something happens or where someone is (location). Common with verbs like nadar (to swim), bañarse (to bathe/swim), estar (to be), and vivir/pasar tiempo (to live/spend time). With other bodies of water you change the noun: en el río (in the river), en el lago (in the lake).
target_language_example: En verano, pasamos mucho tiempo en el mar.
native_language_example: In summer, we spend a lot of time in the sea.

additional_notes: Used for physical location (the center of something) or being caught between two sides/people/situations ("in the middle" of a conflict). Often appears with estar: "estar en el medio".
target_language_example: No me pongas en el medio de su discusión.
native_language_example: Don’t put me in the middle of your argument.

meaning: at the market; in the marketplace.
additional_notes: Used to say where something happens—at a market (a place to buy food/goods). Often follows a verb to indicate location: comprar en el mercado (to buy at the market), ver a alguien en el mercado (to see someone at the market).
target_language_example: Nos vemos en el mercado a las diez.
native_language_example: See you at the market at ten.

additional_notes: Used to say something happens while riding the metro/subway or inside the metro system (stations, trains). Spanish often uses “en” (in) where English uses “on” for public transport: “Voy en el metro” = “I’m going by subway.” You can also say “por metro” to mean “by subway,” but “en el metro” is very common for being in it/using it.
target_language_example: Voy al trabajo en el metro todos los días.
native_language_example: I go to work by subway every day.

additional_notes: Used to say that something happens or is located in the identical location as before, or as another person/thing. You can add details like “de siempre” (the usual place) or “en que...” (where...) to specify which place.
target_language_example: Nos vemos en el mismo lugar a las ocho.
native_language_example: See you in the same place at eight.

additional_notes: Used to introduce a time clause that happens immediately when something else happens. It often takes the subjunctive if the action is in the future/uncertain (e.g., En el momento en que llegues, llámame) and the indicative for past or habitual events.
target_language_example: En el momento en que termine la reunión, te llamo.
native_language_example: The moment the meeting ends, I’ll call you.

additional_notes: Used to talk about something within the whole world (often in comparisons or superlatives: "el/la más ... en el mundo" = "the most ... in the world"). It can also be used more figuratively with "mundo de + noun" to mean a sphere or area, like "en el mundo del arte" (in the art world).
target_language_example: Es el edificio más alto en el mundo.
native_language_example: It’s the tallest building in the world.

additional_notes: Used to call on a person, deity, or authority to support a request, command, oath, prayer, or formal statement. Common in religious or ceremonial contexts (e.g., "En el nombre de Dios..."). You’ll also see it with names of people or institutions. Often appears as a fixed phrase at the start of a sentence.
target_language_example: En el nombre de la ley, deben salir ahora.
native_language_example: In the name of the law, you must leave now.

meaning: “in the eye”; also “in the center of …” (as in en el ojo de la tormenta).
additional_notes: Most often literal: something is in your eye (Tengo algo en el ojo), you got hit in the eye (Me pegó en el ojo), or you have a cut in your eye (un corte en el ojo). In set phrases it can be figurative: en el ojo de la tormenta = “in the eye of the storm / at the center of the trouble.” Related idioms you may see: dar en el ojo can mean “to hit the mark / be exactly right,” and quedarse con la sangre en el ojo means “to hold a grudge / want revenge.”
target_language_example: Tengo algo en el ojo.
native_language_example: I have something in my eye.

additional_notes: Used to say where something happens or where someone/something is located. Often follows verbs like estar (to be), caminar/pasear (to walk/take a stroll), esperar (to wait), jugar (to play), ver (to see).
target_language_example: Nos encontramos en el parque a las cinco.
native_language_example: We’re meeting in the park at five.

additional_notes: Used to talk about a previous time or earlier situation. Often placed at the beginning of a sentence as a time expression: “En el pasado, …”. It can also be used more figuratively to mean leaving something behind (“Dejamos nuestras diferencias en el pasado” = we put our differences behind us).
target_language_example: En el pasado, no teníamos internet en casa.
native_language_example: In the past, we didn’t have internet at home.

meaning: in the hallway / in the corridor.
additional_notes: Used to say someone or something is located in a building’s passageway outside rooms (at home, school, an office, etc.). Often answers the question "¿Dónde?" (Where?).
target_language_example: Nos encontramos en el pasillo antes de entrar a clase.
native_language_example: We’ll meet in the hallway before going into class.

meaning: in the courtyard/yard (outside area of a house or building).
additional_notes: Used to say someone or something is located in the patio—an outdoor space such as a yard, courtyard, or patio area. Often contrasts with being inside (en la casa).
target_language_example: Dejé las sillas en el patio para la cena.
native_language_example: I left the chairs in the yard/patio for dinner.

additional_notes: Used to say where something is located or where someone is hit/injured: *dolor(es) en el pecho* (chest pain), *una masa en el pecho* (a lump in the chest/breast), *una bala en el pecho* (a bullet in the chest). Also common for the general area where the heart and lungs are.
target_language_example: Me dieron un golpe en el pecho y me duele mucho.
native_language_example: They hit me in the chest and it hurts a lot.

additional_notes: Used to say something appears/was published in a newspaper (print or its news outlet). Common with verbs like leer (to read), salir (to appear), and publicar (to publish): “Leí X en el periódico”, “Su foto salió en el periódico”.
target_language_example: Lo vi en el periódico esta mañana.
native_language_example: I saw it in the newspaper this morning.

additional_notes: Used to say something is located or happens on the floor (usually indoors). Common with verbs like estar (to be), poner (to put), caer (to fall), sentarse (to sit), and dormir (to sleep). In some countries, piso can also mean “apartment,” but in this phrase it means “floor.”
target_language_example: Dejé las llaves en el piso.
native_language_example: I left the keys on the floor.

additional_notes: Used to say someone/something is on a lower level inside a building. Often contrasts with “en el piso de arriba” (upstairs/on the floor above). “Piso” can mean “floor” (level) in a building (especially in Spain), and also “apartment,” but here it means a lower floor/level.
target_language_example: El baño está en el piso de abajo, al lado de la cocina.
native_language_example: The bathroom is downstairs, next to the kitchen.

additional_notes: Refers to being located in or within a specific town/village (pueblo can mean either depending on context). It’s commonly used to say someone lives there, was born there, or is known by people there. For “the best in town,” Spanish often says “el mejor del pueblo / del lugar,” but “en el pueblo” is also understandable in casual speech.
target_language_example: Hay un restaurante muy famoso en el pueblo.
native_language_example: There’s a very famous restaurant in town.

additional_notes: A location phrase meaning someone/something is physically on a bridge. Often answers “¿Dónde?” (Where?) or is used to set the scene. Related: “en el puente” (on the bridge), “al puente” (to the bridge), “del puente” (from/of the bridge), “entrando en el puente” (entering onto the bridge).
target_language_example: Nos vemos en el puente a las seis.
native_language_example: See you on the bridge at six.

additional_notes: Used to say something is located at a port (a place where ships dock and cargo is loaded/unloaded). Common with verbs like estar, trabajar, ver, and with ships (barco, buque).
target_language_example: Nos vemos en el puerto a las seis.
native_language_example: See you at the harbor at six.

additional_notes: Used in relative clauses to refer back to a masculine singular antecedent (e.g., el día, el mundo, el hospital, el accidente, el pueblo). Often corresponds to “in which” or sometimes “where” (especially with places). It agrees with the noun: en la que (fem. sing.), en los que (masc. plural), en las que (fem. plural).
target_language_example: El sábado es el día en el que él está libre.
native_language_example: Saturday is the day on which he is free.

additional_notes: Used with "estar" to say where something is located. Common for food/drinks ("La leche está en el refrigerador"), but it can also be used humorously for odd things (like a phone number written on paper and stuck to the fridge/refrigerator).
target_language_example: El jugo está en el refrigerador.
native_language_example: The juice is in the refrigerator.

additional_notes: Used to say where something happens. It’s a very common location phrase: en + el (="in the" + masculine singular) + restaurante. Often placed at the beginning of the sentence for context ("En el restaurante, ..."). You’ll also see it in signs and rules like “No fumar en el restaurante” / “No se puede fumar en el restaurante.”
target_language_example: En el restaurante, pedimos una mesa para dos.
native_language_example: In the restaurant, we asked for a table for two.

additional_notes: Used to say something is located or happens inside the river (water), not just near it. It can answer “Where?” by itself: “¿Dónde?” — “En el río.”
target_language_example: Hay muchos peces en el río.
native_language_example: There are many fish in the river.

meaning: in the living room; in the room/classroom; in the salon (shop).
additional_notes: “Salón” usually means a living room or a large room/hall. In many contexts (especially school), “el salón” can mean the classroom (“salón de clase/aula”). It can also refer to a place of business like a tattoo salon (as in “salón de tatuaje”) or a beauty salon (“salón de belleza”). The meaning depends on context; “en el” means “in the.”
target_language_example: Nos vemos en el salón después de cenar.
native_language_example: See you in the living room after dinner.

additional_notes: Used to say where something is located inside a building. In many Spanish-speaking countries, “segundo piso” is the floor above the ground floor (“planta baja”), which can differ from U.S. usage in some places.
target_language_example: La oficina está en el segundo piso.
native_language_example: The office is on the second floor.

meaning: on the sofa / on the couch.
additional_notes: Used to say someone or something is located, sitting, or lying on the sofa. Common with verbs like estar (está en el sofá), dormir (duerme en el sofá), sentarse (sentado/a en el sofá), acostarse/tumbarse (tumbado/a en el sofá), and quedarse (me quedaré en el sofá).
target_language_example: Hoy voy a dormir en el sofá porque tengo mucho sueño.
native_language_example: Today I'm going to sleep on the sofa because I'm very sleepy.

meaning: on the ground; on the floor.
additional_notes: Used to say something is located on the ground/floor, or to tell someone to be down there (e.g., "¡Al suelo!" = "Get on the ground!"). With objects, it often means something has fallen or been placed there.
target_language_example: Dejé las llaves en el suelo y no las encuentro.
native_language_example: I left the keys on the floor and I can’t find them.

additional_notes: Uses the preposition "en" to say where something happens (location). With places like stores, "en" often translates as either "in" or "at" in English, depending on context. You can add details after it: "en el supermercado de la esquina" (at the corner supermarket).
target_language_example: Nos vemos en el supermercado después del trabajo.
native_language_example: See you at the supermarket after work.

additional_notes: Used to locate a place in the southern part of a larger area (a country, region, city, etc.). It’s a fixed location phrase and is often followed by a place name: en el sur de España / de la ciudad. Variations: en el norte de (in the north of), en el este de (in the east of), en el oeste de (in the west of).
target_language_example: Vivo en el sur de México.
native_language_example: I live in the south of Mexico.

additional_notes: Used to say something (or someone) is located downstairs in the building’s basement. Often answers “¿Dónde?” (Where?). “Sótano” = basement; “en el” = in the.
target_language_example: Las cajas están en el sótano.
native_language_example: The boxes are in the basement.

meaning: at the theater; in the theater.
additional_notes: Used to say where something happens (a location). It can refer to a theater building in general (en el teatro) or a specific one (en el teatro Cavendish). Also used in set phrases like "en el teatro de ópera" (at the opera house).
target_language_example: Nos vemos en el teatro a las ocho.
native_language_example: See you at the theater at eight.

meaning: on the roof; on the ceiling.
additional_notes: “Techo” can mean either the outside top of a building (roof) or the inside top of a room (ceiling). Context makes it clear: vehicles/buildings outdoors → “roof” (paneles solares en el techo); looking up inside a room → “ceiling” (mirar/fijar los ojos en el techo).
target_language_example: Hay una mancha de humedad en el techo.
