native_language_example: There’s a damp stain on the ceiling.

meaning: on the phone (talking on a phone call).
additional_notes: Used to say someone is currently speaking in a phone call or should stay on the line. In some contexts it can also imply spending time using a phone (screen time), but often it’s about being on a call. Common related phrases: “estar en el teléfono” (to be on the phone), “quédate en el teléfono” (stay on the line), “poner a alguien en el teléfono” (put someone on the phone).
target_language_example: No puedo hablar ahora; estoy en el teléfono.
native_language_example: I can’t talk right now; I’m on the phone.

meaning: in time; in the weather; in the (historical) time/era of.
additional_notes: Most commonly relates to time: *congelado en el tiempo* (“frozen in time”), *volver/ir atrás en el tiempo* (“go back in time”), or *en el tiempo de + [period/person]* (“in the time/era of…”). Note that *el tiempo* can also mean “the weather,” so *un cambio en el tiempo* often means “a change in the weather” (not “a change in time”).
target_language_example: Ese edificio parece atrapado en el tiempo.
native_language_example: That building seems stuck in time.

additional_notes: Used to say where something happens (your workplace) or your state of being working. Often follows verbs like estar/ser/trabajar (e.g., Estoy en el trabajo = I’m at work).
target_language_example: No puedo hablar ahora; estoy en el trabajo.
native_language_example: I can’t talk now; I’m at work.

meaning: on the train; in the train.
additional_notes: Used to say where something happens or where someone/something is: en el tren = on/inside the train. With transport, Spanish often uses “en” where English commonly uses “on” (en el tren, en el autobús, en el avión).
target_language_example: Conocí a mi mejor amigo en el tren.
native_language_example: I met my best friend on the train.

additional_notes: Used to talk about the entire cosmos/space (everything that exists). Often appears in science facts ("Hay millones de estrellas en el universo") or in exaggerations/idioms meaning "anywhere in the world/universe" ("el mejor en el universo").
target_language_example: Dicen que es la mejor pizza en el universo.
native_language_example: They say it’s the best pizza in the universe.

additional_notes: Used to talk about things that happen or are true during the summer season. Often interchangeable with "en verano" (without "el"), especially in general statements.
target_language_example: En el verano hace mucho calor aquí.
native_language_example: In the summer it’s very hot here.

additional_notes: Used to say someone/something is located in a building’s lobby/foyer—often in hotels, offices, theaters, etc. It commonly answers “¿Dónde?” (Where?).
target_language_example: Nos vemos en el vestíbulo del hotel a las ocho.
native_language_example: See you in the hotel lobby at eight.

meaning: on the tree; in the tree.
additional_notes: Means “on/in the tree,” depending on context. Use it for something located on the surface of a tree (e.g., a name carved on it) or up in the branches (e.g., a bird singing).
target_language_example: Hay una ardilla en el árbol.
native_language_example: There’s a squirrel in the tree.

meaning: in the area; nearby; in that part/section.
additional_notes: Used to locate something within a certain zone or part of a place. Often followed by a more specific description ("en el área donde...") or a noun ("en el área del..." = "in the area of..."). Depending on context, it can mean nearby (general vicinity) or a specific section inside a building/facility.
target_language_example: Hay un policía en el área, así que ten cuidado.
native_language_example: There’s a police officer in the area, so be careful.

meaning: in the attic (top space under the roof).
additional_notes: Used with estar/haber to say someone or something is located in the attic. "Ático" here means the attic of a house/building (not an apartment/penthouse, which can also be called "ático" in some contexts).
target_language_example: Guardamos las cajas viejas en el ático.
native_language_example: We keep the old boxes in the attic.

meaning: at the last moment (at the last minute).
additional_notes: Used to talk about something that happens right before it’s too late—often a sudden change, cancellation, or idea. Common with verbs like echarse atrás (back out), dejar (leave someone), desaparecer (disappear), ocurrirse (occur to someone).
target_language_example: Llegó en el último momento y alcanzó el tren.
native_language_example: He arrived at the last minute and caught the train.

meaning: "about it" / "on it" (referring to a thing or situation).
additional_notes: Used after verbs that take the preposition "en" (like pensar en, creer en, confiar en, insistir en) to refer back to a previously mentioned idea, object, or situation. "Ello" is a neutral pronoun (not a person); in everyday speech, people often also say "en eso" (more common) with a similar meaning.
target_language_example: No quiero hablar más en ello.
native_language_example: I don’t want to talk about it anymore.

additional_notes: Used to say people do something collaboratively rather than individually. Common with verbs like trabajar (to work), jugar (to play), and colaborar (to collaborate): “trabajar en equipo” = “to work as a team.”
target_language_example: Tenemos que trabajar en equipo para terminar a tiempo.
native_language_example: We have to work as a team to finish on time.

meaning: "in that" (referring to a specific feminine thing/place).
additional_notes: Used with feminine singular nouns (esa + noun) to point to something specific, usually not right next to the speaker: en esa habitación (in that room), en esa caja (in that box), en esa dirección (in that direction). For masculine nouns use "en ese"; for plural use "en esas / en esos".
target_language_example: Dejé mi chaqueta en esa silla.
native_language_example: I left my jacket on that chair.

additional_notes: Used to say something happens or is located at a specific store that’s not here (often one previously mentioned). You can use it with verbs like comprar (to buy), vender (to sell), estar (to be), and hay (there is/are).
target_language_example: Siempre encuentro buenas ofertas en esa tienda.
native_language_example: I always find good deals in that store.

meaning: at that time; in those days.
additional_notes: Used to refer to a particular period in the past that has already been mentioned or is understood from context. Similar to "entonces" or "en aquellos tiempos" (more distant/nostalgic: "in those days").
target_language_example: En esa época no tenía coche, así que iba a todas partes en autobús.
native_language_example: At that time I didn’t have a car, so I went everywhere by bus.

additional_notes: Used to respond to or draw a conclusion from what was just said, often at the beginning of a sentence. Common in both formal and informal speech.
target_language_example: En ese caso, mejor nos vamos ahora.
native_language_example: In that case, we'd better leave now.

additional_notes: Used to refer to a past period or situation already mentioned or understood from context. Often sets the scene for how things were in the past (customs, circumstances, age, relationships). Similar to “en aquel entonces” (a bit more distant/less immediate).
target_language_example: En ese entonces no teníamos coche, así que íbamos a pie a todas partes.
native_language_example: Back then we didn’t have a car, so we walked everywhere.

meaning: at that moment; at that time.
additional_notes: Used to point to a specific time in the past (or in a story) when something was happening. Very common with the imperfect/progressive to set the scene: "En ese momento, estaba..." It can go at the beginning or end of the sentence.
target_language_example: En ese momento no podía contestar el teléfono.
native_language_example: At that moment, I couldn't answer the phone.

additional_notes: Used to talk about a specific period in the past (often a past stage in someone’s life or a historical era). It commonly appears with the imperfect tense (estaba, era) to describe ongoing situations or states during that time. Similar to "en aquella época".
target_language_example: En ese tiempo, no tenía coche y caminaba a todas partes.
native_language_example: Back then, I didn’t have a car and I walked everywhere.

additional_notes: Used to single out someone/something from a group or to say there’s no particular one. Common in questions ("¿... en especial?" = "Any ... in particular?") and negatives ("nada/con nadie en especial" = "nothing/no one in particular"). It can modify a whole sentence ("En especial para usted" = "Especially for you") or be followed by "de" ("en especial de ti" = "especially about you").
target_language_example: ¿Quieres algo en especial o te da igual?
native_language_example: Do you want anything in particular, or do you not care?

additional_notes: Used for something/someone that is waiting or temporarily paused until something happens. Common with calls ("una llamada en espera" = a call on hold) and with "en espera de" meaning "waiting for" (often in more formal contexts).
target_language_example: Estoy en espera de tu respuesta.
native_language_example: I’m waiting for your reply.

meaning: in this house; in this home.
additional_notes: Used to locate something or someone within the speaker’s home/house (physical place). Often appears with verbs like vivir/crecer (to live/grow up), haber (there is/are), estar (to be), or with rules/attitudes: “(no) es bienvenido en esta casa” = “(not) welcome in this house.”
target_language_example: No se permite fumar en esta casa.
native_language_example: Smoking is not allowed in this house.

additional_notes: Used to indicate location within the city you’re currently talking about. Common with expressions like “hay…” (there is/are) and with comparisons (e.g., “el más grande en esta ciudad” = the biggest in this city).
target_language_example: En esta ciudad hay buen transporte público.
native_language_example: In this city there is good public transportation.

additional_notes: Used to say that someone/something is located inside the room you’re currently talking about (often the room you’re in). Common with verbs like estar/haber (está/están, hay).
target_language_example: ¿Hay aire acondicionado en esta habitación?
native_language_example: Is there air conditioning in this room?

additional_notes: Used to say that something is located or happening inside the room you’re currently in (or a specific room being pointed out). Often follows verbs like estar/hacer (e.g., Hace calor en esta sala).
target_language_example: No se puede comer en esta sala.
native_language_example: You can’t eat in this room.

meaning: in this store / in this shop.
additional_notes: Used to say that something happens or is true inside this particular store (esta = “this,” referring to a specific shop you’re in/near or just mentioned). It often comes at the beginning or end of the sentence.
target_language_example: No venden pan en esta tienda.
native_language_example: They don’t sell bread in this store.

additional_notes: Used to locate something or describe rules/conditions within a specific place near the speaker. Often appears in signs and instructions (e.g., "Prohibido... en esta zona"). You can swap in other demonstratives: "en esa zona" (in that area near you) or "en aquella zona" (over there).
target_language_example: No se permite fumar en esta zona.
native_language_example: Smoking is not allowed in this area.

additional_notes: Used to describe the condition something is in, often with an adjective (en estado sólido/líquido) or with de + noun (en estado de ebriedad = drunk/intoxicated). Common in science/technical contexts and in set phrases like en estado de emergencia (in a state of emergency).
target_language_example: El vapor es agua en estado gaseoso.
native_language_example: Steam is water in a gaseous state.

additional_notes: Used mainly for someone’s health/medical status, especially after an accident or serious illness. Often appears with verbs like "estar" or "encontrarse" (to be).
target_language_example: Después del accidente, el conductor está en estado crítico.
native_language_example: After the accident, the driver is in critical condition.

additional_notes: Used to refer to a specific situation, condition, or exception being discussed (often to contrast with other possibilities: "pero no en este caso"). It can also refer to a particular matter or investigation (like a police case), depending on context.
target_language_example: En este caso, vamos a tomar un taxi.
native_language_example: In this case, we’re going to take a taxi.

additional_notes: Used to say where something is or where an action happens. "Cuarto" means "room" (often a bedroom), and "en" means "in/on/at" depending on context.
target_language_example: No hables tan fuerte en este cuarto.
native_language_example: Don’t speak so loudly in this room.

meaning: in this place; here (in this spot).
additional_notes: Used to point to a specific location (physical or sometimes figurative) where something is happening or started. Often appears at the beginning of a sentence to set the scene: “En este lugar…” You can also say “aquí” for a shorter “here,” but “en este lugar” sounds more specific/emphatic.
target_language_example: Nos vemos en este lugar mañana a las ocho.
native_language_example: See you at this place tomorrow at eight.

meaning: right now; at this moment; currently.
additional_notes: Used to talk about what is happening now, or someone’s current situation/location. Common at the start of a sentence for emphasis (often with a comma): “En este momento, …”. Also used to mean someone is unavailable at the moment: “No se encuentra en este momento.”
target_language_example: No puedo hablar en este momento; te llamo luego.
native_language_example: I can’t talk right now; I’ll call you later.

meaning: in this world; in the whole world (for emphasis).
additional_notes: Often used to intensify comparisons and superlatives, especially with phrases like "más que nada" (more than anything) or "lo que más" (what you want most), meaning "above anything else." It can be literal (physically in the world), but in these examples it’s emotional emphasis.
target_language_example: Eres lo que más quiero en este mundo.
native_language_example: You’re what I want most in the whole world.

additional_notes: Used to talk about something that is true (or happens) within the country you’re currently referring to—often the one you’re in now. Common in explanations and comparisons: "En este país..." + a general fact or rule.
target_language_example: En este país la gente cena muy tarde.
native_language_example: In this country people eat dinner very late.

meaning: in this town (here in this town).
additional_notes: Used to locate something happening or being true within the town you’re currently talking about. "Pueblo" often means a small town or village, not a big city. You can swap "este" for "ese/aquel" (that/that over there) or change the noun: "en este barrio" (in this neighborhood).
target_language_example: En este pueblo no hay mucho que hacer por la noche.
native_language_example: In this town there isn’t much to do at night.

additional_notes: Used to talk about the present period of time (not necessarily today—more like “recently/now”). It often comments on current trends or how things are nowadays. You can place it at the beginning of a sentence (“En estos días, …”) or at the end (“… en estos días”).
target_language_example: En estos días estoy muy ocupado con el trabajo.
native_language_example: These days I’m very busy with work.

additional_notes: Used to say something is done more than is healthy, necessary, or appropriate. Common with verbs like beber (to drink), comer (to eat), hablar (to talk). It can also refer to overdoing something in general (e.g., “Lo hice en exceso” = “I overdid it”).
target_language_example: No trabajes en exceso; necesitas descansar.
native_language_example: Don’t work too much; you need to rest.

meaning: 'anyway', 'well', or 'in short' (used to wrap up or move on).
additional_notes: Used as a discourse marker at the start of a sentence (often with a comma) to conclude what was being said, summarize, show resignation, or change topic: “En fin, hay que irse…” ≈ “Anyway, we have to go…”. Depending on tone/context it can also mean “in the end/finally.”
target_language_example: En fin, no vale la pena discutir; vámonos.
native_language_example: Anyway, it’s not worth arguing; let’s go.

meaning: in shape; fit / well-prepared; in the form of.
additional_notes: Common uses: (1) physical condition: "estar/mantenerse/ponerse en forma" = to be/stay/get in shape. (2) "en forma de + noun" = in the shape/form of (often about appearance). (3) More formal: "en forma" can mean "properly/with order" (e.g., explaining something "en forma").
target_language_example: Quiero ponerme en forma antes del verano.
native_language_example: I want to get in shape before summer.

additional_notes: Used to say something is spoken or written using the French language. Often goes with verbs like hablar (to speak), escribir (to write), decir (to say), and aprender (to learn).
target_language_example: ¿Puedes repetírmelo en francés, por favor?
native_language_example: Can you repeat it to me in French, please?

additional_notes: Used to say someone/something is directly before another place or person, or to describe moving past in front of someone (e.g., pasar/correr en frente de alguien). In everyday Spanish, "enfrente de" is also very common and often interchangeable. (Some speakers prefer "delante de" for physical position.)
target_language_example: Nos vemos en frente de la estación a las seis.
native_language_example: See you in front of the station at six.

meaning: "by virtue of" / "on the strength of" (because of a legal or formal basis).
additional_notes: Very formal, often used in legal/administrative writing to cite the authority, reason, or basis for something. It’s similar to "en virtud de". Not commonly used in everyday conversation.
target_language_example: En fuerza de la ley, el contrato queda rescindido.
native_language_example: By virtue of the law, the contract is terminated.

additional_notes: Used to talk about something as a whole, not in specific cases. It can modify a statement (“En general, me gusta este barrio.”) or come after what it describes (“Los precios han caído en general.”). Also used like “generally speaking.”
target_language_example: En general, la gente aquí es amable.
native_language_example: In general, people here are friendly.

meaning: in a big way; big time (to a great extent).
additional_notes: Common as an intensifier meaning “a lot / to the fullest.” Very often used with **pasarlo**: **pasarlo en grande** = “to have a great time.” It can also describe doing something on a large scale: **celebrar en grande** (“celebrate in a big way”). In some contexts it can imply exaggerating or talking big: **hablar en grande** (“to talk big / brag”).
target_language_example: Este fin de semana lo vamos a celebrar en grande.
native_language_example: This weekend we’re going to celebrate in a big way.

meaning: on guard; on the lookout (alert and ready).
additional_notes: Used to tell someone to be alert and prepared (often like a warning or command). Common with verbs like estar/ponerse: “estar en guardia” (to be on guard), “ponerse/pónganse en guardia” (to get on guard). Can also be said alone as an order: “¡En guardia!” (also used in fencing to mean “On guard!”).
target_language_example: Cuando viajes, mantente en guardia con tus pertenencias.
native_language_example: When you travel, stay on guard with your belongings.

additional_notes: Used to say that something is spoken, written, taught, done, or available in the English language (e.g., hablar/escribir/estudiar/estar en inglés).
target_language_example: ¿Puedes explicarlo en inglés, por favor?
native_language_example: Can you explain it in English, please?

additional_notes: Used to say when something happens or is true during the winter season. Often describes typical conditions or what’s advisable/not advisable at that time of year (e.g., weather, activities).
target_language_example: En invierno hace más frío y oscurece temprano.
native_language_example: In winter it’s colder and it gets dark early.

additional_notes: Used with "haber" to say that something important could be gained or lost in a situation (money, lives, reputation, etc.). Common patterns: "Hay mucho en juego" (There’s a lot at stake), "No hay nada en juego" (Nothing is at stake).
target_language_example: En esta decisión hay mucho en juego.
native_language_example: There’s a lot at stake in this decision.

additional_notes: Combination of en + la. Used before feminine singular nouns. Depending on context, en can mean in, on, or at, so en la may be translated as in the, on the, or at the.
target_language_example: Los libros están en la mochila.
native_language_example: The books are in the backpack.

additional_notes: Used to say something is located or happens on/inside sand (typically at the beach, in a sandbox, or on a sandy surface). With verbs like cavar (to dig), correr (to run), sentarse (to sit), or encontrar (to find), it describes where the action takes place. Also appears in the idiom "esconder la cabeza en la arena" = "to bury your head in the sand" (avoid a problem).
target_language_example: Vi una concha en la arena.
native_language_example: I saw a shell in the sand.

additional_notes: Used with "en" to say where something is or where an action happens (location). Common with verbs like "estudiar" (to study), "estar" (to be), "encontrar" (to find), and for meeting plans: "Nos vemos en la biblioteca".
target_language_example: Estoy en la biblioteca hasta las seis.
native_language_example: I'm in the library until six.

meaning: in the mouth; on the lips.
additional_notes: Used for something physically inside someone’s mouth (food, a thermometer, a finger), held between the lips (a pipe), or for a kiss on the lips ("besó... en la boca"). It also appears in fixed expressions like "(dejar) un mal sabor en la boca" = "to leave a bad taste in your mouth" (literal and figurative).
target_language_example: Me puse el chicle en la boca antes de entrar.
native_language_example: I put the gum in my mouth before going in.

meaning: in the bag; in the stock market (on the stock exchange).
additional_notes: With everyday objects, "bolsa" usually means a bag (or a purse), so "en la bolsa" = "in the bag." But "la bolsa" can also mean the stock market/stock exchange (like "la Bolsa de Madrid"), so "invertir/ganar dinero en la bolsa" = "to invest/make money in the stock market." Context tells you which meaning is intended.
target_language_example: Mi hermano invierte en la bolsa desde hace años.
native_language_example: My brother has been investing in the stock market for years.

meaning: in/on the head; in my/your/etc. head (in the mind).
additional_notes: Used for physical location on the head, especially with injuries or contact (golpes, disparos, un bulto): "Le dispararon en la cabeza", "Lo golpeó en la cabeza", "Tiene un bulto en la cabeza". It can also be figurative meaning "in someone’s mind/thoughts" (often with verbs like tener, sentir, pensar): "Tenía otras cosas en la cabeza". The article can change with possession: en mi/tu/su cabeza, but the fixed form "en la cabeza" is common when the possessor is clear from context.
target_language_example: Él lo golpeó en la cabeza.
native_language_example: He hit him on the head.

meaning: in the cafeteria; at the café/coffee shop.
additional_notes: "En" + place is used for location and for where something happens or where you meet someone. "La cafetería" can mean a school/work cafeteria or a casual café/coffee shop (context decides).
target_language_example: Nos vemos en la cafetería a las tres.
native_language_example: See you in the cafeteria/at the café at three.

additional_notes: Used to say that someone or something is located inside a box (a container). With motion verbs you often use it for putting something inside: e.g., "Pon X en la caja" = "Put X in the box."
target_language_example: Guarda las llaves en la caja, por favor.
native_language_example: Put the keys in the box, please.

additional_notes: Used to say someone/something is located in the street (outside, in a public road area). In English, you’ll often say “in the street” (especially British English) or “on the street” (common in American English).
target_language_example: Hay un perro en la calle.
native_language_example: There’s a dog in the street.

additional_notes: Used to say someone is lying/resting/sleeping in bed, or that they should be there (often as advice or an instruction, e.g., when someone is tired or sick).
target_language_example: Estoy en la cama porque no me siento bien.
native_language_example: I’m in bed because I don’t feel well.

meaning: in the face; (figurative) to someone’s face.
additional_notes: Used for physical location (a hit/shot/something on your face) and for direct, confrontational actions like lying or saying something “to someone’s face” (e.g., "Me mintió en la cara"). Also appears in expressions like "Se le ve en la cara" = “You can see it on their face.”
target_language_example: No me lo digas en la cara delante de todos.
native_language_example: Don’t say it to my face in front of everyone.

meaning: on the road; on the highway.
additional_notes: Used to talk about something located or happening on the road (traffic, animals, ice, a truck blocking the road). With verbs of travel it can also mean being out driving/traveling ("Estoy en la carretera" = "I’m on the road").
target_language_example: Ten cuidado: hay un accidente en la carretera.
native_language_example: Be careful: there’s an accident on the road.

additional_notes: Literally “in the house.” Used for being inside a specific house/building (El niño entró… en la casa) or more generally to mean “at home / in the household” (hay paz en la casa). Often followed by “de + person” to mean “in someone’s house” (en la casa del gobernador).
target_language_example: Hoy me quedo en la casa porque hace frío.
native_language_example: Today I'm staying at home because it's cold.

en la casa de al lado

target_language_multi_word_term: en la casa de al lado
additional_notes: Used to say someone or something is located in the neighboring house. Often appears with verbs like vivir (to live), estar (to be), or haber (there is/are): «Vive en la casa de al lado». You can also shorten it to «al lado» (next to) when the place is clear from context.
target_language_example: Mis vecinos viven en la casa de al lado.
native_language_example: My neighbors live in the house next door.

additional_notes: Used to say something happens or is located within a city. Often contrasts with "en el campo" (in the countryside). "En la" = "in the" + a feminine noun (ciudad).
target_language_example: Hay mucho tráfico en la ciudad los lunes.
native_language_example: There is a lot of traffic in the city on Mondays.

meaning: in the class; in the classroom.
additional_notes: Used to say someone/something is physically located in the classroom (e.g., you left something there) or to refer to the group of students in a particular class (e.g., “the only kid of color in the class,” “the best grade in the class”). Often you’ll also hear “en clase” without “la,” especially for general situations like “We can’t use phones in class.”
target_language_example: No hables en la clase, por favor.
native_language_example: Don’t talk in class, please.

meaning: in (someone’s) class for; in the (school) class of.
additional_notes: Used to say which subject/class someone is in: "en la clase de + [subject]" (en la clase de español = in Spanish class). You can also use it with a person to mean their class/group: "en la clase de mi hermano" = in my brother’s class. Often you’ll also hear "en clase de" without the article, especially with subjects ("en clase de matemáticas").
target_language_example: No puedo hablar ahora; estoy en la clase de matemáticas.
native_language_example: I can’t talk right now; I’m in math class.

additional_notes: Used to say someone/something is located inside the kitchen. Often follows verbs like estar/haber (e.g., “Hay alguien en la cocina” = “There’s someone in the kitchen”).
target_language_example: Dejé las llaves en la cocina.
native_language_example: I left the keys in the kitchen.

additional_notes: Used to say something is located on top of or up on a hill. Often comes after a noun to describe it ("la casa en la colina") or at the beginning/end of a sentence to set the scene ("En la colina...").
target_language_example: Hay una iglesia pequeña en la colina.
native_language_example: There is a small church on the hill.

meaning: on the coast; at the seaside.
additional_notes: Used to say something is located or happens by the sea, often referring to coastal towns or the shoreline. It can contrast with inland areas (tierra adentro).
target_language_example: En verano mucha gente trabaja en la costa.
native_language_example: In summer, many people work on the coast.

additional_notes: Uses "en" to mean being inside a place. "La" is "the" (feminine singular) and "cueva" means "cave". You can replace the noun: en la casa (in the house), en la tienda (in the shop).
target_language_example: Nos refugiamos en la cueva porque empezó a llover.
native_language_example: We took shelter in the cave because it started to rain.

additional_notes: Used mainly with babies to say they are located or sleeping in their crib. Common with verbs like dejar (to leave/put), estar (to be), and dormir/quedarse dormido (to sleep/fall asleep).
target_language_example: Pon al bebé en la cuna, por favor.
native_language_example: Put the baby in the crib, please.

additional_notes: Used to say someone is inside prison as a place or situation. Spanish often uses the definite article (la) where English might not: "Está en la cárcel" = "He/She is in jail." You may also see "en cárcel" in some fixed/legal contexts, but "en la cárcel" is the everyday phrase.
target_language_example: Mi primo estuvo en la cárcel por seis meses.
native_language_example: My cousin was in jail for six months.

meaning: in the distance; far away (from where you are).
additional_notes: Used to say that something is visible or perceived far away, usually at some distance from the speaker (often with verbs like ver, mirar, divisar). It can refer to space (a light, a bird, a building far away) and sometimes to time/figuratively, but it’s most commonly physical distance.
target_language_example: Se escuchaban risas en la distancia.
native_language_example: Laughter could be heard in the distance.

additional_notes: Used to say someone is inside the shower area while showering (or doing something while showering). Often with verbs like estar (Estoy en la ducha) and actions like cantar/escuchar (cantar en la ducha, oír a alguien cantar en la ducha).
target_language_example: No puedo contestar ahora; estoy en la ducha.
native_language_example: I can’t answer right now; I’m in the shower.

meaning: at the entrance; at the entryway.
additional_notes: Used to say someone or something is located or waiting at the entrance of a place (a building, a town, a room, etc.). Often followed by “de” + place: “en la entrada del edificio/del pueblo”.
target_language_example: Nos vemos en la entrada del cine.
native_language_example: See you at the entrance of the movie theater.

additional_notes: Used to talk about being physically at the school or doing something there. Often translates as “at school” in English (location), and sometimes “in school” when emphasizing that someone is attending school.
target_language_example: ¿Comes en la escuela o en casa?
native_language_example: Do you eat at school or at home?

additional_notes: Used to say where something happens on someone’s back (pain, a hit, a shot, something placed there). With verbs like doler (to hurt), pegar (to hit), and disparar (to shoot), it marks the location: Me duele en la espalda / Le dispararon en la espalda. Not the same as detrás (behind), which refers to position in space.
target_language_example: Me duele en la espalda desde ayer.
native_language_example: My back has been hurting since yesterday.

additional_notes: Used to say where something is located at an intersection (street corner). Also used in directions: “Gira a la izquierda en la esquina” = “Turn left at the corner.” You’ll often hear it with “de” to specify which corner: “en la esquina de (la calle X y la calle Y)” = “on the corner of (X St and Y St).”
target_language_example: Nos vemos en la esquina de esta calle.
native_language_example: See you on the corner of this street.

additional_notes: Used to say someone/something is located at a station (often a train or bus station). With verbs like esperar (to wait), ver (to see), decir (to say/tell), or parar (to stop), it indicates the action happens there. You can change the article for a specific station: en la estación de Atocha (at Atocha station).
target_language_example: Nos vemos en la estación a las seis.
native_language_example: See you at the station at six.

additional_notes: Used to say where something happens: at the party/event. Often answers “Where?” (¿Dónde?) and can describe what someone wears, does, or who is present at the party.
target_language_example: Nos vemos en la fiesta a las ocho.
native_language_example: See you at the party at eight.

additional_notes: Used with prepositions like "en" to say where something is located or where an action happens (a cut, a kiss, a mark). Often appears with verbs like "tener" (to have) and "besar" (to kiss).
target_language_example: Tengo una cicatriz en la frente desde niño.
native_language_example: I’ve had a scar on my forehead since I was a kid.

meaning: on the farm; at the farm.
additional_notes: Used to say where someone/something is located or where an activity happens. It commonly follows verbs like estar (to be), trabajar (to work), vivir (to live), and hay (there is/are): Está en la granja, Trabajo en la granja. In English you might say “on” or “at” depending on context, but Spanish uses en for both.
target_language_example: Mi tío vive y trabaja en la granja.
native_language_example: My uncle lives and works on the farm.

meaning: in the war; during the war.
additional_notes: Used to place an event or situation within the context of a particular war (time period or setting). With verbs like morir, ser herido, or ser asesinado, it often means someone died/was injured/killed while fighting or as a result of the war. It can also be used more broadly in expressions like “la guerra contra el crimen” (“the war on crime”), meaning a campaign or fight against something, not a literal war.
target_language_example: Muchos soldados perdieron la vida en la guerra.
native_language_example: Many soldiers lost their lives in the war.

additional_notes: Used to say someone/something is located inside a specific room. Often appears with verbs like estar (to be), haber (there is/are), and entrar (to enter): “estar en la habitación”, “hay … en la habitación”, “entrar en la habitación”.
target_language_example: Deja las maletas en la habitación, por favor.
native_language_example: Leave the suitcases in the room, please.

en la habitación de al lado

target_language_multi_word_term: en la habitación de al lado
meaning: in the room next door / in the room next to it.
additional_notes: Used to say someone or something is in the adjacent room. Very common with verbs like estar (to be), oír (to hear), and haber (there is/are). You can also say "la habitación de al lado" by itself as a short answer to "¿Dónde...?" (Where...?).
target_language_example: Estoy en la habitación de al lado; ahora vuelvo.
native_language_example: I’m in the room next door; I’ll be right back.

meaning: in history; in the history (of something).
additional_notes: Used to talk about events or records across time (often with superlatives like "el más alto en la historia"). It can also mean "in the story" depending on context, because "historia" can mean both "history" and "story."
target_language_example: Es uno de los momentos más importantes en la historia del país.
native_language_example: It’s one of the most important moments in the country’s history.

additional_notes: Used to say something happens inside a church building or at a church service/event. Common with events like getting married (casarse en la iglesia) or singing/playing music during a service. In Spanish you usually use "en" for being/doing something in/at a place (en la iglesia).
target_language_example: Nos vemos en la iglesia a las cinco.
native_language_example: See you at the church at five.

meaning: on the list; in the list.
additional_notes: Used to say that something (a name, word, item, etc.) appears as an entry on a list. With people it often means their name is included or their position/rank/order on the list (e.g., "el último en la lista"). In English, "on the list" is more common than "in the list" in many contexts, but Spanish commonly uses "en" either way.
target_language_example: ¿Está tu nombre en la lista?
native_language_example: Is your name on the list?

meaning: on the moon; (figuratively) spaced out / not paying attention.
additional_notes: Literal location: used with being somewhere (e.g., "No hay gente en la luna"). Figurative meaning is common with "estar": "Estás/estoy en la luna" = you're/I’m distracted, daydreaming, not listening.
target_language_example: Perdón, estaba en la luna y no escuché la pregunta.
native_language_example: Sorry, I was spaced out and didn’t hear the question.

meaning: on the line (phone); in line with (a plan/policy).
additional_notes: Common in phone contexts: "Permanezca en la línea" = “Please stay on the line,” and "tener a alguien en la línea" = “to have someone on the line.” With "de" ("en la línea de"), it means “in line with / along the lines of” an idea, policy, or approach.
target_language_example: Un momento, por favor: el doctor está en la línea.
native_language_example: One moment, please: the doctor is on the line.

additional_notes: Used to say someone is holding something. Very common with verbs like tener (to have), llevar (to carry), venir/ir (to come/go), andar/pasear (to walk), estar/quedarse (to be/stay): "con X en la mano" = "with X in (their) hand." Also appears in instructions: "Ponlo en la mano" (Put it in your hand).
target_language_example: Entró en la sala con el teléfono en la mano.
native_language_example: He walked into the room with his phone in his hand.

additional_notes: Common in Latin American Spanish to mean a morning time period, especially with a day reference (e.g., ayer/en la mañana = yesterday morning). In Spain you’ll often hear “por la mañana” for the same idea. Use it to say when something happened during the morning.
target_language_example: Mañana en la mañana tengo una reunión.
native_language_example: Tomorrow morning I have a meeting.

meaning: on the table; at the table.
additional_notes: Literally means “on the table.” With verbs like ver/poner/dejar, it usually means something is physically on the surface (Veo un libro en la mesa). With manners or behavior (modales, comportamiento), it often means “at the table” while eating (malos modales en la mesa).
target_language_example: Deja las llaves en la mesa, por favor.
native_language_example: Leave the keys on the table, please.

meaning: in the mountains; on the mountain.
additional_notes: Used to say someone/something is located in a mountainous area or on a particular mountain. Often translates as “in the mountains” when talking generally about the mountain region, and “on the mountain” when referring to a specific mountain (context usually makes it clear).
target_language_example: Hay un refugio en la montaña donde podemos dormir.
native_language_example: There’s a shelter in the mountains where we can sleep.

additional_notes: Used to say someone or something is located or happens within snowy conditions. Common with verbs like perderse (to get lost), congelarse (to freeze), encontrar (to find), and abandonar (to abandon/leave behind).
target_language_example: Dejé mi mochila en la nieve.
native_language_example: I left my backpack in the snow.

additional_notes: Used to say something happens during the night/evening period. In many places you’ll also hear "por la noche" with the same meaning; "en la noche" can sound a bit more specific (during the night) or more common in some regions. You can add a day: "el lunes en la noche" = "Monday night".
target_language_example: Trabajo en la noche y descanso en la mañana.
native_language_example: I work at night and rest in the morning.

meaning: in the office; at the office.
additional_notes: Used to say where something is happening or where someone/something is located. With "en" + a place, it can mean either physical location ("It’s in the office") or being there as an activity ("I’m at the office/working at the office"), depending on context.
target_language_example: ¿Nos vemos en la oficina mañana por la mañana?
native_language_example: Shall we meet at the office tomorrow morning?

additional_notes: Used literally for situations with little or no light: "buscar algo en la oscuridad" (to look for something in the dark). It also appears in the fixed expression "un tiro en la oscuridad", meaning "a shot in the dark" (a random guess). Similar: "a oscuras" = in the dark.
target_language_example: No puedo leer en la oscuridad.
native_language_example: I can't read in the dark.

additional_notes: Used to say something is located/placed on (or attached to) a wall. Common with verbs like "colgar" (to hang) and "poner" (to put/place): "Está colgado en la pared" / "Ponlo en la pared". You can specify which wall with "la pared de..." (the wall of...): "en la pared de su oficina".
target_language_example: Quiero colgar este cuadro en la pared.
native_language_example: I want to hang this painting on the wall.

additional_notes: Used to say where something happens on the body (pain, an injury, a cut, a burn, etc.). With accidents you’ll often see it after a verb like: cortarse (to cut oneself), quemarse (to burn oneself), hacerse un corte (to get a cut), tener/dar un calambre (to get a cramp).
target_language_example: Me duele en la pierna derecha.
native_language_example: It hurts in my right leg.

meaning: in the pool; at the swimming pool.
additional_notes: Used with "estar", "nadar", "haber", etc. to say someone/something is inside the pool (in the water) or at the pool facility, depending on context. "Piscina" is a swimming pool; in sports contexts, "una calle" means a lane (e.g., "Tuve una calle para mí solo" = "I had a lane to myself").
target_language_example: Nos vemos en la piscina a las cinco.
native_language_example: See you at the pool at five.

additional_notes: Used to say something is written or shown on a classroom board. Often appears with verbs like "escribir" (to write), "poner" (to put), or "estar escrito" (to be written). "Pizarra" can mean a blackboard or a whiteboard depending on the context.
target_language_example: ¿Puedes escribir la fecha en la pizarra?
native_language_example: Can you write the date on the board?

meaning: on the ground floor (first level of a building).
additional_notes: Used to say where something is located within a building. In Spanish, "planta baja" refers to the level at street/entrance level (the ground floor). You’ll often see it on signs or in building directions (e.g., "El ascensor está en la planta baja").
target_language_example: La recepción está en la planta baja, a la derecha.
native_language_example: The reception desk is on the ground floor, on the right.

additional_notes: Used with verbs of location or activities to say something happens at the beach. With a specific beach you can also say “en Playa X” (e.g., “en Playa del Carmen”), but “en la playa” is the general idea of being at the beach.
target_language_example: Vamos a comer en la playa.
native_language_example: We’re going to eat at the beach.

additional_notes: Used to say someone/something is located in the main open public area of a town or neighborhood (la plaza). Often refers to a central square where people gather, walk, and where you might see pigeons, children, markets, etc. You can also specify which one: en la plaza central / en la plaza de la ciudad.
target_language_example: Nos vemos en la plaza a las seis.
native_language_example: See you in the square at six.

meaning: in the first (one); in the front row.
additional_notes: Uses the feminine article because it refers to an implied feminine noun like curva (curve), vuelta (lap), or fila (row): en la primera curva/vuelta/fila. In contexts like seating, it often means “in the front row” (en la primera fila).
target_language_example: ¿Hay asientos en la primera fila?
native_language_example: Are there seats in the front row?

meaning: "in practice"; in real life/in actual use (as opposed to in theory).
additional_notes: Used to introduce what really happens in reality or in everyday use, often contrasting with "en teoría" (in theory). It can also mean "through hands-on experience" in phrases like "aprender en la práctica" (learn by doing).
target_language_example: En teoría suena bien, pero en la práctica no funciona.
native_language_example: In theory it sounds good, but in practice it doesn’t work.

additional_notes: Used to refer to the next place/stop/turn/event in a sequence: en la próxima calle (on the next street), en la próxima parada (at the next stop), en la próxima esquina (at the next corner), en la próxima lección (in the next lesson). In casual conversation, "en la próxima" can be a shortened way to mean "next time" (i.e., next occasion).
target_language_example: Nos vemos en la próxima reunión.
native_language_example: See you at the next meeting.

additional_notes: Used to say someone/something is located right by the door or at the entrance. Often followed by "de" + a place to specify which door ("en la puerta de al lado" = "at the next door / next door").
target_language_example: Hay alguien en la puerta; voy a abrir.
native_language_example: There's someone at the door; I'm going to open it.

en la punta de la lengua

target_language_multi_word_term: en la punta de la lengua
meaning: “on the tip of my tongue” (almost remembered, but not quite).
additional_notes: Used when you feel you’re about to remember a word, name, or piece of information but can’t say it yet. Common with verbs like tener: "Lo tengo en la punta de la lengua" / "Tengo su nombre en la punta de la lengua."
target_language_example: ¡Lo tengo en la punta de la lengua, pero ahora no me sale!
native_language_example: It’s on the tip of my tongue, but I can’t think of it right now!

meaning: "in which" / "where" (referring to a feminine singular noun).
additional_notes: Used in relative clauses after a feminine singular noun (e.g., habitación, época, situación) to mean “in which/where.” It’s the combination of the preposition en + la (feminine singular “the”) + que (relative pronoun). For masculine you often see “en el que,” and for plural “en los/las que.”
target_language_example: Esa es la casa en la que crecí.
native_language_example: That’s the house where I grew up.

additional_notes: Used with verbs like escuchar/oir/sonar/estar to say something was heard or was being broadcast on the radio. It can refer to a specific radio station/program, or to the radio as a device. Contrast: “en la tele” = on TV; “por la radio” can also mean “on/over the radio,” focusing on the medium.
target_language_example: Dicen en la radio que va a llover mañana.
native_language_example: They say on the radio that it’s going to rain tomorrow.

meaning: in the meeting; at the meeting.
additional_notes: Used to say something happened or someone was present during a specific meeting (reunión = meeting). Often used with verbs like estar/ser/decir/hablar/presentarse: “Estuve en la reunión” (I was at the meeting), “Lo dije en la reunión” (I said it in the meeting).
target_language_example: No pude hablar en la reunión porque no levanté la mano.
native_language_example: I couldn’t speak in the meeting because I didn’t raise my hand.

meaning: in the room; in the hall (meeting room).
additional_notes: Used to say someone/something is inside a particular room or hall. "Sala" often means a larger room such as a meeting room, classroom, courtroom, or hall (not necessarily a living room). You’ll also hear "¡Orden en la sala!" as “Order in the court/room!” (a fixed phrase).
target_language_example: Hay mucha gente en la sala, así que hablemos en voz baja.
native_language_example: There are a lot of people in the room, so let’s speak quietly.

additional_notes: Common in transit contexts (bus/metro/train) with verbs like "bajarse" (to get off) or "parar" (to stop). "Siguiente" agrees with the noun: "la siguiente parada" (feminine), but you may also hear "en el siguiente (alto/paradero)" depending on the word used for "stop".
target_language_example: Por favor, avísame cuando estemos en la siguiente parada.
native_language_example: Please let me know when we’re at the next stop.

meaning: in the afternoon; later today (in the afternoon).
additional_notes: Used to say something happens during the afternoon period. With "hoy" it often means "this afternoon" (e.g., "hoy en la tarde"). You may also hear "por la tarde" with the same meaning.
target_language_example: Nos vemos en la tarde para tomar un café.
native_language_example: See you this afternoon to have a coffee.

additional_notes: Used to say you watch something on television, or that someone/something appeared on television (e.g., “salió/apareció en la tele”). Very common in everyday speech; more formal: “en la televisión”.
target_language_example: ¿Lo viste en la tele anoche?
native_language_example: Did you see it on TV last night?

additional_notes: Used to say something is shown, heard, or happens via television (a TV broadcast). Very common with verbs like ver (to see/watch), escuchar (to hear), aparecer (to appear), and poner (to put on). Also used with specific programs: en la televisión / en la tele (more informal).
target_language_example: No lo dieron en la televisión, pero lo vi en internet.
native_language_example: They didn’t show it on TV, but I saw it on the internet.

meaning: in the store; at the shop.
additional_notes: Used to say where someone/something is located or where something happens. Often followed by a type of store: "en la tienda de mascotas" (at the pet store). You can also answer a question about location with just "En la tienda."
target_language_example: Nos vemos en la tienda después de clase.
native_language_example: See you at the store after class.

meaning: on earth; in the ground; on land.
additional_notes: Often refers to (1) being on Earth/in the world (“here on earth”), (2) being in/under the soil (“in the ground”), or (3) being on land (not in the air/sea). In phrases like “un infierno en la tierra,” it means “a hell on earth” (something terrible in real life).
target_language_example: Encontraron agua en la tierra después de cavar un poco.
native_language_example: They found water in the ground after digging a little.

meaning: at the university; in college (as a student).
additional_notes: Used to talk about studying/being a student at a university. Often follows verbs like estudiar (to study), conocer (to meet), and estar + gerund (to be studying). You can add the university name after de: en la universidad de Boston.
target_language_example: Nos conocimos en la universidad y todavía somos amigos.
native_language_example: We met in college and we're still friends.

additional_notes: Used to talk about life in general (your life, people’s lives, or life as a whole). Very common in phrases like "en la vida" (in life), "en la vida futura" (in future life), and "único/a en la vida" (once in a lifetime).
target_language_example: En la vida, lo más importante es aprender de los errores.
native_language_example: In life, the most important thing is to learn from mistakes.

meaning: in the area; in that part/section (of a place).
additional_notes: Used to locate something within a broader place (a city, island, building, venue, etc.). It’s often followed by a direction or descriptor: en la zona norte/este, en la zona alta, en la zona más alejada. You can also specify a designated section: en la zona de no fumadores (“in the non-smoking section”).
target_language_example: Hay un cajero automático en la zona del supermercado.
native_language_example: There’s an ATM in the supermarket area.

additional_notes: Used before feminine plural nouns to say where/when something happens (location, situation, or context): en las sombras = “in the shadows”, en las peores circunstancias = “in the worst circumstances”. It’s the preposition “en” + the feminine plural definite article “las”.
target_language_example: Nos vemos en las oficinas a las nueve.
native_language_example: See you at the offices at nine.

additional_notes: Used to say something is physically on your hands (blood, cracks, calluses), or that someone is holding something (e.g., un arma en las manos = a weapon in their hands). Spanish often uses "en" where English uses "on" (en las manos, en la cara, etc.).
target_language_example: No quiero nada en las manos cuando entremos al museo.
native_language_example: I don’t want anything in my hands when we go into the museum.

additional_notes: Used to say someone or something is located in the mountain area, or that an action happens there. Often answers “where?” (¿Dónde?) and can be used with verbs like estar (to be), vivir (to live), esconderse (to hide), buscar (to look for), pasar (to spend time).
target_language_example: Nos quedamos en las montañas todo el fin de semana.
native_language_example: We stayed in the mountains all weekend.

meaning: 'in the news' (on TV, radio, newspapers, or online news).
additional_notes: Used to say something was reported or mentioned by the news media. Often follows verbs like decir (to say), ver (to see), escuchar (to hear), and salir (to appear).
target_language_example: Lo vi en las noticias esta mañana.
native_language_example: I saw it in the news this morning.

additional_notes: Used with estar (and similar verbs) to say something is burning: “Está/estaba en llamas.” It describes an active fire (flames visible), often in news/emergencies (buildings, cars, forests, areas). It can also appear in titles (e.g., Retrato de una mujer en llamas).
target_language_example: ¡La cocina está en llamas! Llama a los bomberos.
native_language_example: The kitchen is on fire! Call the firefighters.

meaning: "in what" / "in the thing that" (what you do/think/believe/work on).
additional_notes: Used to refer back to an action or idea introduced by the verb that follows, often after verbs like creer (to believe), pensar (to think), trabajar (to work), hacer (to do). Common patterns: “ser bueno en lo que + verb” (to be good at what you do), “pensar en lo que + verb/phrase” (to think about what…), “trabajar en lo que + verb/phrase” (to work on what…).
target_language_example: Estoy concentrado en lo que hago.
native_language_example: I’m focused on what I’m doing.

additional_notes: Used with estar to say someone is right about something: estar en lo cierto. Common in questions (¿Estoy en lo cierto?) and for emphasis (Estás absolutamente en lo cierto). Also: Creo que estoy en lo cierto (“I think I’m right”).
target_language_example: Creo que estás en lo cierto: el museo cierra a las seis.
native_language_example: I think you’re right: the museum closes at six.

meaning: “when it comes to… / as far as… (is concerned)”; also “in whatever / in what”.
additional_notes: Used to limit what you’re talking about to a specific aspect or topic: “en lo que respecta a…” = “when it comes to…”. It can also introduce an open-ended clause with the subjunctive to mean “whatever”: “Te apoyo en lo que decidas” = “I support you in whatever you decide.”
target_language_example: En lo que a mí respecta, todo está bien.
native_language_example: As far as I’m concerned, everything is fine.

additional_notes: Used before a masculine plural noun (los + noun) to mean location, context, or a time period: en los asuntos (in the affairs), en los colegios (in the schools), en los próximos diez segundos (in the next ten seconds).
target_language_example: Encontré las llaves en los cajones de la cocina.
native_language_example: I found the keys in the kitchen drawers.

additional_notes: Used to say something appears/was reported in printed or online newspapers. Often with verbs like ver (to see), leer (to read), salir/estar (to appear/be) + en los periódicos.
target_language_example: Salió en los periódicos esta mañana.
native_language_example: It was in the newspapers this morning.

meaning: 'in the old days' / 'back in the day'.
additional_notes: Used to compare the present to the past, often with a nostalgic feeling. Common in phrases like "como/igual que en los viejos tiempos" (just like in the old days). It refers to a past period in general, not a specific date.
target_language_example: Volvimos a reunirnos y fue como en los viejos tiempos.
native_language_example: We got together again and it was like in the old days.

meaning: in the last (…); over the past (…).
additional_notes: Used with a time period to talk about something that happened within the most recent period up to now: en los últimos dos años (in the last two years). It can also be used with moments/instants: en los últimos momentos (in the final moments).
target_language_example: En los últimos días he estado muy ocupado.
native_language_example: In the last few days, I've been very busy.

additional_notes: Used to express a substitution or choice: you do one thing rather than another. It can be followed by a noun (en lugar de las escaleras), a pronoun (en lugar de ustedes), or an infinitive verb (en lugar de ir a trabajar).
target_language_example: Pedí té en lugar de café.
native_language_example: I ordered tea instead of coffee.

additional_notes: Used to describe something that happens via the internet (e.g., a website, survey, class). With people, it can mean they are spending time connected/using the internet ("estar/pasar tiempo en línea"). Also used for shopping/services done on the internet ("comprar en línea").
target_language_example: Puedes pagar la factura en línea.
native_language_example: You can pay the bill online.

additional_notes: Used with verbs like "estar" to say something has started and is currently happening/operating: "La investigación está en marcha" (the investigation is underway). Also appears in "ponerse en marcha" = to get going / get started (often for people or plans). With machines or systems it can mean "running" or "working". In the idiom "poner ... en marcha" it means to set something in motion / start it (sometimes humorously: "poner la boca en marcha" = start talking).
target_language_example: El plan ya está en marcha, pero todavía falta mucho trabajo.
native_language_example: The plan is already underway, but there’s still a lot of work left.

meaning: en masse; in large numbers (all together).
additional_notes: Used to say many people/things do something at the same time or as a group (often implying a big crowd or a collective action). It can also mean “in bulk” in some contexts (buying/producing large quantities), but most commonly it’s about people doing something together.
target_language_example: La gente salió en masa a la calle después del partido.
native_language_example: People poured out into the street in large numbers after the game.

meaning: in half an hour; in 30 minutes.
additional_notes: Used to say something will happen after 30 minutes from now (a deadline, arrival time, return time, etc.). Also commonly used with future or near-future forms like "volveré", "llegará", "te recojo".
target_language_example: Te llamo en media hora.
native_language_example: I’ll call you in half an hour.

additional_notes: Usually means being located in the center/between things: "el botón de en medio" (the middle button), "en medio del campo" (in the middle of the countryside). In some contexts it means blocking or getting between people/things: "se puso en medio" (he/she got in the way / stepped in between). Very common with "de en medio" to mean "out of the way": "quita de en medio" (move it out of the way), "quítate de en medio" (get out of the way).
target_language_example: La farmacia está en medio de la calle.
native_language_example: The pharmacy is in the middle of the street.

additional_notes: Used to say something happens inside a place/group (a crowd, the street) or during an event/situation (a storm, a class). Often followed by a noun: en medio de la multitud / en medio de una tormenta. Similar to "entre" in some contexts, but focuses on being in the center or surrounded by something.
target_language_example: Nos llamaste en medio de la cena.
native_language_example: You called us in the middle of dinner.

meaning: in the middle of nowhere; far from everything.
additional_notes: Used to describe being in a very isolated place with nothing nearby (no buildings, towns, or people). Often appears after verbs like estar, quedarse, perderse, or despertarse. You can also say "en mitad de la nada" with the same meaning.
target_language_example: Nos quedamos sin gasolina en medio de la nada.
native_language_example: We ran out of gas in the middle of nowhere.

additional_notes: Used to say something happens/exists within a larger place, time period, or situation. It’s followed by a masculine singular noun: en medio del invierno / del campo / del desierto. With feminine singular, use en medio de la (en medio de la noche). Often implies being surrounded by something.
target_language_example: Nos quedamos sin gasolina en medio del camino.
native_language_example: We ran out of gas in the middle of the road.

additional_notes: Used with a time period, quantity, or number to say something happens/exists before that limit is reached: en menos de + number + unit (minutos, horas, días, meses, etc.). Often answers “How long?” or “How much?”
target_language_example: Terminé la tarea en menos de una hora.
native_language_example: I finished the homework in less than an hour.

meaning: in less than an hour; within an hour.
additional_notes: Used to say something will happen before one hour passes, or that something took under an hour to do. It often follows verbs like llegar (to arrive), estar aquí (to be here), or terminar (to finish). You can swap the time unit: en menos de cinco minutos, en menos de dos días.
target_language_example: Podemos hacerlo en menos de una hora.
native_language_example: We can do it in less than an hour.

additional_notes: A very common combination of the preposition en + the possessive mi. It is used before a singular noun: en mi casa, en mi mesa, en mi calendario. Depending on context, en can mean "in," "on," or sometimes "at." Do not confuse en mi ("in/on my") with en mí ("in me"), which has an accent.
target_language_example: Tengo las llaves en mi bolso.
native_language_example: I have the keys in my bag.

additional_notes: Used to say something is located inside your pocket. With verbs like estar/poner/guardar (to be/put/keep), it describes where an item is: «Está en mi bolsillo» (It’s in my pocket), «Lo puso en mi bolsillo» (He/She put it in my pocket). You can swap «mi» for another possessive: «en tu bolsillo», «en su bolsillo», etc.
target_language_example: Tengo las llaves en mi bolsillo.
native_language_example: I have the keys in my pocket.

meaning: “in my head” (literally: “in my head/skull” or “in my mind”).
additional_notes: Often used literally for something physically in/on your head (hair, a sound ringing in your head), and also figuratively for thoughts, imagination, or inner voices (“it’s only in my head”). You can change the possessive: en tu cabeza (in your head), en su cabeza (in his/her head), etc.
target_language_example: No sé si es real o si solo está en mi cabeza.
native_language_example: I don’t know if it’s real or if it’s just in my head.

meaning: in my house; at my place (my home).
additional_notes: Used to say someone or something is inside your home, or that an activity happened at your home. Often translates as “at my place” in English even though it literally means “in my house.”
target_language_example: Vamos a cenar en mi casa esta noche.
native_language_example: Let’s have dinner at my place tonight.

additional_notes: Used to express deep feelings like love, affection, gratitude, or emotional certainty. Common in romantic or emotional contexts (“forever in my heart”), and also with verbs like llevar (“to carry”) or sentir (“to feel”) to show something is emotionally important.
target_language_example: Aunque estés lejos, siempre estás en mi corazón.
native_language_example: Even if you’re far away, you’re always in my heart.

additional_notes: Used to say that someone/something is inside your room. In many contexts, "cuarto" means "bedroom" (especially at home or in a hotel). In hotels, you may also hear "en mi habitación" for the same idea.
target_language_example: Deja la maleta en mi cuarto, por favor.
native_language_example: Leave the suitcase in my room, please.

additional_notes: Used to talk about your family as a group (the people you’re related to). It often introduces a general statement, habit, or fact about your relatives (e.g., “In my family, we say…”, “There are three boys in my family”). You can swap the possessive: en tu familia (in your family), en su familia (in his/her/their family), en nuestra familia (in our family).
target_language_example: En mi familia celebramos los cumpleaños juntos.
native_language_example: In my family, we celebrate birthdays together.

additional_notes: Used to say where something happens. "En" means "in/on/at" depending on context; here it’s typically "in." "Habitación" usually means a bedroom or a room in a home (can also mean a hotel room).
target_language_example: Voy a estar en mi habitación un rato.
native_language_example: I’m going to be in my room for a while.

meaning: in my place; instead of me.
additional_notes: Used when someone does something instead of you (replacement): "Mi hermano hizo eso en mi lugar." It’s also used to ask someone to imagine being you (empathy), often with "ponerse": "Ponte/Póngase en mi lugar" = "Put yourself in my shoes."
target_language_example: ¿Podrías venir en mi lugar mañana?
native_language_example: Could you come instead of me tomorrow?

additional_notes: Used to say someone/something is in your thoughts or imagination. Common with verbs like estar (to be), tener (to have), ver (to see), imaginar (to imagine): "Estás en mi mente" (I’m thinking about you), "Lo vi en mi mente" (I pictured it).
target_language_example: Te tengo en mi mente todo el día.
native_language_example: I have you on my mind all day.

additional_notes: Used to say someone/something is located inside your office, or to tell someone to come to your office for a meeting or conversation. Often appears with verbs like estar (to be), entrar (to enter), volver/regresar (to return), and querer/ver (to want to see).
target_language_example: Nos vemos en mi oficina después de la reunión.
native_language_example: See you in my office after the meeting.

additional_notes: Used to introduce your personal viewpoint. Often comes at the beginning of the sentence (sometimes followed by a comma), but it can also appear later: "Y en mi opinión..." You can change the possessive: "en tu opinión" (in your opinion), "en su opinión" (in his/her/their opinion), "en nuestra opinión" (in our opinion).
target_language_example: En mi opinión, este restaurante es demasiado caro.
native_language_example: In my opinion, this restaurant is too expensive.

additional_notes: Literally means “in my life.” Very common with negation words like "nunca" to emphasize that something has never happened: "Nunca en mi vida" / "No… en mi vida." It can also mean having someone as part of your life (relationships): "Te quiero en mi vida" = “I want you in my life.”
target_language_example: Nunca en mi vida había probado algo tan rico.
native_language_example: Never in my life had I tried something so delicious.

meaning: “in my dreams.” (sometimes: “yeah right,” to show something won’t happen)
additional_notes: Literal meaning: something happens only in your dreams/imagination. Often used sarcastically to reject an idea or express disbelief (like “As if!” / “Yeah right!”). You can also change the possessive: en tus sueños (in your dreams), en sus sueños (in his/her/their dreams).
target_language_example: ¿Que me van a subir el sueldo este mes? En mis sueños.
native_language_example: They’re going to raise my salary this month? Yeah right.

meaning: in the middle of the night.
additional_notes: Used to say something happens at a very late hour, when people are normally asleep. Often implies it’s unexpected, inconvenient, or disturbing (like a call, a knock at the door, crying). You can also hear the simpler version "a mitad de la noche."
target_language_example: Me desperté en mitad de la noche por un ruido.
native_language_example: I woke up in the middle of the night because of a noise.

additional_notes: Used after certain verbs or expressions that take the preposition "en" (very commonly: "confiar en mí" = "to trust me", "fijarse en mí" = "to notice/look at me"). Literal meanings like "in me" are also possible depending on context (e.g., "una impresión duradera en mí" = "a lasting impression on me"; "algo se va a liberar en mí" = "something is going to be released in me"). "mí" (with an accent) is the object form of "yo" after a preposition; don’t confuse it with "mi" (no accent) = "my".
target_language_example: Puedes confiar en mí.
native_language_example: You can trust me.

meaning: in nothing; at all (often in negatives).
additional_notes: Common in negative sentences to emphasize “not … at all” or “not … in any way/thing”: No creo en nada (I don’t believe in anything). No has cambiado en nada (You haven’t changed at all). Also used with verbs like tener éxito/ser bueno/estar de acuerdo: no tener éxito en nada (not succeed at anything), no ser bueno en nada (not be good at anything), no estar de acuerdo en nada (not agree on anything). In “terminar en nada,” it means something “comes to nothing” or “ends up as nothing.”
target_language_example: No estuvimos de acuerdo en nada durante la reunión.
native_language_example: We didn’t agree on anything during the meeting.

additional_notes: Used to say you act, speak, or make a request representing someone/something (“on behalf of”), or to invoke an authority or principle (“in the name of the law/God”). Common in formal contexts (law, religion, official statements). Also used as an emphatic plea: “¡En nombre de Dios!” ≈ “For God’s sake!”.
target_language_example: Hablo en nombre de todo el equipo.
native_language_example: I’m speaking on behalf of the whole team.

meaning: "in our" / "on our" (with a feminine singular noun).
additional_notes: Used with a feminine singular noun: en nuestra casa, en nuestra mesa, en nuestra área. Spanish uses en for several English prepositions (in/on/at), depending on context. It can also be used in expressions like pensar en nuestra situación (“to think about our situation”) or jugar en nuestra contra (“to play against us”).
target_language_example: Hoy comemos en nuestra cocina.
native_language_example: Today we’re eating in our kitchen.

additional_notes: Used to say that something happens or is located at your place (you and your group/family). In Spanish, "casa" often means "home" as well as "house."
target_language_example: ¿Quieres cenar en nuestra casa el sábado?
native_language_example: Do you want to have dinner at our place on Saturday?

additional_notes: Means “in our” and is normally followed by a masculine singular noun (e.g., en nuestro barrio = in our neighborhood). It changes to match the noun: en nuestra (fem. sing.), en nuestros (masc. plural), en nuestras (fem. plural). You may also see it with emphasis words like “propio”: en nuestro propio barrio = in our own neighborhood.
target_language_example: No puedes fumar en nuestro apartamento.
native_language_example: You can't smoke in our apartment.

additional_notes: Used for places (a building, a road, a store) that are being built or repaired. Often seen on signs: “Disculpe las molestias, estamos en obras” (“Sorry for the inconvenience, we’re doing construction work”).
target_language_example: La carretera está en obras, así que hay desvíos.
native_language_example: The road is under construction, so there are detours.

additional_notes: Means something happens from time to time (not always). It can go at the beginning, middle, or end of the sentence. Common variations: "en algunas ocasiones" (sometimes) and "en ocasiones especiales" (on special occasions).
target_language_example: En ocasiones salimos a cenar, pero casi siempre cocinamos en casa.
native_language_example: Sometimes we go out to dinner, but we almost always cook at home.

meaning: in order; organized; OK / all set.
additional_notes: Used to say something is arranged correctly or everything is fine: "Está todo en orden" = "Everything is in order." It can also mean "in sequence" (often with "alfabético": "en orden alfabético" = "in alphabetical order") or "in an orderly way" (e.g., moving/lining up "en orden").
target_language_example: Antes de viajar, quiero tener todo en orden.
native_language_example: Before traveling, I want to have everything in order.

additional_notes: A formal phrase used to express purpose or aim, common in official, legal, or administrative writing. In everyday speech, people more often use "para" or "a fin de" (e.g., "para reducir costos"). It is typically followed by an infinitive or a noun phrase.
target_language_example: Se tomaron medidas en orden a mejorar la seguridad.
native_language_example: Measures were taken in order to improve safety.

additional_notes: Used with "en" to talk about things that happen during the autumn season (general facts, habits, or plans). You can place it at the start of the sentence (often with a comma) or later: "En otoño..." / "... en otoño."
target_language_example: En otoño hace más fresco por las tardes.
native_language_example: In the fall it’s cooler in the afternoons.

additional_notes: Used to postpone something to a different time in the future. Common in polite refusals or to suggest continuing the conversation later (often like “maybe another time”).
target_language_example: Hoy no puedo; mejor en otra ocasión.
native_language_example: I can’t today; better another time.

additional_notes: Used to say that something is (or should be) in a different location, or that you’ll look/find it somewhere else. Often goes with verbs like buscar (to look for), estar (to be), encontrar (to find). It can also be figurative: poner la mente/el cerebro en otra parte = to stop paying attention / to have your mind elsewhere.
target_language_example: Si no lo encuentras aquí, búscalo en otra parte.
native_language_example: If you can’t find it here, look for it somewhere else.

additional_notes: Used to restate the same idea more clearly or more directly, often to explain a conclusion or simplify what was just said. It commonly appears at the start of a sentence and is followed by a comma: "En otras palabras, ...".
target_language_example: No tengo tiempo; en otras palabras, no puedo ir.
native_language_example: I don't have time; in other words, I can't go.

additional_notes: Used to say that something/someone is located elsewhere or should be looked for elsewhere. Common with verbs like buscar (to look for) or estar (to be): “Búscalo en otro lugar” = “Look for it somewhere else.” You can also use it alone as a short answer to mean “Somewhere else.”
target_language_example: Si no hay mesas aquí, podemos comer en otro lugar.
native_language_example: If there are no tables here, we can eat somewhere else.

meaning: in the past; at another time (long ago).
additional_notes: Used to talk about how things were before (often suggesting a long time ago or a previous era). It can refer to a historical period ("España gobernó... en otro tiempo") or to an earlier time in someone’s life. Often interchangeable with "antes" or "en otra época" depending on context.
target_language_example: En otro tiempo, esta calle era mucho más tranquila.
native_language_example: In the past, this street was much quieter.

additional_notes: Literal use: with verbs like "envolver" it means something is wrapped/covered in paper ("Lo envolvió en papel"). Figurative use: "En papel" can mean "on paper"—something is true in theory or according to a plan/document, even if it may not be true in practice (often said alone: "En papel.").
target_language_example: En papel, el plan es perfecto, pero en la práctica es difícil.
native_language_example: On paper, the plan is perfect, but in practice it's difficult.

additional_notes: Used to say something is true/caused/valid only to some degree. Common patterns: "en parte" by itself as a short answer (“Partly.”), and "en parte..., en parte..." to split reasons or descriptions (“partly..., partly...”). Often followed by "por" or "porque" to give a partial reason: "en parte por..." / "en parte porque...".
target_language_example: Lo hice en parte porque quería ayudarte y en parte porque me sentía culpable.
native_language_example: I did it partly because I wanted to help you and partly because I felt guilty.

additional_notes: Used to single out one specific thing/person/reason (sometimes to say there isn’t any specific one: “no… en particular” = “no… in particular”). Common patterns: “en particular” (especially), “nada/ningún(a) … en particular” (nothing/no … in particular).
target_language_example: No busco nada en particular, solo estoy mirando.
native_language_example: I'm not looking for anything in particular; I'm just browsing.

additional_notes: Often used with the verb "dejar" (to leave): "dejar en paz" = to leave someone alone / stop bothering them. In contexts like countries or situations, it means "at peace" (not at war, calm).
target_language_example: Por favor, déjame en paz; estoy trabajando.
native_language_example: Please leave me alone; I’m working.

additional_notes: Used with estar ("estar en peligro") to say someone/something is in danger. Also appears in the causative phrase "poner en peligro" = "to put (someone/something) in danger" or "to endanger".
target_language_example: Los niños estaban en peligro, así que llamamos a la policía.
native_language_example: The children were in danger, so we called the police.

additional_notes: Used to say you will be physically present (not online, not by phone, not through someone else). Often follows verbs like "estar", "ir", "ver", or "conocer": "estar/ir/ver en persona".
target_language_example: Prefiero hablar contigo en persona.
native_language_example: I prefer to talk to you in person.

meaning: standing; on your feet (also: still standing / still going).
