additional_notes: Used to say something/someone is not the same. Often followed by **de** to mean “different from” (e.g., *es diferente de su hermano* = “he’s different from his brother”). In conversation, **eso es diferente** can mean “that’s different/that’s unusual.”
target_language_example: Para mí, este café es diferente del otro.
native_language_example: For me, this coffee is different from the other one.

additional_notes: Used to say that something is hard to do, understand, or achieve. Very often followed by an infinitive, as in "es difícil convencer" = "it's difficult to convince," or by a clause.
target_language_example: A veces es difícil tomar una decisión.
native_language_example: Sometimes it's hard to make a decision.

additional_notes: Used with **ser** to say something (an activity, situation, or even a person) is fun/entertaining: **Es divertido + infinitive** (Es divertido bailar), **[noun] es divertido** (El juego es divertido), **Esto es divertido** (This is fun). With a person it means they are fun/amusing: **Tom es divertido**. Note: **Nadar me es divertido** is grammatical but uncommon; more natural is **Me divierte nadar** (Swimming is fun for me) or **Me parece divertido nadar** (I find swimming fun).
target_language_example: Es divertido aprender español contigo.
native_language_example: It's fun to learn Spanish with you.

meaning: "is where" (used to say/define the place where something happens or exists).
additional_notes: Used to identify or emphasize a location. Often follows a place phrase for emphasis (e.g., "En mi casa es donde...") or starts a sentence to define a place ("Es donde vivo"). It can also be used in general definitions: "Una mina es donde...".
target_language_example: Aquí es donde nos conocimos.
native_language_example: This is where we met.

additional_notes: A very common combination of es ("is") and el ("the"). It is used before a masculine singular noun or title: Es el doctor. In some contexts, el can also stand for "the one," but for beginners the most useful meaning is usually "is the."
target_language_example: Madrid es el centro del país.
native_language_example: Madrid is the center of the country.

additional_notes: Used to compare quantities, prices, or sizes. Often followed by a number (Ocho es el doble de cuatro) or by a clause/noun phrase (Es el doble de lo que pagamos ahora). With adjectives like grande, you commonly add “que” to compare: “es el doble de grande que …” = “is twice as big as …”.
target_language_example: Este apartamento es el doble de caro que el otro.
native_language_example: This apartment is twice as expensive as the other one.

additional_notes: Used both literally (talking about the apocalypse) and, very often, exaggerating to say something feels like a disaster or very serious. Often appears in questions/negatives: «¿Es el fin del mundo si…?» / «No es el fin del mundo» (“It’s not the end of the world”).
target_language_example: Tranquilo, no es el fin del mundo si llegamos tarde.
native_language_example: Relax, it’s not the end of the world if we arrive late.

meaning: 'he is the man' / 'you’re the man' (the right person).
additional_notes: Used to identify someone as the person you mean (e.g., “He’s the man in the photo”) or to say someone is the right person for a job/role (“He’s the man for the job,” “the man of the house,” “the man of my dreams”). It can also be used as praise, especially in direct address: “Usted eres el hombre” ≈ “You’re the man.”
target_language_example: Si alguien puede arreglarlo, él es el hombre.
native_language_example: If anyone can fix it, he’s the man.

additional_notes: Used to say that one masculine singular person or thing is the top one in a group or category. "Mejor" can mean "better" or "best" depending on context; with "el," it means "the best." It is often followed by "de" or "en" (for example, "es el mejor de la clase," "es el mejor en su trabajo"). The form changes with gender and number: "es la mejor," "son los mejores," "son las mejores."
target_language_example: Para mí, este restaurante es el mejor de la ciudad.
native_language_example: For me, this restaurant is the best in the city.

additional_notes: Used to say something or someone is identical to another, or unchanged. Often appears with context that makes the comparison clear (e.g., “but the game is the same”). For people, it can mean “it’s him/the same guy” or “he’s back to being himself again” (e.g., “Tom es el mismo de nuevo”). Changes for gender/number: es la misma, son los mismos, son las mismas.
target_language_example: No te preocupes: este cargador es el mismo que el tuyo.
native_language_example: Don’t worry: this charger is the same as yours.

additional_notes: Used to compare one person (or thing) with a group. Structure: [person/thing] + es + el/la más + adjective + de + [group]. With "alto" it typically refers to height (tall). Adjust gender/number as needed: "es la más alta de…" for a female subject; or swap the adjective: "es el más rápido de…" (the fastest of…).
target_language_example: Tom es el más alto de la clase.
native_language_example: Tom is the tallest in the class.

additional_notes: Used to identify or single out a specific person or thing. In English it often translates as "is the one who/that." The article changes to match what it refers to: es la que, son los que, son las que.
target_language_example: Juan es el que cocina en casa.
native_language_example: Juan is the one who cooks at home.

additional_notes: Used to say that one person or thing is the sole member of a group or the sole option. In this form it is masculine singular; it changes to match the noun: es la única, son los únicos, son las únicas. Although único can also mean "unique," in many everyday sentences like these it means "only."
target_language_example: Este es el único restaurante abierto hoy.
native_language_example: This is the only restaurant open today.

additional_notes: Used to ask or state uncertainty about someone’s nationality. Often appears inside an indirect question with "si" (“whether/if”): "No sé si es español o argentino" = “I don’t know whether he’s Spanish or Argentine.” You can add a subject for clarity: "No sé si él es español o argentino."
target_language_example: No sé si es español o argentino; tiene acento, pero no lo distingo bien.
native_language_example: I don’t know if he’s Spanish or Argentine; he has an accent, but I can’t tell it well.

additional_notes: Used to strongly confirm that something matches your meaning, plan, or expectation. It’s followed by a verb phrase: “Es exactamente lo que quiero decir” (what I mean), “Eso es exactamente lo que voy a hacer” (what I’m going to do). Often appears after “eso” (“that”): “Eso es exactamente lo que…”.
target_language_example: Eso es exactamente lo que necesito ahora.
native_language_example: That’s exactly what I need right now.

additional_notes: Used to intensify an adjective: "Es extremadamente + adjetivo". It’s a formal/neutral way to say something is very intense (peligroso, aburrido, despistado, etc.). Often followed by an adjective, not a noun.
target_language_example: Este examen es extremadamente difícil.
native_language_example: This exam is extremely difficult.

additional_notes: Used to say something is easy. Often followed by an infinitive: “Es fácil + infinitive” (Es fácil viajar). You can also use it with a noun/adjective: “El examen es fácil.”
target_language_example: Es fácil aprender español con práctica.
native_language_example: It's easy to learn Spanish with practice.

additional_notes: Used with an infinitive verb after de: Es fácil de + usar/aprender/decir/hacer. You can change the subject (e.g., Esta cámara es fácil de usar) and gender/number to match it: es fácil (singular), son fáciles (plural).
target_language_example: Este programa es fácil de entender.
native_language_example: This program is easy to understand.

additional_notes: Used to express that something is very good or cool. Often appears with a subject: "Esto es genial" (This is great) or "Eso es genial" (That’s great). You can also use it about people: "Él/ella es genial" = "He/She is great".
target_language_example: ¡Tu idea es genial!
native_language_example: Your idea is awesome!

additional_notes: Used with **ser** to describe size (a general characteristic). **Es** is for singular subjects (El lago/La habitación). For plural: **son grandes**. **Grande** stays the same for masculine/feminine singular (el coche es grande / la casa es grande), and becomes **grandes** in plural. Watch out: **grande** can look like English **grand**, but it usually just means **big/large**.
target_language_example: Tu casa es grande, pero muy acogedora.
native_language_example: Your house is big, but very cozy.

additional_notes: Used to say that the moment has come to do something or that something should happen now. Use **es hora de + infinitive** (Es hora de cerrar.) or **es hora de + noun** (Es hora de la cena.). With a subject/change of action, use **es hora de que + subjunctive** (Es hora de que nos vayamos.). **ya es hora de** often adds emphasis like “it’s about time (to)…”.
target_language_example: Ya es hora de irnos a casa.
native_language_example: It’s about time to go home.

additional_notes: Used to say the moment has come for someone to do something, often as a suggestion, insistence, or a sense of urgency. After "es hora de que," Spanish normally uses the present subjunctive: "Es hora de que vayas," "…salgamos," "…sepas." You can also use "ya" for emphasis: "Ya es hora de que…".
target_language_example: Ya es hora de que empecemos a trabajar.
native_language_example: It’s (really) time for us to start working.

meaning: “is equal to” / “is the same as” / “is like.”
additional_notes: Used to state equality in math (A es igual a B) and also to compare things or people (“Mi respuesta es igual a la tuya” = my answer is the same as yours; “Es igual a su padre” = he/she is like his/her father, very similar). You can change the verb for other subjects/tense: “son iguales a” (they are equal to), “era igual a” (was equal to).
target_language_example: Este número es igual a veinte.
native_language_example: This number is equal to twenty.

additional_notes: Used to say that an action, situation, or thing is not allowed by law. You can change it for number/gender: “es ilegal” (it’s illegal), “son ilegales” (they’re illegal). Common pattern: “Es ilegal + infinitive” (Es ilegal fumar aquí). In “Ningún ser humano es ilegal,” it’s a slogan meaning no person should be considered illegal (often in immigration contexts).
target_language_example: Es ilegal conducir sin licencia.
native_language_example: It’s illegal to drive without a license.

additional_notes: Used to say something matters or is significant. Often followed by an infinitive ("Es importante aprender...") or by "que" + subjunctive to express what is important ("Es importante que todos sepan...").
target_language_example: Es importante llegar a tiempo.
native_language_example: It’s important to arrive on time.

meaning: "it’s important that" (used to stress the importance/necessity of something).
additional_notes: Often followed by the subjunctive because it expresses a recommendation, importance, or necessity: "Es importante que estudies." (not *"estudias"*). You can change the verb to match tense: "Fue/era/será importante que...". You can also add an indirect object: "Es importante que me llames" (It’s important that you call me).
target_language_example: Es importante que llegues a tiempo.
native_language_example: It’s important that you arrive on time.

additional_notes: Used to say something cannot be done or cannot happen. Common patterns: (1) “Es imposible que + subjunctive” to express that something is impossible (e.g., “Es imposible que venga” = “It’s impossible that he/she comes”). (2) “Es imposible de + infinitive” to mean “impossible to + verb” (e.g., “Es imposible de cumplir” = “It’s impossible to fulfill”). Can also be a short stand-alone response: “Es imposible.”
target_language_example: Lo siento, es imposible que lo entregue hoy.
native_language_example: Sorry, it’s impossible for me to deliver it today.

additional_notes: Used to express strong surprise or admiration about a situation or a person. Common patterns: “Es increíble que + (subjunctive)” (It’s unbelievable that...) and “Es increíble lo que + verb” (It’s incredible what...). Can be positive (amazing) or negative (hard to believe). Often used with “¡Dios mío!” for emphasis.
target_language_example: Es increíble lo rápido que aprendes.
native_language_example: It’s incredible how fast you learn.

additional_notes: Used to state that someone did not do something wrong or is not guilty (often in a legal/crime context, but it can also mean someone is naïve). You can change the subject: "Soy inocente" (I’m innocent), "Eres inocente" (you’re innocent).
target_language_example: No cabe la menor duda de que Tom es inocente.
native_language_example: There isn’t the slightest doubt that Tom is innocent.

additional_notes: Used to say something won’t work or isn’t worth doing. Common pattern: “Es inútil + infinitive” (Es inútil discutir / esperar / leer…). Can also describe a thing as not useful: “La televisión … es inútil.”
target_language_example: Es inútil intentarlo otra vez; no hay tiempo.
native_language_example: It’s pointless to try again; there’s no time.

additional_notes: Used to emphasize that something matches perfectly what you need, wanted, expected, or mentioned. It’s commonly followed by a verb in the past or present: Es justo lo que necesitaba / necesito. Similar in meaning to "es exactamente lo que".
target_language_example: ¡Es justo lo que estaba buscando!
native_language_example: It’s exactly what I was looking for!

additional_notes: Comes from es (from ser, “is”) + la (“the” with a feminine singular noun). Use it before a feminine noun or noun phrase: es la regla = “it’s the rule.” In context, English often supplies the subject: “it is the” or “she is the.”
target_language_example: Esta es la mejor opción.
native_language_example: This is the best option.

additional_notes: Used to state that a city is the capital city of a country/region. Structure: [City] + es la capital de + [place]. You can change tense/person: “fue la capital de” (was), “será la capital de” (will be).
target_language_example: Madrid es la capital de España.
native_language_example: Madrid is the capital of Spain.

additional_notes: Used to say something is the most important factor for achieving a result. Often followed by: de + noun (La paciencia es la clave del éxito = Patience is the key to success) or para + infinitive/noun (La práctica es la clave para mejorar = Practice is the key to improving). You can also use the plural: Son la clave = They are the key.
target_language_example: La constancia es la clave para aprender español.
native_language_example: Consistency is the key to learning Spanish.

additional_notes: Used to say that the appropriate or scheduled time has arrived. Very common with **de + noun/verb**: *Es la hora de la cena* (dinner time), *Es la hora de dormir* (time to sleep). With **del/de la** before a noun: *Es la hora del almuerzo / de la siesta*. It can also be used on its own to mean “it’s almost time” or “it’s time (to go/do it).”
target_language_example: Vámonos; ya es la hora.
native_language_example: Let’s go; it’s time.

additional_notes: Used to say something is the best within a group or category. "Mejor" = "better/best"; with "la" it agrees with a feminine noun (la lengua, la medicina, la opción). For a masculine noun, you usually say "es el mejor" (El café es el mejor). You can also add "de" to specify the group: "Es la mejor de la clase" (She/It’s the best in the class).
target_language_example: Para mí, esta película es la mejor.
native_language_example: For me, this movie is the best.

additional_notes: Used to say you’re doing something for the first time. It’s followed by a verb clause; in Spanish you’ll often hear the verb in the present (e.g., "Es la primera vez que veo...") even though in English we often use the present perfect ("it’s the first time I’ve seen...").
target_language_example: Es la primera vez que viajo solo.
native_language_example: It’s the first time I’ve traveled alone.

es la razón por la que

target_language_multi_word_term: es la razón por la que
additional_notes: Used to explain the cause of something. It’s often followed by a verb phrase: “Es la razón por la que + (verb/clause) …”. You can change it for gender/number: “Es la razón por la que…” (la razón, feminine singular) stays the same, but you can also hear “Esa es la razón por la que…”. In more casual speech, “Por eso…” is a common shorter equivalent.
target_language_example: Esa es la razón por la que no puedo ir hoy.
native_language_example: That’s the reason why I can’t go today.

additional_notes: Used to insist that something is true, often as a justification or defense ("Sorry, but it’s the truth"). In your examples it can also mean “what I need is the truth / the truth is the first victim,” where la verdad = “the truth.” Literally “it is the truth.”
target_language_example: No te va a gustar, pero es la verdad.
native_language_example: You’re not going to like it, but it’s the truth.

additional_notes: Used when the thing you’re talking about is feminine and singular (la forma, la manera, la solución). For a masculine noun, use “es el único” (e.g., “Es el único camino”). “Única” looks like “unique,” but here it usually means “only (one).”
target_language_example: Es la única opción que tenemos.
native_language_example: It’s the only option we have.

additional_notes: Used to say that there is just one possible or effective method to achieve a result. It’s commonly followed by an infinitive verb: es la única forma de + infinitive (hacer, aprender, salir, etc.). You can change the subject/tense as needed: Es/Fue/Será la única forma de…
target_language_example: Es la única forma de llegar a tiempo.
native_language_example: It’s the only way to arrive on time.

additional_notes: Used to say that something is the sole option or method to achieve a goal. Typically followed by an infinitive verb (de + infinitive): Es la única manera de escapar / ir / poder quedarme. You can change the verb for tense/person: Fue/Será la única manera de…
target_language_example: Lo siento, es la única manera de llegar a tiempo.
native_language_example: Sorry, it’s the only way to arrive on time.

meaning: “it’s the best” / “it’s the best thing to do.”
additional_notes: Used to say something is the best option or decision in a situation. Often followed by context like “si crees que es lo mejor” (“if you think it’s best”). You can also add “de + noun” to mean “the best part of …” (e.g., “lo mejor de la excursión” = “the best part of the trip”).
target_language_example: Creo que es lo mejor para todos.
native_language_example: I think it’s the best thing for everyone.

additional_notes: Used to point to the specific thing being referred to (“that is what we’ll do / what we need / what you want”). Often follows another clause for emphasis: “...eso es lo que...”. It can also appear in indirect questions meaning “what”: “saben qué es lo que sigue” = “they know what comes next.”
target_language_example: Si es lo que necesitas, puedo ayudarte mañana.
native_language_example: If that’s what you need, I can help you tomorrow.

meaning: “that’s what … to me / that’s what … me.”
additional_notes: Common sentence frame: **Es lo que me + verb**. It introduces “what” (lo que) and then says what happens **to/for me** (me). Examples: **Es lo que me dijo** (“That’s what he told me”), **Es lo que me preocupa** (“That’s what worries me”), **Es lo que me gusta** (“That’s what I like”). You normally need to finish it with a verb phrase.
target_language_example: Es lo que me preocupa más.
native_language_example: That’s what worries me the most.

meaning: "that’s what you want" / "if that’s what you want."
additional_notes: Used to confirm or emphasize someone’s preference/decision. Often appears inside the pattern “(si) es lo que + verb” (e.g., “si es lo que quieres”) meaning “(if) that’s what you want.” It can also be part of a longer question: “Dime qué es lo que quieres” = “Tell me what it is that you want,” where “lo que” means “what/that which.”
target_language_example: Si es lo que quieres, podemos hacerlo mañana.
native_language_example: If that’s what you want, we can do it tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used to say something is the top priority. Often follows a noun with “ser”: “La salud es lo más importante” (“Health is the most important thing”). “Lo más + adjective” means “the most + adjective,” with “lo” turning the adjective into “the … thing” (an abstract idea).
target_language_example: Para mí, pasar tiempo con mi familia es lo más importante.
native_language_example: For me, spending time with my family is the most important thing.

additional_notes: Used to identify or emphasize something (a cleft structure): "X es lo que..." = "X is what...". Often followed by a verb phrase: "Es lo que eres" (It's what you are). You may also see it inside a question: "qué es lo que..." = "what is it that..." (adds emphasis).
target_language_example: Esto es lo que necesito ahora mismo.
native_language_example: This is what I need right now.

meaning: "It is what it is" / "that’s how it is" (accepting a situation).
additional_notes: Used to express resignation or acceptance when something can’t be changed, or when the available options are limited (similar to “that’s all there is”). Often said in a matter-of-fact tone; can sound a bit blunt.
target_language_example: No hay más entradas; es lo que hay.
native_language_example: There are no more tickets; it is what it is.

meaning: “is … enough / sufficiently …” (usually followed by an adjective).
additional_notes: Used with an adjective to say something has enough of a quality to do something or for something to be true. Very often followed by an adjective + “como para” + infinitive: “es lo suficientemente + adj. + como para + verb” (“is + adj. + enough to + verb”). You can also place it before the adjective: “es suficientemente + adj.”
target_language_example: No es lo suficientemente importante como para discutirlo ahora.
native_language_example: It isn’t important enough to discuss it now.

meaning: 'it's the only thing that…' (the only one/thing that…).
additional_notes: Used to emphasize that there is just one option, one fact, or one thing that matters. It’s followed by a clause (usually a verb phrase): “Es lo único que sé” = “It’s the only thing I know.” You can also switch person/tense as needed: “Fue lo único que…” (It was the only thing that…), “Será lo único que…” (It will be the only thing that…).
target_language_example: Es lo único que puedo decir ahora.
native_language_example: It’s the only thing I can say right now.

additional_notes: A very common, literal combination: es = "is/it's" and lo que = "what/that which." It is used to identify, explain, or clarify something: Es lo que pienso = "It's what I think." Very common in patterns like no es lo que... ("it's not what...").
target_language_example: Es lo que necesito ahora.
native_language_example: It's what I need right now.

additional_notes: Used to warn that an activity or habit is unhealthy. Structure: [infinitive/noun] + es malo para la salud. You can also change the verb to match the subject (e.g., Son malos para la salud = “They’re bad for your health”). Similar: es bueno para la salud (“it’s good for your health”).
target_language_example: Fumar es malo para la salud.
native_language_example: Smoking is bad for your health.

meaning: 'it/he/she is wonderful' (talking about a thing or a person).
additional_notes: Use "es maravilloso" to say something is wonderful/amazing in a general or lasting way (using "ser"). It can describe a situation ("Es maravilloso que...") or praise a person ("Tom es maravilloso" / "Él es maravilloso con nosotros"). For a feminine noun/person, use "es maravillosa"; plural: "son maravillosos/as".
target_language_example: Es maravilloso que hayas venido hoy.
native_language_example: It’s wonderful that you came today.

additional_notes: Used in two common ways: for comparison, it means "is better than" (Esta casa es mejor que la otra). Before a clause, it often means "it's better that..." and is usually followed by the subjunctive (Es mejor que vuelvas temprano = It's better that you come back early / You'd better come back early).
target_language_example: Es mejor que salgamos ahora.
native_language_example: It's better that we leave now.

additional_notes: A very common combination of es ("is") and mi ("my"). It is used to say that someone or something is the speaker's, or to identify a relationship: X es mi Y = "X is my Y." Mi does not change for masculine/feminine nouns.
target_language_example: Madrid es mi ciudad favorita.
native_language_example: Madrid is my favorite city.

additional_notes: Used to say that someone is your friend. Spanish often drops the subject pronoun, so “Es mi amigo” can mean “He’s my friend” or “She’s my friend” depending on context. For a female friend, say “Es mi amiga.” You can add a name after it: “Es mi amigo Suzuki.”
target_language_example: Tranquilo, es mi amigo.
native_language_example: Relax, he’s my friend.

additional_notes: Used to take responsibility or blame for something. Often said with an apology: “Lo siento, es mi culpa.” To deny responsibility, use “No es mi culpa” (“It’s not my fault”). “Culpa” = “fault/blame,” so you can change the person: “Es tu culpa” (it’s your fault), “Es su culpa” (it’s his/her/their fault).
target_language_example: Perdón por el retraso; es mi culpa.
native_language_example: Sorry for being late; it’s my fault.

additional_notes: Used to identify someone as your brother. Often followed by extra information: “Es mi hermano el que…” = “It’s my brother who…”. In Spanish you can drop the subject (“él”) because it’s understood from context.
target_language_example: No, no es un amigo: es mi hermano.
native_language_example: No, he’s not a friend: he’s my brother.

additional_notes: Used to identify someone as your son. The subject can be a person’s name (“Tom es mi hijo”) or a pronoun (“Él es mi hijo”). Often said by itself (“Es mi hijo.”) when the subject is clear from context.
target_language_example: Perdón, es mi hijo; se perdió un momento.
native_language_example: Sorry, he’s my son; he got lost for a moment.

additional_notes: Used to say that a language is the one you learned first (your first language). Structure: [Language] + es mi lengua materna. You can also say “mi idioma materno” or “mi lengua nativa.”
target_language_example: El inglés es mi lengua materna, pero estoy aprendiendo español.
native_language_example: English is my native language, but I’m learning Spanish.

additional_notes: Used to say that something is your responsibility or part of what you do for a living. Often followed by an infinitive: “Es mi trabajo + infinitive” (e.g., “Es mi trabajo saber…” = “It’s my job to know…”). Word order can vary: “X es mi trabajo” (“X is my job”).
target_language_example: Es mi trabajo ayudarte con esto.
native_language_example: It’s my job to help you with this.

meaning: 'is much bigger/greater than' or 'is much older than.'
additional_notes: Used to compare two things or people with a strong difference. "mayor" can mean larger/greater (size, quantity, speed, importance) or older (age); context tells you which. Structure: "X es mucho mayor que Y". With nouns, you can avoid repeating the noun: "La población de Japón es mucho mayor que la de Australia" (= than Australia's).
target_language_example: Mi hermano es mucho mayor que yo.
native_language_example: My brother is much older than me.

additional_notes: A very common pattern: **es** + **muy** + adjective. **Es** is the singular form of **ser** ('is') and is used for general or lasting characteristics, descriptions, and qualities: **es muy bonito**, **es muy difícil**, **es muy importante**.
target_language_example: El libro es muy interesante.
native_language_example: The book is very interesting.

additional_notes: Used to describe something you find pleasant or enjoyable (a temperature, a taste, a feeling, an experience, or seeing someone). It can also be a polite way to say you’re happy to meet or see someone: “Es muy agradable verte.”
target_language_example: El clima hoy es muy agradable.
native_language_example: The weather today is very pleasant.

additional_notes: "Alto" means "tall" for people and "high" for prices, numbers, levels, etc. Use "es" (from "ser") for a general/lasting description: "El precio es muy alto" (the price is very high), "Mi hermano es muy alto" (my brother is very tall). For temporary physical location/height you’d more often use "está": "El avión está muy alto" (the plane is very high up).
target_language_example: Ese edificio es muy alto, pero el alquiler también es muy alto.
native_language_example: That building is very tall, but the rent is also very high.

meaning: "(He/She/You) are very kind" / "That’s very kind (of you)."
additional_notes: Used to describe someone as kind/nice, or as a polite response to a compliment, offer, or help (similar to “That’s very kind of you”). With people: "Es muy amable conmigo" = “He/She is very kind to me.” In set polite phrases you may hear "Es/Usted es muy amable" or "Ud. es muy amable". Can also appear as "Es muy amable por su parte" (“That’s very kind of you/It’s very kind on your part”) and "Es muy amable en decirlo" (“That’s very kind of you to say”).
target_language_example: ¿Me puede ayudar? Gracias, es muy amable.
native_language_example: Can you help me? Thanks, that’s very kind of you.

meaning: “is very pretty/beautiful” (describing a feminine person or thing).
additional_notes: Used with the verb ser (“to be”) + muy (“very”) + bonita (“pretty/beautiful,” feminine singular). Use it for women/girls or feminine nouns: “La ciudad es muy bonita.” For masculine nouns, say “es muy bonito.” In Spanish, you often include the subject: “Ella es muy bonita.”
target_language_example: Esa playa es muy bonita.
native_language_example: That beach is very beautiful.

additional_notes: Used to describe how something looks (a place, an object, a sound like singing). Often you’ll swap in a subject: “Aquí es muy bonito” (It’s very pretty here), “El canto … es muy bonito” (The singing is very beautiful). You can change the adjective for gender/number: “es muy bonita” (feminine), “son muy bonitos/bonitas” (plural).
target_language_example: En primavera, este parque es muy bonito.
native_language_example: In spring, this park is very beautiful.

additional_notes: Used to describe something feminine (or “it” referring to a feminine noun) as very good. For masculine nouns, use “es muy bueno”; for plural, “es muy buena(s)/bueno(s).” Often follows the thing being described: “Esta sopa es muy buena.”
target_language_example: La película es muy buena.
native_language_example: The movie is very good.

additional_notes: Used to say that someone/something is very good. With people, it can mean either “a good person” (kind/nice) or “good at” a skill—context matters. Common patterns: “es muy bueno + adjective/noun” (Es muy bueno profesor. / Es muy bueno tocando la guitarra.), “es muy bueno en + field/job/activity” (Es muy bueno en su trabajo.), and “es muy bueno para + activity/thing” (Es muy bueno para el ajedrez.).
target_language_example: Este café es muy bueno, y el servicio también.
native_language_example: This coffee is very good, and the service is too.

additional_notes: Used to say that something costs a lot. The subject can be implied by context (“Es muy caro.” = “It’s very expensive.”). With masculine singular (caro), it matches a masculine noun (e.g., “Este coche es muy caro”) or a general “it.” For feminine or plural subjects, it changes: “es muy cara” (feminine), “son muy caros/caras” (plural).
target_language_example: Lo siento, no lo compro: es muy caro.
native_language_example: Sorry, I’m not buying it: it’s very expensive.

additional_notes: Used to say that an activity, situation, or thing is hard. Often followed by an infinitive: “Es muy difícil + verb” (Es muy difícil aprender ruso / llevarse bien con él). You can change the subject for other nouns: “El ruso es muy difícil.” Feminine: “es muy difícil” stays the same because “difícil” doesn’t change for gender; plural would be “son muy difíciles.”
target_language_example: Es muy difícil entender este acento.
native_language_example: It’s very difficult to understand this accent.

additional_notes: Used with **ser** to give a general opinion that an activity or thing is fun. Often followed by an infinitive: **Es muy divertido + nadar / conducir / jugar**. You can change the subject too: **El baloncesto es muy divertido** (Basketball is very fun).
target_language_example: Es muy divertido jugar con amigos.
native_language_example: It’s really fun to play with friends.

meaning: “it is very strong” / “(he/she) is very strong.”
additional_notes: Used with the verb ser (“to be”) + muy (“very”) + fuerte (“strong”) to describe a person, an object, or a force like wind. Subject pronouns are often omitted in Spanish, so “Es muy fuerte” can mean “It’s very strong,” “He’s very strong,” or “She’s very strong,” depending on context.
target_language_example: Hoy el café es muy fuerte.
native_language_example: Today the coffee is very strong.

additional_notes: Used to say something is very easy, often followed by an infinitive (e.g., "Es muy fácil decir...") or used as a general description ("Esta receta es muy fácil"). It can also sound a bit critical when pointing out that something is easy for someone else to say/do ("Para ti es muy fácil").
target_language_example: Es muy fácil aprender estas palabras.
native_language_example: It’s very easy to learn these words.

additional_notes: Used to describe size (physical or sometimes quantity). The structure is: **[thing] + es + muy + grande**. For plural subjects, use **son muy grandes** (e.g., *Las habitaciones son muy grandes*). *Grande* can also describe age/status in some contexts (like *mi hermano mayor*), but here it’s about size.
target_language_example: La casa es muy grande para nosotros.
native_language_example: The house is very big for us.

additional_notes: Used to stress that something matters a lot. Often followed by an infinitive (Es muy importante estudiar.) or by “que” + subjunctive when what’s important is an action/situation (Es muy importante que hables con ella.).
target_language_example: Es muy importante llegar a tiempo.
native_language_example: It’s very important to arrive on time.

additional_notes: Used with the verb ser (es) to describe someone’s general or lasting trait: “He/She is very intelligent.” You can also add a context with en + noun to mean “very smart at/in (something)” (e.g., en matemáticas, en el agua). For other people, change es to son (they are) or replace it with the right form of ser.
target_language_example: Mi profesor es muy inteligente.
native_language_example: My teacher is very intelligent.

additional_notes: Used to say that something (or someone) is very interesting. Often follows the pattern: [subject] + es muy interesante (e.g., "Este libro es muy interesante"). You can also use it alone as a full sentence to agree or react: "Es muy interesante."
target_language_example: Aprender español es muy interesante.
native_language_example: Learning Spanish is very interesting.

additional_notes: Used to warn or emphasize that an activity or situation is unsafe. Often followed by an infinitive (e.g., nadar, conducir) or used alone as a standalone warning. Gender/number can change depending on what “it” refers to: es muy peligrosa (feminine singular), es muy peligroso (masculine singular/neutral).
target_language_example: No te acerques a la orilla: es muy peligroso.
native_language_example: Don’t go near the shore: it’s very dangerous.

additional_notes: Usually appears in comparisons: es más + adjective/adverb + que = 'is more ... than' (often translated with an -er form in English, like 'is taller than'). It can also appear in the fixed expression lo que es más, meaning 'what's more' or 'moreover'.
target_language_example: Mi hermano es más alto que yo.
native_language_example: My brother is taller than me.

additional_notes: Used to compare prices: **X es más caro que el Y** (“X is more expensive than the Y”). You can change **el** to match the noun: **la** (feminine), **los/las** (plural). Often you’ll also see it without an article before a possessive: **Es más caro que mi coche** (“…than my car”).
target_language_example: Este restaurante es más caro que el de la esquina.
native_language_example: This restaurant is more expensive than the one on the corner.

additional_notes: Used to compare two things, saying the first one is harder than the second. Pattern: **[thing A] es más difícil que [thing B]**. The second part often uses an infinitive verb: *Es más difícil quejarse que actuar.*
target_language_example: Aprender a pronunciar la R es más difícil que memorizar la gramática.
native_language_example: Learning to pronounce the R is more difficult than memorizing the grammar.

additional_notes: Used to compare difficulty: “Es más fácil + infinitive” (Es más fácil hacer…) or “Es más fácil + [thing] + que + [thing]” (…que llevarlos a cabo). Often followed by “de lo que…” to mean “than you think/it seems.”
target_language_example: Es más fácil decirlo que hacerlo.
native_language_example: It’s easier said than done.

meaning: "is easier than" (used to compare two things).
additional_notes: Used in comparisons: "X es más fácil que Y" = "X is easier than Y." After "que," Spanish often repeats the same verb from the first part (it may be omitted): "Enseñar a niños es más fácil que (enseñar) a los adultos." You can also use an indirect object pronoun with an infinitive: "Enseñarle a los niños..." = "To teach the children..."
target_language_example: Para mí, cocinar en casa es más fácil que comer fuera.
native_language_example: For me, cooking at home is easier than eating out.

additional_notes: Used to compare size (physical or sometimes figurative). Pattern: [thing A] + es + más grande que + [thing B]. You can change the verb for other subjects/tenses (e.g., “son más grandes que”, “era más grande que”) and match the adjective to gender/number (grande stays the same in singular; grandes in plural).
target_language_example: Mi casa es más grande que tu apartamento.
native_language_example: My house is bigger than your apartment.

additional_notes: Used with a singular feminine noun (because “mía” agrees with what is owned): *La bicicleta… es mía.* For a masculine noun use *es mío* (*El libro es mío*). For plural: *son mías/míos*. Often used to claim ownership or correct a misunderstanding.
target_language_example: ¿Esa mochila? Sí, es mía.
native_language_example: That backpack? Yes, it’s mine.

additional_notes: Used to say something belongs to you. The possessive pronoun changes to match what you’re talking about: es mío (masc.), es mía (fem.), son míos / son mías (plural). Often used with “lo que” to mean “what is mine”: “Lo que es mío…”.
target_language_example: Ese libro es mío, no tuyo.
native_language_example: That book is mine, not yours.

additional_notes: Used to say something is required/needed. Often followed by an infinitive ("Es necesario + infinitive": Es necesario estudiar) or by "para" to give a purpose ("Es necesario para...": Es necesario para nuestra protección). You can also add "que" + subjunctive: "Es necesario que vengas" (It’s necessary that you come).
target_language_example: Es necesario llevar pasaporte para viajar.
native_language_example: It’s necessary to bring a passport to travel.

additional_notes: Used to say something is required or important. Very often followed by the subjunctive: Es necesario que + (yo) haga, (tú) estudies, (él/ella) vaya, etc.
target_language_example: Es necesario que llegues a tiempo mañana.
native_language_example: You need to arrive on time tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used with a feminine singular noun (e.g., canción, época, costumbre, tecnología, opción, prioridad, profesora). It can mean 'it’s our…' or 'she’s our…' depending on what is being talked about. If the noun is masculine: es nuestro. If plural: son nuestros / son nuestras.
target_language_example: Es nuestra casa, así que cuidémosla.
native_language_example: It’s our house, so let’s take care of it.

additional_notes: A common chunk used before a noun: es nuestro turno = it's our turn. Nuestro changes to match the noun it describes: nuestra, nuestros, nuestras. If there is no noun after it, nuestro can mean "ours" instead: El coche es nuestro.
target_language_example: Hoy es nuestro día.
native_language_example: Today is our day.

additional_notes: Used to contrast with what was just said and signal a change in situation, level, or expectation. Very common in the pattern “Eso ya es otra cosa” (“Now that’s different / that’s another story”), often meaning that with this new detail, your opinion or the outcome changes. It can also be used to contrast two skills or ideas: “Saber es una cosa, enseñar es otra cosa.”
target_language_example: Quería ayudarte, pero si no me lo pides, ya es otra cosa.
native_language_example: I wanted to help you, but if you don’t ask me, that’s a different matter.

additional_notes: Used with "ser para" + person to show who something is intended for, belongs to (as a recipient), or is directed to. Common when handing someone something ("Toma, es para ti") or when a call/message is addressed to them ("El teléfono es para ti"). Can also refer to something being important or special to someone in context ("Sé lo importante que es para ti").
target_language_example: No, no es para mí; es para ti.
native_language_example: No, it’s not for me; it’s for you.

meaning: “is part of” (belongs to; is one component of).
additional_notes: Used to say something belongs to a group, family, organization, or situation, or is one element of a larger whole. It often introduces what something belongs to: “Es parte de esta familia.” You can change the verb for tense/person: “Es/era/será parte de…”, “Somos parte de…”.
target_language_example: Esto es parte de la solución.
native_language_example: This is part of the solution.

additional_notes: Used to say something is one component or element of a larger thing (a contract, a show, a process, etc.). Use with a masculine singular noun: Es parte del contrato / del espectáculo / del proceso. For feminine singular, use “es parte de la …” (Es parte de la experiencia). For plural, use “es parte de los/las …”.
target_language_example: Es parte del trabajo aprender de los errores.
native_language_example: It’s part of the job to learn from mistakes.

additional_notes: Used to say something is ideal, exactly right, or has no flaws. It can describe a general fact ("El reino animal es perfecto"), a quality ("Su acento es perfecto"), or suitability for someone: "Es perfecto para ti" ("It’s perfect for you"). In conversation, "¡Es perfecto!" often means "That’s perfect!" when you approve of a plan or option.
target_language_example: Si llegas a las ocho, es perfecto.
native_language_example: If you arrive at eight, that's perfect.

additional_notes: Used to introduce the reason or explanation for something that was just mentioned. Very common in conversation and writing. You’ll often see it with "y" at the start: "Y es por eso que..." (“And that’s why...”). In more casual speech, people may shorten it to "por eso" (“that’s why”).
target_language_example: Es por eso que no fui a la fiesta.
native_language_example: That’s why I didn’t go to the party.

additional_notes: Used to express possibility or uncertainty. It’s very commonly followed by the subjunctive: Es posible que sea..., Es posible que pueda..., Es posible que se me hayan olvidado...
target_language_example: Es posible que llegue tarde hoy.
native_language_example: It’s possible that I’ll arrive late today.

meaning: "it’s likely/probable that" (often followed by the subjunctive).
additional_notes: Used to express probability/likelihood about something that may happen or may be true. It commonly introduces a clause with the present subjunctive: "Es probable que venga" (not *viene*). You can also use it with past forms for earlier time frames: "Es probable que haya venido" (he has probably come) / "Es probable que viniera" (he was probably coming / would probably come, depending on context).
target_language_example: Es probable que lleguemos tarde por el tráfico.
native_language_example: It’s likely we’ll arrive late because of traffic.

additional_notes: Often used to introduce an explanation, justification, or excuse, especially at the start of a sentence: «Es que no puedo» = «It's just that I can't.» It also commonly introduces a clause after another idea: «Lo bueno es que...» = «The good thing is that...» In «si es que...», it can add doubt or emphasis, like «if there even is/are...».
target_language_example: Es que no sé qué decir.
native_language_example: It's just that I don't know what to say.

meaning: "It’s just that… I don’t / it’s that… (I) don’t" (introduces an explanation or softens a refusal).
additional_notes: Used in conversation to explain yourself, often as a gentle disagreement or excuse. It commonly comes before a negative statement: “Es que no + verb” (e.g., “Es que no puedo”). It can sound like “The thing is, I don’t…” rather than a blunt “No.”
target_language_example: Es que no puedo ir hoy; tengo que trabajar.
native_language_example: It’s just that I can’t go today; I have to work.

additional_notes: Used to say that something is genuine or true (not fake, not a trick, not imaginary). Often appears in negatives: “no es real” = “it’s not real.” You can also change the subject: “eso es real” = “that’s real.”
target_language_example: Tranquilo, es real.
native_language_example: Relax, it’s real.

additional_notes: Used to emphasize that something is important/true in a strong or sincere way. Often followed by an adjective: “es realmente + adjective” (e.g., importante, difícil, bueno).
target_language_example: Este problema es realmente serio.
native_language_example: This problem is really serious.

additional_notes: Used to downplay or limit what something is ("nothing more than"). It’s followed by a masculine singular noun; with a feminine noun it becomes "es solo una" (e.g., "Es solo una idea"). "solo" here means "only/just" (not the English "solo" meaning a performance alone).
target_language_example: No te preocupes: es solo un malentendido.
native_language_example: Don’t worry: it’s just a misunderstanding.

additional_notes: Used to downplay or minimize something: it’s nothing serious/important, just one thing. It’s followed by a feminine singular noun (una intuición, una sombra, una precaución, una reunión). With a masculine noun you use "es solo un" (e.g., "es solo un problema").
target_language_example: Tranquilo, es solo una pregunta.
native_language_example: Relax, it’s just a question.

additional_notes: Used to say something is enough/adequate, often to set a limit or stop something. It commonly appears with “ya” (“Bueno, ya es suficiente” = “Okay, that’s enough/alright, that’s enough”). You can add “para…” to specify for whom/purpose: “Eso es suficiente para mí” = “That’s enough for me.”
target_language_example: Con una explicación es suficiente.
native_language_example: One explanation is enough.

additional_notes: Used to limit or downplay what follows: a thing, reason, amount, or comparison. In many sentences English adds "it" even though Spanish does not say it explicitly. Also common with quantities and comparisons, like "es sólo la mitad..." = "it's only half...".
target_language_example: Es sólo una idea.
native_language_example: It's just an idea.

additional_notes: Used to minimize or downplay something, often to reassure someone or show it’s not important. It’s followed by a masculine singular noun (un + noun): Es sólo un ejercicio. For feminine nouns use “es sólo una…”. You can also drop the “un/una” with other structures (e.g., Es sólo para practicar).
target_language_example: Tranquilo, es sólo un error.
native_language_example: Relax, it’s just a mistake.

meaning: “it’s just a…” (used before a feminine singular noun).
additional_notes: Use to downplay or minimize something: Es sólo una + noun (feminine singular). With a masculine noun, you’d say: Es sólo un… Example: Es sólo un problema. Often followed by nouns like coincidencia (coincidence), formalidad (formality), teoría (theory).
target_language_example: No te preocupes: es sólo una pregunta.
native_language_example: Don’t worry: it’s just a question.

additional_notes: Used with adjectives. "es tan + adjective" means "is so + adjective" (often expressing emphasis). With comparisons, it’s "es tan + adjective + como + (noun/pronoun)" = "is as + adjective + as".
target_language_example: Esta película es tan divertida como la otra.
native_language_example: This movie is as fun as the other one.

additional_notes: Used to compare equal height. It’s the pattern **ser + tan + adjective + como**. Change **alta** to match the person being described: **alto** (masc.), **alta** (fem.), **altos/altas** (plural). For other adjectives, swap in the adjective you need (e.g., *tan rápido como* = as fast as).
target_language_example: Mi hermana es tan alta como yo.
native_language_example: My sister is as tall as me.

additional_notes: Used to compare or emphasize difficulty. Common patterns: **es tan difícil como + noun** (“as difficult as…”): *El latín no es tan difícil como el griego.*; and **es tan difícil que + clause** (“so difficult that…”): *La tarea es tan difícil que no puedo hacerla.* You can change **es** for other forms (e.g., *era tan difícil*, *será tan difícil*) and replace **difícil** with other adjectives (e.g., *es tan caro*).
target_language_example: Aprender a conducir es tan difícil al principio que me estreso.
native_language_example: Learning to drive is so difficult at first that I get stressed.

additional_notes: Used with a noun or situation to express a strong negative opinion: “X es terrible.” It can describe things (a road), events (a war), or abilities/skills (“Mi alemán es terrible” = “My German is terrible”). It’s often an exaggeration in everyday speech. For people, “Eres terrible” can also mean “You’re awful/terrible” (or sometimes “You’re so bad/mischievous,” depending on context).
target_language_example: Lo siento, pero la comida aquí es terrible.
native_language_example: Sorry, but the food here is terrible.

additional_notes: Used to say that something is the only thing (or the full extent) of what follows. It’s typically followed by a clause: “es todo lo que + verb” (e.g., “es todo lo que sé” = “that’s all I know”). In very casual contexts, you may also hear the shorter “es todo” (“that’s all”).
target_language_example: Es todo lo que necesito por hoy.
native_language_example: That’s all I need for today.

additional_notes: Can be used at the end of a statement with an implied subject: “(eso) es todo” = “that’s all.” In other contexts, especially with a noun or with lo, it means “is everything,” as in “La familia lo es todo” = “Family is everything.”
target_language_example: No tengo más preguntas, es todo.
native_language_example: I don't have any more questions, that's all.

additional_notes: Used to wrap up a talk, class, meeting, broadcast, or conversation. Often preceded by filler like “Bueno,” or “Pues,” and sometimes said as “Eso/Esto es todo por hoy” (same meaning).
target_language_example: Bueno, es todo por hoy. Nos vemos mañana.
native_language_example: Well, that’s all for today. See you tomorrow.

additional_notes: Combination of es ('is') and tu ('your'). Usually followed by a noun or noun phrase: es tu auto, es tu turno. tu without an accent means 'your'; tú with an accent means 'you'. Spanish often leaves out the subject pronoun, so es tu... can translate as 'it's your...' in English.
target_language_example: Es tu responsabilidad.
native_language_example: It's your responsibility.

additional_notes: Used with "ser" to say something belongs to the person you’re speaking to. It agrees with the thing owned: es tuyo (masc. singular), es tuya (fem. singular), son tuyos (masc. plural), son tuyas (fem. plural). You can also use it in offers/permission: "Es tuyo si lo quieres" = "You can have it if you want."
target_language_example: Si nadie lo reclama, es tuyo.
native_language_example: If no one claims it, it’s yours.

additional_notes: Used to identify or describe someone or something with a masculine singular noun. Es is a form of ser, and un means "a/an." For feminine nouns, use es una.
target_language_example: Mi padre es un profesor excelente.
native_language_example: My father is an excellent teacher.

additional_notes: Used to identify someone as a friend. Often said about a man or male friend; for a female friend, say “es una amiga.” You can also use it to reassure someone (e.g., “Es un amigo, no?” = “He’s a friend, right?”).
target_language_example: No te preocupes: es un amigo del trabajo.
native_language_example: Don’t worry: he’s a friend from work.

meaning: "is an animal" (literally); also "is a beast" (very intense/strong or very good at something).
additional_notes: Literally it identifies something as an animal: “El delfín es un animal…”. When said about a person, it’s usually informal and figurative: it can be a compliment (someone is incredibly good/strong) or a criticism (someone is brutal/rude). Context and tone make the difference.
target_language_example: En el gimnasio, Juan es un animal: levanta muchísimo peso.
native_language_example: At the gym, Juan is a beast: he lifts a lot of weight.

meaning: "(he) is an artist." / "(she) is an artist." (gendered form shown is masculine)
additional_notes: Used with **ser** to describe someone’s profession or identity: "X es un artista." For a woman, use **"es una artista"**. You can add adjectives after **artista** (e.g., **famoso**, **visual**) or use **"artista nato"** to mean a natural/born artist. "Artista" can refer to a painter, visual artist, performer, etc., depending on context.
target_language_example: Picasso es un artista famoso.
native_language_example: Picasso is a famous artist.

meaning: “it’s a matter/issue (of…)” or “it’s a private affair.”
additional_notes: Used to identify what something is about, often followed by an adjective (serio, trivial, familiar, privado) or by “de” + noun (e.g., es un asunto de dinero). “Asunto” can mean “matter,” “issue,” or “affair,” depending on context.
target_language_example: No te metas: es un asunto privado.
native_language_example: Don’t get involved: it’s a private matter.

meaning: “he is a good man” / “(you) are a good man.”
additional_notes: Used to describe someone’s character positively. It commonly appears after a name or family word (Mi esposo/mi marido/papá/tu padre + es un buen hombre). With no subject, “es” usually refers to “he” (él), but it can also refer to “you” in formal address (Usted es un buen hombre). In Spanish you can drop the subject pronoun because the verb form gives the meaning.
target_language_example: Creo que tu hermano es un buen hombre.
native_language_example: I think your brother is a good man.

meaning: “it’s a good time” / “it’s a good moment.”
additional_notes: Used to say that the timing is good (often with “para + infinitive”): “Es un buen momento para hablar.” In the negative (“no es un buen momento”), it means it’s not a good time right now and can sound like a gentle refusal.
target_language_example: Es un buen momento para hacer una pregunta.
native_language_example: It’s a good time to ask a question.

additional_notes: Used to identify someone as male, often followed by an adjective or description: “Es un chico muy vago” (He’s a very lazy guy). With “de + noun” it can describe a type of person: “un chico de suerte” (a lucky guy). You can also use it with a relative clause: “un chico que…” (a boy/guy who…).
target_language_example: Es un chico muy simpático.
native_language_example: He's a very nice guy.

additional_notes: Used to say something is illegal or morally very wrong. Often appears in statements like “X no es un crimen” (“X isn’t a crime”) to defend or justify something, or “X es un crimen” to strongly condemn it. Common pattern: “Es un crimen + adjective” (e.g., “Es un crimen horrible”).
target_language_example: Robar es un crimen.
native_language_example: Stealing is a crime.

additional_notes: Used to say something is in very bad condition, messy, chaotic, or went very badly. You can use it for places (Esta casa es un desastre), things (La alfombra es un desastre), or situations/results (El vídeo… es un desastre). Often said with emphasis: “Esto sí que es un desastre” = “Now THIS is a disaster.”
target_language_example: Tu cuarto es un desastre; por favor, límpialo hoy.
native_language_example: Your room is a mess; please clean it today.

meaning: “it’s a day” / “it is a (kind of) day”.
additional_notes: Used with **ser** to describe what the day is like or what kind of day it is: **Es un día hermoso / importante / pésimo.** Often followed by an adjective, **de + noun** (**Es un día de viaje** = “It’s a travel day”), or **como...** (**Es un día como cualquier otro** = “It’s a day like any other”). For a specific day (today/that day), Spanish often uses **Hoy es un día...** or **Ese es un día...**
target_language_example: Hoy es un día muy especial para mi familia.
native_language_example: Today is a very special day for my family.

additional_notes: Used to say someone has a high level of knowledge or skill in a topic or field. It agrees with the person: ella es una experta en…, ellos son expertos en…. You can also say “es experto en…” (without un) to sound a bit more formal/neutral.
target_language_example: Tom es un experto en matemáticas.
native_language_example: Tom is an expert in mathematics.

meaning: “(he/she) is a genius” (also: “(he/she) is awesome / really smart”).
additional_notes: Used to praise someone’s intelligence or talent. In context it often means “so smart” or “amazing,” not necessarily a literal IQ/genius claim. You can change the subject: “Soy un genio” (I’m a genius), “Eres un genio” (you’re a genius), “Son unos genios” (they’re geniuses).
target_language_example: ¡Gracias por ayudarme con la tarea! Eres un genio.
native_language_example: Thanks for helping me with the homework! You’re a genius.

additional_notes: Used to describe a masculine singular noun: "Es un gran + noun" (e.g., "Es un gran país"). "Gran" is the shortened form of "grande" and it goes before the noun. With feminine nouns, you say "es una gran + noun" (e.g., "Es una gran idea"). The meaning can be "great" (excellent/important) or "big" (large), depending on context.
target_language_example: Aprender español es un gran paso para mí.
native_language_example: Learning Spanish is a big step for me.

additional_notes: Used to emphasize that something is true and not up for debate. Very common in the pattern “Es un hecho que + [statement]” (“It’s a fact that…”). You can also say “Y eso es un hecho” to strongly underline what you just said.
target_language_example: Es un hecho que necesitamos descansar para estar bien.
native_language_example: It’s a fact that we need to rest to be well.

additional_notes: A straightforward phrase used to identify or describe a male person. In Spanish, the subject pronoun is often omitted, so es can mean "he is," "she is," or "it is" depending on context; with hombre, it refers to a man. It is often followed by an adjective or descriptive phrase, as in es un hombre ocupado or es un hombre de fiar.
target_language_example: Mi abuelo es un hombre muy tranquilo.
native_language_example: My grandfather is a very calm man.

meaning: 'he is a man of…' (used to describe a man’s qualities, appearance, age, etc.).
additional_notes: Common pattern: **Es un hombre de + noun phrase**. It can describe a trait (**un hombre de palabra** = a man who keeps his word), a quality (**de una fe tremenda**), a physical description (**de aspecto agradable**), or age (**de treinta años**). In English you often translate more naturally as “He’s a … man” or “He’s a …-year-old man,” depending on what follows.
target_language_example: Es un hombre de gran paciencia.
native_language_example: He’s a very patient man.

additional_notes: Used to describe a man whose job is in business (often someone who runs or manages companies). You can also say “Es un empresario” (he is an entrepreneur/businessman). For a woman: “Es una mujer de negocios.”
target_language_example: Mi padre es un hombre de negocios y viaja mucho.
native_language_example: My dad is a businessman and travels a lot.

additional_notes: Used in polite/formal situations to express respect, gratitude, or pride. Common patterns: “Es un honor para mí + infinitive” (Es un honor para mí conocerlo = It’s an honor for me to meet you) and “Es un honor + infinitive” (Es un honor poder ayudar = It’s an honor to be able to help). You’ll also hear “Es un honor para nosotros” (for us) or “Es un honor trabajar con usted” (to work with you).
target_language_example: Es un honor para mí estar aquí hoy.
native_language_example: It’s an honor for me to be here today.

additional_notes: Used to say that a language is hard to learn. You can swap in the language name before it: “El japonés es un idioma difícil.” You can also compare difficulty with “pero no tanto como…” (but not as much as…).
target_language_example: Para mí, el alemán es un idioma difícil.
native_language_example: For me, German is a difficult language.

meaning: “he is an idiot” / “(someone) is an idiot.”
additional_notes: A strong insult meaning someone is very stupid or behaves foolishly; can sound harsh/offensive. Often used with a name or subject: “Tom es un idiota.” You can change the verb for other people: “Soy un idiota” (I’m an idiot), “Eres un idiota” (you’re an idiot). Note: *idiota* has the same form for men and women (e.g., “Ella es una idiota”).
target_language_example: No le hagas caso; es un idiota.
native_language_example: Don’t pay attention to him; he’s an idiot.

additional_notes: Used to describe something literally as a game (a sport, chess, etc.) or figuratively as a “game” in the sense of a strategy, trick, or mind game (juego mental). Often followed by details: “Es un juego + adjective” (Es un juego aburrido) or “Es un juego que…” (Es un juego que se juega con tus reglas).
target_language_example: No te preocupes, es un juego; solo estamos practicando.
native_language_example: Don’t worry, it’s a game; we’re just practicing.

meaning: "it’s a place" (used to describe a location).
additional_notes: Used with adjectives to describe a place: “Es un lugar + adjective” (Es un lugar bonito/lindo/agradable). You can add “para + infinitive” to say it’s a good place to do something: “Es un lugar interesante para descubrir” = “It’s an interesting place to discover.”
target_language_example: Es un lugar tranquilo para descansar.
native_language_example: It’s a quiet place to rest.

additional_notes: Used to label a man as someone who lies. Often appears after a name ("Tom es un mentiroso") or after a conditional like "si..." ("Es un mentiroso si dice..."). For a woman: "es una mentirosa." You can also use it with other subjects: "soy un mentiroso" (I’m a liar), "eres un mentiroso" (you’re a liar), "son unos mentirosos" (they’re liars). Strong/accusatory in tone.
target_language_example: No le creas: es un mentiroso.
native_language_example: Don’t believe him: he’s a liar.

meaning: it’s a lot; it’s tons (of something).
additional_notes: Common, informal way to say there is a large amount or that something is very much/very intense. Often used with de + noun: “Es un montón de trabajo” (It’s a ton of work). You can also use “un montón” without “es” as a quantity: “Tengo un montón de amigos” (I have lots of friends).
target_language_example: Es un montón de comida para una sola persona.
native_language_example: That’s a lot of food for one person.

meaning: "(he/she) is a child" or "(he) is a boy."
additional_notes: Used with the verb ser (to be) to state someone’s identity/description: X es un niño. Often you’ll add an adjective after niño: es un niño listo/sensible. For a girl, use es una niña. To specify age, Spanish usually says Tiene X años rather than *Es X años*.
target_language_example: Es un niño muy curioso y siempre hace preguntas.
native_language_example: He’s a very curious kid and he always asks questions.

meaning: "it’s a name" (used to say what type of name something is).
additional_notes: Used to identify something as a name and often to add a description: *Es un nombre + adjective* (Es un nombre bonito.) or *Es un nombre + nationality/language adjective* (Es un nombre español / francés / alemán). For feminine nouns you change it to *es un nombre* anyway, because *nombre* is masculine: *Carmen es un nombre español.*
target_language_example: ¿Sofía? Sí, es un nombre muy común.
native_language_example: "Sofía"? Yes, it’s a very common name.

additional_notes: Used with a place name + “es un país” + adjective or descriptor to say what kind of country it is (e.g., europeo, democrático, rico, hermoso). It can also be followed by a noun phrase: “Es un país de…” (e.g., Es un país de montañas.).
target_language_example: Canadá es un país grande.
native_language_example: Canada is a big country.

additional_notes: Used to describe a country with an adjective after "muy" (very): "Es un país muy seguro/hermoso/bello/poderoso". It commonly comes after a country name: "Colombia es un país muy…".
target_language_example: España es un país muy diverso.
native_language_example: Spain is a very diverse country.

additional_notes: A polite, formal phrase used when meeting someone, welcoming them, or expressing that you’re happy to do something. Often followed by an infinitive ("Es un placer estar aquí") or a verb like conocer/ver/tener + object pronoun ("Es un placer conocerlo/la/los/las"). You can also say "Un placer" as a shorter version.
target_language_example: Es un placer ayudarle.
native_language_example: It’s a pleasure to help you.

additional_notes: Used with adjectives (and some phrases) to soften the description or make it less strong: "Es un poco tarde" = "It’s a bit late." In Spanish you can also use "un poco" without "es" in many contexts (e.g., "Estoy un poco cansado/a" = "I’m a bit tired").
target_language_example: Es un poco caro, pero vale la pena.
native_language_example: It’s a bit expensive, but it’s worth it.

additional_notes: Used to state that something is an issue, difficulty, or concern. Often followed by details like: “es un problema grave” (it’s a serious problem), “es un problema común” (it’s a common problem), or “es un problema que hay que resolver” (it’s a problem that needs to be solved). You can replace “un problema” with “un problema de…” to specify the type (e.g., “de vida o muerte” = life-or-death).
target_language_example: Llegar tarde siempre es un problema en este trabajo.
native_language_example: Being late is always a problem at this job.

additional_notes: Used literally to say something is happening in a dream (e.g., “Sólo es un sueño”). It can also be used figuratively to mean something feels unreal or like a fantasy (“Es un sueño, tiene que serlo”), or to say something used to be only a dream/hope but is becoming real (“ya no es un sueño”).
target_language_example: Ganar este premio es un sueño para mí.
native_language_example: Winning this prize is a dream for me.

additional_notes: Used to describe a man or person, often followed by an adjective: Es un tipo simpático (a nice guy), un tipo rudo (a tough guy). In many contexts, tipo is like "guy" in English: informal and conversational, but not necessarily rude. It can also mean "a kind/type" of something, but with people it usually means "guy/person."
target_language_example: Tu hermano es un tipo muy tranquilo.
native_language_example: Your brother is a very calm guy.

meaning: “it’s a job / it’s work” (a task or a piece of work).
additional_notes: Used to describe something as a task, job, or type of work, often followed by details: “Es un trabajo muy preciso” (It’s very precise work), “Es un trabajo en progreso” (It’s a work in progress). It can also mean “it’s just a job” to downplay its importance: “Sólo es un trabajo.”
target_language_example: No te preocupes, sólo es un trabajo temporal.
native_language_example: Don’t worry, it’s only a temporary job.

meaning: “is a real / a true …” (used to emphasize a noun).
additional_notes: Used to strongly describe what someone/something is: **es un verdadero + noun**. Adjust for gender/number as needed: **es un verdadero** (masc. sing.), **es una verdadera** (fem. sing.), **son unos verdaderos / son unas verdaderas** (plural). Often used for emphasis, sometimes praise (*caballero*, *señor*) or criticism (*pelota*, *psicópata*), depending on the noun.
target_language_example: Tomás es un verdadero caballero.
native_language_example: Tomás is a true gentleman.

additional_notes: Used to identify or describe someone or something with a feminine singular noun. "una" means "a/an" for feminine nouns, so compare "es un" with masculine nouns.
target_language_example: Es una buena idea.
native_language_example: It's a good idea.

additional_notes: Used to say something is a good option/choice/thing, and it normally continues with a feminine noun: Es una buena idea/decisión/elección/apuesta/lección. Because "buena" is feminine, it agrees with feminine nouns; with masculine nouns you’d say: Es un buen plan / Es un buen chico.
target_language_example: Es una buena idea esperar hasta mañana.
native_language_example: It’s a good idea to wait until tomorrow.

meaning: “she is a girl” / “she’s a young woman.”
additional_notes: Used with the verb ser (es = “is”) to describe someone (often followed by an adjective): Es una chica simpática. Chica usually means “girl,” but it can also mean “young woman,” depending on age and context.
target_language_example: Laura es una chica muy inteligente.
native_language_example: Laura is a very smart girl/young woman.

additional_notes: Used to identify/classify a place as a city. It’s a basic structure: **[place] + es + una ciudad (+ adjective)** (e.g., *una ciudad grande* = “a big city”). For plural: *son ciudades*.
target_language_example: Madrid es una ciudad muy bonita.
native_language_example: Madrid is a very beautiful city.

meaning: “is one thing” (used to contrast with something else).
additional_notes: Most commonly used in the pattern “X es una cosa, Y es otra” to highlight a contrast: one action/idea is different from another (often implying “they’re not the same” or “one doesn’t automatically lead to the other”). In English it’s usually “X is one thing; Y is another.”
target_language_example: Decirlo es una cosa; hacerlo es otra.
native_language_example: Saying it is one thing; doing it is another.

meaning: 'it's kind of / sort of' (a type of).
additional_notes: Used to compare or classify something by saying it is similar to, or a type of, something else. Common in definitions and explanations. You can change the verb for other subjects/tense: "son una especie de..." (they are), "era una especie de..." (it was).
target_language_example: Este aparato es una especie de cámara, pero también graba audio.
native_language_example: This device is kind of a camera, but it also records audio.

meaning: "it’s a way of" (doing something); "it’s a form/type of" (something).
additional_notes: Used to define or describe something by comparing it to a broader category ("X es una forma de Y") or to explain a purpose/approach ("es una forma de + infinitive"). Very common for giving explanations: "Es una forma de decir(lo)" = "It’s a way of saying it" (not meant literally).
target_language_example: Para mí, viajar es una forma de aprender.
native_language_example: For me, traveling is a way to learn.

additional_notes: Used to classify something: **X es una fruta** = “X is a fruit.” It’s the verb **ser** (to be) + **una** (a) + **fruta** (fruit). Note: In some contexts, calling a person **una fruta** can be slang/objectifying and may sound rude or inappropriate; for literal descriptions of food, it’s neutral.
target_language_example: La piña es una fruta.
native_language_example: Pineapple is a fruit.

meaning: “it’s a great…” / “he’s a great…” / “she’s a great…”
additional_notes: Used to describe someone or something positively. In Spanish, the adjective "grande" shortens to "gran" before a singular noun (gran chica, gran película, gran manera). You can change "es" to match the subject: "soy" (I’m), "eres" (you are), "es" (he/she/it is), "somos" (we are), "son" (they are).
target_language_example: Es una gran idea.
native_language_example: It’s a great idea.

meaning: "it’s an illusion" (something that seems real but isn’t).
additional_notes: Used to say that a belief, feeling, or appearance is misleading or not real. Often used in philosophical or dramatic statements (e.g., “La seguridad es una ilusión”). You can also use “Todo es una ilusión” = “It’s all an illusion.”
target_language_example: Pensé que tenía el control, pero es una ilusión.
native_language_example: I thought I had control, but it’s an illusion.

additional_notes: Used to classify or describe what something is (often a language): “X es una lengua + adjective” (difficult, beautiful), or “X es una lengua + type” (bereber, construida). You can also use it figuratively, as in “La música es una lengua común…”. Note: “lengua” can mean both “language” and the physical “tongue”; in these examples it means “language”.
target_language_example: El español es una lengua muy hablada en muchos países.
native_language_example: Spanish is a language that is widely spoken in many countries.

additional_notes: Used to say something is wild, unbelievable, chaotic, or unreasonable. Can describe a situation (¡Adentro es una locura! = It’s crazy in there!) or an activity (Es una locura leer esa revista = It’s crazy to read that magazine). Often said with emphasis; can be negative (too much, dangerous) or playful/exaggerated.
target_language_example: Ir sin dormir al trabajo es una locura.
native_language_example: Going to work without sleeping is crazy.

meaning: "it’s a damn/ freaking ..." (strong, rude emphasis before a feminine noun).
additional_notes: Used to intensify a negative opinion or frustration: *Es una maldita redada / película / lástima / tortura.* The adjective *maldita* agrees with a feminine noun (e.g., *una maldita idea*). With a masculine noun, you’d say *es un maldito ...* (e.g., *un maldito problema*). It’s vulgar/insulting in many contexts; use with caution.
target_language_example: Es una maldita pérdida de tiempo.
native_language_example: It’s a damn waste of time.

additional_notes: Used to say that a statement is false. You can add an adjective for nuance: “una mentira blanca” = “a white lie” (a small lie meant to avoid hurting someone). Word order is flexible in speech: “Es una mentira” / “Eso es una mentira” / “¡Es mentira!”
target_language_example: No le creas: es una mentira.
native_language_example: Don’t believe him: it’s a lie.

additional_notes: Strong, vulgar way to say something is very bad, disappointing, or terrible. Often used with a specific subject: “X es una mierda” (“X sucks”). You can intensify it: “es una mierda enorme” (“it’s huge crap / it really sucks”). Not appropriate in polite conversation.
target_language_example: Este trabajo es una mierda, pero tengo que terminarlo.
native_language_example: This job sucks, but I have to finish it.

additional_notes: Used with the verb ser (es = “is”) to identify someone’s gender/identity. Often followed by an adjective: “Es una mujer guapa” (“She’s a pretty woman”). You can add “Sí, por supuesto” to strongly confirm something: “Sí, por supuesto que es una mujer.”
target_language_example: Es una mujer muy inteligente.
native_language_example: She is a very smart woman.

additional_notes: Used with the verb ser (es) to identify someone as a girl/young female (niña). Often followed by an adjective (e.g., es una niña encantadora). Negative form: no es una niña. Can also be used as an announcement like “¡Es una niña!” (It’s a girl!).
target_language_example: Es una niña muy inteligente.
native_language_example: She is a very smart girl.

meaning: “is a person” (used to describe what someone is like).
additional_notes: Used with an adjective or description to talk about someone’s character or qualities: “X es una persona + adjective” (agradable, complicada, decente, honesta, inteligente). In polite/formal contexts, you may see “usted es una persona…”. Often interchangeable with “X es + adjective” (e.g., “Tom es honesto”), but “es una persona…” can feel a bit more descriptive/reflective about the person overall.
target_language_example: Mi jefe es una persona muy justa.
native_language_example: My boss is a very fair person.

additional_notes: Used to describe someone’s personality or qualities. It’s followed by an adjective (independiente, gentil, ocupada, sabia, sensible, trabajadora, simpática). The adjective agrees in gender and number with persona (feminine singular), so you typically use the feminine form: persona muy ocupada / simpática, even if the person is male. For a group: son personas muy amables.
target_language_example: Mi hermano es una persona muy amable.
native_language_example: My brother is a very kind person.

additional_notes: Used to point out that something is a question (often to clarify tone or intent). You can add an adjective after “pregunta” (e.g., “Es una pregunta interesante.”). With “sólo/solo” it can mean “It’s just a question,” to downplay it or say you’re not accusing or insisting.
target_language_example: Tranquilo, sólo es una pregunta.
native_language_example: Relax, it’s just a question.

additional_notes: Used to say an activity, plan, or place isn’t worth doing because it doesn’t bring results or value. Common pattern: "[Something] es una pérdida de tiempo" (e.g., Estudiar eso es una pérdida de tiempo). You can also hear the plural: "son una pérdida de tiempo" for plural subjects.
target_language_example: Discutir otra vez es una pérdida de tiempo.
native_language_example: Arguing again is a waste of time.

additional_notes: Used to say that something is a good moral quality or admirable trait. Often follows an abstract noun (La honestidad es una virtud.) or an infinitive phrase acting as a noun (Aprender de tus errores es una virtud.). You can add emphasis with adjectives: es una gran virtud / es una virtud muy valiosa.
target_language_example: La paciencia es una virtud, especialmente con niños.
native_language_example: Patience is a virtue, especially with kids.

meaning: “it is one of the” (feminine plural noun).
additional_notes: Used to say something belongs to a group: “It’s one of the + [plural noun].” Use **es uno de los** with a masculine plural noun, and **son uno/una de los/las** for plural subjects. Often followed by a superlative or description: **una de las + más + adjective + noun** (e.g., “one of the most beautiful capitals”).
target_language_example: Es una de las mejores razones para aprender español.
