In customer-service contexts, “Ya estoy con usted/ustedes” means “I’ll be right with you.”
target_language_example: Ahora no puedo hablar: estoy con trabajo, pero luego te llamo.
native_language_example: I can’t talk right now: I’m busy with work, but I’ll call you later.

additional_notes: Used with the verb estar (temporary state/location) + en to say where you are physically (en casa, en el mercado, en la India, en el auto) or what situation/event/level you’re currently in (en una cena, en el primer año de instituto). Often translates as “at” for places/events, “in” for countries/rooms/vehicles, and sometimes “on” with transport like en el auto/bus/tren (also common: “in the car”).
target_language_example: Ahora mismo estoy en el trabajo, pero luego estoy en casa.
native_language_example: Right now I’m at work, but later I’m at home.

additional_notes: Used to refer to a meteor streaking across the night sky. You often hear it in the common expression “Pide un deseo” (Make a wish) when someone sees one.
target_language_example: ¡Mira, una estrella fugaz! Pide un deseo.
native_language_example: Look, a shooting star! Make a wish.

additional_notes: Uses the gerund ("estudiando") to say someone is in the process of studying French, often with forms like "estar" ("está/estaba/ha estado... estudiando") to emphasize an ongoing activity. It’s also common with "llevar + time + gerund" to mean "to have been doing something for (time)": "Llevo tres años estudiando francés".
target_language_example: Estoy estudiando francés este semestre.
native_language_example: I’m studying French this semester.

meaning: to study law (as a university major).
additional_notes: In Spanish, "Derecho" (capitalized) commonly refers to the academic field/degree in Law. Without capitalization ("derecho"), it often means "right" (a right/entitlement) or "straight/upright" depending on context. You can also say "estudiar leyes" in a more general sense, but "estudiar Derecho" is the standard way to talk about the major.
target_language_example: Mi hermana va a estudiar Derecho en la universidad.
native_language_example: My sister is going to study law at university.

meaning: to study abroad (in a foreign country).
additional_notes: Used to talk about studying in another country, often as part of a university exchange program, scholarship (beca), or time living overseas. You can also say "ir a estudiar al extranjero" (to go study abroad).
target_language_example: El año que viene quiero estudiar en el extranjero.
native_language_example: Next year I want to study abroad.

additional_notes: Used with verbs like decidir (to decide), comenzar (to start), querer (to want), deber (should), and tener que (to have to). You can swap francés for other subjects/languages: estudiar español, estudiar matemáticas. Note: to say “learn French” in general, Spanish often uses aprender francés, but estudiar francés focuses on studying (classes, books, practice).
target_language_example: Tengo que estudiar francés esta noche.
native_language_example: I have to study French tonight.

additional_notes: A very literal, compositional phrase: "estudiar" = "to study" and "inglés" = "English." You can conjugate "estudiar" (e.g., "estudio/estudiaba/estudiaré inglés") or use it after another verb (e.g., "empecé a estudiar inglés" = "I started studying English").
target_language_example: Voy a estudiar inglés esta tarde.
native_language_example: I’m going to study English this afternoon.

additional_notes: “Estuve” is the preterite (simple past) of **estar** for **yo**. Use **estuve en + place** to say you were somewhere for a finished period of time (even if it was weeks): *Estuve en el hospital por unas semanas.* It can also be used more figuratively: *Una vez estuve en tu lugar* (“I was in your place / I’ve been in your shoes”).
target_language_example: Estuve en casa todo el día ayer.
native_language_example: I was at home all day yesterday.

meaning: 'were here' / 'was here' (hypothetical, wished-for, or expected situation).
additional_notes: Uses the imperfect subjunctive of **estar** (**estuviera**) + **aquí** (“here”). Common after **si** (“if”) for hypothetical situations: *Si (yo) estuviera aquí…* = “If I were here…”. Also appears after expressions of expectation or desire like **esperar que**, **querer que**, **suponerse que** when talking about something that isn’t true/confirmed at the moment: *Esperaba que Tom estuviera aquí* = “I was hoping Tom would be here.”
target_language_example: Si yo estuviera aquí, te ayudaría.
native_language_example: If I were here, I would help you.

additional_notes: Uses the preterite of **estar** (*estuvo*) to talk about someone being here at a specific moment in the past (often a completed, finished time). Common with time expressions like **hace un momento** (a moment ago) or **la semana pasada** (last week).
target_language_example: Lo siento, el doctor estuvo aquí hace unos minutos.
native_language_example: Sorry, the doctor was here a few minutes ago.

additional_notes: Preterite form of **estar**: **él/ella/usted estuvo** + **en** to say someone was in a place at a specific time in the past. Use **en** for locations like cities/countries (**estuvo en Los Ángeles / en Estados Unidos**) and also for being on TV (**estuvo en la TV**). For background/ongoing past situations, Spanish often uses **estaba en** instead.
target_language_example: Mi hermano estuvo en Madrid la semana pasada.
native_language_example: My brother was in Madrid last week.

additional_notes: Used with a conjugated form of estar + a punto de + infinitive to say something will happen very soon (imminently). The specific form "está a punto de" is third-person singular (he/she/it/you-formal). Other forms include: "estoy/estás/está/estamos/están a punto de".
target_language_example: El tren está a punto de llegar.
native_language_example: The train is about to arrive.

additional_notes: Used with estar to say someone/something is safe or protected. Often appears with “de” to mean “safe from” (Está a salvo de un ataque). It can also mean something (like a secret) is secure with someone: “Tu secreto está a salvo conmigo” = “Your secret is safe with me.”
target_language_example: No te preocupes: tu hijo está a salvo.
native_language_example: Don’t worry: your son is safe.

additional_notes: Used with feminine singular nouns (e.g., la tienda, la puerta, la ventana). It’s the present tense of estar + abierta (past participle used as an adjective) to describe a state. For masculine: “está abierto”; for plural: “están abiertos/abiertas”.
target_language_example: La puerta está abierta, pasa por favor.
native_language_example: The door is open; come in, please.

meaning: “she is used to” / “she is accustomed to” (doing something).
additional_notes: Used with a feminine singular subject (ella). It’s the verb phrase estar acostumbrado/a a + infinitive (or a + noun) to talk about a habit or something that feels normal because it’s familiar. For other people: estoy acostumbrado/a a, estás acostumbrado/a a, está acostumbrado/a a, etc.
target_language_example: Ella está acostumbrada a levantarse temprano.
native_language_example: She is used to getting up early.

additional_notes: Used with a person + estar + acostumbrado/a(s) + a + infinitive (habit/action) or noun (something you’re used to). It describes a habitual situation that feels normal to the person. Change gender/number as needed: está acostumbrada a…, están acostumbrados a….
target_language_example: Tom está acostumbrado a hablar en público.
native_language_example: Tom is used to speaking in public.

additional_notes: Uses the present progressive (estar + gerund) to emphasize an ongoing change happening these days/now. Common with numbers, prices, rates, and population. You can also use the more neutral present: “aumenta” = “increases.”
target_language_example: La temperatura está aumentando poco a poco.
native_language_example: The temperature is increasing little by little.

additional_notes: A very common phrase used to say something is acceptable, fine, or good enough. It can describe things ('El barrio está bien' = 'The neighborhood is fine'), show agreement or acceptance ('Está bien, esperaré' = 'Okay, I'll wait'), or reassure someone ('Está bien' = 'It's okay'). Before 'que' and a clause, it can mean 'it's good/right/okay that...'.
target_language_example: Si quieres salir más tarde, está bien.
native_language_example: If you want to leave later, that's fine.

additional_notes: Repetition is common when you want someone to calm down, stop insisting, or when you’re agreeing to end a discussion. Tone matters: it can sound soothing ("Okay, okay, don’t worry") or a bit impatient ("Okay, okay—stop!"). Often used on its own as a response.
target_language_example: Está bien, está bien, ya entendí. No te enojes.
native_language_example: Okay, okay, I got it. Don’t get angry.

additional_notes: Present progressive of "buscar" (to look for/search for): "estar" + "buscando". Often used with "a" before a specific person or pet: "está buscando a Tom"; with things, usually no "a": "está buscando sus zapatos". Pronouns can go before "está" ("Te está buscando") or attached to the gerund ("Está buscándote").
target_language_example: Mi mamá está buscando su teléfono.
native_language_example: My mom is looking for her phone.

meaning: 'is changing' / 'is in the process of changing.'
additional_notes: This is the present progressive: **estar (conjugated) + gerund**. It emphasizes an action happening now or a change currently in progress: *El mundo está cambiando.* With a reflexive pronoun (**se está cambiando**), it can mean “is changing clothes” (*Tom se está cambiando de ropa*), but that extra **se** changes the meaning.
target_language_example: Todo está cambiando muy rápido.
native_language_example: Everything is changing very fast.

additional_notes: Used to say someone (he) is married to a woman. "Está" is from estar (temporary/current state), and "casado" agrees with a male subject; for a female subject you’d say "está casada". The "una" introduces a feminine noun/profession/nationality: "una actriz", "una canadiense", "una profesora". You can also say "está casado con + name": "Está casado con Ana".
target_language_example: Mi hermano está casado con una enfermera.
native_language_example: My brother is married to a nurse.

additional_notes: Used to say someone or something is nearby. Often followed by “de” + place/person: “está cerca de aquí” (it’s near here), “está cerca de ti” (it’s close to you). With masculine singular nouns, “de + el” becomes “del”: “cerca del río” (near the river).
target_language_example: El restaurante está cerca del hotel.
native_language_example: The restaurant is near the hotel.

meaning: “it/she is closed” (feminine; also used for a place being closed).
additional_notes: Used with feminine nouns (la puerta, la botella, la cocina, la oficina, la tapa). It’s the verb estar (a temporary state/condition) + the adjective cerrada (“closed”). Often appears with details like desde el interior (“from the inside”) or con llave (“locked”). For masculine nouns, use está cerrado.
target_language_example: Lo siento, la oficina está cerrada hoy.
native_language_example: Sorry, the office is closed today.

additional_notes: Used with "estar" to describe a current/temporary state: a place/road/business is not open, or something like gas/water/a valve is shut (closed). For permanent/official closure you may also see "está/están clausurado(s)". Agreement changes: "está cerrada" (fem. singular), "están cerrados/cerradas" (plural).
target_language_example: Ahora el museo está cerrado.
native_language_example: The museum is closed right now.

additional_notes: Used to introduce something you consider evident based on facts or the situation. Very common in spoken and written Spanish. You can also hear variations like “está claro” (it’s clear) or “queda claro que” (it becomes clear that).
target_language_example: Está claro que no entiende la pregunta.
native_language_example: It’s clear that he doesn’t understand the question.

additional_notes: Present progressive: estar (conjugated) + gerund (-ando/-iendo) to talk about an action in progress at the moment. Here, "está" matches he/she/it/you (formal) in the present tense; for other subjects: estoy comiendo, estás comiendo, estamos comiendo, están comiendo.
target_language_example: Mi hermano está comiendo en la cocina.
native_language_example: My brother is eating in the kitchen.

additional_notes: Uses the verb estar (“to be,” for states/conditions) + the adverb completamente (“completely”) to strongly emphasize an adjective or past participle: está completamente solo (completely alone), está completamente equivocado (totally wrong), está completamente desconectado (completely disconnected). It’s often translated as “totally,” “completely,” or “entirely,” depending on context.
target_language_example: El teléfono está completamente apagado.
native_language_example: The phone is completely off.

additional_notes: Present progressive of crecer (to grow). Used for people/animals growing up (babies, hair), and also for things that increase or rise over time (the economy, unemployment, the tide, population). Often followed by details like “día a día” (day by day) or “a pasos gigantes” (by leaps and bounds).
target_language_example: La planta está creciendo muy rápido.
native_language_example: The plant is growing very fast.

additional_notes: It’s the present progressive of dar (to give): estar (present) + dando (gerund). Used for actions happening right now. Often appears in set phrases with dar, where the natural English translation may not be literally “give” (e.g., dar una paliza = to beat someone up).
target_language_example: Me está dando una oportunidad.
native_language_example: He/She is giving me a chance.

additional_notes: Used with **estar** to describe a temporary state/condition that’s excessive: **está demasiado + adjective** (e.g., oscuro, salado, débil). Often followed by **para + infinitive** to say “too … to …”: *está demasiado salada para comerse* = “it’s too salty to eat.”
target_language_example: El café está demasiado caliente para tomarlo ahora.
native_language_example: The coffee is too hot to drink right now.

meaning: 'is willing to' / 'is prepared to' (ready to do something).
additional_notes: Used with a person or organization + estar + dispuesto/a/os/as + a + infinitive to express willingness or readiness. Agree in gender/number: está dispuesto a (he/it), está dispuesta a (she), están dispuestos a (they, masc/mixed), están dispuestas a (they, fem).
target_language_example: Tom está dispuesto a hablar.
native_language_example: Tom is willing to talk.

additional_notes: Present progressive: estar (conjugated) + gerund (durmiendo) to talk about an action in progress at this moment. Often used with time words like ahora (“now”) or with a place: está durmiendo en el sofá (“is sleeping on the sofa”).
target_language_example: No hagas ruido; mi hermana está durmiendo.
native_language_example: Don’t make noise; my sister is sleeping.

additional_notes: Used with a verb in the infinitive to say that something has just started or is in the early stages (a change, a process, the weather, feelings, etc.). It’s the present progressive of empezar (estar + empezando), so you can change the subject: estoy empezando a (I’m starting to), estás empezando a (you’re starting to), etc.
target_language_example: Creo que está empezando a llover.
native_language_example: I think it’s starting to rain.

additional_notes: Used with the verb estar + en to say where someone/something is (location). It can also describe being in a certain state or situation: “está en sesión” = “is in session.” With places you’ll often translate it as “in” (Está en Inglaterra = He/She is in England), but with some contexts it becomes “at” or “on” in natural English (está en el coche = is in the car; está en la costa = is on the coast).
target_language_example: Mi hermana está en casa ahora.
native_language_example: My sister is at home now.

meaning: is on the way; is coming.
additional_notes: Used to say someone or something is currently traveling toward a place, or that something is expected to arrive soon (help, a person, a season, the next one in a series). Often used with "ya" for emphasis: "ya está en camino" (it’s already on the way).
target_language_example: No te preocupes: tu pedido ya está en camino.
native_language_example: Don’t worry: your order is already on the way.

additional_notes: Used to say a person or thing is located at home. With people, it can also imply they are home (available) to be seen or visited (e.g., “Ve a ver si… está en casa”). It uses the verb estar for location. You can change the subject: “Estoy/Estás/Está/Estamos/Están en casa.”
target_language_example: Ahora mismo, mi hermana está en casa.
native_language_example: Right now, my sister is at home.

additional_notes: Used to say that something important could be lost or affected by what happens next (often someone’s life, safety, reputation, money, etc.). It commonly follows the thing that’s at risk: "La vida de mi padre está en juego" (My father’s life is at stake). You can also start with "Está en juego..." to emphasize what’s at risk.
target_language_example: Si fallamos, nuestro trabajo está en juego.
native_language_example: If we fail, our job is on the line.

additional_notes: Used with estar + en + peligro to say someone or something is in danger right now or in a risky situation. You can add what is in danger: “Su vida está en peligro” = “His/Her life is in danger.” (Plural: “están en peligro.”)
target_language_example: ¡Cuidado! El niño está en peligro.
native_language_example: Careful! The child is in danger.

additional_notes: Used with the verb estar + enamorado + de to say someone is (currently) in love with a person. Change it for gender/number: está enamorada de (she is in love with), están enamorados/as de (they are in love with). After de, use a person or pronoun: de ella (with her), de él (with him), de mí (with me), de ti (with you), de vos (with you, voseo), de nosotros/as (with us).
target_language_example: Creo que él está enamorado de ti.
native_language_example: I think he’s in love with you.

additional_notes: Used with the verb "estar" (temporary condition) + "enferma" (feminine form of "enfermo"). It refers to a woman or girl who is ill. For a man, say "está enfermo"; for more than one person, "están enfermos/enfermas". Often followed by details like symptoms: "está con fiebre" (she has a fever).
target_language_example: Lo siento, Ana no viene hoy porque está enferma.
native_language_example: Sorry, Ana isn’t coming today because she’s sick.

additional_notes: Uses estar (temporary state) + enfermo (sick). You can use it for people (“Tom está enfermo”) and also metaphorically for things or situations (“El mundo está enfermo” = “The world is sick/broken”). For seriousness, you may hear “está enfermo de gravedad” (“is seriously ill”).
target_language_example: Mi papá está enfermo, así que no va a trabajar hoy.
native_language_example: My dad is sick, so he’s not going to work today.

additional_notes: Present progressive of **esperar**: **estar + esperando**. Use it for (1) waiting for someone/something: **Está esperando a María.** (2) waiting in a place: **Está esperando en la sala.** (3) expecting/hoping that something happens: **Está esperando que María haga algo.** Note: **esperar** can mean “to wait” and also “to hope/expect,” so don’t confuse it with English “to expect” in all cases.
target_language_example: Mi hermano está esperando el autobús.
native_language_example: My brother is waiting for the bus.

additional_notes: Present progressive: **estar** (conjugated) + **estudiando**. Use it for an action in progress or a temporary ongoing situation. The subject can be included (**Ella está estudiando**) or omitted (**Está estudiando**) when it’s clear. Often followed by what someone is studying (**Está estudiando derecho**) or where (**Está estudiando en Harvard**) or for what purpose (**Está estudiando para ser...**).
target_language_example: Ahora no puedo hablar; está estudiando para el examen.
native_language_example: I can’t talk right now; he/she is studying for the exam.

meaning: "is outside/out of" (not within; beyond; away from).
additional_notes: Used with a noun to show that something/someone is not within a limit, range, place, or category. Common uses: **fuera de alcance** (out of reach), **fuera de la ciudad** (out of town), **fuera de curso / fuera de rumbo** (off course), **fuera de tu jurisdicción** (outside your jurisdiction), **fuera de sospecha** (above suspicion / beyond suspicion). Often implies being beyond control or no longer contained (e.g., *El genio está fuera de la botella*).
target_language_example: Lo siento, eso está fuera de mi control.
native_language_example: Sorry, that's out of my control.

additional_notes: Present progressive: estar (3rd person singular: "está") + gerund ("hablando") to describe an action happening now. Often followed by more info, e.g. "está hablando por teléfono" = "he/she is talking on the phone." Can also be used with "dormido": "está hablando dormido" = "he/she is talking in their sleep."
target_language_example: No puedo ayudarte ahora porque está hablando con el médico.
native_language_example: I can't help you now because he/she is talking with the doctor.

additional_notes: Used to say what something is made of. It’s from the verb phrase “estar hecho/a de.” Match gender/number: está hecho de (masc. singular), está hecha de (fem. singular), están hechos de (masc. plural/mixed), están hechas de (fem. plural).
target_language_example: La botella está hecha de vidrio.
native_language_example: The bottle is made of glass.

additional_notes: Used with **estar + hecho** to express either (1) what something is made of (often followed by **de**: *está hecho de plástico*), or (2) that a task is completed: *el trabajo está hecho*. It agrees with the noun: *está hecho* (masc.), *está hecha* (fem.), *están hechos/hechas* (plural).
target_language_example: El trabajo está hecho.
native_language_example: The work is done.

additional_notes: Present progressive of intentar: estar + intentando + infinitive. Used for an action happening around now or in progress (often with adverbs like ahora/siempre). For other subjects: estoy intentando, estás intentando, estamos intentando, etc.
target_language_example: Ahora mismo está intentando llamarte, pero no contesta nadie.
native_language_example: Right now he/she is trying to call you, but nobody is answering.

additional_notes: Used with **estar + jugando** (present progressive) to describe something happening right now. **Con** introduces who/what the person or animal is playing with. You can change the subject and the thing after **con** (e.g., *Estoy/Está/Están jugando con…*).
target_language_example: Mi hermana está jugando con sus amigos en el parque.
native_language_example: My sister is playing with her friends in the park.

additional_notes: Form of the present progressive: estar + gerund (-ando/-iendo) to talk about an action in progress. It agrees with the subject: él/ella está leyendo, yo estoy leyendo, ellos están leyendo. Often used with time words like ahora (now) or siempre (always) to describe a current or habitual ongoing action.
target_language_example: Ahora está leyendo el periódico.
native_language_example: He/She is reading the newspaper now.

additional_notes: Uses estar + adjective to describe a temporary/current state (clean right now), often after cleaning. "Limpia" agrees with a feminine noun (la casa, la camisa, la cocina); for masculine use "está limpio". Can also be used figuratively ("Mi conciencia está limpia" = "My conscience is clear").
target_language_example: No te preocupes: la habitación está limpia.
native_language_example: Don’t worry: the room is clean.

additional_notes: Used with the verb estar to say something is ready/finished (food, a task, a room, etc.). It agrees with what’s ready: está listo (masc. singular), está lista (fem. singular), están listos/listas (plural). Often used with ya (“already”) or ya casi (“almost”).
target_language_example: El té está listo.
native_language_example: The tea is ready.

additional_notes:
Used with a subject (he/she/it/you formal) and then either an infinitive (action) or a noun (event/thing):
- Está listo para + infinitive: Está listo para pelear. (ready to fight)
- Está listo para + noun: Está listo para la fiesta. (ready for the party)
Adjective agreement can change with gender/number: está listo/lista/listos/listas para.
Conjugation changes with subject/tense: estoy/estás/está/estamos/están listo/a/os/as para; estaba/estuvo listo para, etc.
target_language_example: Príncipe Ashitaka, ¿está listo para contemplar su destino?
native_language_example: Prince Ashitaka, are you ready to contemplate your destiny?

additional_notes: Used with feminine singular nouns (e.g., *la habitación*, *la vida*). It describes a place/thing that contains a lot of something: *X está llena de Y*. With masculine nouns use *está lleno de*; plural: *están llenos/as de*. Common both literally (physical contents) and figuratively (ideas, experiences).
target_language_example: La ciudad está llena de historia.
native_language_example: The city is full of history.

additional_notes: Used to say a person/place/thing contains a lot of something. It’s the 3rd-person singular form of "estar" + "lleno"; change it depending on the subject: "estoy lleno/a de" (I’m full of), "están llenos/as de" (they’re full of). Agreement matters: use "lleno" (masc. sing.) or "llena" (fem. sing.) to match the noun (e.g., "El balde está lleno de..." vs. "La sala está llena de..."). Can be literal (containers/places) or figurative ("lleno de secretos", "lleno de maldad").
target_language_example: El cielo está lleno de estrellas.
native_language_example: The sky is full of stars.

additional_notes: Uses the present progressive: estar (está) + gerund (llorando) to emphasize an action happening at this moment. Often used with a reason introduced by porque (“because”).
target_language_example: No puedo hablar ahora; mi hijo está llorando.
native_language_example: I can’t talk right now; my son is crying.

additional_notes: Uses the verb llover (to rain) in the present continuous (estar + gerund) to emphasize that the rain is happening right now. Often appears with time words like ahora (now) or with intensifiers like mucho (a lot). You can also just say Llueve for "It rains/It’s raining" (more general).
target_language_example: No podemos salir; está lloviendo.
native_language_example: We can’t go out; it’s raining.

additional_notes: Used with estar (temporary state/behavior) rather than ser. Often said as an exclamation: “¡Está loco!” = “He/She’s crazy!” To say “crazy about,” you usually add por: “Está loco por ti” = “He’s crazy about you.” It changes for gender/number: está loca, están locos/locas.
target_language_example: Mi hermano está loco por el fútbol.
native_language_example: My brother is crazy about soccer.

additional_notes: Used to judge something as not okay / unacceptable (moral or social) or simply bad quality. Very common in "está mal visto" = "it’s frowned upon". With people, "estar mal" can also mean "to feel unwell / sick". In phrases like "mal herido", "mal" works like "badly" ("badly wounded").
target_language_example: Decir eso está mal; no lo repitas.
native_language_example: Saying that is wrong; don’t repeat it.

additional_notes: Present progressive of "mejorar" (to improve): estar (present) + mejorando. Used to say a situation, a business, or a person’s health/condition is improving right now or over time. You can add words like "poco a poco" (little by little) to emphasize gradual improvement.
target_language_example: Después de la operación, mi abuela está mejorando.
native_language_example: After the operation, my grandma is getting better.

additional_notes: Present progressive of "mentir" (to lie): "estar" (he/she/it is) + "mintiendo" (lying). Used to say someone is lying right now or in this situation. You can add an indirect object: "Te está mintiendo" = "He/She is lying to you."
target_language_example: No le creas: está mintiendo.
native_language_example: Don’t believe him/her: he/she is lying.

additional_notes: Present progressive of mirar: estar (conjugated) + mirando (gerund). Use it for something happening right now: está mirando = he/she/it is watching/looking. Often followed by what someone is looking at with “a” (Está mirando a Tom) or just the thing (Está mirando la pantalla / Plaza Sésamo).
target_language_example: Tom solo está mirando fijamente la pantalla del ordenador.
native_language_example: Tom is just staring at the computer screen.

meaning: “is dead” / “isn’t working anymore” (for things like a battery).
additional_notes: Used with estar (state/result) to say someone has died, or that something (often a device/battery) has stopped functioning. Feminine form (muerta) agrees with a feminine noun (la batería, ella, la reina). For masculine nouns: está muerto.
target_language_example: La batería del auto está muerta; no arranca.
native_language_example: The car battery is dead; it won’t start.

additional_notes: Used with the verb "estar" to describe a state/condition (death). It can also be used figuratively, as in "está muerto para los demás" = "he’s dead to others" (others treat him as if he didn’t exist). You can add "ya" for emphasis: "ya está muerto" = "he’s already dead."
target_language_example: Lo siento, el perro está muerto.
native_language_example: I’m sorry, the dog is dead.

additional_notes: Present progressive of morirse (“to die”), used to talk about something happening right now or currently. Often appears as “se está muriendo” (the most common way to say “he/she is dying”), and it can also be used figuratively for things like a music style or tradition (“Jazz is dying”).
target_language_example: El perro está muriendo y necesitamos un veterinario.
native_language_example: The dog is dying and we need a vet.

additional_notes: Used before an adjective or adverb to describe a state, condition, or location as very something: está muy fría, está muy lejos. Está is from estar, so it is used for how something is, feels, or is situated, often contrasting with es muy for more permanent characteristics.
target_language_example: La sopa está muy caliente.
native_language_example: The soup is very hot.

meaning: “it’s very good / it’s great” (also: “is doing very well”).
additional_notes: Used with estar to evaluate something positively (“This is very good”) or to say someone is doing well/okay (“My family is doing very well”). Often works as a short, approving reaction: “Y está muy bien” = “And that’s fine / that’s great.” Can also mean something is acceptable or appropriate depending on context.
target_language_example: Tu idea está muy bien; podemos empezar mañana.
native_language_example: Your idea is great; we can start tomorrow.

additional_notes: Uses estar (temporary location) + cerca (“close/near”). Often followed by de + place: “Está muy cerca del lago.” You can also use it without de when the place is understood: “El pueblo está muy cerca.” It can be literal distance or figurative proximity (someone standing close enough to hear).
target_language_example: Mi casa está muy cerca de la estación.
native_language_example: My house is very close to the station.

additional_notes: Used with estar to describe a temporary situation (busy right now). You can add what someone is busy doing with a gerund: “Está muy ocupado escribiendo…”, or specify the context with “en”: “en el trabajo.” For plural: “están muy ocupados/ocupadas.”
target_language_example: Lo siento, ahora no puede hablar: está muy ocupado.
native_language_example: Sorry, he can’t talk right now: he’s very busy.

additional_notes: "Estar" + "ocupado/a" describes a temporary state of being busy. Use "está ocupado" for a male subject and "están ocupados/ocupadas" for plural. Common patterns: "estar ocupado/a con" + noun (busy with…), and "estar ocupado/a" + gerund (busy doing…).
target_language_example: Ahora no puedo hablar; está ocupada con una reunión.
native_language_example: I can’t talk right now; she’s busy with a meeting.

additional_notes: Use **estar + ocupado** for temporary states. With **people**, it means “to be busy” (often with **estar ocupado + gerund**: *está ocupado escribiendo...* = “he’s busy writing...”). With **seats/places**, it means “occupied/taken”: *¿Este asiento está ocupado?* = “Is this seat taken?” Match gender/number with the noun or person: **está ocupada** (feminine), **están ocupados/ocupadas** (plural).
target_language_example: Disculpe, ¿este asiento está ocupado?
native_language_example: Excuse me, is this seat taken?

additional_notes: Present progressive: estar + gerundio (pasando). Commonly used for events/situations: “Algo está pasando aquí” = “Something is happening here.” With a direct object pronoun (lo) plus an adverb/phrase like “bien” or “en grande,” it changes meaning: “lo está pasando bien / en grande” = “(he/she) is having a good/great time.” In negative, “No está pasando nada…” = “Nothing is happening…”
target_language_example: ¿Qué está pasando afuera?
native_language_example: What’s happening outside?

additional_notes: Used to state that something is forbidden by a rule or law. Often appears on signs or in formal rules. You can also use it with an infinitive (Está prohibido bailar.) or with a noun phrase (Está prohibido fumar aquí / Fumar está prohibido aquí).
target_language_example: Aquí está prohibido estacionar.
native_language_example: Parking is not allowed here.

additional_notes: Used with the verb estar + the adjective rota (feminine singular of roto) to describe a temporary condition/state: something is broken. If the thing is masculine, use “está roto” (El teléfono está roto). Often used with objects like la ducha, la escalera, etc.
target_language_example: La silla está rota, así que no te sientes ahí.
native_language_example: The chair is broken, so don’t sit there.

additional_notes: Used with **estar** to describe a temporary state or condition. **Está roto** agrees with the noun: **está rota** (feminine), **están rotos/rotas** (plural). It can be literal (an object is damaged) or figurative (**Mi corazón está roto** = 'My heart is broken').
target_language_example: Lo siento, el teléfono está roto.
native_language_example: Sorry, the phone is broken.

meaning: "is coming out / going out"; also "is dating/going out with" (someone).
additional_notes: This is the present progressive of **salir**: **estar + saliendo** = “to be in the process of leaving/coming out.” Common uses: (1) something appearing/emerging: *El sol está saliendo* (“The sun is coming up / rising”); (2) dating: **estar saliendo con + persona** = “to be going out with / dating (someone)”; (3) something slipping out: *Se me está saliendo* (“It’s coming/slipping out on me,” e.g., a thread, a tooth, a word).
target_language_example: Últimamente está saliendo con una compañera de trabajo.
native_language_example: Lately he/she has been dating a coworker.

additional_notes: Used to express certainty about a statement that follows. It’s the verb phrase "estar seguro" + "de que". You can also use other forms: "estoy seguro de que" (I’m sure that), "¿estás seguro de que...?" (Are you sure that...?). Often followed by the present or future tense (e.g., "aprobará").
target_language_example: ¿Está seguro de que esta es la dirección correcta?
native_language_example: Are you sure this is the correct address?

meaning: “is being” (happening right now, often in a passive).
additional_notes: Used to emphasize that something is in progress at this moment. Very common in the passive voice with a past participle: “está siendo + participio” (e.g., “está siendo construido” = “is being built”), and also with adjectives to describe a changing/ongoing state (“está siendo exitoso” = “is being successful/working”). Often sounds more formal/heavy than alternatives like “se está construyendo” or “lo están construyendo,” but it’s correct.
target_language_example: La casa está siendo renovada este mes.
native_language_example: The house is being renovated this month.

additional_notes: Present continuous of the verb “suceder” (to happen). Use it for something happening right now. Very common in questions like “¿Qué está sucediendo?” (= “What’s happening?”). You’ll also often hear “¿Qué está pasando?”, which means the same and is more common in everyday speech.
target_language_example: Algo extraño está sucediendo aquí.
native_language_example: Something strange is happening here.

additional_notes: Used with estar (temporary state/condition) to describe something or someone being dirty right now. Changes for gender/number: está sucia (fem. singular), están sucios/sucias (plural). Often used with objects, clothes, places, and people.
target_language_example: Lo siento, no puedo usarlo: está sucio.
native_language_example: Sorry, I can't use it: it's dirty.

additional_notes: Used with **estar** + **tan** + adjective to describe a temporary state or condition: *Está tan silencioso* = “It’s so quiet.” Often implies an unusual degree. You can also extend it to comparisons: **tan + adj + como** (“as … as”): *Está tan ruidoso como ayer.*
target_language_example: El cuarto está tan oscuro que no puedo ver nada.
native_language_example: The room is so dark that I can’t see anything.

additional_notes: Common check-in or reassurance. Use it as a statement (Está todo bien.) to calm someone down or confirm that things are okay, or as a question (¿Está todo bien?) to ask if there’s a problem. Often said to a person you care about, like “Amor, ¿está todo bien?”
target_language_example: Tranquilo, está todo bien ahora.
native_language_example: Relax, everything is fine now.

additional_notes: This is the present progressive: **estar + gerundio** (e.g., *está tomando*) to talk about an action in progress right now. **Tomar** often means “to take,” but in everyday Spanish it also commonly means “to drink/have” (*tomar café* = “have/drink coffee”), and it appears in set phrases like **tomar el sol** (“to sunbathe”) and **tomar el pelo (a alguien)** (“to tease/mess with someone,” literally “to pull someone’s hair”).
target_language_example: Ahora está tomando una foto.
native_language_example: Right now he/she is taking a photo.

meaning: "is working on" (a project/task) or "is working in/at" (a place).
additional_notes: Present progressive: estar + gerund (trabajando) to talk about something happening now/around now. Use "en" to mean "on" with things like projects/ideas (Está trabajando en eso / en una novela) and to mean "in/at" with locations/workplaces (trabajando en Francia / en el supermercado / en la cochera). Subject can change: "Estoy trabajando en...", "Estamos trabajando en...", etc.
target_language_example: Ahora mismo, Ana está trabajando en un informe.
native_language_example: Right now, Ana is working on a report.

additional_notes: Used with an infinitive: **estar + tratando de + infinitive** to describe an attempt in progress or around now. In many cases it’s similar to **trata de + infinitive** (“tries to”), but **está tratando de** sounds more like “is in the process of trying.”
target_language_example: Ella está tratando de aprender español.
native_language_example: She is trying to learn Spanish.

additional_notes: Used with estar to soften a description of how someone/something is right now (feelings, health, condition, distance). It typically comes before an adjective or adverb: está un poco lejos/preocupado/resfriado. For plural subjects: están un poco...
target_language_example: La estación está un poco lejos, pero podemos ir caminando.
native_language_example: The station is a bit far, but we can walk.

additional_notes: Present progressive: estar (está) + gerund (usando) describes what someone is doing right now. With objects/tools/substances it usually means “is using” (Está usando Internet / drogas). With clothes it often means “is wearing” (Está usando un suéter). You can negate it with “no”: No está usando…
target_language_example: Ahora mismo está usando su teléfono para buscar la dirección.
native_language_example: Right now she’s using her phone to look up the address.

additional_notes: Used with the verb estar to describe a temporary state/condition (something currently has nothing inside). It agrees with the noun’s gender and number: está vacío (masc. singular), está vacía (fem. singular), están vacíos/vacías (plural). Common with objects/places like botella, carpeta, heladera, casa, micro (bus).
target_language_example: La caja está vacía, no hay nada adentro.
native_language_example: The box is empty; there’s nothing inside.

additional_notes: Used with **estar** to describe a temporary state: something has nothing inside it (a place, container, seat, tank, etc.). Also used more figuratively (e.g., someone feels “empty” inside). Feminine form is **está vacía** (e.g., *La nevera está vacía*). Plural: **están vacíos/vacías**.
target_language_example: El tanque está vacío.
native_language_example: The tank is empty.

additional_notes: Used to say that someone (or an animal) is still living/not dead. Refers to a current state, so it commonly appears with “todavía” (still) or “probablemente” (probably). You can also use it hypothetically: “si está vivo…” = “if he’s still alive…”.
target_language_example: ¿Tu abuelo está vivo?
native_language_example: Is your grandfather alive?

meaning: "is there" / "is right there" (it’s present or located in that place).
additional_notes: Used to point out that something/someone is in a specific place or is available/present. Often followed by extra location details ("está ahí, en..."). Can also mean emotional presence/support: "mamá está ahí" = "mom is there for you."
target_language_example: El antídoto está ahí, en la plataforma.
native_language_example: The antidote is there, on the platform.

additional_notes: Used to say someone/something is located in a specific place. "Está" is the he/she/it form of "estar" (to be, for location/temporary states). "Allí" means "there" (usually a bit more specific or farther away than "aquí" = "here"). Can also refer to being present at an event: "Está allí ahora" = "He’s there now."
target_language_example: Mi teléfono está allí, en la mesa.
native_language_example: My phone is there, on the table.

additional_notes: Used with **estar** to say someone/something is located here (physical presence). Spanish often drops the subject, so **Está aquí** can mean “He/She/It is here,” depending on context. You can also use it with time words like **todavía** (still) or **ya no** (no longer): *Todavía está aquí.* / *Ya no está aquí.*
target_language_example: ¿El médico? Sí, está aquí.
native_language_example: The doctor? Yes, he’s here.

meaning: “is with us” (with us / on our side).
additional_notes: Used to say someone is physically with your group (“Tom está con nosotros”) or that someone supports you/your cause (“Dios está con nosotros”). With people, you’ll also hear it in the plural: “Están con nosotros” = “They’re with us.”
target_language_example: ¿Tu hermana está con nosotros o va por su cuenta?
native_language_example: Is your sister with us, or is she going on her own?

additional_notes: Used with locations to say where someone/something is (temporary/state location), from the verb "estar" + "en". Common with rooms/buildings/cities: "está en la habitación", "está en casa", "está en Madrid".
target_language_example: Mi teléfono está en la mochila.
native_language_example: My phone is in the backpack.

additional_notes: Used to say someone/something appears on a list (guest list, to-do list, waitlist, etc.). It uses estar (temporary state/location): está = "is" (he/she/it/you formal), en = "on/in", la lista = "the list". You can change the subject: Estoy en la lista (I’m on the list), Están en la lista (They’re on the list).
target_language_example: Tu nombre está en la lista.
native_language_example: Your name is on the list.

meaning: “it is in/on my …” (talking about location or something being inside you/part of you).
additional_notes: Used with **estar** to say something is located **in** or **on** something that belongs to you: *Está en mi bolso* (“It’s in my bag”), *Está en mi mesa* (“It’s on my table”). It can also be figurative: *Está en mi sangre* (“It’s in my blood,” meaning it’s natural to you) or *Está en mi mente* (“It’s on my mind”). You must add a noun after **mi** (e.g., *mi bolso, mi mente*).
target_language_example: Tu regalo está en mi mochila.
native_language_example: Your gift is in my backpack.

additional_notes: Imperfect tense (estar + gerund) used to describe an ongoing conversation in the past. Commonly followed by a noun/pronoun or a topic: de mi familia (about my family), de ti (about you), de eso (about that). Often used with words like "justo" (just) or "ahora" (right now) to say something happened while you were talking.
target_language_example: Cuando llegaste, estábamos hablando de la fiesta.
native_language_example: When you arrived, we were talking about the party.

meaning: “they are looking for” / “they are searching for.”
additional_notes: Present progressive of buscar (to look for/search for) with ellos/ellas/ustedes. Often followed by a direct object (“están buscando un libro”) or by “a” before a person (“están buscando a alguien”). Can also mean “they are trying to find” in everyday contexts.
target_language_example: ¿A quién están buscando?
native_language_example: Who are they looking for?

meaning: 'they are in/on/at' (they are located in a place or situation).
additional_notes: “Están” is the present tense of “estar” for “they/you all” (ellos/ellas/ustedes). It’s commonly used with “en” to talk about location: están en la cocina (in the kitchen), están en Australia (in Australia). It can also be figurative: están en mi cabeza (in my head), and appear in set phrases like “en proceso” (in progress).
target_language_example: Los libros están en la mochila.
native_language_example: The books are in the backpack.

additional_notes: Present progressive of "esperar" (to wait for / to expect): "estar" (están) + gerund (esperando). Usually used with an object pronoun (lo/la/le/te/me/nos/los/las) to say who they’re waiting for: "Te están esperando" = "They’re waiting for you."
target_language_example: No corras: te están esperando afuera.
native_language_example: Don’t run: they’re waiting for you outside.

additional_notes: Formed with **estar (they)** + **haciendo (doing/making)** to talk about what people are doing right now or around this time. Used with a direct object a lot: *están haciendo su trabajo* (they’re doing their job). In questions, it often appears as **¿Qué están haciendo?** = “What are they doing?”
target_language_example: ¿Qué están haciendo ahora?
native_language_example: What are they doing now?

additional_notes: Form of **estar + listo** (ready). **Están** is used with **ellos/ellas/ustedes** (they/you all). Common as a question: **¿Están listos?** = “Are you (all) ready?” Often followed by **para + noun/infinitive**: **están listos para la batalla / para salir**. In speech, **listos** agrees with the group: **listos** (mixed/men), **listas** (all women).
target_language_example: Chicos, ya es hora: ¿están listos para salir?
native_language_example: Guys, it’s time: are you ready to go?

meaning: “they are crazy” / “you (plural) are crazy”; also “(they/you) are crazy about (love) …” (con + por).
additional_notes: Used with **estar** (temporary state/opinion) + **locos** (plural). It can be literal (“They’re crazy!”) or exaggerated/joking (“You guys are nuts!”). With **estar loco/a por + noun/verb**, it means to be very enthusiastic about something: **Están locos por el jazz** = “They’re crazy about jazz.” Change for gender/number: **está loco**, **está loca**, **están locas**, etc.
target_language_example: Mis amigos están locos por el fútbol.
native_language_example: My friends are crazy about soccer.

additional_notes: Present tense of estar (están) + plural adjective muerto (muertos). Used to state that multiple people/animals are deceased. Often appears with a subject like “mis padres” or “sus padres.” Note: you can also say “han muerto” (“they have died”) to focus more on the event of dying.
target_language_example: Los dos perros están muertos.
native_language_example: Both dogs are dead.

additional_notes: Used with the verb "estar" (3rd person plural: "están") plus "muy" to intensify an adjective or adverb: "están muy + adjective". "Estar" is commonly used for states/conditions (e.g., worried, interested, expensive/cheap, sweet) that are temporary or seen as a current condition. "Están" agrees with a plural subject (ellos/ellas/ustedes/las patatas/los amigos).
target_language_example: Mis padres están muy cansados hoy.
native_language_example: My parents are very tired today.

additional_notes: Used with plural subjects (ellos/ellas/ustedes or a plural noun) to say that people/animals/things are present in this place. Often answers “Where are they?” (¿Dónde están?) or emphasizes arrival: “Ya están aquí” = “They’re here already.” You can add a location after it: “están aquí arriba” (up here), “están aquí abajo” (down here).
target_language_example: Los documentos están aquí, en la mesa.
native_language_example: The documents are here, on the table.

meaning: “they are in / they’re at” (a place), or “they are on it / into it” (a situation or task).
additional_notes: Used with **estar** to talk about a temporary location or situation: **están en + place** ("They’re in/at + place"). With something abstract, **estar en eso** can mean "to be on it" (working on it) or "to be into that" depending on context.
target_language_example: Ahora están en casa, pero luego están en una reunión.
native_language_example: They’re at home now, but later they’re in a meeting.

additional_notes: Uses estar + a salvo to say someone is safe (not in danger). Often appears in negatives (No estás a salvo ahí. = You’re not safe there) and with de to mean “safe from” (No estás a salvo de… = You’re not safe from…). You can change the verb form for other people: estoy a salvo (I’m safe), está a salvo (he/she is safe), están a salvo (they are safe).
target_language_example: Tranquilo, ahora estás a salvo.
native_language_example: Relax, you’re safe now.

additional_notes: Uses the verb estar (temporary state) + bien (“well/fine”). Most often used as a check-in question: ¿Estás bien? = “Are you OK?” It can also be a statement: Estás bien. = “You’re OK / You’re fine.” For a more formal version, use: ¿Está(s) bien? (tú) vs ¿Está usted bien? (formal).
target_language_example: ¿Estás bien? Te ves un poco cansado.
native_language_example: Are you OK? You look a little tired.

additional_notes: Used to tell one person (tú) that their idea, opinion, or statement is incorrect. Often softened with phrases like “creo que…” (I think…) or “sin querer ser grosero…” (without meaning to be rude…). Feminine form: “estás equivocada” (to a woman). For formal “you” (usted): “está equivocado/equivocada”.
target_language_example: Creo que estás equivocado; la reunión es mañana, no hoy.
native_language_example: I think you’re wrong; the meeting is tomorrow, not today.

additional_notes: Present progressive of hacer: estar (tú) + haciendo. Used to ask what someone is doing or to comment on an action in progress. Often followed by a noun (“estás haciendo trampas” = you’re cheating) or used with “lo que” (“sigue con lo que estás haciendo” = keep doing what you’re doing). Can also appear reflexive in some expressions like “hacerse amigas” (“becoming friends / making friends with each other”).
target_language_example: ¿Por qué estás haciendo eso?
native_language_example: Why are you doing that?

meaning: 'You're crazy' / 'Are you crazy?' (said to one person).
additional_notes: Used to tell one person (tú) that you think their idea or behavior is crazy, shocking, or unreasonable; often said as an exclamation. Can be playful between friends or insulting depending on tone and context. In some regions you’ll also hear the voseo form: "vos estás loco". For a woman you may hear "estás loca".
target_language_example: ¿Estás loco? ¡No puedes manejar tan rápido!
native_language_example: Are you crazy? You can't drive that fast!

additional_notes: Direct accusation using estar + gerund (present progressive): estás (you are) + mintiendo (lying). You can add emphasis or specify who is being lied to: “Me estás mintiendo” = “You’re lying to me.” Often used with a tag question like “¿verdad?” (“right?” / “aren’t you?”). In Spain, informal singular “you”; for formal you’d say “está mintiendo (usted)”, and for plural “están mintiendo (ustedes/vosotros)”.
target_language_example: No me engañas: estás mintiendo.
native_language_example: You’re not fooling me: you’re lying.

additional_notes: Used with **tú** to describe someone’s state/condition with **estar + muy + adjective**: *Estás muy cansado/a* (“You’re very tired”). The adjective usually changes for gender/number (*callado/callada; unido/unida*). For a more formal “you,” use **está muy** (usted).
target_language_example: Hoy estás muy ocupada.
native_language_example: Today you’re very busy.

additional_notes: Uses estar (temporary state/location) + ahí (“there,” often meaning “right there/around there”). It can be a question to check if someone is present or listening (e.g., on the phone: “¿Estás ahí?”). It can also describe someone being there physically (“tú estás ahí”) or figuratively (“estar ahí para…” = “to be there for…/to be there just to…”).
target_language_example: ¿Estás ahí? No te escucho bien.
native_language_example: Are you there? I can’t hear you well.

additional_notes: Used to point out or confirm someone’s presence/location. It’s the tú form of estar (temporary state/location): estar + aquí. Often said when you notice someone (“Oh, you’re here.”) or to contrast with before (“But now you’re here.”).
target_language_example: ¡Por fin estás aquí!
native_language_example: You’re finally here!

meaning: 'is/are in' or 'be in/at' (subjunctive of estar + en).
additional_notes: Used after expressions that trigger the present subjunctive (e.g., doubt: "No creo que...", wishes: "Quiero que...", possibility: "Puede que..."). It refers to someone being in a place ("esté en casa" = be at home), being part of something ("esté en esta familia" = be in this family), or being in a situation/state ("esté en lo correcto" = be right/correct).
target_language_example: Dudo que Ana esté en la oficina hoy.
native_language_example: I doubt Ana is at the office today.

additional_notes: Used to emphasize that two situations, thoughts, or things are identical. Common in agreement: "Pensé exactamente lo mismo" (“I thought the exact same thing”) or "A mí me pasó exactamente lo mismo" (“The exact same thing happened to me”). Often followed by "que + (person/thing)": "Quiero exactamente lo mismo que tú".
target_language_example: Yo pensé exactamente lo mismo que tú.
native_language_example: I thought the exact same thing as you.

additional_notes: Used to emphasize that something matches perfectly: “exactly what I mean/need/heard.” It’s often followed by a verb clause (e.g., “exactamente lo que dijiste”). In commands, it can sound firm: “Vas a hacer exactamente lo que te diga” = “You’re going to do exactly what I tell you.”
target_language_example: Dime exactamente lo que necesitas.
native_language_example: Tell me exactly what you need.

additional_notes: Used with the verb extrañar (present tense, "I miss") followed by a person/pet/thing you miss: "Extraño a mi mamá", "Extraño a mi hijo". The personal "a" is common before people (and often pets). Note that "extraño" can also mean "strange" as an adjective, but in these examples it’s the verb "extrañar" (to miss).
target_language_example: Extraño a mi mejor amigo desde que se mudó.
native_language_example: I miss my best friend since he moved away.

additional_notes: Used before a noun to say that something is missing or insufficient: falta de cuidado (lack of care), falta de confianza (lack of confidence), falta de privacidad (lack of privacy). Often used to criticize behavior: falta de respeto (lack of respect), falta de responsabilidad (lack of responsibility). Common pattern: (una/mi/tu/su) falta de + noun.
target_language_example: Lo despidieron por falta de puntualidad.
native_language_example: They fired him for lack of punctuality.

additional_notes: Used mainly in formal written notices, emails, instructions, or customer service (especially in Mexico). It’s usually followed by an infinitive: “Favor de + confirmar/enviar/entregar…”. It can sound more direct/official than “por favor”.
target_language_example: Favor de apagar el celular durante la reunión.
native_language_example: Please turn off your cellphone during the meeting.

meaning: 'faith/confidence in' (to trust/believe in someone or something).
additional_notes: Used with nouns, pronouns, or clauses to express trust or belief: tener fe en + persona/cosa (Tengo fe en ti / en el plan) or perder la fe en (Perdió la fe en su capacidad). Often stronger than just creer en and can refer to confidence as well as religious faith, depending on context.
target_language_example: A veces pierdo la fe en mí, pero sigo intentándolo.
native_language_example: Sometimes I lose faith in myself, but I keep trying.

additional_notes: Used on forms and official documents to ask for someone’s DOB. Often appears with verbs like “escribir” (to write) or “poner” (to put): “Escriba/Escribe/Ponga su/tu fecha de nacimiento…”.
target_language_example: Necesito tu fecha de nacimiento para completar el formulario.
native_language_example: I need your date of birth to complete the form.

additional_notes: Used for the last day/time something must be done or submitted. Common with verbs like "entregar" (to turn in), "presentar" (to submit), "pagar" (to pay), or "cumplir" (to meet). You may also hear "plazo" for a deadline/time limit. Plural: "fechas límite".
target_language_example: La fecha límite para entregar el formulario es el viernes.
native_language_example: The deadline to turn in the form is Friday.

additional_notes: Commonly used to talk about two people in a relationship and how they feel when they are together. It agrees in number and gender with the people: "feliz" (one person) vs. "felices" (two or more people). "Juntos" means "together" and usually implies being together as partners.
target_language_example: Me alegra verlos tan felices juntos.
native_language_example: I’m glad to see them so happy together.

additional_notes: A common Christmas greeting. You can say it by itself (Feliz Navidad, amigo.) or add “a…” to specify who you’re greeting (Feliz Navidad a todos.). With “Que tengan…” it becomes a wish: “Que tengan muy feliz Navidad” = “Have a very merry Christmas.”
target_language_example: ¡Feliz Navidad a tu familia!
native_language_example: Merry Christmas to your family!

meaning: “happy year” (used in greetings, especially “Happy New Year”).
additional_notes: Most commonly appears as part of the New Year greeting “¡Feliz Año Nuevo!” or shortened “¡Feliz año!”. You can also use it in longer wishes like “Te deseo un feliz año”.
target_language_example: ¡Feliz año! Que tengas un gran año.
native_language_example: Happy New Year! Have a great year.

additional_notes: A common New Year greeting said or written around New Year’s Eve/New Year’s Day. Often paired with other holiday wishes (e.g., "Feliz Navidad y feliz año nuevo"). You can also use it after "te deseo" / "les deseo" (“I wish you...”). Capitalization varies; both "Feliz Año Nuevo" and "feliz año nuevo" are common.
target_language_example: ¡Feliz año nuevo! Que tengas un gran año.
native_language_example: Happy New Year! Have a great year.

additional_notes: Used as a birthday greeting, often followed by the person’s name or a family title (e.g., hijo, tía). You can also say it with no extra words as a complete greeting.
target_language_example: ¡Feliz cumpleaños, Marta!
native_language_example: Happy birthday, Marta!

additional_notes: Used as a farewell to someone who is about to travel. You can say it directly ("Feliz viaje") or in a fuller wish like "Que tengas un feliz viaje" or "Te deseo un feliz viaje". The phrase itself is neutral/polite; any rude words around it (e.g., "de mierda") make the whole sentence insulting, not the expression by itself.
target_language_example: ¡Feliz viaje! Avísame cuando llegues.
native_language_example: Have a good trip! Let me know when you arrive.

additional_notes: A common phrase for a party to celebrate someone’s birthday. Often used with possessives (mi/tu/su/nuestra) and with verbs like invitar (to invite), ir (to go), and hacer/organizar (to throw/organize). You can also say "una fiesta de cumpleaños" (a birthday party) or "la fiesta de cumpleaños" (the birthday party).
target_language_example: Vamos a hacer una fiesta de cumpleaños para mi hermana el sábado.
native_language_example: We’re going to throw a birthday party for my sister on Saturday.

additional_notes: Means the weekend (Saturday and Sunday). Often used with articles like "el"/"un": "el fin de semana" (the weekend), "un fin de semana" (a weekend). You can say "este fin de semana" (this weekend) or "el fin de semana pasado" (last weekend).
target_language_example: ¿Qué vas a hacer este fin de semana?
native_language_example: What are you going to do this weekend?

meaning: “the end of the world”; also “the middle of nowhere” (very far away).
additional_notes: Literal meaning is “end of the world.” Often used in expressions like “hasta el fin del mundo” (“to the ends of the earth”) to mean you’d go anywhere for someone. It can also describe a remote place that feels extremely far away (“en el fin del mundo”). You can intensify it with “mismísimo” (“hasta el mismísimo fin del mundo”).
target_language_example: Ese pueblo está en el fin del mundo, pero es muy bonito.
native_language_example: That town is in the middle of nowhere, but it’s very pretty.

additional_notes: Used to say a story, movie, relationship, or situation ends well (often after problems). Common with verbs like "tener" (to have) or "tener/tener un" in the past: "tuvo un final feliz" = "it had a happy ending." You can also say it alone as a short comment: "Final feliz."
target_language_example: Ojalá la película tenga un final feliz.
native_language_example: I hope the movie has a happy ending.

meaning: way of speaking; (also) just an expression/figure of speech.
additional_notes: Often used to describe someone’s speaking style (accent, tone, word choice): "Me gusta su forma de hablar." It can also mean something wasn’t meant literally, similar to “it’s just a way of saying it / a figure of speech”: "Es sólo una forma de hablar."
target_language_example: No te lo tomes literal; era una forma de hablar.
native_language_example: Don’t take it literally; it was just a way of saying it.

additional_notes: Used to talk about how someone lives or the customs/values that define a group (“our way of life”). It can also mean “life form” in a biological sense (e.g., “no form of life is possible without water”). Often appears with possessives: mi/tu/su/nuestra forma de vida.
target_language_example: Para ellos, la música es una forma de vida.
native_language_example: For them, music is a way of life.

additional_notes: Used to say that someone or something is included within a group, organization, category, or larger whole. It’s the 3rd-person singular of the phrase "formar parte de" (to be part of). Negative: "no forma parte de" = "is not part of".
target_language_example: Este programa forma parte del plan de estudios.
native_language_example: This program is part of the curriculum.

meaning: to be part of; to belong to.
additional_notes: Used with "de" + a group/organization/whole: "formar parte de" (to be part of). Often expresses membership or inclusion (a team, club, group, project). It can also be used more generally for something being included as a component of something else.
target_language_example: ¿Te gustaría formar parte de nuestro equipo?
native_language_example: Would you like to be part of our team?

additional_notes: Used to say what the photos are about: fotos de + noun/pronoun (e.g., fotos de mi familia). With verbs like tomar/hacer/sacar fotos (to take photos). Often contrasts with other photo prepositions like "fotos en" (photos taken in a place).
target_language_example: Tengo fotos de mis amigos en mi teléfono.
native_language_example: I have photos of my friends on my phone.

meaning: 'in front of' / 'facing'; also 'when faced with' (in response to).
additional_notes: Used for physical location (something is directly opposite or before something/someone): “Hay un banco frente a la estación.” It can also be used more abstractly to mean “in the face of” or “when confronted with” a situation (often in formal contexts): “procedimiento frente a amenazas…”
target_language_example: Nos quedamos frente a la puerta esperando.
native_language_example: We stayed in front of the door waiting.

meaning: in front of my house; across from my house.
additional_notes: Used to say something is directly in front of your house or on the other side of the street facing it. You can swap the possessive: “frente a tu casa” (your house), “frente a su casa” (his/her/your(formal) house).
target_language_example: Hay una cafetería frente a mi casa.
native_language_example: There’s a café in front of my house / across from my house.

additional_notes: Used to talk about position relative to something/someone. It’s short for **frente a + el** (so before a feminine noun you use **frente a la**: *frente a la estación*). With people, **uno frente al otro** means “facing each other.” It can also describe movement while staying ahead of something: *caminaba frente al auto* (“walking in front of the car”).
target_language_example: La farmacia está frente al supermercado.
native_language_example: The pharmacy is in front of the supermarket.

meaning: to frown; to furrow one’s brow.
additional_notes: Used to describe a facial expression showing displeasure, confusion, concern, or concentration. Commonly conjugated in context (e.g., "frunció el ceño"), but the dictionary form is "fruncir el ceño." It can also appear with an indirect object to indicate who the frown is directed at (e.g., "Le frunció el ceño").
target_language_example: No pude evitar fruncir el ceño cuando escuché la noticia.
native_language_example: I couldn’t help frowning when I heard the news.

additional_notes: In everyday Spanish, **fruto seco** (often used in plural: **frutos secos**) commonly refers to nuts like *nuez* (walnut) and *almendra* (almond), especially as a snack or ingredient. In some contexts it can also include dried fruits like *pasa* (raisin), so you may see it contrasted with or grouped under *fruta deshidratada* (“dried fruit”).
target_language_example: No puedo comer fruto seco por mi alergia.
native_language_example: I can’t eat nuts because of my allergy.

additional_notes: “Fue” is the simple past (preterite) of “ir” (to go) for él/ella/usted. It’s followed by “a” + a place (fue a Japón, fue a la cocina) or by “a” + an infinitive to say someone went somewhere in order to do something (fue a comprar leche, fue a estudiar).
target_language_example: Ella fue a la tienda a comprar pan.
native_language_example: She went to the store to buy bread.

additional_notes: Past passive of **acusar** (“to accuse”). Used with **de + noun/infinitive** to say what someone was accused of: **fue acusado de robo** (“was accused of robbery”) / **fue acusado de robar** (“was accused of stealing”). Can refer to a legal charge or a general accusation.
target_language_example: Fue acusado de mentirle al juez.
native_language_example: He was accused of lying to the judge.

additional_notes: Past, passive form (preterite): ser (fue) + past participle (asesinado). Used to say someone was killed, often implying murder/intentional killing. Change for gender/number: fue asesinada (she was murdered), fueron asesinados/asesinadas (they were murdered).
target_language_example: El periodista fue asesinado en su casa.
native_language_example: The journalist was murdered at his house.

meaning: “was run over by a …” / “was hit by a … (vehicle)”.
additional_notes: Used in the passive voice: **ser + atropellado + por** to say someone or an animal was struck by a vehicle (often implying being run over). The next word is usually a vehicle (auto/carro/camión). You can change **fue** to match tense/person: **es atropellado** (is run over), **fue atropellado** (was), **había sido atropellado** (had been).
target_language_example: El ciclista fue atropellado por un autobús en la esquina.
native_language_example: The cyclist was hit by a bus on the corner.

additional_notes: Past tense (preterite) of "ser capaz de" + infinitive. It expresses that someone succeeded in doing something at a specific moment or situation in the past (often after difficulty). You can change it for other subjects: "fui capaz de" (I was able to), "fue capaz de" (he/she/you formal was able to), "fueron capaces de" (they were able to).
target_language_example: A pesar del cansancio, fue capaz de terminar el trabajo a tiempo.
native_language_example: Despite being tired, he/she was able to finish the work on time.

additional_notes: Used to say someone/something was the first (masculine singular) to do something or to hold a title in the past. It uses the preterite of "ser" ("fue" = "was"). "primer" is the shortened form of "primero" used before a masculine singular noun (e.g., "el primer presidente"). For feminine, use "fue la primera"; for plural, "fueron los primeros / las primeras".
target_language_example: Neil Armstrong fue el primer astronauta en caminar sobre la luna.
native_language_example: Neil Armstrong was the first astronaut to walk on the moon.

meaning: “was expelled from / was kicked out of (the)” (masculine singular).
additional_notes: Past passive form of **expulsar**. Used when someone/something is forced to leave a group, place, or vehicle. **Del** = **de + el** (“from the”). For a woman you’d say **fue expulsada del**; for plural **fueron expulsados/as del**.
target_language_example: Juan fue expulsado del partido por gritarle al árbitro.
native_language_example: Juan was kicked out of the game for yelling at the referee.

additional_notes: "Fue" is the preterite (completed past) of "ser" (“to be”). Use "fue muy" + adjective to describe how something/someone was on a specific occasion or completed event: "El viaje fue muy largo". Often refers to a situation/event (“It was very…”), but can also describe a person’s behavior in that moment: "Tom fue muy grosero". For plural subjects, use "fueron muy".
target_language_example: La película fue muy interesante.
native_language_example: The movie was very interesting.

additional_notes: Very polite, formal-sounding way to thank someone or refer to a courteous action, often followed by "de" + infinitive: "fue tan amable de ayudarme" = "(you) were so kind as to help me." You’ll also see the present tense in requests: "¿Sería tan amable de…?" = "Would you be so kind as to…?"
target_language_example: Fue tan amable de explicármelo otra vez.
native_language_example: You were so kind as to explain it to me again.

additional_notes: Past tense (preterite) of "ser" used with a masculine singular noun: "fue un + noun" = "it/he/she was a + noun". For feminine nouns, use "fue una". Often used to identify or describe what something/someone was in the past, including after "lo que..." ("what...").
target_language_example: Ayer fue un día muy largo.
native_language_example: Yesterday was a very long day.

additional_notes: Common for explaining or insisting that something happened by mistake (often to deny responsibility or intent). Past tense (pretérito) of ser: "fue" = "it was." You’ll often hear it with emphasis: "Te dije/Ya te dije que fue un accidente" ("I told you / I already told you it was an accident").
target_language_example: Perdón, fue un accidente; no quería romperlo.
native_language_example: Sorry, it was an accident; I didn’t mean to break it.

meaning: “it was a day” (used to describe how a day was).
additional_notes: Past tense of "ser" (fue = "was") + "un día" ("a day"). It’s commonly followed by an adjective or description: "Fue un día horrible/ideal/divertido". You can also specify the day with "El lunes fue un día…" or "Hoy fue un día…".
target_language_example: Ayer fue un día muy largo, pero productivo.
native_language_example: Yesterday was a very long day, but productive.

meaning: “it was a mistake / it was an error.”
additional_notes: Past-tense phrase (pretérito of ser: fue) used to say something was wrong or a bad decision. Common patterns: “Fue un error + infinitive” (Fue un error visitar a Tom. = It was a mistake to visit Tom) and “Fue un error de…” (de dedo = a typo / slip of the finger; de su parte = on his/her part). You can also add an adjective: “Fue un error imperdonable” (an unforgivable mistake).
target_language_example: Lo siento: fue un error.
native_language_example: I’m sorry: it was a mistake.

additional_notes: A polite, formal-sounding phrase used to close a conversation after meeting or interacting with someone. Common patterns: “Fue un placer + infinitive” (Fue un placer conocerla = It was a pleasure to meet you) and “Fue un placer + [object pronoun]” (Fue un placer verla = It was a pleasure to see you). You can adjust formality with pronouns: conocerla/verla (formal you, fem.), conocerlo/verlo (formal you, masc.), conocerlos/verlos (you all / them), verte (informal you).
target_language_example: Fue un placer hablar con usted.
native_language_example: It was a pleasure talking with you.

meaning: “It was a pleasure to meet you.”
additional_notes: A polite phrase used when saying goodbye after meeting someone. "Fue" is past tense of "ser" (it was), "un placer" = a pleasure, and "conocerte" = to meet you (informal/singular "tú"). For a more formal version, say "Fue un placer conocerle" (to meet you, formal). You can also use present tense "Es un placer conocerte" when meeting someone.
target_language_example: Gracias por venir; fue un placer conocerte.
native_language_example: Thanks for coming; it was a pleasure to meet you.

additional_notes: Used with **ser** in the **preterite** to describe what something **was** (a completed event or experience). **Una** agrees with a **feminine singular** noun: *Fue una mañana perfecta.* For masculine nouns, use **fue un**: *Fue un día perfecto.* Often followed by a noun phrase or an adjective + noun.
target_language_example: Fue una decisión difícil.
native_language_example: It was a difficult decision.

additional_notes: Used to describe a past situation/event with a feminine singular noun: Fue una gran + noun (fiesta, decepción, pérdida, idea). With masculine nouns: Fue un gran + noun (día, éxito). With plural: Fueron una(s) gran(des) + noun(s). Note: "gran" is the short form of "grande" used before a noun.
target_language_example: Fue una gran sorpresa verte aquí.
native_language_example: It was a big surprise to see you here.

additional_notes: Most commonly used in the plural: “fuegos artificiales” = “fireworks.” In the singular, “fuego artificial” can refer to a single firework or the concept in general. Often appears with verbs like “ver” (to watch) or “lanzar”/“tirar” (to set off).
target_language_example: Ese fuego artificial explotó muy cerca.
native_language_example: That firework exploded very close by.

meaning: crossfire; being caught in the middle of conflicting sides.
additional_notes: Literal meaning is “crossed fire.” Used for gunfire coming from two or more directions, and also figuratively for being trapped between opposing people/groups (e.g., an argument, conflict, or political dispute). Often appears as “quedar/estar en medio del fuego cruzado” (to end up/be in the crossfire).
target_language_example: No quiero que los niños queden en medio del fuego cruzado.
native_language_example: I don’t want the kids to get caught in the crossfire.

additional_notes: Used to talk about being not inside a place (physical or figurative). Often appears in commands like "¡Fuera de aquí!" (Get out of here!) or with verbs like mantener/dejar/sacar + someone + fuera de + place (keep/leave/take someone out of...). Also used more generally for being outside the home/country: "fuera de casa" (outside the home), "fuera de este país" (out of this country). In phrases like "nada fuera de lo ordinario," it means "nothing out of the ordinary."
target_language_example: Deja tus zapatos fuera de la casa, por favor.
native_language_example: Leave your shoes outside the house, please.

additional_notes: Used with estar/parecer to say a person, situation, or thing is no longer being controlled or managed. Often implies things are getting worse or chaotic: «Esto está fuera de control» (This is getting out of hand).
target_language_example: El tráfico hoy está fuera de control.
native_language_example: Traffic today is out of control.

meaning: outside the city; out of town.
additional_notes: Used to say someone/something is not in the city (often traveling) or is located beyond the city limits. Common with estar (temporary: traveling) and vivir (permanent location).
target_language_example: Este fin de semana voy a estar fuera de la ciudad.
native_language_example: This weekend I'm going to be out of town.

additional_notes: Used both literally (things not in their usual position: "everything was out of place") and figuratively (a person looks/feels like they don’t fit in, or a remark is inappropriate: "that comment was out of place"). Often used with "estar", "sentirse", or "verse/lucir".
target_language_example: Creo que mi ropa está fuera de lugar para esta fiesta.
native_language_example: I think my clothes are out of place for this party.

additional_notes: Used with a noun to say something is not in your space, view, or ability to affect it: fuera de mi camino (out of my way), fuera de mi vista (out of my sight), fuera de mi propiedad (off my property), fuera de mi control (out of my control). Note: in writing, "mí" takes an accent when it means "me" (fuera de mí).
target_language_example: Por favor, mantente fuera de mi habitación.
native_language_example: Please stay out of my room.

meaning: out of order; not working; out of service.
additional_notes: Used for things like phones, elevators, machines, or systems that aren’t functioning (often seen on signs: “Fuera de servicio.”). It can also describe people who are “off duty” (e.g., personal fuera de servicio = staff who are not currently working).
target_language_example: El cajero automático está fuera de servicio; vamos a otro.
native_language_example: The ATM is out of order; let’s go to another one.

meaning: 'beside oneself' (out of control from strong emotion).
additional_notes: Used with estar to describe someone overwhelmed by emotion (often anger, but also shock, fear, etc.): «Está fuera de sí». It can also be used in the causative pattern «poner a alguien fuera de sí» = 'to drive someone crazy / to make someone lose control': «Esto puso al alcaide fuera de sí».
