target_language_example: Cuando oyó la noticia, se quedó fuera de sí.
native_language_example: When she heard the news, she was beside herself.

additional_notes: Used to say someone/something is not inside a place/object or is removed from it. It’s also used in the idiom “como un pez fuera del agua” = “like a fish out of water” (feeling uncomfortable or out of place). Grammar note: it’s the contraction of “fuera de + el” (with masculine singular nouns). With feminine singular: “fuera de la”; plural: “fuera de los/las”.
target_language_example: Saca el teléfono fuera del bolsillo, por favor.
native_language_example: Take the phone out of your pocket, please.

additional_notes: Literally “out of the path/road.” Used to describe someone/something being removed so it doesn’t block or interfere (e.g., “Con Linda fuera del camino…” = “With Linda out of the way…”). Very common as an urgent command: “¡Fuera del camino!” = “Out of the way!”
target_language_example: ¡Ponte fuera del camino! Viene un coche.
native_language_example: Get out of the way! A car is coming.

meaning: "were going to" / "was going to" (subjunctive form, often about a possible or imagined future action).
additional_notes: This is the imperfect subjunctive of **ir** used in the structure **fuera a + infinitive** (e.g., *fuera a llover*). It often appears after phrases like **no creí/no pensé que...**, **parece como si...**, or in hypothetical **si**-clauses (**Si él fuera a llegar tarde...**). It talks about something that was expected/feared/imagined to happen (often with doubt or unreality), not a simple past plan.
target_language_example: No esperaba que el examen fuera a ser tan difícil.
native_language_example: I didn’t expect the exam to be so difficult.

additional_notes: Past tense (pretérito) of ir: ellos/ellas/ustedes fueron + a + place/destination. Used for completed trips or movements to a destination (a la playa, a la escuela, a Chicago). You can add how they traveled: “Fueron a Chicago en coche.”
target_language_example: Mis amigos fueron al museo ayer.
native_language_example: My friends went to the museum yesterday.

additional_notes: Used to talk about mental strength to resist temptation, keep habits, or continue despite difficulties. Often appears with verbs like “tener” (to have) and “necesitar” (to need), or with possessives like “su fuerza de voluntad” (his/her willpower).
target_language_example: Necesito mucha fuerza de voluntad para dejar de fumar.
native_language_example: I need a lot of willpower to quit smoking.

additional_notes: "fui" is the simple past (preterite) of "ir" (to go) for "yo" (I). Use "fui a" before a place ("fui a Madrid") or before an infinitive to say you went somewhere in order to do something ("fui a comprar pan" = "I went to buy bread").
target_language_example: Ayer fui a la tienda a comprar leche.
native_language_example: Yesterday I went to the store to buy milk.

additional_notes: "Fui" is the simple past (preterite) of "ir" (to go) for "yo". Use it for a completed action in the past. "A la" = "to the" (a + la). "Tienda" means a store/shop, and you can specify the type: "la tienda de libros" (the bookstore). You can also add a purpose with "a" + infinitive: "Fui a la tienda a comprar..." (I went to the store to buy...).
target_language_example: Ayer fui a la tienda a comprar leche.
native_language_example: Yesterday I went to the store to buy milk.

meaning: It was me / I was the one (who did it).
additional_notes: Used to identify yourself as the person responsible for something (often in answers or clarifications). It uses the preterite of "ser" (fui = I was) plus "yo" for emphasis, similar to saying “It was ME.” Often appears in negatives: "No fui yo" = “It wasn’t me.”
target_language_example: Perdón, fui yo quien rompió el vaso.
native_language_example: Sorry, it was me who broke the glass.

meaning: “we went to” / “we went to (do something)” (past tense).
additional_notes: Past tense (pretérito) of **ir** for **nosotros**: *ir → fuimos*. Use **fuimos a + place** (destination): *Fuimos a Barcelona.* Use **fuimos a + infinitive** (purpose/activity): *Fuimos a nadar.* With specific places you often add **a + el = al**: *Fuimos al lago.*
target_language_example: Anoche fuimos a cenar a un restaurante nuevo.
native_language_example: Last night we went to eat dinner at a new restaurant.

meaning: “we went to the movies / we went to the cinema.”
additional_notes: Past tense (pretérito) of ir: fuimos = “we went.” Used to say that you and others went to a movie theater, often with a time word like ayer, el sábado, luego, etc. Very common in storytelling about completed actions.
target_language_example: Después de cenar, fuimos al cine con unos amigos.
native_language_example: After dinner, we went to the movies with some friends.

fumar es malo para la salud

target_language_multi_word_term: fumar es malo para la salud
meaning: Smoking is bad for your health.
additional_notes: A general statement about the harmful effects of smoking. Very common in health warnings and formal/informative contexts (news, doctors, campaigns). Structure: infinitive as the subject (fumar = “to smoke/smoking”) + es + malo para + noun (“is bad for …”). You can swap in other activities or nouns: “Beber mucho es malo para la salud” (Drinking a lot is bad for your health).
target_language_example: Todo el mundo sabe que fumar es malo para la salud.
native_language_example: Everyone knows that smoking is bad for your health.

additional_notes: Tú imperative of the reflexive verb "fijarse en". It’s used to direct someone’s attention to something (a person, object, detail, etc.). Common in spoken instructions: "Fíjate en este mapa" (pay attention to this map), "Fíjate en mí" (watch me). It can also imply “notice” a detail: "Fíjate en ese charco de sangre" (look/notice that pool of blood).
target_language_example: Fíjate en la señal: dice que está prohibido estacionar.
native_language_example: Look at the sign: it says parking is forbidden.

additional_notes: Used to specify the sport (as opposed to fútbol, which usually means soccer in Spanish). Often appears with verbs like jugar (to play) and ver (to watch), and with nouns like partido/juego (game/match).
target_language_example: ¿Te gusta el fútbol americano?
native_language_example: Do you like American football?

additional_notes: Common everyday term for sunglasses. Typically used in the plural (las gafas de sol). Often appears with verbs like llevar (to wear) or ponerse (to put on): Llevo gafas de sol / Me pongo las gafas de sol.
target_language_example: No olvides tus gafas de sol; hace mucho sol.
native_language_example: Don’t forget your sunglasses; it’s very sunny.

additional_notes: Used to talk about earning income through work or an activity. Often followed by details like how/where ("ganar dinero trabajando") or contrasted with other goals ("no se trata de ganar dinero").
target_language_example: Quiero ganar dinero este verano para pagar mis estudios.
native_language_example: I want to earn money this summer to pay for my studies.

meaning: to buy time; to save time.
additional_notes: Commonly means “to buy time” (delay something to have more time to act or decide): Solo queda ganar tiempo. In more practical contexts it can also mean “to save time” by choosing a faster option: Para ganar tiempo viajamos en avión.
target_language_example: Llamé al técnico para ganar tiempo mientras buscaba la factura.
native_language_example: I called the technician to buy time while I looked for the receipt.

meaning: to earn a living; to make a living.
additional_notes: Used to talk about how someone supports themselves financially, often implying work or a job. Common patterns: “ganarse la vida como + profesión” (to make a living as a + profession) and “ganarse la vida + gerundio” (to make a living doing something). Conjugates as a reflexive verb: me/te/se/nos/os/se gano, ganas, gana, etc., + “la vida”.
target_language_example: La mayoría de las personas tiene que trabajar para ganarse la vida.
native_language_example: Most people have to work to earn a living.

additional_notes: Usually used with the verb "tener": "tener ganas de" + infinitive = to feel like doing something / to want to do something. Common negative: "no tengo ganas de..." = I don’t feel like... It can also be used with a noun: "tener ganas de pizza" (craving pizza). You may also see "quitar las ganas de" = to take away someone’s desire (e.g., "me quitó las ganas de vivir").
target_language_example: Hoy tengo ganas de quedarme en casa y descansar.
native_language_example: Today I feel like staying home and resting.

additional_notes: A common noun phrase: gato = cat, persa = Persian. It usually refers to the long-haired cat breed. Use with articles like el/un and it agrees in number: gato persa / gatos persas.
target_language_example: Mi hermana tiene un gato persa muy tranquilo.
native_language_example: My sister has a very calm Persian cat.

additional_notes: Used to introduce a relative clause that describes a group of people. Very common in speech and writing: "gente que + verb" (e.g., gente que habla, gente que puede ayudar). It’s singular in form (gente) but usually refers to multiple people.
target_language_example: Busco gente que me ayude con la mudanza.
native_language_example: I'm looking for people who can help me with the move.

additional_notes: Used to introduce the person/thing that caused something to happen. Often positive (“thanks to you…”) but it can also be ironic/blaming depending on tone (“Yeah, thanks to you…”). Usually followed by a noun or pronoun: “gracias a Max”, “gracias a la cría”. With a verb clause, Spanish often uses “gracias a que …” (thanks to the fact that …).
target_language_example: Gracias a tu ayuda, terminamos a tiempo.
native_language_example: Thanks to your help, we finished on time.

additional_notes: Used to express gratitude or relief (often like an exclamation: “Thank God!”). It can also literally mean giving thanks to God ("We gave thanks to God"). You’ll often see it at the start of a sentence followed by a comma: "Gracias a Dios, ..."
target_language_example: Gracias a Dios, llegamos a tiempo.
native_language_example: Thank God, we arrived on time.

meaning: 'thanks to you' (because of you; due to you).
additional_notes: Used to give credit to someone for a positive result (“Thanks to you, I can…”). Depending on context and tone, it can also be sarcastic/blaming (“…and it’s all thanks to you” meaning “because of you” in a negative way). Similar to “por tu culpa” when clearly blaming, but “gracias a ti” can be either sincere or sarcastic.
target_language_example: Lo logré, gracias a ti.
native_language_example: I did it, thanks to you.

additional_notes: Used to thank someone for something. It is commonly followed by a noun ("Gracias por tu ayuda") or an infinitive verb ("Gracias por venir"). "Gracias por todo" means "thanks for everything."
target_language_example: Gracias por venir tan temprano.
native_language_example: Thanks for coming so early.

additional_notes: Used to thank someone for a specific thing introduced by the masculine singular definite article el (e.g., el apoyo, el consejo). If the noun is feminine, use “gracias por la …”; if it’s plural, “gracias por los/las …”. You can also say “gracias por + [noun]” without an article in some cases.
target_language_example: Gracias por el regalo.
native_language_example: Thanks for the gift.

additional_notes: Use this to thank someone for a specific thing or action, followed by a feminine noun: Gracias por la información / ayuda / explicación. For masculine nouns, use “gracias por el …” (Gracias por el café). You can also use it to thank someone for an abstract thing like a conversation or correction.
target_language_example: Gracias por la ayuda, de verdad.
native_language_example: Thanks for the help, really.

additional_notes: Used to thank someone politely in formal situations. "Su" is the formal singular "your" (usted). It’s typically followed by a noun: gracias por su tiempo (your time), su atención (your attention), su confianza (your trust). For informal "your," use "gracias por tu …".
target_language_example: Gracias por su ayuda, doctora.
native_language_example: Thank you for your help, doctor.

additional_notes: Used to thank someone politely for assisting you. "Su" is the formal "your" (usted), common in customer service, speaking to strangers, or professional settings. With friends/family you’ll usually hear "gracias por tu ayuda".
target_language_example: Gracias por su ayuda; fue muy amable.
native_language_example: Thank you for your help; that was very kind.

meaning: “Thanks for your …” (to thank someone for something they did/are doing).
additional_notes: Use it before a masculine singular noun to say what you’re thankful for: Gracias por tu + [noun] (e.g., tu ayuda, tu tiempo). If the noun is feminine, use “Gracias por tu” + noun too (tu works for both genders), but the noun changes (e.g., gracias por tu ayuda). In very formal situations, you may see “Gracias por su …” (your = su).
target_language_example: Gracias por tu ayuda.
native_language_example: Thanks for your help.

additional_notes: Used to thank someone for showing up or attending. You can add details with "a + place/event" (Gracias por venir a nuestro cine) or "hasta aquí" to emphasize they came a long way (Gracias por venir hasta aquí). Often said when greeting someone or at the end of a meeting.
target_language_example: Gracias por venir a mi fiesta.
native_language_example: Thanks for coming to my party.

meaning: department store; large store (often selling many types of products).
additional_notes: Common in Spain to refer to big multi-department retail stores (often with clothing, cosmetics, home goods, etc.). It literally means “big warehouse/store,” but it’s usually used like “department store.”
target_language_example: Voy a ir al gran almacén para comprar ropa y un regalo.
native_language_example: I’m going to the department store to buy clothes and a gift.

meaning: “a big deal”; something important or impressive (often sarcastic).
additional_notes: Often used with ser: “Es una gran cosa” = “It’s a big deal / It’s a great thing.” In the negative it downplays something: “No es gran cosa” = “It’s not a big deal / It’s nothing special.” With article “la gran cosa” (or without in some regions) it can be ironic, meaning someone thinks they’re very important: “Se cree la gran cosa” = “She thinks she’s a big deal.”
target_language_example: No es gran cosa, pero me alegra que hayas venido.
native_language_example: It’s not a big deal, but I’m happy you came.

meaning: a small contribution (to help a cause/effort).
additional_notes: Used especially in the phrase "poner/aportar tu grano de arena" to mean doing your small part to help. Literally "grain of sand," and it often refers to contributing time, money, or effort, even if it seems minor.
target_language_example: Cada uno puede poner su grano de arena para cuidar el medio ambiente.
native_language_example: Everyone can do their small part to take care of the environment.

additional_notes: Used to refer to the contemporary Greek language, often to contrast it with "griego antiguo" (Ancient Greek). It can appear in language-learning contexts (classes, books, translations): "estudio griego moderno" / "un diccionario de griego moderno".
target_language_example: Estoy aprendiendo griego moderno para mi viaje a Grecia.
native_language_example: I’m learning modern Greek for my trip to Greece.

additional_notes: A job title for someone who protects a place (a store, warehouse, building, event). Often used with ser/estar (Soy/Es guardia de seguridad) or trabajar como (Trabaja como guardia de seguridad). The article is optional when talking about someone’s profession (Soy guardia de seguridad).
target_language_example: Mi hermano trabaja como guardia de seguridad en un centro comercial.
native_language_example: My brother works as a security guard at a mall.

meaning: civil war (a war within a country).
additional_notes: Used to describe an armed conflict between groups in the same country (not a war between different countries). Often appears with articles like "la guerra civil" or "una guerra civil" and in phrases like "el comienzo de otra guerra civil" (the start of another civil war).
target_language_example: La guerra civil duró varios años y dividió al país.
native_language_example: The civil war lasted several years and divided the country.

additional_notes: Refers to a large war involving many countries (often specifically World War I/II: "la Primera/Segunda Guerra Mundial"). It’s usually used with an article ("la") and can be modified with ordinal numbers (primera, segunda) or "otra" (another).
target_language_example: Mi bisabuelo luchó en la Segunda Guerra Mundial.
native_language_example: My great-grandfather fought in World War II.

additional_notes: A common noun phrase: guitarra = “guitar” + eléctrica = “electric.” Uses feminine agreement (una guitarra eléctrica). In Spanish, you can say Tengo una guitarra eléctrica; adding Yo is optional and usually only for emphasis.
target_language_example: Quiero aprender a tocar la guitarra eléctrica.
native_language_example: I want to learn to play the electric guitar.

additional_notes: Part of the gustar pattern: me/te/le/nos/les gusta el... It is used with a singular masculine noun after it. In Spanish, the thing liked is grammatically the subject, so literally it works more like 'the ... is pleasing to someone' than English 'someone likes the ...'. For plural nouns, Spanish uses gustan instead.
target_language_example: A mi hermano le gusta el fútbol.
native_language_example: My brother likes soccer.

additional_notes: Uses the verb "gustar," which works like "to be pleasing" in English: the thing liked ("el helado") is the grammatical subject, and the person is an indirect object pronoun: "me/te/le/nos/os/les." Often you add "A + person" for clarity or emphasis: "A Tomás le gusta el helado." Use "gusta" (singular) with a singular noun like "el helado," and "gustan" with plural nouns ("Me gustan los helados"). To say you don’t like it: "No me gusta el helado."
target_language_example: A mi hermana le gusta el helado de fresa.
native_language_example: My sister likes strawberry ice cream.

additional_notes: Usually used with an indirect object pronoun + gustar: “Me gusta leer” = “I like to read.” Literally it’s closer to “Reading is pleasing to me,” so the person who likes it is expressed with me/te/le/nos/les (not as the subject). You can swap the pronoun: “Te gusta leer?” = “Do you like to read?”
target_language_example: Me gusta leer antes de dormir.
native_language_example: I like to read before going to sleep.

additional_notes: Used with the verb "gustar" to express what someone likes doing. The person who likes it is often introduced with an indirect object: "me/te/le/nos/les" (or "a + name/pronoun" for clarity or emphasis). The verb agrees with what is liked (here: the activity "leer"), so you use "gusta" (singular).
target_language_example: A mi hermano le gusta leer literatura inglesa.
native_language_example: My brother likes to read English literature.

additional_notes: Used with the verb "gustar" to compare preferences. Common patterns: "Me gusta más X (que Y)" = "I like X more (than Y)"; "¿Qué te gusta más?" = "What do you like more / What do you prefer?" Note that with "gustar," the thing liked is the grammatical subject: "Me gusta más el café" (literally, "Coffee pleases me more").
target_language_example: Me gusta más el té que el café.
native_language_example: I like tea more than coffee.

additional_notes: This phrase is usually used with an indirect object pronoun: me/te/le/nos/les gustan las historias = I/you/he-she/we/they like stories. With gustar, the thing you like (las historias) is the grammatical subject, so the verb is plural (gustan) because historias is plural.
target_language_example: A mi hermana le gustan las historias de misterio.
native_language_example: My sister likes mystery stories.

additional_notes: Uses the verb **gustar**. In Spanish, the thing you like (**las manzanas**) is the grammatical subject, so the verb is **plural**: *gustan*. The person who likes them is shown with an **indirect object pronoun**: *me/te/le/nos/les* (often with emphasis: *a mí, a ti, a él/ella, a nosotros, a ellos*). Example: *Me gustan las manzanas* = “I like apples” (literally, “Apples are pleasing to me”).
target_language_example: A ella le gustan las manzanas, pero a mí no.
native_language_example: She likes apples, but I don't.

additional_notes: Used to say something is over or finished. It’s the present perfect: haber (ha) + past participle (acabado), often translated as “has ended/has finished.” Common with events, periods of time, games, wars, negotiations, etc. Word order can vary: “El juego ha acabado” / “Ha acabado el juego.”
target_language_example: Lo siento, la reunión ya ha acabado.
native_language_example: Sorry, the meeting has already ended.

additional_notes: Present perfect: "ha" (from "haber") + past participle "cambiado". It usually means a change that has happened up to now (often with a present result). "Ha cambiado" is 3rd person singular, so it goes with "él/ella/usted" or singular nouns like "el mundo". It can also take a direct object: "ha cambiado a Japón" = "has changed Japan" ("a" is used before people and sometimes personified groups/places).
target_language_example: Todo ha cambiado desde entonces.
native_language_example: Everything has changed since then.

additional_notes: Present perfect of caer (“to fall”). Used for physical falling (often with se: Se te ha caído algo = “You dropped something / Something fell from you”), for decreases (La temperatura ha caído = “The temperature has dropped”), and for institutions/regimes collapsing (El régimen ha caído = “The regime has fallen”). Also in the expression caer en desgracia = “to fall from favor.”
target_language_example: Se me ha caído el vaso al suelo.
native_language_example: I dropped the glass on the floor.

additional_notes: Present perfect: **haber (ha)** + past participle (**comenzado**) to say something has already started up to now. Often appears with **ya** (“already”) or **ni siquiera** (“not even yet”). Used for events, shows, battles, eclipses, etc.
target_language_example: La reunión ya ha comenzado.
native_language_example: The meeting has already started.

additional_notes: Present perfect (he/she/it/you formal) of crecer (to grow). Used for physical growth (a person, hair, a plant) and for things that increase or expand (size, amount, a city). Often used with intensifiers like mucho/tanto/demasiado and with measurements (p. ej., tres centímetros). In "Cómo ha crecido, ¿eh?" it’s an exclamation meaning “Wow, look how much (someone) has grown.”
target_language_example: Parece que Yuki ha crecido desde la última vez.
native_language_example: It looks like Yuki has grown since the last time.

additional_notes: "Ha dado" is the present perfect of "dar" (to give): "ha" (has) + "dado" (given). It often appears in set phrases like "ha dado comienzo" = "has begun/started". With an indirect object, "le ha dado + [something]" can mean someone suddenly got something (e.g., "Le ha dado un ataque" = "He/She had an attack").
target_language_example: La reunión ya ha dado comienzo.
native_language_example: The meeting has already started.

additional_notes: Present perfect: **ha** (from *haber*) + past participle (**decidido**). Used with a third-person singular subject (él/ella/usted) or a singular noun/name (e.g., *Tom*). Often implies the decision is relevant now or has just been made.
target_language_example: Mi hermana ha decidido cambiar de trabajo.
native_language_example: My sister has decided to change jobs.

additional_notes: Used with an infinitive (dejar de + infinitive) to say an action has stopped. “Ha” is the present perfect (he/she/it has), so it often implies it stopped recently or by now: ha dejado de llover (it has stopped raining). Change the person as needed: he dejado de, has dejado de, hemos dejado de, etc.
target_language_example: Mi móvil ha dejado de cargar.
native_language_example: My phone has stopped charging.

additional_notes: Present perfect of desaparecer (“to disappear”): ha (has) + desaparecido (disappeared). Used for something that is no longer there or has gone away, often with a result that matters now. The subject can come after the verb: Ha desaparecido el dolor (“The pain has disappeared”).
target_language_example: Mi cartera ha desaparecido.
native_language_example: My wallet has disappeared.

additional_notes: Used to report what someone said: "[someone] ha dicho que + clause". It's the present perfect of "decir" (he/she/it has said). Often corresponds to English "said (that)" or "has said (that)" depending on context. You can change the subject and tense: "He dicho que..." (I said...), "dijo que..." (he/she said...).
target_language_example: El guía ha dicho que el museo abre a las diez.
native_language_example: The guide said that the museum opens at ten.

additional_notes: Present perfect of "empezar" + "a" + infinitive. Used to say someone/something has recently begun doing an action: "ha empezado a + infinitive" (ha empezado a nevar, a cantar, a buscar...). Often implies a new change or recent development. Other persons: he empezado a (I’ve started to), has empezado a (you’ve started to), hemos/han empezado a (we/they’ve started to).
target_language_example: Últimamente, mi hermano ha empezado a levantarse temprano.
native_language_example: Lately, my brother has started getting up early.

additional_notes: Used with haber + participle to talk about something found at an unspecified time before now, with a result that matters now. Often followed by a direct object (ha encontrado un diamante) or by "a" with a person (ha encontrado a Mary). Can also appear reflexively as "se ha encontrado" meaning "has been found" (a dagger has been found) or "has run into/come across" depending on context.
target_language_example: La policía ya ha encontrado al sospechoso.
native_language_example: The police have already found the suspect.

additional_notes: Used with the auxiliary verb "haber" (ha) + past participle (escrito) to talk about something someone has done, often with a result or relevance now. It can also be used to talk about life experience (e.g., how many books someone has written). Common with quantities like "tres", "muchos", "cientos de".
target_language_example: María ha escrito un artículo para el periódico.
native_language_example: María has written an article for the newspaper.

additional_notes: Often used as part of the structure **ha estado + gerund (-ando/-iendo)** to mean **“has been (doing something)”**, emphasizing an action that started in the recent past and has continued for a while (sometimes up to now). Example: **te ha estado mirando** = “he/she has been watching you.”
target_language_example: Mi hermano ha estado trabajando mucho esta semana.
native_language_example: My brother has been working a lot this week.

meaning: "has been in / has been to" (has spent time in a place or situation).
additional_notes: Uses the present perfect: **ha** (has) + **estado** (been) + **en** (in/on). It often talks about life experience or repeated visits (**Ha estado en Australia dos veces** = he’s been to Australia twice). It can also mean being in a situation/activity for some time: **ha estado en el teléfono por horas** = he’s been on the phone for hours. With media/activities, it can mean participation: **ha estado en películas** = he has been in movies.
target_language_example: Ella ha estado en España varias veces.
native_language_example: She has been to Spain several times.

additional_notes: It’s the present perfect: **haber (ha)** + past participle **ganado**. Use it for something that has happened (often recently or with a result in the present): *Ha ganado el premio.* With **se ha ganado**, it often means **“has earned/deserved”** something (*Se ha ganado el derecho a pedir más*) or **“has won (someone) over”** (*Me ha ganado* = “it/he/she won me over”). **Ganado** doesn’t change for gender/number in this tense.
target_language_example: Mi equipo ha ganado el partido.
native_language_example: My team has won the match.

meaning: “there has been / there have been” (it has existed/occurred).
additional_notes: Impersonal form of haber used to say something has happened or existed. It’s the present perfect: ha (has) + habido (past participle). It’s always singular (ha), even with plural nouns: “Ha habido muchas quejas” = “There have been many complaints.” Common with events/changes: “Ha habido un accidente/un cambio/dificultades.”
target_language_example: Ha habido varios retrasos esta semana.
native_language_example: There have been several delays this week.

additional_notes: Used with an implied subject (usually “he/she/you (formal)”) to say someone has spoken or has been talking. Common with time expressions (e.g., “No ha hablado en una hora”) and with “de” to mean “has talked about” (“Me ha hablado de tu situación”).
target_language_example: Mi jefe ya ha hablado con el cliente.
native_language_example: My boss has already spoken with the client.

additional_notes: Present perfect: **ha** (from *haber*) + past participle **hecho** (from *hacer*). Used for actions completed in the past with a connection to the present (often similar to English “has done/has made”). Refers to **él/ella/usted** or a thing/idea (3rd person singular). In some set phrases it can mean “has caused” (e.g., *no le ha hecho mal* = “hasn’t harmed him/her”).
target_language_example: ¿Quién ha hecho esto?
native_language_example: Who has done this?

additional_notes: Present perfect form of ir used with él, ella, usted, or a singular thing like esto. It often means someone has gone somewhere, but in English it can also be translated as has been in experience statements. In expressions like te ha ido bien, it means things have gone well for someone.
target_language_example: Mi hermano ha ido al médico esta mañana.
native_language_example: My brother has gone to the doctor this morning.

additional_notes: Used with an implied or stated subject to say someone has made a phone call (or has called someone by a name). It’s the he/she/you-formal form of the present perfect: ha + llamado. Common patterns: “Me ha llamado X” = “X called me / has called me”; “¿Te ha llamado?” = “Has he/she called you?”; “Nadie me ha llamado así” = “No one has called me that (name)”.
target_language_example: ¿Te ha llamado tu jefe hoy?
native_language_example: Has your boss called you today?

meaning: 'it's time to' / 'the moment has come to'.
additional_notes: Used to announce that the right time to do something has arrived. It often introduces an infinitive (ha llegado el momento de + verb: "...de moverse") or a noun phrase ("...de la verdad", "...de los orcos"). Literally "the moment has arrived," but in English you usually translate it as "it's time to...".
target_language_example: Ha llegado el momento de tomar una decisión.
native_language_example: It’s time to make a decision.

additional_notes: It’s the present perfect: haber (ha) + past participle (llevado), used for actions in the past connected to the present. With a person/place as the object, it often means “has taken (someone) (to somewhere)” (e.g., No me ha llevado a Shanghai). With things, it can mean “has carried” or “has taken away.” In the reflexive form (se ha llevado), it often means “has been taken away” or “has carried off” (e.g., by a wave). With “una vida,” it means “has led a life” (Ha llevado una vida emocionante).
target_language_example: Mi hermana me ha llevado al aeropuerto dos veces esta semana.
native_language_example: My sister has taken me to the airport twice this week.

additional_notes: Present perfect: haber (ha) + past participle (mejorado). Used to talk about improvement that happened in the past and is true/relevant now. Often followed by something like “mucho” (a lot) or “desde…” (since…).
target_language_example: Mi situación ha mejorado desde el año pasado.
native_language_example: My situation has improved since last year.

additional_notes: Used to say that someone (or something) has died. Literally it’s the present perfect: "haber" (ha) + past participle (muerto). Common in news/reporting, announcements, or dramatic statements; often followed by details with "en" (place) or "en" + cause (e.g., "en un accidente").
target_language_example: Lo siento mucho, pero tu abuelo ha muerto.
native_language_example: I’m very sorry, but your grandfather has died.

additional_notes: Present perfect of "ocurrir" (to happen). Used to talk about something that happened in the past but is still relevant now, often with words like "jamás", "antes", "hoy", or "desde entonces". In questions: "¿Qué ha ocurrido?" = "What happened?/What has happened?"
target_language_example: No sé qué ha ocurrido, pero todos están preocupados.
native_language_example: I don't know what happened, but everyone is worried.

additional_notes: This exact form is the 3rd-person singular present perfect of pasar. On its own, it often means 'has happened.' With time expressions, it can also mean 'has passed' or 'has spent,' as in ha pasado horas... / ha pasado diez años....
target_language_example: No sé qué ha pasado.
native_language_example: I don't know what has happened.

meaning: "a long time has passed" / "it’s been a long time."
additional_notes: Uses the present perfect (ha pasado) to say that a lot of time has gone by up to now. Very common with "desde" (since) or "desde que" + a verb: "Ha pasado mucho tiempo desde que lo vi" (It’s been a long time since I saw him). It can also stand alone as a full sentence to comment that it’s been a while.
target_language_example: Ha pasado mucho tiempo desde que hablamos por última vez.
native_language_example: It’s been a long time since we last talked.

meaning: “a year has passed” / “it’s been a year.”
additional_notes: Uses the present perfect (ha pasado) to say that one year has elapsed up to now. Very often followed by desde (“since”) or desde que (“since [something happened]”): Ha pasado un año desde entonces (since then); Ha pasado un año desde que ella vino (since she came). You can also use it alone to emphasize the amount of time: Ha pasado un año.
target_language_example: Ha pasado un año desde la última vez que nos vimos.
native_language_example: It’s been a year since the last time we saw each other.

additional_notes: Used with many kinds of “loss”: objects (ha perdido su tarjeta), abilities/health (ha perdido el oído, ha perdido mucha sangre), abstract things (ha perdido la esperanza), and also opportunities/time in set phrases like "no ha perdido el tiempo" (= he/she hasn’t wasted time). It’s formed with "haber" (ha) + past participle (perdido).
target_language_example: Lo siento, ha perdido las llaves.
native_language_example: Sorry, he/she has lost the keys.

additional_notes: "Ha puesto" = haber (ha) + past participle (puesto). It describes something completed in the recent past or with relevance to the present. "Poner" is very common and can mean "to put/place," "to set" (e.g., rules/a date), "to lay" (eggs), or "to make/cause" a feeling (e.g., "me ha puesto nervioso"). "Puesto" is the irregular past participle of "poner."
target_language_example: Él ha puesto las llaves en la mesa.
native_language_example: He has put the keys on the table.

meaning: “has ended up / has been left” (shows the result after something happens).
additional_notes: It’s the present perfect of **quedar** (“to remain / to end up / to be left”). Very common in the pattern **ha quedado + adjective/past participle** to describe the final state: *ha quedado cancelado* (“has ended up canceled”), *ha quedado corto* (“has fallen short / been too short”). Don’t confuse with **se ha quedado**, which often means “has stayed” somewhere or with someone (*Tom se ha quedado conmigo*).
target_language_example: La puerta ha quedado abierta.
native_language_example: The door has been left open.

additional_notes: Used with **haber** to form the present perfect: **(él/ella/usted) ha roto** = “he/she/you (formal) has broken.” With **se** it often means something broke on its own: **Se ha roto** = “It broke / It’s broken.” With people, **ha roto conmigo** means “has broken up with me.”
target_language_example: Mi móvil se ha roto otra vez.
native_language_example: My phone broke again / My phone is broken again.

meaning: "has gone out" / "has come out" / "has left" (depending on context).
additional_notes: This is the present perfect: haber (ha) + past participle (salido). With things like the moon/sun, it means “has come out/appeared” (Ha salido la luna). With transportation or people, it often means “has left/departed” (El avión ya ha salido).
target_language_example: Lo siento, el tren ya ha salido.
native_language_example: Sorry, the train has already left.

additional_notes: Used with a past participle to form the passive voice with ser, often in formal/news contexts: ha sido acusado = "has been accused"; ha sido destruida = "has been destroyed"; ha sido enviado = "has been sent". The subject agrees in gender/number with the participle (acusado/acusada, destruido/destruida, enviados/enviadas).
target_language_example: La carta ha sido enviada hoy.
native_language_example: The letter has been sent today.

additional_notes: Present perfect of **ser** for **él/ella/usted** (and often **eso/esto**): **ha sido** = “has been.” Used to describe what something/someone has been like up to now (e.g., *Ha sido genial* = “It’s been great”). In short answers you may see **lo ha sido** (“it has been”).
target_language_example: La semana ha sido muy larga.
native_language_example: The week has been very long.

meaning: 'it has been a day' / 'it’s been a day' (used to describe how the day was).
additional_notes: Very common with an adjective or description after it: “Ha sido un día duro/perfecto/agotador.” Uses the present perfect (haber + sido), often to talk about how today has gone so far or how a recent day felt. You can also add “Hoy”: “Hoy ha sido un día…”
target_language_example: Ha sido un día largo, pero ya terminó.
native_language_example: It’s been a long day, but it’s over now.

additional_notes: A polite way to end a conversation or meeting, or to thank someone after an interaction. Often followed by an infinitive: “Ha sido un placer + conocerle/conocerla” (to meet you), “hablar con usted” (to speak with you). Uses the present perfect (“has been”), common in Spain; in many Latin American contexts you may also hear “Fue un placer.”
target_language_example: Ha sido un placer hablar con usted. Que tenga un buen día.
native_language_example: It’s been a pleasure speaking with you. Have a good day.

additional_notes: Present perfect: **haber (ha)** + past participle (**sucedido**). Used to talk about something that has happened in the past and is relevant now (often with words like **ya** "already" or **antes** "before"). Also appears in phrases like **lo que ha sucedido** ("what has happened"). Note: **suceder** means "to happen," not "to succeed" (so it can be confused with English "succeeded").
target_language_example: ¿Qué ha sucedido aquí?
native_language_example: What has happened here?

additional_notes: Used with a past participle to talk about past experiences or results that matter now. It’s the third-person singular form (él/ella/usted): "ha tenido". Often followed by a noun: "ha tenido suerte" (has had luck), "ha tenido tiempo" (has had time).
target_language_example: Ella ha tenido un día muy largo.
native_language_example: She has had a very long day.

additional_notes: "Ha terminado" is the present perfect of "terminar" and is used to say something has finished/ended (often with a sense of “it’s done now”). It can refer to events, conversations, battles, etc. With "ya", it can emphasize completion: "Ya ha terminado" = “It’s already over.”
target_language_example: El juego ha terminado, vámonos a casa.
native_language_example: The game is over; let’s go home.

additional_notes: Used with the auxiliary haber + past participle (tomar → tomado) to talk about something that has happened (often recently or with a present connection). Depending on context, tomar can mean “take,” “have (food/drink/medicine),” or “make” (e.g., tomar una decisión = to make a decision). With a reflexive pronoun (se ha tomado), it can appear in set phrases like tomarse molestias (“to go to a lot of trouble”) or tomarse libertades (“to take liberties”).
target_language_example: Él ha tomado una decisión hoy.
native_language_example: He has made a decision today.

additional_notes: Used with the auxiliary verb haber + past participle to talk about something that has happened up to now. "Ha" is the 3rd-person singular form (he/she/it/you-formal: "has"). It often appears with an indirect object pronoun: "me/te/le ha traído" = "has brought me/you/him-her (something)".
target_language_example: El trabajo me ha traído mucha experiencia.
native_language_example: The job has brought me a lot of experience.

meaning: “has come / has arrived” (present perfect, he/she/it has come).
additional_notes: Formed with **haber** (ha) + past participle (**venido**) to talk about something that has happened already. The subject is usually **él/ella/usted** (he/she/you formal) and can be omitted: **Ha venido** = “(He/She) has come.” Negative: **No ha venido** = “hasn’t come.”
target_language_example: ¿Ya ha venido tu hermana?
native_language_example: Has your sister arrived yet?

additional_notes: "Ha visto" is the 3rd-person singular present perfect: "él/ella/usted ha visto" = "he/she/you (formal) has seen". It can refer to something seen at an unspecified time in the past, or to an experience up to now. With a direct object pronoun, it often appears as "le/la/lo ha visto" ("has seen him/her/it").
target_language_example: ¿Usted ha visto mis llaves?
native_language_example: Have you (formal) seen my keys?

additional_notes: Past tense used with haber (present perfect): ha vuelto = “he/she/it has returned.” Very often it’s followed by “a + infinitive” to mean “has done something again” (e.g., ha vuelto a salir = “it has come out again / it’s sunny again”). With the reflexive form (se ha vuelto), it can mean “has become” (e.g., Él se ha vuelto importante = “He has become important”).
target_language_example: Mi hermano ha vuelto a casa tarde.
native_language_example: My brother has come home late again.

additional_notes: Used with an infinitive to say someone has done an action again: **ha vuelto a + infinitive** (e.g., *ha vuelto a ocurrir* = “it happened again,” *ha vuelto a meterlo* = “he/she put it back in”). It can also introduce a return to a place with **ha vuelto a + place** (e.g., *ha vuelto a la ciudad* = “he/she has returned to the city”). It’s the present perfect: **ha** (has) + **vuelto** (returned) + **a** (to), often implying repetition or “back to” a previous state.
target_language_example: Mi hermano ha vuelto a llamar esta mañana.
native_language_example: My brother called again this morning.

additional_notes: Uses the infinitive perfect: haber + past participle (cometido) to talk about a past action with a present result (e.g., realizing now that you made a mistake). Often appears after verbs like deber (must), reconocer (admit), or acusar de (accuse of): “Debo (de) haber cometido…”, “Reconoció haber cometido…”, “Me acusó de haber cometido…”. “Cometer un error” is a common way to say “make a mistake.”
target_language_example: Creo que he/haber cometido un error al escribir la dirección.
native_language_example: I think I made a mistake when writing the address.

additional_notes: Used to talk about being in a place or state *before* another moment in the past, often after another verb (e.g., *debe de*, *tendría que*, *siento*, *dice*). It’s made with **haber** + **estado** (past participle of *estar*).
target_language_example: Me alegra haber estado contigo en ese momento.
native_language_example: I'm glad to have been with you at that moment.

additional_notes: Infinitive perfect progressive: haber (to have) + estado + gerund (esperando). Used after another verb (often a modal or expression like "deber", "poder", "parecer") to talk about an action that started in the past and was ongoing for a while before another point in time.
target_language_example: Debí haber estado esperando dos horas.
native_language_example: I must have been waiting for two hours.

additional_notes: No es una expresión fija ni estándar en español. Normalmente aparece solo en contextos metalingüísticos o gramaticales, al mencionar juntos dos verbos. Más natural sería escribir «haber y estar» si se quiere nombrarlos como elementos de una lista. «Haber» se usa sobre todo como auxiliar y en «hay»; «estar» significa «to be» para ubicación, estado o condición.
target_language_example: La secuencia haber estar no es una expresión fija en español.
native_language_example: The sequence haber estar is not a fixed expression in Spanish.

additional_notes: This is the perfect infinitive: haber + the past participle hecho. It is used to talk about an action that was already completed before another action, feeling, or situation. It often appears after verbs like esperar, sentir, reconocer, and poder, or after prepositions such as sin.
target_language_example: Me alegro de haber hecho esa llamada.
native_language_example: I'm glad I made that call.

additional_notes: Perfect infinitive of "llegar" (haber + past participle). Used after another verb (often a modal like deber/poder, or after prepositions like por) to say the arrival happened before that other action/time: "deben de haber llegado" = "they must have arrived"; "por haber llegado tarde" = "for having arrived late".
target_language_example: No puedo creer que hayas podido haber llegado tan temprano.
native_language_example: I can’t believe you could have arrived so early.

additional_notes: Perfect infinitive of "nacer" (to be born). It’s used after another verb to talk about being born at an earlier time, often in phrases like "estar + adjective + de haber nacido..." (to be [adjective] about having been born...) or "alegrarse de no haber nacido..." (to be glad not to have been born...).
target_language_example: Está orgullosa de haber nacido en México.
native_language_example: She’s proud to have been born in Mexico.

additional_notes: This is the perfect infinitive: "haber" + past participle ("oído"). It means the hearing happened before the time of the main verb (e.g., "Creí haber oído..." = "I thought I had heard..."). Common after verbs like creer (to think/believe), deber (must), recordar (to remember), lamentar (to be sorry), fingir (to pretend), and in phrases like "haber oído acerca de" (to have heard about).
target_language_example: Creo haber oído ese nombre antes.
native_language_example: I think I’ve heard that name before.

additional_notes: Perfect infinitive of "perder" (haber + past participle). It refers to an action that happened before the main verb: "Lamento haber perdido..." = "I regret having lost...". Often used after verbs like lamentar, sentir, esperar, creer, etc., to talk about a past action.
target_language_example: Me alegra no haber perdido el vuelo.
native_language_example: I'm glad I didn't miss the flight.

additional_notes: Used to talk about being something in the past from the perspective of another time. Common after verbs/expressions like lamentar, desear, estar + adjective (e.g., estar desilusionado de…), and in hypotheticals with podría/podían ("could have been"). Also appears in passive constructions like "sin haber sido visto" ("without having been seen").
target_language_example: Me arrepiento de haber sido tan impaciente.
native_language_example: I regret having been so impatient.

additional_notes:
This is the perfect infinitive of "tener" (haber + past participle). It’s commonly used after modal/auxiliary verbs to talk about something in the past (often with regret, criticism, or deduction):
- "deberías/deberíamos haber tenido..." = "you/we should have had..."
- "debe haber tenido..." = "he/she must have had..." (a guess/deduction)
- "quisiera haber tenido..." = "I wish I had had..."
target_language_example: Deberíamos haber tenido más paciencia.
native_language_example: We should have had more patience.

additional_notes: Used after another verb to talk about having already come before that moment (often in regrets, thanks, or wishes): Debería/Deberías/Ojalá pudiera + haber venido. It’s the past infinitive: haber + past participle (venido).
target_language_example: Gracias por haber venido tan temprano.
native_language_example: Thanks for having come so early.

meaning: (no es una combinación estándar en español; normalmente se trata de un error por “haber venido” = “to have come / to have come (perfect infinitive)”, o por “haber de venir” = “to have to come / must come”)
additional_notes:
“Haber venir” por sí solo no se usa de forma natural en español porque *haber* como auxiliar requiere el participio (p. ej., “haber venido”), no el infinitivo (“venir”).

Formas que normalmente se quieren decir:
- “haber venido” (infinitivo perfecto): “to have come / having come”. Ej.: “Gracias por haber venido.”
- “haber de venir” (más formal): expresa obligación, similar a “tener que venir”. Ej.: “He de venir mañana.”
target_language_example: En español no se dice “haber venir”; lo correcto suele ser “haber venido” o “haber de venir”, según el sentido.
native_language_example: In Spanish you don’t say “haber venir”; it’s usually “haber venido” or “haber de venir”, depending on the meaning.

additional_notes: Perfect infinitive of ver. It is used after another verb to talk about a seeing action that happened earlier: debes haber visto = you must have seen, recuerdo haber visto = I remember having seen. With no, it means not to have seen.
target_language_example: Creo haber visto esa película antes.
native_language_example: I think I've seen that movie before.

meaning: to have to say; a nonstandard or dictionary-style shorthand for forms based on haber de decir, such as he de decir ('I must say')
additional_notes: By itself, haber decir is not a standard modern Spanish expression. The usual construction is haber de + infinitive, for example he de decir. It expresses obligation and can sound formal, literary, or rhetorical.
target_language_example: La secuencia «haber decir» no se usa normalmente sin la preposición «de».
native_language_example: The sequence 'haber decir' is not normally used without the preposition 'de'.

meaning: "to be time / to be enough time" (most often: "hay tiempo" = "there’s time").
additional_notes: This is an impersonal use of **haber** (like **hay** = “there is/are”). You’ll most commonly hear it conjugated as **hay tiempo** (“there’s time”) or **no hay tiempo** (“there’s no time”). Often followed by **para + infinitive**: **Hay tiempo para comer** (“There’s time to eat”). Don’t confuse it with **tener tiempo** (“to have time” personally/available in your schedule).
target_language_example: No creo que vaya a haber tiempo para hablar hoy.
native_language_example: I don’t think there’s going to be time to talk today.

meaning: 'there is/there was a' (used to say something exists).
additional_notes: Impersonal use of **haber** + a feminine singular noun (**una**). It means “there is/was a …” (not “to have”). Tense changes with context: **hay una** (there is a), **había una** (there was a/used to be a), **hubo una** (there was a—one-time event), **debería haber una** (there should be a).
target_language_example: En esta ciudad debería haber una estación de tren.
native_language_example: In this city, there should be a train station.

additional_notes: Perfect infinitive of "hacer" (haber + lo + hecho). It talks about an action completed before another time or action. Common after phrases like "deber" (should have) and "arrepentirse de" (regret having done).
target_language_example: Lamento haberlo hecho tan tarde.
native_language_example: I’m sorry I did it so late.

additional_notes: From the verb hablar (to talk) + con (with). "Habla con…" is the tú imperative, used to tell one person you address as tú to talk to someone. For formal you, use "Hable con…"; for plural (Spain), "Hablad con…"; for you all (Latin America), "Hablen con…".
target_language_example: Habla con tu profesora después de clase.
native_language_example: Talk to your teacher after class.

additional_notes: From the verb hablar (to speak) + español (Spanish). It’s often used to say what language someone speaks. Change it depending on the subject: yo hablo español (I speak Spanish), tú hablas español (you speak Spanish), él/ella/usted habla español (he/she/you formal speak Spanish), nosotros hablamos español (we speak Spanish), ellos/ellas/ustedes hablan español (they/you all speak Spanish).
target_language_example: Mi hermano habla español y también inglés.
native_language_example: My brother speaks Spanish and also English.

additional_notes: Used to say someone speaks the French language. Often appears with an explicit subject (Ella habla francés) or implied by context. You can change the subject by changing the verb: yo hablo francés (I speak French), tú hablas francés (you speak French), él/ella habla francés (he/she speaks French), nosotros hablamos francés (we speak French).
target_language_example: Mi hermano habla francés y alemán.
native_language_example: My brother speaks French and German.

additional_notes: From the verb "hablar" (to speak) + the language "inglés" (English). It can describe ability or habit ("speaks English"), and it’s also used to say what language someone is speaking at the moment. "Habla" is the 3rd person singular present (él/ella/usted). Note: "hablar alto" means "to speak loudly" (about volume), not "tall".
target_language_example: Mi jefe habla inglés.
native_language_example: My boss speaks English.

additional_notes: Used to compliment someone’s language ability or how well they express themselves. This is the él/ella/usted form of hablar (habla). You can specify the language (habla muy bien inglés/francés) or leave it implied if context is clear. For informal ‘you’, use ‘hablas muy bien’.
target_language_example: Tom habla muy bien francés.
native_language_example: Tom speaks French very well.

additional_notes: "Hablando" is the gerund (-ing form) of "hablar" (to talk/speak). Use it often with "estar" to talk about something happening right now or in progress: "Estoy hablando con…" = "I’m talking with…". It can also describe someone/something: "La chica hablando con Jim…" = "The girl talking with Jim…". In some contexts, "hablar con + [noun]" can describe the way someone speaks: "hablando con acertijos" = "speaking in riddles."
target_language_example: Estoy hablando con mi mamá ahora.
native_language_example: I’m talking with my mom right now.

additional_notes: Used with estar to say what the conversation/topic is about: “Estamos hablando de una máquina” = “We’re talking about a machine.” It’s also common at the start of a phrase to introduce a topic or make a quick connection/segue: “Hablando de donaciones…” = “Speaking of donations…”. You can also say “Hablando de eso” = “Speaking of that.”
target_language_example: Hablando de eso, ¿ya pagaste la cuenta?
native_language_example: Speaking of that, did you already pay the bill?

meaning: "Speaking of that..." / "By the way..." (to change or return to a topic).
additional_notes: Used to introduce a related topic or to bring the conversation back to something mentioned. It often comes at the start of a sentence: “Hablando de eso, …”. It can also stand alone (“Hablando de eso.”) to signal you’re about to say something connected. Don’t confuse it with “Estoy hablando de eso” (“I’m talking about that”) or “No estoy hablando de eso” (“I’m not talking about that”).
target_language_example: Hablando de eso, ¿ya hablaste con tu jefe?
native_language_example: Speaking of that, did you already talk to your boss?

additional_notes: Uses the gerund (hablando) to describe an action in progress. Often used with estar (está/estoy hablando por teléfono) or to describe someone you saw/heard doing something (lo vi/lo escuché hablando por teléfono).
target_language_example: Ahora no puedo; estoy hablando por teléfono.
native_language_example: I can't right now; I'm talking on the phone.

additional_notes: Used to describe someone who speaks a language as their first language. Often followed by “de + language” (e.g., hablante nativo de español) or used with “un/una” depending on the person (un hablante nativo, una hablante nativa).
target_language_example: Busco un hablante nativo de español para practicar conversación.
native_language_example: I’m looking for a native Spanish speaker to practice conversation.

additional_notes: Used when saying who you are talking to: hablar con alguien. In English this is often "talk to" or "speak with/to" depending on context.
target_language_example: Necesito hablar con mi profesora.
native_language_example: I need to talk to my teacher.

meaning: to talk to her; to speak with her.
additional_notes: "Hablar con" means "to talk to/with." "Ella" = "she/her" (used for a female person). You can change the pronoun: hablar con él (him), hablar con usted (you, formal), hablar con ellos/ellas (them). In "voy a ir a hablar con ella," the "a" marks an action you’re going to do ("I’m going to go talk to her").
target_language_example: Necesito hablar con ella hoy.
native_language_example: I need to talk to her today.

meaning: to talk to them; to speak with them.
additional_notes: Uses the verb "hablar" (to talk/speak) + "con" (with) + "ellos" (them, masculine or mixed-gender group). Common for saying you need/want/are going to talk to a group of people: "Tengo que hablar con ellos" (I have to talk to them), "Voy a hablar con ellos" (I’m going to talk to them).
target_language_example: Después de la reunión, necesito hablar con ellos.
native_language_example: After the meeting, I need to talk to them.

additional_notes: Used when addressing one person politely (e.g., a stranger, an older person, a customer, a boss). It uses the formal "usted" form; with friends or family you’d usually say "hablar contigo" or "hablar con ti" (less common). Often appears in polite phrases like "Quisiera hablar con usted" (I’d like to speak with you).
target_language_example: ¿Podría hablar con usted un momento?
native_language_example: Could I speak with you for a moment?

additional_notes: Used in voseo regions (especially Argentina, Uruguay, and parts of Central America) where “vos” replaces “tú” for informal “you.” It’s the same idea as “hablar contigo,” but with “vos” instead of “ti”/“tú.” Often appears when someone wants a conversation, sometimes a serious one: “Necesito/Tengo que hablar con vos.”
target_language_example: Después de la reunión, quiero hablar con vos un momento.
native_language_example: After the meeting, I want to talk to you for a moment.

additional_notes: Used when you want or need to have a conversation with a male person (“él” = “him”). The preposition “con” means “with,” so it’s very direct: “talk with him.” In speech, you may also hear “hablarle” (“to talk to him”) when “him” is an indirect object, but “hablar con él” is common and clear. Note the accent: “él” (him) vs “el” (the).
target_language_example: Necesito hablar con él antes de la reunión.
native_language_example: I need to talk to him before the meeting.

meaning: to talk to me; to speak with me.
additional_notes: Uses the verb hablar (to talk/speak) + conmigo (with me). Often used for requests or invitations to talk: ¿Puedes hablar conmigo? / Tengo que hablar contigo. If you’re addressing someone informally (tú), you’ll also hear hablar contigo (“talk to you”).
target_language_example: ¿Puedes hablar conmigo un momento?
native_language_example: Can you talk to me for a moment?

additional_notes: Often appears as "hablar consigo mismo/a". "Consigo" is a reflexive prepositional pronoun used mainly with él/ella/usted (and sometimes ellos/ellas/ustedes); with "yo" you would usually say "hablar conmigo mismo/a" instead of "hablar consigo".
target_language_example: A veces él prefiere hablar consigo cuando está nervioso.
native_language_example: Sometimes he prefers to talk to himself when he’s nervous.

additional_notes: Means “to talk/speak with you” (informal singular “you”). Used when addressing one person you’re familiar with (friend, family, etc.). For a formal “you,” use “hablar con usted”; for plural “you,” use “hablar con ustedes” (LatAm) or “hablar con vosotros” (Spain).
target_language_example: ¿Tienes un momento para hablar contigo?
native_language_example: Do you have a moment to talk to you?

additional_notes: Used to introduce the topic of conversation. After hablar, Spanish normally uses de where English often uses about: hablar de un problema, hablar de música, hablar de alguien.
target_language_example: No me gusta hablar de política en la cena.
native_language_example: I don't like talking about politics at dinner.

additional_notes: Used when the thing you’re talking about is already known from context. It’s often used with verbs like preferir (to prefer) or with phrases like no hay necesidad de… (there’s no need to…). You’ll also see the related fixed expression "he oído hablar de ello" = "I’ve heard about it" (literally, "I’ve heard to talk about it").
target_language_example: No quiero hablar de ello ahora.
native_language_example: I don’t want to talk about it right now.

meaning: to talk about that; to discuss that.
additional_notes: Used when referring back to a topic already mentioned or understood from context (eso = “that”). Often appears with “no quiero / no puedo” to refuse or postpone the conversation, or with time phrases like “ahora”, “en otra ocasión”. You can also say “hablar de ello” (more formal) or replace “eso” with a specific topic: “hablar de política”.
target_language_example: No quiero hablar de eso todavía; hablemos mañana.
native_language_example: I don’t want to talk about that yet; let’s talk tomorrow.

meaning: to speak in public; public speaking.
additional_notes: Used for giving a talk or addressing an audience (a class, a meeting, etc.). Often appears with verbs like gustar (no le gusta hablar en público), ser difícil (es difícil hablar en público), and estar acostumbrado/a a (be used to public speaking).
target_language_example: Me da miedo hablar en público, pero necesito hacerlo para la presentación.
native_language_example: I'm afraid of speaking in public, but I need to do it for the presentation.

additional_notes: Uses the verb "hablar" (to speak) + the language name. Often appears with "saber" to express ability: "Sé hablar español" = "I can speak Spanish." You can swap in other languages: "hablar francés", "hablar inglés".
target_language_example: Yo sé hablar español.
native_language_example: I can speak Spanish.

additional_notes: Used to state ability to speak the French language. Often appears with modal verbs (puedo hablar francés = I can speak French) or to describe level (sé hablar francés un poco = I know how to speak a little French).
target_language_example: Apenas puedo hablar francés.
native_language_example: I can barely speak French.

additional_notes: Used to say someone speaks English or needs/refuses to use English in a situation. After "hablar", the language is usually used without an article: "hablar inglés", "hablar español" (not *hablar el inglés* in most everyday contexts).
target_language_example: ¿Puedes hablar inglés conmigo, por favor?
native_language_example: Can you speak English with me, please?

meaning: to talk about; to speak about.
additional_notes: Used with a noun or topic (often introduced by a pronoun like "eso" or by an infinitive phrase) to say what the conversation is about. It’s very close in meaning to "hablar de"; "sobre" can sound a bit more formal or like “on the topic of.”
target_language_example: Podemos hablar sobre el proyecto mañana.
native_language_example: We can talk about the project tomorrow.

additional_notes: Future tense of "hablar" (yo hablaré) + "con". Used to say you will speak with someone later, often to promise or plan to discuss something: "Lo hablaré con…" = "I’ll talk it over with…". You can also use the present for near future in Spanish: "Hablo con ella mañana."
target_language_example: Mañana hablaré con el profesor sobre la tarea.
native_language_example: Tomorrow I’ll talk to the teacher about the homework.

additional_notes: Used to say someone speaks English, often to talk about ability/fluency. It can be a statement (Hablas inglés.) or used in questions and comments: ¿Hablas inglés? (Do you speak English?), No hablas inglés, ¿verdad? (You don’t speak English, right?), ¡Qué bien hablas inglés! (You speak English so well!). Uses the verb hablar (to speak) in the tú form: hablas.
target_language_example: ¿Hablas inglés o español?
native_language_example: Do you speak English or Spanish?

additional_notes: Uses the verb *hablar* in the first-person singular present (*hablo* = “I speak/I talk”). Add details with *con* (“with”), *en* (“in/at”), frequency words like *casi todos los días* (“almost every day”), or combine languages with *e* (used instead of *y* before an *i-* sound: *francés e inglés*). *Ya hablo francés* often means “I already speak French.”
target_language_example: Lo siento, no hablo alemán; hablo francés.
native_language_example: Sorry, I don’t speak German; I speak French.

additional_notes: Used to say you have basic ability in a language. It’s often followed by a language name: “Hablo un poco de español.” You can swap the verb form for other people: “Hablas un poco de…”, “Habla un poco de…”, “Hablamos un poco de…”.
target_language_example: Hablo un poco de italiano, pero entiendo más de lo que hablo.
native_language_example: I speak a little Italian, but I understand more than I speak.

additional_notes: Past tense (preterite) of "hablar": it means you talked to/with someone at a specific time. Use it with a person or group: "Hablé con Ana", "Hablé con ellos". For "I spoke to him/her", use the pronoun after "con": "Hablé con él/ella" (note: "él" has an accent).
target_language_example: Ayer hablé con mi jefe por teléfono.
native_language_example: Yesterday I spoke with my boss on the phone.

additional_notes: "Habló" is the simple past (pretérito) of "hablar" for él/ella/usted. Use "habló con + person" to say someone talked to/with someone. It can also be followed by something like "una sonrisa" to describe the manner (e.g., "spoke with a smile").
target_language_example: Ayer habló con su jefe sobre el problema.
native_language_example: Yesterday he/she spoke with his/her boss about the problem.

meaning: “would have done” (conditional perfect: hypothetical past action).
additional_notes: Used to talk about what someone would have done in a past situation that didn’t happen or is imagined. Often appears with a condition: **Si + imperfect subjunctive** → **habría hecho** (“If…, I would have done…”). Frequently used with object pronouns: **lo/la habría hecho** = “I would have done it.”
target_language_example: Si lo hubiera sabido, lo habría hecho antes.
native_language_example: If I had known, I would have done it earlier.

additional_notes: Conditional perfect of ser (haber in conditional + sido). Used for hypothetical past situations (“It would have been…”), and also for making guesses/speculation about the past (“Yesterday would have been his birthday” = presumably/it would have been).
target_language_example: Sin tu ayuda, habría sido imposible.
native_language_example: Without your help, it would have been impossible.

additional_notes: Used to talk about something that was bought before another past moment/event. Often appears with time expressions like "la semana anterior", "el día antes", or in patterns like "Para cuando llegué, ya había comprado...". You’ll also see it with object pronouns ("lo había comprado" = "I/he/she had bought it") and in relative clauses ("el reloj que había comprado" = "the watch that (I/he/she) had bought").
target_language_example: Cuando empezó la reunión, ya había comprado los boletos.
native_language_example: When the meeting started, I had already bought the tickets.

additional_notes: Uses the past perfect (había + past participle) to talk about something that happened before another past moment. With objects/places it usually means “had left (something somewhere)” or “had left (a person).” With “de” it often means “had stopped/quit” (e.g., había dejado de fumar = had quit smoking). With the reflexive form “se había dejado,” it commonly means “had forgotten/left behind” something (especially at home, on the train, etc.).
target_language_example: Cuando llegué, me di cuenta de que había dejado las llaves en casa.
native_language_example: When I arrived, I realized I had left the keys at home.

additional_notes: Used to report something someone said earlier, before another past event or thought. Common in sentences with another past verb like creí/pensé ("I thought") or a past action: "a pesar de que yo le había dicho que..." = "even though I had told her that...". You can change the person: había dicho (he/she/I had said), habías dicho (you had said), le había dicho (I had told him/her).
target_language_example: Yo creía que él ya había dicho que no podía venir.
native_language_example: I thought he had already said that he couldn’t come.

meaning: 'had been' (past perfect of estar), often used for earlier states or ongoing actions before another past moment.
additional_notes: This is the imperfect subjunctive auxiliary "había" + past participle "estado". It forms the past perfect with estar: "había estado" = "had been". Use it to talk about something that started before and was already true/going on prior to another event in the past (often with "cuando..."). With a gerund it forms the past perfect continuous: "había estado leyendo/trabajando" = "had been reading/working". Also common with adjectives: "había estado enferma" (had been sick), "había estado asustado" (had been scared).
target_language_example: Yo ya había estado aquí antes de mudarme.
native_language_example: I had already been here before I moved.

additional_notes: Past perfect (pluscuamperfecto) of *hacer*: **había** (imperfect of *haber*) + **hecho** (past participle). Used to talk about something completed **before** another moment in the past (often when telling a story or explaining a past feeling/reaction). *Hecho* doesn’t change for gender/number here.
target_language_example: Cuando llegué, ya había hecho la cena.
native_language_example: When I arrived, I had already made dinner.

additional_notes: Used to talk about something that happened before another past moment. Often appears in reported speech (e.g., "me dijo que...") or when explaining earlier past events. With "se" ("se había ido"), it commonly means "had left" / "was gone."
target_language_example: Cuando llegué, ella ya había ido al supermercado.
native_language_example: When I arrived, she had already gone to the supermarket.

additional_notes: Used to say someone died before another past moment or action. It’s common in reported speech (Ella dijo que…) and with time markers like “cuando” (Ya había muerto cuando llegué = he/she was already dead when I arrived). Agree for gender/number: había muerto (he/it), había muerta (she, less common but possible as an adjective), habían muerto (they).
target_language_example: Cuando llegamos al hospital, el abuelo ya había muerto.
native_language_example: When we got to the hospital, Grandpa had already died.

additional_notes: Past perfect (pluscuamperfecto) of olvidar: it talks about something that was already forgotten before another moment in the past. Often used with "(me/te/se/nos) había olvidado" and "de" (to forget about something/someone): "Me había olvidado de él." You may also hear "se me había olvidado" (literally “it had slipped my mind”), which is very common in everyday Spanish.
target_language_example: Cuando llegué al aeropuerto, me di cuenta de que había olvidado mi pasaporte.
native_language_example: When I got to the airport, I realized I had forgotten my passport.

additional_notes: Uses the past perfect (haber + past participle) to talk about something that was heard before another past moment or event. Often appears with "ya" (already) or "hasta que" (until) to show sequence in the past. The participle is "oído" (from "oír"), and the person changes: yo había oído, tú habías oído, él/ella había oído, nosotros habíamos oído, etc.
target_language_example: Cuando llegué, ya había oído la noticia.
native_language_example: When I arrived, I had already heard the news.

additional_notes: Past perfect: había + pasado, used to talk about something that happened before another past moment (e.g., “I wondered what had happened”). Depending on context, pasar can mean “to happen” (¿Qué te había pasado?), “to go by/stop by” (había pasado por la oficina), “to go through/spend time” (dónde había pasado el fin de semana), or “to slip one’s mind” in se me había pasado (“I completely forgot”).
target_language_example: No sabía qué había pasado cuando llegué.
native_language_example: I didn’t know what had happened when I arrived.

additional_notes: Past perfect (pluperfect) of perder (“to lose”): había (imperfect of haber) + perdido (past participle). Used to talk about something that happened before another past event, often in relative clauses like “que había perdido” (“that [someone] had lost”). Person/number can change: yo había perdido, ella había perdido, nosotros habíamos perdido, etc.
target_language_example: Por fin encontré el documento que había perdido ayer.
native_language_example: I finally found the document I had lost yesterday.

additional_notes: Used to say something was already true or had happened before another moment in the past. It’s formed with imperfect haber (había) + past participle (sido). Often followed by a past participle to make the passive voice: había sido destruida = had been destroyed; había sido engañado = had been tricked.
target_language_example: Cuando llegué, la reunión ya había sido cancelada.
native_language_example: When I arrived, the meeting had already been canceled.

additional_notes: Used to talk about a state/identity that was true before another past moment or event. It’s the past perfect: **haber** in the imperfect (**había**) + past participle (**sido**). Common in reported news or when giving background: *La operación había sido un éxito* = it was already a success by that earlier point. With **nunca** or **tan**, it emphasizes experience up to that past point: *Nunca había sido tan feliz* = I had never been so happy (before then).
target_language_example: Cuando llegamos, la tienda ya había sido cerrada.
native_language_example: When we arrived, the store had already been closed.

additional_notes: Past perfect: haber (imperfect) + past participle. "Había terminado" says something was already finished before another past event (often with "cuando"). Used for events ending: a battle, class, meeting, show, etc. You can replace "terminado" with other participles (había llegado, había comido).
target_language_example: Cuando llamaste, la película ya había terminado.
native_language_example: When you called, the movie had already ended.

additional_notes: Past perfect of ver: haber (había) + past participle (visto). Used to talk about something you saw before another moment in the past (often implied or mentioned). Example: Cuando llegué, ya lo había visto = "When I arrived, I had already seen it." You can use object pronouns before the verb: lo/la había visto (I had seen him/it/her), te había visto (I had seen you). In some regions you may hear le había visto for a male person (leísmo).
target_language_example: Ya había visto esa película antes de conocer a mi pareja.
native_language_example: I had already seen that movie before I met my partner.

meaning: (almost always with **no**) “there was nobody / there wasn’t anyone.”
additional_notes: In normal statements you say **no había nadie** (double negative in Spanish is correct): **no** + **haber** (había = “there was”) + **nadie** (“nobody/anyone”). Without **no**, it’s generally only used in questions or very specific contexts.
target_language_example: Cuando llegué a casa, no había nadie.
native_language_example: When I got home, there was nobody (there wasn’t anyone).

additional_notes: Used to say that something existed or was present in the past. It’s the imperfect past of "hay" (there is/are): "había" + a masculine singular noun ("un"). For feminine nouns, use "había una"; for plural, "había" + "unos/unas" or just the plural noun (e.g., "había dos cines").
target_language_example: En la mesa había un libro abierto.
native_language_example: There was an open book on the table.

meaning: "there was a" (referring to a singular feminine noun).
additional_notes: Used with the verb haber (imperfect: había) to say something existed or was present in the past. Common for setting the scene/background or describing what was there. Because it uses "una," it must be followed by a feminine singular noun (e.g., una lluvia, una mezquita, una niebla). For masculine nouns, use "había un"; for plural, "había" + "unos/unas".
target_language_example: Cuando llegamos, había una tienda abierta cerca de la estación.
native_language_example: When we arrived, there was an open shop near the station.

meaning: "Once upon a time" (used to start a story).
additional_notes: Common opening in fairy tales and traditional stories. It literally uses the imperfect of haber ("había" = "there was/were") + "una vez" ("one time"). Typically followed by a noun phrase: "Había una vez un/una...".
target_language_example: Había una vez un niño que soñaba con volar.
native_language_example: Once upon a time there was a boy who dreamed of flying.

meaning: years ago; for years (it’s been years since…).
additional_notes: "Hace" + time period expresses elapsed time. With a specific past event: "pasó/ocurrió hace años" = "it happened years ago." With "Hace años que + present" it means "It’s been years that… / for years…" and often implies "since" (e.g., "Hace años que no nos hablamos" = "We haven’t spoken in years").
target_language_example: Hace años que no veo a mis abuelos.
native_language_example: I haven’t seen my grandparents in years.

additional_notes: Used to talk about the temperature, especially the weather or how a place feels. Spanish commonly uses “hacer” (“to make/do”) in weather expressions: hace calor (it’s hot), hace frío (it’s cold). You can add time phrases: Hoy hace calor (It’s hot today), En verano hace calor (It’s hot in summer).
target_language_example: Hoy hace calor, mejor nos quedamos en casa.
native_language_example: It’s hot today; it’s better we stay home.

meaning: five years ago; five years ago (for)
additional_notes: Used with the present tense to say how long ago something happened: "Me gradué hace cinco años" = "I graduated five years ago." It can also start a sentence: "Hace cinco años, ...". You can swap the number: "hace dos años" (two years ago), "hace diez años" (ten years ago).
target_language_example: Empecé este trabajo hace cinco años.
native_language_example: I started this job five years ago.
