meaning: ten years ago (ten years ago from now / from the time being talked about).
additional_notes: Used to talk about how long ago something happened. It’s built from "hace" (it has been/makes) + a time period. Very common pattern: "hace + [time]" (hace dos días, hace un mes, hace mucho tiempo). In some regions people also say "hace diez años atrás"—it means the same, but "hace diez años" is enough.
target_language_example: Empecé a estudiar español hace diez años.
native_language_example: I started studying Spanish ten years ago.

meaning: two years ago; two years ago/from now (when talking about how long ago something happened).
additional_notes: Used to talk about time elapsed since a past event: "hace + time period" = "... ago" (e.g., hace una semana, hace tres meses). It can appear at the beginning or end of the sentence. With duration, Spanish typically says "Hace dos años que..." or "Desde hace dos años..." (e.g., "Hace dos años que están casados" = "They’ve been married for two years").
target_language_example: Empecé a estudiar español hace dos años.
native_language_example: I started studying Spanish two years ago.

additional_notes: Used with a past action to say how long ago it happened: Hace + time period (hace dos días, hace una semana, hace un año). You can also see the pattern “Hace dos días que + present tense” to mean “It’s been two days since…” (duration up to now): Hace dos días que está ahí. In some regions people add “atrás” (hace dos días atrás), but “hace dos días” is enough and more standard.
target_language_example: Lo vi hace dos días.
native_language_example: I saw him two days ago.

additional_notes: Used to say how long ago something happened. In Spanish you often use **hace + time period** to mean “... ago”: *hace cinco minutos* (five minutes ago), *hace un año* (a year ago). It can appear at the beginning or end of the sentence.
target_language_example: Llegué hace dos horas, pero todavía estoy cansado.
native_language_example: I arrived two hours ago, but I’m still tired.

meaning: two weeks ago; two weeks ago (it has been two weeks).
additional_notes: Used to talk about a point in the past: "hace + time period" = "... ago" (e.g., hace dos semanas = two weeks ago). You can also use it with "que" to mean "it’s been ... since" something happened: "Hace dos semanas que llegué" = "I arrived two weeks ago / It’s been two weeks since I arrived."
target_language_example: Empecé este trabajo hace dos semanas.
native_language_example: I started this job two weeks ago.

meaning: "to be needed" / "to need"; "it’s not necessary" (no hace falta).
additional_notes: Used to talk about necessity or need. Common patterns: (1) "Hace falta + noun/infinitive" = "(It) is necessary/needed" (Hace falta tu sello. / Hace falta firmar.). (2) "A + person + le/te/me/nos hace falta + noun" = "Someone needs/lacks" (Le hace falta disciplina. / Me hace falta dinero.). (3) "Si hace falta" = "if necessary". Very common in everyday speech.
target_language_example: No hace falta que vengas mañana; ya lo resolvimos.
native_language_example: You don’t need to come tomorrow; we already solved it.

additional_notes: Used with the verb hacer to describe the weather: hace frío = it’s cold. You can add time/place: Aquí hace frío. / Hoy hace frío. Negation: No hace frío. Emphasis: Sí que hace frío = It really is cold.
target_language_example: En la montaña hace frío por la noche.
native_language_example: In the mountains it’s cold at night.

additional_notes: This phrase can change meaning depending on context. With hacer in its normal sense, it can mean someone does a lot: Hace mucho por su comunidad = He does a lot for his community. In time expressions, especially with que, it means 'a long time' or 'it's been a long time since.' With no, it often means 'not long ago.'
target_language_example: Hace mucho que no hablo con él.
native_language_example: I haven't spoken to him in a long time.

additional_notes: Used to talk about the weather. Spanish often uses **hacer** (“to make/do”) to describe weather conditions: **hace calor** = “it’s hot,” **hace frío** = “it’s cold.” **mucho** intensifies it (“very/a lot”). You can add time or place: **hace mucho calor hoy** (today), **en verano** (in summer), **en Japón** (in Japan).
target_language_example: En esta ciudad hace mucho calor en agosto.
native_language_example: In this city it’s very hot in August.

meaning: “it’s very hot in …” (talking about a place or time).
additional_notes: Use with a place (en Japón, en Madrid) or a time/season (en verano, en julio). The verb is always 3rd person singular: hace (not *hacen*), because Spanish uses “hacer” to talk about weather/temperature: Hace calor = It’s hot. You can change intensity: hace calor (it’s hot), hace mucho calor (it’s very hot). Word order is flexible: En verano hace mucho calor en Japón / En Japón hace mucho calor en verano.
target_language_example: En mi ciudad hace mucho calor en agosto.
native_language_example: In my city it’s very hot in August.

meaning: a long time ago; (it’s been) a long time.
additional_notes: Used to talk about something that happened far in the past, or to emphasize that a lot of time has passed. Often appears at the start of a sentence (Hace mucho tiempo visité París) or after a time reference (Hace mucho tiempo de eso). By itself (¡Hace mucho tiempo!) it means “It’s been a long time!”
target_language_example: No nos vemos hace mucho tiempo.
native_language_example: We haven’t seen each other in a long time.

meaning: many years ago; for many years (depending on context).
additional_notes: Used with time expressions to say how long ago something happened or how long something has been true. Common patterns: (1) "[Verb] hace muchos años" = "[verb] many years ago" (e.g., Desapareció hace muchos años). (2) "Hace muchos años que + [present]" = "I have been + -ing for many years / It’s been many years since..." (e.g., Hace muchos años que quiero ir...).
target_language_example: Nos conocimos hace muchos años.
native_language_example: We met many years ago.

additional_notes: Used to talk about something that happened not long ago. It often goes at the beginning of the sentence (Hace poco hablé con ella.) or before the verb (Él hace poco regresó.).
target_language_example: Hace poco empecé un trabajo nuevo.
native_language_example: I started a new job recently.

meaning: 'a long time ago' / 'for a long time (already)'.
additional_notes: Literally 'it makes time' (from hacer + tiempo). Used to say that something happened long ago (Hace tiempo, ... / ... hace tiempo) or that something has been true/going on for a long time: "Hace tiempo que" + present tense (Hace tiempo que lo pido = I've been asking for it for a long time). With the imperfect, it means 'it had been a long time since': "Hacía tiempo que no lo veía".
target_language_example: Hace tiempo que no hablamos.
native_language_example: We haven't talked in a long time.

meaning: “It’s been a long time since…” (I haven’t … for a long time).
additional_notes: Used to say that something has not happened for a long time. It’s often followed by a verb (usually in the present: “hace tiempo que no + [present]”, or in the past: “hace tiempo que no + [imperfect/pluperfect]” depending on context). It can also stand alone as a short reply: “Hace tiempo que no.” = “Not in a long time.”
target_language_example: Hace tiempo que no veo a mis amigos.
native_language_example: I haven’t seen my friends in a long time.

additional_notes: Used to say how long ago something happened. It uses "hace + time period" (literally "it makes/does + time"), often placed at the end of the sentence: "Llegué hace tres años." You can change the number/time unit: "hace dos días" (two days ago), "hace un mes" (a month ago), "hace mucho tiempo" (a long time ago).
target_language_example: Empecé a estudiar español hace tres años.
native_language_example: I started studying Spanish three years ago.

additional_notes: Used with a past event to say how long ago it happened. Spanish uses “hace + time period” for “ago”: hace tres días, hace una semana, hace dos años. It can go at the beginning or end of the sentence (Hace tres días ocurrió eso / Eso ocurrió hace tres días). You may also see “Hace tres días que + present tense” to mean “It’s been three days since…”
target_language_example: Llegué a Madrid hace tres días.
native_language_example: I arrived in Madrid three days ago.

additional_notes: Used to say how long ago something happened. It often goes with the past tense: "Se casaron hace tres meses". You may also hear "hace tres meses atrás" (redundant but common in some regions); "hace tres meses" is enough. Pattern: "hace + time period" (e.g., hace dos días, hace un año).
target_language_example: Empecé este trabajo hace tres meses.
native_language_example: I started this job three months ago.

additional_notes: Used to say how long ago something happened. It often appears with the imperfect or preterite (e.g., fue, sucedió, murió). You can swap in other time amounts: hace dos años (two years ago), hace un mes (a month ago), hace una semana (a week ago).
target_language_example: Me mudé aquí hace un año.
native_language_example: I moved here a year ago.

meaning: a month ago; for a month (up to now).
additional_notes: With a completed past action, it means “a month ago”: “Eso fue hace un mes.” With an action/state that continues to the present, Spanish often uses “desde hace un mes” to mean “for a month (now)”: “Está en el hospital desde hace un mes.” (In casual speech you may still hear “Está … hace un mes,” but “desde hace” is the standard form.)
target_language_example: Empecé este trabajo hace un mes.
native_language_example: I started this job a month ago.

meaning: a moment ago; just a moment ago.
additional_notes: Used to talk about something that happened a very short time before now. It commonly appears with the pattern "hace + time period" (e.g., hace dos días = two days ago). You can place it at the beginning or end of the sentence.
target_language_example: Te llamé hace un momento.
native_language_example: I called you a moment ago.

meaning: a little while ago; not long ago.
additional_notes: Used with expressions of time to say something happened recently in the past. Often used with the simple past (pretérito): "Se fue hace un rato" = "He/She left a little while ago." By itself ("Hace un rato."), it’s a short answer meaning “A little while ago.”
target_language_example: Llegué hace un rato, pero todavía no he comido.
native_language_example: I arrived a little while ago, but I still haven’t eaten.

additional_notes: Used to say how long ago something happened. It goes after the verb or at the end of the sentence: "Llamó hace una hora" (He called an hour ago). With other time amounts, you can swap the unit: "hace dos horas" (two hours ago), "hace un minuto" (a minute ago).
target_language_example: Salí de casa hace una hora.
native_language_example: I left home an hour ago.

additional_notes: Used with "hace + time period" to say how long ago something happened: "hace una semana" = "one week ago." It can also appear in "hace una semana que..." meaning "it’s been a week since..." (e.g., "Hoy hace una semana que la vi" = "Today it’s been a week since I saw her").
target_language_example: Empecé este trabajo hace una semana.
native_language_example: I started this job a week ago.

additional_notes: Used with past events to say how long ago something happened. "Hace" + time period works like "ago" in English (e.g., hace dos años = two years ago). Often placed at the end of the sentence: "Lo compramos hace unos años."
target_language_example: Empecé a estudiar español hace unos años.
native_language_example: I started studying Spanish a few years ago.

additional_notes: Used to say how long ago something happened (counting back from now). It often goes at the end of the sentence: “Lo vi hace unos días.” You can also put it at the beginning for emphasis: “Hace unos días, lo vi.”
target_language_example: Hablé con ella hace unos días.
native_language_example: I talked to her a few days ago.

meaning: to leak / to be taking on water; (figuratively) to be failing or falling apart.
additional_notes: Used literally for boats, roofs, pipes, etc. when they let water in or through: «El barco hace agua». Also used figuratively for a plan, argument, system, or team that has clear weaknesses and isn’t working well: «Tu explicación hace agua» (= it doesn’t hold up).
target_language_example: Nuestro plan para ahorrar dinero hace agua.
native_language_example: Our plan to save money is falling apart.

additional_notes: A very common general phrase for taking some action. Here, hacer usually means "do" rather than "make." It can also be used with por + alguien, as in hacer algo por ti, meaning "do something for you."
target_language_example: Tenemos que hacer algo ahora.
native_language_example: We have to do something now.

meaning: 'a few years ago' / 'for a few years' when used in the common time expressions **hace algunos años** ('a few years ago') and **desde hace algunos años** ('for/since a few years').
additional_notes: Although the dictionary form is **hacer algunos años**, in real usage you almost always see it conjugated as **hace algunos años** (3rd person singular present of *hacer*) in time expressions. Pattern: **hace + time period** = '... ago' (e.g., *Llegué hace algunos años* = 'I arrived a few years ago'). With **desde hace + time period**, it indicates duration up to now: 'for/since' (e.g., *Vivo aquí desde hace algunos años* = 'I’ve lived here for a few years').
target_language_example: Dicen que fue al norte por trabajo, después de hacer algunos años aquí.
native_language_example: They say he went north for work, after spending a few years here.

additional_notes: Used for the act of becoming friends with new people. Often appears with verbs like "tratar de" (to try to) or "costar" (to be difficult), e.g., "Me cuesta hacer amigos" = "I have a hard time making friends." You can also say "hacer amigos nuevos" (make new friends).
target_language_example: Me mudé hace poco y quiero hacer amigos en mi barrio.
native_language_example: I moved recently and I want to make friends in my neighborhood.

meaning: to have a birthday; to turn a certain age
additional_notes: A regional expression used in some Spanish-speaking areas for having a birthday or reaching a certain age. In more general Spanish, learners will more often hear cumplir años or cumplir X años.
target_language_example: Mañana voy a hacer años.
native_language_example: Tomorrow is my birthday.

additional_notes:
Common uses:
1) "hacer (algo) bien" = to do something well: "Lo vas a hacer bien" (You’re going to do it well).
2) "hacerle bien a alguien" = to be good for someone / to do someone good (often about health, mood, or stress): "Te va a hacer bien" / "Te va a hacer bien salir…" (It’ll do you good to get out…). The person helped is often an indirect object: me/te/le/nos/les.
target_language_example: Dormir un poco te va a hacer bien.
native_language_example: Sleeping a bit will do you good.

meaning: to do well to; to be right to (do something).
additional_notes: Used to give advice or a recommendation. It’s followed by an infinitive: "hacer bien en + infinitive" (to do well to...). Commonly conjugated: "Haces bien en..." (You’d do well to / You’re right to...), "Hizo bien en..." (He/She did well to...), "Hiciste bien en..." (You did well to...).
target_language_example: Creo que vas a hacer bien en llevar una chaqueta; hace frío.
native_language_example: I think you’d do well to bring a jacket; it’s cold.

additional_notes: Used in an impersonal weather expression, almost always in the 3rd person singular: "Hace buen tiempo" = "The weather is nice." You can also say "hace muy buen tiempo" (it’s very nice out) or use it in the past/future: "Hizo buen tiempo" / "Hará buen tiempo."
target_language_example: Parece que va a hacer buen tiempo mañana.
native_language_example: It looks like the weather is going to be nice tomorrow.

meaning: to redeem / validate (a voucher, coupon, ticket, etc.).
additional_notes: Common in shops and services with things like un vale (voucher), un cupón (coupon), un billete (ticket), un cheque (check): “hacer bueno” means to make it valid by using it or exchanging it for money/credit. It can also be used more figuratively in sports or plans (“hacer bueno el empate/el punto” = make it count), but the redeem/validate meaning is the most concrete.
target_language_example: Puedes hacer bueno este cupón en la caja.
native_language_example: You can redeem this coupon at the register.

additional_notes: Used to talk about the weather/temperature. It commonly appears with time expressions like hoy/mañana and with future forms: "va a hacer calor" (it’s going to be hot), "hará calor" (it will be hot). You can also use "hace calor" for present: "Aquí hace calor" (It’s hot here).
target_language_example: En verano suele hacer calor en esta ciudad.
native_language_example: In summer it’s usually hot in this city.

meaning: to build/pursue a career (in a profession or field).
additional_notes: Used to talk about developing your professional path over time, often with “en” or “como”: “hacer carrera en la medicina” (build a career in medicine), “hacer carrera como abogado/a” (build a career as a lawyer). It can also imply moving up and gaining experience in an organization.
target_language_example: Quiere hacer carrera en la empresa y algún día ser gerente.
native_language_example: He wants to build a career at the company and someday be a manager.

meaning: to pay attention (to); to listen to; to heed.
additional_notes: Often used with "a" + person/thing: "hacer caso a alguien/algo" (pay attention to / listen to someone/something). With "no" it means to ignore: "no hacer caso". You’ll also see it with "de" + noun, especially meaning “without paying attention to / disregarding”: "sin hacer caso del semáforo".
target_language_example: Hoy me tienes que hacer caso: no cruces la calle todavía.
native_language_example: Today you have to listen to me: don’t cross the street yet.

meaning: to wait in line; to queue up.
additional_notes: Used for standing/waiting in a line for something (tickets, a bus, an attraction, etc.). Often appears with "para" + infinitive (e.g., "hacer cola para entrar") or with "sin" to say you don’t have to wait in line ("sin hacer cola").
target_language_example: Tuvimos que hacer cola para comprar las entradas.
native_language_example: We had to wait in line to buy the tickets.

additional_notes: Used with an indirect object pronoun to say who is being tickled: "hacerle cosquillas a alguien" (to tickle someone). The thing that tickles can also be the subject: "Me hace cosquillas" (It tickles / It makes me tickle).
target_language_example: Deja de hacer cosquillas; ¡me da risa!
native_language_example: Stop tickling; it makes me laugh!

additional_notes: Often used with an indirect object pronoun to specify who is harmed: "hacerme daño" (hurt me), "hacerte daño" (hurt you), "hacerle daño" (hurt him/her), "hacernos daño" (hurt us). Can refer to physical or emotional harm. Also used in reassuring phrases like "Nadie te va a hacer daño" (No one is going to hurt you).
target_language_example: Nadie te va a hacer daño.
native_language_example: No one is going to hurt you.

meaning: to pretend; to act as if; to assume (“let’s say”).
additional_notes: Commonly used with "que": "Hacé/Haz de cuenta que..." = “Pretend that...” / “Let’s say that...”. It’s often used to propose an imaginary situation or simplify a problem. More common in Latin America; in Spain you might hear "hacer como si" more.
target_language_example: Vamos a hacer de cuenta que no pasó nada y seguimos.
native_language_example: Let’s pretend nothing happened and keep going.

meaning: to make money; to earn money.
additional_notes: Used for generating income or profit in general. Very common in business contexts, and it can also imply profiting from a situation: “hacer dinero de/con algo” = “to make money off/from something.”
target_language_example: Muchos quieren hacer dinero rápido, pero no es tan fácil.
native_language_example: Many people want to make money fast, but it’s not that easy.

meaning: “two days ago” (talking about how long ago something happened).
additional_notes: Used in an impersonal time expression with the verb “hacer” in the 3rd person singular: “Hace dos días” = “Two days ago.” It can also appear as “Hace dos días que...” = “It’s been two days since...” (e.g., “Hace dos días que no duermo” = “I haven’t slept in two days”). In running text you’ll almost always see it as “hace dos días” rather than the infinitive “hacer dos días.”
target_language_example: Te llamé hace dos días.
native_language_example: I called you two days ago.

additional_notes: In standard Spanish, this time expression is normally used as **hace dos horas** (3rd person singular of **hacer**) to mean “two hours ago” or “it’s been two hours.” The infinitive form **hacer dos horas** can appear after prepositions or in constructions like **debe de hacer dos horas** (“it must have been about two hours”), but **hace dos horas** is by far the most common standalone form.
target_language_example: Debe de hacer dos horas que salí de casa.
native_language_example: It must have been about two hours since I left home.

additional_notes: In real usage this almost always appears as **hace dos meses** (impersonal **hace** from *hacer*) to express elapsed time: **Hace dos meses (que)...** = “It’s been two months (since)...” or “two months ago,” depending on context. The infinitive **hacer dos meses** can appear after another verb (e.g., *van a*, *puede*, *debe*), but **hacer** here still has the special time-elapsed meaning, not “to do/make.”
target_language_example: Va a hacer dos meses que empecé este trabajo.
native_language_example: It’s going to be two months since I started this job.

meaning: 'two weeks ago' (in correct Spanish, this is usually said as: "hace dos semanas").
additional_notes:
In time expressions meaning "ago," Spanish uses the verb "hacer" conjugated in the 3rd person singular present: "hace". So the natural, idiomatic form is "hace dos semanas" (not the infinitive "hacer"). You may see "hacer" in dictionaries or as a base form, but in real sentences you’ll typically use:
- "Hace dos semanas" = two weeks ago
- "Hace dos semanas que + verb" = It’s been two weeks since...
Note: "hacer dos semanas" is not standard as a standalone phrase in a sentence; it would normally be "hace dos semanas".
target_language_example: Decir "hacer dos semanas" no es lo habitual; lo normal es decir "hace dos semanas".
native_language_example: Saying "hacer two weeks" isn’t what’s usual; normally you say "two weeks ago."

meaning: to take effect; to work (e.g., medicine).
additional_notes: Used when something starts producing the intended result. Common with medicine ("El medicamento hace efecto"), rules/laws ("La nueva ley hará efecto el lunes"), or actions like a joke or warning ("No hizo efecto"). Often used with the verb in the 3rd person: "hace efecto" / "hará efecto".
target_language_example: La medicina tardó una hora en hacer efecto.
native_language_example: The medicine took an hour to take effect.

additional_notes: A very common everyday phrase for doing physical activity for fitness/health. You can use it generally (Hago ejercicio) or with frequency words like regularmente/a diario (regularly/daily). Often appears with advice or obligation: Deberías / Debo / Tienes que hacer ejercicio. You can add a place or manner: hacer ejercicio afuera (outside), hacer ejercicio en el gimnasio (at the gym).
target_language_example: Intento hacer ejercicio tres veces por semana.
native_language_example: I try to work out three times a week.

additional_notes: A common, relatively euphemistic way to talk about having sex. It can sound romantic, but in some contexts it can also be direct/explicit. You can use it as: “hacer el amor con alguien” (to make love with someone).
target_language_example: No quiero hacer el amor si no nos sentimos cómodos.
native_language_example: I don't want to make love if we don't feel comfortable.

meaning: to play the role (of); to act as.
additional_notes: Used when someone performs a role in a movie/play, or when someone takes on a role in real life (e.g., “act as the boss/parent/mediator”). Often followed by "de" + noun: "hacer el papel de + profesión/persona".
target_language_example: En la película, ella va a hacer el papel de doctora.
native_language_example: In the movie, she is going to play the role of a doctor.

meaning: to make a fool of yourself; to embarrass yourself.
additional_notes: Used when someone does something that makes them look silly or causes embarrassment (often in public). Common with verbs like "no" (No hagas el ridículo) and in past tense (Hice el ridículo).
target_language_example: No quiero hacer el ridículo delante de todos.
native_language_example: I don't want to embarrass myself in front of everyone.

meaning: to act silly; to fool around; to play dumb.
additional_notes: Common, informal expression used to criticize someone for behaving foolishly or wasting time. Often used as a warning or complaint: "No hagas el tonto" (Stop fooling around). It can also imply pretending not to understand (playing dumb), depending on context.
target_language_example: Deja de hacer el tonto y termina la tarea.
native_language_example: Stop fooling around and finish the homework.

meaning: to do the job/work (complete the task).
additional_notes: Used for carrying out or completing a specific task or piece of work. Often appears with "me fue/resultó imposible" + infinitive ("it was impossible for me to...") or with someone "dispuesto a" + infinitive ("willing/ready to...").
target_language_example: Si quieres, yo puedo hacer el trabajo esta tarde.
native_language_example: If you want, I can do the work this afternoon.

additional_notes: A common, fully transparent phrase: hacer = "do/make" and eso = "that." It refers to an action already mentioned or understood from context. In many situations, English will use "do that."
target_language_example: No quiero hacer eso otra vez.
native_language_example: I don't want to do that again.

meaning: to make (someone) wait; to keep (someone) waiting.
additional_notes: Usually used with a direct object (a person): "Me hiciste esperar" = "You made me wait." In polite contexts you might apologize: "Perdón por hacer esperar a alguien" (sorry for keeping someone waiting). You can also use it in formal address: "hacerlo/la esperar" (to make him/her wait).
target_language_example: Perdón por hacer esperar a todos; el autobús llegó tarde.
native_language_example: Sorry for keeping everyone waiting; the bus arrived late.

additional_notes: Used to refer to performing a specific action that’s clear from context. Often follows verbs/phrases like "poder" (No puedes hacer esto.) or "tener que/deber" (Todo el mundo debe hacer esto.). "Esto" can be swapped with "eso" (that) depending on what you’re pointing to.
target_language_example: No sé cómo hacer esto sin ayuda.
native_language_example: I don’t know how to do this without help.

meaning: to be needed; to be necessary (also: to miss / to need someone, in some contexts)
additional_notes: Often used in an impersonal structure: “hacer falta + noun/infinitive” = “to be necessary/needed (to…)”. With an indirect object pronoun it can mean “(someone) needs (something)”: “me hace falta + noun” = “I need…”. In some regions (especially Latin America), it can also mean “to miss (someone) / to feel someone’s absence”: “me haces falta” = “I miss you / I need you.” Common negative: “no hace falta” = “there’s no need / it’s not necessary.” Note that the verb conjugates (hace, hacen, hacía, etc.), but the dictionary form is “hacer falta.”
target_language_example: No va a hacer falta comprar pan hoy.
native_language_example: We won’t need to buy bread today.

additional_notes: Used with a person (often with an indirect object pronoun like me/te/le/nos/les): “hacer feliz a alguien.” For emphasis you can add “a + name/person”: “hacer feliz a Mary.” In past/future you conjugate hacer: “hizo feliz a…”, “va a hacer feliz a…”, “hará feliz a…”.
target_language_example: Quiero hacer feliz a mi familia.
native_language_example: I want to make my family happy.

meaning: to party; to celebrate (by having a party).
additional_notes: Common in Latin America. It means to have/throw a party or to go out and have fun partying. Often used with a time expression ("el sábado", "esta noche") or a reason ("por mi cumpleaños").
target_language_example: Este fin de semana vamos a hacer fiesta en mi casa.
native_language_example: This weekend we're going to have a party at my house.

meaning: to face; to deal with (a problem).
additional_notes: Used for confronting a difficult situation (stress, a conflict, a challenge): "hacer frente a la ansiedad / al conflicto". It can also mean physically facing someone (standing in front of them), similar to "to face" in English: "hacer frente a los estudiantes". It’s usually followed by "a" + noun/infinitive.
target_language_example: Tenemos que hacer frente a este problema juntos.
native_language_example: We have to face/deal with this problem together.

additional_notes: Used to talk about the weather being cold. It’s an impersonal expression, so you typically say: "Hace frío" (It’s cold), "Va a hacer frío" (It’s going to be cold), "Debe (de) hacer frío" (It must be cold), and you can add time/place: "en invierno", "por la noche", "a la noche" (regional). Not used for people; for a person you’d say "tener frío" (to feel cold).
target_language_example: Debe hacer frío en invierno, así que lleva una chaqueta.
native_language_example: It must be cold in winter, so bring a jacket.

additional_notes: Most commonly used with an indirect object pronoun: "me/te/le/nos/les hace gracia" = "I/you/he/she/we/they find it funny" or "it amuses me/you/...". Depending on context, it can also mean you like something in a light way ("¿Te hace gracia?" = "Do you like it?/Does it appeal to you?").
target_language_example: Ese chiste me hizo hacer gracia.
native_language_example: That joke made me laugh / I found that joke funny.

meaning: to make history (to do something historic).
additional_notes: Used when someone achieves something very important or unprecedented (in politics, sports, science, etc.). Literally it’s “to do history,” but the natural English translation is “to make history.” In examples, the phrase will often be conjugated (e.g., "hizo historia"), but the base term is "hacer historia".
target_language_example: Con esta victoria, el equipo va a hacer historia.
native_language_example: With this victory, the team is going to make history.

meaning: to make someone happy/excited; to look forward to something.
additional_notes: Commonly used with an indirect object pronoun: "me/te/le/nos/os/les hace ilusión". It usually expresses positive anticipation about a plan or future event (similar to “I’m really looking forward to it”), not a literal “making an illusion.”
target_language_example: Me hace ilusión hacer ilusión a mi hermana con esta sorpresa.
native_language_example: I’m excited to make my sister happy with this surprise.

meaning: to match; to go well together (colors/clothes/objects).
additional_notes: Used to say that two things look good together or coordinate in style/color. Very common with the preposition “con”: “hacer juego con” = “to match/go with.” Often used when talking about clothing, accessories, furniture, or decoration.
target_language_example: Estos zapatos van a hacer juego con tu vestido.
native_language_example: These shoes are going to match your dress.

additional_notes: Common daily routine phrase meaning to tidy the bed after sleeping (straighten sheets/blankets and arrange pillows). Not usually about building/assembling a bed.
target_language_example: Todos los días tengo que hacer la cama antes de salir de casa.
native_language_example: Every day I have to make the bed before leaving the house.

additional_notes: Used when you prepare your luggage for a trip. Often said as "Tengo que hacer la maleta" (I have to pack) or "Haz la maleta" (Pack your bag). You can also pluralize it: "hacer las maletas" = to pack (everyone’s bags) / to pack up to leave.
target_language_example: Tengo que hacer la maleta esta noche porque mañana salgo temprano.
native_language_example: I have to pack tonight because I’m leaving early tomorrow.

meaning: to make someone’s life (easy/hard/miserable), typically used with an adjective (e.g., “imposible”, “difícil”, “feliz”) and an indirect object pronoun.
additional_notes: Most commonly appears in the pattern “hacer la vida + adjective + a alguien” or “hacerle la vida + adjective + a alguien” (e.g., “hacerle la vida imposible a alguien”). By itself, “hacer la vida” is uncommon; it usually needs an adjective to sound natural. The indirect object pronoun (me/te/le/nos/les) marks who is affected.
target_language_example: Ese jefe me hace la vida imposible.
native_language_example: That boss makes my life impossible.

additional_notes: A general way to talk about actions or tasks without naming them specifically. Often used with adverbs like mejor (better), bien (well), or rápido (quickly).
target_language_example: Tenemos que hacer las cosas con calma.
native_language_example: We have to do things calmly.

meaning: to make up (after an argument); to reconcile.
additional_notes: Used when two people stop being angry at each other and return to good terms. Often used with "con": "Hice las paces con mi hermano" (I made up with my brother).
target_language_example: Después de discutir, decidimos hacer las paces.
native_language_example: After arguing, we decided to make up.

meaning: to send/forward; to make sure something reaches someone.
additional_notes: Often used when you’re passing along a message or delivering something indirectly (through another person or method). It commonly takes an indirect object pronoun: "hacerle llegar" / "hacerles llegar" = "to get it to him/her/them" / "to pass it on to him/her/them". Frequently used in polite or formal contexts (emails, requests).
target_language_example: ¿Puedes hacer llegar este mensaje a Laura, por favor?
native_language_example: Can you please pass this message on to Laura?

additional_notes: Uses the verb hacer (“to make”) + llorar (“to cry”). It typically takes a direct object (the person who ends up crying): No me hagas llorar. You can also use an indirect object pronoun when the person affected is expressed that way: Me hizo llorar.
target_language_example: No me hagas llorar.
native_language_example: Don’t make me cry.

additional_notes: Used when talking about acting morally or appropriately, even if it’s difficult or unpleasant. Often appears with expressions like "tener que" (have to) or "tratar de" (try to): "Tengo que hacer lo correcto."
target_language_example: Aunque sea difícil, voy a hacer lo correcto.
native_language_example: Even if it’s hard, I’m going to do the right thing.

meaning: to do whatever it takes; to do anything (necessary).
additional_notes: Used to express willingness to do any action needed to achieve a goal or solve a problem. Often followed by a purpose with "para" (e.g., "Voy a hacer lo que sea para ayudarte"). In negative contexts it can also mean “anything at all” ("No haría lo que sea por dinero" = I wouldn’t do just anything for money).
target_language_example: Voy a hacer lo que sea para conseguir ese trabajo.
native_language_example: I’m going to do whatever it takes to get that job.

additional_notes: Used before a clause to mean doing the thing that someone wants, says, or considers best: hacer lo que + clause. It is a compositional phrase built from hacer ('to do/to make') and lo que ('what' / 'that which').
target_language_example: Voy a hacer lo que me dijiste.
native_language_example: I'm going to do what you told me.

meaning: to do my job / to do my work.
additional_notes: Used when you mean doing your responsibilities or tasks (at a job or in a role). Often said to ask someone not to interfere: “Déjame hacer mi trabajo” (Let me do my job). You can swap the possessive to match the person: hacer tu trabajo (your), hacer su trabajo (his/her/their/your formal), hacer nuestro trabajo (our).
target_language_example: Por favor, déjame hacer mi trabajo en paz.
native_language_example: Please, let me do my job in peace.

additional_notes: Used with the verb hacer to talk about weather/temperature: Hace mucho frío. You can change the intensity: hace frío (it’s cold), hace bastante frío (it’s pretty cold), hace muchísimo frío (it’s extremely cold). In questions: ¿Hace mucho frío afuera?
target_language_example: En invierno puede hacer mucho frío en esta ciudad, así que llevo guantes.
native_language_example: In winter it can be very cold in this city, so I carry gloves.

meaning: to make a lot of noise.
additional_notes: Used to talk about people, animals, machines, music, etc. causing loud sounds. The verb is often conjugated (e.g., "no hagas mucho ruido"), but the base expression is "hacer mucho ruido".
target_language_example: Los vecinos suelen hacer mucho ruido por la noche.
native_language_example: The neighbors usually make a lot of noise at night.

meaning: 'a long time ago' / 'it's been a long time'.
additional_notes: Used most commonly in the impersonal construction **hace mucho tiempo** to say how long ago something happened or how long it’s been since something happened. Common patterns: **Hace mucho tiempo, ...** (A long time ago, ...); **Hace mucho tiempo que + present** (It’s been a long time since ...): *Hace mucho tiempo que no lo veo.* Note: here **hacer** is impersonal and means “to have (time)”—it doesn’t literally mean “to make.”
target_language_example: Hacer mucho tiempo sin vernos me pone nostálgico.
native_language_example: Not seeing each other for a long time makes me feel nostalgic.

meaning: 'many years ago' (typically used as: "hace muchos años").
additional_notes: This entry is listed under the infinitive "hacer", but in actual Spanish you almost always use the conjugated impersonal form "hace" in this time expression: "hace + time period" = "... ago". You may see it referenced as "hacer muchos años" in dictionaries/phrase lists, but in sentences it appears as "hace muchos años" (present tense, impersonal). Similar patterns: "hace dos años" (two years ago), "hace mucho" (a long time ago).
target_language_example: Recuerdo haberlo visto por última vez; eso debió de ser hacer muchos años.
native_language_example: I remember having seen him for the last time; that must have been many years ago.

additional_notes: Usually used with "no" to mean "do anything" in negative sentences (e.g., "No puedo hacer nada" = "I can't do anything"). Without "no" it can mean "do nothing" (e.g., "Hice nada" = "I did nothing"), though in everyday Spanish people more often say "No hice nada". Common pattern: "no poder hacer nada" = "can’t do anything / there’s nothing (someone) can do."
target_language_example: Lo siento, ahora mismo no puedo hacer nada para ayudarte.
native_language_example: Sorry, right now I can’t do anything to help you.

meaning: to make (someone) pay; to make (someone) pay for something (often as punishment/revenge).
additional_notes: Commonly used with an indirect object pronoun (me/te/le/nos/les): "hacerle pagar" = "make him/her pay". You can add "por" to specify the reason: "hacer pagar por algo" = "make (someone) pay for something". Can be literal (forcing payment) or figurative (punish/seek revenge).
target_language_example: Te voy a hacer pagar por lo que hiciste.
native_language_example: I’m going to make you pay for what you did.

meaning: to smash/tear to pieces; to destroy completely.
additional_notes: Often used literally for breaking something into many pieces ("Hizo pedazos el vaso") and also figuratively for ruining something or someone (plans, a team, someone’s confidence). Commonly used with pronouns: "hacerlo/hacerla pedazos" = “smash it to pieces.”
target_language_example: El niño empezó a hacer pedazos el juguete sin querer.
native_language_example: The kid started to smash the toy to pieces by accident.

additional_notes: Common everyday way to say you need to urinate. Often used with "tener ganas de" (to feel like/need to) or "tener que" / "necesitar" (to have to / to need to). More casual than "orinar" and less crude than "mear"; used with kids too.
target_language_example: Perdón, ¿dónde puedo hacer pis?
native_language_example: Sorry, where can I pee?

additional_notes: A very common phrase. Use it with a person (often with “a”) or about a topic (with “sobre”). Also used in rules/advice with “no hacer preguntas” (“don’t ask questions”) and in the pattern “sin hacer preguntas” (“without asking questions”).
target_language_example: Si no entiendes, puedes hacer preguntas al profesor.
native_language_example: If you don’t understand, you can ask the teacher questions.

meaning: to make (something) come true; to make real.
additional_notes: Used with hopes, plans, goals, or dreams to mean turning an idea into reality. Often appears as “hacer realidad un sueño” (make a dream come true). Can also be used in passive form: “se hizo realidad” = “it came true.”
target_language_example: Trabajó mucho para hacer realidad su proyecto.
native_language_example: He worked hard to make his project a reality.

additional_notes: Often used with “sin” to mean “without making noise” (quietly), especially as an instruction: “sin hacer ruido”. You can use it for people or things making noise.
target_language_example: Cierra la puerta sin hacer ruido, por favor.
native_language_example: Close the door without making noise, please.

meaning: to be sunny (said about the weather).
additional_notes: Used with impersonal "hacer" to talk about weather: "Hace sol" = "It’s sunny." You can specify time/place: "Hoy hace sol", "Aquí hace sol". Common related patterns: "Hace sol y calor" (sunny and hot), "No hace sol" (it’s not sunny).
target_language_example: Hoy va a hacer sol, así que vamos al parque.
native_language_example: It’s going to be sunny today, so we’re going to the park.

meaning: to make (something) sound; to ring; to sound (an alarm, horn, etc.).
additional_notes: Used with an object (what you make sound): hacer sonar el timbre/la alarma/el teléfono/la bocina. Often implies intentional action to produce a sound (ring a doorbell, sound an alarm, honk a horn).
target_language_example: Por favor, voy a hacer sonar el timbre cuando llegue.
native_language_example: Please, I’m going to ring the doorbell when I arrive.

additional_notes: Commonly used to talk about doing school homework. In many places you’ll also hear "hacer la tarea" (with "la") or "hacer los deberes" (especially in Spain). Without an article, "hacer tarea" can sound more generic or regional, but it’s still understood in context.
target_language_example: Tengo que hacer tarea antes de cenar.
native_language_example: I have to do homework before dinner.

meaning: to do everything possible; to do your best.
additional_notes: Used to say you will make your maximum effort to achieve something or solve a problem. Often followed by "para" + infinitive ("hacer todo lo posible para ayudar") or "por" + infinitive ("hacer todo lo posible por llegar a tiempo").
target_language_example: Voy a hacer todo lo posible para llegar a tiempo.
native_language_example: I’m going to do everything I can to arrive on time.

additional_notes: Used for cheating on a test, in a game, or in any situation where you gain an unfair advantage by not following the rules. Often appears as "hacer trampa en" + activity (e.g., "hacer trampa en el examen").
target_language_example: No puedes hacer trampa en el examen, por favor.
native_language_example: You can’t cheat on the exam, please.

meaning: "to be three months ago" / used to express "three months ago" or "it’s been three months."
additional_notes: Commonly appears as the impersonal time expression "hacer + time period" (most often conjugated as "hace" in the present): "Hace tres meses" = "Three months ago" / "It’s been three months." It can also be used with "que" + clause to mean "It’s been three months since…" Note: the dictionary form "hacer tres meses" is typically seen as an entry, but in real sentences you usually conjugate it (e.g., "hace tres meses", "hacía tres meses").
target_language_example: No nos vemos desde hacer tres meses.
native_language_example: We haven’t seen each other since three months ago.

meaning: “(to be) three weeks ago” / “three weeks (have passed)”.
additional_notes: In real sentences this is almost always used as the impersonal expression **hace tres semanas** (not the infinitive *hacer*): **Hace tres semanas** = “three weeks ago.” The infinitive **hacer tres semanas** most commonly appears after another verb (e.g., *van a*, *pueden*, *deben*) or in more formal/written contexts where an infinitive phrase is needed. You can also use **Hace tres semanas que + verb** to mean “It’s been three weeks since …”: **Hace tres semanas que no te veo** = “I haven’t seen you in three weeks.”
target_language_example: Debe de hacer tres semanas que empecé este trabajo.
native_language_example: It must have been about three weeks since I started this job.

meaning: to make a deal with; to come to an agreement with.
additional_notes: Used when two people or groups agree on an exchange or arrangement (often with conditions). Very common in business, negotiations, or everyday arrangements. You can also say “llegar a un trato con” or simply “hacer un trato” when the other party is clear from context.
target_language_example: Para cerrar el asunto, voy a hacer un trato con el propietario: yo pago hoy y él me da las llaves mañana.
native_language_example: To settle the matter, I'm going to make a deal with the landlord: I pay today and he gives me the keys tomorrow.

additional_notes: A common everyday way to talk about placing a phone call. It often appears with phrases like "Necesito..." (I need to...), "Déjame..." (Let me...), and can be modified: "hacer una llamada urgente" (make an urgent call).
target_language_example: Voy a salir un momento para hacer una llamada.
native_language_example: I’m going to step out for a moment to make a call.

meaning: to work a few hours (often extra hours).
additional_notes: Used when talking about spending some time working, especially picking up a short shift or doing a bit of overtime. You’ll also hear "hacer horas" (to do overtime) and "hacer horas extra" (to work extra hours).
target_language_example: Hoy voy a hacer unas horas en la tienda después de clase.
native_language_example: Today I’m going to work a few hours at the store after class.

meaning: 'a few days ago' (normally used as **hace unos días** in time-elapsed expressions).
additional_notes: This expression is typically used conjugated in the impersonal construction **hace + time period** to mean “... ago.” The infinitive **hacer** is not the most natural form in a full sentence, but it can appear after verbs like *decir*, *recordar*, *creer*, etc., when talking about time elapsed (e.g., *Recuerdo hacer unos días...*). Much more common: *hace unos días*, *hace una semana*, *hace dos horas*.
target_language_example: Recuerdo hacer unos días que no hablaba con ella.
native_language_example: I remember it had been a few days since I’d spoken with her.

meaning: to have a (social) life; to spend time and be active (in a place).
additional_notes: Often used with a place: “hacer vida en + lugar” = to live there in an active way (go out, socialize, have routines), similar to “to have a life” or “to spend time” somewhere. Common in contexts like a new city/neighborhood (“No conozco a nadie aquí, no hago vida”).
target_language_example: Desde que me mudé, intento hacer vida en el barrio.
native_language_example: Since I moved, I’m trying to have a life in the neighborhood.

additional_notes: Weather expression used with "hacer" + a weather noun. It’s typically impersonal: "Hace viento" (not *"hace el viento"*). You can add intensity: "Hace mucho viento" (It’s very windy).
target_language_example: Parece que va a hacer viento, así que lleva una chaqueta.
native_language_example: It looks like it’s going to be windy, so bring a jacket.

additional_notes: “Hacerlo” means “to do it” (hacer + the object pronoun “lo”). “Con” introduces what you do it with, and can express: (1) manner: “hacerlo con prisa” (do it in a hurry), (2) resources/means: “hacerlo con lo que tenemos” (do it with what we have), or (3) accompaniment: “hacerlo con Alberto” (do it with Alberto).
target_language_example: No puedo hacerlo con esta herramienta; necesito otra.
native_language_example: I can’t do it with this tool; I need another.

meaning: to take responsibility for; to take charge of.
additional_notes: Used when someone accepts responsibility for something (a task, a person, a situation, a business). It often appears with "de": "hacerse cargo de" + noun/pronoun. Common in family/work contexts (e.g., taking over a business, taking care of a child).
target_language_example: Ninguno de sus hijos quería hacerse cargo del negocio.
native_language_example: None of his/her children wanted to take responsibility for the business.

meaning: to get dark; for night to fall.
additional_notes: Used to talk about the time of day changing as evening arrives. Often appears with “cuando” or “ya” (e.g., “Cuando se hace de noche…” / “Ya se hace de noche…”). Similar to “anochecer.”
target_language_example: Nos volvemos a casa cuando empieza a hacerse de noche.
native_language_example: We go back home when it starts to get dark.

meaning: to pretend to be; to pose as; to impersonate.
additional_notes: Used when someone presents themselves as another person or as having a certain identity/role, often to deceive. It’s followed by a noun (often a person/role): hacerse pasar por médico / por tu hermano / por un cliente. Conjugates as a pronominal verb (hacerse): me hago pasar por…, se hace pasar por…, se hicieron pasar por…
target_language_example: Para entrar al edificio, se hace pasar por policía.
native_language_example: To get into the building, he pretends to be a police officer.

meaning: to make people like you; to endear yourself
additional_notes: Reflexive expression meaning to win others over and earn their affection through one’s manner or actions. Often appears with a complement indicating by whom or how: “hacerse querer por todos” (to be liked by everyone), “hacerse querer con detalles” (to endear yourself with little gestures). близко по смыслу to “ganarse el cariño (de alguien)” (to win someone’s affection).
target_language_example: En la oficina supo hacerse querer desde el primer día.
native_language_example: At the office, she/he managed to make everyone like her/him from the very first day.

meaning: to get late (time passes and it becomes late).
additional_notes: Used to say that time has gone by and now it’s later than expected, often as a reason to leave or hurry. Common pattern: “Se hace tarde” = “It’s getting late.” You can add “ya” for emphasis: “Ya se hace tarde.”
target_language_example: Se va a hacer tarde si no nos vamos ya.
native_language_example: It’s going to get late if we don’t leave now.

additional_notes: Uses the verb phrase hacer una pregunta (“to ask a question”) plus the indirect object pronoun te (“to you”). Commonly used to politely introduce a question: Quería/Quiero hacerte una pregunta (“I wanted/I want to ask you a question”). You can swap te for other pronouns: hacerle una pregunta (to ask him/her/you [formal] a question), hacerles una pregunta (to ask you all/them a question).
target_language_example: Perdona, ¿puedo hacerte una pregunta?
native_language_example: Sorry, can I ask you a question?

meaning: to ask you a few questions.
additional_notes: Common, polite way to say you want to ask someone some questions. Literally it’s “to make you some questions,” but English uses “ask,” not “make.” Structure: hacer + indirect object pronoun (te = to you) + unas preguntas (“some/a few questions”). You can change the pronoun: hacerle unas preguntas (to ask him/her/you-formal), hacerles unas preguntas (to ask them/you all). Often used with acerca de / sobre / con respecto a (about/regarding).
target_language_example: ¿Puedo hacerte unas preguntas sobre el trabajo?
native_language_example: Can I ask you a few questions about the job?

additional_notes: Used to indicate direction or movement toward something lower. Often follows verbs like presionar (press), mirar (look), apuntar (point), caer (fall). It can describe either motion (push downward) or where you direct your gaze (look down).
target_language_example: Baja la cabeza y mira hacia abajo.
native_language_example: Lower your head and look down.

additional_notes: Used to indicate movement in the direction of the speaker’s location (“here”). Often goes with verbs of motion like venir, ir, correr, caminar. Similar to "para acá", but "hacia acá" focuses more on direction (toward) than destination (to).
target_language_example: Camina hacia acá, por favor.
native_language_example: Walk over here, please.

additional_notes: Used to indicate direction: toward the front or toward what’s in front of you. Common in giving directions ("Sigue hacia adelante") and in physical movement/position (leaning or looking forward). By itself ("Hacia adelante."), it can be a short instruction meaning “Forward.”
target_language_example: Sigue hacia adelante y dobla a la derecha en la esquina.
native_language_example: Go straight ahead and turn right at the corner.

additional_notes: Used to indicate movement or direction toward the speaker’s location (or the place where the speaker is pointing). Common with verbs of motion like venir (to come), empujar (to push), lanzar (to throw), and in commands. Often interchangeable with "para acá" in everyday speech.
target_language_example: Ven hacia aquí un momento, por favor.
native_language_example: Come over here for a moment, please.

additional_notes: Often used with verbs of movement or direction (e.g., mirar/levantar/tirar hacia arriba = look/lift/pull up). It can also mean “up to/alongside” in driving/parking contexts (e.g., tirar hacia arriba hasta el bordillo = pull up to the curb). In expressions like “de cintura hacia arriba,” it means “from the waist up.”
target_language_example: Levanta las manos hacia arriba.
native_language_example: Raise your hands up.

additional_notes: Used to describe movement or direction toward the back (walk/drive/step back) or movement in reverse. Also used as a short directional instruction: “Hacia atrás.” = “Back/Backwards.” In some contexts it can mean something is reversed or the wrong way around (e.g., “Tienes todo hacia atrás.” = “You have everything backwards.”).
target_language_example: Da un paso hacia atrás, por favor.
native_language_example: Take a step back, please.

additional_notes: Used to indicate direction (movement or orientation) toward the north. Often follows verbs of movement like ir, seguir, caminar, conducir: "Vamos/Sigan hacia el norte". Can also be used alone as a short direction: "Hacia el norte."
target_language_example: Camina hacia el norte hasta la próxima calle.
native_language_example: Walk north (toward the north) until the next street.

additional_notes: Used to describe movement or direction in the sense of “heading toward” a place or point on the compass. Often follows verbs like ir, dirigirse, moverse, navegar, poner rumbo, etc. (Note: “al oeste” usually means “to the west (of something),” while “hacia el oeste” emphasizes the direction of travel.)
target_language_example: Conduce hacia el oeste por la autopista.
native_language_example: Drive west on the highway.

additional_notes: Used with movement verbs to show direction (Ir/Volar/Caminar hacia el sur = “go/fly/walk south”). With places/things like windows or a house, it often means the direction they face (Mirar hacia el sur = “to face south”). Often answers “¿Hacia dónde?” (“Which direction?”).
target_language_example: Conduce hacia el sur y verás el mar.
native_language_example: Drive south and you’ll see the sea.

additional_notes: Used to indicate direction or movement/orientation (where to look, turn, or head). Often follows verbs like mirar (to look) or girar (to turn). You can also hear it alone as an instruction: “Hacia la izquierda.”
target_language_example: Gira hacia la izquierda en la próxima calle.
native_language_example: Turn left at the next street.

additional_notes: "Hacia" means "toward" (movement or direction), and "mí" is the object pronoun "me" used after a preposition. It’s used with verbs of movement or gestures: "venir/caminar/correr hacia mí" (come/walk/run toward me), "mirar hacia mí" (look toward me), "tender la mano hacia mí" (reach a hand toward me). Note the accent: "mí" (me) vs. "mi" (my).
target_language_example: El perro corrió hacia mí cuando abrí la puerta.
native_language_example: The dog ran toward me when I opened the door.

additional_notes: Used to say that an action is morally right or the best choice. It often appears with forms of "estar" (estoy/estás/está/estamos) and can be followed by "al" + infinitive to explain what the right action is (e.g., "haciendo lo correcto al ayudar").
target_language_example: Sé que es difícil, pero estás haciendo lo correcto al decir la verdad.
native_language_example: I know it’s hard, but you’re doing the right thing by telling the truth.

additional_notes: Used to describe past weather. "Hacía" is the imperfect of "hacer" used for general conditions (especially weather): "hace frío" (it’s cold), "hacía frío" (it was cold). "Mucho" intensifies it: very/really cold. Often followed by a time expression: "ayer", "por la noche", "durante...".
target_language_example: En la montaña hacía mucho frío, así que nos quedamos en casa.
native_language_example: In the mountains it was very cold, so we stayed home.

additional_notes: Very polite/formal way to ask someone to do something; it uses the usted command form (haga). Often followed by an infinitive (haga el favor de + verb). Common in service situations or when you want to sound extra courteous; with the wrong tone it can also sound a bit stern.
target_language_example: Haga el favor de cerrar la puerta, por favor.
native_language_example: Please close the door.

additional_notes: From the verb cambiar (“to change”) in the present perfect: haber (han) + past participle (cambiado). Used to say that something has changed up to now, often with time expressions like “en los últimos…”, “desde entonces”, or “nunca”. The subject is plural: ellos/ellas/ustedes, or a plural thing (las reglas, las circunstancias).
target_language_example: Desde el año pasado, las cosas han cambiado mucho.
native_language_example: Since last year, things have changed a lot.

additional_notes:
Used with a plural subject to talk about something that has fallen, dropped, decreased, or (for places) been captured/defeated: Las hojas han caído. Los precios han caído. Ciudades han caído a manos de… 
Often appears with an indirect object pronoun and 'se' to show an accidental drop: Se me han caído… (I dropped… / …fell on me by accident), Se te han caído… (you dropped…).
target_language_example: Se nos han caído las llaves en la calle.
native_language_example: We dropped the keys in the street.

meaning: “they have given” / “they gave” (present perfect of dar).
additional_notes: Used with an implied subject (ellos/ellas/ustedes). Common with object pronouns: me/te/le/nos/les han dado… (“they’ve given me/you/him/us/them…”). With "dar a" it can mean “to hit / to shoot (and hit)”: ¿Le han dado a X? = “Did they hit X?”
target_language_example: Me han dado la llave del cuarto.
native_language_example: They gave me the room key.

additional_notes: Present perfect of decidir (to decide): ellos/ellas/ustedes han decidido + infinitive (han decidido no comprar…) or + que + clause (han decidido que…). In many contexts it can be translated as either “have decided” or simple past “decided,” depending on how recent/relevant the decision is.
target_language_example: Mis padres han decidido mudarse a otra ciudad.
native_language_example: My parents have decided to move to another city.

additional_notes: Used with a past participle to describe an activity that has been happening recently or up to now: "Han estado rastreando..." = "They've been tracking...". It can also mean "have been" in a state/situation: "Han estado juntos" (have been together), "han estado casados" (have been married), "nunca han estado con una mujer" (have never been with a woman). Sometimes it's used in set phrases like "ha(n) estado a la venta" = "has/have been on sale".
target_language_example: Últimamente han estado trabajando hasta tarde.
native_language_example: Lately, they've been working late.

additional_notes: Used with the auxiliary verb **haber** (**han**) + past participle **hecho** to talk about something **they** did at an unspecified time in the past that matters now (often used like English “have done”). The subject can be explicit (**ellos/ellas/ustedes**) or implied by context.
target_language_example: No sé qué han hecho, pero están muy felices.
native_language_example: I don’t know what they’ve done, but they’re very happy.

additional_notes: Present perfect of "llegar" (to arrive): haber (han) + past participle (llegado). Used with a plural subject (they/you all). Often followed by "a" + place: "Han llegado a Madrid." You can negate it: "No han llegado todavía" = "They haven't arrived yet."
target_language_example: Ya han llegado los invitados.
native_language_example: The guests have already arrived.

additional_notes: Present perfect of pasar (to pass) with an implied subject like el tiempo / los años / los meses (“time/years/months have passed”). Often used with a time expression (Han pasado cinco años) or with desde que / desde (“since”) to say how much time has passed since something happened. It can also be used more generally with cosas (“things/events have happened”).
target_language_example: Han pasado dos semanas desde que empezé el trabajo.
native_language_example: Two weeks have passed since I started the job.

additional_notes: Present perfect of ser: haber (han) + past participle (sido). Used with plural subjects (ellos/ellas/ustedes) to talk about states or situations that have happened up to now or have present relevance. Often followed by an adjective or past participle (e.g., han sido intensas, han sido leídos).
target_language_example: Este año las clases han sido interesantes.
native_language_example: This year the classes have been interesting.

meaning: "have been" (they/you all have been) — present perfect of *ser*.
additional_notes: Formed by **han** (present of *haber*) + **sido** (past participle of *ser*). It’s used to talk about what someone/something **has been** up to now or in a recent past with relevance to the present: *Han sido muy amables* (They’ve been very kind). It can also appear in impersonal/time expressions: *Han sido necesarias casi dos semanas...* (“It has taken/almost two weeks have been necessary...”). In some contexts it can mean “it was/they were” when identifying who did something: *Seguro que han sido esos delincuentes* (“I’m sure it was those criminals”).
target_language_example: ¿Dónde han sido tus vacaciones este año?
native_language_example: Where have your vacations been this year?

additional_notes: Present perfect: haber (han) + past participle (visto). Used for experiences or things seen up to now. Often means “they have seen” (ellos/ellas/ustedes), with the subject understood from context.
target_language_example: ¿Ya han visto la película?
native_language_example: Have you all seen the movie yet?

additional_notes: Used to introduce a clause with what you will do, often followed by subjunctive (e.g., "haré lo que me pidas"). Common extensions: "haré lo que sea necesario" (I’ll do whatever is necessary), "haré lo que tenga que hacer" (I’ll do what I have to do), "haré lo que usted quiera" (I’ll do what you want).
target_language_example: No te preocupes: haré lo que haga falta.
native_language_example: Don’t worry: I’ll do whatever is needed.

meaning: “you have left” / “you have let (allowed)” (present perfect of *dejar*).
additional_notes: *Has dejado* = **haber (has) + past participle (dejado)**. It’s used for past actions with a connection to the present (“you’ve left/you’ve allowed/you’ve stopped/you’ve abandoned”). Common patterns: **has dejado entrar** (you let [someone] in), **has dejado a alguien** (you left someone / broke up with someone), **has dejado atrás** (you left behind), **has dejado reposar** (you let [it] rest), **te has dejado X** (you left/forgot X), **has dejado plantado** (you stood [someone] up).
target_language_example: ¿Por qué has dejado la puerta abierta?
native_language_example: Why did you leave the door open?

meaning: 'you have said' / 'you said' (present perfect of *decir*, informal singular).
additional_notes: Used with **tú** to talk about what someone has said, often with **que**: *Has dicho que...* (“You said that…”). In many contexts it translates as simple past in English (“you said”), especially when referring to something just said or relevant now. Negative: *No has dicho...*; also common in questions/complaints: *Aún no me has dicho...* (“You still haven’t told me…”).
target_language_example: ¿Por qué has dicho eso?
native_language_example: Why did you say that?

additional_notes: Used with tú to say someone has been in a place or state up to now (or at some time before now that matters in the present). Often followed by an adjective (ausente, enfermo), a place (ahí, en casa), or a gerund to show an ongoing/repeated action (has estado dando vueltas = “you’ve been hanging around/going around”).
target_language_example: ¿Has estado en México alguna vez?
native_language_example: Have you ever been to Mexico?

additional_notes: Present perfect of oír (“to hear”), used to ask if someone heard something or to say they have. Often appears with a direct object: ¿Lo has oído? (“Did you hear it?”) / Has oído lo que he dicho (“You heard what I said”). Can also be followed by de to mean “have you heard from/about”: ¿Has oído de él? / No has oído nada de ella (“You haven’t heard anything from/about her”).
target_language_example: ¿Has oído la noticia?
native_language_example: Have you heard the news?

meaning: “you have passed / you’ve gone through / you’ve spent (time)” (present perfect of pasar, tú).
additional_notes: “Has pasado” is the tú present perfect: haber (has) + pasado. Meaning depends on context: (1) has pasado por… = “you’ve been through…” (difficult experiences); (2) has pasado (toda la noche/el día) = “you’ve spent (all night/the day)…”; (3) has pasado el semáforo en rojo = “you ran the red light / you went through on red”; (4) te has pasado (de la raya) = “you went too far / you overdid it” (common as a standalone: “Te has pasado.”).
target_language_example: Lo siento, pero te has pasado con ese comentario.
native_language_example: I’m sorry, but you went too far with that comment.

additional_notes: Second-person singular present perfect of perder (haber + perdido). Used to say someone has lost a game/competition (“Has perdido”), or that they’ve lost/missed something or a step in a process (“has perdido un paso”). It can also be followed by what was lost: “has perdido la cabeza” = “you’ve lost your mind/head.”
target_language_example: Lo siento, has perdido la llave otra vez.
native_language_example: Sorry, you’ve lost the key again.

meaning: "you have been" (present perfect of ser, tú).
additional_notes: Used to describe what someone has been like up to now (often with adjectives or nouns): Has sido muy amable / Has sido una buena amiga. It uses the tú form: has + sido. For usted, use ha sido; for vosotros, habéis sido.
target_language_example: Has sido muy paciente hoy.
native_language_example: You’ve been very patient today.

additional_notes: Present perfect (tú) of tener: haber (has) + past participle (tenido). Used to talk about something you’ve had/experienced up to now, often with words like alguna vez (ever), ya (already), nunca (never). Depending on context, it can mean having an illness/fever, having time/work, having enough of something, or having had an experience before.
target_language_example: ¿Has tenido tiempo para comer hoy?
native_language_example: Have you had time to eat today?

additional_notes: Present perfect of "venir" (venir → venido) with "tú": "haber" (has) + past participle (venido). It’s used to say that someone has arrived or came (often with a sense of a recent or relevant past), and it can be followed by extra details: "has venido aquí", "has venido en coche", "has venido a + infinitive" (you came to do something), "has venido al lugar adecuado" (you came to the right place).
target_language_example: ¿Por qué has venido tan temprano?
native_language_example: Why did you come so early?

additional_notes: Used with the auxiliary verb haber (has) + past participle (visto) to talk about something you’ve seen at an unspecified time up to now. Common in questions like "¿Has visto...?" and in statements like "Has visto miles de ellos" (You’ve seen thousands of them).
target_language_example: ¿Has visto mis llaves?
native_language_example: Have you seen my keys?

additional_notes: Used to talk about what has happened or what is true from the past up to the present moment. It often implies things could change later. Common as a short reply: “Hasta ahora, bien” = “So far, so good.”
target_language_example: No he tenido problemas hasta ahora.
native_language_example: I haven’t had any problems so far.

meaning: up to there; as far as that point; (figuratively) that’s enough / stop there.
additional_notes: Refers to a limit or endpoint in space, progress, or action. It’s common in directions ("Go up to there...") and also used to set a boundary or stop something: "Hasta ahí está bien" = "That’s fine up to that point" / "That’s enough." Said alone ("Hasta ahí") it can mean "Up to there" or "Stop right there," depending on context and tone.
target_language_example: No sigas discutiendo: hasta ahí.
native_language_example: Don’t keep arguing: that’s enough.

additional_notes: Used to talk about reaching a place or point (physical or figurative): coming all the way here (“venir/llegar hasta aquí”), something extending/reaching here (“llegar hasta aquí”), or to mark a stopping point in a story/presentation (“Hasta aquí…” = “That’s it up to here / So far…”). Often implies effort or distance when used with venir/llegar.
target_language_example: Lo siento por hacerte venir hasta aquí.
native_language_example: Sorry for making you come all the way here.

meaning: to a certain extent; up to a point.
additional_notes: Used to say you agree with something or that something is true/possible, but only partially (not completely). It can go at the end of a sentence or at the beginning for emphasis (Hasta cierto punto, ...). Often contrasted with “pero no del todo” (but not completely).
target_language_example: Me gusta el trabajo, pero solo hasta cierto punto.
native_language_example: I like the job, but only up to a point.

additional_notes: Used to mark a limit or extent (distance, ability, etc.): "hasta donde pude" = "as far as I could." Very common in the expression "hasta donde sé" / "hasta donde yo sé" = "as far as I know" (based on the information I have).
target_language_example: Te acompaño hasta donde pueda.
native_language_example: I’ll come with you as far as I can.

additional_notes: Used to give information with some uncertainty, meaning “based on what I know.” Often followed by a statement about someone/something. You can swap the subject: “Hasta donde yo sé, ella… / ellos… / usted…” or omit it: “Hasta donde yo sé, es honesto.”
target_language_example: Hasta donde yo sé, él trabaja aquí desde 2020.
native_language_example: As far as I know, he has worked here since 2020.

meaning: up to your neck; neck-deep (overwhelmed/in deep).
additional_notes: Used literally for a physical level (e.g., water reaching your neck) and very often figuratively to mean you have too much of something or you’re deeply involved/in trouble (work, debt, problems). Common patterns: "estar hasta el cuello de + noun" ("Estoy hasta el cuello de trabajo") and "estar hasta el cuello con + noun" ("Está hasta el cuello con deudas").
target_language_example: Esta semana estoy hasta el cuello de exámenes.
native_language_example: This week I’m up to my neck in exams.

meaning: until the end; all the way (to the end).
additional_notes: Used to say something continues up to the last moment or the last part of something (a game, meeting, movie, etc.), or up to the end point of a route. Often answers “How long?” (stay until the end) or “How far?” (go all the way to the end of the street). Can also imply persistence: insistir hasta el final (“keep insisting to the very end”).
target_language_example: Me quedé hasta el final de la película.
native_language_example: I stayed until the end of the movie.

additional_notes: Used to talk about everything that has happened up to the present time (or up to a specific time you mention). Very common at the start of a sentence: "Hasta el momento, ...". It can also be followed by "de + event" to mean "up to the time of ..." (e.g., "hasta el momento del crimen").
target_language_example: Hasta el momento, no hemos tenido ningún problema.
native_language_example: So far, we haven’t had any problems.

meaning: until then; up to that time.
additional_notes: Used to refer to the period of time leading up to a specific moment in the future or past that was just mentioned or is understood from context. Often works as a transition at the start of a sentence ("Hasta entonces, ...") or can stand alone as a short goodbye/closing meaning "until then."
target_language_example: Nos vemos el viernes; hasta entonces, cuídate.
native_language_example: See you on Friday; until then, take care.

meaning: up to today; until today (so far).
additional_notes: Used to mark the time limit ending today (up to the present moment). Often implies that something was true/unknown before now, and may change from today onward (e.g., “Nunca había visto uno hasta hoy” = you’re seeing it for the first time today). Can also be a short standalone phrase meaning “Up to today/So far.”
target_language_example: Hasta hoy, no hemos tenido ningún problema.
native_language_example: Up to today, we haven’t had any problem.

additional_notes: Used to mark an end time: something continues up to nighttime. Often appears in the pattern “desde … hasta la noche” (“from … until nighttime”). By itself, it can be a short goodbye meaning “See you tonight.”
target_language_example: Tengo clase hasta la noche.
native_language_example: I have class until nighttime.

additional_notes: A common friendly way to say goodbye, implying you expect to see the person again. Often used at the end of conversations, in person, on the phone, or in messages. You can also hear/see the shorter version: "hasta la próxima" or "hasta la próxima vez" (until the next time).
target_language_example: Bueno, me voy. ¡Hasta la próxima!
native_language_example: Well, I’m going. See you next time!

additional_notes: A common farewell used when leaving, often implying you’ll see the person again. You can say it by itself or with someone’s name ("Hasta la vista, Sara"). It’s a set phrase; literally it’s “until the sight/view,” but it’s used like “see you.”
target_language_example: Me tengo que ir; hasta la vista.
native_language_example: I have to go; see you later.

additional_notes: A common, friendly way to say goodbye, often implying you may see the person again later (today or another time). Used in both formal and informal situations. Often said by itself or after phrases like “bien” (okay) or “de nada” (you’re welcome).
target_language_example: Gracias por venir; hasta luego.
native_language_example: Thanks for coming; see you later.

additional_notes: Most often means "until tomorrow" when talking about how long something lasts (e.g., quedarse hasta mañana = to stay until tomorrow). It can also be used as a goodbye meaning "see you tomorrow". Literally "until tomorrow."
target_language_example: Nos vemos; hasta mañana.
native_language_example: See you tomorrow.

meaning: 'until further notice' (until you hear a new update/instruction).
additional_notes: Used in announcements to say something will continue indefinitely, and will only change when someone informs you. Common with closures, freezes/suspensions, policies, or temporary arrangements.
target_language_example: La reunión queda pospuesta hasta nuevo aviso.
native_language_example: The meeting is postponed until further notice.

additional_notes: A common, polite goodbye used when you expect to see the person again in the near future. Often used on its own ("Hasta pronto.") or with thanks ("Hasta pronto y muchas gracias.").
target_language_example: Me tengo que ir; hasta pronto.
native_language_example: I have to go; see you soon.

additional_notes: Introduces the moment when something happens or changes. It is used before a full clause. With future or expected actions, Spanish often uses the subjunctive after it (for example, "hasta que llegue"). In the pattern "no fue hasta que...", it means "it wasn't until...".
target_language_example: Espera aquí hasta que vuelva.
native_language_example: wait here until I come back.

additional_notes: Used to mark an endpoint in time: an action continues up to the moment when something happens. The "se" is often part of a reflexive verb (e.g., acostarse = to go to bed) or a change-of-state verb (e.g., oscurecerse/oscurecer = to get dark), and it can also appear with passive/impersonal ideas (e.g., hasta que se demuestre = until it is proven). After "hasta que", Spanish often uses the subjunctive when the event is not yet known/hasn’t happened, and the indicative when it’s a completed/past fact.
target_language_example: Esperamos aquí hasta que se abra la tienda.
native_language_example: We’ll wait here until the store opens.

additional_notes: Used to set a condition that lasts up to the moment you do something. It’s often followed by a verb in the present subjunctive (vuelva, llegue, diga, baje) because it refers to a future/unknown moment. In commands, it can sound firm or authoritative: "Nadie sale… hasta que yo lo diga."
target_language_example: Quédate aquí hasta que yo vuelva.
native_language_example: Stay here until I come back.

additional_notes: A strong, often emotional or dramatic goodbye implying you won’t see the person/place again. It’s also used in titles/dedications (e.g., to a country or someone who has died). Less common in everyday casual goodbyes than "hasta luego" or "hasta mañana".
target_language_example: Me voy a otra ciudad; hasta siempre.
native_language_example: I’m moving to another city; farewell forever.

additional_notes: Used to say someone stays awake or something lasts until a late time. Often with verbs like "quedarse" (to stay) and "estar" (to be): "quedarse despierto/a hasta tarde" = "to stay up late."
target_language_example: No puedo salir hoy; me quedé despierto hasta tarde.
