native_language_example: I can’t go out today; I stayed up late.

meaning: "even you" (used to express surprise or emphasis).
additional_notes: Uses "hasta" with a person/pronoun to mean “even …,” often implying “if even you (of all people)…” It’s common in spoken Spanish for emphasis, and it can sound a bit teasing or shocked depending on tone. Often used with exclamations: "¡Hasta tú...!"
target_language_example: ¡Hasta tú lo entiendes!
native_language_example: Even you understand it!

additional_notes: Used to say that someone exists or is present in a place/situation. "Hay" is the impersonal form of "haber" meaning "there is/there are" (it doesn’t change for singular/plural), and it’s often followed by a location: "Hay alguien aquí / ahí / en casa". You can also add "más" for “someone else”: "Hay alguien más".
target_language_example: ¿Hay alguien en casa?
native_language_example: Is there anyone at home?

additional_notes: Uses **hay** (from *haber*) to say that something exists/there is/there are. **Estaciones** here means the seasons of the year (primavera, verano, otoño, invierno). Often used with a place or time: *En Japón hay cuatro estaciones* / *Hay cuatro estaciones al año*.
target_language_example: En mi país hay cuatro estaciones, pero el invierno es muy corto.
native_language_example: In my country there are four seasons, but winter is very short.

additional_notes: Used to say that two of something exist or are present. “Hay” is used for existence/presence (not *estar*). Often followed by a noun or by “que + verb” to describe which two: “Hay dos que…”.
target_language_example: En mi clase hay dos estudiantes nuevos.
native_language_example: In my class there are two new students.

additional_notes: Used to introduce a general statement about some people (not everyone). It’s common for talking about habits, opinions, or beliefs. Verb agreement: "hay" is always singular, but the following verb changes depending on the people mentioned (e.g., "hay gente que cree" / "hay gente que creen").
target_language_example: Hay gente que prefiere caminar en vez de tomar el autobús.
native_language_example: There are people who prefer to walk instead of taking the bus.

additional_notes: Uses the impersonal verb phrase "hay" (from "haber") to say that people exist/are present somewhere. Common with a place: "Hay mucha gente en..."; and with "aquí/allí" (here/there). "Hay" stays the same even if the noun is plural (not *hayn*).
target_language_example: Hoy hay mucha gente en el supermercado.
native_language_example: Today there are a lot of people at the supermarket.

additional_notes: Used with feminine plural nouns (e.g., ventanas, razones, flores, pinturas) to say that many of something exist/are present. It’s the phrase "hay" (there is/are) + "muchas" (many, fem. pl.). You can also use "hay muchos" with masculine plural nouns.
target_language_example: En esta ciudad hay muchas cosas que ver.
native_language_example: In this city there are many things to see.

additional_notes: Used to say that a large amount of something exists. It is common before singular or uncountable nouns, as in hay mucho tiempo or hay mucho trabajo. With plural count nouns, use hay muchos or hay muchas instead.
target_language_example: Hay mucho ruido en esta habitación.
native_language_example: There is a lot of noise in this room.

additional_notes: Used to say that many things exist or are present. "Hay" means "there is/there are" (from haber) and is followed by a noun; "muchos" agrees with a masculine plural noun (e.g., "muchos cuadros"). For feminine plural nouns, use "hay muchas" (e.g., "hay muchas casas").
target_language_example: En esta ciudad hay muchos restaurantes baratos.
native_language_example: In this city there are many cheap restaurants.

additional_notes: Used to say that a larger quantity or number exists. Very common in comparisons with "que" (= than): "hay más X que Y" (there is/are more X than Y). "Hay" is the form of "haber" used for "there is/there are" (it doesn’t change for singular/plural).
target_language_example: En este barrio hay más restaurantes que cafeterías.
native_language_example: In this neighborhood there are more restaurants than cafés.

meaning: “(there is) nothing that …” (usually with **no**: **no hay nada que …**).
additional_notes: This is typically used as part of the negative phrase **no hay nada que + verb (subjunctive)** to mean “there’s nothing (that) … / there’s nothing to …”. Without **no**, it sounds incomplete or unnatural in standard Spanish; in questions, Spanish usually prefers **¿Hay algo que…?** rather than **¿Hay nada que…?**.
target_language_example: No hay nada que podamos hacer ahora.
native_language_example: There’s nothing we can do now.

meaning: "(Is) there anything you can…?" or "there’s nothing you can…" (depending on context).
additional_notes:
This is usually part of a longer sentence, most commonly:
- Question: "¿Hay algo que puedas…?" = “Is there anything you can…?” (In correct Spanish, questions typically use **algo** rather than **nada**.)
- Negative: "No hay nada que puedas…" = “There’s nothing you can…”
It’s followed by an infinitive or verb phrase: "…hacer", "…decir", "…para ayudar", etc.
target_language_example: No hay nada que puedas hacer ahora.
native_language_example: There’s nothing you can do now.

additional_notes: Impersonal expression used with an infinitive to express necessity or obligation in general: hay que + infinitive. It does not usually say exactly who must do it, so depending on context it can sound like "you have to," "we have to," or "it is necessary to."
target_language_example: Para aprender español, hay que practicar todos los días.
native_language_example: To learn Spanish, you have to practice every day.

meaning: you/we must change (or replace) something; it needs to be changed.
additional_notes: “Hay que + infinitive” expresses an impersonal obligation (like “you have to / we have to / one must”). With “cambiar,” it often means “to replace” a part/object (una válvula, la chapa) or “to change” a method/habit (la manera de hacer las cosas). The subject isn’t stated; the context tells who should do it.
target_language_example: Hay que cambiar las pilas del control remoto.
native_language_example: We have to change the remote’s batteries.

meaning: "you/we/one must do"; "it needs to be done".
additional_notes: An impersonal way to talk about obligation or necessity (like English “you have to…” in a general sense). It doesn’t say who specifically must do it. Very common in phrases like “lo que hay que hacer” (= what needs to be done / what must be done). You can also use it with any infinitive: “Hay que estudiar” (You have to study / Studying is necessary).
target_language_example: Hay que hacer la tarea hoy.
native_language_example: We have to do the homework today.

additional_notes: Used to say that something exists or is present. "Hay" means "there is/there are" (it doesn’t change for singular vs. plural), and "un" is "a" for a masculine singular noun. For feminine, you’ll usually see "hay una".
target_language_example: En la mesa hay un libro.
native_language_example: There is a book on the table.

additional_notes: Uses **hay** (from *haber*) to say that someone exists/is present somewhere. Often followed by a place: **hay un hombre aquí/en la puerta/abajo**. For emphasis or clarity you can add **aquí/ahí/allí** (“here/there”).
target_language_example: Hay un hombre afuera que quiere hablar contigo.
native_language_example: There’s a man outside who wants to talk to you.

additional_notes: Used to state that an issue exists. Very common with a location or topic: "Hay un problema en..." (There’s a problem in/at...) or "Hay un problema con..." (There’s a problem with...). You can add emphasis like "Todavía hay un problema" (There’s still a problem).
target_language_example: Perdón, hay un problema con mi reserva.
native_language_example: Sorry, there’s a problem with my reservation.

additional_notes: Used to say that something exists or is present. "Hay" is an impersonal form (it doesn’t change for who/what), and "una" is the feminine singular article, so it’s used before feminine singular nouns: "hay una universidad". For masculine singular, use "hay un".
target_language_example: Hay una tienda cerca de aquí.
native_language_example: There’s a store near here.

additional_notes: Used to introduce a specific (often important) point or topic before adding more information with a clause starting with que. Very common in speech and writing to emphasize “one thing” among others. You can change una cosa to algo (“hay algo que…”) or add emphasis with solo (“solo hay una cosa que…”).
target_language_example: Hay una cosa que tenemos que hablar hoy.
native_language_example: There’s one thing we need to talk about today.

meaning: "has been" / "may have been" (subjunctive, about the past).
additional_notes: This is the present perfect subjunctive of **ser**: **(que) haya sido**. It’s used after triggers like **espero que** (I hope), **no creo que** (I don’t think), **tal vez** (maybe), **ojalá** (I hope/wish) to talk about something in the past with uncertainty, doubt, or a wish. Often translates as “may have been” or “has been,” depending on context.
target_language_example: No creo que haya sido mi culpa.
native_language_example: I don’t think it was my fault.

meaning: "let there be peace" / "let’s have peace" (a call for calm, no arguing).
additional_notes: Used to ask people to stop fighting or arguing and calm down. It often appears as a short, emphatic phrase (sometimes with exclamation marks), similar to saying “peace, everyone” or “let’s keep the peace.”
target_language_example: Ya, por favor, haya paz: podemos hablarlo sin gritar.
native_language_example: Okay, please, let’s have peace: we can talk about it without shouting.

additional_notes: Uses the tú imperative of hacer (haz) + exactamente (“exactly”) + lo que (“what/that which”). It’s followed by a clause like “te diga” (I tell you) or “digo” (I say). Often used to emphasize strict obedience or precision.
target_language_example: Por favor, haz exactamente lo que te expliqué.
native_language_example: Please do exactly what I explained to you.

additional_notes: An instruction using the tú imperative of hacer (haz). lo mismo means “the same (thing)”. Often followed by que + clause to say who/what to copy: Haz lo mismo que yo (“Do the same as me”). It can also refer back to something already done: haz lo mismo de antes (“do the same as before”).
target_language_example: Si yo apago la luz, haz lo mismo.
native_language_example: If I turn off the light, do the same.

additional_notes: Used to tell someone to do a specific thing, often followed by a clause: haz lo que + verb (haz lo que creas / haz lo que te dije). It can also appear in set phrases like haz lo que tienes que hacer (“do what you have to do”) or haz lo que hay que hacer (“do what needs to be done”). Note the command form haz is from hacer (tú).
target_language_example: Haz lo que puedas y no te preocupes.
native_language_example: Do what you can and don’t worry.

additional_notes: Often used to give permission or to show indifference/resignation (“it’s up to you”). It can sound supportive in context, but it can also sound dismissive or a bit annoyed depending on tone. Uses the tú imperative: haz (from hacer) + lo que quieras (“whatever you want”).
target_language_example: Si no te gusta este plan, haz lo que quieras.
native_language_example: If you don’t like this plan, do whatever you want.

additional_notes: An imperative command using the tú form (haz = “do”). Often said firmly to give instructions or orders. You can change the person: “haz lo que te diga él” = “do what he tells you,” “haz lo que te diga ella” = “do what she tells you.” In some regions you may hear it with “nomás/nomás” meaning “just/only”: “Nomás haz lo que te diga.”
target_language_example: Por favor, haz lo que te diga y no te muevas.
native_language_example: Please do what I tell you and don’t move.

additional_notes: Imperative (command) form of *hacer*: **haz** = “do (you)”. Used to tell someone to focus and complete their responsibilities. You can add adverbs like *rápidamente* (“quickly”) or combine it with another command: *Ve y haz tu trabajo* (“Go and do your job”).
target_language_example: Por favor, haz tu trabajo antes de las cinco.
native_language_example: Please do your work before five.

additional_notes: Used to ask someone to do something for you. Very common in spoken Spanish; it can sound polite or a bit demanding depending on tone and what you ask next (e.g., “Hazme un favor y apaga…”). You can also say it alone (“Hazme un favor.”) when the request is implied or will follow. Variants: “hazme el favor (de + infinitive)” and more formal “hágame un favor”.
target_language_example: Hazme un favor y avísame cuando llegues.
native_language_example: Do me a favor and let me know when you arrive.

additional_notes: Present perfect of "acabar" (to finish): "he" + "acabado". It often appears with "de + infinitive" to say you’ve finished doing something: "He acabado de trabajar" (I’ve finished working). With "todavía no" it means you haven’t finished yet: "Todavía no he acabado de desayunar".
target_language_example: Ya he acabado de leer el libro.
native_language_example: I’ve already finished reading the book.

additional_notes: Uses **haber** (he) + past participle (**aprendido**) to talk about something you learned at an unspecified time, often with relevance to the present. Common in Spain for recent/connected past; in much of Latin America, **aprendí** (simple past) is often used in the same situations. The participle **aprendido** does not change for gender/number here.
target_language_example: He aprendido mucho en este curso.
native_language_example: I’ve learned a lot in this course.

additional_notes: Used to talk about something you ate at an unspecified time before now, or about experiences up to now. Common in Spain for recent past (e.g., "He comido mucho esta semana"), while in much of Latin America the simple past is often preferred ("Comí mucho esta semana"). Often appears with time expressions like esta semana, hoy, ya, nunca, todavía.
target_language_example: No me siento bien; creo que es algo que he comido.
native_language_example: I don’t feel well; I think it’s something I ate.

additional_notes: Form of the verb comprar in the pretérito perfecto: he + participle (comprado). Commonly used for recent past actions or actions connected to the present. With reflexive pronouns (me/te/se…), it often means “bought (something) for myself,” e.g., Me he comprado… = “I bought myself…”.
target_language_example: He comprado pan para la cena.
native_language_example: I bought bread for dinner.

additional_notes: This is the present perfect: "he" (I have) + "conocido" (met/known). Use it when you’ve met someone at some point in the past and it’s relevant now. With people, Spanish usually uses the personal "a": "he conocido a Juan". In negative sentences it becomes "no he conocido a..." (I haven’t met/known...).
target_language_example: He conocido a tu hermana, pero no a tu hermano.
native_language_example: I’ve met your sister, but not your brother.

additional_notes: Present perfect: **he** (I have) + **conseguido** (past participle of *conseguir*). Use it to say you’ve succeeded in doing something (*he conseguido verla* = “I’ve managed to see her”) or that you obtained something (*he conseguido dos* = “I’ve gotten two”). Often followed by an infinitive (**he conseguido + infinitive**) or a direct object (**he conseguido + noun/pronoun**).
target_language_example: ¡Por fin lo he conseguido!
native_language_example: I finally managed to do it!

additional_notes: Present perfect of dar (to give): haber (he) + past participle (dado). It’s used with direct/indirect objects (e.g., te he dado algo, no te he dado nada) and in fixed expressions like he dado mi palabra (“I gave my word”). In sentences like Me he dado de alta, the full verb is darse de alta (“to register/sign up; to get discharged”), where he dado is part of the reflexive present perfect (me he dado…).
target_language_example: Te he dado mi palabra.
native_language_example: I've given you my word.

additional_notes: Present perfect of decidir: he (I have) + decidido (decided). It’s used to say you’ve made a decision (often recently) about what you will do. Common patterns: “He decidido + infinitive” (He decidido renunciar.) and “He decidido que + clause” (He decidido que debemos quedarnos aquí.). Negative: “No lo he decidido todavía” = “I haven’t decided yet.”
target_language_example: He decidido que mañana voy a empezar a estudiar español.
native_language_example: I’ve decided that tomorrow I’m going to start studying Spanish.

additional_notes: “He dejado” is the “I have …” form of the verb “dejar” (present perfect). It commonly means (1) “I have left” something somewhere / “I’ve forgotten” something somewhere: “He dejado el pasaporte…”. (2) With “de + infinitive” (“he dejado de fumar”), it means “I have stopped/quit doing (something)”. (3) With an infinitive like “entrar” (“he dejado entrar al gato”), it means “I have let/allowed (someone/something) to (do something)”. Context tells you which meaning fits.
target_language_example: Creo que he dejado las llaves en casa.
native_language_example: I think I’ve left my keys at home.

additional_notes: Present perfect of decir (to say/tell). Often appears with object pronouns to show who you told: les he dicho (I told them), te he dicho (I told you), le he dicho (I told him/her). With que, it introduces reported speech: He dicho que lo dejes (I said to leave it).
target_language_example: Ya te he dicho que no tengo tiempo.
native_language_example: I already told you I don’t have time.

additional_notes: Present perfect: "he" (I have) + "encontrado" (found). Used for something you found/located (often recently). It takes a direct object, which can be replaced by pronouns: "lo he encontrado" (I found it), "la he encontrado" (I found her/it).
target_language_example: ¡Por fin he encontrado mis llaves!
native_language_example: I finally found my keys!

additional_notes: "He escrito" is the yo form of the present perfect: haber (he) + past participle (escrito). It’s used to talk about what you have done up to now, often with words like hoy (today), ya (already), nunca (never), todavía no (not yet). In many parts of Spain it’s especially common for actions in a time period that includes the present (e.g., today/this week).
target_language_example: Esta semana he escrito tres correos importantes.
native_language_example: This week I have written three important emails.

meaning: "I have heard" / "I've heard" (present perfect of escuchar).
additional_notes: Used to say you’ve heard something at least once up to now. Common patterns: he escuchado + [thing] (He escuchado mucho de ti. = I’ve heard a lot about you.); he escuchado a + [person] + [verb] (He escuchado a Roy cantar. = I’ve heard Roy sing.); no he escuchado nada / nunca he escuchado... (I haven’t heard anything / I’ve never heard...). Also used in comparisons like lo más... que he escuchado jamás (the most ... I’ve ever heard).
target_language_example: Ya he escuchado esa historia muchas veces.
native_language_example: I've already heard that story many times.

additional_notes: Present perfect of "estar" (yo): "he estado" = "I have been". Often used to talk about where you’ve been recently ("He estado en su tienda" = "I’ve been in/at his shop"). With a gerund, it can mean an ongoing action over a period of time: "he estado + -ando/-iendo" = "I’ve been (doing)" (e.g., "Me he estado haciendo esa pregunta" = "I’ve been asking myself that question").
target_language_example: He estado muy ocupado esta semana.
native_language_example: I’ve been very busy this week.

additional_notes: Present perfect: "he" (I have) + "estado" (been) + "aquí" (here). Used to say you have been in this place up to now, often with a duration like "por una semana" (for a week) or "toda la noche / todo el día" (all night / all day).
target_language_example: He estado aquí desde esta mañana.
native_language_example: I’ve been here since this morning.

meaning: “I have been to / I’ve been in.”
additional_notes: Present perfect of estar (yo): used to say you have visited a place at least once, or that you have been in a place for a period of time up to now. Often followed by a place name; you can add times like una vez, dos veces, muchas veces. For “I have lived in…,” Spanish more commonly uses “he vivido en…”.
target_language_example: He estado en México tres veces.
native_language_example: I’ve been to Mexico three times.

additional_notes: Present perfect progressive (haber + estado + gerundio) used to say an action started in the past and is still happening now, often with a sense of duration. You can add "por" to say what/whom you’re waiting for: "He estado esperando por ti". It changes with the subject/person: "he" (I), "has" (you), "ha" (he/she/it), "hemos" (we), "han" (they). With object pronouns, they go before "he": "Los he estado esperando" = "I’ve been waiting for you (plural)/them."
target_language_example: Lo siento, he estado esperando por el autobús por veinte minutos.
native_language_example: Sorry, I’ve been waiting for the bus for twenty minutes.

additional_notes: Used to say you talked with someone at an unspecified time in the past that’s relevant now (often “today/recently”). It uses the present perfect: he (haber) + hablado (past participle of hablar). You can add a person or group after con, or use a pronoun (con él/ella/ellos/usted). For negatives: No he hablado con …
target_language_example: Ya he hablado con mi jefe sobre el problema.
native_language_example: I’ve already spoken with my boss about the problem.

additional_notes: "He hecho" is the present perfect of "hacer" (he = "I have" + hecho = "done/made"). It’s used to talk about something you did in the past, often with present relevance (similar to English "I have done/made"). Common in phrases like "lo he hecho" (I’ve done it) and with objects: "he hecho una reserva" (I’ve made a reservation), "te he hecho una pregunta" (I’ve asked you a question).
target_language_example: Lo siento, he hecho todo lo posible.
native_language_example: I’m sorry, I’ve done everything possible.

additional_notes: Used to say you tried to do something in the past and it’s relevant now. Often followed by an infinitive: he intentado + verbo (e.g., he intentado llamarte = I’ve tried to call you). In sentences like “Es/Eso es lo que he intentado decir”, it means “that’s what I’ve been trying to say.”
target_language_example: Lo siento, pero ya he intentado arreglarlo y no pude.
native_language_example: I’m sorry, but I’ve already tried to fix it and I couldn’t.

additional_notes: Present perfect: **haber (he)** + past participle **leído**. Used to talk about something you’ve read at an unspecified time before now, often with an implied or stated object (e.g., *he leído el libro*). The participle **leído** has an accent mark.
target_language_example: He leído ese artículo, pero no lo entendí bien.
native_language_example: I’ve read that article, but I didn’t understand it well.

meaning: 'I’ve killed anyone'—used with a negation to mean 'I haven’t killed anyone / I’ve never killed anyone.'
additional_notes: This phrase is normally used with a negative word before it: **No he matado a nadie** (“I haven’t killed anyone”) or **Nunca he matado a nadie** (“I’ve never killed anyone”). **He matado** is the present perfect (haber + past participle) of **matar** (“to kill”). **A nadie** means “anyone/anybody” and is used for people, especially in negative sentences.
target_language_example: No he matado a nadie, te lo juro.
native_language_example: I haven’t killed anyone, I swear.

additional_notes: Present perfect of **olvidar** (to forget), used to talk about something you forgot (often recently or with a present result): *He olvidado la dirección.* You’ll also hear the reflexive form **me he olvidado de...** (“I forgot ...”): *Me he olvidado de mis gafas.* With **nunca** it becomes negative: **No le he olvidado nunca** = “I have never forgotten him/her.” You can also say **He olvidado traer...** (“I forgot to bring...”).
target_language_example: Lo siento, he olvidado tu nombre.
native_language_example: Sorry, I’ve forgotten your name.

additional_notes: Used to introduce information you heard from someone else (rumor/news), often without confirming it. Literally "I have heard that" (present perfect of oír). Can also sound polite/indirect when bringing up what you know.
target_language_example: He oído que vas a cambiar de trabajo.
native_language_example: I’ve heard that you’re going to change jobs.

additional_notes: Present perfect (haber + past participle) of "pedir" for the first person singular: "he pedido" = "I have asked for / ordered." It’s used for requests (He pedido ayuda), ordering food/drinks (He pedido pan / una copa), or asking someone for something (He pedido a mi jefe un adelanto). With "no", it becomes "I haven’t asked for" (No he pedido tu opinión).
target_language_example: He pedido una mesa para dos.
native_language_example: I’ve asked for a table for two.

meaning: “I have thought about” / “I’ve been thinking about.”
additional_notes: Present perfect of pensar + en. Use it to say you’ve had something on your mind (a plan, idea, person, or possibility). Follow with a noun, pronoun, or infinitive: he pensado en ti; he pensado en volver (to go back). You can also intensify with muchas veces (“many times”).
target_language_example: He pensado en cambiar de trabajo.
native_language_example: I’ve been thinking about changing jobs.

additional_notes: Present perfect: **haber (he)** + past participle (**perdido**). Used for things/people you’ve lost, or for losing track of something: **He perdido a mis amigos** (I’ve lost my friends) / **He perdido la cuenta** (I’ve lost count).
target_language_example: ¡He perdido mis llaves!
native_language_example: I've lost my keys!

meaning: 'I have been able to' / 'I could have' (present perfect of poder).
additional_notes: Used with a past participle or infinitive to say you’ve managed to do something up to now or at some point in the past. Common in phrases like "en cuanto he podido" (as soon as I’ve been able to) and "no he podido + infinitive" (I haven’t been able to...). Also appears in "he podido contar con..." meaning "I’ve been able to rely on...".
target_language_example: Lo siento, no he podido llamarte antes.
native_language_example: Sorry, I haven't been able to call you earlier.

meaning: "I have put" / "I’ve put" (present perfect of poner).
additional_notes: Used to talk about something you placed/added/did in the recent past with a result now: He puesto la dirección al final. In the reflexive form (me he puesto), it often means (1) "I put on" clothing: Me he puesto una falda pantalón. (2) "I became/got" + adjective (especially about health/mood): En cuanto me he puesto mala… It can also be used figuratively: He puesto todo mi empeño = "I’ve put in all my effort."
target_language_example: Ya he puesto tu nombre en la lista.
native_language_example: I’ve already put your name on the list.

additional_notes: This is the present perfect of querer: he (I have) + querido (wanted/loved). Use it to talk about what you have wanted (or felt) up to now or at some point in the past. With people, querer can mean "to love" in a general/affectionate sense, so Nunca te he querido can mean "I’ve never loved you" (or "I’ve never cared for you"). Often appears with words like nunca, siempre, ya, etc.
target_language_example: Siempre he querido aprender español.
native_language_example: I’ve always wanted to learn Spanish.

additional_notes: Present perfect: haber (he) + past participle (recibido). Used to talk about something you have received up to now or recently, often with time expressions like "hasta ahora" (so far).
target_language_example: Ya he recibido el correo, gracias.
native_language_example: I've already received the mail, thanks.

additional_notes: Formed with **haber** (he) + past participle **sido**. Used to talk about what you have been like **up to now** or **at some point in your life**: *He sido bueno* (I’ve been good), *Nunca he sido tan feliz* (I’ve never been so happy). You can add **no** to negate it (*No he sido...*). In *No lo he sido*, **lo** stands for a previously mentioned description (e.g., good, happy, etc.).
target_language_example: Lo siento: hoy no he sido muy paciente.
native_language_example: Sorry: today I haven’t been very patient.

meaning: "I have taken" / "I have had" (present perfect of tomar).
additional_notes: This is the present perfect: haber (he) + past participle (tomado). It’s used for past actions that are relevant to the present (often with ya, nunca, en años, etc.). Tomar is very flexible, so he tomado can mean “I’ve drunk” (He tomado del grifo.), “I’ve made” (He tomado mi decisión.), or more generally “I’ve taken/covered/handled” depending on context.
target_language_example: No he tomado café hoy.
native_language_example: I haven’t had coffee today.

additional_notes: Used to say you brought something/someone and it matters now (you have it with you or the action is relevant to the present). Structure: haber (he) + past participle (traído). With a direct object pronoun, it often goes before the auxiliary: "Le he traído esto" = "I brought this to you/him/her".
target_language_example: He traído tu libro.
native_language_example: I brought your book (I have your book with me).

meaning: "I have come to" / "I came to" (to do something).
additional_notes: Uses the present perfect of venir (he venido) + a + infinitive to say your purpose for coming. In many contexts it translates naturally as "I came to..." (past). You can change the subject: he venido (I), has venido (you), ha venido (he/she), hemos venido (we), han venido (they).
target_language_example: He venido a ayudarte con la tarea.
native_language_example: I came to help you with the homework.

additional_notes: Present perfect: "he" (from haber) + "visto" (past participle of ver). Used to talk about things you’ve seen/experienced at some point up to now (often with words like "alguna vez"). The subject pronoun is optional: "he visto" = "yo he visto". With object pronouns it becomes: "las he visto" = "I’ve seen them".
target_language_example: He visto esa película, pero no recuerdo el final.
native_language_example: I've seen that movie, but I don't remember the ending.

meaning: "I have (done something) again" / "I have returned (to a place)".
additional_notes:
It’s the present perfect of volver (yo): he vuelto. Common patterns:
1) he vuelto a + infinitive = “I’ve done X again” (repeat an action): He vuelto a escribir mi informe. = “I’ve written my report again.”
2) he vuelto a + place = “I’ve returned to (a place)” or simply “I’m back (home)”: He vuelto a casa. = “I’ve returned home / I’m back home.”
With no lo he vuelto a + verb, it often means “I haven’t (done/seen it) again (since…)”: No lo he vuelto a ver desde entonces. = “I haven’t seen him/it again since then.”
target_language_example: No he vuelto a hablar con ella desde ayer.
native_language_example: I haven’t talked to her again since yesterday.

meaning: 'here is/are' (used to present or point out something).
additional_notes: Somewhat formal/literary. Common in writing, speeches, or announcements to introduce something: "He aquí la solución" = "Here is the solution." Often followed by a noun (he aquí + el/la/los/las + noun).
target_language_example: He aquí el informe que me pediste.
native_language_example: Here is the report you asked me for.

additional_notes: Commonly used with forms of "haber" to form compound tenses: "he/has/ha/hemos/habéis/han hecho daño" = "have/has done harm" → usually "have hurt". Often appears with an indirect object: "hacer daño a alguien" = "to hurt someone"; clitic pronouns are common: "me/te/le/nos/os/les has hecho daño" = "you’ve hurt me/you’ve hurt him/her/them". Reflexive "hacerse daño" means "to hurt yourself" or "to get hurt" ("se ha hecho daño").
target_language_example: Me has hecho daño con lo que has hecho.
native_language_example: You’ve hurt me with what you’ve done.

additional_notes: Used to describe items crafted manually (often emphasizing quality or artisanal production). It agrees in gender/number with the noun: hecho a mano (masc. singular), hecha a mano (fem. singular), hechos a mano (masc. plural), hechas a mano (fem. plural). Common with products like ropa, joyas, muebles, artesanías, etc.
target_language_example: Compré un cinturón hecho a mano en el mercado.
native_language_example: I bought a handmade belt at the market.

additional_notes: Present perfect: "hemos" (we have) + "encontrado" (found). Used for something found recently or with a connection to the present. Direct object pronouns often go before it: "lo hemos encontrado" (we’ve found it), "la hemos encontrado" (we’ve found her). The past participle "encontrado" doesn’t change for gender/number.
target_language_example: Ya hemos encontrado la dirección.
native_language_example: We’ve already found the address.

additional_notes: Present perfect (haber + past participle) of estar. Used to say where/what state you have been in at some point up to now: Hemos estado en París (We’ve been to Paris). With a gerund (-ando/-iendo), it can mean an ongoing action up to now: Hemos estado esperando (We’ve been waiting).
target_language_example: Hemos estado muy ocupados esta semana.
native_language_example: We’ve been very busy this week.

meaning: "we have done" / "we have made" (present perfect: haber + hecho).
additional_notes: Used to talk about actions completed in the recent past or with results relevant to the present. "Hacer" can mean "do" (hacer algo bueno, hacer lo mismo) or "make" (hacer un trato = make a deal). With a reflexive pronoun it becomes "hacerse": "Nos hemos hecho amigos" = "We became friends."
target_language_example: Ya hemos hecho la tarea, así que podemos salir.
native_language_example: We’ve already done the homework, so we can go out.

additional_notes: Present perfect of llegar (to arrive): hemos (we have) + llegado (arrived). Used to announce that you’ve reached a place (“Ya hemos llegado”) or figuratively that you’ve made a lot of progress (“Hemos llegado muy lejos” = “We’ve come a long way”). Often appears with ya (“already”) for emphasis.
target_language_example: Tranquilos, hemos llegado al hotel.
native_language_example: Relax, we’ve arrived at the hotel.

additional_notes: Used to say something was lost (contact, a house, a signal, etc.) in a time period connected to the present. With the reflexive pronoun (*nos hemos perdido*), it means “we got lost” (lost our way).
target_language_example: Hemos perdido las llaves.
native_language_example: We’ve lost the keys.

meaning: "we have had" / "we've had" (present perfect of tener).
additional_notes: Used to talk about experiences or situations up to now. Often followed by a noun (hemos tenido mucha lluvia = we've had a lot of rain) or used in expressions like "hemos tenido que + infinitive" = "we have had to + verb".
target_language_example: Este mes hemos tenido mucho trabajo.
native_language_example: This month we've had a lot of work.

additional_notes: Present perfect (haber + participle): hemos + terminado. Used to say a task/activity is completed, often with “ya” to emphasize “already”: “Ya hemos terminado.” You can add what is finished: “Hemos terminado el trabajo…”, or a place/context: “Hemos terminado aquí.”
target_language_example: ¿Podemos irnos? Ya hemos terminado.
native_language_example: Can we leave? We’re already done.

additional_notes: Present perfect of **ver** (to see): **haber (hemos) + visto**. Used to talk about what we’ve seen/experienced up to now (often connected to the present). Also appears in **no hemos visto...** (“we haven’t seen...”) and in the reflexive form **nos hemos visto** meaning “we have seen each other / we’ve met up” (e.g., *No nos hemos visto por mucho tiempo* = “We haven’t seen each other in a long time”).
target_language_example: Ya hemos visto esa película dos veces.
native_language_example: We’ve already seen that movie twice.

meaning: Very offensive insult: “bitch” / “son of a bitch” (literally “daughter of a whore”).
additional_notes: Extremely vulgar and insulting; avoid in polite conversation. Used either as a noun ("Es una hija de puta.") or as an angry exclamation ("¡Hija de puta!"). It’s feminine; the masculine form is "hijo de puta". In English it’s often translated as “son of a bitch” regardless of gender, but Spanish keeps gender agreement.
target_language_example: ¡Eres una hija de puta!
native_language_example: You’re a son of a bitch!

meaning: my daughter (as an affectionate way to address a girl/young woman).
additional_notes: Used as a direct form of address, often to comfort, reassure, or speak gently (similar to “my dear” when talking to a daughter). It can also be used more broadly toward a younger woman (e.g., by an older person) to show warmth or tenderness. In writing, it’s often set off with commas: “Tranquila, hija mía”.
target_language_example: No llores, hija mía; todo va a salir bien.
native_language_example: Don’t cry, my daughter; everything is going to be okay.

additional_notes: Used in Christian/religious contexts. Often refers specifically to Jesus (Jesús es el hijo de Dios). Without an article (un/el), it can also be used more generally to mean a person seen as a “child of God” (Él también es hijo de Dios). Capitalization of Dios is common when referring to the monotheistic God.
target_language_example: Muchos cristianos creen que Jesús es el hijo de Dios.
native_language_example: Many Christians believe that Jesus is the son of God.

additional_notes: Very offensive profanity used to insult someone directly (“Eres un hijo de perra”) or as a stand-alone insult (“¡Hijo de perra!”). Often said in anger or as a threat (“Ven acá, hijo de perra”). In some contexts it can be used jokingly between friends, but it’s still vulgar and risky—best avoided in polite conversation. For a less harsh insult, speakers may use milder alternatives like “idiota” or “imbécil.”
target_language_example: ¡Fuera de aquí, hijo de perra!
native_language_example: Get out of here, you son of a bitch!

meaning: “son of a bitch / motherf***er” (a very strong insult).
additional_notes: Very vulgar profanity used to insult someone directly (often as a shouted address: “¡Hijo de puta!”). Depending on tone and context, it can also be used between friends jokingly, but it’s still offensive and risky. Literally means “son of a whore.”
target_language_example: ¡Eres un hijo de puta!
native_language_example: You’re a son of a bitch!

meaning: “my son” (a tender way to address a boy/young man).
additional_notes: Used as a form of address, often affectionate or protective (parent/older person to a child). It can also be used toward a younger man in a caring or patronizing way depending on tone. The feminine equivalent is “hija mía” (“my daughter”).
target_language_example: Ven aquí, hijo mío, que quiero hablar contigo.
native_language_example: Come here, my son, I want to talk to you.

meaning: only child (a son with no siblings).
additional_notes: Used to say someone has no brothers or sisters. For a girl, you can also say “hija única” (only child, female).
target_language_example: Mi novio es hijo único, así que no tiene hermanos.
native_language_example: My boyfriend is an only child, so he doesn’t have any siblings.

meaning: “sons of bitches / motherfuckers” (a very strong insult).
additional_notes: Very vulgar and aggressive. Used to insult or show anger at people (“Son unos hijos de puta”) or as an exclamation (“¡Qué hijos de puta!” = “What assholes!”). Singular: hijo de puta. Avoid in polite or formal situations.
target_language_example: ¡Esos tipos son unos hijos de puta!
native_language_example: Those guys are a bunch of motherfuckers!

additional_notes: A formal song that represents a country; it’s often played or sung at sports events, ceremonies, official gatherings, and at the end or beginning of public events. Common with verbs like "cantar" (to sing) and "escuchar" (to listen to).
target_language_example: Antes de la ceremonia, todos se pusieron de pie para el himno nacional.
native_language_example: Before the ceremony, everyone stood up for the national anthem.

additional_notes: "Hizo" is the simple past (pretérito) of "hacer" (to do/make) for él/ella/usted. "Eso" means "that" (something not close to the speaker). Often used to refer back to an action already mentioned or understood from context: "¿Por qué hizo eso?" = "Why did he do that?"
target_language_example: No sé por qué hizo eso.
native_language_example: I don't know why he did that.

additional_notes: Used to talk about the weather in the past (preterite of hacer: hizo). Common with time expressions like anoche, ayer, el martes, el mes pasado. You can negate it: no hizo mucho frío (“it wasn’t very cold”).
target_language_example: El sábado hizo mucho frío en la montaña.
native_language_example: On Saturday it was very cold in the mountains.

additional_notes: This is the past (preterite) form of the common expression "hacer una pregunta" = "to ask a question." It’s used for a completed action in the past: "Ella me hizo una pregunta" (She asked me a question). You can also say "preguntar" (to ask), but "hacer una pregunta" is very common.
target_language_example: En la entrevista, me hizo una pregunta difícil.
native_language_example: In the interview, he/she asked me a difficult question.

additional_notes: Use this to greet someone and say your name. After “soy” you usually add your name (Hola, soy Ana). You can also say “Hola, soy yo” to mean “Hi, it’s me.” “Soy” comes from the verb “ser” (to be).
target_language_example: Hola, soy Daniel. Mucho gusto.
native_language_example: Hi, I’m Daniel. Nice to meet you.

additional_notes: Used to describe someone whose job is doing business (often managing companies, investing, making deals). It’s a common, neutral phrase; the feminine form is “mujer de negocios,” and for a group you can say “personas de negocios.”
target_language_example: Mi tío es hombre de negocios y viaja mucho por trabajo.
native_language_example: My uncle is a businessman and travels a lot for work.

meaning: "(the) man is a..." (sentence fragment used to define/describe something).
additional_notes: This is not a complete phrase on its own; it’s the start of a definition or description. You’ll usually see it as **El hombre es un...** (“Man is a... / The man is a...”), followed by a masculine singular noun (because **un** is the masculine singular form of “a”). If you mean a specific man, use **El hombre es un...**; without **el**, it can sound incomplete.
target_language_example: El hombre es un animal social.
native_language_example: Humans are social animals.

additional_notes: Refers to a mythical creature that is both a man and a wolf (a person who turns into a wolf, often at night or during a full moon). Usually used with the article: "un/una" or "el/la" (e.g., "un hombre lobo", "el hombre lobo"). Plural: "hombres lobo".
target_language_example: En la película, el hombre se convierte en hombre lobo cuando hay luna llena.
native_language_example: In the movie, the man turns into a werewolf when there is a full moon.

meaning: 'dead man' / 'a dead man' (often: someone who’s doomed or in big trouble).
additional_notes: Literally means “dead man.” It can be used in a dramatic/figurative way: “Soy/Es hombre muerto” = “I’m/He’s a dead man” (i.e., I’m in serious trouble / there’s no hope). It’s also used in technical phrases like “interruptor de hombre muerto” (“dead man’s switch”). Often you’ll also hear it with an article: “un hombre muerto.”
target_language_example: Si mi madre se entera, soy hombre muerto.
native_language_example: If my mom finds out, I’m a dead man.

additional_notes: Used to introduce a description of a man using a relative clause with que (“who/that …”). It’s common after expressions like “el tipo de…” (the kind/type of…) or after an indefinite article (“un hombre que…” = “a man who…”).
target_language_example: Busco un hombre que sea honesto.
native_language_example: I’m looking for a man who is honest.

additional_notes: Used before a noun or an infinitive. With an infinitive, it means 'time to' (hora de actuar, hora de irse a la cama). With a noun, it can refer to a set time for something (hora de cierre = closing time, hora de comer = mealtime). After a number, it can also mean 'hour of' in expressions like una hora de retraso.
target_language_example: Ya es hora de dormir.
native_language_example: It's time to sleep.

meaning: the moment of truth; the decisive moment.
additional_notes: Used when the key moment has arrived—when you have to act, decide, or see the real outcome (e.g., before an exam, performance, big conversation, or final test). Often appears with verbs like "llegó"/"ha llegado" (it’s arrived) or "es" (it is).
target_language_example: Bueno, llegó la hora de la verdad: ¿vas a decirle lo que sientes?
native_language_example: Well, it’s the moment of truth: are you going to tell them how you feel?

meaning: overtime hour (an extra hour of work).
additional_notes: Used mainly in work contexts to refer to a specific extra hour worked beyond your regular schedule. Often used in plural as "horas extra" when talking about multiple hours. Common with verbs like "hacer" (to do/work) and "pagar" (to pay): "Hice una hora extra" / "Me pagaron la hora extra".
target_language_example: Hoy tengo que hacer una hora extra.
native_language_example: Today I have to work one overtime hour.

meaning: rush hour; peak time (when it’s busiest).
additional_notes: Used for the busiest time of day, especially when traffic is heaviest (commuting times). Commonly appears in phrases like “tráfico de la hora punta” (rush-hour traffic) and “en hora punta” (at peak time).
target_language_example: El metro va llenísimo en la hora punta.
native_language_example: The subway is really packed during rush hour.

meaning: 'and a half hours' (used after a number of hours).
additional_notes: Used to express duration or time amount with half an hour added: "tres horas y media" = 3.5 hours. Agreement changes with the number: "una hora y media" (1.5 hours) but "dos/tres horas y media" (2.5/3.5 hours). With other units you’ll also hear "y medio/a" (e.g., "un minuto y medio" = a minute and a half).
target_language_example: La reunión duró cuatro horas y media.
native_language_example: The meeting lasted four and a half hours.

meaning: "today"; often "nowadays / these days" (in the present time).
additional_notes: Often used like "hoy" to mean "today" (especially in Latin America). In general statements, it can mean "nowadays / these days" (the current era), e.g., describing what is common or what doesn’t happen anymore. Context tells you which meaning fits.
target_language_example: Hoy día casi todo se hace por internet.
native_language_example: Nowadays, almost everything is done online.

meaning: nowadays; these days (in the present time).
additional_notes: Used to talk about how things are in modern times or at the present moment, often comparing with the past. It can appear at the beginning of the sentence or after the subject (e.g., "La gente hoy en día..."). Also common with "incluso": "Incluso hoy en día" = "even nowadays".
target_language_example: Hoy en día mucha gente compra por Internet.
native_language_example: Nowadays a lot of people shop online.

additional_notes: Used to say what the date/day/event is today, or to emphasize that something is happening today: "Hoy es mi cumpleaños" (Today is my birthday). Often followed by a day/date or a noun phrase (el último día del año, la boda de mi hijo).
target_language_example: Hoy es un día importante para nosotros.
native_language_example: Today is an important day for us.

additional_notes: Used to introduce a description of what today is like or what kind of day it is. It’s commonly followed by an adjective (especial, importante, soleado) or by “de + noun” (de celebración, de sol).
target_language_example: Hoy es un día perfecto para quedarnos en casa.
native_language_example: Today is a perfect day to stay at home.

additional_notes: Adds emphasis and urgency to "hoy". It often means "today, without delay / as soon as possible" (especially with requests), and in time expressions it can mean "starting today" or "as of today" (e.g., "desde hoy mismo").
target_language_example: Quiero la respuesta hoy mismo.
native_language_example: I want the answer today (right away).

additional_notes: Used to say something is not happening/true today or that you can’t/won’t do something today. Often comes at the start of a sentence before a verb (“Hoy no tengo…”, “Hoy no es…”) or can stand alone as a short refusal (“Hoy no.”).
target_language_example: ¿Puedes venir a cenar? Hoy no puedo.
native_language_example: Can you come for dinner? I can’t today.

additional_notes: Used in hypothetical, unreal, or wished-for past situations, often with triggers like si (if), como si (as if), ojalá (I wish), and in clauses like de no haber sido por... (if it hadn’t been for...). It typically matches English "had been" in sentences about what would have happened.
target_language_example: Si yo hubiera estado en casa, te habría ayudado.
native_language_example: If I had been at home, I would have helped you.

meaning: “you had done” / “you would have done” (past, hypothetical).
additional_notes: This is the **past perfect subjunctive** of *hacer* (tú): *hubieras* + *hecho*. It’s used for unreal or hypothetical past situations (often implying “but you didn’t”), especially after **como si** (“as if”), **ojalá** (“I wish”), and in regrets/criticisms like **Mejor hubieras hecho...** (“You should’ve done...” / “It would’ve been better if you had done ...”).
target_language_example: Si hubieras hecho caso, no habríamos tenido problemas.
native_language_example: If you had listened, we wouldn’t have had problems.

meaning: “there was a” (for a one-time event in the past).
additional_notes: "Hubo" is the preterite form of "haber" used impersonally (like English "there was/there were") to say something happened or existed at a specific moment in the past. It’s commonly followed by a noun: "hubo un incendio" (there was a fire), "hubo un cambio" (there was a change). For plural, use "hubo unos/unas" or "hubo" + plural noun ("hubo problemas" = there were problems).
target_language_example: En la reunión hubo un problema, pero lo resolvimos.
native_language_example: At the meeting there was a problem, but we solved it.

meaning: "it smells like" / "it smells of"; also "it seems suspicious" ("it smells like a trap").
additional_notes: Used with the verb oler in the 3rd person singular (huele) + a + noun: Huele a café. It can describe a real smell (good or bad) or, with people/situations, a suspicious feeling: Me huele a trampa / a conspiración. You can negate it: No huele a nada (It doesn’t smell like anything).
target_language_example: Esto huele a problema.
native_language_example: This smells like trouble.

additional_notes: From the verb *oler* (“to smell”). Used to say that something has a bad odor: *Algo/Esta carne huele mal.* With a person as the subject (*Él/Ella huele mal*), it means the person smells bad (often body odor).
target_language_example: Creo que la leche huele mal; mejor no la tomes.
native_language_example: I think the milk smells bad; you’d better not drink it.

additional_notes: Used to introduce something obvious or already understood. Commonly followed by "que": "Huelga decir que...". It’s fairly formal and often seen in writing or more careful speech.
target_language_example: Huelga decir que necesitas llevar pasaporte para viajar.
native_language_example: Needless to say, you need to bring a passport to travel.

additional_notes: Used with an infinitive to talk about a repeated behavior: el hábito de fumar (the habit of smoking). With adjectives it often becomes: buen/mal hábito de + infinitive. You’ll also see verbs like tener el hábito de (to have the habit of), coger el hábito de (to pick up the habit of), and librarse del hábito de (to get rid of the habit of).
target_language_example: Estoy tratando de dejar el hábito de comer tarde.
native_language_example: I'm trying to quit the habit of eating late.

additional_notes: Used as the past “going to” future: imperfect of ir (iba) + a + infinitive. It expresses an intention/plan in the past (often something that didn’t happen: “I was going to…, but…”), or something that was just about to happen (“was about to…”). In some contexts it can also describe a repeated past action, similar to “used to” (e.g., “Él iba a verla…” = “He would go see her…”).
target_language_example: Iba a llamarte, pero se me olvidó.
native_language_example: I was going to call you, but I forgot.

additional_notes: Uses the imperfect of ir + a + infinitive (ir a decir) to express an intention in the past: you were planning to say something, were about to say it, or were going to say it but didn’t (because you forgot, got interrupted, or changed your mind). Often used when you’re remembering what you wanted to say (Se me olvidó lo que iba a decir) or when someone else says what you were thinking (Eso es justo lo que iba a decir).
target_language_example: Perdón, se me fue: iba a decir que mañana no puedo.
native_language_example: Sorry, it slipped my mind: I was going to say that I can’t tomorrow.

meaning: “was going to do” / “was about to do.”
additional_notes: Imperfect of ir + a + infinitive ("ir a hacer") used to talk about a plan/intention in the past, or something that was about to happen. It often implies the action didn’t happen or was interrupted (depending on context). Changes with the subject: yo iba a hacer, tú ibas a hacer, él/ella iba a hacer, etc.
target_language_example: Iba a hacer la cena, pero llegaste tarde.
native_language_example: I was going to make dinner, but you arrived late.

meaning: “was going to be” / “would be” (said about the future from a past point of view).
additional_notes: It’s the imperfect of ir a + infinitive (past form of “going to”): iba(s)/iba/íbamos/iban a ser. Used to talk about what you thought, predicted, or planned in the past about something that would happen later (and it may or may not have happened). Often follows verbs like pensar, saber, decir.
target_language_example: No imaginaba que la reunión iba a ser tan larga.
native_language_example: I didn’t imagine the meeting was going to be so long.

meaning: “they were going to” (imperfect past of ir a + infinitive).
additional_notes: Used to talk about a plan, intention, or something expected to happen in the past: iban a + infinitive. It can also suggest something was about to happen (“were about to”). Changes with the subject: yo iba a, tú ibas a, él/ella iba a, nosotros íbamos a, ellos/ellas iban a.
target_language_example: Dijeron que iban a llamar, pero no llamaron.
native_language_example: They said they were going to call, but they didn’t call.

meaning: “you were going to…” (you had the intention/plan, or were about to).
additional_notes: This is the imperfect tense of ir + a + infinitive (the "going to" future) for tú: ibas a + verb. It’s often used in reported speech ("You said you were going to call") or to talk about a plan/intention in the past that may or may not have happened.
target_language_example: Creí que ibas a llegar tarde.
native_language_example: I thought you were going to arrive late.

additional_notes: Used for travel and transportation, especially with tickets: “un billete/pasaje de ida y vuelta” = a round-trip ticket. You can also use it more generally to mean going somewhere and returning.
target_language_example: Quiero un billete de ida y vuelta a Madrid para mañana.
native_language_example: I want a round-trip ticket to Madrid for tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used to talk about a language that is not your native language or not the main language spoken in a place. In Spanish, the adjective usually goes after the noun: idioma (language) + extranjero (foreign). You can also say "lengua extranjera" (same meaning).
target_language_example: Estoy aprendiendo un idioma extranjero para el trabajo.
native_language_example: I'm learning a foreign language for work.

additional_notes: Used to compare two people/things: “igual que tú” = “just like you.” Often followed by a noun or pronoun (“igual que los otros,” “igual que su madre”). In some contexts (with “dar”), it appears in the structure “(no) le/te/me da igual que + subjunctive,” meaning “he/she/you/I (don’t) care that …” (e.g., “Le da igual que se sepa” = “He doesn’t care if it’s known.”).
target_language_example: Mi hermano es igual que mi padre.
native_language_example: My brother is just like my dad.

additional_notes: Used to agree that the same situation/feeling applies to you too. It’s common in casual speech to just say “Igual” meaning “Same here.” You may also hear “Igual para mí” (“same for me”).
target_language_example: —A mí también me da miedo volar. —Igual conmigo.
native_language_example: —I'm also afraid of flying. —Same with me.

meaning: just like; the same as (as… as).
additional_notes: Used to compare two people/things/actions: “X, igual que Y” = “X, just like Y.” With time/frequency words it often means “as (always/before)”: “igual que siempre” = “as always,” “igual que ayer” = “same as yesterday.”
target_language_example: Yo pago igual que tú.
native_language_example: I pay the same as you do.

additional_notes: Used to express a reasonable assumption or expectation, often politely or with some uncertainty. Followed by a clause: Imagino que + verb (often in the present or conditional). It can also stand alone as a short answer: “Imagino que sí/no.”
target_language_example: Imagino que mañana va a llover.
native_language_example: I guess it’s going to rain tomorrow.

meaning: to not give a damn; to not care at all (vulgar).
additional_notes: A very informal and vulgar way to say something doesn’t matter to you. Typically used with a negation and an indirect object pronoun: “No me importa un carajo…”. You can swap the pronoun (te/le/nos/les) depending on who doesn’t care.
target_language_example: A mí no me va a importar un carajo lo que digan.
native_language_example: I’m not going to give a damn what they say.

additional_notes: Used to say someone can’t do something (because they lack the ability, skill, or strength) or that they failed to do it in a specific situation. It’s followed by an infinitive: incapaz de hacer + [verb/noun phrase]. Also common: “ser incapaz de…” (general characteristic) vs. “fui/era incapaz de…” (in a particular moment or time).
target_language_example: Soy incapaz de hacer dos cosas a la vez.
native_language_example: I’m incapable of doing two things at the same time.

meaning: "even if" (introduces a condition that doesn’t change the result).
additional_notes: Used before a clause to mean that something is true or will happen no matter what the condition is. Often followed by the indicative for real/possible situations (Incluso si llueve...) and by the subjunctive for hypothetical or unlikely ones (Incluso si lloviera...).
target_language_example: Iré contigo incluso si no tengo tiempo.
native_language_example: I’ll go with you even if I don’t have time.

additional_notes: A common noun phrase for any instrument used to make music (e.g., la guitarra, el piano, la trompeta). It’s usually used with an article (un/una, el/la) and can be described with adjectives: instrumento musical favorito, instrumento musical nuevo, instrumento musical eléctrico.
target_language_example: ¿Tocas algún instrumento musical?
native_language_example: Do you play any musical instrument?

additional_notes: Used for a person hired to investigate things privately (not a police officer). You’ll often see it with the article: «un/una investigador(a) privado/a». The adjective «privado/a» agrees with the person: «investigador privado» (male) / «investigadora privada» (female).
target_language_example: Necesitamos un investigador privado para este caso.
native_language_example: We need a private investigator for this case.

additional_notes: “Invité” (with an accent) is the yo (I) form of the past tense (preterite) of **invitar**. It’s commonly followed by **a** + an infinitive (invité a cenar = I invited [them] to have dinner) or **a** + a noun/event (invité a María a mi fiesta = I invited María to my party).
target_language_example: Te invité a venir conmigo.
native_language_example: I invited you to come with me.

additional_notes: Past tense (preterite) of "invitar" used with "a" to introduce the person invited: "invitó a María" = "he/she invited María." Very often followed by another "a" + an activity/event: "invitó a María a cenar" (to have dinner) / "invitó a María a una fiesta" (to a party).
target_language_example: Mi vecino me invitó a cenar el sábado.
native_language_example: My neighbor invited me to dinner on Saturday.

additional_notes: Common, conversational way to say you’re doing okay but not great—just managing. Often used when someone asks how you are ("¿Qué tal?", "¿Cómo vas?"). It can also mean you’re continuing despite difficulties: "Vamos tirando" = "We’re hanging in there."
target_language_example: —¿Cómo estás? —Pues, ahí voy, ir tirando.
native_language_example: —How are you? —Well, I’m getting by.

additional_notes: Used to talk about moving toward a place or event: ir a Madrid, ir a la boda. Before el, a contracts to al: ir al cine. It can also be followed by an infinitive to mean 'be going to' do something (for example, voy a comer), but that is a different use.
target_language_example: Queremos ir a la playa mañana.
native_language_example: We want to go to the beach tomorrow.

meaning: to go get; to go pick up; to go fetch (sometimes: to go look for)
additional_notes: Used when you need to physically go somewhere to retrieve someone or something (often like “go and get / go pick up”). It can also mean “go look for,” depending on context. Common pattern: ir a buscar + noun/pronoun (e.g., ir a buscar mi laptop, ir a buscarla). With people, Spanish often uses “a”: ir a buscar a mi hermano.
target_language_example: Necesito ir a buscar mi laptop.
native_language_example: I need to go get my laptop.

additional_notes: A common expression for going back to one's home. In Spanish, casa often means "home" in this pattern, so you usually do not use an article here. You can extend it to a casa de + person to mean "to go to someone's house."
target_language_example: Después de la escuela, quiero ir a casa.
native_language_example: After school, I want to go home.

meaning: to go to sleep; to go to bed.
additional_notes: Common way to say you’re going to sleep (often implying you’re going to bed now). Often used with obligation verbs like tener que / deber: “Tengo que ir a dormir.” You can also pair it with time words such as “ahora”, “ya”, “pronto”.
target_language_example: Tengo que ir a dormir ahora.
native_language_example: I have to go to bed now.

additional_notes: Used for the action of going to bed (getting into bed to sleep), often with time expressions (muy tarde/temprano) or before/after phrases like "antes de ir a la cama". In rules/advice you’ll often see "Hay que ir a la cama" (“You have to go to bed”). You can conjugate "ir" to match the subject: "voy/vas/va/vamos/van a la cama".
target_language_example: Tengo que ir a la cama temprano porque mañana trabajo.
native_language_example: I have to go to bed early because I work tomorrow.

additional_notes: Means attending/going to school. With a destination, Spanish uses "ir a" + place: "voy a la escuela" (I go/I’m going to school), "fui a la escuela" (I went to school). "La" is used because "escuela" is a feminine noun; compare "ir al trabajo" (to go to work).
target_language_example: No puedo ir a la escuela mañana porque estoy enfermo.
native_language_example: I can’t go to school tomorrow because I’m sick.

additional_notes: Uses the verb "ir" (to go) + "a" (to) + "la playa" (the beach). Often used to talk about plans or habits: "Me gusta ir a la playa" (I like going to the beach), "Voy a ir a la playa" (I’m going to go to the beach), "Vamos a ir a la playa" (We’re going to go to the beach).
target_language_example: Este fin de semana vamos a ir a la playa.
native_language_example: This weekend we’re going to go to the beach.

meaning: to go to university (to attend college).
additional_notes: Used to talk about attending university/college in general (often as a life plan), not just physically going to campus today. Common patterns: "poder ir a la universidad" (to be able to go), "decidir no ir" (decide not to go), "planear ir" (plan to go).
target_language_example: Quiero ir a la universidad para estudiar medicina.
native_language_example: I want to go to university to study medicine.

meaning: to go to Mass (a church service).
additional_notes: Used mainly in Catholic contexts. You can specify when: "ir a misa el domingo" (to go to Mass on Sunday). Also common: "ir a misa" (general habit) vs. "ir a la misa" (go to a specific Mass).
target_language_example: Los domingos solemos ir a misa con mi abuela.
native_language_example: On Sundays we usually go to Mass with my grandmother.

additional_notes: Used to talk about what something/someone will be in the (usually near) future. Structure: conjugated form of "ir" + "a" + "ser". Example: "Lo que va a ser difícil" = "What is going to be difficult." Note: In real sentences, "ir" is almost always conjugated, so you’ll commonly see forms like "va a ser", "voy a ser", etc., rather than the infinitive sequence "ir a ser" by itself.
target_language_example: Prometer sin cumplir es ir a ser un problema para el equipo.
native_language_example: Making promises without following through is going to be a problem for the team.

additional_notes: Used with a destination-style structure: ir (conjugated) + a + trabajar. Often expresses routine or obligation with phrases like "tener que" (have to) or a choice like "elegir" (choose). You can add details like how/when: "para ir a trabajar" (in order to go to work), "todos los días" (every day), "solo" (alone).
target_language_example: Mañana tengo que levantarme temprano para ir a trabajar.
native_language_example: Tomorrow I have to get up early to go to work.

meaning: to go ahead; to move forward; to continue.
additional_notes: Used literally for physical movement (“go forward/ahead”) and figuratively to mean continuing or making progress. Often appears as a suggestion or instruction: “Puedes ir adelante” (you can go ahead) or “Sigue adelante” (keep going). Don’t confuse with “salir adelante,” which means “to get by / pull through.”
target_language_example: Puedes ir adelante; yo te alcanzo en un minuto.
native_language_example: You can go ahead; I’ll catch up to you in a minute.

meaning: to go to the bathroom (to use the toilet).
additional_notes: Common, polite everyday way to say you need to use the toilet. Often used with necessity or desire: “necesito ir al baño” (I need to go), “tengo ganas de ir al baño” (I feel like I need to go). You can also say “Voy al baño” (I’m going to the bathroom).
target_language_example: Perdón, ¿puedo ir al baño?
native_language_example: Sorry, can I go to the bathroom?

additional_notes: Used for the activity of going to watch a movie in a movie theater. Conjugate only the verb ir (voy, vas, va, etc.) and keep al cine the same. You can add time expressions: ir al cine hoy, ir al cine los domingos.
target_language_example: ¿Quieres ir al cine conmigo esta noche?
native_language_example: Do you want to go to the movies with me tonight?

additional_notes: Used for attending school (often elementary or middle school). In many countries, "colegio" means "school" (not "college"), so it can be a false friend for English speakers.
target_language_example: Mis hijos tienen que ir al colegio en autobús.
native_language_example: My kids have to go to school by bus.

meaning: to go abroad; to go to a foreign country.
additional_notes: Used with "ir" + "al" (a + el) + "extranjero" to talk about traveling to another country (in general, without naming a specific destination). You can also say "viajar al extranjero" (to travel abroad).
target_language_example: Este verano quiero ir al extranjero con mis amigos.
native_language_example: This summer I want to go abroad with my friends.

meaning: To get to the point; to stop talking generally and say the main thing.
additional_notes: Used when you want to be direct and focus on the most important part of what you’re saying, often after some introduction or small talk. Common with phrases like “Voy a ir al grano” (I’ll get to the point) or “Vamos al grano” (Let’s get to the point).
target_language_example: Mira, voy a ir al grano: necesito una respuesta hoy.
native_language_example: Look, I’ll get to the point: I need an answer today.

additional_notes: Used for going to a hospital building (often for treatment, an emergency, or a visit). In Spanish you usually say "ir al hospital" with the article "al" (= a + el), unlike English where you can say "go to hospital" (UK) without "the".
target_language_example: Si te duele mucho, vamos a ir al hospital.
native_language_example: If it hurts a lot, we’re going to go to the hospital.

additional_notes: Uses the verb "ir" (to go) + "allá" (there/over there, usually a bit farther away or less specific than "allí"). Often refers to going to a place already known from context.
target_language_example: ¿Quieres ir allá conmigo mañana?
native_language_example: Do you want to go there with me tomorrow?

additional_notes: Uses the verb "ir" (to go) + "allí" (there/over there). "Allí" often suggests a specific place at some distance (similar to “over there”); "ahí" is more like “there (near you)”.
target_language_example: No quiero ir allí otra vez.
native_language_example: I don’t want to go there again.

meaning: to go up; to move upward.
additional_notes: Literally “to go” (ir) + “up/above” (arriba). Used for physical movement (going upstairs/up a hill) and also in instructions (e.g., “go up” on a page/menu or “scroll up”). In everyday speech, Spanish often uses “subir” for “to go up.”
target_language_example: Si quieres ver el comienzo, tienes que ir arriba.
native_language_example: If you want to see the beginning, you have to go up (scroll up).

additional_notes: Used to say you accompany someone: "ir con él/ella" = "go with him/her". It can also be used with things like "precaución" to mean "to proceed with" a certain attitude or manner ("ir con precaución" = "go/proceed carefully").
target_language_example: ¿Quieres ir con nosotros al cine?
native_language_example: Do you want to go with us to the movies?

additional_notes: Used to say you will accompany someone somewhere. It’s very common with verbs like ir (to go), venir (to come), and salir (to go out). Note: contigo means “with you” (informal singular tú). For “with you” formal/plural, use con usted / con ustedes.
target_language_example: Si quieres, puedo ir contigo al supermercado.
native_language_example: If you want, I can go with you to the supermarket.

additional_notes: With activity nouns, ir de + noun means "go [activity]-ing" or "go on a/an [activity] trip," as in ir de pesca or ir de acampada. With places, often in the pattern ir de X a Y, it means "go from X to Y."
target_language_example: Los domingos nos gusta ir de pesca al lago.
native_language_example: On Sundays we like to go fishing at the lake.

additional_notes: Used with the verb *ir* (“to go”) + *de compras* (“shopping”). You can add where you’re going with *a/al*: *ir de compras al supermercado* (go shopping to the supermarket).
target_language_example: Vamos a ir de compras después de clase.
native_language_example: We’re going to go shopping after class.

meaning: to go hand in hand (to be closely connected; to go together).
additional_notes: Often used figuratively to say two things are closely linked or tend to occur together ("X and Y go together"). It can also be used literally for two people walking while holding hands. Conjugates as the verb "ir" (e.g., "van de la mano", "fue de la mano").
target_language_example: La seguridad y la confianza suelen ir de la mano.
native_language_example: Safety and trust tend to go hand in hand.

meaning: to go too far (to overdo it or cross a line).
additional_notes: Used both literally (going farther than intended) and very often figuratively (saying/doing something unacceptable or excessive). Common in phrases like “Creo que vas a ir demasiado lejos” (I think you’re going to go too far) or “No debes ir demasiado lejos con eso” (You shouldn’t take it that far).
target_language_example: Perdón, creo que voy a ir demasiado lejos con ese comentario.
native_language_example: Sorry, I think I’m going to go too far with that comment.

meaning: to go toward; to head in the direction of.
additional_notes: Used to express movement (literal or figurative) in the direction of a place, person, or goal. It’s often interchangeable with "ir a" in some contexts, but "hacia" emphasizes direction rather than a specific destination. It can also be used figuratively: "ir hacia un estilo diferente" = move toward a different style.
target_language_example: Vamos a ir hacia la estación de tren.
native_language_example: We’re going to head toward the train station.

additional_notes: Uses the verb ir + adverb tarde to say you’re late or behind schedule: “Voy tarde” (I’m late). Often followed by “a” + place/event: “Voy tarde al trabajo / a clase.” You can also use the imperfect for a repeated situation: “Siempre iba tarde.”
target_language_example: Perdón, no quiero ir tarde a la reunión.
native_language_example: Sorry, I don’t want to be late to the meeting.

meaning: to come and go; to go back and forth.
additional_notes: Used to talk about moving freely between places, often repeatedly. It commonly appears with phrases like "a tu antojo" (as you please), "a voluntad" (at will), or "según le plazca" (as he/she pleases).
target_language_example: Durante el día, los clientes pueden ir y venir sin problema.
native_language_example: During the day, customers can come and go without any problem.

meaning: to go now; to leave right away.
additional_notes: Uses the verb "ir" (to go) with "ya" (now/already) to express urgency: "We should go now" (Hay que ir ya) or as a strong command meaning "Go now!" (¡A ir ya!/¡Ir ya!). More commonly, people use a conjugated form like "Vete ya" or "Vamos ya".
target_language_example: Hay que ir ya; se nos hace tarde.
native_language_example: We need to go now; we’re running late.

meaning: to be doing well; for things to be going well for someone
additional_notes: Used to talk about how things are going for someone (work, life, health, relationships, etc.). The "-le" is an indirect object pronoun that changes depending on the person: irme bien (I’m doing well), irte bien (you’re doing well), irle bien (he/she/you formal is doing well), irnos bien, irles bien (they/you all are doing well). Common in questions like "¿Cómo te va?" / "¿Te va bien?". Note: in many conjugated sentences, the words may split (e.g., "le va bien"), but the dictionary form is "irle bien".
target_language_example: A Marta le está empezando a irle bien en el trabajo.
native_language_example: Things are starting to go well for Marta at work.

meaning: to go home (for me to leave and go to my house).
additional_notes: Uses the verb ir (“to go”) with a reflexive/subject pronoun attached in the infinitive to show who is leaving: irme (for me to leave), irte (for you to leave), irse (for him/her/you formal to leave), irnos (for us to leave), iros (for you all to leave), irse (for them/you all formal to leave). Common after verbs like querer/poder/deber: “Quiero/puedo/debo irme a casa.” In conversation, the equivalent finite form is often “me voy a casa.”
target_language_example: Creo que debería irme a casa.
native_language_example: I think I should go home.

meaning: to leave (to go) to / to leave for; to go off to (do something).
additional_notes: Irse is the reflexive form of ir (“to go”) and emphasizes leaving/going away from a place or situation. It’s commonly used with a destination (irse a Nueva York = “to leave for New York”) or with an infinitive to express leaving in order to do something (irse a trabajar = “to go off to work”). It conjugates like ir, plus a reflexive pronoun: me voy, te vas, se va, nos vamos, se van; in the infinitive it appears as irse.
target_language_example: Ella le pidió que se quedase, pero él tenía que irse a trabajar.
native_language_example: She asked him to stay, but he had to go off to work.

meaning: to go home (to leave for home).
additional_notes: "Irse" emphasizes the act of leaving (often from your current location) rather than simply being en route. It’s common when talking about permission or desire: "Puede irse a casa" (You can go home) and "Estaba deseando irse a casa" (She was looking forward to going home). You’ll also hear conjugated forms like "me voy a casa" for "I’m going home."
target_language_example: Ella estaba deseando irse a casa.
native_language_example: She was looking forward to going home.

additional_notes: Common bedtime phrase. Uses the reflexive verb "irse" (to leave/go away), emphasizing going off to bed (often for the night). Frequently used with expressions like "Es hora de..." (It’s time to...) or "antes de..." (before...).
target_language_example: Es hora de irse a la cama.
native_language_example: It’s time to go to bed.

meaning: to go to hell; to fuck off (vulgar).
additional_notes: Very rude/vulgar expression used in anger or frustration. It can be directed at a person (telling them to leave) or at a situation/plan (meaning it failed or you’re done with it). Uses the reflexive verb: "Me voy al carajo" = "I’m leaving / I’m done." Not appropriate in polite settings.
target_language_example: Dile que no me llame más y que se vaya al carajo.
native_language_example: Tell him not to call me anymore and to fuck off.

meaning: “I will go to …” / “I’m going to …” (future: I will do something).
additional_notes: "Iré" is the future tense of "ir" (to go): "I will go". With "a" + an infinitive, it commonly means you will go somewhere in order to do something, or simply that you will do something in the future (similar to “I’m going to + verb”). In "Te iré a ver mañana", the pronoun "te" (“you”) comes before the verb phrase.
target_language_example: Iré a llamarte más tarde.
native_language_example: I’ll call you later.

additional_notes: Used to talk about going somewhere in the future: *Iré a Irlanda*, *Iré a la universidad*. It can also introduce an action with an infinitive: *Iré a visitarte* (“I’ll go visit you”). In the pattern *ir a por + noun*, it means “to go get/pick up”: *Iré a por el coche* (“I’ll go get the car”).
target_language_example: Esta tarde iré a tu casa.
native_language_example: This afternoon I'll go to your house.

meaning: “Jain” (a person’s name), used to get their attention.
