additional_notes: Used for a lamp or light fixture that gives light (e.g., a bedside lamp, desk lamp). Often followed by an adjective to describe it ("la lámpara vieja", "la lámpara gris"). Related verbs: "encender" (to turn on/light) and "apagar" (to turn off).
target_language_example: ¿Puedes apagar la lámpara, por favor?
native_language_example: Can you turn off the lamp, please?

meaning: the line (mark/row); the line (phone connection); a boundary/limit; a line of thought/approach (“in line with”).
additional_notes: Common uses: (1) a physical line or row on a form/page: "En la línea, sólo tu nombre." (2) a boundary you shouldn’t cross: "Cruzar la línea" = “to cross the line.” (3) telephone connection: "La línea se cortó" = “The line got cut / We got disconnected.” (4) "en la línea de" = “in line with / along the lines of,” often for plans, policies, ideas: "No va en la línea de nuestra política." Also "final de la línea" = “end of the line” (literal or figurative).
target_language_example: Lo que dices no está en la línea de lo que acordamos.
native_language_example: What you’re saying isn’t in line with what we agreed.

additional_notes: Used to talk about someone’s mother and connect her to another person or thing. It’s typically followed by a noun or a possessive phrase: la madre de mi amigo (my friend’s mother), la madre de un amigo mío (a friend of mine’s mother).
target_language_example: La madre de mi hermano trabaja en un hospital.
native_language_example: My brother’s mother works in a hospital.

additional_notes: Used to talk about unlucky events or an unlucky situation. Often appears after "tener" (to have) or with "ser" to describe something as unlucky (e.g., "un número de mala suerte" = an unlucky number). Can also be used alone as an exclamation or short comment: "¡La mala suerte!"
target_language_example: Hoy tengo la mala suerte de perder el autobús.
native_language_example: Today I have the bad luck of missing the bus.

additional_notes: A common noun for a suitcase or piece of luggage (usually for travel). It’s feminine: la maleta, una maleta; plural: las maletas. Often used with verbs like llevar (to carry/take), cerrar (to close), cargar (to load/carry), and perder de vista (to lose sight of).
target_language_example: Puse la maleta en el maletero del coche.
native_language_example: I put the suitcase in the trunk of the car.

additional_notes: Used to introduce how something happens or is done. It’s often followed by a verb: "la manera en que + [someone] + verb". Very similar in meaning to "la forma en que".
target_language_example: No me gustó la manera en que respondió a la pregunta.
native_language_example: I didn’t like the way he/she answered the question.

additional_notes: Means 'hand'. mano is feminine even though it ends in -o, so it takes la and una. With body parts, Spanish often uses the definite article where English uses a possessive: me duele la mano = my hand hurts.
target_language_example: Tengo la mano fría.
native_language_example: My hand is cold.

additional_notes: Used for the left hand specifically (vs. “la mano derecha” = the right hand). With body parts in Spanish, you usually use the definite article (“la”), not a possessive (“my”), even when it’s your own body: “Me duele la mano izquierda” = “My left hand hurts.” It can also appear in fixed/religious expressions like “la mano izquierda de Dios” (“the left hand of God”).
target_language_example: Me duele la mano izquierda desde ayer.
native_language_example: My left hand has hurt since yesterday.

additional_notes: A common noun for the fruit. Uses the feminine singular article “la”; plural: “las manzanas”. You can describe it with adjectives like color ("La manzana es verde") or talk about cutting it ("partió la manzana en dos").
target_language_example: Quiero comerme la manzana después de la cena.
native_language_example: I want to eat the apple after dinner.

meaning: the sea; also (in “la mar de…”) ‘very’ / ‘a lot of’.
additional_notes: “Mar” is often masculine (“el mar”), but “la mar” is also common—especially in poetic or traditional sailor speech. In everyday colloquial Spanish, the fixed pattern “la mar de + adjective/adverb/noun” is used as an intensifier: “la mar de bien” = “very well,” “la mar de ocupados” = “very busy,” “la mar de gente” = “a lot of people.”
target_language_example: Hoy estoy la mar de cansado.
native_language_example: Today I’m very tired.

additional_notes: Used to say that the majority of a person’s time, life, money, etc. is involved. It’s followed by a noun (su vida, su dinero, su tiempo). Note: "su" can mean his, her, your (formal), or their; context tells you which. Also changes for number: "la mayor parte de sus" (most of his/her/your/their + plural noun).
target_language_example: Pasé la mayor parte de su tiempo estudiando.
native_language_example: I spent most of his/her time studying.

additional_notes: Used to talk about more than half of a group. It’s followed by a noun: "la mayoría de + los/las + plural noun" (la mayoría de los alumnos). With an implied noun, you can also use it alone: "La mayoría eran canadienses" (Most were Canadian). Verb agreement can be singular or plural depending on the speaker’s focus (the group as one vs. the individuals), but plural is very common in everyday Spanish.
target_language_example: La mayoría de mis amigos viven cerca de aquí.
native_language_example: Most of my friends live near here.

meaning: most people; the majority of people.
additional_notes: Used to talk about what is true for most people in general (a generalization). It’s often followed by a verb in the singular ("la mayoría ... está/es/hace") because "la mayoría" is the main subject, though plural agreement is sometimes heard in everyday speech.
target_language_example: La mayoría de la gente piensa que es una buena idea.
native_language_example: Most people think it’s a good idea.

additional_notes: Used before a masculine plural noun to mean “most of the …”. It agrees with the noun: la mayoría de las + feminine plural (la mayoría de las personas), and la mayoría de + a singular/uncountable noun (la mayoría del tiempo). It’s often followed by a plural verb (La mayoría de los estudiantes son…), though singular is sometimes used in formal contexts.
target_language_example: La mayoría de los estudiantes viven cerca de la universidad.
native_language_example: Most of the students live near the university.

additional_notes: Refers to the part of the day from dawn until noon. In time expressions, de la mañana means 'in the morning' or 'a.m.' (for example, la una de la mañana = 1 a.m.). Note that mañana by itself can also mean 'tomorrow,' but la mañana specifically means 'the morning.'
target_language_example: La mañana siempre pasa rápido cuando tengo mucho trabajo.
native_language_example: The morning always goes by quickly when I have a lot of work.

additional_notes: Used with prepositions like a (at), hasta (until/by), and pasada (past/after): a la medianoche = at midnight; hasta la medianoche = until/by midnight; pasada la medianoche = after midnight. Usually refers to the transition between one day and the next.
target_language_example: Tenemos que entregar el trabajo hasta la medianoche.
native_language_example: We have to turn in the assignment by midnight.

meaning: medicine; also, the field/practice of medicine.
additional_notes: Usually refers either to (1) a drug/medicine you take (often uncountable in general: "tomar medicina") or (2) the medical profession/science ("la medicina es una profesión"). For a specific dose, Spanish often uses "la medicina" with context or adds a descriptor ("esta medicina", "mi medicina").
target_language_example: Tengo que tomar la medicina dos veces al día.
native_language_example: I have to take the medicine twice a day.

additional_notes: Used with feminine nouns (explicit or implied): la mejor joya, la mejor fiesta. It can also stand alone when the noun is understood: Ella es la mejor (She’s the best). For masculine, use "el mejor"; for plural, "los/las mejores".
target_language_example: Para mí, esa es la mejor opción.
native_language_example: For me, that’s the best option.

additional_notes: Used to introduce the best method or approach for an action that follows, usually with an infinitive (e.g., "la mejor manera de aprender") or with "es" + gerund/infinitive ("la mejor manera de hacerlo es..."). Often interchangeable with "la mejor forma de".
target_language_example: La mejor manera de aprender español es practicar un poco cada día.
native_language_example: The best way to learn Spanish is to practice a little every day.

additional_notes: Common after verbs like tener/en la mente (to have in mind), venir a la mente (to come to mind), and quedarse la mente en blanco (for your mind to go blank). It refers to thinking, remembering, imagining, or mental strength/ability.
target_language_example: No puedo sacarlo de la mente.
native_language_example: I can’t get it out of my mind.

additional_notes: A basic noun phrase: mesa means "table," and la is the feminine singular word for "the." In expressions like poner la mesa, it means "to set the table" for a meal.
target_language_example: La mesa está junto a la ventana.
native_language_example: The table is next to the window.

meaning: “shit” (vulgar); also “this/that shit” or “crap” (vulgar) in a more general sense.
additional_notes: Very vulgar/strong. Literally refers to feces (e.g., it smells bad, cleaning it). It’s also used to refer to something unpleasant or difficult (“la mierda ya es bastante difícil” = “this shit is hard enough”), or as an insult about someone/something (“eres la mierda…” = “you’re shit/you’re a piece of shit”). Often sounds stronger than English “crap.”
target_language_example: No quiero hablar de la mierda de ayer.
native_language_example: I don’t want to talk about yesterday’s shit.

meaning: the mission; a specific task or assignment (often official).
additional_notes: Used for an objective or operation someone must carry out (military, police, work, religious, etc.). Common with verbs like terminar/concluir (finish), llevar a cabo (carry out), cancelar/abortar (cancel/abort), and with phrases like tener luz verde (have the green light).
target_language_example: Tenemos que cumplir la misión antes del amanecer.
native_language_example: We have to complete the mission before dawn.

additional_notes: Used to say two things/people are identical or the very same. It agrees in gender/number with what it refers to: la misma (feminine singular), el mismo (masc. sing.), las mismas (fem. plural), los mismos (masc. plural). Often followed by a noun (la misma persona = the same person) or used on its own when the noun is understood.
target_language_example: Ella y yo tenemos la misma idea.
native_language_example: She and I have the same idea.

additional_notes: Used to say two people/ideas/actions are identical, or to complain that something repeats again and again (often: "siempre es la misma cosa"). It agrees in gender/number with the noun: "la misma cosa" (feminine singular), "el mismo problema", "las mismas cosas", "los mismos días".
target_language_example: No quiero discutir la misma cosa otra vez.
native_language_example: I don’t want to argue about the same thing again.

additional_notes: Used to say two or more people have an equal or very similar age. Often appears with comparison words like “más o menos” (more or less) or “aproximadamente” (approximately), and with “que” to compare: “tener la misma edad que…” = “to be the same age as…”.
target_language_example: Mi hermana y yo tenemos la misma edad.
native_language_example: My sister and I are the same age.

additional_notes: Used before a masculine singular noun: la mitad del alquiler, la mitad del texto. (Before a feminine singular noun, you use “la mitad de la”: la mitad de la casa.) It commonly expresses quantities, portions, or percentages. With people it can be literal (“half the man you are”) or figurative.
target_language_example: Solo necesito la mitad del dinero hoy.
native_language_example: I only need half of the money today.

additional_notes: Refers to a mountain (a large natural elevation). Often used with verbs like "escalar" (to climb) and "subir" (to go up). In names/titles it can be part of a proper noun (e.g., "La montaña de...").
target_language_example: Mañana vamos a caminar por la montaña.
native_language_example: Tomorrow we’re going to hike in the mountains.

additional_notes: Refers to a female, usually a girl or young woman (often a teenager or young adult). Similar to "la chica" (very common) and sometimes older than "la niña" (little girl). Can be used when you don’t know the person’s name: "la muchacha que…".
target_language_example: La muchacha que trabaja aquí es muy amable.
native_language_example: The young woman who works here is very kind.

additional_notes: Refers to death as a general concept or the event of dying. Often used with "de" to talk about someone’s death: "la muerte de su marido" = "her husband’s death."
target_language_example: La noticia de la muerte del actor fue muy triste.
native_language_example: The news of the actor’s death was very sad.

additional_notes: Used to talk about someone’s death, often followed by a name or a possessive phrase: la muerte de Neil Perry; la muerte de su madre. You’ll also see it in expressions like “desde la muerte de…” (“since the death of…”) and with verbs like llorar (to mourn) or superar (to get over).
target_language_example: Nunca olvidaremos la muerte de nuestro abuelo.
native_language_example: We will never forget the death of our grandfather.

meaning: 'death is' (used to define or describe death).
additional_notes: Common sentence starter: “La muerte es + noun/adjective” to say what death is like (e.g., “La muerte es permanente”). You can also add comparisons with “similar a” (“La muerte es similar al sueño”).
target_language_example: Para él, la muerte es parte de la vida.
native_language_example: For him, death is part of life.

additional_notes: uses the feminine singular definite article la with mujer. It refers to a specific woman, either already mentioned or clear from context. In other expressions, mujer can sometimes mean 'wife' (for example, mi mujer = 'my wife'), but la mujer by itself usually means 'the woman'.
target_language_example: La mujer está esperando afuera.
native_language_example: The woman is waiting outside.

meaning: “the woman who/that …” (introduces information describing a woman).
additional_notes: Used to start a relative clause with que (“who/that”) to identify or describe a specific woman: La mujer que + verb/phrase. In Spanish, que is used for both “who” and “that” in this kind of sentence.
target_language_example: La mujer que trabaja aquí es mi profesora.
native_language_example: The woman who works here is my teacher.

additional_notes: Refers to a large group of people gathered in one place (e.g., at a game, concert, or in the street). Often used with verbs like "gritar/chillar" (to shout), "dispersarse" (to disperse), or "perder de vista" (to lose sight of someone) "en medio de la multitud".
target_language_example: Había tanta gente que no podía avanzar por la multitud.
native_language_example: There were so many people that I couldn’t move forward through the crowd.

additional_notes: Used for a physical machine/device (from small appliances to large machines). You’ll often see it with verbs like funcionar (“to work/run”): hacer que la máquina funcione = “make the machine work.”
target_language_example: La máquina no funciona, así que tengo que arreglarla.
native_language_example: The machine doesn’t work, so I have to fix it.

additional_notes: Means “mine” when the thing owned is feminine and usually already understood from context (the noun is often omitted). Common with comparisons and contrasts: “parecida a la mía” = “similar to mine”; “no la mía” = “not mine.” It changes with gender/number: el mío, los míos, las mías.
target_language_example: No encuentro mi llave; ¿has visto la mía?
native_language_example: I can’t find my key; have you seen mine?

additional_notes: This is a sentence fragment used to begin a statement about music. Spanish uses "es el" before a masculine noun (el + noun). With a feminine noun, use "es la" (e.g., "La música es la mejor terapia"). A very common completion is "La música es el lenguaje universal" (music is the universal language).
target_language_example: La música es el lenguaje universal.
native_language_example: Music is the universal language.

additional_notes: A common body-part noun. In Spanish, body parts usually use the definite article (la/ el) instead of a possessive: "Tienes algo en la nariz" (literally “You have something in the nose” = “in your nose”). Also appears in expressions like "tener la nariz enterrada en un libro" (“to have your nose buried in a book” = to be absorbed in reading).
target_language_example: Me duele la nariz.
native_language_example: My nose hurts.

additional_notes: Refers to the natural world in general: plants, animals, landscapes, and the environment. Often used with verbs like gustar (Me gusta la naturaleza) and with topics like protecting the environment (salvar/proteger la naturaleza). Also used in general statements (La naturaleza está llena de...).
target_language_example: Nos encanta pasar tiempo en la naturaleza los fines de semana.
native_language_example: We love spending time in nature on the weekends.

additional_notes: Meaning depends on context. In sci‑fi or travel contexts, it’s usually a ship/spacecraft (e.g., "Hay algo en la nave" = something is on/in the ship). In business/industry contexts, "una nave" often means a large industrial building/warehouse ("nave industrial"). It’s feminine: la nave, una nave.
target_language_example: Hay algo raro en la nave.
native_language_example: There’s something strange on the ship.

additional_notes: Used for the weather phenomenon that reduces visibility. Common with verbs like "haber" (hay la niebla / hay niebla), "aparecer" (to appear), "cubrir" (to cover), and in phrases like "en la niebla" (in the fog). Always feminine: "la niebla".
target_language_example: Nos perdimos en la niebla y tuvimos que volver atrás.
native_language_example: We got lost in the fog and had to turn back.

additional_notes: A feminine noun meaning the white frozen precipitation (“the snow”). Common in comparisons like "blanco/a como la nieve" (“as white as snow”) and with verbs like "caer" (to fall) or "cubrir" (to cover).
target_language_example: En invierno, a veces cae la nieve en las montañas.
native_language_example: In winter, snow sometimes falls in the mountains.

additional_notes: Refers to a female child; often implies she’s young ("little girl"), but it can also mean "girl" more generally depending on context. Uses the feminine singular article "la" (contrast: "el niño" = the boy / the child).
target_language_example: La niña está jugando en el parque.
native_language_example: The little girl is playing in the park.

additional_notes: Refers to the nighttime period after evening and before morning. In context, it can also mean the night of a particular event (for example, la noche del sábado = Saturday night).
target_language_example: La noche está muy tranquila hoy.
native_language_example: The night is very calm today.

additional_notes: Used to refer to the night immediately before a certain day/event mentioned or understood from context. Often followed by “a + [event]” (e.g., “la noche anterior a un vuelo”).
target_language_example: Preparé todo la noche anterior al examen.
native_language_example: I prepared everything the night before the exam.

meaning: the news; the news item (a specific piece of news)
additional_notes: Often refers to a specific news item or piece of information. In Spanish, singular (la noticia) is commonly used for one item; plural (las noticias) often refers to “the news” in general (e.g., the TV news).
target_language_example: Parece que la noticia era falsa.
native_language_example: It seems the news was false.

meaning: “the new” (feminine singular), often meaning “the new one.”
additional_notes: Used before a feminine singular noun (la nueva película = “the new movie”), or by itself when the noun is understood from context (Ella es la nueva = “She’s the new one,” e.g., the new teacher/employee). It must agree with the noun: la nueva (fem. sing.), el nuevo (masc. sing.), las nuevas (fem. pl.), los nuevos (masc. pl.).
target_language_example: Ella es la nueva en la oficina.
native_language_example: She’s the new one in the office.

meaning: “the work” (a piece of art/music/literature, a play, or construction/work being done).
additional_notes: "La obra" is a common way to refer to a creative work (a novel, musical piece, painting, etc.) or specifically a theater play ("una obra de teatro"). It can also mean building/construction work or a job/task in progress, so the exact meaning depends on context.
target_language_example: ¿Has visto la obra en el teatro todavía?
native_language_example: Have you seen the play at the theater yet?

meaning: 'the offer' (a proposal; also a deal/special price).
additional_notes: Common with verbs like aceptar (to accept) and rechazar (to reject). It can refer to an offer of help, an invitation, or a formal proposal (e.g., una oferta de trabajo = a job offer). In stores, una oferta can also mean a special deal/discount.
target_language_example: Acepté la oferta de trabajo.
native_language_example: I accepted the job offer.

additional_notes: Usually refers to a workplace office (a building/room where people work). Also used for an office as a department or someone’s official workplace, e.g. "la oficina del Comandante" = "the Commander’s office". Often used with "ir a" (to go to): "ir a la oficina" = "to go to the office".
target_language_example: Hoy no voy a la oficina porque trabajo desde casa.
native_language_example: Today I’m not going to the office because I work from home.

additional_notes: A common place/building where you send mail and packages. Often used with location verbs like estar/quedar/ubicarse (to be located). You can also say "correos" in some countries to refer to the postal service.
target_language_example: Tengo que ir a la oficina de correos para enviar un paquete.
native_language_example: I have to go to the post office to send a package.

additional_notes: Most commonly used for a medical/surgical operation (a procedure a doctor or surgeon performs). It’s feminine: la operación. You’ll often hear it with verbs like realizar/hacer (to perform/do) and suspender (to suspend/call off). It can also mean a more general “operation” (e.g., a police or military operation), but the examples here are medical.
target_language_example: La operación salió bien y ya está recuperándose.
native_language_example: The operation went well and he/she is already recovering.

additional_notes: Used to talk about the general attitude of society toward an issue, person, or policy—often in politics and the news. Common with verbs like reflejar (to reflect), cambiar (to change), estar a favor de (to be in favor of), and estar en contra de (to be against). Usually singular even though it refers to many people.
target_language_example: Según las encuestas, la opinión pública está en contra de la nueva ley.
native_language_example: According to the polls, public opinion is against the new law.

additional_notes: Used with an infinitive (de + verb) to say someone has/gets/takes a chance to do something: "tener la oportunidad de..." (to have the chance to...), "darle la oportunidad de..." (to give someone the chance to...), "aprovechar la oportunidad de..." (to take advantage of the chance to...).
target_language_example: No tuve la oportunidad de hablar con el doctor.
native_language_example: I didn’t have the chance to talk to the doctor.

meaning: 'the order' (a command or an official instruction); also 'the order' (a purchase/order request).
additional_notes: Most commonly means a command given by someone in authority (e.g., a boss, officer, judge): "Dar la orden" = to give the order; "cumplir la orden" = to carry out/obey the order. In business/shipping contexts it can also mean an order you place (purchase order): "hacer la orden" = to place/make the order. Note: "orden" also exists as "el orden" meaning 'order/organization' (the opposite of chaos), but "la orden" is specifically a command or a purchase order.
target_language_example: El jefe dio la orden de cerrar la tienda.
native_language_example: The boss gave the order to close the store.

meaning: the orchestra (a large group of musicians who play together).
additional_notes: A feminine noun, so it takes "la" (singular) and "las" (plural: "las orquestas"). Used for ensembles that play classical music (symphonies, waltzes, etc.), but it can also refer more generally to a big instrumental group. Common verbs with it: "tocar" (to play), "interpretar" (to perform), "empezar a" (to start to).
target_language_example: La orquesta va a tocar esta noche en el teatro.
native_language_example: The orchestra is going to play tonight at the theater.

additional_notes: Used with verbs like tener miedo de / temer ("to be afraid of") and estar en ("to be in"): tener miedo de la oscuridad, estar en la oscuridad. It can also be used figuratively in poetic or fantasy contexts (e.g., espíritus de la oscuridad = "spirits of darkness").
target_language_example: No puedo ver nada en la oscuridad.
native_language_example: I can't see anything in the dark.

meaning: "the other night" (a recent night in the past).
additional_notes: Used to refer to a past night that happened recently, but not necessarily last night (it could be a few nights ago). Often used when the exact date isn’t important or isn’t specified. Can also be understood as “the other evening,” depending on context.
target_language_example: La otra noche vi una película en casa.
native_language_example: The other night I watched a movie at home.

additional_notes: Used to refer back to the second of two things already mentioned or understood from context. It agrees in gender and number: la otra (fem. sing.), el otro (masc. sing.), las otras (fem. pl.), los otros (masc. pl.). Often used to contrast choices or parts: "Esa camisa no, la otra" (= not that shirt, the other one) or "con la otra (mano)" (= with the other hand). Also appears in fixed patterns like "Una cosa llevó a la otra" (one thing led to another).
target_language_example: No quiero esta taza; prefiero la otra.
native_language_example: I don’t want this cup; I prefer the other one.

additional_notes: Usually means a specific word (a vocabulary item): “No me viene la palabra” = “I can’t think of the word.” Common set phrases: “tomar la palabra” = “to take the floor / speak (in a meeting)”; “tomarle la palabra (a alguien)” = “to take someone at their word”; “esa es la palabra” can mean “that’s the word/right term” (or “exactly”).
target_language_example: No recuerdo la palabra en español para “butterfly”.
native_language_example: I don’t remember the Spanish word for “butterfly”.

additional_notes: Used for the display of a phone, computer, TV, etc.: la pantalla del ordenador (the computer screen). In some contexts it can also mean a projector/movie screen (la pantalla grande = the big screen).
target_language_example: No puedo leer nada en la pantalla porque está muy oscura.
native_language_example: I can’t read anything on the screen because it’s very dark.

additional_notes: Used to talk about the place where you wait for a bus. Often appears with location phrases like "está al lado de..." (it’s next to...), "al otro lado de la calle" (across the street), or "cerca de" (near).
target_language_example: ¿Dónde está la parada de autobús más cercana?
native_language_example: Where is the nearest bus stop?

additional_notes: Refers to a wall of a room/building. Often used with location phrases like "junto a la pared" (next to the wall) or "contra la pared" (against the wall).
target_language_example: Pusimos el sofá contra la pared.
native_language_example: We put the sofa against the wall.

meaning: "the part" (a section, area, or side of something).
additional_notes: Used to talk about a portion of something (la parte que...), a specific area or region (la parte norte), or a position/side (la parte de arriba = the top part; la parte delantera = the front part). Often followed by "de" + noun (la parte del edificio) or by an adjective (la parte norte).
target_language_example: Me gusta la parte del final de la película.
native_language_example: I like the ending part of the movie.

additional_notes: Used for peace in general, often in contexts like countries, treaties, or public order. Common with verbs like mantener la paz (“to keep/maintain the peace”) and desear la paz (“to wish for peace”).
target_language_example: Después de la guerra, todos querían la paz.
native_language_example: After the war, everyone wanted peace.

additional_notes: A very common noun for a ball used in sports or games. It’s feminine singular, so you’ll usually see it with articles like "la" (the) or "una" (a).
target_language_example: ¿Me pasas la pelota, por favor?
native_language_example: Can you pass me the ball, please?

additional_notes: Used to refer to a movie/film. Often used with verbs like ver (to watch/see): “ver la película” = “watch the movie.”
target_language_example: ¿A qué hora empieza la película?
native_language_example: What time does the movie start?

additional_notes: A formal/legal term for the punishment of executing someone for a serious crime. Often used with verbs like abolir (to abolish), imponer (to impose), and aplicar (to apply). Also appears in phrases like condenar a alguien a la pena de muerte (“to sentence someone to death”).
target_language_example: Muchos países han abolido la pena de muerte.
native_language_example: Many countries have abolished the death penalty.

additional_notes: Means “the person” in general. Spanish uses the feminine article “la” because “persona” is grammatically feminine, even when talking about a man (e.g., “Él es la persona adecuada” = “He is the right person”).
target_language_example: Ella es la persona indicada para ayudarte.
native_language_example: She is the right person to help you.

additional_notes: Used to identify or describe a specific person by adding a defining clause after que. It can refer to someone already known (“La persona que vive al lado…”) or to specify who did something (“La persona que me dio esa pintura…”). You’ll also see it in set phrases like “No soy la persona que solía ser” (“I’m not the person I used to be”).
target_language_example: La persona que llamó ayer quiere hablar contigo.
native_language_example: The person who called yesterday wants to talk to you.

additional_notes: Uses the feminine article la because piedra is a feminine noun. Often refers to a particular, known stone in the story or situation (like a magical stone): la piedra = 'the stone' (that everyone is talking about).
target_language_example: La piedra está escondida en la oficina.
native_language_example: The stone is hidden in the office.

additional_notes: Most commonly refers to a person’s skin (the organ covering the body). It can also mean an animal’s hide/skin, sometimes in contexts about materials or money (e.g., selling the hide). Often used with prepositions like en la piel (“on the skin”).
target_language_example: Me puse crema porque tengo la piel muy seca.
native_language_example: I put on cream because my skin is very dry.

additional_notes: Means “the leg.” In Spanish, body parts are often used with the definite article (el/la/los/las) instead of a possessive (mi/tu/su): “Me duele la pierna” = “My leg hurts.” If you mention whose leg it is, Spanish commonly uses an indirect object pronoun (me/te/le/nos/les): “Un perro le mordió la pierna” = “A dog bit his/her leg.”
target_language_example: Me lastimé la pierna jugando al fútbol.
native_language_example: I hurt my leg playing soccer.

additional_notes: In some Latin American countries (especially in the Southern Cone), "pieza" is commonly used to mean a bedroom or a simple room in a house (like a rented room). In other contexts, "pieza" can also mean "piece/part" (e.g., una pieza de pan = a piece of bread), so the meaning depends on context.
target_language_example: Tengo que ordenar la pieza antes de que lleguen.
native_language_example: I have to tidy the room before they arrive.

additional_notes: Often refers to a painting as an artwork (una pintura famosa). It can also mean the activity/art of painting (tener buena mano para la pintura = to be good at painting) or paint as a substance depending on context.
target_language_example: Me gusta la pintura, pero no tengo mucha paciencia para pintar.
native_language_example: I like painting, but I don’t have much patience to paint.

additional_notes: A feminine noun, so it uses "la" (singular) and "las" (plural: "las piscinas"). It can refer to a public/community pool or a private pool at a house/hotel. Common with verbs like "abrir" (to open), "estar cubierta" (to be covered), and "meterse a/en la piscina" (to get into the pool).
target_language_example: En verano vamos a la piscina todos los días.
native_language_example: In summer we go to the pool every day.

meaning: the track; a clue/lead; a runway.
additional_notes: “Pista” is used both literally and figuratively. Literal meanings include a track (sports track, ski slope) or an airport runway (“pista de vuelo”). Figuratively, it can mean a clue/lead in an investigation: “poner a alguien sobre la pista (de…)” = to put someone on the trail of…, “seguir la pista (de/a…)” = to track/follow the trail of…, and “estar en la pista” = to be on the right track.
target_language_example: La policía está siguiendo la pista del sospechoso.
native_language_example: The police are tracking the suspect.

additional_notes: A very common noun. It’s feminine, so it uses the article la (la pizza). With gustar, what is liked goes after the verb: A todos les gusta la pizza. You can describe it with adjectives like fría (cold).
target_language_example: ¿Quieres la pizza con queso extra?
native_language_example: Do you want the pizza with extra cheese?

additional_notes: Refers to the sandy (or rocky) shore by the ocean, sea, or sometimes a lake. Often used with verbs like ir a (to go to): "Vamos a la playa."
target_language_example: Mañana vamos a la playa con unos amigos.
native_language_example: Tomorrow we’re going to the beach with some friends.

additional_notes: Refers to an open public space in a town or city, often a central square where people meet, walk, sit, and events may happen. Common phrases: "plaza de la ciudad" (city square), "plaza central" (main/central square).
target_language_example: Nos vemos en la plaza a las seis.
native_language_example: See you in the square at six.

additional_notes: Used to talk about how many people live in a place (a country, city, region, etc.). It often appears with comparisons (más/menos que) or with numbers/estimates (es…, aproximadamente…). You can also use it with singular verb agreement because it’s a singular noun phrase: “La población de esta ciudad está creciendo.”
target_language_example: La población de México es muy grande.
native_language_example: The population of Mexico is very large.

additional_notes: A noun meaning the condition of being poor or lacking money/resources. Often used with verbs like "vivir en" (to live in), "caer en" / "quedarse en" (to fall into / end up in), and "salir de" (to get out of).
target_language_example: Muchas familias viven en la pobreza en esta región.
native_language_example: Many families live in poverty in this region.

additional_notes: Usually refers to the police as an institution or group. In Spanish, la policía is grammatically singular, so it often takes singular verbs: La policía llegó. For one police officer, Spanish more often uses un policía, una policía, or un agente.
target_language_example: La policía llegó muy rápido.
native_language_example: The police arrived very quickly.

meaning: politics; policy (a set of rules or principles).
additional_notes: Most commonly means “politics” in general (“Me interesa la política”). It can also mean “policy” in the sense of an organization’s rules or approach (e.g., “la política de la empresa” = “the company policy”). In Spanish, context usually makes clear which meaning is intended.
target_language_example: No entiendo mucho de la política, pero quiero votar.
native_language_example: I don’t understand much about politics, but I want to vote.

meaning: the possibility of; the chance to.
additional_notes: Used to talk about something that could happen or be true. Often followed by **de + infinitive** (la posibilidad de ser, de limpiar) or **de que + subjunctive** (la posibilidad de que sea cierto). Common with verbs like **existir**, **dar**, **tener**, **rechazar**, **considerar**.
target_language_example: No descartes la posibilidad de que lleguemos tarde.
native_language_example: Don’t rule out the possibility that we’ll arrive late.

additional_notes: Used to refer to a specific question already known from context. "Pregunta" is a feminine noun, so it takes "la" in the singular and "las" in the plural. Common with verbs like "contestar" (to answer) and "repetir" (to repeat): "contestar la pregunta", "repetir la pregunta". Not related to English "pregnant" (a common confusion).
target_language_example: No entendí la pregunta, ¿puede repetirla?
native_language_example: I didn’t understand the question; can you repeat it?

additional_notes: Used to refer to journalists and media organizations (TV, newspapers, websites) as a group. It can also mean “the printing press,” but in these examples it clearly means the news media (reporters).
target_language_example: No quiero hablar con la prensa ahora mismo.
native_language_example: I don't want to talk to the press right now.

meaning: pressure (often blood pressure or air pressure).
additional_notes: Used in everyday contexts for physical pressure: in weather reports (air/atmospheric pressure) and in health contexts (blood pressure). Common with verbs like subir/bajar (to go up/down) and caer (to fall).
target_language_example: Me tomaron la presión en la farmacia.
native_language_example: They took my blood pressure at the pharmacy.

additional_notes: Used with the feminine article "la". Common with time expressions like "en la primavera" (in spring) and with verbs about weather/season changes (e.g., snow melting, rain, flowers).
target_language_example: En la primavera los días son más largos.
native_language_example: In spring, the days are longer.

additional_notes: Feminine form of “el/la primero/a” (“the first”). Use “la primera” when the noun is feminine (often stated, like “la primera fila/edición/frase”, or implied). With “persona”, Spanish usually matches the article/adjective to the word “persona” (feminine) even if the person is male: “Tom es la primera persona…”.
target_language_example: Esta es la primera vez que vengo aquí.
native_language_example: This is the first time I’ve come here.

additional_notes: Used to introduce a clause about someone’s first experience doing something. Commonly followed by a verb (often in the past: vine/estuviste; or present when talking about a first-time experience happening now: Esta es la primera vez que…).
target_language_example: Es la primera vez que pruebo la comida mexicana.
native_language_example: It’s the first time I’ve tried Mexican food.

meaning: “the princess” (a female royal, usually the daughter of a king/queen).
additional_notes: Used with the feminine definite article “la.” Often appears with “a” + indirect object pronoun when she is the receiver of an action: “A la princesa le gustaba…” = “The princess liked…” (literally, “To the princess, it was pleasing…”).
target_language_example: La princesa vivía en el palacio.
native_language_example: The princess lived in the palace.

meaning: "the test" / "the exam"; also "the trial" or "proof" (depending on context).
additional_notes: Most commonly refers to a test or exam: hacer la prueba (to take/do the test), repetir/volver a hacer la prueba (to retake the test), pasar/superar la prueba (to pass the test). It can also mean a trial/tryout (una prueba física = a physical test) or proof/evidence (una prueba de que... = proof that...).
target_language_example: Tengo que estudiar para la prueba de mañana.
native_language_example: I have to study for tomorrow's test.

additional_notes: Used to refer to the week after the current one. Very common with future plans: "la próxima semana voy a..." It can also be used alone as a question to confirm timing: "¿La próxima semana?"
target_language_example: Nos vemos la próxima semana.
native_language_example: See you next week.

additional_notes: Refers to a physical door. "La" is the feminine singular definite article used with "puerta."
target_language_example: Cierra la puerta, por favor.
native_language_example: Close the door, please.

meaning: the door open; the open door.
additional_notes: Commonly used after verbs like dejar (“to leave”) to say you left the door open: Deja/Dejé/Dejó la puerta abierta. Also appears with other verbs (e.g., regañar por haber dejado… “to scold for having left…”). Adjective agreement: abierta (feminine) matches puerta.
target_language_example: No dejes la puerta abierta, hace frío.
native_language_example: Don’t leave the door open; it’s cold.

meaning: the main door; the main entrance door.
additional_notes: Used to refer to the primary entrance to a building (as opposed to a side or back door). Often used with prepositions like “por” (through) or verbs like “abrir/cerrar/dejar … abierta/cerrada” (open/closed).
target_language_example: Entra por la puerta principal, por favor.
native_language_example: Please go in through the main door.

meaning: a very vulgar exclamation like “fucking hell!”; also used to intensify meaning (“a lot/like hell”).
additional_notes: Extremely offensive profanity. Often said alone to show anger, frustration, surprise, or pain (similar to “Fuck!” / “Fucking hell!”). In phrases like “duele como la puta madre” or “va a doler la puta madre,” it works as an intensifier meaning “it hurts like hell / a ton.” In insults you may hear “la puta madre que te parió,” which is even more aggressive.
target_language_example: ¡La puta madre! Se me cayó el celular.
native_language_example: Fucking hell! I dropped my phone.

meaning: the page (in a book, magazine, website, etc.).
additional_notes: Used to refer to a numbered page in printed material: "por/en la página nueve" = "to/on page nine." With websites, it can mean a web page (e.g., "la página web"), but in these examples it’s a page in a book or newspaper.
target_language_example: Estoy en la página diez.
native_language_example: I’m on page ten.

additional_notes: Refers to a radio device, or to radio as a medium/source of news (“according to the radio…”). Common with verbs like encender (turn on) and apagar (turn off). Note: “radio” can also mean “radius” in other contexts, but “la radio” is usually the device/medium.
target_language_example: Escucho las noticias en la radio todas las mañanas.
native_language_example: I listen to the news on the radio every morning.

additional_notes: Commonly used in two ways: (1) to say someone is right: "Tener la razón" = "to be right"; (2) to give an explanation: "la razón de (que) ..." = "the reason (that) ...". In sentence 2, "la razón de que" introduces the cause/explanation of an action.
target_language_example: No entiendo la razón de su decisión, pero tienes la razón.
native_language_example: I don’t understand the reason for his decision, but you’re right.

additional_notes: Used to introduce an explanation or cause. It’s followed by a clause (usually with a verb): “la razón por la que + [happened/is true]”. In very formal Spanish you may also see “la razón por la cual”.
target_language_example: No sé la razón por la que ella no vino.
native_language_example: I don’t know the reason why she didn’t come.

additional_notes: Used to contrast appearance/ideas with what is actually true (“en realidad” = “actually/in reality”). Often followed by “de…” to mean “the reality of…” (la realidad de la situación).
target_language_example: A veces la realidad es diferente de lo que imaginamos.
native_language_example: Sometimes reality is different from what we imagine.

meaning: "the net" / "the network" (often: the Internet; also: a national network like the power grid).
additional_notes: Common meanings depend on context: (1) a physical net (fishing net, sports net): "Agárrate a la red." / "Él reparó la red." (2) a network/system: "la red nacional" (could be electricity, phone, transport, etc.). (3) very commonly, "la red" means the Internet: "navegar por la red" = to surf/browse the web. Note: Spanish "red" is not the color "red" (that’s "rojo").
target_language_example: No tengo acceso a la red en este momento.
native_language_example: I don’t have access to the network/the Internet right now.

meaning: the region (an area of a country).
additional_notes: Used to refer to a geographic area within a country (or sometimes a broader area) that can be discussed in terms of economy, resources, people, or features. Often used with de + place or a descriptive name (e.g., de la región, de la región Noreste). Plural: las regiones.
target_language_example: La región tiene muchos ríos.
native_language_example: The region has many rivers.

additional_notes: Refers to a female monarch or royal figure (often with a specific queen known in context). It can also be used for a “queen” in other senses, like the queen in a deck of cards (e.g., la reina de picas = the queen of spades). In fixed expressions you may see it repeated for emphasis, e.g., “la reina reina pero no gobierna” (“the queen reigns but does not rule/govern”).
target_language_example: La reina habló con el presidente.
native_language_example: The queen spoke with the president.

additional_notes: Most commonly means “the answer” to a question/problem: “sé la respuesta” (I know the answer). It can also mean a reply/response to what someone said or did. Used in expressions like “la respuesta correcta” (the correct answer).
target_language_example: ¿Cuál es la respuesta a esta pregunta?
native_language_example: What is the answer to this question?

additional_notes: Used for an organized meeting (work, school, etc.). Common with "tener la reunión" (to have the meeting) and "asistir a la reunión" (to attend the meeting).
target_language_example: Esta noche tenemos que cenar más tarde a causa de la reunión.
native_language_example: Tonight we have to eat dinner later because of the meeting.

meaning: the revolution; a major political or social upheaval.
additional_notes: Used to talk about a big, often sudden change—especially an uprising that changes a government or society. It’s a feminine noun, so it uses la/una (la revolución, una revolución). It can also be used more generally for a big change in an area (e.g., la revolución industrial).
target_language_example: La revolución cambió la vida de la gente para siempre.
native_language_example: The revolution changed people’s lives forever.

additional_notes: A body part (feminine noun). You often use it with a possessive or with the definite article instead of a possessive in Spanish: "me lastimé la rodilla" = "I hurt my knee." Common with injuries: "disparar en la rodilla" (shoot in the knee), "lastimarse la rodilla" (hurt your knee).
target_language_example: Me duele la rodilla derecha.
native_language_example: My right knee hurts.

additional_notes: A common general word for clothes in general (not usually one specific item). Often used with verbs like lavar (to wash), quitarse (to take off), and ponerse (to put on).
target_language_example: Voy a lavar la ropa esta noche.
native_language_example: I'm going to wash the clothes tonight.

additional_notes: A feminine noun, so it uses "la" (and "una") and adjectives usually agree in feminine: "la sal blanca". In restaurants and at the table, it’s common to ask for it or pass it: "La sal, por favor" / "Pásame la sal". It can also refer to salt used for practical purposes (e.g., melting snow).
target_language_example: ¿Me pasas la sal, por favor?
native_language_example: Can you pass me the salt, please?

additional_notes: Often refers to the main sitting/common room in a home ("the living room"). Depending on context, sala can also mean a lounge or waiting room (e.g., la sala de espera = “the waiting room”).
target_language_example: Estamos en la sala viendo una película.
native_language_example: We’re in the living room watching a movie.

meaning: the exit; the departure/way out; (in some contexts) the start; sunrise.
additional_notes: Often means “exit” (la salida de emergencia = emergency exit) or “leaving”/“way out” (a place or situation). It can also be used for the “start” of a race (en la salida = at the start line/start), and in fixed phrases like la salida del sol = sunrise (literally “the sun’s rising/outgoing”). “A la salida” commonly means “when it’s over / when you get out” (e.g., after class, after work, after an event).
target_language_example: Nos encontramos a la salida del concierto.
native_language_example: We’ll meet when we get out of the concert (at the exit).

additional_notes: A common noun meaning a person’s physical/mental well-being. It’s often used with verbs like "cuidar" (to take care of) and in phrases like "la salud mental" (mental health) or "la salud pública" (public health).
target_language_example: Nada es más importante que la salud.
native_language_example: Nothing is more important than health.

additional_notes: Most often refers to blood literally (the red liquid in the body). It can also be used figuratively to mean family ties or ancestry ("la sangre" = your bloodline). In commands like "Para la sangre", it means "Stop the bleeding." You may also see it in expressions like "chup(arle) la sangre a alguien" meaning "to drain someone" (take their energy/money).
target_language_example: No puedo ver la sangre; me mareo.
native_language_example: I can’t see blood; I get dizzy.

additional_notes: Used with feminine nouns (often with an implied one), especially in sequences or counts. In the example, it refers to "la segunda vez" (“the second time”). Ordinals agree in gender and number: el segundo / la segunda / los segundos / las segundas.
target_language_example: Es la segunda vez que te lo digo.
native_language_example: It’s the second time I’m telling you.

additional_notes: Used for dense tropical forest (often humid and biodiverse). You’ll commonly see it in phrases like “la selva tropical” (the tropical rainforest). It can be literal (a real jungle) or figurative in expressions like “Bienvenido a la selva” (“Welcome to the jungle,” meaning a tough/chaotic environment).
target_language_example: Vivieron en la selva durante dos meses.
native_language_example: They lived in the jungle for two months.

additional_notes: Used to talk about something that happened in the week before the current one. Often goes at the end of the sentence (as in the examples), but it can also go earlier for emphasis.
target_language_example: Estuve en Madrid la semana pasada.
native_language_example: I was in Madrid last week.

additional_notes: Used to refer to the week after the current one. Very common for plans and appointments; often appears with a day ("el lunes de la semana próxima") or alone ("Hasta la semana próxima" = "See you next week"). You may also hear "la próxima semana" with the same meaning.
target_language_example: Nos vemos la semana próxima para tomar un café.
native_language_example: See you next week to have a coffee.

additional_notes: Used to refer to the week after the current one. Often goes at the end of the sentence (e.g., "Te llamaré la semana que viene"), but it can also appear earlier for emphasis.
target_language_example: Nos vemos la semana que viene.
native_language_example: See you next week.

meaning: the signal; the sign; the cue.
additional_notes: Common meanings: (1) a phone/TV/Wi‑Fi signal (La señal es fuerte. / Se fue la señal.), (2) a sign or indicator (una señal de tráfico = a traffic sign), (3) a cue you give someone to act (Te daré la señal con un pañuelo.). Also used for recorded messages/voicemail: "después de la señal" = after the beep.
target_language_example: La señal es fuerte en este túnel.
native_language_example: The signal is strong in this tunnel.

additional_notes: Used as a polite way to refer to an adult woman. With a surname, it means “Mrs.” (la señora Mak). With no name, it can mean “the lady” or be used respectfully in context. Often paired with el señor (“Mr.”).
target_language_example: No, es de la señora Chan.
native_language_example: No, it’s Mrs. Chan’s.

meaning: "Miss"; a polite title for a young/unmarried woman.
additional_notes: Used before a woman’s last name (or full name) in formal or polite situations (phone calls, introductions, staff addressing someone). In many places it can sound old-fashioned or imply marital status/age; "la señora" is for an older/married woman, and many people prefer "la señor(a)" or just the name in neutral contexts.
target_language_example: ¿Puede pasarme con la señorita López, por favor?
native_language_example: Could you put me through to Miss López, please?

additional_notes: Feminine form of “el/la siguiente” (“the next/following”), used with a feminine noun or with “ser” to mean “you/I am next.” Common in time expressions like “la siguiente vez/semana” (“next time/week”) and in sequences like “la siguiente ronda” (“the next round”). Also used to introduce what comes next: “La escena … es la siguiente” (“The next scene is the following”).
target_language_example: ¿Quién es la siguiente en la fila?
native_language_example: Who’s next in line?

additional_notes: A common feminine noun for a chair (seat with a back). Use it with the definite article: la silla (the chair). In Spanish, furniture is often talked about with articles (la/una). Can also be used in expressions like “sentarse en la silla” (to sit in the chair) or “caer/desplomarse sobre la silla” (to collapse onto the chair).
target_language_example: Deja la mochila en la silla, por favor.
native_language_example: Leave the backpack on the chair, please.

additional_notes: Refers to the state of things at a particular time (a problem, set of circumstances, or what’s going on). Often used when talking about difficulties or explaining context: entender la situación (to understand the situation), resolver la situación (to resolve the situation).
target_language_example: No te preocupes, vamos a manejar la situación juntos.
native_language_example: Don’t worry, we’re going to handle the situation together.

additional_notes: Used to introduce an explanation of what’s going on, often followed by an adjective (La situación es complicada.) or by que + a full clause (La situación es que no tengo dinero.). In casual speech, English often uses “the thing is…”.
target_language_example: La situación es que llegué tarde porque no había autobuses.
native_language_example: The thing is, I arrived late because there were no buses.

meaning: society (people as a group; the community).
additional_notes: Used to talk about people living together as a community and the rules/values that shape it. Often appears with prepositions like “en la sociedad” (in society) or “para la sociedad” (for/to society), and in phrases like “un peligro para la sociedad” (a danger to society).
target_language_example: La sociedad cambia con el tiempo.
native_language_example: Society changes over time.

additional_notes: A common food word. It’s feminine, so it uses "la" (singular) and "las" (plural: "las sopas"). Often used with verbs like "comer" (to eat) or "tomar" (to have/drink, especially soup).
target_language_example: La sopa de pollo está muy rica.
native_language_example: The chicken soup is very tasty.

additional_notes: Refers to fortune/chance in general and can be modified: "la buena suerte" (good luck), "la mala suerte" (bad luck). Common in phrases like "tener la suerte de + infinitivo" (to have the luck/good fortune to...) and "confiar en la suerte" (to rely on luck).
target_language_example: Tuve la suerte de ser tratado por un buen médico.
native_language_example: I was lucky to be treated by a good doctor.

meaning: "his/hers/your/their (one)" (feminine), referring to something that belongs to someone.
additional_notes: “La suya” is a possessive pronoun: la (the feminine thing) + suya (belonging to him/her/you formal/them). It replaces a noun you don’t repeat: mi mesa… la suya = “my table… his/hers.” It can also be used in set comparisons like “mi palabra contra la suya” (“my word against his/hers”) and “haga la suya” (“do your part / do yours”). In “salirse con la suya,” it means “to get your way” (a fixed expression).
target_language_example: Mi respuesta fue clara, pero la suya no.
native_language_example: My answer was clear, but his/hers wasn't.

additional_notes: “La tarde” refers to the part of the day after lunch and before night (“la noche”). In many Spanish-speaking places it can extend later than English “afternoon” (sometimes closer to early evening), so context matters. Used with verbs like pasar (“to spend”): “pasar la tarde” = “to spend the afternoon.”
target_language_example: Mañana paso la tarde en casa.
native_language_example: Tomorrow I’m spending the afternoon at home.

additional_notes: Commonly means school “homework” (often just called “la tarea”). More generally it can mean a duty or job to do (“a task”), and it can be used figuratively to mean something difficult (“la tarea más difícil”).
target_language_example: Todavía no termino la tarea de matemáticas.
native_language_example: I still haven’t finished the math homework.

additional_notes: “Tarta” is a baked dessert. In many places it means “cake” (especially a frosted layer cake), but it can also mean “pie” or “tart” depending on the country and the type (e.g., tarta de manzana). It’s feminine, so it uses “la” (la tarta / una tarta).
target_language_example: La tarta no está envenenada.
native_language_example: The cake isn’t poisoned.

additional_notes: A common noun for technology in general (devices, systems, scientific/technical know-how). Usually used with the definite article: “la tecnología”. You’ll also see it in phrases like “la tecnología funciona” (technology works) or “afecta a…” (affects…).
target_language_example: La tecnología cambia muy rápido.
native_language_example: Technology changes very fast.

additional_notes: Very common informal/colloquial short form of “la televisión”. Used with verbs like ver/mirar (to watch): “ver la tele”, “mirar la tele”. Also in phrases like “en la tele” (on TV) and “por la tele” (on TV/through the TV).
target_language_example: ¿Quieres ver la tele conmigo esta noche?
native_language_example: Do you want to watch TV with me tonight?

additional_notes: Refers to the television as a device or (more generally) television as a medium. Often used with verbs like encender (to turn on) and apagar (to turn off).
target_language_example: ¿Puedes bajar el volumen de la televisión?
native_language_example: Can you turn down the TV volume?

additional_notes: Used for the temperature of the weather or a person’s body. Common verbs: subir/bajar la temperatura (to rise/fall), la temperatura cae/desciende (it drops), estar bajo cero (to be below zero). In a medical context, tomar la temperatura means “to take someone’s temperature.”
target_language_example: Esta mañana, la temperatura ha caído bajo el cero.
native_language_example: This morning, the temperature fell below zero.

meaning: temptation; a strong desire to do something (often something you shouldn’t).
additional_notes: Common with verbs like resistir (to resist) and caer en (to fall into): resistir la tentación = resist temptation; caer en la tentación = give in. Also used in fixed phrases like No nos dejes caer en la tentación (“Lead us not into temptation”).
target_language_example: Tuve la tentación de comerme otro postre, pero me contuve.
native_language_example: I was tempted to eat another dessert, but I held back.

additional_notes: Usually means a place where you buy things (a store/shop). In other contexts, "tienda" can also mean "tent" (e.g., "una tienda de campaña"), but in these examples it’s clearly "store."
target_language_example: Tengo que ir a la tienda a comprar pan.
native_language_example: I have to go to the store to buy bread.

additional_notes: Often means either (1) the planet Earth (especially with verbs like girar, calentarse, ser redonda), or (2) land/property (tierra as a valuable resource, or a piece of land that belongs to someone), or (3) the ground/soil you stand on (e.g., sentir la tierra temblar). Capitalizing "la Tierra" is common when you mean the planet (Earth), but many texts write it in lowercase.
target_language_example: Después del terremoto, todos sentimos la tierra temblar.
native_language_example: After the earthquake, we all felt the ground shake.

additional_notes: A feminine noun meaning “towel” (bath towel, hand towel, etc.). Often used with verbs like "secar" (to dry) and phrases like "estar mojada" (to be wet).
target_language_example: Cogió la toalla y se secó las manos.
native_language_example: He/She grabbed the towel and dried his/her hands.

additional_notes: A common weather noun (feminine). Often used with weather verbs like "haber" (había tormenta), "venir" (viene una tormenta), "durar" (la tormenta duró…), "cesar" (la tormenta cesó), and with "antes/después de" (antes de la tormenta). Can also be used figuratively for a difficult period: "Después de la tormenta viene la calma."
target_language_example: Parece que viene la tormenta; cierra las ventanas.
native_language_example: It looks like the storm is coming; close the windows.

additional_notes: Refers to a tower (a tall structure/building). Often used with location prepositions like “en la torre” (in/at the tower). Noun: torre (feminine) → la torre.
target_language_example: Nos vemos en la torre a las cinco.
native_language_example: See you at the tower at five.

meaning: the crew (the people who operate a ship, plane, spacecraft, etc.).
additional_notes: Used for the group of people who run or work on a vehicle (especially a ship, aircraft, or spacecraft). Often followed by "de" to say which vehicle: "la tripulación del barco" (the ship’s crew). Common verbs: "salvar a la tripulación" (save the crew), "abandonar" (leave/abandon), "prepararse" (get ready).
target_language_example: La tripulación del avión ya está lista para despegar.
native_language_example: The plane’s crew is already ready for takeoff.

meaning: "the sad news" (a piece of bad/sad news).
additional_notes: Used to refer to some specific news that is upsetting (often about a death, illness, accident, etc.). It’s typically followed by reactions like llorar (to cry), quedarse impactado (to be shocked), or quitar el apetito (to take away your appetite).
target_language_example: Cuando me dieron la triste noticia, me quedé sin palabras.
native_language_example: When they gave me the sad news, I was speechless.

additional_notes: Used as a possessive pronoun to replace a noun that’s understood from context: *Mi idea es diferente a la tuya* (“My idea is different from yours”). It agrees with the thing possessed (feminine singular), not with the owner. Other forms: *el tuyo* (masc. sing.), *los tuyos* (masc. pl.), *las tuyas* (fem. pl.). Often used after comparisons: *como la tuya* (“like yours”).
target_language_example: No encuentro mi chaqueta; ¿es esa la tuya?
native_language_example: I can’t find my jacket; is that one yours?

additional_notes: Common meanings depend on context: (1) a "unit" as a group/department (e.g., a military unit, hospital/medical unit, work unit: "mi primer día en la unidad"); (2) "unity" meaning togetherness or being united (often with de: "la unidad de la familia"); (3) a "unit" as the smallest element in a system ("la unidad más pequeña de la sociedad").
target_language_example: La unidad médica revisará a los pacientes antes de salir.
native_language_example: The medical unit will check the patients before they leave.

additional_notes: Refers to an institution of higher education (and often the experience of studying there). In many Spanish-speaking contexts, "universidad" corresponds most closely to "university"; English "college" may be used depending on the country/system. Common with verbs like "ir a la universidad" (to go to university) and "ahorrar para la universidad" (to save for college/university).
target_language_example: Mi hermana estudia en la universidad desde 2023.
native_language_example: My sister has been studying at the university since 2023.

additional_notes: Literally 'the window (that is) open.' Often used with verbs like dejar (to leave): Deja la ventana abierta = 'Leave the window open.' Because it’s feminine, it takes abierta (not abierto). You can add time expressions like un rato ('for a while') or clauses like mientras duerme ('while (someone) sleeps').
target_language_example: ¿Puedes dejar la ventana abierta, por favor?
native_language_example: Can you leave the window open, please?

meaning: "the window and..." (used before adding another action or idea).
additional_notes: "La ventana" means "the window" (feminine: la). The word "y" means "and" and is used to join two actions or clauses: "abre la ventana y espera" = "open the window and wait."
target_language_example: Cierra la ventana y apaga la luz.
native_language_example: Close the window and turn off the light.

additional_notes: Usually means 'the truth' as a noun, especially with verbs like decir, saber, and conocer. At the start of a sentence, la verdad can also be used more loosely to mean 'honestly' or 'to be honest'.
target_language_example: La verdad, no quiero salir hoy.
native_language_example: Honestly, I don't want to go out today.

additional_notes: Used to introduce a truthful clarification, explanation, or correction—often as a softener before saying something direct or disappointing. Very common in speech and writing. Often followed by a full clause: “La verdad es que no sé (…)/La verdad es que ya no viajo”.
target_language_example: La verdad es que no tengo tiempo hoy.
native_language_example: To be honest, I don’t have time today.

meaning: “To be honest, no…” / “The truth is, I don’t…”
additional_notes: Used to introduce an honest answer, often to soften a refusal or disagreement, or to correct expectations. It’s commonly followed by a verb phrase starting with “no” (e.g., “La verdad es que no me acuerdo”). It can also be a standalone reply: “No, la verdad es que no.”
target_language_example: La verdad es que no tengo tiempo hoy.
native_language_example: To be honest, I don’t have time today.

additional_notes: Feminine form of the adjective *verdadero/verdadera* (“true/real”). It agrees with a feminine noun: *la verdadera historia* (“the true story”), *la verdadera felicidad* (“true happiness”). It can also be used on its own as a noun-like phrase to mean “the real/true one” when the feminine person/thing is understood from context: *Ella es la verdadera* (“She’s the real one”). Masculine: *el verdadero*; plural: *los/las verdaderos/verdaderas*.
target_language_example: No creas los rumores: ella es la verdadera.
native_language_example: Don’t believe the rumors: she’s the real one.

additional_notes: Refers to success in a competition, battle, or struggle. Often used with common patterns like "aspirar a la victoria" (to aim for victory), "por la victoria" (for victory), and in expressions about what victory feels like (e.g., "la victoria es amarga" = victory is bittersweet).
target_language_example: Después de tantos intentos, por fin conseguimos la victoria.
native_language_example: After so many attempts, we finally achieved victory.

additional_notes: Usually means "life." Spanish often uses the article here even when English just says "life" in a general sense. It also appears in common expressions such as buscarse la vida (to get by / make a living), dar la vida (to give one's life), and hacer la vida difícil (to make life difficult).
target_language_example: La vida en el campo es tranquila.
native_language_example: Life in the countryside is peaceful.

additional_notes: Used to talk about a person’s life/story or a particular kind of life connected to someone or something. It’s often followed by a noun or name: la vida de mi hijo (my son’s life), la vida de Arwen (Arwen’s life). With an adjective or category, it can mean “the life of a …”: la vida de ciudad (city life), la vida de un pastor (the life of a shepherd). Common expressions: celebrar la vida de… (to celebrate the life of…), la vida de [alguien] está en peligro (someone’s life is in danger), tomar la vida de… (to take someone’s life).
target_language_example: En el documental cuentan la vida de Frida Kahlo.
native_language_example: In the documentary they tell the story of Frida Kahlo’s life.

meaning: the life of a man; a man’s life.
additional_notes: A literal, formal phrase used when talking about someone’s life, often in serious contexts (e.g., risk, responsibility, what’s at stake). Very common with expressions like "estar en juego" (to be at stake) and "se trata de..." (this is about...).
target_language_example: No podemos rendirnos: la vida de un hombre depende de nosotros.
native_language_example: We can’t give up: a man’s life depends on us.

additional_notes: Used to make general statements, descriptions, or reflections about life. It’s often followed by an adjective or noun phrase (e.g., "la vida es hermosa" = “life is beautiful”; "la vida es un sueño" = “life is a dream”).
target_language_example: Para mí, la vida es una aventura.
native_language_example: For me, life is an adventure.

additional_notes: A common, reflective phrase used to express that time passes quickly and you should value your time or enjoy life. You may also hear the slightly more formal/poetic variant “la vida es corta.”
target_language_example: Aprovecha el momento; la vida es breve.
native_language_example: Make the most of the moment; life is short.

meaning: "the old woman / the old lady" (often said informally).
additional_notes: Literally refers to an older woman. In everyday speech, it can also be an informal way to refer to a specific woman everyone knows in the context (e.g., a landlady/neighbor/bossy woman). Depending on tone and region, it may sound rude/pejorative; some people also use it casually to mean “my mom” or “my wife,” but that meaning is highly context-dependent.
target_language_example: La vieja dijo que no podemos entrar sin permiso.
native_language_example: The old lady said we can’t come in without permission.

additional_notes: “Vieja” is the feminine form of “viejo” (old). With a feminine noun, it can mean “the old + noun” (la vieja casa = the old house). It can also be used on its own as a noun meaning “the old woman/old lady,” but in your examples it’s an adjective describing a feminine thing.
target_language_example: Voy a arreglar la vieja bicicleta de mi hermana.
native_language_example: I’m going to fix my sister’s old bicycle.

additional_notes: A noun meaning physical force or aggressive behavior that hurts people, or more generally harsh/abusive treatment. Often used with verbs like odiar (to hate), disgustar (to disgust), or with “decir/darle no a…” (“say no to…”): “Di/Decí no al odio y a la violencia.”
target_language_example: La violencia no es la solución.
native_language_example: Violence is not the solution.

meaning: sight/vision; the view; the gaze/line of sight (what you’re looking at).
additional_notes: “La vista” can mean (1) eyesight/vision: “Perdí la vista” = “I lost my sight.” (2) the view/scenery from a place: “Me encanta la vista desde aquí arriba” = “I love the view from up here.” (3) your gaze/line of sight, often with verbs like “desviar” (avert/turn away) and “mantener” (keep): “Ella desvió la vista” = “She looked away,” “Mantén la vista en…” = “Keep your eyes on…”.
target_language_example: Me encanta la vista desde aquí arriba.
native_language_example: I love the view from up here.

meaning: "the will/desire of"; "the will to" (resolve); also "the will of" (fate/God) in formal/religious contexts.
additional_notes: Used with a noun or infinitive to express determination or intention: la voluntad de + infinitive/noun (e.g., "la voluntad de sobrevivir" = "the will to survive"). With a person or deity, it can mean "the will of" (e.g., "la voluntad de Dios" = "God’s will").
target_language_example: Nada en el mundo es más fuerte que la voluntad de sobrevivir.
native_language_example: Nothing in the world is stronger than the will to survive.

meaning: the voice; the volume (of your voice).
additional_notes: Most commonly means a person’s voice. In commands like "Baja/Baje la voz" or "mantén la voz baja," it refers to speaking more quietly (lowering your volume). It’s also used in the idiom "correrse la voz" = “to spread the word/rumor.”
target_language_example: Por favor, baja la voz; el bebé está durmiendo.
native_language_example: Please lower your voice; the baby is sleeping.

additional_notes: Used to refer to who a voice belongs to (a person, animal, or even a figure like Cristo). It’s followed by a noun or name: la voz de mi madre, la voz de Cristo. With verbs like escuchar/oír (to hear) and imitar (to imitate).
target_language_example: Reconocí la voz de mi hermano por teléfono.
native_language_example: I recognized my brother's voice on the phone.

additional_notes: Common in set phrases: **a la vuelta** = “on the way back / on the return (trip)” (often contrasted with **a la ida** = “on the way there”). **darse la vuelta** = “to turn around” (command: *Daos la vuelta* = “Turn around.”). **darle la vuelta a (algo)** = “to turn/flip (something) over” (e.g., *darle la vuelta al paraguas* = “turn the umbrella inside out” because of wind; *darle la vuelta a la mesa* = “flip/turn the table over”). **dar la vuelta** can also mean “to go around” (walking/driving around a place).
target_language_example: Cuando lleguemos, damos la vuelta y volvemos a casa.
native_language_example: When we get there, we’ll turn around and go back home.

additional_notes: Used to refer to the person who was harmed, attacked, or suffered in a crime, accident, or bad situation. Often used in police/news/medical contexts (e.g., "la víctima" = the victim). Gender: "la víctima" is grammatically feminine even if the victim is male (e.g., "La víctima era un hombre").
target_language_example: La policía habló con la víctima en el hospital.
native_language_example: The police spoke with the victim at the hospital.

meaning: opera (the art form or an opera performance).
additional_notes: Used with the definite article "la" because it’s a feminine noun. Common with verbs like "ir a" (to go to): "ir a la ópera" can mean going to an opera performance/house. It can also refer to opera as a musical genre in general.
target_language_example: Esta noche vamos a la ópera.
native_language_example: Tonight we’re going to the opera.

additional_notes: Means “the last time” something happened. Very commonly used with the imperfect subjunctive after "como si": "como si fuera la última vez" = “as if it were the last time.” You can also use it with "que" to introduce a clause: "la última vez que..." = “the last time that...”. With "por" it can mean “for the last time” (final time): "Te lo digo por última vez."
target_language_example: No recuerdo la última vez que salimos juntos.
native_language_example: I don't remember the last time we went out together.

additional_notes: Used to talk about the most recent occasion when something happened. It’s often followed by a verb: “la última vez que + [verb]” (e.g., “la última vez que lo vi” = “the last time I saw him”). You can compare then vs. now with “más … que la última vez que …” (e.g., “más gordo que la última vez que lo vi”).
target_language_example: La última vez que fui a Madrid, hizo mucho frío.
native_language_example: The last time I went to Madrid, it was very cold.

additional_notes: Used to talk about the most recent occasion when something happened. It’s often followed by a verb phrase (sometimes with the subject included): “La última vez que vine aquí…”. You’ll commonly see it with past tenses (pretérito/pretérito imperfecto) and it can be paired with time expressions like “fue hace un año / fue en la preparatoria”.
target_language_example: La última vez que lo vi, me dijo que estaba muy ocupado.
native_language_example: The last time I saw him, he told me he was very busy.

meaning: "the only family that" (the only relatives who).
additional_notes: Used to say someone is the only family/relatives a person has left. It’s followed by a clause with "que" (= “that/who”), often with "me/te/le/nos queda" (“I/you/he-she/we have left”) or "tiene" (“has”).
target_language_example: Ella es la única familia que me queda.
native_language_example: She is the only family I have left.

meaning: “the one of / that of” (used to avoid repeating a feminine noun).
additional_notes: Used when the noun is understood from context, often in comparisons or descriptions: “parecida a la de…” = “similar to that of…”. It can also mean “the one from/belonging to…” or identify someone by their role: “Rebecca, la de vestuario” = “Rebecca, the wardrobe/costumes one.” You’ll also see time-based contrast: “la de antes” = “the previous/earlier one.”
target_language_example: Mi mochila es más grande que la de Ana.
native_language_example: My backpack is bigger than Ana’s.

additional_notes: Used to refer back to a feminine person/thing already understood from context, and it introduces a clause that describes it. It agrees with what it refers to: la que (fem. sing.), el que (masc. sing.), las que (fem. pl.), los que (masc. pl.). In choices, "la que tú quieras" means "whichever one you want" (feminine).
target_language_example: Elige la que prefieras.
native_language_example: Choose whichever one you prefer.

meaning: "I loved her" (or "I used to love her").
additional_notes: "La" is the direct object pronoun meaning "her" (or sometimes "it" for a feminine noun), and "amaba" is the imperfect past of "amar" ("to love"). The imperfect often describes an ongoing feeling in the past, a repeated/typical situation, or background description: "I loved her / I used to love her / I was in love with her." You can also say "la amaba a ella" to emphasize "her".
target_language_example: Nunca le dije que la amaba.
native_language_example: I never told her that I loved her.

meaning: "I love her" (or "I love it" for a feminine thing).
additional_notes: "La" is a direct object pronoun meaning "her" or "it" (for a feminine noun). "Amo" is the "I" form of "amar" (to love). You can also say "Te amo" (I love you) and "Lo amo" (I love him/it for a masculine noun). In "Le digo que la amo", "le" means "to him/her" (indirect object), while "la" is who/what is loved (direct object).
target_language_example: La amo muchísimo.
native_language_example: I love her very much.
