native_language_example: This book doesn’t belong to Ana.

additional_notes: Used with the verb "pedir" (to ask for / request). "Le" means "to him" or "to her" (indirect object), and "a" introduces the person being asked: "Le pidió a Tom..." = "He/She asked Tom...". Often followed by "que" + subjunctive to say what you asked someone to do: "le pidió a María que comprara...".
target_language_example: Le pidió a su amigo que la ayudara con la tarea.
native_language_example: She asked her friend to help her with the homework.

additional_notes: "Le" is an indirect object pronoun meaning "to him/to her/to you (formal)." You use it with preguntar when you ask someone a question: "Le pregunté si..." (I asked him/her if...). For asking about a topic, you can use "le pregunté sobre..." or "le pregunté por...".
target_language_example: Le pregunté si tenía tiempo para hablar.
native_language_example: I asked him/her if they had time to talk.

additional_notes: Past tense of preguntar (“to ask”). Use **le** for the person you asked (indirect object: “to him/her/you (formal)”), and **a + [person]** to name who you asked: **Le pregunté a Tom…**. Often followed by **si** (if/whether) for yes/no questions, or **por qué** for “why.” You can also say **Le pregunté por...** (“I asked about...”).
target_language_example: Le pregunté a la profesora si había tarea.
native_language_example: I asked the teacher if there was homework.

additional_notes: Used with an indirect object pronoun (le = “to him/her/you (formal)”) plus a + the person asked. Very common in questions with words like por qué (why), cómo (how), dónde (where), quién (who), or si (if/whether). In speech you often include both “le” and “a + name” for clarity: Le preguntó a María…
target_language_example: Le preguntó a su profesor si podía repetir la explicación.
native_language_example: He/She asked his/her teacher if he/she could repeat the explanation.

additional_notes: Past tense (preterite) of robar (“to steal/rob”), used with an indirect object pronoun (le) to show who the victim is: le = to him/her/you (usted). It often appears with what was stolen (Le robaron el bolso) or with the person introduced by a (Le robaron al hombre…).
target_language_example: Le robaron el celular en el metro.
native_language_example: They stole his/her phone on the subway.

additional_notes: From the verb **temer** (“to fear”). In Spanish you often say **temerle a + [thing/person feared]**. The **le** is an indirect object pronoun that refers to what is feared, and it’s often repeated even when the noun is stated: **Él le teme a la oscuridad** (“He’s afraid of the dark”). With plural indirect object, it can be **les teme a...**. Common negative: **No le teme a nada** (“He/She isn’t afraid of anything”).
target_language_example: El niño le teme a la oscuridad.
native_language_example: The child is afraid of the dark.

additional_notes: Uses the verb "leer" (to read) + "el" (the) + "libro" (book). You can change the article and noun as needed: "leer un libro" (read a book), "leer los libros" (read the books). Often used with time/ability expressions like "poder" (can), "tener tiempo" (have time), or "rápidamente" (quickly).
target_language_example: Quiero leer el libro esta noche.
native_language_example: I want to read the book tonight.

meaning: to read between the lines; to understand an implied meaning.
additional_notes: Used when the real message isn’t stated directly and you have to infer it from hints, tone, or context. Common in conversations, emails, and politics when someone is being indirect.
target_language_example: Aunque no lo dijo, pude leer entre líneas que estaba molesto.
native_language_example: Even though he didn’t say it, I could read between the lines that he was upset.

additional_notes: "Leer" means "to read." "Este" is a masculine singular demonstrative meaning "this" and goes before the noun: "este libro" = "this book". You can use it with common structures like "deberías/debes" (you should/you must), "pueden" (can), and time expressions like "Me tomó X" / "Se tarda X" (It took me X / It takes X) + "leer este libro."
target_language_example: ¿Puedes leer este libro conmigo?
native_language_example: Can you read this book with me?

meaning: to read someone’s mind; to know what someone is thinking.
additional_notes: Used when talking about guessing someone’s thoughts or intentions without them saying anything. Often appears in negatives like “No puedo leer la mente” (“I can’t read minds”), meaning “You need to tell me—don’t expect me to guess.” It can also be used literally in the context of a game or trick.
target_language_example: No puedo leer la mente, dime qué quieres.
native_language_example: I can’t read your mind—tell me what you want.

additional_notes: A very common phrase using the verb "leer" (to read) + "libros" (books). After verbs like "gustar" and "preferir," you often use the infinitive: "Me gusta leer libros" (I like to read books). You can also place the infinitive phrase at the start as the subject: "Leer libros es..." / "Leer libros le hará...".
target_language_example: Me gusta leer libros por la noche.
native_language_example: I like to read books at night.

additional_notes: Common verb phrase: "leer" (to read) + "un libro" (a book). You can change the article or add details: "leer el libro" (read the book), "leer libros" (read books), "leer un libro en francés" (read a book in French). Often used with "sentarse a" (sit down to) or "acabar de" (have just) to talk about starting or finishing reading.
target_language_example: Me gusta leer un libro antes de dormir.
native_language_example: I like to read a book before going to sleep.

additional_notes: Used to say something/someone is at a distance from a place or from other people (physical distance). Often appears with verbs like "estar" (to be) or "quedar" (to be located): "está lejos de...", "queda lejos de...". You can soften it with "no tan" (not so) or "no muy" (not very): "no tan lejos de".
target_language_example: Mi oficina está lejos de aquí, así que voy en metro.
native_language_example: My office is far from here, so I take the subway.

additional_notes: Used to say something (a place or person) is at a long distance from where you are now. Often appears with "estar/quedar" (Está/Queda lejos de aquí), and you can intensify with "muy" (muy lejos de aquí) or soften with "no" (no lejos de aquí = not far from here).
target_language_example: Hay un hospital lejos de aquí.
native_language_example: There’s a hospital far from here.

additional_notes: Used to talk about any language that is not your native language (e.g., studying a foreign language at school). Often interchangeable with “idioma extranjero,” with “idioma” being more common in everyday speech.
target_language_example: Estoy aprendiendo una lengua extranjera para viajar.
native_language_example: I'm learning a foreign language to travel.

additional_notes: Used to talk about the language you learned first at home as a child (your first/native language). Often appears with verbs like ser (El urdu es mi lengua materna) or phrases like en mi lengua materna (in my native language).
target_language_example: Aunque hablo inglés, mi lengua materna es el español.
native_language_example: Even though I speak English, my native language is Spanish.

additional_notes: Used to describe a language spoken by a smaller group within a country or region. Often appears in discussions about education, culture, and language rights (e.g., proteger una lengua minoritaria = to protect a minority language).
target_language_example: En esta región, el gobierno apoya la enseñanza de una lengua minoritaria en las escuelas.
native_language_example: In this region, the government supports teaching a minority language in schools.

additional_notes: Plural noun phrase used to talk about languages that are not your native language. Often used in school/learning contexts (e.g., aprender/estudiar lenguas extranjeras). You may also hear the synonym “idiomas extranjeros”; “lengua” and “idioma” are usually interchangeable here.
target_language_example: En mi escuela tenemos que estudiar dos lenguas extranjeras.
native_language_example: At my school we have to study two foreign languages.

additional_notes: Used for the small lens you wear on your eye instead of (or along with) glasses. Often appears in the plural: "lentes de contacto" (contact lenses). Also commonly said as "lentilla" (Spain) for a contact lens.
target_language_example: Voy a comprar un lente de contacto nuevo.
native_language_example: I'm going to buy a new contact lens.

meaning: they love it / they really like it.
additional_notes: Used with verbs like *encantar* (like *gustar*). The person who likes something is introduced with **a + person** (e.g., *A los abuelos...*), and **les** means “to them.” The verb often stays **singular** (*encanta*) when the thing liked is singular or an action (*ver a sus nietos*). Use **les encantan** with plural things (e.g., *Les encantan los libros* = They love books).
target_language_example: A mis amigos les encanta cocinar los fines de semana.
native_language_example: My friends love cooking on weekends.

additional_notes: Used with the verb "gustar" to talk about what people like. Literally it’s closer to "it pleases them," so the thing liked is the grammatical subject: "les gusta el jazz" (jazz pleases them). Use "les gusta" with a singular noun or an infinitive ("les gusta cantar"). With a plural noun, it becomes "les gustan" ("les gustan los perros"). Often appears with "a + person/people" for clarity: "A mis amigos les gusta..."
target_language_example: A mis padres les gusta viajar.
native_language_example: My parents like to travel.

meaning: "I asked them to..." / "I requested that they..."
additional_notes: Used to report a request you made to a group of people ("les" = to them). "Pedí" is the past tense of "pedir" (to ask for/request). After "pedí que", Spanish normally uses the imperfect subjunctive (e.g., "llamaran", "hicieran", "vinieran") to express what you wanted them to do.
target_language_example: Les pedí que me ayudaran con la tarea.
native_language_example: I asked them to help me with the homework.

additional_notes: Used when speaking to two or more people (or to someone you address as ustedes). It’s the verb pedir (“to ask for/request”) in the first person singular (pido = “I ask”), plus les (“to you all / to them”). Often followed by a noun (les pido ayuda/silencio) or by que + subjunctive (les pido que no lo hagan = “I ask you not to do it”). In very formal or public announcements it can sound like “I request your…”.
target_language_example: Por favor, les pido paciencia mientras resolvemos el problema.
native_language_example: Please, I ask you for patience while we solve the problem.

additional_notes: Most often used as **se levanta temprano** (“he/she gets up early”). **Levantarse** is a reflexive verb, so it usually needs a reflexive pronoun: **me/te/se/nos/os/se**. The form **levanta** is the present tense for **él/ella/usted**. For **I**: **me levanto temprano**; for **you (informal)**: **te levantas temprano**.
target_language_example: Él se levanta temprano.
native_language_example: He gets up early.

additional_notes:
Reflexive verb: levantarse = “to get up” (literally “to raise oneself”). Common when talking about routines/habits:
- estar acostumbrado/a a + infinitive = “to be used to (doing)”
- soler + infinitive = “to usually”
- solía + infinitive = “used to”.
Example in first person: “Me levanto temprano.”
target_language_example: Tom está acostumbrado a levantarse temprano.
native_language_example: Tom is used to getting up early.

additional_notes: "Leyendo" is the gerund of "leer" (to read). It’s used to say what someone is doing (often with "estar": "estaba/estoy leyendo...") or how/when something happened (e.g., "Me quedé dormido leyendo un libro" = I fell asleep while reading a book).
target_language_example: Estoy en casa leyendo un libro.
native_language_example: I’m at home reading a book.

additional_notes: Used with the verb **haber** to form the **present perfect**: **he/has/ha/hayamos/habéis/han leído este libro** (“I/you/he… have read this book”). **Leído** is the past participle of **leer** (“to read”). Common with **ya** (“already”) and **antes** (“before”).
target_language_example: ¿Ya has leído este libro?
native_language_example: Have you read this book already?

meaning: “read and written” (intended to mean “able to read and write”).
additional_notes: This is a nonstandard/incorrect phrase in modern standard Spanish. While **leído** is a correct past participle of **leer**, **escribido** is not used; the correct past participle is **escrito**. If you mean literacy, prefer **saber leer y escribir** (“to know how to read and write”) or **leer y escribir** (“to read and write”). If you really need a participle pair, use **leído y escrito**.
target_language_example: Dice en el formulario: «leído y escribido».
native_language_example: It says on the form: “leído y escribido.”

additional_notes: Used for a legal status where someone is released from prison but must follow certain rules/conditions (for example, checking in with an officer, not leaving an area, avoiding certain people). Common with the verb estar: "Estoy/Está en libertad condicional". Also used after prepositions like bajo/en: "Bajo/En libertad condicional".
target_language_example: Salió de la cárcel, pero sigue en libertad condicional.
native_language_example: He got out of prison, but he’s still on parole.

meaning: freedom of speech / freedom of expression.
additional_notes: A common civic/political phrase meaning the right to express opinions and ideas without censorship or punishment. Used in formal contexts (news, debates, laws). Often appears with verbs like proteger (to protect), defender (to defend), respetar (to respect), and limitar (to limit).
target_language_example: La libertad de expresión es un derecho fundamental.
native_language_example: Freedom of speech is a fundamental right.

additional_notes: A literal phrase: "libro" = book, "hechizos" = spells. Used in fantasy/magic contexts; often refers to a magical book that contains spells, instructions, or secrets.
target_language_example: Necesitamos el libro de hechizos para romper la maldición.
native_language_example: We need the spellbook to break the curse.

additional_notes: Used for a school/academic book that teaches a subject (medicine, nursing, math, etc.). Often used with "de" + field: "un libro de texto de enfermería" (a nursing textbook). Plural: "libros de texto".
target_language_example: Necesito comprar el libro de texto para la clase de español.
native_language_example: I need to buy the textbook for Spanish class.

additional_notes: Refers to books used for studying a subject (for a class). Often used in school instructions: abrir/cerrar el libro de texto (open/close the textbook), en la página X (on page X). Singular: "libro de texto".
target_language_example: Necesito comprar los libros de texto para este semestre.
native_language_example: I need to buy the textbooks for this semester.

additional_notes: Used for the official document/permit that allows you to drive. Common in police or traffic stops: “Muéstreme su licencia de conducir” / “Su licencia de conducir y documentos, por favor.” Also appears with other car paperwork like “matrícula” (vehicle registration).
target_language_example: No encuentro mi licencia de conducir; creo que la perdí.
native_language_example: I can’t find my driver’s license; I think I lost it.

meaning: blacklist; a list of people/items you want to block, avoid, or punish.
additional_notes: Used with "estar/poner (a alguien) en la lista negra" to mean someone is (or gets) blacklisted. Often implies being banned, rejected, or treated badly by a person, company, or group.
target_language_example: Si sigues haciendo eso, te van a poner en la lista negra.
native_language_example: If you keep doing that, they’re going to blacklist you.

additional_notes: Used to say someone/something is prepared to do something (listo para + infinitive: "listo para despegar") or prepared for an event/thing (listo para + noun: "listo para el despegue"). Changes for gender/number: listo/lista/listos/listas.
target_language_example: ¿Estás listo para empezar?
native_language_example: Are you ready to start?

additional_notes: Used with an infinitive to say someone is prepared to do an action: "listos para entrar". It can also be followed by a noun to mean ready for an event/situation: "listos para la acción / la batalla". Changes for gender/number: listo/lista/listos/listas.
target_language_example: ¿Están listos para empezar?
native_language_example: Are you ready to start?

meaning: “call” (phone) or “knock on” (a door), addressed to “you” (tú command).
additional_notes: “Llama” is the tú imperative of “llamar” (to call). Use “llama a + person” to tell someone to call a person (the “a” is used before a person). With things like “la puerta,” it means “knock”: “llama a la puerta.”
target_language_example: Si tienes una emergencia, llama a la policía.
native_language_example: If you have an emergency, call the police.

additional_notes: A command using the tú form of llamar (“to call”). Often used in urgent situations; you can add “por favor” to be polite. Also common with “en caso de emergencia” (“in case of emergency”) or “para que…” (“so that…”).
target_language_example: Si ves algo sospechoso, llama a la policía.
native_language_example: If you see something suspicious, call the police.

additional_notes: A common, neutral term for a call made by telephone. Often used with verbs like hacer/recibir/contestar: hacer una llamada telefónica (to make a phone call), recibir una llamada telefónica (to receive a phone call), contestar una llamada telefónica (to answer a phone call).
target_language_example: Tengo que hacer una llamada telefónica ahora.
native_language_example: I have to make a phone call now.

additional_notes: Used when calling a person, especially on the phone: llamar a alguien. The a introduces the person being called, so it is not translated directly in English.
target_language_example: Voy a llamar a mi madre esta noche.
native_language_example: I'm going to call my mother tonight.

additional_notes: Used when you contact the police (usually by phone) because there’s an emergency, a crime, or a serious problem. You can change the tense: tuvimos que llamar a la policía (we had to call the police), iba a llamar a la policía (I was going to call the police), trataré de llamar a la policía (I’ll try to call the police).
target_language_example: Anoche tuvimos que llamar a la policía.
native_language_example: Last night we had to call the police.

meaning: to attract attention; to draw attention (to yourself/something).
additional_notes: Often used when someone is being noticeable on purpose or trying to stand out (sometimes with a negative tone: “stop showing off / stop seeking attention”). It can also be used neutrally to mean that something catches your eye: “Me llamó la atención…” = “It caught my attention…”. In your examples, it refers to drawing attention to yourself, often something you want to avoid.
target_language_example: Intentó hablar en voz baja para no llamar la atención.
native_language_example: He/She tried to speak quietly so as not to draw attention.

additional_notes: Preterite (simple past) of **llamar**. Often means **to call (someone)** on the phone: *Llamó a Mary.* The **a** is used before a person (*llamó a María*). With things like **la puerta**, it commonly means **to knock (at/on)**: *llamó a la puerta.* It can also mean **to call/request** a service: *llamó a un taxi* (called a taxi).
target_language_example: Anoche llamó a mi hermana, pero no contestó.
native_language_example: Last night he/she called my sister, but she didn’t answer.

meaning: to lock the door (with a key).
additional_notes: Usually used in the phrase **ponerle llave a la puerta** (“to put a key/lock on the door” = to lock it). You can also say **cerrar la puerta con llave**. The **le** in **ponerle** refers to *the door* (i.e., “put a lock on it”).
target_language_example: Antes de salir, ponle llave a la puerta.
native_language_example: Before you leave, lock the door.

additional_notes: Used for a key that can open many (or all) doors/locks in a building, like in a school or hotel. In Spanish it’s usually feminine: la llave maestra.
target_language_example: El director tiene la llave maestra para abrir todas las aulas.
native_language_example: The principal has the master key to open all the classrooms.

meaning: “arrives (to/at)”; also “comes to / ends up (doing something)” (with an infinitive).
additional_notes:
From the verb **llegar** (3rd person singular present: **llega**). Common patterns:
- **llegar a + place**: “to arrive (to/at)” → *llega a casa* = “arrives home”, *llega a tiempo* = “arrives on time”.
- **llegar a + infinitive**: “to come to / manage to / even (do)” depending on context → often used for something that happens after some time or as a result (e.g., *me llega a doler la cabeza* ≈ “I end up getting a headache / my head even starts to hurt”).
It conjugates: *llego a, llegas a, llega a, llegan a…*
target_language_example: Sin importar lo que pase, Tom siempre llega a tiempo.
native_language_example: No matter what happens, Tom always arrives on time.

additional_notes: From llegar (to arrive) + tarde (late). Used with people or things (like buses/trains/planes). You can add the destination with a + place: "llega tarde a la escuela". For other subjects: "llego tarde" (I’m late), "llegas tarde" (you’re late), "llegan tarde" (they’re late).
target_language_example: El autobús llega tarde.
native_language_example: The bus arrives late.

additional_notes: Used with places and destinations (Llegamos a la oficina), times (Llegamos a las cinco), and also more figuratively for reaching a person/thing or a point in a story or discussion (Y ahora llegamos a los grandes). It’s the 1st person plural (nosotros) of "llegar" in the past (pretérito): "we arrived / we got".
target_language_example: Llegamos al aeropuerto temprano, pero el vuelo se retrasó.
native_language_example: We got to the airport early, but the flight was delayed.

additional_notes: Used for arriving at a place or reaching a point, goal, result, or even a person/thing figuratively, as in llegar a nuestro corazón ('reach our heart'). In English, this is often translated as 'get to' or 'reach' rather than a literal 'arrive to'.
target_language_example: Queremos llegar a la estación antes de las ocho.
native_language_example: We want to get to the station before eight.

meaning: to get home; to arrive home
additional_notes: Means arriving back at your home. Spanish uses the preposition "a" with "llegar" ("llegar a" + place). With "casa" you normally don’t use an article: "llegar a casa" (not *llegar a la casa* unless you mean a specific house, e.g., someone else’s).
target_language_example: Acabamos de llegar a casa.
native_language_example: We just got home.

meaning: to make it to the end of the month (financially); to make ends meet.
additional_notes: Used when talking about having enough money to cover expenses until the end of the month (often before getting paid). Common with phrases like "no puedo" / "me cuesta" / "tener problemas para" llegar a fin de mes.
target_language_example: Con este alquiler tan caro, me cuesta llegar a fin de mes.
native_language_example: With this rent so expensive, it’s hard for me to make it to the end of the month.

additional_notes: Used for a change over time or achieving a result/role. Often implies a process or effort ("I want to become…", "it can end up being useful"). Common pattern: llegar a ser + noun/adjective (llegar a ser músico / llegar a ser útil).
target_language_example: Con práctica, puedes llegar a ser muy bueno.
native_language_example: With practice, you can become very good.

meaning: to become; to end up being.
additional_notes: Used to describe a change or development over time, often emphasizing the process or eventual outcome (similar to “come to be”). Commonly followed by a noun or adjective: “llegar a ser médico” (become a doctor), “llegar a ser famoso” (become famous). In some past contexts it can imply “ended up being.”
target_language_example: Con el tiempo, llegó a llegar a ser un gran escritor.
native_language_example: Over time, he came to become a great writer.

meaning: to arrive on time; to make it in time.
additional_notes: Used for arriving by a scheduled/expected time (class, work, a meeting). With negatives, it means you were late ("No pude/no conseguí llegar a tiempo"). Also used as “in time” to do something before it’s too late ("Aún podemos llegar a tiempo" = we can still make it in time).
target_language_example: Si salimos ahora, podemos llegar a tiempo a la reunión.
native_language_example: If we leave now, we can make it to the meeting on time.

meaning: to reach an agreement; to come to an agreement.
additional_notes: Used when people negotiate and finally agree on terms (often after discussion or conflict). Common with "con" to say who you agree with: "llegar a un acuerdo con alguien". Also often followed by "sobre" to specify the topic: "llegar a un acuerdo sobre X".
target_language_example: Después de hablar un rato, conseguimos llegar a un acuerdo sobre el precio.
native_language_example: After talking for a while, we managed to reach an agreement on the price.

meaning: to go far; to achieve a lot (be very successful).
additional_notes: Often used literally for physical distance (travel) or figuratively to talk about success, progress, or reaching big goals. Commonly appears in phrases like "vas a llegar lejos" (you’re going to go far / you’ll be very successful).
target_language_example: Con trabajo duro, vas a llegar lejos.
native_language_example: With hard work, you’re going to go far.

additional_notes: Used to say someone arrives after the expected time. Often followed by “a” + an event: “llegar tarde a clase / al trabajo / a comer”. Common with “no” to express an obligation or plan: “no debo llegar tarde” (I mustn’t be late).
target_language_example: Si salimos ahora, no vamos a llegar tarde al cine.
native_language_example: If we leave now, we won’t be late to the movie theater.

additional_notes: Past tense (preterite) of "llegar" for "yo": "llegué" = "I arrived" (a completed action). Used for when you got home at a specific time or as a sequence of events. Often followed by another action: "Llegué a casa y...". You can also add a time: "Llegué a casa a las siete."
target_language_example: Llegué a casa tarde y ya estaban todos dormidos.
native_language_example: I got home late and everyone was already asleep.

additional_notes: Past tense (preterite) of llegar: llegué = “I arrived” + tarde = “late.” Commonly followed by a + place/event (llegué tarde al trabajo / a la escuela). You can also say “llegar tarde” in general: “Siempre llego tarde” = “I’m always late.”
target_language_example: Perdón, llegué tarde porque había mucho tráfico.
native_language_example: Sorry, I arrived late because there was a lot of traffic.

additional_notes: Past tense (preterite) of *llegar a* used to say someone/something arrived at a destination: *llegó a Londres*, *llegó a Brasilia*. It can also be followed by a time to say when it arrived: *llegó a las siete y media*. In *llegó a tiempo*, it means “arrived on time.”
target_language_example: El autobús llegó a la estación a las ocho.
native_language_example: The bus arrived at the station at eight.

additional_notes: Past tense (pretérito) of llegar: llegó = “arrived.” Use it for a completed action in the past. You can add time expressions like hace un momento (a moment ago), poco después (a little later), tan pronto como (as soon as), or describe how someone arrived: cansado/a (tired), exhausto/a (exhausted). For other subjects: llegué a casa (I got home), llegaste (you got home), llegaron (they got home).
target_language_example: Llegó a casa tarde y se fue directo a dormir.
native_language_example: He got home late and went straight to sleep.

additional_notes: Past tense (pretérito) of "llegar" for él/ella/usted. Used for a one-time completed event. Often followed by "a" + destination/event: "llegó tarde a casa / a la reunión". You can change the subject: "llegué tarde" (I), "llegaste tarde" (you), "llegaron tarde" (they).
target_language_example: Él llegó tarde a casa anoche.
native_language_example: He arrived home late last night.

additional_notes: Used with feminine nouns (la bolsa, la cesta, la habitación, etc.). For masculine nouns, use "lleno de" (un bolso lleno de libros). Often follows a noun: "una bolsa llena de manzanas".
target_language_example: La casa está llena de gente.
native_language_example: The house is full of people.

additional_notes: Used to say someone/something contains a lot of something else. Common patterns: "estar lleno de + noun" (temporary/state) and "un/una + noun + lleno/a de + noun" (a thing that is full of something). It agrees with the noun it describes: "lleno" (masc. sing.), "llena" (fem. sing.), "llenos" (masc. pl.), "llenas" (fem. pl.).
target_language_example: El cielo solía estar lleno de ellos.
native_language_example: The sky used to be full of them.

meaning: “full of” (filled with; having a lot of).
additional_notes: Used with estar/quedar and agrees with the noun: lleno (m. sg.), llena (f. sg.), llenos (m. pl.), llenas (f. pl.). Can be literal (full of dust/names) or figurative (full of anger). In insults it can be very vulgar, e.g., “lleno de mierda”.
target_language_example: Después del viaje, estábamos llenos de energía.
native_language_example: After the trip, we were full of energy.

additional_notes: Used with the verb **llevar** + **puesto/puesta/puestos/puestas** (agreeing with what’s being worn) + a noun. It’s a common way to describe clothing or accessories someone has on: **lleva puesto un suéter**, **lleva puesta una chaqueta**, **lleva puestos unos guantes**.
target_language_example: Mi hermano lleva puesto un abrigo negro.
native_language_example: My brother is wearing a black coat.

additional_notes: Used with the imperfect tense (llevaba) to describe what someone had on at a past time or as a habitual past description. It’s followed by a noun; use "un" for masculine singular nouns (un sombrero, un uniforme) and "una" for feminine singular nouns (una camisa, una falda): "llevaba puesta una…". You can also use it with "lo" for masculine items like "un mono".
target_language_example: Cuando lo vi, llevaba puesto un abrigo negro.
native_language_example: When I saw him, he was wearing a black coat.

additional_notes: "Llevaba" is the imperfect past of "llevar". In these examples it means someone had an item on their body (clothes, a mask). It’s often followed by a feminine noun because of "una" (e.g., una chaqueta, una camisa, una máscara). You can also use "llevaba" for carrying/bringing something.
target_language_example: Cuando lo vi, llevaba una chaqueta negra.
native_language_example: When I saw him, he was wearing a black jacket.

meaning: to carry out; to carry through (a plan, task, project).
additional_notes: Used with plans, tasks, projects, procedures, or events to mean completing/implementing them. Often interchangeable with "realizar" or "efectuar" in formal contexts. Literally "to take/carry to completion," so it’s not usually translated word-for-word.
target_language_example: Vamos a llevar a cabo el proyecto este mes.
native_language_example: We’re going to carry out the project this month.

meaning: to take a long time; to have been (doing something) for a long time.
additional_notes: Uses the verb "llevar" to express duration. Common patterns: (1) "Llevar + time + doing something" = "to have been doing something for [time]" (e.g., "Llevo dos horas esperando"). (2) "Llevar mucho tiempo" often means something has been going on for a long time. (3) In questions, "¿Cuánto tiempo llevas... ?" = "How long have you been... ?" Note: the exact form "llevar mucho tiempo" appears when using the infinitive (e.g., "Debe llevar mucho tiempo..."); with a conjugated verb it becomes "llevo/llevas/lleva... mucho tiempo".
target_language_example: Debe llevar mucho tiempo viviendo aquí.
native_language_example: He/She must have been living here for a long time.

meaning: to be wearing; to have on (clothing/accessories).
additional_notes: Used to describe what someone is wearing. It often agrees with the item being worn: puesto (masc. sg.), puesta (fem. sg.), puestos (masc. pl.), puestas (fem. pl.). Common with clothing and accessories (camisa, abrigo, gafas, zapatos). In many real sentences the words may appear separated or inflected (e.g., "llevo puesta"), but the base multi-word term is "llevar puesto".
target_language_example: En la entrevista, debo llevar puesto un traje formal.
native_language_example: At the interview, I should be wearing a formal suit.

meaning: to take time; to take a while; (with a time expression + gerund) to have been doing something for a certain amount of time.
additional_notes: Common uses: (1) "Esto lleva tiempo" / "Llevar tiempo" = something takes time: "Aprender un idioma lleva tiempo" (Learning a language takes time). (2) "Llevar + time period + gerund" expresses duration up to now: "Llevo dos meses estudiando" (I’ve been studying for two months). Note: in the duration pattern, "llevar" must be conjugated, but the base multi-word term is still "llevar tiempo".
target_language_example: Aprender un idioma lleva tiempo.
native_language_example: Learning a language takes time.

additional_notes: Used to say how long an activity will take (duration). Common patterns include: "Eso lleva unos minutos" (That takes a few minutes) and "Me va a llevar unos minutos" (It’s going to take me a few minutes). You can replace "unos minutos" with other time amounts ("unas horas", "un rato").
target_language_example: Esto va a llevar unos minutos.
native_language_example: This is going to take a few minutes.

meaning: 'they took (someone/something) to' or 'they led (someone) to (a result/action)'.
additional_notes: This is the preterite (past) 3rd‑person plural of **llevar**: **ellos/ellas/ustedes llevaron**. Common patterns: **llevar a + place** = “to take to” (Lo llevaron a la cárcel.); **llevar a + noun/result** = “to lead to” (Lo llevaron a su ruina.); **llevar a + infinitive** = “to lead someone to do” (Lo llevaron a beber.). With **se** (**se llevaron a...**) it often means “they took (someone) away.” Note: **llevar a cabo** is a separate fixed expression meaning “to carry out/perform,” and is not the same as **llevaron a** + destination/result.
target_language_example: Sus problemas lo llevaron a beber.
native_language_example: His problems led him to drink.

additional_notes: Used with a person (or group) you have a good relationship with. It’s reflexive, so you conjugate it as "llevarse": me llevo bien, te llevas bien, se lleva bien, nos llevamos bien, se llevan bien. Common pattern: "llevarse bien con + [person]". You can add "muy" or "tan" to strengthen it: "me llevo muy bien con ella".
target_language_example: Es difícil llevarse bien con él.
native_language_example: It’s hard to get along with him.

meaning: to take you home (give you a ride home).
additional_notes: Uses the verb "llevar" (to take/bring) + "te" (you) + "a casa" (home). Common when offering to drive/escort someone home: "Déjame/Puedo/Voy a llevarte a casa." You can change the object pronoun: "llevarme" (take me home), "llevarlo/la" (take him/her home), "llevarnos" (take us home).
target_language_example: Si estás cansado, puedo llevarte a casa.
native_language_example: If you’re tired, I can take you home.

additional_notes: Future tense of llevar (“to take/bring/carry”). It’s often followed by a destination (a + place) or a person’s home (a su casa). When the direct object is a person, Spanish commonly uses the “personal a” (e.g., Llevaré a Juan a casa). With pronouns, you’ll often see it as lo/la llevaré a… (“I’ll take him/her to…”).
target_language_example: Te llevaré al aeropuerto mañana.
native_language_example: I’ll take you to the airport tomorrow.

additional_notes: Past tense (preterite) of the phrase "llevar a cabo" = "to carry out" (to do and finish something planned). Common with nouns like el plan, la misión, el proyecto, la tarea. In other tenses: "lleva a cabo" (carries out), "llevaba a cabo" (was carrying out/used to carry out).
target_language_example: El equipo llevó a cabo el proyecto en tres meses.
native_language_example: The team carried out the project in three months.

additional_notes: Used to say something required more time than expected/than usual. Common patterns: "(Algo) llevó más tiempo de lo que + verb" (…than I expected / than we thought), and "(Algo) me/te/nos llevó más tiempo de lo normal" (it took me/you/us longer than usual). "Llevar" here means "to take (time)".
target_language_example: El trámite llevó más tiempo de lo que pensábamos.
native_language_example: The paperwork took longer than we thought.

meaning: to pour (rain); to rain cats and dogs.
additional_notes: Common idiom for very heavy rain. Often used with the weather verb in the infinitive after expressions like "Va a" or "Parece que va a": "Va a llover a cántaros". The literal image is “raining in pitchers/jugs,” but it’s not translated word-for-word in English.
target_language_example: ¡Coge un paraguas! Va a llover a cántaros.
native_language_example: Grab an umbrella! It’s going to pour.

additional_notes: Uses the neuter article "lo" + an adjective to mean an abstract idea: "what is correct/right." Often used when talking about doing the morally or practically right action (e.g., "hacer lo correcto" = "to do the right thing").
target_language_example: A veces es difícil saber qué es lo correcto.
native_language_example: Sometimes it’s hard to know what the right thing is.

meaning: "which" / "which (fact)" (referring back to what was just said).
additional_notes: Used to refer back to an entire idea, statement, or situation mentioned right before it (not usually a single noun). Often follows a comma: "..., lo cual ...". Related forms: "del cual / de la cual / de los cuales / de las cuales" = "of which"; and "por lo cual" = "which is why / for which reason".
target_language_example: Perdí el autobús, lo cual me hizo llegar tarde.
native_language_example: I missed the bus, which made me arrive late.

additional_notes: used to refer to an identical thing, action, idea, or situation. very common with ser (es lo mismo = it's the same) and hacer (hacer lo mismo = do the same thing). the neuter lo refers to something general, not a specific masculine noun.
target_language_example: Yo quiero lo mismo que tú.
native_language_example: I want the same thing as you.

additional_notes: Used to talk about the least wanted or expected thing, especially in patterns like "lo último que..." = "the last thing that...". In other contexts, it can also mean "the latest" or "the newest."
target_language_example: Lo último que necesito hoy es más trabajo.
native_language_example: The last thing I need today is more work.

additional_notes: Used to express doing something at the earliest possible time. Often follows a verb: “empezar lo antes posible” (start as soon as possible). You can also say “tan pronto como sea posible,” but “lo antes posible” is very common in everyday speech.
target_language_example: Por favor, llámame lo antes posible.
native_language_example: Please call me as soon as possible.

additional_notes: Used to introduce a positive point, advantage, or silver lining, often after mentioning something negative or difficult. It’s commonly followed by a full clause with que (e.g., “lo bueno es que + verb”).
target_language_example: Lo bueno es que mañana no trabajamos.
native_language_example: The good thing is that we don’t work tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used to refer to the opposite of something previously mentioned. Common patterns: “lo contrario de X” = “the opposite of X”, and “pensar/decir lo contrario” = “to think/say the opposite.” It can also stand alone as a short reply meaning “the opposite.”
target_language_example: Yo decía que no iba a llover, pero pasó lo contrario.
native_language_example: I said it wasn’t going to rain, but the opposite happened.

meaning: “the right thing” (the correct/proper thing to do).
additional_notes: Uses the neuter article “lo” + an adjective (“correcto”) to talk about an idea in general: what is right/correct, often in a moral or appropriate-to-do sense. Common with verbs like hacer (“to do”), ser (“to be”), and preguntar (“to ask”).
target_language_example: No sé si esto es lo correcto, pero lo intentaré.
native_language_example: I don’t know if this is the right thing, but I’ll try.

additional_notes: Used to refer to the best part of something or to making the best out of a situation: “sacar lo mejor de…” = “to bring out/get the best out of…”. Common intensifier: “lo mejor de lo mejor” = “the very best (of the best)”.
target_language_example: Tenemos que sacar lo mejor de esta situación.
native_language_example: We have to make the best of this situation.

additional_notes: Used to give advice or recommend the best option in a situation. It’s often followed by an infinitive (Lo mejor es irse) or by “que” + subjunctive (Lo mejor es que tengas un nuevo comienzo).
target_language_example: Lo mejor es hablar con ella mañana.
native_language_example: It’s best to talk to her tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used to introduce a relative clause describing the best option/result among possibilities: “lo mejor que pudo hacer” (the best thing he/she could do), “lo mejor que me pudo haber pasado” (the best thing that could have happened to me). Often appears with verbs like poder (can/could) to express doing your best: “Hago/estoy haciendo lo mejor que puedo”. You’ll also see it with the subjunctive when talking about what is best under a condition or uncertainty: “lo mejor que podamos” (the best we can).
target_language_example: Te llamé porque era lo mejor que podía hacer en ese momento.
native_language_example: I called you because it was the best thing I could do at that moment.

additional_notes: Used to refer to something identical in idea, situation, or result: what is being talked about is the same as something else. The neuter article lo makes it more general/abstract, so lo mismo often means 'the same thing' rather than matching a specific noun. Common in phrases like pensar lo mismo ('think the same thing') and no es lo mismo ('it's not the same').
target_language_example: No quiero lo mismo que tú.
native_language_example: I don't want the same thing as you.

additional_notes: Used to compare two people/things/actions as being equal or identical. Often appears after verbs like "ser" ("es lo mismo que...") or "pensar" ("pienso lo mismo que...") and can be followed by a person, thing, or clause ("lo mismo que a ti", "lo mismo que todo el mundo"). In "pasó lo mismo que...", it means "the same thing happened as..."
target_language_example: Para mí, trabajar desde casa es lo mismo que trabajar en la oficina.
native_language_example: For me, working from home is the same as working in the office.

additional_notes: Used to form the superlative: **lo más + adjective/adverb** = “the most …” (often implying “the most [adjective] thing/part”). Very common in phrases like **lo más … posible** (“as … as possible”) and **lo más que puedo** (“as much as I can / the most I can”).
target_language_example: Hazlo lo más rápido posible, por favor.
native_language_example: Do it as fast as possible, please.

additional_notes: Used to point out the top priority or main point. Often appears in patterns like: “Lo más importante es + infinitive” (Lo más importante es no rendirse), “Lo más importante es que + subjunctive” (Lo más importante es que lo sepas), or “Lo más importante no es X, sino Y” to contrast what truly matters.
target_language_example: Lo más importante es estar bien de salud.
native_language_example: The most important thing is to be in good health.

meaning: the most important thing is that…
additional_notes: Used to emphasize what matters most, often to refocus the conversation or highlight a key point. It is followed by a clause introduced by que. The verb after que can be indicative (fact/goal presented as real or certain: "es que estamos…") or subjunctive when expressing what is important as a desired outcome or requirement ("es que me entiendas", "es que usted acepte").
target_language_example: Lo más importante es que llegues a tiempo.
native_language_example: The most important thing is that you arrive on time.

meaning: as far away as possible; as far as possible.
additional_notes: Used to emphasize maximum distance from something/someone (often for safety or avoiding something). It can be a full phrase by itself, or followed by “de + [noun]” (“as far away as possible from…”).
target_language_example: Quédate lo más lejos posible de la carretera.
native_language_example: Stay as far away from the road as possible.

meaning: (not) at all; even the slightest bit.
additional_notes: Commonly used for emphasis, especially in negatives: “no… lo más mínimo” = “not … at all / not one bit,” and “ni lo más mínimo” = “not even the slightest bit.” It can also appear with verbs like “preocupar” (to worry) or “vacilar” (to hesitate) to mean “in the least.”
target_language_example: No me molesta lo más mínimo.
native_language_example: It doesn’t bother me at all.

meaning: 'as soon as possible' / 'as quickly as possible'.
additional_notes: Used to express urgency: you want something done at the earliest possible time. Often follows what you want done (e.g., "Quiero... lo más pronto posible"). You can also say "lo antes posible" with the same meaning; "pronto" is common in Latin America, while "antes" is very universal.
target_language_example: Por favor, envíame el reporte lo más pronto posible.
native_language_example: Please send me the report as soon as possible.

additional_notes: Used to ask for maximum speed/urgency. It often follows a verb (e.g., "ven lo más rápido posible" = "come as quickly as possible") or can stand alone as a request ("Lo más rápido posible, por favor").
target_language_example: Envíame el informe lo más rápido posible.
native_language_example: Send me the report as quickly as possible.

meaning: "what’s between us" (our relationship) / "our thing" (what we’re doing).
additional_notes: Uses the neuter article **lo** + **nuestro** to mean “the thing that is ours.” Very common to talk about a romantic/close relationship: **¿Lo nuestro ha acabado?** = “Is what we have over?” It’s also used for “our business/our task,” especially in **volver a lo nuestro** = “let’s get back to what we were doing / our topic.”
target_language_example: Bueno, ya basta de hablar de eso; volvamos a lo nuestro.
native_language_example: Okay, enough talking about that; let’s get back to what we were doing.

meaning: “the worst” (the worst thing/situation; the worst-case scenario).
additional_notes: Uses the neuter article “lo” + comparative “peor” to talk about something in general, not a specific masculine/feminine noun. Common patterns: “prepararse para lo peor” (prepare for the worst), “esperar/imaginar lo peor” (expect/imagine the worst), “lo peor de + [situation] es...” (the worst part of ... is ...), “lo peor está por venir” (the worst is yet to come), “ya pasó lo peor” (the worst is over).
target_language_example: Lo peor de este trabajo es levantarse tan temprano.
native_language_example: The worst part of this job is getting up so early.

additional_notes: Used to introduce what happens first in a sequence: lo + adjective (primero) + que + clause. It often appears with ser ("Lo primero que vi fue...") or before a verb phrase ("Lo primero que quiero hacer es..."). You can add time/context phrases like "Cuando..." or "Al..." before it.
target_language_example: Lo primero que hice al llegar a casa fue ducharme.
native_language_example: The first thing I did when I got home was take a shower.

meaning: “what he/she/you say(s)” (the thing that someone says).
additional_notes: Uses the neutral article "lo" + "que" to mean “what/that which.” It introduces a relative clause about someone’s words: "Ten cuidado con lo que dice" = “Be careful about what he says.” It can change with person/tense: "lo que dices" (what you say), "lo que dijo" (what he said), "lo que están diciendo" (what they’re saying).
target_language_example: No entiendo lo que dice el profesor.
native_language_example: I don’t understand what the teacher is saying.

meaning: 'what it was/used to be' or 'which was…'.
additional_notes: Often used with "ya no" to say something is no longer the way it used to be: "ya no es lo que era" = "it’s not what it used to be." It can also introduce a comment about the previous clause, like "which was…": "Dijo que estaba enferma, lo que era mentira" = "…which was a lie."
target_language_example: Este barrio ya no es lo que era.
native_language_example: This neighborhood isn’t what it used to be.

additional_notes: Used to refer to an event in the past, often something already known from context or about to be explained: "Te voy a decir lo que pasó". It can also mean "what happened next/afterward" when followed by time words like "después". Grammatically it’s "lo que" ("what/that which") + "pasó" (past of "pasar").
target_language_example: Nadie entendía lo que pasó en la reunión.
native_language_example: Nobody understood what happened in the meeting.

additional_notes: Uses the structure **lo que + verb (querer)** to mean “whatever/anything that…”. Here **quieras** is the present subjunctive of **querer**, used in open-ended or indefinite statements (not a specific known thing). Often appears after verbs like **hacer, decir, escribir, preguntar, añadir, pensar, ser, tener**. With **todo**: **todo lo que quieras** = “as much/many as you want” / “all you want.”
target_language_example: Elige lo que quieras; yo invito.
native_language_example: Choose whatever you want; it’s on me.

additional_notes: Used to refer to an unspecified thing, without caring which one: “whatever.” With verbs like hacer/comprar/poder, it often means “anything (at all).” You’ll also see the longer form “lo que sea que + verb” (= “whatever …”), e.g., “en lo que sea que haga” = “in whatever I do.”
target_language_example: Elige lo que sea; a mí me da igual.
native_language_example: Choose whatever; I don’t mind.

additional_notes: Used to say something is enough in amount/degree. Often goes after a verb (e.g., "no escuchamos lo suficiente" = "we don’t listen enough"). It can also go before an adjective/adverb as an intensifier (e.g., "lo suficiente bueno" = "good enough"), and it can stand alone as a short answer ("Lo suficiente" = "Enough"). Sometimes followed by "como para" to mean "enough to" ("lo suficiente como para llorar" = "enough to cry").
target_language_example: No tengo lo suficiente dinero para el boleto.
native_language_example: I don’t have enough money for the ticket.

additional_notes: Used before an adjective or adverb to say someone/something meets (or doesn’t meet) a requirement: "lo suficientemente + adj./adv." Often followed by "para" + infinitive ("enough to...") or "como para". In negatives: "no ... lo suficientemente" = "not ... enough".
target_language_example: No estoy lo suficientemente listo para el examen.
native_language_example: I’m not ready enough for the exam.

additional_notes: Used to refer to the final thing in a sequence (the last remaining item, the last thing you remember/heard, or the last thing someone will do/see). Often followed by a verb phrase: “lo último que recuerdo…”, “lo último que supe…”, “lo último que nos quedaba…”.
target_language_example: Lo último que necesito ahora es más problemas.
native_language_example: The last thing I need right now is more problems.

additional_notes: Used to single out one thing as the only one that matters/exists/does something. Often followed by a verb: “lo único que + verb…”. Can also appear in negatives like “no es lo único que…” = “it’s not the only thing that…”.
target_language_example: Lo único que quiero ahora es descansar.
native_language_example: The only thing I want right now is to rest.

meaning: "I met him" / "I got to know him" (in the past).
additional_notes: Preterite (completed past) of conocer + the direct object pronoun lo (“him/it”). Often used for meeting someone for the first time ("I met him"), and sometimes for having known someone ("I knew him"). Contrast: conocer = to know/meet people or be familiar with places/things; saber = to know facts/information.
target_language_example: Lo conocí en una fiesta el año pasado.
native_language_example: I met him at a party last year.

additional_notes: Uses the verb "conocer" (to know/be acquainted with) plus the direct object pronoun "lo" (usually "him" or "it"). It’s used for knowing a person, place, or something you’re familiar with (not for knowing facts—that’s usually "saber"). Common variations you may see: "lo conozco de vista" = "I recognize him / I know him by sight."
target_language_example: Sí, lo conozco de vista, pero nunca hemos hablado.
native_language_example: Yes, I recognize him (I know him by sight), but we’ve never talked.

additional_notes: Used to introduce surprising or hard-to-believe information. It’s addressed to “you” (tú): literally “whether you believe it or not,” with *lo* referring to what comes next or what was just said. Common at the start of a sentence and often set off by commas.
target_language_example: Lo creas o no, hoy terminé el proyecto antes de tiempo.
native_language_example: Believe it or not, today I finished the project ahead of time.

additional_notes: refers to a situation, event, or matter understood from context. With time expressions, it often means "what happened" then: lo de anoche = "what happened last night." With a person or thing, it can mean "the thing about..." or "what happened to/with...": lo de su marido = "what happened with your husband" / "about your husband." It is very common in apologies: siento lo de... = "I'm sorry about..."
target_language_example: No quiero hablar de lo de ayer.
native_language_example: I don't want to talk about what happened yesterday.

additional_notes: Used to refer to something habitual or repeated that both speakers already know from context. Common when ordering food/drinks (meaning “my usual”) or commenting on a recurring situation (often with a tired or resigned tone: “it was the same old thing”).
target_language_example: Ponme lo de siempre, por favor.
native_language_example: Give me the usual, please.

meaning: “you say it / you’re saying it” (referring to something already mentioned).
additional_notes: “Lo” is an object pronoun meaning “it/that.” So “lo dices” literally means “you say it.” It’s common in expressions like “Ahora que lo dices…” (“Now that you mention it…”) and questions like “¿Lo dices en serio?” (“Do you mean it?/Are you serious?”). You’ll often see an extra pronoun added: “me lo dices” = “you tell me (it).”
target_language_example: Si cambias de plan, me lo dices y listo.
native_language_example: If you change your plan, tell me and that’s it.

additional_notes: “Lo” is a direct object pronoun meaning “it/that.” “Diga” is the present subjunctive of “decir” (to say/tell). Very common in time/condition phrases like “cuando/hasta que … lo diga” meaning “when/until … (someone) says so” (often referring to permission or an order). It’s also used as a command: “No lo diga” = “Don’t say it / Don’t tell (them).”
target_language_example: No empieces hasta que el profesor lo diga.
native_language_example: Don’t start until the teacher says so.

additional_notes: Used when you’re stating something and referring to it with the direct object pronoun lo (“it/that”). Often points back to what you just said or are about to say: Por eso lo digo (“That’s why I say it”). Can also sound like “I mean it” or “I’m telling you” depending on context and tone. Literally: lo = it/that, digo = I say.
target_language_example: Lo digo en serio: no voy a ir.
native_language_example: I mean it: I’m not going to go.

meaning: "I’m telling you" / "I say so" (insisting or asserting authority).
additional_notes: Used to emphasize that the speaker is certain or expects to be believed/obeyed. Often sounds firm or bossy depending on tone. Common in answers like: "Porque lo digo yo" ("Because I said so"). You can also add stress: "¡Lo digo yo!" = "I’m telling you!"
target_language_example: No va a llover hoy, lo digo yo.
native_language_example: It’s not going to rain today, I’m telling you.

additional_notes: "Lo" is a direct object pronoun meaning "it/that" (something already known from context). "Dijo" is the past tense (preterite) of "decir" = "to say." You can use it to report who said something: "Lo dijo Goethe" = "Goethe said it."
target_language_example: No es verdad; él mismo lo dijo ayer.
native_language_example: It’s not true; he himself said it yesterday.

additional_notes: Uses the direct object pronoun lo (“it/him”) + encontré (preterite of encontrar). Often means you found something, or you found/ran into someone. Word order in Spanish is commonly object pronoun + verb: lo encontré = “I found it.”
target_language_example: ¡Por fin lo encontré!
native_language_example: I finally found it!

additional_notes: Used to check or confirm someone understands something (“Do you get it?”). "lo" refers to the idea/situation being discussed. Often appears in questions (¿Lo entiendes?), with emphasis (Sí lo entiendes), or with "no" for negation (No lo entiendes).
target_language_example: Explícamelo otra vez si no lo entiendes.
native_language_example: Explain it to me again if you don’t understand it.

additional_notes: Used to say you understand something that was said or explained. "Lo" means "it" (the thing/idea). Often used with emphasis words like "ya" (now/already) or "ahora" (now): "Ya/Ahora lo entiendo." You can also say just "Entiendo" if it's clear what you mean.
target_language_example: No te preocupes, lo entiendo.
native_language_example: Don’t worry, I understand (it).

additional_notes: Uses the present progressive: estar (estás) + gerund (haciendo) to talk about something happening right now. "Lo" is a direct object pronoun meaning "it" (the specific action/thing is understood from context). Often used with words like "de nuevo" or "otra vez" (again) and with intensifiers like "muy bien" (very well) or "bastante bien" (pretty well).
target_language_example: Lo estás haciendo muy bien; sigue así.
native_language_example: You’re doing it very well; keep it up.

meaning: “(he/she/you formal) has said it” / “(someone) told you/us/it.”
additional_notes: Formed with the pronoun **lo** (“it”) + **ha dicho** (present perfect of *decir*: “has said”). It often means “has told (it)” when **lo** refers to some information already known from context. The person who said it is shown by the subject or can be implied: **ella lo ha dicho** = “she has said it.” You can add an indirect object pronoun: **te lo ha dicho** = “(someone) has told you (it),” **nos lo ha dicho** = “has told us (it).”
target_language_example: No te preocupes: el médico lo ha dicho.
native_language_example: Don’t worry: the doctor has said so.

meaning: “(he/she/you formal) has done it” / “has done that”.
additional_notes: Present perfect: **ha hecho** = “has done” (from *hacer*). **Lo** is a direct object pronoun meaning “it/that,” referring to something already known from context. Subject is often omitted in Spanish, so **lo ha hecho** can mean “he has done it,” “she has done it,” or “you (formal) have done it,” depending on context.
target_language_example: ¿De verdad lo ha hecho otra vez?
native_language_example: Has he really done it again?

additional_notes: "Lo" is a direct object pronoun meaning "it" or "him" (also "you" in formal address). "Ha visto" is the present perfect of "ver" (to see): "has/have seen". It’s used to say that someone has seen something/someone, often when the object was already mentioned or is understood from context.
target_language_example: ¿Lo ha visto hoy?
native_language_example: Have you seen him/it today?

additional_notes: Uses the conditional perfect: **haber (habría) + past participle (hecho)** to talk about a hypothetical action in the past (often in “if…” situations, opinions, or regrets). **Lo** is an object pronoun meaning “it/that,” and it goes before **habría**: *Lo habría hecho* = “I would have done it.” You can change the person: *yo lo habría hecho, tú lo habrías hecho, ella lo habría hecho, nosotros lo habríamos hecho*, etc.
target_language_example: Si me lo hubieras pedido, lo habría hecho.
native_language_example: If you had asked me, I would have done it.

additional_notes: "Lo" is a direct-object pronoun meaning "it" or "that" (referring to an action or idea already mentioned). "Hace" is the present tense of "hacer" (to do/make) for él/ella/usted. Often used to avoid repeating the verb phrase: "Dice que no miente, pero lo hace" = "He says he doesn’t lie, but he does."
target_language_example: Dice que no llega tarde, pero lo hace casi todos los días.
native_language_example: He says he isn’t late, but he is almost every day.

additional_notes: Used when the action is already known from context. “lo” is a pronoun meaning “it/that,” and “hacemos” is “we do/make.” Often appears in comparisons ("como lo hacemos...") or to give a reason/purpose ("lo hacemos por/porque...").
target_language_example: Si hay que ayudar, lo hacemos sin dudar.
native_language_example: If we have to help, we do it without hesitation.

additional_notes: "Lo" is a direct object pronoun meaning "it" (the thing/action is understood from context), and "hacen" is the verb "hacer" (to do/make) conjugated for ellos/ellas/ustedes. Often the subject is implied: "Siempre lo hacen" = "They always do it."
target_language_example: Cuando hay mucho trabajo, lo hacen entre todos.
native_language_example: When there’s a lot of work, they do it together.

additional_notes: "Haces" is the present tense (tú) of "hacer" (to do/make). "Lo" is a direct object pronoun meaning "it" (or sometimes "him" in formal/older usage), referring to something already known from context. Word order is usually "lo" + verb: "lo haces" = "you do it".
target_language_example: ¿Lo haces hoy o mañana?
native_language_example: Are you doing it today or tomorrow?

meaning: “(that) he/she/you do it” (subjunctive of hacer + lo = “it”).
additional_notes: Used when talking about an action as uncertain, desired, denied, or not yet happened. Very common after expressions like “que…” (Espero que no lo haga = “I hope he/she doesn’t do it”), “puede que…” (“he/she may do it”), and time clauses like “cuando…” for future actions (“when he/she does it”). Often refers back to an action already mentioned, with lo = “it/that.”
target_language_example: Si te llama, dile que no lo haga.
native_language_example: If he calls you, tell him not to do it.

additional_notes: Used when another word/phrase triggers the present subjunctive, especially after expressions like "quiero que..." (I want you to...), "necesito que..." (I need you to...), "dudo que..." (I doubt that you...), and "a menos que..." (unless...). "Lo" is the direct object pronoun meaning "it" (a thing/idea previously mentioned).
target_language_example: Prefiero que lo hagas hoy.
native_language_example: I’d prefer you do it today.

additional_notes: Used to say you perform an action, where **lo** means “it/that” (a direct object). Often refers back to something already mentioned: *¿Llamas a tu mamá? — Sí, lo hago.* With **ya**, it can mean “I already do it” or “I’ll do it (don’t worry)”: *Ya lo hago yo.* With **ya no**, it means “I don’t do it anymore”: *Ya no lo hago.*
target_language_example: Si quieres, lo hago por ti.
native_language_example: If you want, I’ll do it for you.

additional_notes: Present perfect: han hecho = “have done” (they). Lo is a pronoun meaning “it/that” (a thing or action already understood from context). Very common in phrases like Lo han hecho muy bien (“They’ve done it very well”) or Todos lo han hecho (“Everyone has done it”).
target_language_example: ¿Ya lo han hecho?
native_language_example: Have they done it already?

additional_notes: Future tense of hacer (to do/make): haremos = "we will do/make". Lo is an object pronoun meaning "it" (or "that"), referring to something already known from context. Word order can vary for emphasis: "Lo haremos" and "Nosotros lo haremos" both mean "We’ll do it," but adding "nosotros" stresses "we" (we, not someone else).
target_language_example: No te preocupes: lo haremos mañana.
native_language_example: Don’t worry: we’ll do it tomorrow.

meaning: 'he/she will do it' / 'will do it' (referring to something already known).
additional_notes: "Lo" is an object pronoun meaning "it" (or sometimes "him"), referring to an action or thing mentioned earlier. "Hará" is the future tense of "hacer" (to do/make): "will do/make". Often used to confirm/deny that someone will do something: "No, no lo hará" (No, he/she won’t), "Seguro que lo hará" (I’m sure he/she will). You can add time words: "mañana" (tomorrow), etc.
target_language_example: No te preocupes: él lo hará mañana.
native_language_example: Don’t worry: he’ll do it tomorrow.

additional_notes: Future tense of hacer (harás = 'you will do'). The pronoun lo means 'it' and refers to something already known from context (a task, goal, etc.). Often used to encourage or reassure someone: Creo que lo harás ('I think you’ll do it'), Lo harás bien ('You’ll do it well').
target_language_example: No te preocupes: lo harás muy bien.
native_language_example: Don’t worry: you’ll do it very well.

additional_notes: Uses the future tense of hacer (haré = “I will do”). lo means “it” (a thing/idea already known from context) and usually goes before the verb: lo haré = “I’ll do it.” You can add reasons or emphasis: lo haré por ti (“I’ll do it for you”), lo haré de nuevo (“I’ll do it again”).
target_language_example: Está bien, lo haré mañana.
native_language_example: Okay, I’ll do it tomorrow.

meaning: “I’ll do it.” (emphasizing that *I* will do it).
additional_notes: Uses the pronoun **yo** for emphasis/contrast (often implying “not you” or “if you don’t, I will”). **Lo** = “it” (the thing already mentioned). Common in conditional sentences: **Si no lo haces (tú), lo haré yo** = “If you don’t do it, I’ll do it.”
target_language_example: Déjalo, lo haré yo.
native_language_example: Leave it, I’ll do it.

additional_notes: Conditional tense of hacer (“to do/make”) + the direct object pronoun lo (“it/that”). It often appears in situations like advice (Si yo fuera tú, no lo haría. = If I were you, I wouldn’t do it) or hypotheticals/promises (Nadie más lo haría. = No one else would do it). You can change the subject: yo lo haría (I would do it), él lo haría (he would do it), etc.
target_language_example: Yo lo haría, pero no tengo tiempo.
native_language_example: I would do it, but I don’t have time.

additional_notes: Used to confirm or attribute that someone said something (lo = “it/that”). Often appears in questions like “¿Lo has dicho?” (“Did you say it?”) and with emphasis: “Tú mismo lo has dicho” (“You said it yourself”). Grammatically, it’s the present perfect (haber + participle): has dicho.
target_language_example: ¿Por qué te quejas? Tú mismo lo has dicho.
native_language_example: Why are you complaining? You said it yourself.

meaning: “you have done it” / “you did it” (present perfect).
additional_notes: Uses the pronoun “lo” (“it”) to refer to an action or thing already known from context. “Has hecho” is the tú form of the present perfect of hacer (has + hecho). Often used in speech to talk about something that happened before now, sometimes with emphasis on the result: “Lo has hecho bastante bien” = “You’ve done it pretty well.” In questions it can express surprise or ask for a reason: “¿Por qué lo has hecho?” = “Why did you do it?”
target_language_example: Lo has hecho muy rápido; gracias.
native_language_example: You did it really fast; thanks.

additional_notes: Literally “it, I have done.” Uses the present perfect (he + past participle hecho) to talk about something you have done in the past with relevance to now. With time expressions like “toda mi vida” (all my life) or “por años” (for years), it often means “I’ve been doing it.” “Lo” is a pronoun meaning “it/that” (the thing already mentioned or understood from context).
target_language_example: No te preocupes: lo he hecho antes.
native_language_example: Don’t worry: I’ve done it before.

additional_notes: Uses the present perfect: **he visto** = “I have seen.” **Lo** is a direct object pronoun meaning “it” (or “him” for a masculine person/animal). Often used when the thing/person has already been mentioned: *¿Has visto mi teléfono? — Sí, lo he visto.*
target_language_example: Sí, lo he visto en la mesa.
native_language_example: Yes, I’ve seen it on the table.

additional_notes: "Lo" is a direct object pronoun meaning "it" (or "him" in some contexts), placed before the verb. "Hice" is the preterite (simple past) of "hacer" (to do/to make). Used to say you did something and you’re referring back to it: "Sí, lo hice" = "Yes, I did it."
target_language_example: —¿Terminaste la tarea? —Sí, lo hice anoche.
native_language_example: —Did you finish the homework? —Yes, I did it last night.

meaning: '(that) he/she did it' in the imperfect subjunctive.
additional_notes: Used after triggers like que/para que ("so that"), verbs of wanting/asking/persuading, and expressions like es probable/no es probable, ya era hora de que, etc. It refers to a past or hypothetical action and is commonly equivalent to English "(that) he/she would do it" or "(that) he/she did it," depending on context. Literally it's "it" (lo) + "did" (hiciera), but the subjunctive mood is the key point.
target_language_example: No quería que lo hiciera solo.
native_language_example: I didn’t want him to do it alone.

additional_notes: Preterite (completed past) of hacer ("to do/make") with the direct object pronoun lo ("it/that"). The subject is often implied by context; it can mean "they did it" (ellos/ellas) or "you all did it" (ustedes). You can add the subject for clarity: "Ellos lo hicieron" / "Ustedes lo hicieron". Negative: "No lo hicieron."
target_language_example: No fue fácil, pero lo hicieron.
native_language_example: It wasn’t easy, but you/they did it.

additional_notes: Past tense (pretérito) of hacer: hicimos = “we did/made.” Lo = “it/that,” referring to something already mentioned or understood. Often used to emphasize completion: “And we did it.” Can also mean “we made it” depending on context (e.g., finishing or achieving something).
target_language_example: Lo hicimos al final, aunque fue difícil.
native_language_example: We did it in the end, even though it was difficult.

additional_notes: Uses the direct object pronoun **lo** (“it/that”) before **hiciste** (preterite of **hacer**, “to do/make”). Common for referring back to something already mentioned: *¡Lo hiciste!* = “You did it!” / “You made it!”
target_language_example: ¡Lo hiciste! Terminaste el proyecto a tiempo.
native_language_example: You did it! You finished the project on time.

additional_notes: "Lo" is the direct object pronoun meaning "it" or sometimes "that," and "hizo" is the past tense of "hacer." The full phrase usually means "he/she/you did it," with the subject understood from context or stated separately.
target_language_example: Nadie sabe quién lo hizo.
native_language_example: Nobody knows who did it.

additional_notes: Used to strongly insist you’re telling the truth or making a serious promise. The pronoun "lo" refers to what you’re swearing (e.g., "that"), and "por" introduces what you swear by (often someone very important like "mi madre" or "mi vida"). Common patterns: "Lo juro por mi vida" (I swear on my life), "Te lo juro por mi madre" (I swear to you on my mother’s life).
target_language_example: Lo juro por mi vida: yo no fui.
native_language_example: I swear on my life: it wasn’t me.

additional_notes: Used to apologize or express sympathy/bad news. Literally means “I regret it/that,” with lo = “it/that” and lamento = “I regret” (from lamentar). Common in both formal and informal situations. You can intensify it with muchísimo (“so much/very much”) or add the person’s name: “Lo lamento, Jonny.”
target_language_example: Lo lamento, no puedo ir hoy.
native_language_example: I’m sorry, I can’t go today.

additional_notes: Used to say where you read something. "Lo" = "it" (the thing you read), "leí" = "I read" (past tense of leer), and "en" introduces the source (a book, magazine, interview, the internet, etc.). With websites you can also say "en" (en internet) or "en" + site name (en Wikipedia).
target_language_example: Lo leí en el periódico esta mañana.
native_language_example: I read it in the newspaper this morning.

additional_notes: Used to make a promise about something already understood from context. "Lo" refers to “it/that” (what you’re promising), and "prometo" is “I promise.” Often appears as "Te lo prometo" (I promise you) or "Se lo prometo" (I promise you/formal; or I promise him/her/them). Word order is flexible for emphasis: "Lo prometo" / "Se lo prometo."
target_language_example: No voy a volver a llegar tarde; lo prometo.
native_language_example: I’m not going to be late again; I promise.

additional_notes: "Lo" is a pronoun meaning “it/that” (the thing you’re talking about). "Puedo" is from "poder" (to be able to/can). Word order is flexible; you’ll also hear "puedo hacerlo" (same meaning), and with emphasis "sí lo puedo hacer" (“I *can* do it”).
target_language_example: No es fácil, pero lo puedo hacer.
native_language_example: It’s not easy, but I can do it.

additional_notes: used to refer to a thing, idea, or action: “what” / “the thing that.” It often introduces a clause in statements, as in lo que dices = “what you say.” Unlike direct-question qué, lo que is commonly used inside a longer sentence.
target_language_example: No entiendo lo que dices.
native_language_example: I don't understand what you're saying.

meaning: "what I should do" / "what I have to do."
additional_notes: "Lo que" means "what" or "that which." "Debo" is the "I" form of "deber" (to have to / should). Used to talk about the correct or necessary action, often after verbs like "saber" (to know) or "decir" (to tell). You can change the subject: "lo que debes hacer" (what you should do), "lo que tengo que hacer" (what I have to do).
target_language_example: No estoy seguro de lo que debo hacer ahora.
native_language_example: I'm not sure what I should do now.

additional_notes: Used to refer to the content of someone’s words or of a text/document. It can stand alone (Tengo que revisar lo que dice el contrato) or be part of a longer sentence (Eso es lo que dice). Often followed by who/what is speaking: lo que dice Tom / lo que dice el contrato.
target_language_example: No entiendo lo que dice el mensaje.
native_language_example: I don’t understand what the message says.

additional_notes: Uses the relative pronoun phrase “lo que” (“what / that which”) + “dices” (“you say”) to refer to what someone is saying, often in statements like “I believe what you say,” “I can’t hear what you’re saying,” or “That’s what you say.” It can also be used in comparisons (e.g., “what you do is more important than what you say”).
target_language_example: No entiendo lo que dices.
native_language_example: I don’t understand what you’re saying.

additional_notes: Used to refer back to something you said earlier. Built from **lo que** (“what/that which”) + **dije** (past tense of *decir*, “I said”). Often appears after verbs like *lamentar* (to regret), *recordar* (to remember), or *olvidar* (to forget).
target_language_example: Perdón por lo que dije.
native_language_example: Sorry for what I said.

additional_notes: Used to refer back to someone’s words (the content of what they said). "Dijiste" is the tú (you) form of "decir" (to say) in the simple past (pretérito). Often appears after verbs like "pensar en" (to think about), "recordar" (to remember), or "saber" (to know).
target_language_example: No puedo olvidar lo que dijiste ayer.
native_language_example: I can't forget what you said yesterday.

additional_notes: Refers to the content of what someone said. The subject of dijo is often omitted in Spanish, so depending on context it can also mean "what you said" (formal). Built from lo que ("what" / "that which") + dijo ("said").
target_language_example: No entendí lo que dijo el profesor.
native_language_example: I didn't understand what the teacher said.

additional_notes: Uses "lo que" to mean “what/that which” (the thing that was said). Often appears as a noun-like clause: "Lo que ella dijo no tenía sentido" (subject) or after prepositions: "por lo que ella dijo" (“because of what she said”). You can swap the person/tense: "lo que dijiste" (what you said), "lo que él dijo" (what he said).
target_language_example: No entendí lo que ella dijo.
native_language_example: I didn’t understand what she said.

additional_notes: Used to refer to an action in progress in the past. Often appears after verbs like saber (to know), entender (to understand), or ser consciente de (to be aware of). You can change the subject by changing the verb: lo que estaba haciendo (I/he/she was doing), lo que estabas haciendo (you were doing), lo que estaban haciendo (they were doing).
target_language_example: No me di cuenta de lo que estaba haciendo.
native_language_example: I didn’t realize what I was doing.

additional_notes: Used to refer to the situation or events that are happening right now (often something surprising or important). Common after verbs like saber (to know), ver (to see), decir (to tell): “Sabes lo que está pasando” (You know what’s going on). Also appears in phrases like “Vamos a ver lo que está pasando” (Let’s see what’s happening).
target_language_example: No entiendo lo que está pasando, ¿me lo puedes explicar?
native_language_example: I don’t understand what’s going on—can you explain it to me?

additional_notes: "Lo que" means "what / that which" and introduces a clause; here it refers to the action someone is doing. Used to talk about, appreciate, or comment on someone’s actions. You can swap the verb to match the situation (e.g., "lo que estás diciendo" = "what you’re saying").
target_language_example: No entiendo lo que estás haciendo.
native_language_example: I don’t understand what you’re doing.

meaning: "just what we needed" (often said ironically); literally, "what was missing."
additional_notes: Used to react to a new problem or inconvenience, usually with sarcasm or frustration—like saying “great, that’s the last thing we needed.” Often appears after hearing bad news or when something else goes wrong: “¡Lo que faltaba!”
target_language_example: Se nos pinchó una rueda en la autopista… ¡lo que faltaba!
native_language_example: We got a flat tire on the highway… just what we needed!
