target_language_example: Cualquier cosa puede pasar en el mundo de los sueños.
native_language_example: Anything can happen in the world of dreams.

additional_notes: Uses the possessive pronoun suyos with the article los to replace a noun already mentioned. It can refer to things (e.g., books) or people (“his men,” “her family”). The form matches what is possessed (plural, masculine or mixed group): los suyos (plural), las suyas (plural feminine), el suyo / la suya (singular). Which meaning (his/her/their/your formal) depends on context.
target_language_example: Yo llevé mis documentos y ella llevó los suyos.
native_language_example: I brought my documents and she brought hers.

additional_notes: Use the article + day of the week (los + sábado) to talk about a habitual action that happens every week on that day: Los sábados trabajo / descanso. You can add a time: los sábados por la mañana (on Saturday mornings). To be more specific, for a single, specific Saturday you often say este sábado (this Saturday) or el sábado (on Saturday).
target_language_example: Los sábados por la tarde salimos a caminar.
native_language_example: On Saturdays in the afternoon we go out for a walk.

additional_notes: Plural noun phrase (singular: el trabajador / la trabajadora). Often refers to workers as a group, especially in jobs and labor contexts (salaries, working conditions, strikes: estar de huelga). You can also use it for employees in a company: los trabajadores de la empresa.
target_language_example: Los trabajadores de este restaurante tienen un buen horario.
native_language_example: The workers at this restaurant have a good schedule.

additional_notes: Plural definite form of "el tren" (train). Used to talk about trains in general or specific trains already known from context. Often followed by a location phrase with "en" (e.g., "los trenes en Serbia") and can be the subject of sentences like "Los trenes son..." or "Los trenes van...".
target_language_example: Los trenes aquí llegan tarde con frecuencia.
native_language_example: The trains here often arrive late.

additional_notes: Uses the masculine plural article (los) for a group of three, including mixed-gender groups. Often followed by a noun (los tres vasos = “the three glasses”) or used alone when the noun is understood (por los tres = “for the three of us/them”).
target_language_example: ¿Dónde están los tres libros que compraste?
native_language_example: Where are the three books you bought?

additional_notes:
"Los tuyos" is the masculine plural possessive pronoun for "tú". It replaces a noun that’s understood from context:
- Things: "Mis zapatos... los tuyos" = “my shoes… yours.”
- People (common): "por ti y los tuyos" = “for you and your loved ones/your family.”
It agrees with what’s being replaced: feminine plural = "las tuyas"; singular = "el tuyo / la tuya".
target_language_example: Cuida de ti y de los tuyos.
native_language_example: Take care of yourself and your family/loved ones.

additional_notes: Plural, masculine form of "el vecino". Often refers to people living in the same building, on the same street, or in the surrounding area. You’ll commonly hear it in situations involving shared spaces (e.g., the main door/entrance) or when neighbors complain/call authorities.
target_language_example: Los vecinos hacen mucho ruido por la noche.
native_language_example: The neighbors make a lot of noise at night.

additional_notes: Plural noun phrase. Often used with verbs like ponerse (to put on), quitarse/sacarse (to take off), and with parts like los cordones de los zapatos (shoelaces). In Spanish, clothing items are commonly talked about with the definite article (los/las), where English might use a possessive (my/your).
target_language_example: Quítese los zapatos, por favor.
native_language_example: Please take off your shoes.

additional_notes: Plural of "el árbol" (tree). Used with the definite article "los" to talk about specific trees or trees in general (as a group). Common with verbs like cortar (to cut down), subir(se) a (to climb up), and with location phrases like entre los árboles (among/between the trees).
target_language_example: En otoño, las hojas de los árboles cambian de color.
native_language_example: In autumn, the leaves on the trees change color.

additional_notes: Used with a plural noun (often omitted) to refer to the final ones in a sequence or the most recent period: los últimos años/meses/momentos. Can also contrast with los primeros ('the first ones'). Often followed by a time expression like tres meses, dos semanas, etc.
target_language_example: He estado muy ocupado los últimos días.
native_language_example: I've been very busy the last few days.

meaning: "those from" / "the ones of" (refers to a specific group or set).
additional_notes: Used to talk about "the people/things that belong to" or are "from" a place, group, category, or situation. It often avoids repeating a noun: "Los de la limpieza" = "the cleaning staff"; "los de arriba" = "the ones upstairs"; "idénticos a los de otros" = "identical to other people’s (symptoms)". The feminine form is "las de"; singular is "el/la de".
target_language_example: ¿Ya llegaron los de mantenimiento?
native_language_example: Have the maintenance guys arrived yet?

meaning: “those who” / “the ones who” (plural, masculine or mixed group).
additional_notes: Used to refer to a group of people defined by a relative clause (what comes after que). It often appears at the start of a sentence (“Los que…”) or after a verb as the subject (“…los que…”). For an all-female group, use “las que”. In Spanish you can’t usually drop this the way English sometimes drops “those who” (e.g., Spanish needs “Los que entiendan…”).
target_language_example: Los que tengan preguntas pueden quedarse al final.
native_language_example: Those who have questions can stay at the end.

additional_notes: Uses the present perfect (haber + past participle): "he visto" = "I have seen." "Los" is a direct object pronoun meaning "them" (usually masculine plural, or a mixed group). In Spanish, object pronouns like "los" go before the conjugated verb ("he"). You can also attach the pronoun to an infinitive: "Voy a verlos" ("I’m going to see them").
target_language_example: No te preocupes: los he visto hoy por la mañana.
native_language_example: Don’t worry: I’ve seen them this morning.

additional_notes: “Los” is an object pronoun meaning “them” or “you (plural, formal in Spain; in Latin America it can refer to people you address as ustedes).” “Veo” means “I see.” Depending on context, it can mean (1) literally seeing people/things (“Los veo abajo.” = “I see them downstairs.”) or (2) a goodbye meaning “See you (all) …” (“Los veo mañana.” = “I’ll see you tomorrow.”).
target_language_example: Los veo el lunes.
native_language_example: I’ll see you on Monday.

meaning: to fight against; to struggle against.
additional_notes: Used for fighting an enemy/opponent (literal) or resisting something abstract like bad luck, illness, temptation, etc. It’s followed by a noun/pronoun: luchar contra el mago (fight the wizard), luchar contra ello (fight against it).
target_language_example: Tenemos que luchar contra el miedo.
native_language_example: We have to fight against fear.

additional_notes: Used to indicate that one event happens after another, or that something happens after a period of time. It’s common in more formal or written Spanish; in everyday speech you’ll often hear “después de” with the same meaning. It’s followed by a noun/pronoun (“luego de unos minutos”) or an infinitive (“luego de dar a luz”).
target_language_example: Luego de la reunión, vamos a tomar un café.
native_language_example: After the meeting, we’re going to have a coffee.

additional_notes: Used mainly in Latin America as a conjunction meaning “after” or “once/as soon as.” It’s similar to "después de que" or "en cuanto". It usually introduces an action that happens first: "Luego que termine, ..." (= After/Once I finish, ...).
target_language_example: Luego que termine el trabajo, te llamo.
native_language_example: After I finish the work, I’ll call you.

additional_notes: Used to refer to where someone works (an office, store, factory, etc.). Often appears with possessives: mi/tu/su lugar de trabajo (“my/your/his/her workplace”), and in set phrases like en el lugar de trabajo (“at the workplace”).
target_language_example: No se permite fumar en el lugar de trabajo.
native_language_example: Smoking is not allowed in the workplace.

meaning: “place where” (a place in which something happens or someone does something).
additional_notes: Used to introduce a description of what happens in that place (often followed by a verb in the infinitive or a conjugated verb): “un lugar donde sentarme” = “a place where I can sit / to sit.” It works like “donde” = “where” after “lugar” (place).
target_language_example: Busco un lugar donde estudiar en paz.
native_language_example: I’m looking for a place where I can study in peace.

additional_notes: Used to say there is (or isn’t) space, opportunity, or suitability for something: "hay/no hay lugar para + noun/infinitive". It can be literal (a physical place) or figurative (no room for excuses, miracles, etc.).
target_language_example: En esta casa no hay lugar para discusiones.
native_language_example: In this house, there’s no room for arguments.

additional_notes: Refers to the trip or period right after a wedding when a couple celebrates (often by traveling). Usually used with possessives like "mi/tu/su luna de miel" or with "de" (e.g., "viaje de luna de miel").
target_language_example: Vamos a pasar nuestra luna de miel en México.
native_language_example: We’re going to spend our honeymoon in Mexico.

additional_notes: Refers to the moon when its whole face appears illuminated. Common with the verb haber (Hay luna llena = “There’s a full moon”) or with estar/ser to describe conditions (La luna llena está brillando = “The full moon is shining”). You can also use it for upcoming dates/events: la próxima luna llena (“the next full moon”).
target_language_example: Con luna llena, la playa se ve increíble por la noche.
native_language_example: With a full moon, the beach looks incredible at night.

additional_notes: Used to talk about light that comes from the sun (often through windows), especially when discussing rooms, photography, painting, or spaces that feel bright. Common with verbs like "entrar" (to come in), "dejar pasar" (to let in), and "apenas" (barely) to describe how much daylight a place gets.
target_language_example: Esta habitación tiene mucha luz natural por la mañana.
native_language_example: This room has a lot of natural light in the morning.

meaning: “green light”; permission/approval to start or continue.
additional_notes: Literal meaning is the green traffic light. Figuratively, it means authorization or go-ahead (often used with “dar luz verde (a algo/a alguien)” = “to give the green light (to something/someone)”). You can also say “tener luz verde” = “to have the green light.”
target_language_example: El proyecto ya tiene luz verde, podemos empezar hoy.
native_language_example: The project already has the green light; we can start today.

meaning: '(it’s) bad that…' / 'too bad that…' / 'it’s a shame that…'.
additional_notes: Used with **que** to introduce a clause you’re judging negatively. Common patterns: **Qué mal que + verb** = “How bad that…” / “It’s a shame that…”, **No está mal que + subjunctive** = “It’s not bad that…”, **No vendría mal que + subjunctive** = “It wouldn’t be a bad idea if…” / “It wouldn’t hurt if…”.
target_language_example: Qué mal que no puedas venir hoy.
native_language_example: It’s a shame you can’t come today.

additional_notes: Used with the verb "estar" to describe someone’s mood: "Estoy de mal humor" (I’m in a bad mood). You can also say "tener mal humor" (to be in a bad mood / to be irritable).
target_language_example: Hoy estoy de mal humor, mejor hablamos mañana.
native_language_example: I’m in a bad mood today; we’d better talk tomorrow.

additional_notes: Most commonly refers to bad weather (rain, storms, etc.), often used with por: "por el mal tiempo" (because of the bad weather). In some contexts it can also mean a difficult period in life ("atravesar por un mal tiempo" = to go through a hard time). With hacer: "hace mal tiempo" / "sigue haciendo mal tiempo" = the weather is still bad. With tener: "tuvimos mal tiempo" = we had bad weather (lately).
target_language_example: No podemos ir a la playa porque hace mal tiempo.
native_language_example: We can’t go to the beach because the weather is bad.

additional_notes: Used to talk about how others see a person or thing. Common patterns: "tener mala fama" (to have a bad reputation) and "dar (mala) fama a alguien/algo" / "darle mala fama a..." (to give someone/something a bad reputation; to make them look bad).
target_language_example: Ese restaurante tiene mala fama, pero a mí me gusta.
native_language_example: That restaurant has a bad reputation, but I like it.

meaning: a bad kid; a troublemaker (“bad seed”).
additional_notes: Used to describe someone (often a child/teen) who behaves badly, causes problems, or is considered delinquent. It’s a negative, judgmental label. Literally means “bad weed,” but the idiomatic meaning is closer to “bad seed.”
target_language_example: No te juntes con esos chicos; dicen que son mala hierba.
native_language_example: Don’t hang out with those guys; people say they’re troublemakers.

additional_notes: Common in Spain. Often used with estar/tener: estar de mala leche = to be in a bad mood; tener mala leche = to have a nasty/mean streak or bad temper. Strongly negative and fairly colloquial; tone can be harsh depending on context.
target_language_example: No le hables ahora; está de mala leche.
native_language_example: Don’t talk to him now; he’s in a bad mood.

additional_notes: Used to talk about unlucky events (often with "tener": "tener mala suerte" = to have bad luck). It can also be a dismissive response meaning “too bad” or “tough luck.”
target_language_example: Hoy tengo mala suerte: perdí mis llaves otra vez.
native_language_example: I have bad luck today: I lost my keys again.

additional_notes: Used to introduce or describe unpleasant information. Often said as a short announcement (“Malas noticias...”) before explaining what happened, or in the common pattern “Tengo malas noticias para ti” (“I have bad news for you”).
target_language_example: Tengo malas noticias: el vuelo está cancelado.
native_language_example: I have bad news: the flight is canceled.

additional_notes: A strong curse used to show anger, impatience, or frustration. It can stand alone ("¡Maldita sea!") or be added for emphasis in a sentence ("Lo tengo, maldita sea"). It’s also commonly said before a person’s name ("Maldita sea, Nick") when scolding or snapping at someone. Considered rude/vulgar in many situations—use with caution.
target_language_example: ¡Maldita sea! Se me olvidaron las llaves otra vez.
native_language_example: Damn it! I forgot my keys again.

additional_notes: Used to talk about how something is done or someone’s style/habit (often followed by an infinitive: "manera de explicar", "manera de pensar"). In the pattern "no es manera de + infinitive", it means “that’s no way to…” / “you shouldn’t (do/speak) like that.”
target_language_example: No es manera de responderle al profesor.
native_language_example: That’s no way to answer the teacher.

additional_notes: Most literally it means the right hand (often used for directions or instructions: “gira a mano derecha” = “turn right”). In the figurative sense, “ser mi mano derecha” means to be someone’s most trusted helper (their “right-hand man/person”).
target_language_example: Gira a mano derecha en la próxima esquina.
native_language_example: Turn right at the next corner.

additional_notes: Used to specify the hand on the left side of your body (opposite of "mano derecha"). Often appears with possessives ("mi/tu/su mano izquierda") and with verbs like "agarrar" (to grab/hold), "atrapar" (to catch), "mostrar" (to show), and "girar" (to turn).
target_language_example: Sostén el vaso con la mano izquierda, por favor.
native_language_example: Hold the glass with your left hand, please.

additional_notes: Common expression used to start working on something right away. Often said after agreeing on a plan (like “OK, let’s begin”). Literally “hands to the work,” but it’s used like an idiom in English.
target_language_example: Ya tenemos todo listo; manos a la obra.
native_language_example: We have everything ready; let’s get to work.

meaning: to stay calm; to keep calm.
additional_notes: Common advice or instruction in stressful situations. Uses the verb "mantener" (to keep/maintain) + "la calma" (calm). Often said with "tenés que" (vos, common in Argentina/Uruguay) or "tienes que" (tú) to mean "you have to". Also appears with "Pase lo que pase" = "no matter what happens."
target_language_example: Respirá hondo y tratá de mantener la calma.
native_language_example: Take a deep breath and try to stay calm.

meaning: to stand firm; to hold your ground.
additional_notes: Used when someone doesn’t change their opinion/decision or doesn’t give in under pressure. Often followed by "en" + noun (e.g., "mantenerse firme en su decisión").
target_language_example: Aunque lo criticaron, decidió mantenerse firme en su decisión.
native_language_example: Even though they criticized him, he decided to stand firm in his decision.

meaning: "rotten apple"; (figuratively) a bad influence/person who corrupts others.
additional_notes: Literally refers to a piece of fruit that has gone bad. It’s also used in the common saying "Una manzana podrida (lo) echa a perder todo" to mean that one bad person or element can spoil a whole group. Adjective agreement: manzana (feminine) → podrida.
target_language_example: En ese equipo, una manzana podrida estaba arruinando el ambiente.
native_language_example: On that team, a rotten apple was ruining the atmosphere.

meaning: reverse; go backward; no turning back.
additional_notes: Used with the verb "dar": "dar marcha atrás" = to reverse/back up (a car) or to backtrack on a decision/plan. "No hay marcha atrás" means there’s no going back (it’s final).
target_language_example: Si no te gusta el plan, todavía podemos dar marcha atrás.
native_language_example: If you don’t like the plan, we can still back out.

additional_notes: Used with the verb haber to form the present perfect or past perfect: "he matado a..." = "I have killed..."; "hubiera/hubieran matado a..." = "would have killed...". The "a" is the personal "a" used before a direct object that is a person (or personified being): "He matado a Qiang". With "nadie" you also commonly see: "No he matado a nadie" = "I haven't killed anyone."
target_language_example: No he matado a nadie.
native_language_example: I haven't killed anyone.

additional_notes: Used with the personal a before a specific person or animal that receives the action: matar a alguien, matar a un pájaro. The a is part of the grammar, not part of the English translation.
target_language_example: No quiero matar al mosquito.
native_language_example: I don't want to kill the mosquito.

meaning: to kill time; to pass the time (while waiting).
additional_notes: Used when you do something just to stay busy until something else happens (often while waiting). Common with verbs like "estar" or "para": "Estoy matando el tiempo" / "Para matar el tiempo...". It’s a fixed expression; you’re not literally killing anything.
target_language_example: Para matar el tiempo, voy a leer un poco mientras espero.
native_language_example: To kill time, I’m going to read a little while I wait.

additional_notes: Preterite (simple past) of "matar" for "ellos/ellas/ustedes"; the subject is often omitted in Spanish. The "a" is the personal "a" used before a specific person (and sometimes a specific animal) who is the direct object: "Mataron a André" = "They killed André."
target_language_example: Dicen que mataron a un hombre en el pueblo.
native_language_example: They say they killed a man in the town.

additional_notes: *Mató* is the simple past (preterite) form meaning “(he/she/it) killed.” Spanish uses the **personal a** (*a*) before a **direct object that is a specific person** (and often a pet): *mató a Bill*, *mató a su marido*. With things, you usually don’t use *a*: *Mató el insecto* (“He killed the insect.”).
target_language_example: El ladrón mató a la mujer.
native_language_example: The thief killed the woman.

additional_notes: Fragment: **mató** is the simple past (pretérito) of **matar** (“to kill”). The **a** is the *personal a*, used before a direct object that is a person (or treated as one). **su** means “his/her/your (formal)/their,” so the full meaning depends on context (e.g., *mató a su vecino* = “killed his neighbor”).
target_language_example: El ladrón mató a su vecino.
native_language_example: The thief killed his neighbor.

meaning: "tomorrow in the …" (start of a time expression).
additional_notes: This phrase is incomplete on its own and is normally followed by a time of day: “mañana por la mañana” (tomorrow morning), “mañana por la tarde” (tomorrow afternoon), or “mañana por la noche” (tomorrow night). Use it to say when something will happen tomorrow.
target_language_example: Mañana por la tarde tengo una cita.
native_language_example: Tomorrow afternoon I have an appointment.

additional_notes: Used to specify the morning (por la mañana) of the next day (mañana). Common in plans and appointments (e.g., Nos vemos mañana por la mañana). Often shortened in conversation to just “mañana” if the morning is understood from context.
target_language_example: Tengo una cita con el médico mañana por la mañana.
native_language_example: I have a doctor’s appointment tomorrow morning.

additional_notes: Used to say something will happen tomorrow in the evening/nighttime. Common with plans and future events (e.g., "Te veré mañana por la noche"). You can also say "mañana en la noche" in some regions. Related: "mañana por la mañana" (tomorrow morning), "mañana por la tarde" (tomorrow afternoon).
target_language_example: ¿Puedes llamarme mañana por la noche?
native_language_example: Can you call me tomorrow night?

additional_notes: Used to say something will happen tomorrow during the afternoon (roughly after lunch and before evening). In schedules and appointments, you can also hear/see "mañana en la tarde" in some regions, but "mañana por la tarde" is widely understood.
target_language_example: ¿Puedes llamarme mañana por la tarde?
native_language_example: Can you call me tomorrow afternoon?

additional_notes: Used with the structure: (pronoun) + acabar de (conjugated) + infinitive to talk about the very recent past. The pronoun changes with the person: me acabo de (I), te acabas de (you), se acaba de (he/she/you formal), nos acabamos de (we), se acaban de (they/you all). Example: "Me acabo de casar" = I just got married.
target_language_example: Me acabo de dar cuenta de que dejé las llaves adentro.
native_language_example: I just realized I left the keys inside.

additional_notes: Used with the verb acordarse de (reflexive), so it takes a reflexive pronoun (me/te/se/nos/os/se) and is followed by de + a noun/pronoun or a clause. Common pattern: Me acuerdo de él/ella/usted; Me acuerdo de lo que dijiste.
target_language_example: No me acuerdo de su nombre.
native_language_example: I don’t remember his/her name.

additional_notes: Uses the verb agradar: the thing/person you like is the subject (e.g., "Ella me agrada" = "I like her"). Often sounds a bit more formal or restrained than "me gusta". You can also use it with an infinitive: "Me agrada trabajar aquí" (I like working here).
target_language_example: Me agrada mucho tu idea.
native_language_example: I really like your idea.

additional_notes: Used to express happiness or pleasure about something. Very often followed by an infinitive or a clause with que: me alegra saberlo = 'I'm glad to know that', me alegra que estés bien = 'I'm glad you're well'. Grammatically, alegrar works like gustar: the thing that causes the feeling is the subject, so literally it is closer to 'it makes me happy'.
target_language_example: Me alegra que estés aquí.
native_language_example: I'm glad you're here.

meaning: “I’m very happy (to hear/see/that…)” / “That makes me very happy.”
additional_notes: Used to express strong happiness about something. It literally means “it makes me very glad,” with an implied “it” (the situation). Common patterns: “Me alegra mucho + infinitive” (Me alegra mucho verte = I’m very happy to see you), “Me alegra mucho que + verb” (Me alegra mucho que estés aquí = I’m very happy that you’re here), and “Me alegra mucho por ti” (= I’m very happy for you). You can swap “mucho” for “tanto” (Me alegra tanto) or make it formal with “Nos alegra mucho…” (We’re very happy…).
target_language_example: Me alegra mucho que hayas venido hoy.
native_language_example: I’m very happy you came today.

additional_notes: Used to react positively to news or information. It’s often followed by "eso" (that), "de" + noun (e.g., "de tu éxito"), or "que" + a full clause ("me alegra oír que..."). You can also say "Me alegra oírlo" = "I’m glad to hear it."
target_language_example: Me alegra oír que te sientes mejor.
native_language_example: I’m glad to hear that you’re feeling better.

meaning: “I’m happy/glad that …” (followed by a verb in the subjunctive).
additional_notes: Used to express your feelings about a situation or someone else’s action/state. It’s most commonly followed by the subjunctive: Me alegra que estés aquí. It can also be adjusted for different people: Nos alegra que…, Le alegra que…, etc.
target_language_example: Me alegra que hayas venido hoy.
native_language_example: I’m glad you came today.

additional_notes: Used to express happiness about something. Common patterns: (1) "me alegro de" + infinitive: "Me alegro de verte" (I’m glad to see you). (2) "me alegro de que" + subjunctive: "Me alegro de que hayas venido" (I’m glad you came).
target_language_example: Me alegro de conocerte.
native_language_example: I’m glad to meet you.

additional_notes: Used to express happiness about a situation. It’s followed by a verb in the subjunctive (me alegro de que + subjunctive), because it expresses an emotion/reaction: “Me alegro de que hayas empezado” (I’m glad you started). Often used with present subjunctive for past events with present relevance, and imperfect subjunctive after past contexts: “Me alegré de que vinieran” (I was glad they came).
target_language_example: Me alegro de que estés aquí.
native_language_example: I’m glad you’re here.

meaning: I’m happy to see you / I’m glad to see you.
additional_notes: Common friendly greeting when you meet someone (again). Literally “I rejoice to see you,” but in everyday English it’s “I’m glad/happy to see you.” You can change the pronoun: “me alegro de verlo/la verla” (formal you) or “me alegro de verlos/las verlas” (plural). Often followed by “de nuevo” (again) or used with “yo también” (me too).
target_language_example: ¡Qué bueno verte! Me alegro de verte de nuevo.
native_language_example: It’s great to see you! I’m glad to see you again.

additional_notes: From the verb "amar" (to love): "amas" = "you love" (informal singular "tú"), and "me" = "me". Used to talk about romantic love, often in questions like "¿Me amas?" (Do you love me?). Compare: "te amo" = "I love you," and "me quieres" is often a softer/more common way to say "you love me" in everyday Spanish.
target_language_example: Dime la verdad: ¿me amas?
native_language_example: Tell me the truth: do you love me?

meaning: “I feel like … / I’m in the mood for …” (I’d like …).
additional_notes: Used to express a spontaneous desire, often for food, drinks, or an activity. Structure: "Me apetece" + infinitive (Me apetece beber...) or + noun (Me apetece un café). Verb agrees with what you want: "Me apetece" (singular thing) / "Me apetecen" (plural things).
target_language_example: Me apetece un café ahora.
native_language_example: I feel like a coffee now.

additional_notes: Used to say someone helped you do an action. Structure: [person] + me ayudó a + infinitive (e.g., llevar, hacer, pintar). In speech, English often drops “to”: “He helped me carry…”. You can change the pronoun: te ayudó a (helped you), le ayudó a (helped him/her), nos ayudó a (helped us).
target_language_example: Mi amiga me ayudó a estudiar para el examen.
native_language_example: My friend helped me study for the exam.

additional_notes: Past tense (preterite) of the reflexive verb "casarse" (to get married), used to talk about a completed event. Often followed by "con" + the person ("Me casé con ella/él"), or used with time expressions like "hace ocho años" (eight years ago) or ages ("cuando tenía diecinueve años").
target_language_example: Me casé con mi pareja en 2018.
native_language_example: I got married to my partner in 2018.

additional_notes: Preterite (completed past) of the reflexive verb caerse (to fall). It uses the reflexive pronoun me. Often followed by de/del/de la + place/vehicle to say where you fell from: Me caí de la moto (I fell off the motorcycle).
target_language_example: Me caí de la bicicleta y me lastimé la rodilla.
native_language_example: I fell off the bike and hurt my knee.

additional_notes: Reflexive verb phrase: (yo) me cepillo = “I brush” (for myself). It’s commonly used with time expressions like cada mañana (“every morning”) or después de… (“after…”). You can also say: Me cepillo los dientes con un cepillo de dientes (“…with a toothbrush”).
target_language_example: Antes de dormir, me cepillo los dientes.
native_language_example: Before going to sleep, I brush my teeth.

additional_notes: "Me comí" is the preterite (completed past) of "comerse" (to eat). The "me" is a reflexive pronoun often used to emphasize finishing or consuming something (similar to "ate it all" / "ate it up"), though in everyday Spanish it can also simply mean "I ate". Common pattern: "Me comí + (un/una/unos/unas) + food".
target_language_example: Ayer me comí una pizza entera.
native_language_example: Yesterday I ate a whole pizza.

additional_notes: From the verb **contar** (“to tell”). **Me** = “to me.” Used when someone told you information or a story. Often followed by **que + clause** (“me contó que…” = “told me that…”) or by a noun (“me contó una historia” = “told me a story”).
target_language_example: Mi hermana me contó que mañana no viene.
native_language_example: My sister told me that she’s not coming tomorrow.

meaning: "it was hard for me" / "it cost me" (past).
additional_notes: From the verb "costar" (preterite: costó). It’s used in two very common ways: (1) with an infinitive to talk about difficulty: "Me costó encontrar..." = "It was hard for me to find..."; in the negative, it means it was easy: "No me costó..." = "It wasn’t hard for me...". (2) with a price or amount to talk about cost: "Me costó trescientos dólares" = "It cost me 300 dollars."
target_language_example: Me costó mucho aprender a pronunciar la "rr".
native_language_example: It was really hard for me to learn to pronounce the “rr.”

meaning: "I find it hard" / "it’s difficult for me" (to do something).
additional_notes: From the verb "costar" + an indirect object pronoun. It’s commonly used to say something takes effort or is hard for you: "Me cuesta + infinitive" (Me cuesta hablar...) or "Me cuesta + noun" (Me cuesta trabajo) or "Me cuesta creer + que..." (I have a hard time believing...). You can change the pronoun: "te cuesta" (you find it hard), "le cuesta" (he/she finds it hard), "nos cuesta" (we find it hard).
target_language_example: Me cuesta levantarme temprano los lunes.
native_language_example: I find it hard to get up early on Mondays.

additional_notes: Literally “it gives me pleasure,” used to express happiness about what you hear/see or about meeting someone. Common patterns: “Me da gusto + infinitive” (Me da gusto verte = I’m glad to see you) and “Me da gusto + noun/pronoun” (Me da gusto tu llamada = I’m happy about your call). Often interchangeable with “Me alegra…”.
target_language_example: Me da gusto verte de nuevo.
native_language_example: I’m glad to see you again.

meaning: “I’m happy to see you.” / “It’s nice to see you.”
additional_notes: A common, friendly way to say you’re glad to see someone. Literally “it gives me pleasure to see you.” You can add time words like “de nuevo” or “otra vez” (“again”), or intensifiers like “mucho” (“Me da mucho gusto verte”). You’ll also hear “Me da gusto” by itself when the rest is understood.
target_language_example: Me da gusto verte hoy; ¿cómo has estado?
native_language_example: I’m happy to see you today; how have you been?

meaning: "I don't care" / "it’s all the same to me."
additional_notes: Used to say you have no preference between options or that something doesn’t matter to you. It can be followed by a noun (Me da lo mismo la pizza), or by a clause with "que" or "si" (Me da lo mismo que vengas / Me da lo mismo si vienes). Very similar to "me da igual."
target_language_example: Me da lo mismo si vamos en coche o en bus.
native_language_example: I don’t care whether we go by car or by bus.

additional_notes: Literally “it gives me fear.” Used with a person/thing as the subject: “(Él/Ella/Eso) me da miedo” = “He/She/That scares me.” Also common with an infinitive to say you’re afraid to do something: “Me da miedo + infinitive” (e.g., “Me da miedo caer” = “I’m afraid of falling”).
target_language_example: Me da miedo hablar en público.
native_language_example: I’m afraid to speak in public.

meaning: "they give me" / "they make me feel" (used for reactions like fear, disgust, etc.).
additional_notes: “Me” is an indirect object pronoun meaning “to me.” “Dan” is the 3rd-person plural of “dar” (they give). It’s very common in expressions where something causes a feeling or reaction: “me dan miedo” (they scare me), “me dan asco” (they disgust me), “me dan igual” (I don’t care about them). The verb agrees with the thing causing the feeling: singular “me da…” vs plural “me dan…”.
target_language_example: Las arañas me dan miedo.
native_language_example: Spiders scare me.

meaning: "I feel like..." / "I get the urge to..."
additional_notes: Used to express a sudden desire/urge to do something: **me dan ganas de + infinitive**. It’s commonly used in the pattern **(me/te/le/nos/les) dan ganas de...** (e.g., *te dan ganas de salir* = you feel like going out). Similar to **tener ganas de**, but **dar ganas** often sounds more like an urge that comes over you.
target_language_example: Cuando veo esa película, me dan ganas de llorar.
native_language_example: When I watch that movie, I feel like crying.

additional_notes: From the verb dar (to give): “me” = “to me,” “das” = “you give” (informal singular tú). It can mean literally giving something (Me das eso / Me das un beso) or causing a feeling/reaction (Me das lástima = You make me feel sorry for you; No me das miedo = You don’t scare me; Me das envidia/asco = You make me feel envy/disgust). For formal “you,” use me da (usted).
target_language_example: ¿Me das tu número de teléfono, por favor?
native_language_example: Can you give me your phone number, please?

meaning: “you owe me” (money, something, or a favor).
additional_notes: Used with the verb deber (to owe). Common patterns: “Me debes + noun” (Me debes dinero/una disculpa/un auto) and “Me debes una” = “You owe me one” (a favor). With “nada,” it means “You don’t owe me anything.”
target_language_example: Me debes cincuenta dólares.
native_language_example: You owe me fifty dollars.

additional_notes: From the verb "dejar" (past: "dejó"), with the object pronoun "me" (= me). Common patterns: (1) "dejar + infinitive" = "let/allow me to..." (Me dejó entrar = He let me in). (2) "dejar + adjective/past participle" = "left me" in a state (Me dejó esperando/solo/inconsciente = He left me waiting/alone/unconscious). (3) "dejar + something" can also mean "left me" something in the sense of "gave/left behind" (Me dejó esto / Me dejó algunos bienes).
target_language_example: No me dejó hablar durante la reunión.
native_language_example: He/She didn’t let me speak during the meeting.

additional_notes: Preterite (completed past) of despertarse: “to wake up.” The “me” shows it’s reflexive (you woke yourself up / you woke up). Common with time words (temprano, ayer) and with “y…” to continue the story. Also used with “de…” to describe your mood: “Me desperté de mal humor.”
target_language_example: Me desperté a las siete y salí de casa.
native_language_example: I woke up at seven and left the house.

additional_notes: Past tense (pretérito) of darse cuenta de: "to realize/notice." Often used when something suddenly becomes clear (De repente/De pronto) or when you realize it later (Recién). It’s followed by que + a full clause (verb). You can change the person: "me di cuenta", "te diste cuenta", "se dio cuenta", etc.
target_language_example: Me di cuenta de que había olvidado las llaves en casa.
native_language_example: I realized that I had forgotten my keys at home.

additional_notes: From the verb phrase “darse cuenta (de)”. In more careful/standard Spanish it’s very common to say “me di cuenta de que …” (with “de”), especially before a clause, but in everyday speech many people also say “me di cuenta que …”. It’s used when you suddenly understand or become aware of something.
target_language_example: Me di cuenta que había dejado mi bolso en el tren.
native_language_example: I realized I had left my bag on the train.

additional_notes: “Me” = “to me,” and “dieron” is the simple past (preterite) of **dar** for **ellos/ellas/ustedes** (“they/you all gave”). Spanish often drops the subject, so **me dieron** can mean “they gave me” without saying who. It’s also used in common patterns like **me dieron ganas de + infinitive** (“I felt like / got the urge to …”).
target_language_example: Me dieron una cita para el lunes.
native_language_example: They gave me an appointment for Monday.

meaning: "they told me that" / "I was told that".
additional_notes: Used to report information someone else gave you. Literally: "to me" (me) + "they said/told" (dijeron) + "that" (que). In conversation it often implies you’re repeating what you heard (not necessarily confirming it’s true). You can also change the person: "me dijo que" (one person told me that).
target_language_example: Me dijeron que la reunión empieza a las ocho.
native_language_example: They told me that the meeting starts at eight.

additional_notes: Used when reminding someone of what they said in the past (dijiste = you told [informal tú, preterite]). Follow it with a statement ("…era un ladrón"), or with a verb in the subjunctive after giving instructions/requests ("…que hiciera esto", "…que regresara").
target_language_example: Me dijiste que hoy no venías, ¿recuerdas?
native_language_example: You told me you weren’t coming today, remember?

additional_notes: Used to report what someone said to you. The subject is not included in the phrase, so it can mean 'he/she/you (formal) told me...'. dijo is the preterite of decir. With a statement after que, it usually means 'told me that...'; with the subjunctive, it often means 'told me to...'.
target_language_example: Laura me dijo que llegaría tarde.
native_language_example: Laura told me that she would arrive late.

meaning: “(He/She) told me no”; “(He/She) told me not to …”.
additional_notes: Used when someone refuses a request ("He/She said no") or gives you a negative instruction ("told me not to"). Structure: "me dijo" = "told me" + "que no" + verb (often in the subjunctive): "Me dijo que no nadara" = "He/She told me not to swim."
target_language_example: Le pedí ayuda, pero me dijo que no.
native_language_example: I asked him for help, but he told me no.

additional_notes: Past tense of dar with me: literally 'gave me.' It is used when someone or something gave something to you. In common expressions with feelings or physical reactions, it can also mean 'made me feel...' or 'I got...,' as in me dio sed ('I got thirsty') or me dio asco ('it disgusted me').
target_language_example: El profesor me dio más tiempo para terminar.
native_language_example: The teacher gave me more time to finish.

additional_notes: Past tense of "dar una patada" (to kick). "Me" is the indirect object pronoun (“to me”), and the subject is understood from context (él/ella/eso). Often followed by where: "me dio una patada en la pierna" (in the leg). "En las pelotas / en los huevos" are vulgar ways to say “in the balls/testicles.” You can add intensity: "una patada dura" (a hard kick) or intention: "a propósito" (on purpose).
target_language_example: El niño me dio una patada sin querer.
native_language_example: The kid kicked me by accident.

additional_notes: Uses the preterite tense of "dar" (to give): "diste" = "you gave" (tú). "Me" is an indirect object pronoun meaning "to me" or "me." Common with things you give (un beso, tu teléfono, tu palabra, una alternativa, una contusión). For the formal 'you,' say "me dio" (usted).
target_language_example: Me diste tu palabra, y yo te creí.
native_language_example: You gave me your word, and I believed you.

additional_notes: Used to express that you suddenly notice, understand, or come to a conclusion. It’s the reflexive verb phrase "darse cuenta de" + "que" (for a clause). You can change the person: "me doy cuenta" (I realize), "te das cuenta" (you realize), "se da cuenta" (he/she/you formal realizes), "nos damos cuenta" (we realize), "se dan cuenta" (they/you all realize). Often used when something becomes clear after thinking, observing, or hearing something.
target_language_example: Me doy cuenta de que olvidé mi pasaporte.
native_language_example: I realize that I forgot my passport.

additional_notes: Used to say you feel pain in a specific body part. Pattern: "me duele + singular" (Me duele la cabeza / el estómago) and "me duelen + plural" (Me duelen los ojos). You can add intensity with "mucho", "un poco", etc.
target_language_example: Me duele la espalda desde ayer.
native_language_example: My back has been hurting since yesterday.

additional_notes: Used to say you feel pain in your head. Structure: "me" (to me) + "duele" (hurts, from doler) + "la cabeza" (the head). You can add a reason with "de" (e.g., "de tanto trabajar" = "from working so much") or use it as a request/complaint ("Paren de gritar, me duele la cabeza").
target_language_example: No puedo concentrarme; me duele la cabeza desde esta mañana.
native_language_example: I can’t concentrate; I’ve had a headache since this morning.

meaning: it hurts a lot / I’m in a lot of pain.
additional_notes: Used to say that a body part hurts a lot. Pattern: "Me duele mucho + el/la + [body part]" (e.g., Me duele mucho la cabeza). You can also put the body part first for emphasis: "La cabeza me duele mucho" or "Mi pierna me duele mucho". For more than one thing hurting, Spanish often uses "me duelen" (plural): "Me duelen mucho los pies".
target_language_example: Me duele mucho la muela.
native_language_example: My tooth hurts a lot.

additional_notes: Past tense (pretérito) of enamorarse de (“to fall in love with”). Use it with a person (me enamoré de ella/él/ti) or with a quality/thing (me enamoré de su encanto = “I fell in love with his/her charm”). Other persons: te enamoraste de (you), se enamoró de (he/she/you formal).
target_language_example: Me enamoré de él cuando lo vi por primera vez.
native_language_example: I fell in love with him when I saw him for the first time.

additional_notes: A very common way to say you love something. Literally it works like 'it delights me,' so Spanish uses encanta with a singular thing or an infinitive: Me encanta el té; Me encanta caminar. With plural things, Spanish usually uses me encantan.
target_language_example: Me encanta esta canción.
native_language_example: I love this song.

additional_notes: Used to say you really like something that belongs to the person you’re talking to. Grammatically it works like “(It) enchants/delights me, your …”: the thing you love is the subject (tu vestido/tu acento/tu sombrero), and “me” means “to me.” Often followed by a noun; if the noun is plural, use **Me encantan tus …**.
target_language_example: Me encanta tu camisa.
native_language_example: I love your shirt.

meaning: “I love (them)” / “I’m delighted by (them)” (used with plural nouns).
additional_notes: From the verb "encantar" (“to love/to really like”). "Me" marks who feels it (me), and "encantan" agrees with the thing(s) loved, so it’s used when what you love is plural: "Me encantan las naranjas". With a singular noun, use "me encanta": "Me encanta el café". It’s stronger than "me gustan" (“I like”).
target_language_example: Me encantan tus ideas.
native_language_example: I love your ideas.

meaning: “I’d love to” / “I would really like to.”
additional_notes: A polite, enthusiastic way to say you would like to do something (often in response to an invitation or suggestion). It’s the conditional form of “encantar” (“to love/delight”), so it often implies “I’d be delighted.” Use it with an infinitive (me encantaría ir) or with a noun (me encantaría una pizza).
target_language_example: Me encantaría ir contigo al cine.
native_language_example: I’d love to go to the movies with you.

additional_notes: Used to say you will be responsible for doing something in the future. It’s the future tense of “encargarse de” + the reflexive pronoun “me.” It can be followed by a noun/pronoun (de eso, de este problema) or by “que” + subjunctive to mean you will make sure something happens (Me encargaré de que la conozcas…).
target_language_example: No te preocupes: me encargaré de hablar con el profesor mañana.
native_language_example: Don’t worry: I’ll take care of talking to the teacher tomorrow.

meaning: “I ran into / met up with (someone),” often by chance.
additional_notes: Past tense (preterite) of reflexive "encontrarse con". Used when you unexpectedly meet someone (or happen to see them) in a place. Common pattern: "Me encontré con + person"; you can also add where/when: "Me encontré con Ana en el metro."
target_language_example: Ayer me encontré con mi profesor en el supermercado.
native_language_example: Yesterday I ran into my teacher at the supermarket.

additional_notes: Used in two common ways: (1) without “con”, it means how you are feeling/doing: “Me encuentro bien” = “I feel good / I’m doing well.” (2) with “con + person”, it means meeting up with someone: “Me encuentro con ella” = “I meet up with her / I run into her.” It comes from “encontrarse” (literally “to find oneself”), but it’s usually translated as “to feel” or “to meet (up)”, depending on context.
target_language_example: Hoy me encuentro con Carlos después del trabajo.
native_language_example: Today I’m meeting up with Carlos after work.

additional_notes: “Me” = “to me.” “Enseñó” is the past tense (preterite) of “enseñar.” It’s used for a completed action in the past. It can mean teaching a skill or lesson (often with “a” + infinitive: “me enseñó a hacer…”) or showing something (“me enseñó la cámara”).
target_language_example: Mi abuelo me enseñó a manejar.
native_language_example: My grandpa taught me to drive.

additional_notes: Used to say that someone taught you how to do an action. "Me" = to me, "enseñó" = (he/she) taught (past), and "a" is followed by an infinitive verb (e.g., leer, manejar, usar). You can change "me" to another indirect object pronoun (te/nos/le/les) and "enseñó" to another tense/person (me enseña, me enseñaron, etc.).
target_language_example: Mi mamá me enseñó a cocinar.
native_language_example: My mom taught me to cook.

additional_notes: Used before a gerund (-ando/-iendo) to form the present progressive with reflexive or pronominal verbs: me estoy poniendo, me estoy divirtiendo. Here, me refers to the speaker, but it often is not translated as "myself" in English. You can also often say this with the pronoun attached to the gerund instead: estoy divirtiéndome.
target_language_example: Me estoy preparando para el examen.
native_language_example: I'm getting ready for the exam.

meaning: "it’s driving me crazy" / "it’s making me go crazy."
additional_notes: Used to complain that something is really annoying, stressful, or overwhelming. Literally it’s “(it) is turning me crazy”: *volver(se)* + adjective. Change the pronoun/person as needed: *me/te/le/nos/les está(n) volviendo loco/loca/locos/locas*.
target_language_example: ¡Ese pitido constante me está volviendo loco!
native_language_example: That constant beeping is driving me crazy!

additional_notes: Past tense (preterite) of "irse" = "to leave". It often means you left a place: "Me fui de la fiesta" (I left the party). It can also be used with a destination using "a": "Me fui a tu escuela" (I went to your school). You can add how you left: "Me fui corriendo" (I ran off / I left running).
target_language_example: Cuando terminó la reunión, me fui a casa.
native_language_example: When the meeting ended, I went home.

meaning: "I went to sleep" / "I went to bed."
additional_notes: Common way to say you decided to go to bed (often after finishing something or because it’s late). Literally "I went myself to sleep": *me fui* is the preterite of *irse* (to leave/go away) used like "I went," and *a dormir* means "to sleep." You’ll often hear variations like *me voy a dormir* (I’m going to bed / I’m going to sleep) and *me fui a la cama* (I went to bed).
target_language_example: Me fui a dormir temprano porque estaba muy cansado.
native_language_example: I went to bed early because I was very tired.

additional_notes: Uses the preterite of irse (me fui) to talk about going to bed at a specific moment in the past. Often appears with time words like temprano (early) or after another action: después de…, en cuanto… (as soon as…). Also common: irse a la cama (to go to bed) / ir a la cama (to go to bed, more neutral).
target_language_example: Anoche me fui a la cama a las diez porque estaba muy cansado.
native_language_example: Last night I went to bed at ten because I was very tired.

additional_notes: Used to say you like something. Literally it means "it pleases me," so the thing you like is the grammatical subject. Use me gusta with a singular noun or an infinitive; with plural nouns, Spanish usually uses me gustan.
target_language_example: Me gusta mucho esta canción.
native_language_example: I like this song a lot.

additional_notes: Uses the verb gustar: literally "eating is pleasing to me." The thing you like is the subject (comer + food/activity). You can add what you like to eat after comer: "Me gusta comer pizza." For emphasis, you can add "a mí": "A mí me gusta comer..."
target_language_example: Me gusta comer pasta los domingos.
native_language_example: I like to eat pasta on Sundays.

additional_notes: Used to say you like something that happens in a particular situation or at a particular time. It’s a common pattern: (No) me gusta cuando + verb (present tense). You can also change the person: te gusta cuando… (“you like it when…”), le gusta cuando… (“he/she likes it when…”).
target_language_example: Me gusta cuando me llamas por mi nombre.
native_language_example: I like it when you call me by my name.

additional_notes: Used to say you like the way someone does something or the way something looks/sounds/feels. Structure: Me gusta cómo + verb (present tense): “Me gusta cómo caminas” = “I like how you walk.” You can also use it with something: “Me gusta cómo suena” = “I like how it sounds.”
target_language_example: Me gusta cómo cocinas.
native_language_example: I like how you cook.

additional_notes: Used to say you like a singular masculine noun: me gusta el café, me gusta el libro. Spanish uses gustar differently from English: literally, the thing is pleasing to you. For feminine nouns, use me gusta la; for plural nouns, use me gustan los/las.
target_language_example: Me gusta el café por la mañana.
native_language_example: I like coffee in the morning.

additional_notes: Uses the verb "gustar" (literally, "to be pleasing"). "Me" = to me, and "gusta" stays singular because the thing you like ("la música") is singular. You can add details after it (e.g., "moderna", "especialmente el rock").
target_language_example: Me gusta la música, pero hoy prefiero el silencio.
native_language_example: I like music, but today I prefer silence.

meaning: I like it a lot / I really like it.
additional_notes: Used with the verb gustar to express strong liking. The thing you like is the subject: Me gusta mucho esta fotografía. With plural nouns, use gustan: Me gustan mucho las películas. You can also use it before an infinitive to say you really like doing something: Me gusta mucho estudiar idiomas.
target_language_example: Me gusta mucho este lugar.
native_language_example: I really like this place.

additional_notes: Used with comparisons to say you like one thing more than another. Common patterns: (1) "Me gusta más X que Y" = I like X more than Y. (2) "De + plural group + me gusta más + singular" = Of the group, I like this one the most. (3) "Cada vez me gusta más + (noun/clause)" = I like it more and more / increasingly.
target_language_example: Me gusta más esta película que la otra.
native_language_example: I like this movie more than the other one.

additional_notes: Used to say you like something that belongs to the person you’re talking to. The full pattern is: "Me gusta" + singular noun + "tu" + noun (e.g., "Me gusta tu collar"). With plural nouns, use "Me gustan": "Me gustan tus ideas". Literally it’s closer to "Your ___ pleases me," so the verb agrees with the thing you like (gusta/gustan), not with "me."
target_language_example: Me gusta tu estilo.
native_language_example: I like your style.

additional_notes: From the verb phrase "gustar" (literally "to be pleasing"). "Me" = "to me"; "gustaba" is imperfect past, used for ongoing states in the past, repeated past feelings, or "used to". The thing/person you liked is the grammatical subject: "Me gustaba eso" = "That used to please me" → "I liked that." Often used with emphasis: "A mí me gustaba..." (= "I" as opposed to others).
target_language_example: No me gustaba el café, pero ahora me encanta.
native_language_example: I didn’t use to like coffee, but now I love it.

additional_notes: Uses the verb gustar to express preferences. Literally “girls are pleasing to me.” The thing you like (las chicas) is grammatically the subject, so the verb is plural: gustan. You can add adjectives after chicas (e.g., chicas japonesas) to specify what kind of girls you like.
target_language_example: Me gustan las chicas inteligentes.
native_language_example: I like smart girls.

meaning: "I like" (for plural masculine nouns; also used for mixed-gender groups).
additional_notes: Used with the verb gustar to say you like things. Literally closer to "(they) are pleasing to me." Use it before a plural noun with los (e.g., los pasteles). For plural feminine nouns, use "me gustan las" (e.g., Me gustan las flores). For a singular thing: "me gusta el/la".
target_language_example: Me gustan los libros de misterio.
native_language_example: I like mystery books.

additional_notes: A common, polite way to express desire or preference. It is the conditional form of gustar, so it literally means something like 'it would please me.' It can be followed by a noun (me gustaría un helado) or an infinitive (me gustaría ser más grande).
target_language_example: Me gustaría aprender español.
native_language_example: I'd like to learn Spanish.

meaning: "I would like to be able to" / "I'd like to be able to."
additional_notes: Used to express a wish or desire about having the ability or opportunity to do something. It’s polite and a bit more tentative than "quiero" (I want). Follow it with an infinitive: "me gustaría poder + infinitive" (e.g., "viajar", "comprar", "hablar").
target_language_example: Me gustaría poder ayudarte más.
native_language_example: I'd like to be able to help you more.

meaning: “I would like (it) that…” / “I wish that…” (followed by a verb in the imperfect subjunctive).
additional_notes: Used to express a wish or preference about a situation, often hypothetical or not true right now. It’s commonly followed by the imperfect subjunctive (e.g., estuviera/estuviese, fuera, hubiera/hubiese, tuvieras). Often refers to someone else’s actions or a change in circumstances: “Me gustaría que vinieras” = “I’d like you to come.”
target_language_example: Me gustaría que me ayudaras mañana.
native_language_example: I’d like you to help me tomorrow.

meaning: “I would like to know how (to)… / I’d like to know how (to)…”.
additional_notes: A polite way to ask for instructions or an explanation. Often followed by an infinitive (cómo instalar…, cómo hacer…) or by a full clause (cómo el cuerpo absorbe…). More formal/indirect than “¿Cómo…?” and similar in tone to “Quisiera saber cómo…”.
target_language_example: Me gustaría saber cómo llegar al centro en autobús.
native_language_example: I’d like to know how to get downtown by bus.

meaning: “I’d like to know what…” (polite way to ask for information).
additional_notes: Used to introduce an indirect question with qué (“what”), often to sound softer or more polite than directly asking. After qué, use normal statement word order (e.g., “qué dijo,” not “qué dijo él?”). You can also use it to express curiosity rather than demand an answer.
target_language_example: Me gustaría saber qué hora es.
native_language_example: I’d like to know what time it is.

meaning: "I would like to have" / "I'd like to have."
additional_notes: A polite way to express a wish or desire. It uses the conditional of gustar (gustaría) + infinitive (tener) + the thing you want. Often used for hypothetical wants (e.g., better memory, more time) as well as polite requests or wishes.
target_language_example: Me gustaría tener una semana libre para descansar.
native_language_example: I’d like to have a week off to rest.

additional_notes: Used when speaking to one person (tú). With people, it often suggests romantic interest, though context can make it softer. Literally, the structure is closer to “you are pleasing to me,” which is why Spanish uses me + gustas instead of a direct word-for-word version of English “I like you.”
target_language_example: Me gustas mucho.
native_language_example: I like you a lot.

meaning: I liked it / I liked him/her (in the past).
additional_notes: Past (preterite) form of "gustar" for a specific moment or completed experience. Literally it’s closer to “it pleased me,” so the thing/person you liked is the grammatical subject: "Me gustó la película" (the movie pleased me). You can add emphasis with "mucho": "Me gustó mucho".
target_language_example: Me gustó la comida, pero no me gustó el postre.
native_language_example: I liked the food, but I didn’t like the dessert.

additional_notes: Used with a past participle to form the present perfect when the action affects you: me means "me" or "to me," and ha means "has" with a he/she/it or usted subject. For example: me ha sorprendido = "has surprised me," me ha explicado = "has explained to me."
target_language_example: El profesor me ha enviado un correo.
native_language_example: The teacher has sent me an email.

meaning: "has given me" / "has done to me" (with dar).
additional_notes: "Me ha dado" is the present perfect of dar with the indirect object pronoun me: "(he/she/it) has given me". It often introduces what someone gave you (Me ha dado un libro / una carta), but dar is also used in common set phrases like "me ha dado un susto" ("it gave me a scare") and "me ha dado por + noun/infinitive" meaning you suddenly got into something or started doing it ("Me ha dado por la música" = "I’ve gotten into music").
target_language_example: Mi amiga me ha dado un consejo muy útil.
native_language_example: My friend has given me very useful advice.

additional_notes: Used to report what someone said to you. It’s the verb decir in the present perfect (ha dicho) plus the indirect object pronoun me (to me). After que, Spanish often uses the subjunctive when the person told you to do something: me ha dicho que deje / vaya / lo haga.
target_language_example: Mi jefe me ha dicho que llegue temprano mañana.
native_language_example: My boss has told me to arrive early tomorrow.

additional_notes: From the verb "gustar" in the present perfect: "ha gustado" = "has/have pleased." Spanish often frames likes as something pleasing you: "Me ha gustado" literally means "It has pleased me." Use it to say you liked something (a book, movie, food, etc.), often with "mucho" (a lot). You can add the thing you liked as the subject: "Este libro me ha gustado" (This book, I liked it).
target_language_example: La película me ha gustado mucho.
native_language_example: I liked the movie a lot.

additional_notes: Present perfect of hacer with the indirect object pronoun me (“to me”). Often used for cause/result: (1) me ha hecho + adjective (“has made me [adjective]”), (2) me ha hecho + infinitive (“has made me [do]”), or (3) me ha hecho + noun/role (“has made me [something]”). In exclamations like "¡Mira lo que me ha hecho!", it means “Look what he/she did to me!” (something done to you).
target_language_example: Esa experiencia me ha hecho más fuerte.
native_language_example: That experience has made me stronger.

meaning: "I had" (past perfect), used with a past participle.
additional_notes: This is the imperfect form of haber (había) + the pronoun me. It’s used to form the past perfect: me había + participle (e.g., me había dormido = I had fallen asleep). The pronoun me can be reflexive (about yourself: me había levantado = I had gotten up) or an indirect object with se (se me había caído = it had fallen (on me)/I had dropped it). It describes an action that happened before another moment in the past.
target_language_example: Cuando llegaste, ya me había ido.
native_language_example: When you arrived, I had already left.

additional_notes:
"Me" is an indirect object pronoun meaning “to me.” It’s used with hacer in many common expressions: 
- hacer una visita = to pay a visit (De vez en cuando él me hace una visita.)
- hacer una pregunta = to ask a question (Tom me hace la misma pregunta cada día.)
- hacer ruido = to make noise (Me hace ruido el estómago.)
A related and very common pattern is "se me hace" = “it seems to me / it feels (to me)” (Esto se me hace familiar.)
target_language_example: Mi jefe me hace muchas preguntas en la reunión.
native_language_example: My boss asks me a lot of questions in the meeting.

additional_notes: Used to say that something or someone causes an emotion or physical feeling in you. It comes from "hacer sentir" (to make someone feel). The subject can be a thing (Esto/La música) or a person (Tom), and you can add an adjective or phrase after it: "bien", "incómodo", "viejo", "como en casa", etc.
target_language_example: Esa canción me hace sentir feliz.
native_language_example: That song makes me feel happy.

meaning: 'they have (done to me)' / 'I have been …' (with a past participle).
additional_notes: "Me" is an object pronoun meaning "to me" or "me." "Han" is the "they/you all" form of "haber" used to make the present perfect: han + past participle (ofrecido, atacado, insultado, mantenido). It’s used when someone (often an unspecified "they") has done something to you: "Me han insultado" = "They’ve insulted me" / "I’ve been insulted."
target_language_example: Me han llamado esta mañana, pero no pude contestar.
native_language_example: They called me this morning, but I couldn’t answer.

meaning: I've been told that / they told me that.
additional_notes: Used to report information you heard from other people. It’s the present perfect of "decir" (han dicho = "have said/told"), with "me" = "to me". Often implies the source isn’t important or you don’t want to name who said it. Similar: "Me dijeron que" (they told me; simple past).
target_language_example: Me han dicho que mañana va a llover.
native_language_example: I've been told that it's going to rain tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used with a past participle to talk about something you have done to the speaker: me has ayudado (you’ve helped me), me has confundido (you’ve confused me). Word order: object pronoun + has + participle. In questions: ¿me has llamado? = have you called me?
target_language_example: Me has ayudado mucho hoy.
native_language_example: You’ve helped me a lot today.

meaning: “I hurt myself in/on (a body part)” / “I injured my (body part).”
additional_notes: Used with a body part to say you got hurt there: “Me hice daño en el pie” = “I hurt my foot.” Common with en + el/la + body part. In the past tense (hice), it refers to a specific moment when the injury happened; the infinitive is “hacerse daño (en) …”.
target_language_example: Me hice daño en la rodilla jugando al fútbol.
native_language_example: I hurt my knee playing soccer.

additional_notes: "me hizo" is the preterite form of hacer with me, so it usually means "made me" or "caused me to" + verb: Ella me hizo esperar = "She made me wait." With some nouns, it can also mean "did me" or "gave me," as in me hizo un cumplido = "he paid me a compliment."
target_language_example: La profesora me hizo repetir la frase.
native_language_example: The teacher made me repeat the sentence.

meaning: "I would have liked (to)…" / "I wish I had…" (past regret).
additional_notes: Used to express that something did not happen, and you regret it or would have preferred it in the past. Often followed by an infinitive (me hubiera gustado ir, verlo) or by "que" + past subjunctive (me hubiera gustado que vinieras). It’s a common, polite way to talk about missed opportunities.
target_language_example: Me hubiera gustado llamarte antes, pero no tuve tiempo.
native_language_example: I would have liked to call you earlier, but I didn’t have time.

meaning: "I was going to" / "I was about to" (followed by an infinitive).
additional_notes: Uses the imperfect of ir (iba) + a + infinitive to talk about an intention, plan, or something that was expected to happen in the past (often "future in the past"). Common pattern: me iba a + infinitive (I was going to...), te ibas a (you were going to...), se iba a (he/she was going to...), etc. It can also mean "was about to" when something almost happened but didn’t.
target_language_example: Me iba a llamar, pero se le olvidó.
native_language_example: He was going to call me, but he forgot.

additional_notes: Used to make an assumption or inference without sounding too direct—similar to “I suppose…” or “I take it…”. Often followed by a full clause (me imagino que + verb), and it can also stand alone as a short reply: “Me imagino que sí” = “I guess so.”
target_language_example: Me imagino que mañana va a llover, así que llevo paraguas.
native_language_example: I’m guessing it’s going to rain tomorrow, so I’m bringing an umbrella.

additional_notes: From the verb *impedir* (to prevent/stop). *Me* is an indirect object pronoun meaning “to me / for me,” so *me impidió + infinitive* is used to say something prevented you from doing an action: *La nieve me impidió salir* (“The snow prevented me from leaving”). Also common: *impedir que + subjunctive* (e.g., *Me impidió que saliera*).
target_language_example: El tráfico me impidió llegar a tiempo.
native_language_example: Traffic prevented me from arriving on time.

additional_notes: Used with the verb **importar** to say something matters to you or you care about it: **me importa** = “I care / it matters to me.” You often add **lo que…** to mean “what…”: **Me importa lo que pienses** (“I care what you think”). **Sí me importa** emphasizes the feeling (“I do care”). With strong slang like **me importa una mierda**, it means “I don’t give a damn” (very rude).
target_language_example: Me importa mucho tu opinión.
native_language_example: I really care about your opinion.

additional_notes: Used to say something interests you or matters to you. Literally means "it interests me" (from interesar). The thing you’re interested in is usually the subject: "Me interesa la música" = "Music interests me" (not "I interest music"). You can add intensity: "me interesa mucho" (I’m very interested), or negate it: "no me interesa" (I’m not interested / I don’t care). You can also use it with a clause: "Me interesa cómo..." (I’m interested in how...).
target_language_example: No me interesa ese plan, pero me interesa la idea.
native_language_example: I’m not interested in that plan, but I’m interested in the idea.

additional_notes: Future tense of the verb "irse" (to leave/go away): "yo me iré". Often used with "de" + place ("me iré de aquí" = I’ll leave here) or with "a" + infinitive for going to do something ("me iré a dormir" = I’ll go to sleep).
target_language_example: Si no cambia nada, me iré mañana.
native_language_example: If nothing changes, I’ll leave tomorrow.

additional_notes: This is a very common pronoun combo: **me** (to/for me) + **la** (it / her / the feminine thing). It goes **before** a conjugated verb: *me la das* (you give it to me). With an infinitive or -ando/-iendo form, it can go before or attach to the end: *me la quieres dar* / *quieres dármela*; *me la estás enseñando* / *estás enseñándomela*. **La** usually replaces a feminine noun (e.g., *la foto, la llave*) or “her.”
target_language_example: ¿Me la puedes pasar, por favor?
native_language_example: Can you pass it to me, please?

meaning: “I brush my teeth” / “I wash my teeth.”
additional_notes: A common reflexive phrase with **lavarse** (“to wash oneself”). **Me** = “myself” and **los dientes** = “(my) teeth” (Spanish often uses **the** instead of “my” with body parts). Often used with time expressions like **cada mañana** (every morning) or **todos los días** (every day).
target_language_example: Después de cenar, me lavo los dientes.
native_language_example: After dinner, I brush my teeth.

additional_notes: From the reflexive verb "levantarse" (to get up). It’s the present tense for "yo": "me levanto" = I get up / I wake up and get out of bed. Often used with time expressions like "temprano" (early), "tarde" (late), and "pronto" (soon/early). In the idiom "me levanto con el pie izquierdo", it means you start the day in a bad mood or with bad luck.
target_language_example: Me levanto a las siete todos los días.
native_language_example: I get up at seven every day.

additional_notes: Preterite of the reflexive verb "levantarse" (to get up). Commonly used for getting out of bed: "Me levanté temprano." In some expressions it can also be part of a different meaning, e.g., "me levanté el ánimo" = "I cheered myself up" (literally 'I lifted my spirits').
target_language_example: Hoy me levanté a las seis.
native_language_example: Today I got up at six.

meaning: 'they call me' / 'my name is (as people call me)'.
additional_notes: Literally means “they call me.” Use it to say what people call you (a name/nickname/label): "Me llaman X." It can also appear as "si me llaman" meaning “if they call me (on the phone or to get my attention).”
target_language_example: En el trabajo me llaman Ana.
native_language_example: At work they call me Ana.

additional_notes: Common way to say your name: me llamo Ana = 'my name is Ana.' It comes from the reflexive verb llamarse ('to be called,' literally 'to call oneself'), so it can also appear in phrases like cómo me llamo ('what my name is').
target_language_example: Hola, me llamo Ana y soy de Texas.
native_language_example: Hi, my name is Ana and I'm from Texas.

meaning: 'he/she called me' (by phone) or 'he/she called me [something]' (named/insulted me).
additional_notes: Past tense (preterite) of llamar. "Me" is an indirect object pronoun meaning "to me"/"me." It’s used both for phone calls (Me llamó anoche. = He/She called me last night.) and for what someone called you (Me llamó cobarde. = He/She called me a coward.).
target_language_example: Me llamó para preguntarme si estaba bien.
native_language_example: He/She called me to ask if I was okay.

additional_notes: From the verb “llevar” (to take/bring/carry). “Me llevó a…” often means someone took you somewhere: “me llevó al cine” = “he took me to the movies.” With time expressions, “me llevó + amount of time + infinitive” means “it took me…”: “me llevó cinco minutos resolverlo” = “it took me five minutes to solve it.” It can also mean “carried me” in the sense of physically carrying/transporting you (e.g., “me llevó en hombros”).
target_language_example: Me llevó dos horas terminar la tarea.
native_language_example: It took me two hours to finish the homework.

additional_notes: A combination of object pronouns: me usually means "to me" or "for me," and lo usually means "it" (or sometimes "him"). In English, the order is usually different: me lo explicó = "explained it to me." It appears before a conjugated verb, or attached to an infinitive/gerund in some structures.
target_language_example: ¿Me lo puedes repetir, por favor?
native_language_example: Can you repeat it to me, please?

additional_notes: Common Spanish pronoun pattern: **me** = “to me”, **lo** = “it” (the thing/information), **dijo** = “told/said” (preterite of *decir*). It usually refers to something already known from context (what “it” is). You can swap the subject (who told you) before or after: *Mi papá me lo dijo* / *Me lo dijo mi papá*.
target_language_example: No sé cómo pasó; mi hermana me lo dijo ayer.
native_language_example: I don’t know how it happened; my sister told me yesterday.

meaning: I got into; I got myself into.
additional_notes: From the verb "meterse (en)", used to talk about entering/starting something (a game, an activity, a situation) or getting involved—often with an unintended negative result ("meterse en problemas" = to get into trouble). It can also mean intruding in someone’s personal affairs: "meterse en la vida de alguien" = to meddle in someone’s life. Past tense, first person singular ("I").
target_language_example: Me metí en un lío por llegar tarde.
native_language_example: I got myself into a mess for arriving late.

additional_notes: Past tense (preterite) of "mirar". "Me" is the object pronoun "me." It’s often followed by an adverb or phrase that describes how they looked at you: "me miró fijamente" (stared at me), "me miró de lado" (looked at me sideways), "me miró y sonrió" (looked at me and smiled).
target_language_example: Cuando dije su nombre, me miró y se quedó callado.
native_language_example: When I said his name, he looked at me and stayed quiet.

additional_notes: From the verb **molestar** (“to bother/annoy”). **Me** is an indirect object pronoun (“to me”), and **molesta** is often used like “it bothers” (present tense, 3rd person singular): *Me molesta el ruido* = “The noise bothers me.” You can also use it with a clause: *Me molesta que…* = “It bothers me that…”. Note: it looks like English **molest**, but in Spanish it usually just means “bother/annoy,” not sexual harassment.
target_language_example: Me molesta que me interrumpas todo el tiempo.
native_language_example: It bothers me that you interrupt me all the time.

meaning: “I can’t wait to…” / “I’m dying to…” (really want to).
additional_notes: Used to express strong desire or excitement to do something (followed by an infinitive: ver, escucharte, hacerlo, ir, volver) or to have something (often with a noun: una bebida helada). It’s common and informal-sounding but not rude; it’s an exaggeration for emphasis.
target_language_example: Me muero por probar esa comida.
native_language_example: I can’t wait to try that food.

additional_notes: Used to strongly reject doing something or accepting/believing something. It’s the verb negarse a (to refuse to) in the first person: me niego a + infinitive (me niego a aceptar, me niego a contestar). It can also be followed by “creer” (me niego a creer...) to mean “I refuse to believe...”.
target_language_example: Me niego a hacerlo sin tu permiso.
native_language_example: I refuse to do it without your permission.

additional_notes: Reflexive construction: "odiar" (to hate) + "me" (myself). "a mí mismo" adds emphasis and can be omitted: "Me odio" = "I hate myself," but "Me odio a mí mismo" sounds more emphatic. Use "mismo" if the speaker is male; "misma" if female: "Me odio a mí misma." "Te odias a ti mismo/a" = "You hate yourself."
target_language_example: A veces me odio a mí mismo, pero intento perdonarme y seguir adelante.
native_language_example: Sometimes I hate myself, but I try to forgive myself and keep going.

additional_notes: Past tense (pretérito) of "olvidarse de". Use it with an infinitive to say you forgot to do something: "Me olvidé de apagar...". Use it with a noun/pronoun to say you forgot about something or left something behind: "Me olvidé de eso" / "Me olvidé de mi bufanda". Often interchangeable with "se me olvidó" in everyday speech.
target_language_example: Me olvidé de enviar el correo.
native_language_example: I forgot to send the email.

meaning: “can you hear me?” / “do you hear me?”
additional_notes: Used to check if someone can hear you (in person or on the phone), or to emphasize a command/statement (“you hear me?”). It’s the present tense of oír: ¿Me oyes? (informal tú). For a more formal version: ¿Me oye?
target_language_example: ¿Me oyes? Estoy en la entrada del edificio.
native_language_example: Can you hear me? I’m at the building entrance.

additional_notes: Used to give your opinion or impression, often with some uncertainty (like “it seems…”). Literally “it seems to me that,” from parecer (“to seem”). It’s common in conversation and can sound a bit softer/more polite than stating something as a fact.
target_language_example: Me parece que hoy va a llover.
native_language_example: I think it’s going to rain today.

additional_notes: Used to give your personal impression or opinion about something in the past. It’s the preterite of “parecer” with an indirect object pronoun: me pareció = it seemed to me. Often followed by an adjective (Me pareció interesante) or by an infinitive (Me pareció oír…).
target_language_example: La película me pareció muy aburrida.
native_language_example: I thought the movie was very boring.

meaning: "it seemed to me that" / "I thought that" (at that moment).
additional_notes: Uses the verb "parecer" in the preterite (pareció), so it often describes a first impression or what you believed at a specific moment in the past. Commonly followed by a clause with "que": "Me pareció que era tarde" (It seemed to me that it was late). In many contexts it’s close to "creí que" (I thought) but can sound a bit more like an impression than a firm belief.
target_language_example: Me pareció que nadie entendía la pregunta.
native_language_example: It seemed to me that nobody understood the question.

meaning: "(he/she) asked me to" (followed by a verb).
additional_notes: Used to report a request someone made to you. After "pedir que", Spanish typically uses the subjunctive (often the imperfect subjunctive in the past): "me pidió que fuera/esperara/pusiera". You can change "me" to other pronouns: "te pidió que" (asked you to), "le pidió que" (asked him/her to), "nos pidió que" (asked us to).
target_language_example: El jefe me pidió que llegara temprano mañana.
