native_language_example: My boss asked me to arrive early tomorrow.

meaning: “(He/She) asked me to (do something) for him/her.”
additional_notes: Used with **pedir** to report a request: **me pidió que + [verb in the imperfect subjunctive]**. **le** is an indirect object pronoun meaning “to/for him/her/you (formal)” depending on context (who benefits or receives the action). Often followed by verbs like *hiciera, enseñara, comprara, trajera, pasara*.
target_language_example: El jefe me pidió que le enviara el informe hoy.
native_language_example: My boss asked me to send him the report today.

meaning: “it makes me” (puts me into a certain mood/feeling).
additional_notes: Used with a thing/situation as the subject: “Eso/Esta canción/No verlos…” + me pone + adjective (contento, nervioso, triste, feliz) to say it causes that emotion. Very common with “me pone nervioso/a” and the fixed phrase “me pone de los nervios” = “it drives me crazy / gets on my nerves.” Agreement: contento/contenta, nervioso/nerviosa, etc.
target_language_example: Los cambios de última hora me ponen nervioso.
native_language_example: Last-minute changes make me nervous.

meaning: “I put on” (clothes) / “I get” (a state or mood) / “I place myself” (in a position).
additional_notes: From the verb ponerse (reflexive). Common patterns: (1) me pongo + adjective to talk about becoming a temporary state: me pongo nervioso/sentimental (“I get nervous/sentimental”); (2) me pongo + clothing item to mean “I put on”: me pongo ropa cómoda (“I put on comfy clothes”); (3) me pongo + de + noun to mean putting yourself in a position: me pongo de rodillas (“I kneel”); (4) me pongo a + infinitive to mean starting to do something: me pongo a estudiar (“I start studying”); (5) me pongo a mí + [adverb/adjective] emphasizes yourself: me pongo a mí primero (“I put myself first”).
target_language_example: Cuando tengo frío, me pongo un suéter.
native_language_example: When I’m cold, I put on a sweater.

meaning: “I was wondering if…” (polite way to ask).
additional_notes: Uses the imperfect of preguntar (preguntaba) to sound less direct and more polite than a simple question. Often used to introduce a request or a sensitive question. You can also hear it in other persons: “Te/Se preguntaba si…”.
target_language_example: Me preguntaba si me podrías ayudar con esto.
native_language_example: I was wondering if you could help me with this.

additional_notes: Used to express curiosity or uncertainty about the way something is/was/will be. It’s often followed by a verb in the future, past, or subjunctive depending on context (e.g., me pregunto cómo será / cómo pasó / cómo les irá).
target_language_example: Me pregunto cómo lo vas a resolver.
native_language_example: I wonder how you’re going to solve it.

additional_notes: Used to introduce an indirect question about a place or location. It’s often followed by a verb in the past/present (e.g., escondió, juega) or by a guess/speculation with future perfect (habrá..., se habrá...). Spanish keeps the question word (dónde) but does not use question marks in indirect questions.
target_language_example: Me pregunto dónde dejé mi teléfono.
native_language_example: I wonder where I left my phone.

additional_notes: Used to express curiosity or confusion about a reason. It introduces an indirect question, so por qué keeps the accent (like in questions). You can change the tense: Me preguntaba por qué… (“I was wondering why…”).
target_language_example: Me pregunto por qué no me llamó ayer.
native_language_example: I wonder why he/she didn’t call me yesterday.

additional_notes: Used to introduce an indirect question about a person’s identity. It’s followed by a verb clause (often in the subjunctive or with future/conditional) and no question marks are needed unless the whole sentence is a direct question.
target_language_example: Me pregunto quién va a venir a la fiesta.
native_language_example: I wonder who is going to come to the party.

additional_notes: Used to express curiosity or uncertainty before an indirect question. It’s formed from "me pregunto" (I ask myself / I wonder) + "qué" (what). Often followed by the subjunctive or future forms to show uncertainty (e.g., "qué habrá pasado", "qué será").
target_language_example: Me pregunto qué vas a decirle.
native_language_example: I wonder what you’re going to tell him/her.

additional_notes: Used to express that you’re unsure and thinking about a question. It’s followed by a clause starting with "si" (= "if/whether"). Often used when politely asking yourself (or indirectly asking someone) about a possibility.
target_language_example: Me pregunto si mañana va a llover.
native_language_example: I wonder if it’s going to rain tomorrow.

meaning: “(He/She) asked me what had …” (an indirect question about the past).
additional_notes: Used to report someone’s question (indirect speech). “Me preguntó” = “he/she asked me.” After “qué” (“what”), “había” is the imperfect of haber and often appears: (1) with a past participle to form the past perfect (pluscuamperfecto): “qué había comprado” = “what (I/you/he) had bought,” “qué había estado haciendo” = “what (I/you/he) had been doing”; (2) in the expression “qué había sido de + person” meaning “what had become of … / what happened to …”.
target_language_example: El detective me preguntó qué había visto esa noche.
native_language_example: The detective asked me what I had seen that night.

additional_notes: Used to introduce an indirect yes/no question. "Me" = "to me" and "preguntó" is the past tense (pretérito) of "preguntar" (to ask). "Si" here means "if/whether" (not "yes").
target_language_example: El profesor me preguntó si entendía la lección.
native_language_example: The teacher asked me if I understood the lesson.

additional_notes: Used with the verb "preocupar" (to worry/concern). The thing that causes the worry is the subject: "Me preocupa eso" = "That worries me." Very common pattern: "Me preocupa que + subjunctive" to express concern about something that may happen: "Me preocupa que vayas..." = "I’m worried that you’ll go..."
target_language_example: Me preocupa que no llegues a tiempo.
native_language_example: I’m worried that you won’t arrive on time.

additional_notes: Used to report a promise someone made to you. "Me" = "to me". "Prometió" is past tense (he/she promised). "Que vendría" uses the conditional tense to mean "would come" (future-in-the-past), often with a time: "a las tres" (at three), "temprano" (early), or a place: "aquí" (here).
target_language_example: Mi jefe me prometió que vendría a la reunión.
native_language_example: My boss promised me that he would come to the meeting.

meaning: “he/she proposed marriage to me” (i.e., proposed to me).
additional_notes: From **proponer matrimonio** = “to propose marriage.” **Me** is an indirect object pronoun meaning “to me.” It’s typically said about a marriage proposal (often with a ring): *Me propuso matrimonio anoche.* You can change the pronoun/person: **te propuso matrimonio** (to you), **le propuso matrimonio** (to him/her), **nos propuso matrimonio** (to us).
target_language_example: Me propuso matrimonio en la playa.
native_language_example: He proposed to me on the beach.

additional_notes: Past tense (preterite) of the verb phrase “ponerse” (yo me puse). Common uses: (1) “me puse + clothing” = “I put on …” (Me puse los zapatos). (2) “me puse + adjective” = “I got/became …” (Me puse enfermo/a, me puse rubio/a). (3) “me puse del lado de …” = “I took (someone’s) side.” The adjective often agrees with the speaker (enfermo/enferma, rubio/rubia).
target_language_example: Cuando empezó a llover, me puse la chaqueta.
native_language_example: When it started to rain, I put on my jacket.

additional_notes:
From the verb **quedar**. Common uses:
- **Clothing fit:** *Este abrigo me queda corto/grande/bien* = “This coat fits me short/big/well.”
- **Time/quantity remaining:** *Me queda poco tiempo / me queda dinero* = “I have little time left / I have money left.”
- With **se me queda...** (like in the example *se me queda la mente en blanco*), it means something “ends up/stays” in a certain state: “my mind goes blank.”
target_language_example: Me queda poco dinero este mes.
native_language_example: I have little money left this month.

additional_notes: Future tense of quedarse (“to stay/remain”). Used to say you’re not leaving and will remain in this place for some time. Often followed by a time expression (un rato, unos días, por un tiempo corto) or by “contigo” (“with you”).
target_language_example: Si tú te vas, yo me quedaré aquí.
native_language_example: If you leave, I’ll stay here.

additional_notes: Future tense of "quedarse con". Most often means choosing to remain in someone’s company ("I’ll stay with him/her"). With objects, it can mean keeping something ("I’ll keep it"). You can change the subject: "me quedaré con" (I), "te quedarás con" (you), "se quedará con" (he/she), etc.
target_language_example: No te preocupes: yo me quedaré con los niños esta noche.
native_language_example: Don’t worry: I’ll stay with the kids tonight.

additional_notes: Uses the verb phrase "quedarse" (to stay/remain) in the simple future: "me quedaré" = "I will stay". You can add time words like "hoy" (today), "mañana" (tomorrow), or "todo el día" (all day).
target_language_example: Estoy cansado, así que me quedaré en casa esta noche.
native_language_example: I’m tired, so I’ll stay at home tonight.

meaning: 'I stay' / 'I'm staying' (also used with an adjective: 'I become / end up').
additional_notes: From the verb quedarse (reflexive). Often means “to stay/remain” somewhere: “Yo también me quedo” = “I’m staying too.” It can also be used with an adjective to describe a change of state, especially common: “me quedo dormido” = “I fall asleep.”
target_language_example: Si quieres, me quedo contigo un rato.
native_language_example: If you want, I’ll stay with you for a while.

additional_notes: From the verb phrase “quedarse con (algo)”. Used when choosing one option from several (“I’ll go with…”) or when deciding to keep something (“I’ll keep it”). Often followed by a noun or option: “Me quedo con este/esa opción.”
target_language_example: De los dos, me quedo con el azul.
native_language_example: Of the two, I’ll take the blue one.

additional_notes: First-person singular preterite of quedarse. It is used to say that you stayed somewhere, remained in a place, or were left in a situation. Depending on context, it can also sound like 'I ended up' or 'I was left.'
target_language_example: Me quedé en casa toda la tarde.
native_language_example: I stayed at home all afternoon.

additional_notes: Used when sleep happens unintentionally or sooner than planned. It’s the preterite (past) form of "quedarse dormido" = "to fall asleep." Change "me" for other people: "te quedaste dormido/a" (you fell asleep), "se quedó dormido/a" (he/she fell asleep). "Dormido" changes to match gender: "dormido" (male), "dormida" (female).
target_language_example: Me quedé dormido en el sofá y no escuché el teléfono.
native_language_example: I fell asleep on the couch and didn’t hear the phone.

additional_notes: Uses the verb quedarse (to stay/remain). Me quedé is the preterite (completed past) form: 'I stayed' (e.g., last night/that day). Often followed by a reason with porque (because), por (due to), or para + infinitive (in order to).
target_language_example: Hoy estaba cansado, así que me quedé en casa.
native_language_example: Today I was tired, so I stayed home.

additional_notes: Used when a person, thing, smell, photo, etc. makes you think of someone or something else. Structure: [X] me recuerda a [Y] = "[X] reminds me of [Y]." You can change the indirect object pronoun: te recuerda a (reminds you of), le recuerda a (reminds him/her of), nos recuerda a (reminds us of).
target_language_example: Esta canción me recuerda a mi infancia.
native_language_example: This song reminds me of my childhood.

additional_notes: Used to compare someone to another person/thing. Structure: **Tú + me recuerdas a + [alguien/algo]**. For other subjects: **me recuerda a** (he/she/it reminds me of), **me recuerdan a** (they remind me of).
target_language_example: Me recuerdas a mi madre.
native_language_example: You remind me of my mother.

additional_notes: Used to clarify what you meant earlier. It’s the imperfect of "referirse a" (to refer to), so it often sounds like “I was referring to…” in English, especially when correcting a misunderstanding: "No, no me refería a usted" (No, I didn’t mean you). Follow it with a noun, person, or time: "me refería a la comida / a ti / a antes".
target_language_example: Perdón, me refería a la reunión de mañana, no a la de hoy.
native_language_example: Sorry, I meant tomorrow’s meeting, not today’s.

additional_notes: Used to clarify what you’re talking about. Often followed by a noun or pronoun (me refiero a eso, me refiero a ahora, me refiero a uno pequeño) or by “que” + a whole idea (me refiero a que… = “I mean that…”). Negative: no me refiero a… = “I don’t mean…” / “I’m not referring to…”.
target_language_example: No, me refiero a mañana, no a hoy.
native_language_example: No, I mean tomorrow, not today.

meaning: “It seems familiar to me” / “It rings a bell.”
additional_notes: Used when something (a name, face, place, idea, etc.) feels familiar but you may not remember exactly from where. The thing that seems familiar is the subject: “Tu nombre me resulta familiar” = “Your name seems familiar to me.” You can change the person: te/le/nos/les resulta familiar (it seems familiar to you/him/her/us/them).
target_language_example: Ese lugar me resulta familiar, pero no recuerdo de dónde.
native_language_example: That place seems familiar to me, but I don’t remember from where.

meaning: “they stole from me” / “I got robbed” (something was stolen from me).
additional_notes: "Me" is the indirect object pronoun (“from me”), and "robaron" is the simple past (preterite) “they stole.” It’s used when someone stole something that belonged to you: "Me robaron el coche" = “They stole my car.” The subject (who stole it) is often unknown or not mentioned. You can also use it for non-physical things like ideas: "Me robaron la idea" = “They stole my idea.”
target_language_example: Me robaron el celular en el metro.
native_language_example: My phone was stolen from me on the subway.

meaning: “(He/She/It) saved my life.” (often: “it was a lifesaver” / “it saved me”).
additional_notes: Literally “(someone/something) saved my life.” Used both for real, life-threatening situations (a person or animal rescues you) and exaggeration for something that helped a lot at the right moment (like coffee, a favor, advice). Verb is in the past (salvó). You can change the indirect object: “te salvó la vida” (saved your life), “nos salvó la vida” (saved our lives), etc.
target_language_example: Gracias por traerme agua; me salvó la vida.
native_language_example: Thanks for bringing me water; you saved my life.

additional_notes: Preterite (completed past) of the reflexive verb "sentarse". Often followed by a place or position: "me senté a su lado" (I sat next to him/her), "me senté entre..." (I sat between...). The "me" is the reflexive pronoun used with "sentarse".
target_language_example: Me senté en la primera fila para ver mejor.
native_language_example: I sat in the front row to see better.

additional_notes: Preterite (simple past) form of **sentirse** (“to feel”). Used with emotions or physical states, often followed by an adjective: **me sentí cansado/a, feliz, mal**. The adjective agrees with the speaker (cansado = male speaker, cansada = female speaker).
target_language_example: Me sentí mal después de la cena.
native_language_example: I felt sick after dinner.

additional_notes: Past (imperfect) form of "sentirse" used to describe how you felt over a period of time, repeatedly, or as background in a story. It’s often followed by an adjective (me sentía solo/enfermo/orgulloso) or by "como" + a phrase (me sentía como en un sueño).
target_language_example: Ayer me sentía muy cansado, pero hoy estoy mejor.
native_language_example: Yesterday I was feeling very tired, but today I’m better.

additional_notes: Used to talk about your emotional or physical state, often followed by an adjective or adverb: me siento feliz, me siento mal. In other contexts, me siento can also mean "I sit down" from sentarse, but with adjectives like in the examples it means "I feel."
target_language_example: Hoy me siento mejor.
native_language_example: I feel better today.

additional_notes: Used to talk about how you feel physically or emotionally. It comes from the verb "sentirse" (to feel, about yourself), and it changes with the subject: "me siento" (I feel), "te sientes" (you feel), "se siente" (he/she/it feels), "nos sentimos" (we feel). For the negative, say "No me siento bien" (I don’t feel well).
target_language_example: Gracias por preguntar; hoy me siento bien.
native_language_example: Thanks for asking; today I feel good.

meaning: "I feel bad for" / "I feel bad about".
additional_notes: Used to express guilt, regret, or sympathy. Use **por + person** for sympathy (Me siento mal por él = I feel bad for him) and **por + (verb in infinitive / haber + past participle / lo que + verb)** for regret about something you did or didn’t do (Me siento mal por haber dicho eso = I feel bad about having said that). Often interchangeable with **me sabe mal** in some regions.
target_language_example: Me siento mal por no haberte llamado antes.
native_language_example: I feel bad about not calling you earlier.

additional_notes: Used to say you’re feeling improved (often health/mood). It comes from the reflexive verb sentirse (“to feel”): me siento = “I feel,” mejor = “better.” You can add time words like ya (“already”), cada día (“every day”), or gracias (“thanks”).
target_language_example: Después de descansar un poco, me siento mejor.
native_language_example: After resting a bit, I feel better.

additional_notes: Used with an adjective to describe your current physical or emotional state. The verb is pronominal: "sentirse" (to feel). You usually complete it with an adjective: "Me siento muy bien/mal/cómodo(a)/cansado(a)". The adjective agrees with the speaker (cómodo/cómoda).
target_language_example: Me siento muy cansado hoy.
native_language_example: I feel very tired today.

meaning: "I feel very well" / "I feel really good."
additional_notes: Used to talk about how you feel physically or emotionally. Often appears with "no": "No me siento muy bien" = "I don’t feel very well" (common way to say you’re not feeling well). You can also add context with "con" + noun/phrase: "Me siento muy bien con esto" = "I feel really good about this."
target_language_example: Hoy me siento muy bien, gracias.
native_language_example: Today I feel very well, thanks.

additional_notes: Used to express that something is unexpected to you. Often followed by **que + verb** (“I’m surprised that…”): *Me sorprende que…*. You can also use it with an infinitive: *Me sorprende verte…* (“I’m surprised to see you…”).
target_language_example: Me sorprende que no me lo hayas dicho antes.
native_language_example: I’m surprised you didn’t tell me earlier.

additional_notes: Uses the indirect object pronoun "me" (= to me). The subject is the thing that caused the surprise: "Me sorprendió su perseverancia" (His/Her perseverance surprised me). You can also use it with a clause: "Me sorprendió que viniera."
target_language_example: Me sorprendió lo rápido que aprendiste español.
native_language_example: I was surprised by how quickly you learned Spanish.

additional_notes: Used to introduce bad news, a refusal, or something disappointing in a polite/softened way. Often followed by a negative ("me temo que no…"). You can also use it alone to answer politely: "Me temo que no."
target_language_example: Me temo que hoy no puedo reunirme contigo.
native_language_example: I'm afraid I can't meet with you today.

meaning: "I'm afraid (that) not..." / "I'm afraid (that)..." (introducing bad news or a correction).
additional_notes: Used to politely (often gently) disagree, correct someone, or deliver disappointing news. It’s more formal and softer than just saying "no". Often followed by a verb ("me temo que no entiendes...") or by "hay" ("me temo que no hay..."). You can also use "Me temo que sí" for "I’m afraid so."
target_language_example: Me temo que no podemos hacerlo hoy.
native_language_example: I'm afraid we can't do it today.

meaning: "I have to go" / "I need to leave."
additional_notes: Used to say you must leave (often because of an obligation or situation). Very common when saying goodbye: "Lo siento, me tengo que ir". You can change the time word: "me tengo que ir pronto/temprano/ahora". In everyday speech, you’ll also hear "me tengo que ir" shortened to "me tengo que ir ya" or "me tengo que ir" with the subject implied (it always means 'I').
target_language_example: Perdón, me tengo que ir ya; hablamos luego.
native_language_example: Sorry, I have to go now; we’ll talk later.

additional_notes:
From the verb **tomar** (to take). Very common patterns:
- **Me tomó + (time)** = “It took me + (time)” (the subject is often an activity: *Escribir el ensayo me tomó dos horas* / *Me tomó dos horas escribir el ensayo*).
- **Me tomó + noun** = “(Someone) took (something) from/on me,” especially in set phrases like **tomar la temperatura** (“take someone’s temperature”).
- **Me tomó en sus brazos** = “He/She took me in his/her arms” (picked me up/held me).
target_language_example: Me tomó tres horas terminar la tarea.
native_language_example: It took me three hours to finish the homework.

additional_notes: Used to say how long an activity took you. The pattern is: "Me tomó + amount of time + (infinitive)". You can add the task as an infinitive (e.g., "lavarlo", "repararlo") or with "para" ("para escribirlo"), though "para" is often optional in everyday Spanish.
target_language_example: Me tomó varias horas terminar el informe.
native_language_example: It took me several hours to finish the report.

additional_notes: Preterite (past) of **traer**. **Me** is an indirect object pronoun meaning “to/for me.” The subject is often omitted in Spanish (e.g., *mi tía* can be understood from context). You’ll often see it with a thing: **Me trajo** + noun (*Me trajo flores* = “She brought me flowers”), or with a destination: **Me trajo a/al** + place (*Me trajo al lago* = “It brought me to the lake,” e.g., a walk or path).
target_language_example: Mi hermano me trajo un café.
native_language_example: My brother brought me a coffee.

meaning: "They’re going to kill me" (often: "I’m going to be in big trouble").
additional_notes: Literally means someone is going to kill you, but very often it’s used exaggeratively to mean you expect a strong reaction (anger, punishment, getting fired, etc.), especially with people like your boss, parents, or partner. The person is the subject: "Mi padre me va a matar" = "My dad is going to kill me." You can change the person: "Te va a matar" (he/she is going to kill you), "Nos van a matar" (they’re going to kill us).
target_language_example: Llegué tarde otra vez; mi jefe me va a matar.
native_language_example: I was late again; my boss is going to kill me.

additional_notes: Uses the near-future construction **ir a + infinitive**: **van a + verb** = “are going to + verb.” **Me** is an object pronoun meaning “me/to me,” showing who the action affects (e.g., *me van a despedir* = “they’re going to fire me”). The subject is usually “they” (explicit or implied), and it changes with the verb **ir**: *me va a* (he/she is going to…), *me vas a* (you are going to…), *me voy a* (I’m going to…).
target_language_example: Me van a llamar mañana.
native_language_example: They’re going to call me tomorrow.

meaning: "you are going to" (do something) to/for me.
additional_notes: This is the near-future structure: "ir (vas) + a + infinitive" with the indirect object pronoun "me". It can be a neutral question ("¿Qué me vas a regalar?") or sound like a strong demand/threat depending on tone ("Me vas a ayudar"). The verb after "a" stays in the infinitive: "me vas a ayudar / dar / llevar / poner".
target_language_example: Me vas a decir la verdad ahora.
native_language_example: You’re going to tell me the truth now.

additional_notes: Past tense (preterite) of "ver" (to see): "vio" = "he/she/it saw." "Me" is the object pronoun "me." Often used in storytelling with "cuando" or "en el momento en que" to mean "when (someone) saw me" and describe what happened next.
target_language_example: Cuando me vio, me saludó.
native_language_example: When he saw me, he said hello.

additional_notes: Used before an infinitive to say what the speaker is going to do. This is the first-person form of ir a + infinitive. The me often belongs to the following verb, especially with reflexive verbs: me voy a morir = voy a morirme. Don't confuse it with me voy by itself, which means 'I'm leaving.'
target_language_example: Me voy a lavar las manos.
native_language_example: I'm going to wash my hands.

meaning: “I’m going to stay” / “I’m going to keep it.”
additional_notes:
From **quedarse** (“to stay/remain”). Often used with:
- **quedarse en + lugar** = “to stay (in/at) + place”: *Me voy a quedar en casa.*
- **quedarse con + cosa** = “to keep + thing” (instead of giving it back or sharing): *Me voy a quedar con esto.*
Literally it’s “I’m going to remain,” but in everyday Spanish it commonly means “I’m going to stay.”
target_language_example: Está lloviendo, así que me voy a quedar aquí.
native_language_example: It’s raining, so I’m going to stay here.

additional_notes: Usually means you are leaving or going away from where you are. It comes from the verb irse, which often means "to leave" rather than just "to go." Beginners often compare it with voy: voy focuses more on going somewhere, while me voy often focuses on departing.
target_language_example: Ya es tarde, me voy a casa.
native_language_example: It's late, I'm going home.

meaning: “I’m going home” / “I’m going to my house.”
additional_notes: Uses irse (“to leave/go away”) in the reflexive: me voy = “I’m leaving / I’m going.” Add destinations with a: me voy a casa (home). You can also specify whose home with de: me voy a casa de mi madre = “I’m going to my mom’s (house).” Often used when you’re leaving a place: “Well, I’m going home.”
target_language_example: Bueno, ya es tarde: me voy a casa.
native_language_example: Well, it’s late: I’m going home.

meaning: "I'm leaving here" / "I'm getting out of here."
additional_notes: Used to say you are leaving your current place. It uses the verb "irse" (to leave/go away): "me voy" = "I’m leaving". "de aquí" means "from here." Often used with time words for emphasis: "ahora mismo" (right now), "ya" (already/now). In the negative it means you refuse to leave: "No me voy de aquí" = "I’m not leaving here."
target_language_example: Si siguen gritando, me voy de aquí.
native_language_example: If you keep yelling, I'm getting out of here.

additional_notes: Used for the first-place award in competitions (sports, contests, Olympics). Often appears with verbs like ganar (to win), conseguir (to obtain), or obtener (to get).
target_language_example: Ella ganó la medalla de oro en natación.
native_language_example: She won the gold medal in swimming.

additional_notes: Often used with the verb "dar": "dar media vuelta" = to turn around and go back. It can describe a physical half-turn (180°) or changing direction to return the way you came.
target_language_example: Cuando escuché mi nombre, di media vuelta.
native_language_example: When I heard my name, I turned around.

additional_notes: Used to talk about a duration of 30 minutes (e.g., waiting, walking time) or a time difference: "media hora temprano/tarde" = "half an hour early/late." Often appears without "una": "espera media hora".
target_language_example: La reunión empieza en media hora.
native_language_example: The meeting starts in half an hour.

additional_notes: Used to talk about a duration or waiting time: “Dame media hora” (give me half an hour). With “hace (más de) …” it means “(more than) … ago”: “hace más de media hora” = “more than half an hour ago.” You can also soften it with “como” to mean “about/roughly”: “como media hora.”
target_language_example: Espérame media hora, por favor.
native_language_example: Wait for me for half an hour, please.

additional_notes: Used to talk about actions, rules, or equipment meant to prevent danger, accidents, or crime (e.g., in a building, workplace, event, airport, or online). Often used with verbs like tomar/implementar/reforzar (take/implement/strengthen) and revisar/verificar (review/check).
target_language_example: El hotel tiene medidas de seguridad muy estrictas.
native_language_example: The hotel has very strict security measures.

additional_notes: Most commonly means “part-time” when talking about jobs (trabajar a medio tiempo, un trabajo de medio tiempo). It can also mean “halftime” or the “half-time break” in sports contexts (el medio tiempo). In some contexts it can mean a “half-length” interval, like a mid-point segment (e.g., a planned half-time speech/show).
target_language_example: Estoy buscando un trabajo a medio tiempo mientras estudio.
native_language_example: I’m looking for a part-time job while I study.

additional_notes: Common in news, school, and policy contexts to talk about nature and environmental protection (e.g., contaminación del medio ambiente, proteger/cuidar el medio ambiente). Often used with the article: el medio ambiente.
target_language_example: Tenemos que cuidar el medio ambiente.
native_language_example: We have to take care of the environment.

meaning: the middle of the (with a feminine noun).
additional_notes: By itself, this chunk is most commonly seen inside larger phrases like **en medio de la...** (“in the middle of the...”) or **por medio de la...** (“by means of the.../through the...”). **La** is used because the following noun is feminine (e.g., *la calle, la reunión*).
target_language_example: Estaba en medio de la calle cuando empezó a llover.
native_language_example: I was in the middle of the street when it started to rain.

additional_notes: Used to say a place is very remote, far from towns, people, or anything nearby. Common with "en" (en medio de la nada). You may also hear it without "el": "en medio de la nada".
target_language_example: Nos quedamos sin gasolina en medio de la nada.
native_language_example: We ran out of gas in the middle of nowhere.

additional_notes: Used to compare two things, people, or options. It can compare nouns (Este escritorio es mejor que ése) or whole ideas/infinitives (Es mejor que no hacer nada). Often paired with "más" (más mejor is incorrect in standard Spanish).
target_language_example: Esta opción es mejor que la otra.
native_language_example: This option is better than the other one.

additional_notes: This is usually the start of a warning or strong suggestion, followed by a verb (often in the present subjunctive): “Mejor que te vayas” = “You’d better leave.” It commonly appears with reflexive/indirect object pronouns like te (“you”). By itself, “mejor que te” is incomplete—you need the verb after it.
target_language_example: Mejor que te vayas ahora.
native_language_example: You’d better leave now.

additional_notes: Used to add an improved option, suggestion, or piece of information compared to what was just said. Often follows a statement and can introduce a new idea: "Podemos ir mañana; mejor aún, el sábado". You may also see "aún mejor" with the same meaning.
target_language_example: Podemos pedir pizza; mejor aún, cocinamos en casa.
native_language_example: We can order pizza; better yet, we’ll cook at home.

meaning: better to leave / it’s better to go.
additional_notes: Used to suggest or advise that leaving is the best option. Often appears as a standalone recommendation (like “We’d better leave”) or with a subject for clarity: “Mejor nos vamos” / “Mejor me voy.” You can also use it after a reason: “Si no hay taxis, mejor irse.”
target_language_example: Está muy tarde; mejor irse ya.
native_language_example: It’s very late; we’d better leave now.

additional_notes: Most commonly used in comparisons: X es mejor que Y = X is better than Y. In some contexts, especially before a subjunctive verb, it can be short for es mejor que..., meaning 'it's better that...' or 'you'd better...'.
target_language_example: Este restaurante es mejor que el otro.
native_language_example: This restaurant is better than the other one.

meaning: "better than me" (I do/know/understand it less well).
additional_notes: Used to compare abilities, knowledge, or understanding with yours. Very often follows a verb or phrase like hacerlo (to do it), saber (to know), or comprender (to understand): hacerlo mejor que yo = do it better than me. In careful Spanish, some speakers prefer "mejor que yo" (implying "...que yo [lo hago/lo sé]") rather than "mejor que mí".
target_language_example: Nadie conoce esta ciudad mejor que yo.
native_language_example: Nobody knows this city better than me.

meaning: underage; a minor (not legally an adult).
additional_notes: Used to say someone is below the legal age of adulthood (often 18, depending on the country). Often appears with the verb “ser”: “Es menor de edad.” The opposite is “mayor de edad” (of legal age).
target_language_example: No puede entrar al club porque es menor de edad.
native_language_example: He/She can’t enter the club because he/she is underage.

additional_notes: Used to say an amount is below a number (price, weight, time, age, etc.): "menos de 15 dólares". With "no" ("no ... menos de"), it often emphasizes a large number and means "no fewer than" / "at least": "No tiene menos de 500 libros".
target_language_example: Llegamos en menos de una hora.
native_language_example: We arrived in less than an hour.

additional_notes: Used to express relief that something bad didn’t happen or that a situation turned out well. Common patterns: (1) on its own: “Menos mal.” = “Thank goodness.” (2) with que + clause: “Menos mal que…” = “It’s a good thing that…” / “Luckily…” Often said at the end of a sentence as a reaction.
target_language_example: Menos mal que llegaste a tiempo.
native_language_example: Thank goodness you arrived on time.

additional_notes: Used to express relief about something that happened (or didn’t happen). It’s often followed by a verb phrase: "Menos mal que vino" (Good thing he came), "Menos mal que no pasó nada" (Luckily nothing happened). You can also hear it without "que" as a standalone reaction: "¡Menos mal!" (Thank goodness!).
target_language_example: Menos mal que llegaste a tiempo.
native_language_example: Good thing you arrived on time.

additional_notes: Used to compare quantity, degree, or value: A es menos que B (“A is less than B”). It can be literal (numbers, amounts) or figurative to show inferiority or self-deprecation (“I’m less than…”).
target_language_example: Esta mochila pesa menos que la tuya.
native_language_example: This backpack weighs less than yours.

meaning: except once; all but one time.
additional_notes: Used to subtract one occurrence from a total or to say something happened every time except on one occasion. Often placed after a time expression: "Fui todos los días, menos una vez" (I went every day except once). In more math-like contexts it can be understood literally as “minus one time/one occurrence.”
target_language_example: He venido todos los días esta semana, menos una vez.
native_language_example: I’ve come every day this week, except once.

additional_notes: Used for a message sent/received by phone text. Very common with verbs like enviar (to send), recibir (to receive), and ignorar (to ignore): “Te envié un mensaje de texto.” Also shortened in everyday speech to “mensaje” when context is clear.
target_language_example: Te mando un mensaje de texto cuando llegue.
native_language_example: I’ll text you when I arrive.

additional_notes: Used to describe being willing to consider new ideas or different opinions. Common with the verb "tener" (to have) or "mantener" (to keep): "tener la mente abierta", "mantener la mente abierta". You may also hear the adjective form "de mente abierta" (“open-minded”).
target_language_example: Trata de mantener la mente abierta cuando escuches otras opiniones.
native_language_example: Try to keep an open mind when you listen to other opinions.

additional_notes: Used to talk about buying or selling goods or currency illegally or unofficially, often to avoid regulations, taxes, or price controls. Common with things like dollars/foreign currency, stolen goods, or restricted items. Often used with verbs like comprar/vender (to buy/sell) and prepositions like en (in) or al (to the).
target_language_example: No compres medicamentos en el mercado negro.
native_language_example: Don’t buy medicine on the black market.

additional_notes: Mostly used in the fixed phrase «a merced a» meaning “thanks to” or “due to,” often in more formal or written Spanish. In everyday speech, «gracias a» is more common. Don’t confuse it with «a merced de» (“at the mercy of”).
target_language_example: A merced a tu ayuda, terminamos el proyecto a tiempo.
native_language_example: Thanks to your help, we finished the project on time.

additional_notes: Used to say something is worth the effort, time, cost, or risk. Often followed by an infinitive: “Merece la pena ver/ir/hacer…” (It’s worth seeing/going/doing…). You can also use it alone: “Merece la pena.”
target_language_example: Aunque está lejos, merece la pena ir.
native_language_example: Even though it’s far, it’s worth going.

additional_notes: Used to specify where a month falls within the calendar year, often with ordinal numbers: el primer/segundo/último mes del año. Note the contraction: de + el → del.
target_language_example: Marzo es el tercer mes del año.
native_language_example: March is the third month of the year.

meaning: to mess up; to put your foot in it (say/do something embarrassing).
additional_notes: Common idiom used when you make a mistake, especially a social blunder (e.g., saying the wrong thing). Often used with phrases like "perdón" or "creo que" to soften it: "Perdón, creo que voy a meter la pata." Although it’s a fixed expression, it conjugates normally (voy a meter la pata / meto la pata / metí la pata).
target_language_example: Perdón, creo que voy a meter la pata con este comentario, pero necesito decirlo.
native_language_example: Sorry, I think I’m going to put my foot in it with this comment, but I need to say it.

meaning: to get into; to put oneself into (a place or a situation, often trouble).
additional_notes: Used for entering a physical place (e.g., a pool) or getting involved in a situation (very commonly: "meterse en problemas" = "to get into trouble"). It often implies doing it oneself (sometimes carelessly or as a result of one’s actions).
target_language_example: Los que hablan mucho suelen meterse en problemas.
native_language_example: People who talk a lot often get into trouble.

additional_notes: “Mi” means “my” and “abogado” is “lawyer/attorney” (male; for a female lawyer: “mi abogada”). Often used with verbs like hablar con (to speak with) and llamar a (to call). In formal address you may see “Ud.” = “usted” (“you”).
target_language_example: Quiero hablar con mi abogado antes de firmar.
native_language_example: I want to speak with my lawyer before signing.

additional_notes: "Mi" means "my" and "abuela" means "grandmother" (paternal or maternal). You can swap the possessive: "tu abuela" (your grandmother), "su abuela" (his/her/your(formal) grandmother), "nuestra abuela" (our grandmother).
target_language_example: Voy a visitar a mi abuela este fin de semana.
native_language_example: I'm going to visit my grandmother this weekend.

additional_notes: Used to talk about your (male) grandparent. "Mi" means "my" and "abuelo" means "grandfather"; you can change "mi" to other possessives (e.g., "tu abuelo" = your grandfather, "su abuelo" = his/her/their grandfather).
target_language_example: Mi abuelo vive cerca de aquí.
native_language_example: My grandfather lives near here.

meaning: "my soul"; also an affectionate way to address someone (like "dear").
additional_notes: Most literally refers to your soul/spirit (often in emotional, religious, or poetic contexts: "save my soul"). In some places it’s also used as a term of endearment when speaking to someone directly ("Lo siento, mi alma" = "I’m sorry, dear").
target_language_example: No te preocupes, mi alma, todo va a salir bien.
native_language_example: Don’t worry, dear, everything is going to be fine.

additional_notes: “Mi” means “my.” “Amiga” is a female friend (or you use it if the friend is a woman/girl). It can also be used to address a woman directly in a friendly way (like “my friend”), depending on tone and context. For a male friend, use “mi amigo.”
target_language_example: Hoy voy a cenar con mi amiga.
native_language_example: Today I'm going to have dinner with my (female) friend.

additional_notes: Used to refer to a male friend. For a female friend, say mi amiga. The possessive mi means "my" before both masculine and feminine singular nouns.
target_language_example: Pedro es mi amigo desde la escuela.
native_language_example: Pedro is my friend from school.

meaning: "my love" (a term of affection; also literally "my love" as a feeling).
additional_notes: Used as an affectionate way to address a partner (like “honey,” “sweetheart”). It can also mean “my love for (someone)” as a noun phrase: "Mi amor por ella...". Common in romantic contexts; tone depends on relationship and can sound overly intimate if used with strangers.
target_language_example: Mi amor, ¿puedes esperarme un momento?
native_language_example: My love, can you wait for me a moment?

additional_notes: Common in much of Latin America. In Spain, "mi coche" is more common. Used to talk about your personal vehicle (ownership or the one you use).
target_language_example: No puedo ir hoy porque mi auto está en el taller.
native_language_example: I can’t go today because my car is at the mechanic’s.

additional_notes: Used to say that a bicycle belongs to you. "Mi" changes with the owner (mi = my, tu = your, su = his/her/your/their).
target_language_example: Voy a ir al trabajo en mi bicicleta.
native_language_example: I’m going to go to work on my bike.

additional_notes: Possessive phrase: "mi" (my) + "brazo" (arm). Used when talking about your own arm, especially in everyday situations (pain/injury) or when someone is holding your arm. Common with verbs like "agarrarse a/de" (hold on to), "doler" (to hurt), and commands like "Suelta/Suelte" (let go) or "Toma" (take).
target_language_example: Me duele mi brazo derecho.
native_language_example: My right arm hurts.

additional_notes: Literally refers to your head (body part), often used when talking about pain: “Ay, mi cabeza” = “Ow, my head.” It can also be used more figuratively to mean thoughts or imagination, especially with “en”: “en mi cabeza” = “in my head.”
target_language_example: No puedo concentrarme; tengo demasiadas cosas en mi cabeza.
native_language_example: I can’t concentrate; I have too many things in my head.

additional_notes: A straightforward phrase meaning your own house or home. In Spanish, casa can mean both "house" and "home" depending on context, so mi casa may translate either way. After verbs of movement, as in ir a mi casa, it often means "go to my house/home."
target_language_example: Mañana vienen unos amigos a mi casa.
native_language_example: Some friends are coming to my house tomorrow.

additional_notes: Uses the possessive adjective **mi** (“my”) before the noun **coche** (“car”). Common in everyday contexts to talk about your own car, including describing it (*Mi coche es azul*), saying something is wrong (*Le pasa algo a mi coche*), giving permission (*Puedes coger mi coche*), or telling someone to get out (*Sal de mi coche*).
target_language_example: No puedo ir hoy; mi coche está en el taller.
native_language_example: I can't go today; my car is at the mechanic.

additional_notes: Uses the possessive adjective "mi" (my) before the noun. "Computadora" is common in Latin America; in Spain you’ll often hear "mi ordenador". You can refer to a desktop or laptop depending on context.
target_language_example: No encuentro mi computadora; creo que la dejé en la oficina.
native_language_example: I can’t find my computer; I think I left it at the office.

additional_notes: Used to offer or refer to advice you gave. Often appears with verbs like seguir (to follow): «seguir mi consejo» = “follow my advice.” Also common in formal commands: «Siga mi consejo.»
target_language_example: Mi consejo es que hables con el profesor cuanto antes.
native_language_example: My advice is that you talk to the teacher as soon as possible.

additional_notes: Literally refers to the heart (the organ), but very commonly used in a figurative/emotional sense (love, sadness, heartbreak). Often appears in phrases like “con todo mi corazón” (“with all my heart”) and “mi corazón está roto” (“my heart is broken”).
target_language_example: Te lo digo de todo mi corazón.
native_language_example: I’m telling you this with all my heart.

additional_notes: Uses the possessive adjective mi (“my”) + cuarto (“room”). In many contexts, mi cuarto specifically refers to your bedroom in a home. Cuarto can also mean “quarter” (1/4) in other contexts, but with mi and sentences about keys/cleaning/location, it means a room.
target_language_example: Voy a estar en mi cuarto estudiando.
native_language_example: I’m going to be in my room studying.

additional_notes: A common possessive phrase: **mi** (my) + **cuerpo** (body). Used to talk about your physical body, health, sensations, or injuries. It can also refer to your body as a whole (e.g., after death: *quemen mi cuerpo* = “burn my body”). In Spanish you may also hear **el cuerpo** instead of **mi cuerpo** when speaking generally about the body.
target_language_example: Me duele mi cuerpo después de correr.
native_language_example: My body hurts after running.

additional_notes: Very informal/vulgar. Can be literal (talking about your butt) or used as a rude way to show disbelief/contempt, similar to English “my ass!” (meaning “yeah, right / no way”). Because it’s crude, avoid it in polite or formal situations.
target_language_example: ¿Que él es muy honesto? ¡Mi culo!
native_language_example: That he's very honest? My ass!

additional_notes: Used to talk about the date you were born and the yearly celebration. With dates you’ll often see: “Mi cumpleaños es el 20 de julio” (specific day) or “Mi cumpleaños es en noviembre” (month). It can also be used figuratively for an anniversary, e.g., “mi cumpleaños de sobriedad” = “my sobriety anniversary.”
target_language_example: ¿Qué quieres hacer por mi cumpleaños?
native_language_example: What do you want to do for my birthday?

additional_notes: Used to refer to your female spouse. "Mi" changes with the owner (mi = my, tu = your, su = his/her/your formal/their). You can also say "la esposa de + name/pronoun" (e.g., "la esposa de Tom").
target_language_example: Voy a cenar con mi esposa esta noche.
native_language_example: I’m going to have dinner with my wife tonight.

additional_notes: Used to refer to your wife. "Mi" changes depending on the person (mi = my, tu = your, su = his/her/your/their). "Esposa" is feminine; the masculine equivalent is "mi esposo" (my husband).
target_language_example: Voy a cenar con mi esposa esta noche.
native_language_example: I’m going to have dinner with my wife tonight.

additional_notes: Used to refer to your spouse (male). Often appears after prepositions like "para mi esposo" (for my husband) or "con mi esposo" (with my husband). You can also say "mi marido" with the same meaning in many contexts.
target_language_example: Voy a llamar a mi esposo para avisarle que llego tarde.
native_language_example: I'm going to call my husband to let him know I'm arriving late.

additional_notes: Possessive phrase used to refer to your family. "Mi" changes to match the noun: "mi" (singular) and "mis" (plural), e.g., "mi familia" / "mis amigos".
target_language_example: Voy a visitar a mi familia este fin de semana.
native_language_example: I'm going to visit my family this weekend.

additional_notes: Used to talk about your own pet cat. "Mi" means "my" (before a masculine singular noun), and "gato" means "cat" (male cat, or cat in general). For a female cat you can say "mi gata."
target_language_example: No puedo salir hoy; mi gato está enfermo.
native_language_example: I can’t go out today; my cat is sick.

meaning: "my people" (my group: family, friends, community, or team).
additional_notes: Used to refer to the people you identify with or feel loyal to—often your close circle (family/friends) or your group/community. It can sound warm and personal, and it doesn’t imply literal ownership.
target_language_example: Hoy salgo con mi gente después del trabajo.
native_language_example: Today I'm going out with my people (my friends) after work.

meaning: my room (bedroom or a room you’re staying in).
additional_notes: “Mi” means “my” and “habitación” is “room.” It’s commonly used for your bedroom at home or your room in a hotel (“mi habitación de hotel”). Use it with location/description verbs like “estar” (Mi habitación está arriba / está llena de…).
target_language_example: Voy a dejar mi maleta en mi habitación.
native_language_example: I’m going to leave my suitcase in my room.

additional_notes: Used to refer to your sister. "Mi" changes to match the noun: mi hermano (my brother), mis hermanas (my sisters), mis hermanos (my siblings / my brothers).
target_language_example: Voy a cenar con mi hermana esta noche.
native_language_example: I'm going to have dinner with my sister tonight.

additional_notes: Used to specify that your sister is older than you. You can swap the possessive: "tu/su/nuestra hermana mayor" (“your/his-her/our older sister”). "Mayor" goes after the noun ("hermana").
target_language_example: Voy a cenar con mi hermana mayor esta noche.
native_language_example: I’m going to have dinner with my older sister tonight.

additional_notes: Used to refer to your younger sister (not necessarily physically small). In Spanish, the possessive (mi) comes before the noun, and the adjective (pequeña) usually comes after: mi hermana pequeña. You can also hear mi hermana menor with the same meaning.
target_language_example: Voy a recoger a mi hermana pequeña al colegio.
native_language_example: I’m going to pick up my little sister from school.

additional_notes: Past tense (pretérito) of reflexive verb "casarse" = "to get married." Use "se casó" for a completed event in the past. Add "con" + person to say who she married: "Se casó con un doctor." You can add time expressions like "hace unos años" (a few years ago).
target_language_example: Mi hermana se casó el año pasado.
native_language_example: My sister got married last year.

additional_notes: Uses **tener** (“to have”) to talk about having things (classes, a job, good handwriting, etc.). In Spanish, **age is expressed with tener**: *Mi hermana tiene tres años* = “My sister is three (years old)” (not “has three years” in natural English). You can also use it for age differences: *tiene tres años menos que yo* = “she’s three years younger than me.”
target_language_example: Mi hermana tiene 25 años y tiene un buen trabajo.
native_language_example: My sister is 25 years old and has a good job.

additional_notes: A straightforward possessive phrase: mi = "my" and hermano = "brother." It refers to a male sibling. Use mis hermanos for "my brothers" or "my siblings" in a mixed group.
target_language_example: Mi hermano vive cerca de aquí.
native_language_example: My brother lives near here.

additional_notes: Used to state your brother’s current location, state/condition, or an action in progress. In Spanish, "está" (from "estar") is commonly used for temporary states, locations, and the present progressive ("está" + gerund: "está viendo", "está regresando"). Note: for identity or more permanent characteristics, Spanish often uses "ser" ("mi hermano es...") instead.
target_language_example: Mi hermano está trabajando ahora mismo.
native_language_example: My brother is working right now.

additional_notes: Used to talk about your oldest/older brother. In Spanish, "mayor" means "older" (not "bigger"); it agrees with the noun: "hermano mayor" (older brother) / "hermana mayor" (older sister). You can also say "mi hermano mayor" by itself as a short answer or when introducing him.
target_language_example: Mi hermano mayor trabaja en una oficina cerca de aquí.
native_language_example: My older brother works in an office near here.

additional_notes: Used to talk about your younger brother. In Spanish, "menor" means younger (opposite of "mayor" = older). It can describe siblings and also minors (under 18). You can swap "mi" for other possessives: "tu hermano menor" (your younger brother), "su hermano menor" (his/her/their younger brother).
target_language_example: Voy a recoger a mi hermano menor después de la escuela.
native_language_example: I'm going to pick up my younger brother after school.

additional_notes: A common way to talk about your younger brother. In Spanish, family members are often referred to with a possessive (mi/tu/su) + noun, and adjectives like pequeño usually come after the noun. "Hermano pequeño" can mean either the younger brother (relative age) or simply the smaller/younger kid brother; if you mean strictly “the youngest,” you can also say "mi hermano menor".
target_language_example: Mi hermano pequeño estudia en la universidad.
native_language_example: My younger brother studies at the university.

additional_notes: Possessive phrase: "mi" (my) + "hija" (daughter). Used to talk about your (female) child. For "my son," say "mi hijo." With "a" (to) it can become "a mi hija" (to my daughter), as in "Vine a ver a mi hija."
target_language_example: Hoy voy a recoger a mi hija de la escuela.
native_language_example: Today I’m going to pick up my daughter from school.

additional_notes: A basic possessive phrase: mi means "my" and hijo means "son." For a daughter, use mi hija. Mi stays the same with masculine and feminine singular nouns.
target_language_example: Mi hijo tiene ocho años.
native_language_example: My son is eight years old.

meaning: "my home" (the place you live, often with an emotional sense of belonging).
additional_notes: "Hogar" can mean your physical home, but it often emphasizes warmth, family, and the feeling of belonging more than "casa". You can use "mi hogar" to talk about where you live now or a place you consider home (including your hometown or country).
target_language_example: Después de viajar, por fin vuelvo a mi hogar.
native_language_example: After traveling, I’m finally coming back home.

additional_notes: Used to talk about your life when you were a child. It often appears with memories and nostalgia verbs like recordar (to remember), pensar en (to think about), or phrases like durante/todo el día de mi infancia (during/all through my childhood). It can be used in emotional descriptions: Mi infancia fue feliz/triste/difícil.
target_language_example: A veces extraño mi infancia.
native_language_example: Sometimes I miss my childhood.

additional_notes: Used to refer to the person who is your superior at work. In many workplaces you can also hear it used more generally for the person in charge (e.g., a leader), but the most common meaning is “boss.” If you’re speaking directly to your boss, you’d usually say "mi jefe" only when talking about them to someone else (not to their face).
target_language_example: Mañana tengo una reunión con mi jefe.
native_language_example: Tomorrow I have a meeting with my boss.

additional_notes: A common possessive phrase meaning your own mother. Madre is a neutral standard word; in everyday speech, many speakers also say mi mamá.
target_language_example: mi madre vive en Madrid.
native_language_example: my mother lives in Madrid.

additional_notes: Used to describe your mother with a profession (often without an article: "Mi madre es profesora"), an adjective ("Mi madre es activa"), or nationality/origin ("Mi madre es griega"). You can also add more information after it (e.g., family relationships or job type).
target_language_example: Mi madre es enfermera.
native_language_example: My mother is a nurse.

meaning: "my mother is" (using estar: location or a state/condition).
additional_notes: Use "mi madre está" with "estar" to talk about where your mother is (location) or how she is (health, mood, condition): "Mi madre está muy bien." You can also use it with opinions/stances using expressions like "estar en contra de" (to be against). "Mi madre está en el cielo" is a common, polite way to say someone has passed away (literally "in heaven").
target_language_example: Mi madre está en casa ahora.
native_language_example: My mother is at home now.

meaning: “my mother … me” (my mom does something to/for me).
additional_notes: Often used with the pronoun **me** before the verb to show that **I** am the person affected by the action. In sentences like *Mi madre me regaló… / me preparó… / me regañó*, **me** usually means **“to me/for me”** (indirect object), though with some verbs it can be closer to **“me”** as a direct object (e.g., *Mi madre me regañó* = “My mom scolded me”). Word order: **Mi madre me + verb**.
target_language_example: Mi madre me llamó anoche.
native_language_example: My mother called me last night.

additional_notes: "Mi madre" means "my mother." The "se" is a very common little word that goes with certain verbs: (1) reflexive actions (she does something to herself: "se estaba preparando" = she was getting herself ready), (2) change of state/emotion ("se alegrará" = she’ll be happy/glad), and (3) verbs that simply require "se" ("se preocupa" = she worries). In English, "se" is often not translated as a separate word.
target_language_example: Mi madre se levanta temprano todos los días.
native_language_example: My mother gets up early every day.

additional_notes: Used to talk about your suitcase/luggage. Common in travel situations (airports, hotels). Often appears with verbs like robar (to steal), llevar (to carry/take), dejar (to leave), and with location phrases (aquí/allá). "Mi maleta está hecha" means "My suitcase is packed."
target_language_example: ¿Has visto mi maleta? No la encuentro.
native_language_example: Have you seen my suitcase? I can’t find it.

additional_notes: A common, informal way to say “my mother.” It’s more affectionate/colloquial than “mi madre” and is used in everyday speech.
target_language_example: Mi mamá trabaja mañana, así que hoy cenamos temprano.
native_language_example: My mom works tomorrow, so today we’re having dinner early.

additional_notes: Possessive phrase: **mi** (my) + **mano** (hand). Used for physical touch/holding and also in set expressions like **tomar/agarrar mi mano** (“take/hold my hand”). Note: **mano** is feminine in Spanish, so adjectives agree: *mi mano derecha/izquierda*.
target_language_example: ¿Puedes sostener mi mano un momento?
native_language_example: Can you hold my hand for a moment?

additional_notes: Used by a woman to refer to her husband. "Mi" means "my" and "marido" means "husband" (so it’s straightforward and literal). You can also say "esposo" in many contexts; both mean "husband."
target_language_example: Mi marido trabaja desde casa los viernes.
native_language_example: My husband works from home on Fridays.

additional_notes: Used to refer to your closest female friend. You can also say "mi mejor amigo" for a male friend. "Mejor" is the comparative form of "bueno" (good), so it’s literally "my better friend" → "my best friend."
target_language_example: Voy al cine con mi mejor amiga esta noche.
native_language_example: I’m going to the movies with my best friend tonight.

additional_notes: Used to refer to the closest friend. For a female friend, say "mi mejor amiga". In Spanish you can drop the subject pronoun: "Es mi mejor amigo" = "He is my best friend."
target_language_example: Él es mi mejor amigo desde la escuela.
native_language_example: He has been my best friend since school.

additional_notes: Refers to your thoughts, memory, imagination, or mental state. Common in expressions like "liberar mi mente" (to free my mind), "mi mente está en blanco" (my mind is blank), and with verbs like "venir a mi mente" / "vino a mi mente" meaning "to come to mind".
target_language_example: Necesito descansar; mi mente no para.
native_language_example: I need to rest; my mind won’t stop.

additional_notes: Most commonly means “my wife” (spouse). It can sometimes also mean “my woman” (girlfriend/partner) depending on context, but that use can sound possessive or old-fashioned in some situations. In sentence 1 (“Eres mi mujer.”), it usually implies a serious/committed relationship and often marriage.
target_language_example: Voy al cine con mi mujer esta noche.
native_language_example: I’m going to the movies with my wife tonight.

additional_notes: Means a typewriter that belongs to the speaker. It uses the possessive adjective "mi" (my) + the noun phrase "máquina de escribir" (typewriter). "De escribir" literally means "of writing" (a machine for writing).
target_language_example: Mi máquina de escribir está en el escritorio.
native_language_example: My typewriter is on the desk.

additional_notes: "Nieto" means a grandson (male grandchild). For a granddaughter, use "mi nieta". It’s used to talk about your child’s child. In Spanish, family words are often used with a possessive like "mi" (my), "tu" (your), "su" (his/her/their).
target_language_example: Mi nieto vive con mis hijos.
native_language_example: My grandson lives with my children.

additional_notes: Means “my name.” Often used in introductions: “Mi nombre es…” = “My name is…”. Can also mean “in my name / on my behalf” in phrases like “en mi nombre” (someone acts for you or represents you).
target_language_example: Hola, mi nombre es Ana.
native_language_example: Hi, my name is Ana.

additional_notes: A common, polite way to introduce yourself. Often used with "Hola" (Hello): "Hola, mi nombre es..." In everyday conversation you can also say "Me llamo..." (I’m called/I’m named...).
target_language_example: Hola, mi nombre es Ana.
native_language_example: Hi, my name is Ana.

meaning: "my girlfriend" (or "my bride" in a wedding context).
additional_notes: Most commonly means “my girlfriend” (your female romantic partner). It can also mean “my fiancée/bride” when talking about marriage or a wedding (novio/novia = engaged couple or bride/groom). Used with a feminine partner; for a male partner, say “mi novio.”
target_language_example: Ella es mi novia desde hace dos años.
native_language_example: She’s been my girlfriend for two years.

additional_notes: Used to refer to your male romantic partner. "Novio" can mean "boyfriend" (or "fiancé" if you’re engaged), so context matters. The feminine form is "mi novia" (my girlfriend).
target_language_example: Voy a cenar con mi novio esta noche.
native_language_example: I'm going to have dinner with my boyfriend tonight.

additional_notes: Used to refer to the speaker’s office or workspace (a room at work, or a home office). It’s possessive: mi (my) + oficina (office). Often used with estar/ser for location or identification: “Está en mi oficina” (It’s in my office) / “Esta es mi oficina” (This is my office).
target_language_example: Mañana tengo una reunión en mi oficina.
native_language_example: Tomorrow I have a meeting in my office.

additional_notes: Used to give your personal view or judgment. Often appears after verbs like pedir (to ask for): "Me pidieron mi opinión." You can also use it in the pattern "Mi opinión es..." to compare or state your view.
target_language_example: En mi opinión, es una buena idea.
native_language_example: In my opinion, it’s a good idea.

additional_notes: A common way to refer to your father. It is neutral and standard; mi papá is often more affectionate or informal.
target_language_example: Mi padre trabaja en un hospital.
native_language_example: My father works in a hospital.

additional_notes: Uses the imperfect past tense (era) to describe what your father was like, his profession/role, or a past state/background description. Often followed by a noun or adjective: “Mi padre era escritor / un gran hombre”.
target_language_example: Mi padre era maestro cuando yo era niño.
native_language_example: My father was a teacher when I was a child.

additional_notes: Used to describe your father with an adjective or noun. With jobs/roles, Spanish often drops the article: "Mi padre es profesor" (not *un profesor*). With other nouns, you usually include an article or other determiner: "Mi padre es un poco anticuado" / "Mi padre es un diccionario ambulante".
target_language_example: Mi padre es muy paciente.
native_language_example: My father is very patient.

meaning: "my father is" (using *estar* for location or a temporary state/condition).
additional_notes: Use **mi padre está** with **estar** to talk about where your father is (**está en casa**, **está afuera**) or how he is/what condition he’s in (**está ocupado**, **está interesado en...**). For more permanent characteristics, Spanish often uses **ser** instead (*Mi padre es alto* = “My father is tall”).
target_language_example: Mi padre está cansado hoy.
native_language_example: My father is tired today.

additional_notes: Used when your father does something to/for you. In Spanish, the pronoun **me** usually goes **before** the conjugated verb: *Mi padre me ayudó* (“My father helped me”). It can be a **direct object** (“me” = the person receiving the action, e.g., *me mima*) or an **indirect object** (“to/for me,” e.g., *me hizo un almuerzo*, *me llevó*).
target_language_example: Mi padre me llamó esta mañana.
native_language_example: My father called me this morning.

additional_notes: A complete sentence using the preterite (murió) to talk about a finished event in the past. Often used with time expressions like "hace tres aos" (three years ago) or "cuando yo tena..." (when I was...).
target_language_example: Mi padre murió en 2018.
native_language_example: My father died in 2018.

meaning: "my father" + "se" (a pronoun used with many verbs; often like "my father *got/left/recovered*...").
additional_notes: "Mi padre" = "my father." The "se" here is a pronoun that goes with *pronominal/reflexive* verbs (verbs that commonly appear with "se"). It doesn’t translate as a separate word in English in many cases, but it’s required in Spanish and can change the verb’s meaning: **enterar** = to inform vs **enterarse (de)** = to find out; **retirar** = to withdraw something vs **retirarse** = to retire/step away; **recuperar** = to recover something vs **recuperarse** = to recover (get better). Word order: subject + se + verb ("Mi padre se enterará...").
target_language_example: Mi padre se fue a casa temprano.
native_language_example: My father went home early.

additional_notes: Used to talk about your father possessing/owning something, or having something as a characteristic. "Tiene" is the 3rd-person singular form of "tener" (to have). Often followed by a noun: "Mi padre tiene un restaurante."
target_language_example: Mi padre tiene dos perros.
native_language_example: My father has two dogs.

additional_notes: "Papá" is a common, everyday way to say "dad" (often warmer/more casual than "padre"). Use it with a possessive like "mi" (my): "mi papá" = "my dad."
target_language_example: Hoy voy a cenar con mi papá.
native_language_example: Today I'm going to have dinner with my dad.

meaning: "my dad" + "(to/for) me" (he did something to me or for me).
additional_notes: Used before a verb to say what your dad did, with "me" showing that *you* are the person affected. The "me" can mean he did something *to you* (Mi papá me mandó… = My dad sent/ordered me…) or *for you* (Mi papá me compró… = My dad bought me…). It’s very common with verbs like "dijo" (told), "compró" (bought), "regaló" (gave as a gift), "mandó" (ordered/sent).
target_language_example: Mi papá me ayudó con la tarea.
native_language_example: My dad helped me with my homework.

additional_notes: Used to talk about the portion that belongs to you (your share of something) or the responsibility/task you are supposed to do (“I did my part”). In music or performance, it can also mean “my part” (the part you play/sing): “No va a tocar mi parte.”
target_language_example: Yo ya hice mi parte; ahora te toca a ti.
native_language_example: I already did my part; now it’s your turn.

additional_notes: Used to talk about the country you belong to (by nationality/citizenship) or feel you come from. It’s a possessive phrase: mi (my) + país (country). In Spanish, the possessive changes with the owner (mi/mis, tu/tus, su/sus, nuestro/a/s, etc.), not with the noun’s gender.
target_language_example: Echo de menos mi país cuando estoy en el extranjero.
native_language_example: I miss my country when I'm abroad.

additional_notes: Literally refers to the speaker’s dog. It can be used in a joking/insulting way in comparisons (e.g., saying someone looks like your dog). In Spanish, possessives agree with the thing owned: mi perro (masc.), mi perra (fem.).
target_language_example: Voy a pasear a mi perro después de cenar.
native_language_example: I’m going to walk my dog after dinner.

additional_notes: Used to talk about your cousin who is a woman/girl. Spanish distinguishes gender: mi primo = my (male) cousin, mi prima = my (female) cousin. Often used with a name in apposition: “Mi prima, Sandra.”
target_language_example: Mi prima vive en Madrid.
native_language_example: My cousin lives in Madrid.

additional_notes: Used before a singular masculine noun to say it’s the first one you have/had (mi primer hijo, mi primer viaje). It’s the shortened form of "primero" that’s used before a masculine noun; with feminine nouns use "mi primera" (mi primera vez).
target_language_example: Mi primer día en la universidad fue emocionante.
native_language_example: My first day at university was exciting.

additional_notes: Used to refer to your male cousin. For a female cousin, use "mi prima". You can also add a name after it: "mi primo Balin" = "my cousin Balin".
target_language_example: Mi primo vive en Madrid.
native_language_example: My cousin lives in Madrid.

additional_notes: Used to emphasize that something/someone belongs to you or is personally yours. It must agree with a feminine noun: mi propia casa, mi propia familia. For masculine nouns use **mi propio** (mi propio plan). Often adds emphasis like “my very own.” It also appears in set phrases like **de mi propia cosecha** (“of my own making / my own invention”) and **a mi propia salud** (“to my own health,” as in a toast).
target_language_example: Quiero abrir mi propia tienda.
native_language_example: I want to open my own shop.

additional_notes: Used to emphasize that something belongs to you personally or is done by you (not borrowed, shared, or someone else’s). It agrees with the noun: mi propio + masculine singular noun (mi propio plan), mi propia + feminine singular noun (mi propia casa), mis propios/mis propias for plural.
target_language_example: Necesito mi propio espacio para estudiar.
native_language_example: I need my own space to study.

additional_notes: Means “my watch” when you’re talking about a wristwatch, and “my clock” when it’s a clock (for example, an alarm clock). Used with verbs like ser/estar/parecer (“is/seems”), adelantarse/atrasarse (“runs fast/slow”), and arreglar (“to fix”).
target_language_example: No encuentro mi reloj; creo que lo dejé en casa.
native_language_example: I can’t find my watch; I think I left it at home.

additional_notes: Used to identify a male family member who is the son of your brother or sister. Spanish distinguishes gender: "mi sobrino" (nephew) vs. "mi sobrina" (niece). Often appears with "Es" or "Ese es" to introduce or point someone out ("Es mi sobrino", "Ese es mi sobrino").
target_language_example: Mi sobrino vive con mi hermana.
native_language_example: My nephew lives with my sister.

additional_notes: Most commonly refers to school homework. It’s made of mi (my) + tarea (task/homework). You’ll also hear "hacer la tarea" = to do homework. With animals, both "El perro comió mi tarea" and "Mi perro se comió mi tarea" mean the dog ate it; "se comió" often emphasizes that it ate it up.
target_language_example: No puedo salir; todavía no termino mi tarea.
native_language_example: I can’t go out; I still haven’t finished my homework.

additional_notes: Uses the possessive adjective "mi" (my) before the noun. In context it usually means a mobile phone. Common with "estar" for states/conditions: "Mi teléfono está mojado" (is wet) and "Mi teléfono está muerto" (is dead = has no battery / isn’t working).
target_language_example: No encuentro mi teléfono.
native_language_example: I can’t find my phone.

additional_notes: Usually means the speaker’s job or the work they’re responsible for. It can refer both to a paid job ("my job") and to a task/role they must do ("my work"), as in "Solo hice mi trabajo" = "I just did my job."
target_language_example: No puedo hablar ahora; estoy haciendo mi trabajo.
native_language_example: I can't talk right now; I'm doing my job.

meaning: 'my job/work is…' (used to describe your job or what your job involves).
additional_notes: Often followed by an adjective (Mi trabajo es aburrido/sencillo) or by an infinitive to say your responsibility (Mi trabajo es mantener el orden). You can also use it more broadly to mean 'my task/role is…' in a specific situation, not only your employment.
target_language_example: Mi trabajo es ayudar a los clientes.
native_language_example: My job is to help customers.

additional_notes: Used to talk about your aunt (your parent’s sister, or sometimes your uncle’s wife). You can change the possessive: mi tía (my aunt), tu tía (your aunt), su tía (his/her/your formal/their aunt). The accent matters: tía (aunt) vs tia (not correct).
target_language_example: Mi tía vive en México.
native_language_example: My aunt lives in Mexico.

additional_notes: Means “my uncle” (your dad’s or mom’s brother). It can also be used for an uncle by marriage. Like many family terms in Spanish, it can be used when talking about family members even without naming them (e.g., “Mi tío vive en México.”).
target_language_example: Mi tío vive cerca de aquí, pero casi no lo veo.
native_language_example: My uncle lives near here, but I hardly ever see him.

meaning: my neighbor (male) / the man who lives near me.
additional_notes: Used to talk about a male neighbor; for a female neighbor, say "mi vecina". You’ll often use it with "de" to specify: "mi vecino de arriba" (my upstairs neighbor) or "mi vecino de al lado" (my next-door neighbor).
target_language_example: Mi vecino de al lado siempre saluda cuando nos vemos.
native_language_example: My next-door neighbor always says hello when we see each other.

additional_notes: Literal phrase made of mi + vida. It usually refers to someone's life in general. In other contexts, especially when speaking directly to someone, mi vida can also be an affectionate term like “my love” or “darling.”
target_language_example: Quiero cambiar mi vida.
native_language_example: I want to change my life.

additional_notes: Used to set the background of an event that happened during an ongoing action. "Mientras" = "while" and "caminaba" is the imperfect tense of "caminar" (to walk), suggesting something in progress in the past. "por el" usually means "through the" or "along the" (masculine singular), and it needs a noun after it (e.g., "bosque", "parque", "río"). For a feminine noun, use "por la" (e.g., "por la calle").
target_language_example: Mientras caminaba por el centro, empezó a llover.
native_language_example: While I was walking through downtown, it started to rain.

additional_notes: Often used to contrast two people/things or two situations: "X..., mientras que Y..." = "X..., whereas Y...". It can also mean "while" in the time sense: "...mientras que yo estaba fuera" = "...while I was out."
target_language_example: Yo trabajo de noche, mientras que mi esposo trabaja de día.
native_language_example: I work at night, whereas my spouse works during the day.

additional_notes: Used to say that something happens during the time before another event happens, or at the same time as something else. Often placed at the beginning of a sentence and followed by a comma: “Mientras tanto, …”.
target_language_example: Mientras tanto, voy preparando la cena.
native_language_example: Meanwhile, I’ll start preparing dinner.

additional_notes: Used to talk about an amount of money: 1,000 dollars. In Spanish, large numbers are often written with a space or a period (1.000 or 1 000) rather than a comma. You can also use it with time phrases like “por día” (per day).
target_language_example: Ese celular cuesta mil dólares.
native_language_example: That cellphone costs a thousand dollars.

additional_notes: In most Spanish-speaking contexts, "mil millones" is the unambiguous way to say 1,000,000,000 (a thousand millions). This avoids confusion because "un billón" in Spanish usually means 1,000,000,000,000 (a trillion in US English). Used in news, money, and statistics: "mil millones de dólares" = "one billion dollars."
target_language_example: La empresa vale mil millones de dólares.
native_language_example: The company is worth one billion dollars.

additional_notes: In most Spanish-speaking countries, "mil millones" = 1,000,000,000 (English: "a billion"), not "a million million". Used in statistics and big numbers (population, speakers, etc.). Often appears as "X mil millones de personas" (e.g., "dos mil millones...") or without "de" when used as a subject: "Mil millones de personas hablan...".
target_language_example: En 2050 podría haber casi diez mil millones de personas en el planeta.
native_language_example: In 2050 there could be almost ten billion people on the planet.

additional_notes: Used to talk about prices, costs, allowances, or amounts of money in Japanese yen. You often see it with another number before it: dos mil yenes (2,000 yen), diez mil yenes (10,000 yen), cincuenta mil yenes (50,000 yen). With larger numbers, Spanish also uses mil as part of the number phrase: cinco mil yenes = 5,000 yen.
target_language_example: Este bolso cuesta tres mil yenes.
native_language_example: This bag costs three thousand yen.

additional_notes: Used before a noun to express a very large number: miles de años (thousands of years), miles de cosas (thousands of things). Often implies “a lot,” not an exact count.
target_language_example: Hay miles de personas en el concierto.
native_language_example: There are thousands of people at the concert.

additional_notes: Uses the plural noun "miles" (thousands) + "de" + a plural noun to express a large number. Common with past-tense events: "Miles de personas fueron/visitaron...". You can swap "personas" for other nouns: "miles de dólares", "miles de años".
target_language_example: Miles de personas asistieron al concierto.
