native_language_example: Thousands of people attended the concert.

meaning: (a) gold mine; figuratively, a goldmine (a very valuable source of money or information).
additional_notes: Literal meaning: a mine where gold is extracted. Very commonly used figuratively to mean something that produces a lot of value, profit, or useful information (like “a goldmine”/“a treasure trove” in English). Often used with ser: “Esto es una mina de oro.”
target_language_example: Este negocio es una mina de oro.
native_language_example: This business is a goldmine.

meaning: Look, no… / Listen, no… (used to start a refusal or correction).
additional_notes: Used at the beginning of a sentence to get attention and introduce a negative response (disagreeing, refusing, or clarifying). Often sounds a bit firm or defensive depending on tone. Very common in spoken Spanish; you can also hear “Mira, es que…” or “Oye, no…”.
target_language_example: Mira, no puedo ir hoy; tengo mucho trabajo.
native_language_example: Look, I can’t go today; I have a lot of work.

additional_notes: Imperative phrase used to tell someone to observe their surroundings (often to notice what’s happening or what’s nearby). You can also say "Mira alrededor" (less common) or "Mira a su alrededor" (formal: "look around you," addressing usted).
target_language_example: Antes de decidir, mira a tu alrededor y piensa.
native_language_example: Before you decide, look around you and think.

meaning: “Look how…” / “Just look at how…” (often to point out or criticize something).
additional_notes: Uses the tú command form of mirar (“mira”) + cómo (“how”) to draw attention to someone’s behavior, appearance, or what is happening. Very common in scolding or expressing disapproval: “Mira cómo te comportas” = “Look at how you’re behaving.”
target_language_example: Mira cómo hablas con tu hermano.
native_language_example: Look at how you’re talking to your brother.

additional_notes: Used to draw someone’s attention to something you’re about to show or point out. Common in conversation as a lead-in (e.g., Ahora/Bien/Pero/Vaya, mira esto...). You can also use it to express surprise: “Mira esto, ¡un cigarro entero!”
target_language_example: Ven aquí y mira esto: encontré tus llaves.
native_language_example: Come here and look at this: I found your keys.

additional_notes: Used to call someone’s attention to something you’re about to show or point out: “Mira lo que he encontrado.” With verbs like “te digo,” it can also mean “listen to what I’m telling you / pay attention,” not necessarily literally “look.” Often followed by a verb in the present perfect (he encontrado, ha hecho) or another clause.
target_language_example: ¡Mira lo que compré en el mercado!
native_language_example: Look what I bought at the market!

meaning: "Watch what you're doing!" / "Look what you're doing!"
additional_notes: Used to warn someone to be careful or to scold them because they’re making a mistake or causing a problem. It's an informal/neutral command in the tú form (mira = "look/watch"). You can also hear variations like “¡Mira lo que has hecho!” (Look what you’ve done!).
target_language_example: ¡Mira lo que haces! Vas a romper el vaso.
native_language_example: Watch what you're doing! You're going to break the glass.

meaning: "Look what you’ve done." (said to blame or scold someone for the result of their actions).
additional_notes: Uses the informal command "mira" (look) plus "lo que has hecho" (what you have done). Often said in an annoyed or disappointed tone after something goes wrong. You can add words like "ahora" (now) for emphasis. In sentences like "Mira lo que has hecho a tu madre", it means "Look what you’ve done to your mother" (i.e., the effect you caused).
target_language_example: ¡Mira lo que has hecho! Ahora tenemos que limpiar todo.
native_language_example: Look what you’ve done! Now we have to clean everything.

additional_notes: Used to point out who someone is or who has arrived/is present. Often expresses surprise, recognition, or irony (e.g., "Look who's being dramatic now"). Usually followed by a verb (mira quién ha venido, mira quién está ahí) or a clause (mira quién se pone dramático).
target_language_example: ¡Mira quién apareció de repente!
native_language_example: Look who showed up all of a sudden!

additional_notes: Used mainly when the direct object is a person (or sometimes an animal/personified thing). Spanish often adds the personal “a” before people: mirar a alguien = “to look at someone.” With things, you usually say mirar algo (no “a”): mirar la tele = “to watch TV.”
target_language_example: No puedo mirar a mi jefe a los ojos.
native_language_example: I can’t look my boss in the eyes.

meaning: to look (someone) in the eyes; to make eye contact.
additional_notes: Used to express making direct eye contact with someone. Common in requests/commands like "Mírame a los ojos" or "No me mires a los ojos." You can specify the person with an indirect object pronoun: "mírame" (look at me), "míralo" (look at him), etc. As an infinitive phrase, it often appears after another verb (e.g., "quiero", "puedes", "debes").
target_language_example: Tienes que mirar a los ojos cuando hables con alguien.
native_language_example: You have to look people in the eyes when you speak with someone.

additional_notes: Used when you turn your head/eyes to see what’s nearby or to take in a place. Common in directions and when exploring: “Vamos a mirar alrededor” (Let’s look around).
target_language_example: Cuando llegues, puedes mirar alrededor y buscar la entrada.
native_language_example: When you arrive, you can look around and look for the entrance.

additional_notes: Used for physically directing your gaze upward (e.g., to the sky, a sign, the ceiling). In instructions, it can also mean to look at something located above (for example, on a page or screen). Often you’ll also hear: "mirar hacia arriba" (look upward).
target_language_example: Tienes que mirar arriba: hay un avión en el cielo.
native_language_example: You have to look up—there’s a plane in the sky.

additional_notes: Used to introduce what you want to find out or verify: mirar qué + verb/clause (e.g., mirar qué pasa = see what happens). You may also see it as an instruction in signs/notes using the infinitive (Mirar qué...) or as a command: Mira qué... / Mire qué... (Look what... / See what...).
target_language_example: Vamos a mirar qué opciones hay.
native_language_example: Let’s see what options there are.

additional_notes: A possessive phrase: "mis" (my, plural) + "abuelos" (grandparents). It can refer to both grandparents together, or to grandparents in general. For an indirect object like "to my grandparents," use "a mis abuelos" (often with "les" as in "A mis abuelos nunca les gustó...").
target_language_example: Siempre llamo a mis abuelos los fines de semana.
native_language_example: I always call my grandparents on weekends.

additional_notes: Plural of “mi amiga” (my female friend). “Mis” = my (plural), and “amigas” is the feminine plural form, used when the group is all women/girls (or a group of mixed genders that you’re referring to with feminine nouns).
target_language_example: Esta noche voy a cenar con mis amigas.
native_language_example: Tonight I’m going to have dinner with my (female) friends.

additional_notes: Possessive phrase: **mis** = “my” (plural) + **amigos** = “friends” (masculine plural). **Amigos** can refer to a mixed-gender group; for an all-female group you can say **mis amigas**. It’s used to talk about your friends as a group or to introduce them (e.g., *Ven a ver a mis amigos*).
target_language_example: Esta noche voy a cenar con mis amigos.
native_language_example: Tonight I’m going to have dinner with my friends.

additional_notes: Used to refer to your belongings or personal items. In context it can mean physical objects (clothes, a bag, etc.) or more generally “my personal business/private matters” (e.g., “Don’t get into my stuff”). Often used with verbs like recoger (pick up), traer (bring), dejar (leave), or meterse en (mess with/get into).
target_language_example: Tengo que ir por mis cosas antes de irme.
native_language_example: I have to go get my things before I leave.

additional_notes: Possessive phrase: **mis** (“my”, plural) + **hermanos** (“brothers”; can also mean “siblings/brothers” in mixed groups depending on context). Used to say who someone is to you (e.g., *Ellos son mis hermanos*) or to talk about your brothers in general (*Amo a mis hermanos*).
target_language_example: Voy a ver a mis hermanos este fin de semana.
native_language_example: I’m going to see my brothers this weekend.

additional_notes: "Mis" is the plural form of "my" (used with plural nouns). "Hijas" is the plural of "hija" (daughter). Use "mis hijas" when talking about your daughters; if you have one daughter, say "mi hija".
target_language_example: Voy a recoger a mis hijas a la escuela.
native_language_example: I’m going to pick up my daughters from school.

additional_notes: "Mis" means "my" (plural), and "hijos" can mean "sons" or "children" depending on context. Use it to talk about your kids in general or your sons specifically. For daughters only, say "mis hijas."
target_language_example: Mis hijos van a la escuela en autobús.
native_language_example: My kids go to school by bus.

meaning: my men (the men who work for me / are under my command).
additional_notes: Used to refer to a group of male people associated with the speaker, often subordinates (guards, soldiers, employees, team members). It sounds possessive/authoritative in contexts like orders or control. Singular: "mi hombre" (my man / my husband in some contexts).
target_language_example: Mis hombres ya están buscando al sospechoso.
native_language_example: My men are already looking for the suspect.

additional_notes: Uses the possessive adjective "mis" (my) with the plural noun "libros" (books). It agrees in number: "mi libro" (singular) vs. "mis libros" (plural). Often contrasted with other possessives: "tus libros" (your books), "sus libros" (his/her/their books), or with the possessive pronouns "los míos/los tuyos/los suyos" (mine/yours/his-hers-theirs).
target_language_example: No encuentro mis libros; ¿los viste?
native_language_example: I can’t find my books; did you see them?

additional_notes:
Literal meaning: your own hands (body part): "Mis manos están temblando" (My hands are shaking). It also appears in common expressions: 
- "(No) está en mis manos" = "It’s (not) in my hands" / "(I) can’t do anything about it".
- "De mis manos" can mean "from my hands" (someone took something away from you).
target_language_example: Lo siento, pero la decisión final no está en mis manos.
native_language_example: I’m sorry, but the final decision isn’t in my hands.

additional_notes: Literally the plural possessive phrase “my eyes.” Used both literally (opening your eyes, something getting in your eyes, seeing through someone’s eyes) and in the common expression “como a las niñas de mis ojos,” meaning “like the apple of my eye” (to protect/care for something very much).
target_language_example: ¡Cuidado! Me entró polvo en mis ojos.
native_language_example: Careful! Dust got into my eyes.

additional_notes: “Mis” means “my” (plural), and “padres” means “parents.” Used to talk about your own parents. If you mean only your father, you’d say “mi padre”; only your mother: “mi madre.”
target_language_example: Mis padres viven cerca de aquí.
native_language_example: My parents live near here.

additional_notes: Possessive phrase: **mis** = “my” (plural), **pies** = “feet” (plural of *pie*). Used for physical descriptions (*Mis pies están fríos*) and in expressions like **bajo mis pies** = “under my feet/beneath my feet.”
target_language_example: Después de caminar mucho, mis pies me duelen.
native_language_example: After walking a lot, my feet hurt.

additional_notes: Used to talk about your emotions, including being hurt or how you feel about someone romantically (e.g., "mis sentimientos por ti" = "my feelings for you"). Often appears with verbs like importar (to matter), hablar de (to talk about), cambiar (to change), saber de (to know about), and herir (to hurt).
target_language_example: Necesito que respetes mis sentimientos.
native_language_example: I need you to respect my feelings.

additional_notes: Refers to dreams you have while sleeping or your hopes/aspirations for the future. It uses the possessive adjective "mis" (my) with the plural noun "sueños" (dreams). In phrases like "hacer realidad mis sueños", it means goals/wishes coming true.
target_language_example: Quiero cumplir mis sueños algún día.
native_language_example: I want to achieve my dreams someday.

additional_notes: Used to talk about shoes that belong to you. It’s the plural possessive: mi (my) → mis (my, plural) + zapatos (shoes). Often appears as a full sentence in context (e.g., pointing: “Mis zapatos.” = “My shoes.”).
target_language_example: ¿Has visto mis zapatos?
native_language_example: Have you seen my shoes?

additional_notes: Used when someone in authority (a boss, officer, commander, etc.) is giving commands that must be followed. Common with verbs like **recibir** (to receive), **seguir** (to follow), **obedecer** (to obey), and **hacer caso a** (to pay attention to). In more formal or military-style speech you may also hear **a mis órdenes** meaning “at your service / ready to obey.”
target_language_example: Quiero que sigas mis órdenes al pie de la letra.
native_language_example: I want you to follow my orders exactly.

additional_notes: Used to say two people/things are in, going to, or coming from an identical location. Very often appears with the article: "el mismo lugar" (to the same place / in the same place).
target_language_example: Nos vemos en el mismo lugar de siempre.
native_language_example: See you at the same place as always.

meaning: "moment of truth" (the decisive moment when you find out what’s really true or whether something will work).
additional_notes: Used when results are about to be revealed or a crucial test/decision is happening: an exam result, trying a plan, giving a presentation, asking an important question, etc. Often appears with verbs like "llegó" (it arrived) or "es" (it is): "Llegó el momento de la verdad."
target_language_example: Llegó el momento de la verdad: vamos a ver si el coche arranca.
native_language_example: The moment of truth has arrived: let’s see if the car starts.

additional_notes: Commonly used when talking about coin collecting (coleccionar monedas antiguas). "Monedas" = coins; "antiguas" = old/ancient (feminine plural to match "monedas"). Depending on context, it can mean historical coins or just old coins.
target_language_example: Mi abuelo colecciona monedas antiguas desde hace años.
native_language_example: My grandpa has been collecting old coins for years.

meaning: to starve (to death); to be extremely hungry.
additional_notes: Literally “to die of hunger.” It can be used literally (lack of food, potentially life-threatening) or more loosely/hyperbolically depending on context. Common with estar a punto de (“to be about to”): estar a punto de morir de hambre.
target_language_example: Sus hijos están a punto de morir de hambre.
native_language_example: Their children are about to starve to death.

additional_notes: Used to talk about a large quantity of water (for drinking, watering plants, or describing how much water there is somewhere). It’s the feminine form: mucha + agua (agua is feminine, but takes el in singular: el agua; in plural: las aguas). You can also use it in questions: ¿Hay mucha agua?
target_language_example: No hay mucha agua en la botella, pero podemos comprar más.
native_language_example: There isn’t much water in the bottle, but we can buy more.

additional_notes: Common way to say there are many people. It can be used as the subject or object of a sentence (e.g., “Mucha gente viene…” / “Veo a mucha gente…”). You’ll also see it in plural as “muchas gentes,” but “mucha gente” is the most common.
target_language_example: En verano, hay mucha gente en la playa.
native_language_example: In summer, there are lots of people at the beach.

additional_notes: Used to talk about having been lucky (tener/tener + mucha suerte) or to wish someone luck (desear + mucha suerte). As a standalone phrase ("Mucha suerte."), it’s a common way to say “Good luck.”
target_language_example: ¡Mucha suerte en tu examen!
native_language_example: Good luck on your exam!

additional_notes: Used to talk about a large number of things in general. "Muchas" agrees with the plural feminine noun "cosas". Often followed by "para" + infinitive to mean "many things to (do/see/etc.)": "muchas cosas para hacer".
target_language_example: Todavía tengo muchas cosas que hacer hoy.
native_language_example: I still have many things to do today.

additional_notes: Used to say someone has faced or is facing many problems/challenges. Often appears with verbs like superar (to overcome) and pasar por (to go through). Usually refers to serious obstacles (life, work, health, etc.).
target_language_example: Hemos tenido muchas dificultades, pero seguimos adelante.
native_language_example: We’ve had many difficulties, but we’re moving forward.

additional_notes: A very common, polite way to say “thank you” with extra emphasis. Often followed by: “por + noun/infinitive” (Muchas gracias por venir = “Thanks a lot for coming”) or “a + person” (Muchas gracias a todos = “Thank you very much, everyone”). Also used directly when addressing someone: “Muchas gracias, profesor.”
target_language_example: Muchas gracias por tu ayuda.
native_language_example: Thank you very much for your help.

additional_notes: Use this to thank someone for a specific thing or action. It’s followed by a noun (Muchas gracias por la cena), a pronoun (por esto), or an infinitive/perfect infinitive to thank for an action (por llamar, por haberme invitado). In formal situations you may use "su" (Muchas gracias por su ayuda).
target_language_example: Muchas gracias por venir tan rápido.
native_language_example: Thank you very much for coming so quickly.

meaning: many people; a lot of people.
additional_notes: Plural phrase used to talk about a large number of people in general or in a place/event. It often comes at the beginning of the sentence as the subject ("Muchas personas..."), or after a verb to say an event attracted/required many people ("atrajo a muchas personas", "se requieren muchas personas"). "Muchas" agrees in gender/number with the noun (many = "muchos/muchas").
target_language_example: Muchas personas quieren un trabajo mejor.
native_language_example: Many people want a better job.

additional_notes: Used to say that someone has (or is asking) many questions. It often implies curiosity, but depending on tone it can also suggest someone is asking too many or being a bit interrogative. In Spanish you can also say “tengo muchas preguntas” (I have a lot of questions) or “hacer muchas preguntas” (to ask a lot of questions).
target_language_example: Antes de empezar, tengo muchas preguntas.
native_language_example: Before we start, I have a lot of questions.

additional_notes: Used to say something happens repeatedly. It can go at the beginning or end of the sentence ("Muchas veces..." / "...muchas veces").
target_language_example: He visto esa película muchas veces.
native_language_example: I’ve seen that movie many times.

additional_notes: Used to say something is true to a high degree (mucho) and then add a limitation or exception with pero. The comma often matches a pause in speech: "Te quiero mucho, pero…". You can use it with verbs (te quiero, me gusta), reactions (me asustaste), or what someone can do/knows (puedo hacer, sé).
target_language_example: Me gusta mucho, pero es demasiado caro.
native_language_example: I like it a lot, but it’s too expensive.

additional_notes: Used to emphasize that something happened significantly earlier than another time/event. Often followed by “de” + infinitive or noun (“mucho antes de conocernos”), and it can also appear in comparisons with “de lo que…” (“mucho antes de lo que creéis” = much sooner/earlier than you think).
target_language_example: Llegamos mucho antes de que empezara la reunión.
native_language_example: We arrived much earlier than the meeting started.

meaning: 'a lot / very much' (used with *echar de menos* = 'to miss').
additional_notes: You’ll most often hear this as **echar mucho de menos**: *Te echo mucho de menos* = “I miss you a lot.” The key expression is **echar de menos** (“to miss”); **mucho** intensifies it. Word order is usually *echar* + (object pronoun) + *mucho de menos*: *Te echamos mucho de menos*.
target_language_example: Echo mucho de menos a mi familia.
native_language_example: I miss my family a lot.

additional_notes: Used to strongly intensify a comparison. Common with "que" to compare two people/things: "mucho mejor que..." (= much better than...). You can also use it without "que" when the comparison is implied: "Estoy mucho mejor" (= I’m much better).
target_language_example: Con este mapa, llegaremos mucho mejor.
native_language_example: With this map, we’ll get there much better.

additional_notes: Used to compare two things, people, or moments in time. It can compare with another noun/pronoun (Mucho mejor que ella), with time expressions like antes/ayer/la última vez, or in set phrases like mucho mejor que antes (“much better than before”). In sentences like “sabe mucho mejor que…”, saber means “to taste,” not “to know.”
target_language_example: Con esta medicina me siento mucho mejor que ayer.
native_language_example: With this medicine I feel much better than yesterday.

additional_notes: Often used to intensify a negative statement: “not X, much less Y” (Y is even harder/less likely). Common patterns: “no…, y mucho menos …” / “no…, mucho menos …”. It can also mean simply “much less/a lot less” with verbs like gastar, trabajar, estudiar.
target_language_example: No puedo pagar el alquiler, y mucho menos comprar una casa.
native_language_example: I can’t pay the rent, much less buy a house.

additional_notes: Used to make a comparison (more than expected/than something else). Often followed by a comparison phrase like “de lo que…” (than what…). Example pattern: “X vale/cuesta/es mucho más (de lo que…)”.
target_language_example: Este hotel es mucho más caro de lo que pensaba.
native_language_example: This hotel is much more expensive than I thought.

meaning: "a lot to me"; "means a lot to me."
additional_notes: Used to express that someone/something is very important or valuable to you, often with verbs like "significar" (to mean) or "valer" (to be worth). The verb changes with tense/person: "significa" (means), "significó" (meant), "vale" (is worth).
target_language_example: Gracias por tu ayuda; significa mucho para mí.
native_language_example: Thanks for your help; it means a lot to me.

additional_notes: Means a large amount of money. "Mucho" agrees in gender/number with the noun: "mucho dinero" (money is treated as singular masculine), but "muchas" + feminine plural nouns (e.g., "muchas cosas"). Often used after verbs like "tener" (to have), "ganar" (to earn/win), "costar" (to cost), and "deber" (to owe).
target_language_example: Necesito mucho dinero para pagar el alquiler.
native_language_example: I need a lot of money to pay the rent.

meaning: “Nice to meet you.”; also “good taste” (in art/style/choices).
additional_notes: Most commonly used as a polite greeting when you meet someone (often short for “Mucho gusto en conocerte”). You can also use it literally to talk about someone’s taste: “tener mucho gusto” = to have good taste. In that sense, it’s about preferences/style, not pleasure.
target_language_example: Encantado, mucho gusto. ¿Cómo te llamas?
native_language_example: Nice to meet you. What’s your name?

meaning: a lot of fear; very afraid.
additional_notes: Used to intensify fear. Common patterns: (1) "tener mucho miedo (de + noun/verb)" = to be very afraid (of): "Tengo mucho miedo de volar." (2) "dar mucho miedo" = to scare someone a lot / to really frighten someone: "Las serpientes me dan mucho miedo." With "dar miedo", the thing causing fear is the subject; the person afraid is an indirect object (me/te/le/nos/les).
target_language_example: Los truenos me dan mucho miedo por la noche.
native_language_example: Thunder really scares me at night.

additional_notes: Used to say something is very noisy. Often with verbs like hacer (to make): “Hace mucho ruido” = “It makes a lot of noise.” You can also use it to explain why you can’t hear/understand: “Hay mucho ruido aquí” = “There’s a lot of noise here.”
target_language_example: No puedo concentrarme; hay mucho ruido en la calle.
native_language_example: I can’t concentrate; there’s a lot of noise in the street.

additional_notes: Used to talk about either the amount of time spent on something or a long duration. In natural English, it often becomes 'a lot of time' or 'for a long time' depending on the sentence.
target_language_example: Paso mucho tiempo estudiando español.
native_language_example: I spend a lot of time studying Spanish.

additional_notes: Used to say there is a large amount of work to do. It can refer to being busy at a job (Tenemos mucho trabajo) or to effort required in general (Necesita mucho trabajo). Common patterns: “hay mucho trabajo” (there’s a lot of work), “tener mucho trabajo” (to have a lot of work), “mucho trabajo por delante” (a lot of work ahead), and “causar/ahorrar mucho trabajo” (to cause/save a lot of work).
target_language_example: Esta semana tengo mucho trabajo, así que no puedo salir.
native_language_example: This week I have a lot of work, so I can’t go out.

additional_notes: Used to say someone still needs to learn a lot (often with todavía/aún = “still”). The structure is “mucho” + “que” + infinitive (aprender), meaning “a lot to [verb]”: e.g., mucho que hacer (a lot to do), mucho que decir (a lot to say). You can add “de” + person/thing: Tengo mucho que aprender de ti (“I have a lot to learn from you”).
target_language_example: Todavía tenemos mucho que aprender.
native_language_example: We still have a lot to learn.

meaning: “a lot to do” / “many things to do.”
additional_notes: Used to say you’re busy or have many tasks ahead. Often appears with tener (“to have”): Tengo/Tienes/Tenemos mucho que hacer. It can also be used with hay (“there is/are”): Hay mucho que hacer. Also common with time words like hoy (“today”).
target_language_example: No puedo salir ahora; tengo mucho que hacer.
native_language_example: I can’t go out now; I have a lot to do.

additional_notes: "Muchos" agrees in gender and number with the noun (muchos amigos, muchas amigas). Often used with the verb "tener" (to have): "Tengo muchos amigos." You can also say "hacer amigos" (to make friends) or "hacer muchos amigos" (to make many friends).
target_language_example: En la universidad hice muchos amigos.
native_language_example: In college I made many friends.

additional_notes: Used to talk about a long period of time, often with verbs like pasar (to pass) or llevar (to have been doing something for). It agrees in gender and number: muchos años (masc. plural); manyas would be muchos años anyway because año is masculine.
target_language_example: Viví en México muchos años.
native_language_example: I lived in Mexico for many years.

additional_notes: Used to talk about a large number of students (plural). You can place it before the verb as the subject ("Muchos estudiantes están...") or after "a" with an indirect object pronoun to mean "to many students" ("A muchos estudiantes les gusta..."). "Muchos" must match the noun: muchos estudiantes (masculine plural); muchas estudiantes (feminine plural).
target_language_example: Muchos estudiantes estudian en la biblioteca después de clase.
native_language_example: Many students study in the library after class.

additional_notes: "Muchos" agrees with the noun: muchos (masculine plural) + libros. You can use it after verbs like tener (to have), comprar (to buy), leer (to read), or with hay to say something exists: "Hay muchos libros...". For feminine nouns, it changes to "muchas" (e.g., "muchas revistas").
target_language_example: En mi casa hay muchos libros, pero no tengo tiempo para leerlos.
native_language_example: In my house there are many books, but I don’t have time to read them.

additional_notes: Used to say there are many children in a place (hay/había muchos niños...). With "tener" (tiene muchos niños), it means "to have many children" (to be the parent of many kids). "Muchos" agrees with the plural masculine noun "niños"; if it’s all girls, you can say "muchas niñas".
target_language_example: En esta escuela hay muchos niños.
native_language_example: There are many children at this school.

additional_notes: Plural phrase: "muchos" (many, masculine plural) + "países" (countries). Common after verbs like "hay" (there are) and with phrases like "en muchos países" (in many countries) or "de muchos países" (from many countries).
target_language_example: Esta costumbre existe en muchos países.
native_language_example: This tradition exists in many countries.

additional_notes: Used to say that someone has lots of difficulties or issues. Often appears with tener (to have): “tener muchos problemas.” Can also be followed by de + noun (“problemas de planificación” = planning problems) or con + noun (“problemas con sus dientes” = problems with her teeth).
target_language_example: Últimamente tengo muchos problemas en el trabajo.
native_language_example: Lately I’ve been having a lot of problems at work.

additional_notes: A very strong, enthusiastic way to say thanks. Common in both formal and informal situations. Often followed by something like "de verdad" (really) or "por..." (for...).
target_language_example: Muchísimas gracias por la ayuda.
native_language_example: Thanks a lot for the help.

additional_notes: Often used as an exaggeration to mean “really hungry.” It agrees with the person: muerto (male) / muerta (female). You can also hear “medio muerto de hambre” = “half-starved,” often describing someone who looks underfed or very thin.
target_language_example: Después del viaje, yo estaba muerto de hambre y pedí pizza.
native_language_example: After the trip, I was starving and ordered pizza.

additional_notes: A fixed pairing meaning “women and children,” often used when talking about a group of people (e.g., victims, evacuees). In Spanish it’s common to omit the article in lists or general statements (“Mujeres y niños…”), though you may also hear “las mujeres y los niños” when referring to specific people.
target_language_example: Primero evacuaron a mujeres y niños.
native_language_example: They evacuated women and children first.

meaning: the real world (everyday life, outside of fantasy/online/a protected environment).
additional_notes: Used to contrast real life with an imaginary world, a virtual/online space, or a sheltered environment (like school). Often appears with “en el mundo real” (“in the real world”) and in expressions like “volver/al mundo real” (“to return to the real world”) or “te veo en el mundo real” (“see you in real life”).
target_language_example: Cuando termine la universidad, tendré que enfrentarme al mundo real.
native_language_example: When I finish university, I’ll have to face the real world.

additional_notes: “Murió” is the past tense (preterite) of *morir* (“to die”) for él/ella/usted. Use **morir de + illness/cause** to say what someone died from: *murió de cáncer*, *murió de un infarto*. You can specify the type: **cáncer de + body part** (e.g., *cáncer de estómago*). For plural or other persons: *morí* (I died), *murieron* (they died).
target_language_example: Mi tía murió de cáncer hace dos años.
native_language_example: My aunt died of cancer two years ago.

additional_notes: Used to say where (or sometimes when) someone died. "Murió" is the preterite (simple past) form of "morir" for él/ella/usted (he/she/you formal): "murió" = "(he/she) died." Often followed by a place ("murió en Madrid") or a year/time period ("murió en 1998").
target_language_example: Mi abuelo murió en 2010.
native_language_example: My grandfather died in 2010.

murió en un accidente de tránsito

target_language_multi_word_term: murió en un accidente de tránsito
additional_notes: Used to state that someone’s cause of death was a road/traffic accident. It’s neutral in tone and often used in news or serious contexts. The subject can change (e.g., *Mi amigo murió...*, *Murieron...*). In Spain, you’ll also commonly hear *accidente de tráfico* instead of *accidente de tránsito*.
target_language_example: Lamentablemente, el actor murió en un accidente de tránsito.
native_language_example: Sadly, the actor died in a traffic accident.

additional_notes: "Murió" is the simple past (pretérito) of "morir" for he/she/you-formal: "murió" = "he/she died." "Hace + time" expresses how long ago something happened: "hace tres años" = "three years ago." You can replace the time: "murió hace dos días" (died two days ago), "murió hace mucho" (died a long time ago).
target_language_example: Mi perro murió hace tres años.
native_language_example: My dog died three years ago.

additional_notes: You repeat "muy" to strongly intensify an adjective or adverb. In writing it’s often separated by commas ("muy, muy"), and in speech it’s said with emphasis. You can repeat it more times for even stronger emphasis ("muy, muy, muy importante").
target_language_example: Estoy muy, muy cansado hoy.
native_language_example: I’m very, very tired today.

additional_notes: Used to say something happens with high frequency. It commonly goes near the verb (before or after it): “La llamo muy a menudo” / “Muy a menudo voy a esquiar.” You can negate it with “no” to mean “not very often.”
target_language_example: Muy a menudo llego tarde al trabajo.
native_language_example: Very often I arrive late to work.

additional_notes: Used to say someone has good luck or is in a favorable situation. It can describe a person (Eres muy afortunado) or an event/situation (un encuentro muy afortunado). You can change the gender/number: muy afortunada, muy afortunados, muy afortunadas.
target_language_example: Me siento muy afortunado de tener amigos como ustedes.
native_language_example: I feel very lucky to have friends like you.

additional_notes: Used to describe experiences, places, weather, or people as pleasant/enjoyable. Often used politely about someone ("Es una persona muy agradable") or about an event/visit ("Fue muy agradable hablar contigo").
target_language_example: Fue muy agradable conocerte.
native_language_example: It was very nice to meet you.

additional_notes: Used to describe someone’s kind, polite, or helpful behavior. Often said directly to a person as a compliment (“Eres muy amable.”) or as a polite way to thank someone (“Gracias, ha sido muy amable.” / “Muy amable por su parte.”). “Amable” is also used for being courteous (e.g., in customer service).
target_language_example: Muchas gracias; es usted muy amable.
native_language_example: Thank you very much; you’re very kind.

meaning: “very kind of (someone) to …” / “that’s very kind of you.”
additional_notes: Used to thank someone politely for doing something or offering help. It’s often followed by a person or phrase like: “Muy amable de tu parte” (That’s very kind of you) or “Muy amable de usted” (very kind of you—formal). You can also add an infinitive: “Muy amable de tu parte ayudarme” (Very kind of you to help me).
target_language_example: Es muy amable de tu parte ayudarme con esto.
native_language_example: It’s very kind of you to help me with this.

additional_notes: A polite, somewhat formal way to thank someone for a favor, help, or a nice gesture. Uses the formal “su” (you, formal), so it’s common with strangers, customers, older people, or in professional settings. Often said on its own, or after “Gracias”: “Gracias, muy amable de su parte.”
target_language_example: —Le guardé un asiento. —Gracias, muy amable de su parte.
native_language_example: —I saved you a seat. —Thank you, that’s very kind of you.

additional_notes: Used to describe people’s behavior as kind, polite, or helpful. Often appears after a form of "ser" (son/fueron/han sido): "Son muy amables" = "They are very kind." It can also be said by itself as a brief polite comment (e.g., after someone helps you): "Muy amables."
target_language_example: Muchas gracias por su ayuda; han sido muy amables.
native_language_example: Thank you very much for your help; you’ve been very kind.

additional_notes: Usually means 'very well' and can also mean 'very good' in English depending on the verb: Suena muy bien = 'That sounds very good.' With verbs like conocer, it means doing or knowing something very well. With clothing or appearance, te queda muy bien means 'it suits you very well' or 'it looks great on you.' At the start of a sentence, Muy bien can also be a conversational phrase meaning 'all right' or 'very well' before continuing.
target_language_example: Hablas español muy bien.
native_language_example: You speak Spanish very well.

meaning: “Alright/OK, but…” (agreement followed by an objection or condition).
additional_notes: Used to acknowledge what someone said (“muy bien” = OK/fine) and then introduce a limitation, disagreement, or next requirement with “pero” (but). Common in conversation to soften a contradiction. You’ll often hear it at the start of a reply.
target_language_example: Muy bien, pero primero necesito tu dirección.
native_language_example: Alright, but first I need your address.

additional_notes: Used to describe a feminine noun (or a woman/girl) as very pretty/beautiful. It agrees in gender and number: muy bonito (masc.), muy bonitos / muy bonitas (plural). Can describe people, things, places, or qualities like handwriting: “una letra muy bonita”. With people you’ll also hear “Qué bonita” or “Te ves muy bonita” (“You look very pretty”).
target_language_example: Tu casa es muy bonita.
native_language_example: Your house is very pretty.

meaning: very pretty; very nice; really beautiful
additional_notes: Used to say something is especially attractive or pleasant. It can describe places, views, objects, or gestures (e.g., Un gesto muy bonito). With actions like singing, it means “very nicely/beautifully” (e.g., Estabas cantando muy bonito). Note: in Spanish, adjectives agree in gender/number, so you may also see “muy bonita/muy bonitos/muy bonitas” depending on the noun.
target_language_example: Es un lugar muy bonito.
native_language_example: It’s a very beautiful place.

additional_notes: Used with feminine plural nouns. Buenas is the feminine plural form of bueno, so it matches nouns like ideas, comidas, or carreteras. Compare: muy bueno (masculine singular), muy buena (feminine singular), muy buenos (masculine plural).
target_language_example: Tus ideas son muy buenas.
native_language_example: Your ideas are very good.

additional_notes: Used to strongly praise a person, thing, or situation. It agrees in gender/number with the noun it describes: muy bueno (masc. sing.), muy buena (fem. sing.), muy buenos (masc. plural), muy buenas (fem. plural). With verbs like ser/estar: Es muy bueno. / Está muy bueno (often means “it tastes really good”; when talking about a person, it can also mean “really attractive” in some contexts).
target_language_example: Eres un niño muy bueno.
native_language_example: You are a very good boy.

additional_notes: Used to describe multiple people or things as high quality or strongly positive. It agrees in number/gender with the noun: muy buenos (masc. plural) / muy buenas (fem. plural). Often used with nouns like recuerdos (memories), maestros (teachers), fideos (noodles), géneros (fabrics).
target_language_example: Esos restaurantes son muy buenos.
native_language_example: Those restaurants are very good.

additional_notes: Used with estar or parecer to describe how someone feels/looks right now: "Estoy muy cansado" (I’m very tired), "Pareces muy cansado" (You look very tired). Agree in gender/number: muy cansado (masc. sing.), muy cansada (fem. sing.), muy cansados/cansadas (plural).
target_language_example: Hoy estoy muy cansado.
native_language_example: Today I’m very tired.

additional_notes: Used to talk about physical distance (Muy cerca de + place: “very close to…”) or being close to reaching a goal (“We’re very close”). It can also be used by itself as an adverbial phrase (“Muy cerca, ya.” = “Very close now/almost there.”).
target_language_example: Estamos muy cerca de la estación.
native_language_example: We’re very close to the station.

additional_notes: Used to emphasize that something is not the same as before or not the same as something/someone else. Often followed by "de" to compare: "muy diferente de..." (very different from...). It can describe people, places, situations, or how someone looks ("Luzco muy diferente").
target_language_example: Este restaurante es muy diferente de los demás.
native_language_example: This restaurant is very different from the others.

additional_notes: Used to intensify the adjective difícil (“difficult/hard”) with muy (“very”). It describes tasks, situations, or experiences that are hard to do or deal with. You can also use it with other adjectives in the same pattern (muy importante, muy fácil, etc.).
target_language_example: Fue muy difícil tomar esa decisión.
native_language_example: It was very difficult to make that decision.

additional_notes: Used to describe something as highly entertaining or enjoyable. Can be said on its own ("Muy divertido.") or with ser ("Es/Fue/Será muy divertido"). "Divertido" changes to agree with the noun it describes (divertida, divertidos, divertidas), but the fixed term here is the masculine singular form "muy divertido."
target_language_example: Ha sido muy divertido.
native_language_example: It has been very fun.

meaning: very hard (a lot); very hard/strongly (with impact).
additional_notes: "Muy" intensifies "duro". With verbs like trabajar/estudiar, it means putting in a lot of effort ("work/study very hard"). With verbs like golpear/caer, it means with great force ("hit very hard"). It can also describe something physically hard (e.g., "La cama es muy dura" = "The bed is very hard/firm").
target_language_example: Tengo un examen mañana, así que estoy estudiando muy duro.
native_language_example: I have an exam tomorrow, so I’m studying very hard.

additional_notes: Used to emphasize that something or someone stands out as particularly important or different in a positive way. Often describes events (una noche muy especial), people/groups, or a purpose/role in life. In conversation you can also say it alone (“Muy especial.”) as a short, emphatic comment.
target_language_example: Para mí, este día es muy especial.
native_language_example: For me, this day is very special.

additional_notes: Used to describe something that feels unusual, odd, or hard to explain (a situation, sound, dream, person, moment, etc.). "Extraño" can also mean "foreign" or "I miss" (as in "Te extraño") in other contexts, but in this phrase it means "strange/weird." Note: Spanish adjectives agree in gender/number; you’ll also see "muy extraña" (feminine) and "muy extraños/extrañas" (plural).
target_language_example: Esto es muy extraño.
native_language_example: This is very strange.

additional_notes: “Muy” is an adverb meaning “very.” “Felices” is the plural form of “feliz” (happy) and is used with plural subjects (nosotros/nosotras, ellos/ellas, ustedes, etc.). You’ll often see it after verbs like ser, estar, parecer, or verse: “Somos/Estamos/Parecen/Se ven muy felices.”
target_language_example: Mis amigos y yo estamos muy felices hoy.
native_language_example: My friends and I are very happy today.

additional_notes: Used with adjectives to mean “very strong” (e.g., a strong wind, a strong person/animal). With verbs it often means “very hard/intensely,” describing how something is done: soplar muy fuerte = “to blow very hard,” abrazar/besar muy fuerte = “to hug/kiss very tightly.”
target_language_example: Agárralo muy fuerte para que no se caiga.
native_language_example: Hold it very tightly so it doesn’t fall.

additional_notes: Used to emphasize that something is easy. With verbs like "ser" or "parecer," it describes how easy something is: "Fue muy fácil" (It was very easy). In phrases like "Lo tiene muy fácil," it means someone has it easy / is in a very easy situation. "Ponerlo muy fácil" means to make it very easy for someone (often by simplifying things or helping).
target_language_example: Con esta guía, el examen será muy fácil.
native_language_example: With this guide, the exam will be very easy.

additional_notes: Used to intensify size/extent: "muy" (very) + "grande" (big/large). It can describe physical size (un cuarto muy grande, un país muy grande) or more general magnitude. In some contexts it can imply something figurative or important (e.g., "Te debo una muy grande" = "I owe you a big one / a big favor" for helping me out).
target_language_example: Ese perro es muy grande, pero es muy tranquilo.
native_language_example: That dog is very big, but it’s very calm.

additional_notes: “Guapa” is the feminine form of “guapo” and is used to compliment a girl or woman on her looks (pretty/attractive). It agrees with the person described: “muy guapa” (female), “muy guapo” (male). You can use it with “ser/estar” (e.g., “Ella es…” / “Estás…”).
target_language_example: ¡Qué vestido tan bonito! Estás muy guapa hoy.
native_language_example: What a nice dress! You look very pretty today.

meaning: "very beautiful" (talking about a woman or feminine noun).
additional_notes: Muy = “very” and hermosa = “beautiful” in the feminine form. Use it to compliment a woman/girl (“Eres muy hermosa”) or to describe a feminine noun (“La casa es muy hermosa”). For a man/masculine noun, use “muy hermoso”.
target_language_example: La playa es muy hermosa al atardecer.
native_language_example: The beach is very beautiful at sunset.

additional_notes: Used to strongly emphasize that something matters a lot. "Muy" intensifies the adjective "importante"; it can be repeated for extra emphasis ("muy, muy importante"). It agrees with the noun only in number: "muy importante" (singular), "muy importantes" (plural).
target_language_example: Es muy importante llegar a tiempo.
native_language_example: It’s very important to arrive on time.

additional_notes: Used to strongly describe a person, animal, or idea as smart. It goes before the adjective: muy + adjective (muy inteligente, muy interesante, etc.). Often said as a compliment: Eres muy inteligente. Note the different forms of “you are” in the examples: ella es…, tú eres…, vos sos… (common in Argentina/Uruguay), vosotros sois… (Spain).
target_language_example: Tu hermana es muy inteligente y aprende rápido.
native_language_example: Your sister is very intelligent and learns quickly.

additional_notes: Used to emphasize that something is interesting. "Muy" is an intensifier meaning "very" and goes before adjectives like "interesante." You can use it to describe things (a book, a movie, a class, a person’s idea).
target_language_example: La clase de hoy fue muy interesante.
native_language_example: Today's class was very interesting.

additional_notes: Used to describe someone’s age or how young they look/are considered. Often followed by "para" + infinitive to say someone is too young to do something ("muy joven para viajar solo").
target_language_example: Eres muy joven para conducir.
native_language_example: You’re too young to drive.

additional_notes: Used to say someone isn’t old/mature/experienced enough for an action or situation. Structure: "ser/parecer + muy joven para + infinitive" (Ella es muy joven para casarse) or "muy joven para + eso/esto" (Eres muy joven para eso).
target_language_example: Creo que soy muy joven para tomar una decisión tan grande.
native_language_example: I think I’m too young to make such a big decision.

additional_notes: Used to talk about distance in space (physically far away) and sometimes figuratively to mean achieving a lot or going a long way ("llegar muy lejos"). Often follows verbs like estar/queda (location), venir (origin), and llegar (progress). You may also see it with de: "No está muy lejos de..." = "It’s not very far from...".
target_language_example: El restaurante no está muy lejos de aquí.
native_language_example: The restaurant isn’t very far from here.

additional_notes: Used to describe a female person or a feminine noun (e.g., una chica, una hija) as very pretty or nice. It’s the feminine form of “muy lindo”; plural is “muy lindas.” Often said alone as a short compliment: “Muy linda.”
target_language_example: Tu hija es muy linda.
native_language_example: Your daughter is very pretty.

meaning: very nice; very pretty; really sweet (about someone).
additional_notes: Used to compliment people, things, places, moments, or events. With people it often means “really sweet/cute/kind” (tone depends on context). It can also be used alone as a reaction (“Muy lindo.” = “Very nice.”). Common structure: ser + muy lindo/a (Es muy lindo. / Eres muy linda.).
target_language_example: Gracias por venir; fue muy lindo verte.
native_language_example: Thanks for coming; it was really nice to see you.

additional_notes: Used (1) to say something is really wrong/bad: "Esto está muy mal" = "This is very wrong/bad." (2) with verbs to mean you do something poorly: "Hablo muy mal" = "I speak very badly." (3) with sentirse/estar to say you feel unwell or emotionally terrible: "Me siento muy mal". It can also sound like a warning about a negative outcome: "Te va a ir muy mal" = "Things will go very badly for you."
target_language_example: Después de comer, me sentí muy mal.
native_language_example: After eating, I felt very sick.

additional_notes: Used to say you don’t have time to do something. "Ocupado" often means "busy" in Spanish (e.g., with work or plans), even though it looks like English "occupied".
target_language_example: Lo siento, hoy estoy muy ocupado.
native_language_example: Sorry, today I’m very busy.

meaning: very proud of you (said by a woman).
additional_notes: “Orgullosa” agrees with the speaker (female). A male speaker would say “muy orgulloso de ti.” Used to praise or congratulate someone for what they did or who they are. You can also change “ti” to another person: “de él/ella/usted/nosotros.”
target_language_example: Estoy muy orgullosa de ti por todo tu esfuerzo.
native_language_example: I’m very proud of you for all your effort.

additional_notes: Used to describe a person, thing, situation, or activity that could cause serious harm or risk. It can modify a noun ("un hombre muy peligroso") or be used after the verb ser/estar ("es muy peligroso").
target_language_example: Es muy peligroso nadar aquí por la corriente.
native_language_example: It’s very dangerous to swim here because of the current.

meaning: very little; very few; not much.
additional_notes: "Muy" intensifies "poco". Use it with verbs to mean “hardly / not much” (Se enoja muy poco = He/she rarely gets angry; Come muy poco = He eats very little). With nouns, it means “very little/few” (Tengo muy poco tiempo = I have very little time). With adjectives, "muy poco" can also mean “not very” (Es muy poco común = It’s not very common). In time expressions, "dentro de muy poco" means “very soon / in a short time.”
target_language_example: Nos queda muy poco dinero, así que hoy vamos a gastar muy poco.
native_language_example: We have very little money left, so today we’re going to spend very little.

additional_notes: Used to say something will happen in the near future ("very soon") or that something happened earlier than expected ("quite early"). Often with future tense (Sabrás/Entenderás...) or with past tense to describe quick adaptation or an early event.
target_language_example: Volveré muy pronto.
native_language_example: I’ll be back very soon.

additional_notes: "Raro" can mean either (1) unusual/strange/weird (common with people’s behavior, situations, sounds: "Eso es muy raro", "Me suena muy raro", "Se comporta muy raro") or (2) rare/uncommon (common with objects/materials: "un diamante muy raro"). "Muy" = “very.”
target_language_example: Eso es muy raro.
native_language_example: That is very strange.

additional_notes: "Muy" intensifies an adverb or adjective. With "rápido" it describes the speed of an action (often like English "quickly"): "habla muy rápido", "condujo muy rápido". In everyday speech, Spanish often uses "rápido" as an adverb instead of "rápidamente".
target_language_example: No corras muy rápido, es peligroso.
native_language_example: Don’t run too fast; it’s dangerous.

additional_notes: Used to say something happens later than usual or later than is reasonable/expected. Common with times of day and routines: quedarse afuera/despierto hasta muy tarde (stay out/awake very late), volver a casa muy tarde (come home very late), llamar muy tarde (call very late). Also appears in the expression “Se está haciendo muy tarde” = “It’s getting very late.”
target_language_example: Mañana trabajo temprano, así que no puedo quedarme despierto hasta muy tarde.
native_language_example: I work early tomorrow, so I can’t stay up very late.

additional_notes: Used to intensify the adjective "triste" (sad). Common with "estar" for how someone feels right now: "Estoy muy triste" = "I’m very sad." It can also describe something as sad or depressing: "un espectáculo muy triste".
target_language_example: Me siento muy triste hoy.
native_language_example: I feel very sad today.

additional_notes: "Muy" intensifies the adjective "valiente" (brave). Used to praise someone’s courage, often for doing or saying something difficult. Matches gender/number: "muy valiente" (singular, masculine or feminine), "muy valientes" (plural).
target_language_example: Fuiste muy valiente al hablar en público.
native_language_example: You were very brave to speak in public.

additional_notes: Used to strongly say something is useful or helpful. It often comes after a noun or after the verb ("es/será muy útil"), and it can also be said alone as a short, positive reaction (like “Very useful.”).
target_language_example: Tu consejo fue muy útil.
native_language_example: Your advice was very useful.

additional_notes: A common noun for the figure you build out of snow. Usually used with an article: “un/una muñeco(a) de nieve” or “el muñeco de nieve.”
target_language_example: Hicimos un muñeco de nieve en el parque.
native_language_example: We made a snowman in the park.

additional_notes: A common everyday noun phrase for a device used to sew fabric (make or repair clothes). It’s usually feminine: la máquina de coser; plural: las máquinas de coser. Often used with comprar (to buy), usar (to use), and regalar (to give as a gift).
target_language_example: ¿Tienes una máquina de coser para arreglar este pantalón?
native_language_example: Do you have a sewing machine to fix these pants?

additional_notes: A noun phrase for the machine used to type on paper. Literally “machine to write” (máquina + de + escribir). Often used with articles: la máquina de escribir / una máquina de escribir.
target_language_example: Encontré una máquina de escribir antigua en el ático.
native_language_example: I found an old typewriter in the attic.

additional_notes: A noun phrase for a (usually fictional) machine that lets you travel through time. Often used with articles like “la” or “una”: “la máquina del tiempo” (the time machine), “una máquina del tiempo” (a time machine).
target_language_example: Si tuviera una máquina del tiempo, volvería al pasado.
native_language_example: If I had a time machine, I would go back to the past.

additional_notes: Used for time (later, at a later point) or for location/direction (further ahead on a road/path). Often appears in phrases like "nos vemos más adelante" (see you later) and can be intensified: "un poco más adelante" (a little further ahead).
target_language_example: Hablemos de eso más adelante; ahora no puedo.
native_language_example: Let’s talk about that later; I can’t right now.

meaning: beyond; further than; beyond (in the sense of “more than / exceeding”).
additional_notes: Used for physical location (“beyond X”) and for figurative limits (“beyond description/doubt/measure”). Common fixed phrases: “más allá de toda descripción” = “beyond all description,” “más allá de toda duda” = “beyond any doubt,” “más allá de toda medida” = “beyond measure.”
target_language_example: Su generosidad está más allá de toda duda.
native_language_example: His/Her generosity is beyond any doubt.

additional_notes: Used to talk about going past a physical limit (distance, a line, a floor, the horizon) or past an abstract limit (ability, understanding, contempt). It often implies a boundary that cannot be reached or is exceeded. The full phrase is commonly "más allá de" + noun; it changes with the article (del = de + el; de la; de los; de las).
target_language_example: No puedo ver más allá del río.
native_language_example: I can’t see beyond the river.

additional_notes: Comparative structure: más + adjective + que = “more … than.” Use alta with feminine nouns (una mujer, una pared, una temperatura, una torre). With masculine nouns use más alto que, and for plural use más altas que / más altos que. Can refer to physical height (taller) or figurative/abstract “higher.”
target_language_example: Mi casa es más alta que la tuya.
native_language_example: My house is taller/higher than yours.

additional_notes: Used as a comparative with adjectives: más alto = “higher/taller.” It can refer to height (taller person/building) or position/volume (jump higher, speak louder—often also said as “más fuerte”). Common superlatives: “el más alto” = “the tallest (male)” and “lo más alto (que puedas)” = “as high as (you can).”
target_language_example: ¿Puedes hablar más alto, por favor?
native_language_example: Can you speak louder, please?

additional_notes: Comparative and superlative of "barato" (cheap). Use "más barato" to compare two options ("This one is cheaper"), and "el/la más barato/a" to mean "the cheapest" among several (it agrees in gender/number: "la más barata", "los más baratos"). Often used with "sale más barato" = "it works out cheaper / it ends up being cheaper."
target_language_example: Si compras dos, sale más barato.
native_language_example: If you buy two, it works out cheaper.

meaning: "rather" / "more like" (to soften or correct what you mean).
additional_notes: Used to say something is more accurate or closer to the truth than another option (“more of a…”). It often softens a statement: *Es más bien tímido* = “He’s rather shy.” Also used when you’re correcting yourself or choosing a better description: *No es un jefe; es más bien un maestro* (“…more like a teacher”).
target_language_example: No estoy enojado; estoy más bien preocupado.
native_language_example: I’m not angry; I’m more worried.

additional_notes: Comparative of "cercano" (near/close). Used to express greater proximity in space, time, or relationships. Often appears after a noun ("un restaurante más cercano") or with an article to mean "the nearest" (e.g., "el planeta más cercano"). "Lo más cercano" means "the closest thing (to it)" when there isn’t an exact equivalent. Agreement changes with gender/number: "más cercano" (m. sg.), "más cercana" (f. sg.), "más cercanos" (m. pl.), "más cercanas" (f. pl.).
target_language_example: Ese restaurante está lejos; mejor vamos a otro más cercano.
native_language_example: That restaurant is far; we’d better go to another, closer one.

additional_notes: Comparative form of cuidadoso (“careful”). Often used with ser (Sé más cuidadoso…), or with subjunctive after advice/wishes (que sea/fuera/fuese más cuidadoso). You’ll commonly see it followed by: con (“with/about”), en (“in/with what you do”), or cuando + verb (“when you…”).
target_language_example: Por favor, sé más cuidadoso con el vaso; es de vidrio.
native_language_example: Please be more careful with the glass; it’s made of glass.

additional_notes: Usually used with numbers or amounts to indicate a quantity above a limit: más de dos horas = more than two hours. It can also mean more of before a noun or pronoun: más de esto = more of this.
target_language_example: Necesito más de tres días para terminarlo.
native_language_example: I need more than three days to finish it.

additional_notes: Used to say something is excessive (more than what’s appropriate or advisable). Common with verbs like hablar (talk), dormir (sleep), comer (eat), beber (drink). In contexts like "ya ha tenido más de la cuenta", it often means someone has had too much to drink.
target_language_example: No comas más de la cuenta, luego te va a doler el estómago.
native_language_example: Don’t eat too much, or your stomach will hurt later.

additional_notes: Used to compare an amount, degree, or extent with a clause introduced by “lo que” (“what/that which”). Common pattern: “más + (adjective/adverb/verb) + de lo que + clause”. Example: “Te quiero más de lo que crees” = “I love you more than you think.” Often implies a surprise or stronger-than-expected comparison (“more than you imagine/than I know/than she can pay”).
target_language_example: Sé más de lo que dije.
native_language_example: I know more than I said.

meaning: “more than” (what/that) — used to compare amounts or degree.
additional_notes: Used in comparisons to say something is greater than another thing, often introducing a clause with a verb: “más de lo que + verb” (more than I/you/he/she/they + verb). It can be followed by a statement that sets the comparison (sometimes implied): “Más de lo que puedes imaginar” = “More than you can imagine.”
target_language_example: Te quiero más de lo que crees.
native_language_example: I love you more than you think.

additional_notes: Used to ask someone to slow down, especially when speaking (e.g., "Hable/Hablen más despacio"), but also for walking or driving. Often used alone as a short request: "Más despacio." You can soften it with "por favor" or "un poco" (a bit).
target_language_example: ¿Puedes hablar más despacio, por favor?
native_language_example: Can you speak more slowly, please?

meaning: 'more difficult' / 'harder' (also: 'the most difficult' depending on context).
additional_notes: Used for comparisons: "más difícil" = harder than something else (often with "que": "más difícil que..."). With "el/la/lo" it becomes a superlative: "el/la/lo más difícil" = the hardest / most difficult part/thing. Agree "difícil" with gender/number only when it becomes plural: "más difíciles".
target_language_example: Para mí, lo más difícil es levantarme temprano.
native_language_example: For me, the hardest thing is getting up early.

additional_notes: Used after a verb to say someone should put in more effort or intensity, especially with work or studying: “estudiar/trabajar más duro.” You can also hear “más fuerte” or “con más empeño” with a similar idea.
target_language_example: Tengo que entrenar más duro si quiero ganar.
native_language_example: I have to train harder if I want to win.

additional_notes: Comparative form of feliz (“happy”). Use it to compare how happy someone is (often with que: más feliz que… = “happier than…”). Common with verbs like sentirse (“to feel”): sentir(se) más feliz = “to feel happier,” and with verse (“to look/seem”): verse más feliz = “to look happier.”
target_language_example: Desde que cambió de trabajo, está más feliz.
native_language_example: Since he changed jobs, he’s happier.

additional_notes: Comparative form of "fuerte" (strong/loud). Used to compare strength, intensity, or volume: "más fuerte que" = "stronger/louder than." Also common in the pattern "más fuerte de lo que..." = "stronger/more intense than (what) ...".
target_language_example: Habla más fuerte, por favor; no te oigo.
native_language_example: Speak louder, please; I can’t hear you.

additional_notes: Comparative form of grande. Usually refers to physical size: más grande = bigger/larger. For people, it can also mean older or more grown-up. With an article, as in el más grande or la más grande, it often means the biggest/largest.
target_language_example: Necesitamos una mesa más grande.
native_language_example: We need a bigger table.

additional_notes: Used to say something is the largest worldwide. Structure: "el/la/los/las + [noun] + más grande del mundo" (superlative). It agrees in gender/number with the noun: el coche…, la ciudad…, los bancos…, las ciudades…
target_language_example: Barcelona no es la ciudad más grande del mundo, pero es muy bonita.
native_language_example: Barcelona isn’t the biggest city in the world, but it’s very beautiful.

additional_notes: Used to compare something feminine (often a noun like "casa" or "mochila") with something you own. "La mía" means "mine" (feminine singular). The structure is: "más + adjective + que + [possessive pronoun]". If the thing is masculine, you’d say "más grande que el mío"; plural: "los míos / las mías".
target_language_example: Tu casa es más grande que la mía.
native_language_example: Your house is bigger than mine.

additional_notes: Comparative form of "grande" (big/large). Used with "que" to compare two things: "más grandes que..." = "bigger/larger than...". It agrees in gender and number with the noun: "más grande" (sing.), "más grandes" (plural).
target_language_example: Necesitamos zapatos más grandes.
native_language_example: We need bigger shoes.

additional_notes: Used to compare importance: “X es más importante que Y” = “X is more important than Y.” With an article it can express a superlative: “la cosa más importante” = “the most important thing.” The meaning depends on context (comparison vs. superlative).
target_language_example: Para mí, es más importante tu salud que el trabajo.
native_language_example: For me, your health is more important than work.

additional_notes: Used to form the superlative with plural nouns ("the most important ..."). It agrees in number and gender: "más importante" (singular), "más importantes" (plural). Often appears after the noun it describes ("los puntos más importantes").
target_language_example: Tenemos que hablar de las cosas más importantes primero.
native_language_example: We have to talk about the most important things first.

additional_notes:
Used to compare interest level. 
- With a comparison: "más interesante que..." = "more interesting than..." 
- With "de lo que": "más interesante de lo que esperaba" = "more interesting than I expected." 
- With "el/la/lo" it becomes a superlative: "el libro más interesante" = "the most interesting book." 
- Often appears with "cada vez más" to show a change over time: "cada vez más interesante" = "more and more interesting."
target_language_example: La conversación se está volviendo cada vez más interesante.
native_language_example: The conversation is becoming more and more interesting.

additional_notes: Comparative form of "joven" (young): "más joven (que...)" = "younger (than...)". It can describe age or how someone looks: "parece más joven" = "looks younger". Often used with "de lo que" to compare with an expectation: "más joven de lo que piensas" = "younger than you think."
target_language_example: Mi hermano es más joven que yo.
native_language_example: My brother is younger than me.

additional_notes: Used to compare distance or how far something goes (physical or sometimes figurative). Often appears with comparisons like “más lejos que…” (farther than…) and with the superlative: “lo más lejos (posible/que puedas)” = “as far as possible / as far as you can.”
target_language_example: Camina más lejos y luego me llamas.
native_language_example: Walk farther and then call me.

additional_notes: Used to compare two people/things: **más + listo/a/os/as + que + ...**. *Listo* often means “smart/clever” (sometimes “quick-witted”). It agrees with the noun/pronoun being described: *más listo que*, *más lista que*, *más listos que*, *más listas que*.
target_language_example: Tom era más listo que Mary.
native_language_example: Tom was smarter than Mary.

additional_notes: Often written with a comma (“más, más”) in standard punctuation, but it can also appear as “más más” in casual writing or speech transcription. It’s a repeated “más” for emphasis when requesting more of something (food, volume, time, etc.).
target_language_example: ¡Más más, por favor!
native_language_example: More, more, please!

additional_notes: Used to give an approximate amount/time (“about/around”), or to say something is only OK/average (“so-so”). It can go at the beginning, middle, or end of a sentence, and is often set off by commas when it comments on the whole statement.
target_language_example: —¿Cómo estás? —Más o menos.
native_language_example: —How are you? —So-so.

additional_notes: Comparative form of "profundo" (deep). Used to compare depth (literal or figurative): "más profundo que..." = "deeper than...". Often follows a verb like "ir", "llegar" or "cavar": "ir más profundo" (go deeper), "cavar más profundo" (dig deeper). "Profundo" can look like English "profound"; in Spanish it commonly means "deep".
target_language_example: Tenemos que cavar más profundo para encontrar agua.
native_language_example: We have to dig deeper to find water.

additional_notes: Usually used to make comparisons: cuesta más que..., cuenta más que.... In negative expressions like no ... más que, it means 'only' or 'nothing but'.
target_language_example: Este teléfono cuesta más que el otro.
native_language_example: This phone costs more than the other one.

additional_notes: Used to say that something is not enough or that there’s something additional/bigger beyond what was mentioned. Often appears after a statement (Pero es más que eso.) or as a warning (Vas a necesitar más que eso.)
target_language_example: No basta con pedir perdón: es más que eso.
native_language_example: It’s not enough to apologize: it’s more than that.

additional_notes: Used to emphasize that the amount/quality is not just enough, but plenty (sometimes implying “so stop/that’s all we need”). It can stand alone as a short answer (Más que suficiente.) or modify a noun: más que suficiente comida/evidencia/dinero. With people (Eres más que suficiente), it often means “you are enough / you’re more than enough” in an emotional/relationship sense.
target_language_example: No te preocupes: con tres botellas de agua es más que suficiente.
native_language_example: Don’t worry: three bottles of water is more than enough.

additional_notes: Used to compare how much/many or how often someone does/has something, with tú as the comparison point. Common patterns: (verb) + más que tú (Trabajo más que tú = I work more than you); (noun) + más que tú (Tengo diez bolígrafos más que tú = I have ten more pens than you); (me importa/te quiero) + más que tú (+ a mí) for comparisons in feelings (Nadie me importa más que tú = No one matters to me more than you).
target_language_example: Yo estudio más que tú, pero tú duermes más que yo.
native_language_example: I study more than you, but you sleep more than me.

additional_notes: Used in comparisons to say someone has/does something to a greater degree than you. Common with verbs like necesitar (to need) or saber (to know): "Tú lo necesitas más que yo" = "You need it more than I do." In casual speech, "más que yo" is often used instead of the more formal "más que yo lo hago" (more than I do).
target_language_example: Creo que te gusta el café más que yo.
native_language_example: I think you like coffee more than I do.

additional_notes: Used to compare speed: “más rápido que …” = “faster than …”. It can describe how someone/something is (“Es más rápido”) or how an action is done (“Así es más rápido” = “That way it’s faster/quicker”). Superlatives also appear: “el/ la/ los/ las más rápido(s)” = “the fastest” (e.g., “el segundo más rápido” = “the second fastest”).
target_language_example: Si vas por aquí, es más rápido.
native_language_example: If you go this way, it’s faster.

additional_notes: Used to compare speed: *más rápido (que ...)* = “faster (than ...)”. It can modify an action (meaning “more quickly”) or a noun/subject (meaning “faster”). Often used as a command: *¡Más rápido!* = “Faster!” / “Hurry up!”.
target_language_example: Hazlo más rápido que ayer, por favor.
native_language_example: Do it faster than yesterday, please.

additional_notes: Comparative form of "seguro" (safe/secure). Often used with "ser" or "estar": "Es/Está más seguro" = "It’s safer." With "el/la/los/las" it means "the safest" (e.g., "el camino más seguro"). With "lo", it can mean "the safest thing" or, in predictions, "the most likely" ("Lo más seguro es que…" = "Most likely…").
target_language_example: Lo más seguro es que lleguemos tarde si salimos ahora.
native_language_example: Most likely we’ll arrive late if we leave now.

additional_notes: Used to say something will happen at a later time. Common in plans and conversations: "Hablamos más tarde" = "We’ll talk later." It can refer to later the same day or a more general time in the future (e.g., "unos meses más tarde" = "a few months later").
target_language_example: No puedo ahora; lo hago más tarde.
native_language_example: I can't right now; I'll do it later.

additional_notes: Used to compare times or to say something happens earlier than usual (often with "que": "más temprano que nosotros/de costumbre"). Also common in requests like "Ven más temprano" (Come earlier).
target_language_example: Si salimos más temprano, llegaremos a tiempo.
native_language_example: If we leave earlier, we’ll arrive on time.

meaning: "You'd better..." / "It’d be best if..." (a warning or strong advice).
additional_notes: Used to warn someone or strongly recommend an action, often implying consequences if they don’t do it. It commonly introduces a verb in the present subjunctive: "Más vale que te vayas". You can also hear "más vale" + infinitive: "Más vale irse" (It’s better to leave).
target_language_example: Más vale que me llames cuando llegues.
native_language_example: You’d better call me when you get there.

additional_notes: Used to show a gradual increase over time. It often comes before an adjective/adverb ("más y más difícil" = "more and more difficult") or after a verb to emphasize continuing change ("creció más y más" = "he grew more and more").
target_language_example: Cada día me gusta más y más este barrio.
native_language_example: Every day I like this neighborhood more and more.

additional_notes: Usually used in the pattern **(no) tener más alternativa que + infinitive** to express that someone is forced to do something because there are no other options. Very common with **no**: *No tuve más alternativa que…*
target_language_example: No tenemos más alternativa que cancelar el viaje.
native_language_example: We have no choice but to cancel the trip.

additional_notes: Used to talk about an additional amount of money (often meaning “extra” or “a larger amount than before”). Typically follows verbs like conseguir (to get), ganar (to earn), necesitar (to need), or haber (there is/are): “conseguir más dinero”, “tiene que haber más dinero”.
target_language_example: Necesito más dinero para pagar el alquiler.
native_language_example: I need more money to pay the rent.

additional_notes: Used to talk about an increase in the number of people in general (not a specific group). Very common in patterns like: “cada vez más gente...” (more and more people...), “ojalá hubiera más gente como tú” (I wish there were more people like you), and “donde haya más gente” (where there are more people). Note: “gente” is singular in Spanish, so you say “más gente es...” / “más gente tiene...”, not *“más gente son...”*.
target_language_example: En verano hay más gente en la playa.
native_language_example: In the summer there are more people at the beach.

additional_notes: Used to ask for or point someone to additional details (common in signs, emails, websites: “Para más información…” / “Haga clic aquí para más información”). Often used without an article: “más información” (not usually “la más información”).
target_language_example: Si necesitas más información, envíame un correo.
native_language_example: If you need more information, send me an email.

additional_notes: Used in the fixed pattern "(no) tener más opción que + infinitive" to say someone is forced to do something. It’s usually preceded by "no" ("no tengo más opción que...") and followed by an infinitive verb.
target_language_example: No tenemos más opción que esperar.
native_language_example: We have no choice but to wait.

additional_notes: Used to ask for or talk about needing additional time. Common with verbs like necesitar (to need), tener (to have), esperar (to wait), and durar (to last): Necesito más tiempo (I need more time); La reunión duró más tiempo de lo esperado (The meeting lasted longer than expected).
target_language_example: Necesito más tiempo para terminar la tarea.
native_language_example: I need more time to finish the homework.

additional_notes: A genre label used like an uncountable noun: me gusta la música pop (“I like pop music”). You can add an adjective or origin after it (música pop rusa = “Russian pop music”).
target_language_example: ¿Te gusta la música pop o prefieres el rock?
native_language_example: Do you like pop music or do you prefer rock?

additional_notes: Used to say where someone was born. It’s the 3rd-person singular, past tense of "nacer" (to be born): "él/ella/usted nació". Follow it with a place (city, country, etc.). For "I was born in...": "nací en..."
target_language_example: Mi abuela nació en México.
native_language_example: My grandmother was born in Mexico.

additional_notes: "Nací" is the preterite (simple past) of "nacer" (to be born) for "yo". Use "nací en" before a location: a country, city, or even an unusual place ("en un taxi").
target_language_example: Nací en Nueva York, pero vivo en Miami.
native_language_example: I was born in New York, but I live in Miami.

meaning: not good at all; not well.
additional_notes: Used to strongly negate “bien” (well/good). Common with **estar** for health or how something is going: *No está nada bien* (“He/She isn’t well at all”). Also used to say something doesn’t look promising, often with verbs like **pintar**: *Esto no pinta nada bien* (“This doesn’t look good at all”).
target_language_example: Después de la noticia, estoy nada bien.
native_language_example: After the news, I’m not doing well at all.

additional_notes: Used for emphasis to highlight something surprising, impressive, or exact. Common patterns: **nada menos (que) + noun/clause** ("nothing less than...") and **nada menos que + number/amount** ("no less than..."). It can also appear after a name/title for dramatic emphasis ("Andrés Salgado, no less!").
target_language_example: Pagó nada menos que cien dólares por eso.
native_language_example: He paid no less than one hundred dollars for that.

meaning: 'only / just' (and with an infinitive: 'as soon as').
additional_notes: Used to limit or emphasize that something is the only thing/amount ("Eso es su opinión nada más" = "That’s just his opinion").
