In expressions like "nada más + infinitive" it means "as soon as" ("nada más llegar" = "as soon as (someone) arrived"). With "así nada más" it means "just like that / for no special reason".
target_language_example: Te llamo nada más llegar a casa.
native_language_example: I’ll call you as soon as I get home.

meaning: “nothing to anyone” / “anything to anyone” (used with negation).
additional_notes: Common pattern with a negative verb: no + verb + nada a nadie (e.g., no le dije nada a nadie = “I didn’t tell anyone anything”). Often appears with verbs like decir (to say/tell), deber (to owe), demostrar (to prove), and is frequently paired with an indirect object pronoun (le/les) to show who would receive it (a él/ella/usted).
target_language_example: No tengo que explicarle nada a nadie.
native_language_example: I don’t have to explain anything to anyone.

meaning: “nothing about it/that” (no information or comment regarding something).
additional_notes: Used with verbs like saber, decir, comentar, or negar to mean you know/say/comment “nothing about” a topic. Often appears with another negative word (no, nadie) in Spanish: “no… nada al respecto”, “nadie… nada al respecto”.
target_language_example: No sé nada al respecto, lo siento.
native_language_example: I don’t know anything about it, sorry.

additional_notes: Used to say that there is not any amount or part of something: nada de lo que dijo = "none of what he said." Before a noun, especially in exclamations, it can mean "no" or "none of": ¡Nada de excusas! = "No excuses!"
target_language_example: Nada de eso es verdad.
native_language_example: None of that is true.

additional_notes: Used to deny or reject something that was said, suggested, or assumed (“Not that / none of that”). It can also refer back to a category of things: “ni nada de eso” = “or anything like that.” Often appears with “no” for emphasis: “No, nada de eso.”
target_language_example: —¿Te enojaste con ella? —No, nada de eso.
native_language_example: —Did you get mad at her? —No, nothing like that.

additional_notes: Used to say that no part of the current situation/thing(s) is included or matters. Often appears in negative or emotional statements (e.g., nada de esto importa; nada de esto hubiera pasado). You can also say it alone (“Nada de esto.”) to reject or dismiss what’s being discussed.
target_language_example: No entiendo nada de esto.
native_language_example: I don’t understand any of this.

additional_notes: Used to say that from everything that was said/heard/done, not a single part applies or had an effect. Common with verbs like escuchar (to hear), decir (to say), entender (to understand), ver (to see). It’s often followed by a verb clause: “Nada de lo que + (verb)…”.
target_language_example: Nada de lo que me dijiste me convenció.
native_language_example: Nothing you told me convinced me.

additional_notes: Emphatic way to say there is zero of something or you didn’t do/see/know anything. Often used after a negative (e.g., “No vi nada de nada”) or as a stand-alone answer (“Nada de nada.”). Common in spoken Spanish and can sound blunt.
target_language_example: Cuando llegamos, no había nadie: nada de nada.
native_language_example: When we arrived, there was nobody: absolutely no one.

additional_notes: Common after a negative: "no hizo nada malo" = "he/she didn’t do anything wrong." It can also be used in predictions: "nada malo pasaría" = "nothing bad would happen."
target_language_example: Tranquilo, no has hecho nada malo.
native_language_example: Relax, you haven’t done anything wrong.

additional_notes: Often used to limit what you’re saying/asking: “Nada más dime…” = “Just tell me…”. It can also mean “nothing else / nothing more” (e.g., “No hallaron nada más.”, “No puedo decir nada más.”). With an infinitive, it can mean “as soon as”: “Nada más llegar…” = “As soon as (he) arrived…”.
target_language_example: Nada más termine, te llamo.
native_language_example: As soon as I finish, I’ll call you.

additional_notes: Used to limit something to just one thing. Common patterns: **no... nada más que + infinitive** ("do nothing but...") and **no... nada más que + noun** ("have nothing but..."). **Nada más que** can also mean "nothing more than" to downplay something ("he was nothing more than a liar").
target_language_example: Hoy no hice nada más que trabajar.
native_language_example: Today I did nothing but work.

additional_notes: A common, reassuring phrase used to excuse small mistakes or imperfections (yours or someone else’s). You can add details after it, e.g. “nadie es perfecto en eso” (“nobody is perfect at that”).
target_language_example: Tranquilo, nadie es perfecto; la próxima vez te saldrá mejor.
native_language_example: Don’t worry, nobody is perfect; next time you’ll do better.

additional_notes: Used when **nadie** (“nobody”) is followed by the indirect object pronoun **le** (“to him/her/you [formal]”). It often appears in negative contexts and **le** comes before the verb: *nadie le escucha* = “nobody listens to him/her.” Depending on the verb, English may translate it as “nobody **helps him/her**,” “nobody **listens to him/her**,” “nobody **bothers him/her**,” etc.
target_language_example: A nadie le importa lo que digo.
native_language_example: Nobody cares about what I say.

additional_notes: Used when you are the person affected and “no one” does something to you. It’s typically followed by a verb: “nadie me contestó” (no one answered me), “nadie me reconocía” (no one recognized me), “nadie me creyó” (no one believed me), “nadie me escuchó” (no one listened to me).
target_language_example: Llamé varias veces, pero nadie me respondió.
native_language_example: I called several times, but no one answered me.

additional_notes: Used to say that no other person (besides the one already mentioned or implied) will do something or is affected. It often appears with a verb in the negative sense (e.g., Nadie más lo haría = No one else would do it). It can also be used in warnings/requests to prevent further harm: Nadie más tiene que salir herido = No one else has to get hurt.
target_language_example: No se lo digas a nadie más.
native_language_example: Don’t tell anyone else.

additional_notes: Used to say that it’s impossible for any person to do something. In Spanish, the negative subject “nadie” typically goes before the verb: “nadie puede + infinitive” (e.g., nadie puede entender, nadie puede negar). In a more dramatic/incomplete sentence, it can stand alone: “Nadie puede, después de…” (“No one can, after…”).
target_language_example: Nadie puede entrar sin permiso.
native_language_example: Nobody can come in without permission.

additional_notes: Used to say that no person wants something. Often followed by an infinitive ("Nadie quiere morir"), a noun ("Nadie quiere una guerra"), or "que" + subjunctive to express what nobody wants to happen ("Nadie quiere que pase eso").
target_language_example: Nadie quiere esperar tanto tiempo.
native_language_example: Nobody wants to wait that long.

additional_notes: Used to say that there is no person who has the information. Often followed by a question word or clause: “nadie sabe dónde/cuándo/por qué…”, or “nadie sabe lo que…”. You can also add an indirect object to say who doesn’t know: “nadie sabe + me/te/le/nos/les…”.
target_language_example: Nadie sabe cuándo va a llegar el tren.
native_language_example: No one knows when the train is going to arrive.

additional_notes: Used to say that something is unknown or uncertain, followed by a clause (often with future: "pasará", "será", etc.). You can add an indirect object pronoun to specify who it will happen to: "Nadie sabe lo que *le* pasará" (to him/her/you formal), "…*me* pasará" (to me).
target_language_example: Nadie sabe lo que va a pasar después.
native_language_example: No one knows what will happen next.

additional_notes: This is the start of a sentence/clause meaning “nobody/no one …” when the verb uses **se**. The **se** can be reflexive or part of a pronominal verb (a verb that commonly goes with se), and it comes before the conjugated verb: *Nadie se rió* (Nobody laughed), *Nadie se dio cuenta* (Nobody realized). If there are extra pronouns like **lo/la/los/las**, they also go before the verb: *Nadie se lo cree* (Nobody believes it).
target_language_example: Nadie se acordó de llamarme.
native_language_example: Nobody remembered to call me.

additional_notes: "Nadie" is a negative pronoun meaning "no one." "Te" is the object pronoun for "you" (tú), meaning "you" as the person receiving the action ("you," "to you"). It’s commonly followed by another object pronoun: e.g., "Nadie te lo ha dicho" = "No one has told you (it)." With "nadie" before the verb, you normally don’t add "no" ("Nadie te obliga," not *"No nadie te obliga").
target_language_example: Nadie te entiende cuando hablas tan rápido.
native_language_example: No one understands you when you talk so fast.

additional_notes: Used to say that nobody will do a future action. It’s formed with nadie (“no one”) + ir a + infinitive (a very common way to talk about the near future). Often used to reassure someone (Nadie va a buscarte) or to emphasize that something won’t happen.
target_language_example: Nadie va a ayudarte si no lo pides.
native_language_example: No one is going to help you if you don’t ask for it.

additional_notes: "Necesita" is the usted (formal you) form and also the he/she form of "necesitar" (to need). Used to say someone needs help or to politely offer help: "Si necesita ayuda, dígame" = "If you need help, tell me." For "I need help": "Necesito ayuda." For "Do you (informal) need help?": "¿Necesitas ayuda?"
target_language_example: Si necesita ayuda, puedo explicárselo otra vez.
native_language_example: If you need help, I can explain it to you again.

additional_notes: Used with the verb necesitar in the third-person singular (necesita) to say that someone or something needs one of something. Usually followed by a masculine singular noun (un trabajo) or by a noun phrase like "un poco de" (un poco de aire). For feminine nouns, use "necesita una" (e.g., "necesita una pausa").
target_language_example: Mi coche necesita un lavado.
native_language_example: My car needs a wash.

additional_notes: Used to say that a group (including the speaker) needs a greater amount of something. It’s “necesitamos” (we need) + “más” (more), and it’s usually followed by a noun (más dinero, más tiempo) or can stand alone if the thing is understood from context.
target_language_example: Para terminar hoy, necesitamos más tiempo.
native_language_example: To finish today, we need more time.

additional_notes: Used to say that you (a group including the speaker) need one thing: Necesitamos un + noun (usually a masculine singular noun). If the noun is feminine, use "necesitamos una" (Necesitamos una habitación). With plural nouns, use "necesitamos unos/unas" (Necesitamos unos datos). You can also use it with some quantity phrases: "necesitamos un poco de..." (we need a bit of...).
target_language_example: Necesitamos un taxi para ir al aeropuerto.
native_language_example: We need a taxi to go to the airport.

additional_notes: Used to say that a group of people (ellos/ellas/ustedes) needs assistance. From necesitar (to need) in the present tense: necesitan = “they/you all need,” plus ayuda = “help.” Often the subject is omitted: “Necesitan ayuda.”
target_language_example: ¿Necesitan ayuda con esto?
native_language_example: Do you need help with this?

additional_notes: Uses the verb "necesitar" (to need) in the tú form: "necesitas". It can be a statement (Necesitas ayuda.) or a question (¿Necesitas ayuda?). Often used to offer help or to point out that someone needs assistance; you can add names or softeners like "¿...?," "si..." (e.g., "Llámame si necesitas ayuda").
target_language_example: ¿Necesitas ayuda con la tarea?
native_language_example: Do you need help with the homework?

additional_notes: Used to ask for assistance. Often followed by **con** + noun (necesito ayuda con mi trabajo = I need help with my work) or **para** + infinitive (necesito ayuda para entender = I need help to understand). You can also specify the type of help: *ayuda médica* (medical help).
target_language_example: Necesito ayuda con esta tarea, por favor.
native_language_example: I need help with this homework assignment, please.

meaning: "I need to talk to / speak with" (someone).
additional_notes: Used to say you must speak with a specific person or group. Follow it with a person, pronoun (él/ella/ellos/ellas/usted/ustedes), or an institution (la policía, mi abogado). You can add time/urgency words like "primero" (first) or "ahora mismo" (right now).
target_language_example: Necesito hablar con usted un momento.
native_language_example: I need to talk to you for a moment.

additional_notes: Used to say you need someone else to do something. It’s typically followed by a verb in the subjunctive: “Necesito que firmes… / que veas… / que te vayas…”. In English this often becomes “I need you to + verb.”
target_language_example: Necesito que me ayudes con esto.
native_language_example: I need you to help me with this.

meaning: "I need you to" (do something to/for me).
additional_notes: Used to ask for something you need, followed by a verb in the present subjunctive because it comes after "necesitar que". The "me" is an indirect object pronoun meaning "to/for me" (or sometimes the person affected). Common patterns: "Necesito que me + verb" (Necesito que me ayudes / llamen / dejen / lleven). You can often drop "me" if the action isn’t directed at you: "Necesito que respondas" vs. "Necesito que me respondas" (answer me).
target_language_example: Necesito que me ayudes con esto, por favor.
native_language_example: I need you to help me with this, please.

additional_notes: Used to say you need information. Commonly followed by a question word (dónde, por qué, qué, cómo) or a noun phrase: “Necesito saber dónde vives” (I need to know where you live), “Necesito saber tu nombre” (I need to know your name). You can change the subject by changing the verb: “necesitas saber” (you need to know), “necesita saber” (he/she/you formal needs to know), “necesitamos saber” (we need to know).
target_language_example: Necesito saber a qué hora empieza la reunión.
native_language_example: I need to know what time the meeting starts.

additional_notes: Use “su” to be polite or formal (usted). Common with strangers, customers, or older people. With friends/family you usually say “necesito tu ayuda.” You can also soften it: “Necesito su ayuda, por favor.”
target_language_example: Disculpe, necesito su ayuda para encontrar la estación.
native_language_example: Excuse me, I need your help to find the station.

additional_notes: Used to ask someone directly for help. "Necesito" = "I need" (from necesitar), and "tu ayuda" = "your help." You can swap in another possessive: "necesito su ayuda" (formal or plural "your"), "necesito nuestra ayuda" (I need our help).
target_language_example: Lo siento, necesito tu ayuda con esta tarea.
native_language_example: Sorry, I need your help with this assignment.

additional_notes: Used to say that you need one masculine singular thing: necesito un bolígrafo, necesito un cable. Before a feminine noun, use necesito una instead.
target_language_example: Necesito un minuto para pensar.
native_language_example: I need a minute to think.

additional_notes: Use it to ask for or state you need a small amount of something. It’s followed by a noun (usually uncountable: jabón, papel, información; but it can also be abstract like tiempo). You can make it more polite by adding “por favor”: “Necesito un poco de agua, por favor.”
target_language_example: Necesito un poco de ayuda con esta tarea.
native_language_example: I need a little help with this homework.

additional_notes: Used to say you need something: necesito (I need) + una (a/an). Use it before feminine singular nouns: una ambulancia, una bicicleta, una habitación. For masculine nouns, use "necesito un" (e.g., necesito un médico). You can drop "yo" because the verb form already shows who needs it.
target_language_example: Necesito una mesa para la cocina.
native_language_example: I need a table for the kitchen.

additional_notes: Used to deny a past action or experience: **negar + haber + past participle**. The verb **negar** is conjugated (here, **negó** = 'he/she denied'), and **haber** introduces a completed past action (like English 'having done'). Common after this: *negó haber dicho* (denied having said), *negó haber sabido* (denied having known).
target_language_example: Ella negó haber tomado el dinero.
native_language_example: She denied having taken the money.

additional_notes: Used to emphasize that something is far from being true/achieved. Very common in comparisons like “no estar ni cerca de + noun/infinitive” (to be nowhere near + noun/doing something). It can also appear in contrasts like “ni cerca ni lejos” (neither close nor far).
target_language_example: Todavía no está ni cerca de terminar el proyecto.
native_language_example: He’s still not even close to finishing the project.

meaning: "No way!" / "Not a chance." (also: "Don’t even talk/mention it.")
additional_notes: Common, colloquial expression used to strongly reject an idea or proposal: “De eso, ni hablar” = “Absolutely not / No way.” It can also mean “let’s not even talk about that” or “don’t mention that,” often with “de” + topic: “ni hablar de eso.”
target_language_example: ¿Prestarte mi coche? Ni hablar.
native_language_example: Lend you my car? No way.

additional_notes: Common, informal-sounding way to say you don’t know or had no knowledge about something. Often used alone as a short answer (“¿Sabes quién fue?” “¡Ni idea!”) or in longer phrases like “no tener ni idea de…” (to have no idea about…) and “no tener ni idea que…” (to have no idea that…).
target_language_example: ¿A qué hora llega? Ni idea, todavía no me han dicho nada.
native_language_example: What time is it arriving? No idea—they still haven’t told me anything.

meaning: not at all; far from it.
additional_notes: Used to strongly emphasize a negative idea or to correct an assumption: “not even close.” Often follows a negative statement (e.g., “no…, ni mucho menos”) or can stand alone as a firm reply meaning “Definitely not.” Also common in the pattern “(no) … ni mucho menos …” = “(not) … much less … / let alone …”.
target_language_example: ¿Te molesta? No, ni mucho menos.
native_language_example: Does it bother you? No, not at all.

additional_notes: Used to connect two (or more) negative options, repeating ni before each item: No quiero ni té ni café. It often appears with no before the verb, but it can also be used by itself to add another negative idea: No vino, ni llamó. (Also, in informal speech, un/una ni-ni can mean a person who neither studies nor works.)
target_language_example: No tengo ni ni tiempo ni dinero.
native_language_example: I have neither time nor money.

additional_notes: Used to strongly refuse something or shut down an idea. Often appears after a suggestion or request: "¿Me prestas tu coche? —Ni pensarlo." It’s also common as "¡Ni lo pienses!" (same idea).
target_language_example: ¿Puedo salir hoy aunque tenga examen mañana? —Ni pensarlo.
native_language_example: Can I go out today even though I have an exam tomorrow? —Don’t even think about it.

meaning: "as if" / "like" (showing disbelief or rejecting an idea).
additional_notes: Usually followed by the subjunctive and often used in exclamations to say something is NOT true or NOT a good excuse: "¡Ni que fuera tonto!" = "As if I were stupid!" It can also appear in shortened/elliptical phrases like "Ni que lo menciones" meaning "Don’t even mention it." This use is common in spoken, informal Spanish.
target_language_example: ¿Por qué corres? ¡Ni que llegáramos tarde!
native_language_example: Why are you running? It’s not like we’re late!

additional_notes: Used for emphasis to show that something is surprising because it does not happen in the most basic or expected case. It often comes before the verb: ni siquiera puedo = I can't even. If it comes after the verb, Spanish often uses no earlier in the sentence: no puedo ni siquiera hablar.
target_language_example: Ni siquiera tengo tiempo para comer.
native_language_example: I don't even have time to eat.

additional_notes: Used to emphasize that something doesn’t happen at all, not even in the most basic or expected way. It’s often followed by a verb: “ni siquiera me conoces” (you don’t even know me), “ni siquiera me miras” (you don’t even look at me), “ni siquiera me estás escuchando” (you’re not even listening to me). You can move it for emphasis: “Tú ni siquiera me conoces.”
target_language_example: Ni siquiera me llamaste para avisar.
native_language_example: You didn’t even call me to let me know.

meaning: "I don't even know" / "I don't even know (that...)"
additional_notes: Used to emphasize that you don’t know something at all, often showing surprise, frustration, or that you lack basic information. It’s commonly followed by a question word or clause: "ni siquiera sé qué...", "ni siquiera sé lo que...", "ni siquiera sé cómo...", "ni siquiera sé a qué...".
target_language_example: Ni siquiera sé dónde dejé las llaves.
native_language_example: I don't even know where I left the keys.

additional_notes: Used to emphasize a negative idea (often with another negative like “no”): “Eso no te lo crees ni tú” = “Not even you believe that.” It also appears in “ni... ni...” structures to mean “neither... nor...” (“Ni tú ni yo” = “Neither you nor I”), and can be used alone as a short, emphatic reply (“Ni tú.” = “Not even you.” / “You neither.”).
target_language_example: Eso no lo entiendes ni tú.
native_language_example: Not even you understand that.

meaning: not a single person; nobody (at all).
additional_notes: Used for emphasis to say that there are zero people present. Common after "no hay" or "no había" ("there isn’t/wasn’t"), and it can also be said alone as a short answer: "Ni un alma."
target_language_example: Fui al parque temprano y no había ni un alma.
native_language_example: I went to the park early and there wasn’t a single person there.

meaning: not even a single; not a single (one).
additional_notes: Used to emphasize zero quantity, often with a negative idea (no, nunca, nadie, etc.) or in negative contexts. It’s a strong way to say “not one” of something: “No vi ni un solo… / Nunca… ni un solo…”. It agrees in gender/number with the noun: ni un solo día (masc.), ni una sola vez (fem.).
target_language_example: No tengo ni un solo minuto libre hoy.
native_language_example: I don’t have a single free minute today.

meaning: not a word; not a single word.
additional_notes: Used to emphasize total silence or that someone said nothing at all, often with negatives like "no" ("No dijo ni una palabra"). It can also be used as a command: "Ni una palabra más" = "Not another word."
target_language_example: No digas ni una palabra hasta que lleguemos a casa.
native_language_example: Don’t say a word until we get home.

additional_notes: Used to emphasize zero quantity: “ni uno” = “not even one / not a single one.” Common in phrases like “ni uno más” (not one more) and “ni uno solo” (not a single one). It’s also used in the pattern “ni X ni Y” = “neither X nor Y” (e.g., “ni uno ni lo otro” = “neither one nor the other”).
target_language_example: No tengo ni uno.
native_language_example: I don’t have a single one.

additional_notes: Used to emphasize certainty. Often appears in set phrases like “sin ninguna duda” (without a doubt) and “no hay/tengo ninguna duda (de que…)” (there is/I have no doubt (that…)). It agrees in gender/number with the noun: “ninguna duda” (fem. singular).
target_language_example: Sin ninguna duda, este es el mejor camino.
native_language_example: Without a doubt, this is the best route.

additional_notes: Used to talk about a group of people/things and say that zero of them do something or apply. Often appears with “no” in the sentence (double negative in Spanish): “No conozco a ninguno de ellos.” You can also use it as a subject: “Ninguno de ellos sabe…”. For feminine groups, use “ninguna de ellas” (none of them, women/things).
target_language_example: Ninguno de ellos quiere ir hoy.
native_language_example: None of them want to go today.

meaning: none of us; not one of us.
additional_notes: Used to say that zero people in the group “we/us” did something or are something. It’s normally followed by a singular verb (Ninguno de nosotros es / puede / tiene), although plural agreement can appear in some contexts. For mixed genders, Spanish typically uses the masculine form ninguno; for an all-female group you may hear ninguna de nosotras (“none of us [women]”).
target_language_example: Ninguno de nosotros entiende la pregunta.
native_language_example: None of us understand the question.

additional_notes: Used to say something isn’t an issue or to reassure someone you won’t cause trouble. Usually appears with negation (no / no hay / no es / no tenemos) because ningún means “no/none” before a masculine singular noun (problema). For feminine nouns, use ninguna (e.g., ninguna duda).
target_language_example: No hay ningún problema; puedo hacerlo mañana.
native_language_example: No problem; I can do it tomorrow.

meaning: a little girl; a young girl.
additional_notes: Used to refer to a female child. "Niña" means "girl" and "pequeña" means "small/little"; together it’s a common way to emphasize that the girl is young. You can also say "una niña" or "una niña chica" in some regions.
target_language_example: Esa niña pequeña está jugando en el parque.
native_language_example: That little girl is playing in the park.

additional_notes: Used to strongly deny or correct something. The first “No,” answers (or reacts), and the second “no” is the normal negation before the verb (often with a different subject): “No, no está aquí” = “No, he/she isn’t here.” In Spanish it’s normal to have “No,” + another “no” when the next sentence is negative.
target_language_example: No, no quiero ir hoy.
native_language_example: No, I don't want to go today.

additional_notes: Used to strongly deny or correct something, often after someone suggests the opposite: “No, no lo comprendo” = “No, I don’t understand it.” The "lo" is a direct object pronoun meaning “it/that,” referring to a masculine noun or to an idea/statement already understood from context. With forms like "no lo soy" or "no lo está," "lo" can mean “that” (e.g., “I’m not that,” “it’s not that/like that”).
target_language_example: —¿Lo entiendes? —No, no lo entiendo.
native_language_example: —Do you understand it? —No, I don’t understand it.

meaning: “can’t take it anymore” / “can’t stand it anymore.”
additional_notes: Used to say you’ve reached your limit (physically or emotionally). Often followed by what you can’t tolerate: “No aguantar más el ruido” (to not be able to stand the noise anymore), or used alone. Very close in meaning to “¡No puedo más!” depending on context.
target_language_example: No aguantar más este calor es imposible; vámonos a casa.
native_language_example: Not being able to take this heat anymore is impossible; let’s go home.

meaning: "not like that" / "not so" (used to contrast with what was just said).
additional_notes: Used to say that a statement applies to one thing/person but does NOT apply to another. It often appears in contrast structures like: “X sí…, no así Y” (“X does…, but Y doesn’t”) or “X es…, no así Y” (“X is…, but Y isn’t”). It can sound a bit formal/literary in this contrastive use.
target_language_example: A Ana le encanta viajar; no así a su hermano.
native_language_example: Ana loves to travel; her brother doesn’t.

additional_notes: Used mainly in formal or written Spanish to mean that one action happens immediately after another. It typically introduces a clause with a past tense verb: "No bien + preterite/compound past…, (ya) + verb…". It does NOT mean "not well" in this use.
target_language_example: No bien llegué a casa, me llamó mi madre.
native_language_example: As soon as I got home, my mom called me.

additional_notes: Used to say you don’t understand something (an idea, situation, or what someone said). Often followed by a question word like cómo (how) or por qué (why): “No comprendo cómo…” / “No comprendo por qué…”. You can add nada for emphasis: “No comprendo nada” = “I don’t understand anything.”
target_language_example: Perdón, no comprendo lo que dices.
native_language_example: Sorry, I don’t understand what you’re saying.

additional_notes: Used to express doubt or disagreement: “I don’t think that…”. It is normally followed by the subjunctive (no creo que sea / haga / debas…). Often used to soften an opinion or refusal.
target_language_example: No creo que podamos ir hoy.
native_language_example: I don't think we can go today.

meaning: "I don’t think there is/are" (I doubt there’s…).
additional_notes: Used to express doubt or belief that something doesn’t exist or isn’t the case. "Haya" is the present subjunctive of "haber" (impersonal “there is/are”), triggered by "no creo que". It’s commonly followed by: alguien/nadie (someone/no one), ningún/ninguna (any/none), mucho/a (much/many).
target_language_example: No creo que haya suficiente tiempo para hacerlo hoy.
native_language_example: I don’t think there’s enough time to do it today.

meaning: "I don’t think it is" / "I don’t believe it is" (followed by the subjunctive).
additional_notes: Used to express doubt or disbelief about something. Because "creer" is negated ("no creo"), Spanish normally uses the present subjunctive after "que" (here: "sea" from "ser"). Often followed by an adjective or a noun clause: "No creo que sea correcto" / "No creo que sea eso."
target_language_example: No creo que sea una buena idea.
native_language_example: I don’t think it’s a good idea.

additional_notes: Uses the conditional of deber (“should/ought to”) with no to say something is not recommended, not appropriate, or not expected. Often followed by an infinitive: no debería hacerlo (“I/you/he/she shouldn’t do it”). The subject can be clear from context or added (Yo/Tú/Él/Ella no debería...).
target_language_example: No debería decir eso en voz alta.
native_language_example: You/I shouldn’t say that out loud.

additional_notes: Used to give advice, a recommendation, or a mild warning/reproach. It uses the conditional of deber (deberías), which often sounds like a suggestion rather than a strict order. Followed by an infinitive: “No deberías + infinitive” (e.g., no deberías decir, venir, hacer).
target_language_example: No deberías conducir tan rápido.
native_language_example: You shouldn’t drive so fast.

additional_notes: Used with an infinitive to tell one person (tú) not to do something: no debes + verb. It can express advice ('you shouldn't') or a stronger rule/prohibition ('you must not'), depending on context.
target_language_example: No debes salir tan tarde.
native_language_example: You shouldn't go out so late.

meaning: to not say anything; to stay quiet.
additional_notes: Uses the infinitive after another verb or expression (e.g., es mejor / prometí / sabía que era mejor). Often implies choosing to keep silent (sometimes to avoid problems or keep a secret).
target_language_example: En la reunión, preferí no decir nada.
native_language_example: In the meeting, I preferred not to say anything.

meaning: to not say a word; to stay completely silent.
additional_notes: Used to emphasize total silence, often in situations where someone refuses to speak, is upset, or is shocked. Very similar variants include “no decir ni una palabra” (not to say even one word) and “sin decir palabra” (without saying a word). Neutral in tone and common in everyday speech.
target_language_example: Cuando le preguntaron qué había pasado, decidió no decir palabra.
native_language_example: When they asked him what had happened, he decided not to say a word.

additional_notes: Used to tell someone to prevent something from happening. It’s the negative command (tú) of **dejar** (“to let/allow”) + **que** + a verb in the **subjunctive**: *No dejes que entre.* (“Don’t let him/her come in.”).
target_language_example: No dejes que te hablen así.
native_language_example: Don’t let them talk to you like that.

additional_notes: Used as a negative tú command of “decir” (to say/tell): “no digas + (something)”. It can also be an exclamation of surprise (“¡No digas!”) meaning “No way!” / “You’re kidding!” (similar to “You don’t say!”).
target_language_example: No digas eso, por favor.
native_language_example: Don’t say that, please.

additional_notes: Past tense (pretérito) of decir: no + dijo + nada. Often used to describe someone staying silent or not commenting in a specific moment. You can add context with phrases like “en absoluto” (at all) or “con respecto a…” (regarding…).
target_language_example: Le pregunté qué pasó, pero no dijo nada.
native_language_example: I asked him/her what happened, but he/she didn’t say anything.

additional_notes: Used to say you don’t understand something. Often followed by what you don’t understand: “No entiendo las preguntas” (I don’t understand the questions). You can add emphasis with “nada”: “No entiendo nada” (I don’t understand anything / I don’t get it at all). Can also be used alone as a reaction: “No entiendo.”
target_language_example: Perdón, no entiendo esta palabra.
native_language_example: Sorry, I don’t understand this word.

additional_notes: "No era" is the negative imperfect past of "ser" (to be). Use it for past descriptions, background information, or things that were generally true at that time (not a one-time event). Example: "Tom no era bueno" = "Tom wasn't good" (by nature / at that time). Note: "era" looks like English "era" (a time period), but here it means "was".
target_language_example: Pensé que era fácil, pero no era.
native_language_example: I thought it was easy, but it wasn't.

additional_notes: Used to negate the verb **ser** in the **tú** form (**eres**). It’s commonly followed by a noun or adjective: **No eres estudiante** (“You’re not a student”), **No eres creativo/a** (“You’re not creative”). For emphasis you may see **no eres más que...** (“you’re nothing more than...”).
target_language_example: No eres mi jefe.
native_language_example: You're not my boss.

additional_notes: Negative form of es (from ser). It can mean "he/she/it is not" or "you are not" (formal). Use it with ser for identity, origin, description, time, and similar general facts, not usually for temporary states.
target_language_example: No es una buena idea.
native_language_example: It's not a good idea.

additional_notes: Used to tell someone something doesn’t concern them. Often sounds firm or rude, especially said alone (“No es asunto tuyo.”). You can also use it with a clause: “No es asunto tuyo dónde estoy” = “Where I am is none of your business.” Variations: “no es asunto mío” (none of my business), “no es asunto nuestro” (none of our business).
target_language_example: No es asunto tuyo con quién salgo.
native_language_example: It’s none of your business who I’m dating.

additional_notes: Used to deny or correct something (“No, that’s not true / not the case”). Often also appears as a tag question: “¿no es así?” = “isn’t that right?” / “right?”
target_language_example: No, no es así; te entendí mal.
native_language_example: No, it’s not like that; I misunderstood you.

meaning: “it’s not good” / “it’s not a good idea.”
additional_notes: Used to say something is bad quality (a road, a referee, a product) or to warn that an action is unhealthy, unsafe, or inappropriate. Often followed by an infinitive: “No es bueno + verb” (No es bueno fumar). You can add “para” to specify for whom: “No es bueno para ti.”
target_language_example: No es bueno conducir cuando estás cansado.
native_language_example: It’s not good to drive when you’re tired.

additional_notes: Used to say something has a negative effect on a person, thing, or situation. Follow it with a noun or pronoun (para el bebé, para mí, para los negocios). You can also use it with an infinitive as the subject: "Fumar no es bueno para la salud."
target_language_example: Comer demasiada azúcar no es bueno para los dientes.
native_language_example: Eating too much sugar isn’t good for your teeth.

additional_notes: Used to deny or correct something that was said or implied. Often appears with a tag question like “¿verdad?” or “¿no es cierto?” (similar to “right?” / “isn’t that so?”). You can also say “Eso no es cierto” = “That isn’t true.”
target_language_example: No es cierto; yo nunca dije eso.
native_language_example: That’s not true; I never said that.

additional_notes: Used to say that something is difficult. Often followed by an infinitive (e.g., “No es fácil estudiar”) or a clause about an activity (“No es fácil hablar una lengua extranjera”). You can also use it to comment on a person or situation: “No es fácil lidiar contigo.”
target_language_example: No es fácil levantarse temprano todos los días.
native_language_example: It’s not easy to get up early every day.

meaning: “it’s not what…” / “it’s not the same as…” (often: “it’s not what it used to be”).
additional_notes: Used to say something has changed or isn’t as good as before: “No es lo que era” = “It’s not what it used to be.” Also used to correct someone or clarify a misunderstanding: “No es lo que pregunté/oí” = “That’s not what I asked/heard.” It’s typically followed by a clause (e.g., “no es lo que pensé”) or by “era / solía ser.”
target_language_example: Este restaurante ya no es lo que era.
native_language_example: This restaurant isn’t what it used to be anymore.

additional_notes: Used to say something does not belong to you or is not your responsibility/area. It’s typically followed by a noun: “no es mi culpa” (it’s not my fault), “no es mi especialidad” (it’s not my specialty). You can also say “no son mis …” for plural nouns (they aren’t my …).
target_language_example: Lo siento, pero no es mi problema.
native_language_example: Sorry, but it’s not my problem.

additional_notes: Used with an adjective (or sometimes an adverb) to soften a negative evaluation: *no es muy + adj.* It can mean “not very” or, depending on tone, “not particularly.” You can change **es** to match the subject: *no soy muy*, *no eres muy*, *no somos muy*, etc.
target_language_example: La película no es muy buena, pero vale la pena verla.
native_language_example: The movie isn’t very good, but it’s worth watching.

additional_notes: Used to downplay or minimize something, often followed by a noun: No es más que + un/una + noun. Can sound dismissive depending on context (e.g., “No es más que una niña” = “She’s just a girl”).
target_language_example: No te preocupes: no es más que un rumor.
native_language_example: Don’t worry: it’s just a rumor.

meaning: “it’s nothing more than a” / “it’s just a”.
additional_notes: Used to downplay or reduce something/someone to what the speaker considers its true or lesser nature. Often has a dismissive tone. It agrees with gender/number: no es más que un (masc. sing.), no es más que una (fem. sing.), no es más que unos/unas (plural).
target_language_example: No te preocupes: no es más que un malentendido.
native_language_example: Don’t worry: it’s just a misunderstanding.

additional_notes: Used to downplay something or reassure someone. Common in phrases like “No es nada personal” (“It’s nothing personal”) and as a response to thanks (“No es nada” = “You’re welcome / It’s nothing”).
target_language_example: Gracias por tu ayuda. — No es nada.
native_language_example: Thanks for your help. — It’s nothing / You’re welcome.

additional_notes: Used to say something isn’t required. Often followed by a noun (No es necesario el algodón.) or by “que” + subjunctive to talk about an action (No es necesario que estés sola.). You can change the verb for other subjects/tense: No era necesario…, No será necesario….
target_language_example: No es necesario que vengas mañana.
native_language_example: You don’t need to come tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used to say something cannot happen or cannot be done. Often followed by an infinitive (No es posible + verbo: “No es posible concebir…”) or by “que” + clause (No es posible que…: “It’s not possible that…” / “You can’t possibly…”).
target_language_example: Lo siento, hoy no es posible terminar el proyecto.
native_language_example: Sorry, it’s not possible to finish the project today.

additional_notes: Used to say that something doesn’t meet a need, requirement, or expectation. Often followed by “para” + someone/something: “No es suficiente para mí” (It’s not enough for me). Can also be used alone as a complete sentence: “No es suficiente.”
target_language_example: Lo siento, pero eso no es suficiente para aprobar el examen.
native_language_example: Sorry, but that’s not enough to pass the exam.

additional_notes: Used to compare and say something does not reach the same degree. It’s usually followed by an adjective/adverb and often completed with "como" + comparison: "no es tan + adj./adv. + como..." ("isn't as ... as...").
target_language_example: Esta película no es tan interesante como la otra.
native_language_example: This movie isn't as interesting as the other one.

additional_notes: Used with ser to say that someone or something is not a masculine singular noun or category. Before feminine singular nouns, use no es una instead.
target_language_example: Eso no es un problema.
native_language_example: That is not a problem.

additional_notes: Used to say that something/someone does not belong to a category or is not described by a certain label: “No es una opción / excepción / vergüenza…”. It’s the negative form of “es una …”. For masculine nouns, you say “no es un …” (e.g., “No es un problema”).
target_language_example: Eso no es una buena idea.
native_language_example: That isn’t a good idea.

additional_notes: Used to say something is false or to contradict what someone said. Often followed by what isn’t true: “Lo que dijiste no es verdad” (“What you said isn’t true”). You can also use it on its own as a direct denial: “No es verdad, señor.”
target_language_example: No es verdad; yo no dije eso.
native_language_example: That’s not true; I didn’t say that.

additional_notes: Used with the verb **estar** in the **yo** (I) form to say you are not in a temporary state or condition (busy, working, interested, etc.). Often followed by an adjective or a gerund (-ando/-iendo): **no estoy ocupado** (I'm not busy), **no estoy trabajando** (I'm not working).
target_language_example: Lo siento, ahora no estoy disponible.
native_language_example: Sorry, I'm not available right now.

additional_notes: Use it to express disagreement. It’s the negative of “estoy de acuerdo con” (“I agree with”). Follow it with a person or thing: “No estoy de acuerdo con mi jefe” (I don’t agree with my boss). If you want to disagree with an idea in a full clause, you often use “No estoy de acuerdo con que + subjunctive”: “No estoy de acuerdo con que salgas tan tarde.”
target_language_example: No estoy de acuerdo con esa decisión.
native_language_example: I don’t agree with that decision.

additional_notes:
Used to express uncertainty. It’s followed by:
- a noun/idea: No estoy seguro de la hora.
- an indirect question: No estoy seguro de cuándo / qué / cómo…
- an infinitive: No estoy seguro de poder / ir / ganar…
- “que” + verb (often subjunctive): No estoy seguro de que me guste… (very common in speech). You can change the subject/person: No estamos seguros de…, ¿Estás seguro de…?
target_language_example: No estoy seguro de si mañana tenemos clase.
native_language_example: I’m not sure if we have class tomorrow.

additional_notes: Negative form of está, from estar. It is used to say that someone or something is not in a certain place, state, condition, or situation. Depending on context, it can also mean "you are not" with formal usted.
target_language_example: Mi hermana no está en casa.
native_language_example: My sister isn't at home.

meaning: "It’s not OK / it’s not right" or "it’s not well (in good condition)."
additional_notes: Used for (1) things that aren’t working or aren’t in good condition: "La mira no está bien" (the sight/scope isn’t working right), "La carretera no está bien" (the road isn’t in good condition); (2) people who don’t feel well: "No está bien, no quiere comer" (he/she isn’t well; he/she doesn’t want to eat); and (3) to say something is wrong or unacceptable: "No está bien mentir" (it’s not right to lie).
target_language_example: Lo que hiciste no está bien.
native_language_example: What you did isn’t OK.

additional_notes: Used to state that something is prohibited by a rule, law, or policy. Often followed by an infinitive (No está permitido fumar / aparcar / nadar) or by a clause with que + subjunctive (No está permitido que nadie vaya allá). Also common as a short standalone answer: No está permitido.
target_language_example: No está permitido entrar sin identificación.
native_language_example: It’s not allowed to enter without ID.

meaning: “isn’t / is not (here/there)” or “isn’t (in a certain state/condition)” (about someone/something).
additional_notes: Used with **estar** to say someone/something is not present or not in a specific place/state. Often implies absence: **No está aquí** = “He/She isn’t here.” Can also be used alone as a short answer meaning “He/She/It isn’t (here/available).” In some contexts (like **No está ni ahí**) it can be part of an idiom meaning someone doesn’t care.
target_language_example: Lo busqué, pero no está en casa.
native_language_example: I looked for him, but he isn’t at home.

additional_notes: Uses **estar** (not *ser*) to talk about someone’s location. The subject is often understood from context (e.g., *El gerente no está aquí* or just *No está aquí*). **Aquí** means “here” (near the speaker); compare **allí/ahí** for “there.”
target_language_example: Lo siento, el doctor no está aquí ahora.
native_language_example: Sorry, the doctor isn’t here right now.

additional_notes: Used to say someone/something is not located somewhere or not included in something. It’s the negative of “está en” (from “estar” for location/temporary state). “en” often translates as “in,” but can also mean “on” or “at” depending on context (e.g., “en la lista” = “on the list”).
target_language_example: Mi teléfono no está en mi bolso.
native_language_example: My phone isn't in my bag.

additional_notes: Used to negate the verb "estar" for "tú" (you). Common with adjectives or states/conditions: "No estás listo" (You’re not ready), "No estás seguro" (You’re not sure). You can also use it to negate an ongoing action with the gerund: "No estás comiendo" (You’re not eating). Often appears without the subject "tú" because it’s understood.
target_language_example: Ahora no estás en casa.
native_language_example: You’re not at home right now.

additional_notes: Used to say that something is not real, not present, or not available. Often followed by a noun: “No existe la persona perfecta” (“The perfect person doesn’t exist”). Also used with ideas/concepts (“Dios no existe”) or things that used to exist (“ya no existe” = “no longer exists”).
target_language_example: En esta ciudad no existe el metro.
native_language_example: In this city, there is no subway.

additional_notes: Preterite (simple past) of "no ser". Used to say something wasn’t true/pleasant/a coincidence, etc.: "No fue cierto" = "It wasn’t true." Common set phrases: "No fue hasta que…" = "It wasn’t until…" and "No fue mucho antes de que…" = "It wasn’t long before…".
target_language_example: No fue mi culpa; fue un error.
native_language_example: It wasn’t my fault; it was a mistake.

additional_notes: Used as an infinitive phrase after many verbs (e.g., aconsejar, preferir, prometer) to say that someone should/chooses/promises not to smoke. It can also appear on signs as a prohibition (e.g., «No fumar» = “No smoking”).
target_language_example: En este restaurante está prohibido no fumar.
native_language_example: In this restaurant it’s forbidden not to smoke.

additional_notes: Used with devices, machines, services, or systems to say they aren’t operating properly (e.g., elevator, phone, printer, TV). Also used more generally to mean “it doesn’t work” in the sense of “it won’t work / it doesn’t work out” (an idea, method, relationship, plan). Present tense of funcionar; for a temporary situation you can also hear “no está funcionando.”
target_language_example: Lo siento, mi tarjeta no funciona aquí.
native_language_example: Sorry, my card doesn’t work here.

meaning: "there hasn’t been" / "there haven’t been" (there has not been).
additional_notes: Used with the verb "haber" to say something did not exist or did not occur up to now (present perfect). It’s often followed by a noun: "no ha habido noticias" (there hasn’t been any news), "no ha habido agua caliente" (there hasn’t been hot water). For plural nouns, English uses "haven’t," but Spanish still uses "ha": "no ha habido problemas".
target_language_example: Hoy no ha habido clases.
native_language_example: There haven’t been classes today.

additional_notes: Negative present perfect of **ser** for **él/ella/usted** (and also used with things: **esto/eso**). Common in polite set phrases like **No ha sido molestia** = “It wasn’t any trouble.”
target_language_example: Lo siento, no ha sido mi intención.
native_language_example: I'm sorry, it hasn't been my intention.

additional_notes: Used to say someone has not come (often meaning "not yet" up to now). It’s built with haber (ha) + past participle (venido). Common with negatives like "nadie" (no one): "No ha venido nadie" = "No one has come," and "nada" (nothing): "No ha venido nada" = "Nothing came/was included" (e.g., in a newspaper).
target_language_example: Todavía no ha venido el médico.
native_language_example: The doctor still hasn’t come.

meaning: “to just have to” / “there is/was nothing but” (only).
additional_notes:
Used mainly in two common patterns:
1) **No hay (no había / no habrá) más que + infinitive** = “You just have to…” / “All you have to do is…”.
2) **No hay (no había) más que + noun** = “There is/was nothing but…” (only that thing exists/was there). In phrasebook form it’s often listed as **no haber más que**, but in real sentences it appears conjugated (e.g., **no hay más que**, **no había más que**).
target_language_example: En este caso, no haber más que llamarme si necesitas ayuda.
native_language_example: In this case, you just have to call me if you need help.

additional_notes: Use this to tell someone you can’t speak English. You can swap in other languages: “No hablo español/francés/alemán.” If you’re addressing someone formally, you can add “(lo) siento” to be polite: “Lo siento, no hablo inglés.”
target_language_example: Lo siento, no hablo inglés. ¿Habla español?
native_language_example: Sorry, I don’t speak English. Do you speak Spanish?

meaning: “there won’t be / there will not be” (future of “there is/are”).
additional_notes: Used to say that something will not exist or be present in the future. It’s the negative form of “habrá” (from haber). Common with nouns: “no habrá clase” (there won’t be class), “no habrá nadie” (there won’t be anyone), “no habrá más…” (there won’t be any more…).
target_language_example: Si llueve, no habrá partido.
native_language_example: If it rains, there won’t be a game.

additional_notes: Uses the imperfect of "haber" (impersonal/existential) to say something did not exist/was not available in the past. It doesn’t change for singular/plural: "no había un problema" and "no había problemas" are both correct. Common patterns: "no había + noun" (there wasn’t/weren’t…), "no había + dónde/qué/cuándo + infinitive" (there was nowhere/nothing/no time to...).
target_language_example: Cuando llegamos, no había asientos libres.
native_language_example: When we arrived, there were no free seats.

additional_notes: Uses the imperfect of haber (había) to say that at a certain time, nobody was present somewhere. Often followed by a place: “No había nadie en casa/en el parque.” “Nadie” is negative here, so it goes with “no” (double negative is normal in Spanish).
target_language_example: Cuando llegué, no había nadie en la oficina.
native_language_example: When I arrived, there was nobody in the office.

meaning: “there was nobody/no one in …” (in the past).
additional_notes: Used to say a place was empty at a past moment. The verb is imperfect: “había” = “there was/there were” (background description). Common pattern: “No había nadie en + place” (No había nadie en la casa / en el auto). You can also add details: “No había nadie en la habitación además de…” = “There was no one in the room besides…”.
target_language_example: Cuando llegamos, no había nadie en el restaurante.
native_language_example: When we arrived, there was nobody in the restaurant.

meaning: "there was no reason to" / "there was no reason for".
additional_notes: Used to say something wasn’t necessary or justified in the past. Common patterns: + infinitive (No había razón para preocuparse = no reason to worry) and + "para que" + subjunctive when it’s about another person/action (No había razón para que usted se enfadara = no reason for you to get angry).
target_language_example: No había razón para salir tan temprano.
native_language_example: There was no reason to leave so early.

additional_notes: Used to say something is unnecessary. Common patterns: **No hace falta + infinitive** (No hace falta decirlo.) and **No hace falta que + subjunctive** (No hace falta que te quedes.). Often implies “it’s obvious” with **(ni) decirlo**: *No hace falta (ni) decirlo* = “it goes without saying.”
target_language_example: No hace falta que vengas mañana.
native_language_example: You don’t have to come tomorrow.

meaning: “you don’t need to (do) it” / “there’s no need for you to … it.”
additional_notes: Used to say something is not necessary. It’s usually followed by a verb in the subjunctive (e.g., “No hace falta que lo hagas / compres / digas”). “Lo” is an object pronoun meaning “it” (referring to something already mentioned).
target_language_example: No hace falta que lo repitas; ya entendí.
native_language_example: You don’t need to repeat it; I already understood.

meaning: to do nothing; not to do anything.
additional_notes: Used to say that someone takes no action or is inactive. Often appears after verbs like "estar cansado de" (to be tired of), "mejor" (better), "preferir" (to prefer), or "antes de" (before). You can also add "más" for emphasis: "no hacer nada más" = "not do anything else".
target_language_example: Si no sabes qué decir, es mejor no hacer nada.
native_language_example: If you don’t know what to say, it’s better to do nothing.

additional_notes: A negative infinitive phrase. hacerlo means “to do it,” and lo refers to something already mentioned or understood from context. Common after verbs like decidir, elegir, or preferir, and after para: para no hacerlo = “in order not to do it.”
target_language_example: Quería decir la verdad, pero decidí no hacerlo.
native_language_example: I wanted to tell the truth, but I decided not to do it.

additional_notes: Used to tell one person (tú) not to do something: no + hagas (present subjunctive of hacer). Often followed by a noun (No hagas ruido/tonterías) or by “eso/esto” (No hagas eso/esto). For the formal singular (usted), use “No haga…”. For plural: “No hagáis…” (Spain) / “No hagan…” (Latin America).
target_language_example: Por favor, no hagas eso aquí.
native_language_example: Please, don’t do that here.

additional_notes: Negative form of hay, used to say that something does not exist or is not available. Hay stays the same with singular and plural nouns: no hay una mesa / no hay mesas.
target_language_example: No hay tiempo para esperar.
native_language_example: There is no time to wait.

additional_notes: Used with the verb "hay" (from "haber") to say that nothing exists or is available in a situation. Often followed by "que" + verb to mean "there's nothing (that) ..." / "there's nothing I/you can do" (e.g., "No hay nada que hacer").
target_language_example: Lo siento, no hay nada que yo pueda hacer ahora.
native_language_example: I'm sorry, there's nothing I can do now.

additional_notes: Used to say something is the best, most comforting, or most enjoyable option. It’s often followed by a noun (No hay nada como el hogar.) or by an infinitive/reflexive verb to talk about an action (No hay nada como descansar / darse un baño.).
target_language_example: Después de un día largo, no hay nada como dormir bien.
native_language_example: After a long day, there’s nothing like sleeping well.

additional_notes: Used to say that no thing/action exists that can (or should) be done. Very often followed by a verb in the subjunctive: “No hay nada que pueda hacer” = “There’s nothing I can do.” It can also introduce a strong statement with a double negative: “No hay nada que no pueda pasar” = “There’s nothing that can’t happen.”
target_language_example: Lo siento, no hay nada que pueda hacer para cambiar la decisión.
native_language_example: I'm sorry, there's nothing I can do to change the decision.

meaning: "There’s nothing to do" / "There’s nothing we can do."
additional_notes: Used to say there are no activities available (bored) or that a situation can’t be changed (resigned/helpless tone). Often followed by details: "No hay nada que hacer al respecto" = "There’s nothing we can do about it."
target_language_example: Lo intentamos todo, pero no hay nada que hacer.
native_language_example: We tried everything, but there’s nothing we can do.

additional_notes: Used to say nobody is present or nobody exists in a place/situation. Often followed by a location (no hay nadie aquí/en casa). It can also be used in comparisons to mean “there’s nobody (better/smarter) than…” (no hay nadie mejor que tú), or with a clause: no hay nadie que + verb (“there’s no one who…”).
target_language_example: Lo siento, no hay nadie en casa ahora.
native_language_example: Sorry, there’s no one at home right now.

meaning: "there’s no need to" / "you don’t have to".
additional_notes: Used to say something isn’t necessary. It’s typically followed by an infinitive verb (e.g., no hay necesidad de + esperar/explicarlo). You can also use it with a noun: No hay necesidad de eso. Common in polite reassurance or to calm someone down.
target_language_example: No hay necesidad de preocuparte; todo está bajo control.
native_language_example: There’s no need to worry; everything is under control.

meaning: “There isn’t any / there are no (female noun).”
additional_notes: Used to say that something does not exist or is not present. It’s the negative form of “hay” (there is/are) + “ninguna” (not any, none) and it agrees with a feminine singular noun: “No hay ninguna duda” (duda is feminine). With masculine nouns you use “no hay ningún …” and with plural nouns: “no hay ningunas / ningunos …” (less common) or more naturally “no hay …” + plural noun: “No hay reglas.”
target_language_example: No hay ninguna solución fácil.
native_language_example: There isn’t any easy solution.

meaning: “there isn’t any” / “there are no” (with a masculine singular noun).
additional_notes: Used to say something does not exist or is not present. It’s the negative form of “hay” (there is/are) + “ningún” (any/no) before a masculine singular noun: “No hay ningún error.” For feminine nouns use “no hay ninguna …” (e.g., “No hay ninguna razón.”). For plural, use “no hay …” + plural noun, often with “ningunos/ningunas” depending on the context (e.g., “No hay ningunos planes” or more commonly “No hay planes”).
target_language_example: No hay ningún café en la cocina.
native_language_example: There isn’t any coffee in the kitchen.

additional_notes: Literally “there isn’t a problem.” Common to reassure someone, accept a request, or respond to thanks/apologies. It can also be used literally to mean “there is no problem” (nothing is wrong).
target_language_example: —Perdón por llegar tarde. —No hay problema.
native_language_example: “Sorry for being late.” “No problem.”

meaning: “you don’t have to …” / “one shouldn’t …” (it’s not necessary; don’t).
additional_notes: Used before an infinitive (verb in the “to ___” form): no hay que + infinitive. It gives general advice or a rule (like English “you don’t have to” or “you shouldn’t”), and the subject is usually general/impersonal rather than a specific person. Similar idea to “no es necesario (que) …”.
target_language_example: No hay que preocuparse tanto.
native_language_example: You don’t have to worry so much.

meaning: "no one can" / "there’s no way to" (it’s impossible or very hard to do).
additional_notes: Commonly followed by a verb in the subjunctive (e.g., "no hay quien duerma/entienda/salga"). It expresses that something is unbearable, impossible, or extremely difficult, often due to circumstances (noise, heat, a situation). Also used with an object pronoun: "No hay quien lo/la aguante" = "No one can stand him/her/it."
target_language_example: Con tanto ruido, no hay quien estudie.
native_language_example: With so much noise, there’s no way anyone can study.

meaning: "I haven't been able to" (up to now).
additional_notes: Present perfect of poder (yo): no + he podido + infinitive. It means you were unable to do something during a period that includes the present (e.g., today/this week/up to now). Often followed by an infinitive: no he podido dormir/encontrar/hacer/ver.
target_language_example: Lo siento, no he podido llamarte hoy.
native_language_example: Sorry, I haven't been able to call you today.

meaning: “wasn’t going to” (not going to do something; not going to happen).
additional_notes: Uses the imperfect of **ir** + **a** to talk about a future action from a past point of view (“was going to…”). With **no**, it means someone didn’t intend to do it, or it wasn’t going to happen (often suggesting it was impossible or inevitable). Common before an infinitive: **no iba a volver / no iba a luchar / no iba a dejarte / no iba a ir / no iba a parar**.
target_language_example: Pensé que no iba a llegar a tiempo.
native_language_example: I thought I wasn’t going to arrive on time.

meaning: "it doesn't matter" / "never mind"; also "no matter (what/when/how much)".
additional_notes: Used to say something is not important ("Está bien, no importa" = "It’s okay, never mind"). It can also introduce an idea meaning "regardless of": no importa qué = no matter what, no importa cuándo = no matter when, no importa cuánto = no matter how much. Often followed by subjunctive in the "no matter..." pattern: "No importa lo que digas" (No matter what you say).
target_language_example: No importa lo que pase, estaré aquí.
native_language_example: No matter what happens, I’ll be here.

additional_notes: Very informal and often vulgar (from the verb *joder*). Common in Spain; can sound rude/aggressive depending on tone. Used as an exclamation of surprise/disbelief (“No way!”) or as a warning/complaint (“Don’t mess with me / Don’t screw around”). Not appropriate in polite settings.
target_language_example: —Me robaron el celular. —¡No jodas!
native_language_example: —They stole my phone. —No way!

additional_notes: “No” makes the verb negative, and “la” is the direct object pronoun meaning “her” or “it” (for a feminine noun). It normally goes right before a conjugated verb: “No la traerán” = “They won’t bring her/it.” With an infinitive, you can place it before the infinitive or attach it: “No la voy a traer” / “No voy a traerla.” Meaning depends on context (a woman/girl = “her”; a feminine thing = “it”).
target_language_example: No la conozco, pero quiero hablar con ella.
native_language_example: I don’t know her, but I want to talk to her.

meaning: "I haven’t seen her in…" (for a period of time).
additional_notes: Uses the present perfect: no + la (her) + he visto (I have seen) + en + time period. Common with durations like "en diez años" (in ten years), "en una semana" (in a week), or phrases like "en mi vida" (in my life = never). You can swap "la" for other direct-object pronouns: "no lo he visto en…" (I haven’t seen him/it in…).
target_language_example: No la he visto en dos meses.
native_language_example: I haven’t seen her in two months.

additional_notes: `no` negates the verb, and `le` is an object pronoun placed before it. `le` usually means 'to him/her/it' or 'to you' (formal), so the exact English translation depends on the verb: `no le gusta` = 'he/she doesn't like it', `no le hablo` = 'I don't speak to him/her'. With `gustar`-type verbs, it marks the person affected. In some varieties, `le` can also be used for a male person where many other speakers use `lo`.
target_language_example: No le escribo a Ana todos los días.
native_language_example: I don't write to Ana every day.

additional_notes: Command telling someone to keep something secret. It’s the negative tú imperative of decir: no digas. "le" often means “to him/her/you (formal),” but in this phrase it can sound natural even when it basically means “don’t tell anyone.” You can add what should be kept secret with de + noun (de esto), dónde + verb (dónde estoy), or que + clause (que te lo dije).
target_language_example: No le digas a nadie que vamos a mudarnos.
native_language_example: Don’t tell anyone that we’re going to move.

meaning: "he/she doesn’t like it" (it doesn’t please him/her).
additional_notes: Used with the verb gustar. The person who dislikes something is expressed with an indirect object pronoun: me/te/le/nos/les. The thing disliked is the grammatical subject: No le gusta hablar… = “Speaking… doesn’t please him/her.” Common pattern: A + person + no + (me/te/le/nos/les) + gusta + infinitive / noun; or No le gusta que + subjunctive for actions by others (e.g., “he doesn’t like that they tell him what to do”).
target_language_example: A Marta no le gusta levantarse temprano.
native_language_example: Marta doesn’t like getting up early.

meaning: "he/she doesn’t care" / "it doesn’t matter to him/her".
additional_notes: Used with the verb "importar" (to matter). Spanish commonly phrases this as: "(A alguien) le importa (algo)" = "(To someone) something matters." So "no le importa" means the person referred to by "le" (to him/her/you-formal) doesn’t care. You can add the person with "a + person": "A Juan no le importa" (Juan doesn’t care).
target_language_example: A Marta no le importa llegar tarde.
native_language_example: Marta doesn’t care about arriving late.

additional_notes: "Les" is an indirect object pronoun meaning "to them" (or "to you" plural formal, in Spain). "No" goes right before it to negate the verb: "No les dije nada" = "I didn’t tell them anything." Common with verbs like "decir" (to tell), "importar" (to matter to), "dar" (to give), "gustar" (to be pleasing to).
target_language_example: No les voy a decir la verdad.
native_language_example: I’m not going to tell them the truth.

additional_notes: A very common combination of no + lo. Here lo usually means "it" (sometimes "him" or "that") and comes before the verb in Spanish: No lo necesito = "I don't need it." With negative commands, no lo + verb means "don't [verb] it": No lo hagas = "Don't do it." In some expressions like no lo es, lo refers more generally to a quality or idea, so the translation may be less literal.
target_language_example: No lo entiendo.
native_language_example: I don't understand it.

meaning: “I don’t think so” / “I don’t believe it.”
additional_notes: Used to disagree or to say something is unlikely. “Lo” refers to the idea or situation being discussed (“it/that”). You can use it alone as a short reply (“—¿Vienes? —No lo creo.”).
target_language_example: —¿Crees que va a llover? —No lo creo.
native_language_example: —Do you think it’s going to rain? —I don’t think so.

additional_notes: Used to tell someone they don’t understand a situation or idea (often with emphasis or frustration). "Lo" is a direct-object pronoun meaning “it/that” (the thing being discussed). Also common: "No entiendes" (“You don’t understand”), "No lo entiendo" (“I don’t understand it”).
target_language_example: No lo entiendes: no se trata de dinero, se trata de confianza.
native_language_example: You don’t understand it: it’s not about money, it’s about trust.

additional_notes: Uses the conditional perfect (haber in conditional + past participle) to talk about a hypothetical past: something that did NOT happen, often because of different conditions. The pronoun "lo" means "it/that" (a previously mentioned thing). The subject is implied and depends on context: "yo no lo habría hecho" = "I wouldn’t have done it"; "él no lo habría hecho" = "he wouldn’t have done it." Common with "si...": "Si lo hubiera sabido, no lo habría hecho" (If I had known, I wouldn’t have done it).
target_language_example: Si hubiera entendido las reglas, no lo habría hecho.
native_language_example: If I had understood the rules, I wouldn’t have done it.

additional_notes: Used to tell someone (tú) not to do something. Literally: “don’t do it,” where lo = “it/that.” Often used with names or with por favor (“please”): «Por favor, no lo hagas». You can also hear «no lo haga» (formal usted) and «no lo hagáis/no lo hagan» (plural).
target_language_example: Si es peligroso, no lo hagas.
native_language_example: If it’s dangerous, don’t do it.

additional_notes: Used to say you don’t do a particular action that’s already known from context. "lo" = “it” (a thing/idea/action previously mentioned), and "hago" is the present tense of "hacer" (to do/make). Often appears with emphasis or frequency words: "nunca" (never), "tampoco" (either/neither), "yo" (to stress “I” in contrast to someone else).
target_language_example: Lo siento, pero no lo hago.
native_language_example: Sorry, but I don’t do it.

meaning: "I haven’t (done/seen) it" (used before a past participle).
additional_notes: This is a common fragment of the present perfect: **no** (not) + **lo** (it) + **he** (I have). It normally needs a **past participle** right after it: *no lo he visto* (I haven’t seen it), *no lo he hecho* (I haven’t done it). The **lo** refers to a masculine thing/idea or to an unspecified “it/that.”
target_language_example: No lo he visto todavía.
native_language_example: I haven’t seen it yet.

additional_notes: Used to deny having done something. "Lo" is a direct-object pronoun meaning "it/that" (something understood from context), and "hice" is the preterite (completed past) of "hacer" for "I". You can add emphasis with words like "yo" (I) or "yo mismo" (myself): "No lo hice yo" / "No lo hice yo mismo."
target_language_example: Te lo juro: no lo hice.
native_language_example: I swear: I didn’t do it.

additional_notes: Uses the past tense of hacer (“hizo” = “did”) with “lo” meaning “it/that” (a thing or action already mentioned). Often answers a question like “¿Lo hizo?” or emphasizes denial: “Por supuesto que no lo hizo.” You can replace the subject with a name: “Tom no lo hizo.”
target_language_example: Te dije que lo haría, pero al final no lo hizo.
native_language_example: I told you he would do it, but in the end he didn’t.

additional_notes: Used to say you don’t remember a specific thing already mentioned (the direct object “lo” = “it/that”). You can change the pronoun for other objects: “no la recuerdo” (I don’t remember her/it-fem), “no los recuerdo” (I don’t remember them). Often used with fillers like “para ser honesto” (to be honest) or “si…” (if…).
target_language_example: Lo siento, pero no lo recuerdo.
native_language_example: Sorry, but I don’t remember it.

additional_notes: Used to say that someone doesn’t know a specific thing (lo = “it/that”). The verb is saber (“to know” a fact/information), and sabe can mean “he/she knows” or “you know” (usted). Often appears with emphasis or with words like nadie (“no one”) or bien (“well/really”).
target_language_example: No lo sabe nadie todavía.
native_language_example: Nobody knows it yet.

meaning: “you have no idea” / “you don’t know (just) how much.”
additional_notes: Often used as an emphatic reply after someone says something that’s true but understated. Literally it’s “you don’t know it well,” but in conversation it usually means “you really don’t know the extent of it” or “you don’t know the half of it.”
target_language_example: —Estoy cansado. —No lo sabes bien; hoy fue un día larguísimo.
native_language_example: —I’m tired. —You have no idea; today was a really long day.

additional_notes: Used to say you lacked that information. "Lo" means "it/that" and refers to something already mentioned or understood from context. "Sabía" is the imperfect past of "saber" (to know), often used for background knowledge in the past. It can change with the subject: "No lo sabía nadie" = "Nobody knew."
target_language_example: Perdón, no lo sabía; nadie me lo dijo.
native_language_example: Sorry, I didn't know; nobody told me.

additional_notes: Common way to say you don’t know. Literally “I don’t know it,” where “lo” refers to the thing you’re being asked about. You can also say “no sé” for short.
target_language_example: Lo siento, no lo sé.
native_language_example: Sorry, I don’t know.

additional_notes: Used to admit you don’t know something (No lo sé) and then add a guess, opinion, or contrast (pero = “but”). Often followed by creo que… (“I think…”) or a statement you do know.
target_language_example: No lo sé, pero creo que mañana va a llover.
native_language_example: I don’t know, but I think it’s going to rain tomorrow.

meaning: "don’t/doesn’t" + "them" (masculine plural direct object), before a verb.
additional_notes: "No" negates the verb, and "los" is a direct object pronoun meaning "them" (or sometimes "you" plural, formal, in some regions). It goes before a conjugated verb: "No los tengo" (I don’t have them). With infinitives/gerunds, it can go before the first verb or attached to the end: "No los puedo dejar" / "No puedo dejarlos" (I can’t leave them).
target_language_example: No los encuentro por ninguna parte.
native_language_example: I can’t find them anywhere.

additional_notes: A very common combination of no + me. By itself it literally means "not me," but before a verb it often means "doesn't ... me," "don't ... me," or "not to me," depending on the verb: no me dice = "he/she doesn't tell me," no me mires = "don't look at me."
target_language_example: No me hables así.
native_language_example: Don't talk to me like that.

meaning: “don’t tell me” / “don’t say that to me”; also “no way!” (surprise).
additional_notes: Literally “don’t tell me.” Used in two common ways: (1) as a request/complaint meaning “don’t talk to me like that / don’t say that to me” (often with something after it: “No me digas así.”), and (2) as an exclamation or question showing surprise or disbelief (“No me digas!” / “¿No me digas?” = “No way!” / “Really?”).
target_language_example: —Me ascendieron hoy. —¿No me digas? ¡Felicidades!
native_language_example: —I got promoted today. —No way? Congratulations!

additional_notes: Used to react to what you’ve just heard or to push back on an idea. Often implies “I can’t believe it” or “surely not,” and it can also be used to emphasize a complaint (e.g., “don’t tell me you didn’t hear it”). Common in exclamations; can be followed by indicative: "No me digas que perdiste..."
target_language_example: ¡No me digas que ya se fueron sin mí!
native_language_example: Don’t tell me they already left without me!

additional_notes: Used with the verb gustar to express that you don’t like something. Literally it’s closer to “it doesn’t please me,” so the thing you don’t like goes after gusta (e.g., “No me gusta la lluvia” = “I don’t like the rain”). You can also use it with an infinitive: “No me gusta esperar” (I don’t like to wait).
target_language_example: No me gusta esta película.
native_language_example: I don't like this movie.

meaning: “don’t make me…” / “don’t do that to me…”
additional_notes: Used to tell someone not to force you to do something or not to put you in a difficult situation. Often followed by an infinitive (no me hagas + verb: “No me hagas esperar”) or by “esto/eso” (“No me hagas esto”). It uses the tú command form of hacer (hagas) with an indirect object pronoun (me).
target_language_example: No me hagas esperarte otra vez.
native_language_example: Don’t make me wait for you again.

meaning: "I don't care" / "it doesn't matter to me."
additional_notes: Used to say something doesn’t matter to you or you’re not interested. You can add what you don’t care about: "No me importa + noun" (No me importa el Alfaverso). You can also emphasize it: "No me importa en lo más mínimo" = “I don’t care at all / in the slightest.” Common variant: "A mí no me importa" adds emphasis (“As for me, I don’t care”).
target_language_example: Si quieres ir hoy o mañana, no me importa.
native_language_example: If you want to go today or tomorrow, I don't care / it doesn't matter to me.

additional_notes: Used to say something doesn’t interest you or doesn’t matter to you. Often followed by a noun: “No me interesa la política.” You can also use it alone as a complete sentence: “No me interesa.” (tone can sound dismissive depending on context).
target_language_example: Lo siento, no me interesa ese trabajo.
native_language_example: Sorry, I’m not interested in that job.

meaning: "don’t … it to/for me" / "I didn’t … it" (with object pronouns "me" + "lo").
additional_notes: This is a very common pronoun cluster used before a verb: **no** (not) + **me** (to/for me) + **lo** (it). The exact translation depends on the verb: *No me lo agradezcas* = “Don’t thank me for it”; *No me lo esperaba* = “I didn’t expect it”; *No me lo perdería* = “I wouldn’t miss it.” **Lo** refers to an idea/thing already known from context.
target_language_example: No me lo digas todavía.
native_language_example: Don’t tell me yet.

meaning: "It doesn’t seem to me" / "I don’t think so."
additional_notes: Used to give your opinion or politely disagree. It’s based on the verb "parecer" (to seem). The "me" shows who it seems to (to me). Common patterns: (1) "No me parece + adjective/noun" (No me parece buena idea.), (2) "No me parece que + subjunctive" (No me parece que sea verdad.), and (3) "No me parece + infinitive" (No me parece haber entendido.). You can add emphasis with "A mí": "A mí no me parece..."
target_language_example: No me parece que sea necesario.
native_language_example: I don’t think it’s necessary.

additional_notes: Used to tell someone something is not necessary. Common patterns: “no necesitas + noun” (No necesitas eso. = You don’t need that.) and “no necesitas + infinitive” (No necesitas hacerlo. = You don’t need to do it / You don’t have to do it.). Often followed by “ya” or “ya no” to mean “(not) anymore” (Ya no necesitas hacer eso. = You don’t need to do that anymore.).
target_language_example: No necesitas preocuparte; yo me encargo.
native_language_example: You don’t need to worry; I’ll take care of it.

additional_notes: "No" is the negation (not / don't / didn't), and "nos" means "us" (object pronoun). Together, "no nos" is used before a verb to say something did not happen to us, or someone did not do something to/for us: "No nos aplaudieron" (They didn’t applaud us), "No nos avisaron" (They didn’t notify us).
