It normally goes right before the conjugated verb, or before the auxiliary in a compound tense: "No nos hemos visto..." (We haven’t seen each other...).
target_language_example: No nos escuchan en esta reunión.
native_language_example: They aren't listening to us in this meeting.

additional_notes: Uses the negative tú imperative of "olvidar" to remind someone to do something: "No olvides + infinitive" (No olvides llamar = Don’t forget to call) or "No olvides + noun" (No olvides las llaves = Don’t forget the keys). For formal you’d say "No olvide" (usted), and for plural "No olviden" (ustedes).
target_language_example: No olvides traer tu pasaporte mañana.
native_language_example: Don’t forget to bring your passport tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used to say something continues nonstop or repeatedly. It’s the negative of "parar de" (to stop doing something). Common patterns: "No para de + infinitive" (No para de llover = It keeps raining) and with reflexive verbs: "No para de quejarse" (He/She keeps complaining).
target_language_example: Desde esta mañana no para de sonar el teléfono.
native_language_example: Since this morning, the phone hasn’t stopped ringing.

additional_notes: Common reassuring phrase meaning nothing bad is happening or that something isn’t a big deal (e.g., after a small mistake, delay, or apology). Often followed by something calming like “tranquilo/a.” Literally “nothing happens,” but used like “it’s fine.”
target_language_example: —Perdón por llegar tarde. —No pasa nada, todavía tenemos tiempo.
native_language_example: —Sorry for arriving late. —No problem, we still have time.

additional_notes: Used to say you didn’t expect something or you were wrong about what would happen. It’s the preterite (past) of pensar: pensé = “I thought.” After que, Spanish commonly uses the imperfect subjunctive (e.g., estuvieras, fuera, fueras) for something you didn’t believe/expect, and sometimes the conditional (e.g., vendrías) or imperfect (e.g., volvería) depending on meaning and context.
target_language_example: No pensé que fuera tan tarde.
native_language_example: I didn’t think it was so late.

additional_notes: Used to strongly refuse to allow something to happen. It’s followed by a verb, usually in the subjunctive (e.g., No permitiré que ocurra / suceda / vuelva a pasar). Often used as a firm promise or warning.
target_language_example: No permitiré que me hables así.
native_language_example: I won’t let you talk to me like that.

additional_notes: Used to say that ‘we’ are not able to do something or that something isn’t allowed/possible. It’s the negative of “podemos” (we can), with “no” placed directly before the verb. The subject pronoun “nosotros/nosotras” is often omitted: “No podemos ir” = “We can’t go.”
target_language_example: Lo siento, hoy no podemos ayudarte.
native_language_example: Sorry, we can't help you today.

meaning: to not be able to stand (someone/something).
additional_notes: Often used with a direct object (usually a person) to mean you really dislike them or can’t tolerate them. Common pattern: «No poder ver a + person» (e.g., «No puedo ver a mi jefe»). It can also be literal (“can’t see”), but in everyday speech it frequently means “can’t stand.”
target_language_example: No poder ver a ese tipo es imposible para mí; siempre está criticando a todo el mundo.
native_language_example: I can’t stand that guy; he’s always criticizing everyone.

additional_notes: This is the negative future of poder: no + podré (yo) = “I won’t be able to.” It’s often used for consequences or inability in the future, followed by an infinitive: no podré ayudarte, no podré descargar…, no podré levantarme. In some contexts it can sound like “I can’t (do it)” in general, but grammatically it points to a future moment.
target_language_example: Si no me dices la contraseña, no podré entrar.
native_language_example: If you don’t tell me the password, I won’t be able to log in.

additional_notes: Used to say someone was unable to do something in the past. It’s the imperfect tense of "poder" ("podía" = "could/was able to"), often describing an ongoing difficulty or repeated inability (not a single completed moment). Typically followed by an infinitive ("no podía ir") or sometimes by another verb phrase ("no podía encontrarlo").
target_language_example: Lo intenté muchas veces, pero no podía abrir la puerta.
native_language_example: I tried many times, but I couldn't open the door.

additional_notes: Uses the imperfect tense (podía) to describe an ongoing situation or repeated difficulty sleeping in the past. Often followed by a reason with por (e.g., por el calor = because of the heat) or with tan...que (e.g., tan nervioso que... = so nervous that...).
target_language_example: Anoche no podía dormir porque tenía mucho trabajo en la cabeza.
native_language_example: Last night I couldn't sleep because I had a lot of work on my mind.

additional_notes: From the verb poder (“to be able to”). "No pude" is the simple past (preterite) for “I couldn’t,” often used for a specific situation that happened and finished in the past. It’s commonly followed by an infinitive: "no pude dormir" (I couldn’t sleep), "no pude resistir" (I couldn’t resist), "no pude contener" (I couldn’t hold back).
target_language_example: Lo intenté, pero no pude abrir la puerta.
native_language_example: I tried, but I couldn’t open the door.

additional_notes: Past tense (preterite) of *no poder* for a completed situation in the past: *no pudo + infinitive* (no pudo llegar, no pudo abrir). Often implies a specific failure at that moment, rather than a general inability. Used for he/she/it/you (formal) and also *él/ella/usted no pudo*.
target_language_example: Lo intenté, pero ella no pudo venir.
native_language_example: I tried, but she couldn’t come.

additional_notes: Used to say someone is not able to do something or it’s not possible. "Puede" is the he/she/you(formal)/it form of "poder" (to be able to). It can also express a strong conclusion: "no puede haber + past participle" = "can’t have + past participle" (e.g., "Él no puede haber ido" = "He can’t have gone").
target_language_example: Lo siento, pero no puede entrar sin identificación.
native_language_example: Sorry, but you can’t come in without ID.

meaning: "there can't be" / "there cannot be" (it isn't possible for there to be).
additional_notes: Used to say something is impossible or cannot exist in a situation. It’s the impersonal structure: no (not) + puede (can) + haber (to be/there to be). Often followed by a noun phrase: "no puede haber + [noun]" (e.g., "no puede haber excusas"). In general statements it can be like "Without X, there can’t be Y": "Sin agua no puede haber vida."
target_language_example: En este lugar no puede haber silencio con tanta gente.
native_language_example: In this place, there can’t be silence with so many people.

meaning: "it can't be" / "that can't be" (not possible; can't be true).
additional_notes: Used to say something is impossible or not true, or that someone/something can't be a certain identity ("It can't be him/your teacher/yours"). Often followed by an adjective ("No puede ser correcto") or a noun/pronoun ("No puede ser él"). As an exclamation—"¡No puede ser!"—it can mean "No way!" or "I can't believe it!"
target_language_example: No puede ser verdad.
native_language_example: That can't be true.

meaning: "It can't be" / "It can't be possible"; also "Now isn't possible" (not now).
additional_notes: Literally "it can't be." Often used to say something is impossible or unacceptable ("No, this can’t be"). In conversations it can also mean "not now" or "it can’t happen (at that time)" (e.g., "Ahora no puede ser" = "Now won’t work / now isn’t possible"). You can add a subject for clarity: "Eso no puede ser" (That can’t be) or "Ahora no puede ser" (Now isn’t possible).
target_language_example: Lo siento, hoy no puede ser; mañana sí.
native_language_example: Sorry, it won’t work today; tomorrow it will.

additional_notes: Means that “they/you all can’t” do something. It’s formed with **no** + **pueden** (present tense of **poder**, “to be able to”). **Pueden** is used for **ellos/ellas/ustedes**.
target_language_example: No pueden entrar aquí.
native_language_example: They can’t come in here.

additional_notes: Used with tú (2nd person singular) to say someone is not allowed to do something or is unable to do it: “No puedes + infinitive.” For ustedes (you plural), use “no pueden.”
target_language_example: Lo siento, no puedes entrar aquí.
native_language_example: Sorry, you can't come in here.

additional_notes: First-person singular present of poder. It means that the speaker cannot do something, and it is usually followed by an infinitive: no puedo venir = I can't come. It can also stand alone when the action is understood from context.
target_language_example: Lo siento, no puedo ir contigo hoy.
native_language_example: Sorry, I can't go with you today.

additional_notes: Used to refuse or say something is unacceptable. Often followed by a noun (un regalo, estas condiciones, una excusa), or said alone as a complete statement: “No puedo aceptar.” It can express a polite refusal (e.g., of a gift) or a firm rejection (e.g., of terms or an excuse).
target_language_example: Lo siento, no puedo aceptar tu oferta.
native_language_example: I'm sorry, I can't accept your offer.

additional_notes: Used to express strong surprise, shock, disbelief, or indignation. It’s commonly followed by a verb in the subjunctive (e.g., “no puedo creer que estés…”), though you may also hear the indicative in casual speech.
target_language_example: No puedo creer que hayas hecho eso.
native_language_example: I can’t believe you did that.

additional_notes: Used to say something is involuntary or hard to control. Common patterns: (1) no puedo evitar + infinitive: "No puedo evitar pensar..." / "No puedo evitar reírme..."; (2) no puedo evitar + noun/pronoun: "No puedo evitar eso." Often implies "even if I want to".
target_language_example: No puedo evitar preocuparme cuando no me respondes.
native_language_example: I can't help worrying when you don't reply to me.

additional_notes: Used to say you’re unable to talk (right now or in general), or that you can’t speak a certain way or language. It can also extend to what you can’t talk about (e.g., “sobre eso” = “about that”). For “I can’t speak for him,” Spanish uses “No puedo hablar por él.”
target_language_example: Lo siento, ahora mismo no puedo hablar; te llamo luego.
native_language_example: Sorry, I can’t talk right now; I’ll call you later.

additional_notes: Used to say you’re unable to go somewhere or leave. Often followed by a place with "a" (e.g., "no puedo ir a la fiesta") or by a time word like "ahora". The verb "poder" changes with the subject: "no puedo" (I can’t), "no puedes" (you can’t), "no puede" (he/she/you-formal can’t), etc.
target_language_example: Lo siento, no puedo ir hoy.
native_language_example: Sorry, I can't go today.

additional_notes: Used to say you won’t let something happen or you won’t accept something. It’s often followed by a noun or by “que” + subjunctive: “No puedo permitir que me hablen así” (I can’t allow them to talk to me like that).
target_language_example: Lo siento, pero no puedo permitir que entres sin identificación.
native_language_example: Sorry, but I can’t allow you to enter without ID.

meaning: "I can't continue" / "I can't go on"; also "I can't follow."
additional_notes: With "seguir con + noun/verb" it means to continue doing something: "No puedo seguir con esto" (I can’t continue with this). With a direct object, "seguir" often means to follow (track/understand): "No puedo seguir la bola" (I can’t follow the ball) or "No puedo seguir su lógica" (I can’t follow his/her logic). By itself, "No puedo seguir" can mean "I can’t go on" (continue).
target_language_example: Lo siento, estoy muy cansado; no puedo seguir.
native_language_example: Sorry, I’m very tired; I can’t go on.

additional_notes: Used to say you’re unable to see something (because of darkness, distance, poor eyesight, an obstacle, etc.). Often followed by what you can’t see: "No puedo ver la torre" (I can’t see the tower), "No puedo ver nada" (I can’t see anything). With people, Spanish commonly uses "ver a" + person: "No puedo ver a nadie" (I can’t see anyone). It can be intensified with informal/vulgar expressions like "No puedo ver un carajo" (I can’t see a damn thing).
target_language_example: Perdón, no puedo ver el menú sin mis gafas.
native_language_example: Sorry, I can’t see the menu without my glasses.

additional_notes: Used to say you really need someone or something, often for strong feelings (love, dependence, or exaggeration). After "sin" you use a noun or a pronoun: "sin ti" (without you), "sin él" (without him), "sin ella" (without her), "sin esto" (without this). You can change the verb for other people/tense: "no puedes vivir sin..." (you can't live without...), "no podía vivir sin..." (I couldn't live without...).
target_language_example: No puedo vivir sin café por la mañana.
native_language_example: I can’t live without coffee in the morning.

additional_notes: From the verb "poder" (to be able to). Used to say you can’t do something, either because it’s impossible, too hard, or you don’t have the strength/energy. Common patterns: "no puedo + infinitive" (No puedo ir = I can’t go), "no puedo más" (I can’t take it anymore), and "no puedo con + noun/pronoun" (I can’t handle it/them).
target_language_example: Lo siento, no puedo ir hoy.
native_language_example: Sorry, I can’t go today.

additional_notes: Uses the imperfect of querer (quería) to talk about not wanting to do something in the past, often as background, a repeated feeling, or a polite/softened way to introduce what you’re about to say ("I didn’t mean to..."). Common pattern: "No quería + infinitive" (no quería interrumpir / mentirte / decir nada). Subject depends on context: yo no quería, él/ella no quería.
target_language_example: Perdón, no quería molestarte.
native_language_example: Sorry, I didn’t want to bother you.

additional_notes: Used to express that someone did not want another action to happen. After "querer que", Spanish normally uses the subjunctive: "no quería que fueras" (I didn't want you to go), "no quería que lo supiera" (didn't want him/her to know). The subject often changes after "que" (I didn’t want YOU to…), but it can also refer to fate/things: "El destino no quería que…" = "Fate didn't want…".
target_language_example: No quería que me esperaran tan tarde.
native_language_example: I didn’t want them to wait for me so late.

meaning: “(he/she/it) doesn’t want to” / “(you formal) don’t want to.”
additional_notes: From the verb **querer** (to want). **No quiere + infinitive** = “doesn’t want to + verb” (No quiere ver a nadie = He/She doesn’t want to see anyone). **No quiere que + subjunctive** = “doesn’t want (that)…” (No quiere que se sepa = He/She doesn’t want it to be known). Can refer to **él/ella/usted** depending on context.
target_language_example: No quiere salir hoy.
native_language_example: He/She doesn’t want to go out today.

additional_notes: Negative form of quiero from querer. Use it to say you do not want something (No quiero nada) or do not want to do something when followed by an infinitive (No quiero salir). It can sound direct, especially on its own.
target_language_example: Hoy no quiero salir.
native_language_example: I don't want to go out today.

additional_notes: Used to express that you don’t want someone (or something) to do an action. It’s normally followed by a verb in the present subjunctive: “no quiero que entres / lleguen / sigas…”. You can also add a person to clarify: “no quiero que tú…”, “no quiero que ellos…”.
target_language_example: No quiero que me llames después de las diez.
native_language_example: I don't want you to call me after ten.

meaning: "I don’t want you to…" (said to someone informally).
additional_notes: Used to express what you don’t want the other person (tú) to do or to have happen to them. It’s followed by a verb in the present subjunctive: no quiero que te vayas, no quiero que te preocupes. The "te" is an object/reflexive pronoun that depends on the next verb (te vayas, te pase, te escapes, te muestres).
target_language_example: No quiero que te vayas todavía.
native_language_example: I don’t want you to leave yet.

additional_notes: Used to say you don’t want to become something (a job/role/identity) or don’t want to act as something in a situation. Often followed by a noun ("No quiero ser cura"), an article + noun ("No quiero ser tu niñera"), or an adjective/idea ("No quiero ser humano").
target_language_example: Lo siento, pero no quiero ser parte de esto.
native_language_example: Sorry, but I don't want to be part of this.

additional_notes: Uses the verb **recordar** in the 1st person present (**recuerdo** = “I remember”) with **no** to make it negative. You can use it with a noun (**No recuerdo este lugar.**) or with a clause, often introduced by **qué** (“what”), **cuándo** (“when”), **dónde** (“where”), etc. It can also stand alone as a complete answer (**Ya no recuerdo.** = “I don’t remember anymore.”).
target_language_example: Lo siento, no recuerdo tu nombre.
native_language_example: Sorry, I don’t remember your name.

additional_notes: Used to say you have no memory of what happened (often after an event, shock, alcohol, sleep, an accident, etc.). In the present tense: "(yo) no recuerdo nada". You can add a time reference: "de ayer", "de anoche", "después de eso".
target_language_example: Me golpeé la cabeza y no recuerdo nada.
native_language_example: I hit my head and I don’t remember anything.

additional_notes: “No sabe” is the negation of “sabe” (3rd-person singular, present tense of *saber*). It’s used for not knowing information (No sabe con qué está jugando.) and also for not knowing how to do something / not being able to do it (No sabe nadar.). The subject can be a name (Cleo no sabe…) or implied (No sabe…).
target_language_example: Mi hermano no sabe cocinar.
native_language_example: My brother can’t cook. / My brother doesn’t know how to cook.

additional_notes: Used to say that you (a group including the speaker) lack information or are unsure. Often followed by a question word (si, qué, para qué, en qué, etc.) to introduce what is unknown: "No sabemos si..." (we don’t know whether...), "No sabemos para qué..." (we don’t know what for/why...).
target_language_example: Lo siento, no sabemos a qué hora llega el tren.
native_language_example: Sorry, we don’t know what time the train arrives.

additional_notes: Uses tú (sabes) and is addressed to one person. Common before question words: “no sabes quién…” (you don’t know who…), “no sabes lo que…” (you don’t know what…), “no sabes qué…” (you don’t know what/which…). Often used to say someone lacks information or doesn’t know what to do; by itself (“No sabes.”) it can sound blunt/critical depending on tone.
target_language_example: No sabes lo mucho que te agradezco tu ayuda.
native_language_example: You don’t know how much I appreciate your help.

additional_notes: Used to say someone has no knowledge/understanding of a person, topic, or situation. Often sounds critical or accusatory. Usually followed by a noun, pronoun (mí, ella, nosotros), or an infinitive: "No sabes nada de ser...". Note: you normally say either "no sabes nada de mí" or "no sabes nada acerca de mí" (not *"de acerca de").
target_language_example: No sabes nada de mi trabajo, así que no opines.
native_language_example: You don’t know anything about my job, so don’t give your opinion.

additional_notes: Used to introduce something you didn’t know in the past. "Sabía" is the imperfect past of "saber" (to know), often implying you lacked the information at that time. It’s commonly followed by a clause with "que"; after "no sabía que", Spanish often uses the subjunctive (e.g., "fuera") when the information is new/unknown to the speaker.
target_language_example: No sabía que vivías tan lejos.
native_language_example: I didn’t know you lived so far away.

additional_notes: Without the accent, this is not no sé ('I don't know'). no se is not one fixed expression: se can change function depending on the verb. In these examples, it can make an impersonal or passive meaning (No se permiten perros = Dogs aren't allowed), be part of a reflexive/pronominal command (No se meta... = Don't put...), or replace le/les before lo/la/los/las (No se la cuentes = Don't tell it to him/her/them).
target_language_example: Aquí no se puede fumar.
native_language_example: You can't smoke here.

meaning: Don’t come closer; don’t approach. (formal command)
additional_notes: Negative command in the usted form of acercarse (to come closer/approach). Often used with “a” + person/place: “No se acerque a la puerta.” You can add distance words like “mucho/demasiado”: “No se acerque demasiado.”
target_language_example: Por favor, no se acerque a la ventana.
native_language_example: Please, don’t go near the window.

additional_notes: Used before a verb to show a negative action with two object pronouns: **se** + **lo**. Here **se** usually stands for **le/les** (to him/her/you formal/them) because **le/les** changes to **se** when it comes before **lo/la/los/las** (e.g., *No se lo pedí* = *No le lo pedí* ❌). The exact meaning depends on the verb: *no se lo comió* (he didn’t eat it), *no se lo pedí* (I didn’t ask him/her for it), *no se lo pregunté* (I didn’t ask him/her), *no se lo tome* (don’t take it), *no se lo mostrará* (he won’t show it).
target_language_example: No se lo dije a mi jefe.
native_language_example: I didn’t tell it to my boss (I didn’t tell my boss).

meaning: “I can’t think of (anything/any reason/what to say).”
additional_notes: Literally “it doesn’t occur to me.” Uses the verb **ocurrirse** with an indirect object pronoun: **no se me ocurre** (to me), **no se te ocurre** (to you), **no se le ocurre** (to him/her/you formal). Often followed by **nada** (“anything”), **ninguna + noun** (“any + noun”), or a question word: **qué decir**, **por qué**, **cómo**.
target_language_example: Lo siento, no se me ocurre qué responder.
native_language_example: Sorry, I can’t think of what to say.

additional_notes: Used to reassure someone or tell them not to be concerned. It uses the formal usted form (preocupe), so it’s appropriate with strangers, customers, older people, or in polite situations. Informal version: “no te preocupes.” You can also add “por eso/por ello” = “about that.”
target_language_example: No se preocupe, yo me encargo de todo.
native_language_example: Don’t worry, I’ll take care of everything.

additional_notes: Very common expression meaning something is not possible or not allowed. Often used with an infinitive: «no se puede + infinitive» (e.g., «no se puede saber» = “you can’t know / it’s impossible to know”). It can be general (“you/one can’t…”) rather than referring to a specific person.
target_language_example: Aquí no se puede fumar.
native_language_example: You can’t smoke here.

additional_notes: Impersonal expression with **se** (no specific person is doing the knowing). It’s used when the information is unknown or uncertain, often followed by a question word or clause: **no se sabe qué/cuál/lo que…**.
target_language_example: No se sabe a qué hora llegará el autobús.
native_language_example: Nobody knows what time the bus will arrive.

additional_notes: Used to clarify the real point of a situation and correct a misunderstanding. Often followed by a noun ("No se trata de mí") or an infinitive verb ("No se trata de ganar dinero"). You can also use it to reject an interpretation: "No se trata de un chiste" (It’s not a joke).
target_language_example: No se trata de quién tiene la culpa; se trata de cómo lo vamos a arreglar.
native_language_example: It’s not about who’s to blame; it’s about how we’re going to fix it.

meaning: "You can't see it" / "it isn't visible"; also "it doesn't look (like)".
additional_notes:
Used with an implicit subject (it/that/he/she): 
- Visibility: "El avión no se ve" = the plane can’t be seen.
- Appearance/impression: "No se ve feliz" = he/she doesn’t look happy; "No se ve nada bien" = it doesn’t look good at all.
Often expanded as "no se ve + adjective" (doesn’t look + adjective) or "no se ve nada" (you can’t see anything).
target_language_example: Con esta niebla, la montaña no se ve.
native_language_example: With this fog, you can’t see the mountain.

meaning: "may not be" / "isn't" (subjunctive form of "ser", to be).
additional_notes: “Sea” is the present subjunctive of “ser” (to be). You often see “no sea” after expressions that trigger the subjunctive (uncertainty, doubt, wishes), like “ojalá que…”, “puede que…”, “quizás/tal vez…”. It also appears in phrases like “no tenemos otra opción que no sea…” meaning “we have no other option but to… / other than…”.
target_language_example: Espero que no sea demasiado tarde.
native_language_example: I hope it isn’t too late.

meaning: “don’t be …” (telling someone not to act a certain way).
additional_notes: Used to tell one person (tú) not to be something or not to behave in a certain way. It’s the negative tú command of ser: no seas + adjective/noun (No seas ridículo / No seas un bebé). In other contexts it can also be part of a subjunctive clause meaning “that you are not …” (Es bueno que no seas parte…).
target_language_example: No seas tan impaciente; ya casi llegamos.
native_language_example: Don’t be so impatient; we’re almost there.

meaning: “don’t be so…” (telling someone to stop being so ___).
additional_notes: Used as an informal/neutral way to criticize or scold someone. Grammatically it’s the negative tú command of **ser** (“no seas”) + **tan** (“so/as”), followed by an adjective: **No seas tan + adj.** The adjective agrees with the person you’re talking to (e.g., *tan malo/tan mala*).
target_language_example: No seas tan impaciente; ya voy.
native_language_example: Don’t be so impatient; I’m coming.

meaning: to be nothing; to be no big deal.
additional_notes: Used to minimize the importance of something or to say something isn’t serious. Often used to downplay a favor, apology, or minor issue. Because it’s an infinitive phrase, it commonly appears after a conjugated verb like «Es/era/va a/puede no ser nada» (“It is/was/it might not be anything”).
target_language_example: No te preocupes: puede no ser nada.
native_language_example: Don’t worry: it might be nothing.

meaning: “it means nothing to me” / “it doesn’t matter to me.”
additional_notes: Used to say something has no importance, value, or emotional significance for you. With people ("Él/Ella no significa nada para mí"), it can sound cold and implies you don’t care about them or don’t have feelings for them. Pattern: [subject] + no significa nada para mí.
target_language_example: Ese comentario no significa nada para mí.
native_language_example: That comment means nothing to me.

additional_notes: Used to say that you and others ("we") are not something. "Somos" is the present tense of "ser" (to be) for "nosotros/nosotras"; "no" goes directly before the verb to make it negative. Often followed by a noun/adjective: "No somos ricos" (We’re not rich), or with "los/las": "No somos los únicos" (We’re not the only ones).
target_language_example: No somos de aquí, somos de Texas.
native_language_example: We’re not from here; we’re from Texas.

additional_notes: Used to negate the verb "son" (they/you all are), from "ser". It’s followed by an adjective or a noun: "no son suficientes" (are not enough), "no son peces" (are not fish).
target_language_example: Mis llaves no son negras; son plateadas.
native_language_example: My keys aren’t black; they’re silver.

additional_notes: "No soy" is "(yo) no soy" ("I am not") and uses **ser** (soy) to talk about identity, professions, nationality, or general characteristics. It’s followed by a noun or adjective, and the adjective agrees with the speaker: *no soy sordo/sorda*, *no soy rico/rica*.
target_language_example: Lo siento, pero no soy la persona que buscas.
native_language_example: Sorry, but I'm not the person you're looking for.

meaning: "I’m not a" (said by a male speaker).
additional_notes: Used to deny being a specific kind of person/thing before a masculine singular noun: No soy un + noun/adjective phrase. For a female speaker, use “no soy una”. If the noun is feminine but the speaker is male, you still use the noun’s gender: “No soy una persona…”
target_language_example: No soy un experto, pero puedo ayudarte.
native_language_example: I’m not an expert, but I can help you.

additional_notes: Literally 'I don't know.' It is the 1st-person singular of saber. You can use it by itself as a complete response, or before a noun, infinitive, or clause: no sé los pasos, no sé decirlo, no sé qué es. With de + person, it can mean 'I haven't heard from' or 'I don't know anything about' someone.
target_language_example: No sé qué hacer ahora.
native_language_example: I don't know what to do now.

additional_notes: Used as a conversational filler to show uncertainty or soften what you’re about to say, then add a guess, opinion, contrast, or warning. Often implies “I’m not sure, but…” or “I don’t know (the full story), but…”.
target_language_example: No sé, pero creo que deberíamos irnos ya.
native_language_example: I don’t know, but I think we should leave now.

meaning: "I don’t know how many"; by extension, "so-and-so / countless" (an unknown or unspecified number).
additional_notes: Used when you don’t know (or don’t want to specify) an exact number. It can also suggest “a lot” in a casual way. It’s commonly followed by a plural noun: "no sé cuántos años" (I don’t know how many years), "no sé cuántos libros" (I don’t know how many books). It agrees with the noun in gender/number: "cuántos" (masc. plural) / "cuántas" (fem. plural).
target_language_example: He esperado no sé cuántos días para que me contestes.
native_language_example: I’ve waited I don’t know how many days for you to reply to me.

additional_notes: Used to say you don’t know the way/method to do something, or you can’t explain how something happened. It’s often followed by an infinitive (No sé cómo usarla) or by a clause (No sé cómo lo hace / No sé cómo encontró la casa). In conversation it can also express worry or uncertainty about what you’ll do next (No sé cómo voy a...).
target_language_example: No sé cómo decirle la verdad.
native_language_example: I don’t know how to tell him/her the truth.

meaning: "I don’t know anything about" / "I know nothing about".
additional_notes: Used to say you have no knowledge or information about a topic, situation, or person. The part after de can be a subject (de ciencia), a person (de él/ella), or an event (de ningún secuestro). Often implies ignorance or denial of involvement: No sé nada de eso = “I know nothing about that.”
target_language_example: Lo siento, no sé nada de este tema.
native_language_example: Sorry, I don’t know anything about this topic.

additional_notes: Used to say you have zero knowledge/information about a topic. Follow it with a noun (no sé nada sobre arte), a pronoun (no sé nada sobre eso/ello), or a person (no sé nada sobre él). In speech you can also hear the same idea as “No sé nada de …” (e.g., No sé nada de Linux).
target_language_example: Lo siento, no sé nada sobre ese tema.
native_language_example: Sorry, I don’t know anything about that topic.

additional_notes: Used to express that you don’t know the reason for something. Often followed by a full clause ("No sé por qué dijo eso"), but it can also be said alone as a complete answer ("No sé por qué."). You’ll also hear the variant "No sé por qué + infinitive" (e.g., "No sé por qué ir"), meaning “I don’t know why (to) …”.
target_language_example: No sé por qué no me contestas.
native_language_example: I don’t know why you’re not answering me.

additional_notes: Most commonly used to introduce an indirect question: “No sé qué significa” = “I don’t know what it means.” In casual speech it can also work like a vague filler after a name or description, similar to “so-and-so” or “whatever”: “Freddy no sé qué” (like “Freddy what’s-his-name / Freddy something-or-other”). Often appears with other words like “no sé qué más…” = “I don’t know what else…”.
target_language_example: No sé qué decir en esta situación.
native_language_example: I don't know what to say in this situation.

meaning: I don’t know what to do.
additional_notes: Used to express uncertainty or being stuck about what action to take. You can add extra details with "con + [person/thing]" (e.g., "no sé qué hacer con ella" = "I don’t know what to do with her"). Often said on its own as a complete sentence, and you may hear it with fillers like "es que" to sound more natural in conversation.
target_language_example: Estoy muy nervioso y no sé qué hacer.
native_language_example: I’m very nervous and I don’t know what to do.

additional_notes: Used to express uncertainty about whether something is true or will happen. It’s often followed by a verb in the indicative (No sé si llueve / lloverá) and can also be used to soften an opinion or question (No sé si es buena idea…).
target_language_example: No sé si tengo tiempo hoy.
native_language_example: I don't know if I have time today.

additional_notes: Used to express uncertainty about what something is (or whether it has a certain quality). It’s often followed by an adjective or noun: “No sé si es seguro” (safe), “No sé si es amor” (love). You can also add “una buena idea” (a good idea).
target_language_example: No sé si es el momento adecuado para hablar.
native_language_example: I don’t know if it’s the right time to talk.

additional_notes: A very common combination of no + te. Before a verb, it often means 'you don't' in statements (no te veo = I don't see you) or helps form a negative tú command (no te acerques = don't come near). Depending on the verb, te can mean 'you,' 'to you,' or 'yourself.'
target_language_example: No te preocupes por eso.
native_language_example: Don't worry about that.

additional_notes: A strong warning/command telling someone not to do something. Uses the verb "atreverse" (to dare) in the present subjunctive: "te atrevas". It’s followed by an infinitive: "no te atrevas a decir / hablar / ponerte...". Common in arguments and can sound threatening or very firm.
target_language_example: No te atrevas a tocar eso.
native_language_example: Don’t you dare touch that.

meaning: “Don’t hold back / don’t be shy; go ahead.” (Also literally: “Don’t cut yourself.”)
additional_notes: It’s the negative tú command of the reflexive verb cortarse. In everyday speech, cortarse often means “to feel shy/embarrassed” or “to hold back,” so no te cortes is used to encourage someone to act/speak without hesitation (similar to “go for it”). In a physical context (e.g., with paper, knives), it can mean “don’t cut yourself.”
target_language_example: No te cortes y pregúntale al profesor si no entiendes algo.
native_language_example: Don’t be shy—ask the teacher if you don’t understand something.

meaning: "don’t think so" / "not really" (used to correct or downplay something).
additional_notes: Common in conversation to disagree gently or to say something isn’t as true/important as it seems. Literally it comes from "creerse" (to believe/think), but in practice it often means “actually, no” or “don’t assume that.” Sometimes it can also mean “don’t believe it,” depending on context.
target_language_example: ¿Crees que soy muy bueno en español? No te creas, todavía me falta mucho.
native_language_example: Do you think I’m really good at Spanish? Not really—I still have a long way to go.

additional_notes: Commonly used to call someone out for pretending or acting innocent: “No te hagas (el/la) + noun/adjective” (e.g., “No te hagas el listo” = don’t act smart). It also appears with reflexive idioms like “no te hagas ilusiones” (don’t get your hopes up) and other “hacerse + …” expressions (e.g., “no te hagas explotar” = don’t blow yourself up / don’t get yourself blown up). Often sounds colloquial in the standalone form “No te hagas.”
target_language_example: No te hagas; sé que tú también quieres ir.
native_language_example: Don’t pretend; I know you also want to go.

additional_notes: With "si" + verb, it’s a common way to ask permission or check if something is okay: "¿No te importa si…?" = "Do you mind if…?" (often polite). Said on its own, it can mean "You don’t care" or, in a sharper tone, "It’s none of your business." Uses "te" (tú), so it’s informal in the sense of being the tú form (vs. "no le importa").
target_language_example: ¿No te importa si abro la ventana?
native_language_example: Do you mind if I open the window?

meaning: “don’t … it / you can’t … it” (no + te + lo before a verb).
additional_notes: This is a common pronoun cluster used before a verb: **no** (not/don’t) + **te** (“to you” or “for yourself”) + **lo** (“it”). It depends on the verb that follows: **No te lo pienses** = “Don’t think about it,” **No te lo pierdas** = “Don’t miss it,” **No te lo puedes imaginar** = “You can’t imagine it,” **No te lo tomes a pecho** = “Don’t take it so personally.”
target_language_example: No te lo digas a nadie.
native_language_example: Don’t tell it to anyone.

additional_notes: Used to tell someone (informally) not to interfere, not to get involved, or not to poke their nose into a situation or someone else’s business. It’s the negative tú command of meterse en (“to get into / get involved in”). Often followed by esto/eso (“this/that”), mis asuntos (“my business”), la vida de los demás (“other people’s lives”), lo que no te importa (“what doesn’t concern you”).
target_language_example: No te metas en mis asuntos; yo lo arreglo.
native_language_example: Don’t meddle in my business; I’ll handle it.

additional_notes: An informal command using the negative tú imperative of "moverse" (to move). Common in urgent situations (e.g., during a photo, when someone might be in danger). You can add location: "No te muevas de ahí" = "Don’t move from there / Stay right there."
target_language_example: No te muevas, ya vuelvo.
native_language_example: Don’t move; I’ll be right back.

meaning: "Don’t get" / "don’t become" (in a certain mood or state).
additional_notes: Used to tell someone not to start feeling or acting a certain way, especially with emotions or reactions: no te pongas celoso/a (don’t get jealous), no te pongas histérico/a (don’t get hysterical), no te pongas así (don’t get like that). It comes from the verb ponerse (“to get/become” in a temporary state). Often followed by an adjective or “así.”
target_language_example: No te pongas nervioso, todo va a salir bien.
native_language_example: Don’t get nervous; everything is going to be fine.

additional_notes: Used to reassure someone or tell them not to be concerned. It’s the informal (tú) negative command of "preocuparse" (to worry). Common in responses like "No te preocupes, yo me encargo" (Don’t worry, I’ll take care of it) or "No te preocupes, está cubierto" (Don’t worry, it’s covered/it’s on me).
target_language_example: No te preocupes, lo arreglo en un momento.
native_language_example: Don’t worry, I’ll fix it in a moment.

additional_notes: Used to reassure someone and tell them not to worry about a person/thing/situation. Often followed by a noun or pronoun (por él, por eso, por el problema). You can also hear: “No te preocupes” = “Don’t worry.”
target_language_example: No te preocupes por mí; estoy bien.
native_language_example: Don’t worry about me; I’m fine.

additional_notes:
Negative tú command of **quedarse** (“to stay/remain/end up”). It’s often followed by:
- **a place/position**: *No te quedes ahí sentado* (“Don’t stay sitting there.”)
- **an adjective/state**: *No te quedes dormido / hambriento* (“Don’t fall asleep / don’t end up hungry.”)
- **a gerund (-ando/-iendo)**: *No te quedes mirando* (“Don’t keep staring/watching.”)
- **an adverb**: *No te quedes atrás* (“Don’t fall behind.”)
target_language_example: No te quedes callado; dime qué pasó.
native_language_example: Don’t stay quiet; tell me what happened.

meaning: Don’t just stand (sit) there; don’t stay there.
additional_notes: An informal-sounding imperative using quedar(se) (“to stay/remain”) + ahí (“there”). It’s used to urge someone to move or take action instead of remaining where they are. Often expanded with an adjective/participle that agrees with the person: no te quedes ahí parado/parada (standing), sentado/sentada (sitting).
target_language_example: ¡No te quedes ahí, ven a ayudarme!
native_language_example: Don’t just stand there—come help me!

additional_notes: Negative command (tú) of the verb irse (“to leave/go away”). Often used to ask someone to stay, sometimes with extra details: no te vayas sin mí (“don’t go without me”), no te vayas a ninguna parte / a ningún lado (“don’t go anywhere”).
target_language_example: No te vayas todavía, por favor.
native_language_example: Don’t leave yet, please.

additional_notes: “No” + “tenemos” (we have). Used to say that “we” lack something or don’t possess something. Often followed by a noun (“no tenemos clase/comida”), or by “nada” (“no tenemos nada en común”), or by fixed phrases like “no tenemos más remedio” / “no tenemos otra opción” (= we have no choice).
target_language_example: Lo siento, no tenemos tiempo para ir hoy.
native_language_example: Sorry, we don’t have time to go today.

meaning: to have no idea; to not know (at all).
additional_notes: Commonly used to say you don’t know something. Conjugate “tener” to match the subject/tense (e.g., “no tengo idea”, “no tenía idea”, “no tendrás idea”). Often followed by a question word or by “de” + clause/infinitive: “no tener idea de qué… / de cómo…”. You can also say “no tener ni idea” for extra emphasis.
target_language_example: A esta hora, yo digo que no tener idea de dónde está mi teléfono es un problema.
native_language_example: At this point, I’d say that having no idea where my phone is is a problem.

meaning: to have no idea; to have no clue.
additional_notes: Used to say you don’t know something at all. Often followed by "de" + noun/infinitive: "No tener ni idea de dónde está" (to have no idea where it is). You can change the verb to match the subject/tense: "No tengo ni idea" / "No tenía ni idea" / "No tendríamos ni idea".
target_language_example: No tener ni idea de cómo se hace esto es normal al principio.
native_language_example: Having no idea how this is done is normal at the beginning.

meaning: to be speechless; to not know what to say.
additional_notes: Used when something surprises, shocks, moves, or amazes you so much that you can’t find the words. Very common in the structure “No tengo palabras para + infinitive” (e.g., “No tengo palabras para agradecerte”).
target_language_example: No tengo palabras para agradecerte todo lo que hiciste.
native_language_example: I’m speechless—I don’t have words to thank you for everything you did.

meaning: to be beyond help; to have no solution (it can’t be helped).
additional_notes: Used to say a situation (or a person’s behavior) is hopeless, inevitable, or won’t change. Often used in the phrase “No tiene remedio.” Can also be used jokingly about yourself: “Yo no tengo remedio.”
target_language_example: Lo siento, pero esta situación va a empeorar: no tener remedio.
native_language_example: I’m sorry, but this situation is going to get worse: it has no solution / it can’t be helped.

additional_notes: Negative tú command of tener (“tengas” is the present subjunctive): literally “don’t have fear.” Used to reassure someone. Often followed by a reason with porque (e.g., “No tengas miedo, porque…”). Common with affectionate words like bebé or cariño.
target_language_example: No tengas miedo, estoy aquí contigo.
native_language_example: Don’t be afraid, I’m here with you.

additional_notes: Used to say that you do not have something. It is the negative form of tengo, the first-person singular of tener (“to have”). It can refer to physical things, people, places to go, or abstract things like time or money.
target_language_example: No tengo coche.
native_language_example: I don't have a car.

meaning: "I have no idea (about)…" / "I don’t know… (at all)."
additional_notes: Used to say you don’t know something (often strongly). It’s followed by a question word like cómo (how), dónde (where), por qué (why), quién (who), or qué (what/which/what it means). You can also say: "No tengo idea" by itself.
target_language_example: No tengo idea de a qué hora empieza la reunión.
native_language_example: I have no idea what time the meeting starts.

additional_notes: Literally “I don’t have nothing/anything.” Used to say you don’t possess something or don’t have something to give/offer. It can also be used in expressions like “No tengo nada en contra de…” = “I have nothing against …” (meaning you don’t dislike or oppose someone/something).
target_language_example: Lo siento, no tengo nada de dinero ahora.
native_language_example: Sorry, I don’t have any money right now.

additional_notes: Used to say you don’t have anything to do/say/eat/add/etc. It’s followed by an infinitive verb: “no tengo nada que + infinitive” (e.g., no tengo nada que hacer, no tengo nada que decir). You can change “tengo” to match the person: “no tienes nada que…”, “no tiene nada que…”, “no tenemos nada que…”.
target_language_example: Lo siento, no tengo nada que mostrarte hoy.
native_language_example: Sorry, I don't have anything to show you today.

meaning: “I have no idea (about)…” / “I don’t know at all…”
additional_notes: Used to strongly say you don’t know something. Often followed by a question word (adónde, cuáles, cuántos, dónde, qué) or by “lo que…”. You can also hear it without “de” when the next word is a question word: “No tengo ni idea qué es esto.”
target_language_example: No tengo ni idea de dónde está mi móvil.
native_language_example: I have no idea where my phone is.

meaning: “I don’t have to” / “I have no reason to.”
additional_notes: Used to say you don’t feel obligated or you don’t see any justification for doing something. Often followed by an infinitive: “No tengo por qué + infinitive” (e.g., disculparme, hacerlo). It can also be used alone to mean “I don’t have to (do that).”
target_language_example: No tengo por qué explicarte nada.
native_language_example: I don’t have to explain anything to you.

additional_notes: Used to say you’re too busy to do something. Follow it with a noun (para eso/esto), an infinitive (para ayudarte), or a person/pronoun (para ti/para mí). You can change the verb to match the subject: no tengo (I), no tienes (you), no tiene (he/she/you formal), no tenemos (we).
target_language_example: Lo siento, no tengo tiempo para hablar ahora.
native_language_example: Sorry, I don’t have time to talk right now.

additional_notes: Negative of «tenía» (imperfect of «tener»). Used for ongoing situations in the past (“didn’t have”), background description, or habitual past (“used to not have”). Often followed by a noun (no tenía agua), an infinitive phrase (no tenía dónde esconderme = “I had nowhere to hide”), or expressions like «no tenía otro remedio» (“I had no other choice”).
target_language_example: Cuando era niño, no tenía dinero para comprar helado.
native_language_example: When I was a kid, I didn’t have money to buy ice cream.

additional_notes: Used with a singular third-person subject: él, ella, usted, or a thing/idea. It comes from tener ('to have') and is commonly used to say that someone or something lacks something.
target_language_example: Este hotel no tiene piscina.
native_language_example: This hotel doesn't have a pool.

additional_notes: Common (especially in Mexico and some parts of Latin America) to say an action is useless or won’t change anything. It’s usually followed by an infinitive: "No tiene caso + discutir/quejarse/intentarlo". Also used as a stand-alone comment to mean "it’s pointless." Similar to "no vale la pena" and "no tiene sentido."
target_language_example: No tiene caso intentarlo otra vez; ya es demasiado tarde.
native_language_example: There’s no point trying again; it’s already too late.

no tiene nada que ver con

target_language_multi_word_term: no tiene nada que ver con
meaning: “has nothing to do with” / “is not related to”.
additional_notes: Used to say there is no connection or relevance between two things. The basic structure is: (subject) + no tiene nada que ver con + noun / person / situation. It can change for tense and person: no tengo nada que ver con… (I have nothing to do with…), no tiene nada que ver con… (it has nothing to do with…).
target_language_example: Eso no tiene nada que ver con mi decisión.
native_language_example: That has nothing to do with my decision.

additional_notes: Used to say something is not necessary or not required. Often followed by an infinitive ("No tiene por qué ir") or by "ser" + adjective ("No tiene por qué ser así"). It can also suggest “there’s no reason why it should be that way.”
target_language_example: No tiene por qué preocuparte ahora.
native_language_example: You don’t have to worry right now.

meaning: “It doesn’t make sense.” / “It has no meaning.”
additional_notes: Used to say something is illogical, unclear, or pointless. It can refer to an idea/explanation/story (“Esto no tiene sentido.”) or to life having (or lacking) meaning (“Mi vida no tiene sentido sin ti.”). Also appears as “no tiene sentido de…” meaning someone lacks a certain quality or attitude (e.g., “no tiene sentido de la aventura” = “has no sense of adventure”).
target_language_example: Lo que dices no tiene sentido.
native_language_example: What you’re saying doesn’t make sense.

additional_notes: Present-tense negative of “tener” (to have) for “ellos/ellas/ustedes” (they / you all). Used to say someone lacks something (“no tienen cerebro” = they don’t have a brain) or doesn’t possess it (“no tienen el expediente” = they don’t have the file).
target_language_example: No tienen tiempo hoy, así que lo hacemos mañana.
native_language_example: They don’t have time today, so we’ll do it tomorrow.

additional_notes: Literally means “you don’t have” (to a person you address as tú). Very commonly used in fixed patterns: (1) “no tienes que + infinitive” = “you don’t have to …” / “you’re not required to …” (No tienes que ser mi amiga.); (2) “no tienes nada que + infinitive” = “you have nothing to …” (No tienes nada que temer.); (3) “no tienes más que + infinitive” = “you only have to …” / “all you have to do is …” (No tienes más que pulsar el botón.).
target_language_example: No tienes que venir hoy si estás cansado.
native_language_example: You don’t have to come today if you’re tired.

additional_notes: Used to tell someone they don’t understand something or don’t know important information. Very often followed by a question word clause: no tienes idea de qué/quién/cuál/cuánto…, or by “lo que…” / “en qué…”. You can also use other subjects: no tengo idea de… (I have no idea), no tiene idea de… (he/she/you formal has no idea).
target_language_example: No tienes idea de cuánto trabajo me costó terminar esto.
native_language_example: You have no idea how much work it took me to finish this.

meaning: "you don’t have to" / "there’s no need for you to".
additional_notes: Used to tell someone they are not obliged to do something, or that there’s no reason/need to do it. It’s often followed by an infinitive (no tienes por qué + decir/hacer/quejarte) and can sound reassuring or slightly firm depending on tone. You can change the person: no tengo por qué, no tienes por qué, no tiene por qué, etc.
target_language_example: No tienes por qué preocuparte; yo me encargo.
native_language_example: You don’t have to worry; I’ll take care of it.

additional_notes: Used to tell one person (tú) that something is not necessary or not required. It’s often followed by an infinitive: "no tienes que + infinitive" (no tienes que hacer / decir / preocuparte). For other people: "no tengo que" (I don’t have to), "no tiene que" (he/she/you formal), "no tenemos que" (we), "no tienen que" (they/you plural).
target_language_example: No tienes que venir mañana si estás cansado.
native_language_example: You don't have to come tomorrow if you're tired.

additional_notes: Used to say that a statement doesn’t apply to every member of a group. It’s typically followed by a plural noun ("no todos los errores") or by "que" + verb ("No todos los que vienen..."), and often contrasts with a generalization.
target_language_example: No todos los estudiantes tienen tiempo para estudiar hoy.
native_language_example: Not all (the) students have time to study today.

meaning: “is not going to” (negative of *ir a* + infinitive).
additional_notes: Used before an infinitive to talk about a future plan or something expected to happen (often in the near future). Conjugate **ir** for the subject: *no voy a*, *no vas a*, *no va a*, *no vamos a*, *no van a* + infinitive. Example: *No va a llegar* = “He/She isn’t going to arrive / won’t make it.”
target_language_example: Lo siento, no va a poder venir hoy.
native_language_example: Sorry, he/she isn’t going to be able to come today.

additional_notes: Idiomatic phrase meaning that nothing else can be added or done—there’s no room/time for more. Common in the context of gambling (roulette/casino) as “no more bets,” and also used more generally to mean “that’s it, end of story” or “it can’t get any better / any further.”
target_language_example: Lo siento, no va más: ya no aceptamos más pedidos hoy.
native_language_example: Sorry, that’s it: we’re not taking any more orders today.

meaning: “it’s not worth it / it’s not worth the trouble.”
additional_notes: Used to say something isn’t worth doing (because it’s too much effort, risk, time, money, etc.). Often followed by an infinitive: “No vale la pena + infinitive” (No vale la pena discutir / hablar). You can also use it alone as a reaction: “¡No vale la pena!”
target_language_example: No vale la pena preocuparse por eso.
native_language_example: It’s not worth worrying about that.

meaning: “we’re not going to …” / “we’re not going to (do something).”
additional_notes: Used with an infinitive to talk about a future plan/intention that won’t happen, or to refuse/deny doing something: no vamos a + infinitive (ir, trabajar, volver, etc.). In speech it can sound like a firm decision (“we won’t…”).
target_language_example: No vamos a hablar de eso hoy.
native_language_example: We’re not going to talk about that today.

meaning: "you’re not going to..." (near future; tú form).
additional_notes: Used with an infinitive to say something will not happen (or someone won’t be able to do it): no vas a + infinitive. It’s the negative of the common future structure ir a + infinitive (“to be going to”). This is for tú; other forms include: no voy a (I’m not going to), no va a (he/she isn’t going to), no vamos a (we aren’t going to), no van a (they aren’t going to).
target_language_example: No vas a entender si no escuchas.
native_language_example: You’re not going to understand if you don’t listen.

additional_notes: Used before an infinitive to say what the speaker is not going to do. It is the negative first-person singular of the ir a + infinitive future construction, and it can also sound like a firm refusal or decision depending on context.
target_language_example: No voy a comprar eso.
native_language_example: I'm not going to buy that.

additional_notes: Used to tell someone not to repeat an action. It’s a negative command with "volver a" (to do something again). After "a" you use an infinitive: "No vuelvas a decir...", "No vuelvas a hacer...". It can sound strict or threatening depending on context and tone.
target_language_example: No vuelvas a hablarme así.
native_language_example: Don’t talk to me like that again.

meaning: "No, the…" (correcting/clarifying which masculine thing you mean).
additional_notes: Used when you say “no” and then specify the correct option with a masculine noun: “No, el metro”, “No, el grande”. It often answers a misunderstanding and is said with a short pause (written with a comma). Use **el** with masculine nouns; for feminine nouns you’d use **no, la**. You can also add an adjective or pronoun after **el** when the noun is understood from context (e.g., **No, el mío** = “No, mine”).
target_language_example: —¿Quieres el pequeño? —No, el grande.
native_language_example: —Do you want the small one? —No, the big one.

additional_notes: Used at the start of a reply to contradict what was just said or assumed, then give the correct information. Often followed by a noun/adjective clause: “No, es de…”, “No, es en serio”, “No, es que…”. In speech it’s a common correction/clarification marker.
target_language_example: No, es que no tengo tiempo ahora.
native_language_example: No, it’s just that I don’t have time right now.

meaning: "No, I am…" (used to correct or contradict).
additional_notes: Used to say that something is NOT the case and then state your situation with the verb estar (yo estoy). Common patterns: (1) + adjective: "No, estoy cansado" (I’m tired). (2) + en + place/location: "No, estoy en…" (I’m in/at…). (3) + gerund to describe what you’re doing right now: "No, estoy hablando…" (I’m speaking…).
target_language_example: No, estoy ocupado ahora.
native_language_example: No, I’m busy right now.

meaning: "No, it’s…" / "No, he/she is…" (correcting someone: "No, it is/isn’t…").
additional_notes: Used to correct or contradict what someone just said, followed by a description of the situation or someone’s state/location. "Está" is from **estar** (temporary state, location, condition): *No, está bien / cerca / preocupado / roto.* Don’t confuse **está** (verb, with accent) with **esta** ("this" feminine, no accent): *No, esta puede ser nuestra única oportunidad…* ("No, this might be our only chance…").
target_language_example: No, está en casa; no puede venir ahora.
native_language_example: No, he’s at home; he can’t come right now.

additional_notes: A polite way to refuse or decline an offer or invitation. Often said as a full response by itself, or followed by a reason (e.g., “No, gracias. Estoy bien.”). You may also hear it without the comma: “No gracias.”
target_language_example: No, gracias. No quiero nada más.
native_language_example: No, thanks. I don’t want anything else.

additional_notes: "No," is often used to answer or correct someone, followed by a sentence. "Lo" is a direct object pronoun meaning "it" (or "him"), referring to something already known from context. It usually goes right before a conjugated verb: "No, lo hice" = "No, I did it." (In "No, lo que...", "lo que" means "what/that which"—a different use of "lo".)
target_language_example: No, lo compré ayer.
native_language_example: No, I bought it yesterday.

meaning: “No, …” followed by “me” (“me / myself”) starting the next clause.
additional_notes: This isn’t a set phrase; it’s just a very common pattern in conversation: you say “No,” and then your next sentence begins with the object/reflexive pronoun **me**. You’ll see it with verbs like **gustar** (**No, me gusta…** = “No, I like…”), with accidents/things happening to you (**No, me lo perdí** = “No, I missed it”), or with reflexive verbs (**No, me voy** = “No, I’m leaving”). The comma is a pause in speech; in writing it may or may not appear.
target_language_example: No, me siento bien hoy.
native_language_example: No, I don’t feel well today.

additional_notes: Repeating “no” is very common in spoken Spanish to sound firmer, more certain, or to correct/deny something quickly (similar to “No, no…” / “No, not at all…” in English). It can be followed by an explanation (No, no puedo, porque…) or used alone (No, no mucho.). Intonation matters: it can sound polite but definite, or strongly insistent depending on tone.
target_language_example: No, no puedo ir hoy; tengo que trabajar.
native_language_example: No, I can’t go today; I have to work.

additional_notes: Used to correct or deny a statement about what something is. Often followed by a noun (No, no es gato.), an article + noun (No, no es la verdad.), or a negative word like nada/ninguno for emphasis (No, no es nada. / No, no es ninguna prueba.). In Spanish, double negatives are normal and correct.
target_language_example: —¿Es tuyo este libro? —No, no es mío.
native_language_example: —Is this book yours? —No, it isn't mine.

meaning: “No, no…” (a firm or emphatic “no”; also used to correct or disagree).
additional_notes: Repeating “no” adds emphasis. It can sound like: (1) a stronger refusal (“No, no, eso no va a pasar.”), (2) a correction/clarification (“No, no, eso es lo que no quiero que hagas.”), or (3) mild disagreement, sometimes with a surprised/admiring tone depending on context (“No, no, ese sí que es un buen truco…”). Intonation matters: it can be friendly or more forceful.
target_language_example: No, no, gracias; prefiero quedarme en casa.
native_language_example: No, no, thanks; I’d rather stay home.

additional_notes: Repeating “no” is a common way to make a refusal stronger, show disagreement, or stop/correct someone (similar to “No, no, no!” in English). The number of “no”s varies with emotion/urgency. Often followed by a term of address like “cariño” (honey) or “hombre” (man/dude) to soften it or make it more conversational.
target_language_example: No, no, no, gracias; hoy no puedo.
native_language_example: No, no, no, thanks; I can’t today.

meaning: “No, no, …” (followed by a phrase starting with “por” to add emphasis or direction).
additional_notes: This is a common spoken pattern: you repeat “no” to strongly reject, interrupt, or correct someone, and then add a “por + …” phrase depending on what you mean. Examples: “por Dios” = “for God’s sake,” “por favor” = “please,” “por aquí” = “this way / over here,” “por si acaso” = “just in case.” The exact meaning comes from what follows “por.”
target_language_example: No, no, por favor, no lo toques.
native_language_example: No, no, please, don’t touch it.

meaning: “No, but …” (a refusal/disagreement followed by a contrast, correction, or extra point).
additional_notes: Used at the start of a reply to reject or disagree with what was said or implied, then add a contrasting idea or important detail. Often sets up a correction (“No, pero…”), an exception (“No, pero…”), or a request after saying no (“No, pero dame detalles.”). In speech it’s usually said with a brief pause after “no”.
target_language_example: No, pero mañana sí puedo ayudarte.
native_language_example: No, but tomorrow I can help you.

meaning: “No, because …” (a negative reply followed by the reason).
additional_notes: Used to answer a question or reject an idea, then immediately explain why. In speech it often has a slight pause after “no” (shown by the comma), and the reason comes after “porque.” You can also hear it used defensively or to correct someone’s assumption: “No, porque…” = “No, that’s not it—because…”.
target_language_example: ¿Vienes hoy? No, porque tengo que trabajar.
native_language_example: Are you coming today? No, because I have to work.

additional_notes: Used to answer "no" and then add a small correction/clarification: you’re saying it’s not what the other person thinks—it's only this. In these examples, **solo** means **only/just** (not "alone"). You may also see **sólo** with an accent in older writing, but **solo** is standard now.
target_language_example: No, solo quiero ayudarte un momento.
native_language_example: No, I just want to help you for a moment.

meaning: “No, I’m…” (used to deny or correct who/what you are).
additional_notes: Used to correct an assumption about your identity, job/role, relationship, nationality, etc. It uses **soy** (1st person singular of **ser**, “to be”). Often followed by a noun or adjective: *No, soy doctor.* / *No, soy español.* The comma is optional in writing: *No soy…*
target_language_example: No, soy tu profesor; soy tu compañero de clase.
native_language_example: No, I’m not your teacher; I’m your classmate.

additional_notes: Used at the start of a reply to correct what someone assumed or to downplay something. It’s often followed by an explanation: “No, sólo quería charlar” (“No, I just wanted to chat”). Note: Spanish “sólo/solo” usually means “only/just” in this use, not English “solo” (alone), so it can be confusing.
target_language_example: No, sólo estaba preguntando.
native_language_example: No, I was just asking.

meaning: “No, you…” / “No, to you…” (starting a reply and addressing someone directly).
additional_notes: Used at the start of a sentence to contradict or correct someone: “No, te…” + verb. The comma is common in writing because it’s like “No, listen…” “Te” is an object pronoun meaning “to you” (or sometimes just “you” depending on the verb), and it normally goes right before the conjugated verb: “No, te entiendo” = “No, I understand you.”
target_language_example: No, te lo dije ayer.
native_language_example: No, I told you yesterday.

additional_notes: Used to start an answer that corrects or reassures someone by saying something has already happened or is already true (often with the sense of “don’t worry/it’s taken care of”). Common with verbs like: “No, ya he comido” (I’ve already eaten), “No, ya lo sé” (I already know), “No, ya los tengo” (I already have them). It can also introduce something expected soon: “No, ya vendrá …” (She’ll come later / She’ll show up). The comma reflects a pause; in speech it’s the intonation that matters.
target_language_example: —¿Te llamo un taxi? —No, ya viene mi hermano.
native_language_example: “Should I call you a taxi?” “No, my brother is already coming.”

additional_notes: Used to contradict or correct someone and emphasize that *you* (not someone else) will/won’t do something. In Spanish you can omit the subject pronoun, so adding "yo" here is for emphasis or contrast: "No, (yo) no..." = "No, *I* don't..."
target_language_example: No, yo no dije eso.
native_language_example: No, I didn't say that.

additional_notes: Used to strongly deny, disagree, or correct what was just said or suggested. The second "no" adds emphasis and can also sound reassuring in replies like "No, no fue nada" ("No, it was nothing"). Common in conversation.
target_language_example: No, no puedo ir hoy.
native_language_example: No, I can't go today.

additional_notes: Often used on its own to gently disagree with what someone has just said or assumed. Literally it comes from creer ('to believe/think'), so before que it can also mean 'don't think that...': No creas que es fácil.
target_language_example: —¿Es un examen fácil? —No creas.
native_language_example: —Is it an easy exam? —Not really.

meaning: “there isn’t/aren’t any more” or “so there won’t be any more.”
additional_notes: Uses the present subjunctive of **haber** (**haya**) after **no**. Common after expressions of purpose or prevention: **para que no haya más + noun** (“so there won’t be any more + noun”), e.g., problems, mistakes, confusion. It can also be used in firm instructions with **que**: **¡Que no haya más ruido!** (“No more noise!”).
target_language_example: Hablemos ahora para que no haya más malentendidos.
native_language_example: Let’s talk now so there won’t be any more misunderstandings.

additional_notes: Used to say something is not important. Common patterns: “No importa si + clause” = “It doesn’t matter if…”. Often used alone (“No importa.”) meaning “It doesn’t matter / No worries.” In this phrase, “importa” comes from “importar” = “to matter” (not “to import”).
target_language_example: No importa si llegas tarde; empezamos cuando puedas.
native_language_example: It doesn’t matter if you arrive late; we’ll start when you can.

additional_notes: Negative tú command (informal singular) from the verb "llorar" (to cry). Used to tell one person not to cry, often to comfort them. You may also see it in the proverb "No llores sobre la leche derramada" (“Don’t cry over spilled milk”). For a formal or plural command: "no llore" (usted) / "no lloren" (ustedes).
target_language_example: No llores; todo va a estar bien.
native_language_example: Don’t cry; everything is going to be okay.

additional_notes: Often used in many Latin American varieties to mean “only” or “just,” usually after the word or phrase it limits: uno no más = “just one.” Depending on context, it can also keep its more literal sense of “no more.”
target_language_example: Quiero uno no más.
native_language_example: I only want one.

meaning: to not stop; to keep (doing something).
additional_notes: Often used with **de + infinitive**: **no parar de + verb** = “to keep on / can’t stop (doing something)”. It can describe repeated actions, activity, or movement.
target_language_example: Esta semana prometí no parar de trabajar hasta terminar el proyecto.
native_language_example: This week I promised not to stop working until I finish the project.

additional_notes: Very common, friendly phrase used to reassure someone or downplay an issue (after an apology, a small mistake, bad news, or an inconvenience). Literally “nothing happens,” but it usually means “it’s not a big deal.” Often used on its own as a complete response.
target_language_example: Perdón por llegar tarde. —No pasa nada.
native_language_example: Sorry for arriving late. —No problem.

meaning: to not be able to take it anymore; to be at your limit (often: exhausted).
additional_notes: Used to express that you’ve reached your physical or emotional limit. Often followed by a cause: “No puedo más con este calor” (I can’t take this heat anymore) or used alone: “No puedo más” (I can’t go on / I can’t take it anymore). With “ya” it emphasizes “anymore”: “Ya no puedo más.”
target_language_example: Después de tantas horas sin dormir, ya no poder más me tenía desesperado.
native_language_example: After so many hours without sleep, not being able to take it anymore had me desperate.

additional_notes: Often a negative command meaning “don’t look/watch” + [noun] (“No veas la televisión.” = “Don’t watch TV.”). In Spain it’s also a very common colloquial expression used to emphasize how intense/surprising something is, similar to “wow” or “you have no idea” (“No veas los gritos que pegaba.” ≈ “You should’ve heard the screams he was letting out.”). It can be used on its own: “No veas.”
target_language_example: ¡No veas el frío que hace hoy!
native_language_example: Wow, it’s so cold today!

additional_notes: Used to refer to the night of a wedding (often the first night the couple spends together as married partners). It’s usually said with a possessive: "mi/tu/nuestra noche de bodas". "Bodas" is plural in Spanish here.
target_language_example: Reservaron una suite para su noche de bodas.
native_language_example: They booked a suite for their wedding night.

additional_notes: Used on forms and in official contexts to ask for or state your full legal name (first name + both last names in many Spanish-speaking countries). You may see it as a label by itself: “Nombre completo:”.
target_language_example: Por favor, escriba su nombre completo aquí.
native_language_example: Please write your full name here.

additional_notes: Used to refer to someone’s given name (the name you receive at birth/baptism), as opposed to surnames (apellidos). Common in more formal contexts; in everyday speech people also say “nombre” when it’s clear they mean first name.
target_language_example: ¿Cuál es tu nombre de pila?
native_language_example: What is your first name?

meaning: proper name / proper noun; (on forms) first name (given name).
additional_notes: In grammar, a "nombre propio" is a name that identifies a specific person, place, organization, etc. (e.g., Ana, Madrid) and is usually capitalized. In everyday contexts (especially on forms), "nombre propio" can mean your given name (first name), often contrasted with "apellido" (last name).
target_language_example: Escribe tu nombre propio y tu apellido aquí.
native_language_example: Write your first name and your last name here.

additional_notes: Used on forms, registrations, deliveries, and official requests when someone needs your identifying info. Often appears as a prompt by itself (e.g., “Nombre y dirección, por favor.”).
target_language_example: Para enviar el paquete, necesito tu nombre y dirección.
native_language_example: To send the package, I need your name and address.

additional_notes: From the verb casarse (to get married). Nos is the “we/us” reflexive pronoun here (“we marry ourselves” → “we get married”). Often used with time phrases like hace siete años (seven years ago) or with places like en Las Vegas. Without context, it can mean either past (“we got married”) or present/future for a planned event (“we’re getting married”).
target_language_example: Nos casamos el próximo sábado.
native_language_example: We’re getting married next Saturday.

additional_notes: Used when two people are familiar with each other (not “I know you” in the sense of knowing information). It’s the reciprocal form of conocer: conocer = to meet/know (a person), conocerse = to know each other. Often used with time/degree words: Hace mucho que nos conocemos (We’ve known each other for a long time), Apenas nos conocemos (We barely know each other).
target_language_example: ¿De verdad? Pensé que nos conocemos desde la escuela.
native_language_example: Really? I thought we’ve known each other since school.

meaning: "we've known each other for" (a period of time).
additional_notes: Used to say how long two people have known each other. It’s typically followed by a duration (e.g., "cinco años", "mucho tiempo"). "Desde hace" combines: "desde" (since) + "hace" (ago) to express “for (how long)”. You can change "nos" to other pronouns: "se conocen desde hace..." (they’ve known each other for...), "os conocéis desde hace..." (you all have known each other for...).
target_language_example: Mi mejor amiga y yo nos conocemos desde hace tres años.
native_language_example: My best friend and I have known each other for three years.

meaning: “we met” (we got to know each other).
additional_notes: Past tense (pretérito) of "conocerse" for "we" (nosotros). Use it to talk about the moment two people first met: "Nos conocimos ayer/en la universidad". Often used with time expressions like "desde el día en que nos conocimos" (“since the day we met”) or "aquí es donde nos conocimos" (“this is where we met”).
target_language_example: Nos conocimos en una fiesta hace dos años.
native_language_example: We met at a party two years ago.

additional_notes: "Nos" is the indirect object pronoun meaning "to us." It’s used with the verb "dar" (to give): "(alguien/ algo) nos da + noun". In Spanish the subject can be omitted, so "Nos da..." often means "It gives us..." or "He/She gives us..." depending on context.
target_language_example: Nos da las llaves mañana.
native_language_example: He/She will give us the keys tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used to report what someone said to the speaker and other people (nos = “to us”). The verb is usually in past tense (dijo = “said/told”), and que introduces the message/clause. You’ll often need to infer who the subject is from context (e.g., Ella/Tom).
target_language_example: El profesor nos dijo que no había clase hoy.
native_language_example: The teacher told us that there was no class today.

additional_notes: From the verb dar (to give) in the simple past (preterite): dio = “gave”. Nos is an object pronoun meaning “to us / us.” Often followed by a thing (Nos dio todo) or used more generally for what something caused (Eso nos dio motivos... = “That gave us reasons...”).
target_language_example: La película nos dio muchas ideas para el proyecto.
native_language_example: The movie gave us many ideas for the project.

additional_notes: From the verb "encontrarse" (to meet). It often implies meeting in a place or bumping into each other unexpectedly. You’ll commonly add a location with "en" (Nos encontramos en...).
target_language_example: Nos encontramos en la estación a las seis.
native_language_example: We’ll meet at the station at six.

additional_notes: Used with the verb gustar to say what “we” like. The thing liked is the grammatical subject: Nos gusta el jazz. (“We like jazz.”) With verbs/activities you usually use an infinitive: Nos gusta compartir. If you like more than one thing, use the plural: Nos gustan los perros. To say “we don’t like,” add no: No nos gusta.
target_language_example: No nos gusta levantarnos temprano.
native_language_example: We don’t like getting up early.

additional_notes: "Nos" means "us" (object pronoun), and "ha" means "has" (from "haber"). Together they commonly appear in the present perfect: **nos ha + past participle** (e.g., *nos ha olvidado* = "has forgotten us"). The pronoun **nos** goes before **ha**: *Ella nos ha...*.
target_language_example: El ruido nos ha despertado temprano.
native_language_example: The noise has woken us up early.

meaning: "have" (to us): they have + past participle (present perfect).
additional_notes: "nos" is the object pronoun meaning "us" (to/for us). "han" is the 3rd person plural of "haber" used to form the present perfect: "(ellos/ellas/ustedes) han" = "they/you all have". Together, "nos han" is used before a past participle: "nos han dicho" (they’ve told us), "nos han robado" (they’ve robbed us).
target_language_example: Nos han llamado esta mañana.
native_language_example: They called us this morning / They’ve called us this morning.

additional_notes: Used with a past participle to talk about something “we” have done/recently did. It’s the present tense of the auxiliary verb haber (hemos) plus the object/reflexive pronoun nos. Common with reflexive/pronominal verbs: nos hemos mudado (we’ve moved), nos hemos perdido (we got lost), nos hemos divertido (we had fun), no nos hemos decidido (we haven’t decided). Word order: Nos hemos + participle; in questions you can invert: ¿Nos hemos perdido?
target_language_example: Nos hemos levantado temprano hoy.
native_language_example: We got up early today.

additional_notes: Future tense of ir (“to go”). It’s used when you’re talking about you + others leaving a place or going somewhere in the future. Common patterns: nos iremos pronto (we’ll leave soon), nos iremos de aquí (we’ll get out of here), nos iremos a casa (we’ll go home), nos iremos en cuanto... (we’ll leave/go as soon as...).
target_language_example: Si no mejora el clima, nos iremos mañana por la mañana.
native_language_example: If the weather doesn’t improve, we’ll leave tomorrow morning.

additional_notes: Used to say what remains for “us” (time, options, things, feelings). Common patterns: “nos queda + noun” (Nos queda un minuto), “sólo nos queda + infinitive / cosa” (Sólo nos queda esperar / una cosa), “ya no nos queda otra alternativa” (we have no other choice). Verb is "quedar" in the sense of “to remain.”
target_language_example: Nos queda poco tiempo, así que vamos rápido.
native_language_example: We have little time left, so let’s go quickly.

additional_notes: From quedarse (to stay/remain). Depending on context, "nos quedamos" can be present ("we stay / we’re staying") or preterite ("we stayed"). Here it means staying in a place (not "we meet up"—that’s usually "quedamos" without "nos").
target_language_example: Mejor nos quedamos en casa esta noche.
native_language_example: We’d better stay home tonight.
