additional_notes: Used when an experience, situation, or action tests a person’s abilities, patience, or the quality of something: "poner a prueba la paciencia" (test someone’s patience), "poner a prueba un plan" (test a plan). You can also use the reflexive form "ponerse a prueba" = to challenge oneself / test oneself.
target_language_example: Este trabajo va a poner a prueba tu paciencia.
native_language_example: This job is going to test your patience.

additional_notes: Used to indicate placing something in a specific location (“allí” = “there,” typically more specific/farther than “ahí”). Commonly appears with direct object pronouns (lo/la = “it”) and with polite/neutral forms like puede/pueden.
target_language_example: Lo puede poner allí.
native_language_example: You can put it there.

meaning: to pay attention; to pay close attention.
additional_notes: Commonly used as an instruction or request. Often followed by **a** + noun or clause: *poner atención a la explicación* / *poner atención a lo que dices*. You may also hear **prestar atención**, which means the same thing.
target_language_example: Tienes que poner atención a lo que te digo, por favor.
native_language_example: You have to pay attention to what I’m telling you, please.

meaning: to drive someone crazy; to get on someone’s nerves (to make them very nervous/irritated).
additional_notes: Usually used with an indirect object pronoun: "Me/Te/Le/Nos/Os/Les pone de los nervios" (or with a noun: "A Juan lo/le pone de los nervios"). It often describes repeated annoying behavior or a stressful situation. Stronger than "poner nervioso/a" (more like "make me lose patience").
target_language_example: Ese ruido me pone de los nervios.
native_language_example: That noise drives me crazy / gets on my nerves.

additional_notes: Often used with a location or surface: “poner el dedo aquí/en la pantalla/en el botón”. In many idioms it appears as part of a longer phrase, e.g. “poner el dedo en la llaga” (to touch on a sensitive point).
target_language_example: Tienes que poner el dedo aquí para desbloquear el teléfono.
native_language_example: You have to put your finger here to unlock the phone.

meaning: to start; to set in motion; to get going (a plan, project, machine, etc.).
additional_notes: Used for initiating something that will run or develop—like starting a machine/engine, launching a project, or implementing a plan. Very common in formal and everyday contexts. Often appears with nouns like: un proyecto, un plan, una iniciativa, una campaña, una máquina, el motor. Similar idea to “arrancar” for machines, but “poner en marcha” is broader and can be used for plans/projects too.
target_language_example: Mañana vamos a poner en marcha el nuevo proyecto.
native_language_example: Tomorrow we’re going to launch/get the new project started.

meaning: to put (someone/something) in danger; to endanger.
additional_notes: Used to talk about causing risk or harm. Common patterns: "poner en peligro a alguien" (to endanger someone) and "poner en peligro algo" (to jeopardize something). You can also use it in passive-like statements: "Se puso en peligro la vida de..." (Someone’s life was put at risk).
target_language_example: No debes poner en peligro a tus amigos; maneja con cuidado.
native_language_example: You shouldn’t put your friends in danger; drive carefully.

additional_notes: Used for preparing the table before a meal (placing plates, cutlery, glasses, napkins, etc.). Common with verbs like ayudar a (to help), dejarme (let me), and expressions of time (me tomó unos minutos…).
target_language_example: ¿Puedes poner la mesa mientras yo cocino?
native_language_example: Can you set the table while I cook?

meaning: to cheat on (a partner); to be unfaithful.
additional_notes: A common idiom meaning to have an affair while in a relationship. It’s used with a direct object (the person being cheated on): "Le puso los cuernos a Ana" = "He cheated on Ana." You may also hear the noun phrase "los cuernos" alone ("Me puso los cuernos" = "She cheated on me").
target_language_example: Dicen que él suele poner los cuernos a sus parejas.
native_language_example: They say he tends to cheat on his partners.

meaning: to catch up; to get up to date.
additional_notes: Used for catching up on missed information, work, messages, news, or someone’s life: "ponerse al día con el trabajo / con las noticias / con alguien". It’s reflexive (me/te/se/nos/os/se) and the verb changes with the subject (pongo/pones/pone/ponemos/ponéis/ponen).
target_language_example: Es importante ponerse al día con el trabajo antes del lunes.
native_language_example: It’s important to catch up on work before Monday.

meaning: to agree; to come to an agreement.
additional_notes: Used when two or more people reach an agreement after discussing something. Very common with "con" (with someone) and "en/sobre" (on/about something): "ponerse de acuerdo con alguien" / "ponerse de acuerdo en algo". Can also mean to coordinate plans: "Nos ponemos de acuerdo" = “We’ll work it out / we’ll agree on a plan.”
target_language_example: Tenemos que ponerse de acuerdo en la hora para vernos.
native_language_example: We have to agree on the time to meet.

meaning: To stand up (to get to a standing position).
additional_notes: Uses reflexive "ponerse" to mean "to get" into a new state/position. Often used when someone moves from sitting/lying down to standing. Common with requests and instructions: "Ponte de pie" (stand up) and formal "Póngase de pie" (stand up).
target_language_example: Es hora de ponerse de pie.
native_language_example: It's time to stand up.

additional_notes: Used to tell someone to place an object somewhere. "Ponlo" = "put it" (command to tú). Use "en" for putting it in/into a container or space ("ponlo en un sobre" = put it in an envelope) and also commonly for placing it on a surface/location ("ponlo en la mesa / en la pared" = put it on the table / on the wall).
target_language_example: Ponlo en la mochila, por favor.
native_language_example: Put it in the backpack, please.

meaning: "for God's sake" / "oh my God" (an exclamation for emphasis).
additional_notes: Used to show frustration, surprise, or urgency, often when asking someone to do something: “Por Dios, dime…” It can also be used more literally in religious contexts meaning “by God” or “from God,” e.g., “enviado por Dios” (“sent by God”).
target_language_example: Por Dios, por lo menos contéstame.
native_language_example: For God's sake, at least answer me.

additional_notes: Used to say something happened unintentionally (not on purpose). Common with verbs like tirar (throw away), borrar (delete), encontrar (find), golpear/pegar (hit), and with reflexive constructions like “me encontré con…” (I ran into…).
target_language_example: Lo hice por accidente, perdón.
native_language_example: I did it by accident, sorry.

additional_notes: Used to talk about a place near where the speaker is, often a general area rather than an exact spot: "vive por acá" = "lives around here." It can also be used to guide someone: "Venga por acá" = "Come this way." Contrast with "por allá" (over there / that way, farther from the speaker).
target_language_example: Si pasas por acá mañana, llámame.
native_language_example: If you come by here tomorrow, call me.

additional_notes: Used to say something happens before the expected time. Common with thanks and apologies: “Gracias por adelantado” = “Thanks in advance,” and “disculparse por adelantado” = “to apologize in advance.” Also used with payments: “pagar por adelantado” = “to pay in advance/upfront.”
target_language_example: ¿Puedes enviarme la información por adelantado?
native_language_example: Can you send me the information in advance?

additional_notes: Used to say something is true or will be done temporarily, up to a later change or decision. Often placed at the beginning of the sentence for emphasis (Por ahora, ...), or after what it modifies (Es suficiente por ahora.).
target_language_example: Por ahora, vamos a esperar aquí.
native_language_example: For now, we’re going to wait here.

additional_notes: Used to mean someone/something is in the general area (not an exact place): “Está por ahí.” It can also mean “here and there / hanging around,” often describing moving around without a specific destination: “Anduve por ahí.” With verbs like “preguntar,” it can mean asking around (asking different people/places): “Preguntaré por ahí.”
target_language_example: Si ves a Marta por ahí, dile que me llame.
native_language_example: If you see Marta around, tell her to call me.

meaning: for some reason; for something (a specific thing).
additional_notes:
Two common uses:
1) "for some reason" (often implying there’s a reason behind it): "Por algo preguntas" = "You’re asking for a reason."
2) "for something" meaning “to get/to fetch something”: "Fue a la cocina por algo de café" = "He went to the kitchen for some coffee."
Context tells you which meaning is intended.
target_language_example: Si estás nervioso, por algo será.
native_language_example: If you’re nervous, there must be a reason.

additional_notes: Used when you don’t know the exact reason, or when you suggest there may be a (possibly meaningful) reason. It can go at the beginning of the sentence ("Por alguna razón, ...") or after the verb ("... por alguna razón"). In expressions like "Todo pasa por alguna razón," it can imply "everything happens for a reason."
target_language_example: Por alguna razón, hoy estoy de buen humor.
native_language_example: For some reason, I’m in a good mood today.

meaning: 'over there' / 'over that way' (in that direction, at some distance).
additional_notes: Used to point out a place or thing that’s not close to the speaker. Often goes with gestures or words like "mira" (look). "Allá" implies farther away than "aquí" (here) or "ahí" (there/near you). You’ll commonly hear it at the end of a sentence: "Está… por allá."
target_language_example: El baño está por allá, al fondo.
native_language_example: The bathroom is over there, at the back.

meaning: over there; around there (in that area).
additional_notes: Used to indicate an imprecise location or direction away from the speaker, often when pointing or giving directions. It can also mean “around there” in the sense of “in that area/nearby,” and with verbs of movement it means going/passing “through/that way” (e.g., pasar por allí = to pass by there).
target_language_example: La tienda queda por allí, cerca de la plaza.
native_language_example: The store is over there, near the plaza.

meaning: “for God’s sake” / “for the love of God” (used to show frustration, disbelief, or to beg).
additional_notes: Common exclamation used to emphasize what you’re saying—often when you’re annoyed, shocked, or pleading. It can appear alone (“¡Por amor de Dios!”) or before/after a request (“Por amor de Dios, vístete.” / “Vístete, por amor de Dios.”). Can sound dramatic or rude depending on tone; not necessarily religious in intent.
target_language_example: Por amor de Dios, baja la música, que estoy trabajando.
native_language_example: For God’s sake, turn the music down—I’m working.

additional_notes: Used to refer to a past period that the speaker has in mind (often something already mentioned or understood from context). It’s common in storytelling or when comparing the past with the present. Similar to “en aquel tiempo” or “en esa época.”
target_language_example: Por aquel entonces no había internet en casa.
native_language_example: Back then we didn’t have internet at home.

additional_notes: Used for a nearby area or for a route/direction. With movement verbs, it often means 'through here' or 'this way'; in more general statements, it means 'around here' or 'near here'.
target_language_example: Siéntate por aquí, por favor.
native_language_example: Sit around here, please.

additional_notes: Used to politely direct someone to come or go through a specific place, often while guiding them (e.g., in an office, store, or waiting room). Common with verbs like pase/pasen (“come in/go ahead”), venga (“come”), or just said alone as an instruction.
target_language_example: Por aquí, por favor. La doctora lo atenderá enseguida.
native_language_example: This way, please. The doctor will see you right away.

meaning: "so to speak" (in a manner of speaking).
additional_notes: Used to soften or qualify what you just said, often to show it’s not meant literally, it’s an approximation, or you’re using a metaphor/figure of speech. It can appear in the middle or at the end of a sentence, and can also be used alone as a short response meaning “so to speak.”
target_language_example: Es mi jefe, por así decirlo, aunque no trabaja en mi oficina.
native_language_example: He’s my boss, so to speak, even though he doesn’t work in my office.

meaning: peacefully / nicely; without forcing (usually in the phrase “por las buenas”).
additional_notes: Most commonly appears with the definite article: “por las buenas”, often contrasted with “por las malas” in “por las buenas o por las malas” (= ‘one way or another’, ‘nicely or by force’). Without the article (“por buenas”) can occur in some contexts, but it may sound less standard to many speakers. It conveys doing something through cooperation, good manners, or persuasion rather than threats or force.
target_language_example: Intenté convencerlo por buenas, pero no quiso escuchar.
native_language_example: I tried to persuade him nicely, but he wouldn’t listen.

additional_notes: Used to say something happened without planning it or without expecting it. It often answers the question “How did it happen?” (not because of a reason, just coincidence). You can also use it in questions: “¿Por casualidad tienes…?” = “Do you happen to have…?”
target_language_example: Lo vi por casualidad en el supermercado.
native_language_example: I saw him by chance at the supermarket.

additional_notes: Used to give the reason for something, usually with a noun or noun phrase: "por causa de + [reason]". It often sounds a bit formal; in everyday speech, "por" or "a causa de" are also common. For negative reasons you may also hear "a causa de" more often, but "por causa de" works too.
target_language_example: Cancelaron el partido por causa de la lluvia.
native_language_example: They canceled the game because of the rain.

additional_notes: Used after a number to express a percentage. It’s often followed by "de" when you say percent of something: "X por ciento de + noun". You can also say "el/lo que es" to clarify: "el 10 por ciento" = “10 percent.”
target_language_example: El veinte por ciento de descuento es solo hoy.
native_language_example: The twenty percent discount is only today.

additional_notes: Used as a conversational aside to add extra information, change topic slightly, or mention something you just remembered. It often appears at the beginning of a sentence, but it can also come at the end (like “..., by the way”). Although it literally looks like “for certain,” that is usually not the meaning in everyday speech.
target_language_example: Por cierto, ¿ya le escribiste a tu mamá?
native_language_example: By the way, did you already text your mom?

meaning: “By the way, have you…?” (to bring up something casually).
additional_notes: Used to introduce an extra question that’s not the main topic, often as a quick reminder or a change of subject. “Por cierto” = “by the way,” and “¿has…?” is the start of a question with haber (present perfect), typically followed by a past participle: ¿has encontrado/hecho/oído/probado…?
target_language_example: Por cierto, ¿has visto mis llaves?
native_language_example: By the way, have you seen my keys?

additional_notes: Used as an adverbial phrase to emphasize that something is total/whole (no part left out). Common with verbs like cambiar (change), ignorar (ignore), rendirse (give up), and expressions like pasar desapercibido (go unnoticed). It can also be used alone as a short answer meaning “completely.”
target_language_example: Lo entiendo por completo.
native_language_example: I understand it completely.

additional_notes: Used as an adverb to emphasize that something is total or finished (often with verbs like "olvidarse" = to forget, or to describe something being fully covered). It usually comes after the verb or at the end of the clause: "Me olvidé por completo" / "Cubrió la ciudad por completo."
target_language_example: Se me borró por completo la contraseña.
native_language_example: I completely forgot my password.

meaning: on behalf of; paid for by (at the expense of).
additional_notes: Used to say who is responsible for something or who pays for it (common in business/finance). Often followed by a person, company, or institution: "por cuenta de la empresa" = paid by the company / on the company’s account. In some contexts it can also mean "because of" (more formal), but the most common beginner-use is responsibility/payment.
target_language_example: La cena corre por cuenta de la empresa.
native_language_example: Dinner is paid for by the company.

meaning: on the house; paid for by the establishment.
additional_notes: Used in restaurants, bars, hotels, etc. to say something is free because the business (“la casa”) is paying. Often appears with verbs like “va” or “corre”: “Eso va/corre por cuenta de la casa.” You can also say it alone as a short answer: “Por cuenta de la casa.”
target_language_example: El postre va por cuenta de la casa.
native_language_example: Dessert is on the house.

additional_notes: Used to say someone does something without help or without being told (independently), or that someone works for themselves (is self-employed). Often appears with verbs like hacer, actuar, venir/ir, and trabajar.
target_language_example: Prefiero resolverlo por cuenta propia.
native_language_example: I prefer to solve it on my own.

additional_notes: Used to assign blame or responsibility for a negative result: *por culpa de + noun/pronoun*. It often has a judgmental/accusatory tone. For neutral “because of” without blame, Spanish often uses *por* or *a causa de* instead.
target_language_example: Cancelamos el viaje por culpa del mal tiempo.
native_language_example: We canceled the trip because of the bad weather.

additional_notes: Used for physical position (under/beneath something: “por debajo de nosotros”) and for comparisons/levels (“por debajo de mis expectativas” = not meeting expectations; “por debajo de tu peso” = underweight). Often implies being less than a desired or expected level.
target_language_example: La temperatura está por debajo de cero.
native_language_example: The temperature is below zero.

additional_notes: Used to soften or qualify what you just said, often to signal it’s an approximate description, a metaphor, or not meant literally. It can be inserted mid-sentence between commas, or said alone as a quick clarification.
target_language_example: Es, por decirlo así, el jefe del equipo.
native_language_example: He’s, so to speak, the team’s boss.

additional_notes: Often used to compare position in space or time: "un paso por delante" = "one step ahead." With "poner" it means to prioritize something: "poner X por delante" = "to put X first" (ahead of other things).
target_language_example: En el trabajo, pongo por delante a mi familia.
native_language_example: At work, I put my family first.

additional_notes: Used to introduce bad news or an undesirable situation. Commonly placed at the beginning of a sentence (often followed by a comma), but it can also appear mid-sentence.
target_language_example: Por desgracia, no puedo ir a la fiesta.
native_language_example: Unfortunately, I can’t go to the party.

additional_notes: Used for position or movement: someone grabs you from behind ("me agarró por detrás"), or you go/enter via the back to avoid a mess or crowd ("Ve por detrás", "te llevo por detrás"). Depending on context, it can also mean doing something behind someone’s back/secretly.
target_language_example: Si hay mucha gente, entramos por detrás.
native_language_example: If there are lots of people, we’ll go in through the back.

additional_notes: Used to express duration (how long something lasts). Common with actions like esperar (to wait), estudiar (to study), trabajar (to work), caminar (to walk). Often interchangeable with “durante dos horas.”
target_language_example: Estuve esperando por dos horas.
native_language_example: I was waiting for two hours.

additional_notes: Used to introduce an example or illustration. It can go at the beginning of the sentence or after what you’re referring to: “Por ejemplo, …” / “…, por ejemplo.” Often followed by a comma in writing.
target_language_example: Puedes visitar muchos lugares; por ejemplo, el museo y el parque.
native_language_example: You can visit many places; for example, the museum and the park.

additional_notes: Not a fixed idiom, but the common combination por + el. The exact English translation depends on context: it can also mean "through the" or "by the." It is used for cause (por el mal tiempo = because of the bad weather), movement through a place (por el campus = through the campus), or something wanted or competed for (por el puesto = for the position). Unlike a + el = al, por + el does not contract. Don't confuse por el with por él, which means "for him" or "because of him."
target_language_example: Pasamos por el túnel para llegar más rápido.
native_language_example: We went through the tunnel to get there faster.

meaning: “for the love of God!” (an urgent plea; “please!”)
additional_notes: Used as a strong exclamation to beg someone to stop, not do something, or to show frustration/urgency. Often placed at the beginning or in the middle of a sentence. It can sound intense and emotional (sometimes bordering on rude depending on tone), even though it’s religious in wording.
target_language_example: Por el amor de Dios, baja la música.
native_language_example: For the love of God, turn the music down.

meaning: for the good of; for the sake of.
additional_notes: Used to say you do something to benefit someone/something (a person, a group, your health, etc.). It’s often followed by a noun or pronoun: por el bien de todos / por el bien de mi salud / por el bien de los dos. Similar to “por el beneficio de,” but much more common.
target_language_example: Lo hice por el bien de mi familia.
native_language_example: I did it for the good of my family.

meaning: through the forest; in/around the forest.
additional_notes: Used with verbs of movement or activity (caminar, pasar, pasear, dar vueltas) to say someone goes or does something in/through a forest. "Por" often means "through" or "along" when talking about movement through a place.
target_language_example: Fuimos por el bosque para llegar al lago.
native_language_example: We went through the forest to get to the lake.

meaning: along the way; via/on the path/road.
additional_notes: Used with verbs of movement (ir, venir, pasar, perderse, irse) to say someone goes/comes/travels via a path/road, or that something happens or is lost “along the way.” Often followed by a more specific path: "por el camino del oeste" (along the western road).
target_language_example: Nos detuvimos por el camino para comprar agua.
native_language_example: We stopped along the way to buy water.

meaning: for the money; because of money (as the motive).
additional_notes: Used to say that money is the reason someone does something (often implying a selfish or purely financial motive). Common with phrases like "solo/sólo por el dinero" (only for the money) or in negatives like "No lo hago por el dinero" (I’m not doing it for the money).
target_language_example: No acepté el trabajo por el dinero, sino por la experiencia.
native_language_example: I didn’t take the job for the money, but for the experience.

additional_notes: Used after an example to mean “and similar things” or “something along those lines.” Common patterns: “algo por el estilo” (something like that), “cosas por el estilo” (things like that), “o … por el estilo” (or … like that). In negatives, “nada por el estilo” means “nothing like that / nothing of the sort.”
target_language_example: Podemos comer pizza, tacos o algo por el estilo.
native_language_example: We can eat pizza, tacos, or something like that.

meaning: for now; at the moment (for the time being).
additional_notes: Used to talk about a situation that is true temporarily and may change later. Common in announcements, plans, and updates (e.g., number of people, current status). Similar to "por ahora" and "de momento".
target_language_example: Por el momento no tengo más información.
native_language_example: For now, I don’t have any more information.

meaning: through/around the park; in the park (moving around).
additional_notes: Uses por to express movement through a place or along an area (not a fixed location). Common with verbs like caminar, pasear, correr, and guiar. Contrast: en el parque = located in the park (no focus on movement).
target_language_example: Fuimos por el parque para llegar más rápido.
native_language_example: We went through the park to get there faster.

meaning: on the floor/ground; along the floor/ground.
additional_notes: Used for movement happening in contact with the floor/ground (crawl, drag yourself, roll), or for something spread on the floor (like blood). It can also mean something is lying around on the floor (often implying it’s messy or not put away).
target_language_example: Mi móvil estaba por el suelo debajo de la mesa.
native_language_example: My phone was on the floor under the table.

additional_notes: Uses "por" + "ello" (“that/it”) to refer back to something already mentioned. Common with feelings or thanks ("gracias por ello", "mi gratitud por ello" = “thanks for that/it”), and with causes/consequences ("y por ello..." = “and because of that...”).
target_language_example: No estudié y, por ello, no aprobé el examen.
native_language_example: I didn’t study and, because of that, I didn’t pass the exam.

additional_notes: Often expresses movement across/over something: pasar por encima de (to go over/step over). It can also mean doing something quickly without details: contar por encima (to summarize, to go over it briefly). With "por encima de" it can also mean physically above something.
target_language_example: ¿Me lo puedes explicar por encima?
native_language_example: Can you explain it to me briefly?

additional_notes: Used to indicate position or movement at a higher level than something else. Often used with verbs of movement (volar, pasar, trepar, saltar). Similar to "sobre" in many cases, but "por encima de" often emphasizes going across/over something (like an obstacle).
target_language_example: El gato saltó por encima de la mesa.
native_language_example: The cat jumped over the table.

meaning: above all; more than anything else.
additional_notes: Used to say something is the top priority or most important thing. Often set off with commas as a comment (“..., por encima de todo, ...”). You can also use it after a noun/idea to emphasize priority (“X por encima de todo”).
target_language_example: Tu seguridad está por encima de todo.
native_language_example: Your safety is above all else.

additional_notes: Used to say something happened unintentionally. It commonly goes with verbs like coger/tomar (take), enviar (send), decir (say), or hacer (do): “Lo hice por error” = “I did it by mistake.” Similar to “accidentalmente” and “sin querer.”
target_language_example: Lo borré por error, ¿puedes enviármelo otra vez?
native_language_example: I deleted it by mistake—can you send it to me again?

meaning: through that door; out/in via that door.
additional_notes: Uses **por** to indicate movement *through* a doorway (entering or leaving). It can also be used to point out where something is located/where you should go (e.g., “it’s that way—through that door”). Often appears with verbs like **entrar (por)**, **salir (por)**, **pasar (por)**.
target_language_example: Tienes que entrar por esa puerta para llegar a la oficina.
native_language_example: You have to go through that door to get to the office.

additional_notes: Used to say something should be provided as a written document/message (not just spoken). Common in instructions and formal requests: enviar/mandar/poner algo por escrito, dejar algo por escrito.
target_language_example: ¿Me lo puedes confirmar por escrito, por favor?
native_language_example: Can you confirm it in writing, please?

additional_notes: Used to refer back to a reason already mentioned. It often connects two ideas, especially at the start of a sentence, and is very common for explaining a result or consequence.
target_language_example: Está lloviendo; por eso no salgo hoy.
native_language_example: It's raining; that's why I'm not going out today.

additional_notes: Used to explain a refusal or negative action by linking it to a reason just mentioned or understood from context. Often appears before a verb: "Por eso no + verbo" (e.g., por eso no fui, por eso no dije nada).
target_language_example: No tenía dinero; por eso no fui al cine.
native_language_example: I didn’t have money; that’s why I didn’t go to the movies.

meaning: because of a lack of; due to not having enough (of something).
additional_notes: Used to give the reason something happened: there wasn’t enough of a necessary thing (money, water, oxygen, time, etc.). It’s typically followed by a noun: por falta de dinero/agua/fondos. Often implies a negative outcome (couldn’t continue, failed, died).
target_language_example: Llegamos tarde por falta de tiempo.
native_language_example: We arrived late because of lack of time.

additional_notes: Used to make requests more polite. It can also express pleading or urgency, as in por favor no hagas eso ('please don't do that'). It can appear at the beginning, middle, or end of a sentence.
target_language_example: Pásame la sal, por favor.
native_language_example: Pass me the salt, please.

additional_notes: Uses the formal command form of abrir (“to open”): abra (usted). Common in polite requests from strangers, staff, police, etc. Often followed by what to open: la puerta (the door), el maletero (the trunk), su bolsa (your bag). By itself (“Por favor, abra.”) it means “Please open (it/the door).”
target_language_example: Por favor, abra la ventana.
native_language_example: Please open the window.

additional_notes: Used in polite, formal situations with usted (acepte = usted command form of aceptar). Common with apologies, condolences, congratulations, invitations, and formal requests: "Por favor, acepte mis disculpas / mis condolencias / mis felicitaciones". For an informal version (tú), you’d say: "Por favor, acepta...".
target_language_example: Por favor, acepte este obsequio como muestra de agradecimiento.
native_language_example: Please accept this gift as a token of gratitude.

additional_notes: Used to politely ask someone to hand you something or to give you something (an object, a photo, a drink, etc.). Use it before a noun: "Por favor, dame + [thing]". "Dame" is the informal (tú) command form of "dar"; with someone you address as "usted," say "Por favor, deme ...".
target_language_example: Por favor, dame un vaso de agua.
native_language_example: Please, give me a glass of water.

additional_notes: Used to politely ask for instructions or an explanation. Often followed by an infinitive (cómo + arreglar/hacer/llegar) or by a full clause (cómo puedo… / cómo se…). You can also change the person: “dime” (tell me, informal tú); formal: “dígame” (usted).
target_language_example: Por favor, dime cómo usar esta aplicación.
native_language_example: Please tell me how to use this app.

meaning: “please, let me…” (asking someone to allow you to do something / stop bothering you).
additional_notes: Used to politely (sometimes firmly) ask for permission or space. "Déjame" is the informal (tú) command of "dejar" + "me" (“let me / leave me”). Common patterns: "Por favor, déjame + infinitive" (déjame ir/entrar/comer) and "Por favor, déjame en paz" (“please leave me alone”). For a more formal version, use "Por favor, déjeme" (usted).
target_language_example: Por favor, déjame terminar de hablar.
native_language_example: Please, let me finish speaking.

additional_notes: Used to politely ask someone not to do something. "No" goes right before the verb: "Por favor, no entren" (Please don’t come in). It can also be used by itself to express a polite objection or refusal: "Por favor, no" (Please, no). "Por favor" may sometimes be used as a general plea (like “please”) even when the next words aren’t a command.
target_language_example: Por favor, no hagas ruido en la biblioteca.
native_language_example: Please, don’t make noise in the library.

additional_notes: Used to politely ask someone to come (often to a place like your home, or to come see you). "Ven" is the informal (tú) command form of "venir"; for a more formal request to one person, use "por favor, venga" (usted).
target_language_example: Por favor, ven conmigo un momento.
native_language_example: Please, come with me for a moment.

additional_notes: Used when something expected, delayed, or difficult happens after a long time. Often placed at the beginning of the sentence for emphasis (Por fin...), or before the verb (por fin terminé / él por fin aprobó).
target_language_example: Por fin encontramos un buen restaurante cerca de casa.
native_language_example: We finally found a good restaurant near home.

meaning: for no reason; just because; for fun/for free (without being paid).
additional_notes: Often implies something was unnecessary or pointless ("Llamaste por gusto" = you called for nothing). It can also mean doing something simply for enjoyment ("solo por gusto" = just for fun) or doing it without charging (teaching/helping "por gusto" = not for money).
target_language_example: Fui al centro por gusto; no tenía nada que comprar.
native_language_example: I went downtown for no reason; I didn’t have anything to buy.

additional_notes: Used to talk about rates or payment calculated for each hour of work (hourly). Often appears with verbs like "pagar" (to pay) or "cobrar" (to charge): "pagar/cobrar por hora". In some contexts it can also mean "hourly" (happening every hour).
target_language_example: Cobro por hora.
native_language_example: I charge by the hour.

additional_notes: Used to say something is finished or will stop for the rest of today (often implies you’ll continue another day). Common with verbs like "terminar" (to finish), "dejar" (to leave/stop), or "basta" (enough).
target_language_example: Eso es todo por hoy.
native_language_example: That’s all for today.

additional_notes: Used to say someone/animals act automatically, without thinking or planning, guided by instinct. It can describe how an action is done (actuar por instinto) or be used at the start of a sentence as an adverbial phrase (Por instinto, ...).
target_language_example: Me aparté por instinto cuando vi venir la pelota.
native_language_example: I moved out of the way instinctively when I saw the ball coming.

meaning: in the street; along/down the street.
additional_notes: Used with movement verbs (caminar, correr, marchar) to show that something happens out on the street or along it. It can also mean “out and about/on the street” when you run into someone by chance (Me lo encontré por la calle). In Spain you’ll also hear it used to mean “in public” (e.g., No lo digas por la calle = don’t say it publicly).
target_language_example: Me encontré a Ana por la calle y hablamos un rato.
native_language_example: I ran into Ana on the street and we talked for a while.

additional_notes: Literal meaning is “by/through the back,” often used with violence (e.g., apuñalar/disparar por la espalda = stab/shoot from behind). Figuratively, it can mean doing something without the person knowing, often in a negative way: criticar a alguien por la espalda = criticize someone behind their back.
target_language_example: No hables de mí por la espalda.
native_language_example: Don’t talk about me behind my back.

additional_notes: Used to say that something happens during the morning. Often refers to a habitual time (e.g., todos los días por la mañana = every day in the morning). Contrast: por la tarde (in the afternoon), por la noche (at night).
target_language_example: Normalmente desayuno por la mañana antes de salir.
native_language_example: I usually eat breakfast in the morning before leaving.

meaning: in half; by half (half the amount/price).
additional_notes: Used after verbs like cortar/partir/dividir to mean splitting something into two equal parts: «Córtalo por la mitad». It can also describe a reduction by 50% (often with prices): «por la mitad (de precio)». In casual speech it can be a short answer meaning “in half.”
target_language_example: Si esperas a las rebajas, lo puedes comprar por la mitad de precio.
native_language_example: If you wait for the sales, you can buy it for half the price.

additional_notes: Means during the night hours (when it’s dark). In everyday Spanish it can also cover the late evening period; for “tonight” (this specific night), Spanish often uses “esta noche”. Often contrasts with “por la mañana” (in the morning) and “por la tarde” (in the afternoon/evening).
target_language_example: Prefiero estudiar por la noche porque hay menos ruido.
native_language_example: I prefer to study at night because there’s less noise.

meaning: along the beach; on/through the beach area.
additional_notes: Uses por to express movement or an activity happening in a place/area (route or location): caminar/pasear/correr por la playa = to walk/stroll/run along the beach. Different from en la playa (being/located on the beach) and a la playa (going to the beach).
target_language_example: Nos gusta caminar por la playa al atardecer.
native_language_example: We like to walk along the beach at sunset.

meaning: through the back door; via the back (entrance/exit).
additional_notes: Used with verbs of movement (salir, entrar, irse, escaparse) to say someone goes in/out using the back door/entrance. It can be literal (a physical back door) or imply leaving/entering discreetly or avoiding attention.
target_language_example: Si no quieres que te vean, sal por la puerta de atrás.
native_language_example: If you don’t want them to see you, go out through the back door.

additional_notes: Used in relative clauses with a feminine singular noun (la mujer, la persona, la razón, la parte) to mean “the one/thing that… for which/for whom…”. It’s por + la que, where que refers back to the noun. Variations: por el que (masc. sing.), por los que / por las que (plural). Often used with reasons, motives, and people you do something for (e.g., “la razón por la que…” = “the reason why…”).
target_language_example: Esta es la razón por la que no fui ayer.
native_language_example: This is the reason why I didn’t go yesterday.

meaning: in the afternoon; in the evening (before night).
additional_notes: Used to say when something happens during the later part of the day, after the morning (por la mañana). In many contexts it covers both “afternoon” and the earlier “evening,” depending on local usage and the time of year. You can use it with routines or schedules: Trabajo/Estudio por la tarde.
target_language_example: Nos vemos por la tarde.
native_language_example: See you in the afternoon.

additional_notes: Used with verbs of motion (especially "saltar" = to jump) to say movement goes through and out of a window. "Por" here indicates the route/way something happens (passing through the window opening).
target_language_example: El gato salió por la ventana cuando abrí las cortinas.
native_language_example: The cat went out the window when I opened the curtains.

meaning: through/along the streets; around the streets.
additional_notes: Used with verbs of movement or activity (e.g., caminar, correr, pasear, dar vueltas) to say someone is moving or spending time in the streets in a general, non-specific way (not on one particular street). Often implies going around different streets.
target_language_example: Estuvimos caminando por las calles toda la tarde.
native_language_example: We were walking around the streets all afternoon.

meaning: up/down the stairs; via the stairs.
additional_notes: Used with movement verbs to show the path taken (not using the elevator). Often appears with verbs like subir (to go up), bajar (to go down), caer(se) (to fall), and llevar/subir/bajar something (to carry something up/down).
target_language_example: Subimos por las escaleras porque el ascensor no funcionaba.
native_language_example: We went up the stairs because the elevator wasn’t working.

meaning: at night; in the evenings (as a usual time).
additional_notes: Used to talk about what someone typically does at night/in the evenings. It often implies a routine or repeated habit ("I usually… at night"), not just one specific night. You’ll also hear the singular "por la noche" for a particular night or a more general “at night.”
target_language_example: Por las noches, me gusta leer antes de dormir.
native_language_example: At night, I like to read before going to sleep.

additional_notes: Used to add a final comment after mentioning an exception, problem, or special detail. Common after talking about one issue, then saying that everything else is fine: "Por lo demás, todo bien."
target_language_example: El hotel era caro, pero por lo demás estuvo muy bien.
native_language_example: The hotel was expensive, but otherwise it was very good.

additional_notes: Used to talk about what typically happens or what is true most of the time. Often placed at the beginning of the sentence and can be followed by a comma: "Por lo general, ...". Similar to "generalmente" and "normalmente".
target_language_example: Por lo general, tomamos el autobús al trabajo.
native_language_example: We usually take the bus to work.

additional_notes: Used to express a minimum amount/limit, or to soften a statement by offering the least that’s true. It can modify a whole sentence (Por lo menos, así lo dice él = “At least, that’s what he says”) or appear before a time/quantity (Por lo menos no hoy = “At least not today”). Often interchangeable with "al menos" in many contexts.
target_language_example: Por lo menos avísame si vas a llegar tarde.
native_language_example: At least let me know if you’re going to be late.

additional_notes:
Common uses:
1) In relative clauses, it means “for what / because of what / through what,” referring to the thing or reason: "Entiendo por lo que estás pasando" = “I understand what you’re going through.”
2) As a connector, it can mean “which is why / so,” introducing a consequence: "No tenía dinero, por lo que no fui" = “I had no money, so I didn’t go.”
3) In expressions like "por lo que sabemos", it often means “as far as we know.”
target_language_example: No contestó, por lo que pensamos que estaba ocupado.
native_language_example: He didn’t answer, so we thought he was busy.

additional_notes: Used to introduce a conclusion or consequence based on what was just said. Often set off by commas, and it can appear at the beginning of a sentence ("Por lo tanto,") or in the middle after a clause. It’s a fairly formal connector; in casual speech you’ll also hear "así que" or "entonces".
target_language_example: No estudió; por lo tanto, no aprobó el examen.
native_language_example: He didn’t study; therefore, he didn’t pass the exam.

additional_notes: Used to introduce a consequence or conclusion from what was just said. It’s a linking phrase common in formal writing and speeches, and it’s often set off by commas (e.g., "..., por lo tanto, ..."). Similar in meaning to "por eso" (more common in everyday speech).
target_language_example: No trajiste tu identificación; por lo tanto, no puedes entrar.
native_language_example: You didn’t bring your ID; therefore, you can’t enter.

meaning: "apparently" / "it seems" (based on what’s been seen or heard).
additional_notes: Used to introduce a conclusion or assumption from evidence, appearances, or what someone said. Often goes at the beginning of the sentence (“Por lo visto, …”), but it can also appear mid-sentence. Slight nuance: it often suggests “from what I can tell / from what I’ve heard.”
target_language_example: Por lo visto, la reunión se canceló.
native_language_example: Apparently, the meeting got cancelled.

additional_notes: Used to mark a minimum number/amount/frequency ("at least four," "at least once a week"). It can also mean "if nothing else" to soften a request or highlight a small positive point ("Por lo menos dime..." / "Por lo menos nos lo pasamos bien"). Often interchangeable with "al menos" in everyday speech.
target_language_example: Por lo menos llámame cuando llegues.
native_language_example: At least call me when you arrive.

additional_notes: Used to express a minimum amount/number (Por lo menos, cinco minutos.) or to soften/qualify a statement (Por lo menos, lo intenté = At least I tried). Often interchangeable with "al menos" in everyday speech.
target_language_example: Necesito por lo menos una hora para terminar.
native_language_example: I need at least an hour to finish.

meaning: "because of what" / "for what"; also "from what (I see/hear)".
additional_notes: Used to refer to a specific thing or event (often introduced by a clause): "pagarás por lo que me hiciste" = you’ll pay for what you did to me; "responsable por lo que has hecho" = responsible for what you’ve done. With verbs like "ver", "oír", "decir" it often means "from what I see/hear/they said": "Por lo que veo..." / "..., por lo que decían."
target_language_example: Por lo que entiendo, la reunión es mañana.
native_language_example: From what I understand, the meeting is tomorrow.

meaning: “as far as I know” / “from what I know.”
additional_notes: Used to limit what you’re saying to your current knowledge (you’re not 100% sure). Often placed at the beginning of a sentence as an opener: “Por lo que sé, …”. It can also be said alone (“Por lo que sé.”) meaning “As far as I know.”
target_language_example: Por lo que sé, la reunión es mañana a las diez.
native_language_example: As far as I know, the meeting is tomorrow at ten.

additional_notes: Used to refer back to something specific (usually a thing someone said or did). Common after words like agradecer (to thank), pedir perdón/disculpas (to apologize), sentirse culpable (to feel guilty), etc.: "Gracias por lo que hiciste" = “Thanks for what you did.” It’s often followed by a verb in the past (dijo, hizo, había hecho).
target_language_example: Lo siento por lo que dije ayer.
native_language_example: I'm sorry for what I said yesterday.

meaning: around the year(s) of; back around (that time).
additional_notes: Used to place something approximately in time (not an exact date). It’s often followed by a year or a time period: “por los años de 1998”, “por los años de la universidad” (= around the time of college).
target_language_example: Nos conocimos por los años de 2010.
native_language_example: We met around the year 2010.

additional_notes: Used to say someone barely succeeded or narrowly avoided something bad (often with verbs like aprobar, escapar, librarse). It means “at the last moment / by the skin of your teeth,” not literally “because of the hairs.”
target_language_example: Llegamos por los pelos antes de que cerraran la puerta.
native_language_example: We arrived just in time, right before they closed the door.

meaning: by means of; through (using something as an intermediary).
additional_notes: Used to say something is done using a tool, method, or intermediary person/thing (similar to “via” or “through”). It often appears with a noun after it: por medio de + un/una/el/la + noun (e.g., por medio de un intérprete). In many cases it can be replaced by “a través de” or “mediante.”
target_language_example: Pagamos por medio de una transferencia bancaria.
native_language_example: We paid by means of a bank transfer.

meaning: on my own; on my tab (I’ll pay).
additional_notes: Often means doing something independently (“by myself/without help”): Lo hice por mi cuenta. With verbs like ir/venir/estar + por mi cuenta, it commonly means you will cover the cost (“it’s on me/my treat”): Las bebidas van por mi cuenta / Va por mi cuenta. Changes with the person: por tu cuenta (on your own), por su cuenta (on his/her/their own).
target_language_example: Tranquilo, la cena va por mi cuenta.
native_language_example: Don’t worry, dinner is on me.

meaning: for my part; as far as I’m concerned.
additional_notes: Used to give your personal viewpoint or responsibility. Common in polite statements like “Por mi parte, no hay problema” (“As far as I’m concerned, no problem”). It can also mean “on my part” in phrases like “Fue un error por mi parte” (“It was a mistake on my part”). Often appears at the start of a sentence with a comma.
target_language_example: Por mi parte, estoy de acuerdo con el plan.
native_language_example: For my part, I agree with the plan.

meaning: “for my life” (fearing for your life / to save your life); also “on my life” (I swear).
additional_notes: Used in two common ways: (1) with verbs like luchar, huir/correr, temer: it means you’re in serious danger and are fighting/running because your life is at risk (“I ran for my life”). Often appears as “por tu/su/nuestra vida”. (2) In oaths: “Te lo juro por mi vida” = “I swear on my life.”
target_language_example: Cuando vi el incendio, corrí por mi vida.
native_language_example: When I saw the fire, I ran for my life.

additional_notes: Used to say something happens intermittently or changes from one moment to the next. Often describes feelings, situations, or intensity that comes and goes (similar to “at times” / “moment by moment”).
target_language_example: Por momentos, pensé que no íbamos a llegar a tiempo.
native_language_example: At times, I thought we weren’t going to make it on time.

additional_notes: A formal, somewhat old-fashioned way to give a reason or cause, similar to "a causa de" or "debido a". It’s most often used to mean "because of" (cause), and less commonly to mean "for the sake of" (purpose).
target_language_example: Se canceló el evento por mor de la tormenta.
native_language_example: The event was canceled because of the storm.

meaning: no matter how much; however much (even if you try a lot).
additional_notes: Used to express concession: the result doesn’t change despite a lot of effort or intensity (“however much…”). It’s often followed by the subjunctive when talking about attempts in general or hypothetical situations (por mucho que lo intentes / lo intente), and it can be followed by the indicative when referring to a specific real past effort (por mucho que lo buscaron).
target_language_example: Por mucho que estudie, me cuesta entender esta lección.
native_language_example: No matter how much I study, I have trouble understanding this lesson.

meaning: for a long time; for long.
additional_notes: Used to talk about a long duration of time (how long something lasts or has been happening). Often goes with the present perfect to mean “for a long time” up to now (e.g., "He estado... por mucho tiempo"), and with "no" it can mean “not for a long time” / “in a long time” (e.g., "No nos hemos visto por mucho tiempo").
target_language_example: No puedo quedarme por mucho tiempo porque tengo que trabajar.
native_language_example: I can't stay for long because I have to work.

meaning: 'no matter how much' / 'however much' (often in "por mucho que...").
additional_notes: Most common in the pattern "por mucho que + subjunctive", meaning that the result stays the same despite the effort/amount: "Por mucho que lo intentes, ..." = "No matter how much you try, ...". It can also appear without "que" as an intensifier meaning "by far" or "a lot" (especially in comparisons), and in negatives like "ni/no por mucho" meaning "not by any means / not at all" depending on context.
target_language_example: Por mucho que corras, no vas a llegar a tiempo.
native_language_example: No matter how much you run, you won't get there on time.

additional_notes: Used to ask someone to do something for your benefit (a favor). Often appears after an imperative: “Hazlo por mí” / “Hágalo por mí.” You can swap the pronoun: por ti (for you), por él/ella (for him/her), por nosotros (for us).
target_language_example: ¿Puedes llamarlo por mí?
native_language_example: Can you call him for me?

meaning: by myself; on my own (for myself).
additional_notes: Used to say you will do something alone or without help, or that you want to see/check something personally. It changes with the person and gender: por ti mismo/a, por sí mismo/a, por nosotros/as mismos/as, etc. You can also say "yo mismo/a" for emphasis ("I myself").
target_language_example: Prefiero hacerlo por mí mismo.
native_language_example: I prefer to do it by myself.

meaning: for nothing; for no reason; (with verbs like preocupar) about nothing.
additional_notes: Common meanings depend on context: (1) "por nada" = "for no reason" (often with emotions like enfadarse: "get mad over nothing"); (2) "por nada" = "for almost nothing/very cheaply" (prices, selling: "I’m selling everything for next to nothing"); (3) in negative contexts it can mean "for nothing in the world" (= under no circumstances), e.g., "no ... por nada (en este mundo)"; (4) with preocupar/temer, it often means "about nothing" ("No necesitas preocuparte por nada").
target_language_example: No me voy a rendir por nada en el mundo.
native_language_example: I won’t give up for anything in the world.

meaning: “not for anything in the world” / “no way” (absolutely not).
additional_notes: Used to strongly emphasize refusal or that you would never do something, often with “no” or “nunca”: “No… por nada del mundo”, “Nunca… por nada del mundo.” It can also stand alone as an emphatic answer: “¿Vas a hacerlo?” “Por nada del mundo.”
target_language_example: No lo haría por nada del mundo.
native_language_example: I wouldn’t do it for anything in the world.

meaning: nowhere (to be found/seen); in no place.
additional_notes: Used with negation (often "no") to emphasize that something/someone can’t be found or seen anywhere: "No lo veo por ningún lado". Common with verbs like ver (to see), encontrar (to find), estar/haber (to be/there is), aparecer (to appear). Similar to "en ninguna parte" and "en ningún sitio".
target_language_example: Busqué mis llaves por ningún lado, así que llamé a mi hermano.
native_language_example: I couldn’t find my keys anywhere, so I called my brother.

meaning: "through the work of" / "by" (as the cause or agent).
additional_notes: Used to attribute something to someone/something as the agent or cause, often in formal or literary contexts. Common in set phrases like "por obra de Dios" or "por obra y gracia de..." (often meaning something happened thanks to, or because of, someone/something—sometimes said ironically).
target_language_example: El cambio se logró por obra de la comunidad.
native_language_example: The change was achieved through the work of the community.

additional_notes: Used to add a contrasting or additional consideration—often similar to “however,” “also,” or “besides.” It can appear at the beginning of a sentence or between commas. Common in spoken and written Spanish when weighing two sides of something.
target_language_example: Me gustaría ir; por otra parte, tengo que trabajar mañana.
native_language_example: I’d like to go; on the other hand, I have to work tomorrow.

meaning: "on the other hand"; also "on the other side" (literally/physically).
additional_notes: Often used to contrast two ideas (similar to "however" / "on the other hand"). It can also be used literally to mean the other side of a place (e.g., the other side of the street). Common pattern: "Por un lado..., pero por otro lado..."
target_language_example: Por otro lado, podríamos ir mañana si hoy estás ocupado.
native_language_example: On the other hand, we could go tomorrow if you're busy today.

additional_notes: Used to attribute an action, attitude, or responsibility to a person or group: "Fue amable por parte de ella" (It was kind of her). It can also mean "on [someone’s] side of the family" in phrases like "por parte de padre/madre" (on my father’s/mother’s side).
target_language_example: Fue un gesto muy generoso por parte de ellos.
native_language_example: It was a very generous gesture on their part.

meaning: step by step; one thing at a time.
additional_notes: Often used to suggest breaking a topic or task into smaller pieces, especially when explaining something: “Vamos por partes” = “Let’s take it step by step.” It can also mean “in parts/pieces,” depending on context.
target_language_example: Vamos por partes: primero revisamos el contrato y luego hablamos del precio.
native_language_example: Let’s take it step by step: first we’ll review the contract and then we’ll talk about the price.

additional_notes: Used to say something almost happened but didn’t. Very common pattern: “por poco + no + verb” = “I almost didn’t … / I nearly didn’t …” (e.g., “Por poco no llego a tiempo” = “I almost didn’t arrive on time”). Also used with accidents/mistakes: “Por poco me caigo” = “I almost fell.”
target_language_example: Por poco pierdo el tren.
native_language_example: I almost missed the train.

additional_notes: Used to say something is happening/happened on someone’s first occasion of doing it. Often placed after the verb phrase: "Fuimos... por primera vez", "Lo hice por primera vez". It can also refer to the first time you met someone: "conocí a mi esposa por primera vez".
target_language_example: Probé sushi por primera vez ayer.
native_language_example: I tried sushi for the first time yesterday.

meaning: for the first time in (a period/place).
additional_notes: Used to say something happens for the first time within a time span (en cinco años, en meses, en su vida) or in a location/context (en Australia). Often followed by a time expression or place, and it can start a sentence for emphasis: «Por primera vez en su vida, ...».
target_language_example: Por primera vez en mucho tiempo, me sentí tranquilo.
native_language_example: For the first time in a long time, I felt calm.

por primera vez en mi vida

target_language_multi_word_term: por primera vez en mi vida
meaning: for the first time in my life.
additional_notes: Used to emphasize that something has never happened to you before, and this is your very first experience of it. It can go at the beginning of the sentence (often with a comma) or at the end. You can swap the pronoun to match the person: por primera vez en tu/su/nuestra vida.
target_language_example: Por primera vez en mi vida, llegué temprano al trabajo.
native_language_example: For the first time in my life, I arrived early to work.

additional_notes: This phrase is grammatically possible but uncommon on its own in everyday Spanish; speakers typically use an article: **por la puerta** (through the door) or **por las puertas** (through the doors). You may still see **por puertas** in telegraphic/sign-style wording, instructions, or when emphasizing “by way of doors” in general rather than specific doors. Common with verbs like **entrar/salir/pasar**.
target_language_example: En caso de emergencia, salgan por puertas laterales.
native_language_example: In case of emergency, exit through side doors.

additional_notes: Used in direct and indirect questions to ask for the reason. It is written as two words with an accent on qué when it means "why" (compare porque = "because"). It can also appear inside expressions like no tener por qué, meaning there is no reason to or no need to.
target_language_example: No entiendo por qué estás enojado.
native_language_example: I don't understand why you're angry.

meaning: "why not?" / "how come (we/you) don't...?" (a suggestion or question).
additional_notes: Used to propose an idea politely or challenge a situation: ¿Por qué no + verb (present)? = “Why don’t we/you...?” It can also be a standalone response meaning “Why not?” Note: with accent (por qué) it’s a question; without accent (porque) it means “because.”
target_language_example: ¿Por qué no vamos al cine después de cenar?
native_language_example: Why don’t we go to the movies after dinner?

additional_notes: Used to say people do something individually rather than as a group (llegar/pagar por separado). Also common in shopping/product info to mean an item is not included and must be bought separately (Se vende por separado / Los accesorios se venden por separado).
target_language_example: ¿Podemos pagar por separado, por favor?
native_language_example: Can we pay separately, please?

additional_notes: Used to talk about a possible situation and what you do now to be prepared for it. It’s commonly followed by a verb (often in the present indicative): "por si vuelve" (in case he/she comes back), "por si pasa algo" (in case something happens). It can also introduce a reason for bringing/keeping something: "Lo llevo por si lo necesito" (I’m taking it in case I need it).
target_language_example: Lleva una chaqueta por si hace frío.
native_language_example: Bring a jacket just in case it gets cold.

additional_notes: Used to express a precaution: you do something now because something might happen later. It can go before a clause (Por si acaso lo necesita...) or stand alone as a short reply meaning “just in case.” Often implies “better safe than sorry.”
target_language_example: Trae una chaqueta por si acaso hace frío.
native_language_example: Bring a jacket just in case it’s cold.

additional_notes: Means something lasts indefinitely. Common in emotional or poetic contexts (por siempre en mi corazón / en mi memoria). In casual speech it can also be used for emphasis, similar to “forever” in English (“fiestas por siempre”). Often interchangeable with “para siempre,” though “para siempre” is more common for “forever” in many situations.
target_language_example: Te voy a querer por siempre.
native_language_example: I'm going to love you forever.

additional_notes: A compositional phrase: por + su. The word su can mean his, her, your (formal), or their, so context tells you whose thing it refers to. Depending on the verb or expression, por su may also sound more natural in English as "by," "about," "because of," or even "after," as in por su acento = "by his accent" and gracias por su cooperación = "thank you for your cooperation."
target_language_example: Lo reconocí por su voz.
native_language_example: I recognized him by his voice.

additional_notes: Used to say someone does something without help, supervision, or support from others. It can also suggest acting independently of a group or instructions. Variants with other possessives are common (por mi cuenta, por tu cuenta, por nuestra cuenta), but "por su cuenta" is used for he/she/you formal/they.
target_language_example: Tom investigó por su cuenta.
native_language_example: Tom investigated on his own.

additional_notes: Used to express relief or that something turned out well. Common at the start of a sentence (Por suerte, …). In some regions you may hear/see it followed by "que" ("Por suerte que…") with the same meaning: "Luckily, …".
target_language_example: Por suerte, llegamos a tiempo.
native_language_example: Luckily, we arrived on time.

additional_notes: Used to strongly confirm/agree with what someone said or asked, similar to “of course” in English. Often set off with commas (“Por supuesto, …”) and it can also be used alone as a full reply (“—¿Vienes? —Por supuesto.”). Sometimes said with tone for emphasis or mild irony, depending on context.
target_language_example: —¿Puedes ayudarme mañana? —Por supuesto.
native_language_example: —Can you help me tomorrow? —Of course.

additional_notes: Used to strongly agree, confirm, or say something is obvious/expected. Common as a short reply (“Por supuesto.”) or inserted into a sentence to emphasize certainty.
target_language_example: ¿Puedes ayudarme mañana? Por supuesto, cuenta conmigo.
native_language_example: Can you help me tomorrow? Of course—count on me.

additional_notes: Used to strongly confirm or agree with what was just said or asked. It often comes at the start of the sentence, and the "que" introduces the clause that follows (similar to "of course (that) ..." in English). You can also say "por supuesto" without "que" when answering briefly.
target_language_example: —¿Vienes mañana? —Por supuesto que sí.
native_language_example: —Are you coming tomorrow? —Of course.

additional_notes: “Por supuesto” means “of course/certainly.” Adding “que” introduces the clause, and “lo” is a direct object pronoun meaning “it” (or sometimes “him/that”), referring to something already known from context: Por supuesto que lo conozco. = “Of course I know him/it.” You can swap the verb to fit the situation: por supuesto que lo tengo (I have it), lo era (it was), lo ha hecho (he/she has done it), etc.
target_language_example: Por supuesto que lo entiendo.
native_language_example: Of course I understand it.

meaning: for his/her/their; because of his/her/their; by his/her/their.
additional_notes: "Por" has several common meanings (often "for," "because of," or "by"), and "sus" means "his/her/their" (plural: used with plural nouns, or with singular nouns in some regions). Together, "por sus" introduces the reason/cause ("because of their..."), what someone is fighting/doing something for ("for their..."), or the means of identification ("by their..."). The exact translation depends on context: e.g., "luchar por sus derechos" = "fight for their rights"; "identificar por sus huellas" = "identify by their fingerprints."
target_language_example: Lo conocen por sus buenos modales.
native_language_example: They know him for his good manners.

additional_notes: Used to say someone does something alone/independently, without help or influence from others. It’s the feminine form; for a man: “por sí mismo,” for a group: “por sí mismos/as.” It can also mean “in itself” (e.g., “La victoria por sí misma…” = “Victory in itself…”).
target_language_example: María aprendió a cocinar por sí misma.
native_language_example: María learned to cook by herself.

meaning: by himself; on his own; for himself (i.e., independently).
additional_notes: Used to express that someone acts independently, without help or outside direction; also used for thinking/deciding independently (“for himself”). It agrees with gender/number: por sí misma (she), por sí mismos (they, masc./mixed), por sí mismas (they, fem.). Common with verbs like hacer, decidir, pensar.
target_language_example: Tom lo hizo por sí mismo.
native_language_example: Tom did it by himself.

meaning: by himself/itself; on his/its own; (also) speaks for itself.
additional_notes: Used to say someone does something alone/without help, or that something is self-evident (“it speaks for itself”). It agrees with the subject: por sí solo (masc. sing.), por sí sola (fem. sing.), por sí solos / por sí solas (plural). Often corresponds to “alone” or “on your own” in English.
target_language_example: Tom pintó la casa por sí solo.
native_language_example: Tom painted the house by himself.

additional_notes: A very common phrase meaning "for you," often expressing doing something for someone's benefit or sake. In some contexts, it can also mean "because of you." Note that Spanish uses the pronoun "ti" after the preposition "por," not "tú."
target_language_example: Haría cualquier cosa por ti.
native_language_example: I would do anything for you.

additional_notes: Used to emphasize that you personally do something, decide, or experience something without relying on others (“see for yourself,” “decide for yourself,” “do it yourself,” “think for yourself”). It can also mean “for yourself” in the sense of self-respect ("respeto por ti mismo"). Variation by gender/number: por ti misma (female), por vosotros mismos/mismas (you all, Spain), por ustedes mismos/mismas (you all, Latin America).
target_language_example: No te lo creas; compruébalo por ti mismo.
native_language_example: Don’t just believe it; check it for yourself.

additional_notes: Used to say something/someone is in many places, spread around, or happening in many areas. Often follows verbs like "hay" (there is/are), "estar" (to be), or "ver" (to see): "Hay ___ por todas partes" = "There are ___ everywhere."
target_language_example: Después de la fiesta, había vasos por todas partes.
native_language_example: After the party, there were cups everywhere.

meaning: all over the world; around the world.
additional_notes: Used to say something happens/exists in many places worldwide. Common with verbs like viajar (to travel), conocer (to know), haber (there is/there was), and tener (to have): “viajó por todo el mundo” = “she traveled around the world,” “había paz por todo el mundo” = “there was peace all over the world.”
target_language_example: Hay fans de esa banda por todo el mundo.
native_language_example: There are fans of that band all over the world.

additional_notes: Used with "por" to mean "for everything" when thanking, apologizing, or taking responsibility (e.g., "Gracias por todo", "Perdóname por todo", "Pagar por todo"). With verbs like "preocuparse" it often means "about everything" (worry about everything).
target_language_example: Lo siento por todo.
native_language_example: I’m sorry for everything.

additional_notes: Used to say something is present in many places, or that you looked in every place you could. Often with verbs like buscar (to look for) or hay (there is/are).
target_language_example: Después de la fiesta, había vasos por todos lados.
native_language_example: After the party, there were cups everywhere.

meaning: by all means; by any means possible.
additional_notes: Used to say you will do everything possible to achieve something (sometimes with a sense of urgency or determination). Often follows a verb like intentar, hacer, conseguir, salvar, evitar. It can also be used alone as an emphatic reply meaning “Absolutely / By all means.”
target_language_example: Tengo que encontrar mis llaves por todos los medios.
native_language_example: I have to find my keys by any means possible.

additional_notes: Used with the informal possessive "tu" (= "your" when speaking to one person you address as "tú"). "Por" has several common meanings, so "por tu" can mean "for your" (Te agradezco por tu ayuda), "because of your" (Estamos preocupados por tu futuro), "on/for the occasion of" (por tu cumpleaños), or sometimes "through/out of" with places/openings (Mira por tu ventana = "Look out (through) your window").
target_language_example: Gracias por tu paciencia.
native_language_example: Thanks for your patience.

additional_notes: Used to say someone is responsible for a bad result. Often has an angry or accusatory tone. You can change the person: por mi culpa (my fault), por su culpa (your fault—formal / his/her fault), por nuestra culpa (our fault). Similar: es tu culpa (it's your fault).
target_language_example: Llegamos tarde por tu culpa.
native_language_example: We’re late because of you / It’s your fault we’re late.

additional_notes: Used to say you did or said something to help someone, even if it feels unpleasant or they don’t like it. Often appears with advice or warnings (e.g., “Te lo digo por tu propio bien”). You can change the person: “por mi propio bien” (for my own good), “por su propio bien” (for his/her/their own good), “por nuestro propio bien” (for our own good).
target_language_example: Tienes que descansar un poco; es por tu propio bien.
native_language_example: You have to rest a bit; it’s for your own good.

additional_notes: Not a fixed expression. This is just por + un, so the exact translation depends on context. It can mean things like "by/because of a" (por un ruido fuerte), "through a" (por un cielo azul), or "for" with time or purpose (por un par de meses, por un café). un changes to una with feminine nouns.
target_language_example: Estuve en México por un mes.
native_language_example: I was in Mexico for a month.

additional_notes: Used to introduce one side of an argument, comparison, or situation. It’s often paired with "por otro lado" ("on the other hand") to show contrast, but it can also appear alone to present a first point before adding more context.
target_language_example: Por un lado quiero ir, pero por otro lado no tengo tiempo.
native_language_example: On the one hand I want to go, but on the other hand I don’t have time.

meaning: 'for a minute' (for a short time; sometimes 'by a minute').
additional_notes: Used to say something will last a short time: Déjame pensar por un minuto. It can also mean 'only for a moment' when asking for someone’s time: Solo necesito a Tom por un minuto. With times/being late, it can mean 'by a minute' (difference of one minute): Se me pasó el tren por un minuto (I missed the train by a minute).
target_language_example: Espera por un minuto, por favor.
native_language_example: Wait for a minute, please.

meaning: for a moment; for a short time.
additional_notes: Used to talk about something that lasts briefly. Often with commands/requests (Quédate..., Espera...) meaning “for a moment.” In negative expressions like “ni por un momento,” it means “not even for a moment” (not at all).
target_language_example: Espera por un momento, por favor.
native_language_example: Wait for a moment, please.

meaning: for a couple of days (for a few days).
additional_notes: Used to say something will last a short time, usually around two days (but it can also mean “a few days” in casual speech). Often used with verbs like irse, quedarse, estar, dejar, or vivir to talk about being somewhere temporarily.
target_language_example: Voy a quedarme aquí por un par de días.
native_language_example: I'm going to stay here for a couple of days.

meaning: for a while; for a short time.
additional_notes: Used to say something lasts temporarily. It can refer to minutes or longer, but it usually implies “not permanently.” Common with verbs like estar, quedarse, sentarse, esperar, dejar (a alguien) solo. You can add “más” to mean “a little longer”: por un rato más.
target_language_example: Quédate conmigo por un rato, por favor.
native_language_example: Stay with me for a while, please.

meaning: for a while; for some time.
additional_notes: Used to say something lasts/continues for a period of time (often temporary). Common with past or ongoing actions: "funcionó por un tiempo" (it worked for a while), "ha estado... por un tiempo" (has been... for some time), "sólo será por un tiempo" (it’ll only be for a while).
target_language_example: Voy a quedarme aquí por un tiempo.
native_language_example: I’m going to stay here for a while.

additional_notes: Used to express duration (how long something lasts). It often appears with activities or states: "leer por una hora" (read for an hour), "descansar por una hora" (rest for an hour). In everyday speech, "durante una hora" is a very common alternative with the same meaning.
target_language_example: Estudié por una hora antes del examen.
native_language_example: I studied for an hour before the exam.

meaning: for a reason; for a purpose.
additional_notes: Used to say that something has a specific cause, explanation, or purpose—often implying it’s not accidental. Very common in reflective phrases like “Todo pasa por una razón” (“Everything happens for a reason”). You can also use it to emphasize why something is the way it is: “Es el número dos por una razón.”
target_language_example: Todo pasa por una razón, aunque no lo entendamos ahora.
native_language_example: Everything happens for a reason, even if we don’t understand it now.

additional_notes: Used with time expressions after "por" to say how long something lasts or has lasted (duration). Often used with estar + past participle/adjective: "He estado aquí por una semana". In many situations, especially with "llevar" or in some regions, you may also hear "una semana" or "desde hace una semana" depending on whether you mean duration vs. since a starting point.
target_language_example: He trabajado aquí por una semana.
native_language_example: I’ve worked here for a week.

meaning: for once; just this one time.
additional_notes: Used to emphasize that something should happen at least one time, especially if it usually doesn’t. Often appears in commands or complaints: “Hazlo por una vez” (do it for once). It can sound frustrated or critical depending on tone.
target_language_example: Por una vez, escúchame antes de decidir.
native_language_example: For once, listen to me before you decide.

meaning: 'defeated' (in the phrase “darse por vencido” = 'to give up').
additional_notes: Almost always used with the reflexive verb “darse”: “me doy por vencido” (I give up), “se dio por vencido” (he/she gave up). It means to stop trying because you think you can’t win or succeed.
target_language_example: No me doy por vencido; voy a intentarlo otra vez.
native_language_example: I’m not giving up; I’m going to try again.

meaning: 'yet to come' / 'still to come' (in the future).
additional_notes: Used to talk about something that hasn’t happened yet. Common patterns: **estar por venir** (“to be yet to come”): *Lo peor está por venir.* It can also describe a future thing like an adjective after a noun: *una tarea por venir* (“a task still to come”). Note: **por + infinitive** can also mean “for + -ing” in other contexts (e.g., *Gracias por venir* = “Thanks for coming”), but **por venir** in *está por venir* means “yet to come,” not “for coming.”
target_language_example: Lo más difícil todavía está por venir.
native_language_example: The hardest part is still to come.

additional_notes: Used to say how many things happen or are done in each single occasion. Often appears with a number: "dos por vez" (= two at a time) or in instructions/limits: "solo una persona por vez" (= only one person at a time). In many contexts, Spanish also uses "a la vez" for “at the same time,” but "por vez" focuses on a per-occasion limit.
target_language_example: Solo se permite una persona por vez.
native_language_example: Only one person is allowed at a time.

additional_notes: Used to emphasize that you won’t ask/say/do something again (often as a warning or to show impatience). Common with verbs like pedir (to ask for/request), preguntar (to ask), and hablar (to talk).
target_language_example: Te lo digo por última vez: no entres aquí.
native_language_example: I’m telling you for the last time: don’t come in here.

additional_notes: Used to introduce the final point in a list, sequence, or explanation (similar to “lastly” or “and finally”). It can stand alone as a short transition (“Por último.”). Often followed by a comma: “Por último, …”.
target_language_example: Y por último, vamos a pagar la cuenta.
native_language_example: And finally, we’re going to pay the bill.

additional_notes: Used to give the reason for something, followed by a description/identity of “you” with the verb **ser** (eres = “you are”). It introduces a cause: **[result] + porque eres + [adjective/noun]**. (Don’t confuse **por qué** = “why?” with **porque** = “because”.)
target_language_example: No voy a cambiar de plan porque eres mi invitado.
native_language_example: I’m not going to change the plan because you’re my guest.

meaning: “because I …” / “because (of) me …” (giving a reason that involves the speaker).
