additional_notes: Used at the start of a reason clause: **porque** + **me** (object pronoun) + verb. Often followed by more pronouns, like **porque me lo dijo** (“because he/she told me”). In English you usually translate the whole clause, not word-for-word (“because me” is not natural in English).
target_language_example: No fui porque me sentía cansado.
native_language_example: I didn’t go because I felt tired.

additional_notes: Used to introduce a reason where the clause is negative: porque no + verb (e.g., porque no hay…, porque no era…, porque no puede…). Usually written as one word: porque. Don’t confuse it with the question ¿por qué no? (“why not?”).
target_language_example: No fui a la fiesta porque no tenía tiempo.
native_language_example: I didn’t go to the party because I didn’t have time.

additional_notes: Used to say there’s no clear reason or explanation, or that someone did/feels something without a specific cause. It can also be a short, slightly dismissive answer to “¿Por qué?” (Why?): “—¿Por qué? —Porque sí.”
target_language_example: No quiero salir hoy, porque sí.
native_language_example: I don't want to go out today, just because.

additional_notes: Used when speaking politely to someone you address as usted. Structure: preguntarle + algo + a + [person] (optional). The "le" is an indirect object pronoun meaning “to you (formal), to him, to her.” For an informal “you,” use preguntarte algo.
target_language_example: Disculpe, ¿puedo preguntarle algo?
native_language_example: Excuse me, can I ask you something?

additional_notes: Used to introduce a question (often polite or a bit serious). It’s the infinitive phrase “preguntar” (to ask) + “-te” (to you) + “algo” (something). Commonly appears after verbs like “quiero/debo/tengo que” (I want/must/have to) or in questions like “¿Puedo preguntarte algo?”
target_language_example: ¿Te puedo preguntarte algo rápido?
native_language_example: Can I ask you something quickly?

additional_notes: Used to tell someone to ask a person for information. It’s the tú command of “preguntar” + “le” (to him/her/you formal) + “a” + the person being asked: “Pregúntale a Tom…”. In some set/idiomatic phrases (e.g., “Pregúntale a mis labios”), it can be used humorously to mean “don’t ask me / I’m not telling.”
target_language_example: Pregúntale a tu profesor cuándo es el examen.
native_language_example: Ask your teacher when the exam is.

meaning: to catch fire; to set on fire.
additional_notes: Used for something starting to burn on its own (La casa prendió fuego = “The house caught fire”) or for causing something to burn (Prendió fuego a la basura = “He/She set the trash on fire”). Often appears as "prenderse fuego" (to catch fire) and with "a" before the thing set on fire: "prender fuego a + noun".
target_language_example: La sartén empezó a prender fuego, pero la apagamos rápido.
native_language_example: The frying pan started to catch fire, but we put it out quickly.

additional_notes: Used with estar (or sentirse) to describe feeling worried/anxious about a situation or thing. It’s often followed by a noun or an infinitive (e.g., preocupado por tener que...).
target_language_example: Estoy preocupado por el examen de mañana.
native_language_example: I'm worried about tomorrow's exam.

additional_notes: Common command form (tú) of the verb phrase "prestar atención a". It’s followed by "a" + the person/thing you should focus on: "a ella", "a él", "a ellos", "a las bicicletas". You can also use it in other forms, e.g., "Presto atención a..." (I pay attention to...), "Presta atención" (Pay attention).
target_language_example: Presta atención a lo que dice el profesor.
native_language_example: Pay attention to what the teacher is saying.

additional_notes: Common construction: (subject) + prestar + atención. Often followed by “a” to specify what you’re paying attention to: “Prestar atención a las instrucciones / a lo que dice.” Frequently used with “tener que” (to have to): “Tienes que prestar atención.” Imperatives use “presta atención” (tú) or “presten atención” (ustedes).
target_language_example: Tienes que prestar atención a lo que te digo, por favor.
native_language_example: You have to pay attention to what I’m telling you, please.

additional_notes: Refers to the first person you ever loved romantically (often your first serious crush or relationship). Common in phrases like “Mi primer amor” (my first love) and “nunca se olvida al primer amor” (you never forget your first love).
target_language_example: Nunca voy a olvidar a mi primer amor.
native_language_example: I’m never going to forget my first love.

meaning: first year (of school, a program, or a period of time).
additional_notes: Used to talk about someone’s first year in a school level or program: "de primer año" = "first-year" (often "freshman" in a college context, depending on the country). With "en/el" it means being in the first year: "Estoy en el primer año..." Also used more generally for the first year of something: "durante el primer año" = "during the first year."
target_language_example: Mi hermana es de primer año y todavía se está adaptando.
native_language_example: My sister is a first-year student and she’s still adjusting.

additional_notes: Title for the head of government in many countries (not the same as the president/monarch). Used with or without an article: “el primer ministro” (the prime minister) or as a direct form of address: “Bienvenido, primer ministro.” Often capitalized in English; in Spanish it may appear in lowercase unless used as part of an official title in context.
target_language_example: El primer ministro dará un discurso esta noche.
native_language_example: The prime minister will give a speech tonight.

meaning: (1) first class (travel/service); (2) first class / first lesson (in a course).
additional_notes: Meaning depends on context: in transport/hospitality it refers to a higher, more expensive category of service (often said as "en primera clase" or "boleto en primera clase"). In school or a course, "mi/nuestra primera clase" means the first session/lesson with a teacher or group.
target_language_example: Compré un boleto en primera clase para el tren.
native_language_example: I bought a first-class ticket for the train.

additional_notes: Usually refers to the Catholic sacrament/ceremony when a child receives Communion for the first time. It’s commonly preceded by "la" (la primera comunión) and used with "de" to say whose it is (la primera comunión de mi hermana). People often talk about preparing/studying for it and about special clothes (e.g., a dress or suit).
target_language_example: Mis primos vienen a mi primera comunión este sábado.
native_language_example: My cousins are coming to my First Communion this Saturday.

additional_notes: Used in grammar and storytelling. In Spanish, "primera persona" refers to speaking from the point of view of the speaker (yo/nosotros). Common phrases: "en primera persona" (in the first person) and "narrado/escrito en primera persona" (told/written in the first person).
target_language_example: La novela está escrita en primera persona.
native_language_example: The novel is written in the first person.

additional_notes: Used to talk about doing/experiencing something for the first time. Often appears as “la primera vez” (“the first time”) or “por primera vez” (“for the first time”). In sentence 1, “Primera vez que…” is a shortened way of saying “Es la primera vez que…” (“It’s the first time that…”).
target_language_example: Es la primera vez que visito Madrid.
native_language_example: It’s the first time I’ve visited Madrid.

meaning: "the first to" (do something) / "first in" (a place or list).
additional_notes: Used with an infinitive to say someone is the first person to do something: "el primero en + infinitive" (e.g., "el primero en moverse"). It can also be used with places/lists to mean first in a location or order ("el primero en la escena", "el primero en la lista"). Changes for gender/number: "el primero / la primera / los primeros / las primeras en".
target_language_example: Hayes es el primero en moverse.
native_language_example: Hayes is the first to move.

additional_notes: Used for basic medical help given right away in an emergency (before a doctor/ambulance). Often appears with words like curso (course), equipo/kit (kit), or maletín (case): “un curso de primeros auxilios”, “un kit de primeros auxilios”. Usually plural in Spanish.
target_language_example: ¿Hay alguien que sepa dar primeros auxilios?
native_language_example: Is there anyone who knows first aid?

additional_notes: Most commonly you’ll see this as **tan pronto como** (“as soon as”). It introduces the moment something happens: *Tan pronto como llegue…* In sentences about the future, Spanish often uses the **subjunctive** after it: *Tan pronto como puedas, llámame* (“As soon as you can, call me”).
target_language_example: Tan pronto como termine la clase, te llamo.
native_language_example: As soon as class ends, I’ll call you.

additional_notes: Used to talk about the forecast for upcoming weather (rain, temperature, wind, etc.). Very common in news and everyday conversation: “¿Cuál es el pronóstico del tiempo?” You can also say “el pronóstico” when the context is clearly weather.
target_language_example: Según el pronóstico del tiempo, mañana va a llover.
native_language_example: According to the weather forecast, it's going to rain tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used to say that a place or object belongs to a private person or company and is not public. Common on signs and warnings (often implying “no trespassing” or “no public access”). You can say: Es/Esto/Esta es propiedad privada ("This is private property") or Estás en propiedad privada ("You’re on private property").
target_language_example: No entres: es propiedad privada.
native_language_example: Don’t go in: it’s private property.

additional_notes: Use "proteger" with the personal "a" before a direct object that is a person (or a pet): "proteger a mi hijo", "proteger a Tom". With things, you usually don’t use "a": "proteger la casa". You can add "de" to say what you’re protecting someone from: "proteger a alguien de algo".
target_language_example: Quiero proteger a mis amigos de cualquier peligro.
native_language_example: I want to protect my friends from any danger.

additional_notes: Used in politics and government for a law that is being proposed and discussed/voted on, but hasn’t become law yet. You’ll often see it with verbs like aprobar (to pass/approve), votar (to vote), and estar en contra / a favor (to be against / in favor).
target_language_example: El Congreso debatirá el proyecto de ley mañana.
native_language_example: Congress will debate the bill tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used as a holiday greeting/wish around New Year’s (often in the set phrase “Feliz y próspero año nuevo”). You can say it on its own or after a greeting like “¡Que tengas un…!”
target_language_example: ¡Feliz y próspero año nuevo para ti y tu familia!
native_language_example: Happy and prosperous New Year to you and your family!

additional_notes: Used to talk about something that was possible in the past, often when you’re not sure what really happened. It’s the past tense of “poder” (pudo) + “haber” + past participle: “pudo haber sido” (could have been), “pudo haber pasado” (could have happened). Also used in questions about unknown causes or responsible people: “¿Quién pudo haber…?” (Who could have…?).
target_language_example: Pudo haber sido un error, pero no estoy seguro.
native_language_example: It could have been a mistake, but I’m not sure.

additional_notes: Formed with the present subjunctive of poder (pueda) + infinitive hacer. It’s commonly used after expressions like "algo/nada que..." (something/nothing that...), and after verbs/phrases of doubt, fear, or uncertainty (e.g., dudo que..., me temo que...). In these contexts Spanish uses the subjunctive because it’s not stated as a certain fact.
target_language_example: Si hay algo que pueda hacer, dímelo.
native_language_example: If there's anything I can do, tell me.

additional_notes: Often used as a polite request with an implied “usted” (formal “you”): “¿Puede ayudarme…?” = “Can you help me…?” In statements, it can also mean “(he/she/it/you-formal) can help me,” depending on context (e.g., “Nadie puede ayudarme” = “Nobody can help me”).
target_language_example: ¿Puede ayudarme con esta maleta, por favor?
native_language_example: Can you help me with this suitcase, please?

additional_notes: Formed with the verb poder in the present tense (puede) + an infinitive (cambiar). It’s used to say something is possible: “can change.” The subject is often “él/ella/eso” or “esto” (it/this), and it can also be used with an indirect object like “te” (“puede cambiarte la vida” = “can change your life”).
target_language_example: Todo puede cambiar de un día para otro.
native_language_example: Everything can change from one day to the next.

meaning: "might be" / "could be" (it/he/she might be in a place or state).
additional_notes: Present tense of poder + estar (3rd person singular). Used to express possibility about someone’s location or condition/state: Puede estar en casa. / Puede estar enfermo. It can also mean "can be" in general statements: Puede estar en cualquier parte. Negative: No puede estar lejos ("It can’t be far").
target_language_example: No contesta; puede estar durmiendo.
native_language_example: He’s not answering; he might be sleeping.

meaning: “there may be / there can be” (it’s possible that there is/are).
additional_notes: From "poder" (can/may) + "haber" (there is/are). Used to express possibility about existence or occurrence: "puede haber cambios" = “there may be changes.” In negative form: "no puede haber" = “there can’t be / there must not be.” "Haber" stays in the singular even if what follows is plural: "puede haber doce cadáveres" (not *pueden haber*).
target_language_example: Puede haber un problema con la reserva, así que llega temprano.
native_language_example: There may be a problem with the reservation, so arrive early.

meaning: "can do" / "is able to do" (also: "may do" in the sense of permission).
additional_notes: Formed with poder (to be able to / can) + infinitive hacer (to do / to make). "Puede" is for él/ella/usted (he/she/you formal). Often followed by "lo que" to mean "whatever" (e.g., "Puede hacer lo que quiera" = He/She can do whatever he/she wants). In negative form, "no puede hacer" means "can’t do" (or "mustn’t" depending on context).
target_language_example: ¿Puede hacer una copia de este documento?
native_language_example: Can you make a copy of this document?

meaning: “can do it” / “is able to do it.”
additional_notes: Made of "puede" (he/she/you-formal can) + "hacerlo" (to do it). Used to say someone has the ability or permission to do something. The subject can be explicit (Él/ella/usted) or implied by context.
target_language_example: ¿Crees que ella puede hacerlo sola?
native_language_example: Do you think she can do it by herself?

additional_notes: From poder (can/may) + irse (to leave/go away). Often used to give permission or to dismiss someone politely, usually addressing usted. Common with a destination: “Puede irse a casa” (You may go home). With “ya” it means “you can leave now / you may go now.”
target_language_example: Gracias, ya puede irse.
native_language_example: Thank you, you may leave now.

additional_notes: Used to talk about someone’s ability to swim. It’s the verb poder (to be able to/can) + nadar (to swim). Puede is the “he/she/you (formal)” present-tense form: él/ella/usted puede nadar. For “I can swim,” say: Yo puedo nadar. You can add adverbs or comparisons: puede nadar bien (swim well), puede nadar más lejos (swim farther), puede nadar una milla (swim a mile).
target_language_example: Él puede nadar bien.
native_language_example: He can swim well.

additional_notes: Means that something is possible/uncertain: “it could happen.” Common in phrases like “todo puede pasar” (anything can happen), “nunca se sabe qué puede pasar” (you never know what could happen), and “le puede pasar a cualquiera” (it can happen to anyone). Literally it’s “(it) can pass,” but in most contexts it’s closer to “happen.”
target_language_example: No te preocupes; puede pasarle a cualquiera.
native_language_example: Don’t worry; it can happen to anyone.

additional_notes: Expresses possibility or a possible state/identity. It is often followed by a noun or adjective, as in puede ser útil ('can be useful') or puede ser joven ('may be young'). In impersonal phrases like no se puede ser..., it means 'you/one can't be...'. On its own in conversation, puede ser can also mean 'maybe' or 'possibly'.
target_language_example: No todo puede ser perfecto.
native_language_example: Not everything can be perfect.

meaning: "it can be / it could be"; also "maybe."
additional_notes: From the verb phrase "poder ser" ("to be able to be"). It’s used (1) to express possibility about what something is or might happen: "Puede ser esta noche" (It could be tonight); (2) in the pattern "Puede ser que + subjunctive" to mean "It may be that...": "Puede ser que eso tenga..."; and (3) as a short reply meaning "maybe" or "could be": "Puede ser, sí." In negatives like "no puede ser", it often means "it can’t be" or "that can’t be" (sometimes like "no way").
target_language_example: —¿Es verdad? —Puede ser, no estoy seguro.
native_language_example: —Is it true? —Maybe, I’m not sure.

meaning: "it may be that" / "it could be that".
additional_notes: Used to express possibility or uncertainty. It’s typically followed by the subjunctive (e.g., "Puede ser que venga"). You’ll also hear the shorter version "puede que" with the same meaning.
target_language_example: Puede ser que lleguemos tarde por el tráfico.
native_language_example: We might arrive late because of traffic.

additional_notes: Formed with the verb poder + infinitive: puede (he/she/it/you formal) + tener (to have). Use it to express possibility, ability, or permission to have something. In negative form (no puede tener), it often means "cannot have" (impossible or not allowed), and it can also be used for logical deduction: "Él no puede tener hambre" = "He can’t be hungry" (it doesn’t make sense given the situation). For other subjects: puedo/podemos/pueden tener, etc.
target_language_example: El estrés puede tener un gran impacto negativo en tu salud.
native_language_example: Stress can have a big negative impact on your health.

additional_notes: Form of **poder + infinitive**: **puede ver** is 3rd person singular (“he/she can see”) and also the **usted** form (“you can see,” formal). Common in the impersonal/passive **se puede ver** = “you can see / it can be seen.”
target_language_example: Desde aquí, puede ver toda la ciudad.
native_language_example: From here, you can see the whole city.

additional_notes: Used to express possibility or uncertainty. It is normally followed by the subjunctive, as in "Puede que llegue tarde" (He/She may arrive late).
target_language_example: Puede que mañana llueva.
native_language_example: It might rain tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used to express possibility or uncertainty about a past event. It’s the structure "puede que" + present subjunctive; with "haya" (from "haber") it’s followed by a past participle to form the present perfect subjunctive (e.g., "puede que haya llovido" = "it may have rained"). Often interchangeable with "quizá(s)" or "tal vez" in similar meanings.
target_language_example: Puede que haya olvidado las llaves en casa.
native_language_example: I may have forgotten my keys at home.

additional_notes: Used to express possibility or uncertainty. It’s the structure: "puede que" + verb in the present subjunctive; here "haya" is the subjunctive of "haber" (to exist/there to be). Often followed by a noun: "puede que haya una salida" (there may be an exit), "puede que haya otros" (there may be others).
target_language_example: Puede que haya un error en la dirección.
native_language_example: There may be a mistake in the address.

additional_notes: Used to express possibility in the negative. It’s short for the structure **puede que + subjunctive**: *Puede que no estemos...*, *Puede que no esté...*. Common in conversation to hedge or show uncertainty, like “might not.”
target_language_example: Puede que no tenga tiempo hoy.
native_language_example: I might not have time today.

additional_notes: Used to express possibility or uncertainty. It’s built from **puede que** (“it’s possible that”) + **sea** (subjunctive of *ser*, “to be”), so it’s normally followed by the **subjunctive**: *Puede que sea así.* You can change the verb to match the meaning: *Puede que esté…* (from *estar*), *Puede que tenga…* (from *tener*), etc.
target_language_example: Puede que sea verdad, pero no estoy seguro.
native_language_example: It might be true, but I’m not sure.

additional_notes: "Pueden" is the present tense of "poder" for "they" or "you (plural, Spain)", and it’s followed by an infinitive like "hacer". It talks about ability or possibility: "pueden hacer eso" = "they can do that." Often used in phrases like "pueden hacer mucho" (they can do a lot) or "¿qué pueden hacer?" (what can they do?).
target_language_example: Mis amigos pueden hacer la tarea después de cenar.
native_language_example: My friends can do the homework after dinner.

additional_notes: Formed by **pueden** (they/you-plural can) + **ser** (to be). Used to talk about possibilities or general truths about a plural subject: *Las gaviotas pueden ser…* You can often translate it as “can be” (ability/possibility) or “may be” (possibility).
target_language_example: Las reglas pueden ser diferentes en cada país.
native_language_example: The rules can be different in each country.

additional_notes: Formed with **poder** (to be able to/can) + infinitive: **pueden + ver**. It can refer to **they** (e.g., *Los gatos pueden ver...* = “Cats can see...”) or **you all** (Spain: *ustedes pueden ver...*). Very often it appears with **se** in an impersonal/passive sense: **se pueden ver...** = “you can see...” / “...can be seen.”
target_language_example: Desde aquí pueden ver el mar.
native_language_example: From here, they/you all can see the sea.

additional_notes: Used to say someone is trustworthy. It’s the verb phrase "confiar en" (to trust in/on) with "puedes" (you can). Add a person or pronoun after "en": "puedes confiar en mí / él / ella / ellos". You can also limit it with phrases like "hasta cierto punto" (up to a point).
target_language_example: Puedes confiar en nosotros; no vamos a decir nada.
native_language_example: You can trust us; we won’t say anything.

additional_notes: Formed from poder (to be able to) + hacer (to do/make). Used to say what someone is allowed or able to do. It’s often followed by an infinitive or by “lo” (it): “Lo puedes hacer…” = “You can do it…”. You’ll also see it in fixed phrases like “puedes hacer uso de…” = “you can make use of…”, and in role/option lists: “Puedes hacer de…” = “You can play/act as…”.
target_language_example: Si tienes tiempo, lo puedes hacer mañana.
native_language_example: If you have time, you can do it tomorrow.

meaning: "you can do it" / "you can do that".
additional_notes: Used to encourage someone or say they’re capable of doing something. "Puedes" can be "you can" (ability) or "you may" (permission), but in this phrase it’s usually about ability/encouragement. "Hacerlo" = "do it" (hacer + lo). You can add emphasis with the subject pronoun: "Tú puedes hacerlo."
target_language_example: No te rindas: puedes hacerlo.
native_language_example: Don’t give up: you can do it.

meaning: “you can leave” / “you can go (away)” (also: “you may leave”).
additional_notes: From poder (you can/are allowed to) + irte (to go away/leave; ir + te). Used to give permission (“Puedes irte ahora.”), to say it’s possible to leave, or in the negative to forbid it (“No puedes irte.” = “You can’t/you’re not allowed to leave.”). Often implies leaving the place or going away from the speaker. Can be followed by details: “por…” (by/through a route), “si quieres” (if you want).
target_language_example: Si ya terminaste, puedes irte.
native_language_example: If you’re done already, you can leave.

meaning: “you can call me …” or “you can phone/call me.”
additional_notes: From poder (you can) + llamar (to call) + me (me). With a name or nickname, it means how you’d like to be addressed: “Puedes llamarme Vanya” = “You can call me Vanya.” With time/conditions (cuando, esta tarde, si necesitas ayuda), it means to call on the phone: “Puedes llamarme cuando quieras” = “You can call me whenever you want.” Often softened with por favor.
target_language_example: Si tienes alguna pregunta, puedes llamarme mañana.
native_language_example: If you have any questions, you can call me tomorrow.

meaning: "you can stay here" / "you may stay here."
additional_notes: Used to give permission or allow someone to remain in a place. "Puedes" can mean either "can" (ability) or "may" (permission); in this phrase it usually means permission. Often followed by extra details like "conmigo" (with me), "en casa" (at home), "el tiempo que quieras" (as long as you want), "si quieres" (if you want), or conditions like "siempre que..." (as long as/provided that...).
target_language_example: Si no tienes dónde ir, puedes quedarte aquí esta noche.
native_language_example: If you have nowhere to go, you can stay here tonight.

additional_notes: Used to give someone permission to keep something or take possession of it. Very common with objects and money: “Puedes quedarte con el cambio” = “Keep the change.” With people, it can mean “you can stay with” or “you can take care of” someone (“Puedes quedarte con Colin” = “You can stay with Colin / You can keep Colin (with you)”), depending on context.
target_language_example: No te preocupes, puedes quedarte con mi paraguas.
native_language_example: Don’t worry, you can keep my umbrella.

additional_notes: Used to offer permission (“You may use…”) or describe an available option (“You can use…”). Often followed by a thing (puedes usar el diccionario) or by “o” to present choices (puedes usar X o Y). In more formal Spanish, “puede usar” can be used for “you can use” (formal you).
target_language_example: Si no tienes efectivo, puedes usar mi tarjeta.
native_language_example: If you don’t have cash, you can use my card.

meaning: "you can use my..." (giving permission to use something of mine).
additional_notes: Used to offer or allow someone to use something that belongs to you. It’s typically followed by a noun: “Puedes usar mi coche/bolígrafo/ordenador…”. You can add “cuando quieras” (whenever you want) or “si quieres” (if you want) to soften it.
target_language_example: Puedes usar mi cargador si quieres.
native_language_example: You can use my charger if you want.

additional_notes: From poder (to be able to / can) + venir (to come). It can mean ability (“can you come?” / “if you can come”) or permission (“you may come”), depending on context. Used with conditions like si… (“if…”) and siempre que… (“as long as / provided that…”).
target_language_example: ¿Puedes venir a mi casa esta tarde?
native_language_example: Can you come to my house this afternoon?

additional_notes: Uses the verb "poder" (you can/are able to) + "ver" (to see). It can refer to physical sight (what is visible from a place, seeing in the dark, etc.) or to understanding/realizing something, especially with "que": "Puedes ver que es un error" = "You can see/tell it’s a mistake."
target_language_example: Desde aquí puedes ver el mar.
native_language_example: From here you can see the sea.

meaning: “I can help you.” / “Can I help you?”
additional_notes: From the verb phrase **poder + infinitive** (“can + verb”) plus **ayudar** (“to help”) and **te** (“you”). Often used as an offer of help (**¿Cómo puedo ayudarte?** = “How can I help you?”). With **no**, it becomes **No puedo ayudarte** (“I can’t help you”). You may also hear **puedo ayudarle** (formal “you”) or **puedo ayudarte con + noun** (“help you with…”).
target_language_example: ¿Puedo ayudarte con las bolsas?
native_language_example: Can I help you with the bags?

meaning: "I can get" / "I can obtain" / "I can manage to get."
additional_notes: Used to say you’re able to obtain, arrange, or make something happen. With a noun: "puedo conseguir mesa" = "I can get a table." With an infinitive or clause (often with "que"): "puedo conseguir que..." = "I can get (someone) to..." / "I can arrange for..." (e.g., to have it done by Monday).
target_language_example: No te preocupes: puedo conseguir entradas para el concierto.
native_language_example: Don’t worry: I can get tickets for the concert.

additional_notes: Used to say what you are able/allowed to give someone. It’s made of "puedo" ("I can") + "darte" ("to give you"). Often appears in negatives: "no puedo darte..." = "I can’t give you...". You’ll usually add what you can give: "puedo darte información" (I can give you information).
target_language_example: Puedo darte más información mañana.
native_language_example: I can give you more information tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used to express that you are able/allowed to say something. Often appears with an object pronoun: “te lo puedo decir” = “I can tell you (it)”. Also commonly used in negatives: “no lo puedo decir” = “I can’t say/tell it.” Word order can vary: “puedo decir” / “te puedo decir” / “puedo decírtelo” (same idea).
target_language_example: Todavía no te lo puedo decir, pero mañana sí.
native_language_example: I still can’t tell you, but tomorrow I can.

additional_notes: From the verb "esperar" (to wait / to hope / to expect). In this phrase it usually means you’re able/willing to wait. You’ll often add what you’re waiting for with "por": "Puedo esperar por ti" = "I can wait for you." Be careful: "No puedo esperar" is often used like English "I can’t wait" (impatient or excited), especially when followed by "a" + infinitive: "No puedo esperar a verte" = "I can’t wait to see you."
target_language_example: Si estás ocupada, puedo esperar un poco más.
native_language_example: If you’re busy, I can wait a little longer.

meaning: "I can speak" / "I’m able to talk (to someone)".
additional_notes: Uses the verb poder (to be able to) + infinitive hablar (to speak/to talk). Commonly followed by con + person (puedo hablar con ellos = I can talk with them) or by a language (puedo hablar chino = I can speak Chinese). Subject pronouns like yo are optional and mainly used for emphasis: Yo puedo hablar…
target_language_example: ¿Puedo hablar contigo un momento?
native_language_example: Can I talk to you for a moment?

additional_notes: “Puedo” = “I can” (from poder) + “hacerlo” = “do it” (hacer + lo = “it”). Used to say you’re able to do something. It can be followed by an adverb like “mejor” (better): “Puedo hacerlo mejor.” Negative is “No puedo hacerlo” = “I can’t do it.” You can add emphasis with a subject or pronoun: “Yo puedo hacerlo” (I can do it), “Puedo hacerlo yo sola” (I can do it myself / on my own—said by a woman).
target_language_example: No te preocupes: puedo hacerlo.
native_language_example: Don’t worry: I can do it.

additional_notes: Used to say you’re able to hear a sound. Often followed by a noun (puedo oír el viento), “algo” (I can hear something), or “a + person” when you can hear someone (Puedo oír a Tom roncar…). Negative: “No puedo oír” = “I can’t hear.”
target_language_example: No puedo oír bien; ¿puedes hablar más alto?
native_language_example: I can’t hear well; can you speak louder?

additional_notes: From the verb phrase "poder" (to be able to) + "ver" (to see). Use it to say you’re able to see something, often because it’s visible, close enough, or you have what you need (like glasses). You can add what you can see right after it: "Puedo ver + [thing]". Negative: "No puedo ver" = "I can’t see."
target_language_example: No puedo ver bien sin mis gafas.
native_language_example: I can’t see well without my glasses.

meaning: "I can handle/deal with" (it); "I’m able to manage".
additional_notes: Used with a noun or pronoun: "poder con + algo/alguien" means being able to cope with, carry, or overcome something (physically or mentally). In the negative, "no puedo con..." often means "I can’t handle it" or "it’s too much for me."
target_language_example: No te preocupes: puedo con la maleta yo solo.
native_language_example: Don’t worry: I can handle the suitcase by myself.

meaning: back door; (figuratively) a loophole/weak point someone can use to get in.
additional_notes: Literally, it’s the door at the back of a building/home (often opposite the main/front door). Figuratively, it can mean a vulnerability or “backdoor” access—something that lets someone bypass normal defenses or rules.
target_language_example: No dejes la puerta trasera abierta por la noche.
native_language_example: Don’t leave the back door open at night.

additional_notes: Literally “setting of the sun.” Used to talk about the time when the sun goes down or the view/scene of the sky at that time. Common with verbs like ver/mirar/admirar (to watch/admire) and expressions like hasta la puesta de sol (“until sunset”).
target_language_example: Vamos a la playa para ver la puesta de sol.
native_language_example: Let’s go to the beach to watch the sunset.

additional_notes: Used literally for the area you can’t see (especially when driving, around the side/rear of a car), and figuratively for something you don’t notice or understand (a weakness or gap in awareness). Often appears with verbs like estar (“to be”) or quedar (“to be located”): “Está en el punto ciego.”
target_language_example: Cuidado: la moto está en tu punto ciego.
native_language_example: Careful: the motorcycle is in your blind spot.

additional_notes: Used to name the specific place where people agree to meet (friends, a group, protesters, etc.). Often appears with verbs like "ser" (Ese es nuestro punto de encuentro), "necesitar" (Necesito el punto de encuentro), "conocer" (Conocen el punto de encuentro), and "ver(se)" (Nos vemos en el punto de encuentro).
target_language_example: Quedamos en el punto de encuentro a las seis.
native_language_example: Let’s meet at the meeting point at six.

meaning: starting point; the place or idea you begin from.
additional_notes: Used both literally (the place where a trip starts) and figuratively (the initial idea, situation, or baseline for a process). Common in phrases like "el punto de partida de..." (the starting point of...) and "volver al punto de partida" (to go back to square one).
target_language_example: Para mí, aprender lo básico es el punto de partida para hablar bien español.
native_language_example: For me, learning the basics is the starting point for speaking Spanish well.

additional_notes: Used to talk about someone’s opinion or the way they see/interpret a situation. Common with "desde mi/tu/su punto de vista" (from my/your/his/her point of view) and "depende del punto de vista" (it depends on the perspective).
target_language_example: Desde mi punto de vista, es mejor esperar un poco.
native_language_example: From my point of view, it’s better to wait a little.

additional_notes: Used for a person, thing, plan, or place to mean its main weakness or vulnerability. Common with "tener" (to have) and "ser" (to be): "tiene un punto débil", "es su punto débil". It can be physical (a weak point in a wall/defense) or figurative (a subject you’re bad at, or something you’re sensitive about).
target_language_example: La organización tiene un punto débil: depende de una sola persona.
native_language_example: The organization has a weak point: it depends on just one person.

additional_notes: Literally “end point.” Used for the punctuation mark (a period) in writing: "Falta el punto final." Also used figuratively to mean ending something or stopping it: "ponerle punto final a esto" = “put an end to this.” As a standalone phrase or with "y punto final," it emphasizes a firm decision: “and that’s that / end of discussion.”
target_language_example: Se acabó, y punto final.
native_language_example: It’s over, and that’s final.

meaning: strong point; strength (something you’re good at).
additional_notes: Used to talk about an advantage or the area where a person (or thing) is strongest: "X es mi/tu/su punto fuerte". It can also mean a strong/strategic position (especially in military or defensive contexts), as in "abandonamos nuestro punto fuerte".
target_language_example: Las matemáticas no son mi punto fuerte.
native_language_example: Math isn’t my strong point.

additional_notes: "Puso" is the simple past (preterite) of "poner" (to put/place). "Su" means "his/her/your/their" depending on context; here it’s usually "his" (e.g., Tom). It’s commonly followed by the thing being placed and a location phrase like "en" (in/into), "sobre" (on), or "debajo de" (under).
target_language_example: Ella puso su mochila en el suelo.
native_language_example: She put her backpack on the floor.

meaning: “Fuck!” / “Goddamn it!” (very vulgar expletive expressing anger, frustration, or surprise).
additional_notes: Often said on its own as an emotional reaction (like an interjection). It’s highly offensive/vulgar in most contexts, so avoid it in polite situations or with people you don’t know well. Note: in a different structure, **de puta madre** can mean “awesome/great,” but **puta madre** by itself is usually negative.
target_language_example: ¡Puta madre, perdí el tren!
native_language_example: Fuck, I missed the train!

additional_notes: Common everyday term for a website (often used even when referring to a whole site, not just a single page). Usually used with a possessive or de + noun: "nuestra página web", "la página web de la empresa". You may also hear "sitio web" with a similar meaning.
target_language_example: ¿Tienes la página web del hotel?
native_language_example: Do you have the hotel's website?

additional_notes: Used in a relative clause after a noun to add information about it (“…that I know”). Very common with superlatives like “el mejor/la mejor/lo mejor” or “la persona más…” to mean “the best… I know” / “the smartest person I know.” Here, “conozco” is the “I know (people/places/things)” verb form of conocer.
target_language_example: Es la ciudad más bonita que conozco.
native_language_example: It’s the most beautiful city I know.

additional_notes: Used after a noun or pronoun to mean “that exists/that there is,” often to point out what is available or what the situation is: “el mejor … que hay” = “the best … there is,” “lo único que hay es…” = “the only thing there is is…”. It’s different from the question “¿Qué hay?” (“What’s up?/What’s there?”), which includes an accent on qué and usually has question marks.
target_language_example: Es el restaurante más barato que hay en esta zona.
native_language_example: It’s the cheapest restaurant there is in this area.

additional_notes: Used after a noun (often with a superlative like el/la más…, el/la mejor…) to say someone is the most/least something in your personal experience: “the … that I’ve met.” It comes from conocer (“to meet/know someone”). You can change the verb for other people/tenses: que has conocido (you’ve met), que he visto (that I’ve seen).
target_language_example: Es el profesor más amable que he conocido.
native_language_example: He’s the kindest teacher I’ve ever met.

additional_notes: Uses the present perfect (he oído = “I’ve heard”). Very common after a superlative or similar phrase: lo más + adjective / la cosa más + adjective + que he oído = “the most … I’ve heard (in my life).” You can add emphasis with “nunca” (“ever”): que he oído nunca = “that I’ve ever heard.”
target_language_example: Es la mejor noticia que he oído en mucho tiempo.
native_language_example: It’s the best news I’ve heard in a long time.

additional_notes: Used after a noun with **que** (“that/which”) to add information about it: *el mejor trabajo que he tenido* = “the best job I’ve had.” **He tenido** is the present perfect of *tener* (“to have had”), often used for experiences up to now (sometimes with words like *hoy*, *nunca*).
target_language_example: Es el mejor restaurante que he tenido cerca de casa.
native_language_example: It’s the best restaurant I’ve had near my house.

additional_notes: Used in a relative clause to describe a noun, often after a superlative (lo más…, el/la peor…, el/la mejor…, el/la más…). It adds your personal experience: “the most/least … that I’ve seen (so far).” In Spanish you can use present perfect (he visto) even when English often prefers simple past (“that I’ve ever seen” / “that I’ve seen”).
target_language_example: Es la mejor comida que he visto en este restaurante.
native_language_example: It’s the best food I’ve seen at this restaurant.

meaning: "that we have" / "which we have" (introduces a clause about something we did).
additional_notes: Used to start a relative clause describing a noun: "el/la/los/las + noun + que hemos + past participle". Here, "hemos" is the 1st-person plural of "haber" used to form the present perfect (we have done/seen/kept, etc.), and it’s followed by a past participle (visto, guardado, trabajado, soñado...). Often translates as "that we have" or "which we have" depending on context.
target_language_example: Esta es la película que hemos visto dos veces.
native_language_example: This is the movie that we’ve seen twice.

meaning: 'that I did' / 'that I made' (past: 'I did' or 'I made').
additional_notes: Often introduces a clause describing something you did in the past, especially after a noun: ruidos que hice (noises I made), trabajos que hice (jobs/works I did), juramento/promesas que hice (oath/promises I made). It can also appear in the fixed pattern "lo que hice" = "what I did".
target_language_example: No olvides las promesas que hice.
native_language_example: Don’t forget the promises I made.

meaning: “who did” / “that did” (past tense, in a relative clause).
additional_notes: Used after a noun to identify the person/thing by an action in the past: “el hombre que hizo esto” = “the man who did this.” With neuter "lo que" it becomes "lo que hizo" = “what he/she did.”
target_language_example: La mujer que hizo la llamada ya se fue.
native_language_example: The woman who made the call already left.

additional_notes: Used after a superlative (el/la/lo más + adjective) to emphasize that something is the most extreme in your entire experience: “the ___est I’ve ever seen.” It commonly uses the present perfect subjunctive (haya visto). You’ll also hear “que nunca haya visto” with a similar meaning.
target_language_example: Es la película más extraña que jamás haya visto.
native_language_example: It’s the strangest movie I’ve ever seen.

meaning: “that I’ve ever seen” / “that I’ve never seen before.”
additional_notes: Used after a noun phrase (often with a superlative like “el/la/lo más …”) to emphasize that something is the best/most beautiful/etc. you have ever seen. “Jamás” is a stronger, more emphatic version of “nunca” (“never”).
target_language_example: Es el paisaje más impresionante que jamás he visto.
native_language_example: It’s the most impressive landscape I’ve ever seen.

meaning: "that/which ... to him/her" (relative clause using indirect object pronouns: "that/which I gave/told/paid to him/her").
additional_notes: Used in relative clauses. "que" refers to the person/thing mentioned ("that/which"), and "le" marks the indirect object (usually "to him/to her/to you (formal)"). Often appears after prepositions or expressions like "la persona a la que le...". In many cases you can think of it as English "the one that I ... to" (e.g., "los aretes que le diste" = "the earrings (that) you gave her").
target_language_example: La amiga que le presté el libro ya lo terminó.
native_language_example: The friend I lent the book to has already finished it.

additional_notes: This is not a fixed expression; it’s the relative word **que** (“that/which/who”) followed by **les** (indirect object pronoun meaning “to them” or “to you all” in Spain). It often introduces a description of a person/thing and then shows that an action is done *to/for them*: **El chico del que les hablé** = “the boy (that) I told you (all) about”; **alguien que les quiere** = “someone who loves them.”
target_language_example: Esa es la idea que les expliqué ayer.
native_language_example: That’s the idea that I explained to you (all) yesterday.

additional_notes: Used in a relative clause: "que" = "that/which/who" referring back to a person or thing mentioned just before, and "me" = "me" as an object pronoun (often meaning "to me" or "me" depending on the verb). Very common pattern: "(noun) que me + verb" (e.g., "el chico que me ayudó" = "the boy who helped me").
target_language_example: Busco un libro que me explique esto claramente.
native_language_example: I’m looking for a book that explains this clearly to me.

meaning: "that you gave me" / "which you gave me".
additional_notes: Used after a noun to introduce a relative clause describing it: "el libro que me diste" = "the book that you gave me." It’s made of: que (that/which) + me (to me) + diste (you gave, informal past of dar). Often refers to a specific item/information someone previously gave you.
target_language_example: Gracias por el consejo que me diste ayer.
native_language_example: Thanks for the advice you gave me yesterday.

additional_notes:
Used in a relative clause after words like "lo" or "todo":
- "todo lo que necesitaba" = "everything (that) I needed"
- "lo que necesitaba oír" = "what I needed to hear"
"Necesitaba" is the imperfect past of "necesitar" (I/he/she needed; used for ongoing needs in the past). The subject (I/he/she) comes from context.
target_language_example: Encontré lo que necesitaba para el viaje.
native_language_example: I found what I needed for the trip.

additional_notes: Used in relative clauses to talk about a person/thing that does NOT do something or is NOT something ("that doesn’t...", "which isn’t...", "who doesn’t..."). Often comes after a noun (e.g., "un lugar que no conozco" = "a place that I don’t know"). It can also appear after "el hecho" or similar phrases: "el hecho de que no..." = "the fact that...").
target_language_example: Busco un restaurante que no sea muy caro.
native_language_example: I’m looking for a restaurant that isn’t very expensive.

meaning: “that/which … us” or “that we …” (introduces a clause involving “us”).
additional_notes: Used when **que** (“that/which/who”) introduces a relative or subordinate clause and **nos** refers to “us.” Depending on the verb, **nos** can mean **us** (que nos vio = “who saw us”), **to us** (que nos ha pasado = “that has happened to us”), **each other** (que nos veamos = “that we see each other”), or **ourselves** (que nos hacemos = “that we ask ourselves”).
target_language_example: Es algo que nos preocupa mucho.
native_language_example: It’s something that worries us a lot.

additional_notes: Usually appears in a relative clause. pueda is the present subjunctive of poder, so this often refers to someone or something that is able to do something, or to something possible or not yet certain. Depending on context, it can also mean 'that I can' or, with lo que, 'what may/might'.
target_language_example: Necesitamos a alguien que pueda venir mañana.
native_language_example: We need someone who can come tomorrow.

meaning: “(that) I/he/she/you want(s)” / “as much as (someone) want(s)” (subjunctive of querer).
additional_notes: Used after a noun or expression like "todo", "lo", "el tiempo", "los/las + noun" to mean "whatever/whichever/as much as someone wants". It’s common in relative clauses: "todo lo que quiera" (anything you want), "el que quiera" (whoever wants), "el tiempo que quiera" (as long as you want). In these patterns, Spanish uses the present subjunctive "quiera" because the person/thing is not specific or is open-ended.
target_language_example: Puedes quedarte el tiempo que quieras.
native_language_example: You can stay as long as you want.

additional_notes: Usually follows a noun or pronoun: el que quieras, la que quieras, lo que quieras, algo que quieras. It often refers to an unknown or freely chosen thing, so Spanish uses the subjunctive quieras. Depending on context, it can mean 'that you want,' 'whatever you want,' or 'whichever ... you want.'
target_language_example: Puedes pedir lo que quieras.
native_language_example: You can order whatever you want.

additional_notes: Used to introduce a relative clause with **que** (“who/that/which”) + **quiere** (3rd person singular of *querer*, “to want”). It describes a person or thing: *una señora que quiere hablar contigo* (“a woman who wants to talk to you”), *lo que quiere la gente* (“what people want”). It can refer to he/she/it (and sometimes a singular formal “you,” *usted*). For plural, use **que quieren**.
target_language_example: Tengo un amigo que quiere aprender español.
native_language_example: I have a friend who wants to learn Spanish.

additional_notes: Often appears in relative clauses: **que** = “that/which/who” + **se** marking a reflexive/reciprocal action (**se llama** = “is called”), or an impersonal/passive idea (**se destruyeron** = “were destroyed”). It’s not usually a fixed phrase by itself; the meaning depends on the verb that follows.
target_language_example: Es la única canción que se escucha en todas partes.
native_language_example: It’s the only song that is heard everywhere.

additional_notes: "que" introduces a relative clause ("who/that/which"), and "te" is the object pronoun meaning "you" (often "to you" or "you" depending on the verb). It commonly appears after a noun: "la mujer que te dio..." = "the woman who gave you...". Also in fixed patterns like "lo que te..." = "what ... you / what ... to you" (e.g., "Eso es lo que te preocupa" = "That's what worries you").
target_language_example: Conoce a alguien que te pueda ayudar.
native_language_example: Meet someone who can help you.

additional_notes: Used after expressions that trigger the subjunctive, especially when talking about what you want, prefer, recommend, or need someone to like. It comes from the verb “gustar,” which is usually phrased like “to be pleasing to” (e.g., “Me gusta…” = “I like…”). Here, “te” = “to you,” and “guste” is the subjunctive form.
target_language_example: Quiero que te guste este libro.
native_language_example: I want you to like this book.

additional_notes: Used after a noun to add a relative clause describing what you have: "el único amigo que tengo" (the only friend I have), "las armas que tengo" (the weapons I have). Often appears with "único/a(s)" or "lo que": "Es todo lo que tengo" (It’s all I have). Word order can change for emphasis: "la misma raqueta que tengo yo" = "the same racket that I have" (yo is added to stress who has it).
target_language_example: Estos son los únicos zapatos que tengo.
native_language_example: These are the only shoes I have.

additional_notes: Used in a relative clause: **que** = “that/which” + **tenía** (imperfect of *tener*) = “had/used to have.” The subject is understood from context (yo, él/ella, etc.). Often refers back to something mentioned before: *lo único que tenía* (“the only thing I had”), *la otra que tenía* (“the other one I had”).
target_language_example: Esta es la única foto que tenía en mi teléfono.
native_language_example: This is the only photo I had on my phone.

additional_notes: Used with the relative pronoun "que" to describe a person or thing: "el/la que tiene..." = "the one who has..." and "(algo) que tiene..." = "something that has...". The verb is "tener" (to have) in the "él/ella/usted" form: "tiene". It can also be used in expressions like "para la edad que tiene" = "for the age (that) she/he is".
target_language_example: El chico que tiene el celular es mi hermano.
native_language_example: The boy who has the cellphone is my brother.

additional_notes: Usually used with the verb "tener": "tener que ver con..." = "to have to do with / be related to...". Very common in questions and negatives: "¿Qué tiene que ver con el... ?" (What does it have to do with the...?), "No tiene nada que ver con el..." (It has nothing to do with the...). The "el" changes with the noun: con el (masc.), con la (fem.), con los/las (plural).
target_language_example: Eso no tiene nada que ver con el problema.
native_language_example: That has nothing to do with the problem.

additional_notes: Used after a noun to add information about where a person/animal/thing lives. It introduces a relative clause with que (“who/that”): mi tío que vive en Osaka (“my uncle who lives in Osaka”).
target_language_example: Conozco a una chica que vive en Madrid.
native_language_example: I know a girl who lives in Madrid.

additional_notes: Used in relative clauses after a noun or pronoun to specify something about yourself (yo). Very often it’s just emphasizing the subject (“I”), and in many cases Spanish can also drop it (e.g., “algo que pueda hacer”). Common patterns: “algo que yo pueda hacer” = “something (that) I can do”; “el/la único/a que yo…” = “the only one (that) I…”.
target_language_example: No hay nada que yo pueda decir para cambiar tu decisión.
native_language_example: There’s nothing that I can say to change your decision.

additional_notes: A common religious well-wish used when saying goodbye, wishing someone luck, or showing affection/care. Literally means “(may it be) that God bless you,” using the subjunctive (bendiga) to express a wish. Often followed by a term of endearment like cariño (dear), hermano (brother), or hijo (son).
target_language_example: Cuídate mucho y que Dios te bendiga.
native_language_example: Take good care of yourself, and may God bless you.

additional_notes: Often introduces a clause where you want/ask/need someone to do something: "que alguien + verb" (usually in the subjunctive), like "Que alguien llame..." = "Someone call..." / "Can someone call...?". It can also appear after another "que" (e.g., "quiero que alguien..."). In statements like "por supuesto que alguien...", "que" is an emphatic connector and the verb is not necessarily subjunctive.
target_language_example: Necesito que alguien me ayude con esta tarea.
native_language_example: I need someone to help me with this task.

meaning: “that you trust me” / “for you to trust me.”
additional_notes: Used after verbs like necesito/quiero/te pido to introduce what you want the other person to do. confíes is the present subjunctive of confiar (used after expressions of desire, need, or requests). en mí means “in me” → “trust me.”
target_language_example: Solo te pido que confíes en mí un poco más.
native_language_example: I’m only asking you to trust me a little more.

additional_notes: Used to make something clear and officially/explicitly stated. Often appears as: (1) “Que conste que + clause” to emphasize a point (sometimes as a warning or clarification): “Que conste que te lo dije.” (2) “Para que conste (en acta)” in formal/legal contexts meaning “so that it is put on record,” e.g., in meetings, documents, or testimony.
target_language_example: Que conste que no estoy de acuerdo con esa decisión.
native_language_example: For the record, I don’t agree with that decision.

meaning: 'to have to choose between' (used after verbs like tener/haber).
additional_notes: Most often appears in phrases like “tener que elegir entre A y B” or “hay que elegir entre A y B.” Here, “que” introduces an obligation (“have to”), “elegir” means “to choose,” and “entre” is “between.” Use “entre” + two options joined by “y/e.”
target_language_example: Tengo que elegir entre quedarme en casa o salir con mis amigos.
native_language_example: I have to choose between staying home or going out with my friends.

additional_notes: A compositional phrase made of que + ella. Most often it means “that she” when introducing a clause: Me dijo que ella venía = “He told me that she was coming.” In comparisons, que ella can also mean “than/as her” or more naturally “than/as she does,” depending on the full sentence.
target_language_example: Creo que ella no sabe la respuesta.
native_language_example: I think that she doesn't know the answer.

additional_notes: This chunk usually appears as part of a bigger phrase like “hay que encontrar a …” (we have to find …) or “tengo que encontrar a …” (I have to find …). The “a” is the personal a: it’s used before a direct object that is a specific person (e.g., “encontrar a Marta” = to find Marta).
target_language_example: Tengo que encontrar a mi hermano antes de las seis.
native_language_example: I have to find my brother before six.

additional_notes: Used after verbs like decir (to say), saber (to know), pensar (to think), ver (to see), reconocer (to recognize), confesar (to confess) to introduce reported information or a fact. It’s the conjunction que (“that”) + the imperfect of ser, era (“was/used to be”). Often describes identity or a state in the past, or sets background (e.g., “I recognized … that he was American”).
target_language_example: Sabía que era tarde, pero no quería irme.
native_language_example: I knew it was late, but I didn’t want to leave.

meaning: "that you are" (introduces a clause saying what someone is).
additional_notes: Used after verbs/expressions like saber (to know), decir (to say/tell), confirmar (to confirm), ver (to see), recordar (to remember): e.g., “Sé que eres…” = “I know (that) you are…”. In English, “that” is often optional, but in Spanish “que” is typically required. Note: with some expressions you may see the subjunctive “que seas” instead of “que eres” (e.g., “No es que seas…”).
target_language_example: Sé que eres una buena persona.
native_language_example: I know you’re a good person.

additional_notes: Used after a comparison (often with mejor/peor = “better/worse”) to introduce an action in the infinitive: mejor/peor + que + infinitive. Example: “Es mejor irse que esperar” = “It’s better to leave than to wait.”
target_language_example: Es mejor salir ahora que esperar más.
native_language_example: It’s better to leave now than to wait longer.

additional_notes: Used when a clause introduced by **que** needs the **subjunctive** of *estar* (**esté**)—often after expressions of feelings/opinions or evaluation (**Lástima que…**, **Entiendo que…**), negation/doubt (**No digo que…**), or with time expressions like **hasta que** (“until”) when the action is not yet completed (**hasta que esté listo**). It refers to a temporary state/location (the meanings of *estar*).
target_language_example: Me alegra que esté aquí contigo.
native_language_example: I’m happy that he/she is here with you.

additional_notes: Used with "que" to introduce a clause where Spanish typically requires the subjunctive ("esté"): after expressions of emotion/opinion (Me alegra que esté aquí), wishes/hope (Espero que esté ahí), necessity/commands, and some time/condition phrases (Espera hasta que esté a bordo). It often implies uncertainty, a wish, or a subjective reaction rather than stating a fact.
target_language_example: Espero que esté en casa ahora.
native_language_example: I hope he/she is at home now.

meaning: "that you are" / "for you to be" (subjunctive of estar).
additional_notes: Used after expressions that trigger the subjunctive (que + estés), especially to talk about a desired, necessary, uncertain, or hypothetical state. Common patterns: "Es importante que estés..." (It’s important that you be...), "Quiero que estés..." (I want you to be...), "Será mejor que estés..." (You’d better be...), and "Para que estés..." (So that you are...). "Estés" is the tú present subjunctive of "estar" (to be, temporary/state).
target_language_example: Quiero que estés aquí a las ocho.
native_language_example: I want you to be here at eight.

additional_notes: Used after verbs/expressions that trigger the subjunctive (doubt, wanting, insisting, being surprised, opposing, etc.). It introduces a subordinate clause: que + fuera (imperfect subjunctive of ir) + al (= a + el, “to the” + masculine singular place). Often translates as “that he/she go” (requested/expected) or “that he/she went” (reported/uncertain) depending on context and tense sequence.
target_language_example: El jefe pidió que fuera al despacho a primera hora.
native_language_example: The boss asked that I go to the office first thing.

additional_notes: Used after expressions like antes de que, para que, parecer que, pedir/aconsejar que, sorprendería que, nunca pensamos que, decidir que. It introduces a clause in the imperfect subjunctive (fuera from ser/ir). It often refers to: (1) a past/hypothetical situation: Me sorprendería que fuera culpable. (2) a goal/purpose: Lo hizo para que fuera… (3) a request/advice: Me pidió que fuera más atento. With antes de que, it commonly means “before it became…”.
target_language_example: Me pidió que fuera temprano a la reunión.
native_language_example: He asked me to be early to the meeting.

additional_notes: Used with the subjunctive (funcione) after expressions like "hacer que..." (to make/cause ... to happen) and often after verbs of perception or doubt when what you perceive/expect isn’t confirmed. Common with things like devices, plans, relationships, or systems: "No creo que funcione" (I don’t think it works), "Haz que funcione" (Make it work).
target_language_example: Necesitamos que funcione antes de mañana.
native_language_example: We need it to work before tomorrow.

meaning: not a standard Spanish expression; possibly intended as ¿qué hay? ('what's up?' / 'what is there?')
additional_notes: As written, que haber is not a normal surface form in Spanish. It appears to be a citation-form or mistaken combination of que and haber. Learners often mean ¿qué hay?, where hay is a conjugated form of haber. Because the requested term is nonstandard, the example below mentions the exact string rather than using it as a natural phrase.
target_language_example: La secuencia "que haber" no es una expresión idiomática en español.
native_language_example: The sequence "que haber" is not an idiomatic expression in Spanish.

meaning: “to do it” (usually after tener que: “have to do it”).
additional_notes: Most commonly appears as part of the expression **tener que + infinitive** (“to have to / must”). Here, **hacerlo** = “to do it” (hacer + lo). With **no** in front, it means you *don’t* have to do it: **No tengo que hacerlo** = “I don’t have to do it.”
target_language_example: No tienes que hacerlo hoy.
native_language_example: You don’t have to do it today.

additional_notes: Used to introduce an action someone wants, tells, allows, or requires another person to do. It’s very often part of patterns like: querer que haga (to want [me/him/her] to do), decirle que haga (to tell [someone] to do), dejarme que haga (to let me do), sin importar lo que ... que haga (no matter what ... [I] do), and siempre que haga... (as long as [he] does...). The verb is in the present subjunctive: haga = “(that) I/he/she do.”
target_language_example: Mi jefe quiere que haga el informe hoy.
native_language_example: My boss wants me to do the report today.

additional_notes: This is a subjunctive clause (hagas) used after expressions like querer, pedir, necesitar, or es importante, when one person wants/asks another person to do something. Often appears as part of a longer sentence: “Quiero/Puedo pedirte que hagas algo por mí…”. The pronoun “mí” (with accent) means “me” after a preposition like por/para.
target_language_example: ¿Puedo pedirte que hagas algo por mí?
native_language_example: Can I ask you to do something for me?

additional_notes: Used after expressions that trigger the subjunctive (e.g., hope, doubt, feelings, luck): "Esperamos que...", "Me alegra que...", "Es posible que...". Very often it’s followed by a past participle to form the present perfect subjunctive: "que haya tenido" = "that (someone) has had", "que haya pasado" = "that (someone) has passed". It can also mean "that there is/are" (existence): "No creo que haya tiempo" = "I don’t think there’s time."
target_language_example: Me alegra que haya venido hoy.
native_language_example: I’m glad you came today. / I’m glad that you’ve come today.

additional_notes: Used to introduce a clause with the subjunctive after expressions like: es normal que..., espero que..., no puedo creer que..., quieren que.... It often means “that there be…” or “that there is/are…,” usually expressing desire, possibility, doubt, or reaction rather than stating a fact. “Haya” is the present subjunctive of “haber” used impersonally (like English “there is/are”).
target_language_example: Me alegra que haya más opciones.
native_language_example: I’m glad there are more options.

meaning: “that you came / that you have come” (used after expressions of feelings or thanks).
additional_notes: This is the present perfect subjunctive of “venir” (hayas venido). It commonly follows phrases like “me alegro…”, “estoy feliz…”, “aprecio…”, “te agradezco…”, and “qué bueno/gusto…”, expressing a reaction (happiness, gratitude, etc.) to the fact that someone came. Often translated naturally as “that you came” in English, even though Spanish uses a perfect tense.
target_language_example: Me alegro mucho de que hayas venido hoy.
native_language_example: I’m really glad you came today.

additional_notes: Used with "que" to introduce a subordinate clause in the imperfect subjunctive of "hacer" (hiciera). Common after expressions of doubt/opinion/emotion (e.g., "Es increíble que...") and after requests/orders (e.g., "Me pidieron que..."). Often refers to an action that was expected, requested, or viewed subjectively (not stated as a simple fact).
target_language_example: No quería que hiciera tanto ruido.
native_language_example: I didn’t want him/her to make so much noise.

meaning: “(to) have to go to the …” (used after verbs like *tener* or *hay*).
additional_notes: This chunk is most commonly part of **tener que ir a la + place** (“to have to go to the + place”) or **hay que ir a la + place** (“you/we have to go to the + place”). *A la* = *a + la* (“to the”, feminine singular). For masculine places, use **ir al** (*a + el*): *Tengo que ir al banco.*
target_language_example: Tengo que ir a la farmacia.
native_language_example: I have to go to the pharmacy.

meaning: "that people…" / "that the people…" (introduces a clause about what people do or feel).
additional_notes: Used with **que** to introduce a subordinate clause, often after verbs/expressions like *decir* (to say), *esperar* (to hope/expect), *hacer* (to make), *poner nervioso* (to make nervous): *Espero que la gente…*, *Me pone nervioso que la gente…*, *Hacer que la gente…*. It can also start a sentence for emphasis or as a wish/command, in which case Spanish typically uses the **subjunctive**: *¡Que la gente sea respetuosa!* (“May people be respectful!”).
target_language_example: Me alegra que la gente venga a ayudarnos.
native_language_example: I'm glad that people come to help us.

additional_notes: Used after comparisons with "más/menos... que" ("bigger than yours") or sameness with "la misma... que" ("the same as yours"). "La tuya" refers back to a feminine singular noun already mentioned (e.g., la cámara, la habitación, la opinión). You can swap the article and possessive to match gender/number: "que el tuyo" (masc. sing.), "que las tuyas" (fem. pl.), "que los tuyos" (masc. pl.).
target_language_example: Mi mochila es más pesada que la tuya.
native_language_example: My backpack is heavier than yours.

meaning: “that + her/it (feminine)” (introduces a clause where **la** is the object).
additional_notes: **Que** often means “that” after verbs like *prometer, decir, querer, encargarse de* and introduces a subordinate clause. **La** is a direct object pronoun meaning “her” or “it” (for a feminine noun). Together, **que la + verb** commonly translates to “that I/you/he/she… + her/it + verb”: *Dijo que la conocía* = “He said (that) he knew her.” Word order: **la** normally goes right before the conjugated verb (*que la conoces*), or before the auxiliary in compound tenses (*que la había conocido*).
target_language_example: Te llamo para asegurarme de que la entiendes.
native_language_example: I’m calling to make sure you understand it (her).

additional_notes: Used to introduce a subordinate clause about how things are, happen, or should be. Often follows verbs/expressions like "ver" (to see), "gustar" (to like), "dar a entender" (to imply), and "hacer que" (to make/ensure that). The verb that follows can change tense: "que las cosas van..." (things are going...), "que las cosas sean..." (that things be...), etc.
target_language_example: Quiero que las cosas salgan bien.
native_language_example: I want things to go well.

meaning: that ... to/for him, her, or you (formal)
additional_notes: Not a fixed idiom, but a very common combination. que usually introduces a following clause ('that'), and le is an object pronoun meaning 'to/for him, her, or you (formal)'. After verbs like decir, pedir, querer, aconsejar, or expressions like está bien que, English often drops 'that' or changes the word order. In some varieties, especially in Spain, le can also mean 'him' as a direct object (for example, que le quiere = 'that she loves him').
target_language_example: Quiero que le compres un regalo.
native_language_example: I want you to buy him/her a gift.

additional_notes: Not a fixed expression. Here, que usually introduces a subordinate clause ('that'), and lo is usually a direct object pronoun meaning 'it' or 'him' before the next verb: que lo prueben = 'that they try it', que lo habían encarcelado = 'that they had imprisoned him'. In sequences like que lo que..., lo may instead belong to lo que ('what' / 'that which').
target_language_example: Creo que lo entienden.
native_language_example: I think they understand it.

additional_notes: Uses the present subjunctive of hacer (haga) after verbs like dejar (let), querer (want), decir (tell), or hacer (make). “Lo” means “it,” and “que” often translates as “that.” The subject is understood from context: que lo haga yo = “that I do it,” que lo haga él/ella = “that he/she do it.”
target_language_example: ¿Quieres que lo haga ahora o más tarde?
native_language_example: Do you want me to do it now or later?

additional_notes: Used after expressions like creo que, quieren que, me alegro de que, no dejaré que to talk about someone doing something, often expressing desire, emotion, permission, or prevention. Lo = “it” (a thing already known); hagas is the tú present subjunctive of hacer. Often follows another verb: “Quieren que lo hagas” = “They want you to do it.”
target_language_example: Es importante que lo hagas hoy.
native_language_example: It’s important that you do it today.

meaning: “that he/she do it” (subjunctive), referring to some previously mentioned action.
additional_notes: Used in a dependent clause after verbs/expressions like ordenar (to order), querer (to want), decir (to tell), pedir (to ask), etc. “Lo” means “it” (the thing/action already understood). “Hiciera” is the imperfect subjunctive of hacer, often used because the main verb is in the past (e.g., quería/ordenó/dijo) or conditional (habría querido).
target_language_example: Mi mamá quería que lo hiciera hoy.
native_language_example: My mom wanted me to do it today.

meaning: "that what" / "that which" (introduces what someone said, knew, heard, etc.).
additional_notes: This is the sequence **que + lo que**. It often appears after verbs like *demostrar, admitir, decir, contar, saber, oír* to introduce a clause meaning “what …”. In English you usually translate it as **“that what …”** or more naturally just **“what …”** (e.g., *Admitió que lo que dije era verdad* = “He admitted that what I said was true.”).
target_language_example: Ella explicó que lo que necesitaba era más tiempo.
native_language_example: She explained that what she needed was more time.

meaning: “than others / than everyone else” or “that others …” (depending on context).
additional_notes: “Los demás” means “the others / everyone else.” With “más/menos … que los demás,” it’s used for comparisons (“… than others”). With verbs like “querer/esperar/pedir + que …,” it introduces a clause: “(I want/expect/ask) that others …”.
target_language_example: No quiero ser mejor que los demás; solo quiero mejorar cada día.
native_language_example: I don’t want to be better than others; I just want to improve every day.

additional_notes: Used to introduce a clause where the verb takes a masculine plural direct object pronoun (los = “them/it,” referring to masculine plural nouns or a mixed group, or to plural masculine things like documentos, ojos, etc.). Very common after verbs of saying/asking/ordering/wanting/expecting (e.g., decir, ordenar, querer, necesitar, esperar) and in expressions like “hasta que…”. In commands and recommendations you may see the order flipped: “Que los…” (roughly “Have them…” / “Let them…”).
target_language_example: Necesito que los termines hoy.
native_language_example: I need you to finish them today.

additional_notes: Not a fixed expression: it is simply que + me. It introduces a clause involving me. With reflexive verbs, English often translates it as 'that I ...' (for example, que me siento = 'that I feel'); with other verbs, it can mean 'that ... me' (for example, que me llaman = 'that they call me').
target_language_example: Sé que me conoces.
native_language_example: I know you know me.

additional_notes: Used after verbs like decirle, pedirle, or rogarle to report a request: “Tell/ask him/her to call me.” It’s the present subjunctive (llame) because it’s something you want someone else to do. Often appears with an implied subject (“él/ella”) and can also be used by itself as a demand: “Have him call me!”
target_language_example: Por favor, dile que me llame cuando tenga un momento.
native_language_example: Please tell him to call me when he has a moment.

additional_notes: Literally “that they kill me,” using *que* + subjunctive (*maten*). You’ll often hear it as a dramatic exclamation of frustration, embarrassment, or disbelief: *¡Que me maten!* (“Just kill me!”). It can also appear after words like *antes de* or *para que*: *antes de que me maten* (“before they kill me”).
target_language_example: ¡Que me maten! Se me olvidó su nombre otra vez.
native_language_example: Kill me. I forgot his name again.

additional_notes: Often appears in clauses that use the subjunctive after expressions like "es interesante que..." or "no se permite que...": "que nadie" = “that nobody” (i.e., no person). Also common after "sin": "sin que nadie..." = “without anyone...” (typically with the subjunctive). In comparisons with "más/menos", it means “than anyone (else)”: "más que nadie" = “more than anyone.”
target_language_example: Cerró la puerta sin que nadie lo viera.
native_language_example: He closed the door without anyone seeing him.

additional_notes: Used to introduce a negative clause: dijo que no venía = 'he said that he wasn't coming.' After verbs like decir or contestar, it can also mean simply 'no' (dijo que no = 'he said no'). In expressions like hace mucho que no..., it means 'for/since someone hasn't ...'.
target_language_example: Ella dice que no quiere café.
native_language_example: She says she doesn't want coffee.

additional_notes: Used after verbs like decir (to say/tell), saber (to know), asegurarse (to make sure), etc., to introduce a clause where the subject is someone else and the object is "me": e.g., "Dile que no me llame" = "Tell him/her not to call me." The verb that follows changes to match the subject (no me busca, no me seguían, no me casaré, etc.).
target_language_example: Te pido que no me interrumpas.
native_language_example: I’m asking you not to interrupt me.

meaning: "that we don't / that doesn't (happen) to us" (introduces a clause with "we/us" + negation).
additional_notes: This is a common sequence, not a fixed idiom: **que** introduces a subordinate clause (“that…”), **no** negates it, and **nos** refers to “us” (often as the object, or reflexive “each other” with verbs like *vernos* / *hablarnos*). Examples: *Es preferible que no nos veamos más* (“It’s better that we don’t see each other anymore”), *Hace años que no nos hablamos* (“We haven’t spoken to each other in years”). Word order is typically **que + no + pronoun + verb**.
target_language_example: Me preocupa que no nos entiendan.
native_language_example: I'm worried that they won't understand us.

additional_notes: Used to introduce a negative clause (often with the subjunctive) after expressions like cuidado, dile, asegúrate, etc. The "se" is commonly part of a reflexive verb (e.g., caerse, olvidarse) or a passive/impersonal construction. It’s often followed by pronouns like te/le/lo: "que no se te caiga" = “so you don’t drop it / so it doesn’t fall on you.”
target_language_example: Asegúrate de cerrar la puerta, que no se quede abierta.
native_language_example: Make sure you close the door so it doesn’t stay open.

additional_notes: Used after verbs of hoping/wishing like (espero/esperamos/esperemos) to express concern that something will happen in time. It uses the present subjunctive (sea) because it refers to something uncertain. Often appears as: “Espero que no sea demasiado tarde.”
target_language_example: Date prisa; espero que no sea demasiado tarde.
native_language_example: Hurry up; I hope it’s not too late.

meaning: 'that you don’t…' / 'so that they don’t… (to) you'.
additional_notes: This is a common sequence, not a fixed idiom: **que** introduces a clause (“that/so that”), **no** makes it negative, and **te** is the informal singular object pronoun (“you”). The verb that follows changes depending on meaning and subject: *que no te diga* (“that he/she doesn’t tell you”), *que no te vean* (“so they don’t see you”), *que no te cogen* (“they won’t catch you”). Often after phrases like **me dijo que…** (he told me that…), **para que…** (so that…), or **cuidar(se) de que…** (to make sure that…).
target_language_example: Asegúrate de que no te vean aquí.
native_language_example: Make sure they don’t see you here.

additional_notes: Used very often after verbs like hacer, decir, pedir, querer, necesitar, encantar, etc., to introduce what happens to/for “us.” The pronoun “nos” can mean “us” as a direct object (“make us…”) or indirect object (“tell us… / accept us…”), depending on the verb. Word order in English usually changes (you don’t normally say “that us”).
target_language_example: Necesito que nos ayudes con la tarea.
native_language_example: I need you to help us with the homework.

additional_notes: Most commonly used in comparisons with "más" (or other comparatives) to mean "than ever": "más ... que nunca" = "more ... than ever". It can also introduce a clause meaning "that ... never" after verbs like "apostar", "decir", "prometer", "parecer": "Apuesto que nunca..." = "I bet you never...". Note: "que nunca" is different from "nunca" by itself; "que" here usually links to what was said/thought/promised, or it completes a comparison.
target_language_example: Hoy me siento más cansado que nunca.
native_language_example: Today I feel more tired than ever.

additional_notes: "Pase" is the present subjunctive (and also the formal usted command) of pasar.
