target_language_example: Sus padres no están en casa ahora.
native_language_example: His/Her/Their parents aren’t home right now.

additional_notes: “Sus” is a possessive that can mean “his,” “her,” “their,” or formal “your,” so the meaning depends on context. Often used when talking about what someone said and its effect; in phrases like “Sus palabras se hicieron realidad,” it means what they said came true.
target_language_example: No olvidé sus palabras.
native_language_example: I didn’t forget his/her/their words.

meaning: their legs / your (plural, formal) legs / his/her legs.
additional_notes: "Sus" is a possessive that can mean "his," "her," "their," or "your" (plural "ustedes" or formal "usted"), depending on context. It’s usually clarified by the verb form or by adding: "las piernas de él/de ella/de ellos" if needed.
target_language_example: Después de correr, sus piernas estaban muy cansadas.
native_language_example: After running, their legs were very tired.

additional_notes: “Sus” is a possessive that can mean “his,” “her,” “your (formal),” or “their,” so the context tells you whose plans they are. “Planes” are intentions or arrangements (often for the future), like travel plans or what someone is going to do.
target_language_example: No entiendo cuáles son sus planes para este fin de semana.
native_language_example: I don’t understand what his/her/their plans are for this weekend.

additional_notes: “Sus” can mean “his,” “her,” “your (formal),” or “their,” depending on context. With “problemas,” it refers to the difficulties or personal issues belonging to someone else (or to the person you’re addressing formally).
target_language_example: No puedo resolver sus problemas, pero puedo escucharte.
native_language_example: I can’t solve your problems, but I can listen to you.

additional_notes: Uses the possessive adjective “sus” (for él/ella/ellos/ellas/usted/ustedes) + plural noun “promesas.” Often appears with verbs like “romper sus promesas” (to break his/her/their promises) and “cumplir con sus promesas” (to keep/fulfill his/her/their promises). Context tells you whose promises they are.
target_language_example: No confío en él porque siempre rompe sus promesas.
native_language_example: I don’t trust him because he always breaks his promises.

additional_notes: Used with a possessive (sus) + propio/a(s) to emphasize that something belongs to the subject (not someone else’s). It must agree with the noun: sus propios (masc. plural), sus propia (fem. singular), sus propio (masc. singular). Often used with things like mentiras, experiencias, capacidades, deudas, etc.
target_language_example: Cada uno debe aprender de sus propias experiencias.
native_language_example: Everyone has to learn from their own experiences.

meaning: "their/his/her own" (emphasizes that something belongs to them).
additional_notes: Used before a noun to stress that the thing is someone’s own (not shared or someone else’s): sus propios errores/ problemas/ sentimientos. It agrees with the noun: propios (masc. plural), propias (fem. plural). For singular: su propio / su propia. Often appears with body parts too: sus propios pies = “his own feet.”
target_language_example: Cada uno debe traer sus propios materiales.
native_language_example: Each person must bring their own materials.

additional_notes: "Sus" is a possessive that can mean "his," "her," "their," or "your" (formal, singular: usted). "Sentimientos" are feelings/emotions, often deeper or more personal; common in phrases like "herir sus sentimientos" (to hurt their feelings), "ocultar sus sentimientos" (to hide their feelings), and "expresar sus sentimientos" (to express their feelings).
target_language_example: No quiero herir sus sentimientos.
native_language_example: I don't want to hurt their feelings.

additional_notes: “Sus” is a possessive that can mean “his/her/its/their/your (formal).” In context, “sus vidas” usually means “their lives,” but it can also mean “your lives” when talking to someone with usted/ustedes. It’s used both literally (saving/escaping with their lives) and figuratively ("la oportunidad de sus vidas" = the opportunity of a lifetime; "mejorar sus vidas" = improve their lives).
target_language_example: Tienen que proteger sus vidas.
native_language_example: They have to protect their lives.

additional_notes: “Sus” is a possessive adjective that changes with the thing owned, not with the owner: sus + plural noun (zapatos). It can mean “his,” “her,” “their,” or “your” (usted/ustedes), so context clarifies who the owner is. Often used with prepositions: “para sus zapatos” (for his/her/their shoes), “con sus zapatos” (with his/her/their shoes).
target_language_example: No encuentro sus zapatos por ninguna parte.
native_language_example: I can't find his/her/their shoes anywhere.

meaning: “I know what you mean / what you’re referring to.”
additional_notes: Used to show you understand someone’s point or reference. Very common with “ya” for emphasis (“Ya sé a qué te refieres” = “I know what you mean”). Often appears in the negative: “No sé a qué te refieres” (“I don’t know what you mean”). Neutral register.
target_language_example: Sí, sé a qué te refieres, pero no estoy de acuerdo.
native_language_example: Yes, I know what you mean, but I don’t agree.

meaning: "I know how" / "I know what it’s like".
additional_notes: Used with the verb *saber* (yo: *sé*) + *cómo* to say you know the way something is/works/happened (*Sé cómo llegaron* = “I know how they got here”). It can also mean you understand someone’s experience or feelings (*Sé cómo te sientes* = “I know how you feel”). Often followed by a verb or by *es/son*.
target_language_example: Sé cómo hacerlo, no te preocupes.
native_language_example: I know how to do it, don’t worry.

meaning: "I know exactly" (used to emphasize you understand precisely).
additional_notes: Uses the verb "sé" (from "saber") for knowing facts or understanding something clearly. It’s often followed by "lo que..." or "de lo que..." ("what..." / "what...about") to specify what you know exactly.
target_language_example: Sé exactamente dónde está la llave.
native_language_example: I know exactly where the key is.

meaning: "I know what it is" / "I know what it’s like."
additional_notes: Used to say you can identify something (an object, a smell, a situation): “I know what that is.” It can also mean you have personal experience with something: “I know what it’s like to…”. The word “lo” refers to “it/that” (the thing or situation you’re talking about). Often appears as “Sé lo que es eso/esto” (I know what that is/this is).
target_language_example: Tranquilo, sé lo que es perder un trabajo.
native_language_example: Don’t worry, I know what it’s like to lose a job.

meaning: I know what’s happening (what’s going on).
additional_notes: Used to say you understand the situation. Often appears with or without a place word like “aquí” (here). The negative version is “no sé lo que está pasando” = “I don’t know what’s happening.” In conversation you may also hear “Sé lo que pasa,” which is slightly shorter but very similar.
target_language_example: Tranquilo, sé lo que está pasando y lo voy a arreglar.
native_language_example: Don’t worry, I know what’s happening and I’m going to fix it.

meaning: "I know very well" / "I know perfectly well."
additional_notes: Used to emphasize that you know something clearly or for sure. Often followed by a question word or clause: "sé muy bien quién..." (I know very well who...), "sé muy bien lo que..." (I know very well what...). It can sound firm or defensive depending on tone.
target_language_example: No te preocupes: sé muy bien cómo llegar allí.
native_language_example: Don’t worry: I know very well how to get there.

additional_notes: Used to introduce something the speaker knows to be true. sé is the first-person singular of saber ("to know"), and que introduces the following clause. In English, "that" is often omitted: "I know ..."
target_language_example: Sé que mañana será un día largo.
native_language_example: I know that tomorrow will be a long day.

meaning: "I know that I know nothing." (I admit I don't really know.)
additional_notes: A well-known philosophical quote (often attributed to Socrates) expressing humility: you recognize your own ignorance or lack of certainty. In everyday speech it can be used seriously or jokingly to mean “I have no idea” or “I’m not sure about anything here.” Often appears as “Solo/Sólo sé que no sé nada.”
target_language_example: Con este tema me pierdo; solo sé que no sé nada.
native_language_example: I’m lost on this topic; I only know that I know nothing.

additional_notes: Imperative form of ser (sé) + amable (“kind”) + con (“to/with”). Used to tell one person informally (tú) to treat someone nicely: Sé amable con él/ella/los demás. For a formal command (usted), use: Sea amable con…
target_language_example: Por favor, sé amable con tu hermano.
native_language_example: Please, be kind to your brother.

additional_notes: Used to partially agree and then add a reservation, correction, or opposing idea. Often sets up a contrast between two people/things ("Él sí, pero ella…") or between what you might think and what’s likely true ("Podría pensar que sí, pero…"). In speech it can sound like hedging or backtracking: "Pues sí, pero…".
target_language_example: Sí, pero no tengo tiempo ahora.
native_language_example: Yes, but I don’t have time right now.

additional_notes: Used to add strong emphasis to what you’re saying (often like “really/indeed/actually” in English). Common when confirming something strongly, showing surprise, or contradicting an expectation (e.g., “Pues sí que…” = “Well, it really is…”). It often goes before the verb (Sí que lo entiendo) or in the pattern “X sí que…” to highlight X (Ese sí que es un buen truco).
target_language_example: Esa película sí que da miedo.
native_language_example: That movie is really scary.

additional_notes: Used with **ser/estar** to strongly confirm or contradict what was said before (similar to “I sure am,” “yes, I am,” “he really was”). **Lo** refers back to the idea/adjective/state already mentioned (e.g., listo, cansado, culpable). Word order is fixed: **Sí que lo + soy/eres/es/fui/era/estoy/estaba**, etc.
target_language_example: —¿Estás cansado? —Sí que lo estoy.
native_language_example: —Are you tired? —I sure am.

meaning: “Yes, that’s how it is / yes, like that.”
additional_notes: Used to agree with someone and confirm the way something is/was/should be (“that’s right”, “exactly like that”). Often followed by verbs like ser/estar (“Sí, así es/está”) or by a pronoun (“Sí, así lo creo” = “Yes, that’s what I think”).
target_language_example: —¿Lo dejamos así? —Sí, así está perfecto.
native_language_example: “Should we leave it like this?” “Yes, like that it’s perfect.”

meaning: "yeah, well…" (a hesitant/softening reply; sometimes mildly dismissive).
additional_notes: Used at the start of an answer to pause, soften what you’re about to say, or show you’re not fully agreeing. It can introduce a counterpoint (often followed by "pero"), an excuse, or a reluctant acceptance: "Sí, bueno, a veces." Similar to English "Yeah, well…" or "Well, yes, but…".
target_language_example: Sí, bueno, entiendo tu punto, pero no estoy de acuerdo.
native_language_example: Yeah, well, I get your point, but I don’t agree.

additional_notes: Used to agree or confirm something. Tone depends on context: it can be genuinely polite/enthusiastic, or (with a certain intonation) slightly sarcastic like “yeah, sure.” Often followed by things like “por supuesto” (of course) or “lo siento” (sorry).
target_language_example: —¿Me ayudas un momento? —Sí, claro.
native_language_example: —Can you help me for a moment? —Sure.

additional_notes: Used to agree or respond positively while giving your opinion. Often followed by a full clause (e.g., “sí, creo que deberíamos…”). In casual speech it can also sound a bit hesitant/softened, like “yeah, I think…”.
target_language_example: Sí, creo que tienes razón.
native_language_example: Yes, I think you’re right.

meaning: "Yes, in/on..." (confirming something and giving a location or context).
additional_notes: Used when you answer “yes” and immediately add where/what context with en. En often means “in” or “on” depending on the noun (en la mesa = on the table; en una caja = in a box; en verdad = truly/indeed). Common pattern: “Sí, en + [place/thing]”.
target_language_example: —¿Está el libro aquí? —Sí, en mi mochila.
native_language_example: —Is the book here? —Yes, in my backpack.

additional_notes: Used to confirm or agree with something someone just said or asked. Often followed by a noun/adjective ("Sí, es perfecto") or by "lo que..." ("Sí, es lo que pensaba" = “Yes, that’s what I thought”).
target_language_example: —¿Es tuyo este libro? —Sí, es mío.
native_language_example: —Is this book yours? —Yes, it’s mine.

additional_notes: Used to agree with or confirm a specific thing that was just mentioned or is understood from context. It often sounds like you’re pointing back to an idea: “Yes—THAT (thing).” You’ll also see it before verbs to mean “Yes, I do/it does”: “Sí, eso ayuda” (Yes, that helps), “Sí, eso dije” (Yes, that’s what I said). In conversation it can work as a brief “Yep, that’s it,” and it can also be used to correct or emphasize: “Sí, eso sí” (“Yes, that one / that part, yes”).
target_language_example: —¿Quieres decir que el problema es la batería? —Sí, eso.
native_language_example: —Do you mean the problem is the battery? —Yes, that's it.

additional_notes: Used to confirm that something is true or matches what you meant/thought/said/did. Common before a verb phrase: “Sí, eso es lo que + estaba/estoy + [verb in -ando]” (Yes, that’s what I was/am doing), or “Sí, eso es lo que + [imperfect]” (Yes, that’s what I thought). Often shortened in speech to “Sí, eso es.” or “Eso es lo que…”.
target_language_example: Sí, eso es lo que quería decir.
native_language_example: Yes, that’s what I meant to say.

additional_notes: Used to answer a yes/no question or confirm something about yourself with the verb estar (“to be” for temporary states, feelings, conditions, locations). It’s commonly followed by an adjective or phrase: estoy bien (I’m fine), estoy listo (I’m ready), estoy de acuerdo (I agree), estoy seguro (I’m sure), estoy llorando (I’m crying). For permanent identity (e.g., “I’m American”), Spanish typically uses ser (sí, soy…).
target_language_example: —¿Estás listo? —Sí, estoy listo.
native_language_example: —Are you ready? —Yes, I’m ready.

meaning: “Yes, it is/yes, he/she is” (agreeing with a statement using estar).
additional_notes: Used to confirm something is true when the verb is **estar** (temporary state/condition, location, being alive). Often followed by an adjective or phrase: **Sí, está bueno** (“Yes, it’s good”), **Sí, está vivo** (“Yes, he’s alive”). You can also specify who/what with a subject: **Sí, está aquí** (“Yes, he’s here”).
target_language_example: —¿El café está caliente? —Sí, está caliente.
native_language_example: —Is the coffee hot? —Yes, it’s hot.

additional_notes: Used when answering “yes” and referring back to a feminine singular direct object with **la** (“it” for a feminine noun, or “her” for a woman). Common with verbs like *ver* (to see), *tener* (to have), *amar* (to love): **Sí, la veo** = “Yes, I see her/it.” The **la** usually refers to something already mentioned in the conversation.
target_language_example: —¿Tienes la llave? —Sí, la tengo.
native_language_example: —Do you have the key? —Yes, I have it.

additional_notes: Used to confirm something already mentioned. "Lo" is the direct object pronoun meaning “it/that,” referring back to a previous action/idea: “Sí, lo ha hecho” = “Yes, he/she has done it.” With "estar" it often stands for the implied situation (e.g., “Sí, lo estabas” ≈ “Yes, you were (doing that / in that state)”), and with the near future "ir a" it confirms an intended action (“Sí, lo vas a hacer” = “Yes, you’re going to do it”). In English you usually don’t say “Yes, it”; you say “Yes, I did / Yes, he has / Yes, you will.”
target_language_example: —¿Vas a llamar a tu mamá? —Sí, lo voy a hacer ahora.
native_language_example: —Are you going to call your mom? —Yes, I’m going to do it now.

meaning: "Yes, I..." (starting an affirmative reply, often with a reflexive verb).
additional_notes: Used when you answer “yes” and then continue the sentence with a verb that takes the pronoun “me” (often reflexive): me acuerdo = I remember, me casaré = I will get married, me queda bien = it fits me/it looks good on me. In English you usually don’t keep “me” after “yes”; you’d say “Yes, I remember / Yes, I will / Yes, it fits me.”
target_language_example: Sí, me gusta esa canción.
native_language_example: Yes, I like that song.

additional_notes: Used to confirm what someone just said and then intensify it with an adverb or adjective: “Sí, muy en serio” = “Yes, very seriously.” Often sounds a bit emphatic, like you’re strongly agreeing.
target_language_example: —¿Te gustó la película? —Sí, muy mucho.
native_language_example: —Did you like the movie? —Yes, very much.

meaning: "Yeah, no" (a hesitant/softened way to say "no"; sometimes ironic).
additional_notes: Used as a discourse marker, often at the start of a reply. It can soften disagreement or refusal, show hesitation, or add sarcasm/irony. It’s commonly followed by a negative statement (e.g., "sí, no creo...", "sí, no puedo...").
target_language_example: Sí, no puedo ir hoy; tengo mucho trabajo.
native_language_example: Yeah, no, I can’t go today; I have a lot of work.

additional_notes: Used to acknowledge what someone said (“yes”) and then introduce a contrast, objection, or limitation (“but”). Often used to soften disagreement or to add an important exception.
target_language_example: Sí, pero prefiero hacerlo mañana.
native_language_example: Yes, but I’d rather do it tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used to acknowledge something (“sí”) and immediately add a contrast or limitation (“pero no…”). It often softens disagreement or introduces a correction. Common patterns: “Sí, pero no creo que…” (Yes, but I don’t think…), “Sí, pero no necesitas…” (Yes, but you don’t need to…).
target_language_example: Sí, pero no puedo hoy; mejor mañana.
native_language_example: Yes, but I can’t today; tomorrow is better.

additional_notes: Used to answer a question or respond to someone and immediately justify your “yes” with an explanation. Often followed by a full clause: “Sí, porque + [reason]”. In speech, the pause/comma after “sí” is common.
target_language_example: —¿Vas a ir mañana? —Sí, porque necesito hablar con el jefe.
native_language_example: —Are you going tomorrow? —Yes, because I need to talk to the boss.

meaning: "Yes, it/that/one…" (a common way to start answers with "sí" + "se" + verb).
additional_notes: In these answers, **se** is usually the **impersonal/passive se** (not “himself/itself”). It’s used when the subject is general or not mentioned, similar to English **“it is/was…,” “you can…,” “it shows/you can see…”**. Examples: *Se acabó* = “It’s over,” *se lo he dicho* = “I’ve told him/her/you,” *se nota* = “It shows,” *se podría decir* = “you could say,” *se ve (claramente)* = “you can see (clearly) / it looks (good).”
target_language_example: Sí, se entiende perfectamente.
native_language_example: Yes, it’s perfectly understandable / You can understand it perfectly.

additional_notes: Used to show respect, politeness, or obedience when replying to a man (or someone you address as “señor”). You’ll hear it in formal situations (customers/staff, police, military) and also jokingly or enthusiastically (“Yes, sir!”). For a woman, you’d say “sí, señora.” Often repeated for emphasis: “Sí, señor, sí, señor.”
target_language_example: —¿Puedes hacerlo hoy? —Sí, señor, ahora mismo.
native_language_example: —Can you do it today? —Yes, sir, right now.

additional_notes: Used to confirm your identity or a characteristic about yourself. “Soy” is the 1st-person singular (“I am”) of the verb “ser” (to be), often followed by a name, “yo” (me), or a noun/adjective: “Sí, soy Ana.” / “Sí, soy yo.” / “Sí, soy consciente.”
target_language_example: —¿Eres tú el profesor? —Sí, soy yo.
native_language_example: —Are you the teacher? —Yes, I am.

meaning: “Yes, yes.” (used to agree, confirm, or show you’re listening)
additional_notes: Common in conversation to strongly confirm something (“Yes, that’s it”), to reassure (“Yes, I’m fine”), or to show active listening before continuing. Depending on tone, it can also sound a bit impatient, like “yeah, yeah.”
target_language_example: Sí, sí, entiendo; ahora te explico lo que sigue.
native_language_example: Yes, yes, I understand; now I’ll explain what comes next.

meaning: “Yes, I/they … you” (introduces a verb with the pronoun te = “you”).
additional_notes:
Used at the start of a reply to confirm something and then continue with a verb that takes te. 
- te is an object pronoun meaning “you” (informal singular), as in: Sí, te llamaré… (“Yes, I’ll call you…”).
- With reflexive verbs it can mean “yourself,” as in: te llamas… (“your name is…” / literally “you call yourself…”).
Often followed by other pronouns too: Sí, te lo prometo (“Yes, I promise it to you”).
target_language_example: Sí, te ayudo con la tarea.
native_language_example: Yes, I’ll help you with the homework.

meaning: “Yes, and …” / “Yeah, and …” (adding something else, sometimes with a sharp or sarcastic tone).
additional_notes: Used after agreeing (“sí”) to continue the idea with extra information (“y”). Depending on intonation and context, it can sound neutral (simply adding details) or confrontational/sarcastic (like “Yeah, and?” or “Yes—and you’re going to stop it right now.”). Often followed by a full sentence.
target_language_example: Sí, y mañana te llamo para confirmarlo.
native_language_example: Yes, and I’ll call you tomorrow to confirm it.

additional_notes: Used to confirm something and add that it has happened already (or is done). Here, ya emphasizes that the action is completed. In other contexts, "ya" can also mean "now" or "soon," depending on the sentence.
target_language_example: Sí, ya lo hice.
native_language_example: Yes, I already did it.

additional_notes: Used to confirm something and add that it’s not new information: “yes, I already know/heard/believe (it).” **Ya** = “already,” and **lo** is an object pronoun meaning “it/that” (referring to the idea or information being discussed). You typically complete it with a verb: *sí, ya lo sé* (I already know), *sí, ya lo oí* (I already heard it), *sí, ya lo creo* (I do believe so).
target_language_example: Sí, ya lo sé, pero gracias por decírmelo.
native_language_example: Yes, I already know, but thanks for telling me.

additional_notes: Used to answer and then emphasize that *you* (not someone else) did/think/remember something: “Yes, I did.” In Spanish, the subject pronoun **yo** is often omitted (“Sí, lo vi”), but adding **yo** can sound more emphatic or contrastive (“Sí, yo lo vi, pero él no”).
target_language_example: —¿Tú lo hiciste? —Sí, yo lo hice.
native_language_example: —Did you do it? —Yes, I did.

meaning: "Yeah, and...?" / "Okay, so what?" (often skeptical); also "Yes, and what about...?"
additional_notes: Used in conversation to push back or challenge what someone just said (similar to "Yeah, and?" meaning "So what?"). It can also introduce a follow-up topic or concern: "Sí, ¿y ahora?" (Okay, and now what?), "Sí, ¿y la biblioteca...?" (Yes, and what about the library...?). Tone depends on context and can sound dismissive.
target_language_example: Sí, ¿y qué hacemos si no funciona?
native_language_example: Yeah, and what do we do if it doesn’t work?

additional_notes: Used to answer a man respectfully (often to a boss/authority) or to strongly confirm what you just said. In some contexts it can be ironic or mocking, depending on tone. For a woman, you’d say “sí señora.” You may also hear it repeated (“sí señor, sí señor”) for extra emphasis.
target_language_example: —¿Puedes enviarlo hoy? —Sí señor, ahora mismo.
native_language_example: —Can you send it today? —Yes, sir, right away.

additional_notes: Reflexive form meaning “(to/for/by) himself/herself/itself/yourself (formal).” It changes with the person and gender/number: mí mismo/a (myself), ti mismo/a (yourself, informal), sí mismo/a (himself/herself/itself/yourself formal), nosotros/as mismos/as (ourselves), vosotros/as mismos/as (yourselves), sí mismos/as (themselves). Common after prepositions like a, para, por: a sí mismo (to himself), para sí mismo (to himself/privately), por sí mismo (by himself/on his own).
target_language_example: Sólo piensa en sí mismo.
native_language_example: He only thinks about himself.

additional_notes: Used to emphasize limitation or exclusivity: that something is the only thing available/possible, or that the quantity is limited. It’s the verb phrase "hay" (there is/are) with "sólo" (only/just) placed before it. In modern spelling, "solo hay" is also common; both are understood.
target_language_example: En la nevera sólo hay leche y huevos.
native_language_example: In the fridge there are only milk and eggs.

additional_notes: Used to soften what you’re about to say, often to explain your intention, make a polite request, or downplay something (“only/just”). It’s the imperfect past of querer, so it commonly refers to what you wanted a moment ago or in a past situation. Often followed by an infinitive (sólo quería hablar…) or by que + imperfect subjunctive (sólo quería que me ayudaras…).
target_language_example: Sólo quería preguntarte una cosa.
native_language_example: I just wanted to ask you one thing.

meaning: "you just have to" / "all you have to do is".
additional_notes: Used to say that something is the only necessary step. It’s followed by an infinitive (e.g., creer, empezar, llamar). You can also hear it without the accent: "solo tienes que".
target_language_example: Sólo tienes que decirme la verdad.
native_language_example: You just have to tell me the truth.

additional_notes: Used to ask someone to wait briefly or to say something will take a very short time. Common in polite requests with “por favor”: “Sólo un momento, por favor.” You’ll also see it written without the accent as “solo un momento.”
target_language_example: Disculpa, sólo un momento; ahora te ayudo.
native_language_example: Sorry, just a moment; I’ll help you now.

meaning: 'just a few minutes' / 'only a few minutes.'
additional_notes: Used to say something will take a short amount of time, or that the difference was very small (e.g., you missed something by only a few minutes). Often appears as “sólo unos minutos más” = “just a few more minutes.” In modern Spanish, it’s also common to write it without the accent: “solo unos minutos.”
target_language_example: Espera, por favor: sólo unos minutos.
native_language_example: Please wait: just a few minutes.

meaning: just as; exactly how; the way (that).
additional_notes: Used to compare something with a reference or expectation: “in the same way as” or “exactly as.” Often followed by a clause (Tal como nos dijo), or used with words like antes (“as before”), puedes ver (“as you can see”), lo dijo (“exactly as he said it”), estaba previsto (“as planned”).
target_language_example: Déjalo tal como está, por favor.
native_language_example: Leave it just as it is, please.

meaning: exactly like that; just as it is.
additional_notes: Used to emphasize that something is unchanged or exactly the same as stated ("just like that"). Often used to agree/confirm: “Sí, tal cual.” It can also describe something unmodified: “Lo quiero tal cual (está).”
target_language_example: Sí, tal cual: no hay nada que añadir.
native_language_example: Yes, exactly—there’s nothing to add.

meaning: just as; exactly as (in the way that).
additional_notes: Used to compare with or refer to the same manner/way something happened or is/should be. Very common with verbs like "decir" (as he/she said) and "ser" (accept/love someone as they are). Often interchangeable with "como" in casual speech, but "tal y como" sounds a bit more emphatic/formal (“exactly as”).
target_language_example: Hazlo tal y como te lo expliqué.
native_language_example: Do it exactly as I explained it to you.

additional_notes: Used to refer to something previously mentioned or to a hypothetical/uncertain thing. Often appears in expressions like “si es que existe tal cosa” (“if such a thing even exists”).
target_language_example: No entiendo cómo alguien puede decir tal cosa.
native_language_example: I don’t understand how someone can say such a thing.

additional_notes: Used to express possibility or uncertainty. It is often followed by the subjunctive when the speaker is unsure, as in the example: tal vez haya sido. In everyday speech, it can also appear with the indicative.
target_language_example: Tal vez llueva mañana.
native_language_example: Maybe it will rain tomorrow.

meaning: "maybe, but…" (conceding something, then giving a counterpoint).
additional_notes: Used to partially agree or admit a possibility (tal vez = maybe/perhaps) and then contrast it with another idea (pero = but). Often implies "That could be true, but…". You’ll also see it without the comma: "Tal vez pero…"; in speech the pause can replace the comma.
target_language_example: Tal vez, pero no creo que sea una buena idea.
native_language_example: Maybe, but I don’t think it’s a good idea.

additional_notes: Used to gently suggest a possible action for yourself (a tentative recommendation). "Tal vez" = "maybe/perhaps" and "debería" is the conditional of "deber" ("should/ought to"). Often followed by an infinitive: "tal vez debería + infinitive" (e.g., descansar, hacerlo, irme).
target_language_example: Tal vez debería llamar a mi mamá.
native_language_example: Maybe I should call my mom.

additional_notes: Used to suggest an action in a tentative, polite way. "Tal vez" = "maybe/perhaps" and "deberíamos" is the conditional of "deber" ("we should/ought to"), often implying a recommendation rather than an obligation.
target_language_example: Tal vez deberíamos pedir ayuda.
native_language_example: Maybe we should ask for help.

additional_notes: Used to express uncertainty in a negative way (you think something might not be true or might not happen). It often comes before a verb: "Tal vez no venga" (“Maybe he/she won’t come”). With "tal vez", Spanish commonly uses the subjunctive for uncertainty ("tal vez no venga"), though you may also hear the indicative in some contexts. It can also stand alone as a short answer: "—¿Vienes? —Tal vez no."
target_language_example: Tal vez no podamos ir mañana.
native_language_example: Maybe we won’t be able to go tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used to express uncertainty about something being true. "Sea" is the present subjunctive of "ser" (to be), often used after "tal vez" to sound more doubtful or tentative. In casual speech you may also hear "tal vez es", but "tal vez sea" is very common and slightly more cautious.
target_language_example: Tal vez sea una buena idea esperar.
native_language_example: Maybe it's a good idea to wait.

meaning: "perfect for each other"; "a perfect match" (often said with irony).
additional_notes: Used to say two people (or things) are very similar and go well together—either positively (they’re made for each other) or sarcastically/negatively (they deserve each other because they’re the same, often in a bad way). Often used on its own as a comment: “Tal para cual.”
target_language_example: Esos dos son tal para cual: siempre llegan tarde y nunca se disculpan.
native_language_example: Those two are a perfect match: they’re always late and never apologize.

meaning: “also/too + it/that” (referring back to something already mentioned).
additional_notes: “Lo” is a direct object pronoun meaning “it/that” (or sometimes “him,” for a male person) and it refers to something understood from context: Lo sé (I know it), lo hice (I did it), lo eran (they were it/that way). “También” means “also/too” and often comes right before object pronouns: “también lo + verb” = “also/too + verb + it/that.” In English you usually won’t translate it word-for-word as “also it.”
target_language_example: Yo también lo entiendo.
native_language_example: I understand it too.

additional_notes: Used to compare the degree of how well something happens or is done. Often appears in patterns like: "tan bien que..." (so well that...), "tan bien como..." (as well as...), and "ir(te/le) tan bien" (to go so well / for someone to do so well).
target_language_example: Lo hiciste tan bien que todos aplaudieron.
native_language_example: You did it so well that everyone applauded.

meaning: as well as (someone/ something); just as well as.
additional_notes: Used to compare how well two people do something, or to say someone does something to the best of their ability. Structure: "tan bien como + noun/pronoun" (Lo sabes tan bien como yo.) or "tan bien como + verb" (Lo hicimos tan bien como pudimos / como pudimos hacerlo.). After "como" you may see the subjunctive when talking about ability/possibility ("tan bien como podamos").
target_language_example: Intentaré explicarlo tan bien como pueda.
native_language_example: I’ll try to explain it as well as I can.

additional_notes: Uses "tan" + adverb to intensify: "cerca" = close/near, so "tan cerca" = so close. It can refer to distance (Estamos tan cerca.) or closeness to a person (Me siento tan cerca de ti.). Often appears in contrasts like "Tan cerca, pero tan lejos" (“So close, yet so far”).
target_language_example: Faltan solo dos días; estamos tan cerca de terminar.
native_language_example: Only two days left; we’re so close to finishing.

additional_notes: In standard Spanish, tan and como are usually separated by an adjective or adverb: tan + adjective/adverb + como, as in tan alto como ('as tall as') or tan rápido como ('as fast as'). Because of that, the exact contiguous string tan como is uncommon in ordinary sentences; it is best understood as the comparison frame itself. For nouns or amounts, Spanish usually uses tanto ... como instead.
target_language_example: La estructura «tan como» se usa para hacer comparaciones de igualdad.
native_language_example: The structure 'tan como' is used to make comparisons of equality.

additional_notes: Used with "tan" + adjective to emphasize the degree of a feeling or quality. Often followed by "de" + infinitive to say what you’re happy about: "Estoy tan feliz de verte". Common in comparisons with "como": "tan feliz como tú" (“as happy as you”).
target_language_example: Estoy tan feliz de verte otra vez.
native_language_example: I’m so happy to see you again.

additional_notes: Tan + adjective/adverb means "so" or "that" (degree). With fuerte it can describe strength (fuerte = strong) or volume (hablar fuerte = to speak loudly). Common patterns: "Eres tan fuerte" = "You’re so strong"; "No hables tan fuerte" = "Don’t speak so loudly"; "Depende de qué tan fuerte..." = "It depends on how strong/loud...".
target_language_example: No pongas la música tan fuerte, por favor.
native_language_example: Don’t play the music so loud, please.

meaning: so big; that big; as big (as).
additional_notes: Used to emphasize size or degree (physical or figurative). Often appears in comparisons with "como" ("tan grande como" = "as big as"). It can also mean "so great" in a non-physical sense (e.g., emotions, importance).
target_language_example: No pensé que el problema fuera tan grande.
native_language_example: I didn’t think the problem was so big.

additional_notes: Used to emphasize the degree of youth, often implying surprise, admiration, or sadness. It usually comes after the noun it describes: "alguien tan joven" (someone so young), "un chaval tan joven" (a boy/kid that young).
target_language_example: No puedo creer que tenga un trabajo tan bueno siendo tan joven.
native_language_example: I can’t believe he has such a good job being so young.

additional_notes: Used with "tan" + adverb to express degree: "tan lejos" = a great distance (physical) or how far you’ve progressed/come (figurative). Often appears with comparisons or contrasts ("tan cerca pero tan lejos"), and in negatives as "no tan lejos" = "not so far" / "not that far away."
target_language_example: Está tan lejos que tardamos dos horas en llegar.
native_language_example: It’s so far away that it took us two hours to get there.

additional_notes: Used to soften a negative judgment, often in the pattern "no (está / se ve / suena) tan mal" = "it’s not that bad / it doesn’t look/sound so bad." It compares the current situation to a worse expectation or to how it was before ("no tan mal como...").
target_language_example: La comida no está tan mal, ¿verdad?
native_language_example: The food isn’t that bad, right?

meaning: “as busy as” (used to compare how busy someone is).
additional_notes: Pattern: **tan + adjective/adverb + como** = “as + adjective/adverb + as”. Here **ocupado/a** agrees with the person: **tan ocupado como yo** (male) / **tan ocupada como yo** (female). You can add **siempre** (“as always”) or use it with names/pronouns: **tan ocupado como Mary / como nosotros**.
target_language_example: Esta semana estoy tan ocupado como tú.
native_language_example: This week I’m as busy as you.

additional_notes: Often used to talk about something happening immediately after something else: “tan pronto + verb/clause” = “as soon as …” (e.g., “Tan pronto llegues, llámame.”). It can also mean “so soon” in the sense of “too early/earlier than expected” (“No te vayas tan pronto.”). In comparisons you may see “tan pronto … como …” meaning “as … as …” (e.g., “Tan pronto estaba alegre como triste” = “He/She was as happy as sad”).
target_language_example: Te llamaré tan pronto llegue a casa.
native_language_example: I’ll call you as soon as I get home.

additional_notes: Used to say that one action happens immediately after another. It introduces a clause (often with subjunctive when referring to the future: "Tan pronto como llegue..."; indicative for past/habitual: "Tan pronto como llegué...").
target_language_example: Tan pronto como termines, avísame.
native_language_example: As soon as you finish, let me know.

meaning: as soon as I can (as soon as possible).
additional_notes: Used to promise you’ll do something at the earliest moment you’re able to. It commonly follows a future statement (e.g., devolveré/estaré/regresaré...). Grammar note: "pueda" is the present subjunctive of "poder" after "tan pronto como" when referring to an uncertain future action. You can change the person: "tan pronto como puedas" (you can), "tan pronto como pueda" (I/he/she/you formal can).
target_language_example: Te llamo tan pronto como pueda.
native_language_example: I'll call you as soon as I can.

additional_notes: Used to express urgency: you want something done at the earliest possible time. Often shortened in conversation to “Tan pronto como sea posible.” or “Tan pronto como puedas/pueda” (“as soon as you can/I can”). Uses the subjunctive (“sea”) because it refers to an unspecified future time.
target_language_example: Envíame los documentos tan pronto como sea posible, por favor.
native_language_example: Send me the documents as soon as possible, please.

additional_notes: Used to compare speed: **tan + adverb (rápido) + como** = “as … as”. Very common with **poder** (“can”): **tan rápido como pude** = “as fast as I could,” and with **ser posible**: **tan rápido como sea posible** / **tan rápido como te sea posible** = “as fast as possible” / “as fast as you can.”
target_language_example: Hazlo tan rápido como puedas, por favor.
native_language_example: Do it as fast as you can, please.

additional_notes: Commonly used to emphasize how small/limited something is (often with time/amounts): “en tan solo unos años” = “in only a few years.” In wishes/regrets, it often appears as “si tan solo…” meaning “if only…/if only (I/he/she) had…”
target_language_example: Llegamos en tan solo diez minutos.
native_language_example: We arrived in just ten minutes.

meaning: only; just. (Also: “if only…” in “si tan sólo…”)
additional_notes: Used to emphasize a small amount, a limitation, or “nothing more than”: “tan sólo tres horas” = “only three hours,” “es tan sólo un niño” = “he’s just a child.” With “si tan sólo + imperfect subjunctive,” it expresses a wish/regret: “Si tan sólo pudiera…” = “If only I could…”. You may also see it written without the accent: “tan solo.”
target_language_example: Tan sólo tenemos dos entradas.
native_language_example: We only have two tickets.

meaning: "as much as" / "as … as" (to compare amount or degree).
additional_notes: Used to compare quantity or intensity: tanto como + verb ("Corrí tanto como pude" = I ran as much as I could). It can also compare two people/things: "Tom puede hacer tanto como Mary" (Tom can do as much as Mary). Often appears with querer/poder: "tanto como quieras/puedas" (as much as you want/can), and with "sea posible" (as much as possible).
target_language_example: No puedo ayudarte tanto como quisiera.
native_language_example: I can’t help you as much as I would like.

meaning: “so much/so long that” (to the point that).
additional_notes: Used to show a consequence caused by a very strong degree or a long duration. Common patterns: adjective/adverb + “tanto que” (Me cansé tanto que…) or verb + “tanto que” (Me reí tanto que…). With time/length, it often means “so long that” (Duró tanto que…).
target_language_example: Me reí tanto que me dolía el estómago.
native_language_example: I laughed so much that my stomach hurt.

meaning: so much time; such a long time.
additional_notes: Used to emphasize a long duration. Common with expressions like "hace tanto tiempo" (so long ago), "ha pasado tanto tiempo" (so much time has passed), "por tanto tiempo" (for so long), and "en tanto tiempo" (in such a long time).
target_language_example: No te veo desde hace tanto tiempo.
native_language_example: I haven’t seen you in such a long time.

additional_notes: Used with verbs like llegar/ir: "Llegar tarde a la escuela" = to arrive late to school. "Tarde" means "late" (as in not on time), and "a la escuela" means "to school." Often you’ll hear "llegar tarde" on its own when the destination is clear.
target_language_example: Si sigues así, vas a llegar tarde a la escuela.
native_language_example: If you keep going like that, you're going to be late to school.

additional_notes: Used to say something is inevitable and will happen at some point, even if you don’t know when. Often placed at the beginning or end of a sentence, sometimes set off with commas.
target_language_example: Tarde o temprano, tendrás que hablar con tu jefe.
native_language_example: Sooner or later, you’ll have to talk to your boss.

meaning: 'card for' / '... card' (used to name what kind of card it is).
additional_notes: Used before a noun to specify the purpose/type of a card: tarjeta de estudiante (student ID), tarjeta de acceso (access card/badge), tarjeta de crédito (credit card), tarjeta de regalo (gift card). Often translates as “[noun] card” in English rather than “card of …”.
target_language_example: ¿Tienes una tarjeta de crédito?
native_language_example: Do you have a credit card?

additional_notes: Used to talk about paying with a credit card or your credit-card account/balance. Often appears with verbs like pagar (to pay), usar (to use), and with (con) to mean 'by/with credit card': pagar con tarjeta de crédito. You can also say la tarjeta (the card) when the context is clear.
target_language_example: ¿Puedo pagar con tarjeta de crédito?
native_language_example: Can I pay with a credit card?

additional_notes: A card you send by mail (often with a photo on one side and a short message on the other), usually without an envelope. Common with the verb "enviar" (to send): "enviar una tarjeta postal".
target_language_example: Voy a comprar una tarjeta postal y enviársela a mi mamá.
native_language_example: I’m going to buy a postcard and send it to my mom.

additional_notes: A common dessert. Also often said as "pastel de manzana" (especially in some countries). With food, you’ll often see "un poco de" = “a little (bit) of.”
target_language_example: ¿Quieres un trozo de tarta de manzana?
native_language_example: Do you want a slice of apple pie?

additional_notes: Used to talk about (1) the amount of coffee you drink (una/dos/tres tazas de café) or (2) the physical cups/mugs themselves (e.g., collecting or buying coffee cups). Singular: taza de café.
target_language_example: ¿Cuántas tazas de café tomas al día?
native_language_example: How many cups of coffee do you drink a day?

additional_notes: Used to express deep love (romantic, or very strong affection—also possible with close family like a parent/child). It’s stronger and more intense than "te quiero" in many contexts. "Te" = "you" (to you) and "amo" = "(I) love".
target_language_example: Te amo con todo mi corazón.
native_language_example: I love you with all my heart.

additional_notes: Future tense of ayudar (“to help”) with te (“you” as an indirect object). Common for offering help or making a promise: Te ayudaré (a + infinitive) = “I’ll help you (to do something).” You can also add conditions: Te ayudaré, con la condición de que… (“I’ll help you, on the condition that…”).
target_language_example: No te preocupes: te ayudaré a estudiar para el examen.
native_language_example: Don’t worry: I’ll help you study for the exam.

additional_notes: From the verb conocer (to know/be acquainted with) + te (you). Used for knowing a person, recognizing someone, or being familiar with them (not for knowing facts—use saber for that). Common patterns: "Te conozco de..." (I know you from...), "Te conozco de toda la vida" (I’ve known you my whole life), "Te conozco desde..." (I’ve known you since...).
target_language_example: No te preocupes: te conozco bien y sé que lo vas a lograr.
native_language_example: Don’t worry: I know you well and I know you’ll do it.

additional_notes: *Te* is an indirect object pronoun (“to you”). *Da* is “he/she/it gives.” So it often means “(someone/something) gives you …” (e.g., *La vida te da limones* = “Life gives you lemons”). It also appears in common expressions where the meaning is more like “causes you” (*Te da sueño* = “It makes you sleepy”) or “gives you (a quality)” (*Te da cierto encanto* = “It gives you a certain charm”). Related patterns you may see: *Se te da bien* (“You’re good at it”) and *Te da lo mismo* (“It’s all the same to you / you don’t care”).
target_language_example: Esta medicina te da sueño.
native_language_example: This medicine makes you sleepy.

additional_notes: Future expression from dar (“to give”): daré means “I will give,” and te means “to you.” It is used when promising or saying you will give someone something later.
target_language_example: Mañana te daré la respuesta.
native_language_example: Tomorrow I'll give you the answer.

additional_notes: Used to say you owe someone money, a specific item (un almuerzo, un favor), or that you feel you owe them gratitude/an apology. Very common in casual speech: “Te debo una” = “I owe you one” (you helped me, so I’ll return the favor).
target_language_example: Gracias por ayudarme ayer; te debo una.
native_language_example: Thanks for helping me yesterday; I owe you one.

meaning: "I will leave you" or "I will let you".
additional_notes: Future tense of "dejar" + "te" ("you"). It can mean (1) leaving someone somewhere or ending/abandoning a relationship ("Te dejaré aquí." / "Nunca te dejaré."), or (2) allowing someone to do something, often with an infinitive ("Te dejaré ver eso." = "I’ll let you see that"). Context tells you which meaning is intended. With "no", it commonly means "I won’t let you" or "I won’t leave you."
target_language_example: Te dejaré quedarte un rato más.
native_language_example: I’ll let you stay a little longer.

meaning: "I leave you" / "I let you" (depending on context).
additional_notes: From the verb "dejar" (to leave; to let/allow). Common uses: (1) allow someone to do something: "Te dejo entrar" = I’ll let you in; (2) stop bothering/leave someone alone: "Te dejo solo" = I’ll leave you alone; (3) leave something for someone: "Te dejo el regalo aquí" = I’ll leave the gift here for you; (4) end a relationship: "Te dejo" = I’m leaving you / I’m breaking up with you. Often followed by an infinitive ("te dejo + verb") or by "solo/a".
target_language_example: Te dejo el dinero en la mesa.
native_language_example: I’ll leave the money on the table for you.

additional_notes:
Two common uses:
1) Desire/attraction: "Te deseo" = "I desire you / I want you" (often romantic or sexual).
2) Good wishes: "Te deseo" + a noun phrase = "I wish you…" (e.g., "te deseo toda la felicidad", "te deseo buena suerte").
Grammar note: "te" = "to you/you" (object pronoun), and "deseo" = "I desire / I wish".
target_language_example: Te deseo lo mejor en tu nuevo trabajo.
native_language_example: I wish you the best in your new job.

meaning: "I tell you" / "(that) I tell you" (to you).
additional_notes: From the verb *decir* (to say/tell). *Te* = “to you” (informal singular). *Diga* is the present subjunctive (yo diga). It often appears after expressions like **deja que...** (let...) and **haz lo que...** (do what...), and in commands/promises: **Haz/Vas a hacer exactamente lo que te diga** = “Do/You will do exactly what I tell you.” Contrast with **te digo** (present indicative: “I tell you” as a statement).
target_language_example: No te vayas hasta que te diga.
native_language_example: Don’t leave until I tell you.

meaning: "I’m telling you that…" (often used for emphasis).
additional_notes: Used to introduce what you want the other person to believe or understand. It can sound insistent or reassuring depending on tone: Te digo que es él. / Te digo que te va a encantar. Often followed by a full clause (subject + verb).
target_language_example: Te digo que mañana lo terminamos.
native_language_example: I’m telling you we’ll finish it tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used to remind someone of something you already said. Often has the tone of “I told you so,” especially when pointing out you were right (Te dije que eso pasaría). It’s followed by a clause; with requests/commands it’s common to use the imperfect subjunctive: “Te dije que salieras…” = “I told you to leave…”.
target_language_example: Te dije que no quería ir.
native_language_example: I told you I didn’t want to go.

additional_notes: Used to remind someone that you already said something before. "Te" = “to you,” "dije" = “I said/told,” "que" introduces the clause, and "era" is the imperfect of "ser" (“was”). What follows often agrees in gender/number: "era bueno" (it/he was good), "era buena" (she/it was good), "era falso" (it was false).
target_language_example: Te dije que era una mala idea.
native_language_example: I told you it was a bad idea.

meaning: "I told you no" / "I told you not to".
additional_notes: Used to remind someone that you previously said “no” or warned them not to do something. Often followed by a verb in the imperfect subjunctive (e.g., fueras, llamaras, vinieras) to mean “I told you not to + verb.” Can also be used before a longer clause: “Te dije que no deberíamos…” = “I told you we shouldn’t…”.
target_language_example: Te dije que no tocaras eso.
native_language_example: I told you not to touch that.

meaning: “I told you not to …” / “I told you you shouldn’t …”
additional_notes:
Used to remind someone of a warning or instruction you already gave them. The phrase is usually followed by a verb: 
- Te dije que no te acercaras. (I told you not to come closer.)
- Te dije que no te fiaras de él. (I told you not to trust him.)
In everyday speech, Spanish often uses imperfect subjunctive after “te dije que…”, especially for telling someone not to do something.
target_language_example: Te dije que no te metieras en problemas.
native_language_example: I told you not to get into trouble.

additional_notes: Used to introduce what you’re about to say, often as a preface to advice, a comment, or an important point. Literally: “I will tell you something” (future tense of decir + indirect object te = “to you”). Commonly preceded by fillers like “Bueno” or “Muy bien.”
target_language_example: Te diré algo: tienes que descansar más.
native_language_example: I’ll tell you something: you need to rest more.

additional_notes: Used to introduce what you are about to explain, predict, or instruct someone to do. It’s often followed by a verb phrase (e.g., "te diré lo que debes hacer" = “I’ll tell you what you must do”). Similar to English "I’ll tell you what" as a lead-in, not necessarily the idiomatic exclamation.
target_language_example: Te diré lo que pienso sobre eso.
native_language_example: I’ll tell you what I think about that.

additional_notes: "Te" means "to you" (informal singular), and "doy" is "I give" (from *dar*). Used for giving something (money, help, a gift) and also in set phrases like **Te doy mi palabra** = "I give you my word" (I promise).
target_language_example: Te doy mi palabra de que voy a estar allí.
native_language_example: I give you my word that I’ll be there.

additional_notes: Used to tell someone you miss them. It can be said to a partner, family member, or friend; adding terms like cariño/tesoro makes it more affectionate. You can change the object pronoun: "Te echo de menos" (I miss you), "Os echo de menos" (I miss you all), "La/Lo echo de menos" (I miss her/him/it).
target_language_example: Te echo de menos desde que te fuiste.
native_language_example: I’ve missed you since you left.

additional_notes: From the verb *equivocarse* (“to be mistaken”), used with **tú** (informal singular “you”). Often appears as **No, te equivocas** (“No, you’re wrong”) or **No te equivocas** (“You’re not wrong”). You can change the person: **me equivoco** (I’m wrong), **se equivoca** (you formal/he/she is wrong), **nos equivocamos** (we’re wrong).
target_language_example: Lo siento, te equivocas: la reunión es mañana, no hoy.
native_language_example: Sorry, you’re mistaken: the meeting is tomorrow, not today.

additional_notes: Used to show you’re paying attention and ready for the other person to speak. Common in conversation and also as a radio/phone-style response (like “This is Vlad, I read you / go ahead”). Repetition (“Te escucho, te escucho”) can add emphasis or signal urgency/connection-check.
target_language_example: Ya estoy listo; te escucho.
native_language_example: I’m ready; I’m listening.

additional_notes: Used to emphasize that you are addressing the person (te = “to you”) and that it’s happening in the moment (estoy hablando). Often said to get someone’s attention, especially if they’re ignoring you or you’re annoyed. You can add “a ti” for extra emphasis: “Te estoy hablando a ti.”
target_language_example: Oye, te estoy hablando; mírame un segundo.
native_language_example: Hey, I’m talking to you; look at me for a second.

additional_notes: Used with the verb "esperar" (to wait for). "Te" is the object pronoun "you" (informal singular). "Está esperando" is the present progressive: "is waiting". You can swap the subject depending on who is waiting: "Él/Ella/La vida te está esperando."
target_language_example: Tranquilo, tu hermana te está esperando en la entrada.
native_language_example: Relax, your sister is waiting for you at the entrance.

additional_notes: Past tense (preterite) of extrañar: it means you missed someone (felt their absence). Te is the direct object pronoun (“you”). Often strengthened with mucho (“a lot”): Te extrañé mucho. Not related to extraño (“strange”)—different meaning.
target_language_example: Te extrañé cuando no estabas aquí.
native_language_example: I missed you when you weren’t here.

additional_notes: Past tense (pretérito) of ir for “tú”: fuiste. With te, it often implies leaving a place or going away (sometimes like “you left/you took off”). Common in clauses with desde que (“since”): desde que te fuiste = “since you left.”
target_language_example: Me llamaron cuando te fuiste.
native_language_example: They called me when you left.

additional_notes: Used with the verb gustar to say what someone likes. Grammatically it works like “it pleases you”: the thing you like is the subject, so the verb often matches that thing (e.g., te gusta el café; te gustan los libros). Often followed by a noun or an infinitive (Te gusta bailar).
target_language_example: Te gusta esta canción, ¿verdad?
native_language_example: You like this song, right?

additional_notes: From the verb "gustar" in the imperfect tense. Spanish uses the pattern "A alguien le gusta/gustaba algo": literally, "Something was pleasing to someone." So in "Te gustaba el chocolate", the subject is "el chocolate" (the thing liked), and "te" means "to you." Often used for past habits/ongoing past feelings ("you used to like...", "you liked...").
target_language_example: De niño, te gustaba jugar al fútbol.
native_language_example: As a kid, you used to like playing soccer.

meaning: “you’ll like it” / “you’re going to like it.”
additional_notes: Future tense of "gustar" (3rd person singular: gustará) with "te" = "to you." Used to predict or promise that someone will like something, or to guess (“No te gustará, ¿verdad?” = “You won’t like it, right?”). Often followed by a thing: "Te gustará esto" or "Te gustará Alemania."
target_language_example: Creo que te gustará esta película.
native_language_example: I think you’ll like this movie.

meaning: "has (to you)" — used in the present perfect to say someone has done something to/for you (e.g., "has heard you," "has lied to you").
additional_notes: This is the combination of the indirect object pronoun "te" (to you) + "ha" (he/she/it has, from "haber") + a past participle: "te ha + participle". The pronoun goes before "ha": "Te ha oído" = "(He/She) has heard you"; "Te ha mentido" = "(He/She) has lied to you". In "se te ha metido en la cabeza," "te" marks who it happened to: "it’s gotten into your head" / "you’ve gotten it into your head."
target_language_example: ¿Quién te ha dicho eso?
native_language_example: Who told you that? / Who has told you that?

additional_notes: Uses the past perfect: haber (había) + past participle (visto). It refers to something that happened before another past moment (often implied). Very common with negation: "No te había visto" = "I hadn't seen you" / "I didn't see you (until now)." Can also be used with "nunca": "Nunca te había visto..." = "I had never seen you...".
target_language_example: Perdona, no te había visto en la esquina.
native_language_example: Sorry, I hadn't seen you on the corner.

additional_notes: Past perfect (pluscuamperfecto) of irse (to leave/go away): habías ido = "you had gone"; with te it becomes reflexive irse, often meaning "to leave". Used to talk about an action completed before another past moment (e.g., Pensé que... = "I thought that..."). Often appears with ya to mean "already."
target_language_example: Cuando llegué, te habías ido.
native_language_example: When I arrived, you had left.

additional_notes: Used with a thing/situation as the subject + hacer + indirect object pronoun (te) to say something causes an effect on you: "Eso te hace feliz" = "That makes you happy." It’s often followed by an adjective (te hace feliz), an infinitive (te hace pensar), or a verb like "ver" to mean “make you look” (te hace ver como…).
target_language_example: Ese comentario te hace sentir mal.
native_language_example: That comment makes you feel bad.

additional_notes: Used to say someone needs something or lacks it. It can refer to an object (Te hace falta un cinturón nuevo.) or an action (Solo te hace falta practicar más.). Literally it’s like “it makes lack to you,” but in natural English it’s “you need…”. Often interchangeable with “necesitas,” especially in everyday speech.
target_language_example: Si quieres aprobar, te hace falta estudiar un poco cada día.
native_language_example: If you want to pass, you need to study a little every day.

additional_notes: From "hacer" in the future tense: "haré" = "I will do/make" and "te" = "to you/for you" (or "you" as the object). It’s used to promise, threaten, or offer to do something: "te haré daño" (I’ll hurt you), "te haré un sándwich" (I’ll make you a sandwich), "te haré saber" (I’ll let you know). Often followed by a noun ("te haré un té") or an infinitive/phrase ("te haré caer" = I’ll make you fall; "te haré arrestar" = I’ll have you arrested).
target_language_example: Si quieres, te haré una lista de compras.
native_language_example: If you want, I’ll make you a shopping list.

meaning: "you have" (used with a past participle; often with reflexive verbs).
additional_notes: Made of the reflexive/indirect pronoun **te** (you) + **has** (you have, from *haber*). It’s used to form the **present perfect**: **te has + participle** (e.g., *te has cortado*, *te has dado cuenta*). Very common with reflexive or idiomatic verbs like **pasarse** (to go too far: *te has pasado*), **darse cuenta** (to realize: *te has dado cuenta*), **portarse** (to behave: *te has portado*), **reírse (de)** (to laugh at: *te has reído de mí*).
target_language_example: ¿Te has olvidado de llamarme?
native_language_example: Have you forgotten to call me?

additional_notes: Not a fixed expression: te is the informal singular object pronoun for tú ('you,' 'to you,' or 'for you'), and he means 'I have.' It is used before a past participle to form the present perfect, as in Te he dicho ('I've told you') or Te he enviado un mensaje ('I've sent you a message'). English usually does not translate this word-for-word.
target_language_example: Te he enviado un mensaje.
native_language_example: I've sent you a message.

meaning: “I’ve told you that…” / “I told you…” (often: “I already told you…”).
additional_notes: Uses the present perfect (he dicho) with the indirect object pronoun te (“to you”). It introduces what you told someone and often sounds firm or impatient, especially when repeating yourself: “Te he dicho que no…” = “I told you not to…”. In Spain it’s very common; in much of Latin America you may also hear “Te dije que…”.
target_language_example: Te he dicho que no toques eso.
native_language_example: I told you not to touch that.

additional_notes: Uses the present perfect: "he llamado" (haber + past participle) to talk about calls made in the recent past or up to now. "Te" means "you" (informal singular) and is the object pronoun: "I called you" (on the phone). You can add how many times: "Te he llamado dos/seis veces"; "un par de veces" = "a couple of times."
target_language_example: Te he llamado esta mañana, pero no contestaste.
native_language_example: I called you this morning, but you didn’t answer.

additional_notes: Uses the present perfect (he visto) with the object pronoun te (“you”). Common for saying you’ve seen someone doing something (Te he visto bailar = “I’ve seen you dance”) or in a place (Te he visto por aquí = “I’ve seen you around here”). With todavía no (“still not”), it means you haven’t seen the person yet: Todavía no te he visto = “I still haven’t seen you.”
target_language_example: Te he visto hoy en el supermercado.
native_language_example: I saw you today at the supermarket.

meaning: 'do you mind?' / 'do you care?' / 'does it matter to you?'
additional_notes: From the verb "importar" (to matter). Used to say something matters to someone ("no te importa" = "you don't care"), or as a polite question with "¿Te importa si...?" = "Do you mind if...?". It can also sound challenging in questions like "¿Qué te importa?" = "What’s it to you?". Note: "importar" usually does NOT mean "to import" here (false friend).
target_language_example: ¿Te importa si abro la ventana?
native_language_example: Do you mind if I open the window?

meaning: “I swear (to you) that…” (strong emphasis that you’re telling the truth or really will do something).
additional_notes: Used to strongly insist something is true or to make a serious promise. You can also hear it as “te lo juro” (“I swear it / I swear to you”), and it often appears in emotional or defensive situations.
target_language_example: Te juro que mañana te llamo.
native_language_example: I swear I’ll call you tomorrow.

additional_notes: This is a very common pronoun combination: **te** is an indirect object pronoun (“to/for you”), and **la** is a direct object pronoun referring to a feminine noun (“it/her/that”). It often translates as “I’ll give it to you,” “I owe it to you,” “Take it off,” etc., with the exact meaning depending on the verb and what **la** refers to. The order is fixed: **te** comes before **la**. It can go before a conjugated verb (Te la doy) or attach to an infinitive/gerund/affirmative command (Voy a dártela / Estoy dándotela / Dámela).
target_language_example: Si quieres, te la presto mañana.
native_language_example: If you want, I'll lend it to you tomorrow.

additional_notes: Common way to say you will call someone in the future. "Te" = "you" (the person being called) and "llamaré" is the future tense of "llamar" (to call). Often used to promise a call later or to say you’ll call if something happens.
target_language_example: Cuando termine la reunión, te llamaré.
native_language_example: When the meeting ends, I'll call you.

additional_notes: Literally “I call you,” but in everyday Spanish it usually means you’ll call the person soon or later (a promise/plan): Ahora te llamo (I’ll call you now/in a moment), Después te llamo (I’ll call you later), Te llamo mañana (I’ll call you tomorrow). You can also use it as a question to check if it’s okay: ¿Te llamo mañana?
target_language_example: Estoy saliendo del trabajo; te llamo en cinco minutos.
native_language_example: I’m leaving work; I’ll call you in five minutes.

additional_notes: Past tense (preterite) of llamar + te (“you”). Used for a completed phone call attempt: it can mean you successfully reached the person or simply that you tried calling. Often followed by when/how many times: anoche (last night), dos veces (twice), en cuanto… (as soon as…).
target_language_example: Te llamé, pero no contestaste.
native_language_example: I called you, but you didn’t answer.

meaning: “I’ll take you to …” / “I’ll bring you to …” (future).
additional_notes: Used to promise that you will take someone to a place or to an activity. It’s the future tense of llevar: yo llevaré = “I will take/bring,” and te = “you” (informal singular). Usually followed by a destination (a casa, a la escuela) or an action in the infinitive (a nadar, a ver…).
target_language_example: No te preocupes, te llevaré al aeropuerto mañana.
native_language_example: Don’t worry, I’ll take you to the airport tomorrow.

additional_notes: Combination of te ('to you', informal singular) and lo ('it/this/that'). It usually comes before a conjugated verb: te lo explico = 'I explain it to you', te lo devolveré = 'I'll return it to you'. Lo can refer to a masculine noun or to a whole idea/situation, and English usually uses a different word order.
target_language_example: Mañana te lo mando.
native_language_example: I'll send it to you tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used to express gratitude for something the other person did or said. Literally “I thank it to you”: te = to you, lo = it (the thing you’re grateful for), agradezco = I appreciate/thank. Often appears after “Gracias” and can be strengthened with “mucho” (“Te lo agradezco mucho”).
target_language_example: Si puedes ayudarme con esto, te lo agradezco mucho.
native_language_example: If you can help me with this, I’d really appreciate it.

additional_notes: Made of te (to you) + lo (it) + digo (I say/tell). It’s often used to emphasize that you mean what you’re saying, or to introduce advice, a warning, or an honest opinion: Te lo digo como amigo (I’m telling you as a friend), Te lo digo de frente (I’m telling you straight), Te lo digo por tu propio bien (I’m telling you for your own good). You can add what you’re telling after it: Te lo digo ahora. (I’m telling you now.)
target_language_example: Te lo digo en serio: no vayas.
native_language_example: I’m telling you seriously: don’t go.

additional_notes: Common way to remind someone that you already said something (often when you were right). Literally: “I told it to you” (te = to you, lo = it/that, dije = I said/told). Can sound a bit insistent depending on tone; you may also hear it with emphasis: “¡Te lo dije!”
target_language_example: Te lo dije: esa calle está cerrada.
native_language_example: I told you: that street is closed.

additional_notes: Future tense of decir (“to tell/say”) with pronouns: te = “to you” and lo = “it/that.” Used when you’ll give someone information later (often with después, luego, en un minuto). You can also add a time or condition: Te lo diré mañana / cuando llegue.
target_language_example: No puedo explicarlo ahora, pero te lo diré más tarde.
native_language_example: I can’t explain it now, but I’ll tell you later.

additional_notes: Future tense of explicar (to explain). Te = “to you” (informal singular), lo = “it” (or “that”), explicaré = “I will explain.” Often used with time words like luego/más tarde (later) or todo (everything). In Latin America, “luego” can also mean “soon,” depending on the context.
target_language_example: No te preocupes: te lo explicaré cuando lleguemos a casa.
native_language_example: Don’t worry: I’ll explain it to you when we get home.

meaning: "I had told you (it/that)" / "I told you so."
additional_notes: Uses the past perfect (había dicho) to talk about something you told someone before another past moment. "Te" = "to you" and "lo" = "it/that" (the thing you said). Often used to remind someone that you already told them, sometimes with an "I told you so" tone depending on context.
target_language_example: Te lo había dicho, pero no me escuchaste.
native_language_example: I had told you, but you didn’t listen to me.

additional_notes: Used to reassure someone or emphasize that you’re telling the truth. "Te" = to you (informal singular), "lo" = it/that, "prometo" = I promise. Often placed at the end of a sentence: "Todo va a salir bien, te lo prometo." With a different person it changes (e.g., "se lo prometo" = I promise you [formal] / I promise him/her).
target_language_example: No te voy a mentir, te lo prometo.
native_language_example: I’m not going to lie to you, I promise.

additional_notes: A strong, often emotional way to ask someone to do (or stop doing) something. It’s more intense than “por favor” and can sound dramatic or very polite in serious situations. Grammar: “te” = “to you,” “lo” = “it/this,” from the verb “rogar” (to beg/plead). You can also say “Te ruego que…” (“I beg you to…”).
target_language_example: Por favor, escúchame, te lo ruego.
native_language_example: Please, listen to me—I beg you.

meaning: "I’m going to (do it) to you / for you."
additional_notes: Used before an infinitive to talk about the near future with the structure **ir a + infinitive**. **Te** = “to you / for you,” and **lo** = “it” (a masculine thing/idea, or a generic “it”). Common in promises, warnings, or offers: *Te lo voy a explicar* (“I’m going to explain it to you”). Word order is fixed: **te lo** comes before **voy a**.
target_language_example: Te lo voy a enviar mañana.
native_language_example: I’m going to send it to you tomorrow.

additional_notes: Very strong and aggressive. Literally uses the verb "matar" (to kill) in the simple future "mataré" (I will kill) plus "te" (you, as a direct object). It can sometimes be said jokingly to mean “I’m going to kill you!” (e.g., when someone breaks something), but it’s still harsh and can easily be taken as a real threat.
target_language_example: Si me vuelves a mentir, te mataré.
native_language_example: If you lie to me again, I'll kill you.

additional_notes: From the verb "merecer(se)" (to deserve). "Te" is the object pronoun meaning "you" (informal singular), so it changes with the person: "me merezco" (I deserve), "te mereces" (you deserve), "se merece" (he/she/you formal deserves), "nos merecemos" (we deserve). It can be used positively ("You deserve the best") or negatively/ironically ("That’s more than you deserve").
target_language_example: Te mereces una oportunidad.
native_language_example: You deserve a chance.

additional_notes: Future tense of mostrar (“to show”) with te (“to you”). Used to promise/offer to show someone something later or in a moment. Often followed by what you’ll show: te mostraré el lugar/la ciudad/algunas fotos, or te mostraré lo que…
target_language_example: Espera un segundo y te mostraré cómo funciona.
native_language_example: Wait a second and I’ll show you how it works.

additional_notes: Used when speaking directly to someone (“te” = you). Often said on the phone or in a noisy place to confirm you can hear the other person, or in the negative (No te oigo / Casi no te oigo) to say you can’t (really) hear them. From the verb oír (to hear).
target_language_example: Espera, hay mucho ruido: casi no te oigo.
native_language_example: Wait, there’s a lot of noise: I can barely hear you.

additional_notes: Used to say someone resembles another person (or even an animal/thing). It comes from the verb "parecerse a" (to resemble) and requires "a": "Te pareces a tu madre". You can replace "te" with other pronouns: "Me parezco a...", "Se parece a...", "Nos parecemos a...".
target_language_example: Te pareces a tu hermana cuando sonríes.
native_language_example: You look like your sister when you smile.

meaning: "I asked you to" (informal: "I told you to").
additional_notes: "Pedir" + indirect object pronoun (te = to you) + "que" introduces what you asked someone to do, followed by a verb in the imperfect subjunctive (e.g., hicieras, llamaras, vinieras). Used to remind someone of a request or to deny you made that request ("No te pedí que...").
target_language_example: Te pedí que llegaras temprano, pero no viniste.
native_language_example: I asked you to arrive early, but you didn’t come.

meaning: “I ask you to…” / “I’m asking you to…”
additional_notes: Used to make a request to someone (often serious or emotional). It’s followed by a verb in the present subjunctive: te pido que + escuches / vengas / no vayas. You can change the indirect object: le pido que (I ask him/her/you formal to), les pido que (I ask you all / them to).
target_language_example: Te pido que me perdones.
native_language_example: I’m asking you to forgive me.

meaning: “Let me introduce you to …” / “This is …” (introducing someone).
additional_notes: Used when you introduce a person to someone else. Literally “I introduce (someone) to you”: te = “to you,” presento = “I introduce,” a is used before a person. You can change te to other pronouns: les presento a… (to you all), le presento a… (to you, formal).
target_language_example: Hola, Carlos, te presento a mi hermana, Laura.
native_language_example: Hi, Carlos, let me introduce you to my sister, Laura.

additional_notes: Used to make a strong, personal promise to someone. "Te" = "to you" (informal singular), "prometo" = "I promise", and "que" introduces what you’re promising. Often followed by the future (protegerá, encontraré) or by "no" to promise not to do something.
target_language_example: Te prometo que voy a llegar a tiempo.
native_language_example: I promise you I’m going to arrive on time.

additional_notes: From the verb "quedarse" (to stay/remain). "Te puedes quedar" is commonly used to give permission or allow someone to stay somewhere, often as an invitation. It can be followed by a place or time: "te puedes quedar aquí", "te puedes quedar el tiempo que quieras", "te puedes quedar a pasar la noche". "Tú" is often omitted: "(Tú) te puedes quedar".
target_language_example: Si quieres, te puedes quedar aquí hasta mañana.
native_language_example: If you want, you can stay here until tomorrow.

additional_notes: From the verb quedar. Commonly used in two main ways: (1) With clothes/colors/hairstyles to say something looks good on you or fits you: “Esa chaqueta te queda muy bien” = “That jacket looks great on you.” (2) With time/quantity to say how much remains: “Te queda poco tiempo” = “You don’t have much time left.” Often followed by adverbs like bien/mal, muy bien, mejor, or by amounts like poco/mucho, un minuto, etc.
target_language_example: Ese color te queda muy bien, pero te queda poco tiempo para cambiarte.
native_language_example: That color looks great on you, but you don’t have much time left to change.

meaning: “It looks good on you” / “It fits you well.”
additional_notes: Used to say that clothing (or a color/style) suits someone or fits them nicely. It comes from the verb "quedar" (to fit/suit): "me/te/le queda bien" = it looks good on me/you/him/her. For size/fit problems you’ll often hear "te queda grande" (too big) or "te queda chico" (too small).
target_language_example: ¡Ese vestido te queda bien!
native_language_example: That dress looks good on you!

additional_notes: From the verb "quedarse" (to stay / to remain). In conversation, "te quedas" is often used like a firm instruction meaning “you’re staying” (similar to an imperative). With "quedarse con + [thing]", it means “to keep” something (often implying you keep it for yourself): "te quedas con el dinero" = “you keep the money.”
target_language_example: No salgas; te quedas aquí conmigo.
native_language_example: Don’t go out; you’re staying here with me.

additional_notes: As a complete phrase, te quiero usually means 'I love you' or 'I care about you,' often less intense than te amo. In longer sentences, it can also be part of a structure meaning 'I want...' with te as 'you': te quiero abrazar = 'I want to hug you,' te quiero en mi vida = 'I want you in my life.'
target_language_example: Te quiero mucho.
native_language_example: I love you very much.

additional_notes: From the verb "referirse (a)" = “to refer to / to mean.” Very often used in questions to clarify: “¿A qué te refieres (con eso)?” = “What do you mean (by that)?” It typically takes "a": "Te refieres a junio" (You mean June). You can also hear: "Sé a lo que te refieres" = “I know what you mean / I know what you’re referring to.”
target_language_example: Perdón, ¿a qué te refieres con "más tarde"?
native_language_example: Sorry, what do you mean by “later”?

meaning: 'it looks good on you' / 'it suits you (well)'.
additional_notes: Used to say that something (often clothes, a color, a hairstyle, or even a habit like exercise) has a good effect on someone or makes them look good. Literally from "sentar" = "to suit/to agree with" in this sense. You can swap the indirect object pronoun: "me sienta bien" (it suits me), "le sienta bien" (it suits him/her/you formal), "nos sienta bien" (it suits us), etc.
target_language_example: Ese vestido te sienta bien.
native_language_example: That dress looks good on you.

additional_notes: “Te sientas” can come from two different reflexive verbs: (1) sentirse = “to feel” (common with emotions/conditions, often after triggers like cuando, es normal que, etc.: “cuando te sientas triste…”), and (2) sentarse = “to sit down / to sit” (talking about where someone sits: “donde te sientas…”). It’s a reflexive form (te + verb), used with tú.
target_language_example: Si te sientas cansado, descansa un rato.
native_language_example: If you feel tired, rest for a while.
