additional_notes: From the verb "tener" (to have). "Tiene" is used with él/ella/usted (he/she/you formal). Often followed by an adjective (e.g., "un perro grande") or combined with other pets ("y seis gatos").
target_language_example: Mi vecino tiene un perro muy amable.
native_language_example: My neighbor has a very friendly dog.

additional_notes: From the verb phrase **tener un problema** (“to have a problem”). **Tiene** is the 3rd-person singular form (he/she/it/you-formal). Use it for a general issue (“Tiene un problema”) or specify what kind: **tiene un problema de** + noun (e.g., *de acné*), **tiene un problema con** + thing/person (e.g., *con la bebida* = with alcohol/drinking), or **tiene un problema en/al** + body part (common in some regions: *al corazón*).
target_language_example: Mi coche tiene un problema, no arranca.
native_language_example: My car has a problem; it won’t start.

additional_notes: "tiene" is the present tense of "tener" for he/she/you (formal)/it: "(él/ella/usted) tiene" = "has." "una" means "a" or "one" and is used with feminine singular nouns (una frontera, una sartén, una esposa, una vaca). Often the subject is implied from context.
target_language_example: Mi hermano tiene una bicicleta nueva.
native_language_example: My brother has a new bicycle.

additional_notes: From the verb "tener" (to have). "Tiene" is the third-person singular form, used with él/ella/usted or a name (e.g., Tom). Often followed by a location ("en el sur", "en Italia") or by a description introduced by "que" ("una casa que..."). In many contexts it implies ownership, but it can also simply mean someone has access to a house.
target_language_example: María tiene una casa cerca del mar.
native_language_example: María has a house near the sea.

additional_notes: Used to describe where someone’s scar is located. After en, you usually give a body part or place: en la cara (on the face), en el brazo (on the arm). Possession is expressed with tener (“to have”), and articles are common with body parts (el/la). You may also hear en su brazo (“on his/her arm”) for emphasis or clarity.
target_language_example: Ella tiene una cicatriz en la pierna.
native_language_example: She has a scar on her leg.

meaning: "(He/She) has a personality" (often followed by an adjective).
additional_notes: Used with "tener" to describe what someone’s personality is like: "Tiene una personalidad fuerte / maravillosa / dócil". You can add adjectives to specify the type of personality. To make it plural or change tense/person, conjugate "tener": "tengo", "tienes", "tenemos", "tenía", etc.
target_language_example: Mi jefe tiene una personalidad muy fuerte, pero es buena persona.
native_language_example: My boss has a very strong personality, but he’s a good person.

meaning: "has a (… ) voice" (used to describe someone’s voice).
additional_notes: Use "tener" + "una voz" + an adjective to describe the quality of someone’s voice (e.g., dulce = sweet, suave = soft, hermosa = beautiful, agradable = pleasant, baja = low, profunda = deep). You can also use "voz" with "de" + noun: "Tiene voz de niño" (He has a childlike voice).
target_language_example: Ella tiene una voz muy tranquila.
native_language_example: She has a very calm voice.

additional_notes: From the verb tener (“to have”) + hambre (“hunger”). Spanish commonly uses tener + hambre to express hunger (literally “to have hunger”). Tienen is the present tense for ellos/ellas/ustedes (“they/you all”).
target_language_example: Mis amigos tienen hambre, así que vamos a comer.
native_language_example: My friends are hungry, so we’re going to eat.

additional_notes: Form of the obligation expression "tener que" (to have to / must). "Tienen" is used with "ellos/ellas" (they) and also with "ustedes" (you all) in Latin America. It’s followed by an infinitive: "tienen que + verbo" (e.g., "tienen que ir" = they/you all have to go).
target_language_example: Ustedes tienen que estudiar hoy.
native_language_example: You all have to study today.

meaning: "they have a" (plural form of "tener" + masculine singular "un").
additional_notes: Used to say that "they" (a group of people or things) possess or have something: "Ellos/ellas/ustedes tienen un...". It’s the present tense of "tener" (yo tengo, tú tienes, él/ella tiene, nosotros tenemos, vosotros tenéis, ellos/ellas/ustedes tienen). "Un" is used with a masculine singular noun (use "una" for feminine nouns: "tienen una idea").
target_language_example: Esas casas tienen un jardín grande.
native_language_example: Those houses have a big yard/garden.

additional_notes: Form of the verb "tener" for "they" (ellos/ellas/ustedes). Used before a feminine singular noun (una + noun): "tienen una casa", "tienen una pista". For a masculine noun, use "tienen un".
target_language_example: Mis vecinos tienen una perra muy tranquila.
native_language_example: My neighbors have a very calm (female) dog.

additional_notes: Used before an infinitive to express obligation or necessity: tienes que + verb. This is the informal singular tú form, used when talking to one person you address as tú.
target_language_example: Tienes que salir ahora.
native_language_example: You have to leave now.

meaning: "you have to understand" / "you need to understand."
additional_notes: Used to emphasize that understanding something is necessary. It uses the verb phrase "tener que" (to have to) + an infinitive ("entender"). "Tienes" is the tú form, so it’s said to one person you address as "tú." Often followed by "que" + a full idea: "Tienes que entender que..." (You have to understand that...).
target_language_example: Tienes que entender que no puedo ir hoy.
native_language_example: You have to understand that I can’t go today.

meaning: “you have to be” / “you need to be.”
additional_notes: Used to say someone is required/expected to be in a place or in a certain state/condition. It combines tener que (to have to) + estar (to be, for location/temporary state). You can follow it with a place (en casa), an adjective (listo), or a situation (aquí, allí).
target_language_example: Tienes que estar aquí a las ocho.
native_language_example: You have to be here at eight.

meaning: "you have to do it" / "you must do it."
additional_notes: Used to say someone is required or obligated to do something. It’s the phrase "tener que" (to have to) + "hacerlo" (to do it). Often followed by emphasis words like "ya" (right now), "inmediatamente" (immediately), or "tú mismo / tú" (you yourself) to stress urgency or who must do it.
target_language_example: Lo siento, pero tienes que hacerlo hoy.
native_language_example: Sorry, but you have to do it today.

meaning: “you have to go to …” / “you need to go to …”
additional_notes: Used to tell someone an obligation or requirement: tienes que (you have to) + ir a (to go to) + a place or an action. Common with destinations (la corte, la fábrica, la policía) or an infinitive after "ir a" (e.g., ir a presentar cargos = to go file/press charges).
target_language_example: Tienes que ir a la oficina mañana.
native_language_example: You have to go to the office tomorrow.

meaning: “you have to leave” / “you need to go (away)” (said to one person).
additional_notes: Used to tell or remind one person (tú) that they must leave. It’s very common with places or destinations: “Tienes que irte a casa / a la oficina…”. It can also mean “go to (do something)” with an infinitive phrase: “Tienes que irte a dormir” = “You have to go to sleep.” Often strengthened with time words like “ahora” (now) or “ya” (right away).
target_language_example: Lo siento, pero tienes que irte ya.
native_language_example: I’m sorry, but you have to leave right now.

meaning: you have to pay (you must pay).
additional_notes: "Tienes que" + infinitive expresses obligation/necessity. "Tienes que pagar" is used when telling one person (tú) they are required to pay, either for a bill/service ("pagar el teléfono") or as a consequence ("pagar por ello" = pay for it / face the consequences).
target_language_example: Lo siento, tienes que pagar antes de entrar.
native_language_example: Sorry, you have to pay before going in.

meaning: "you have to keep (doing something)" / "you have to follow".
additional_notes: "Tienes que" = "you have to" (obligation). "Seguir" can mean (1) "to continue/keep doing" + a gerund: "seguir cantando/comiendo" = "keep singing/eating"; or (2) "to follow" + a noun: "seguir las instrucciones/el guión" = "follow the instructions/the script".
target_language_example: Tienes que seguir estudiando todos los días.
native_language_example: You have to keep studying every day.

meaning: you have to be / you must be.
additional_notes: Used to tell one person (tú) that it’s necessary to be a certain way. It can be advice, a rule, or an obligation. Uses tener que (to have to) + infinitive ser (to be). For other people: tengo que ser (I have to be), tienes que ser (you), tiene que ser (he/she/you formal), tenemos que ser (we), tienen que ser (they/you all).
target_language_example: Si quieres el trabajo, tienes que ser puntual.
native_language_example: If you want the job, you have to be on time.

additional_notes: Used to agree with someone or admit they were correct (often after realizing a mistake). It can sound more direct than “sí” and is commonly used with intensifiers like “sí,” “lo siento,” or “claro.” You can change the verb to match the person: “tiene razón” (you formal/he/she), “tengo razón” (I’m right), “tienen razón” (you all/they).
target_language_example: Perdón, tienes razón: me equivoqué.
native_language_example: Sorry, you’re right: I was wrong.

additional_notes: Used with the verb tener (to have) to say someone has/possesses something or has something happening (like a visitor). It’s addressed to “tú” (informal singular “you”). Use **tienes una** before singular feminine nouns (e.g., *Tienes una idea*).
target_language_example: Tienes un problema.
native_language_example: You have a problem.

meaning: 'you have a' (to talk to one person informally, before a feminine noun).
additional_notes: Used with tú (informal 'you') in the present tense of tener: tú tienes. 'Una' is the feminine form of 'a/an' and must match a feminine singular noun (una habitación, una elección, una pluma). For formal 'you', use 'tiene una'.
target_language_example: ¿Tienes una pregunta?
native_language_example: Do you have a question?

meaning: dry land; solid ground (as opposed to the sea).
additional_notes: Used especially in sea/travel contexts to mean “land” you can reach from the water (the shore/coast). Common with verbs like llegar a (to reach), ver (to see), alcanzar (to reach), and the phrase poner un pie en tierra firme (“set foot on land”).
target_language_example: Después de la tormenta, por fin llegamos a tierra firme.
native_language_example: After the storm, we finally reached dry land.

meaning: a tough guy; someone who acts/claims to be tough.
additional_notes: Used to describe someone who is physically or emotionally tough, or who wants to look tough. Often slightly mocking or ironic in questions like “¿Te crees un tipo duro?” (“You think you’re a tough guy?”).
target_language_example: No te hagas el tipo duro; si necesitas ayuda, pídela.
native_language_example: Don’t act like a tough guy; if you need help, ask for it.

additional_notes: Very informal and a bit crude; common in casual speech. Often used in everyday casual conversation. Variants include "echarse un pedo". Avoid in formal situations.
target_language_example: Perdón, voy a tirarse un pedo sin querer.
native_language_example: Sorry, I’m going to fart by accident.

additional_notes: From the verb **tocar** (to play an instrument) + **el piano** (the piano). It agrees with the subject: **yo toco**, **tú tocas**, **él/ella/usted toca**, **nosotros tocamos**, **ellos tocan**. Often used with adverbs like **muy bien** (very well).
target_language_example: Mi hermana toca el piano en una banda.
native_language_example: My sister plays the piano in a band.

additional_notes: From the verb "tocar" (to play an instrument). Here it’s conjugated in the present tense for él/ella/usted: "toca". To talk about yourself, use "(yo) toco la guitarra"; for you (informal), "(tú) tocas la guitarra". Spanish uses the article: "la guitarra" (the guitar).
target_language_example: Mi padre toca la guitarra en una banda.
native_language_example: My dad plays the guitar in a band.

additional_notes: Uses the verb “tocar” (to play an instrument / to touch). With musical instruments in Spanish, you usually say “tocar” + the instrument: “tocar el piano”, “tocar la guitarra”.
target_language_example: ¿Sabes tocar el piano?
native_language_example: Do you know how to play the piano?

additional_notes: Used with instruments to mean “to play” (not “to touch”). With verbs like gustar: “A Einstein le gustaba tocar el violín” = “Einstein liked playing the violin.” You can also use it after verbs of hearing/seeing: “Oímos al niño tocar el violín” = “We heard the boy play the violin.”
target_language_example: Mi hermana está aprendiendo a tocar el violín.
native_language_example: My sister is learning to play the violin.

additional_notes: Tocar is the verb used for playing musical instruments in Spanish (tocar la guitarra, tocar el piano). It’s often used with saber/poder to talk about ability: saber tocar la flauta = “to know how to play the flute.”
target_language_example: ¿Sabes tocar la flauta?
native_language_example: Do you know how to play the flute?

additional_notes: Use "tocar" for playing musical instruments in Spanish (tocar el piano, tocar la batería, etc.). Often used after verbs like "querer", "poder", "aprender a", and "oír" (e.g., "Quiero aprender a tocar la guitarra").
target_language_example: Mi hobby es tocar la guitarra.
native_language_example: My hobby is playing the guitar.

additional_notes: Very informal and vulgar slang (common in Spain). Used to complain that someone is pestering you or being a pain: "Me estás tocando las pelotas" = "You’re really annoying me." Often appears with an indirect object pronoun: me/te/le/nos/os/les. Not suitable for polite situations.
target_language_example: Deja de tocar las pelotas, que estoy trabajando.
native_language_example: Stop bothering me, I’m working.

additional_notes: Used before a noun to mean a wide variety of things. It agrees with the idea of “all” (toda) + “type/kind” (clase) + “of” (de). Often interchangeable with "todo tipo de".
target_language_example: En esta tienda venden toda clase de productos.
native_language_example: In this store they sell all kinds of products.

meaning: the whole house; all over the house.
additional_notes: Means the entire house (as a space). Often used with prepositions: "por toda la casa" = "all over/throughout the house" (searching or things scattered everywhere); "en toda la casa" = "in the whole house". "Tener toda la casa para (uno) solo" means having the whole house to yourself.
target_language_example: Busqué mis llaves por toda la casa.
native_language_example: I looked for my keys all over the house.

meaning: the whole city; the entire city.
additional_notes: Means all parts of the city as a single whole. Often appears with "por" ("por toda la ciudad") to mean "all over/throughout the city." "Toda" agrees with the feminine noun "la ciudad."
target_language_example: Hay carteles por toda la ciudad.
native_language_example: There are posters all over the city.

meaning: the whole family; everyone in the family.
additional_notes: Used to include every family member (not just one person). Often appears with a preposition, e.g. “a toda la familia” (to the whole family). It can also be used more emotionally/figuratively: “Eres toda la familia que tengo” = “You’re the only family I have.”
target_language_example: Voy a invitar a toda la familia a la fiesta.
native_language_example: I’m going to invite the whole family to the party.

additional_notes: Means “all the people” in a group or place, often like “everyone.” It’s feminine singular (gente), so it goes with singular verbs: “toda la gente está/anda/quedó…”.
target_language_example: En el concierto, toda la gente cantaba la misma canción.
native_language_example: At the concert, everyone was singing the same song.

additional_notes: Used to say something lasted for the entire morning. Often appears at the end of the sentence as a time expression (e.g., "He estado... toda la mañana"). You can also change it to match other times: "toda la tarde" (all afternoon), "toda la noche" (all night), "todo el día" (all day).
target_language_example: Estuve trabajando toda la mañana.
native_language_example: I was working all morning.

additional_notes: Means something lasts for the entire night (from night until morning). You can also change it for other time periods: toda la mañana (all morning), toda la tarde (all afternoon), todo el día (all day).
target_language_example: Estudié toda la noche para el examen.
native_language_example: I studied all night for the exam.

additional_notes: Means the entire week (from beginning to end), often implying a continuous situation. Common with time expressions like estar, pasar, llevar + gerund (to have been doing something). Can also be used for emphasis on its own: “Toda la semana.”
target_language_example: Voy a trabajar en casa toda la semana.
native_language_example: I’m going to work from home all week.

additional_notes: Used to say an activity lasted for the entire afternoon (for a long stretch of time). It commonly goes after the verb phrase: "Estuve/He estado + gerundio + toda la tarde" (I was/I've been + -ing + all afternoon). Can also be used with "llevar" to mean something took all afternoon: "Le llevó toda la tarde (hacer algo)".
target_language_example: Estuve trabajando toda la tarde y terminé muy cansado.
native_language_example: I worked all afternoon and ended up very tired.

additional_notes: Used to refer to the whole span of a person's life. In everyday speech, it can also be used more loosely to mean 'for a very long time' or 'forever,' depending on context.
target_language_example: Vivió en ese pueblo toda la vida.
native_language_example: She lived in that town all her life.

additional_notes: Used to say someone is young or has plenty of time and opportunities in the future. It’s common as encouragement or reassurance, and it changes with the subject (tengo/tienes/tiene/tenemos/tienen). Often used with “aún” (still): “Tienes aún toda la vida por delante.”
target_language_example: No te preocupes: tienes toda la vida por delante.
native_language_example: Don’t worry: you have your whole life ahead of you.

additional_notes: Used to emphasize that something has been true for your entire life or for as long as you can remember. Often goes at the end of a sentence (e.g., “He vivido aquí toda mi vida.”). It can also be said alone as a short, emotional response.
target_language_example: He vivido en esta ciudad toda mi vida.
native_language_example: I’ve lived in this city my whole life.

meaning: his/her/their/your (formal) whole life; all his/her/their life.
additional_notes: Means “for one’s entire life (up to now or until death).” The possessive changes with the person: toda mi vida (my whole life), toda tu vida, toda su vida (his/her/your formal/their whole life), toda nuestra vida, toda vuestra vida. Very common with the preposition en: en toda su vida (“in all their life/ever”), often used in negatives for emphasis: No ha sido puntual en toda su vida = “He’s never been on time in his life.”
target_language_example: Ella trabajó en Francia toda su vida.
native_language_example: She worked in France her whole life.

meaning: your whole life; all your life.
additional_notes: Used to talk about a person’s entire lifetime, often for emphasis. You’ll also see the same pattern with other possessives: toda mi vida (my whole life), toda su vida (his/her/your whole life), toda la vida (all my life / forever, depending on context).
target_language_example: He vivido aquí toda tu vida.
native_language_example: I’ve lived here your whole life.

additional_notes: Used before a feminine plural noun (explicit or implied): todas esas chicas/fotos/personas. It can also refer back to a previously mentioned idea in a casual way: “y todas esas tonterías” = “and all that nonsense/that kind of thing.” Contrast: masculine is “todos esos.”
target_language_example: No quiero hablar de todas esas cosas ahora.
native_language_example: I don’t want to talk about all those things right now.

additional_notes: Used before a feminine plural noun to mean “all the.” It agrees in gender and number with the noun: todas las familias/sillas. For masculine plural, use “todos los.”
target_language_example: Todas las tiendas están cerradas hoy.
native_language_example: All the stores are closed today.

additional_notes: Means the whole group of girls. Often used with "a" + people to mean "to all (of them)": "a todas las chicas" = "to all the girls." You can also add "de..." to specify which group: "todas las chicas de la clase" = "all the girls in the class."
target_language_example: Invité a todas las chicas a la fiesta.
native_language_example: I invited all the girls to the party.

additional_notes: Used to refer broadly to everything (objects, events, situations). Often appears with negation to mean “not everything”: “No todas las cosas…” = “Not all things…”. It can also be followed by an adjective or phrase to narrow it down: “todas las cosas bonitas” (all the beautiful things), “todas las cosas de buen aspecto” (all the good-looking things).
target_language_example: No puedo hacerlo todo hoy; tengo demasiadas cosas, pero haré todas las cosas importantes primero.
native_language_example: I can’t do everything today; I have too many things, but I’ll do all the important things first.

additional_notes: Used to refer to every light in a place (e.g., in a house: lamps, ceiling lights). It can also refer to all traffic lights on a route, as in “Todas las luces estaban en verde” (“All the lights were green”).
target_language_example: Por favor, apaga todas las luces cuando te vayas.
native_language_example: Please turn off all the lights when you leave.

additional_notes: Uses the feminine plural form of “todo” (todas) because “manzanas” is feminine plural. Commonly used to talk about the entire set of apples in a group. Word order is typically: todas + las + noun (plural).
target_language_example: En el mercado, todas las manzanas estaban muy caras.
native_language_example: At the market, all the apples were very expensive.

additional_notes: Means something happens each morning as a habit or routine. Often used with the present tense to talk about regular actions (e.g., "Voy al trabajo todas las mañanas").
target_language_example: Me levanto temprano todas las mañanas.
native_language_example: I get up early every morning.

additional_notes: Means every woman in a group. Use **todas** because *mujeres* is feminine plural. Often followed by **de + place/group**: *todas las mujeres del mundo* (“all the women in the world”).
target_language_example: En esta clase, todas las mujeres tienen que llevar casco.
native_language_example: In this class, all the women have to wear a helmet.

additional_notes: Used to talk about something that happens each night as a habit or routine. It’s a time expression and often goes at the end of the sentence (but it can also come earlier for emphasis).
target_language_example: Me acuesto temprano todas las noches.
native_language_example: I go to bed early every night.

additional_notes: Means the whole group of people in general. Often used in general statements ("Todas las personas..."). With "de" ("De todas las personas...") it means "of all people..."—often expressing surprise or emphasis (like "Of all people, you!").
target_language_example: Todas las personas merecen respeto.
native_language_example: Everyone deserves respect.

additional_notes: Used to talk about something that happens regularly each week. Often used with the present tense for routines (e.g., voy, escribe). You can also say "cada semana" with the same meaning.
target_language_example: Hacemos la compra todas las semanas.
native_language_example: We do the grocery shopping every week.

additional_notes: Used to say something hasn’t happened or isn’t true up to now, but you expect it to change later. Often goes right before the verb: “todavía no ha llegado” = “hasn’t arrived yet.” You can also place it at the start of the sentence for emphasis: “Todavía no puedo…” = “I still can’t / I can’t yet…”.
target_language_example: Todavía no he terminado la tarea.
native_language_example: I haven’t finished the homework yet.

additional_notes: Commonly used in directions to mean “keep going straight” (often the same idea as "todo recto"). It does not mean “all right” in English; "derecho" here means “straight” (or “straight ahead”), not “right” as a direction.
target_language_example: Sigue todo derecho y verás el banco a la izquierda.
native_language_example: Keep going straight and you’ll see the bank on the left.

additional_notes: Used to say something happens or is true throughout the entire year (in every season). Often placed at the end of the sentence: "hace frío todo el año". Literally "all the year".
target_language_example: Este restaurante está abierto todo el año.
native_language_example: This restaurant is open all year round.

additional_notes: Often used with an indirect object pronoun (me/te/le/nos/les) in phrases like: Me duele todo el cuerpo (My whole body hurts). With sensations like picar (to itch), doler (to hurt), temblar (to tremble), or with locations using en: en todo el cuerpo (all over the body).
target_language_example: Después del entrenamiento, me dolía todo el cuerpo.
native_language_example: After the workout, my whole body hurt.

additional_notes: Means the entire amount of money (in a place, in someone’s possession, or in general). It’s often used with verbs like dar (to give), dejar (to leave/inherit), traer (to bring), or robar (to steal).
target_language_example: Necesito todo el dinero antes del viernes.
native_language_example: I need all the money before Friday.

additional_notes: Used to say that something happens, continues, or is true during the entire day. It commonly goes after the verb or at the end of the sentence.
target_language_example: Estuve ocupado todo el día.
native_language_example: I was busy all day.

additional_notes: A very common way to refer to all people in general. Although it refers to many people, it usually takes a singular verb in Spanish: todo el mundo sabe, todo el mundo quiere.
target_language_example: Todo el mundo quiere ser feliz.
native_language_example: Everyone wants to be happy.

additional_notes: Used to say that something is generally known. Often followed by a direct object (todo el mundo conoce las reglas) or by a person with "a" (todo el mundo conoce a María). You can make it negative with "No todo el mundo conoce..." (= not everyone knows...).
target_language_example: Todo el mundo conoce ese truco.
native_language_example: Everyone knows that trick.

additional_notes: Used to make a general statement about people in general. It’s built from "todo el mundo" (everyone) + "necesita" (needs). What comes next can be an infinitive ("necesita creer/dejar...") or a noun ("necesita una segunda oportunidad").
target_language_example: Todo el mundo necesita descansar de vez en cuando.
native_language_example: Everyone needs to rest from time to time.

additional_notes: Used to make a general statement about all people. "Todo el mundo" literally means "the whole world" but is commonly used to mean "everyone." Follow it with a noun or phrase: "Todo el mundo tiene + sustantivo" (Everyone has + a/an ...).
target_language_example: Todo el mundo tiene un secreto.
native_language_example: Everyone has a secret.

additional_notes: Used to address or refer to everyone who works in an organization (employees, crew, team members). Common in announcements, warnings, and instructions: “Atención a todo el personal…”, “Todo el personal debe…”. Often followed by a verb in singular (personal is a collective noun): “Todo el personal debe evacuar…”.
target_language_example: Atención a todo el personal: la reunión empieza en cinco minutos.
native_language_example: Attention all staff: the meeting starts in five minutes.

additional_notes: Used to say something happens repeatedly or continuously. Often goes at the end of the sentence: "Habla todo el rato" = "He talks all the time." It can also stand alone as a short answer for emphasis: "¿Te molestó?" — "Todo el rato." = "The whole time."
target_language_example: Estuvo lloviendo todo el rato.
native_language_example: It was raining the whole time.

additional_notes: Used to say something happens very often or continuously. In everyday speech, it often means 'constantly' or 'very often,' not necessarily every single second.
target_language_example: Mi hermano habla de fútbol todo el tiempo.
native_language_example: My brother talks about soccer all the time.

meaning: all the time in the world (plenty of time; no hurry).
additional_notes: Used to say you have lots of time and don’t need to rush. Often appears with tener: "Tengo todo el tiempo del mundo" (I’ve got all the time in the world), including the warm/romantic "Para ti, tengo todo el tiempo del mundo". It can also be said by itself as a short reassurance: "Todo el tiempo del mundo."
target_language_example: Tranquilo, hoy tenemos todo el tiempo del mundo.
native_language_example: Relax, today we have all the time in the world.

meaning: all the work; the whole job.
additional_notes: Means the entire amount of work that needs to be done. Often used with verbs like hacer (to do), terminar/acabar (to finish), and estar hecho (to be done): “Está casi todo el trabajo hecho” = “Almost all the work is done.” You can also say “todo el trabajo” without “el” in some contexts, but “todo el trabajo” is the common phrase for “all the work.”
target_language_example: No puedo salir todavía: tengo que terminar todo el trabajo.
native_language_example: I can’t go out yet: I have to finish all the work.

additional_notes: Used to refer back to things already mentioned (events, details, information, etc.). Often comes after describing several things: “Un número te dice todo eso” = “A number tells you all that.”
target_language_example: No quiero hablar de todo eso ahora.
native_language_example: I don’t want to talk about all that right now.

additional_notes: Used to emphasize that something has been happening continuously up to now, or during a period that has just passed. It can refer to a long time (“all this time”) or highlight a surprising realization (“this whole time”). Often goes at the end of the clause for emphasis: "He estado esperando todo este tiempo".
target_language_example: He estado buscándote todo este tiempo.
native_language_example: I’ve been looking for you all this time.

additional_notes: Refers to the whole situation, set of things, or what was just mentioned/experienced. Often used to react to events or information (e.g., giving an opinion: “todo esto me parece…”, expressing suspicion: “todo esto me huele a…”).
target_language_example: No entiendo todo esto; ¿puedes explicármelo otra vez?
native_language_example: I don’t understand all this; can you explain it to me again?

additional_notes: Refers to the whole situation/thing(s) being talked about. Often used when reacting to something happening (“¿Qué es todo esto?” = “What is all this?”) or when explaining a reason (“por todo esto” = “because of all this / for all these reasons”).
target_language_example: No entiendo todo esto, ¿me lo explicas?
native_language_example: I don't understand all this—can you explain it to me?

additional_notes: Used to describe or judge a whole situation you’ve just mentioned (“all of this”). It’s often followed by a noun or adjective: Todo esto es + extraño/hipocresía/un malentendido. You can also say “todo esto está…” for temporary states (e.g., Todo esto está listo = All this is ready).
target_language_example: Todo esto es demasiado complicado para mí.
native_language_example: All of this is too complicated for me.

additional_notes: Used to correct someone or to emphasize that the reality is the opposite of what was said or expected. Often stands alone as a short reply (e.g., “De hecho, todo lo contrario.”). You can also use it after verbs like hacer: “hacer todo lo contrario” = “to do the exact opposite.”
target_language_example: Pensé que ibas a enojarte, pero fue todo lo contrario.
native_language_example: I thought you were going to get angry, but it was the complete opposite.

additional_notes: Used to refer to the rest of the things not already mentioned (often after listing one or two items: “X y todo lo demás”). It can also be used to contrast with something important: “Olvida todo lo demás menos…” (“Forget everything else except…”).
target_language_example: Ya compré el pan; tú encárgate de todo lo demás.
native_language_example: I already bought the bread; you take care of everything else.

additional_notes: Used to refer to the rest of things not already mentioned. Often contrasts with one specific thing: "X está bien, pero todo lo demás..." It agrees with what it refers to in gender/number if needed (e.g., "todas las demás" for feminine plural).
target_language_example: Me gusta este lugar; todo lo demás es demasiado caro.
native_language_example: I like this place; everything else is too expensive.

meaning: at most; at the very most.
additional_notes: Used to set an upper limit (maximum), often with numbers, time, or quantities. It’s similar to (and often interchangeable with) “a lo más” and “como mucho”. You may also see it followed by “que”: “todo lo más que puedo hacer…” = “the most I can do…”.
target_language_example: Tardará todo lo más diez minutos.
native_language_example: It’ll take at most ten minutes.

meaning: as much as possible; everything possible.
additional_notes: Used to express maximum effort or the greatest possible amount. Common patterns: “hacer todo lo posible (para/por + infinitive)” = “to do everything possible (to…)” and with verbs like “tratar de…” to mean “as much as possible” (e.g., “ahorrar todo lo posible” = “save as much as possible”).
target_language_example: Voy a hacer todo lo posible por llegar a tiempo.
native_language_example: I’m going to do everything possible to arrive on time.

additional_notes: Used to refer to the full set of things, ideas, or actions in a following clause. Very common before a verb: todo lo que + verb, as in todo lo que sé ('everything that I know').
target_language_example: No entiendo todo lo que dice el profesor.
native_language_example: I don't understand everything that the teacher says.

additional_notes: Used to say that nothing else is needed. It often appears in sentences like “Es todo lo que necesita…” (“It’s all you need…”) or “Todo lo que necesita es…” (“All you need is…”). The verb changes with the person: todo lo que necesito (I need), todo lo que necesitas (you need), todo lo que necesitan (they/you all need).
target_language_example: Aquí está todo lo que necesita para empezar.
native_language_example: Here is everything you need to get started.

additional_notes: Used to say there are no other options available. Often followed by an infinitive (es esperar / es rezar), or used alone after es (Es todo lo que podemos hacer). You can add time phrases like ahora or en este momento.
target_language_example: Lo siento, pero es todo lo que podemos hacer por hoy.
native_language_example: I’m sorry, but it’s all we can do for today.

meaning: “whatever you want” / “as much as you want.”
additional_notes: Uses querer (to want) in the present subjunctive: quieras. Often follows an imperative or a verb like poder/hacer/decir/decirme to mean “anything/whatever you want” (freedom of choice) or “as much as you want” with food/drink. You can change it by person: todo lo que quieras (you, tú), todo lo que quiera (you, usted), todo lo que quieran (you all), todo lo que quiera (he/she).
target_language_example: Pregúntame todo lo que quieras.
native_language_example: Ask me anything you want.

additional_notes: Used to say you’ve told the complete set of details you can recall. Often appears with **es** (“That’s all I remember”) or after a verb like **contar** (“I told you everything I remember”). You can add **que** + a clause to specify the only detail you remember: **Todo lo que recuerdo es que…**
target_language_example: Eso es todo lo que recuerdo de aquella noche.
native_language_example: That’s all I remember about that night.

additional_notes: Used to emphasize you’re sharing the full amount of information you have. Common after verbs like decir (to tell), saber (to know), enseñar (to teach/show), or in the phrase “Eso es todo lo que sé” (“That’s all I know”). Literally: “all that (which) I know.”
target_language_example: Eso es todo lo que sé sobre el problema.
native_language_example: That’s everything I know about the problem.

additional_notes: Used to say that the only thing(s) you possess or have available is what comes next. It’s often followed by a noun phrase (esto, un libro, algo de ropa) or can be used more emotionally/figuratively (“all I have left is…”). In speech it can also appear as “lo único que tengo es …”.
target_language_example: Todo lo que tengo es mi teléfono y cinco euros.
native_language_example: All I have is my phone and five euros.

todo lo que tienes que hacer es

target_language_multi_word_term: todo lo que tienes que hacer es
additional_notes: Used to introduce a simple action or instruction that’s enough to achieve something. It’s often followed by an infinitive (mirar, obedecer, pulsar, seguir, sentarte). You can change the subject: "todo lo que tengo que hacer es..." (I), "todo lo que tienes que hacer es..." (you), "todo lo que tiene que hacer es..." (he/she/you formal).
target_language_example: Todo lo que tienes que hacer es escribir tu nombre aquí.
native_language_example: All you have to do is write your name here.

additional_notes: Used to refer to the total set of things that follow in a relative clause. Often appears at the start of a sentence (“Todo lo que + verb...”) or before another clause (“...todo lo que el profesor dijo”). It can also be used with verbs like “hacer”, “decir”, “tener”, “necesitar”.
target_language_example: Anoté todo lo que dijiste.
native_language_example: I wrote down everything you said.

additional_notes: Common way to refer to all people in general (similar to "todo el mundo"). It usually takes singular verb agreement: "Todo mundo estaba..." / "Todo mundo ha...".
target_language_example: En esta ciudad, todo mundo se conoce.
native_language_example: In this city, everyone knows each other.

additional_notes: "Todo" = "all" + "su" = "his/her/their" + "dinero" = "money." It means the person’s entire amount of money. "Su" can be singular or plural (their), and the meaning depends on context. Often used with verbs like "robar" (to steal), "gastar" (to spend), "traer" (to bring), and "dar" (to give).
target_language_example: Perdió todo su dinero en el viaje.
native_language_example: He/She lost all his/her money on the trip.

meaning: all kinds of; every kind of.
additional_notes: Used before a plural noun to talk generally about a wide variety within a category: todo tipo de deportes/personas/ropa. It often means “many different kinds of,” not necessarily literally every single kind.
target_language_example: En esta tienda hay todo tipo de regalos.
native_language_example: In this store there are all kinds of gifts.

additional_notes: Used to check if someone is okay (“¿Todo bien?” / “¿Va todo bien?”) or to reassure that things are fine (“Está todo bien”, “Va a estar todo bien”, “Saldrá todo bien”). Very common in casual speech; you can answer simply “Sí, todo bien.”
target_language_example: ¿Todo bien? Si necesitas algo, dime.
native_language_example: All good? If you need anything, tell me.

additional_notes: Used to say the result or decision is determined by something else. It’s followed by a noun or pronoun: «Todo depende de los resultados», «Todo depende de ti». You can also hear «Depende de…» without «todo» when the context is clear.
target_language_example: Todo depende de lo que diga el médico.
native_language_example: It all depends on what the doctor says.

additional_notes: Used to express optimism or to say that an outcome isn’t ruled out. Often appears after giving a reason or condition: “Con la tecnología, todo es posible” (with technology, anything is possible). Can also be said on its own to mean “you never know.”
target_language_example: Si trabajas duro, todo es posible.
native_language_example: If you work hard, anything is possible.

additional_notes: A reassuring phrase about the future (estar in the future tense: estará). Often said to comfort someone or express confidence that things will work out. You can also hear the near-future version: "todo va a estar bien."
target_language_example: No te preocupes, todo estará bien mañana.
native_language_example: Don’t worry, everything will be fine tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used to say that the whole situation or everything in a set is in a certain state or condition. Here todo means "everything," so it takes singular está, not están. Common in phrases like todo está bien, todo está bajo control, and todo está perdido.
target_language_example: No te preocupes, todo está listo.
native_language_example: Don't worry, everything is ready.

additional_notes: Used to reassure someone or to say a situation is under control. Often said on its own as a calming response (similar to “It’s okay”). You can also hear it as a check-in question: “¿Todo está bien?” = “Is everything okay?”
target_language_example: Tranquilo, todo está bien; ya llamé al médico.
native_language_example: Relax, everything is okay; I already called the doctor.

meaning: “everything will be fine / everything will go well.”
additional_notes: A reassuring phrase used to comfort someone or express confidence about the future. Uses the future tense of ir (irá = “will go”). Often said as a complete sentence, sometimes with a comma + a term of endearment (e.g., “cariño”).
target_language_example: No te preocupes: todo irá bien.
native_language_example: Don’t worry: everything will be fine.

additional_notes: Literally “everything together.” Used to mean things are combined/mixed in the same place (“put it all together”). It can also mean “overall / taken as a whole,” often at the start of a sentence: “Todo junto, no es muy complicado” = “All in all, it’s not very complicated.”
target_language_example: Metí la ropa y los zapatos todo junto en la maleta.
native_language_example: I put the clothes and the shoes all together in the suitcase.

additional_notes: Used to refer to the totality of things in a clause: “everything that + verb.” Very common in sentences like “Todo lo que (yo) sé es…” (“All I know is…”), “Todo lo que dijiste…” (“Everything you said…”). Note: “Todo lo que” (everything that) is different from “todo” alone (“everything/all”).
target_language_example: Todo lo que necesito es un poco de tiempo.
native_language_example: All I need is a little time.

additional_notes: Used to exclude one thing from “everything.” With people/adjectives it often means “anything but” (strong emphasis): “Es de todo menos tonto” = “He’s anything but stupid.” Often appears as “todo menos + noun” or “de todo menos + adjective/noun.”
target_language_example: Quiero ir a cualquier lugar, pero a casa todo menos.
native_language_example: I want to go anywhere, but home is the one place I don’t want to go.

additional_notes: Used to express an extreme choice with no middle ground: either complete success/commitment or complete failure/no commitment. Often said on its own as a slogan or attitude (e.g., in sports, business, relationships). You may also see it as "o todo o nada" for emphasis.
target_language_example: En este proyecto vamos a por todo: es todo o nada.
native_language_example: In this project we’re going for it: it’s all or nothing.

meaning: Everything will be fine / everything will work out.
additional_notes: Used to reassure or comfort someone when they’re worried. It’s in the future tense of “salir” (to turn out), so it literally means “everything will turn out well.” Commonly followed by phrases like “al final” (in the end) or “confía en mí” (trust me).
target_language_example: Tranquila, todo saldrá bien al final.
native_language_example: Relax, everything will work out in the end.

additional_notes: Used to say you know, tell, hear, or forget all the information/details about something. It’s often used after verbs like saber (to know), contar (to tell), oír (to hear), and olvidar (to forget): “Sé todo sobre…”, “Cuéntame todo sobre…”. You can also use “todo acerca de” with the same meaning.
target_language_example: Cuéntame todo sobre tu nuevo trabajo.
native_language_example: Tell me everything about your new job.

additional_notes: A reassuring phrase used to comfort someone or calm a situation. It’s often said with emphasis (e.g., “Te lo prometo” = “I promise you”) and can be placed at the start or end of a sentence (e.g., “Ahora todo va a estar bien”).
target_language_example: Tranquila, todo va a estar bien.
native_language_example: Don’t worry, everything will be fine.

meaning: “Everything is going to be okay / turn out fine.”
additional_notes: A reassuring phrase used to comfort someone or express optimism about the future. Very common in stressful situations; often said with “te lo prometo” (“I promise”) or as “va a salir todo bien” (same meaning).
target_language_example: No te preocupes: todo va a salir bien.
native_language_example: Don’t worry: everything is going to be okay.

additional_notes: Used to reassure someone that the situation is okay or progressing smoothly (at work, at home, during a trip, etc.). Often said as a response to questions like “¿Cómo va todo?” (How’s everything going?) or to confirm there are no problems.
target_language_example: No te preocupes, todo va bien.
native_language_example: Don’t worry, everything is fine.

meaning: all of them (masculine or mixed-gender group).
additional_notes: Used to refer back to a specific group of people or things already mentioned. For an all-female group, use "todas ellas". You can also say "todos" alone when "them" is understood from context.
target_language_example: Todos ellos llegaron temprano a la reunión.
native_language_example: All of them arrived early to the meeting.

additional_notes: Used before a plural noun to refer to a specific group/amount already known from context or pointed out: todos esos + noun (e.g., todos esos televisores). It can also refer to a period of time: todos esos años = “all those years.” Contrast: todos estos = “all these” (near the speaker).
target_language_example: No puedo creer que hayas guardado todos esos papeles.
native_language_example: I can’t believe you kept all those papers.

additional_notes: Used to emphasize that something has been true or happening for a long time up to now (often with emotion like surprise, frustration, or nostalgia). Common in phrases like “Después de todos estos años…” (“After all these years…”) and “Todos estos años creí que…” (“All these years I thought…”).
target_language_example: No puedo creer que hayas guardado ese secreto todos estos años.
native_language_example: I can’t believe you kept that secret all these years.

additional_notes: Used before a plural masculine noun to mean "all the." It also applies to mixed-gender groups. For feminine plural nouns, use "todas las." In some expressions like "todos los días," it can correspond to "every."
target_language_example: Todos los estudiantes necesitan un libro.
native_language_example: All the students need a book.

additional_notes: Means the entire group of animals being talked about. Often used as the subject of a sentence: “Todos los animales son…” = “All animals are…”. In negative sentences you may see “No todos los animales…” = “Not all animals…”.
target_language_example: Todos los animales necesitan agua.
native_language_example: All animals need water.

additional_notes: Used to talk about something that happens annually or regularly once a year. Often placed at the end of the sentence, but it can also go near the verb for emphasis.
target_language_example: Mis abuelos nos visitan todos los años en verano.
native_language_example: My grandparents visit us every year in the summer.

additional_notes: Used to refer to the rest of a group, excluding the person/people already mentioned. It agrees in gender/number with the group: todos los demás (masc./mixed plural), todas las demás (fem. plural), todo lo demás (everything else, neutral/unspecified things), toda la demás (rare; feminine singular in specific contexts). Often follows a noun implicitly: "como todos los demás" = like everyone else.
target_language_example: No quiero ser como todos los demás.
native_language_example: I don’t want to be like everyone else.

additional_notes: Used to say you know/need/have every piece of information. Often appears with verbs like saber/conocer (to know), tener (to have), recordar (to remember), and escuchar (to listen to someone who has the information).
target_language_example: Si quieres ayudar, necesito todos los detalles.
native_language_example: If you want to help, I need all the details.

additional_notes: Used to talk about something you do regularly on Sundays. The plural "domingos" is used in Spanish to mean "every Sunday" (a repeated habit), not multiple specific Sundays. Often goes at the end of the sentence, but it can also be placed earlier for emphasis.
target_language_example: Salgo a caminar todos los domingos.
native_language_example: I go for a walk every Sunday.

additional_notes: Used to talk about habits, routines, or something that happens each day. It's very common with the present tense. Compare it with "todo el día," which means "all day."
target_language_example: Leo un poco todos los días.
native_language_example: I read a little every day.

additional_notes: Refers to the entire group of students. With a verb it often means “every student” in the sense that the statement applies to the whole group (e.g., “Todos los estudiantes aplaudieron.”). It can also be part of expressions like “a todos los estudiantes” (“to all the students”).
target_language_example: La profesora saludó a todos los estudiantes al entrar en clase.
native_language_example: The teacher greeted all the students when she walked into class.

additional_notes: "Todos" means "all" and agrees in gender/number with the noun: todos los hombres (masculine plural). It’s used to make a general statement about men in a group or in general. For "all people" (mixed/unspecified gender), Spanish often uses "todas las personas" or "todo el mundo".
target_language_example: En esta empresa, todos los hombres y todas las mujeres tienen las mismas oportunidades.
native_language_example: In this company, all the men and all the women have the same opportunities.

additional_notes: A set phrase meaning that every person (often understood as everyone, regardless of differences) should have the same rights or be treated the same. Common in legal, moral, and religious contexts: "ante" or "a los ojos de" (before / in the eyes of) + Dios; "de acuerdo a" (according to) + la ley. Note: "hombres" can mean "men" literally, but in older/formal usage it can also mean "human beings" (people).
target_language_example: En una democracia, todos los hombres son iguales ante la ley.
native_language_example: In a democracy, all people are equal before the law.

additional_notes: Used to say something happens regularly on Mondays. Place it after the verb ("Lo hago todos los lunes") or at the beginning for emphasis ("Todos los lunes lo hago").
target_language_example: Voy al gimnasio todos los lunes.
native_language_example: I go to the gym every Monday.

additional_notes: Means the entire group of children being talked about. "Todos" is plural masculine and is used for mixed-gender groups; for an all-girls group you can say "todas las niñas". You’ll often see it with "a" when the children are the direct object: "a todos los niños" (e.g., "les gusta" / "vi a").
target_language_example: Todos los niños del barrio juegan en el parque después de la escuela.
native_language_example: All the kids in the neighborhood play in the park after school.

meaning: all living things; all living beings.
additional_notes: Used to talk about every organism collectively (people, animals, plants, etc.). Often appears in scientific or general statements about life and nature. Grammar: plural phrase—"todos" (all) + "los" (the) + "seres vivos" (living beings).
target_language_example: El agua es esencial para todos los seres vivos.
native_language_example: Water is essential for all living things.

additional_notes: Used to talk about something that happens regularly each summer (a habitual routine). Often used with the present tense for habits ("Voy todos los veranos...") or with the imperfect/past to describe a repeated action in the past ("Iba todos los veranos...").
target_language_example: Visitamos a mis abuelos todos los veranos.
native_language_example: We visit my grandparents every summer.

additional_notes: Used to talk about your entire group of friends. It often comes before a verb: “Todos mis amigos están…” (All my friends are…). In comparisons you may see “De todos mis amigos…” = “Out of all my friends…”.
target_language_example: Todos mis amigos viven cerca de aquí.
native_language_example: All my friends live near here.

additional_notes: Most commonly used as "de todos modos" to mean that something is true or will happen regardless of what was just said (similar to “anyway” or “in any case”). You can also hear "de todas maneras" with the same meaning. On its own, "todos modos" is less common than the full phrase with "de".
target_language_example: No tengo mucho tiempo, pero de todos modos voy a ayudarte.
native_language_example: I don’t have much time, but I’m going to help you anyway.

additional_notes: Means “all of us” (a group that includes the speaker). Often used after prepositions: “entre todos nosotros” (among all of us), “de todos nosotros” (of all of us), “para todos nosotros” (for all of us), “por todos nosotros” (for all of us / on behalf of all of us). You can also say “todos nosotros” for emphasis; otherwise Spanish often just uses “todos” when “us” is already clear.
target_language_example: Esto es un logro de todos nosotros.
native_language_example: This is an achievement of all of us.

additional_notes: Used before a masculine plural noun to mean that every one of the things belongs to 'us': todos nuestros planes/asuntos. For feminine plural nouns, use "todas nuestras" (todas nuestras ideas).
target_language_example: Todos nuestros amigos llegaron temprano.
native_language_example: All of our friends arrived early.

additional_notes: Means the entire group of someone’s friends. The pronoun "sus" can mean "his," "her," "your" (formal), or "their" depending on context; often you clarify with "de él" or "de ella" (e.g., "todos sus amigos (de ella)"). Used frequently with preposition "a" when the friends are the indirect object: "Invitó a todos sus amigos".
target_language_example: Invitó a todos sus amigos a cenar.
native_language_example: He invited all his friends to dinner.

additional_notes: Used to address a group of people with the pronoun "ustedes" (common in Latin America and also used formally in Spain). "Todos" agrees in gender/number: use "todas ustedes" for an all-female group. Often used for emphasis; you can also just say "ustedes" (= you all).
target_language_example: Gracias a todos ustedes por venir hoy.
native_language_example: Thank you all for coming today.

additional_notes: Used to say that all the people in a group were in a certain state or doing something. It’s the imperfect tense of estar (estaban), often describing an ongoing situation in the past (e.g., emotions, conditions, actions in progress). Typically followed by an adjective (felices, satisfechos) or a gerund (escuchando).
target_language_example: Cuando llegué, todos estaban nerviosos.
native_language_example: When I arrived, everyone was nervous.

additional_notes: "Todos" refers to all people in a group, and "están" is the present tense of estar (used for states/conditions, locations, or temporary situations). Often followed by an adjective or phrase: "Todos están bien" (everyone is fine), "Todos están de acuerdo" (everyone agrees), "Todos están en casa" (everyone is at home).
target_language_example: En la reunión, todos están de acuerdo con el plan.
native_language_example: In the meeting, everyone agrees with the plan.

additional_notes: Used to say that a whole group does something at the same time or stays/comes/returns as a group (not separately). It often goes with verbs like ir (to go), volver (to return), estar (to be), and vivir (to live).
target_language_example: Vamos a entrar todos juntos.
native_language_example: Let's go in all together.

additional_notes: Often appears as **a todos nos** + verb to mean “to all of us / for all of us”: *A todos nos pasa* (“It happens to all of us”). It can also be **Todos nos...** as the subject (“All of us...”): *Todos nos están mirando* (“They’re looking at all of us”). In an all-female group you may hear **todas nos**. With reflexive verbs you’ll see it before the verb: *todos nos reunimos* (“we all meet / we all get together”).
target_language_example: A todos nos gusta esa canción.
native_language_example: All of us like that song.

additional_notes: Used to include the speaker and a group ("we"). Often placed at the start for emphasis: "Todos nosotros..." You’ll also see it after a preposition as "de/para todos nosotros" ("of/for all of us"). Feminine group: "todas nosotras"; mixed/masculine group: "todos nosotros".
target_language_example: Todos nosotros tenemos que ayudar.
native_language_example: All of us have to help.

additional_notes: “Todos” means “everyone/all (people)” and “quieren” is the present tense of “querer” (to want/to love). It’s used to say that all people in a group want something: Todos quieren + noun (dinero), or Todos quieren + infinitive (creer, sentarse). With a person, “querer a + person” means “to love” or “to care about”: Todos quieren a Tom. You can negate it with “No todos quieren…” = “Not everyone wants…”.
target_language_example: No todos quieren lo mismo.
native_language_example: Not everyone wants the same thing.

additional_notes: Used to introduce something presented as common knowledge or obvious. Typically followed by a clause (indicative): “Todos saben que + [statement].” In speech you may also hear “Todo el mundo sabe que …” with the same meaning.
target_language_example: Todos saben que mañana es el examen.
native_language_example: Everyone knows that the exam is tomorrow.

meaning: “everyone” / “they all” (used before a verb with se).
additional_notes: Use **todos** as the subject meaning “everyone/they all,” and **se** is the pronoun required by many verbs (often reflexive or describing a change of state): *levantarse* (to get up), *dormirse* (to fall asleep), *irse* (to leave), *reírse* (to laugh), etc. In English you usually translate it as **“everyone”** or **“they all,”** not word-for-word as “all themselves.”
target_language_example: Todos se fueron temprano.
native_language_example: They all left early.

additional_notes: Used to make a general statement that includes everyone in a group (“all of us”). It’s often followed by an adjective or noun: “todos somos responsables” (we’re all responsible). You can also say “todas somos” if the group is all female, and “todos somos” can also be used for mixed groups.
target_language_example: En esta familia, todos somos importantes.
native_language_example: In this family, we are all important.

additional_notes: Used to say that every person/thing in a group has the same quality. It’s the plural of “todo es” (everything is). Often followed by an adjective or a noun: “Todos son altos” (They’re all tall), “Todos son hackers” (They’re all hackers).
target_language_example: En esta clase, todos son muy inteligentes.
native_language_example: In this class, they’re all very smart.

additional_notes: Used to make a general statement about everyone (including the speaker). Often followed by a noun ("todos tenemos problemas") or by "que" + infinitive to express obligation/inevitability ("todos tenemos que morir"). Spanish commonly drops the subject pronoun "nosotros" because "tenemos" already shows it's "we".
target_language_example: Todos tenemos días buenos y días malos.
native_language_example: We all have good days and bad days.

additional_notes: From "todos" (everyone/all) + "tienen" (they have). Used to say that something is true for every person in a group. Often followed by a noun ("Todos tienen secretos") or by "que" to mean "everyone has to" ("Todos tienen que saber...").
target_language_example: Todos tienen que llevar identificación.
native_language_example: Everyone has to carry ID.

additional_notes: Emphatic way to refer to every single person or thing in a group, highlighting individuals one by one. Often used with “de”: “todos y cada uno de ellos/de ustedes/de los sabores.”
target_language_example: Quiero agradecer a todos y cada uno de ustedes por su ayuda.
native_language_example: I want to thank each and every one of you for your help.

meaning: to get some fresh air; to take a breath.
additional_notes: Used when you step outside or pause to breathe and recover (physically or emotionally). In Spanish it’s a common, natural expression; in English you usually say “get some air” or “take a breath” rather than “take air.”
target_language_example: Voy a salir un momento a tomar aire.
native_language_example: I’m going to step out for a moment to get some fresh air.

meaning: to have something (to drink); or to take/pick up something.
additional_notes: Very common phrase. With food/drinks, tomar means “to have” (especially “to drink”): Me gustaría tomar algo = “I’d like to have something (to drink).” With objects, tomar means “to take/grab/pick up”: Necesito tomar algo del auto = “I need to get something from the car.” Context usually makes the meaning clear.
target_language_example: Después del trabajo, podemos tomar algo en un bar.
native_language_example: After work, we can have a drink at a bar.

additional_notes: Common polite phrase used by hosts, receptionists, or staff to invite someone to sit. Often said as an imperative: "Tome asiento" (formal you) or "Toma asiento" (informal you). Also used with "puede": "Puede tomar asiento".
target_language_example: Puede tomar asiento, por favor.
native_language_example: You can take a seat, please.

meaning: to go out for some fresh air.
additional_notes: Used when you step outside (often briefly) to breathe fresh air, get a break, or clear your head. Very common with ir/venir/salir: «Voy a tomar el aire», «Vamos a tomar el aire». It’s not about “taking” air literally; it means going outside for air.
target_language_example: Después de estar todo el día en casa, salí a tomar el aire.
native_language_example: After being at home all day, I went out to get some fresh air.

meaning: to tease someone; to pull someone’s leg (to joke/trick them).
additional_notes: Common in Spain and Latin America. It usually implies you’re joking or making someone believe something that isn’t true. Often used as a question or denial: “¿Me estás tomando el pelo?” / “No te estoy tomando el pelo.” It’s not literally about hair.
target_language_example: ¿Es verdad, o solo quieres tomar el pelo?
native_language_example: Is it true, or are you just pulling my leg?

additional_notes: Used to say you will consider a factor, suggestion, or information when making a decision. Very common with an object (e.g., “tomar en cuenta algo” = to take something into account). In many regions you’ll also hear “tener en cuenta” with the same meaning.
target_language_example: Vamos a tomar en cuenta tu opinión antes de decidir.
native_language_example: We’re going to take your opinion into account before deciding.

meaning: to take the floor; to speak up (in a meeting or group).
additional_notes: Used when someone begins speaking after being given a turn, or when they decide to address a group. Common in formal or semi-formal contexts (meetings, classes, presentations): “Ahora va a tomar la palabra…” = “Now … will speak.” Often contrasted with “pedir la palabra” (to ask to speak).
target_language_example: Al final de la reunión, Marta decidió tomar la palabra para hacer una pregunta.
native_language_example: At the end of the meeting, Marta decided to take the floor to ask a question.

meaning: to take note; to write down.
additional_notes: Used when you want to record information so you don’t forget it. Often followed by "de" + what you’re noting ("Tomé nota de su número"). In polite requests you’ll hear "Tome nota" (formal) or "Toma nota" (informal).
target_language_example: Voy a tomar nota de tu dirección.
native_language_example: I’m going to write down your address.

meaning: to take by surprise; to catch off guard.
additional_notes: Used when something happens unexpectedly and surprises someone. Commonly used in the past tense (e.g., "me tomó por sorpresa") with an event/person as the subject: "La noticia/lluvia/decisión me tomó por sorpresa." Similar in meaning to "sorprender" or "pillar desprevenido/a".
target_language_example: La lluvia nos tomó por sorpresa cuando salimos sin paraguas.
native_language_example: The rain took us by surprise when we went out without an umbrella.

additional_notes: Often used in an impersonal way: "Tomar tiempo + infinitive" or "Tomar tiempo + noun" ("It takes time to…" / "It takes time for…"). In some contexts, it can also mean “to time/measure” something (e.g., timing a race), but beginners most often see it as “to take time.” Related: "tomarse tiempo" = “to take your time.”
target_language_example: Aprender español puede tomar tiempo.
native_language_example: Learning Spanish can take time.

additional_notes: Common with tener que / deber / es hora de to express obligation or urgency: “Tengo que / Debes / Es hora de tomar una decisión.” In the past, it’s often “tuve que tomar una decisión” (“I had to make a decision”).
target_language_example: Necesito más información antes de tomar una decisión.
native_language_example: I need more information before making a decision.

additional_notes: Common way to say you nap, especially a short rest during the day (often after lunch). Uses the verb "tomar" (to take) + "una siesta" (a nap).
target_language_example: Después de comer, voy a tomar una siesta.
native_language_example: After eating, I'm going to take a nap.

meaning: curfew (a required time to be off the streets / at home).
additional_notes: Used to say that authorities have declared or imposed a restriction on movement at certain hours. Common verbs: haber (Hay toque de queda), declarar (Se ha declarado el toque de queda), imponer (Se impuso un toque de queda), cumplir (Tengo que cumplir con el toque de queda).
target_language_example: Durante la emergencia, impusieron un toque de queda a las 10 de la noche.
native_language_example: During the emergency, they imposed a curfew at 10 p.m.

meaning: "works as" (has the job of); also "works like" (in the manner of).
additional_notes: Used with a noun to say someone’s role or profession: "Trabaja como cajero" = "He works as a cashier." With "como + un/una" it can also describe how someone works (a comparison): "trabaja como una hormiga" = "works like an ant" (works very hard). You can change the subject and tense: "Trabajo como…", "Ella trabajaba como…", etc.
target_language_example: Ella trabaja como profesora en una escuela primaria.
native_language_example: She works as a teacher at an elementary school.

meaning: 'works hard' (third-person singular: he/she/it works hard) or 'work hard' (as a command).
additional_notes: From "trabajar" (to work) + "duro" (hard). It can describe what someone does ("Él trabaja duro") or be used as an instruction/encouragement ("¡Trabaja duro!"). You can also change the subject: "Yo trabajo duro", "Nosotros trabajamos duro", "Ellos trabajan duro".
target_language_example: Mi hermana trabaja duro todos los días.
native_language_example: My sister works hard every day.

meaning: 'works in' / 'works at' (a place, company, country, etc.).
additional_notes: Used with "en" to say where someone works: a workplace (en una escuela), a company/store (en Walmart), a field/area (en la televisión), or a location (en Francia). For working *for* a person/company as an employer, Spanish often uses "trabajar para" (e.g., "Trabajo para Google").
target_language_example: Mi mamá trabaja en un hospital.
native_language_example: My mom works at a hospital.

meaning: working hard in the field (doing farm work).
additional_notes: Uses the gerund "trabajando" (working) plus the adverb "duro" (hard) to describe an ongoing activity. Common with forms of "estar" to express what someone is/was/will be doing: "está/estuvo/estará trabajando...". "En el campo" usually refers to the countryside or farm fields.
target_language_example: Estamos trabajando duro en el campo para terminar antes de que anochezca.
native_language_example: We’re working hard in the field to finish before it gets dark.

meaning: to work as; to work like (very hard, like…).
additional_notes: Use **trabajar como + noun** to say someone’s job (**Trabaja como médico** = “He works as a doctor”) or to compare how someone works (**trabajar como esclavo** = “to work like a slave,” i.e., extremely hard). In comparisons, **como** means “like/as,” not a job title.
target_language_example: Es terrible verlos **trabajar como** esclavos en este calor.
native_language_example: It’s terrible to see them work like slaves in this heat.

additional_notes: A common, neutral phrase for putting in a lot of effort at work or toward a goal. Uses the verb trabajar (to work) + duro (hard). You can change the subject/tense: Trabajo duro. / Trabajé duro. / Tengo que trabajar duro.
target_language_example: Si quieres aprobar el examen, tienes que trabajar duro.
native_language_example: If you want to pass the exam, you have to work hard.

additional_notes: Used with places or institutions to say where someone works, and with tasks, projects, or problems to say what someone is working on. In English, this often becomes "work in/at" for places and "work on" for things.
target_language_example: Ella quiere trabajar en un hospital.
native_language_example: She wants to work in a hospital.

additional_notes: Used when two or more people cooperate or collaborate on a task or goal (often on a project). It can describe a one-time effort (Vamos a trabajar juntos en esto) or an ongoing situation (Solíamos trabajar juntos). You can also use it as advice/command: Debéis trabajar juntos.
target_language_example: Si queremos terminar a tiempo, tenemos que trabajar juntos.
native_language_example: If we want to finish on time, we have to work together.

additional_notes: Used to emphasize that someone worked for the whole day (often implying it was tiring). It can refer to working continuously or with only short breaks, depending on context. Common with phrases like "sin parar" (without stopping) and with being tired: "estar cansado/agotado".
target_language_example: No puedo salir esta noche; tengo que trabajar todo el día.
native_language_example: I can’t go out tonight; I have to work all day.

meaning: “I work in/at/on …” (to say where you work or what you work on).
additional_notes: Used with places and organizations: “Trabajo en un supermercado” = “I work at a supermarket.” With projects/areas it can mean “work on/in”: “Trabajo en marketing” / “Trabajo en un proyecto.” Note: “Trabajo en equipo” means “teamwork” or “working as a team.”
target_language_example: Trabajo en una oficina cerca del centro.
native_language_example: I work in an office near downtown.

additional_notes: A common noun phrase meaning people working together as a team toward a shared goal. Often used with verbs like existir (to exist), contar (to matter), and with adjectives like perfecto (perfect).
target_language_example: Para terminar el proyecto a tiempo, necesitamos trabajo en equipo.
native_language_example: To finish the project on time, we need teamwork.

meaning: (some) work to do; tasks that need to be done.
additional_notes: Used with the verb tener to say you have work to do: "Tengo trabajo que hacer". You can add quantity/degree words like "mucho", "tanto", "un montón de", or adjectives like "importante": "Tengo mucho trabajo que hacer", "Tenemos importante trabajo que hacer". Similar to "cosas que hacer" (things to do).
target_language_example: No puedo salir hoy; tengo trabajo que hacer.
native_language_example: I can’t go out today; I have work to do.

additional_notes: Common way to refer to swimwear in general. Used for both men’s and women’s swimwear (one-piece, bikini, swim trunks), depending on context. Plural: "trajes de baño".
target_language_example: ¿Dónde está mi traje de baño?
native_language_example: Where is my swimsuit?

additional_notes:
Two common uses:
1) **Tratar de + noun** = “to deal with / to be about” (often in definitions or explanations): *La ética... trata de la conducta humana.*
2) **Tratar de + infinitive** = “to try to (do something)”: *Trata de dormir*, *Él trata de ver...*. In commands, **Trata de...** means “Try to...”. (Very common with **no**: *Trata de no preocuparte* = “Try not to worry.”)
target_language_example: Trata de llegar temprano mañana.
native_language_example: Try to arrive early tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used to give advice or a gentle command: trata de (infinitive) = “try to …”, and trata de no (infinitive) = “try not to …”. It’s the tú (informal singular) command form of tratar; for a more formal/polite version use “trate de no …”. Common with reflexive verbs: “trata de no preocuparte / ponerte tenso(a)” = “try not to worry / get tense.”
target_language_example: Trata de no contestar sin pensar.
native_language_example: Try not to answer without thinking.

additional_notes: Used with an infinitive (verb in the "to + verb" form): "tratando de + verbo" (e.g., tratando de ahorrar, tratando de averiguar). Often appears with "estar" for an action in progress: "estoy/está/están tratando de..." It can also follow time expressions to show ongoing effort: "Pasé toda la tarde tratando de..."
target_language_example: Estoy tratando de aprender español, pero es difícil.
native_language_example: I'm trying to learn Spanish, but it's hard.

meaning: to deal with (a person or situation).
additional_notes: Often used for handling a difficult person or managing a problem/situation. Common patterns: "tratar con alguien" (deal with someone) and "tratar con algo/esto" (deal with something/this).
target_language_example: No sé cómo tratar con este problema.
native_language_example: I don’t know how to deal with this problem.

additional_notes: Used before an infinitive to say someone makes an effort to do something: tratar de + infinitive. Don't confuse it with other uses of tratar, which can mean things like 'to deal with' or 'to be about.'
target_language_example: Voy a tratar de llegar temprano.
native_language_example: I'm going to try to arrive early.

meaning: 'try to' (usted form); also, in 'se trate de', 'be about / be a'.
additional_notes: From the verb "tratar de". "Trate de + infinitive" is often a polite/formal command to one person (usted): "Trate de comprender" = "Try to understand." It can also appear after expressions like "Es posible que..." with the present subjunctive: "Es posible que trate de hacerlo". With "se trate de + noun", it means "it may be about / it may be a": "Puede que se trate de un bandido" = "It might be a bandit."
target_language_example: Trate de llegar temprano, por favor.
native_language_example: Try to arrive early, please.

additional_notes: Used with an infinitive (trato de + verb) to talk about making an effort to do something. Often implies the action is difficult or not guaranteed: Trato de no pensar en eso. In many contexts you may also hear "trato" without "de" (Trato de ayudar / Trato ayudar), but "trato de" is very common.
target_language_example: Trato de llegar temprano, pero siempre hay tráfico.
native_language_example: I try to arrive early, but there’s always traffic.

additional_notes: Used to confirm that an agreement has been reached (often after negotiating). Similar to saying “Deal!” or “You’ve got a deal.” You’ll also hear it as a question: “¿Trato hecho?” = “Deal?”
target_language_example: Si tú traes la comida, yo pongo las bebidas: trato hecho.
native_language_example: If you bring the food, I’ll bring the drinks: it’s a deal.

additional_notes: "traté de" is the preterite (simple past) first-person singular of "tratar de" + infinitive. It describes an attempt you made at a specific moment in the past; it doesn’t necessarily imply success. Common pattern: "traté de" + infinitive (hacer, conseguir, escribir, no reírme, etc.).
target_language_example: Ayer traté de llamarte, pero no contestaste.
native_language_example: Yesterday I tried to call you, but you didn’t answer.

additional_notes: Past tense (preterite) of the phrase “tratar de + infinitive” = “to try to do something.” It’s followed by an infinitive: “trató de convencer”, “trató de consolar”. Often used when you want to say someone made an effort, whether or not they succeeded. Note: “tratar” can look like English “treat,” but “tratar de” usually means “to try to,” not “to treat.”
target_language_example: Ella trató de llamarte, pero no pudo.
native_language_example: She tried to call you, but she couldn’t.

additional_notes: Most commonly used as **a través de** (with **a**): *a través de internet* (via the internet), *a través de la ventana* (through the window). It can refer to a physical path (“through”) or a method/channel (“via/by means of”).
target_language_example: Te enviaré los documentos a través de correo electrónico.
native_language_example: I’ll send you the documents via email.

meaning: through / via / by means of the.
additional_notes: In standard Spanish you almost always say **a través de la** (with **a**): *a través de* + noun. It’s used for physical movement (*through the window*), but very commonly for methods or channels (*via the internet*, *through the company*). For plural, use **a través de las**.
target_language_example: Te enviaré el documento a través de la aplicación.
native_language_example: I’ll send you the document through the app.

additional_notes: Used mainly to talk about someone’s age with the verb "tener": "Tengo trece años" = "I’m thirteen." Also used with "cuando tenía trece años" to mean "when I was thirteen." In Spanish you generally say you "have" years, not "are" years old.
target_language_example: Tengo trece años y estoy en octavo grado.
native_language_example: I’m thirteen years old and I’m in eighth grade.

meaning: "thirty years" (an age or a length of time).
