additional_notes: Used to introduce the items that follow (often with a noun or an infinitive clause): una lista de cosas, una lista de precios, una lista de lo que me debes. It’s also common with verbs like hacer (to make), tener (to have), mantener (to keep), and mostrar/enseñar (to show).
target_language_example: Necesito una lista de invitados para la fiesta.
native_language_example: I need a list of guests for the party.

additional_notes: Usually refers to a telephone call. Common with verbs like hacer (to make): "hacer una llamada", and recibir (to receive/get): "recibir una llamada". You may also hear it for a "call" in a meeting/work sense (a scheduled phone/video call): "Tenemos una llamada". "Una llamada en espera" means a call on hold/call waiting.
target_language_example: Voy a hacer una llamada y vuelvo enseguida.
native_language_example: I'm going to make a call and I'll be right back.

meaning: “crazy” / “madness”; something unbelievable or out of control.
additional_notes: Used to describe a situation, idea, or place as very chaotic, intense, unreasonable, or hard to believe. Often appears as “Es una locura” (It’s crazy) or “Es toda una locura” (It’s totally crazy). Also common: “Se está volviendo una locura” = “It’s becoming crazy here.”
target_language_example: ¡Este tráfico es una locura!
native_language_example: This traffic is crazy!

additional_notes: Used to judge someone’s character as bad or unkind. It’s strong and insulting in direct statements like “Eres/Sos una mala persona.” You can negate it with “No soy…” and it also appears after “ser” in past stories: “resultó ser una mala persona” (“turned out to be a bad person”). “Eres” is common in Spain; “Sos” is common in Argentina/Uruguay.
target_language_example: No creo que seas una mala persona; solo cometiste un error.
native_language_example: I don’t think you’re a bad person; you just made a mistake.

additional_notes: Used before a feminine noun (or a feminine adjective used like a noun) to add anger, emphasis, or insult: "una maldita infección" = "a damn infection." The masculine form is "un maldito" (e.g., "un maldito problema"). Very vulgar in many contexts; avoid in polite conversation.
target_language_example: No puedo encontrar una maldita llave.
native_language_example: I can’t find a damn key.

additional_notes: Used to talk about a method/approach for doing something: "una manera de + infinitive" (una manera de salir, evitar, describir). It can also be used more generally to mean "a way of saying/describing something" and may sound a bit like "that's one way to put it."
target_language_example: ¿Hay una manera de pagar con tarjeta?
native_language_example: Is there a way to pay by card?

additional_notes: Literally means “a hand” (part of the body), as in holding something with one hand. Very commonly used in the expression «echar una mano (a alguien)», meaning “to give someone a hand / to help someone.”
target_language_example: ¿Me echas una mano con estas cajas?
native_language_example: Can you give me a hand with these boxes?

additional_notes: Refers to the fruit. "Una" is the feminine form of "a/an" because "manzana" is feminine. In some contexts, "manzana" can also mean a city block, but the examples here clearly mean the fruit.
target_language_example: ¿Quieres una manzana?
native_language_example: Do you want an apple?

additional_notes: A feminine noun meaning a false statement. Commonly used with verbs like decir (to tell) or contar (to tell). Contrast: una verdad (a truth).
target_language_example: No digas una mentira; dime la verdad.
native_language_example: Don’t tell a lie; tell me the truth.

additional_notes: Used to refer to a (usually unspecified) table. Common in restaurants when asking someone to find/get a table: “¿Nos buscas una mesa?” = “Can you find us a table?”
target_language_example: ¿Hay una mesa para dos?
native_language_example: Is there a table for two?

additional_notes: Very vulgar and insulting. Used to call a person or thing “worthless” (Eres una mierda; Mis amigos, una mierda) or to refer to something bad that happened (una mierda atroz). In negative sentences it can mean “nothing at all” (no ver una mierda = not see a thing). As a standalone exclamation (¡Una mierda!) it expresses strong disgust or dismissal (“This is bullshit/This sucks”).
target_language_example: No entiendo una mierda de lo que estás diciendo.
native_language_example: I don’t understand a damn thing of what you’re saying.

additional_notes: Often used with verbs like echar/dar (“to take a look”) and with an indirect object pronoun: échale/dale una mirada ("take a look at it/him/her"). Can also be made more specific: una mirada de cerca ("a closer look").
target_language_example: ¿Puedes echarle una mirada a este documento, por favor?
native_language_example: Can you take a look at this document, please?

meaning: a mission; an important task (sometimes secret).
additional_notes: Used for a purposeful assignment or job you’ve been given (often with a sense of importance). It can be everyday (“a task”) or more dramatic/official (“a mission”), and it’s common to add adjectives like importante, secreta, especial. With estar/en: “Estoy en una misión” = “I’m on a mission.”
target_language_example: Mañana salgo temprano porque estoy en una misión especial.
native_language_example: Tomorrow I’m leaving early because I’m on a special mission.

additional_notes: Refers to a single coin (physical money). Often used when you need change (e.g., for a pay phone, vending machine) or when something costs very little. Plural: "monedas". Also note: "moneda" can sometimes mean "currency" in general depending on context (e.g., "la moneda local"), but "una moneda" usually means one coin.
target_language_example: ¿Tienes una moneda de un euro para la máquina?
native_language_example: Do you have a one-euro coin for the machine?

additional_notes: Used with the indefinite article "una" to mean "a fly". Very common in everyday situations (finding an insect in food/drinks, swatting a fly, etc.). Plural: "moscas".
target_language_example: Hay una mosca en la sopa.
native_language_example: There’s a fly in the soup.

additional_notes: Used for (1) a physical sample taken for testing (often with verbs like tomar/sacar una muestra: una muestra de sangre/orina/ADN) and (2) an expression of a feeling or intention (una muestra de amor/cariño/agradecimiento).
target_language_example: El médico tomó una muestra de sangre para el análisis.
native_language_example: The doctor took a blood sample for the test.

additional_notes: Most commonly refers to a toy doll (as in the examples). Note: “muñeca” can also mean “wrist” in other contexts (e.g., “Me duele la muñeca” = “My wrist hurts”).
target_language_example: Compré una muñeca para mi sobrina.
native_language_example: I bought a doll for my niece.

additional_notes: Used for a physical machine or piece of equipment in general (una máquina en la fábrica). It can also mean a specific device used for a purpose, especially in medical/technical contexts (una máquina para ayudarle a respirar; una máquina que transmite páginas por teléfono = a fax machine). In casual speech, "Es una máquina" can also mean someone is amazingly skilled or efficient (“He/She’s a machine”).
target_language_example: Necesitamos una máquina nueva para cortar la madera.
native_language_example: We need a new machine to cut the wood.

additional_notes: “Naranja” is the fruit (and also the color “orange,” as in “color naranja”). With “una,” it means one orange. You’ll often hear comparisons like “como una naranja” to describe something round (e.g., “forma parecida a la de una naranja” = a shape similar to an orange’s).
target_language_example: ¿Quieres una naranja?
native_language_example: Do you want an orange?

additional_notes: Means “a girl” (often a child). It uses the indefinite article una (“a/an”) + niña (“girl”). In some contexts it can imply “young/childlike,” depending on tone (e.g., vestir como una niña = dress like a little girl). You may also see fixed expressions like niña de iglesia (“church girl,” i.e., a very proper/religious girl).
target_language_example: Hay una niña jugando en el parque.
native_language_example: There’s a girl playing in the park.

meaning: a night; one night (a single night).
additional_notes: Used to talk about nighttime in general ("Es una noche hermosa") or to emphasize that something happened on a single night ("una noche extraña"). With weather, Spanish often uses "Hace una noche..." to mean “It’s a ... night” (e.g., "Hace una noche preciosa"). In "la aventura de una noche", it means a “one-night” adventure/stand (something that lasts only that night).
target_language_example: Solo fue una noche, pero no la voy a olvidar.
native_language_example: It was only one night, but I’m not going to forget it.

additional_notes: Often used with verbs like "dejar" (to leave) or "escribir" (to write): "Te dejé una nota" = "I left you a note." It usually means a short written message (on paper, a sticky note, etc.), not a grade.
target_language_example: Si no estás, te dejo una nota en la mesa.
native_language_example: If you’re not there, I’ll leave you a note on the table.

additional_notes: Used for a long story in book form, usually fiction. You can use it with verbs like escribir (to write) and leer (to read): escribir una novela, leer una novela. For a soap opera on TV, Spanish often uses telenovela instead.
target_language_example: Estoy leyendo una novela nueva esta semana.
native_language_example: I’m reading a new novel this week.

meaning: a cloud; a cloud (of dust/smoke, etc.).
additional_notes: Most commonly means a cloud in the sky. It’s also used figuratively for a large mass of something in the air: una nube de polvo (a cloud of dust), una nube de humo (a cloud of smoke). Often used with prepositions like tras (behind) or por (across/through) when describing movement or position.
target_language_example: Salió una nube de humo de la chimenea.
native_language_example: A cloud of smoke came out of the chimney.

additional_notes: Used before a feminine noun to mean “a new …”: una nueva estrella (a new star), una nueva estrategia (a new strategy). The adjective agrees in gender/number: una nueva (feminine singular), un nuevo (masculine singular), unas nuevas (feminine plural), unos nuevos (masculine plural). It can also be used as “a new one” when the noun is understood from context.
target_language_example: Necesito una nueva porque la vieja ya no funciona.
native_language_example: I need a new one because the old one doesn’t work anymore.

meaning: a new life; a fresh start.
additional_notes: Used when someone begins living in a different way (often after a big change like moving, changing jobs, or leaving a past situation). Very common with verbs like empezar/comenzar (to start), comenzar de nuevo (to start again), or mudarse (to move).
target_language_example: Después de la separación, ella decidió empezar una nueva vida en otra ciudad.
native_language_example: After the separation, she decided to start a new life in another city.

meaning: once or twice; a few times.
additional_notes: Used to say something happened a small number of times, often approximate (not necessarily exactly one or exactly two). It can soften what you’re saying ("I’ve only seen her a couple of times").
target_language_example: He estado en Madrid una o dos veces, pero quiero volver.
native_language_example: I’ve been to Madrid once or twice, but I want to go back.

meaning: a play; a work (piece of art/creation).
additional_notes: Often means a theatrical play (una obra de teatro), especially with verbs like escribir (to write) or ver (to see). More generally, obra can mean a creative work (book, artwork, music), depending on context.
target_language_example: Vamos a ver una obra esta noche.
native_language_example: We’re going to see a play tonight.

additional_notes: Used for a chance to do something (often with verbs like dar/den/darle: "to give (someone) a chance"). Very common in requests: "Dame una oportunidad" = "Give me a chance." You can add más (more), otra (another), or describe it: "una oportunidad única" (a unique opportunity).
target_language_example: ¿Me das una oportunidad de explicarlo?
native_language_example: Will you give me a chance to explain it?

meaning: an order; a command; (legal) an order/warrant.
additional_notes: Often means an instruction that must be obeyed: «Esto es una orden» (“This is an order”). In legal/police contexts it can mean an official document/authorization, like «una orden de registro» (“a search warrant”).
target_language_example: El jefe dio una orden clara: nadie sale hasta terminar el trabajo.
native_language_example: The boss gave a clear order: nobody leaves until the work is finished.

additional_notes: Used to refer to a single word in general, often when talking about vocabulary, what someone said, or the power of language. Also appears in expressions like “Una palabra llevó a la otra” (“One word led to another”), meaning a conversation developed from one thing said to the next.
target_language_example: Solo necesito una palabra para describirlo: increíble.
native_language_example: I only need one word to describe it: incredible.

additional_notes: Usually means a physical beating (someone hits someone else a lot): Darle una paliza a alguien = to beat someone up. It can also be used more generally for a severe defeat (especially in sports/games): Dar una paliza (al equipo rival) = to crush them.
target_language_example: Si sigues molestándolo, te van a dar una paliza.
native_language_example: If you keep bothering him, they’re going to beat you up.

meaning: a couple (two people together, often romantic).
additional_notes: Commonly used for two people in a relationship ("Son una pareja" = they’re a couple). It can also refer to any pair of beings/animals ("una pareja de gorriones" = a pair of sparrows). For “partner” as a person, Spanish also uses "mi pareja" (my partner), especially in more neutral/inclusive contexts.
target_language_example: Ellos son una pareja desde hace dos años.
native_language_example: They’ve been a couple for two years.

meaning: (informal) “amazing / awesome”; also “a (mean) trick / prank” (in: jugar/hacer una pasada).
additional_notes: Very common in Spain as an exclamation or short comment: “¡Una pasada!” = “So awesome!” Used with ser (“Es una pasada”) or with eso/esto (“Eso es una pasada”). In the pattern “jugarle/hacerle una pasada a alguien,” it means to play a trick on someone or do something sneaky to them.
target_language_example: ¡El concierto fue una pasada!
native_language_example: The concert was awesome!

additional_notes: Used for a physical fight (sometimes like a boxing match) or for a verbal disagreement between people. Common with verbs like "tener" (to have) and "pelear" (to fight).
target_language_example: No quiero tener una pelea contigo.
native_language_example: I don’t want to have a fight with you.

additional_notes: Use it to talk about a single movie/film. Película is feminine, so it goes with una/la/esta/esa: una película (a movie), la película (the movie). For plural: películas (movies).
target_language_example: ¿Quieres ver una película esta noche?
native_language_example: Do you want to watch a movie tonight?

additional_notes: Used before a feminine singular noun: una pequeña ciudad (a small city), una pequeña linterna (a small flashlight). It agrees in gender/number: un pequeño (masc.), unas pequeñas (fem. plural), unos pequeños (masc. plural). On its own, la/una pequeña can also mean “the/a little girl” depending on context.
target_language_example: Compré una pequeña libreta para tomar notas.
native_language_example: I bought a small notebook to take notes.

additional_notes: Means “a person” (one human being). It’s often used to describe someone with an adjective (e.g., “una persona inteligente” = “an intelligent person”). The article changes with gender/number: “una persona” (a person), “la persona” (the person), “personas” (people). Note: “persona” is grammatically feminine, so you say “una persona buena/mala/inteligente” even if the person is male.
target_language_example: Es una persona muy amable y siempre ayuda a los demás.
native_language_example: He/She is a very kind person and always helps others.

additional_notes: Most often means a bad dream (Tener una pesadilla = “to have a nightmare”). It’s also commonly used figuratively to describe something very unpleasant or stressful: “Fue una pesadilla” = “It was a nightmare.”
target_language_example: El examen fue una pesadilla, pero al final lo pasé.
native_language_example: The exam was a nightmare, but in the end I passed it.

additional_notes: Usually literal (a physical stone/rock): tropezarse con una piedra (to trip over a stone), levantar una piedra (to pick up a stone). It can also be used in comparisons to describe someone/something as hard, cold, or emotionless (e.g., frío como una piedra = “cold as a stone”).
target_language_example: Cuidado, hay una piedra en el camino.
native_language_example: Careful, there’s a rock on the path.

additional_notes: Used when you have (or give) a piece of information that helps you discover something or solve a mystery/problem. Common with verbs like tener (to have), dar (to give), encontrar (to find), and ser (to be): «Tengo una pista», «Te doy una pista».
target_language_example: Si te doy una pista, ¿puedes adivinar la respuesta?
native_language_example: If I give you a hint, can you guess the answer?

additional_notes: Usually refers to a handgun. It’s a feminine noun: una pistola; la pistola; dos pistolas. In negative sentences: no tengo una pistola (“I don’t have a gun”).
target_language_example: No quiero tener una pistola en casa.
native_language_example: I don’t want to have a gun at home.

additional_notes: Most commonly, **pluma** means a **pen** (especially in Latin America; in Spain you may hear **bolígrafo** more). It can also mean a **feather**, as in **ligero(a) como una pluma** (“as light as a feather”) or when talking about a feather stuck in someone’s hair/clothes. Context usually makes the meaning clear.
target_language_example: Necesito una pluma para firmar este documento.
native_language_example: I need a pen to sign this document.

additional_notes: Means “a question” (something you ask to get information). Very common with the verbs tener (“to have”) and hacer (“to ask” / literally “to make”): Tengo una pregunta. / Quiero hacerte una pregunta. Use un/una depending on gender; pregunta is feminine, so it’s una pregunta.
target_language_example: Perdón, tengo una pregunta sobre la tarea.
native_language_example: Sorry, I have a question about the homework.

additional_notes: Used when someone commits to doing (or not doing) something. With hacer: hacer una promesa = "to make a promise". In your examples, haga/hagas are from hacer (subjunctive) after quiero que...: Quiero que me haga/hagas una promesa = "I want you to promise me (something)."
target_language_example: Te hago una promesa: mañana te llamo.
native_language_example: I promise you: I’ll call you tomorrow.

additional_notes: A very common noun meaning a “test” in many contexts. Often used with “de” + noun: “una prueba de fe” (a test of faith), “una prueba de sonido” (a soundcheck). With “hacer una prueba” it can mean doing a tryout/audition or running a test.
target_language_example: Mañana tengo una prueba de matemáticas.
native_language_example: Tomorrow I have a math test.

additional_notes: A common noun for the animal. Feminine: la rata / una rata. Plural: las ratas / unas ratas. Often used with colors or descriptions (una rata blanca, una rata grande).
target_language_example: En el sótano hay una rata.
native_language_example: There is a rat in the basement.

additional_notes: Most commonly means a romantic relationship (e.g., "Estoy en una relación" = "I’m in a relationship"). It can also mean a non-romantic connection or bond: "una relación de amistad" (a friendship) or "tener una relación con" someone (to have a connection/relationship with). In some contexts it can imply an affair or inappropriate relationship ("tuvo una relación inapropiada").
target_language_example: No quiero tener una relación a larga distancia.
native_language_example: I don’t want to have a long-distance relationship.

meaning: an answer; a reply; a response.
additional_notes: Used for answers to questions (una respuesta a cada pregunta) and for replies to messages/letters/emails (una respuesta a su carta / a este correo). Often followed by "a" + what it answers/replies to ("una respuesta a..."), or described with an adjective ("una respuesta amable").
target_language_example: Todavía no tengo una respuesta a mi solicitud.
native_language_example: I still don’t have a response to my request.

additional_notes: Common noun for a planned gathering—often for work (una reunión de oficina), but it can also be private or informal. Often used with tener to say you have a meeting: “Tengo una reunión esta tarde.” You can modify it with adjectives like importante (important), larga (long), or secreta (secret).
target_language_example: Tengo una reunión esta tarde.
native_language_example: I have a meeting this afternoon.

additional_notes: Use it to talk about a printed or digital magazine. It’s a feminine noun: la revista (the magazine), una revista (a magazine). Common verbs with it: comprar una revista (to buy a magazine), leer una revista (to read a magazine), ver algo en una revista (to see something in a magazine).
target_language_example: Estoy leyendo una revista en el tren.
native_language_example: I’m reading a magazine on the train.

meaning: a rock; (figurative) someone/something very hard or very solid.
additional_notes: Literal meaning: a physical rock/stone. Very common in comparisons: “duro como una roca” (hard as a rock), “firme y sólido como una roca” (steady/solid as a rock). It can also be used insultingly to mean someone is not intelligent: “tener el intelecto de una roca” (to have the intellect of a rock).
target_language_example: La puerta es tan pesada como una roca.
native_language_example: The door is as heavy as a rock.

additional_notes: Used to refer to one rose. Often appears with color adjectives (e.g., "una rosa roja" = "a red rose"). Common with prepositions like "en" (una rosa en la mano / en el florero) and with "dar" in gift-giving contexts (darle una rosa a alguien = to give someone a rose).
target_language_example: Compré una rosa para mi amiga.
native_language_example: I bought a rose for my friend.

meaning: an exit; a way out (a solution).
additional_notes: Often means a physical exit (like a door out of a building): "Hay una salida." It can also be used more figuratively to mean a solution or escape from a problem: "Siempre encuentra una salida" = he always finds a way out. Common sign: "Salida" (Exit).
target_language_example: No te preocupes, siempre hay una salida.
native_language_example: Don’t worry, there’s always a way out.

additional_notes: Used to ask for or talk about getting another opportunity to try again, usually after a mistake or failure. Very common with verbs like dar (to give) and tener (to have): “Dame una segunda oportunidad” (Give me a second chance), “tener una segunda oportunidad” (to have a second chance).
target_language_example: Por favor, dame una segunda oportunidad.
native_language_example: Please, give me a second chance.

additional_notes: Means a period of seven days. Often used with expressions like "para una semana" (for a week; enough to last a week), "tras una semana" (after a week), and "una semana antes" (a week before).
target_language_example: Voy a estar fuera una semana.
native_language_example: I’m going to be away for a week.

meaning: a series of; a number of.
additional_notes: Used before a plural noun to talk about multiple things happening or existing, often in sequence (events, concerts, explosions) or as a set (rules). It’s common in both formal and neutral contexts.
target_language_example: Hubo una serie de problemas durante el viaje.
native_language_example: There were a series of problems during the trip.

additional_notes: Literally refers to the animal. It’s feminine: una serpiente / la serpiente. You can add adjectives after it (una serpiente gigante) or describe a type with “de” (una serpiente de X).
target_language_example: Hay una serpiente en el jardín.
native_language_example: There’s a snake in the garden.

additional_notes: Used for a physical signal (a gesture, sound, light, etc.) or for a “sign” that you interpret as meaning something (“I’ll take it as a sign”). Common verbs: hacer una señal (to signal/make a sign), dar una señal (to give a signal), tomar algo como una señal (to take something as a sign).
target_language_example: Si llegas, hazme una señal.
native_language_example: If you arrive, give me a signal.

additional_notes: Often used with verbs like echarse/tomarse/darse una siesta (to take a nap). Very common in Spain and some Spanish-speaking countries as a short rest after lunch. You can also say: Tengo ganas de echarme una siesta (I feel like taking a nap).
target_language_example: Después de comer, me voy a echar una siesta.
native_language_example: After lunch, I'm going to take a nap.

additional_notes: Refers to a single chair; "una" is the feminine form of "a/an" used with feminine nouns like "silla". Common with verbs like "sentarse" (to sit down) and phrases like "sentado/a en una silla" (sitting on a chair).
target_language_example: ¿Me puedes traer una silla, por favor?
native_language_example: Can you bring me a chair, please?

meaning: a situation; a set of circumstances (often a problem).
additional_notes: Used for any circumstance or state of affairs, but very often implies something difficult, urgent, or problematic: “Tenemos una situación.” Common patterns: “una situación peligrosa/seria/absurda”, “estar en una situación (mejor/peor)”.
target_language_example: Estamos en una situación complicada y necesitamos ayuda.
native_language_example: We’re in a complicated situation and we need help.

additional_notes: Used before a feminine noun to emphasize that there is only one of something (e.g., una sola pierna, una sola maleta). It can also mean “only one” in expressions like una sola dirección (“a single direction”) or una sola cosa más (“just one more thing”). Masculine form: un solo.
target_language_example: Solo tengo una sola pregunta.
native_language_example: I only have one question.

meaning: a solution (an answer or way to fix a problem).
additional_notes: Used with verbs like hay/no hay (“there is/isn’t”) or buscar/encontrar (“to look for/find”) when talking about solving a problem. Often followed by an adjective: una solución simple/rápida/definitiva (“a simple/quick/final solution”).
target_language_example: Estamos buscando una solución para este problema.
native_language_example: We’re looking for a solution to this problem.

additional_notes: A common noun phrase used to describe someone’s facial expression. Often used with verbs like tener (to have) and with (con) to describe how someone speaks or acts: con una sonrisa = “with a smile.” It can also be used figuratively (e.g., hiding sadness behind a smile).
target_language_example: Me saludó con una sonrisa.
native_language_example: He/She greeted me with a smile.

additional_notes: A common noun phrase used with the verb ser: "Fue/Es una sorpresa" = "It was/is a surprise." You may also hear "toda una sorpresa" to emphasize that something was really surprising. "Sorpresa agradable" means "pleasant/nice surprise."
target_language_example: Tu llamada fue una sorpresa agradable.
native_language_example: Your call was a nice surprise.

meaning: a cake; sometimes a tart/pie (depending on the country).
additional_notes: In many places, *tarta* commonly means a cake (often decorated, like a birthday cake). It can also refer to a tart/pie, especially when followed by *de + flavor/ingredient* (e.g., *tarta de manzana*). The exact meaning varies by region; in Mexico, *pastel* is more common for “cake.”
target_language_example: Para mi cumpleaños quiero una tarta de chocolate.
native_language_example: For my birthday I want a chocolate cake.

additional_notes: A very common, literal phrase: una (a) + taza (cup) + de (of) + café (coffee). Used when offering, ordering, or asking someone to make coffee. With hot drinks, Spanish often uses “taza” (cup/mug). You can also hear “un café” in cafés/restaurants to mean “a coffee” in general, but “una taza de café” is more specific.
target_language_example: ¿Te apetece una taza de café?
native_language_example: Do you feel like a cup of coffee?

additional_notes: Used when ordering, offering, or talking about drinking tea. Common with verbs like querer (to want), beber/tomar (to drink), traer (to bring), and preparar (to prepare).
target_language_example: ¿Me puedes preparar una taza de té, por favor?
native_language_example: Can you make me a cup of tea, please?

additional_notes: Used to refer to a towel (bath towel, hand towel, etc.). It often appears with adjectives like seca (dry) or húmeda (damp/wet), or with a material: de algodón (cotton). You can also specify the type: una toalla de papel = a paper towel.
target_language_example: Después de nadar, necesito una toalla limpia.
native_language_example: After swimming, I need a clean towel.

additional_notes: A common noun phrase used to talk about bad weather; often appears with verbs like "se aproxima" (is approaching) or "es inminente" (is imminent). Can refer to a strong storm that is dangerous or causes damage.
target_language_example: Cancelaron el partido por una tormenta.
native_language_example: They canceled the game because of a storm.

additional_notes: Used for a physical device that catches something (like a mousetrap) and also for a situation meant to deceive someone ("It could be a trap"). Often used with "ser" or "parecer": "Es una trampa" / "Podría ser una trampa".
target_language_example: No entres ahí: podría ser una trampa.
native_language_example: Don’t go in there: it could be a trap.

additional_notes: Used before a feminine noun to emphasize that something really is that thing (often like English “a real…” or “a true…”): “una verdadera lata” = “a real pain/annoyance.” It can also be used for strong praise (“una verdadera máquina” = “a real machine”) or to say something doesn’t fully qualify (“No es una verdadera mansión” = “It’s not a real mansion”). Feminine form: use it with feminine nouns; with masculine nouns you’d say “un verdadero”.
target_language_example: Es una verdadera sorpresa.
native_language_example: It’s a real surprise.

additional_notes: Literally means "one time." It often refers to a single occasion in the past ("I once saw..."). It can also introduce a time condition meaning "once" or "when," as in "una vez adentro" = "once inside."
target_language_example: Una vez fui a México con my familia.
native_language_example: I went to Mexico once with my family.

additional_notes: Used to talk about how often something happens (frequency). You can swap the time period: una vez al día (once a day), una vez al mes (once a month). Often placed at the end of the sentence.
target_language_example: Voy al gimnasio una vez a la semana.
native_language_example: I go to the gym once a week.

additional_notes: Used to say how often something happens. You can swap the time period: una vez al mes (once a month), una vez a la semana (once a week), una vez al día (once a day).
target_language_example: Voy al dentista una vez al año.
native_language_example: I go to the dentist once a year.

additional_notes: Used to say how often something happens. It often goes at the end of the sentence, but it can also be placed at the beginning for emphasis.
target_language_example: Pago la renta una vez al mes.
native_language_example: I pay rent once a month.

additional_notes: Used to indicate repetition (doing/saying something again). Very common in everyday speech and works in many contexts: asking again, checking again, explaining again, etc. It can also stand alone for emphasis (e.g., “Y una vez más.” = “And once again.”).
target_language_example: ¿Puedes decirlo una vez más, por favor?
native_language_example: Can you say it one more time, please?

additional_notes: Used to say that one action happens after another is completed. It introduces a clause, typically in the subjunctive when referring to the future (Una vez que lleguemos...) and often in the past/indicative for completed events (Una vez que terminó...). Similar to "después de que" (after).
target_language_example: Una vez que termines tu tarea, puedes salir.
native_language_example: Once you finish your homework, you can go out.

additional_notes: Means “a life” in general. Often used with an adjective to describe someone’s way of living: una vida normal (a normal life), una vida decente (a decent life), una vida mejor (a better life), una vida fácil (an easy life).
target_language_example: Ella quiere llevar una vida tranquila.
native_language_example: She wants to live a quiet life.

meaning: "an old" (feminine), used before a feminine noun (e.g., una vieja foto = an old photo).
additional_notes: In your examples, "vieja" is an adjective meaning "old" and it agrees with a feminine noun: una vieja cabaña / una vieja foto / una vieja librería / una vieja canción. Spanish often places some adjectives (like "viejo/a") before the noun; it can sound more descriptive, familiar, or subjective. Be careful: "una vieja" by itself can also mean "an old woman" and can sound rude depending on context (more neutral: "una señora mayor").
target_language_example: Encontré una vieja carta en una caja.
native_language_example: I found an old letter in a box.

additional_notes: Used for the act of visiting someone/somewhere, or for the stay/occasion itself. Common patterns: “hacer una visita” = “to pay/make a visit”; “una visita de + person” = “a visit from/by + person”; “estar/ir a + place + por una visita” = “to be/go to + place for a visit.”
target_language_example: ¿Quieres venir a casa para una visita este fin de semana?
native_language_example: Do you want to come to my place for a visit this weekend?

meaning: a vision; a view/perspective (an idea of how something is or should be).
additional_notes: Used for (1) a literal/supernatural or imagined “vision” (a scene you see in your mind), and (2) a figurative “vision” meaning an outlook, perspective, or guiding idea/plan (e.g., una visión de la vida / una visión nueva). It can also mean a representation or portrait of something (e.g., una visión de la sociedad).
target_language_example: Necesitamos una visión clara para el futuro del proyecto.
native_language_example: We need a clear vision for the future of the project.

additional_notes: Used to talk about someone’s speaking or singing voice ("una voz hermosa", "una voz maravillosa"), or a voice you hear ("una voz en la cabeza"). In some places you’ll also hear informal expressions like "dar/pegar una voz" meaning “to give someone a shout / call out to someone” (e.g., "Si necesitas algo, pégame una voz").
target_language_example: Ella tiene una voz muy suave.
native_language_example: She has a very soft voice.

meaning: a walk/ride around; a turn; (with "darle una vuelta") to think it over.
additional_notes: "Dar una vuelta" is very common and means to go for a walk/drive/ride around (often casually or for a short time): "Doy una vuelta". "Dar una vuelta" can also mean to turn something over/around. With an object pronoun + "darle una vuelta (a algo)", it often means "to think about it again / to reconsider": "Dale una vuelta" (Think it over).
target_language_example: Voy a dar una vuelta por el barrio y vuelvo.
native_language_example: I’m going to take a walk around the neighborhood and I’ll be back.

additional_notes: Used to emphasize repetition (doing/saying/experiencing the same thing many times). Often goes at the end of the sentence, but it can also appear earlier for emphasis.
target_language_example: Te lo he explicado una y otra vez.
native_language_example: I’ve explained it to you again and again.

additional_notes: Usually means 'one of' when referring to a feminine noun or to a group: una de ustedes = one of you. It can also refer back to a feminine noun understood from context, as in Hay una de Madagascar = There's one from Madagascar. In time expressions, it appears in longer phrases such as la una de la mañana (1 a.m.).
target_language_example: Una de mis amigas vive en Sevilla.
native_language_example: One of my friends lives in Seville.

additional_notes: Used when there are only two possible choices or outcomes. Often followed by two alternatives: “Una de dos: o vienes tú, o voy yo.” It can also be used alone to mean “it’s got to be one of the two.”
target_language_example: Una de dos: o me llamas hoy, o lo dejamos para mañana.
native_language_example: One of two: either you call me today, or we leave it for tomorrow.

meaning: “one of them” (referring to a group of females or feminine things).
additional_notes: Used to pick out a single item/person from a previously mentioned group. It agrees in gender and number: “uno de ellos” (one of them, masculine/mixed group), “una de ellos” (a woman speaking about a mixed/masculine group), “una de ellas” (a woman/thing from an all-female or feminine group). Often follows words like “al menos” (at least) or “todas y cada una de” (each and every one of).
target_language_example: En mi clase hay muchas chicas; yo soy una de ellas.
native_language_example: In my class there are many girls; I’m one of them.

meaning: “one of those” (referring to a person/thing of that type).
additional_notes: Used to pick one item/person/option from a group already known or implied. Often followed by a noun: “una de esas veces” (one of those times), “una de esas personas” (one of those people). Also common with “una de esas dos…” = “one of those two…”. You can use “uno de esos” with masculine nouns (e.g., “uno de esos días”).
target_language_example: Hoy es una de esas noches en las que no puedo dormir.
native_language_example: Today is one of those nights when I can’t sleep.

additional_notes: Used before a feminine plural noun to mean a single item/person from a group: una de las sillas (one of the chairs), una de las cosas (one of the things). For masculine plural nouns, use “uno de los”.
target_language_example: Este es uno de los libros que más me gustan, y esta es una de las canciones más famosas.
native_language_example: This is one of the books I like the most, and this is one of the most famous songs.

additional_notes: Used to say that something/someone is one item/person from your group of possessions, relatives, favorites, etc. It’s followed by a feminine plural noun (mis + noun): una de mis maletas / primas / canciones / llantas. For masculine nouns, use "uno de mis" (uno de mis amigos).
target_language_example: Una de mis amigas vive en Chicago.
native_language_example: One of my (female) friends lives in Chicago.

additional_notes: Used before feminine plural nouns to mean an unspecified small number: unas cuantas veces/palabras/copas. With context or tone, it can suggest “quite a few” rather than just “a few.” Masculine form: unos cuantos (unos cuantos libros).
target_language_example: Necesito unas cuantas cosas del supermercado.
native_language_example: I need a few things from the supermarket.

additional_notes: Used to talk about an approximate, small number of hours. Common in time expressions like "hace unas horas" (a few hours ago), "en unas horas" (in a few hours), and "por unas horas" (for a few hours).
target_language_example: Vuelvo en unas horas.
native_language_example: I’ll be back in a few hours.

additional_notes: Feminine plural form used before a feminine plural noun (e.g., unas pocas páginas, unas pocas palabras). It implies a small number. For masculine nouns, use “unos pocos” (unos pocos libros).
target_language_example: Solo necesito unas pocas cosas del supermercado.
native_language_example: I only need a few things from the supermarket.

meaning: a few people (some, but not many).
additional_notes: Used to say the number of people is small. "Unas" agrees with the feminine plural noun "personas" (you can also say "unas cuantas personas" = quite a few / several people). Often appears with "solo" to emphasize "only a few."
target_language_example: En la fiesta había unas pocas personas, pero lo pasamos bien.
native_language_example: There were a few people at the party, but we had a good time.

additional_notes: "Unas" is the plural feminine form of "uno/una" used to mean an approximate, small number. With time expressions, "en unas semanas" usually means "in a few weeks" (from now), while "hace unas semanas" means "a few weeks ago," and "por unas semanas" means "for a few weeks."
target_language_example: Vuelvo a verte en unas semanas.
native_language_example: I’ll see you again in a few weeks.

meaning: a vacation; some time off (from work/school).
additional_notes: Very common with the verb "tomarse" (to take time off): "tomarte unas vacaciones". With a duration, use "de": "unas vacaciones de dos semanas". Often used to suggest rest or say someone deserves a break.
target_language_example: Después de este proyecto, voy a tomarme unas vacaciones.
native_language_example: After this project, I'm going to take a vacation.

additional_notes: Used to pick a single person/thing from a group: "uno de mis amigos" (one of my friends), "uno de éstos" (one of these). It agrees in gender and number when needed: "uno de" (masc.), "una de" (fem.); plural: "unos de", "unas de" (some of). Often followed by a plural noun or pronoun (e.g., "mis padres", "éstos").
target_language_example: Quiero uno de esos libros, por favor.
native_language_example: I want one of those books, please.

additional_notes: Used to identify a single person/thing as part of a group: *Eres uno de ellos* = you’re one of them. For an all-female group, use **una de ellas**. With objects, Spanish still uses **ellos/ellas** depending on the grammatical gender of the group (often **ellos** for mixed or masculine nouns).
target_language_example: Solo conozco a uno de ellos.
native_language_example: I only know one of them.

additional_notes: Used to point to one item/person/thing within a group that’s already known, visible, or just mentioned. It’s the masculine singular form; for feminine use “una de esas” (e.g., “una de esas casas”). Often followed by a noun: “uno de esos troncos / pianos / accidentes.”
target_language_example: ¿Me pasas uno de esos vasos, por favor?
native_language_example: Can you pass me one of those glasses, please?

additional_notes: Used when things are going wrong or it’s been stressful/irritating. Often said with the verb ser: “Es/Ha sido/Va a ser uno de esos días.” You can add details after it (e.g., “de lluvia”, “de mucho trabajo”) to specify what kind of day.
target_language_example: Perdí el autobús y se me cayó el café… es uno de esos días.
native_language_example: I missed the bus and I spilled my coffee… it’s one of those days.

additional_notes: Used to refer to one item from a group that’s already known or visible in the context. It often stands in for a noun you don’t repeat (e.g., "uno de esos (sándwiches)"). Changes for gender/number: "una de esas" (fem.), "unos de esos" / "unas de esas" (plural).
target_language_example: ¿Me das uno de esos, por favor?
native_language_example: Can you give me one of those, please?

meaning: "one of these days" (sometime soon; at some point in the near future).
additional_notes: Used to talk about something you expect or plan to do in the near future, but without a specific date. It can also be used as a warning/teasing threat ("One of these days, they'll..."), and it often implies procrastination or delay (e.g., "Uno de estos días" can mean "not today" in practice).
target_language_example: Uno de estos días tengo que llamar a mi abuela.
native_language_example: One of these days I have to call my grandma.

additional_notes: Used to pick a single item/person from a group of masculine or mixed-gender plural nouns (los). For feminine plural nouns, use "una de las" (e.g., "una de las casas"). Often followed by a plural noun: "uno de los + plural noun".
target_language_example: Uno de los estudiantes llegó tarde a clase.
native_language_example: One of the students arrived late to class.

additional_notes: Used to say that someone or something belongs to the top group in a category. It agrees with gender and number: "uno de los mejores" (masc. plural), "una de las mejores" (fem. plural). Often followed by a noun ("uno de los mejores alumnos") or used on its own when the category is understood ("Eres uno de los mejores").
target_language_example: Yo era uno de los mejores alumnos de la clase.
native_language_example: I was one of the best students in the class.

meaning: “one of us” / “one of our people” (part of our group).
additional_notes: Used to say someone belongs to your group/team/community (“in the in-group”). It agrees with the person: uno de los nuestros (male or mixed group), una de las nuestras (female), and plural: unos de los nuestros / unas de las nuestras. Often said with emphasis to show acceptance, loyalty, or solidarity.
target_language_example: Él es uno de los nuestros.
native_language_example: He’s one of us.

additional_notes: Used to include someone in a group (“You’re one of us now”) or to say that only one person from the group will do something (“Solo puede llevarse a uno de nosotros” = “He can only take one of us”). You can change it to match the group: “uno de ustedes” (one of you), “una de nosotras” (one of us, all-female group), “uno de ellos/ellas” (one of them).
target_language_example: Si vienes con nosotros, serás uno de nosotros.
native_language_example: If you come with us, you’ll be one of us.

additional_notes: Used to refer to a single male person or masculine noun chosen from a group that belongs to someone. It’s the masculine form (uno); before a feminine noun it becomes “una de sus” (una de sus amigas). “Sus” can mean his, her, your (formal), or their—context clarifies whose.
target_language_example: El profesor acusó a uno de sus alumnos de hacer ruido en clase.
native_language_example: The teacher accused one of his/her students of making noise in class.

meaning: oneself; oneself (as the same person as the subject).
additional_notes: Used to refer back to the subject (the reflexive idea “yourself/myself/himself…”), often for emphasis or clarity. Common with reflexive verbs: «conocerse a uno mismo» (to know oneself), «hacerse daño a uno mismo» (to hurt oneself). It can agree with gender/number: «uno mismo» (m.), «una misma» (f.), «uno(s) mismo(s)/una(s) misma(s)» (plural). In many contexts you may also see «yo mismo/a», «tú mismo/a», etc., but «uno mismo» is more general (“oneself/one”).
target_language_example: Conocerse a uno mismo no es fácil.
native_language_example: Getting to know oneself is not easy.

additional_notes: Used to describe doing something or something happening with each person/thing separately, in sequence (not all at once). It often goes with verbs like sacar (to take out), pasar (to go in), entrar (to enter), morir (to die), contar (to tell). It can appear after the verb (sacó los huevos uno por uno) or at the start for emphasis (Uno por uno, ...).
target_language_example: Revisamos los documentos uno por uno para no cometer errores.
native_language_example: We reviewed the documents one by one so we wouldn’t make mistakes.

meaning: one after another; one by one (in sequence).
additional_notes: Used to show that people or things do the same action in a line or sequence, with little or no time in between. It can describe events happening successively (Vinieron uno tras otro) or repeated outcomes (Murieron uno tras otro). You can also say "una tras otra" for feminine nouns (e.g., "las personas, las visitas"), and "uno tras otro" for masculine or mixed groups.
target_language_example: Los clientes entraron uno tras otro.
native_language_example: The customers came in one after another.

additional_notes: Used to talk about an approximate, not exact, number of years (often 2–5, depending on context). Common with time expressions like "hace unos años" (a few years ago), "durante unos años" (for a few years), and "en unos años" (in a few years). "Unos" here means “some/a few” (plural, masculine).
target_language_example: Viví en Madrid unos años antes de mudarme a Londres.
native_language_example: I lived in Madrid for a few years before moving to London.

meaning: a few; quite a few (an unspecified small number).
additional_notes: Used before a plural noun or on its own to mean “some/a few” (not an exact number). Often implies “several” depending on context. You can also use it with "de" + a plural noun/pronoun: "unos cuantos de éstos" = "a few of these."
target_language_example: Voy a comprar unos cuantos regalos.
native_language_example: I'm going to buy a few gifts.

additional_notes: Used to give an approximate quantity. "Unos/unas" + number means “around/approximately” that number (e.g., "unos dos minutos" = about two minutes). Use "unos" with masculine or mixed nouns and "unas" with feminine nouns ("unas dos horas").
target_language_example: Tardo unos dos minutos en llegar.
native_language_example: It takes me about two minutes to get there.

additional_notes: Used to talk about an approximate number of days (not exact). It can refer to a short stay or a short time until something happens. Often translated as “a few days” when it means a small number (e.g., 2–5), and “some days” when it means an unspecified number.
target_language_example: Voy a descansar unos días antes de empezar el trabajo nuevo.
native_language_example: I’m going to rest for a few days before starting the new job.

additional_notes: "Unos/unas" is used with time expressions to mean an approximate amount (not an exact number): "unos meses" = "a few months". In the future it often means "in a few months" (En unos meses...), and with "hace" it means "a few months ago" (Hace unos meses...). It can also mean "for a few months" when describing duration (Pasó unos meses...).
target_language_example: Nos mudamos en unos meses.
native_language_example: We’re moving in a few months.

additional_notes: Used to mean an approximate, short amount of time (not an exact number). Often used in requests (Dame unos minutos.) or to say you’ll be gone briefly (por unos minutos). With "más tarde" it means "a few minutes later."
target_language_example: Espérame unos minutos, por favor.
native_language_example: Wait for me a few minutes, please.

meaning: a few; a small number of.
additional_notes: Used with plural countable nouns to mean “a small number of” (unos pocos años, unos pocos meses, unos pocos errores). It can also stand alone when the noun is understood (Solo envía unos pocos). Often suggests “a handful,” not many.
target_language_example: Solo necesito unos pocos minutos para terminar.
native_language_example: I only need a few minutes to finish.

additional_notes: Used before a number to show it’s an estimate, not an exact count. It agrees in gender/number with the implied noun: "unos" with masculine plural nouns (unos tres días) and "unas" with feminine plural nouns (unas tres horas). Often interchangeable with "aproximadamente" or "más o menos".
target_language_example: Estaré allí en unos tres minutos.
native_language_example: I’ll be there in about three minutes.

meaning: to use your head; to think (before acting).
additional_notes: Commonly used as advice or a mild scolding, often in the imperative: «¡Usa la cabeza!» = “Use your head!” / “Think!” It can also be used more generally to mean “to think logically” or “to be sensible.”
target_language_example: Antes de contestar, debes usar la cabeza.
native_language_example: Before you answer, you should use your head.

additional_notes: A common, literal phrase used to give someone permission to use your dictionary. The verb changes with the person/formality: puedes (you, informal), puede (you, formal), podés (you, informal—common in Argentina/Uruguay), pueden (you all). Often used with "siempre" (always) or "siempre que quieras/quiera" (whenever you want).
target_language_example: Si no sabes la palabra, puedes usar mi diccionario.
native_language_example: If you don’t know the word, you can use my dictionary.

additional_notes: Used to speak directly to a man in a polite/formal way. Often appears as a form of address set off by commas (e.g., "Es para usted, señor"). You can add a name or title after "señor" ("señor Anthony"). In writing, "Usted" is often capitalized at the start of a sentence, but it’s not required in the middle of a sentence.
target_language_example: Disculpe, ¿puede ayudarme, usted, señor?
native_language_example: Excuse me, can you help me, sir?

additional_notes: Used with the formal "you" (usted) to express obligation or strong advice: "Usted debe escoger" = "You must choose." In some regions, "debe de" can also express a deduction or probability (similar to "must be"): "Usted debe de ser la señorita Kenny" = "You must be Miss Kenny."
target_language_example: Usted debe llenar este formulario antes de entrar.
native_language_example: You must fill out this form before entering.

additional_notes: "Usted" is the formal/polite way to say "you" (used with strangers, customers, older people, or in professional settings). It uses the third-person singular verb form: "usted es" (not *usted eres*). In questions you’ll often see it as "¿Usted es ...?" (“Are you ...?”).
target_language_example: Disculpe, ¿usted es la doctora Pérez?
native_language_example: Excuse me, are you Dr. Pérez?

additional_notes: Used with the formal “you” (usted) + the verb “to be” (es) + an indefinite article (un/una) + a noun (often a label or description): “Usted es un maestro.” Use “una” with feminine nouns (“Usted es una doctora.”). Often sounds direct/strong in Spanish, especially with insults (some examples like “dolor en el culo” are very vulgar).
target_language_example: Usted es un buen amigo.
native_language_example: You are a good friend.

additional_notes: Used to emphasize that the person addressed (usted) should do something personally, without help. Often appears in instructions or polite requests (e.g., Hágalo… / Sírvase…). The feminine form is “usted misma” when addressing a woman.
target_language_example: Puede llamarlo usted mismo si quiere.
native_language_example: You can call him yourself if you want.

additional_notes: Used to make a negative statement about someone you address formally (usted). It comes before the verb: “Usted no sabe” = “You don’t know.” With verbs like ser/estar, it often means “you are not”: “Usted no es…” = “You are not…”. You may also see it as “a usted no …” when “usted” is an indirect object for emphasis: “Yo pensé que a usted no le interesaba” = “I thought you weren’t interested.”
target_language_example: Usted no puede entrar aquí.
native_language_example: You can’t come in here.

meaning: formal: "you don’t have" / "you do not have."
additional_notes: Used with the formal subject pronoun "usted" when speaking politely to one person. "No" goes before the verb to make it negative. It can mean (1) not possessing something ("Usted no tiene niños") or (2) not having a certain quality/idea ("Usted no tiene idea..."). Note that "usted no tiene que + infinitive" means "you don’t have to + verb" (not obligation).
target_language_example: Usted no tiene que venir mañana.
native_language_example: You don’t have to come tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used to speak directly to two people at once, especially in Latin American Spanish where "ustedes" is the normal plural "you". It’s often used for emphasis or clarity (making it explicit it’s exactly two people). In Spain, you’ll more commonly hear "vosotros dos" in informal situations and "ustedes dos" in formal ones.
target_language_example: ¿Ustedes dos pueden venir conmigo, por favor?
native_language_example: Can you two come with me, please?

additional_notes: Used to describe two or more people you’re addressing. “Ustedes” is the standard plural “you” in Latin America (formal/neutral), and it can also be used in Spain in formal situations (informal plural there is usually “vosotros”). “Son” is the “they/you all are” form of ser, used for identity, descriptions, relationships, and general qualities.
target_language_example: Ustedes son muy amables.
native_language_example: You all are very kind.

additional_notes: Used before an infinitive to talk about what someone/something is going to do in the near future. This is the él/ella/usted form of the pattern ir a + infinitive, so the first word changes with the subject: voy a, vas a, va a, etc.
target_language_example: Mi hermana va a llegar mañana.
native_language_example: My sister is going to arrive tomorrow.

additional_notes: Uses the near-future structure **ir a + infinitive**. **Va** is the 3rd-person singular present of **ir** (“to go”), so it matches **él/ella/usted/eso/esto** (and names like Tom). For other subjects: **voy a cambiar** (I), **vas a cambiar** (you), **vamos a cambiar** (we), **van a cambiar** (they). Often used for predictions or things expected to happen soon, but it can also mean “will” in general.
target_language_example: Con el tiempo, todo va a cambiar.
native_language_example: With time, everything is going to change.

meaning: "there is/are going to be" (there will be).
additional_notes: Future of "haber" used in the sense of "there is/are": "va a haber" + noun. You can change it for other persons: "va a haber" (there is/are going to be), "van a haber" is commonly heard but in standard Spanish "va a haber" is used even with plural nouns ("Va a haber muchas personas"). Often used to announce events or say something will exist/occur.
target_language_example: Va a haber mucha gente en la fiesta.
native_language_example: There are going to be a lot of people at the party.

meaning: "is going to do" / "will do" (he/she/it is going to do).
additional_notes: This is the near-future structure **ir a + infinitive**: **va a hacer** = “is going to do/make.” It’s the **third-person singular** form (for *él/ella/usted*). For other subjects: *voy a hacer* (I’m going to do), *vas a hacer* (you’re going to do), *vamos a hacer* (we’re going to do), *van a hacer* (they’re going to do). In questions you’ll often see: **¿Y qué va a hacer?** = “So what’s he/she going to do?”
target_language_example: Creo que va a hacer una llamada ahora.
native_language_example: I think he/she is going to make a call now.

additional_notes: Form of the near-future construction **ir a + infinitive**. **Va a ir** literally means “is going to go” (often just “will go”). In **te va a ir (bien/mal)**, it means “things will go (well/badly) for you.” In **se me va a ir...**, it can mean something is about to “get away” from you (e.g., **Se me va a ir el avión** = “I’m going to miss the plane”).
target_language_example: Si no sales ya, te va a ir muy mal en el examen.
native_language_example: If you don’t leave now, you’re going to do very badly on the exam.

additional_notes: Common weather phrase. Literally “(it) goes to rain,” using **ir a + infinitive** (va a + llover) to talk about the near future or a prediction. Often used with time words like **mañana** (tomorrow) or with sources like **según el pronóstico** (according to the forecast).
target_language_example: Creo que va a llover esta tarde, así que lleva un paraguas.
native_language_example: I think it’s going to rain this afternoon, so bring an umbrella.

additional_notes: Formed with **ir a + infinitive** to talk about a near-future action. **Va a matar** is 3rd-person singular (he/she/it is going to kill). Often used as a threat or warning (**Te va a matar** = “He/She’s going to kill you”), and it can also be figurative (**Tu adicción te va a matar** = “Your addiction will kill you”). Change **va** depending on the subject: **voy a matar** (I’m going to kill), **vas a matar** (you’re going to kill), **van a matar** (they’re going to kill).
target_language_example: Tu adicción te va a matar.
native_language_example: Your addiction is going to kill you.

additional_notes: Uses the construction **ir a + infinitive** (morir) to express an expected future event. **Va** is the 3rd person singular present of *ir* (él/ella/usted **va**). Change *ir* to match the subject: *yo voy a morir, tú vas a morir, él/ella/usted va a morir, nosotros vamos a morir*, etc. Can sound neutral and factual, or dramatic depending on context.
target_language_example: Dice no, y es el día en que va a morir.
native_language_example: He says no, and it’s the day he’s going to die.

additional_notes: Form of **ir a + infinitive** (near future): **(something) va a pasar** = something is going to happen. Often used to talk about predictions or expectations. It can also mean "is going to pass (by)" in other contexts, but in these examples it means "happen." You can change the subject: **voy a pasar** (I’m going to happen / pass — usually "pass"), **te va a pasar** (it’s going to happen to you), **nos va a pasar** (it’s going to happen to us).
target_language_example: Si sigues así, algo malo va a pasar.
native_language_example: If you keep going like this, something bad is going to happen.

additional_notes: Form of the near-future: **ir (to go) + a + infinitive**. **Va** agrees with the subject (**él/ella/usted va**). Other common forms: **voy a ser** (I’m going to be), **vas a ser** (you’re going to be), **van a ser** (they’re going to be). Often appears in phrases like **A ver qué va a ser** = “Let’s see what’s going to happen / what it’s going to be.”
target_language_example: Mañana va a ser un día largo.
native_language_example: Tomorrow is going to be a long day.

meaning: "will have to" / "is going to have to" (will be required to).
additional_notes: Used to express obligation or necessity in the near or expected future. It’s built from the near-future construction "ir a" + infinitive plus the obligation phrase "tener que": "va a" + "tener que" + infinitive. You can change "va" depending on the subject: "voy a tener que" (I’m going to have to), "vas a tener que" (you’re going to have to), "van a tener que" (they’re going to have to).
target_language_example: Si no estudia, va a tener que repetir el curso.
native_language_example: If he/she doesn’t study, he/she is going to have to repeat the course.

additional_notes: Form of **ir a + infinitive** to talk about the near future. **Va** is the “he/she/it/you (formal)” form of *ir* (to go) + **a** + **venir** (to come). Often used when you expect something to happen soon or you’re fairly sure. Can also appear with additions like **por mí** (“to pick me up”).
target_language_example: Mi hermana va a venir mañana.
native_language_example: My sister is going to come tomorrow.

additional_notes: Uses the near-future structure **ir a + infinitive**: **(él/ella/usted) va a volver** = “he/she/you (formal) is going to return.” Often followed by a time phrase (**a las cinco**, **en tres horas**) or a clause with **cuando** (“when”). For other subjects: **voy a volver** (I’m going to return), **vas a volver** (you’re going to return), **vamos a volver** (we’re going to return).
target_language_example: Va a volver mañana por la mañana.
native_language_example: He/She is going to come back tomorrow morning.

additional_notes: Form of the verb **ir** (to go): **va** = “(he/she/it/you formal) goes.” Used as **ir + a + place** (“go to [a place]”): *Va a la oficina.* Also used as **ir a + infinitive** to talk about the near future (“going to do”): *Va a estudiar.* With **se** (**se va a ...**) it often means “leave/go away,” especially with a time: *Se va a las nueve* = “He leaves at nine.”
target_language_example: Marta va al supermercado y luego va a cocinar en casa.
native_language_example: Marta goes to the supermarket and then she’s going to cook at home.

additional_notes: "Va" is the he/she/you(formal) form of "ir" (to go) in the present tense. "A" means "to," and "la escuela" means "the school." Use it to say that someone attends/goes to school (often as a routine).
target_language_example: Mi hermano va a la escuela todos los días.
native_language_example: My brother goes to school every day.

additional_notes: Used with "ir" to talk about how something is going (El negocio va bien; Me va bien; No va bien). With indirect object pronouns (me/te/le/nos/les) it means someone is doing well. With clothing or style it means something suits someone or fits them well: "Le va bien" (it looks good on them) and "Te va bien" (it fits you/looks good on you). You’ll also hear it alone as a short reply meaning “Okay / Sounds good / All right.”
target_language_example: ¿Cómo te va? — Me va bien, gracias.
native_language_example: How’s it going? — It’s going well for me, thanks.

meaning: (It) is going very well; (someone) is doing very well.
additional_notes: Used with the verb "ir" to talk about how things are going for someone or something (work, life, a project, etc.). Common patterns: "me/te/le/nos/les va muy bien" = "it’s going very well for me/you/him-her/us/them".
target_language_example: Con el nuevo trabajo, me va muy bien.
native_language_example: With the new job, I’m doing very well.

additional_notes: Used when ordering or choosing something and you want one unit (a drink, a ticket, a portion, etc.). It’s common in casual speech: someone offers options and you respond with “va uno” to mean you want one. Often followed by what it is: “Va uno de pollo.” Although “va” literally means “goes,” here it functions more like “make it” / “I’ll have.” Note: In practice, speakers often match gender with the noun (e.g., “va una” for *cerveza*), but “va uno” is used when the implied item is masculine or generic (e.g., *uno* = one [item/order]).
target_language_example: ¿Quieres un boleto para el tour? —Sí, va uno.
native_language_example: Do you want a ticket for the tour? —Yes, I’ll take one.

meaning: “it’s worth it / it’s worth the effort.”
additional_notes: Used to say something is worthwhile (the benefit is worth the time, cost, or effort). Often followed by an infinitive: “Vale la pena + verb” (Vale la pena estudiar). You can also say “No vale la pena” = “It’s not worth it.”
target_language_example: Vale la pena intentarlo otra vez.
native_language_example: It’s worth trying again.

additional_notes: Used to compare value or importance. It can mean literal monetary value (e.g., “the frame is worth more than the painting”) or figurative importance (e.g., “health matters more than gold”). Common pattern: [thing] vale más que [other thing].
target_language_example: Tu amistad vale más que cualquier regalo.
native_language_example: Your friendship is worth more than any gift.

meaning: to be worth it; to be worthwhile.
additional_notes: Used to say that an effort, cost, or experience is worth doing because the result/benefit is good. Common patterns: “Valer la pena + infinitive” (Puede valer la pena esperar = It may be worth waiting) and “Valer la pena + noun” (Puede valer la pena el viaje = The trip may be worth it). Often used in questions/negatives: “¿Puede valer la pena…?” / “No puede valer la pena…”.
target_language_example: ¿Crees que puede valer la pena visitar este museo?
native_language_example: Do you think it might be worth visiting this museum?

additional_notes: Used before an infinitive. It is the first-person plural form of ir a + infinitive. Most often it means a planned or near-future action ('we're going to...'), but in context it can also be used like a suggestion or encouragement ('let's...'). Object pronouns can appear before vamos, as in 'los vamos a ver' = 'we're going to see them'.
target_language_example: Vamos a comer ahora.
native_language_example: We're going to eat now.

additional_notes: Used to suggest or announce that it’s time to eat. Literally “we go to eat” = “we’re going to eat,” but in conversation it often works like an invitation: “Let’s eat.” In a different context, it can also be literal (“We’re going to eat couscous / in the kitchen”). Related idiom: “No te vamos a comer” means “We’re not going to hurt you” (literally “We’re not going to eat you”).
target_language_example: Si ya estás listo, vamos a comer.
native_language_example: If you’re ready, let’s eat.

meaning: “we’re going to do/make” (we are going to do).
additional_notes: Formed from "vamos a" (we’re going to) + "hacer" (to do/make). Used to talk about a plan or what you and others will do next. In questions like "¿Qué vamos a hacer?" it means “What are we going to do?”
target_language_example: ¿Qué vamos a hacer mañana?
native_language_example: What are we going to do tomorrow?

meaning: “let’s do it” / “we’re going to do it.”
additional_notes: From "vamos a" (let’s / we’re going to) + "hacerlo" (do it). Often used to suggest starting an action together (“Let’s do it”), but it can also simply state a plan (“We’re going to do it”). Add-ons like "juntos" (together), "otra vez" (again), or "a tu modo" (your way) are very common.
target_language_example: Está bien, vamos a hacerlo ahora.
native_language_example: Okay, let’s do it now.

additional_notes: Often used as a conversational filler meaning “let’s see / we’ll see,” especially at the start of a sentence or after a pause: “Bueno, vamos a ver…”, “Vamos a ver, escúchame…”. It can also be literal: (1) “we’re going to see/visit (someone)” = “Vamos a ver a tu mamá.” (2) “we’re going to see each other” (meet again / see each other often) = “Nos vamos a ver mucho.”
target_language_example: Vamos a ver cómo lo resolvemos.
native_language_example: Let’s see how we can solve it.

additional_notes: Common, informal way to end a conversation or to say you’ll stay in contact as plans develop. Often implies “we’ll check in and update each other.” You may also hear it as “vamos viendo” (“we’ll see / we’ll play it by ear”).
target_language_example: No sé si podré ir mañana, pero vamos hablando.
native_language_example: I’m not sure if I can go tomorrow, but we’ll keep in touch.

meaning: "Come on" / "let’s go" (urging someone to move or continue).
additional_notes: Repetition adds emphasis and impatience/encouragement, like “come on, come on” or “hurry up.” It’s common in speech when pushing someone to act, keep going, or speed things up.
target_language_example: Vamos, vamos, que llegamos tarde.
native_language_example: Come on, come on—we’re going to be late.

additional_notes: From the verb "ir" (to go): "vamos" = "we go". Often used to suggest an action like “let’s…” when followed by a place (Vamos a tu casa = Let’s go to your house). It’s also used for the near future when followed by an infinitive (Vamos a comer = We’re going to eat). With "a por" it means “go get / go after” someone or something: "Vamos a por ellos" = Let’s go after them / Let’s go get them.
target_language_example: Vamos al parque.
native_language_example: Let’s go to the park.

meaning: “we go to the” / “let’s go to the”.
additional_notes: "Vamos" can mean either (1) "we go/are going" (present tense) or (2) "let’s go" as a suggestion/command. "Al" = "a" (to) + "el" (the), used before a masculine singular noun (e.g., al valle).
target_language_example: Vamos al supermercado después de clase.
native_language_example: Let’s go to the supermarket after class.

meaning: “Come on, don’t …” (used to urge, encourage, or scold).
additional_notes: Used in speech to push someone to stop doing something or to react differently: encouragement (Vamos, no llores…), impatience/scolding (Vamos, no molestes…), or disbelief (Vamos, no me digas…). Often followed by a verb in the imperative or by a statement. Very common in conversational Spanish.
target_language_example: Vamos, no te rindas; ya casi terminamos.
native_language_example: Come on, don’t give up; we’re almost done.

additional_notes: "Van a" is the 3rd-person plural form of "ir a" + infinitive, used to talk about plans, intentions, or near-future actions (a common way to form the future in Spanish). It’s used with an infinitive: "van a quedarse" (they’re going to stay), "van a aumentar" (they’re going to increase). With pronouns, the pronoun can go before "van" ("se van a encontrar") or attached to the infinitive ("van a encontrarse").
target_language_example: Creo que van a llegar tarde.
native_language_example: I think they’re going to arrive late.

additional_notes: Form of **ir a + infinitive** (“to be going to…”). **van** is from *ir* (to go) and matches **ellos/ellas/ustedes** (they/you all). **hacer** means “to do/make.” Often used to talk about plans or what will happen soon; in questions it can be **¿Qué van a hacer?** (“What are they/you all going to do?”).
target_language_example: ¿Qué van a hacer este fin de semana?
native_language_example: What are you all going to do this weekend?

additional_notes: This is the near-future construction **ir a + infinitive**. **Van** is the **ellos/ellas/ustedes** form of **ir** (to go), and **ser** is “to be.” It’s used to talk about what something/someone will be like: *Van a ser famosos* (They’re going to be famous).
target_language_example: Van a ser días muy largos.
native_language_example: They’re going to be very long days.

meaning: “you/they are going to see” (and sometimes “you’ll see.”).
additional_notes: Form of the near-future: **ir (van) + a + infinitive (ver)**. **Van** is used with **ustedes** (“you all”) or **ellos/ellas** (“they”). It can also be said on its own (**Van a ver.**) meaning “You’ll see.” to build suspense or as a warning/promise depending on tone.
target_language_example: Si no me crees, van a ver lo que pasa mañana.
native_language_example: If you don’t believe me, you’ll see what happens tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used to say an action happened repeatedly (more than once, not an exact number). It often comes after the verb ("Lo intenté varias veces") but can also appear earlier for emphasis ("Varias veces me pasó eso").
target_language_example: Te lo dije varias veces, pero no me escuchaste.
native_language_example: I told you several times, but you didn’t listen to me.

additional_notes: Means an indefinite number of days (more than one), often implying “a few” days rather than a specific count. Common after time expressions like por (for) or en (in/within): por varios días = for several days; en varios días = in several days / over several days. Note: you may also hear unos días (“a few days”).
target_language_example: Voy a estar fuera por varios días.
native_language_example: I'm going to be away for several days.

meaning: "you are going to do" / "you will do" (informal singular).
additional_notes: From **ir a + infinitive** (near future): **vas a hacer** = **you’re going to do/make**. It’s used with **tú** (informal “you”); formal would be **va a hacer** (usted) and plural **van a hacer** (ustedes). **Hacer** can mean “to do” or “to make,” depending on context.
target_language_example: ¿Qué vas a hacer mañana?
native_language_example: What are you going to do tomorrow?

additional_notes: Uses **ir a + infinitive** (“vas a llegar”) to talk about something that will likely happen soon. **Llegar tarde a/al + place/event** = “to arrive late to…”. Often used as a warning or reminder: *Vete… o vas a llegar tarde* (“Leave… or you’ll be late”).
target_language_example: Si no sales ahora, vas a llegar tarde.
native_language_example: If you don’t leave now, you’re going to be late.

additional_notes: Literally the near-future form of "morir" (to die): "vas a" + infinitive. Often used as a dramatic statement or a threat ("¡Vas a morir!"), and very commonly in the negative to reassure someone: "No te vas a morir" = "You’re not going to die" / "You’ll be fine."
target_language_example: Tranquilo, no te vas a morir; solo es una inyección.
native_language_example: Relax, you’re not going to die; it’s just a shot.

additional_notes: From **ir a + infinitive** (“to be going to…”) + **necesitar** (“to need”). **Vas** is the *tú* form of **ir**. It often appears with an object: **Vas a necesitar esto** (“You’re going to need this”), or with a pronoun before the verb: **La vas a necesitar** (“You’re going to need it/her”). Can also be used for emphasis like “You’re going to need more than that.”
target_language_example: Vas a necesitar ayuda para terminar a tiempo.
native_language_example: You’re going to need help to finish on time.

meaning: “you are going to be” / “you will be.”
additional_notes: Formed with ir (vas) + a + infinitive (ser) to talk about the future. It can describe a future identity/state (“Vas a ser padre”) or a future event affecting you (“Vas a ser arrestado”). Often translates naturally as “you’ll be…” in English.
target_language_example: Si estudias mucho, vas a ser un gran médico.
native_language_example: If you study a lot, you’re going to be a great doctor.

meaning: 'you're going to have to' / 'you'll have to' (you must).
additional_notes: Common way to express obligation or necessity directed at "tú" (you, informal). It’s the near-future structure "vas a" + "tener que" + infinitive: "Vas a tener que confiar" = "You’ll have to trust." Can sound firm or like a warning depending on tone. For "usted": "va a tener que"; for "ustedes": "van a tener que".
target_language_example: Vas a tener que estudiar si quieres aprobar el examen.
native_language_example: You’re going to have to study if you want to pass the exam.

meaning: 'is/are going to' (subjunctive) / 'might' (about something that may happen).
additional_notes: “Vaya” is the present subjunctive form of “ir” (to go). “Vaya a + infinitive” is used in dependent clauses—often after expressions like dudar que (to doubt), no creer que (to not think), tener miedo de que (to be afraid), esperar que (to hope)—to talk about a possible or expected action, often in the near future: “No creo que eso vaya a pasar” = “I don’t think that’s going to happen.”
target_language_example: No creo que ella vaya a venir hoy.
native_language_example: I don’t think she’s going to come today.

meaning: “(that I/you/he/she) go to…” (present subjunctive of ir); also “Go to…” (formal command).
additional_notes: “Vaya” comes from the verb “ir” (to go). It’s used as a subjunctive form after words like “que”, “cuando” (talking about the future), “quizá(s)”, “puede que”, etc.: “Quieren que vaya a ayudar”, “Cuando vaya a…”. It’s also the formal (usted) command: “Vaya a la parte de atrás” = “Go to the back.” Often followed by a place (a la cárcel, a tu fiesta) or an action with an infinitive (a ayudar).
target_language_example: Quizá no vaya a la reunión mañana.
native_language_example: Maybe I won’t go to the meeting tomorrow.

additional_notes: "Vayamos" is the present subjunctive of "ir" for "nosotros" and is commonly used to propose an action (“Let’s …”) or as a polite command. It’s usually followed by (1) a place: "Vayamos a la cocina" (Let’s go to the kitchen), or (2) an infinitive: "Vayamos a comer" (Let’s go eat / Let’s eat). You’ll also see it in phrases like "Es hora de que nos vayamos a casa" (“It’s time for us to go home”), where "que" triggers the subjunctive.
target_language_example: Vayamos a tomar un café.
native_language_example: Let’s go have a coffee.
